en: Śrīḥ! *Tattvasaṅgraha*, together with the *Pañjikā*.
The first part of the *Tattvasaṅgraha*: Introductory Verses (1–6).
It is devoid of activity belonging to either primordial matter (prakṛti) or a Lord (īśvara), yet it is mobile;

it is the locus for the systematic arrangement of the connection between action and its fruit, and so forth, through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of qualities (guṇa), substances (dravya), actions (kriyā), universals (jāti), inherence (samavāya), and the like. || 1 ||
It is empty of the superimposed forms that are the objects of words and conceptual cognitions;
it is ascertained by the two means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) endowed with clear characteristics;
and it is not mixed with anything else, even in its most subtle part.
Without transition, without beginning or end, resembling a reflection and the like,
free from the entire mass of conceptual proliferation, and unattainable by others; independent, detached from the scriptures, and desiring to act for the welfare of the world.

Having prostrated before that Omniscient One, the best among speakers, who proclaimed dependent origination and whose great compassion became his very nature over many incalculable eons, this *Tattvasaṃgraha* is composed.

(Pañjikā) Having bowed with reverence to that foremost among the knowers of reality— who, out of compassion, gratified the world with the nectar of truth obtained from churning the ocean of the knowable, which pacifies the sufferings of birth, disease, old age, and so forth— I shall here commence a most lucid Pañjikā for the compendium of realities within this treatise.

Persons like me, dull-witted as I am, are never capable of speaking of a subject that has not been previously known; nor is there any path here that has not been traversed in many ways by the wise day after day. However, my mind—intent on its own purpose yet desiring the rise of merit—is now fully resolved to undertake this practice of reality, which has the attainment of auspiciousness as its fruit.

For in this treatise, the engagement of discerning persons is preceded by an ascertainment of the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*); and since devotion toward great beings is the primary cause for attaining all that is most auspicious, [the author], having reflected on this, first offers worship to his own Teacher as a preliminary rite to this treatise. This is done to generate devotion toward the Blessed One and to ensure the listener engages with this treatise with respect. By means of these verses beginning with "The primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) and ending with "The Compendium of Reality" (*Tattvasaṅgraha*), he states the subject matter and the purpose.

For instance: if its subject matter (*abhidheya*) were not stated, a discerning person, suspecting it to be as meaningless as the speech of a madman or the like, would not even endeavor to listen; therefore, its subject matter must necessarily be stated. Furthermore, even if the subject matter exists, discerning people will not care to listen to a treatise that lacks a desired purpose (*prayojana*), such as a treatise investigating the teeth of crows; thus, for the sake of inducing them to engage with it, the purpose must be stated at the outset. Indeed, the purpose itself is the primary factor that serves as a limb (*aṅga*) for engagement.

Since the audience engages with treatises solely out of a desire for that [purpose], and since it is impossible to achieve that through a treatise devoid of a subject matter (*abhidheya*), the subject matter is stated in order to demonstrate that the treatise is a means to the purpose.
Furthermore, that purpose must be shown as having a compatible means; it should not be one whose accomplishment is impossible to practice.

Otherwise, like a treatise instructing one on the ornament of Takṣaka’s crest-jewel as a means to neutralize poison, a discerning person would not engage [with it], realizing that even if a purpose exists, its accomplishment is impossible;

for this very reason it has been said: "Therefore, no other [type of] statement is superior to one that is coherent, possesses a suitable means, declares a human goal, and remains unimpaired by critical examination."
Thus,
for this reason, the statement of the subject matter and so forth is made in the treatises in order to induce engagement;
for indeed, the engagement of discerning persons arises only from certainty.
Certainty arises from valid cognition alone;
however, this introductory statement possesses no authority regarding external objects such as its subject matter and so forth,
because there is no necessary connection between it and those objects.
For instance: first of all, there is no relation characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), because the difference [between the speaker and the word] has arisen and because they are absolutely distinct;
nor is there a relation characterized by origination (*tadutpatti*), because a sentence is dependent solely upon the speaker's intention.

Furthermore, it is not logical that knowledge produced regarding an object of inquiry from a sentence that lacks such a relation should be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
And although a sentence possesses authority when there is an intention to speak, nevertheless, that [authority] is not a factor for the engagement of a discerning person;
for those who intend to say something in one way do not necessarily act accordingly at the time of performance, due to the possibility of a deceptive intention.

Otherwise, it would be impossible to compose a treatise that differs from its own thesis; furthermore, for one who has already understood the purpose of the treatise through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the presentation of a statement of purpose is entirely useless,
since such a person has already been prompted to act by those very other means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, for one whose purpose for the scripture is sublated by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the scripture] is all the more useless; for, precisely because it is sublated by another means of valid cognition, engagement with it is impossible. And while these two points are stated assuming [such a case], there is no means of valid cognition—neither establishing a purpose and so forth nor subverting it—that exists for those of limited vision prior to their engagement.
Since those people would understand the existence or non-existence of that [purpose] through their own activity, which is accessible to them,
this statement is commenced for the sake of one who has not yet understood the purpose and other elements of the treatise.
And for that discerning person, only doubt arises from this statement, not certainty, because it lacks authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇatva*).

Furthermore, since that doubt already existed even prior to the presentation of the statement regarding the purpose and so forth, the presentation of such a statement is useless. To this, it is replied:
As for the claim that the activity of discerning persons occurs only through certainty, that is incorrect,
because activity is observed even through doubt, as in the case of farmers and others.
It might be argued that although farmers and others have doubt regarding a future result, they nevertheless possess certainty regarding the means to achieve that result;
therefore, their activity is preceded by certainty. This is incorrect.
For it is only this much that is relevant here: that when a person's activity is directed toward a certain object, that activity occurs even when there is doubt regarding that object.

Furthermore, farmers and others do not engage in their activities for the sake of the means themselves, such that their activity could be described as preceded by certainty on the grounds that certainty exists regarding the means;
rather, what is the case?

They engage in that [activity] for the sake of the result, yet because obstacles and the like may arise regarding that result, there is no certainty; therefore, their engagement is preceded solely by doubt.
Furthermore, even that initial engagement of theirs which aims at the ascertainment of the means is likewise [preceded by doubt].

Even in that case, there is no certainty regarding the means (*sādhana*), precisely because activity proceeds for the sake of that [result]. Furthermore, even their ascertainment of the means would necessarily take one of two forms: either it would be of the nature "this will certainly accomplish such a future result," or it would be of the nature "provided that obstacles and deficiencies in auxiliary factors do not occur, this is certainly sufficient for the production of the desired result."

In that regard, the first [alternative] is not tenable; for even in the case of rice and other crops where a deficiency of auxiliary causes or the occurrence of an obstacle might be suspected, it is observed that they lack the capacity to produce their future fruit despite having produced such a fruit previously. Since this suspicion cannot be excluded in all cases, as it has been said: "There is inconclusiveness regarding the effect in what is connected to the transformation of the potencies of the causal complex, because of the possibility of obstacles and the like."
If, on the other hand, it is the second [alternative], then this is even more appropriate,
because every activity preceded by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is of such a nature;
for this very reason, the teachers provide a qualification there by means of an inference of capability (yogyatā).
In the absence of an obstacle, this [means] is indeed capable;
however, since the result is also ascertained by means of this form, it is not merely the ascertainment of the means.
Furthermore, in such an engagement, an engagement preceded by the ascertainment of the result is not established from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Because other schools of thought are unable to ascertain the very non-existence of an impediment and so forth.

It might be argued as follows: although it is impossible to ascertain the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), nevertheless, in an activity preceded by valid cognition (*pramāṇa-pūrvikā pravṛtti*), there certainly exists a certainty of this kind: "If there were no necessary connection, then the attainment of the result from this [cause] would necessarily not occur. This is not the case, however, in an activity not preceded by valid cognition; otherwise, there would be no distinction between activities preceded by valid cognition and those preceded by what is not valid cognition. Furthermore, even such a certainty cannot arise from a verbal statement, because with respect to an external object, that [statement] lacks validity due to the absence of a necessary connection. This is indeed true.

However—if it were established that no discerning person ever acts on the basis of a statement, then all this [criticism] would hold true; but as a matter of fact, we see some people who, hearing of great benefits or calamities resulting from certain actions whose fruits are not perceptible, are unable to remain without relying on the authority of scripture (*āgama*) and proceed to act according to its words. Yet, their status as discerning persons is not thereby lost, because they act by means of a valid method; for indeed, there is no other method available for action regarding objects that are entirely beyond the senses except through scripture.
One must necessarily proceed on the basis of scripture;

for those who adopt a scripture that is contradicted would be acting without due deliberation, whereas by proceeding with reliance upon a non-contradicted scripture, how could they not be considered discerning? For that alone is the correct means.

Nor is it reasonable to say that people act toward scripture solely because they have ascertained its truthfulness by virtue of its being composed by a superior person, for such a superior person cannot be ascertained by those of limited vision; yet, even discerning individuals do not fail to act on the basis of scripture.
Similarly here as well,
those who act with foresight will engage in the treatises upon hearing the statements regarding the unimpeded purpose and so forth,
because their engagement occurs precisely through such means.
For even in this case of engagement, there is no other means [of knowledge],
because the meaning of the treatise is absolutely beyond the senses prior to one's engagement with it;
and as for what was also said regarding the intention to speak— that although it possesses validity, and so forth— [that too is untenable].

That too is without substance, because we observe that treatises are sometimes completed even with a meaning other than what was intended to be expressed; likewise here, by whom could the engagement of discerning persons be prevented, considering that the completion of the intended subject matter might still occur? Nor is it proper to desist from activity due to a suspicion of impossibility; for activity proceeds even from doubt regarding the goal, otherwise, since a suspicion of the non-attainment of the fruit is possible even in the case of activity preceded by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be no engagement whatsoever anywhere.
Nor is there any apprehension of encountering an undesirable result, because it is impossible to obtain an undesired fruit from a treatise (*śāstra*).

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that there is an apprehension of encountering an undesirable result characterized by the non-attainment of a desired fruit, since such an apprehension would be equally present in all cases of engagement [with any activity].
As for what was said—that this statement is commenced for one who has not yet understood the purpose of the treatise—[that too is incorrect].
We also say this,
however: although there is doubt regarding it prior to the presentation of the statement of purpose,
that doubt concerns the purpose in general— namely, whether this [treatise] possesses a purpose or not.

Nor is it reasonable to engage in activity based merely on a doubt regarding the purpose, for that would entail engaging in every possible action, and a mere purpose is not what is sought; rather, engagement is observed to arise from a doubt concerning a specific purpose, which serves as the cause for employing specific means.
Since seekers engage in a particular means of accomplishment only when a specific purpose is desired,

and since there is no other cause for the arising of doubt regarding a specific purpose prior to the statement of that purpose— by which one might abandon other treatises and undertake this specific treatise—
it may be argued that the very desire for a specific purpose already exists in a person as the cause for the arising of doubt regarding that specific purpose.

For instance, the mind of one who is possessed by an expectancy for a specific purpose first thinks thus: "Is this [treatise] purposeful by virtue of the purpose we already know? Or is it by another? Or is it purposeless? Since, in the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to establish or refute that [purpose], such a doubt is logically established, and because other treatises explaining a specific purpose are observed, a doubt regarding the object of a specific purpose certainly arises even beforehand. Therefore, the presentation of a statement of purpose is redundant.
This is not so;
for although the desire for a specific purpose may indeed be a cause for a specific doubt, nevertheless, it does not manifest for everyone.

Because for certain people of dull intellect who have not mastered the goals of human life (puruṣārtha), [the desire for liberation] does not manifest before them; for instance, although liberation is established as the supreme goal of human life, there are nevertheless some unenlightened persons who do not recognize even that supreme goal as a human goal,
and thus they will not seek it at all.

Nor is it logical that a desire for a specific purpose, when not present before one, can be the cause for the arising of doubt regarding the object of that specific purpose; for effects are dependent upon the existence of their causes.

Even if such a desire were to manifest in some cases, it still cannot be the cause of a specific doubt that leads to the adoption of a particular means while abandoning other means; for since the absence of both proving and refuting evidence applies everywhere, it follows by logic that such a desire is not the cause of that [specific doubt]. Furthermore, activity is not justified by this much alone.

Since it would follow that [activity] would occur everywhere, and since it is not possible for anyone to act everywhere, those who seek a specific result would remain indifferent due to the absence of a basis for adopting specific means; therefore, just as one composes a scripture concerning objects that are entirely beyond the senses in order to produce a doubt regarding a specific object— the cause for adopting specific means— one must indeed state a statement of purpose (*prayojana-vākya*) so that those seeking a specific result may adopt specific means.
For it is by this [statement] that the specific subject matter of this very treatise is demonstrated, and not that of any other;

thus, a doubt is produced regarding the specific object—the particular means, the goal to be accomplished, and the result—which is restricted [to this work]. And the listener might proceed even from a doubt concerning that specific purpose generated by the statement of the purpose, thinking, "Perhaps this specific purpose of mine will be accomplished," just as one might proceed from a doubt concerning an extremely remote object generated by scripture (āgama). Therefore, the statement of the purpose is presented.

This must necessarily be understood in this way; otherwise, even the composition of scriptures concerning objects that are entirely beyond the senses would be useless. For even prior to the composition of the scriptures, doubt regarding [the existence of results] would persist among those seeking specific fruits in acts such as giving, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to either prove or disprove it.
However, such doubt does not arise at all for those who are unacquainted with fruits such as heaven, because the desire for specific fruits—which is the cause of that doubt—is not present in them.

Furthermore, since that [desire] which arises in them is common to all as a cause for engaging even in the eating of stones and the like, it cannot—by avoiding such acts—be the cause for undertaking specific activities such as giving; considering this, the authors of the scriptures compose their works for that purpose. Likewise, there is no objection to the statement of the purpose by the authors of treatises.
Moreover, no other treatise has been found that establishes a specific purpose one might wish to know, by the power of whose discovery a doubt regarding a specific desired purpose might arise.

For when another treatise is available for accomplishing a specific desired purpose, no discerning person would undertake yet another treatise, as that would entail the loss of their status as a discerning person;
therefore, even the perception of another treatise does not become a cause for doubt regarding the specific intended purpose.
Therefore, it is established that the presentation of the statement concerning the purpose and so forth is for the sake of inducing the audience to engage [with the work].

As for one who thinks that the statement of the purpose and so forth is not for the sake of inducing the audience to engage—on the grounds that doubt arises from it, and because engagement by a discerning person is impossible through mere doubt—that view is incorrect.

However, that which is devoid of purpose or is useless should not be undertaken, such as the examination of a crow’s teeth or the speech of a madman; since this treatise is likewise devoid of purpose, it should not be begun for the sake of listening or composition. For one who objects in this manner by means of the non-perception of a pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), the statement regarding the purpose and so forth is introduced at the outset in order to point out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of that reason. This appears somewhat incorrect, because it has already been established that activity occurs even through doubt.
And because pointing out the unestablished nature [of the reason] would be futile;
for it would indeed be meaningful only if, on account of that statement, activity were to arise in that opponent.
As long as the lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) regarding this statement has been pointed out, no certain knowledge of the aforementioned pervader can arise for a discerning person from this statement—

by which he might be prompted to act— because, as before, this statement lacks authority (*apramāṇatva*); and because, according to your own view, it is impossible for a prudent person to act based on doubt.
Therefore, pointing out the "unestablished" (asiddha) nature [of the reason] is entirely fruitless.
Furthermore, no discerning person who is unaware of the body of the treatise would suddenly conclude that the pervader is absent and thereby oppose it;

nor, because of such opposition, would the author of the treatise—though himself knowing the purpose of the treatise—not begin to compose it, or the listener—a person acting with foresight—not desist from it. For it is for the sake of inducing their engagement that the "unestablished" nature would need to be pointed out.

Furthermore, it might be argued that one who acts without foresight might grasp the aforementioned absence of the pervader even without a basis and without cause, and might even cause others to grasp it; therefore, the pointing out of its being unestablished (*asiddha*) is directed toward him. This too is incorrect.

If that [pointing out] is not a factor for their engagement with the treatises, then pointing out its being unestablished toward them is entirely fruitless; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For there are indeed many who engage in incoherent chatter; in order to demonstrate that even they are speaking improperly, one would have to state a great deal that is not useful for the undertaking of the treatise. Therefore, the pointing out of the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetvasiddhatā*) at the beginning of the treatise must certainly be described solely as having the fruit of motivating the audience, lest it be fruitless or lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Consequently, would this [statement of purpose] not also be meaningful for one who does not object by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), and who would not proceed to act without having heard the purpose?
Since it has been previously analyzed that the statement of the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and so forth is solely for the purpose of engaging the audience—
and not for its own sake— it follows that, because [the author] would not engage [in the work] on their own accord otherwise, it would be as disconnected as the ravings of a madman.

Furthermore, as for what was stated by the Master in the *Nyāyabindu*— "one's own understanding also occurs in this way"— and thus its formulation exists even in inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), that does not refer to a formulation external [to cognition]; rather, it refers precisely to internal discourse (*antarjalpa*),
because inference for oneself consists of cognition.

And as for what was said previously regarding "the ordinary powers" and so forth, that too was stated by way of indirect speech (*vakrokti*) for the purpose of making those whose minds are afflicted by impurities such as envy into suitable vessels; enough of this elaboration.

As for the performance of worship to the Teacher, it is for the purpose of generating serene confidence (*prasāda*) toward the Blessed One, which is the cause for attaining all that is most auspicious.
For in this manner, by the method of proclaiming the multitude of the Blessed One’s qualities, his majesty is manifested;
and upon hearing that, for those whose minds follow through faith, a sudden clarity of heart toward the Blessed One undoubtedly arises.

Even those who follow through wisdom (prajñānusārin), seeing no contradiction in such [scriptures] and perceiving the excellence resulting from the cultivation of qualities such as wisdom, conclude that such sages certainly exist in the world based on the very means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to be described which establishes the perception of supersensuous objects; having thus determined this, they indeed generate faith toward the Blessed One.

And through that [great beings'] grace, their qualities are respected in their teachings and in the treatises based upon them, for the purpose of undertaking their study and so forth after first subjecting them to critical examination; then, by means of the gradual arising of the wisdom consisting of hearing and the rest, one attains the supreme good. Thus, devotion toward the great is the primary cause for the attainment of all excellence. For this very reason, when treatises are composed based on the teachings of renowned masters, the authors of those treatises first perform worship of their own master at the beginning of the work.
Even when that [other cause] is active, its status as an auxiliary factor (aṅga) exists to some degree;
for this very reason it was said: "Desiring to compose the treatise, he undertook the salutation to his Teacher in order to make known the greatness of his Teacher.
Therefore, it is established that the performance of worship to the Teacher is not purposeless.
In this context, everything up to the words "having bowed to him" indicates the performance of worship to the Teacher.

With the phrase "the *Tattvasaṃgraha* is being composed," he states the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*). For the subject matter of this treatise consists of those realities (*tattva*) which are the specific characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), such as its being devoid of activity through intrinsic nature (*prakṛti*) and so forth;
and these are indeed indicated by the word "reality" (*tattva*) itself through the force of the context, since it is untenable for anything else to possess the status of reality.

Now, it might be argued that the principle is that only a sentence possesses a denotable meaning (abhidheya) and nothing else; and since an entire treatise (*śāstra*) is not a single sentence but rather a collection of sentences, how could such a work possess a denotable meaning?
This is not so;

for although a treatise consists of a collection of sentences, those sentences nonetheless exist in a state of mutual dependence and connection. Otherwise, like a collection of sentences uttered by a madman or the like, it would be entirely incoherent in its meaning.
Furthermore, because it consists of a collection of many mutually connected words, the treatise (*śāstra*) is indeed a sentence (*vākya*), just like any other sentence;
for a sentence is not composed of words alone, but also of sentences.
Therefore, since it is a great sentence (*mahāvākya*), it follows that the treatise possesses a subject matter (*abhidheya*); thus, there is no room for objection.
The purpose (*prayojana*), however, has been indicated by the word "compendium" (*saṅgraha*).

For it is thus: when the purpose is being demonstrated for those desiring to engage with treatises (*śāstra*), it must be shown as residing within that very treatise and not elsewhere; otherwise, there would be an irrelevant statement.
And it has been said: "For a speaker who wishes to incite others toward treatises states the purpose at the beginning of the treatise, not out of mere habit."
And how is it that another person is incited to engage with the treatises through the instruction of a purpose,
if only the purpose residing therein is stated and not one residing elsewhere?
For a discerning person would not engage with one thing based on the statement of a purpose residing in something else.

A discourse capable of conveying a distinguished meaning is called a *śāstra*, neither the mere subject matter nor the mere words devoid of the capacity to convey meaning. Therefore, it is not necessary to point out a purpose residing in the subject matter and so forth; rather, that which consists in the accomplishment of one's goal through omniscience preceded by right knowledge—this is [the purpose].
With this intention, [one might ask] why there is no statement of the purpose (*prayojana*).

However, the statement of the purpose does not refer to the purpose of the subject matter (*abhidheya*); for by the word "correct knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*), it is intended precisely as the mastery of correct knowledge.
Since the attainment of omniscience is established only when that mastery of correct knowledge is the goal, this statement of the purpose would be logically consistent.
Otherwise, it would indeed be poorly constructed;

and that purpose of the treatise is threefold: the form of the action, the fruit of the action, and the fruit of the fruit of the action. For instance, there may be the status of being the cause for a treatise that is commenced for the sake of instructing others.

Alternatively, there is the status of being an agent; and since both the agent and the instrument are means (*sādhana*), there is no purpose other than the one already stated. Because a means depends upon action, and because all three types of action and so forth are invariably concomitant with it, it is entirely logical that they have that [action] as their purpose; the distinction, however, is merely whether it is direct or indirect.
However, the purpose designated as the "fruit" (phala) is the primary one, because the undertaking of action is for its sake.

In that regard, the common function of all sentences—namely, the act of communicating their own respective meanings—is so well-known that it need not be presented as a [specific] purpose; for there is no deviation of the scripture from that function.
If it is argued that [the definition] must be presented for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that [the object] is inexpressible, we say no;
for that very doubt is already dispelled by the mere statement of what is expressible.
Nor is its presentation intended for the purpose of making known a specific subject matter, since that has already been established by the mere statement of the specific subject matter itself.

Therefore, it is the unique activity (*asādhāraṇā kriyā*) that ought to be presented; and such an activity certainly exists in this treatise, characterized as the "Compendium of Principles" (*Tattvasaṅgraha*).
For by means of this treatise, a compendium is effected—consisting in the gathering together within a single cognition those principles which were previously scattered here and there.
Therefore, he has indicated that very [work] by the word "compendium" (*saṃgraha*).
Furthermore, the fruit of this activity of composing the *Tattvasaṃgraha*— which is the easy understanding of reality within the mental continuum of those to be instructed—
is also clearly revealed by the word "compendium."

For when a condensed reality (*tattva*) is presented in one place, its comprehension arises easily for the practitioner, whereas that which is scattered about leads to difficulty; therefore, by employing the term "compendium" (*saṃgraha*) to indicate this condensation as the cause of easy comprehension, he demonstrates that this work is undertaken for the sake of the easy understanding of reality.

However, the mere understanding of reality is not its sole fruit, for in that case the composition of the treatise would be rendered useless, since the determination of reality has already been accomplished by previous teachers.
Furthermore, there exists a specific benefit of favoring others [through this work].
Furthermore, because the treatise is for the sake of others, [the author]—

considering that even though the principles have been set forth by previous teachers, this work, the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, being undertaken for the sake of easy comprehension by one of dull intellect who is unable to easily grasp them due to their extreme dispersion, will not be in vain— commences this treatise;
for this very reason, he calls it the *Tattvasaṅgraha*.
Otherwise, it would have been said that "the determination of reality is being performed";

for in this way, the presentation of the intended meaning would indeed have been made clearly. Therefore, the easy comprehension of reality is the very fruit of the composition of the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, and the purpose of that easy comprehension is the attainment of prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) without delay.

And that [fact] is so well known that it was not stated, because it is established for all those who accept the existence of reality (*sarvāstika*) that the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) results from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Alternatively, since the phrase "with the desire to promote the welfare of the world" recurs later on, that too has already been shown;
for when that phrase recurs, the meaning of the sentence becomes: "The *Tattvasaṅgraha* is being composed with the desire to promote the welfare of the world."

And how does the desire to bring about the welfare of the world (*jagaddhitavidhitsā*) become the cause for the composition of the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, if the accomplishment of the welfare of the world were the fruit of that composition?

Just as in the expression "one brings water because of thirst," where drinking the water is understood to be the fruit of the act of bringing it, so it is here as well. Consequently, the meaning established is: "The *Tattvasaṅgraha* is composed for the sake of accomplishing the welfare of the world."

And this very purpose has been shown as being accompanied by the appropriate means; for the attainment of higher rebirth (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is called the welfare of the world (*jagaddhita*),
and its cause is non-perversion (*aviparyāsa*), because all affliction (*saṃkleśa*) is rooted in perversion, and because the welfare of the world is the opposite of affliction.
Therefore, its cause is established as being the opposite of that [cause of error];

and non-perversion consists in the firm conviction regarding the connection between actions and their fruits as they truly are, as well as the realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena. This [non-perversion] arises from this treatise which correctly elucidates dependent origination, through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and meditation; thus, it is understood that by the composition of the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, the welfare of the world is also accomplished.

And when the attainment of both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) has occurred, the person’s desire is severed by the completion of their desired goal; therefore, no further purpose beyond this need be sought, and thus there is a finality regarding the purpose.
As for the relationship (*sambandha*), it should not be presented separately from the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*), because it would be fruitless.

For if it were to be demonstrated, it must be shown as the relationship characterized by the state of being the means and the end between the treatise and its purpose, and not another [relationship] characterized by the lineage of teachers and so forth, since such a thing does not lead to the engagement of those seeking the goal.
And that relationship of the probandum and the probans is shown precisely by the statement of the purpose;
for, when one demonstrates that "this is the purpose of this," it follows that it has been demonstrated that "this is the means of accomplishing this.
Indeed, that which does not accomplish something cannot be its purpose, because that would lead to an over-extension [of the term].

Therefore, because it is obtained through implication (*sāmarthya*), this [connection] need not be mentioned separately from the subject matter (*abhidheya*) and the purpose (*prayojana*). Indeed, that alone deserves to be mentioned separately from another when, even though that other has been stated, it is not understood; for instance, when either one of the two—subject matter or purpose—is mentioned, the other is not understood. Furthermore, there is no possibility that the aforementioned connection would not be expressed even when the purpose is stated. Thus, only the subject matter and the purpose are to be explicitly stated.

Furthermore, this subject matter and so forth have not been divided by us as constituent parts of the sentence-meaning; rather, having extracted the members from the sentence, they are treated as its meanings,
whereas the sentence-meaning itself is precisely the aforementioned act of synthesis.

Since even that which has become subordinate (guṇībhūta), such as the expressed meaning (abhidheya) and so forth, is perceived from this sentence, its status as the sentence-meaning (vākyārthatva) is entirely uncontradicted;
for while it is contradictory for a single sentence to express multiple meanings as primary (prādhānyena), it is not so when they exist in a relationship of subordinate and primary.
Now, one might ask: why is praise expressed toward the Blessed One—who is the locus of an immeasurable multitude of qualities—by means of the teaching on dependent origination alone?
This is not a valid objection, for the same line of questioning would apply equally in every case.

And since it is not possible to perform a description of worship by means of manifesting all immeasurable qualities, that worship must be performed by manifesting only a single portion of those qualities;
therefore, whether it is performed by manifesting the teaching of dependent origination or otherwise, there is no difference whatsoever.
Nevertheless, a distinction is stated as follows:

For instance: because he possesses the perfection of qualities as they truly are, and because he brings about worldly prosperity and the supreme good for the world, the Blessed One is the Teacher; he alone is to be declared as the cause for those seeking prosperity and the supreme good to go for refuge to the Blessed One and so forth, and through his teaching of dependent origination, the Blessed One is the one who procures prosperity and the like.

For instance: from the teaching of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) as it truly is, and from the ascertainment of its meaning, there arises a correct conviction regarding the connection between actions and their results and so forth, which is the cause for a happy rebirth (*sugati*); and the realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), which is the cause for the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), arises through the sequence of hearing, reflection, and cultivation. Upon its arising, ignorance—the cause of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*)—is ceased; and when that ceases, all afflictive and cognitive obscurations (*kleśa-jñeyāvaraṇa*) rooted in it are also ceased. Thus, through the removal of all obscurations, the attainment of liberation (*apavarga*) occurs.

Therefore, since this jewel of the Blessed One’s teaching has dependent origination as its primary focus, the expression of praise for the Blessed One consists precisely in his being the one who teaches dependent origination without error.

Furthermore, because others maintain that this dependent origination has discordant causes and serves as the locus for categories of existence contradicted by valid cognition, [the author] employs many of the aforementioned qualifiers of dependent origination for the following purposes: to demonstrate that it is exactly as taught by the Blessed One through the refutation of those [other views], and to introduce the reality of the subject matter to be established by the entire treatise that follows. This is the collective meaning.
The meaning of the individual components is now stated:

in every instance, such as "devoid of the activity of primordial matter (*prakṛti*), God (*īśa*), both [together], the Self (*ātman*), and so forth," the connection is with the one who taught dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). In this context, *prakṛti* refers to the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) postulated by the Sāṅkhyas, consisting of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. *Īśa* means Īśvara (God). *Ubhaya* (both) refers to these two together. *Ātman* refers to a single Puruṣa who is the agent of creation and dissolution, as well as other transmigrating beings. By the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), time (*kāla*) and other factors are encompassed. Their "activity" (*vyāpāra*) means their status as causes; "devoid of that" means empty of such causal activity. This is the meaning.

In this regard, it was said by the Blessed One: "And this sprout is not made by itself, nor made by both [itself and another], nor created by Īśvara, nor produced from primordial matter (*prakṛti*), nor dependent on a single cause, nor has it arisen without a cause.
By this, there is an introduction to the examinations of Primordial Matter, Īśvara, Both, the Causeless, the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*), and the Self (*ātman*).
Now, did he declare that such dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) is non-momentary? No, he says: "It is moving" (*calam*).
"Moving" (cala) means unstable, that is to say, momentary; the sense is that it is impossible for anything else to possess movement.
Regarding this, it was said by the Blessed One: "All conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) are momentary; how can there be action in things that are unstable?"
"Existence itself is their action, and that very same thing is called the causal factor"—this is an introductory objection regarding the examination of permanent entities.

If this were so, it would follow that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) could not serve as the basis for the established order of the relationship between actions and their fruits, because [permanent entities] lack mobility; therefore, he says "action," and so forth.

The intention is that we shall establish this point later. In this context, "action" (*karman*) refers to the auspicious and inauspicious; its "fruit" (*phala*) refers to the desirable and undesirable; their "relation" (*sambandha*) is characterized by the nature of the produced and the producer; and the "establishment" (*vyavasthā*) of that relation means its fixed order, which is to say, its conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is included the establishment of memory, recognition, doubt, certainty, the searching for what was hidden by oneself, curiosity regarding seen objects, cessation [of activity], the relation of cause and effect, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends them, bondage, liberation, and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: "the common substratum (*samāśraya*) of these."

Regarding this, it was said by the Blessed One: "Thus, monks, there is action and there is its fruit, but an agent is not found who abandons these aggregates and takes up other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṃketa*). In this regard, the conventional designation of phenomena is as follows: 'When this exists, that comes to be,' and so forth.
And this is the introduction to the examination of the connection between action and its fruit.

Furthermore, this dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is to be understood as pertaining to the aggregates (skandha), elements (dhātu), and sense-bases (āyatana), because it is precisely these that are dependently originated.

One might ask: "Are not substances (dravya), qualities (guṇa), actions (karman), and so forth, real entities? Why does [dependent origination] not apply to them? To this, he says: "Qualities," and so forth.
The compound consists of qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), actions (*kriyā*), genus (*jāti*), and inherence (*samavāya*).
By the word "genus" (*jāti*), both types of generality—higher and lower—are included.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the ultimate particularities (*viśeṣa*) residing in eternal substances, as well as those properties (*dharma*) described by some as distinct from the substratum (*dharmī*), such as the existence (*astitva*) of all six categories, defined as being the object of a means of valid cognition that apprehends the existent (*sadupalambhaka-pramāṇa-viṣayatva*), and so forth.

The term *guṇādyupādhi-viśeṣaṇa-samāsa* is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) meaning "qualities and so forth which are adjuncts and qualifiers"; the meaning is that [the Tathāgata] is empty of, or devoid of, those.

Regarding this, it was said by the Blessed One: "O Brahmin, 'everything, everything'—how far does that extend? It extends only as far as the five aggregates (*skandha*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*)."
This is the introduction to the examination of the six categories (ṣaṭpadārtha). Now, one might ask:

in the absence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi), how can dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) be made an object of verbal expression and conceptual thought? For it cannot be denoted by those two if it is not made their object, and there is no functioning of words or conceptual thought without limiting adjuncts; so how did the Blessed One speak of it? To this he says: "Having a superimposed form," and so forth.

"Superimposed"—that is, that whose nature (svabhāva) is an aspect (ākāra) superimposed as being external; such is the object of words and cognitions. That dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) in which the object (gocara)—the domain—of words and cognitions has a superimposed aspect is so described.

The word "pratyaya" should be understood here as a specific conceptual cognition (vikalpa) consisting of intended verbal expression, because it occurs in proximity to the word "śabda" and because it is invariably concomitant with them due to sharing a single object.
By this, the following is meant:

Even though limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) do not exist, there nevertheless exists a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which is of the nature of a logical connection (*pratibandha*)—that has arrived by way of the perception of objects mutually excluded from one another, and which is determined as having an external form; this is the meaning of words.
For, in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), this is not the domain of words, because all conceptual constructions have transcended it.

However, just as word-meanings are established in the world through their being pleasing when left unexamined, so too are they revealed by the Blessed Ones—who, while disregarding the ultimate reality, adopt the "closed-eye" posture of the elephant for the sake of introducing others to the supreme truth—by means of the conventional reality of cultivating those [meanings]. Since there is no other means [to realization], even though the word-meaning possesses a superimposed form, it certainly serves as a cause for attaining that [reality] because it is indirectly connected to the actual thing. Thus, such a reality is indeed revealed by them through the power of [their teaching]; therefore, there is no possibility of deception.

In this regard, it was said by the Protector (Tāyin): "For by whatever name each phenomenon (dharma) is expressed, that [phenomenon] does not exist therein; for such is the true nature (dharmatā) of phenomena."
And this is the introduction to the examination of words and their meanings.

Now, is this [treatise] merely substantial in its verbal composition, lacking the wealth of valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could establish it like the categories of reality imagined by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), or does it possess some valid means of cognition to establish its subject matter? He says "it exists," beginning with the words "clearly" (*spaṣṭa*) and so forth.

The term *spaṣṭa-lakṣaṇam* is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*) meaning "that which has a clear definition. The clarity of the definition is due to its being free from the defects of impossibility (*asaṃbhava*), under-extension (*avyāpti*), and over-extension (*ativyāpti*). He states "clear definition" in order to demonstrate that the definitions of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) provided by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) are, by contrast, unclear.
That which is conjoined with—that is, endowed with—the two means of valid cognition known as perception and inference, and determined by them;

this he will demonstrate in all his investigations, and this too is approved by the Blessed One, as it has been said: "Just as gold is [tested] by the wise through heating, cutting, and rubbing on a touchstone."
"O monks, my words are to be accepted after critical examination, and not out of reverence"—
in this regard, the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is its being free from error and conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
And that has indeed been stated by the Blessed One, as he said: "One who is attached to visual consciousness cognizes blue, but does not [cognize] 'it is blue'.

For, by the phrase "cognizes blue," non-delusion is expressed through the demonstration that the object is not inverted; and by the phrase "but not 'it is blue'," the absence of conceptual construction is expressed through the rejection of grasping an object permeated by a name.
The definition of inference has indeed already been stated by demonstrating the logical mark (*liṅga*) which is the basis of inference.

For instance: "A logical mark that is ascertained as being inseparably connected (*avinābhūta*) with the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is the cause of inferential knowledge; and this [inseparable connection] is clearly revealed by one who demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason (*hetu*) by the probandum, as follows: 'O monks, whatever is of the nature of arising is everywhere of the nature of cessation. Thus, it has been made most evident.
As it has been said: "The basis of inference is the mark (liṅga), characterized by inseparable connection (avinābhāva);
because the pervasion (vyāpti) is seen through the reason, that [mark] which is to be established is not explicitly stated, yet it is clear."
And that *liṅga* (logical mark) is divided into three types according to the specific distinctions of essential nature (*svabhāva*), effect (*kārya*), and non-perception (*anupalambha*).
Among these, by the statement, "O monks, whatever has the nature of arising," the *liṅga* called essential nature has indeed been demonstrated;
and the one called effect is likewise shown: "Fire is known by smoke, and water by the crane."

By stating, "The lineage of the wise Bodhisattva is known by means of signs," it has been shown that even that which is called the "distinction of non-apprehension" is indeed demonstrated; for one who rejects the validity of mere non-apprehension [has thereby implicitly accepted it].

As it has been said: "O monks, let not one person judge another, nor grasp a measure for another person; for, O monks, a person who judges another person is ruined, as am I if I were to judge another person, or whoever else might be like me.

By this, the validity of mere non-perception regarding things remote by nature (*svabhāva-viprakṛṣṭa*) is rejected. Furthermore, by saying "as am I," etc., it is even more clearly demonstrated that validity belongs only to a specific kind of non-perception.
And this is an introduction to the examination of perception, inference, and other means of valid cognition.

Now, is this dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) endowed with a commonality (*anvaya*) through some form such as substantiality (*vastutva*), as the proponents of the *syādvāda* say? Or is it of an unmixed nature? What follows from this? If it were endowed with a commonality, there would be a confusion of the definitions of perception and the other means of valid cognition; furthermore, because there would be no difference in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between cause and effect, there would be neither production nor being produced. Consequently, the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) characterized by clear definitions could not be established with certainty, nor would the meaning of dependent origination itself be tenable.

Even if their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are unmixed, because there is no distinction among the auxiliaries (*sahakārin*), they would not possess the capacity for a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*), just like those things considered non-producers; to this he replies with the words "not even by the slightest" (*aṇīyasāpi*) and so forth. He thinks as follows: the latter position alone is correct here, and there is no occasion for the aforementioned fault; we shall demonstrate this later. The analysis of the compound is: that in which another nature (*aparātmā*) has become mixed—that is, commingled—is what is meant by "intermingled" (*miśrībhūta*).
The meaning is that there is not even the slightest trace of the nature of another cause or the like following into the essence of the effect and so forth.

By the word "even by the most minute" (*aṇīyasāpi*), he shows that this is true not only with respect to many properties such as existence (*satva*) and knowability (*jñeyatva*), but also with respect to even the most subtle ones.
The point is that if even a single form were to persist, there would have to be persistence in its entirety;
this he will demonstrate later. And this very point was stated by the Blessed One: "How indeed could the sprout be eternal, since the sprout is one thing and the seed is another?"
But it is not the case that the sprout is the very same as the seed; rather, the sprout is dissimilar to the seed, and therefore it does not transmigrate—
this is an introduction to the examination of the *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifold aspects).

Now, do the aggregates (*skandhas*) and so forth, even though they possess unmixed intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), exist throughout the time-periods (*adhvan*) without ever abandoning that nature? Regarding this, some Sarvāstivādins who advocate for "transmigration" (*saṃkrānti*) say they do; [the author] says "it is not so," stating: "there is no transmigration. The point is that if there were transmigration, then because the entity would exist in its entirety [at all times], nothing at all could be produced, and thus dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) itself would be impossible.
There is no transmigration—that is, no movement of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth across the time-periods (*adhvan*).
This has been stated by the Blessed One as follows: "The eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation."
"Thus, monks, the eye, having not been, comes to be; and having been, it passes away.
This is an introduction to the examination of the three times.
Now, does this [eye] exist only for the duration of being seen? As the Cārvākas say: "When one has been reduced to ashes and is extinguished, how can there be a return?"
"No," he says; "without beginning or end" (*anādyanta*) is the analysis of the compound, meaning that within it, a beginning and an end do not exist.
This too has been pointed out by the Blessed One: "Monks, the cycle of births (*jātisaṃsāra*) is indeed without end or beginning," and so forth.
The term "inferior" (avara) refers to the end, and "superior" (agra) refers to the beginning; because both are negated, it is called "without inferior or superior" (anavarāgra).
This was stated with reference to those who have not yet produced the Noble Path; for those who have produced the Noble Path, cyclic existence (saṃsāra) is indeed peaceful.
Therefore it has been said: "Long is the saṃsāra of the fool who does not understand the True Dharma."
And this is the introduction to the examination of the Lokāyata:
now, is this dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) of the nature of external objects, or does it have the body of mind-only (cittamātra)? He says: "It is like a reflection and so forth.
By this, he shows that it has the nature of mind-only alone.
For this is what is meant:
just as reflections, fire-wheels, cities of the Gandharvas, and so forth, have mind alone as their body, so too does this [external world].
And this was said by the Blessed One: "No external object exists in the way it is conceptualized by the ignorant."
"The mind, stirred by latent impressions (vāsanā), proceeds as the appearance of objects"—
this is the introduction to the examination of external objects.

Thus, having established that dependent origination is free from the web of conceptual constructions regarding unreal objects as previously described, he concludes by saying "all conceptual proliferation," and so forth.

The "mass" (*sandoha*) refers to the collection of all the aforementioned conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*), such as [theories of] primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and [divine] causality; it is "freed from" that.
Now, was this also fully realized (*abhisambuddha*) by others, such as Hari, Hara, and Hiranyagarbha? No; he says: "not attained by others."
Because all other systems are characterized by adherence to the false view of a self, this perfect awakening belongs exclusively to the Blessed One;
he will demonstrate this in all his investigations.

Now, regarding this dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) as it has been described: did the Blessed One proclaim it after having personally awakened to it himself, or rather on the basis of the non-human Vedas favored by others, as the followers of Jaimini say: "Therefore, there exists no direct seer of supersensuous objects; but he who sees through the eternal word, he truly sees"?

He says "not so": "unattached to independent scripture. Independent scripture means the Veda, which is a source of valid knowledge by itself—that is to say, eternal speech. "Unattached" to it means free from reliance; the meaning is that he, as a direct perceiver, taught dependent origination while being entirely independent of that [scripture]. Furthermore, there is no such thing as a non-human (apauruṣeya) sentence.
As it was said by the Blessed One: "Thus, Ānanda, these ancient great sages were the authors of the Vedas and the promulgators of the mantras. The sense is that we shall establish this point later;
and this constitutes an introduction to the examination of the Vedas (*śrutiparīkṣā*) and the examination of independent authority (*svatantraprāmāṇyaparīkṣā*).

Now, one might ask: since the Blessed One has already attained the perfection of all his own goals, for what purpose is this teaching on dependent origination? To this he says: "Out of a desire to bring about the welfare of the world. Welfare for the world (*jagaddhita*) is that which is beneficial to the world;

furthermore, it consists in the abandonment of all afflictive and cognitive obscurations through the means of awakening to the unerring nature of dependent origination. The desire to bring about that welfare is the "desire to bring about the welfare of the world" (*jagaddhitavidhitsā*), and that is the cause for this teaching.
He explains how that desire to promote the welfare of the world arises in him with the words beginning "analpa" (not small), etc.
The analysis of the compound is: "he whose great compassion has become his very nature through many incalculable eons.

Furthermore, that great compassion of the Blessed One is understood from the fact that he does not abandon his activity for the sake of others, even though he has attained the perfection of all his own goals.
Now, he explains what that one, whose great compassion had become his very nature, did—starting with the words "He who," and so forth.
Although the word "he" is a general term, it refers specifically to the Blessed Buddha, because such qualities as those described cannot possibly belong to anyone else.
"Dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) means that which is the arising of the aggregates and so forth, having depended upon— that is, having relied upon— causes (hetu) and conditions (pratyaya);
this is what is meant.

Although the term "dependent origination" (*samutpāda*) is taught as if it were a distinct entity by saying, "he who proclaimed the aggregates and so forth, which have arisen through the power of causes and conditions," nevertheless, it is precisely the dependently originated thing itself that is designated in that way when there is a desire to exclude other distinctions.
Alternatively, *samutpāda* means "that which originates" (*samutpadyate*), according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*, whereby the suffix *ghañ* is used in the sense of the agent.
Therefore, the term *pratītya* forms a compound with *śabda* either according to the rule *sup-supā* or by virtue of belonging to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* group; or else it remains uncompounded.
By all of this, the Blessed One’s perfection in the accomplishment of the welfare of others, together with its means, is fully illuminated.
For instance: by the statement, "He who taught such dependent origination," the Blessed One’s practice for the benefit of others is shown as it truly is.
This very practice for the benefit of others consists in the Blessed One’s instruction to others regarding the unerring path to heaven and liberation.
As it has been said: "The Tathāgatas are merely proclaimers; you yourselves must do the work."

And the means for this perfection of practicing the welfare of others without error consists in direct vision regarding all phenomena (*dharma*) and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*). For even one who is compassionate is not capable of correctly teaching the welfare of others if they lack knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*); and one who possesses such knowledge, if devoid of compassion, would simply not teach at all, or if they were to teach, they might teach what is harmful.
Therefore, both wisdom (*prajñā*) and compassion are the means for the Blessed One’s correct practice of the welfare of others.

Furthermore, that direct vision is demonstrated by his independence from [reliance on] scripture (*śruti*), and the possession of great compassion is demonstrated by the fact that it has become his very nature (*sātmībhūta*).

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) has been taught without error even by Bodhisattvas, Śrāvakas, and others? What, then, is the excellence of the Blessed One in this regard? To this he says: "The best among speakers" (*gadatāmvara*). Although those Śrāvakas and others do indeed speak of dependent origination, the Blessed One alone is the best among those who speak;

for it is only the reality of phenomena (*dharmatattva*) as taught by the Blessed One that they reveal, since they themselves lack the power to teach dependent origination exactly as described on their own authority.
Alternatively, because he is the locus of the ultimate excellence and deficiency of all virtues and faults, the Blessed One alone is supreme and not the others, since they are the opposite of that;

and by this demonstration of the Blessed One’s distinction from the disciples and others, his own perfection of wisdom— characterized by the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions and the knowable, including their residual latencies— is fully illuminated.
Otherwise, how could he be distinguished from them? For if the Blessed One did not possess the aforementioned qualities, he would not be superior.
Therefore, he says: "Him, the omniscient.
And this is an introductory statement for the proof of his omniscience.
Then, having prostrated to him, he asks what is being done: "The *Tattvasaṅgraha* (Compendium of Principles) is composed.

The principles (*tattva*) are indeed those very specific characteristics of dependent origination as previously described, because they are non-erroneous. A "compendium" (*saṅgraha*) is the collection (*saṅkṣepa*) of these [principles] which are scattered here and there into one place; and because the treatise explains them, it is designated by that same name, just as the poem [entitled] *Sītāharaṇa*.

Alternatively, *saṃgraha* (compendium) refers to the very text itself, because by means of it the principles (*tattva*) are correctly or completely grasped; the use of the present tense—“it is being made”—is intended with reference to the time when the work has begun but is not yet finished.

In that context, in order to demonstrate that primordial nature (*prakṛti*) is devoid of activity, he sets forth the Sāṃkhya doctrine, beginning with the words: “From that which is accumulated with all powers,” and so forth.

An Examination of Primordial Matter (Prakṛti): From primordial matter alone, which is accumulated with all powers, the various effects proceed; they exist in reality as having that very same nature. (7)

When the *pradhāna*—which is characterized by the state of equilibrium among *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—is "accumulated," meaning endowed with all its inherent powers (*śakti*) that produce the entire collection of effects beginning with the *mahat*, it is from that very source that these various effects, such as the *mahat* and so forth, proceed; thus say the followers of Kapila.
The restrictive phrase "from the *pradhāna* alone" is intended to exclude time, the *puruṣa*, and other such factors.
The expression "from the *kevala*" (the isolated) is for the purpose of refuting the Lord (*īśvara*) postulated by the theistic Sāṅkhya.
"Evolve" means that they arise either directly or through a succession;
for their process is as follows:

from *pradhāna*, the intellect (*buddhi*) arises first; from the intellect, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); and from the ego-sense, the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*) consisting of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell, as well as the eleven organs, arise.

The five sense organs (buddhīndriyas) are characterized as hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell; the five organs of action (karmendriyas) are speech, hands, feet, the anus, and the genitals; and with the mind as the eleventh, there are eleven.
Furthermore, from the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements arise:
from sound comes space (ākāśa), from touch comes air (vāyu), from form comes fire (tejas), from taste come waters (āpaḥ), and from smell comes earth (pṛthivī).
As it was stated by Īśvarakṛṣṇa: "From primordial nature (prakṛti) arises the Great One (mahat); from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen;
and from five of that group of sixteen, the five gross elements arise."
In this context, "the Great One" (mahat) is a designation for the intellect (*buddhi*);
and this intellect is characterized by the determination of objects, such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth.
The ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), however, is characterized by expressions such as "I am fortunate" or "I am handsome."
The mind (*manas*), however, has the characteristic of volition (*saṅkalpa*).

For example, suppose a certain young student hears that there is a meal in another village; he would then form a volition regarding it, thinking, "I shall go there," and further, "Will there be molasses and curds there, or perhaps only curds?
In this way, the mind functions through volition.
Thus, in this manner, the mutual distinction between intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*manas*) should be understood;
the rest is easily comprehensible.
These—the great principle (*mahat*) and so forth—along with primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*), constitute these twenty-five principles (*tattvas*).

As it has been said: "One who knows the twenty-five principles, in whatever stage of life he may be engaged—whether wearing matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot—is liberated; of this there is no doubt."

These aforementioned varieties of effects, proceeding from Pradhāna, do not—as the varieties of effects favored by the Buddhists and others do—become absolutely different from their cause; rather, they are of its very nature. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that" (tat) refers to Pradhāna, and "having that as their form" (rūpa) means having that as their essence (ātman). Thus, they are essentially identical with Prakṛti by way of possessing the nature of the three *guṇas* and so forth. For instance, in the world, whatever the nature of the cause may be, an effect of that same nature is observed.

Just as a cloth produced from black threads is black, and one produced from white threads is white, so too the *pradhāna* consists of the three *guṇas*; likewise, the manifest (*vyakta*)—consisting of intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the senses (*indriya*), and the gross elements (*bhūta*)—is also perceived as having the three *guṇas*, and therefore it possesses that same nature.
Furthermore, it is non-discriminative (*aviveki*).
For instance, these [qualities] such as *sattva* and so forth, and this manifest [world] beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), cannot be made separate;
rather, those qualities are that manifest, and that which is manifest is those qualities.
Furthermore, both the manifest and the unmanifest are objects of experience.
And it is common to all persons because its nature is that of an object of experience,
owing to its being experienced by all.
And it is insentient in nature, like a female slave in a brothel, because it does not experience pleasure, pain, or delusion.

And it possesses the nature of productivity; for instance, primordial matter (pradhāna) produces the intellect (buddhi), the intellect produces the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the ego-sense produces the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the eleven organs, and the subtle elements produce the gross elements (mahābhūtas).
Therefore, these various effects proceed as having that very same nature, in the form of the three qualities (guṇas) and so forth.

As it has been said: "The manifest is composed of the three qualities, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and productive; so too is the Pradhāna. The Puruṣa is the opposite of that, and likewise [the Pradhāna is the opposite of the Puruṣa]."

Now, if the various effects are indeed of that same nature [as their cause], how is it that the distinction between the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) is described in the treatise?

For instance, it was stated by Īśvarakṛṣṇa: "The manifest is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composed of parts, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite."
Thus, the meaning here is as follows: "possessing a cause" means having a cause; that is, it is indeed manifest. For instance:

the intellect (*buddhi*) has the primary matter (*pradhāna*) as its cause; the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) has the intellect as its cause; the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the eleven organs have the ego-sense as their cause; and the gross elements have the subtle elements as their causes.
But the unmanifest is not thus, because it does not arise from anything whatsoever;
likewise, the manifest is impermanent, because its nature is to originate.

But the Unmanifest is not like this, because it is devoid of origination. Furthermore, just as Pradhāna and Puruṣa exist everywhere—pervading heaven, earth, and the intermediate space—the Manifest does not exist in such a manner; rather, it is non-pervasive. Moreover, during the period of transmigratory existence (saṃsāra), the Manifest migrates, being conjoined with the thirteenfold body-instrument characterized by intellect, ego, and the senses, and residing within the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra); but the Unmanifest does not migrate in this way, because, being all-pervasive, it cannot possess activity.

The manifest is perceived as manifold through the distinctions of intellect (*buddhi*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and so forth, whereas the unmanifest is not; for that which is singular is the cause of the three worlds.

Furthermore, the manifest is dependent, because whatever arises from something else is dependent upon it, but the unmanifest is not so, because it is not an effect. Moreover, the manifest is a sign (*liṅga*), in the sense that it undergoes dissolution (*laya*).

For instance: at the time of dissolution, the gross elements dissolve into their respective subtle elements (*tanmātras*); the subtle elements and the sense organs dissolve into the ego (*ahaṅkāra*); the ego dissolves into the intellect (*buddhi*); and the intellect dissolves into the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*). However, the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) never undergoes dissolution anywhere; this is because it has no further cause.
Furthermore, the Manifest (*vyakta*) possesses parts, as it is composed of the constituent elements of sound, touch, taste, form, and smell;
but the Unmanifest is not so, because sound and the other qualities are not perceived within the nature of the Primal Matter.

Furthermore: just as a son is not independent while his father is alive, so too the manifest (vyakta) is always dependent on its cause and thus lacks autonomy; however, the unmanifest (avyakta) is not like this, because it is eternally independent of any cause.
Anticipating all these objections, he says: "In reality" (bhāvataḥ)—that is, from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārthataḥ), there is identity with that [unmanifest].

The meaning is that the distinction as previously stated is not contradicted by the specific transformation resulting from the difference between the primal nature (*prakṛti*) and its modifications (*vikāra*).
Alternatively, "by way of being" (*bhāvataḥ*) means by way of their own nature (*svabhāvataḥ*); thus, they proceed in the very form of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*).

The meaning is that the diversity of creation, through the distinctions of the predominance or non-predominance of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, is entirely consistent with the differentiation into the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the subsequent evolutes.
By this, it is asserted that the effect exists within the causal self.

In this regard, how is it understood that the effect exists prior to its production? He says: "If," and so forth—"If the effect were non-existent [prior to production], it could not be produced from the power residing in the nature of the cause, because of its lack of essence, like a sky-lotus. (8)

To establish that the effect exists [in the cause], five reasons have been stated by others: "Because what is non-existent cannot be produced; because there is the grasping of a material cause; because there is no production of everything from everything; because the potent produces only that which it is capable of producing; and because of the nature of the instrument—the effect exists. To support the first of these reasons, this is said: "If, however, the effect were non-existent... and so forth.

For if the effect did not exist within the nature of the cause prior to its production, then it would not have been produced by anyone, just like a sky-lotus. The formal argument is as follows: that which is non-existent is not produced by anyone, just like a lotus in the sky.

According to the opponent's view, the effect does not exist prior to its production; this entails the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving something that contradicts the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), for such is not the case.
Therefore, it is established that whatever effect, such as oil, is produced from causes such as sesame seeds, that effect exists even prior to [its production] from them.

"According to its capacity" means in the form of potentiality (*śakti*); for even by the followers of Kapila (*kāpila*), existence prior [to manifestation] is not accepted in the form of manifestation (*vyakti*),
because it would be devoid of nature (*nairūpyāt*).
Because they lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva), he says "And why? and so forth, in order to support the second reason.

And for what reason do [beings] take up only specific material causes (*upādāna*), such as the distinct varieties of rice seeds and so forth, when [all things] are equal in their existence? [Otherwise], if the effect were non-existent, there would be no such thing as the taking up of specific material causes by individuals.
(Verse 9) If the effect were non-existent, then there would be no such thing as the taking up of specific material causes by individuals.
To explain: those seeking the fruit of *śāli* rice take up only the *śāli* seed, not the *kodrava* seed;
likewise, those seeking curd, thinking "the Brahmins shall eat tomorrow," take up milk, not water.

In this regard, just as the *śāli* and other grains are non-existent within the *śāli* seeds and so forth, they are equally non-existent within the *kodrava* seeds and so forth. Why, then, even though the non-existence of the *śāli* fruit and so on is equal everywhere, are only specific *śāli* seeds and the like taken up?

To whatever extent even *kodrava* and other grains might be taken up by those seeking the fruit of *śāli*, since there is no difference in their being non-existent; or if it is argued that they are not taken up because they are devoid of that fruit— then likewise, the *śāli* seed also should not be taken up by one seeking the fruit of *śāli*, because it too is devoid of that fruit.
And it is not the case that it is like the seed of *kodrava* [grain];
therefore, it is understood that its effect exists therein.

To support the third reason, he says: "And all," and so forth: "And everything would possess the property of arising from everything, because here, the absence of identity (tādātmyavigama) is without distinction in respect to everything. (10)

If it is your view that an effect arises only from what is non-existent, then every effect—such as gold, silver, and so forth—would arise from every entity, such as grass, dust, clods of earth, and the like.
Why? Because the absence of identity (tādātmyavigama) is indistinguishable in all cases;
that is to say, the lack of the nature of the intended entities, such as grass and so on, is equally present in every entity that is subject to arising.
Previously, the argument was stated by way of the cause (*kāraṇa*), whereas now it is stated by way of the effect (*kārya*); this is the distinction.
Furthermore, everything does not arise from everything;
therefore, it is understood that this restriction exists because that [effect] is possible only from that [cause].

It might be argued: "The potencies of causes are restricted to specific effects; therefore, even though the effect does not yet exist, only a particular effect is produced and not a sky-lotus; only a specific material cause is employed, namely that which is capable, and not just anything; and only a specific thing arises from a specific source, rather than everything arising from everything.
