Having raised this objection, the author says "of the potencies," etc., under the guise of providing a reply, in order to support the fourth reason.
Regarding the restriction of these powers, the objection that "it is not so" is not a valid answer,
because causes perform their effects by virtue of being capable [of doing so].
(11) "Of these" refers to...
The meaning is that for those entities considered to be causes, the aforementioned refutation does not apply.

Why is this [system] unsurpassed compared to that of the Buddhists and others? Because even potent causes, when producing an effect, produce only that which is capable of being produced, not that which is incapable.

Now, it might be asked: "Who has said that they perform the impossible, such that you would prohibit this? Rather, it is merely stated that they produce an effect even though it is non-existent, and that [production] is indeed possible for them. To this, he says: "That which lacks a produced excellence," and so forth: "That which lacks a produced excellence, is formless, and is immutable..."
"How indeed could that [destruction] be brought about by them, since it would result in the destruction of the self in the modification?"—
thus he thinks:
by the very admission that they produce an effect that does not pre-exist, it is implied that they are performing what is impossible to perform.

To explain: that which is non-existent is formless and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); and that which is formless, like the horn of a hare and so forth, lacks any excellence of effect—that is, it is incapable of having an excellence added to it (*anādheyātiśaya*). And that which cannot have an excellence added to it is immutable, like space.
How then can such a thing, being of that nature and not having acquired any specific form, be made [into something else] by anyone?

Furthermore, one might argue that it certainly undergoes modification because it attains a state of existence; to this he says: "Because in the case of modification, there would be the loss of its own self-nature."
Because when modification is intended, that which is described as its essence or intrinsic nature— the so-called "formless"— would necessarily undergo loss;
for it is not logical that something non-existent can attain that state of being without abandoning its own nature,
nor, if it were to abandon it, could it be established that the non-existent has simply attained the form of the existent.

For the nature of existence is one thing, and the nature of non-existence is another; because these two are established through mutual exclusion, that which is non-existent is simply incapable of being produced.
Indeed, if one were to admit the production of such an entity, one would effectively be admitting that causes are capable of producing the impossible.
Furthermore, nothing that is impossible can be produced by anyone, just like a lotus in the sky;
therefore, this argument based on the restriction of capacity is not a valid response.
To establish the five reasons, he says: "And because the effect is thus impossible," and so forth. Since the effect is thus impossible, what could the cause be doing?
Therefore, even the status of being a cause for the seed and so on is not tenable. (13)
In this way— that is, by the principle just mentioned, or rather, because of the four reasons already stated,
since the effect is in every respect impossible under the theory that the effect is non-existent (asatkāryavāda)— what could a cause such as a seed do to become a cause?
And thus, one might argue as follows:
"The seed and other such causes are not [true] causes because their effects do not exist [prior to production], just like a lotus in the sky";
yet, this is not the case.
Therefore, it is established that because of the contrary [evidence], the effect exists prior to its production.
One might object: "Granted that the effect exists [prior to production] is thus established..."
To explain how it is established that these various effects proceed from the Pradhāna alone, he says: "Pervaded by pleasure, etc.
This manifest world is observed to be pervaded by pleasure and so forth, because its effects—such as serenity, distress, and dejection—are perceived here [in experience]. (14)
In that regard, these five applications of inference for the proof of the existence of the Pradhāna have been stated by others,
as it has been said: "Because of the finite measure of distinct objects, because of their commonality, because of activity proceeding from power,
because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-differentiation of the manifold universe."
The meaning is that the unmanifest (avyakta) exists as the cause.
Pradhāna exists, because of the finite measure of differentiated effects;
for in this world, whatever has a maker is seen to have a finite measure,
just as a potter produces from a finite lump of clay a finite jar that holds a *prastha* or an *āḍhaka*.

Furthermore, this manifest world, beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), is observed to be finite: there is one intellect (*buddhi*), one ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), eleven organs, and five gross elements.
Therefore, we establish through inference that the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*) exists, which produces this finite manifest world;
for if the Primal Nature did not exist, this manifest world would be infinite.
For this reason as well, the Pradhāna exists: because we observe a commonality among diverse objects.
For whatever is perceived as being permeated by a certain genus is produced from a cause consisting of that [genus].
Just as diverse objects such as jars, bowls, and the like, which are permeated by the genus "clay," are produced from a cause whose nature is clay.

And why is it that this manifest world is perceived as being endowed with the classes [of qualities] such as pleasure, pain, and delusion? Because effects such as serenity, distress, and dejection are observed;
for instance, serenity, buoyancy, attachment, exhilaration, and joy are the effects of *sattva*.
That which is called "pleasure" is in fact only sattva;
while heat, emaciation, piercing pain, stiffness, agitation, and distress are the effects of rajas,
and rajas is suffering.
The effects of *tamas* are dejection (*dainya*), obstruction (*āvaraṇa*), depression (*sādana*), destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), repulsiveness (*bībhatsa*), and heaviness (*gaurava*);
and *tamas* is expressed by the word "delusion" (*moha*).
Furthermore, the effects of these [qualities], beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*), such as clarity (*prasāda*), distress (*tāpa*), and dejection (*dainya*), are perceived.

Therefore, it is inferred that these [objects] are specific arrangements of the three—pleasure, pain, and delusion. By this, it is established through their effects such as clarity (*prasāda*) and so forth that they are permeated by pleasure and the rest; and from that permeation, it is established that they originate from a primordial nature (*prakṛti*) composed of those [qualities]. Once that is established, it follows by implication that this primordial nature is *pradhāna*; thus, it is established that *pradhāna* exists because the commonality among diverse objects is observed. Furthermore, *pradhāna* exists because activity proceeds from power (*śakti*).
In this world, whoever engages in a particular activity is capable of it, just as a weaver is capable of making cloth;
therefore, we establish that the Pradhāna possesses a power by which it produces the manifest.
Furthermore, that power cannot exist without a substratum;
therefore, the Pradhāna exists as that in which power resides.
For this reason also, the Pradhāna exists: because of the distinction between cause and effect.

In this world, a distinction between cause and effect is observed; for instance, a lump of clay is the cause and a jar is the effect, and the latter possesses a nature distinct from the former. To explain: a jar is capable of holding honey, water, and milk, whereas a lump of clay is not. Observing such effects as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, we establish that the Pradhāna exists, from which these effects such as the Great Principle have arisen.
Furthermore, the Pradhāna exists because of the non-differentiation of the manifold forms of the universe.
The term *vaiśvarūpya* refers to the three worlds;
for these indeed attain a state of non-distinction (*avibhāga*) somewhere at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*).

To explain: the five gross elements merge into the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*); the subtle elements and the five sense organs merge into the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); the ego-sense merges into the intellect (*buddhi*); and the intellect merges into primordial matter (*pradhāna*). Thus, at the time of dissolution, the three worlds attain a state of non-distinction.

"Non-distinction" (avibhāga) means non-separation (aviveka). Just as in the state of milk it is impossible to make a distinction such that "the milk is one thing and the curd is another," so too at the time of dissolution it is impossible to make a distinction such that "this is the manifest and this is the unmanifest.
Therefore, we conclude that the Pradhāna exists, wherein the differentiation of the marks (liṅga) beginning with the Mahat occurs.
This very reason—"on account of homogeneity" (samanvayāt)—has been stated by the Teacher here as an illustration for the remaining reasons.
In that context, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "pleasure and so forth," suffering and delusion are included; thus,
the manifest (*vyakta*)— from the Great Principle (*mahat*) down to the primary elements (*bhūta*)—
is observed as the manifest.
The meaning is that it is clearly perceived.
To the question "How so?", he says: "prasāda" and so forth;
the word "ādi" (and so forth) is connected with each [term].
And this has already been explained by us previously.
(14) Having thus demonstrated the establishment of the reason "because of being endowed with" (*samanvayāt*), he states the formal proof (*pramāṇa*), beginning with "therefore" (*tataḥ*).

"Therefore, because it is observed that [the effect] arises from that [cause] and follows its genus, the followers of Kapila maintain that the Pradhāna is like the various distinctions such as jars and so forth, being produced from that which consists of it.
Regarding the phrase "produced from that which consists of it":
The meaning is that it has arisen from that cause which consists of pleasure and so forth;
this is the statement of the thesis (*sādhyanirdeśa*), and "because the concomitance of its genus is observed" is the reason (*hetu*).
The meaning is: because it is observed to be followed by that genus characterized by the three qualities (traiguṇya);
"like the various types of *kuṭa* and so forth" means like the various types of jars and so forth.
And that which is the cause consisting of that [effect] is called *pradhāna*— thus the followers of Kapila, the Sāṅkhyas, describe it.
With the words "In this regard" (*tadatra*) and so forth, he begins the refutation.

Regarding this, the wise have said: "The injunction regarding the existence [of the cause] is equal for both sides; therefore, whatever answer you have for that, it will be equally applicable to the wise as well.
In this regard, concerning what was first stated—that these various effects proceed from the Pradhāna and so forth as being of its very same nature—the following is investigated.
If these various effects are of the very same nature as the Pradhāna, how can their emergence from it as effects occur?
For it is not logical that something which is non-different from another should be either its cause or its effect, because cause and effect possess distinct characteristics;
otherwise, how could there be an unconfused determination such as "this is the effect" and "this is the cause"?

Furthermore, the systematic arrangement you have established—that the primal nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is exclusively a cause; that the group of sixteen, characterized by the elements and the senses, is exclusively an effect; and that intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are both effects and causes depending on their relation to what precedes or follows them—that would not be possible.
As it has been stated: "The primal nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (*mahat*), are both evolvents and evolved;
the group of sixteen is only evolved; and the Person (*puruṣa*) is neither evolvent nor evolved."
Thus, because all things are indeed non-distinct from one another, it would follow that everything is both an effect and a cause;

or else, since the relationship of cause and effect is relative and there is no other distinct form to be depended upon, nothing would possess the nature of a primal source (*prakṛti*) nor the nature of a modification (*vikṛti*), just like the Puruṣa.
Otherwise, even the Puruṣa would be designated as a modification of Prakṛti;

and it has been said: "That which is curd is that which is milk, and that which is milk is that which is curd"—by saying this, Rudrila himself has revealed his status as a dweller of the Vindhya mountains.
Furthermore, that which was described as "the manifest possesses properties such as having a cause, while the unmanifest is the opposite," is merely the prattle of a child;
for it is not logical that something which is non-different in its essential nature from another should be its opposite, since opposition is characterized by a difference in form.
Otherwise, the conventional usage of distinction would be utterly destroyed.
Furthermore, the admission of a mutual distinction between the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* on the one hand and consciousness (*caitanya*) on the other would be entirely groundless;
indeed, the entire universe would become uniform in nature.

Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of their simultaneous arising and destruction, because the definition of non-difference is the sharing of a single destiny (*ekayogakṣema*). Therefore, since it is not distinct from the manifest form, the unmanifest (*avyakta*) also follows as being endowed with properties such as having a cause, just like the manifest (*vyakta*); or else, the manifest would be endowed with properties such as having a cause, because it is not distinct from the unmanifest form, just like its own nature—this is an absolute certainty.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the principle];
moreover, in the world, the relationship between cause and effect is well-known as being ascertainable through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka),
and there is no such conventional usage regarding the production of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest from Primordial Matter (pradhāna) and so forth.
Furthermore, an eternal entity cannot possess the nature of a cause by which the production of diverse effects from the Pradhāna could be established,
because for that which is eternal, causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is contradictory whether it occurs successively or simultaneously.

It might be argued as follows: "We do not maintain that the causal relation consists in the production of a previously non-existent nature (apūrva-svabhāva), such that it would be contradicted when there is no difference in essential nature (svarūpa). Rather, Primordial Matter (pradhāna), undergoing transformation (pariṇāma) into the forms of the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth—just like a snake transforming into the form of a coil and so on—is designated as the cause of those [evolutes] such as the Great Principle. And since those [evolutes] such as the Great Principle are of the nature of its transformations, they are designated as its effects. Furthermore, because transformation has a single substance as its substratum, it is not contradictory even when there is non-difference. This, however, is incorrect.
Because transformation is not established;
for transformation would have to occur either through the abandonment of the previous form or without its abandonment.
If it were without abandonment, then there would be a confusion of states, because even in the state of old age and so forth, the state of youth and so forth would necessarily be perceived.

Furthermore, if it were through abandonment [of its previous nature], then there would be the consequence of the loss of its own-nature (*svabhāva*); and consequently, since a previous distinct nature would have ceased and a new, unprecedented nature would have arisen, the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of anything whatsoever could not be established.
Moreover, transformation is described as the characteristic of that very thing becoming otherwise; and that state of being otherwise would have to occur either partially or in its entirety.
It cannot occur partially, because a single entity cannot possess parts.
Nor can it be by way of its entire self, because if another entity were to arise [in place of it], it would follow that the previous one has perished;
therefore, it is not logical for that very same thing to undergo alteration, since such a change is based on the arising of a different intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Furthermore, it might be argued that transformation (*pariṇāma*) is described as the manifestation of a different property through the cessation of another property within a persisting substratum (*dharmin*), and not due to an alteration in the intrinsic nature itself.
This is incorrect;

for instance, a property (dharma), whether it is evolving or ceasing, must be either distinct from its substratum (dharmin) or non-distinct from it. If it were distinct, then the substratum would remain in that very same state; how, then, could it be said to have undergone transformation?

For when the production and destruction of two things that are distinct entities— such as a cloth and a horse— occur, there can be no transformation of a jar or similar object whose own essential nature remains unshaken, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
If it is argued that the Spirit (puruṣa) would likewise be subject to transformation,
since its transformation is established through the production and destruction of the two qualities (dharma) connected to it, and not for anything else— that is not so.
Because there is no relationship between the existent and the non-existent, their mutual connection is not established;
for instance, a relationship would have to belong either to the existent or to the non-existent.
It cannot first belong to the existent, because since it has attained the perfection of its entire nature, it is independent and thus incapable of dependence upon anything else.
Nor can it belong to that which is non-existent, because, being characterized by the absence of all descriptive attributes (*upākhyā*), it is impossible for it to be dependent upon anything;
for it is not logical that the horn of a hare or the like should be dependent on anything.
Furthermore, you do not establish "transformation" (*pariṇāma*) as occurring when there is the production and destruction of distinct, separate properties.

What then? Where there is the persistence of a single essential nature that constitutes the very self of the entity, along with a difference in its states, there your [Vaiśeṣika] doctrine of transformation (pariṇāma) is established.
However, when two properties are distinct from the substratum (dharmin), there can be no persistence of a single essential nature;

for the substratum itself would be their single essence, and since that [substratum] is distinct [from the properties], there is no persistence of a single essential nature that constitutes their very self.

Furthermore, no entity distinct from the two properties of "occurring" and "ceasing," which meets the conditions for perception, ever enters the range of vision for anyone; therefore, such a thing is simply an object of the conventional designation of non-existence for the wise.

Moreover, if the position is taken that it is not a separate entity [from the substratum], then because the two properties—destruction and arising—are non-different from the single nature of the substratum, they too would possess only oneness, just like the nature of the substratum itself. On what basis, then, could the substratum undergo transformation, or the properties themselves?

Furthermore, because the two properties are not distinct from the substrate that persists, there can be neither their disappearance nor their appearance, just as there is none for the nature of the persisting substrate itself.

And since the substrate is non-different from its properties, there would be the production of something new and the destruction of something prior, just as with the nature of the properties themselves; thus, the transformation of any single entity is not established.
Therefore, even on the basis of transformation, your account of the causal relationship is not tenable.

Considering that this [previous argument] is an obvious refutation, he sets it aside; thinking, "We shall later provide a counter-argument to that fault which has been stated by others regarding the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*)," he first refutes the theory of the existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) under the guise of attributing an equal fault to it: "In this regard," and so forth.
The wise ones—the Buddhists—say:
"This fivefold objection that was formulated, beginning with 'because what is non-existent cannot be produced,' is equally applicable even to the position of the theory of the existent effect."
For instance— it can be stated as follows: "The effect exists [prior to its production],
because (1) what is non-existent cannot be produced, (2) there is the grasping of a specific material cause, (3) there is no possibility of everything arising from everything,
(4) the efficient cause produces only that for which it has the capacity, and (5) because the effect is of the same nature as the cause."

The phrase "the effect does not exist [in the cause]" is connected with what follows; why? Because of the reasons such as "because the cause exists" and "because there is the grasping of the material cause.
The intention is that it is not proper for one person to raise an objection that results in a fault common to both parties.

But how can this be equality, given that there is the objection: "In one case it is because of not producing what is non-existent," while in the other case it is "because of not producing what is existent"?
It is not so.

This was stated with the intention of merely expressing the non-occurrence [of production], the necessity [of production], and the grasping of the material cause (*upādāna*), because these factors— non-occurrence and so forth— are equally applicable even in the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). This was said due to a failure to understand the underlying intention.

And regarding that objection, whatever answer belongs to you, the proponents of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavādins*), will also belong to the wise Buddhists, the proponents of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavādins*).
To explain how this [objection] is equal, he says: "If," and so forth.

If curds and so forth already exist within the nature of milk and so forth, then since they are already present, what is there to be produced for those things whose nature is identical to their causes and other factors?
This [verse] is intended to establish the principle that "what is existent cannot be produced."

If effects characterized as curds and so forth already exist in every way and in their entirety within the natures of milk and so forth—which possess the essence of milk and the like—in a distinct form consisting of specific tastes, potencies, post-digestive transformations, and so on, just as they do in the intermediate state, then what form remains to be produced among those [already] existing things, by virtue of which they would be generated by causes such as milk?
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose self (ātman) is similar to the cause and so forth.

Here, "cause" (hetu) refers to *prakṛti* (primordial nature), and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), consciousness (*caitanya*) is included; and of these, the "form" (*rūpa*) is understood as that which is already accomplished and not to be produced again in the intermediate state.
By this, the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish the consequence of the destruction of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) have been indicated.
Now, providing the proof explicitly, he says: "That which is produced by a cause," and so forth.
That effect is not produced by its cause, because it exists [already], just like the cognition of the cause;
therefore, the intended cause is not a true cause because it is not something to be proven, like the self of another.
(18) "Cause" refers to the primary cause (pradhāna) and that which is well-known in the world, such as milk.
"That which has it as its effect" refers to the well-known worldly entities such as the Great One (mahat) and so forth, as well as curd and the like, by virtue of their existence.
The reason is: "because of existence," as in the case of the knowledge of causes;
[the examples are] primordial matter (pradhāna) and that which is well-known in the world, such as milk.
Vittiḥ—consciousness.
The application [of the reason] is like that of "cause-consciousness" (hetuvittivat), meaning it exists as equal to those two.
Whatever exists in every respect is not produced by anything, just as primordial nature (prakṛti) or consciousness (caitanya).
Furthermore, if the effect were already existent in its intermediate state,

and if, according to the opponent's view, it were to exist as curds and so forth in its entirety, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving something contradictory to the pervader;
nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Even for that which possesses no excellence to be produced, if it were subject to being produced, there would follow the undesirable consequence that everything would be produced, as well as the consequence of infinite regress; these serve as subverting proofs (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), because it would follow that even what has already been produced must be produced again.
Thus, the demonstration has been made that those things considered to be effects would, in fact, result in not being effects.
Now, demonstrating the consequence that those things considered to be causes would actually be non-causes, he says: "Therefore, [the cause] is not what is intended," and so forth.
The word "intended" (abhimata) implies "a category-entity" (padārtha);
thus, the meaning is as follows.

The intended category of things, such as primordial matter (*mūlaprakṛti*) and so forth, or seeds, milk, and so forth, does not serve as a cause for that which is intended to be produced, such as the "great one" (*mahat*) and so forth, or curd and so forth—that is to say, it does not attain the status of being fit for the conventional usage of being a "producer.

Why? Because it is "unprovable" (*asādhyatvāt*); it is "unprovable" because it has nothing to be proven (*sādhya*), and its state of being so is its "nature" (*tattva*). This is established by the negation of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) mentioned immediately prior.
For this very reason, it is said "from this," meaning "like the supreme self" (parātman),
that is, like something of a different nature.
The meaning is: "like the intrinsic nature of a category of entity considered to be without cause.

And the category of entity considered to be without cause is consciousness (caitanya), because of the statement: "The Puruṣa is neither a primordial material cause (prakṛti) nor a modification (vikṛti)."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which lacks an existing effect is not a cause, just like consciousness (*caitanya*); and the entity under discussion is one whose effect is not [yet] existing. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Since both of these are proofs by reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*), there is no need for an example established for both parties.
But as for the Sāṅkhya who maintains that even the *puruṣa* possesses agency with respect to experience by way of the principle of the arising of a reflection,
for him the explanation is as follows:
"para" and "ātman"— the meaning is "the liberated one."
For since he is liberated, he possesses no agency even with respect to experience; thus, there is no lack of proof for the example.
Now, with the words "atha" and so forth, [the author] raises the objection that the two reasons are unestablished according to the opponent's view.
Now, suppose there is some excellence characterized by manifestation and so forth,
which the causes produce and for which they do not incur censure.
In that case, if the first reason is formulated with a qualification as "because it exists in its entirety even in the form of manifestation and so forth," then it is not established.
For we do not maintain that the effect exists even in the form of manifestation and so forth;
rather,
it exists in the form of a potentiality (śakti).

Now, if [the reason] is stated generally without qualification, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because an excellence (*atiśaya*) characterized by manifestation and so forth is being produced; thus, there will be no undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everything must be an effect.
For this very reason, the second reason is also unestablished (*asiddha*), because the probandum exists [in the form of] "characterized by manifestation and so forth."
By the word "etc. (ādi), specific states such as "excess" (udreka) and so forth are included.
"Yam" refers to excellence (atiśaya);
"vacanīyatām" refers to being subject to verbal expression (vācyatā).
The meaning is that the fault— that the intended reason is unproven (*asādhyatva*), and so forth— does not occur.
[The author] responds with the words beginning "it existed previously" (*prāgāsīt*).
If he existed previously in this manner, why was no answer given to us? Otherwise, how could he attain manifestation from those things that are non-existent? (20)

In this regard, there are two alternatives: either this excellence existed even in the state of primordial nature (*prakṛti*) prior to the state of manifestation and so forth, or it did not. If it did exist, then you have offered no answer to the charge that both of your reasons are unestablished (*asiddha*) and the like. If, on the other hand, it did not exist previously, then how could that excellence come into being from those causes? According to your own logic—that "the non-existent cannot arise from a cause"—this is not tenable; such is the intended meaning. Thus, the reason "because of the non-production of the existent" (*sadakaraṇāt*) has been established.
Now, for the purpose of establishing the fourfold set of reasons beginning with "due to the grasping of appropriation" (upādānaparigrahāt), he says: "Therefore, there is no probandum," and so forth:
"Therefore, since no probandum exists, there is no grasping of appropriation; nor is there birth from something determinate, nor potentiality, nor activity. (21)

According to the principle stated, since there is no object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the appropriation of material causes (*upādāna*) would not occur; furthermore, because those [causes] are appropriated by discerning persons precisely out of a desire for the fruit to be accomplished, the fact that curds and so forth arise specifically from milk and so forth would also not obtain, simply because the object to be accomplished is impossible.
This [point] is the substantiation of the statement "because there is no arising of anything at all."

For instance—the absence of arising from everything is precisely what is called "birth from a specific cause," and that is not tenable under the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) because of the absence of the thing to be produced;
likewise, the two principles "of the capable" and "the production of the possible" are also not tenable for the very same reason: the absence of the thing to be produced.
For if something were produced by someone, then the power of the producer could be established and the instrument of the produced would be proven;
it is not otherwise.
He demonstrates this with the words: "And there is neither power nor action" (verse 21).
Even the state of being a cause among entities is not tenable, precisely because of the absence of anything to be accomplished.
He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "sarvātmanā" and so forth: "Because it is produced as the self of all, there is no effect whatsoever here;
therefore, even the designation 'cause' is not at all tenable. (22)

And this is the support for the reason "because of the existence of the cause," namely: "it is not so; therefore, the effect does not exist [prior to its production]. This application of the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) should be joined to all the reasons.
Again, refuting the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) by means of another method, he says: "And all," and so forth.
All means of proof that have been set forth—which turn back error and produce certainty—are not thus consistent with reason. (23)
The term "occurrence" (*vṛtta*) refers to what has arisen;
by the inclusion of "error," doubt is also included, because it is possible for doubt to function as a superimposition by relying upon both sides [of its object].
For every means of valid cognition (sādhana), when it operates upon its own object, performs a twofold function:
when it operates upon the object of knowledge (prameya-artha), it eliminates doubt and error, and it produces a certain determination regarding that object.
This [process] is not logically consistent with the doctrine of pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda).
To the question "How so?", he says: "There is no doubt," and so forth;
for doubt and error are never to be removed, as they are always present.
Nor does the birth of certainty arise from that [consciousness]; therefore, everything is in vain.
To explain: according to your view, doubt and error must either consist of consciousness itself or have the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the mind (*manas*).
In either case, their cessation is not possible.
Furthermore, because consciousness, intellect, and mind are eternal, those two [certainty and uncertainty] would also be eternal; thus,
the arising of certainty cannot result from a means of knowledge,
precisely because that [means] would exist at all times.
Therefore, this entire proof that has been stated by you is entirely in vain;
by this, a contradiction with your own words is revealed.
For instance, by one who states a proof for the sake of producing certainty, the production of a non-existent certainty would have to be admitted.
Furthermore, by asserting the thesis that "the effect exists [in the cause]," that very [thesis] is negated; thus, there is a contradiction with one's own words (svavacanavyāghāta).
(24) Moreover, if it were the case that a certain determination arises from a means of proof (sādhana)...
But surely, by that very [reasoning], all these [arguments] would be fallacious.
Now, lest the application of the means of proof be rendered futile, if it is accepted that a non-existent certainty—one that did not previously exist—arises from the means of proof; [then...]

In that case, the entire collection of reasons beginning with "because of not producing what is non-existent" would become inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since there is no contradiction in the production of even a non-existent thing, just as in the case of certainty (*niścaya*). Consequently, just as there is the production of certainty despite its being non-existent, and just as there is the employment of specific means for its accomplishment; and just as it does not arise from every kind of fallacious means; and just as, although it is non-existent, it is produced by efficacious causes, and therein the causal status of those causes exists—so too will it be in other cases as well.
If it is argued that "the unmanifest becomes manifest through those [means]," then what is its manifestation?
It cannot be the production of an excellence of form (*rūpātiśaya*), because there is no differentiation and no connection [between the means and the object].

(26) Furthermore, even if it were the case that the ascertainment (*niścaya*) already exists prior to the application of the means, nevertheless the means would not be useless; for it might be that this [ascertainment], though previously unmanifest, attains manifestation later through those means.

"Therefore, since means of accomplishment are employed for the sake of manifestation, they are not purposeless"—this [argument] is incorrect, because manifestation is unestablished. To explain: manifestation must be either the production of an excellence in its own nature, or the cognition directed toward it, or the removal of the obstruction to its perception.
In this regard, there is first of all no production of an excellence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvātiśaya*).
To explain: this excellence of intrinsic nature must be either non-different from the nature of the ascertainment (*niścaya*) itself, or different from it.

If it were non-different, then because it would be inseparable and non-distinct from that ascertainment, it would persist at all times just like the nature of the ascertainment; thus, its production is not logical.

If, on the other hand, they are separate entities, even so, the relationship expressed as "this belongs to that" is untenable. To explain: the relationship must either be characterized by the relation of substratum and superstratum, or characterized by the relation of producer and produced.
It cannot be the first, because that is impossible between two things that do not stand in a mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary.
Alternatively, if that assistance (*upakāra*) is distinct from the [substratum], a relationship cannot be established because it would lead to an infinite regress;

and if it is not distinct, the employment of the means of proof (*sādhana*) is redundant, since the excellence (*atiśaya*)—which is non-distinct from the assistance—would arise simply from the certainty [of the cause]. Furthermore, because excellence is immaterial, its downward movement is impossible, and thus no substratum for it is logical, given that a substratum is defined as that which prevents downward motion.

Nor can it be characterized by the relationship of produced and producer, because since the cause called "ascertainment" (niścaya) is always present, there would be the undesirable consequence of the constant production of excellence;
furthermore, it is not logical for ascertainment to produce excellence in dependence upon the application of a means,
because dependence on that which provides no assistance is impossible.
Alternatively, if there is assistance, the same fault as before applies and there is an infinite regress.
Furthermore, regarding that excellence which is produced as something distinct, the two alternatives—whether it is non-existent or existent—certainly arise here as well.
In that case, if it were non-existent, the means of proof would incur the fallacy of being inconclusive, just as before.
Furthermore, if [the manifestation] were already existent, the effort of the means of production would be futile;
and if manifestation is also desired to be manifested there, the consequence of an infinite regress—namely, "what is this manifestation?"—is difficult to avoid.
Therefore, even in the view that [manifestation] is distinct [from the entity], since it is unconnected and lacks a relationship, the production of a superior quality of form is not tenable.
26–27. There is neither cognition of that object nor the destruction of the veil over perception,
because perception is eternal and a second [perception] is impossible.

Nor is manifestation characterized by the arising of a cognition having that [object] as its object tenable, because the consciousness of that object is eternal according to you who maintain the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*).
For, since that consciousness of the object is eternal in your view, what could there be for it to be produced?
Furthermore, because a second perception is impossible, manifestation characterized by the arising of a cognition having that object is not tenable.
The word *api* (also/even) serves as a conjunction (*samuccaya*) and its position is displaced; it should be understood as following immediately after the word *asambhavāt* (due to impossibility).
By this, the following is stated:

according to your view, consciousness is one alone, because of your established doctrine that "cognition is one from the beginning of creation until the dissolution of the world. And that [consciousness] itself is the ascertainment (*niścaya*). In that case, what other "perception" called "manifestation" could there be, which could be produced by means (*sādhana*)?
It might be argued that the cognition of its object does not have the nature of *buddhi*,
but rather the nature of the *manas*;
however, this is incorrect, because *buddhi*, *upalabdhi*, *adhyavasāya*, and *manaḥsaṃvitti* do not denote different things.
And this will be explained later;

nor is it a manifestation characterized by the destruction of the obscuration to the perception of that object. For these two reasons, namely: as for that obscuration to its perception, its destruction is not possible because it is eternal.
Nor is destruction characterized by disappearance (tirobhāva) logical, because disappearance is impossible for that which has not abandoned its prior nature,
and because there is no concealment of perception since a second perception is impossible;
for concealment is not possible for what is non-existent, as it must have a real entity as its object.
Therefore, its destruction is not logical.

Alternatively, because of its permanence—that is, because the consciousness whose object is that [self] is permanent—an obscuration is impossible; since that is impossible, its destruction is not logical.
Furthermore, the destruction of an obscuration is not brought about by anyone.
Because that [effect] lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*),

not only is the application of a proof (*sādhanaprayoga*) futile under the position of the theory of pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*), but the unavoidable consequence of the non-existence of bondage and liberation, as well as the annihilation of all worldly conventions, follows. For instance, you maintain that liberation occurs when there arises the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), characterized by the perception of the isolation (*kaivalya*) of both *pradhāna* and *puruṣa*.
Furthermore, since that knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) would be eternally present, all embodied beings would be liberated at all times; consequently, there would be no bondage.

Bondage is held to result from false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), and if that were eternally present, everyone would be bound forever—so how could there be liberation? Moreover, people engage in activity for the sake of attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful; yet under the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), there is nothing unattainable or unrejectable, and thus the world would be devoid of effort. Ultimately, this leads to the undesirable consequence of the total cessation of all worldly transaction.

Having thus refuted the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), [the author] says "In the case of the three qualities," etc., in order to avoid the faults that arise from the position of the theory of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*):
"Even though there is no difference in the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), not everything is the producer of everything."

Just as [in the case of the existent], so too, even though the effect is non-existent, not everything is the producer of everything. (28) Since the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has been refuted, it is established by implication that the effect is non-existent (*asatkārya*); for, since existence and non-existence are defined by mutual exclusion, no other alternative is possible. Nevertheless, this is stated in order to demonstrate that the objection raised by the opponent is merely a fallacious refutation (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*).

Regarding that which was stated—that it would be impossible to produce [an effect] because of its formlessness—that is unproven, because we accept that it is precisely the intrinsic nature (*vastusvabhāva*) of the thing that is being produced, and because that intrinsic nature of the thing is not established as being formless.
If it is argued that "prior to its production, it is indeed devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)," [we reply: no.
Because it is impossible for that very [entity] to be without intrinsic nature;
for it is not logical that intrinsic nature itself be without intrinsic nature, since being without intrinsic nature is defined as the negation of the intrinsic nature of a thing,
and furthermore, it does not exist prior to its arising.
If that very entity by which an object is being produced were established as lacking intrinsic nature, then [the argument fails].

Alternatively, if one takes as the subject (pakṣa) a formless substratum characterized precisely by the absence of an entity, and employs "because of being formless" as the reason (hetu), then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā);
for the absence of an entity is not accepted by anyone as something being produced.
Moreover, the reason is not even inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because no subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) has been shown regarding the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

For, due to the specific restriction of causal power (*kāraṇaśaktipratiniyama*), only that which is non-existent is produced for which a producing cause exists; however, that for which no cause exists—such as a sky-lotus (*viyadabja*) and the like—is not produced. Thus, the reason remains inconclusive.
For it is not accepted that everything is the cause of everything, nor is it accepted as a universal rule that whatever is non-existent must necessarily be produced; what then?

That which is produced must be non-existent prior to its production—this might be argued. Even if causes are equal in their capacity to produce what is non-existent, why is it that everything does not become the cause of every non-existent thing?
This same objection applies equally to you as well; for if causes were equal in their capacity to produce what is existent, why would everything not be the cause of every existent thing?

If it is argued that, according to your view, there is nothing non-existent that could be produced— since even existent things such as a rabbit’s horn are not produced due to the specific restriction of causal power—
that argument applies equally to the other case as well.

Furthermore, just as for you [the Sāṃkhyas], although the three qualities (triguṇya) are present everywhere without distinction, not everything is the producer of everything— due to the specific restriction of capacities (śakti)— whether one analyzes the compound as "the producer of everything" or "everything is its producer," so too, even if the effect does not exist [prior to production], nothing will be the producer of everything, because there is some persisting form [of the cause] that follows through [into the effect].
This has been stated while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position] by saying "just as... so too," but it is not actually a case of equality;
for even when there is a difference, only a specific thing serves as the cause for a specific effect.

This is not contradictory because, due to the nature of illusion (*māyātattva*), there is a specific determination of the distinctions in the intrinsic natures of things based on a succession of their own causes.
However, if there were no distinction, how could it be possible for a single thing at one and the same time to be both a cause and a non-cause, given that they are mutually exclusive?
For the distinction between entities is necessarily grounded in the imposition of contradictory properties.

And so it has been said: "For if there were difference, some cause would exist by virtue of being a property of the entity; but if there were non-difference, both action and non-action would be precluded for that single [entity]."
With the words "of the limits" (avadhīnām) and so forth, the opponent objects, conceiving of a restriction of powers: "Since limits are not established, those [powers] are not restricted."

But for you, the Buddhist who maintains the doctrine of the non-existence of the effect (*asatkāryavāda*), a restriction regarding those [powers] would not be possible with a fixed limit. Why? Because the limits, which are the effects themselves, have not yet been produced.

For there is no existence of that which possesses a limit (the limited) without a limit (the limiting). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things that are devoid of a real limit consisting of an effect do not possess restricted capacities, such as, for example, a rabbit’s horn; and entities such as rice seeds are devoid of a real limit consisting of an effect. Thus, by means of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), he says "existence" (*sattve*) while demonstrating the firmness of his own position.
The meaning is "when the effects exist";
"of them" refers to the powers (śaktis).
With the words "not so" and so forth, he states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the reason:
"It is not so; let it be that because those [qualities] are unestablished, the word [denoting them] does not exist in that way;
yet there is no harm to the nature of the real entity (*vasturūpa*) which is devoid of all adventitious adjuncts (*upādhi*). (30)

For instance—if, due to the non-establishment of those limits, there were merely the absence of such a designation as "the milk has the power to produce curd," then there would be no denial of that reality which is devoid of all adjuncts (*upādhi*), neither superimposed nor non-superimposed, and immediately after which another previously unseen entity arises.

[Objection: One might argue that where words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) do not function, the very nature of the thing (*vastu-svabhāva*) also ceases to exist. To this he says: "Neither name nor form," and so forth.

Indeed, names and forms, as well as conceptual constructions and designations, do not constitute the reality of things; rather, diverse conceptualizations proceed according to habituation toward that which is non-differentiated.

For it is the essential nature (svabhāva) itself, being pervasive, which, when excluded, excludes its own pervaded (vyāpya), or the cause excludes the effect, because of the existence of a necessary connection (pratibandha).

Nothing else [is the nature], for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the fact that curd possesses the capacity for milk and so forth— which is a designation based on names— is not the form or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things,
such that its absence would cause the thing itself to cease to exist.
The mention of "name" is an illustration;
conceptual construction associated with it is also included.
Furthermore, the mention of "form" is likewise an illustration.
(The cause is taken up: Even the cause of things does not truly exist as a name, for things can occur even without it; here he states the reason: "conceptual constructions" and so forth.

Because conceptual constructions—which possess association with names—and denotative words are "various conceptualizations"—that is, of manifold kinds—they function according to habituation toward that which is non-differentiated, an entity whose nature is partless and unitary.
For instance—a single entity such as sound is conceptualized and designated by proponents existing at different times as having various forms, such as being eternal and so forth.
If those verbal conceptualizations were identical with the object or had it as their referent, then the object would necessarily possess manifoldness;
or else, like the nature of the object itself, the verbal conceptualizations would result in being of a single form.
For it is not logical that a single thing be variegated, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, because of the specific restriction of capacities (*śaktipratiniyama*), only a certain non-existent [effect] is produced and not everything; thus, the reason "because of being formless" (*nairūpyāt*) is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For this very reason, the fourfold set of reasons beginning with "because of the appropriation of the material cause" (*upādānagrahaṇāt*) is also inconclusive.
For instance: if it were established anywhere that the apprehension of specific material causes is produced solely by the existence of the effect, then this [argument] would hold;
however, the apprehension of specific material causes is indeed consistent even when produced by the restriction of the causal capacity.

And it is precisely because of the specific restriction of causal capacity that everything does not arise from everything, since it is impossible for everything to possess the nature of performing every purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Furthermore, as for what was stated— "that which is an excellence beyond action," and so forth— that too was said through a failure to understand our intention;
for we do not assert that "non-existence" is produced,
such that there would be the undesirable consequence of its losing its own nature when a transformation occurs.
However, it was previously established that it is indeed the entity itself that is produced.

And since that entity cannot be produced because it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception, and because what is already accomplished cannot logically be an effect, it is said to be non-existent prior to its arising. That cause by whose mere presence such an entity arises is designated as "producing" it; yet nothing is produced by anything through the application of an activity, because all phenomena are devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*).
Nor does there exist anything called "non-existent" that could undergo transformation, nor is it the nature of a real entity, because non-existence is characterized solely by negation.

Furthermore, if it is asserted that the non-existent is not produced because it lacks any excellence of effect (*akāryātiśaya*), then the existent as well lacks any excellence of effect precisely because its own nature is already established; so how could it be produced?
Therefore, because that which is capable produces only what it is capable of producing, the reason "because of the capacity" (*śaktasya śakyakaraṇāt*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, since the state of being a cause is logically possible even under the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*), the reason "because of the state of being a cause" (*kāraṇabhāvāt*) is also inconclusive.

Alternatively, since it has already been demonstrated that it is impossible for that which exists previously to be an effect, and since the restriction regarding the selection of a material cause (*upādānagrahaṇa*) and so forth is only logical under the theory that the effect is non-existent, these four reasons beginning with "because of the selection of a material cause" are contradictory (*viruddha*), as they prove the opposite of the thesis.
Now, if it is your view that only the non-existent arises, how is it that the arising of both the existent and the non-existent is refuted in the Sūtra?
As it has been said: "O Mahāmati, all phenomena are unarisen, because neither the existent nor the non-existent arises. To this, he replies: "Arising," and so forth.

Arising, however, is the existence of a thing; it is not connected with either the non-existent or the existent in that way, but rather [it is connected] solely with a non-existent conceptualizing cognition. (32) The word "tu" (however) has the sense of restriction.

The very intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of things, which exists for only a single moment and is empty of prior and posterior limits, is called "arising" (utpāda) when there is a desire to know that alone, by way of excluding other distinctions; however,
it is not the "birth" (jāti) as a characteristic of the conditioned (saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa) imagined by the Vaibhāṣikas.

Since that [inherence] is about to be refuted, neither the inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*) nor the inherence in its own cause (*svakāraṇa-samavāya*) postulated by the Vaiśeṣikas is [the cause], for both of those will also be refuted, and according to their own doctrine,
both of those are eternal.

Furthermore, birth is impossible for that which is eternal, as it has been said: "Since it is the cause that effects the connection of existence with its own cause, that existence is indeed [eternal];
and since both that [existence] and the relation are eternal, what then is the effect here?"
Thus,
this origination, being of such a nature, is not connected with non-existence through identity,
because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence.
For that which is non-existent does not exist,
nor is it connected with an existent thing that precedes it, because that [existent] was previously non-existent.

He says "by a conceptualizing [intellect]" (*kalpikayā*) and so forth to address the question: "How is it that you are now proponents of the theory that the effect is non-existent" (*asatkāryavādinaḥ*)?

By means of a conceptualizing intellect, whether acting as the agent (*kartṛ*) or the instrument (*karaṇa*), it is connected solely with a non-existent agent—the meaning is that it is brought into a relationship [with it]. For there is no such thing as a non-existent that could enter into production; rather, this is merely a conventional usage based on imagination, namely, that "the non-existent is produced. This is the sense.

But what, then, is the seed of this conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) by which such conventional usage is accepted? To this he says: "That which is this," and so forth—that is, this form of the object which is perceived immediately [after the sensation].
"It did not exist previously"—this is the seed [of that notion];

for this [object], which is perceived as a new form of reality immediately following some specific, determinate thing, did not exist prior to its intermediate state, because it was not perceived despite having reached the conditions for perception.
Therefore, the seed of this conceptualization—that "this, being previously non-existent, arises"—is established.
He asks "Why? and says: "Because it existed previously," and so forth.

Prior to the middle state, while the nature of the entity—which has become that [middle state]—is already present, this basis for conceptual construction, namely "this arises," does not exist. For instance, by the term "arises," only a specific intrinsic nature (svarūpa) that is to be realized in the middle state is expressed.

And if its existence were to occur even prior [to that state], then its very nature—which is necessarily characterized by its intermediate state—would be lost; for, like space, that which exists eternally lacks prior, posterior, and intermediate states. Consequently, one would have to designate that everything is produced at all times, since there is no distinction [between the states].
Furthermore, refuting the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) by another method, he says: "And in milk, etc.
and so forth; that which is considered to exist in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*) within milk and other such substances as curd and the like.
What power is there in that [curd and so forth] if it were seen like milk?
Regarding what you say—that the effect exists in the cause—what is the intended meaning there?
Is it in the form of manifestation? That is not so.

Because there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving curds and so forth even during the state of milk and so on, as one does later; or, if you say they exist in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), even then, is that form of potentiality of the curds and so forth something other than their manifest effect-form which has reached the conditions for perception, or is it that very same thing? If it is that very same thing, then there is the same undesirable consequence of its being perceived as before.
Furthermore, if it were otherwise, how could one thing be said to exist through the non-existence of another?
For the existence of sattva is not the existence of rajas and tamas. 35. [And] the existence of rajas and tamas is not the existence of sattva.

If, on the other hand, the position is that [the effect] is something else, then the position that "the effect exists within the nature of the cause" would be abandoned; for it is admitted that there exists a distinct entity called "power" (*śakti*) which is different from the effect.
To explain: that very form which has manifested, endowed with specific qualities such as taste, potency, and post-digestive transformation, is called the effect, such as curd and the like;
and since that is not perceived during the state of milk, even though it is capable of being perceived, it is the object of the conventional designation "non-existent."

Furthermore, whatever else exists in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*) is not itself the effect, nor does one thing exist because of the presence of another, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [An objection is raised: "But surely we see other things being spoken of in relation to the existence of others, such as 'clarified butter is longevity' (*āyur ghṛtam*) or 'water from a reed-bed is a foot disease' (*naḍvalodakaṃ pādaroga*). To this he replies: "Not figuratively" (*abhaktyā*).
"Without devotion"— the meaning is "without figurative application";
for when it is said, "Clarified butter is life," this is due to the figurative application of the effect to the cause,
not in a primary sense.

If, however, you also say that the effect exists in the cause by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), then there is no contradiction; but it is said that there is a contradiction in the primary sense.
Demonstrating this very point through an example, he says: "For not... and so forth.
For that which has the nature of *sattva* is not established by you as being the same as suffering (*duḥkha*) and delusion (*moha*), since their characteristics are established as mutually distinct.

Now, demonstrating the unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) of the reason "because a continuity of differences is observed," he says: "That which is permeated by *sattva*, etc. (*sattvādyanugatam*, etc.).
The manifest (vyakta), which is accompanied by sattva and the other [guṇas], is not established for us in any way;
because pleasure and the rest are internal, and because they are manifest through their own self-awareness.
The manifest characterized by sound and so forth—that is, having the nature of pleasure and the rest—is not established for us, that is, for us [Sāṃkhyas].

Why? Because pleasure and the like are internal—that is, they are of the nature of consciousness—whereas sound and the like are insentient; how, then, could these [latter] be endowed with pleasure and the like?
The formal argument is as follows: those things which are not of the nature of consciousness are not composed of pleasure and the like, just like the insentient person accepted by the opponent.
And since sound and the other objects are devoid of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), this would be a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

This [objection] might be raised: "If the pervasion of being composed of pleasure and so forth by the nature of consciousness were established, then that [nature of consciousness], being excluded, would exclude the state of being composed of pleasure and so forth from sound and the rest; however, that very [pervasion] is not established, because it is accepted that only the *puruṣa* possesses the nature of consciousness. To this he says: "Because of its manifestation through its own consciousness" (*vyaktatvāt tatsvasaṃvidaḥ*). That is to say, the nature of consciousness in pleasure and the rest is established. Why? Because of the manifestation of the "own-consciousness" (*svasaṃvit*)—that is, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—of pleasure and the rest.

This self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), characterized as being self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*) and independent of any other light, is extremely evident in the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth, whether or not objects such as sound are present.

For that which is established by itself through its own nature as pleasure and so on, independent of any other light, is called by synonyms such as "consciousness" (*caitanya*), "pleasure," "experience" (*saṃvedana*), and "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

If the manifestation of experience for pleasure and the like were due to their being experienced by another cognition, then their experience would be of a nature that is not pleasure and so on, because they themselves do not possess that nature.

Otherwise, when a yogin or an inferer perceives the pleasure and so forth belonging to another, those yogins and others would become afflicted just like those who directly experience pleasure and so forth; or else, like the yogins,
there would be no benefit or harm for others either, since there would be no distinction between them.

And if it is admitted that cognition (*saṃvedana*) has the nature of being pleasant (*sāta*) and so forth, then the fact that pleasure (*sukha*) and the like are of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*) is established;
for this alone is our pleasure and pain, namely, cognition that is pleasant and unpleasant.
Therefore, the reason is neither inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) nor unestablished (*asiddha*).
Since for all proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādins), it is established that sounds and other phenomena are devoid of the nature of consciousness,
otherwise they would be accepting the very position of the Vijñānavādins, which is indeed their intended view.

Nor is the reason contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa). One might object: "Just as a cognition, though not having the nature of blue and so forth, appears in the form of blue and so forth due to the proximity of external objects such as blue, so too, by the influence of external adjuncts such as pleasure, that which is not of the nature of pleasure appears as if it were of the nature of pleasure. Therefore, even if cognition possesses the nature of pleasure and so forth, it does not follow that pleasure and the rest have the nature of consciousness; thus, the primary reason is not inconclusive. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In one [instance]," and so forth.
And in a single instance, such as sound and so forth, attachment and the other [afflictions] are clearly observed to occur with necessity according to the distinctions in their cultivation and types.
(37) "According to the distinctions in their cultivation and types" means:
"Bhāvanās" means repeated practices; "jāti" means one's innate nature. The "difference" between these two refers to specific distinctions such as attachment (saṅga) and so forth.

Here, "attachment" (saṅga) means longing; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the groups of effects of the three guṇas are included, such as affection and the like, aversion, agitation and the like, and dejection, obscuration and the like.
Furthermore, they are "determined" (niyata) and uniform in form;

for instance, due to specific mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*), pleasure and other states arise as restricted to certain individuals—such as lustful persons who have cultivated the notions of purity or impurity regarding wine, women, and so forth—and due to specific birth (*jāti*), such as deer, young elephants, and others, [pleasure] arises in some but not in all. This would not be logical if sound and the other objects were inherently of the nature of pleasure and so on.
He asks "Why? and says: "Because of subsisting in a single object," and so forth;
for if [cognition] were to subsist in a single object, it would follow that cognition is variegated (*citrā*).
If it is argued that [the cognition] does not [perceive all aspects] due to the influence of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) and so forth, then [cognition] would not follow the reality [as it is].

For since all of those [aspects] have a single, non-different object as their domain, it would follow that for each individual [aspect], there would be a variegated consciousness (citrasaṃvit), just like the perception of objects such as blue and so on.

This might be the case: although the object consists of three natures, nevertheless, by the power of auxiliary factors characterized as the unseen (adṛṣṭa), merit (dharma), and so forth, only a certain form appears to someone, and not every [form] to everyone.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of [factors] such as the distinction between types of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and the desire to grasp [an object].

The point is this: if it were not so, that consciousness—which follows after an object—that is, which has an object as its support (*ālambana*), would not be attained, because it would be devoid of that object's form (*tadākāra*).

Demonstrating that very emptiness of those forms, he says: "The form of the object has three aspects, but the cognitions of it have only one aspect; how could those [cognitions], which are future and distinct from it, be applicable to that [object]? (39)

The meaning is that the cognitions (*vidas*)— that is, the consciousnesses (*saṃvittayas*)— of those knowers (*tadvidaḥ*), namely the *puruṣas*, are perceived as having a single form, because each is restricted to a single nature consisting solely of attachment and so forth toward the forms of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
"Those"—meaning cognitions; "there"—meaning in sound and so forth; "future"—meaning ultimate or real;
why are they not tenable? He says: "because they are different from that," meaning they are different from the object which serves as their support.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever does not possess the cognition of a particular form is not an object of that [form], just as visual cognition does not have sound as its object;

and the aforementioned cognitions are devoid of the forms of the three-natured reality (*tryātmakavastu*). This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), which serves as a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the opposite position by way of the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

It might be argued: "Just as even when an object such as sound is grasped by perception in its entirety, a determinate ascertainment (*niścaya*) arises only with respect to certain aspects like momentariness due to the force of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, and not with respect to everything; likewise, due to the force of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, a cognition may arise with only a single form."
This is incorrect;
for we do not maintain that conceptual constructions such as "momentariness" have, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), a real entity (*vastu*) as their object,
because the ultimate reality transcends all conceptual construction.
However, its validity is established through a mediated connection to the object, by virtue of being the cause for attaining such an object.
As for pleasure and so forth, others maintain that they have the real object as their domain in the ultimate sense;

otherwise, if they were without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), then the manifestation of the experience of pleasure and so on could not occur from the experience of sounds and other objects which are themselves of the nature of pleasure and so on.

And since those [mental states] such as joy and so forth are conceptual (*savikalpaka*), there is no form whatsoever that remains undetermined; thus, there would be a manifestation of experience in its entirety.
For this indeed is the comprehension of an object by determinate cognitions: namely, that which is called "ascertainment" (*niścayana*).

Regarding what was stated—that the accompaniment of sound and other objects by pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth is established because effects such as serenity (*prasāda*), agitation (*udvega*), and depression (*dainya*) are observed—he says "serenity, agitation, and concealment... and so on, demonstrating that this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*):
"Serenity, agitation, and concealment [occur] in a single person for yogins."
And yet, a person of that nature is not accepted by our opponents.

For instance, among the followers of Kapila’s Yoga who meditate upon the Puruṣa as distinct from Prakṛti, there arises clarity and joy for those whose yoga is well-practiced by taking the Puruṣa as their object;
for those whose yoga is unmastered and who do not perceive it quickly, there arises agitation; and for those whose intellects are dull by nature, a covering (of ignorance) arises.
Furthermore, that person (puruṣa) is not accepted by the opponents as being of that nature—that is, consisting of the three guṇas.
Therefore, because effects such as serenity, distress, and dejection are observed, this [argument] is inconclusive.
If it is argued that those states, such as joy and so forth, arise from volition (saṅkalpa) and not from the person;
This is the same in the case of sound and the other objects; consequently, if they were produced by mere mental construction (*saṅkalpa*), external pleasures and so forth would not be established,
because mental construction is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid*).
For this very reason, the claim that consciousness possesses the nature of pleasure and so forth due to the influence of external objects such as pleasure is also fallacious;
for we observe the arising of joy and the like by taking a person as its object even without the influence of an external object.

Furthermore, how could that well-known experience of pleasure and so forth—which occurs through the conceptualization of the desirable and undesirable without depending on the proximity of an external object—arise from the influence of another?
If it is argued that the mind (*manas*) is also composed of the three *guṇas* because it arises from them as its substrate, we say no;

for its nature as consciousness (*saṃvidrūpatva*) has already been established by such statements as: "Indeed, that which does not depend on another light [to be perceived] is itself self-established," and so forth.
Therefore, the reason "because of [the presence of] samanvaya" is unestablished (asiddha).
Now, while provisionally accepting the establishment of the reason, [the author] states the following to demonstrate its inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva): "Even if it is established," and so forth.
Even if the manifest (vyakta) is established as consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa), the Pradhāna is not thereby proven;
for that [proposed] cause is not one, eternal, and endowed with a single genus.
(41) Even if it were granted that the manifest is composed of the three qualities, nevertheless, its postulated cause called Pradhāna is not established.
The meaning is that, because of such a nature [of the probandum], the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of the reason is not established anywhere.
To explain: one intends to prove a cause that consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), is unitary, eternal, and all-pervading;
however, no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the reason with such a cause has been established anywhere.
Nor is it necessarily the case that whatever nature an effect is observed to have, its cause must possess that same nature, because there is a distinction between cause and effect.

To illustrate: you maintain that the manifest effect is endowed with properties such as having a cause, impermanence, and non-pervasiveness; yet you do not accept that its cause possesses those same characteristics. Therefore, your reason is inconclusive.

Showing that [the argument] is also contradictory because it involves a conceptualization contrary to the specific nature of the property (*dharma-viśeṣa-viparīta-bhāvanā*), he says: "That cause is one," and so forth. A single, eternal, and three-constituent (*triguṇātmaka*) causal property is intended to be proven; however, such a thing is not established, but rather its opposite—this is the sense. Why? He says: "For that is not endowed with a single genus (*jāti*)."
The word "hi" (for/indeed) indicates the reason;
therefore, that effect called "the manifest" is not established as being endowed with a single genus consisting of the three *guṇas* which is its own essence.
What then? It is perceived as being endowed precisely with attributes such as multiplicity, impermanence, and so forth.

For if the manifest entity were indeed endowed with a single universal (jāti) as previously described, then its cause would also be established as characterized by those same aforementioned properties; however,
since the effect is observed to possess the properties of impermanence and multiplicity, its cause is likewise inferred to be so, because for that which is eternal,
causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is contradictory whether it occurs successively or simultaneously.
Furthermore, because the diversity of effects is produced by a difference in causes—
otherwise, it would follow that they are causeless—
it is therefore not established that *pradhāna* is eternal and of a single uniform nature.
If, however, the cause were designated as *pradhāna* (the primal matter) being merely impermanent and manifold in form, then there would be no dispute; this is the sense.
Why, then, is the manifest (*vyakta*) not endowed with a single common genus? To this he says: "like iron rods," and so forth.
For all individual manifestations are seen to be like iron rods, whose forms are joined only in succession, and whose natures are intermingled with conceptual construction (kalpanā).

Just as iron rods are not connected to one another, so too these manifestations of sound and the rest— being established in their own respective natures— do not enter into mutual connection due to differences in place, time, capacity, appearance, and so forth.
By this, their multiplicity has been established.
To establish their impermanence, he says: "those whose forms are joined in a sequence.
The analysis of the compound is: those whose forms (*mūrti*) are joined—that is, embraced—by the sequence of arising.

How then are entities determined as being followed by a single form such as "earth" and so forth, and likewise by a stable nature such that one thinks, "this is that very same thing"? To this he says: "having a nature mixed with conceptual construction.
