This means that this grasping of a single identity among objects is a false conceptualization (*mithyāvikalpa*);
and this will be demonstrated later in the section on momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth.

Thus, the fallacies of being unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) regarding the reason "because of concomitance" (*samanvayāt*) have been demonstrated. Now, demonstrating that the example "like the various types of jars and so forth" lacks the concomitance of the properties of the probandum and the probans, he says: "The various modifications of clay and so forth," etc.—just as the various modifications of clay and so forth are not endowed with a single genus (*ekajāti*).
And [the arguments] are established as having multiple causes due to the distinction between a lump of clay and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), modifications such as gold and the like are included.
The word "tathā" (likewise) serves either to aggregate another refutation or to indicate similarity.
By the phrase "not endowed with a single genus," the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanadharma*) is shown;
and the phrase "nor having a single cause" is connected to the subject under discussion, namely, that they are established [as such].
By this, the lack of concomitance with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) has been shown.

Now, one might object: "But surely a single cause, such as a lump of clay or gold, is established for these [products]; likewise, a genus such as 'clay-ness' or 'gold-ness' is observed to follow them. So how can there be a deficiency in both respects? To this he says: "Because of the difference from the lump of clay, etc.
For there is no single composite whole (*avayavin*) such as a lump of clay; otherwise, if it were covered in one part, it would follow that it is entirely covered.
Nor is there a single genus [applying] to every individual, because there is a difference in their manifestation;
furthermore, demonstrating that the reason "because of recurrence" (*samanvayāt*) is inherently inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "consciousness," and so forth.

Even though they possess consciousness and other such qualities, it is not accepted that persons have a single prior cause; if you claim that [the oneness] is secondary, why is it not the same in this case as well? (44) For instance, persons are held to be endowed with immeasurable attributes such as sentience and being an enjoyer, yet you do not accept that they are preceded by a single cause of that kind.

Furthermore, it might be argued that the possession of consciousness (*caitanya*) and so forth by the *puruṣas* is not intended in a primary sense; rather, it is secondary (*gauṇa*). For all *puruṣas* are excluded from non-consciousness and the like; therefore, consciousness is postulated as a genus (*jāti*) consisting in the exclusion of other things (*arthāntara-vyāvṛtti*), which follows after them, but there is no single, real entity [of consciousness] existing [independently]. If this is so, then that is secondary. Likewise, even in the absence of being preceded by a single such cause, why is the possession of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth not similarly postulated here for the individual? Why is it not considered equal? Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The mention of "of persons" (puruṣāṇām) is an elliptical indication [for other categories as well].

Likewise, pleasure and the rest, which exist in the state of primordial nature (mūlaprakṛti), are endowed with qualities such as being attributes (guṇatva), insentience (acetanatva), and non-enjoyership (abhoktṛtva); and both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa) are possessed of properties such as eternality (nityatva). Yet, these are not preceded by a single cause of that same nature; thus, [the reason] is indeed inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Thus, the reason "because of concomitance" has been refuted;

now, under the guise of a conclusion, he states a mere indication for the purpose of refuting the remaining reasons: "Even in the absence of a primary cause," and so forth, meaning that even in the absence of a primary cause, everything is produced from that [nature].

The diversity [of the world], consisting of the relation of cause and effect and so forth, arises from the differentiation of power (*śakti*). Regarding that which was stated— that the Pradhāna exists because of its limited dimensions, because activity proceeds from power, and because of the relation of cause and effect—
all three of these reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to the opposite of the thesis.

Since no subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*) has been presented, there is no contradiction among these [reasons], such as "limited magnitude" (*parimāṇa*), even in the absence of the cause called *pradhāna*.

To explain: if it is merely the existence of a cause that is being proven, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), for we do not maintain that the production of an effect occurs without a cause; and if one applies the designation "Primal Matter" (*pradhāna*) to the mere cause, nothing is contradicted.

Now, if it is argued as follows: "There exists an intelligent cause (prekṣāvat-kāraṇa), because this [world] produces manifest entities of a fixed dimension and proceeds from [its own] capacity"—then that argument is inconclusive (anaikāntikatā). For even without an intelligent agent, there is no contradiction in the production of things endowed with fixed dimensions and so forth, due to the specific restriction of the power of their own causes; moreover, it is not logical for Pradhāna to be intelligent, because it is insentient (acetana).
Furthermore, since "prekṣā" (contemplation) is a synonym for consciousness (*caitanya*), and moreover:
if by the statement "because of activity from power" you intend to prove merely a cause endowed with non-distinct powers, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*);
but if you mean a single, eternal cause endowed with distinct and diverse powers, then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, because positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is not established for such a [cause] anywhere, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). For it is not proven that the activity of any cause toward any effect occurs by virtue of a distinct power (*śakti*), since powers are identical with the essence of the thing itself.

As for what was stated—that "the manifold world arises from non-differentiation"—that is unestablished, because the dissolution of all entities into anything whatsoever is unproven, given that all things possess the nature of perishing without leaving a trace (*niranvayavināśadharman*).

For instance: if dissolution occurs, it must happen either upon the loss of the previous nature or without such loss. If it occurs upon the loss of that nature, then the consequence is total destruction without residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*). If, however, it occurs without such loss, then dissolution is logically impossible; for dissolution is not tenable for anyone who continues to experience their own essential nature in its entirety, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the argument.
Therefore, this [proposition]—"the manifoldness of the universe is non-differentiated"—is mutually contradictory.

Thus, even in the absence of a primary cause (pradhāna), the diversity of the effect—such as its limited magnitude—and the distinction between cause and effect arise through the cause consisting of the specific capacities of the causal substance; therefore, the reasons [adduced by the opponent] are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the phrase "proceeding from capacity" (*śaktitaḥ pravṛtteḥ*) is included.
Alternatively, in the phrase "even in the absence of a primary cause," the particle "even" (*api*) is used for emphasis.
Therefore, the meaning is this:

because the diversity of the effect—in the form of its limited dimensions and so forth—and the relationship of cause and effect are established precisely by the reason of the differentiation of causal potencies (which exists only in the absence of a primal cause), the reasons [adduced by the Sāṃkhya] are contradictory.
For instance, if Pradhāna were the cause of the manifest world, then, being of its very nature, the entire universe would be a single substance, identical in character to it.
Furthermore, there would be no division of dimensions such as "one intellect," "ego," or "the five subtle elements";
and that being the case, the world would be entirely without dimension.
Likewise, the activity of potters and others in producing jars and so forth through their capacity would be possible only in the absence of a primary cause (pradhāna), but not when it exists.
As stated previously, neither potentiality nor activity exists;
thus, the very distinction between cause and effect is only logical when the Pradhāna as a cause is absent.
Furthermore, the manifold diversity previously mentioned is simply not possible if the Pradhāna exists.

It has been stated that because the entire world would, by virtue of being identical with that [Brahman], result in being one with its own nature, there would consequently be no manifoldness (vaiśvarūpya) from the very beginning; how then could there be its non-differentiation? Thus ends the examination of Primordial Matter (prakṛti).

In the *Īśvaraparīkṣā*, now demonstrating that [the world] is devoid of the activity of a Lord (*īśa*), he says: "Others declare the Lord to be the cause of all things that have an origin," and so forth.
"Indeed, that which is insentient does not initiate its own effects by itself.
(46) Since atoms, space, and so forth, being unproduced, are eternal and thus have no cause, the term "of those that are produced" (*utpattimatām*) was used.
"The Lord" (*īśam*) means the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*).
"Others" refers to the Naiyāyikas and others.
Among them, some hold that the creator of the entire world is the Lord (Īśvara), who is omniscient and possesses specific qualities distinct from [ordinary] selves.

Others maintain that he is a separate substance (dravyāntara) indeed, because his qualities are different [from those of other substances], owing to his being endowed with an eternal, unitary cognition whose object is all things.

[Objection: Surely merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), atoms, and so forth, do indeed exist as the causes of the world; for what purpose, then, do you postulate a further cause in the form of a Lord (*īśvara*)? [Response: To this he says, "Not that which is insentient," and so on. Although merit and the rest are causes, nevertheless, because they are insentient (*acetana*), they are not capable of initiating their own effects by themselves without a presiding controller. Therefore, there must be some agent who presides over them; for no insentient thing is ever observed to be an independent presiding controller.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is insentient does not begin its own effect without a presiding controller, just as a lump of clay, a staff, water, thread, and so forth [cannot produce] a jar without a potter; and since dharma, adharma, and the rest are insentient, this is an "observation of the contrary of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Therefore, it is established that he who is this presiding controller is God (*Īśvara*).
Nor, this being the case, are dharma, adharma, and the rest rendered useless, because God is their instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
It might be argued that since merit and demerit are inherent in the self, that very self will be the controller; what then is the use of postulating a Lord? That is incorrect.

Because that self is then ignorant, as long as its aggregate of effects and causes—namely the body, senses, and so forth—is not produced, this ignorant being does not perceive even perceptible objects such as forms; how then could it perceive dharma and adharma, which are imperceptible?
As it has been said: "This living being is ignorant and not master of its own pleasure and pain;
impelled by the Lord, it goes either to heaven or indeed to hell."

46. In that regard, he states the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) presented by Aviddhakarṇa for proving the Lord (*īśvara*), beginning with "that which possesses a specific arrangement of its own constituent parts" (*yatsvārambhaka-avayava-sanniveśa-viśeṣavat*).
That which is understood through an intelligent cause is such as a jar and the like.
Such a subject of dispute—whether perceptible by two sense organs or imperceptible—is preceded by an intelligent agent; therefore, atoms are considered [to be] dissimilar [to this].

As it has been stated: "That which is perceptible by two sense organs and that which is imperceptible, when taken as the subject of dispute, are preceded by an intelligent cause, because they possess a specific arrangement of their own constituent parts, like a jar; by contrast, atoms [are not].

In this context, "perceptible by two sense organs" refers to the three kinds of substances known as earth, water, and fire, which are perceptible by both the visual and tactile organs, being endowed with the causes for the perception of magnitude, possession of multiple substances, color, and so forth.

Air and the like are ungraspable, because largeness (*mahattva*), the state of possessing multiple substances (*anekadravyavattva*), and inherence of color (*rūpasamavāya*) are held to be the causes of perception; and these do not exist in air and the like, as it has been stated: "Perception occurs due to largeness, due to the possession of multiple large [substances], and due to color;
there is no perception of atoms and the like because they do not possess [multiple] substances."
Due to the absence of the formative factor of color (*rūpa-saṃskāra*), there is no perception of air;
"formative factor of color" means the inherence of color,
while the non-perception of dyads (*dvy-aṇuka*) and so forth is due to their lack of magnitude (*amahattva*).

In this context, if one were to prove generally that whatever is perceptible by two sense-faculties or imperceptible by them is preceded by an intelligent cause, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because in the case of jars and the like,
both [the property and its cause] are admitted and there is no dispute.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with what has been accepted, because atoms, space, and so forth are not accepted as being such [non-eternal],
and since they are eternal, there would be a contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition;
therefore, for that reason, the phrase "those which have entered into the state of being the subject of dispute" is included.
"Vividhā matiḥ" means diversity of opinion, that is to say, disagreement; the meaning is that this [diversity] has become the substratum, i.e., the subject of dispute.
When such is the case, the body, the senses, the worlds, and so forth, are alone made the subject (*pakṣīkṛta*); thus there is no over-extension (*prasaṅga*) to atoms and the like.

Furthermore, even if the probandum were merely "having a cause as its antecedent," it would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); therefore, the term "intelligent cause" (*buddhimatkāraṇa*) is employed.

With respect to the Sāṃkhya, there is no proving of what is already established [by us], because the existence of the intellect (*buddhi*) as a distinct entity is untenable; for the Sāṃkhyas maintain that the intellect is non-different from primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and a thing cannot possess its own nature by means of itself alone. Furthermore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) consists in the accumulation (*pracaya*) of the arrangement of the constituent parts that originate it.
That which is distinguished and delimited by that [quality], its state [is "being distinguished by that"];

therefore, because being distinguished by the arrangement of constituent parts (*avayava-sanniveśa*) is subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*) with respect to "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, the term "its own" (*sva-*) is included [in the definition].
For "cowness" and the like are distinguished by the arrangement of parts that originate a substance (*dravya*), but not by the arrangement of parts that originate themselves.
Therefore, that which is intelligent is God;
this very point has been indicated by the two verses beginning with "That which... and so forth.
The "distinction" (viśeṣa) is precisely the particular arrangement of its own constituent parts; because He possesses this [distinction], He is described as such.
The meaning is that it is distinguished by that;
by this, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason has been shown.
Demonstrating the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, he says: "by two sense-faculties," and so on.
"Subject of dispute" (vivādapada) means that which has become the basis for a legal dispute (vivādādhikaraṇāpanna).

And secondly, demonstrating that [the aforementioned] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "The material cause (*upādāna*) of the principles (*tattva*) and so forth, such as the *ātman* and so forth, is presided over by an intelligent being," and so on.
The material cause of the principles and so forth is presided over by one who possesses consciousness.

"Because they possess color and other qualities, just as threads and the like are observed to produce their own effects. [Verse 49] The connection is as follows: the material causes (*upādāna*) of the body and so forth—namely, atoms and the like—are producers of their own effects when presided over by a conscious cause. "Because they possess color and other qualities" is the logical reason (*hetu*). The phrase "of atoms and the like" refers to the material causes of the body and so forth. "Threads and the like" refers to what is observed [in experience]. "Producing their own effects" is the predicate. "Presided over by a conscious cause" qualifies the subject. Thus, the meaning is that atoms and the like, being the material causes of bodies and so forth, produce their own effects when they are presided over by a conscious cause, because they possess color and other qualities, just as threads and the like are observed to do.
The example begins with "the threads" and so forth,
as it has been stated: "We maintain that the material causes of the body, the world, and the instruments are presided over by an intelligent being while producing their own effects,
because they possess form and other qualities, just like threads and the like."

Uddyotakara, however, offers this proof: "The causes of the world—namely *pradhāna*, atoms, and *adṛṣṭa*—require a controller possessed of superior intelligence for the production of their own effects, because they proceed after having remained inactive, like threads, a shuttle, and so forth.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "merit, demerit, and atoms," etc.
All atoms of dharma and adharma, presided over by a conscious being, initiate their own effects after having remained [inactive], because of their subsequent activity, like a weaver’s thread.
(50) This is easily understood.

Praśastamati, however, says: At the beginning of creation, the linguistic usage of persons must have been preceded by the instruction of another, because at a later time it is restricted to specific objects for those who have become awakened; just as the linguistic usage of children, who have not yet mastered the conventional use of words, regarding cows and other things, is restricted to specific objects and is preceded by the instruction of their mothers and others.
"Because for the awakened ones there is a restriction to each respective object"—this means that because for those who are awakened there is a restriction to each respective object.

He demonstrates the established conclusion that he whose teaching precedes worldly activity at the beginning of creation is the Lord (Īśvara), whose excellence of knowledge remains unimpaired even at the time of dissolution: "At the beginning of creation," and so forth.
And at the beginning of creation, the linguistic usage of persons arises from the instruction of others,
because it is regulated, like the usage of children by those who are grown and awakened.
(51) "Sarga" means creation or origination.
Its beginning is the first period;
the rest, however, is easily understood.

Likewise, he demonstrates these other, further, illuminating, and colored arguments: "The manifest world, consisting of the great elements and so forth, being presided over by an intelligent cause, serves as the instrument for pleasure and pain, because it is insentient, because it is an effect, because it is perishable, and because it possesses form and other qualities, like a shuttle and similar tools.
This is shown in the passage beginning with "the great elements and so forth."
The manifest world, consisting of the great elements and so forth, being presided over by an intelligent cause, becomes the cause of pleasure and pain for the entire world,
because of such reasons as its insentience, its being an effect, and its perishability. (52)
As in the case of an axe and other tools, everything regarding that [world] is clearly understood from his [the author's] speech.
(Buddhimaddhetvadhiṣṭhitam— ) Therefore, it is presided over by an intelligent being.
From the aforementioned collection of reasons,
"of him" refers to Īśvara, the cause of the entire world.

Now, how is his omniscience established, by virtue of which he may become an object of devotion for those who desire both ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) and worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*)? To this, he says: "And when his status as the creator of all is established," and so forth.
And once his status as the creator of all things is established, his omniscience is proven without effort, because a creator must be one who perceives the form and other qualities of his effects.
Thus, Praśastamati and others have said: "Precisely because he is the cause of the entire universe, his omniscience is established."
Because of the agent’s thorough knowledge of the material cause, the instruments, the purpose, and the recipient of the action;
for in this world, whoever is the agent of something knows its material cause and so forth.

Just as it is well known that a potter, the maker of jars and other vessels, knows their material cause—the lump of clay—as well as the instruments such as the wheel, the purpose—such as the fetching of water—and the recipient, namely the householder; in the same way, Īśvara, the creator of all worlds, knows their material causes characterized by atoms and so forth, their instruments such as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), space (*dik*), and time (*kāla*), the instruments of worldly transaction characterized by generality (*sāmānya*), particularity (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*), the purpose—which is experience—and the persons designated as recipients.
Therefore, his omniscience is established;
that is, he is "the knower of the form and so forth of the effect.

The compound means: those which are the form and so forth of the effect—where "form" refers to its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and the like, and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the material cause (*upādāna*) and other factors—the knower of these.

Because the suffix *ṇat* in *yājaka* and similar words belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa*, this [suffix] is prescribed after a verbal root (*karman*) with the addition of the self-referential (*svārthika*) suffix *ka*;
the remainder is easily understood.
Likewise, another collection of proofs has been stated by them:

"That which is the locus of diverse arisings and fluctuations, yet is not their locus; which has entered into the state of being the subject of dispute; and which is delimited by a means of valid cognition other than the five beginning with the second [perception], because it possesses the nature of being a real entity (*vastutva*) and so forth, like color and other qualities (*rūpa*)."
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), [the examples] such as "tortoise-hair" and so forth are given;

therein, the category of quality (*guṇa-padārtha*) is said to have a manifold arising (*vicitrodaya*), because its arising is manifold. Motion (*prasyanda*) is the category of action (*karma-padārtha*). The substratum (*āspada*) of these two is substance (*dravya*), which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); the non-substrata are the five beginning with quality and ending with inherence (*samavāya*). The second through the fifth means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—starting from inference (*anumāna*) and ending with non-existence (*abhāva*)—are distinct from those; the other means of valid cognition is perception (*pratyakṣa*). The rest is easily understood. This is another reason stated by them.

That which is pervaded by the six non-differentiating properties (*aviśeṣa*) beginning with "existence" (*sat*), as well as that which is not so pervaded, when taken as the subject of dispute, is perceptible to someone because it exists, like color-form (*rūpa*) and other such things.

In this context, the six non-differentiating properties are: existence, impermanence, possession of substance (*dravyavat*), being an effect, being a cause, and possessing generality and particularity (*sāmānyaviśeṣavat*). These are the differentiators of substances, qualities, and actions. That which is pervaded—that is, occupied—by these, according to their respective possibilities, consists of the three categories of substances, qualities, and actions; that which is not so pervaded consists of the remaining categories, beginning with generality, which are easy to understand.

He demonstrates this collection of proofs as follows: "The object that is the locus of dispute is clearly perceived by someone, because it is a real entity and so forth, like the distinction between pleasure and pain. (55)

Thus, he begins the refutation here with the words "In this case, the reason is unestablished," and so forth: "In the first proof, since the arrangement called 'conjunction' is not established, neither is the composite [substance] established in that way. (56)

In this regard, the meaning is as follows: since there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the reason in the initial formulation—"that which is insentient does not begin its own effect without a controller"—the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful.

Furthermore, as for the reason "because it possesses a specific arrangement of its constituent parts" used in the first proof-statement, that is unestablished (*asiddha*). To explain how it is so, he says: "Since," and so forth.

For by the term "arrangement of parts" (avayava-saṃniveśa), a specific kind of conjunction (saṃyoga-viśeṣa) is intended, and [the second reason] refers to the state of being qualified by that [conjunction] in the substance known as the "whole" (avayavin). Since both of these—the qualifier and the qualified—are unestablished, the reason is unestablished in two ways. To the question, "How, then, are both unestablished? he says: "By virtue of being visible," and so forth.
"Because the two things accepted as being visible are not perceived, this example is also devoid of the probans (sādhana). Therefore,
[the author] states here in brief the subverting proof, which is precisely called the non-perception of the essential nature (svabhāvānupalambha)."

The refutation of these two will be stated in detail in the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*—namely, that of both "configuration" (*saṃniveśa*) and the "composite whole" (*avayavin*), as it is said: "Configuration is accepted as being visible; for it is stated that number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and action are perceptible by the eye because they are inherent in colored substances."

Furthermore, the whole (*avayavin*) is intended to be perceptible, according to the statement: "Perception occurs because of magnitude, because of being composed of multiple large substances, and because of color.

Since no other entity such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or a whole appears in cognition apart from color and the rest, and since that which meets the conditions for perception is not perceived, it follows that it is an object of the conventional designation of non-existence, like the horn of a hare.

Nor does it follow that color and other qualities would be unperceivable because atoms are beyond the senses, for since we accept that atoms in their specific state are accessible to the senses, their being beyond the senses is unproven.

For this very reason, he shows that the pot, as an example based on similarity, is devoid of the probans (the property to be proven) due to the non-existence of conjunction and the composite whole—by stating "not connected with the probans," and so forth.

Thus far, the non-establishment of the reason (*hetu*) by way of its own nature has been demonstrated through the non-establishment of the qualifier and the qualified; now, it is shown that it is also unestablished due to the non-establishment of a portion of its locus—beginning with "the eye," etc.:
"The visual and tactile cognitions arise with distinct appearances; there is no single objective basis for the two, just as in the case of the cognition of odor and so forth. (58)
For here, two kinds of subjects (*dharmin*) have been indicated: that which is perceptible by two sense-faculties and that which is imperceptible.
Among these, no subject perceptible by two sense-faculties is established.

To explain: visual cognition and tactile cognition both arise with distinct appearances, because they respectively manifest only the form of blue and so forth, and are established as manifesting only the various types of tangibles such as hardness and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no single object for those two cognitions—visual and tactile—because they have different appearances, just like the cognitions of smell, taste, and so forth.

This is the formal argument: two cognitions that have different manifestations do not have a single object, as in the case of the cognitions of smell and taste; and the visual and tactile cognitions have different manifestations. This is the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Moreover, if there were a single object despite the difference in appearance, it would follow that the cognitions of color, sound, and so forth would also have a single object; this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in this case.
If, then, these two do not have the same object, how can there be this synthetic cognition (*pratisandhāna-jñāna*) such as:

"The very same jar that was seen by me in the light is now being touched in the dark"? Therefore, this proposition is sublated by inference. In this regard, the following inference was stated by Uddyotakara: "The two cognitions of seeing and touching, which are the subject of dispute, have one and the same object because they are being synthesized, like the cognition of a blue lotus. To this, he replies: "By its capacity," and so forth.

The synthetic cognition (*pratisandhānavijñāna*), whose nature is accompanied by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) arising from the power of those [sensory perceptions], determines the collection [of atoms].
Therefore, this [collection] such as water or fire does not exist as something graspable by two sense-faculties.
The reason is unestablished due to the non-establishment of its locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*), because of the subject (*dharmin*) as it has been described.

[The analysis of the compound is as follows: "of those two"—namely, the visual and tactile cognitions which manifest only color-form and tangible objects; their "capacity" (*sāmarthya*) means their power (*śakti*); that from which [the cognition] arises is "produced from that"; and "that which has a nature (*ātman*) followed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)" is the analysis of the term.
By this, it is established that the synthesizing cognition (*pratisandhāna-pratyaya*) is not a perception (*apratyakṣatva*).

Because it is an error due to the determination of multiplicity as unity, and because its nature conforms to conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), it is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, since it determines an object already delimited by a prior cognition, it apprehends what has already been grasped; and because it is erroneous, the reason "because it is being synthesized" (*pratisaṃdhīyamānatvāt*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For if the validity of the cognition that links [past and present] were established, then the reason would not be inconclusive; however, in the case of those forms and so forth for which conventional designations such as "pot" are made to manifest their common capacity, once they have been experienced respectively by sight and touch, there subsequently arises this memory-cognition—which is by nature erroneous—determining a unity while possessing distinct mental impressions deposited by corresponding conventions regarding the objects as they were previously perceived.
For instance: when there is such a mental coordination (*samanvāhāra*), even a color such as blue appears therein;

yet, it is not logical for a color to appear in tactile consciousness (*sparśanavijñāna*), because that [color] is the object of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Therefore, what was stated by the Teachers—that after perceiving distinct objects through the eyes and touch according to their respective domains, a distinct memorial cognition (*smārta-bhedajñāna*) arises which has the aggregate (*samudāya*) as its object—is alone reasonable.

Now, if the aggregate (*samudāya*) had been previously experienced, then it would be appropriate for this [cognition] to be a memory (*smārta*); however, you do not accept an aggregate distinct from color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest by which it might be experienced. Furthermore, when color-form and the rest are experienced, there would be the cognition "color-form" and so on, but not "pot. Nor is memory appropriate regarding that which has not been experienced. Therefore, how does this memory-cognition arise having the aggregate as its object? This is not so.

It is not said that a composite (*samudāya*) distinct from color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest has been previously experienced, such that this [memory] could arise; rather, those very elements—color-form and the rest—which perform the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of holding water and so forth, are designated as the "pot" (*ghaṭa*), which is the composite.
And when these have been individually experienced by sensory cognitions, it is asserted that a memory arises in accordance with convention, namely, "this is a pot.

Alternatively, since the conceptualized composite consists of the nature of conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), it is indeed experienced through self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*); so why should its memory not arise?

Therefore, he asks why the reason "because of being characterized by a specific arrangement of its own constituent parts" suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*). He says: "Because of the non-establishment of the subject as it has been stated.

This means that because the subject, as it was described—namely, that which is perceptible by two sense organs—is not established, the reason is unestablished due to the non-establishment of a portion of its locus.

Thus, the threefold non-establishment (*asiddhatā*) of the reason has been stated due to the non-establishment of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*), the qualifier (*viśe�ṣaṇa*), and their substratum (*āśraya*). Now, he states the fourth type of non-establishment pointed out by the Teacher, beginning with the words "sanniveśa" (structure) and so forth:
"The kind of distinctness of structure (*sanniveśaviśiṣṭatva*) which is found in things such as temples..."

If, even when the agent is not perceived, the cognition of an intelligent cause arises upon seeing such [effects] as these, then it would be appropriate that the same kind of thing be observed in the case of subjects such as bodies and so forth;
thus, from this proof, there would be the proof of what is desired. (61–62)

For that specific configuration which is well-known in the world—as in temples and the like—to be preceded by the activity of an intelligent person, such that from the sight of it one understands an intelligent cause even when the maker is not seen; if such a configuration is adduced as the reason (*hetu*) in the case of the subjects of proof (*sādhyadharmin*), such as those minute trees and mountains, then there would be the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) desired by you.

Indeed, an effect that has been clearly determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) does not deviate from its cause, for that would entail the consequence of it being causeless.
Furthermore, such a specific configuration (sanniveśaviśeṣa) is not well-known in trees, mountains, and so forth; rather, it is merely the vague babble "configuration" that is known.

Moreover, even if a property (dharma) is established as being distinct from others by its very nature, it is not sufficient for establishing the desired probandum when it is employed as a reason based solely on the identity of the word, because there is no contradiction in its existence even in the opposite of the probandum.

The collective meaning is as follows: just as when "being a modification of clay" is adduced as a reason to establish that an anthill is the work of a potter, even though the subject (the anthill) is present;
the meaning of the individual parts is now stated:
"upon seeing which, there occurs the cognition of an intelligent agent."
The meaning is that when the arrangement of something is perceived, there occurs an inference of an intelligent cause;
"in bodies and so forth" means: *tanu* is the body, *agāḥ* are mountains or trees, and by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), oceans and other such things are included.
"Of that which is desired" means it is the proof for [the fact that the world] is preceded by an intelligent being.
Success 61 62
He asks, "How is this logical? and replies with the verse beginning "anvaya" and so forth:

"That which is ascertained to be the effect of something through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)—the certainty regarding that [effect] arises upon seeing that [cause]; such is the established principle. (63)
However, such a specific arrangement does not exist among these [trees] at all; rather, in the case of various distinctions such as trees and so forth, there is only the word itself.
When such [a word] is uttered, its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) becomes doubtful.
One encounters [the effect] in things such as those made by a potter on an anthill.
Regarding "that which is the effect"— such as smoke— and "that of which it is the effect"— such as fire.
"His certainty is thus"—that is, [the certainty] regarding fire and so forth arises precisely from the perception of that [effect], meaning when the effect such as smoke is perceived.
[The opponent] says, "If it is so here as well," and so on, [anticipating the objection]: "But the specific arrangement... and so forth.
If it is argued that the very arrangement which is established through the generality of the word will serve as the reason, he says: "of such a kind," and so forth.
"Of such a kind" means non-differentiated by the mere word, like [the arrangement] produced by a potter.
The remainder [of the argument] is that it is merely a state of being a modification of clay;
thus, it has been demonstrated that the specific configuration is unestablished, whereas the mere configuration is inconclusive.
With the words beginning with "nanu," the opponent raises a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*).
Is this not a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*), since it establishes that the cause, such as the effect, is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*) by means of a conceptual differentiation of its properties?
This is the futile rejoinder known as "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*).
For instance, when it is stated that "sound is impermanent because it is produced," the proponent of the genus (*jāti*) objects:
"Is this 'producedness' being adduced as the reason (hetu) that which resides in jars and the like,
or that which resides in sound, or that which resides in both?"
In the first case, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*),
for a property of one thing does not exist in another;
in the second case as well, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) lacks the probans (*sādhanavikala*).
In the third case as well, these same two faults apply;
thus it has been established that this is the futile rejoinder (jātyuttara) named "balancing the effect" (kāryasama).
As it has been stated: "Balancing the effect is the demonstration of the non-establishment of the probandum by means of a slight difference in the nature of being an effect."
Since the inference of impermanence is intended by grasping only the generality (*sāmānya*) of being an effect (*kāryatva*) and not its specific particulars (*viśeṣa*),

it is established that when such a generality is accepted as the probans (*sādhana*), any rejoinder based on a conceptual differentiation of the specific properties of that dharma is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) known as "balancing the effect" (*kāryasama*).
And because this is a conceptual differentiation based on the distinction of properties, it is therefore a futile rejoinder.
He refutes [this objection] with the verse beginning "atadrūpa" (not having that nature), stating that the mere thing itself, as excluded from what is not of that nature, is impermanence.
This logical principle does not establish identity here in this proof;
for it is correct that the mere fact of being produced establishes impermanence.

The meaning is as follows: because in that case there exists a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), whereas here, in the mere proof of being distinguished by the arrangement of its own constituent parts, this logic does not apply.

This is because the necessary connection is unestablished, since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) against the contrary regarding the generality of "arrangement" (*sanniveśasāmānya*). Thus, the point is that the necessary connection characterized by origination (*tadutpatti*)—by the perception of which even one who has not seen the action would form the cognition that it was made—is unestablished for this [subject].

Now, showing that if one sets aside the specific feature of the non-obstruction of its arising and asserts only the general property as the logical mark (*liṅga*), then it would be fallacious (*vyabhicārin*), he says: "Smoke," and so forth—"The white substance that is smoke is seen to be invariably concomitant with fire."
"From the mere fact of being denotable by the word 'white,' there is no understanding of that [snow] even from the word 'snow'.

He asks, "How then is *kāryasama* cited as a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*)? and says: "But when there is a connection with a generality (*sāmānya*), one resorts to a particular (*viśeṣa*)," and so forth.
When an objection (*codanā*) is raised there, it is cited as a "pseudo-refutation" (*jātyuttara*).

Even though the connection of the probans-property with the probandum through their commonality is established by the operation of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), when an objection is raised by resorting to a specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*), that is a pseudo-refutation. However, in this case, no such connection has been established through a generality; rather, that which possesses a connection to a specific configuration (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*) remains unproven. Therefore, this is not a pseudo-refutation.
Now, showing that if even an unrelated universal were a signifier, it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), he says: "From the mere fact of being denotable by the word 'cow'... and so forth.
Otherwise, if this principle were not accepted, then the possession of horns would be established for directions and other such things merely because they are denotable by the word 'cow'. (70)

For in this way, there would follow the undesirable consequence that even heaven, the directions, speech, eyes, rays, thunderbolts, and water would possess horns, simply because they are denoted by the word *go*, just like Bāhuleya and other [bulls].

One might argue: "Just as with 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, this [property of] being characterized by a specific arrangement (*saṃniveśaviśiṣṭatva*) is indeed necessarily connected to having an intelligent cause; thus, the invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) exists. To this, he says: "If, however," and so forth.

If, however, no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established for this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then there would be no dispute for anyone regarding its establishment through reasoning.
But showing that this very connection is not established, he says: "But rather," and so forth.

However, because it lacks pervasion due to the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*), [the argument] does not achieve proof: "But [the world] has as its basis an eternal, single, omniscient, and eternal intellect.

For you do not merely wish to prove that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent agent; rather, you wish to prove that it is preceded by that entity called God, who is an intelligent cause of the entire universe and the basis of an eternal, single, and omniscient intellect.
Because that very [subject] is the locus of dispute, and such a thing does not attain proof;
why? Because of the deficiency of the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) and because of the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*);

for the reason (*hetu*) lacks the aforementioned similarity with the similar instance (*sādharmyadṛṣṭānta*), such as a jar, and thus the pervasion of the reason by the probandum-property (*sādhyadharma*) in that manner remains unestablished.

For there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of the logical reason (*hetu*) with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) as it has been described in any instance of an example; this is what is meant.
Demonstrating that very point, he says: "For instance," and so forth.
For instance, palaces, staircases, gate-towers, watchtowers, and so forth,
are ascertained to be preceded by many impermanent cognitions.

Furthermore, he shows that the reason is not only unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), but also contradictory (*viruddha*)— this is indicated by the words "for this very reason," and so on.
For this very reason, even though it causes the destruction of what is desired,
it is still accepted, because it establishes that [the world] is preceded by many impermanent cognitions.
"For this very reason" means...

By the word "also" (api), he indicates that [the reason] is not only unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) according to the method previously stated, but is also [invalid] because it is pervaded by a property contrary to the probandum (*sādhyaviparītadharma*). 74

But surely, a contradictory [reason] would occur only when there is a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the opposite; yet, in this case, there is no necessary connection even with the mere fact of being preceded by an intelligent agent. So how could it exist in its specific form? To this he says: "For regarding the mere cause consisting of an intelligent agent," and so forth.
For you have asserted a necessary connection only with respect to the mere cause consisting of an intelligent agent.
Furthermore, in the second [case], we state it quite clearly:
By you, who maintain the existence of a Lord (Īśvara), a necessary connection has been described as consisting solely of an intelligent cause;
otherwise, if the connection were not established even in a general sense, how could the fact that entities have the Lord as their cause be proven?

Therefore, having accepted the established nature of the mere fact that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent being—a point already proven according to your own view—we clearly state the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) of our reason with this second specific property of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣa*), which is the opposite of what you desire: namely, the characteristic of being preceded by multiple impermanent cognitions.
(75) To the question, "How is this clearly stated?", he says: "Succession and simultaneity," and so forth.
Eternal entities do not produce effects, because there is a contradiction between succession and non-succession;
since objects possess succession, there is likewise succession in the cognitions of them.
(76) Indeed, eternal entities such as God and the like do not produce effects, because for an eternal thing, causal efficiency is contradicted by both succession and simultaneity.

Therefore, it is established that only impermanent things are capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and since these possess different intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) at every moment, their impermanence and multiplicity are proven; thus, there is no intelligent creator.
Furthermore, demonstrating that the thesis asserting that the Lord (*Īśvara*) is endowed with a single, eternal cognition is also contradicted by inference, he says: "Of objects," and so forth.
He provides proof with the verse beginning "occurring in succession" (*kramabhāvī*): God’s cognition occurs in succession because it is connected to objects of knowledge that occur in succession.
Just as the cognition of Devadatta and others has flames and so forth as its object.

Whatever cognition has a sequential object of knowledge is itself sequential, just as the cognition of Devadatta and others has flames and so forth as its object; and since the cognition of Īśvara has a sequential object of knowledge, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason) formulated as a *prasaṅgasādhana* (reductio ad absurdum).

Therefore, one should not suspect that the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*), because the cognition of Devadatta and others regarding categories such as "generality" (*sāmānya*) is devoid of the property to be proven; thus, the example given is that which has flames and the like as its object.

But what here is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*)? It is said: if that cognition of God were produced with its own internal representation by means of an object possessing succession, then succession would indeed be established.

If, on the other hand, it is not produced [by the object], then, due to the absence of a basis for proximity (*pratyāsatti*), it would not cognize that object; furthermore, your accepted validity (*prāmāṇya*)— which occurs even in the absence of an object— would be lost, and there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cognition being objectless (*nirviṣayatva*) with respect to an object that has either perished or not yet arisen.
This is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) here.

Furthermore, as for what was stated— that "atoms are considered [to be] by way of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyeṇāṇavo matāḥ*)— he says, beginning with "merely an aggregation of atoms," etc., demonstrating that even that example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-udāharaṇa*) does not exclude the property to be proven (*anivṛtta-sādhyadharma*).
Since we maintain that a jar or the like is merely an aggregation of atoms, the potter and other such agents are the agents of the atoms themselves.
Therefore, the property desired as the probandum is not excluded from those [atoms]. (78)

Because of this example of an atom (*aṇu*) which has been illustrated by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), and because the whole (*avayavin*) will be refuted in detail and has already been refuted, it is established that the potter and others are merely the agents of the atoms. Therefore, the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*)—namely, "having an intelligent precursor"—is not excluded from the atoms as they have been presented by way of dissimilarity; thus, the example of dissimilarity suffers from the fault of having a non-excluded property to be proven (*avyāvṛttasādhyadharmatā*).

It might be argued as follows: "If we intended to prove a specific [creator], then the previously mentioned deficiency of the example by similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) regarding the probandum (*sādhya*) would indeed apply. However, since we are proving merely that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent agent (*buddhimat-pūrvakatva*) in a general sense, once that is established, it follows by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) that God is the creator of trees and so forth. For it is not possible for them to have a potter or similar artisan as their creator, as is the case with jars and the like. Therefore, because the general property is qualified by a specific [creator], and because no other creator is conceivable for trees and such, it follows by implication—even without explicitly grasping a specific [creator]—that God alone is established as their creator. To this, he says: "Because it is preceded by an intelligent [agent]," and so forth.
And if it is asserted in a general sense that [the world] is preceded by an intelligent being, we have no dispute at all; for the manifold diversity of the universe arises from karma.
For in this way, there would be the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

He asks "Why? and says: "For the manifoldness," and so forth. "Manifoldness" (*vaiśvarūpya*) refers to the diversity of the world of sentient beings and their environment; it is "born of karma," meaning it is produced by common and uncommon, auspicious and inauspicious karma.

Therefore, since intelligent persons who perform auspicious and inauspicious karma become the causes of this [world], the argument commits the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
If it is argued that [the probandum] is then established specifically, he says: "eternal," etc.;
in the proof that [the world] is preceded by a single eternal intellect, there is a lack of the probandum.
Furthermore, there is the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), because palaces and the like are seen to be constructed by many [agents].
Although this has been stated previously, it is mentioned again for the sake of the conclusion (*nigamana*).
The analysis of the compound is as follows: "one cognition regarding this" is *ekabuddhiḥ*; he who is eternal and possesses such a single cognition is *nitya-ekabuddhiḥ*.
Alternatively— the compound means "one whose cognition is eternal and unitary"—
the ellipsis is that this constitutes a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhya-śūnyatā*) of the corroborative instance based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
And there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*);
the word "of the reason" (*hetoh*) is to be supplied [to the sentence].
To the question "How so?", he says: "The palace," and so forth.
Regarding what was stated beginning with "of trees and so forth," he says: "This very same [argument applies]," and so on;
that is, this very same [reasoning] applies as appropriate to the remaining reasons.
Another refutation is also to be applied; however, a mere portion of it is being revealed here.

For even in those proofs such as "because of possessing form and so forth," this very same refutation should be stated according to the circumstances; that is precisely what is meant by "this very [refutation]."

Unestablishedness, deviation due to the absence of a necessary connection, contradiction when a connection exists, deficiency in the probandum, proving what is already established by way of generality, and so forth.

For instance—even there, the kind of possession of form and so forth that is presided over by a conscious agent is not established in trees and the like. Since the mere possession of form and so forth lacks a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*). If a necessary connection were admitted, it would be contradictory (*viruddha*) because it would prove the opposite of what is intended. Furthermore, the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because an anvaya (positive concomitance) with the probandum—namely, being presided over by a single, eternal conscious being—is not established. If [the probandum] is stated in general terms, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); if in specific terms, there is deviation because things such as pots are seen to be otherwise. This same reasoning should be applied to other reasons as well. 82
Regarding the proof stated as "because [an agent] acts after having remained stationary," he states a further refutation: "Having remained stationary," etc.
The activity of atoms and so forth after having remained stationary is not established, because of their momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Furthermore, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by that very [reason], since even those [atoms] possess sequential activity. (83)

Since all entities perish immediately upon their arising, there is no stability even for a single moment; therefore, how could there be activity after having first remained stable? Consequently, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished for the respondent and is inconclusive because of that very Īśvara. For Īśvara, while engaging in successive effects, does so after remaining stable, yet he is not presided over by another conscious being, as that would lead to an infinite regress.

Now, if the reason is formulated with a qualification as "being insentient," as was done by Praśastamati, even then its inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) remains unavoidable because its exclusion from the counter-example (vipakṣa) is doubtful. For only that qualification is logical which actually excludes the reason from the counter-example; however, that which does not remove doubt regarding the counter-example is as good as non-existent even if it is included.
Furthermore, the previously mentioned defects such as being unestablished (asiddhatā) remain exactly as they were, even when the reason is qualified.
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "and at the beginning of creation there is worldly convention," he says: "In dissolution... and so forth;
for us, persons do not have their consciousness and memory destroyed during dissolution.
Because of the arising from the Ābhāsvara heaven and so forth, and because of the subsequent arising here [in this world]. || 84 ||

The qualification "of those who have awakened at a later time" is unestablished; for, according to our view, it is not the case that at the time of dissolution (pralaya) persons remain with their knowledge and memory obliterated and devoid of body and sense organs. Rather, they are reborn among the classes of gods in the Ābhāsvara and other realms who possess an excellence of clear knowledge. As for those whose karma is conducive to the ripening of specific hells and so forth, they are reborn in other world-systems. Thus, even at the time of evolution (vivarta), they arise from those very realms such as Ābhāsvara with their knowledge and memory unimpaired.

Therefore, the qualification "of those who have awakened at a subsequent time" is unestablished (*asiddha*), and the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because its exclusion from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. Furthermore,

if the probandum (*sādhya*) is merely "being preceded by the instruction of another," it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), since it is accepted by all that beginningless worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) is preceded by the instruction of another.

If it is being proved that [the Veda] is preceded by the instruction of a person characterized as a Lord (īśvara), then there is the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), because linguistic usage is possible even otherwise; furthermore, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*). And this general refutation has already been stated previously.

Showing that the reason is contradictory and that the thesis is sublated by what has been accepted, he says: "If the teaching of one who is turned away [from the truth] is to be understood only through faith," and so forth.
If the status of being a teacher for one who is averse [to the truth] is something to be accepted solely on the basis of faith...
Aversion [to teaching] arises from the absence of a body, due to the lack of discrimination between dharma and adharma.

(85) If worldly activity were preceded by the instruction of a Lord, then the reason [for the Lord's non-existence] would not be contradictory; however, because he is devoid of a face—that is, a mouth—he is not fit to be an instructor. And that state of being "faceless" is due to his being bodiless—the meaning being that he lacks a physical form.

And as to how this attenuation of doubt is established for him, he says: "from the discrimination between dharma and adharma," which means from the absence of dharma and adharma, the causes of the body;
thus it has been stated by Uddyotakara.

Just as there is no possibility of proof for the existence of God in relation to the existence of consciousness (*buddhi*), so too there is no proof for the existence of *dharma* and the like; therefore, since it is impossible for God to be a teacher, the fact that linguistic usage is preceded by His instruction is not established. Rather, [linguistic usage] is preceded by the instruction of other persons distinct from God; thus, because it subverts what is desired, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*).

Alternatively, if God’s status as a teacher is accepted, then the [previously] admitted quality of being "turned away" (*vimukhatva*) is abandoned, which constitutes a contradiction with one's own tenets (*abhyupetabādha*).

In the formulation beginning with "the manifest, such as the great elements (*mahābhūta*), [is produced by a creator]," the reasons (*hetu*) are, as before, inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because there is no subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). Furthermore, it should be applied that [the reason] proves what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in a general sense, whereas in a specific sense, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).

(85) Having thus refuted in detail the proofs establishing Īśvara, he now states—beginning with "contradiction by inference" (*anumānavirodha*)—the proof that subverts that [position] by way of exposing defects in the pervasion (*vyāpti*), in order to establish his own position.
And there is contradiction with inference: in every case of a probans, a pervasion by a contradictory property is not possible for the reason.
(86) In every such aforementioned probans, the pervasion of the reason by the probandum—that is what will be described as the contradiction with inference.

Now, why is contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*) not raised against the thesis (*pratijñā*)? If the thesis were a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the proof (*sādhana*), then its defect would indeed be pointed out; however, since it—either directly or indirectly—does not attain the status of being a constituent for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*), then when the statement of defects in the proof is under discussion, the pointing out of a defect in the thesis would constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the proponent due to the pointing out of a non-defect. Therefore, no defect of the thesis should be stated during the employment of the proof.

However, wherever a contradiction with the proposition (*pratijñāvirodha*) is raised, it should be understood that by means of that very [contradiction], the pervasion (*vyāpti*) itself is being undermined. Alternatively, this should be seen as occurring elsewhere than in the actual application of the proof (*sādhanaprayoga*).
Now, he explains how there can be a contradiction with inference even at the time of establishing the pervasion: "Not by the contradictory," and so forth.

"By the contradictory" means by that which is sublated by a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); since such [a contradictory] is impossible, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not logical, for pervasion cannot be conceived with that which is non-existent—this is the meaning.

"What is that inference by which the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is sublated? To this he says: "God is not the cause of living beings," and so forth: "God is not the cause of living beings because he is devoid of origination, like a sky-lotus; otherwise, everything would come into existence simultaneously. (87)

That which is devoid of origination cannot be the cause of anything, just like a sky-lotus; and since Īśvara is devoid of origination, this is an "apprehension of the contradictory of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Furthermore, this is a *prasaṅga*-proof; therefore, one should not raise the objection that it is "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*), for otherwise everything would arise simultaneously.
The meaning is that, because the cause possesses unimpeded capacity, everything would arise simultaneously, like a collection of effects intended to occur at one time;
this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) here, or rather, this is merely an explanation of the sense. However, the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-sādhana*) should be formulated as follows:
Whatever has its complete causes necessarily comes into being,
just as a sprout, when its causes are complete upon reaching the final stage of the causal complex, necessarily arises;
and since the entire world has God as its cause with all causes complete, it would have to come into being simultaneously.

It might be argued: "The Lord alone is not the sole cause; rather, He acts in dependence upon other auxiliary causes such as *dharma* and so forth, because the Lord is merely the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). Therefore, due to the deficiency of those other causes like *dharma*, it is unproven that the cause is complete. This is incorrect.

For if some benefit were to be produced for that [permanent entity] by its auxiliaries through some assistance, then it would have a dependence upon those auxiliaries; however, since it is eternal and no excellence can be imparted to it by others, there is nothing whatsoever for it to obtain from its auxiliaries—so why would it depend upon such unbeneficial auxiliaries?
Furthermore, even those auxiliaries, since their very birth depends upon Īśvara, are always already present together with him; thus, how could the reason [of the opponent] be unestablished?

Nor is there any lack of certainty [in the reason], because it would entail the loss of the status of having its causes complete; for if that which has all its causes complete were not to arise, it would follow that nothing would ever arise, since there is no distinction [between them].

Uddyotakara, however, says: "Even though the eternal cause called God is always present and complete with respect to entities, there is nevertheless no simultaneous production, because God acts preceded by intelligence."
If God were the producer of things without prior intelligence merely by His existence, then this objection would hold;
but when He acts with prior intelligence, there is no fault, because He engages in effects according to His own will.
Therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is indeed inconclusive.

This is incorrect; for the activity or cessation of effects does not depend upon the presence or absence of the will of their cause, such that one could claim they do not arise because of the absence of His will even though the cause called Īśvara is always present with unimpeded power. What then? Entities conform to the presence or absence of the capacity residing in their cause.

For instance: effects do not arise from an agent who possesses the desire [to act] but lacks the capacity; yet they do arise from seeds and the like which possess the capacity even in the absence of desire.

In this regard, if the cause called "God" were always present with unimpeded power, just as it is at the time of producing an effect, why would entities depend upon that desire of His, which provides them no assistance, such that they would not arise simultaneously, just as they do at the time of production? For in this way, they would demonstrate that their own causes are complete, if they were to arise all at once.
Furthermore, since God is not assisted by others, He has no dependence whatsoever such that He would require desire;

moreover, there is no desire other than His intellect (*buddhi*), and you maintain that God’s intellect is eternally uniform. Consequently, even if God acts preceded by intellect, why do entities not arise simultaneously, given that like God, His intellect is also ever-present?

Furthermore, even if it is admitted that his intellect is non-eternal, since it arises merely from the existence of God, it would necessarily exist eternally just like God; thus, the same fault remains.

Therefore, the qualification "because of being intelligent" is entirely ineffective. Consequently, the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). And since this is not the case, there is a reversal [of the opponent's position].

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever does not exist at a particular time does not have its causes complete at that time, just as a sprout that is not yet produced while in the state of remaining as a seed within a granary.
And at the time of the production of a single entity, the entire universe does not exist [simultaneously]. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Nor is this a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because it has already been demonstrated that if God were the cause, it would be impossible for his causal conditions to be incomplete.
He states another proof as well: "Or those which arise in succession," and so forth;
those which arise in succession do not have God as their cause.
Like the cognitions of the dull-witted produced by the aforementioned means,
even if those [cognitions] were to arise from that [means], the statement of the proof would be fruitless;
for because it is eternal and thus incurable, that [statement] can never be a cooperative cause.

From the aforementioned probans, such as "being characterized by a specific arrangement of its own constituent parts," there arise cognitions—meaning certainties, as it were—concerning the desired subject of proof for those dull-witted people who are intent upon God as the cause.

[Objection: But since these are tainted by the aforementioned defects, no cognitions regarding the desired probandum arise from them; thus, the property of the example-subject is not established. [Reply:
This is true.

For this very reason, it was stated "of insentient things" (*jaḍānām*). For since insentient things lack the capacity for discrimination regarding the means [of knowledge], cognitions indeed arise in them even from fallacious means. Now, one might object: "Even so, the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), because even those insentient cognitions are accepted as having God as their efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*. To this, he says: "Of those too," and so forth.

For those [effects] as well—which are insentient cognitions—if their arising is held to be from God (*īśvara*), then the statement of the means (*sādhanābhidhā*) would be fruitless; that is to say, the mention of a means would be useless because they would arise from God alone. This is the intended meaning.

[Objection: "But surely God will be their producer by depending on the expression of the means [of proof] as a cooperative cause; thus, He will not be fruitless through that alone. To this he says: "Because of eternality," and so forth. If that expression of the means were to remove the incapable nature of that God and instill a capable one, then it might be His cooperative cause. However, since God is eternal, His nature is unproduced and irreversible, and thus nothing can be brought about in Him by anything. Therefore, it is not logical for the expression of the means to be His cooperative cause. (88)

Furthermore: Just as when the causal status of a Lord (*īśvara*) whose capacity is not perceived is postulated in addition to causes such as the means of accomplishment whose capacity is observed, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) follows for you; because even after having postulated that Lord, another [cause] such as a *ḍheṭaka* or a *ṣakādika* would necessarily have to be postulated as well, since there is no distinction [between them]. Demonstrating this, he says: "In those... and so forth. However, in those cases where [the cause] exists, your [proposed] effect occurs, and where it does not exist, it never occurs at any time.
"If you postulate another cause for that [cause], how is it that there is no infinite regress for you?"— the phrase "that which is seen by you" is the necessary supplement; thus,
"in the postulation of another cause."

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "anyahetutā" (the state of being another cause) refers to a cause other than those whose causal capacity has been observed; "klṛpti" means the postulation (*kalpanā*) of that [state].
Regarding what was stated previously, beginning with "and for the sake of establishing [his] omnicausality," he says: "kartṛtva... and so forth.
And by the refutation of his agency, his omniscience must be understood as likewise rejected, because it is precisely through the power of that [agency] that omniscience is established.
(91) You maintain that he is omniscient by virtue of being the creator of all; therefore, by the refutation of that [agency], his omniscience is also refuted without effort.

91. Having accepted that the means of proof (*sādhana*) are free from defects, he states another refutation: "As has been stated," etc.; [he says this] so that the means of proof may not be corrupted by the aforementioned faults.
Nevertheless, the oneness of the creator is not established, because of the demonstration of deviation [in the reason].
And since a single creator is unproven, upon what could omniscience be based?
The aforementioned defects, ending with the contradiction of inference, [apply here as well].
This is the collective meaning here:

although an intelligent creator is established by these proofs such as the body, the mountains, and so forth, it is not yet certain that he who is the cause of one is necessarily the cause of another. Since it is possible for there to be different creators for each individual effect—given that even a single structure like a palace is seen to be built by many—it is impossible to establish a single creator. And as long as a single creator is not established, how can omniscience be proven?
Here, Praśastamati provides a proof for the establishment of a single creator:

"Brahmā and the others, down to the Piśācas, have a single presiding authority because they exist in a state of mutual superiority; for in this world, it is observed that those who exist in a state of mutual superiority are dependent upon one [authority], just as in this world the lords of houses, villages, towns, and regions are dependent upon a single sovereign king. And since such is the case with snakes, Rākṣasas, Yakṣas, and so forth, who exist in a state of mutual superiority, we conclude that they too are dependent upon a single Lord."
In this regard, if the intended point to be proven is that these [things] are presided over by one called "God," then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
because there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary and thus the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established.
Furthermore, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).

If it is argued that [the world] is "possessed of a presider" merely by virtue of having a presider, then this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because we ourselves accept that the entire world is presided over by the Blessed One, the Perfectly Awakened One, the crest-jewel of all the worlds, out of his compassion;
it is through his power that virtuous people even today attain the wealth of worldly prosperity and the supreme good.
And this other proof was stated by that same [author]:
"The seven worlds were created by a single intellect, because they are contained within a single entity,
like the rooms contained within a single house."

Just as it is observed that the various apartments contained within a single dwelling are the product of the intellect of a single architect, so too, since the seven worlds are contained within one and the same world,
it is determined that they also are the product of a single intellect;
and he whose intellect produced these is the Blessed Lord Maheśvara, the sole architect of all the worlds.

In this regard, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), for there exists no single world (*bhuvana*) or dwelling (*āvasatha*) and so forth; rather, this designation was applied to many things for the sake of brevity in common usage (*vyavahāra*).
For this very reason, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is also devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*).
Furthermore, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it is observed that the apartments (*apavarakādi*) within a single mansion are constructed by many architects.
In this same way, refutations should be stated as appropriate for other proofs as well.
As for what was said regarding "the object that is the locus of dispute," and so forth:

Regarding this, he says: "The means for establishing that [is now stated]"; thus, the examination of God concludes with the verse: "The means for establishing that has been proclaimed; it shines forth among the followers of Jaimini. (93) Thus ends the Examination of God.
If you are proving in a general sense that "there exists someone who is omniscient," then this proof of yours does not shine before us,
due to the fallacy of proving what is already established; rather,
it is only effective against those followers of Jaimini who deny the existence of an omniscient being.

If it is intended here to prove an omniscient being called Īśvara, then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is unestablished, and the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*);
thus, the sense is that this proof does not appear valid to us.
Furthermore, as for the qualification of the subject (*dharmin*) employed in the phrase "the arising of diverse [effects]," etc., it serves no purpose whatsoever.
