This proclamation of your own system is made by you solely for the purpose of deluding others;

for instance: if the probans (*sādhana*) is free from defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*) even without such qualifiers as "belonging to the subject" (*dharmī*), then the desired probandum (*sādhya*) is indeed established.

But if the probans is vitiated by defects such as being unestablished, then even with the inclusion of such qualifiers, there is no establishment of the probandum. Thus, the qualifier is entirely useless in every respect.
Furthermore, that qualification alone is logical which excludes the reason from the counter-position (*vipakṣa*).

Moreover, the reason would be unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), for the subject (*dharmin*) as qualified by the aforementioned qualification is not established for the opponent; therefore, a subject established merely by the authority of a treatise (*śāstra*) should not be employed.
Thus concludes the examination of the Lord;
[this is] the twofold examination.

In order to demonstrate that both [Prakṛti and Īśvara] are devoid of agency, he says: "Because the causality of both Prakṛti and Īśvara has thus been negated, neither of them individually nor together is the creator of these living beings. (94)
Regarding this, some Sāṅkhyas say: "These various effects do not proceed from the *pradhāna* alone, because it is insentient;
for an insentient entity is never seen to begin its own work without a directing agent.
Nor is it logical that the *puruṣa* be the director, because at that time he is devoid of knowledge."
For instance—the Puruṣa perceives only that object which has been determined by the intellect (buddhi);
moreover, prior to contact with the intellect, he is indeed devoid of cognition and never knows any object at all;
and since no one is capable of acting upon an unknown object, he is not the agent.
Therefore, it is established that God alone, in dependence upon primordial matter (*pradhāna*), is the creator of the various effects, neither by Himself alone nor by primordial matter alone;
for Devadatta and others do not produce a son by themselves, nor does a potter make a jar by himself.

Thus, since the causality of both primordial matter and God has been individually refuted, it follows that this pair—consisting of God and primordial matter—is not the creator or progenitor of "those who are born," that is, of things subject to origination.

94. Now, one might object: "Even if the agency of these two individually has been refuted, nevertheless, their agency when combined is certainly not refuted; for it is not the case that because the eyes and other [faculties] lack the capacity to produce visual cognition individually, they likewise lack it when combined. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Sāhityam," etc.—"The combination (*sāhitya*) of these two, which is conceived as their state of being co-operative (*sahakāritva*), is also merely conceptualized (*kalpyate*)."
That [causality] would have to arise either from the imparting of a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) or from the performance of a single purposeful action.
Of these two, the first conception is not tenable because [the cause] is immutable;
nor is the second, because it would entail the simultaneous production of all effects.

What is called "sāhitya" (association) is the state of being a co-operative cause (*sahakāritva*), and that is of two kinds: either through the mutual imparting of excellence or through the performance of a single purpose.

In this regard, first of all, the postulation of the first kind of co-operation—characterized by the imparting of excellence—is not tenable. Why? Because those two, namely Īśvara and Pradhāna, being eternal, are devoid of modification;
nor is the postulation of the second kind tenable. This is to be connected with the subject at hand.
Why? Because it would follow that all effects would arise simultaneously;
for since the cause—designated as Īśvara and Pradhāna—possesses unimpaired and unobstructed capacity and is eternally present, the causes would be complete at all times.
In this regard, as before, the reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*) beginning with "that which has complete causes" and so forth should be stated.
Now, with the words "If it is said," etc., he points out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason "that which has its causes complete" according to the opinion of another.
Now it is said: the threefold nature of the Pradhāna is established;
therein, this Maheśvara, joined with *rajas*, is the cause of creation.
But when he again resorts to *sattva* whose function has become manifest, [he becomes the cause of dissolution].
Then it becomes the cause for the stability of the entire world.
When it is joined with *tamas* in the form of emergent power (*udbhūta-śakti*), it indeed brings about the dissolution of the whole universe. (98–99)

Thus, since its auxiliaries—consisting of *rajas*, *sattva*, and so forth, as well as form and the rest—occur only in succession, the effects do not arise simultaneously; therefore, there is no lack of sequence.
Even though these two causes are eternally present, [the effects still follow a temporal order].

Nevertheless, these various effects will proceed only in a sequential order; for the three qualities (*guṇas*) residing in *pradhāna*—namely *sattva* and the others—are the auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) of Īśvara. Since they function sequentially, there is also a sequence in their effects. For instance: when Maheśvara is joined with *rajas*, whose activity has become manifest, he then becomes the cause of the creation of living beings, because *rajas* has the nature of producing.
But when he resorts to *sattva*, whose activity has become manifest, he then becomes the cause of the maintenance of the worlds, because *sattva* is the cause of stability.

But when he is joined with the power arisen from *tamas*, then he effects the dissolution and destruction of the entire world, because *tamas* is the cause of dissolution. As it has been said: "Salutation to the Unborn, who is the soul of the three qualities (*triguṇātman*) and consists of the three Vedas (*trayīmaya*), who is the master of creation, maintenance, and destruction; who touches *tamas* at the dissolution of beings, *sattva* for their maintenance, and *rajas* for their birth."
The word *kila* is used here to express incredulity.
99–100 He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said here," and so forth.
To this it is replied: At the time of their single activity, does that capacity for the production of other effects exist or not?
If it exists, then even at the time of creation, both [other effects] would likewise arise.
In this way, if the existence of one [of these two] were established, the other two would follow as a consequence;
"of those two" refers to primordial matter (prakṛti) and the Lord (īśvara).
Regarding the phrase "at the time of a single activity":

there are two alternatives as to whether, at the time of any one of the activities of creation (*sarga*), maintenance (*sthiti*), or dissolution (*pralaya*), the capacity to produce the other two effects exists or does not exist.

In that regard, if it does exist, then because the cause would be unimpaired during the times of creation, the other two effects consisting of maintenance and dissolution would come into being just like the effect of creation.
In this way, even during the time of stability, origination and destruction would occur;
and at the time of dissolution, stability and origination would exist.
But this is not tenable.
For it is not logical that things existing through mutual exclusion should coexist at one time in a single substratum.

It might be argued that at the time of producing that single effect, those two—Prakṛti and Īśvara—do not possess another form for the production of the other two effects; therefore, there is no contingency of them [producing those] at that time. To this he says: "For indeed," and so forth:
"For indeed, it does not become the producer of another by means of its other form, and its own nature is precisely that [same one]; how then could there be a cessation of that activity? (103)
The word "that" refers to the cause known as primordial matter (prakṛti) and the Lord (īśvara)— namely, of the other two subsequent effects.
It is not by way of another nature; rather, the intended meaning is that it is a cause precisely by way of its own nature.
(103) It might be argued: "Even if it is not a cause by way of another nature, nevertheless, at the time of producing one effect, it lacks the capacity to produce the remaining two effects."
Therefore, he says that at that time there is no production of the two effects: "But in the absence of that capacity," and so forth.
"However, in the absence of that capacity, it would not be a producer of those [effects] at all, because at other times it is devoid of power, like a sky-lotus and the like. (104)
"At another time" means at the time of commencing the desired activity.

It might be argued: "Even though all potentialities (*śakti*) are present in the Pradhāna, nevertheless, only that whose activity (*vṛtti*) has become manifest attains the status of being the cause, and no other; therefore, there will be no simultaneity of effects. To this he says: "If that which is predominant," and so forth—"If that which is predominant and in the form of a potentiality were the sole cause..."
Because of its proximity to that which is eternal in form, it would exist at all times.
(105) Indeed, it is not tenable to say that this intense form of [qualities] such as sattva is eternal, because it occurs only occasionally.

Consequently, there are three possible alternatives regarding its occasional existence: it must arise either from causes such as *prakṛti* and *Īśvara*, or from some other cause, or it must be independent.
In that regard, in the first position, that predominant form would exist at all times, because the cause known as *prakṛti* and *Īśvara* is eternally present due to its eternal nature.
Regarding the second position as well, he says: "And not another," and so forth.
Nor is it desired [to arise] from a succession of others; therefore, it does not come from anything else either.
Nor is this [arising] independent, because its occurrence is only occasional (kādācitkatva).
For no other cause is accepted apart from Primordial Matter (prakṛti) and God (īśvara), from which it might otherwise originate.
Nor is the third position tenable; thus he says, "Nor also," and so forth (verse 106).
Now, if there is independence [of the cause], what contradiction is there in its being occasional? To this he says, "From itself," and so forth.
If existence were from itself, there would necessarily be causelessness, because it is contradictory for something to act upon itself;
for it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible.
(107) "From itself" means from its own nature; "if existence," meaning if there is birth, [then] there would necessarily be causelessness.

[Objection: But how can that which arises from its own nature (*svabhāva*) be causeless, given that its very nature is understood to be its cause? [Reply: He says: "Because of the contradiction with its own activity" (*svakriyāyā virodhataḥ*). This means because of the contradiction of an entity’s causal status (*hetubhāva*) existing within its own essential form (*svarūpa*). It might be argued: "Granted that there is this lack of a cause, why is occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatva*) not tenable? To this he says: "For, by depending on... and so forth. For it is logical that entities whose existence depends upon other natures (*svabhāvāntara*) should be occasional.

Because their existence and non-existence are dependent upon the presence or absence of other factors, why would those things whose mode of being is independent of anything else ever exist at any time, given that there is nothing for them to depend upon?
Now, he asks how this very contradiction with its own activity is established, and says: "For instance," and so forth.
For indeed, no activity of non-existence upon itself is admitted, because even for that which has already come into being, its self-nature is already established in this state. (108)
For when an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) produces itself, is it already established or not?
It cannot be that it is already established;

because at that stage, since the self (*ātman*) is also known as being non-different from the established form, it would follow that the self is already established, just like the intrinsic nature itself.
And consequently, since an effect is impossible, where could this entity exert its activity?
(108) He shows that it is not even unestablished with the words beginning "unestablished," etc.
But one whose nature is unestablished does not engage in any activity whatsoever,
because of being devoid of all causal power, like a sky-lotus and so forth.
(109) Thus ends the examination of both.
The term "in some cases" is a general statement;
the meaning is that [the action] exists neither as identical with its own self nor as something other.
If there were an activity, it would necessarily be of a nature already accomplished.
The meaning is that the perfected [nature] has precisely this much as its defining characteristic. (109) Thus concludes the examination of both.
In the examination of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikavāda*),

[the author], while refuting the arguments of the proponents of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*) included under the word "etcetera" by disregarding their sequence due to the brevity of what needs to be said, says: "All," and so forth—
"The birth of entities is described as being independent of all causes."
For those proponents of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādin*) do not even say that [intrinsic nature] is its own cause.
Although the doctrine of the self-existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvasvatobhāvavāda*) was not explicitly mentioned here by the word "etc.
(*ādi*), it is nonetheless indicated by the inclusion of the proponents of intrinsic nature.
In this regard, those who maintain that entities arise from themselves have already been refuted by the argument beginning with "because of the contradiction of self-action" (*svakriyā-virodhāt*);
now, the proponents of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādins*) are being refuted.
They say this: "The birth of entities is neither from themselves nor from another; what then? It is independent of all causes"—meaning it is independent of its own or any other cause.
Now, one might ask: "What is the difference between these [entities] and those who describe them as arising from themselves alone? To this he says: "Those," and so forth.
"Those" refers to the proponents of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavādins*). "From themselves" means...
The word "also" (api) implies that their own nature (svarūpa), as well as the nature of another (pararūpa),
is intended; whereas the former [schools] maintain that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is the cause, these [latter schools] do not accept even that— this is the distinction.

110 And here they set forth the reasoning: that which meets the conditions for perception but whose existence is not perceived is, for discerning persons, an object of the conventional usage of "non-existent," just as a hare's horn; and since the cause of entities is [such] a thing whose existence is not perceived, this is a non-perception of essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
And showing that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "The lotus," and so forth:
"Who indeed creates the variety of the lotus filaments and other parts? Or by whom was the variegated eye-pattern on the peacock's tail fashioned? (111)
*Rājīva* means a lotus; the analysis of the compound is "the filaments and so forth of that.
By the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the stalk, petals, pericarp, and the like, as well as the sharpness of the thorns and so on.
This constitutes the "variety" (*vaicitrya*).
Who creates the distinctions of shape, color, hardness, and so forth?
No one at all.
The meaning is that this is because a cause such as Īśvara (God) is not perceived.

(111) It might be argued: "Granted that the lack of a cause is established for external entities due to the non-perception of their causes, how is it established for internal entities? To this, he says: "Just as... and so forth.
Just as the sharpness and so forth of thorns and the like are without cause because they occur only occasionally, in the same way, suffering and the rest are without cause.
(112) Even if the causelessness of suffering and the rest is not established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is nonetheless established by inference (*anumāna*).

For instance: whatever is occasional is determined to be causeless, such as the sharpness of thorns; and since suffering and so forth are occasional, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, it is not logical to say that "that whose presence or absence necessarily results in the presence or absence of another is the cause of that," because of the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
For example, visual consciousness occurs when there is touch and does not occur when there is no touch.
And yet, that [object] is not the cause of visual consciousness;
therefore, this definition of the relationship between cause and effect is fallacious. Consequently, it is established that the arising of entities is independent of any cause whatsoever.

He provides a rebuttal with the verse beginning "sarojakesarādīnām" [of the lotus filaments, etc.]: "The seeds, mud, water, and so forth, which possess positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), are subject to a specific state characterized by excellence. (113)
"When a cause has been ascertained through perception and non-perception, why is another cause for these [effects] then asked about? (114).
By this, he demonstrates both the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetu*) and the contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*) regarding the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

As for the claim that no cause for the lotus, its filaments, and so forth is perceived, that is unproven; for by means of perception and non-perception, seeds, mud, water, and the like are ascertained to be causes through their possession of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
To explain: when the birth of something occurs only when another thing exists, and when a modification of one follows a modification of another, that [latter] is called the cause of the former.

Such things as seeds, having reached specific states characterized by swelling and so forth, possess positive and negative concomitance with respect to the lotus, its filaments, and the rest—that is, they exhibit the presence and absence [of the effect].
The reason [you provide]—that [the relationship] is ascertained through perception and non-perception—is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, as for what was said regarding the definition of cause and effect being subject to deviation (*vyabhicārin*), that too is unestablished;
for even touch is accepted as a causal factor for visual consciousness by virtue of being a cause of form (*rūpa*).
For instance— the term "contact" (sparśa) refers to the primary elements (bhūta),
and form (rūpa) exists by depending upon them; therefore, contact certainly possesses the status of a causal condition (nimittabhāva) with respect to visual consciousness,
the only distinction being whether it is produced directly or through a succession.
Nor do we accept mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone as the cause for determining the relationship of cause and effect;
rather, it is a specific kind [of concomitance].
For instance, when other causes capable [of producing the effect] are present, that single thing whose absence prevents the effect from occurring is described as its cause.
But it is not mere negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) in the sense that "in the absence of X, Y does not occur";

otherwise, there would be the absurd consequence that the *piṇḍakharjūra* fruit—which grows in a region where the marriage of one's mother is customary—would cease to exist in the absence of such a marriage.
Furthermore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to touch in the case of such a negative concomitance.

For instance—if it were shown that visual consciousness does not arise because, despite the presence of visible form (*rūpa*) and the other [sensory objects], there is an absence of the single factor of tangible contact (*sparśa*), then there would be a deviation [in the causal rule]. However, this cannot be demonstrated;
therefore, there is no deviation in the definition of the relationship between cause and effect.
He demonstrates that not only are seeds and so forth determined as causes of entities, but that place and time as well are determined as restricted: "niyatau" and so forth.
How is it that place and time are also restricted for entities?
If these [causes] were not the causes of those [effects], they would occur everywhere and at all times;
yet, since they occur only occasionally, in certain places, and in relation to something specific,
they are necessarily dependent upon that [specific condition], by way of excluding everything else.

For if lotuses and other such things did not have that causality—that is, causality restricted to specific places and times—then their occurrence only in specific locations such as water while avoiding places like stones, and their occurrence only during seasons such as summer while avoiding seasons such as winter, would not be possible;
rather, those entities like lotuses would exist everywhere in all places and at all times, because they would be independent of those [specific conditions].
However, since they occur with necessity only in specific places and so forth by avoiding other places and times, it is certain that they are dependent upon them.
[Objection: But for entities that are devoid of intention, what is this "dependence"? [Response: He says: "Dependence on that is such an occurrence."
Dependence on that [cause], which is a functioning in such a manner, is called "dependence" (apekṣā), and this is what is meant by "being an effect.
Furthermore, such functioning is directly perceived; therefore, the reasons (hetu) are established here.
This very functioning, which occurs in a restricted place and so forth by excluding other places and so forth, is what is called "dependence."

It might be argued that [the dependence] consists of intention; even if they indeed have that [intention] as their object, how is it determined that they are its effects? To this he says: "Dependence is called being an effect.
For being an effect is not something other than this; what then? That very dependence, characterized by such a mode of operation, is called being an effect.
If it is asked how such a behavior of theirs is established, he says: "By perception," and so forth.
This doctrine of their inherent nature is contradicted by direct perception.
Because the nature of the cause is ascertained through perception and non-perception;
"tad" means therefore.
The compound "the doctrine of intrinsic nature (*svābhāvikavāda*) regarding those [lotuses] such as the *rājīva*" is sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*),
because even non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is essentially of the nature of perception insofar as it consists in the apprehension of something else.

Furthermore, the reason stated as "because of being occasional" (*kādācitkatvāt*) in order to prove that pleasure and so forth are causeless is contradictory, because it proves the opposite of what is to be proven;
for it is impossible for that which is causeless and independent to be occasional,
and the meaning is that the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
Thus far, the contradiction of the thesis with perception and the unestablished nature of the reason have been pointed out;
now, while provisionally accepting the establishment of the reason, [the author] demonstrates its inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva), saying "mā vā" and so forth.

Or, let there be no existence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the sake of establishing the existence of a reason; nevertheless, by the mere absence of a means of valid cognition, there is certainly no ascertainment of the non-existence of an object. (119) If mere non-apprehension were taken as the reason, then it would be inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Since the non-existence of an object cannot be determined merely by the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) due to the absence of a [corresponding] cognition (*mānābhāva*),
he asks why this is not the case and says: "Because," and so forth.

Because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is neither the pervader (*vyāpaka*) nor the cause (*kāraṇa*) of the existence of an object, due to the existence of difference [between them] and because of its deviation and its arising from that [object].
For it is a pervading nature (*svabhāva*) that, when ceasing, causes its own pervaded (*vyāpya*) to cease, or a cause that [causes its] effect to cease.
In that regard, because the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the effect (*kārya*) are restricted by identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*), respectively,

there is no non-difference between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the existence of the object (*arthasattā*), since they appear as distinct; nor is the means of valid cognition the cause of the object, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Because existence occurs even in the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
for instance, the existence of objects remote in space, time, or nature is entirely non-contradictory even when they have not been made an object of a *pramāṇa*.
Furthermore, it is not logical that something which exists even without another thing should have that other as its cause, for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Alternatively, if one accepts that [the object] is the cause [of the means of valid cognition], one abandons one's own position;
and because it arises from that, the means of valid cognition is not the cause of the existence of the object.
For instance, the means of valid cognition arises precisely from the object itself, which serves as its objective domain.
Furthermore, the object of cognition is not [established] by means of the instrument of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Now, it might be argued that even an unconnected instrument of valid cognition will exclude the existence of the object; to this he says: "And that which... and so forth.
And for that entity which is not of such a nature, the exclusion of another is understood through its own cessation, because there is no necessary connection [between them].
"Not of such a nature" means...
It is neither a cause nor a pervader;
for it is not logical that the necessary cessation of one thing should follow from the cessation of another that is not related to it, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For in that case, upon the cessation of a horse, there would also have to be the cessation of a cow.
Non-perception by everyone is doubtful, while non-perception by oneself is inconclusive;
for instance, even though [grass] such as dūrvā in the hollows of the Vindhya mountains is not perceived, it nonetheless exists.

Furthermore, when non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is adduced as a reason, is it adduced as characterized by the cessation of apprehension by all persons, or as characterized by the cessation of one's own apprehension? It cannot be the first, because that is doubtful due to its impossibility of being ascertained by one of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*); for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) available to one of limited vision to establish that the cause [of a peacock’s eye-pattern] is not apprehended by all persons.

Even that non-perception by oneself is inconclusive. Why? Because of the existence—even when not perceived—of things such as sprouts of *dūrvā* grass or fragments of stone located within mountain caves; the meaning is that there is no contradiction with their existence.
In that case, non-existence is not certain due to doubt.
If a reason is not employed for the sake of establishing causelessness, then since there is no proof without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the thesis is not established.
And if a reason were employed for its establishment, even so, it would not [be established]. || 123 ||

Since that accomplishment (*siddhi*) is produced by its cause, your position is thereby established. Furthermore, you should be questioned as follows: in order to establish your own position—that entities are without cause—do you employ some reason (*hetu*), or not?
In that regard, if it is not accepted, then your thesis is not established;
for there is no establishment of an object without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Or, if it is accepted, even so, your thesis is not fully established—this is the connection with what is to be said hereafter.
Why?
Because accomplishment is produced by that cause—since accomplishment, which is the ascertainment of an object of knowledge as its domain, is generated by that cause;
and so it has been stated by the venerable teacher Sūri:

"One who says 'nothing exists' surely undermines his own thesis by making it causeless; moreover, if he were to be lazy in adducing a reason, what would be gained for him by the mere thesis alone? (123)
It might be argued: "I employ a probans (*hetu*) that is indicative (*jñāpaka*), not productive (*kāraka*);
so why is my thesis (*pakṣa*) not established? To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.
For instance, a probans (*hetu*) that makes known, or a statement that illuminates it,
is called a "knower of the probandum" (*sādhyajñāpaka*) when it serves as the cause for its establishment. [Verse 125] Regarding the phrase "a probans that makes known":
The logical mark possessing the three characteristics exists either at the time of inference for oneself,
or as a verbal statement at the time of inference for others.
"It illuminates that" means it is the illuminator of that cause,
for the sake of its establishment.
If the determination of the object of cognition were not to serve as the cause for its establishment in any other way, then how could it not be a communicator? Indeed,
in that case, it would follow that everything would be a communicator of everything.

125. If this is so, why do the Teachers make this distinction between the *kāraka* (the producer) and the *jñāpaka* (the indicator)? And here, he says that the designation of the object (*artha*) is by virtue of cognition, and not by virtue of the actual state of the object as it is produced: [The verse: “Just as a lamp illuminates forms, so too does knowledge illuminate objects; for it is through the power of cognition that objects are designated, not by virtue of their being produced. Therefore, this very [reason] is called an indicative cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*) precisely because it is a causal factor (*kāraka*); however, it is not designated as a causal factor in the sense of being a producer, because it does not produce the probandum (*sādhya*).

It is called "indicative" rather than "causal" because it does not produce the probandum; whereas that which produces the probandum, such as a sprout and so forth, is called a "causal factor"—thus there is no fault.
By all of this, the objection that arises against the refutation stated by the Teacher Sūri is answered;
for instance, the following objection might be raised:
"Even one who asserts that [the world] has a cause, why would he undermine his own proposition by saying that there is no cause?"

For he asserts a probative cause (*jñāpaka-hetu*) while rejecting the productive cause (*kāraka*); to this, the following is the reply: even the probative cause is indeed a productive cause, because it has cognition as its cause. By this, a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) is exposed.
However, there is no reason whatsoever that establishes the absence of a cause, because such a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is sublated by perception and other means of valid cognition (sūtra 126).
With the words "Therefore," etc., he demonstrates, under the guise of a conclusion, that the meaning of the proposition is also sublated by inference (*anumāna*).

Therefore, other entities as well possess causes, because their arising is restricted, just like the cognition directed toward the object to be proven which arises for you from its means of accomplishment. (127) Thus ends the examination of the doctrine of the natural spontaneity of the world.
"Others too" refers to the lotus filaments and so forth, which are distinct from the cognition whose object is the thing to be proven;
they possess a restricted birth.
The application [of the argument] is as follows, with the phrase "given the presence of fixed entities" being understood:

those things which have a fixed birth when there is the presence of fixed entities are possessed of causes; for example, the cognition whose object is the thing to be proven arising from the presence of your [opponent's] means of proof; and likewise, entities such as lotuses [arise under fixed conditions]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
127. Thus concludes the examination of the doctrine of intrinsic nature (svābhāvikavāda) and the examination of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahma).
With the words "destruction, origination," and so forth, the proponents of Śabdabrahman (the doctrine of the Word-Brahman) say:
"The supreme Brahman, consisting of sound, is untouched by destruction or origination; it is the transformation of that [Brahman] which is perceived as this entire collection of entities. (128)

This collection of entities, such as form and so forth, is perceived as the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of that Brahman which consists of sound, is devoid of distinctions such as prior and posterior, unarisen, and indestructible; as it has been said:
"Brahman, whose beginning and end are not, is the imperishable essence of sound (*śabdatattva*);
it manifests (*vivartate*) in the form of objects, from which the process of the world proceeds."
Thus,
in this context— "beginning" means origination, and "end" means destruction; because it lacks these two, it is the imperishable (akṣara) that is without beginning or end.
Because the letters beginning with 'a' serve as the cause,

the manifestation (*vivarta*) in the form of the signifier is shown by this; furthermore, the manifestation of the signified is shown by the phrase "in the form of the object" (*arthabhāvena*), and so forth.
"Evolution" refers to the various distinctions, while "Brahman" is the proclamation of its name;
he points out the meaning of this very verse with the words: "untouched by destruction or origination."

This mention of destruction and origination is also to be understood here as an illustration; for it is stated therein that [the Self] is devoid of the distinction between prior and posterior locations, and likewise that it is without beginning or end.
"Consisting of sound" means having sound as its intrinsic nature; for this very reason, sound is its reality (tattva), and thus it is called "the reality of sound" (śabdatattva);
the meaning is that sound is its non-erroneous form.
"Param" means consisting of the *praṇava*;
for indeed, the *praṇava* is the source of all words and all meanings, and it is the Veda.
But this Veda, established through the sequence of phonemes and words, stands as the means for its comprehension, existing by way of being its facsimile;
and those whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are graced by dharma, which has as its fruit both worldly prosperity and the supreme good, perceive that Supreme Brahman—
this is what they establish here as their authority.

Whatever things are permeated by a certain form are composed of that [form], just as transformations of clay— such as jars, bowls, and water-pots— which follow the form of clay, are well-known to be "made of clay" (mṛṇmaya) because they conform to the form of clay;
and since all entities are permeated by the form of the word, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason),
for it is established through direct perception itself that all objects conform to the form of the word.
For instance: a cognition arising with respect to objects arises as being accompanied by the verbal expression of the word itself, as it has been said:
"There is no cognition in the world that occurs without the accompaniment of words;
every knowledge proceeds as if permeated by speech."
Thus,
the designation of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things is based upon the form of cognition;

therefore, it is established that these [things] are permeated by the form of words, and once that is established, their being composed of that [form] is also necessarily established, because being composed of something consists in arising from nothing but that.
With the words "those [who say] 'they are to be stated,'" etc., he refutes the meaning of the proposition;
thus they explain: "even those who say this must be asked: what is this of their own?"

Having abandoned its form as sound, it attains the state of being blue and so forth; or else it does not. If the first position is adopted, then there would be a loss of its imperishable nature due to the destruction of its prior self.

Furthermore, in the immediately following position, even for one who does not accept [the doctrine of the transformation of sound], the cognition of the nature of sound would clearly occur during the perception of blue and other objects.
(131) In this regard, either the world's being composed of sound is intended as the thesis because the world is sometimes of the nature of a transformation of sound, or because it arises from sound.

Just as in the expression "the vital breaths consist of food" (*annamayāḥ prāṇāḥ*), the suffix *mayaṭ* is prescribed in the sense of a cause, here the first position [that Brahman undergoes transformation] is not tenable, because transformation itself is untenable. To explain: when Brahman, whose nature is sound, assumes the form of blue and so forth, does it do so by abandoning its own inherent nature of sound, or without abandoning it?

In this regard, if the first position— that [the cognition] "abandons" [its object]— is adopted, then there would be a loss of that imperishability and indestructibility which was accepted by the statement "without beginning or end," because its subsequent nature would have perished. If, on the other hand, the next position— that it does not abandon [its object]— is taken, then even at the time of the perception of blue and so forth, sound would become perceptible to a deaf person,
since it is non-different from that [perception of blue], just like the perception of blue itself.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is non-different from something is perceived when that thing is being perceived, just as the nature of that very blue object is perceived during the state of perceiving the blue. And sound is non-different from the blue; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Otherwise, because they would possess distinct fates (*bhinnayogakṣema*), its being of that very nature would be established [as impossible]; this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in this case. 129
Explaining this very point in detail, he says: "By which," and so forth.
"By which [reason] everything is established as consisting of sound in its primary sense,
because there is no abandonment of the form of sound, whether through transformation (pariṇāma) or through designation (abhidhāna).
(132) "By which"— that is, because you describe the world as being essentially of the nature of sound in its very primary sense.
He asks "Why? and says: "Because there is no abandonment of the form of sound" (verse 132).
If it is indeed established as being primarily composed of sound, then what follows? He says: "And because it is not figurative," and so forth.
And since non-figurative oneness is thus established for blue and the other [objects],
how could there not be the cognition of this [object] at the time of its cognition?
(133) [The phrase] "in the oneness of blue and the others" [is used].
The phrase "together with the word" is to be supplied;
"at the time of their cognition" means at the state of cognizing those [objects], such as blue and so forth.

The intention is that as for the claim "he has no sensation," since that too meets the conditions for perception— just like the intrinsic nature of blue and so forth— it is indeed logical that there is cognition.
For if this [consciousness] were not cognized, there would be no cognition even of blue and so forth;
because they would be of one essence, it would follow that their distinct properties are absolutely different.
(134) Now, if the cognition of this [consciousness] is not admitted, then it follows that blue and so forth would likewise be uncognized, just like the nature of the word itself.
"Because of identity"—the meaning is that blue and so forth possess a single nature together with the word;
otherwise, if it were admitted that blue and so forth have distinct properties from the word, an absolute difference would have to be accepted.
He asks "Why? and says:

"For the association with contradictory properties is the defining characteristic of the difference among many; otherwise, even an imagined [difference] would not exist for individual manifestations. (135)
For it is not logical for a single entity to be both perceived and not perceived from the perspective of individual perceivers,
as this would entail the loss of its unity.

Otherwise, if unity were to persist even when contradictory properties are superimposed, then even the imagined distinction between individuals that is accepted for jars and other such things would not exist.
The word "also" (api) implies that not only is there no difference in the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of Brahman;

for it is an established tenet (*siddhānta*) that there is no difference in Him who is established in His own self, since any such difference would fall within the domain of modification (*vikāra*). To illustrate: His state of being without beginning or end is not asserted in the form of [limited objects] such as jars and the like.
What then?
Since jars and other objects are perceived as having visible arising and passing away and as being limited in space by the Supreme Self,

this consequence— that there would be a clear verbal cognition [of Brahman] from the mere hearing [of the word "Brahman"]— which was stated, must be considered only if the form of Brahman is held to have reached the conditions for perceptibility.
If, on the other hand, it is described as being extremely subtle and beyond the senses, then this fault does not apply;

however, since blue and other colors would likewise possess that same nature, the consequence would be that they too could not be perceived, just like its own nature—this is the fault that must be stated.
Consequently, this established rule is not tenable.
Those of inferior vision perceive only the object as possessing arising and passing away;

it might be argued that just as for you [Yogācārins] momentariness—which is non-different from blue and so forth—is not perceived even when blue and so forth are experienced, so too is the nature of sound. But this is incorrect.

For it is not the case that momentariness is not perceived in the cognition of blue and so forth; rather, although it is grasped by a non-conceptual mind, it is said not to be ascertained because of the superimposition of other qualities due to a cause of error. Thus, with respect to direct experience (*anubhava*), it is indeed grasped, but with respect to determinative cognition (*niścaya-jñāna*), it is ungrasped. Therefore, due to the distinction between types of cognition, the state of being grasped and ungrasped regarding a single object is entirely non-contradictory.
Furthermore, in your view, the apprehension and non-apprehension of sound are not tenable,
because you admit that all cognitions are conceptual (savikalpaka),
and thus sound would be determined in its entirety by a single cognition alone.
Because it is impossible for there to be another intrinsic nature that has not been apprehended,
as it has been said: "How can that form which is not determined by determinations be their object?"
Now, if it is admitted that there is some knowledge even that is free from conceptual construction,
then one should not say: "There is no cognition in the world that is devoid of the accompaniment of words."
Furthermore, the reason "because they are permeated by the form of sound" would not be established;
consequently, due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the determination that entities consist of the nature of sound would be entirely groundless.
Moreover, since the momentariness of entities is established through another means of valid cognition, it is said that even though it has been experienced, it is not [simply] ascertained.
But from what is the nature of things as being identical with sound established, such that it could be posited in this way?
(135) He states another line of criticism, beginning with "And for every thing," etc.

And if it is maintained that the single essence of the word is distinct for every manifestation (*pratibhāva*), then all things would occupy the same location and cognition would take on a single form.
For that essence of the word, undergoing transformation, either attains distinction with respect to each object or does not;
in that case, if the position is taken that it is not distinct, then it follows that all [objects] such as blue and so forth would occupy the same location.
The term "being a single part" is an illustration;
it should also include time, transformation, activity, specific states, and so forth.
And [the cognition] would have a single form, namely, the appearance as a whole (vita-pratibhāsa). It "would be"—that is, it obtains.
Because all [things] such as blue and so forth are not distinct from the single form of the word,
if there were a difference in this [word] for every individual instance, it would follow that Brahman is manifold.
Because it would consist of the nature of many distinct entities, just like individual particulars (vyakti).
If, on the other hand, a difference in this word-nature is admitted for each individual, then multiplicity would result for Brahman.

"Because its nature consists of many distinct entities"—the analysis of the compound is as follows: that whose nature (*rūpa*), or intrinsic character (*svabhāva*), is a manifold essence consisting of many distinct entities; the state of being so is "that-ness. Since the one Supreme Brahman is thus asserted, the meaning is that there is a contradiction with what has been accepted in the thesis.
137 He states another refutation as well: "And if [the world] consisted of eternal words," and so forth;
for if things consisted of eternal words, then even entities would be eternal.
If the world has the nature of eternal sound— that is, if its intrinsic essence is eternal sound— then it follows that all entities must also be eternal. Consequently,
because all entities would be established simultaneously with sound at all times, the nature of transformation (pariṇāma) could not be attained.
The word *tat* means "therefore" (*tasmāt*); alternatively, the analysis of the compound is: "the simultaneity (*yaugapadya*) of those [objects] such as blue and so forth is *tadyaugapadyam*.
(138) Now, he asks: even though it is established through simultaneity, why does transformation not occur? He replies with the verse beginning "of a single form," etc.
For transformation would be established in the case of clay and the like, where one form disappears and another form arises;
however, it is not established in the case of a non-sequential [entity]. The word "tu" (but/however) indicates a shift in the sequence.
Thus, first of all, it is not logical that entities consist of sound by way of transformation (pariṇāma).
Furthermore, showing that the second position is also not tenable, he says: "But even if... and so forth.
Moreover, even if the world consists of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*) in the form of effects,

nevertheless, because it is changeless, there can be no sequential emergence from it. (140) Even so, since the Word is eternal and thus immutable, the sequential arising of effects and so forth cannot be established from it.

All effects would arise simultaneously, because their causes possess complete and unimpeded capacity; for effects depend upon the deficiency of their causes, and if those causes are complete, what else could they require by which they would not arise all at once?
Since [the world] arises from the mutual manifestation of various forms, how indeed can it be said that it has evolved into the form of objects from a state of single-naturedness? 141.

Moreover—if it is admitted that from that single-natured essence of sound (*śabda-ātman*) there arises another and yet another nature, then the claim that "that Brahman has evolved (*vivṛtta*) in the form of objects" would not be established; for when a different entity is produced, it is not logical that something else which does not enter into its nature should evolve into that very form.
Therefore, in every respect, the meaning of the proposition is untenable.

Showing that the reason "because it is permeated by the form of sound" is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "atadrūpa," etc.—Because of the perception of the nature of clay as excluded from what is not that [nature], a single essence of clay is postulated here amidst the various differences such as pots, jars, and so forth. (142)
However, such [a common nature] is not perceived in the case of entities such as blue, yellow, and so forth;
therefore, even that conceptualization—which lacks a seed and consists in the exclusion of what is other than the nature of sound—is groundless.
For, in the ultimate sense, there is no persistence of a single form among entities.

Since all things, by virtue of being established in their own respective natures, possess a nature that is excluded from those of the same class, a conceptual unity—consisting in the exclusion of dissimilar things—is attributed to them because they are permeated by a single form. For example, although jars, bowls, water-pots, and so forth are ultimately distinct, the nature of "clay" is conceptually attributed to them because they are excluded from objects that do not consist of clay. This is how it is established in that case.
Furthermore, that imagined state of these [cognitions] such as blue being permeated by the form of a word is not possible;
for we do not perceive the nature of sound within blue, yellow, and so forth.
And not perceiving it, how can we imagine that they are permeated by the form of a word based on the exclusion of what is non-linguistic in nature?
Therefore, this conceptual construction is seedless; thus, the reason is unestablished. 142–143.

Regarding what was stated— that all [individuals] would occupy the same location and consciousness would be of a single form— the author raises an objection based on the view of others, beginning with "Now, if this reality of Brahman is indeed indivisible": "Now, if this reality of Brahman has always existed as entirely indivisible..."
Due to the affliction of ignorance, the world conceives of things as manifold.
(144) Nevertheless, it may be that the reality consisting of Brahman is always undivided, changeless, and established as the ultimate truth;

there is no transformation of it in the ultimate sense. Rather, those whose eyes of intellect are struck by the cataract of ignorance perceive it as if it were manifold through distinctions such as blue and so forth.
As it has been said: "Just as a person afflicted by cataracts perceives the pure sky as if it were filled with various specks,
so too is this immutable, immortal Brahman [perceived] through ignorance."
"Since it manifests as differentiation while having fallen, as it were, into a state of turbidity,
there will be no consequence of all things occupying the same location, because they are not real entities."
Furthermore, there will be a distinction between cognitions, because that [distinction] is produced by the affliction of ignorance; this is the intended meaning.
(144) He offers a rebuttal with the words "In that case as well," and so forth:
Even there, form is perceived by people overwhelmed by ignorance in the manner of blue and so forth, serving as the basis for rejection and acquisition;
yet apart from that form, the nature of Brahman remains unperceived.
How can it be perceived as existing by those whose minds have emerged [from meditation]?

For the establishment of the existence of an object of knowledge depends upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and there is no such means of valid cognition for the proof of Brahman in its formless nature.
To explain: first of all, its proof is not through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For indeed, no other form of Brahman appears apart from blue and so forth, which serve as the basis for attaining the beneficial and avoiding the harmful;
and how could that which does not appear be perceived as existing by those whose minds have emerged [from meditation] and who abide on the path of logic?
That [unity] is not established through perception, because it does not appear as undivided;
nor is there an inferential mark based on an effect, since production from an eternal [cause] is impossible.
But because the subject (*dharmin*) is not established, an essential nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be a prover;
nor, apart from this, can a logical mark (*liṅga*) be a prover of existence.
This might be argued: [148]
That [light] is established by self-cognizing perception alone, because its nature is that of knowledge;
for it is indeed light, because its essence is sound and its form is consciousness.
Thus, this [position of yours] contradicts self-cognition.
For indeed, even when the mind is directed elsewhere, one who perceives a form with the eye experiences a cognition of blue and so forth that is not accompanied by verbal expression;
this will be demonstrated in detail.
By this, what was stated—"There is no such cognition in the world," and so forth—is also refuted.
Therefore, Brahman, which is undivided and consists of sound, is not established through direct perception,
because such a thing does not manifest to the senses;
nor is it established through inference.

For instance, would this inference have as its logical mark (*liṅga*) an effect (*kārya*), or an essential nature (*svabhāva*)? Since non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) has negation as its object, it has no authority regarding affirmation;

thus, it cannot first be an effect as a logical mark, because the production of any effect from an eternal entity is impossible, since for an eternal thing, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradicted by both succession and simultaneity.
Nor is there an essential nature as a logical mark.

Since that very subject (dharmin) called "Brahman" is unestablished, a property (dharma) that constitutes its own nature cannot be established independently when the subject is unestablished. To the objection that there might then be some other logical mark (liṅga), he says: "Nor this," and so forth.
Since there is no connection with the object to be proven for anything other than its own nature (*svabhāva*) or its effect (*kārya*),
it is not logical for a sign (*liṅga*) that lacks such a connection to be valid, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, as for what was stated regarding the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of entities with the form of words:
Because that [reason] is unestablished and because it is false, it is not capable of proving that Brahman has the nature of sound as its ultimate reality;
nor can its establishment come from scripture, because that is unstable,
even though there exists a logical mark known as non-perception (anupalabdhi).
The point is that this [reason] is included within the essential nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*) itself;
or rather, because what is intended here is that which establishes existence, for this very reason he says: "that which establishes existence" (147).
Furthermore: Let it be understood that Brahman is incapable even of performing the function of being an object of cognition; by virtue of that incapacity, its form is characterized by unreality.
Establishing this point, he says: "Knowledge is established through the sequence of the objects of knowledge," and so forth.

Knowledge is established through the sequence of the objects of knowledge; otherwise, if it were not so, all of it would result in simultaneity, and the cognition of its effects would follow accordingly. (149)
Even if it were mere cognition, its form could not exist beyond that;
consequently, it would follow that it is equivalent to the son of a barren woman.
This has already been established previously in the "Examination of God" (Īśvaraparīkṣā).
The meaning of "tataḥ param" (beyond that) is that it is something other than blue and so forth, which are based on the acts of abandoning and taking up;
alternatively, "tataḥ" serves as a conclusion.
"Beyond" (param) means something other than blue and so forth, which are based on grasping and rejecting;
or alternatively, "beyond" (param) refers to the ultimate (tātvikam), while "therefrom" (tataḥ) serves as the conclusion.

"Being equal to the son of a barren woman" means that there is no basis for establishing the non-reality of the son of a barren woman other than his lack of causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). 149

Now, it is said that only yogins whose internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*) are graced by *dharma*, which has as its fruit both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), perceive that Supreme Brahman, the Self; however, [the author] demonstrates that this too is not tenable, beginning with the words "purified" (*viśuddha*), etc.
Even yogins, whose mental continua consist of pure knowledge,
do not perceive that form of Brahman because they are conjoined with their engagement in cognition.
For if its operation were present within the yoga-born cognition, then it would follow that the yogins see its form.
To the extent that, because there is no activity of that [object] within cognition in the manner described, this would be untenable;
it might be argued that yogis perceive it through the arising of a cognition having that as its object— but this is not so,
because of the non-existence of a yogi distinct from that [object] and of a yogic cognition [distinct from it].
However, it is said that in the state of being a yogi, yogis perceive their own self as having the form of light and as shining;
if this is so, it must be stated what its nature was prior to the state of being a yogi.
If it were always of the nature of light, then there would never be a state of non-yoga, because Brahman is eternally of the nature of the light of the Self;
consequently, liberation would result effortlessly for everyone.

Or, it might be argued that just as for you, even non-dual cognition appears in the states of dreaming and so forth by assuming various forms, so too that non-dual [Brahman] appears in such a manner to those with impure mental continuums due to the power of ignorance.
That is incorrect,
for there are no others whatsoever apart from that [consciousness] who possess an impure continuum such that it appears as such to them;
if you argue that it appears as such to itself, then in that case, it follows that liberation is impossible.
Since Brahman is at all times of the nature of the manifestation of non-dual form,
liberation is indeed possible for us through the arising of another pure cognition;
moreover, for you, there exists no ignorance distinct from that [Brahman].

If it were the case that "it appears as such by virtue of that [ignorance]," then since there is no distinction [between the appearance and ignorance], it would be poorly argued to say that "by virtue of that [ignorance], that very thing appears as such. Furthermore,
one might argue that by the statement "it appears by virtue of ignorance," its very nature as ignorance is being made known.
If this were so, it would clearly demonstrate the very consequence of the total absence of liberation;
for as long as Brahman— consisting of ignorance and remaining eternally of a single nature— persists, the disappearance of that ignorance which constitutes its essence is impossible,
such that liberation could occur through the disappearance of ignorance.

Now, if it is admitted that ignorance (*avidyā*) is distinct [from Brahman], even so, since Brahman is eternal and incapable of having any excellence added to it, that [ignorance] does nothing to it; thus, it is not logical that it appears as such by virtue of ignorance.
Consequently, because there would be no connection between it and ignorance, the undesirable consequence follows that transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) would be non-existent.
Nor is it reasonable to say that it cannot be described as either identical to or different from reality, for there is no other possible mode of being for a real entity.

Otherwise, it would not even possess the nature of a real entity (*vastutva*); nor is it logical for such a thing to appear as it does by virtue of being a non-entity, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, there is no dispute regarding the designation of the name "abiding" for a nature that is thus constituted and capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*).
For us, however, ignorance (*avidyā*) is simply the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) for adherence to the unreal; and that predisposition is called a "power" (*śakti*).

Since this power is essentially of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*) in its causal form, it follows that from each preceding cognition—which serves as the cause and consists in the nature of ignorance—there arises a subsequent effect-cognition characterized by adherence to an unreal form. Therefore, it is logical that there is such an appearance [of objects] due to the power of ignorance.

Through the practice of yoga, that ignorance (*avidyā*) is removed by a process of producing moments that are progressively less potent; consequently, a continuum of purified knowledge arises, leading to the attainment of liberation (*apavarga*). Thus, the distinction between bondage and liberation is logically consistent.

However, this is not possible for you [the proponents of Brahman], because Brahman is eternal and of a single uniform nature, making two distinct states impossible. Furthermore, since that Brahman is one, if one were liberated, it would follow that all are liberated; and if one were not liberated, it would follow that all are not liberated—a consequence that cannot be avoided.
Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition to establish that the self possesses the nature of light even in the state of non-yoga;
for while knowledge is well-established through self-awareness as having the nature of illumination,
it has already been demonstrated that the word-nature is not perceived in this way within every cognitive state.

If, on the other hand, its nature as the light of the Self is not admitted during the state of unfitness, then it must be explained from where that nature as the light of the Self—which was previously non-existent—arises later in the state of fitness for Brahman, which has not abandoned its prior form.
Therefore, this doctrine of yours regarding the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahma*) is a false proclamation; enough of this prolixity.
With the words "by the primary cause" (pradhāna) and so forth, he extends the previously stated method of refutation here as well:
"The view of Brahman is equal to the transformation of the primary cause;
the refutation here is to be understood according to that [previous] refutation. (152)
Thus concludes the examination of the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*).
In this regard, the following refutation should be stated: that effect is not produced by the word, because it exists [prior to its production], just like the cognition of the reason;
therefore, the intended reason is not a valid reason because it is not something to be proven, like the self of another.
And so forth.
152 Thus concludes the Examination of the Word-Brahman (śabdabrahma).
With the words "Others [say]... the Person," and so forth, he introduces the view of the proponents of the Veda:
"But others [hold that] the Person, who possesses qualities similar to those of Īśvara, is the cause of the world."
Those whose intellects follow doctrines poorly expounded imagine [this]:
"Even when all things are dissolved, he who possesses unimpaired power of knowledge is indeed the cause of living beings, like a spider to its threads. (153-154)

They speak as follows: "The Puruṣa alone is the cause of the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of the entire world; even in dissolution, his excellence of knowledge and power remains undiminished.
And so it has been said: "As a spider is to its threads, as a moonstone is to its waters, as the Plakṣa tree is to its shoots, so is he the cause of all living beings."
Thus, the Puruṣa alone is all this— whatever has been and whatever is to be—
as possessing the same attributes as the Lord (īśasadharmāṇam), because both possess the same attributes in being the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe.

However, this is the distinction: those who follow the doctrine of the Person (puruṣavādins) maintain that, apart from God, other factors such as the Self and so forth serve as inherent and other types of causes, whereas for those whose intellects follow poorly expounded tenets, the Person alone is the cause; yet, in both cases, the state of being the instrumental cause for the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe is the same.
The analysis of the compound is: "those whose intellect follows poorly expounded doctrines.
*Ūrṇanābha* refers to a spider.
With the words "of this too" and so forth, he begins the refutation: "Like Īśvara"—
everything that was to be said regarding Īśvara must also be stated here as a negation.
And for what purpose does he perform such an activity?

(155) Here too, the following refutation should be stated using the suffix *vati* after a word ending in the genitive case: "The Person is not the cause of living beings, because he is devoid of birth."
"If everything were otherwise, it would all exist simultaneously like a lotus in the sky," and so forth—
these are the arguments stated by others to establish the existence of Īśvara.

In the same way, when [the existence of] the person (*puruṣa*) is asserted by those who maintain the doctrine of the person (*puruṣavādin*), then, just as before, defects such as being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) must be stated;
he states another mode of refutation as well, beginning with "And for what purpose," and so forth.
Since the activity of one who acts with foresight is invariably concomitant with a purpose, it must be stated for what purpose this Person performs such an operation as the creation of the world;
otherwise, if he were impelled by another, his independence would not exist.
If, out of compassion, he were to make the world entirely happy;
yet, for one who creates beings afflicted by various hardships such as mental anguish, poverty, and grief—what kind of compassion can that be perceived to be? (156–157)
If he acts even against his will because he is impelled by another, such as Īśvara, then that independence which was admitted of him would be lost.

Alternatively, if he acts out of compassion for the sake of favoring others, then he should not create beings suffering in hell and so forth; rather, he should create only those who are exclusively happy.
157–158. Prior to creation, since those who are to be objects of compassion do not exist, compassion itself is not possible; yet it is on account of that [compassion] that this Creator is postulated.

Furthermore, prior to creation—that is, before the act of emanation—there would be no sentient beings to be objects of compassion; therefore, on whose account could this Creator—the Progenitor—be postulated?
Moreover, he would not bring about dissolution for those who are always endowed with prosperity;
for if [his action] depends upon their unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), his sovereignty is lost.
Furthermore, if he acts out of compassion, then why does he bring about dissolution for those very humans who are always endowed with prosperity?
The meaning is that he should, at his pleasure, bring about the destruction of those very beings who belong to the miserable realms and possess afflicted continuums.

Furthermore, it might be argued that he creates a world endowed with pleasure and pain in dependence upon the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) characterized by dharma and adharma belonging to those objects of compassion;
however, this is not the case.
For in this way, the independence [of the Lord] that has been accepted is lost;
nor is there any dependence on anything else for one who is capable,
and if he were incapable, his status as the cause would be lost because the world would arise from that very thing upon which he depends.
And for what purpose would he take into account an unseen cause of suffering?
On the contrary, in that case, equanimity alone is appropriate for him when compassion is present.

Granted that there may be a dependence on the unseen (adṛṣṭa) for that [suffering], nevertheless, it is not fitting for a compassionate person to depend upon that unseen force consisting of merit and demerit which is the cause of affliction; rather, it is fitting for him, being subservient to compassion, to simply disregard it.
For those who possess compassion do not seek out the very causes of others' suffering, since their activity proceeds solely from the desire to separate others from suffering.
If his activity were for the sake of play, he would not be the master of that play,
because of his dependence on various means of amusement, just like a child. (160–161)
Now, if he does not act out of compassion, what then? It is for the sake of sport.
This too is incorrect;
for in this way, he would lack independence in producing his play, since he would have to depend upon the various means of play consisting of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.
If one possesses the power to perform it, one should perform all that which constitutes the means for that pleasure which is to be accomplished through play simultaneously;
otherwise, if one were not capable at the outset, one would not be capable even in succession.
For it is not logical for a single, undivided entity to possess both power and powerlessness simultaneously.
Furthermore, regarding those various means of play: if he possesses the power to produce them, he would produce them all at once;
if, however, he lacks that power initially, then he could not produce them even sequentially.

Because the state of incapacity is indistinguishable [from its opposite], for it is not logical that two mutually contradictory properties—capacity and incapacity—should belong to a single entity with respect to a single object.
Furthermore, every such conceptual objection as "for what purpose does he undertake such an activity? applies equally to the case of Īśvara as well.
By this [he means]: as Praśastamati said—"The Lord acts for the sake of favoring others;

just as some sage who has accomplished his own purpose gives instruction for the benefit of others even when there is no possibility of attaining or avoiding anything beneficial or harmful for himself, so too the Lord acts, desiring to favor living beings by making manifest His own sovereign power."

Alternatively, it may be due to the inherent nature of power (*śakti-svābhāvyāt*), just as, for example, the production of transformations in stationary and moving beings occurs by their very nature through the sequential manifestation of time (*kāla*) in the form of spring and other seasons; likewise, the Lord’s causality regarding the birth, maintenance, and dissolution of living beings results from the sequential manifestation of his powers of manifestation, grace, and withdrawal.
This [objection] too has been refuted by this very same [argument].
For instance, regarding the claim that "He acts for the sake of favoring others," this very same rebuttal applies;
and regarding the claim that "The Supreme Being would make the world exclusively happy through the nature of His power," this same refutation applies here as well.

If he possessed manifest power, he would effect the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world simultaneously; if he did not do so, his power would be unmanifest. Yet it is not logical that this Lord possesses manifest power even in succession.
If it is argued that the manifestation of power is something other than the entity itself, then how could there be only one entity?
This same fault applies even regarding time, for when time manifests as spring and so forth in a successive sequence, this very defect remains.
However, it will be demonstrated later that time is simply the entities themselves— which possess distinctions based on cold, heat, and succession— and which perish at every moment. (162–163)
Now, he raises the objection representing the view of Uddyotakara, beginning with "If its operation [is] by way of intrinsic nature," and so forth:
"Or else, its operation at the beginning of creation is described as being due to its own intrinsic nature, just as fire and the like possess their actions such as burning by their very nature. (164)
If all things were thus to arise simultaneously, that would be because of the presence of the causes endowed with the capacity to produce them.
For he [the Lord] said: "The activity of the Blessed One is certainly not for the sake of sport."

Furthermore, it is entirely untenable to claim that the nature of the Lord is such that He acts toward His effects in the same way that the great elements, such as earth and the rest, act toward their own effects;
for if this were so, all things— which arise solely through His activity— would necessarily be produced simultaneously, since their capable and unimpaired causes would be present at once.
Furthermore, it has already been established by us that intelligence (*buddhimattva*) is not a valid differentiator.
If this is so, why does simultaneity not also occur for effects such as fire? To this he says: "Produced by the power of their own causes," and so forth.
The powers produced by the power of their own causes are indeed restricted; they do not exist at all times in things such as flames. (166)
Otherwise, all effects would arise simultaneously, if this restriction is not admitted even for them.
Regarding the word "teṣām" (of them): it refers to those [causes].
The word "also" (api) indicates that this rule applies not only to fire and the like, but to the Lord as well.
Produced by the power of its own causes. 166–167.
It might be argued: "Why does the spider, though active by its own nature, not produce its effects such as webs simultaneously? To this he says: "By nature alone," and so forth.
Even in the case of the spider, being the cause of the threads is not admitted to be due to its nature alone;
rather, it produces the web of saliva because of its greed for devouring living beings. (168)
The spider (*ūrṇanābha*) also does not act by its own nature;
rather, the intention is that it acts due to an occasional and specific cause arising from a craving to devour living beings.
For it is not eternally of a single form, since even its power is occasional, being produced by the force of its own causes.

Now, it might be argued that [the action] proceeds in some way or another not out of compassion, nor for sport, but simply without prior deliberation; to this he says: "In some way or another," and so forth.
If his activity were merely arbitrary, what kind of intelligence would he possess,
since even a child does not engage in action without first considering the task?
For if this were so, how could his word be worthy of attention by discerning people, given that he is utterly ignorant even of commoners such as fishermen?
"Buddhimatā" means being discerning;
"śanakaḥ" refers to a fisherman.

By this very refutation of the person (puruṣa), it should be understood that those such as Śauri and others who are imagined by others to be the creators of the world are also refuted; thus he shows [this].
The commentator [says]: "Śauryātmaja and others," etc.; those who are conceived as creators, such as Śauryātmaja and the rest.
In this very manner, they too are in fact refuted.
Thus concludes the examination of the Puruṣa;
therein, Śauri is Viṣṇu.
Brahmā is the self-born;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of that which is accepted by others as the intelligent time (kāla),
as it has been said:
Thus ends the examination of the person,
which is the examination of the self.
An Examination of the Self as Conceived by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas:
Others, however, here maintain that the self is the substratum of desire and the rest, being inherently insentient in nature, eternal, and likewise all-pervading. (171)
It is the agent of auspicious and inauspicious actions and the enjoyer of their fruit; it is conscious due to its association with consciousness, not by its own nature.
Its agency is said to consist in its connection with knowledge, effort, and so forth. (172)

The state of being an enjoyer consists in the inherence of the cognition of pleasure, pain, and so forth. Birth is defined as its conjunction with a specific class of novel cognitions and sensations. (173–174)
Separation from those [faculties] previously acquired is death, whereas life is the conjunction of the mind with the body, consecrated by merit and demerit.
Indeed, injury (hiṃsā) is attributed to this [self] through the destruction of the body, eyes, and so forth.
In this way, even though the Person (puruṣa) is eternal, this process is observed to be pure.

The specific types of cognition—namely, perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, knowledge established by observation, and intuitive knowledge; as well as doubt, error, dream, and the dream-within-a-dream—are objects of experience for a cognizer distinct from my own body and so forth. This is because they possess the properties of having an origin dependent on their own causes, possessing both general and particular characteristics, being of the nature of consciousness, being subject to immediate destruction, producing mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and being of the nature of cognition, just like the cognitions of another person. By contrast, [the objects] such as jars, which are either excellently measured or unmeasured, are not so.
Among those, the six non-specific categories beginning with "Being" have been explained previously;
the objects of these six, beginning with "Being," are substance, quality, and action,
