while their non-objects are generality, particularity, and inherence.
This object of knowledge, which consists of both [the internal and external], is the domain of specific cognitions such as perception and the rest; these have been so described.

The compound expression beginning with "perception, inference, and analogy" is a dvandva (copulative) construction, while "siddhadarśana" refers to that which is set forth in the science of astrology and similar fields.
For that is called "siddhadarśana" (the vision of the perfected ones) because it is either the vision belonging to the perfected ones (*siddha*) or it is a vision that has been perfected;
whereas intuitive knowledge (*prātibhajñāna*) is called "ārṣa" (of the seers), as in "my brother, the horse, will go"— for this generally occurs to the seers (*ṛṣi*), and thus it is called ārṣa.
Doubt is uncertainty;
error is perversion;
a dream is a cognition occurring during the state of the first stage of sleep.
That other knowledge which occurs even in a dream having that [same] object is the "dream-end" (svapnāntika);
these alone are the specific types of higher knowledge (prajñāna),
while the rest is easily understood.
Pointing out this very means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) by way of its meaning, he says: "And my cognitions," and so forth.
My cognitions are to be known by an experiencing subject distinct from the objects such as reality (tattva) and the rest, because they are cognitions, like any other [cognition]. (177)
In the phrase "because they are preceded by reality," etc., the word "etc. includes the sense-faculties and sensations;
"because they are conditions" is an illustration, and other reasons—such as having an origin dependent upon their own causes—should also be understood.

Śaṅkarasvāmin, however, provides another proof: "Desire and the rest must be supported by something, because, while being entities, they are effects, like color and so forth. He demonstrates this with the words "Desire and the rest," etc.:
"All these, beginning with desire, are supported by something."
Since it possesses substantiality and is an effect, it [the self] must have form, like a pot; and for us, that [self] is indeed the person (puruṣa).

Because of the inclusion of "substantiality," this [reason] does not suffer from the fallacy of deviance (vyabhicāra) in the case of destruction, since destruction, even though it possesses a cause, lacks substantiality.

By the passage beginning with "because of the apprehension of being a real entity" (vastutvagrahaṇāt), he demonstrates the efficacy of the qualification "provided that it is a real entity" (vastutve sati).

Uddyotakara, however, offers this proof: "Devadatta’s cognitions of color, taste, smell, and touch have a single and multiple cause, because they are synthesized by the cognition 'by me,' just like the simultaneous cognitions of many persons regarding a single movement of the eyebrows of a dancer among those who have made a prior agreement."

This is its meaning: Just as, for example, among many people who have made an agreement that "the garments must be thrown [to us] immediately after the dancer’s brow-frown," various cognitions produced by different agents and having diverse objects are synthesized as "it was seen by me, it was seen by me" because the cause—the brow-frown—is one; so too here, cognitions with various objects will be synthesized because the cause is one, and that which is the single cause is the Self.
Furthermore, *pratisandhāna* (synthetic unification) is the joining together of cognitions—such as "I have seen" and "I have heard"—by virtue of their having a single knower as their cause.
However, in the case of a dancer’s brow-flick, it is the bringing about of a single object for the cognitions;
in every respect, *pratisandhāna* is defined as the connecting of cognitions by taking a single object as their basis.

Demonstrating this very proof, he says: "The cognitions of form and so forth"—all cognitions of form and so forth have both a single and multiple causes, because there is a synthesis of these [cognitions] by means of the cognition "by me. (180)
Just as there are many cognitions regarding the movement of a dancer’s creeper-like eyebrows,
otherwise, recognition would not arise without a basis.
(181) This is easily understood.

180–181 This is another of his arguments: the word "ātman" denotes something distinct from the aggregate of body, sense-faculties, mind, intellect, and sensations; for, while being distinct from well-known synonyms, it is a single term, like the word "jar" and others.
Regarding this, he says: "The term 'ātman' is considered a single word because it denotes something distinct from the aggregate of the sense-faculties of cognition and so forth. (182)
And that which is thus ascertained as being distinct from the synonyms of "established" (siddha) by means of the property as specified is endowed with [that property], like the word "cloth" (paṭa).
Regarding the phrase "distinct from the synonyms of 'established'":
The meaning is: "while being distinct from those established synonyms of the intellect, sense organs, and so forth, such as 'cognition' (dhī) and the rest";
and "that which is thus determined" means while being distinct from the established synonyms, it is expressed by a single word.
"By means of the property as previously specified" means by way of denoting an object distinct from cognition and the like.
Furthermore, he himself employed a negative-only (vyatirekin) reason to establish his own position:
"This living body is not soulless, because [if it were], it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth, like a jar."
He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "by the vital breaths," etc.:
"If this living body were devoid of the vital breaths and so forth, it would be like a jar due to its lack of self; therefore, it does not have the nature of being soulless. (184)
"His lack of selfhood"— that is, the living body lacks a self;
or rather, this self has no lack of selfhood, meaning it is not devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā), but rather its existence is established.

Now, as to how its eternity and omnipresence are to be understood, Aviddhakarṇa first offers this proof: "My cognitions at times other than that [present time] are cognizable by the same cognizer who cognized my first cognition immediately after emerging from my mother’s womb, because they are my cognitions, just like my first cognition.
In the same way, suffering and the rest should also be made the subject of the inference.
And this is the inference for [the soul's] eternity; he demonstrates it as follows: "By the knower of the consciousness of Sadyojāta and so forth," and so on.
Every subsequent consciousness is known by that very knower of the consciousness of Sadyojāta and so forth, because it is my consciousness, just like that first [consciousness]. (185)
The phrase "beginning with that" (tadādyavat) means that which begins with that [first cognition], namely, the cognition occurring at a subsequent time.

To establish [his] mastery (*vibhutva*), he provides the following proof: "Earth, water, air, and mind, which have become objects of dispute and are situated at a great distance, are connected with my self because they possess corporeality, velocity, priority and posteriority, and mutual conjunction and disjunction, just like my own body and so forth."

He demonstrates this with the words beginning "madīya" (my own): even though it resides in a distant place, [the earth and so forth] are joined with my own self because they possess corporeality and other such qualities, just like our own bodies. || 186 ||
He concludes with the words "In this way" and so forth:
"And thus, when the permanence, omnipresence, and existence of sentient beings have been definitively established, it remains a settled conclusion that all phenomena are not devoid of a self. (187)
He offers a rebuttal with the words "tadatra" and so forth:

"In this regard, first of all, regarding the first proof, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because it is accepted that your own cognition is knowable by an omniscient being and others. (188)
Regarding the first [point], "the means of proof," and [the statement] "and my cognitions," and so forth: therein,

there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because we admit that your cognitions are known by us— by those who are omniscient and distinct from your body and so forth, as well as by Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and others who perceive the minds and mental states of others.

Furthermore, demonstrating that the concordant example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta) "like the cognition of another person" is deficient in the probandum (sādhyavikala), he says: "And independent of an illuminator," and so forth;
"and its own nature as consciousness arises independent of an illuminator."
In the same way, another cognition is also devoid of the property to be proven [in the example].
Since even a cognition belonging to another person arises as having the nature of self-awareness (svasaṃvit) without depending on another illuminator,
this example is devoid of the property to be proven— that it is cognizable by a cognizer distinct from the object such as a pot.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "It is not another's mind alone that is intended as the example; rather, the object upon which consciousness arises having assumed its form is what is intended here as the example. To this he says:
"By that which is colored by its form," and so forth—that which is cognized by another [consciousness] as being colored by its form.
Even if that [example] were used as an illustration, there would still be doubt due to another [reason].

(190) That is to say, even so, since cognition arises as having the very nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpa*) and is devoid of being cognized by another cognition, doubt would arise; therefore, the reason is not conclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Now, suppose it is argued that even that [cognition] is to be cognized by a cognizer distinct from itself, because—like its object—it possesses the properties of arising and passing away (*udayavyayadharmaka*), is an object of knowledge (*prameya*), and is subject to being remembered as a means of valid cognition (*smaryamāṇapramāṇatva*).

Therefore, in this case as well, because there is no subverting argument against the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaye bādhakābhāvāt*), the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not certain;
furthermore, if one were to experience each subsequent cognition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*),
for an object cannot be established if it is not manifested by a manifestation itself.
Furthermore, for one who pursues a succession of cognitions in order to establish a single object, an entire human lifespan would be required.
Even if some cognition were to arise as self-cognized in order to avoid the fear of infinite regress,
even so, by that very fact, the reasons— such as having the nature of arising and passing away— would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

In the same way, what aversion can there be toward accepting the self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) of other cognitions as well? If, on the other hand, it is maintained that they exist in a form that is not cognized by themselves,
even so, since that [self-awareness] is unestablished, all preceding cognitions remain unestablished, because their manifestation would lack a manifesting agent.
Furthermore, even the object would not be established.

For those Vijñānavādins who hold the view that all cognition is self-luminous because it is devoid of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper—and is not known by another cognition—the flaw of the "lack of the probandum" (*sādhyavikalatā*) remains unshakable against them.
In this same way, regarding other proofs such as "having an origin dependent on causes," one should state the flaws such as "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Furthermore, the qualification of the subject (*dharmin*) made as "always perceived" and so forth is useless, just as before; for it does not serve as a factor in establishing the probandum under discussion. To explain: what is not already established by this much? By the mere statement, "my cognitions such as perception are to be known by a cognizer distinct from my body and so forth," the differentiation of the subject—even through the distinction between perception, inference, and so on—is entirely useless, since the point is already reached by the phrase "my cognitions."

Furthermore, since the subject (dharmin) qualified by the aforementioned specifications is not established for the opponent, the reasons suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhatā). Alternatively,

if one adopts those specifications in vain and states a different proof altogether to establish them, then, because it concerns a matter unrelated to the original topic, it constitutes the point of defeat known as "irrelevance" (arthāntara).

Furthermore, if it is sought to prove that desire and so forth possess a substratum (samāśritatva), and if the "substratum" is postulated as being merely a cause (kāraṇamātra), [then the argument fails]. 191.
If you consider that which supports them to be their locus (*āśraya*), then the desired conclusion is already established;
for even so, the postulation of a locus for that which lacks motion is fruitless.

As for what was stated—"desire and the rest," etc.—if you are proving merely that there is a cause as the locus of desire and the rest, then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), for we do not maintain that desire and the rest are without a cause.
The meaning is that because of the statement, "Mind and mental factors [arise] from four [conditions]," they are described as being conceptually constructed (*parikalpyate*).

Now, he demonstrates that even if the substratum (*āśraya*) characterized as a support (*ādhāra*) is established, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by that [substratum] is not proven, because the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) is sublated by inference—starting with the words "tadādhāra" and so forth. "Tadādhāra" means the support of those [qualities] such as desire and the rest.
For indeed, the postulation of a support would apply to material entities (*mūrta-bhāva*) that possess the property of moving, in order to prevent their downward fall.
But as for those things such as pleasure and so forth which are devoid of motion, since they cannot possibly fall downward, what could the self or other [entities] do to serve as their support?

One might object: "Just as jars and the like are supports for jujube fruits and so forth even though they do nothing for them, in the same way, the self will be the support for pleasure and the rest. To this he says: "The support," and so on.
"A support such as a bowl is appropriate for jujube fruits and the like because it either acts as an obstacle to their movement or produces a specific change [in them]. (193)
Because it creates an obstacle to movement; or, according to the theory of momentariness, because it produces a specific change— namely, that [change] which, in the case of momentary entities,
consists in the production [of an effect] in the same location as its material cause.
Since neither of these two types is possible for desire and the rest, it is not logical that they have any substratum (ādhāra).

Furthermore, showing that the qualification "provided it exists as a real entity" (vastutve sati) is entirely meaningless because there is nothing to be excluded by it, he says: "Of that which is formless," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not at all logical for destruction, being formless, to possess the nature of an effect;
therefore, the qualification stated here by the opponents in their reason is redundant.
For if the status of destruction as an effect were possible, then the qualification "while being a real entity" would be meaningful for the purpose of excluding that [destruction].
To the extent that, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), nothing can be produced by causes, how could there be causality?
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is a non-entity is not the effect of anything, just like a rabbit's horn;
and destruction is a non-entity. This is established through the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).
The subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) here is that if [the self] were an effect, it would follow that it is a real entity (*vastu*), just like pleasure and so forth;
furthermore, there is a contradiction with your own tenets.

For instance, the designation and cognition "an effect" arise either from its acquisition of its own nature (*ātmalābha*), or from its inherence in its own causes, or from its inherence in existence (*sattā*).
Furthermore, there can be no inherence (samavāya) of destruction— which is devoid of the nature of substance and so forth— either in its own cause or in existence (sattā),
because it lacks any formal character (nīrūpatva).
Otherwise, it would be both dependent—like substance (*dravya*) and so forth—and a real entity (*vastu*); thus, it could not be excluded by the qualification of the reason.
Therefore, the qualification "provided it is a real entity" would be redundant.
Regarding the passage beginning with "having form and so forth as their conditions," he says: "By me," and so on.
The synthesis expressed as "by me" is due to the affliction of ignorance;
even though all things are momentary, this [synthesis] appears because of the identity of the agent and so forth. (195)
Furthermore, because it arises from false conceptualization, the establishment of reality [based on it] is not tenable.
Even though [the cognitions] are distinct due to differences in their capacities, they become unified by having a single basis.
The synthesis characterized by the reconnection of cognitions—such as "I have seen" or "I have heard"—on the grounds that they have a single knower as their cause, is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Since even in the case of momentary entities, a connection [of recognition] is possible due to the deluded conceit of a single agent, a real ontological determination cannot be justified on the basis of such a connection. To the question, "How then do your moments come to serve as the cause for connection? he says: "Because of a difference in capacity," and so forth.

Due to a difference in capacity—that is, due to a specific capacity—even multiple objects can be the cause (nibandhana)—the basis—for a single effect such as a uniform conceptual determination (parāmarśa), just as *guḍūcī* and other herbs are the cause for the alleviation of fever and so forth; this he will demonstrate in detail later.

196. Now, as to how its very erroneous nature is determined, he says: "If it were an effect that follows a single [cause]," and so forth; in that case, the sequence of priority and posteriority would be contradicted.
Because of the proximity of capable causes for cognitions of form, sound, and so forth.

(197) For if these cognitions of blue and so on were the effects of a single, eternal self that persists through prior and subsequent times, then their occurrence in a temporal sequence would be contradicted;
for, since their cause would be unimpaired, it would follow that they must arise simultaneously.
Furthermore, that which is eternal has no dependence on another, because it cannot be assisted by anything whatsoever.

Furthermore, he shows that if one were merely establishing in a general sense that [cognition] is preceded by a cause, then it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*)—with the verse beginning "From an immediately preceding cognition," etc.: "The arising of the six cognitions from an immediately preceding cognition is clearly perceived simultaneously; therefore, this is the establishment of what is already accepted. (198)

Since the arising of the six consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness and the rest, from a single immediately preceding consciousness acting as the *samanantara-pratyaya* (immediately preceding condition) is clearly experienced—

as follows: at the very moment one sees the form of a dancer, one simultaneously hears the sound of drums and other instruments, smells the fragrance of blue lotuses and the like, tastes the flavor of camphor and other substances, experiences the touch of a fan’s breeze and so forth, and thinks with the mind of taking up a garment or similar object—
it is not reasonable to claim that this perception is due to rapid movement, as in the case of seeing a whirling firebrand (*alātacakra*).
Because it would follow that [the object] appears indistinctly;
for you describe this conceit of simultaneous apprehension as resulting from the synthesis of visual perceptions,
and such synthesis is performed by memory.
Furthermore, that [cognition] is indistinct because its object is past,
whereas this simultaneous manifestation of color-form and so forth is experienced as distinct;
moreover, in cases such as "sara" and "rasa," there is an even more rapid arising of cognitions grasping the phonemes *sa* and so forth.
In this case as well, there would be the conceit of simultaneous apprehension,
and consequently, no sequence whatsoever would be determined;
this will be demonstrated in detail later.
But here, by the statement "it is manifest," the direction for the refutation has already been shown.

Now, if it is sought to establish that these [effects] have a single cause because they are caused by an entity that is eternal and of a single nature, then he shows that this inference is contradicted by the pervasion (*vyāpti*)— starting with the words "of those occurring in succession," and so forth.
However, it was stated immediately prior that for successive [causes], there can be no single causality;
therefore, a contradiction with inference (anumāna) regarding the pervasion (vyāpti) in this case is clearly observed.
"Immediately prior" refers to [verse 198].
Regarding the phrase "following one" and so forth,
the refutation here is as follows: those things that are present and possess unimpeded causal capacity arise simultaneously,
just as sprouts and the like, which possess a complete causal complex, arise all at once.
Furthermore, Devadatta and the cognitions of objects such as form possess causes whose capacities are present and unimpeded; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
However, since this is not possible [in the case of the opponent's view], there is a reversal of the logical mark.
199. He shows that the example is also devoid of the property to be proven (sādhyavikala) with the words "the dancer," and so forth:
"The movement of the creeper-like eyebrow of a dancer is not at all one [in reality] from the perspective of ultimate truth."
Because it is an aggregate of many atoms, its oneness is merely conceptualized.
For indeed, the dancer’s brow-creeper and so forth are not one, since they consist of an aggregate of many atoms.
If this is so, how can it become the object of a single word? To this he says: "Its oneness is conceptualized."
Now, he asks: what is the basis for this conceptual construction? He says: "Because of their utility toward a single effect," and so forth;
because they are useful toward a single effect, they fall within the scope of a single word.
"If such a [property] is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*), then it is the proof of what is already established.

Since this [single action], such as the movement of the eyebrows, is employed for a single effect, such as visual consciousness and so forth, therefore, even though it is distinct, it becomes the object of a single word.

Now, one might argue: "We intend such a [property] as the probandum, wherein unity is merely conceptualized; thus, there is no deficiency of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) with respect to the probandum. To this he says: "The probandum also," and so forth.

For in this way, there is the proving of what is already established, because the conditioned factors (saṃskāra) existing in a temporal sequence are the objective referents for the designation of multiple sentient beings based on a single cognition.
Regarding what was stated [in the objection], beginning with "intellect, sense-faculties," and so forth, he says here: "intellect, mind," and so forth.

For us, words such as *buddhi*, *citta*, and so forth, do not possess the capacity to denote something distinct [from consciousness], even though they are single words; this is because they are synonyms.
Therefore, the reason [you have provided] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). But was it not stated that there is a qualification [to the reason]?
It is said: That is not at all established, because it remains a synonym for "mind" (citta).
By way of conventional truth, the mind is called the "self" (ātman) because it is the locus of the ego (ahaṅkāra); however, in terms of the ultimate reality, no object of this [ego] exists. (203–204)

The reason "because it consists of a single word" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, although terms such as *buddhi*, *citta*, *jñāna*, *indriya*, *akṣa*, *vedanā*, *cittanu*, *kāya*, *śarīra*, and so forth—which are synonyms for intellect, sense-faculty, sensation, and body—are single words, they do not, in our view, denote a category of reality distinct [from those they signify]. Thus, because its exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is unestablished, the reason is inconclusive.

[Objection: But surely, having anticipated this very objection, the qualification "provided that it is not different from established synonyms" was stated for that reason; how then can there be inconclusiveness? To this, it is replied:

This qualification of the reason is unestablished; why? Because of the established status of "ātman" as a synonym for consciousness (*citta*), as it has been stated: "It is consciousness alone that is metaphorically designated as 'ātman' because it is the locus of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*)."
"It is metaphorically designated (*upacaryate*)"—the meaning is that it is conventionally expressed (*vyavahriyate*).

Therefore, what was stated by Uddyotakara—that a metaphorical designation is not tenable because a primary [meaning] is impossible—should be understood as resulting from his failure to grasp the intended meaning.
He clarifies this very point with the words "this alone is sung."
Therefore, the reason has an unestablished qualification (*asiddhaviśeṣaṇa*).

This [point] was stated as the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of this reason by accepting its having an object conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*); however, if it were established in the ultimate sense (*paramārthena*) that [the word] denotes an object distinct from cognition and so forth, then this reason would be entirely improper because its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is sublated by inference. Showing this, he says: "In terms of the actual state of things" (*vastuvṛttyā*), and so forth.

The meaning is this: since all verbal usage has as its object a superimposed entity, as will be demonstrated later, there is therefore no object for this word "self" at all; how, then, could there be a pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason by the probandum? 202
Showing that even a reason accompanied by a qualification is inconclusive, he says: "In the case of a lotus in the sky, etc. and so forth.

When a single word such as "agent" (*kāraka*) and so forth is applied to things like a lotus in the sky, a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed. For instance, when someone applies a word such as "agent" to something like a "sky-flower" (*gaganakusuma*), which is absolutely non-existent, then—since that [application] is established for both parties—that thing possesses the property of being a single word while being distinct from words denoting the body and so forth; yet it does not have as its object a real entity distinct from the body and so forth. Thus, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
But how, then, can words such as "agent" (kāraka) be applied to that which is devoid of any defining characteristic? To this he says: "Existing by mere convention," and so forth.
Where indeed are words, which exist by mere convention, not applicable?
Nor is there an inherent illumination of meaning by words such as "self" (ātman) and so forth.
For convention arises solely from independent whim, and words denote only that [conventional] object; how then could there be any obstruction to their application anywhere?

Furthermore, if it is intended that the reason [in the argument] is "because they consist of single words not based on convention," and thus there will be no deviation (vyabhicāra), he says: "Nor indeed... and so forth.

For words do not possess an inherent capacity to reveal meaning independently of convention; otherwise, it would follow that even one who has not learned the language would understand the meaning from them, it would follow that there could be no restriction [of usage] by one's own will,
and it would follow that convention would be rendered useless.
Therefore, it is not established that words such as "self" (ātman) and so forth reveal their meaning by their very nature; thus, the reason [adduced] is unestablished (asiddha).
Alternatively, if another qualification is added—namely, "provided they have as their object a knowable thing included within a category that is not a locus for distinctions"—as stated by Bhāvivikta:

Even so, because the aforementioned qualification is unestablished, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); and because there is an absence of pervasion (*vyāpti*), it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Regarding what was stated, "separated from breath and so forth," etc., he says: "And of breath and so forth," etc.
If the connection of the vital breaths and so forth with the self were established, then this consequence would be appropriate; otherwise, it is inconsistent.
For the living body does not follow as a consequence from the emptiness of the son of a barren woman.
Indeed, this same consequence would apply to you as well in the absence of [the relationship between] the vital breaths and so forth.

(208) For if some relation—characterized either by identity (*tādātmya*) or by origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—between the vital breaths and the like and the self were established, then the consequence that the vital breaths and so forth must cease in the body upon the cessation of the self would be logical.

Otherwise, the consequence that the cessation of one thing entails the cessation of another when there is no necessary connection would be entirely inconsistent, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For indeed, upon the cessation of the son of a barren woman, there is no cessation of breath and so forth that are unrelated to him;

therefore, just as one might raise the objection that upon the cessation of the son of a barren woman, the cessation of breath and so forth would follow—even though they are unrelated to him—just like a jar or similar objects, such a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) is inconclusive (anaikāntika). Likewise, your own attempt to entail the cessation of breath and so forth upon the cessation of this self is also strictly inconclusive, because the relationship [between them] is unestablished. This is the sense.
208. Furthermore, as to how the connection is unestablished, he says: "Not indeed," and so forth—"Not indeed, in this case, is there identity [between the two], because their difference is admitted."
Nor can there be a causal relationship [between the self and the body], because that would entail the consequence of simultaneity.
For when that [self] ceases to exist, would these vital breaths—inspiration, expiration, and so forth—cease from the body, being devoid of any connection to it? (209–210)

"Because their difference is admitted"—thus, between those two, namely the self and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), there is no relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), since a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is accepted.
To explain: the vital breaths and so forth are impermanent, non-pervasive, and corporeal, whereas the self is the opposite of that.

Nor is it characterized by origination from that [the body], because since the causes such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are unimpaired, there would follow the consequence of their simultaneous occurrence;
and apart from these, no other relation exists.
Therefore, being devoid of any relation, why do the vital breaths and so forth cease from the body—that is, from the physical frame qualified by life?
The meaning is that for this reason, the logical reason (hetu) is not inconclusive (anaikāntika).

By this, those things such as desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition which have been stated by others to be marks of the self (ātman) should be understood as refuted, because the relationship [between them and the self] is unestablished.

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: those things which are not invariably concomitant (pratibaddha) with something else do not serve as indicators (gamaka) of that thing, just as cranes and the like are not indicators of sesame seeds and the like; and vital functions (prāṇa) and so forth are not invariably concomitant with the self. This is an inference based on the non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi).
Nor is the reason (hetu) unestablished (asiddha), because both types of relationship have already been refuted.
Nor is it inconclusive, because that would entail the absurd consequence that everything would prove everything;
nor is it contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Furthermore, as for what [the opponent] says—that the establishment of the agent follows from the establishment of the instrument—that is unestablished.
For the status of the eyes and so forth as instruments is not established in the ultimate sense, because in the arising of consciousness all [factors] are equal in being causes,
and because the conventional distinction between agent and instrument is merely imagined by one's own whim.
Thus, in proving mere agency, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), since that which is imagined has not been refuted.
There is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) in proving ultimate agency,
because a connection with such an agent is not established anywhere in the case of the eyes and other sense organs.
Regarding what was stated [in the objection], beginning with "sadyojātādyavijñāna" and so forth, he says: "And thus," etc.;
and thus, because the existence of a self is not established by any of these means of proof.
"The example cited for [the properties of] permanence and omnipresence is devoid of the probandum (sādhyahīna).
Regarding the examples stated—namely, 'like the first cognition' and 'like my own body'—those are deficient in the aforementioned property to be proven because the self (ātman) is unestablished;
therefore, the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika)."
With the words "by others," etc., he again raises the objection regarding the view of Uddyotakara, Bhāvivikta, and others:
"The self has been postulated by others as being established through direct perception."
"For the ego (ahaṅkāra) is self-cognizable, and its object is considered to be the Self.

(212) For they say this: "The Self is established through direct perception itself; for instance, the cognition 'I' is a direct perception, like the cognition of color and so forth, because it does not depend on the recollection of the relationship between a mark and the bearer of the mark.
And its object is not color and so forth, because it appears as distinct from the cognition of those [objects]."
Therefore, [the opponent's claim] that "the object is indeed something else" is incorrect;
he refutes this with the words beginning with "that is improper."
Therefore, that [claim] is incorrect, because that form does not appear in the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra);
for the manifestation of eternality, omnipresence, and so forth is not observed therein.
Rather, the manifestation of [qualities such as] fair complexion and so on is clearly present there.

The self is not accepted as having that [ego-consciousness] as its intrinsic nature; therefore, this [consciousness] does not have it as its object. (214) Thus, the fact that ego-consciousness has the self as its object is unestablished, because it is devoid of the form of that [self]. The formal argument is: whatever is devoid of the form of something does not have that thing as its object.

Just as visual cognition does not have sound as its object and is devoid of the form of a self, so too is the cognition "I"; this is an inference based on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
He shows that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*) with the words beginning "for not" (*na hi*).
For instance—the self is held to be endowed with qualities such as eternity, omnipresence, and consciousness;
yet, in this notion of "I," no manifestation of eternity and so forth is observed.

Rather, because it arises in contact with the states of the body—as in "I am fair-complexioned," "I have weak eyes," "I am emaciated," or "I am pierced by intense pain"—the manifestation perceived is characterized by features such as fair complexion.

Therefore, it is clearly known— that is, it is evident— that the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which arises through contact with the states of the body and so forth, has the body and such as its objective support,
because its functioning is unerring and manifest.

Consequently, that which was stated by Uddyotakara and others— that this is a metaphorical designation of the self (*ātman*) with respect to the body as the locus of experience, just as a king says of a compliant servant, "He who is I, he is this very servant of mine"—
is thereby refuted; for if this were figurative, its application would be faltering.

If it is argued that in the world, although both the primary and the metaphorical [uses] of the term "lion"— as in "the lion" applied to a lion and a young boy— give rise to an unerring cognition, yet the application of the term "lion" to one's own body and so forth is a "slipping" usage because one perceives their difference (vyatireka) through the thought "these are my body and so forth," we say:
no.
Because it would follow that its application would even falter with respect to the self;
for even there, the distinction "my self" is observed,
and if it is argued that the difference here is merely imagined—

[Objection: Let it be the same in the other case as well; even though the cognition "I am fair" (gaura) and so forth is primary, why then is the self not its object? [Reply: He says: "having that nature," meaning having the nature of being fair and so forth.
Because of the impossibility of qualities such as form and so forth belonging to it.
Thus, it has been described that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) cannot have the self as its object because it lacks the form [of a self];
furthermore, he shows that it is not tenable [as such] because it would follow that there could be no dispute regarding it—starting with "If," etc.:
"If the person were truly accessible through direct perception..."
Therefore, for what purpose does this dispute proceed regarding the existence and other attributes of that [Self]?
[It proceeds] regarding that Self's existence, permanence, omnipresence, and so forth.

It might be argued: "Just as for you there arises a dispute regarding momentariness and so forth—which are not distinct from the nature of blue and other objects—even though they have been directly perceived, so too will it be with respect to the self. To this he says: "For thus," and so on; for this ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*) proceeds as being of the nature of a certainty.
And the relationship of sublated and sublator is established between a cognition of certainty and a cognition of superimposition.

(216) For it is logical that there should be dispute regarding momentariness and so forth—which are non-different from [the object] blue and the like—even when that object is apprehended by perception; this is because, on your view, that perception is non-conceptual and thus not determinative, leaving momentariness and the rest undetermined.
However, in your case, such dispute is not logical, because the notion of "I" is conceptual and thus determinative in nature, and therefore the self is already determined.

Furthermore, once an object has been made the focus of a definitive cognition (*niścaya*), there can be no occurrence of a superimposing cognition (*samāropa-pratyaya*) that grasps a contrary aspect, by which a dispute between the two could arise due to their relationship as sublated and sublator through their coexistence.

For this indeed is the comprehension of their own objects by definitive cognitions: namely, their very act of definitively determining it; if they do not determine it, it follows that they do not grasp it at all.
Having thus refuted the opposing position and establishing his own position, he says: "Therefore," and so forth;
therefore, desire and all the rest do not indeed inhere in the self.
Because they arise in a sequence, like a seed, a sprout, and a creeper. Or else, all internal [phenomena] have their forms pervaded by selflessness,
because of reasons such as being functional entities and existing as things, just like external objects such as jars.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things that arise successively do not inhere in a self (*ātman*), such as seeds, sprouts, creepers, and so forth; and pleasure (*sukha*) and other mental states arise successively. This is because of the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). Since successive arising is pervaded by non-inherence in a self—which is the opposite of inherence in a self—the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary position is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that they would arise simultaneously, given that their complete causes are present.

Alternatively: all those things endowed with properties such as substantiality, being produced, and having an origin are devoid of a self (*nirātman*), just like external objects such as jars; and internal entities such as the living soul, the body, the living body, the mind, intellect, pain, and pleasure are likewise endowed with properties such as substantiality. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
But how is pervasion established here? He says: "If there were a self," and so forth.

For if there were a self, it would follow that its causes are eternal; and since eternal things are incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), existence and other such properties cannot possibly occur [in them]. (219)
If there were "possession of a self"—meaning that the body and so forth were presided over by a self—then the self would be their cause;
for it is not logical that a non-cause should be a presiding agent, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Consequently, because their causes—the body and so forth—would have the self as their cause, it would follow that they are eternal—that is, they would lack succession due to having their causes fully present.

It might be argued: "Even if their eternality were indeed entailed, nevertheless, properties such as being a real entity (*vastutva*) would still persist. To this he says: "And [if] eternal," and so forth.

The meaning is that if bodies and the like were eternal while existing, they would follow as being incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); the word "follow" (*prasajyante*) from the context is connected here by a change of grammatical number.
The point is that for an eternal thing, causal efficiency is contradictory with both succession and simultaneity.

And when the capacity for causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya) ceases, the status of being a real entity (vastutva) also ceases, because a real entity is defined by that very capacity for causal efficiency.
When the status of being a real entity ceases, there is also the cessation of existence and other such properties of real entities; thus, the pervasion (vyāpti) is established.
Uddyotakara, however, says: Now, what is the meaning intended as the probandum by the term "selfless"?
If it means "that which does not benefit the self," then there is no corroborative instance (dṛṣṭānta), for there is nothing whatsoever that does not benefit the self.

Now, regarding the negation of the self (*ātman*): [the claim] that "the self is not the body" implies whose self the body would be; furthermore, because the prefix *nis-* has as its scope the subsequent word (*uttarapada*), one must state what it is that possesses a self (*sātmaka*). Indeed, we do not observe the use of *nis-* when there is no subsequent word, as in the case of *nirmakṣika* ("free from flies").
If you are negating the body-self (*śarīrātman*), you are proving what is already established;
for to whom does a "body-self" belong?
Or, [if you mean] that the body is not related to the self—
Furthermore, there is no further example;
all these are negations of specific instances, and from the negation of specific instances, the general is indeed understood.
This being so, that which was intended to be negated becomes effectively admitted.
Furthermore, if it is argued that the word "self" has an impermanent object because it is a word,

even so, this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of eternal words; moreover, since [terms like] "body" and so forth are metaphorically designated as "self," this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

Now, if it is argued that the word "self" (ātman) has as its object something impermanent, distinct from the body and so forth, and is thus established as having an impermanent object, even so, there is a contradiction because one would be admitting an object distinct from form (rūpa) and the other aggregates;
to this, he provides the following rebuttal: "In the case of jars and so forth," and so on.
And that very same [argument] which is common to pots and other things— whereby non-selfhood (*nairātmya*) is denied by others regarding the living body— is what we are establishing here.
Thus, this objection is equally applicable to you as well.

For instance: you yourselves indeed accept that external objects such as jars possess selflessness (*nairātmya*), either because they are not presided over by a self or because they are not the locus for the experience of that self; otherwise, they could not be cited as examples in the following reductio argument: "This living body is not devoid of a self, for if it were, it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth, like a jar. Consequently, the same objection applies to those [jars] as well: how can they be devoid of a self? If [you say it is] because they do not benefit the self, and so forth.

Therefore, in whatever manner you yourselves accept that selflessness (*nairātmya*) is common to all those external things such as jars and so forth—whether by way of their not being presided over by a self or by way of their not being the locus for its enjoyment—and which [selflessness] you deny in the case of the living body, saying "this living body is not without a self," [denying it] so that by that denial the living body alone is accepted as having a self and not dead bodies, jars, and so forth—that very point is what we establish: that the living body is without a self because of its being a functional entity (*vastutva*), and so on.

Therefore, the conceptual distinction that [the body] is of no benefit to the self and so forth is entirely groundless, since even for you [Buddhists], the absence of self (*nairātmya*) is well-established. Furthermore, as for what was said—that there is no example to prove that the self is not benefited—that is incorrect. For it can be established as follows: whatever does not bestow a specific excellence of nature upon something else is not a benefactor of that thing, just as the Vindhya mountains are not a benefactor of the Himālayas; and the body and other such things do not bestow a specific excellence of nature upon the self, which is eternal and of a single form. This is because of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Nor is the reason unestablished,
because the excellence of intrinsic nature is not distinct from the self; therefore,
when that [excellence] is produced, it would be the production of the self itself.
Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of [the cause] being impermanent;

and if it were distinct [from the effect], since there would be no basis for a relationship between the excellence of its own nature and that [effect], the relationship "this belongs to that" could not be established.
Therefore, nothing can be a benefactor to what is eternal, because [the eternal] renders nothing whatsoever to it.
And as for what was said— "To whom does the body belong?"— that too is incorrect, for there are indeed some who describe the body and so forth as being transformations of the self (*ātman*),
such as the proponents of the Upaniṣads.
Therefore,

that which was stated— namely, that since the prefix *nis-* has as its object the meaning of the subsequent word, one must specify whether it is "with self" (*sātmaka*) or not— that too is inconsistent.
For it is not the actual referent of the second member that is negated;
rather,
what is negated is that which has been superimposed.
Because that which exists cannot be negated, the object superimposed by the opponent through delusion becomes precisely the referent of the subsequent term;
for it is by restating that very object that the negation is performed in order to demonstrate the falsity of the opponent’s cognition.

Otherwise, when you are negating the momentariness imagined by the Buddhists in such statements as "lamps and the like are non-momentary," this very objection would indeed apply: for we do not observe the use of the negative particle (*nañ*) without a following noun, as was said in the question, "In whose body does the self exist? That too is incorrect; for according to those whose view is that the self is the size of a thumb-joint or half a *śyāmāka* grain, the self possesses form (*mūrta*) and therefore its residence in the body certainly exists. For them, the negation is entirely appropriate.
As for what was said—that there is no illustrative example for the negation of the body’s relation to the self—that is unproven;

for it can be established, as before, that there is no relation between the self and the body, just as there is none between the Vindhya and Himālaya mountains, due to the absence of mutual benefit and benefaction.
Furthermore, as for the claim that a general principle is understood from the negation of specific instances, that is inconclusive.
Even though you have refuted the momentariness of lamps and the like, you do not accept the momentariness of anything by way of a general property (*sāmānya*).

However, it might be argued that we indeed accept the application of the term "momentary" to lamps and so forth based on their enduring for only a short time; therefore, momentariness is established as a general property.
If this is so, then we also accept the application of the term "self" (*ātman*) to the mind when it is conjoined with the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); thus, the self is established as a general property.
As for what was stated— the two positions beginning with "now, the word 'self' has impermanence as its object"— that too is entirely inconsistent, because it is not accepted;
for no object of the word "self" is accepted as existing in an ultimate sense.
Nor is it the case that [the word "eternal"] exists apart from form and so forth;
nor is the application of the word "eternal" to any eternal entity established in the ultimate sense, such that there would be a deviation [from the rule].

Nor has it been stated that the word "self" applies to the body and so forth by way of metaphorical usage because its application is unerring; therefore, this is not a proof of what is already established.
Thus, since the self is unestablished, every systematic analysis performed regarding it is entirely without foundation, standing like the son of a barren woman. 221. [End of verse 221]
Thus concludes the examination of the self as conceived by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas.

Since the substratum called the "self" is unestablished because it is contradicted by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), the framework of agency, enjoyership, and so forth that you have metaphorically attributed to it is groundless—like the son of a barren woman—and therefore no separate refutation of it is made;
for it has already been rejected by the very refutation of its locus.

Furthermore, how the faults of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) do not arise will be demonstrated in the "Examination of the Connection between Action and its Fruit" (Chapter 221).
Thus concludes the examination of the self as conceived by the Naiyāyikas and Vaiśeṣikas.

The examination of the self as conceived by the Mīmāṃsakas, and the refutation of that self conceived by the Mīmāṃsakas, is stated as follows: "Others, moreover, [assert] a self whose nature consists of both exclusion and inclusion," and so forth.
They maintain that consciousness is of the nature of sentience (*caitanya*), which is characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*).

*Vyāvṛtti* (exclusion) refers to the mutual differences between states such as pleasure and pain; *anugama* (concomitance) refers to the persistence of [qualities] such as sentience, substantiality, and existence. The analysis of the compound is: "that whose own-nature (*svabhāva*) consists of these two, exclusion and concomitance. What is meant is this: other followers of Jaimini describe the self as being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), excluded in the form of pleasure and so forth, yet concomitant in the form of existence and so forth.

And that consciousness is not something other than the intellect (*buddhi*) as it is maintained by the Sāṅkhyas; rather, he shows that it is the intellect itself—by stating "consciousness has the intellect as its characteristic. This means it has the intellect as its defining mark; the sense is that no form of consciousness is perceived apart from the intellect.

But how, one might ask, is it possible for a single self to possess two mutually contradictory natures—one characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and the other by inclusion (*anugama*)? To this he says: "Just as of a snake," and so forth;
just as the coiled state of a snake departs, immediately after which...
The state of straightness arises, yet the nature of being a serpent persists;
in exactly the same way, for the Self whose nature is eternal consciousness, there is neither a total disappearance of its form nor a persistence of every [transient] aspect. (223–224)
However, its states characterized by pleasure, pain, and so forth, cease and arise; yet consciousness persists throughout. || 225 ||

Just as, for instance, in the case of a serpent—a single snake—even when its coiled state ceases and its straightened state appears, its nature as a serpent persists through both states; so too, although the Self is a single entity whose nature is eternal consciousness, there is neither a total disappearance of all its attributes nor, as imagined by the Naiyāyikas and others, a persistence of every attribute. Rather, states such as pleasure and the like cease and arise, while the form of consciousness persists throughout. Therefore, there is no contradiction; this is the collective meaning.

The meaning of the individual components is now stated: "of that whose nature is eternal consciousness" (*nityacaitanyasvabhāvasya*) is a *vigraha* compound meaning "that of which eternal consciousness is the nature.
[This refers to] "of all" (*sarvasya*).
"Of form" (rūpasya) is the ellipsis; "or even following" (anugamo 'pi vā)— the word "not" (na) is to be connected with what has been stated in the context.
And these are the states of pleasure, pain, and so forth.

Now, why is it that one does not exclusively adopt the position of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), as is desired by the Buddhists who maintain the doctrine of destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśavāda*), or why is it that one does not exclusively adopt the position of inclusion (*anvaya*), as is adopted by the Naiyāyikas and others? To this he says: "They might both be," and so forth.
For if there were absolute destruction, there would indeed be the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done,
as well as the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, would not occur for one who is of a single, unchanging nature.
(226) For if destruction were without any continuity, then there would be the destruction of the action performed, because the agent would have no connection with the fruit.
Furthermore, there would be the arrival of what was not done, because the non-doer would be connected with the fruit;
and if the self were of a single uniform nature, there could be no experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, because— as in the case of space—
there would be no distinction between its state as a non-experiencer and its state as an experiencer.

And so it has been said by Kumārila: "Therefore, by abandoning both [extremes], the person must be accepted as having the nature of both exclusion and inclusion, like a snake in relation to its coils and other states. (226)

[Objection: But surely, if the person (*pums*) possesses both forms [of agency and enjoyment], then that state which is the agent is not the enjoyer; thus, the faults of the destruction of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) would apply here as well. To this he says: "And not," etc. And agency and enjoyment do not depend upon the states of the person; therefore, because of the identity (*tattva*) of those very states within the person, the agent alone obtains that fruit. (227)
For agency and enjoyment do not depend upon a state; rather, they belong to the person alone, because it is the person himself who acts and enjoys, and not the state.
Therefore, since that person who possesses the states does not abandon his prior nature, he remains the agent and thus receives the fruit of that action—this is free from fault.
Furthermore, what is the proof that establishes the existence of this self? He says: "The person," and so forth; such a person exists because of the presence of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).
For by this very [recognition], the self is established and the doctrine of no-self (nairātmya) imagined by the Buddhists and others is refuted.
This is because recognition—which has a single agent as its object, such as "I myself have known" and "I myself know"—exists in reality;
thus the self is well-known, and by this very recognition, the refutation of the doctrine of no-self is also established.
As it has been said: "Therefore, from this recognition established by all the world, there would be a sublation of the doctrine of selflessness. (228)
Furthermore, he explains how these two [the self and knowledge] are established through the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) with the words beginning "I know":
"The cognition 'I'—as in 'I know'—apprehends a knower;
and that [knower] must be either the self (*ātman*) or knowledge (*jñāna*), [but not] that which is absolutely transitory. (229)
If the self were the object of that [cognition], then everything would be consistent;
however, under the doctrine of momentary cognition, everything is utterly untenable.
For instance: "I myself previously knew this, and now [I know it]."
Regarding the cognition that arises [in the form], "I myself know," what object is postulated for that moment of knowledge?
Is it the past, or the present, or is it rather the continuum? (231–232)
In that regard, when the object is known in the past, it is appropriate to say "I have known," but it is not appropriate to say "I know"; for he does not know it now.
However, when the object is present, it is logical to say "I perceive."
The claim that "he knew" is indeed false, because this [object] did not exist previously at all.
For this very reason, it is not postulated that both [the self and the object] are the objects of apprehension for that [cognition];
for neither of them had known [it] before, nor do they know it now.
The continuum is also not external to that [consciousness], nor is it its object, because both are impossible;
for it was not previously known due to its non-substantiality, nor is it so now.
Therefore, this ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) exists within whatever sphere of experience [it occupies].
Established as something other than what was stated [previously], this self possesses an eternal nature.

Regarding the point that "I know"—this notion of 'I' (ahaṃpratyaya) refers to a knower—there is no dispute here. Since it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the agentive notion "I know," that which is the knower must be either the self or the cognition imagined by you to be exclusively perishable and momentary; such is the twofold conceptualization.
In this regard, if the position is that [the self] is the "self," then everything is consistent, since the intended object is established.

However, if the position is that it is "cognition," then everything is extremely difficult to maintain. To explain: regarding this "I-consciousness" (*ahambuddhi*) which arises through the reflective awareness of a single agent—"I have known" and "I myself now know"—if one considers the moment of cognition as its object, there are four possible positions: it may be conceived as (1) past, or (2) present, or (3) both past and present, or (4) a continuum (*santati*).

Regarding the first [alternative]: the determination of the form "I have known" (*jñātavān*) is appropriate when the past cognition is postulated as the object, because it was previously known by that [cognition]; however, "I know now" (*saṃprati jānāmi*) is not appropriate, for this [subject] does not know at the present time—that is, during the moment of the past cognition—since that [past cognition] has already ceased. Now, if the second position is taken, namely that the object is present, then "I know" (*vedmi*) is appropriate, because it is currently performing the act of knowing.
However, grasping the form "he has known" (jñātavān) is not tenable;
why? Because [the object] did not exist before, whereas "this" (idam) refers to present knowledge.

For this very reason—it is established that because this cognition proceeds by way of turning away [from its object], the two cognitions, the past and the present, are not its objects of apprehension;
for neither both the present and the past, characterized as cognitions, have known [the object] nor do they know it at present.
What then? One has known it, and the other knows it.
For this very reason, the continuum (*santāna*) also cannot be grasped by that "I-consciousness," because a duality—the pair of past and present cognitive acts—is impossible.

To explain: that continuum did not know previously, nor does it know now, since it is a conceptual construction and thus lacks substantial reality; and a non-substantial entity cannot possess the status of a knower, as that is a property of real entities. Therefore, it is established that the object upon which this ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) operates, apart from the aforementioned cognitions, is the Self (*ātman*).
Now, he explains how its eternal nature is established:
"The knower who transcended the ego-conception at the beginning continues to persist even now," because it is accessible through the notion of "I," just like a cognizer in the present. (238)

Indeed, this [present] knower is the same as yesterday’s knower because of its nature as a knower; for that very reason, it is like yesterday’s knower, and thus those cognitions are established as being proven.
That "I" which was understood through the cognition of "I" in the past continues even today, just like the cognizer of the present moment.
"And this present cognizer is accessible through the notion of 'I'"; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
"This one" refers to the present cognizer.
"From that very [source]" means because it is accessible through the notion of "I"; thus, having established the knower as the subject (dharmin), the formal argument (prayoga) has been shown.
Now, making the "I-notions" (ahaṃpratyaya) of the present the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), he says "of those," etc., while demonstrating another formal argument (*prayoga*).
"Of those" refers to the past and present "I-notions"; "the state of being the thesis" (*sādhyatā*) means the state of being the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmitā*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "Belonging to a single continuum," and so forth.
Because they are "I-notions" belonging to a knower connected to a single continuum,
all "I-notions" of yesterday and today have the same object, like a single cognition.
(240) "All 'I-notions' of yesterday and today"— this is the statement of the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).

"Having the same object" means that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) has a single objective domain; that is, those "I-notions" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) belonging to a cognizer who is connected with a single continuum—such as that of Devadatta and so forth—are the "I-notions of a cognizer connected with one continuum. Their state of being such is their "nature" (*tattva*).
And this statement of the reason— namely,

"the state of being the object of the notion of 'I'"— is qualified by the phrase "having as its object a knower connected to a single continuum," in order to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva), since that mere state of being the object of the notion of 'I' occurs even in the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) belonging to other persons;
the example provided is "like a single cognition."
The meaning is: "among those very notions of 'I', like a single intended cognition.
With the words "tadatra" (in this regard) and so forth, he begins the counter-argument.
In this regard, it is considered: if eternal and unitary consciousness (*caitanya*) is accepted, then it follows that even the intellect (*buddhi*) must be of that same nature.

For if consciousness is admitted to be eternal and of a single form, then the intellect, being non-different from the nature of consciousness, would likewise result in being eternal and of a single form.
And this is not desired; therefore, there is a contradiction with the thesis due to the acceptance [of the opposite].
For it has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "For that [cognition] is momentary; it does not persist until the time of another cognition.
Likewise, it was also stated by Jaimini: "When there is contact of a person's sense organs with an existing object, the arising of cognition is perception (pratyakṣa)."

Furthermore, Kumārila’s own statement involves a contradiction with his own words, because birth is impossible if [cognition] were eternal; as he himself has said: "For it does not remain even for a moment, nor is it born as something non-valid, such that it might later function in the apprehension of an object like the sense organs and so forth."
Thus,
because cognition is unitary, there is a contradiction with the accepted doctrine of the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

as well as a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for when one reflects upon various objects superimposed in immediate succession, cognitions characterized by arising and passing away are experienced with extreme clarity.
But Kumārila, seeing no such mass of contradictions at all, says: "And because cognitions, like the person, have consciousness as their inherent nature," and so forth.
Eternity, unity, and activity [belong] to both; if there is difference, it has its locus in the objects.

(242) Eternity, unity, and activity belong to the cognitions and the Person. Why? Because of their nature as consciousness—that is to say, according to our view, because the Person has the nature of consciousness characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*). If so, how is the distinction perceived, such as "the cognition of color" or "the cognition of taste"? To this he says: "If there is difference, it has its locus in the objects."
The word "cet" (if) is used to concede the opponent's position;
the meaning is: "if it is postulated in this way.
It might be argued: "If cognition is eternal and unitary, then why does it apprehend form and other objects sequentially?

It should rather apprehend them all at once, since there is no difference [in its nature]. To this he says: "By its own nature," and so forth; "just as fire is eternally characterized by the property of burning."
Fire burns only that which is brought near to it as fuel, and nothing else; nor does it burn anything at all times.
Just as fire, though its nature is eternally to burn, does not burn everything at every moment—what then? It burns only what is "brought near," meaning what is presented to it;
and even there, it burns only that which is fit to be burned (dāhya), such as wood, and not things like clouds. Therefore, he specifies "that which is fit to be burned."
With the words "Or as," and so forth, he states another example: "Or as a mirror is clear, or as a crystal stone is."
Whatever is placed there, it assumes the reflection of that;
in the same way, the souls, which are eternally conscious, assume the functions of the body and perceive forms and other objects brought to them by the instruments— this, O wise one, is our view.
Because that which is impure lacks the capacity for receiving a reflection, it is described as "clear";
the term *ādhīyate* means "is brought near" (*ḍhaukyate*).
The phrase "in the same way" indicates the application of the illustration:

although individual souls (*puruṣas*) are all-pervading, nevertheless, by the power of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), they reside only within the body and perceive objects brought to them by the instruments such as the eyes; they do not perceive elsewhere.
Furthermore, that which is this eternal consciousness is our *dhī*—that is, *buddhi* (intellect); it is not a *buddhi* distinct from that [consciousness] as it is for the Sāṅkhyas.

Anticipating the objection, "If this is so, how is it well-known that this cognition is momentary (bhaṅginī)? he demonstrates the very reason indicated by the words beginning with "by that" (*tena*), thereby establishing the momentariness of cognition.

Therefore, because the activity of the bringers [of objects] is perishable, cognition is observed to be perishable, just as fire, though eternally a burner, does not burn in the absence of combustible fuel.

(246) The "bringers" are the eyes and other [senses], which cause the objects such as form and so forth to reach [the senses]. Their "activity" is their operation; because that is perishable—that is, subject to destruction—the cognition is characterized as being perishable.

"But if that [cognition] is not perishable by itself, then if it is not perishable by itself, it would perceive every object; thus the objection remains exactly as before. To this he says: "It is not eternally a burner," and so forth.
Likewise, cognition does not eternally perceive every object, because at all times not every object is present; such is the meaning.
Now, as to how its permanence is understood, he says: "In that regard," and so forth: "In that case, cognition is recognized as being of the nature of awareness."
The status of cognitions such as those of a jar or an elephant is accepted by the world as being distinct based on their differences;
in this context, the phrase "in that regard" introduces the statement:
because it is recognized as "cognition, cognition" through its nature as consciousness, cognition is eternal, just like sound.

If this is so, how is it that this distinction between cognitions—such as "this is the cognition of a jar" and "this is the cognition of a cloth"—is accepted by perceivers in the world? To this he says: "The jar," and so forth;
"due to their difference" means due to the difference between the jar, the elephant, and so on.
With the words "That very [intellect]," and so forth, he clarifies this very point:
"That very [intellect] is not what is called 'buddhi' by those who follow the distinctions among objects."
And there is no non-recognition [of the object] when a distinction between objects is not resorted to as a means.
(248) "By those who follow the distinction between objects" refers to the cognizers.
By means of this positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), he demonstrates that the difference in cognition is caused solely by the difference in the object;
and as for the phrase "there is no non-recognition," it means that recognition certainly does exist.
He replies with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely):
"But surely, on a ground devoid of elephants and so forth, for one who imposes [such a notion]..."

If the distinctions among cognitions arise solely from the distinction of objects, then what would be the basis for the distinction among those cognitions that occur when one sequentially superimposes elephants, horses, and so forth upon a ground devoid of them? What basis for the determination of distinction could be perceived therein?
The meaning is that there is no basis whatsoever for establishing such a distinction.
For instance: there is no difference among all cognitions *per se*, because their unity is admitted;
nor [is there difference] due to the multiplicity of objects serving as adjuncts (*upadhāna*), because in that case there exists no object whatsoever that could serve as such an adjunct.

It might be argued: "The claim that [consciousness] is devoid of an object is unproven; for it has been stated by Kumārila: 'In cognitions such as dreams, an external object is certainly not denied in every respect;
rather, in all cases, there is an external objective support (*ālambana*), though its nature is altered in terms of place and time.'"
Thus, he raises this doubt: "If individuals existing in other places and so forth," and so on.
"If individuals existing in other places and so forth are the basis, then because the object of apprehension everywhere consists of a different place, time, and nature. (250)
The term *nibandhana* means the cause for the determination of the distinctions of cognition.

It is described as such because its nature (*ātman*) is otherwise—that is, of a different kind—regarding space and time; or, according to the analysis of the compound, it is that whose nature is otherwise than [the nature of] space and time.
He answers with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely):
"But surely, their connection with that place does not exist in that manner."
Why do they appear there in that form?

For those individuals (*vyakti*) which were superimposed in a certain place and in a certain sequence appear at that time with that spatial location; however, for those [individuals] situated in other places and other times, such a connection with that [original] place and sequence does not exist at all. Why, then, do they appear in that form superimposed by one's own will rather than appearing in some other form?
Indeed, it is not logical for one thing to appear in the form of another, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For in this way, it would follow that all cognition has everything as its object;
consequently, the established order of specific objects would be utterly destroyed.
For in your view, the form does not belong to the cognition; rather, it is described as being external.
Furthermore, the elephant, the staff, and so forth do not exist in the specific location intended [by the cognition].
Moreover, in your Mīmāṃsaka view, that form which appears does not belong to the cognition, but is instead described as having the nature of an external object.

Regarding the statement that "the external object possesses form while cognition is formless," if this is indeed the case, [the author] asks, "What follows from that? and says: "Not intended," and so forth;
"intended" refers to the location where its superimposition was made.
Furthermore, those elephants and other objects, being connected to specific places and times, would appear only as connected to those very places;
why then do they appear in other places and at other times when they are absent from their own?

Therefore, it is established that these cognitions are indeed without external support (*nirālambana*), because in ultimate reality they possess unmixed natures and are mobile in nature, owing to their occasional occurrence.

And since it is established that the person (*puruṣa*), whose nature is that [of consciousness], is impermanent and manifold, the following might be thought: "Cognition is an attribute (*dharma*) of that person; therefore, even though there is a distinction in that [attribute], there is no distinction in the person, because the person is the substratum (*dharmin*).
This is incorrect.
Pratyaya, consciousness (caitanya), intellect (buddhi), and knowledge (jñāna) are not different in meaning;
for the nature of things does not change merely by a difference in names.
Furthermore, even though they have different names, it is indeed accepted that these cognitions possess a single, underlying form consisting of consciousness.
And since that consciousness is non-different, there must likewise be no division among the cognitions, which have that very nature as their essence;
for otherwise, due to the imposition of contradictory attributes, there would necessarily be absolute difference.
By this very demonstration that cognitions are without an external object, the non-perceptibility of cognition is refuted.

For instance—it has been established that this manifesting form is not something external, such as an elephant; therefore, cognitions, which apprehend that manifesting form as being identical with themselves, are established as being self-cognizing because they are of the nature of self-luminosity. Furthermore, regarding what was stated—"just as fire [is known] by its own nature," etc.—he says "sarvārtha... and so forth, adding further support right here in order to refute that argument.
And if cognition, whose nature is the awareness of all objects, were always present,
then why is there not a constant perception of everything?
(253) If cognition were always established as having the nature of the awareness of all objects, then it would follow that there must be knowledge of all objects at all times.
To the question "How so?", he says: "That cognition which has sound as its adjunct," and so forth;
[this refers to] that cognition which has taste, color, and so on as its object, [and] which has sound as its adjunct.
"It is that very same [cognition]," if you say this, then the distinctions [between objects] have been established by you yourself.
