For instance: the cognition which has sound as its adjunct—that is, which has sound as its object—is the very same [cognition] that has taste, color, and so forth as its objects, and not another. Consequently, at the time of experiencing one object, there would follow the undesirable consequence of experiencing all objects, because the cognition whose nature is the apprehension of those [objects] is always present. As it has been said: "If multiple things were known by a single [cognition], then that [cognition] would perceive them all simultaneously."
"Because there would be no distinction, let it not be even in succession; for that [distinction] would likewise be absent"—
this is what is meant by "if not."

If it is not admitted that the very cognition which has sound as its adjunct is itself the one whose object is taste and so forth, then in that case, you yourself have established by your own words the difference between cognitions (254).
Furthermore, demonstrating that this example of fire is also unestablished, he says: "samasta... and so forth.
Even fire, which has burning as its nature, does not eternally burn all combustible forms; otherwise, everything would be reduced to ashes without exception.

(255) For fire, whose nature is to burn all combustible things, does not remain eternally present; otherwise, the entire mass of combustibles would be reduced to ashes, because its own power to burn—just like the combustible matter already in contact with the flames of fire—would be perpetually proximate.
By the word "also" (api), he shows that it is not only the case that cognition does not have the nature of perceiving all objects;
[he asks] if fire is thus not eternally of the nature of burning, how then could it burn an object even when brought near? To this he says: "In the presence of the object to be burned," and so forth.
It is logical that its nature as a burner of that [object] exists only when the object to be burned is present; for otherwise, the burning of all objects would occur simultaneously.
(256) "Thus" means...
If the meaning just stated were accepted, the burning of all objects would not result simultaneously— meaning it would not follow as a consequence. 156
Furthermore, regarding what was said— "Just as in the case of a mirror," and so forth—
he says [verse 156] to show that even this is not tenable, given that the mirror and other such things possess a permanent and uniform nature.
He says: "Due to the connection with the blue lotus and so forth," etc.;
that is, due to the connection with the blue lotus and so forth, mirrors, crystals, and the like [assume their colors].
These [atoms], which are the causes for the production of the illusion of its shadow, are subject to momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅgin).

Since it is a single entity existing in states both with and without an adjunct (sopadhāna), it would always be seen either possessing that shadow or devoid of it; otherwise, it could not be so. || 257–258 ||

A crystal, a mirror, and the like, being subject to destruction at every moment, exercise a dominant influence (*ādhipatya*) in the production of erroneous cognitions through contact with blue lotuses and other objects; otherwise—if they were non-momentary and could cast a reflection—then that very same entity which exists in the state of having an adjunct would remain in the state of lacking an adjunct. Consequently, even when separated from an adjunct such as a blue object, it would still be perceived as having the reflection of blue and so forth, because it has not abandoned its prior nature;
or else, even while in the state of having an adjunct, it would be seen devoid of the form of blue and so forth, since there is no difference from its prior nature.
By this, the apprehension of reflections by all things whatsoever— such as crystals, mirrors, and the like— is generally refuted under the non-momentary (akṣaṇika) position.
Now, he refutes the perception of a reflection according to each of the two positions—that it is momentary or non-momentary—beginning with "Because of stability," and so forth:
"Because of its stability, because of its indivisibility, and because material objects cannot coexist, the surface of a mirror never bears a reflection. (259)
Because of its stability—that is, because it is not momentary—the surface of the mirror bears the prior reflection; this is the connection.
Even if it were momentary, one must understand that it does not bear [the reflection] because it lacks internal divisions.

For instance, a reflection is perceived as being situated within the surface of the mirror, like water inside a well; yet there is no division or cavity in the mirror's surface, owing to the extremely dense arrangement of its constituent parts. Therefore, this is an illusion.
Alternatively— the cause here for the state of being indivisible and the absence of difference between the prior and subsequent states is its stability;
by this, the following meaning is established.
Because it is partless due to its stability— the meaning being that it is devoid of prior and subsequent states—
and furthermore, because corporeal objects cannot coexist in the same place, it follows that the surface of a mirror does not actually bear a reflection; for indeed,

reflections of mountains and the like are perceived on the mirror's surface as occupying that very same space, yet corporeal entities never attain the state of occupying a single location, as that would entail the consequence of their identity.
And this is a refutation common to both the positions of momentariness and non-momentariness.
[The author] demonstrates that even for a crystal, there is no actual apprehension of the reflection of an adjunct in reality, by means of the verse beginning with "pārśva" and so forth.

Furthermore, those situated on both sides perceive the crystal stone as perfectly white; thus, even this [crystal] has not acquired the shadow [of redness]. For instance: at the very moment the observer standing in front perceives the crystal as red due to contact with a *japā* flower, those situated on both sides perceive the entire crystal stone as perfectly white, and not in parts.

Furthermore, if there were a cognition of a shadow, then, just as in the case of a person standing in front, there would also have been a cognition appearing red for the two persons standing on either side;
and this is a defect common to both the positions of momentariness and non-momentariness.
With the words "there would be difference with each substrate" and so forth, he states the fault specifically in the case of non-momentariness:
"Difference with each substrate would follow for the crystal and so on, if its apprehension of their reflection were real. (261)

For if, in an ultimate sense, there were a cognition of the coloring by an adjunct (upadhāna) in the case of a crystal and the like, then—just as the various reflections produced by successive adjuncts would not possess a single nature due to the difference in their own natures—likewise, a differentiation of the crystal itself would follow with respect to each and every adjunct.
However, if it is admitted that this is an illusion, then this fault does not arise; it is for the purpose of making this known that he says "real" (tātvikī).
Therefore, this is an illusion regarding those [entities] which possess diverse and inconceivable powers;
and since, in both cases, the apprehension of a reflection is not tenable, it is established that this is an illusion.

If this is so, why does that illusion occur only in the case of crystal and the like, and not in the case of a wall and so forth? To this he says: "In those possessing diverse and inconceivable powers.
"Diverse" means of various kinds; "inconceivable" refers to those things which possess such powers.
Indeed, the specific determination of the powers of entities does not admit of questioning, because it is produced by their own successive chain of causes.
Furthermore, you yourselves have no dispute on this point, as it has been said: "Fire burns, but space does not; who here could be questioned about this?"

If this is so, then even in the case of cognition (*buddhi*), let the apprehension of the reflection of an object be merely an error; let there not be an actual apprehension of a reflection. To this he says:
"In cognition, even the existence of error is not tenable, because of the absence of differentiation. (262) The existence of error in cognition is not tenable.
The word "also" implies that not only is the apprehension of a reflection untenable;
why? Because of the absence of difference—that is, due to the lack of distinction.

For an illusion is possible in the case of crystals and the like, because an illusory cognition can arise as something distinct from them; however, there is no such other cognition in the form of an illusion within cognition itself, since cognition is held to be unitary.
Nor is it reasonable to say that cognition arises as something inherently delusive in nature, because you accept the eternity of the intellect (*buddhi*).

Furthermore, regarding the statement made there—that "the intellect is recognized through its nature as consciousness" (*bodhātmakatva*)—in order to prove its unity and eternity, he says: "But [cognition] which has a distinction consisting of non-consciousness," and so forth.
However, by superimposing a common difference from the nature of non-cognition upon all cognitions,

recognition proceeds even though there is multiplicity. This recognition is inconclusive, because it is not contradictory for recognition to proceed among all cognitions despite their multiplicity, once one has superimposed— i.e., attributed— the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) from objects such as jars, which are of the nature of non-cognition.

This must necessarily be understood: that this recognition is produced based on the exclusion of heterogeneous things (*vijātīya-vyāvṛtti*) only when there is indeed multiplicity (*nānātva*), and not when there is non-multiplicity.

For instance, in the case of superimposed cognitions (*samāropa-buddhi*) which are without a real objective basis (*nirālambana*), recognition does not occur even though no difference in objects is relied upon; for it does not happen there that "the very cognition that was of an elephant is the same as the cognition of a horse or a chariot.
Furthermore, the fact that these cognitions lack an objective basis has already been established and need not be stated again.
Therefore, what was stated— that "there is no non-recognition when a difference in objects is not admitted"— must be understood as unproven.
Furthermore, if you maintain that the self is eternal and of a single nature, then a distinction between states such as pleasure and so forth would not be possible.
Now, if a distinction between states such as pleasure and so forth is admitted, then its being eternal and of a single uniform nature must not be admitted;
for it is not logical that a single entity should possess two mutually contradictory natures, namely difference and non-difference.
Introducing the refutation of what was stated by Kumārila in order to answer this objection, he says: "By means of the distinction between the differences of states," and so forth.

Even though the void and the non-void are established as being absolutely situated within a stable self through the distinction of different states, that which is imagined by others [is not found there]. (264) "Of the states"—meaning pleasure and so forth; "distinction"—meaning their multiplicity; "through that, the distinction"—meaning the very multiplicity of the person; "void of that."
The meaning is that even though there is a plurality of states, it possesses but a single intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
He states the reason for this: "in that which has a stable self" (*sthirātmani*).
"Stable" (*sthira*) means eternal (*nitya*); "self" (*ātman*) means intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); that whose self is thus [described] is called "that which has a stable self."

Alternatively, "distinctions of state" refers to specific states such as pleasure and so forth; "absolute difference" from them means a separate existence. The meaning is that [the self] is devoid of that [difference], even though it is not distinct from it.
To the question, "What is it that is thus conceptualized? he says: "pleasure," and so forth.
Even while passing through states such as pleasure and pain, a person never abandons my nature consisting of consciousness, substance, existence, and so forth.
(265) "Even while passing" means...
Even while practicing,
the person is the self.

By the word "existence" (*sattva*) and so forth, there is the inclusion of general properties such as knowability (*jñeyatva*), cognizability (*prameyatva*), agency (*kartṛtva*), and enjoyership (*bhoktṛtva*).
Furthermore, showing that there is no absolute eradication even of specific properties (*viśeṣadharma*), he says: "And not... and so forth.

And upon the arising of another state, the preceding one does not perish utterly; rather, it dissolves into the universal essence (sāmānyātman) for the sake of conforming to the subsequent state. (266) "The preceding," etc.

If this is the case regarding states such as pleasure, one might ask: why is the state of suffering not perceived even during a state of pleasure? To this he says: "For the sake of conforming to what follows," and so forth.

For while the state of pleasure remains in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), the subsequent state of suffering does not arise; therefore, that [state of pleasure], dissolving into the universal self—which permeates all states and is characterized by consciousness, substantiality, and so on—becomes conducive to the arising of the subsequent state of suffering. It is for that purpose that it dissolves therein.

Anticipating the objection that, "If this is so, then just as in the case of different states, it is illogical for the states to dissolve even into the nature of the universal because of contradiction," he says: "For by their own nature... and so forth;
"for there is mutual contradiction among the states by their very nature."
But that which is non-contradictory in all states is perceived as the universal self.

(267) Since the various states, in their own forms such as pleasure and so forth, are mutually contradictory, their dissolution into one another is not logical; however, what contradiction could there be in their dissolution into the universal self, which is a different state, such that it would not exist therein? For this universal self is seen to be non-contradictory and persistent across all states, since consciousness and the like are perceived in every state.
He offers a rebuttal with the words beginning "In that case," etc.:
"In that case, if there were not an absolute difference between the states..."
If there were absolute difference [of the states] from the person, then upon their destruction and origination, those two [destruction and origination] would likewise belong to him as well.

(268) For if an absolute difference of the states from the person is not admitted, then upon their destruction and origination—that is, when the destruction and origination of those states occur—those two, destruction and origination, would also belong to this person absolutely.
The statement [is made] for the purpose of making it known that if there is no distinction whatsoever, the consequence of arising and passing away, just like the states, is unavoidable.

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: whatever is non-different from something else undergoes production and destruction when that [other thing] undergoes production and destruction; for example, the essential nature of those very things such as pleasure.
And the Person (puruṣa) has a nature non-different from pleasure and the rest. This is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).

And showing that this reason is not inconclusive (anaikāntika), he says: "But when there is a conjunction of contradictory properties, there would be an absolute difference, as among men, because each is restricted by its own individual nature. (269)

If it is accepted that origination and destruction belong only to the states (*avasthā*) and not to the person (*puruṣa*), such that a conjunction of contradictory properties characterized by origination and non-origination is admitted, then the consequence of difference (*bheda*) follows. The sense is this: just as among many persons there is mutual difference due to their own respective, fixed natures—each determined individually—and because the conventional usage of "difference" is based solely on this much; for even among persons, there is no mutual difference in terms of being a "real entity" (*vastu*) and so forth. Therefore, the phrase "determined individually" (*pratisvaṃ niyatena*) was stated in order to avoid the fallacy of the example being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).

The form restricted to each individual self (*pratyātmaniyata-rūpa*) is absolutely distinct [in each case]; otherwise, due to the absence of specific determination in experience, memory, and so forth, there would be a confusion of established order.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not share the same acquisition and preservation (*ekayogakṣema*) cannot be non-different from that; for example, persons are mutually distinct by virtue of their forms restricted to each individual self, and the states of pleasure and so forth do not share the same acquisition and preservation as the person. This is because of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Regarding what was said— that "this [entity] does not perish absolutely when another state arises"— he says in response: "If, for you, the states dissolve into the person by their very own nature," and so forth.
Even suffering and so forth would be experienced when pleasure and so forth arise.
(270) For the various states, in dissolving into the universal self, must dissolve either by way of their own nature or by way of another's nature.

If the first alternative is held, then even upon the arising of pleasure—that is, even during the experience of a state of pleasure—that suffering would also be experienced, because it has reached the conditions for perception.

Now, regarding the position that [the cognition occurs] "by means of another form," he says: "And not" (na ca), etc.—and when there is a transition into another form, a transition into something else is impossible.

And if there were a transference by way of identity (tādātmya), then the self would be subject to arising. Furthermore, the transference of pleasure and so forth into the person is held to occur precisely through identity;
consequently, because it is non-different from them—just like pain and so forth—the self, that is, the person, would be subject to arising, meaning it would be something produced.
Regarding what was said— "Agency and enjoyment do not depend upon a state [of the self]"— he says "If," and so forth:
"If agency and enjoyment did not indeed depend upon a state..."
Because it remains in that same state, agency and so forth are impossible [for the Self].
(272) For if agency and the rest were dependent upon the person alone, they could not belong to a Self that has not abandoned its prior nature.

The formal argument is as follows: whatever does not abandon the state of being neither an agent nor an enjoyer does not act, nor does it experience—as is the case with space; and the person is always such that it does not abandon the state of being neither an agent nor an enjoyer. This is an observation of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Regarding what was stated by the venerable teacher Diṅnāga—"If there is modification in a person at the time of the arising of cognition, then there is impermanence; but if there is no modification, then it is not tenable that the so-called self is the cognizer"—Kumārila replied to this: "It is not denied that the self is denotable by the word 'impermanent'."
Because it expresses merely the state of undergoing modification (*vikriyā*), that [text] displays this error as *ttvāttadvyu tve* [sic]. For there is no annihilation of this [self] by that much.
Thus, under the guise of a conclusion, he states the fault: "That," and so forth;
that which is denoted by the word "eternal" is not denied of the self.

Because it possesses modification of its own nature, its discontinuity exists. (273) "That"—therefore, we do not deny that [consciousness] is denotable by the word "eternal," because consciousness, preceded by its own material cause and perishing at every moment, continues without interruption throughout the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

However, because its own nature—that is, its essential character—is subject to modification, meaning it necessarily abandons its previous nature and a different nature emerges, its discontinuity—that is, its destruction—is most clearly established.
Furthermore, demonstrating that even the example of the serpent and so forth that was cited does not establish a permanent, unitary nature, he says: "The serpent also," and so on;
"the serpent also, because of its momentary disintegration, undergoes states such as coiling."
But in the case of a stable form, there can be no connection with a different state, as in the case of a person.

For just as it is not logical for a change of state to occur in a person because of his stable and uniform nature, so too it would not be logical for a snake either; however, if this [snake] were subject to momentary destruction, then the occurrence of a different state would be logical, since the manifestation of a different state is characterized by the arising of a different intrinsic nature (svabhāva).
Regarding what was stated—that the cognition "I know" refers to a knower—that is unproven; demonstrating this, he says: "This ego-sense proceeds without any objective support," and so forth.
This ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) indeed functions without any objective support.
Indeed, due to the power of the seed of the vision of sentient beings since beginningless time, [the ego-sense] occurs only in certain instances.
For this *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense) has no object of perception whatsoever from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), by which it could have a knower as its objective domain.
If this is so, what is the cause for its arising? To this he says: "Since beginningless time," and so forth.

*Sattvadṛk* means the view of a self-entity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). Its "seed" means its latent impression (*vāsanā*) or capacity; the analysis of the compound is: that which is both beginningless and the seed of the view of a self-entity. Its "power" means its sovereign influence (*ādhipatya*).
"In some cases only" means restricted solely to the six sense-bases within the internal [person].
Now, he asks why [this] does not occur everywhere, and says: "For only some," and so forth.
For only certain conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) attain sovereignty (*ādhipatya*) with respect to the determination of that form; therefore, it does not occur everywhere. || 276 ||
"Resolving that form" means resolving upon the nature of the knower which persists through prior and subsequent times; this applies to the *ahaṃkāra*,
but not everywhere.
Otherwise, this same objection would apply equally to you regarding other continua, such as jars, and even regarding the person.
Because of the existence of a distinction in that power, everything is entirely free from confusion.
Furthermore, even if the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense) has the self as its objective support, the same objection applies: why does it not function with respect to another self?

If you argue that this is not so because of the specific restriction of power (*śakti-pratiniyama*), then for us as well, due to the restriction of power, it functions only with respect to a certain internal object and not everywhere; thus, the established order remains entirely free from confusion.
It might be argued: "Let this distinction be granted; however, how is its lack of an objective basis established? To this he says: "In the case of an eternal object," and so forth;
for if the object were eternal, then all forms of ego-conception would arise from that [eternal source].
They would all arise at once, because the efficient cause is established as being present.
Even if they have impermanent objects, subsequent cognitions would then be clearly manifest; thus, they pointlessly question the existence of an external object as a support.
For its object must be either permanent or impermanent.

If it were permanent, then all instances of *ahaṅkṛti*—that is, all acts of egoism—would arise simultaneously, because their cause would be present in its entirety; for it is not logical that an object which is not a cause [of a specific cognition] should serve as its objective support, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, it has been repeatedly demonstrated that a potent cause does not require auxiliary causes.

Nor can it be said that this ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is a single entity, because its plurality is established by its occasional nature. For instance, the ego-sense is not perceived during deep sleep, intoxication, or fainting, whereas it is perceived at other times; thus, its occasional occurrence is proven by its non-perception at all other times.

Furthermore, because [the object] occurs only occasionally, its multiplicity is also established; thus, all instances of ego-grasping (*ahaṅkṛti*), which exist solely in dependence upon that [object], would arise simultaneously.

Alternatively, if the position is taken that the objective support (*ālambana*) is impermanent, then, like visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions, all instances of ego-grasping would result in being extremely vivid appearances, because they would directly apprehend the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the real entity.

Therefore—from that reason—the other non-Buddhist outsiders, such as Kumārila and others, fruitlessly interrogate its objective support, asking such things as: "What kind of object, characterized by ignorance, has been imagined for this [cognition]?

Regarding that which was stated—that this ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*) proceeds as an error, being indeed without an objective basis (*anālambana*) due to the force of the beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)—here he anticipates the objection raised by Kumārila, beginning with the words "In the knower," etc. (*jñātari* ityādi).
Recognition can produce a latent impression (vāsanā) only in the knower, not in that which is not the knower; for it [the object] is not the cause of error regarding the notion "this is that.
Therefore, if the notion of "I" were held to be an error, it would be untenable, as there is no sublation of it.

For a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is capable of producing a recognition whose object is the knower, but it cannot produce a cognition—that is, a knowledge—in which there is a notion that "he" (the knower) exists in one who is not the knower; this is the connection [of the sentence].
Why? Because such an impression is not a cause of error; rather, its meaning is that it generates a cognition whose object is precisely the thing as it was experienced, and not an erroneous one.

If it is argued that this ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*) is not logically a delusion because it arises from latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and because there is an absence of any subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), [we reply:
the word "and" (*ca*) is out of its proper order and should be understood as following immediately after the phrase "due to the avoidance of subversion" (*bādhavarjanāt*).
He replies with the words "No," and so forth, because the refutation of that [position] has been demonstrated by the reasoning just stated. || 281 ||
The reasoning just mentioned, beginning with "But in the case of the position that [the object] is eternal," etc.,

has been stated. Furthermore, regarding what was said— that "the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is not the cause of error"— he says "In the case of Īśvara and so forth," etc., demonstrating that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

How is it that various delusions regarding the causality and other attributes of Īśvara and so forth arise for devotees, given that they exist merely as latent impressions (vāsanā)? Furthermore, when the state of being without objective support (nirālambanatā) is thus established even in the case of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
Therefore, no cognizer exists that is graspable by the notion of "I.

Consequently, among all means of valid cognition, there is no supporting instance (dṛṣṭānta) that possesses established proof; and the reasons (hetus), as they have been stated according to their respective applications, are unestablished in their substratum (āśrayāsiddha).
Regarding the examination of the self as conceived by the Mīmāṃsakas:

if habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) were not the cause of error, then how could such delusions as "the Lord (*īśvara*) is the cause of all produced things," "he is omniscient," and "he is the substratum of eternal cognition" arise from the mere occurrence of habitual tendencies?
For indeed, even Kumārila has refuted that the Lord and others are the creator of the world.

And because [the self] exists as a mere latent impression (*vāsanā*), the inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding an object that is [perceived as] existing in such a way [i.e., as an external reality].
Therefore, since the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), there is no well-established knower who is its object; thus, the self is not established on that basis.
Regarding the proof of permanence that was stated, beginning with "that which is graspable by a past ego-sense," he says: "That," and so forth.

The term "anyone" refers to a cognizer who is either eternal or non-eternal; since no such subject exists in the example, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*). For instance, in the first and second syllogisms, the defect of the example is the non-establishment of the subject (*dharmin*), because there is no cognizer whatsoever—whether present or past—that is accessible through the notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*).

Regarding the third application, the example "like a single cognition" is deficient in both the probandum and the probans; for it is unestablished that the intended "single cognition" possesses the nature of an "I-notion" belonging to a cognizer connected to a single continuum, and it is also unestablished that it has a single object.
Therefore, by way of the non-establishment of these two properties, its own lack of establishment is stated.
"Adduced as appropriate" means that those reasons which were previously set forth have been adduced— i.e., introduced— as appropriate, meaning according to their possibility,
such as the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*).

For instance: the reasons presented in the first and second syllogisms are unestablished with respect to their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*), because no subject (*dharmin*) whatsoever that is apprehended by the notion of "I" as a knower is established;
however, in the third syllogism there is no unestablishedness of the substratum, because the cognitions themselves, which serve as the subjects, are established.
However, the qualification "a specific cognizer connected to a single continuum" is unestablished for them,
because the absence of an objective support (*nirālambanatva*) is well-established;
therefore, it was stated [in the verse] that this applies "as appropriate."
Thus concludes the examination of the self as conceived by the Mīmāṃsakas.
Now, for the purpose of refuting the self as conceived by the followers of Kapila, he says: "Consciousness," and so forth.

Others consider consciousness to be distinct from the nature of the intellect; they conceive of consciousness as the innate form of the self. He alone experiences the fruit brought forth by primordial matter (pradhāna).
"It has no agency at all; that [agency] is considered to belong to primordial matter (prakṛti) alone"—thus say the Sāṃkhyas. 286.
"It is other [than the self]"—so the Sāṃkhyas maintain.

For they postulate that consciousness distinct from the intellect (*buddhi*) is the innate nature of the self (*ātman*), since their doctrine holds that the intellect is of the nature of primordial matter (*pradhāna*), whereas consciousness is the very essence of the person (*puruṣa*). Furthermore,

that *puruṣa* is the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) of the fruits of auspicious and inauspicious actions brought forth by primordial matter, but not the agent (*kartṛ*) of those actions, because agency is accepted as belonging solely to primordial matter, which consists of the transformation of the entire world.

And here they provide the following proof: whatever entity is composite in nature is seen to exist for the sake of another, such as a bed and so forth; and the eye and other [faculties] are composite in nature. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
And that "other" which exists is, by implication, the self (*ātman*); thus is the position of the opponent established.
In that regard, with the words "tatrāpi" and so forth, he first refutes the meaning of the thesis.
Even in that case, how could the distinct forms of cognitions regarding color, sound, and so forth be clearly perceived if consciousness is held to be one?

For instance, by one who asserts that "consciousness is the innate nature of the person," it is effectively claimed that consciousness is eternal and of a single form, because it is non-different from the person, who is eternal and of a single form.

And this is contradicted by direct perception; for it is very clearly—and indeed most distinctly—perceived through self-awareness that the cognitions of form, sound, and so forth possess a differentiated nature, that is, distinct intrinsic characters.
And that [differentiation] would not be possible if consciousness were a single unity.

And demonstrating the contradiction with their own tenets, he says: "If consciousness were of a single form and remained constant at all times, how indeed could its state of being the enjoyer of various kinds of objects be logically possible? (288)
Furthermore, that the self is of a single form and yet the enjoyer of manifold objects is mutually contradictory,
because it is indistinguishable from the state of not being an enjoyer.
If it is argued that there is no contradiction because of the connection with the desire to see (*didṛkṣā*) and so forth, he says: "No," and so on.
Desires to see and the like, being distinct [from the Self], do not constitute the basis for its experience; for if that were the case, the person would be subject to birth. || 289 ||

If the desires to see, hear, and so forth regarding form and other objects—which are conceived as the basis for his experience—are distinct from one another, they do not belong to this Self; that is, they do not arise [as its own].

For if they were to arise, then, by virtue of their distinction and their existence—that is, their birth—the person would be subject to origination, because he would be non-different from them, just like the desire to see and the rest.
Clarifying this very point, he says: "For there exists nothing such as the desire to see that is distinct from consciousness," and so forth.
Indeed, no desire to see or the like exists apart from consciousness.
When there is the occurrence of its arising and passing away, this [transformation] is unavoidable even in the case of the Person (puruṣa).
For if there were a difference [between them], the relation expressed as "his" would be untenable,
because there would be no basis for a relationship such as "benefit."
The application [of the argument] is as follows: "This" refers to the occurrence of arising and passing away.
That for which there is no basis for establishing its existence cannot be established by a discerning person as having that nature, just as space cannot be established as possessing material form.
And there is no basis for establishing an enjoyer, such as the Puruṣa or the desire to see, because no such cause is perceived;
furthermore, it has already been demonstrated that this reason is not unestablished (asiddha).
Furthermore, he demonstrates that because agency is absent, its state of being an enjoyer is also untenable: "And auspicious and inauspicious... and so forth.
If auspicious and inauspicious karma has not been performed by the self at all, then from what source does this variety of experience arise for it? (291)
For no one experiences the fruit of an action not performed, as that would entail the logical fallacies of encountering what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and so forth.
(291) Here, the opponent anticipates an objection: "In accordance with one's desire," and so on.

If Nature bestows [the fruit] in accordance with one's desire, then this relationship between the two is established like that of the lame man and the blind man. (292) Even though the Puruṣa is not the agent of actions, nevertheless Nature brings him the object as he has desired; he enjoys that, and thus there is no fault.

Now, one might ask: since *prakṛti* is insentient, how can it be the agent of auspicious and other kinds of actions, by which it brings about for the *puruṣa* the fruits of action according to his desire? To this he says: "Like the lame and the blind," and so forth. Just as, indeed, a blind person’s engagement with objects occurs through connection with a sighted man, so too the subtle body (*liṅga*), consisting of the great principle (*mahat*) and the rest, through contact with the sentient *puruṣa*, performs determination regarding effects such as merit (*dharma*) and the like, as if it were itself sentient; thus there is no fault. And so it has been said: "For the sake of the *puruṣa*'s perception, and likewise for the sake of the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *pradhāna*."
"The union of both is like that of the lame and the blind; from that [union] arises creation" (292).
He provides a rebuttal with the words "If it be so," and so forth.

If this is so, why is it that even when there is a desire for what is wished for, it is not accomplished? For if Prakṛti were to bring about the desired fruit even of an action that has not been performed, then why would the desired object not always be achieved for every person whenever there is a wish for what is desired?
It might be thought: "Because of the absence of its cause, *dharma*, [the result] is not established. To this he says: "Nature (*prakṛti*) is not [the cause]," and so forth.

For *dharma* is the effect of nature; and since that [effect] is non-different from it, it exists at all times. Thus, the desired fruit would indeed come to be. For instance: all this is nothing other than nature and the self (*puruṣa*), and these two are always in close proximity.
Therefore, the fruit would have to be eternal;
moreover, if Nature bestows whatever object is desired, then why would it bestow what is undesirable? For no one ever desires what is undesirable.

Moreover, even if it were the case that primordial nature (prakṛti) brings objects to him, nevertheless his state of being an enjoyer is untenable because he is changeless; this is shown in the passage beginning with "And at the time of enjoying objects," etc., which means:
"And if, at the time of enjoying objects, there is no modification (vikriyā) in him..."
It could not possibly be an enjoyer, nor would nature be its benefactor.
Furthermore, if modification were to exist, its eternity would be lost;
for modification is indeed a change of state, and how could that occur while its essential condition remains the same?

For if [the Self] were not brought into a modification consisting of joy, distress, and so forth by means of pleasure, pain, and the like, then it would be a non-enjoyer just like space, and Nature (prakṛti) would not be its benefactor; such is the connection [of the argument],
because it is impossible to effect a benefit upon an unchanging Self.
Now, if its state of being subject to modification is admitted, then there follows the undesirable consequence of the loss of its permanence;
for we define impermanence as precisely this lack of stability in one's own state,
and since that exists when there is modification, how could it possess permanence?
Because eternity consists in remaining in that same state.

With the words "It might be thought" (*syānmatam*) and so forth, he raises another objection regarding the nature of the enjoyer according to the view of others: "It might be thought that first the intellect (*buddhi*), assuming the form of the object, undergoes transformation (*vivartate*); and the person (*puruṣa*) perceives the object as determined by that [intellect]. (296)
And thus, by way of the arising of a reflection, this [Puruṣa] possesses the state of being an enjoyer;

yet this Puruṣa never abandons his own essential nature (svarūpa). For his state of being an enjoyer is not accepted as resulting from undergoing modification; rather, it occurs through the principle of the arising of a reflection of the object determined by the intellect (buddhi).

For instance—the reflection of an object mounted upon the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*) is transferred to the *puruṣa*, who is like a second mirror; that alone constitutes his state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), but not the occurrence of any modification (*vikāra*).

Nor does the *puruṣa* abandon its own nature even when there is a mere transfer of a reflection, because, like a mirror, it remains in its original condition. Therefore, in the argument "that which is indistinguishable from its non-enjoying state [is] non-enjoying," the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said," and so forth.

It is said: If the reflection arises through identity (*tādātmya*) [with the Puruṣa], then it follows that the Puruṣa itself possesses the quality of arising and passing away; however, if there is a difference, then there is no state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*).

(298) If it is maintained that the reflection of the object mounted upon the mirror of the intellect (*buddhi*) is transferred into the Puruṣa, who is like a second mirror, then if that reflection were non-different from the Puruṣa, it would follow—just as was stated immediately above—that the Puruṣa itself possesses the quality of arising and passing away.
Because it is non-different from that which possesses the nature of a reflection associated with arising and passing away;
if, on the other hand, the position is that it is different, then the status of being an enjoyer does not obtain, because there would be no distinction whatsoever from its state as a non-enjoyer.

Nor is it logical for the person's status as an enjoyer to arise from a connection with the reflection of the object, since a connection cannot be established between two things that do not mutually benefit one another.

Primordial matter (pradhāna) proceeds toward activity in accordance with the desire to see [the Puruṣa] and other such factors; otherwise, how could that which is insentient by nature produce such a variety of diverse arrangements?

Furthermore, if the Pradhāna were to know the desire to see [the Puruṣa] and so forth on the part of the Puruṣa, then its activity toward the goal of that Puruṣa would be appropriate as a form of compliance; however, because it is insentient in nature, even though there is a connection with the sentient being—like the case of the lame man and the blind man—such activity is not logical. For instance, although the blind man may not perceive the path, he certainly perceives the intention of the lame man because he possesses sentience; yet the Pradhāna does not know the desire to see and so forth of the Puruṣa, because, being composed of non-sentience, it is insentient in nature.
Furthermore, since those two do not assist one another, there is no relationship between them— like that of a cripple and a blind man—
such that the *pradhāna* could indeed bring about the manifestation of the *vyañjana* and so forth.
And it does not know how to enjoy; what could be more improper than this?
Now, if it is maintained that the Pradhāna knows the Puruṣa’s desire to see and so forth, then, that being the case, the status of being an enjoyer would also follow for the Puruṣa.
For how could one who indeed knows how to act not also know how to enjoy?

Therefore, what could be more improper than to say that he knows how to act but does not know how to enjoy? The meaning is that there is nothing at all [improper in this]; for surely a cook, the maker of condiments and such, does not fail to know how to eat them.
The word "iti" is to be supplied here;
with the words "because of being intelligent," etc., he anticipates the opponent's reply.

If it is argued that because the *pradhāna* possesses intelligence (*buddhimattva*), everything is consistent for it, then by virtue of that very intelligence, it would follow that it possesses consciousness (*caitanya*), just as it does in the case of the *puruṣas*.
For intelligence is indeed determination (*adhyavasāya*), as well as cognition (*saṃvit*) and the act of perceiving (*saṃvedana*).
"Consciousness" (saṃvitti) and "volition" (cetanā)— all these are synonyms for sentience (caitanya).
The word "all" refers to the engagement [of the senses] in accordance with the desire to see and so forth.
This refers to the Pradhāna;

the meaning is as follows: even if the Pradhāna is not of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), nevertheless, because it is endowed with the intellect (*buddhi*) characterized by determination (*adhyavasāya*), it will proceed after having fully understood the desire to see (*didṛkṣā*) and other states residing in the Puruṣa; therefore, everything is consistent.
To this, he states the following reply: "By being endowed with intelligence," and so forth.

For if the Pradhāna were admitted to possess intelligence, then it would follow that it possesses consciousness (*caitanya*), just like the Puruṣa, because terms such as "intellect" (*buddhi*) and the like are synonymous with "consciousness."

For instance—that which, by its nature as light, is self-cognized and shines forth independently of anything else is called consciousness (*caitanya*). Since that essence exists even in the intellect (*buddhi*), why should the intellect not be of the nature of consciousness?
Nor do we perceive any other form of consciousness apart from the intellect, by means of which the existence of a *puruṣa* distinct from it could be established.
Here, in order to establish the difference between consciousness (*cit*) and the intellect (*buddhi*), he says: "The intellect is insentient by nature," and so forth.

If it is held that the intellect (*buddhi*) is insentient by nature, like sound, smell, taste, and so forth, on the grounds of the reasons of having an origin and being subject to destruction; the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever possesses properties such as having an origin and being subject to destruction is insentient, just like taste and the rest; and the intellect is likewise [subject to these properties]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
He replies with the verse beginning "Not these two," etc.:
"These two reasons are not established for both [parties] when an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*) is intended."
There is no sublation by the opposite [thesis] even when a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) is intended to be stated.
(304) This might sometimes be an independent proof or a *prasaṅga*-proof;
if it were an independent proof, then the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished for one of the two parties.

For instance: the kind of "possessing an origin" characterized by the production of what was previously non-existent, or the kind of "perishability" consisting of absolute annihilation, which is well-known to the Buddhist, is not accepted by you, the Sāṅkhya, because you maintain that those two consist respectively of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and concealment (*tirodhāna*); and the kind [of these properties] accepted by you is not established for the Buddhist. Thus, the reason is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*).

Nor is the reason established merely by the establishment of the word; for the establishment of a real entity follows from the establishment of a real entity, since only a real entity can serve as a reason.

As it has been said: "Even when there is non-deviation in the word, the means of proof should be known as defective if there is deviation in the [real] object itself, because the establishment of a real entity [depends on] the real entity."
Thus,

even if the position is that this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum), the two reasons remain inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been presented against the opposite of the probandum (*sādhya-viparyaya*).
For what necessary connection (*pratibandha*) exists here such that consciousness (*caitanya*) must not possess the properties of being produced (*utpattimattva*) and being perishable (*nāśitva*)?
Furthermore, this conception— that the activity of the Pradhāna is for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa, just as the activity of insentient milk is for the sake of the growth of the calf—
is itself merely a false conception.
For milk does not proceed independently as the cause for the growth of the calf;
rather, it arises from its own specific causes and conditions that occur at particular times.
Once produced, it becomes the cause for the calf’s growth; thus, it is described as "proceeding" even though it is insentient.
Furthermore, such an activity of the *pradhāna* is not logical;

for instance, because it is eternal and lacks any other cause, its occasional power cannot depend on the occasional proximity of other causes, nor can it be inherent. For if it were inherent, since the complete causes would always be present, there would follow the absurd consequence that all human goals—characterized by worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*)—would arise simultaneously.

304. Furthermore, it might be argued: "Let there be non-difference between cognition and consciousness; nevertheless, its status as the self remains unrefuted. To this he says: "In consciousness," and so forth.
Even if the word "self" is applied to consciousness, there is no harm to our position.
Its permanence is difficult to establish, because the sense organs and so forth possess efficacy;
for if consciousness were eternal, the sense organs and their objects would be fruitless.
If fire were eternal, there would be no need for fuel. (205–206)

For we do not deny consciousness itself merely by applying the word "self" (ātman) to it; what then? That superimposed property characterized as permanence which is attributed to it is what is denied.
Why? Because of the efficacy of the eyes, light, mental attention, and so forth;
otherwise, if consciousness were eternal and permanent, then the eyes and other such factors would be rendered useless.
Since those [scriptures] have the purpose of producing that [knowledge],
and since production is impossible for that which is eternal, he provides an illustration for this very point, beginning with the words "it would not exist," and so forth.
If fire were eternal, then people would never take up fuel for the sake of fire; therefore, it is not logical that consciousness is of a single, unchanging nature. 305–306.
Regarding the statement that "whatever is composite matter is seen to be for the sake of another," and so forth—
he says "pārārthya" (being for the sake of another) and so on, while investigating what this "other" intended therein is,
as he further explains the fact that the eyes and other [senses] are for the sake of another.
If it is argued that, by the reason of being an aggregate— just like a bed, a seat, and so forth—
these [atoms] possess the quality of having something to which excellence is imparted, then this is a proof of what we already accept; for we maintain that they are benefactors of cognition.
In proving that [the atoms] are benefactors despite being unchanging, the example would be devoid of the probandum, since only things that are mobile can be benefactors.
However, if their "being for the sake of another" is being established in a general sense, [then there is no fault].

"Nevertheless, the proof is futile, for [the self] is already established as being useful to the mind. (310) Thus ends the examination of the self as conceived by the followers of Kapila. There are three possible alternatives: either the "other" intended is one to whom an excellence can be imparted (*ādheyātiśaya*); or, because its nature is such that no excellence can be imparted, it is immutable (*avikārī*); or else, what is being proved is merely the state of being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) in a general sense, which is charming only so long as it is not scrutinized. These are the three options.

In that regard, in the first position, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because we ourselves accept that the eyes and so forth are assistants to consciousness, according to the scriptural statement: "Dependent upon the eye and forms, visual consciousness arises," up to "dependent upon the body and tangibles, tactile consciousness arises.
Now, showing that in the second position the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddhatā*), he says: "Because they assist without being modified," and so forth.

"Benefiting an unchanging eternal entity" means benefiting that which is unchangeable. Since the eyes and other organs are established as such [benefactors], the reason is contradictory because it is pervaded by the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) in the example; for those things, such as beds and so forth, are logically beneficial only to something mobile and impermanent, since it is impossible to produce an excellence (*atiśaya*) in that which is unchanging. Now, if the third position is taken—that setting aside the alternatives regarding whether an excellence is produced or not, one merely proves "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*) in general—then even in that case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the eyes and other organs are accepted as being beneficial to the mind.

Now, even if the mind (*citta*) is accepted as the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), as it is accepted by the Naiyāyikas, even so, your desired conclusion is not established, because you do not accept a self (*ātman*) distinct from the mind;
nor is the intended object of the Naiyāyikas established, because they accept that the eyes and other sense organs possess "benefiting others" (*paropakāritva*) by virtue of their mutual assistance.

Since "otherness" (*paratva*) is relative—just like the concepts of "this shore" and "the other shore"—and since the mind arises by receiving assistance produced by multiple causes, its nature as a composite (*saṃghātatva*) is indeed established as a conceptual construct; therefore, the reason [adduced] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Thus concludes the examination of the self as conceived by the followers of Kapila.
Now, for the purpose of refuting the self as conceived by the Digambaras, he says: "Like the Jaiminīyas," and so forth.
Like the Jaiminīyas, the Jainas assert that the person (*nara*) is characterized by consciousness (*cillakṣaṇa*),
consisting of both substance (*dravya*) and modification (*paryāya*), and having the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anugama*).
(311) "The Jainas" refers to...
The Digambaras speak thus:

the self is characterized by consciousness; and because it is non-different in its substantial form (*dravya-rūpa*) across all states, it is of the nature of persistence (*anugama*); whereas because it is different in each state in its modal form (*paryāya-rūpa*), it is of the nature of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
This twofold nature of the self is established through direct perception itself, and thus need not be proven by any other means of valid cognition.

For instance—the opponent's position is as follows: even amidst the differences in states such as pleasure and so forth, that which persists as the substratum throughout all states and is perceived as consciousness is the substance (*dravya*);
whereas the various successive states, such as pleasure and so forth, are the modes (*paryāya*), and these are established by direct perception itself.
To this, he replies with the verse beginning "tatrāpi" and so forth:
"In that case as well, if the unmodified substance were conjoined with its modifications..."

"There is no distinction in it; therefore, it would not be subject to transformation" (312). Herein there are two positions: either that substance whose nature is consciousness, when conjoined with its modes (*paryāya*s), is conjoined while remaining unmodified and never abandoning its prior form as consciousness and so forth; or else, it is conjoined having abandoned its prior form. If the latter position were held, it would entail the loss of its permanence, because there would be no persisting entity whatsoever.

Now, if the first position—that it is unchanging—is maintained, then there would be no distinction between its prior and subsequent states; that is, there would be no "otherwise-ness" (anyathātva). Consequently, that consciousness could not be transformative (pariṇāmin), for transformation is defined by the characteristic of otherwise-ness, and yet it is accepted [by you] as being transformative.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not differ between its prior and subsequent states does not undergo transformation (*pariṇāmin*), just like space; and consciousness (*caitanya*) does not differ in any of its states. [This is established] through the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
With the words "of place, time, and nature," etc., he anticipates the objection that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) according to the opponent's view.
Oneness is asserted because there is no difference in place, time, and intrinsic nature;
however, difference is described due to differences in number, characteristic, name, and purpose.
For example, "color and so forth" and "the jar" are distinguished by their difference in number and name.
The persistence and cessation of activity constitute the distinction between the definition and the purpose [of substance and mode].
Thus, for both substance and mode, there is no absolute non-distinction;
for the substance itself undergoes differentiation through the form of its modes. (314–315)

For instance: if the substance were absolutely distinct from its modes, then it would possess some distinction [from them]; however, since the identity of substance and mode is accepted due to the non-difference of their location, time, and nature, whereas their difference is established through differences such as number and so forth—in that regard, "number" refers to oneness, plurality, and the like.
To explain: substance is endowed with the number one, whereas the modes (paryāyas), such as pleasure and the like, are characterized by multiple numbers.

Their defining characteristics (lakṣaṇa) are also distinct, since substance is characterized by persistence (anuvṛtti), while the modes are characterized by differentiation (vyāvṛtti). Furthermore, their designations (saṃjñā)—that is, names—and their purposes (artha)—that is, functions—are different.

And so it has been said: "There is non-difference between the property-bearer (*dharmin*) and its properties (*dharma*) due to the non-difference of place, time, and intrinsic nature; however, there is difference due to the difference in number, designation, characteristic, and function, as in the case of a jar and its color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth. For instance, there is non-difference between the jar and its color-form etc. with respect to place and so on, because whatever is the place, time, and intrinsic nature of the jar is the very same for its color-form etc.; yet there is difference between them and the jar with respect to number and so on, for while the jar is one, the color-form etc. are many—this is the difference in number.
The distinction in designation is that "the jar" and "color and so forth" are different names;

the distinction in characteristic is that the substance, such as the jar, is characterized by persistence (*anuvṛtti*), whereas the modes (*paryāya*), such as color and so forth, are characterized by exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*);
and the distinction in function is that the task of fetching water is performed by the jar, while the dyeing of cloth and so forth is performed by color and the other qualities.

In this same way, it should be understood that even in the case of the self-substance (*ātman-dravya*), which consists of consciousness (*caitanya*), there is a distinction of effects among its modes (*paryāya*) such as pleasure and pain;

this distinction of effects therein should be understood as follows: through consciousness, the experience of objects is produced, whereas through pleasure and so forth, affliction, favor, and the like are produced.
He demonstrates this with the words "form and so forth," etc.
The phrase "distinguished by number and designation" is connected with what will be stated later regarding substance and mode,
while "distinguished by purpose as the persistence and exclusion of effects" refers to their defining characteristics.
The connection is as follows:
"the relation [consists in] the differentiation of effects, the differentiation of objects, and the differentiation of characteristics, namely persistence and exclusion";
this is the syntactical division in the phrase "of substance and mode."
With the words "In this way," etc., he concludes the proof of the reason's lack of establishment (*asiddhi*).
And having established this, substance (*dravya*) is not absolutely undifferentiated; rather, it attains distinction through the differentiation of its modes (*paryāya*).

Therefore, because there is no absolute difference between substance and its modes, and because they are non-different due to their identity, the reason [stated by the opponent] is unestablished (*asiddha*).
He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "non-difference of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvābheda*) and so forth:

"If there is oneness due to the non-difference of intrinsic nature, then difference is difficult to establish in any way whatsoever, just as in the case of the essential nature of synonymous terms (*paryāya*). (316)

For if the non-difference between substance and mode is also accepted, then this non-difference would have to be absolute in every respect; and how could difference, which is the opposite of that, exist? Indeed, it is not logical for affirmation and negation, which are mutually contradictory, to belong to one and the same thing at one and the same time. Thus, by the term "one," an identity of nature is expressed, which is inseparable from the negation of difference. And when that identity of nature exists, how could there be difference at that very same time, since difference consists in the negation of that [identity]?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Where there is non-difference (*abheda*), its opposite, difference (*bheda*), finds no room; for example, in the case of those very modes (*paryāya*) and the substance (*dravya*), there is no difference from their own nature regarding that specific, unique, essential form (*ātmarūpa*) which belongs to them. And since non-difference between substance and mode is established, [difference is excluded] by the perception of a contradictory [property]. (316) Consequently, when there is non-difference between substance and mode in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), he demonstrates that even a difference in defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) does not obtain.
And thus, in the case of the non-figurative [identity], and so forth:
"When such unity of substance and mode is established as non-figurative, the substance would possess exclusion [from others], just like the intrinsic nature of the modes. (317)
Alternatively, if all those modes were also of a pervasive nature, they would necessarily result in being like the substance, because their identity with the substance remains constant.

Whatever has a nature non-different from that which possesses exclusion is itself excluded; for example, the intrinsic nature of the modes. And since the substance is not distinct from that which possesses exclusion, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Alternatively: whatever is not distinct from that which possesses a pervasive nature must itself possess that pervasive nature, just as the nature of a substance [is pervasive]. And since the modes (paryāyas) such as pleasure and so forth have a nature inseparable from that which possesses a pervasive nature, this is indeed a reason based on essential identity (svabhāvahetu).
Otherwise, because their acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema) would be distinct, there would be nothing but difference.

Furthermore, if there were unity even for that which is characterized by contradictory properties, the conventional usage of "difference" would be utterly destroyed; this is the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the contrary position.
He concludes with the words beginning "tata" (therefore) and so forth.

Therefore, no substance such as the self (*ātman*) exists that is not situated [within change], because it is not distinct from its modifications (*paryāya*), just like the nature of the modifications themselves.
(319) "The self, etc. means...
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of jars, rice, and so forth is intended.
With the words beginning with "nor" (*na ca*), he states the result of establishing the second undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*).
Nor are even the modes (*paryāya*) subject to arising and passing away,
because they are not distinct from the substance (*dravya*), just like the fixed nature of that very substance.

Since that substance is also accepted as being subject to arising and passing away in the form of its modes, the phrase "like its fixed nature" was stated so that there would be no contingency of the probandum being deficient.
This self (ātman) is fixed as having the nature (svabhāva) of being a substance (dravya) and so forth; thus, it is a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa).
Then, with the words "therefore, it is without continuity" and so on, he concludes.
Therefore, either destruction must be admitted as being without a residue (*niranvaya-dhvaṃsa*), or everything must be accepted as permanent;
for these two—exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and inclusion (*anugama*)—cannot both exist within a single self-nature.

Not only is there no proof for the existence of a substance-nature that is non-different from its successive states (*paryāya*) because of its inclusive character, but for this reason as well, since it is not perceived apart from the successive states despite meeting the conditions for perception, it is simply an object of the conventional usage of "non-existent. Demonstrating this, he says: "And not... and so forth.

Furthermore, there is no manifestation of a substance (*dravya*) that possesses a perceptible form and a nature following through its various states (*paryāya*); therefore, it does not exist, like a lotus in the sky.
Consequently, what was stated—that the nature of the substance is established as persisting through [the states] by means of perception itself—is unproven.

For indeed, in any cognition accepted as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), no persisting single-natured substantial self (*dravyātman*) is observed whose body is not distinct from its modes (*paryāya*).
(322) If this is so—if there is no substantial self apart from the modes—then how is the distinction between number and so forth established? To this he says: "Vivid objects," etc.

They are capable of various purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*), they are the causes of cognitions such as "similar" and so forth, and they are the objects of words and concepts based on conventions regarding such things. (323) The analysis of the compound is as follows: "various" means of many kinds; "purposeful actions" refers to the functions of [objects] such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so on, which are divided into similar and dissimilar types. Among these, the similar ones are characterized by such things as holding water, while the dissimilar ones are characterized by the production of cognitions such as the coloring of cloth or the perception by the eye. "Capable" means efficacious with respect to those [actions].

In that regard, since all [atoms] contribute simultaneously to a common effect, in order to indicate that they are all causes as a collective, those very atoms—even though they are distinct—are expressed by a word such as "jar" as qualified by a single number (*ekasaṅkhyā*), despite the absence of a non-differentiated substantial form. However, when there is an intention to express their utility toward a specific, uncommon effect, they possess various numbers; thus, a distinction in number and a distinction in effect are established among them.
To the question, "If so, how is there a distinction in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)?", he says: "They are the causes of cognitions such as 'similar'."

Even though entities perish at every moment throughout states such as being raw or cooked, these very particulars—arising with similar configurations and being experienced as objects of non-conceptual perception—become the causes of similar cognitions, such as "this is a jar, this is a jar," across all states. However, when they arise with differences in color, such as dark or red, they become the causes of dissimilar cognitions. Thus, even in the absence of a persistence of a single form, these things function as causes for both similar and dissimilar cognitions; consequently, they are established by way of inclusion and exclusion, and their distinction of characteristics is thereby determined.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "similar etcetera" (*tulyādi*), dissimilar cognition (*atulyajñāna*) is also included.
To the question, "What then is the difference in designation? he says: "Of such a kind," and so forth.

"Of such a kind" (*tathāvidha*) refers to an object such as color (*rūpa*) and so on, which is capable of various purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) and is the cause of cognitions of similarity and the like. That which has this as its "object" (*artha*)—that is, its referent (*viṣaya*)—is the conventional designation (*saṅketa*) such as "jar" or "color and so on. That is what was stated [previously]. Those words and cognitions which have such objects as their conventional designations are described as such; the analysis of the compound is: "those which are the range (*gocara*) of those [words and cognitions]."
He demonstrates through a conclusion that the selflessness of entities is established by direct perception itself: "Arising," and so forth;
[entities] are merely modalities characterized by the nature of arising and passing away.
From that, selflessness and extreme purity are clearly experienced.
(324) "Successive states" refers to form and so forth, as well as suffering and so forth, which have the nature of being self-cognized.
"Kevalāḥ" means those devoid of the nature of a single, undivided substance;
and because for that which is eternal, purposeful activity (*arthakriyā*) is contradictory whether it occurs successively or simultaneously.

The capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) of these [entities] is only possible when they possess the nature of arising and passing away; thus, through inference as well, their selflessness (*nairātmya*) is established by the mark (*liṅga*) of their existence as causal agents.
(324) Regarding what was stated previously—"nor of that which has a perceptible form," etc.—the author anticipates the opponent's rebuttal with the words "Now then" (*atha*), and so forth.

Now, the form that exists as a fusion (*samūrchita*) of substance and mode is indeed held to be twofold yet indivisible, like [the being] Narasiṃha. "Fused" means become a single unified whole; therefore, the meaning is that even though it exists, the form of the substance does not appear through differentiation.
He states the reason for its being a composite whole (*saṃmūrchita*): "For that, being of two forms," and so forth.

Since that entity, such as the self (*ātman*) and so on, is held to be partless even while possessing two forms—just like Narasiṃha—it is therefore a composite of both forms due to its partlessness, and thus it is not perceived separately.
Showing that this which you assert is mutually contradictory, he says: "But surely," and so forth—
"But surely, the very fact that [the word] has two forms is the basis for its having multiple meanings."
The designation "having two forms" (*dvirūpa*) is due to the expression of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) by the word "form" (*rūpa*).
For if it were partless, then the statement "it has two forms" would be contradictory, because this designation is based on multiple objects. Why? Because the word "form" denotes intrinsic nature;
thus, that which has two forms is said to have two intrinsic natures. And it is not logical for a single thing to possess two intrinsic natures, as that would entail the loss of its unity.
You have established only two natures; however, a single entity cannot possess two forms, because unity and multiplicity are defined by their mutual exclusion.
Furthermore, he demonstrates that even Narasiṃha, while being one, is not established as having two forms, using the words "Even Narasiṃha... and so forth.
Nor is it logical for Narasiṃha to be either a single entity or dual in nature;
for he is perceived as being composed of a collection of many atoms. (327) This concludes the examination of the self as conceived by the Digambaras.
The word "also" (api) indicates that not only is that which has become the subject of dispute untenable, but that [other thing] as well; thus says Narasiṃha.
"So be it";
[it is] by way of the variety of its parts and by way of occupying a more extensive space that it would not otherwise appear in such a manner.
Furthermore, if it were covered even by as much as the space occupied by a fly, it would follow that such a thing [the whole] would be obscured;
by this, [objections regarding] color and so forth being like a dark-blue gem (*mecakamaṇi*) are refuted.
The intention is that we shall demonstrate this in detail during the refutation of the composite whole (*avayavin*).
Thus concludes the examination of the self as conceived by the Digambaras;
[now follows] the examination of the self according to the Upaniṣads.

Furthermore, others who follow the Advaita philosophy and are followers of the Upaniṣads postulate a self whose nature is eternal, unitary consciousness, and which consists of the transformations of earth and the other elements;
thus, pointing out their very view, he says: "This [world] consisting of earth, fire, water, and so forth, is an evolution of eternal consciousness," and so on.
Others, moreover, assert that "the Self is of the nature of that.
By "of the nature of that" is meant that its essence consists of eternal, unitary consciousness in the form of the transformations of earth and the other elements.
"Others" refers to the followers of the Upaniṣads.
"What is the proof for this? he says: "Nothing here exists that is endowed with the characteristics of an object of apprehension;
therefore, all this is observed as a transformation of consciousness. (329)

For earth and the other elements do not exist apart from cognition as things possessing the characteristic of being perceivable, such that they might appear [as external objects]; since neither wholes nor atoms exist,
it is therefore determined by implication that these [elements], such as earth and the rest, are merely forms appearing within consciousness.
"This" refers to earth and the other [elements].
He refutes them with the verse beginning "teṣām" and so forth:
"However, their view is only slightly flawed because of their assertion of permanence;
for in the cognitions of form, sound, and so on, a clear distinction is perceived. (330)
But if they were of the nature of a single cognition, it would follow that form, sound, taste, and so forth are perceived simultaneously; moreover, there can be no change of state in what is eternal.
[This is considered] a minor fault.

Since he accepts mere cognition endowed with reasoning, one might ask: "If this is so, why is even a slight fault attributed to that [position]? To this he says: "Because of the assertion of permanence," and so forth.
Furthermore, to the question, "Why is the acceptance of permanence not logical? he says: "Form, sound, and so forth," and so forth.

For permanence (*nityatā*) is defined as remaining in the same state (*tādavasthya*), whereas impermanence (*anityatā*) is the lack of such a state. Now, the cognition appearing as form, sound, and so forth, is never experienced as remaining in a single state; rather, it appears sequentially, sometimes as the appearance of form and at other times as the appearance of sound and so on. Therefore, if these sounds and the rest were essentially the appearance of a single, permanent cognition, they would have to appear all at once—just like the appearance of a multicolored rug—because the cognition whose essence consists of those appearances would be constantly present.

Furthermore, it might be argued that this change of state arises in the cognition sequentially through the appearance of sound and so forth, and therefore there will be no simultaneous perception of sound and the rest. To this he says: "If [the cognition] were eternal, there would be no change of state.
Since the states are not different from the possessor of the states, the destruction and arising of the states would entail the destruction and arising of the possessor of the states as well.
Alternatively, just as the substratum [is eternal], it would follow that the states are also eternal; furthermore,
if the states were distinct [from the substratum], the relationship expressed as "these belong to that" could not be established due to the absence of any mutual benefit,
and there would be a contradiction with the accepted doctrine of a single, eternal consciousness alone.

Furthermore— regarding the eternal self whose nature is consciousness, its establishment must occur either through perception or through inference; first, he shows that it is not established through perception by means of the verse beginning with "rūpa" (form), etc.
No cognition distinct from the cognitions of form and so forth is perceived;
since that [cognition] differs at every moment, what remains established as non-different?
