(332) Indeed, apart from the cognitions of form and so forth appearing in succession, no cognition is experienced that persists as eternal and unitary, by which its establishment through direct perception might occur.
And since it is established that this cognition of form and so forth, being experienced sequentially, perishes at every moment, one must state what else remains as an undifferentiated entity.

Therefore, the point is that because such a nature consisting of cognition—which has reached the moment of perception—is not perceived, it is simply an object of the conventional designation "non-existent.
Nor, he considers, is there establishment [of its existence] through inference.

For inference must have either an essential nature (*svabhāva*) as its logical mark (*liṅga*) or an effect (*kārya*). First of all, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes such an essential nature for the self consisting of knowledge; on the contrary, subverting evidence such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) does exist. Thus, the transformation (*vivarta*) of eternal knowledge is untenable.
Furthermore, he shows that under this view, the distinction between bondage and liberation would not be established, beginning with the words "one who is deluded" (*viparyasta*), etc.
In a person whose nature is that of a single cognition, no distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cognition exists; therefore, how could bondage and liberation occur?

For one who holds the position that cognition—which perishes at every moment—is indeed manifold for each individual and proceeds as a distinct continuum, it is logical to establish the system of bondage and liberation based on the arising of a series of erroneous or non-erroneous cognitions.

Furthermore, through the gradual practice of yoga, as ever-purer knowledge arises and the continuum of impure knowledge ceases, liberation (*apavarga*) is attained; thus, the exertion for the attainment of liberation is fruitful. However, for you, O Bhavatrāta, who hold the position that the self (*ātman*) has the nature of a single, eternal cognition, how can bondage and liberation occur in a person whose essence is that single cognition?
For instance, if that single cognition were always of a distorted nature, then, because there would be no other state, the distinction of liberation could not exist.
If, on the other hand, it were non-erroneous, then because its nature would be eternally pure, there could be no bondage.

For us, however, representation (vijñapti) is held to be both defiled and pure according to the distinction of mental continua (santāna); thus, the established order of bondage and liberation is logical, as it has been said: "It is both defiled and purified, with stains and without stains."
If it were not defiled, all embodied beings would be liberated;
if it were not pure, effort would be fruitless.
Furthermore, it might be argued that bondage and liberation are merely conceptual constructs and not ultimate realities; in that case, the basis for such a conceptualization must also be stated.
However, in the view that cognition is impermanent, the basis has already been demonstrated.

And thus, he shows that this effort of yours toward the cultivation of reality (*tattva-bhāvanā*) for the sake of attaining liberation and transcending cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) results in nothing but exhaustion—expressing this with the words "Or what," and so forth:
"Or what could the yogi eliminate? What could he accomplish through the practice of yoga? For that which consists of error (*viparyāsa*) cannot possibly be abandoned. (334)
Furthermore, the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna) is not something to be produced, because it exists eternally through identity [with the self];
therefore, this entire practice of yoga is likewise fruitless.
[This concludes] the Examination of the Self as Conceived by the Followers of the Upaniṣads.

For if the yogin were to cause anything to cease or bring anything into being through the cultivation of reality (*tattvabhāvanā*), then his effort would be fruitful; however, he does not first cause error (*viparyāsa*) to cease, because that error is of the nature of that [Self]—namely, of the nature of eternal consciousness. Therefore, it cannot be abandoned, since abandonment is impossible for that which is eternal and indestructible.
Nor does he accomplish the knowledge of reality through cultivation, because the knowledge of reality is already present at all times by virtue of being the nature of eternal consciousness.
Therefore, this is not tenable.
Thus concludes the examination of the self according to the Upaniṣads.
Now, for the purpose of refuting the *pudgala* (person) as conceived by the Vātsīputrīyas, he says: "But some," and so forth.

"But some, though considering themselves followers of the Sugata, describe themselves by the designation of a 'person' (pudgala) as being devoid of identity with or difference from [the aggregates], etc.
Regarding the word "some":

The Vātsīputrīyas, for they, though considering themselves sons of the Sugata, nevertheless postulate a self under the guise of the *pudgala* as being inexpressible in terms of identity with or difference from the aggregates.

Showing how those who have indeed accepted the status of being sons of the Blessed One, the Sugata who teaches selflessness, could possibly be so intent upon the false view of a self, [the author] states a point of derision: "even those who consider themselves followers of the Sugata."

For instance, this is the definition of the self (ātman): that which is the agent of various wholesome and unwholesome karmas, the experiencer of the desired and undesired fruits of its own actions, and that which transmigrates by abandoning the preceding aggregates and taking up other subsequent aggregates, as well as the experiencer—that is the self.
Since all of this is accepted even regarding the person (pudgala), there is merely a dispute over names.
Now, as to what the reasoning is for the inexpressibility of the person (*pudgala*), he says: "From the aggregates... and so forth.
The person is not other than the aggregates, because that would entail the views of the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
Nor is it non-other, because that would entail [the faults of] multiplicity and so forth. Therefore, its inexpressibility is correct. (337)

If the person (*pudgala*) were other than the aggregates (*skandhas*), then there would be the view of a self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*) as imagined by the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*); consequently, the fallacy of an eternal self would follow.
Furthermore, it is not logical for an eternal self to possess agency, enjoyership, and so forth, because like space, it would be forever devoid of distinction.
Moreover, the eternal self has been refuted by the Blessed One, and the statement "all phenomena are selfless" (*nirātmānaḥ sarve dharmāḥ*) would be contradicted.
If it is argued that "then let [the person] be non-different [from the aggregates]," he says: "It is not non-different," and so forth.

For if the person were merely the aggregates such as form and the rest, then, because of being non-different from the many aggregates, the person would result in being manifold, just like their own nature; yet the person is held to be one.
As it has been said: "A single person (pudgala), when arising in the world, arises just like a Tathāgata," and by the word "etcetera" (ādi), qualities such as impermanence are included;
this being the case, the person would likewise be subject to annihilation, just like the aggregates (skandhas).

Furthermore, it would follow that performed actions are lost, and the doctrine of annihilationism has been refuted by your Blessed One; therefore, it is established that the *pudgala* exists as something inexpressible (337).

By the words "they [the Vaibhāṣikas] should be asked," etc., he demonstrates that you yourselves have established—by your own very statement—that the *pudgala* is not a real entity because it is inexpressible.

They should be addressed as follows: "The person (*pudgala*) does not exist in an ultimate sense, because it is inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different from [the aggregates], like a sky-lotus and so forth.

(338) The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is not expressible in terms of identity or difference with respect to a given thing is not that thing, just like a lotus in the sky; and the person is not expressible [in those terms]. This is due to the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Regarding the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*) such as sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, [the author] asks:
"How, then, is pervasion (*vyāpti*) established here? and replies with the words beginning "otherness" (*anyatva*).
Whether as otherness or non-otherness, a real entity does not transcend these two states in reality; however, that which is formless is conceived as being inexpressible.
(339) For a real entity never transcends being either identical to or different from another real entity, as there is no other possible alternative.
Otherwise, even form and the other [sensory objects] would be inexpressible in relation to one another;
therefore, it is the formless and essence-less itself that is conceived as inexpressible, and not the actual entity.

To the question "How so?", he says: "Because the conceptual construction of difference and non-difference has a real entity as its substratum, the inability to designate [an entity] as being either identical to or different from reality is appropriate only in the case of things that lack intrinsic nature. (340)
For when there is a negation of a thing in the form "this is not that," it is clearly stated to be a difference [from] another entity;
and the negation of its being something other than that is itself designated as its true nature.
That object does not transcend either its reality (*tattva*) or its differentiation (*bheda*).
(342) For it is the very object that serves as the basis for the conceptual constructions of difference and non-difference, not a non-object;

therefore, the inability to designate [it] as identical to or different from [another], and so forth, is appropriate only in the case of things lacking intrinsic nature—that is, in those devoid of self-nature.
The connection [of the sentence] is that it is not tenable for there to be no designation of identity, difference, and so forth with respect to a real entity (*vastu*).

Since there is no other possible mode of existence apart from difference and non-difference, he asks: "How, then, is there no other mode of existence? and replies with the words beginning "For this... (*yad etad dhi*, etc.).

To explain: this negation—that the person (*pudgala*) does not have the nature (*svabhāva*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth—precisely expresses its difference from that form and the rest. This is because the negation of the existence of one thing in another thing is invariably concomitant with the affirmation of a different nature. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever thing is devoid of the nature of a given thing is other than it; for example, form is other than sensation (*vedanā*). And the thing called "person" is devoid of the nature of form and the rest. Thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, this negation of a thing’s being otherwise—the negation of its not having that nature—is itself designated as its very essence (tattva), because it is inseparable from the affirmation of that essence; for the negation of a real entity’s being something else is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of its own essence.
Otherwise, if no intrinsic nature were affirmed of it, then, due to the negation of all natures, it would simply be a non-entity.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: because non-substantiality (*avastutva*) is characterized by the negation of all intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*). Whatever is a real entity whose essential nature is negated as being distinct from something else, that is precisely that [negation]; for example, just as form (*rūpa*) has its essential nature negated as being distinct from itself.
And since the person (*pudgala*) has its essential nature negated as being distinct from form and the other aggregates, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Therefore, since a thing does not transcend being either identical to or different from that very entity, the pervasion of the fundamental reason is established.
Thus, it has first been demonstrated that if one accepts the inexpressibility [of the person], it follows that the person is merely a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisat*).

Now, considering that if one accepts the person as a real entity (*vastu*), its inexpressibility is untenable, otherwise there would be a contradiction with one's own words regarding the proposition, the author concludes with the verse beginning "From the aggregates," and so forth.
"The person (*pudgala*) is not other than the aggregates (*skandha*): this indicates its non-otherness;
yet [the statement] 'the aggregate is not the person' clearly demonstrates its otherness.

(443) Furthermore, he shows that by saying "the person is inexpressible," you have actually proclaimed with even greater clarity the distinctness of the person from the aggregates: "For there is an association with contradictory properties," and so forth.

For the association with contradictory properties is said to be the difference between things; does this difference not indeed exist between the aggregates (*skandha*) and the person (*pudgala*)? (344) The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those two things which are characterized by properties existing through mutual exclusion are mutually distinct, just as form (*rūpa*) and sensation (*vedanā*), which are endowed with the properties of being material and being immaterial. And the aggregates and the person are characterized by such mutually contradictory properties as "being expressible" and "being inexpressible. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
And showing that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "For instance," and so forth;
for indeed, the person (*pudgala*) is said to be inexpressible in relation to feeling (*vedanā*) and the other aggregates.
Therefore, form, perception, and so forth must be expressible as being either identical to or different from [the person].

For instance, while the person is held to be inexpressible in terms of identity or difference from feeling, perception, and so on, form, feeling, and the rest are, on the contrary, expressible as being mutually different from one another. Consequently, the reason [adduced] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
He demonstrates that the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) is established for this reason as well—starting with "by way of impermanence" and so forth:
"The aggregates of form (*rūpaskandha*) and the rest are considered to be denotable by [the term] 'impermanence'."
But the person (*pudgala*) is not so; therefore, its distinctness is perfectly clear.

(346) For, according to the statement "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent," form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates must indeed be described as being impermanent. However, the person is not intended to be described in that way—as impermanent—in any manner whatsoever, because it is held to be inexpressible (*avācya*). Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since the conventional usage of distinction is based solely on this much [namely, the difference in their modes of description]. Otherwise, the entire universe would be a single entity, and consequently, there would follow the absurd consequence of simultaneous arising and destruction.

It has been demonstrated that this *pudgala* is not a real entity because it cannot be described as either identical to or different from [the aggregates]; furthermore, demonstrating that it is not a real entity precisely because it cannot be described as impermanent, he says: "In causal efficacies... and so forth.
And the capacity for causal efficacies is the defining characteristic of existence.
Thus, reality is restricted to momentary things alone, and likewise, it does not belong to that which is inexpressible.

For this very capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is the defining characteristic of existence and the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a real entity; since the definition of unreality is the absence of all capacity, it follows by implication that reality is defined solely by the capacity for causal efficiency. And that causal efficiency is restricted exclusively to momentary things.
The meaning is that [existence] is pervaded by momentariness alone;
because for a permanent entity, causal efficiency is contradicted by both succession and simultaneity, there is no substantial reality in a person (*pudgala*) that cannot be described as momentary.

In that case, because its pervader, momentariness, is absent, it is like the absence of "śiṃśapā-ness" when "tree-ness" is absent—as it has been said: "That which cannot be described as impermanent is not the cause of anything.

This might be the case if the *pudgala* were permanent; for then there would be a contradiction regarding its causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity. However, since it is inexpressible as impermanent, it is likewise inexpressible as permanent; therefore, its capacity for causal efficiency is indeed not contradicted.

That is incorrect; for it is not logical that a thing (*vastu*) as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) should be devoid of both aspects, because permanence and impermanence are defined by their mutual exclusion. This is because the rejection or acceptance of one aspect in a thing is necessarily concomitant with the acceptance or rejection of the other aspect.

We do not deny the application of the term "ineffable" (*avācya*) to the person (*pudgala*), for it is impossible for anyone to deny what is introduced merely by one's own independent whim; rather, we are here examining the actual nature of this entity.

Is this nature of the entity called "person" (pudgala) existent at all times, or rather non-existent? If it exists, then it is indeed eternal; for that which is called "eternal" is nothing other than this: whatever nature remains forever and does not perish is termed "eternal," as it has been said: "The wise call that eternal whose nature does not perish.
On the other hand, if the position is that it does not exist, then it is likewise impermanent, because the characteristic of the impermanent is its lack of a persisting nature.

Therefore, since there is no other alternative between being momentary and non-momentary, and since for a non-momentary entity there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (arthakriyā) due to its inability to act either successively or simultaneously, existence—which is defined by the capacity for causal efficiency—is pervaded by momentariness. Thus, it is established that when momentariness is excluded from the *pudgala*, existence is also excluded.

If this is so, and if the *pudgala* does not exist at all, why did the Blessed One, when asked whether "the soul is the same as the body" or "the soul is one thing and the body another," say that "this is undeclared" (*avyākṛta*) rather than simply stating that it does not exist? To this he says: "But in the case of a contradiction with the meaning of the scriptures... and so forth.
Regarding the contradiction with the meaning of the scriptures, however, the Great Beings have exerted themselves;
the diverse words of the Compassionate One were intended to refute nihilism.

For if the person (*pudgala*) were established as a real entity (*dharmin*), then its properties—such as being identical to or different from [the aggregates]—would deserve to be declared indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
To the extent that the very subject (*dharmin*) itself is not established, how could its property (*dharma*) be specified?
For sharpness and so forth are not possible for non-existent things such as a donkey’s horn, by which it might be described;
therefore, making known that it exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñaptisattva*), the Blessed One stated, "This [question] regarding the person (*pudgala*) is undeclared (*avyākṛta*)."
However, it was not stated simply that "it does not exist," because the opponent had not asked about the intrinsic nature of the subject (*dharmisvarūpa*).

Alternatively, even regarding that which exists as a mere designation (*prajñaptisat*), the teaching of emptiness was not expressed as "it does not exist" in order to avoid the dogmatic adherence to non-existence, having regard for the disposition of disciples who were unfit for such a teaching.
And as it has been said: "Having considered the piercing by the fangs of the 'view-fanged' one, and the ruin of [wholesome] actions..."

"The Victors teach the Dharma like a tigress carrying away her cub"—thus, masters such as Ācārya Vasubandhu have exerted themselves in works such as the *Abhidharmakośa* and the *Paramārthasaptatikā* to reveal this underlying intention (*abhiprāya*). Therefore, it should be understood from those very sources;
however, for fear of excessive prolixity, it is not written here—this is the sense.
If this is so, how is the statement "there is a being who is reborn" to be interpreted? He says: "By way of [avoiding] nihilism," and so forth.
The remainder of the sentence is: "For the various teachings of the Compassionate One asserting the existence of a being are not contradictory.

For when there is the designation of a "being" with respect to a particular continuum of consciousness, the Blessed One said "there is a being" with the underlying intention that it is not subject to annihilation.

Otherwise, because one would understand the non-existence of even those formative forces (*saṃskāra*) whose succession of cause-and-effect moments has not ceased, the disciples would fall into a nihilistic view, thinking: "Since there is no self that transmigrates to another world, the next world is unestablished. (129-27) [The list of corrections displays this error as *māt pa*, omitting *ra*.]
As for that which was said: "O monks, I shall teach you the burden, the taking up of the burden, the laying down of the burden, and the bearer of the burden;

therein, the burden is the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandhāḥ*), the taking up of the burden is craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the laying down of the burden is liberation (*mokṣa*), and the bearer of the burden is the person (*pudgala*)," how is this to be interpreted? For it is not logical that the burden itself should be the bearer of the burden. To this he says: "Because of the collection," and so forth.

The teaching on the bearer of the burden and so forth, as well as the specific negations, shine forth by means of a mind that regards [the person] as a collection and so on, directed toward those who hold such views.
(349) Thus ends the examination of the self as conceived by the Vātsīputrīyas.

In this context, the aggregates (*skandhas*) themselves, existing at the same time and intended as a totality, receive the designation "collection" (*samudāya*). These very same [aggregates], when occurring simultaneously as cause and effect, are designated as a "continuum" (*santāna*). Furthermore, when they exist as the basis for a single conceptual reflection (*ekākāraparāmarśa*), they are indicated by the terms "possessor of the continuum" (*santānin*) and "constituent of the collection" (*samudāyin*). Therefore, the teaching regarding the bearer of the burden (*bhārahāra*) and so forth is not contradictory, provided it is understood with the intention of a "collection" and so on. The word "etc. (*ādi*) in the first instance includes "continuum" and so forth; in the second instance, it includes "burden" and so forth. This is the remainder [of the sentence].

In this context, those very aggregates (*skandhas*), when intended in the form of a collection, a continuum, and so forth, are designated as the "person" (*pudgala*) and the "bearer of the burden" (*bhārahāra*).
This is because, in common worldly usage, the term "person" is applied precisely to that [collection].

For this very reason, after the Blessed One asked, "Who is the bearer of the burden? It is the person," he explained the person by saying: "O Venerable One, he who has such a name, such a birth, such a clan, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a long life," and so forth.

This [person], characterized as a collection of aggregates (*skandha-samudāya-lakṣaṇa*), exists as a mere designation (*prajñapti*); it is taught so that one might understand it otherwise—as neither something else, nor as permanent, nor as a substantial entity (*dravya*) as imagined by others. Furthermore, this must necessarily be understood in this way; otherwise, since the burden (*bhāra*) and so forth are also taught separately from the aggregates, they would—like the person (*pudgala*)—not be included within the aggregates.
Therefore, those very aggregates which exist for the sake of producing subsequent aggregates are spoken of as "the burden" when considered as preceding states.

Those who will enter [into nirvana] as the result [of their practice] are called "bearers of the burden"; thus, this [scriptural passage] is not a proof [for the existence of a self]. However, Uddyotakara says: "For one who does not accept a self, this word of the Tathāgata cannot be established as meaningful, because it has been said:

'Venerable sir, form is not I; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, venerable sir, are not I. Likewise, O monk, this form is not you; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not you."
For by this, the aggregates such as form and so forth have been refuted as being objects of the notion of "I";
moreover, this is a specific refutation and not a general refutation,
whereas one who does not accept a self must refute it only in a general sense.
A specific negation such as "you are not this" is invariably concomitant with an affirmation of something else;
just as when it is said, "I do not see with my left eye," it is understood that one does see with the right eye.
In that case as well, if there were no perception, the mention of "either" would be meaningless; one should simply say, "I do not see.
Similarly here too, when it is stated that "form is not the self," up to "consciousness is not the self," it is indicated that there exists a self distinct from those.
Whether that [self] is inexpressible or something else, in any case, the self exists.
Here he says: "And the negation of particulars," and so forth;
this is what is meant:
this mountain of the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), rising with its twenty peaks, prevails among those of poor intellect.
Namely: "form is the self," up to "consciousness is the self"; "the self possesses form," up to "the self possesses consciousness"; or "form is in the self," up to "consciousness is in the self.

Regarding these, for the sake of refuting the first five views, a specific refutation directed toward those who hold such views is appropriate. Those who possess the views beginning with "form is the self" are called "those who hold such views" (*taddṛṣṭikāḥ*).
For it is precisely that which is a ground for doubt for one of deluded intellect that is restated and then negated;
no injunction of anything whatsoever is intended here.
Otherwise, a proponent who utters a sentence that fails to refine the understanding of the listener would indeed be lacking in foresight.
Thus ends the examination of the self according to the Vātsīputrīyas,
and the examination of the permanence of entities.
To justify this qualification [of the calamity], he says: "Or rather," and so forth.

Or rather, this effort is being made in the wrong place, since by the very establishment of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the rest have already been refuted. (350)

In order to negate, without distinction, that which has been stated and that which will be stated—such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth—the momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is clearly established here. The sense is this: since momentary destruction, which pervades all things without exception, is being established, even though the entire mass of entities postulated by others—such as Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*), God (*īśvara*), and the like—is being refuted with a single stroke, our undertaking of a refutation by articulating each point individually through an excessively voluminous composition of text results solely in exhaustion. This is because that [mass of entities] has already been refuted by a very brief means.

For instance—it is not accepted by others that everything, beginning with primordial matter (prakṛti), perishes immediately after its arising, nor is it accepted by some that it possesses the property of ceasing without leaving a trace (niranvayanirodha).

Therefore, considering that all these [theories] are refuted by the very establishment of the momentariness (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) that pervades all things, we shall clearly establish momentariness specifically in order to refute: (1) the categories beginning with "primordial nature" (*prakṛti*) and ending with the "person" (*pudgala*) as stated [by the Sāṃkhyas]; (2) the genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), and substance (*dravya*) etc. to be discussed [by the Vaiśeṣikas]; (3) the referent of words; (4) the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of valid cognition (*prameya*); (5) the variegated entity resembling a multi-colored gem; (6) the entity persisting through the three times; (7) the four elements accepted by the Cārvākas and others; and (8) the collection of Vedic words desired by the followers of Jaimini. Thus it is said.
Because the three-fold logical reason that establishes this is demonstrated herein,
it is thereby stated that the completion of the entire purpose of the treatise occurs within this very examination of the permanence of entities.
How is this established? He says: "By way of being produced or unproduced," and so forth;
some maintain that there is a twofold division by way of being produced or unproduced.
"Others maintain that entities are both momentary and non-momentary.
(352) For here, the Naiyāyikas and others, holding that not even a single entity is momentary, establish a twofold classification of entities based on being produced or unproduced.
In this regard—some are produced, such as jars and the like; some are unproduced, such as atoms, space, and so forth.

Furthermore, other schools such as the Vātsīputrīyas maintain that entities are divided into two categories based on whether they are momentary or non-momentary; for according to their view, things such as cognitions, sounds, and flames are momentary, whereas earth, space, and so forth are non-momentary. (352)

Thus, the classification of the views being established, [the author], demonstrating that the proof is stated by first taking as the subject (pakṣa) those very things intended to be produced, says "In that regard," and so forth:
"In that regard, whatever entities are produced, they are all subject to momentary destruction, because they exist without dependence on anything else with respect to their perishing. (353)

Because all things stand in relation to their destruction without depending on any other cause, a three-featured logical reason (*trilakṣaṇa-hetu*) is indicated by this; clarifying that very point, he says: "Whatever state [a thing] does not depend upon any other cause for, it should be known as restricted to that state, because it arises from its own causes in such a manner. (354)
For the causal complex is indeed independent in producing its own effect, just as all things that are born are independent with respect to their own destruction.
(355) The formal argument is: those things which are independent of the existence of something else are necessarily restricted to that state of being.

Just as a causal complex is necessarily fixed toward the production of its own effect immediately following [its assembly], and all produced entities that possess birth are independent with respect to their destruction— this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason); this is another reason (*hetvantara*).
He states the reason why [the effect] is necessarily non-different from its cause: "from their own causes," meaning that it arises in such a way— that is, in that determined form.

Furthermore, those things which are not restricted to a particular state do not become independent even with respect to that state; for example, unbaked jars and the like [do not become independent] regarding the process of baking and so forth—this is the illustration here by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya).

But is it not the case that the reason is inconclusive? For even if entities are indeed independent of other causes with respect to their destruction, nevertheless, since the destruction of an entity is possible after it has endured for some time and in another place, it is not established that one can prove these [entities] to have their cessation immediately following their arising. To this he says: "Even if independent," and so forth:
"Even if this [destruction] were independent, if it were to occur at another place or at another time..."
Because it depends on that, this [destruction] does not result in being independent;
"this" refers to destruction.
"By virtue of dependence on that" means by virtue of dependence on another place or time.

For if something were independent with respect to a certain [place or time], yet were to exist in some place or at some time, then—because of its dependence on that place and time—it would not be independent at all; so how could there be any deviation?

For instance: how can that which exists in another place, time, and so forth, without abandoning its own place and time, be called "independent" (*anapekṣa*)? Because such existence itself is its dependence; it is not an active striving, since [the entity] is devoid of intention.
If, then, the intended meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is "because of being entirely independent," then that reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For instance: some things are observed to depend upon a hammer or similar instruments for their destruction, such as jars and the like.

Even those things well known to be independent, such as cognitions and sounds, do not indeed depend on hammers and the like; nevertheless, they still depend upon place and time. Anticipating the objection that the reason [of the argument] is therefore unestablished (*asiddha*), the author says "In all cases," etc., in order to refute it.
"And all produced things are everywhere independent regarding their destruction,
because in every respect the causes of destruction are incapable of acting upon them.
(Verse 357) "Everywhere" means...
The meaning is that produced things are independent of all causes of destruction, such as place, time, and so forth;

for those [factors] accepted as causes of destruction are incapable of acting and provide no assistance, and it is not logical for something to depend on what provides no assistance, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
He asks, "How is it that [the cause of destruction] is ineffective? and says: "For instance," and so forth.
For indeed, it is not logical for a cause of destruction to be the producer of a destruction that is not distinct from the entity itself, because the entity is produced by its own cause. (358)

For destruction, when being produced, must be either an entity (*vastu*) or a non-entity (*avastu*). In that regard, if it were an entity, then this destruction would be produced by a cause of destruction as either non-different from that [entity] or different from it;

for there is no escaping these two alternatives regarding an existing entity. A position of both or neither is simply untenable, because in the case of an entity, the abandonment or acceptance of one aspect is necessarily concomitant with the acceptance or abandonment of its other aspects.
It has been stated that for a single entity, both affirmation and negation are untenable; in that regard,
the position that [negation] is not a distinct thing from the entity itself is not tenable, because the nature of an entity arises solely from its own causes at the very moment of its production,
and since it is inseparable from that [entity], it is already established just like the entity itself.
Furthermore, a cause for that which is already produced is not logical, because it would entail the consequence of the cause never ceasing its activity.

It might be argued: "This entity is not produced in its entirety from its own cause; therefore, it acquires another nature called 'destruction' from another cause. To this, he says: "And [it is] not partless," and so forth.
Furthermore, when a partless entity has arisen from its own cause as having the nature of both existence and non-existence, that very nature cannot subsequently be made to perish by other factors.

(359) For a single thing cannot possess two natures such that it might be produced in one part; rather, an entity is indeed partless, and since it arises from its own cause as being produced in its entirety, how could another nature be imparted to it at a later time by other causes?

For it is not logical that something which is not established when another is being established should be its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), because non-difference is characterized by sharing the same fate (*ekayogakṣema*). Therefore, that entity whose nature is destruction which arises at a later time is a different intrinsic nature; and how could that which is different belong to it? Thus, this [objection] is trivial.

(359) Now, regarding the position that [destruction] is a distinct entity (*arthāntarabhūta*), he shows that even there the cause of destruction is utterly ineffective for the entity—starting with "distinct from the category of things" (*padārthavyatirikta*), etc.
But when that which is called "destruction" is established as something distinct from the entity itself, nothing at all is produced in that entity by other causes.
Therefore, its perception, its causal efficiency, and so forth, persist exactly as before.

Furthermore, because it remains in that same state, it is not logical for [the destruction] to benefit it even through its own occurrence. For when one thing is produced, another cannot truly be benefited, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor is it reasonable to say that an entity is benefited by the production of a destruction related to it, because such a relationship is unestablished.

For instance: because difference is admitted, there can be no relation characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), nor one characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*), since [the entity] originates precisely from the cause of its own destruction; nor is there any other real relation.
Even if a relation were to exist, since the entity would remain as it was, the same consequences regarding perception and other effects would follow;
for perception itself is the effect.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the retention of water, the breaking of the shanks, and so forth are included.

If it is argued that [the entity] does not perform its effects, such as perception, because it is covered or obstructed by that distinct destruction, he replies: "Because of its remaining in that same state," and so on.

For it is not logical that something which neither destroys nor produces a specific excellence of the entity's own nature (*svabhāva*) should be its coverer or its obstructor, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, because its prior nature is unrenounced, unobscured, and unimpeded, neither obscuration nor obstruction is tenable. 360–361.

It might be argued that the aforementioned consequence regarding perception and so forth does not apply, because the entity is destroyed by that destruction which is distinct from it. To this he says: "By the entity named 'destruction,' etc.
It is false that an entity is destroyed by an entity called "destruction," because the same alternatives—such as whether it is different [from the entity] and so forth—apply there as well. (362)

For does destruction, while destroying an entity, destroy something other than it or non-other? Or rather, does it destroy by producing a destruction characterized as total annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*), like a mallet and so forth? In this case as well, the same alternatives recur, and the fault already mentioned applies there;
and it will be stated that the same fault applies to that other destruction which is produced under the name "destruction. Regarding that [other destruction] as well:
"By way of following the meaning" means by way of the persistence of conceptual constructions such as otherness and so forth;
thus, it has first been demonstrated that [the effect] is not produced as a real entity.
Showing that it is not even a non-entity, he says: "Consisting of both existence and non-existence," and so forth;
destruction, which is known by another name as *pradhvaṃsa*, consists of the nature of both existence and non-existence.
If it is argued that [non-existence] is produced, then its production is not logically consistent.
For if non-existence were an effect, it would follow that it is a real entity, like a sprout and so forth, because that which is of an unproduced nature arises through the power of a cause.

For there is the production of an existent (*bhāva*), not of a non-existent (*abhāva*); because it is characterized by the absence of all intrinsic nature that could be made its cause, there is no form whatsoever to be produced.

Therefore, destruction—which consists of the non-existence of an existent and is of the nature of the negation of an existent—is not produced by anything, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), like the horn of a donkey.
Otherwise, due to being an effect, it would necessarily be an entity, like a sprout and so forth.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is an effect must necessarily perish, just like sprouts and the like; and destruction is indeed an effect. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
To establish its pervasion (*vyāpti*), he says: "Because it arises through the power of a cause"; for that alone is called an "effect."

For by the power of a cause, an object attains a specific excellence of its own nature (*ātmātiśaya*), and it is only when that excellence has been attained that the object [is said to have been produced];
and on this point, there is no dispute even among the Naiyāyikas and others.
For instance: "being an effect" is defined as either inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*) or inherence in its own cause (*svakāraṇa-samavāya*);

however, neither inherence in existence nor inherence in its own cause applies to destruction, because that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that destruction, like substances and so forth, would be a locus of existence (*astitva*). (363)
If this is so, let there be substantiality (*vastutva*) in destruction; what fault is there in that? To this he says: "By affirmation alone," and so forth:
"And thus non-existence is established by affirmation alone, because it relies upon exclusion (*paryudāsa*)."
Furthermore, regarding the conceptual constructions such as exclusion (*vyatireka*) that arise therein:

in response to the inquiry, "How can there be the production of a non-entity (*abhāva*) by way of affirmation (*vidhi*)?", this was stated— "by resorting to *paryudāsa*," which means by taking recourse to *paryudāsa*.

For, by the power of intention (*vivakṣā*), a very real entity (*bhāva*) that is distinct from some other entity is designated as "non-existence" (*abhāva*). In that case, the aforementioned fault recurs regarding the conceptual alternatives of difference (*vyatireka*) and so forth.

(365) Now, if—out of fear of this fault—it is not admitted that non-existence consisting of exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is produced by causes of destruction; what then? It is accepted that it consists of absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

Showing that even in that case, the utter inefficacy of a cause of destruction has been demonstrated, he says: "Now," and so forth: "Now, this negation of activity certainly does not produce the entity; nevertheless, the lack of causality is established because the agent loses its status as a cause. (366)

For instance: if it were a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), because the negative particle would be connected with the verb "to do," it would mean "he effects non-existence" or "he does not effect existence. Thus, by negating the action, the cause of destruction would be established as a non-agent; and how could that which is a non-agent be a cause? Therefore, there is no cause whatsoever for destruction. (366) Here, wishing to point out the proofs stated by Aviddhakarṇa for establishing that destruction possesses a cause, he says: "But surely," and so forth.
Now, this destruction does not exist at the time of the entity’s existence, nor before it, nor long after; rather, it occurs immediately following the entity.
And thus, being restricted to a specific time, it is logical that this destruction possesses a cause.

For the occurrence of occasionality is refuted in the case of that which is independent. To explain: destruction does not occur at the time of a thing's existence, because it would follow that even a thing lasting for only a single moment would be non-existent; nor does it occur prior to its production, because it is impossible for that which has not yet arisen to perish—for indeed, the sons of barren women and the like do not perish while remaining unproduced. Nor does it occur later, because it occurs immediately [after arising]; for it is impossible for that which has already perished in the third and subsequent moments to perish again, just as a fire that has been reduced to ashes cannot burn once more. Rather, destruction occurs in the second moment immediately following the existence of the thing.
Consequently, it is established that destruction possesses a cause because it is restricted in time, like a sprout and so forth;
"because it is restricted in time" means because it occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatvāt*).

Establishing its pervasion (vyāpti), he says: "For the connection with occasional occurrence... and so forth. Indeed, occasional occurrence is not possible for that which is independent, because it would follow that such a thing must exist eternally.
Therefore, by virtue of its occasional occurrence, its possession of a cause is established.
He shows that [the point] is established from this as well: "And because it occurs immediately after a real entity," and so forth;
for only that which has a cause is logically consistent with occurring immediately after a real entity.
And because it exists after having not existed, it is considered to be just like any other moment.

(369) Thus, these three reasons have been stated for destruction being caused: because it occurs only occasionally, because it is accepted by the Buddhists as occurring immediately after the arising of the entity, and because it acquires its own nature after previously not existing—just like a subsequent moment.
He also states the reasoning expressed by Uddyotakara, "by way of dissimilarity, such as the horns of a hare," beginning with the words "because of being without a cause," etc. (369).

Furthermore, because it lacks a cause, this [non-existence] must either be non-existent like the son of a barren woman and so forth, or else it must be eternal like space; for there is no other alternative.
If all things were non-existent, they would possess eternity due to their lack of destruction.
The cognition that all conditioned phenomena are subject to destruction is signless (animittaka).
Even if [the self] were eternal, its coexistence with destruction would not be contradictory; furthermore, the assertion of the destruction of that which is unarisen does not conform to reason.

For he spoke thus: one who asserts that "there is no cause for destruction" must be questioned as follows: "Is destruction non-existent because it lacks a cause, like a sky-lotus and the like, or is it eternal because it lacks a cause, like space and the like? For in your own position, that which is causeless is seen to be of two kinds: either eternal or non-existent; indeed, there is no other category apart from existence and non-existence.

In that regard, if destruction were non-existent because it lacks a cause, then it would follow that all entities are eternal, since there would be no destruction; furthermore, the cognition that "all conditioned phenomena perish" would become groundless, for it is not the case that one says "he is going" when there is no act of going. On the other hand, if it were eternal, then it would follow that an entity coexists with its own destruction, because it would persist at all times.
And this is not logical, because existence and non-existence are characterized by being mutually exclusive.
If simultaneous coexistence is not admitted, then the arising of an effect would not be possible, because its opposite, destruction, would be eternally present.

Consequently, the destruction of that which has not arisen is also untenable; for it is not observed in the world that unarisen things, such as the horns of a hare, undergo destruction. Therefore, the statement that "there is destruction of the unarisen" does not conform to reason at all.
With the words "In this regard," and so forth, he refutes everything: "In this matter, what kind of destruction do the opponents inquire about—
is it the very entity itself, which has the nature of existing for a moment, that is described as such?"
Now, regarding the cessation of the nature of an entity, which is designated as "destruction," nothing at all is contradicted by the preceding inquiry.
For destruction is of two kinds: that characterized as an affirmation and that characterized as a negation.
To explain: since an entity whose nature is momentary existence is itself mobile and perishing, it is designated as "destruction" (*vināśa*);
or else, destruction is the process of perishing, also known by the name "annihilation" (*pradhvaṃsa*), characterized by the departure from the entity's own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Regarding the former kind of destruction, if this inquiry into the proof of its having a cause is made by means of the aforementioned reasons, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
He demonstrates that very same state of the proven being already established with the words beginning "yo hi" (for he...).
For we maintain that whatever entity exists for a moment is designated as "destruction" and is thus caused; however, because of the non-existence of another [entity], destruction is uncaused.
To the question, "If this is so, how is it that destruction is understood by you to be uncaused? he says: "However, because of the non-existence of another, it is uncaused."

The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: because there is no destroyer such as a hammer that is distinct from its own causes and occurs at a later time, we maintain that destruction is causeless.

And in this case, regarding destruction as the locus (*dharmī*), these two reasons—namely, "because it is occasional" and "because it acquires its own nature after previously not existing"—are established.

If "occurring immediately after another entity" is intended in a general sense, then it is already established, since its existence is well-known to follow immediately after an entity that serves as its cause.

However, if what is intended is its occurrence immediately after an entity that is essentially perishable, then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). He demonstrates this with the words "occurring immediately after another entity," etc.:
"In such [an entity], there is no occurrence immediately after another entity."
Because that which has the nature of a mobile entity arises simultaneously with the entity itself,
it is "of such a kind"— that is, non-different from the very nature of the mobile object.
Indeed, for a partless entity, there is no distinct part by which its existence could be subsequent to that [entity].

Since destruction, which possesses that same nature and is non-different from it, is established at the very moment that [the entity] is established, otherwise its very nature as such would not exist; this has already been stated. (376)
Regarding what was stated—that "the cognition of the perishability of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) is itself causeless"—he shows that this too is refuted by the very same reasoning:
"Therefore," because destruction exists, all conditioned things are not eternal, and it does not follow that the cognition of their perishability is without a cause. (377)

For it is precisely because things have the property of existing for only a moment, and their forms are thus determined by that cognition, that they serve as the cause (*nimitta*) for that cognition; therefore, there is no consequence of [the cognition] being without a cause.

Now, if destruction characterized by annihilation (*pradhvaṃsa*) is intended as the property-bearer (*dharmin*), then all three reasons are unestablished (*asiddha*); this he demonstrates with the words "of annihilation," etc.
However, because cessation (*pradhvaṃsa*) is devoid of self-nature (*nairātmya*), it lacks the quality of being "subsequent" (*anantarabhāvitā*);
it does not possess the connection of "coming into existence after having not existed," just like a sky-lotus and the like.

(378) For properties such as being subsequent are based only on real entities (*vastu*) and not on non-entities (*avastu*), as in the case of a rabbit's horn and so forth; and since cessation is devoid of self-nature—that is, it is without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)—how could properties such as being subsequent be possible for it?
And by the word "ca" (and), the inclusion of the fact that [the effect] occurs only occasionally (*kādācitkatva*)— rather than arising from what did not previously exist— is intended.

If this is so—if destruction does not possess the quality of occurring immediately after [the entity]—then how could it be said that "the destruction of the entity occurs"? For it would not be logical to say that something "occurs" for that which never exists at all. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Destruction," and so forth;
[the meaning is that] when it is said "destruction occurs," it is not the case that the entity itself occurs.
But here it is the meaning that is conveyed, not the injunction of anything, according to the opinion of some (v. 379).

Even though destruction is indicated as being enjoined, nevertheless only the negation of an existing entity is perceived; there is, in the ultimate sense, no injunction of any positive thing whatsoever.

One might object: "Just as in the case of [the sentence] 'Caitra has a son,' the use of the verb 'to be' (bhavati) implies that here too, only the act of coming into being is being enjoined. To this he replies with the words "For not," and so on:
"For when a name such as 'son of Bālā' is merely applied, not every property of a donkey becomes applicable to that person. (380)
For the existence or non-existence of things does not conform merely to the application of words, since the operation of such words is dependent solely upon one's own will;
otherwise, if some person were to apply the name "bāleya" to a certain man by the force of his own desire, it would follow that all the properties of a donkey would apply to him,
for the words *bāleya* and *rāsabha* are synonyms for "donkey."
And this must necessarily be understood: namely, that there is only the negation of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of a thing, and nothing at all is being affirmed.
For if a category of entity named "destruction" were itself affirmed, then for that [destruction], there would again be no...
If something arises from a thing, why does that thing cease?
Otherwise, if another distinct entity called "destruction" were established, nothing would have arisen from the thing; so why would that thing cease? (381)
Regarding what was stated previously—that "all things would be non-existent" and so forth—he replies: "And thus, for that which consists in the destruction of an entity," and so on.

And thus, the non-existence of destruction, which consists in the annihilation of an entity, is accepted because of its separation from the nature of a real thing (*vastu*), not because it is of the nature of the absence of an entity (*bhāvābhāva*). (382)

"Thus" means because it consists in the dissociation from the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things; it does not mean that there is non-existence due to the cessation of the essential form of an existing entity. For if their destruction, characterized by the negation of intrinsic nature, were itself non-existent, then these things would be eternal.
However, since destruction—characterized by the negation of intrinsic nature—is itself of a non-existent form and yet exists for them, how could they be eternal?
However, the cause for the cognition that all conditioned phenomena are subject to destruction has already been stated.
As for what was said regarding their coexistence even if they were eternal, and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "Because it is of the nature of cessation," and so on.
In this [system], even the nature of cessation is not denoted by an injunction (*vidhi*),
and the persistence of a positive entity (*vastu-rūpa*) beyond a single moment is negated.
Therefore, no established form whatsoever is prescribed for it.
Thus, any conceptualization of permanence regarding this [destruction] is groundless (384).

Even by this statement, "there is cessation," it is not asserted that the nature of cessation is expressed in a positive form within this destruction; for it has no form whatsoever that could be enjoined.
What then? It is the persistence of the entity’s own nature beyond a single moment that is negated.

Therefore, the conceptual construction of permanence—on the grounds that this [unconditioned] is exclusively of the nature of non-existence—is entirely without foundation, because, due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), it cannot possess a form established at all times;
for properties tied to the nature of permanence or impermanence are necessarily bound to intrinsic nature.

Furthermore, as for what you have stated—that for you [Buddhists], that which is causeless is twofold, namely permanent and non-existent—that arises from ignorance of the tenets of others, since for the Buddhists who argue according to logic (*nyāya*), that which is causeless is simply non-existent.

As it was said by the Blessed One: "A Bodhisattva dwelling in the contemplation of phenomena within all phenomena does not perceive even the slightest phenomenon that is exempt from dependent origination. Therefore, those Vaibhāṣikas who conceptualize entities such as space as being substantially real are relegated to your own side and are not followers of the Son of the Śākya; thus, the presentation of their views is not appropriate here.

Thus, because all causes of destruction are incapable of producing any effect, the reason [in our argument] is not unestablished. Furthermore, the incapacity of the causes of destruction must be stated as follows:
when an entity arises from its own cause, it arises either by its very nature as something inherently perishable, or as something inherently imperishable.
If it is perishable, it has no cause for its destruction, because it perishes by virtue of having that very nature inherently.

For whatever is the nature of a thing, that thing arises from its own causes as being of such a nature; it does not require another cause for that state, just as luminosity, fluidity, heat, and solidity, having arisen with those as their very essence, do not require another cause for their state of luminosity and so forth.

It might be argued: "Just as seeds and the like, though possessing the inherent nature (*svabhāva*) of producing sprouts and so forth, do not produce them alone because they depend on other causes such as water, in the same way, an entity (*bhāva*), even if it possesses both non-perishable and perishable natures, will require another cause for its destruction. This is incorrect, because we admit that only that which has reached its final state possesses the nature of being a producer, and nothing else.
Therefore, that which possesses that nature necessarily produces [the effect] and does not depend on anything else;
however, that which remains in a granary or similar location and does not produce it does not possess that nature.
Because it is the cause of the cause, it is designated as a "cause" only figuratively and not in the primary sense; thus, there is no deviation [in the rule].
Now, if the position is that the self is imperishable, even then a cause of destruction is entirely ineffective,
because it is impossible for its nature to be altered by anything;
for instance:

If an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) did not perish immediately after its arising, then even later that very same nature would remain its state of persistence; thus, what could a cause of destruction do to it such that it would perish?

Furthermore, one might argue: "Just as copper and other substances, though possessing a solid form, undergo a change of state through contact with fire and so forth, likewise, although a thing possesses an imperishable intrinsic nature, a change is produced in it by a cause of destruction."
"Therefore, it perishes upon encountering a cause of destruction"—
this is incorrect,
for that very same thing does not become something else.

Because alteration is characterized by the arising of another intrinsic nature (svabhāva), it is as follows: that which is called "alteration"—is it something other than the entity (bhāva) or is it the entity itself? It cannot be the entity itself, because that was already produced previously from its own causes.

If, on the other hand, it were something other [than the entity], then the entity would remain established exactly as it was with the property of non-departure; thus, there would be no alteration of it.

The example of copper and so forth is likewise unestablished; for instance, when the preceding moment of hardness in copper and such things perishes due to its own inherent cessation (*svarasanirodha*), another distinct nature called "liquidity" arises from a different collection of causes consisting of fire and other auxiliary conditions as well as its own material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

Then, when that nature of liquidity perishes again through its own inherent cessation, another distinct nature called "hardness" arises from a different set of auxiliary conditions and its own material cause. Thus, there is no alteration of a single entity.
Therefore, the cause of destruction is in every way entirely ineffective; thus, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*),
nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in our own position,
nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as this has been demonstrated previously.

It might be argued: "Just as space does not depend on anything else for its corporeality, yet it is not invariably present there, so too an entity, though produced, will not necessarily be subject to destruction. This is incorrect, for there is no such thing as a produced entity that is not accepted by others as impermanent.

Since it is accepted that everything possessing a cause is impermanent, and since only those [things] are here made the subject (*pakṣa*) and no others, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*). As for those who might imagine that even though they are produced, they will nonetheless be eternal because they are indestructible—it should be understood that such things are, in the ultimate sense, included within the category of the unproduced (*akṛtaka*); therefore, by the very refutation of that [category], their refutation is also accomplished, and thus there is no fault.

Nor is it established that space and so forth are independent with respect to properties such as corporeality; for whatever property a thing lacks, it is necessarily dependent upon that very property. Indeed, no dependence of entities is posited toward a property already possessed; rather, it is only toward a property not yet attained. Thus, the example is unestablished. (384) Now, with reference to the category of the uncreated, he says: "But those which... and so forth.
However, those entities such as space which are considered uncreated do not exist at all in reality, because they are devoid of causal capacity; therefore,
the conceptual alternatives of momentariness or non-momentariness have no footing in them.
Then it would be the entity itself that might be momentary or otherwise.

(386) For if entities such as space were established as having real existence, then the consideration of properties such as momentariness could apply to them; for properties do not have independent establishment. Otherwise, their very status as properties would be lost.

Furthermore, space and the like cannot be unproduced subjects, because, being devoid of all causal efficiency (*sāmarthya*), they are objects of the conventional designation of non-existence, like the son of a barren woman.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is devoid of all causal efficiency is a non-entity (*avastu*), just like the son of a barren woman; and space and so forth are devoid of all causal efficiency. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), or rather, in reality, it is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Nor is this reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the conventional usage of "non-existent" is based solely upon this [absence of causal efficiency]; nor is it unestablished (*asiddha*), as we shall demonstrate later.
Because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa), it is not contradictory (viruddha) either.
Why, then, does the conceptual distinction between momentary and non-momentary not apply to a non-entity? To this he says: "For that whose form persists for a moment," and so forth.
For an entity whose form persists for a moment is called momentary; conversely, an entity that is pervaded by a stable form is called non-momentary. (387)
This is easily understood.

(387) Uddyotakara, however, says: "The suffix expressing possession (*matvarthīya*) is untenable in the word 'momentary' (*kṣaṇika*). For instance, if it is understood that 'momentary' means 'that which has a moment (*kṣaṇa*), where a moment is defined by the aforementioned logic as destruction (*kṣaya*'), then that is not correct because of the difference in time. For when there is destruction, the thing subject to destruction (*kṣayin*) does not exist; the possessive suffix is never seen to apply to two things existing at different times."

Furthermore, if it is said that a "moment" (kṣaṇa) is defined by the destruction immediately following the existence [of a thing], then even in that case, the thing does not possess that [moment] by means of itself; thus, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is not logical.

Alternatively, if "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) refers to things whose duration lasts for a moment—since the moment is indeed the ultimate limit of time—then those which endure for that [duration] are momentary.

This too is not tenable, because time is accepted as a mere designation (*saṃjñāmātra*), and it is not logical for a mere designation to serve as a qualifier of a real entity; to this he replies: "That which does not persist immediately after its arising," and so forth.
That nature of an entity which does not persist even for a moment after its arising is called a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*). That which possesses such [a nature] is considered "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).
(388) The moment of an entity is said to be its intrinsic nature that perishes immediately after arising; that which has this [nature] is "momentary."
And so it has been said: "A moment (kṣaṇa) is that which perishes immediately after attaining its own existence; that which possesses this [moment] is 'momentary' (kṣaṇika).

(388) Now, even if this is so, since the nature [of the thing] is not something distinct from the thing itself, the cognition "this belongs to it"—which is based on a distinction—is not tenable. To this, he says: "Even though [it is not distinct]," and so forth.
And even when there is no difference in the object, the expression "this belongs to that" is not contradicted, for a signifier arises solely through a convention established by desire.

Just as in cases such as "the nature of itself" (*svasya svabhāvaḥ*) or "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrakasya śarīram*), where although no real difference exists, the genitive case of separation (*vyatireka-ṣaṣṭhī-vibhakti*) occurs by relying on a difference imagined by the intellect, so too will it be here; for words do not necessarily conform to the actual nature of things.
What then? [They] conform to the speaker’s intention (389).

Furthermore: to whatever extent a sound is employed by speakers for a particular meaning, to that same extent it conveys that meaning by virtue of convention; however, in an ultimate sense, there is no such thing as a "base" (*prakṛti*) or an "affix" (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, this term "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*) has been applied by the learned to any entity whatsoever that does not persist beyond its arising.

Regarding such an entity intended by the word "momentary," whether the term *kṣaṇika* is used with its suffix (*sapratyaya*) or without its suffix (*pratyayarahita*), we have no great regard for this conventional expression which follows mere whim; thus he shows this with the words "not persisting beyond its arising," etc., meaning that the entity itself, which does not persist beyond its arising, is what is intended.
In that case, let a word be employed, whether it be meaningful or meaningless;
[this applies] by the phrase "thus" (evam) and "momentary" (kṣaṇikam). || 390 ||
The term *sapratyaya* means "that which exists together with a suffix (*pratyaya*) expressing possession.

(390) Thus, it has been demonstrated that if one accepts that space (*vyoman*) and so forth are unproduced, they necessarily fall within the scope of the conventional designation "non-existent. Now, demonstrating that if one instead accepts their existence, the consequence is that they must be momentary, [the author] says: "If, however," and so forth.

But if space, time, and so forth were existent, then even they would not escape this momentary destruction, as if they had been created. Regarding the phrase "as if they had been created": it means that, just like things produced by causes, they too would be subject to the same nature of momentary flux.
The meaning is "as if produced";
by this, the reason "because of existence" (sattvāt) is indicated.
Clarifying that very point, he says: "For instance," and so forth.
For instance, all those things which are indeed existent are subject to momentary destruction; this is established immediately thereafter, just like conditioned phenomena. (392)
Moreover, you accept that these things—such as space, time, and the Lord—are existent; yet, if they were devoid of momentariness, their existence would not be possible.
This is because they would be incapable of performing causal efficiency (arthakriyā), whether successively or simultaneously.
Entities are not stable; therefore, they are considered to be devoid of intrinsic substance (*niḥsattva*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever exists is all momentary, just like the momentary things established immediately prior; and you yourself accept that entities such as space (*vyoman*) and so forth exist. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), and it is thus established.
By this [term] "momentariness," one should not suspect that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*), because it has already been established;
thus he shows by the words "are intended by you" that this is a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) argument.
Otherwise, the reason would be unestablished for one of the two parties.
To explain how the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this reason is established, he says: "But if there were an absence of momentariness," and so forth.
Here, existence is intended as the reason, characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*); and that [existence] ceases when momentariness is absent.

For instance: entities perform causal efficiency either successively or simultaneously; indeed, no other mode besides succession and simultaneity is possible, because those two consist in mutual exclusion.
And this is established by direct perception itself.

For example, a jar, while successively bringing honey, water, and so forth—which are distinct from other substances—is perceived by direct perception as performing its own cognition and the fetching of water, and not simultaneously.

In this regard, it is established by direct perception that when a jar is perceived as sequentially performing various functions, or when a potter is perceived as sequentially producing bowls, jars, and so forth, he is not capable of producing them simultaneously at that very time;

nor is a jar perceived as simultaneously producing cognitions and other effects regarding its own object at that very time, rather than producing them sequentially—all of this is determined through direct perception.

Therefore, since succession is determined precisely by the exclusion of simultaneity, and simultaneity is determined precisely by the exclusion of succession, the operation of a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) determines one of the two while simultaneously excluding its opposite and indicating the absence of any other alternative. Thus, the contradiction between these two—defined by their existence through the mutual exclusion of each other's mode of occurrence—is established solely by the means of direct perception (pratyakṣa).
Consequently, because there is no third possibility, causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is pervaded by both succession and simultaneity.

And that [non-existence], ceasing when its own pervader ceases in the case of stable entities, causes their existence—defined by that [pervader]—to cease; thus, the pervasion is established. Nor can it be said that "the succession and simultaneity of entities are not established because a distinct category of time is not accepted," for we do not claim that the succession and simultaneity of entities are produced by a category of time that is a separate entity.
What then? It is produced by arising in such and such a manner;

for instance, if one [entity] experiences existence at the very same time that others experience it in exactly the same way, then all of them, arising in this manner, become the basis for the designation of simultaneity (*akrama*), just as many sprouts arise together when their causal conditions are complete.
By contrast, those things that possess a sequential designation, such as the sprout, the stalk, and the leaf,
are established through direct perception and are designated as such by people; likewise,

although the operation of a cause has for its object an entity of that same nature, it is designated according to the sequence or simultaneity pertaining to that object— thus, this objection is not valid.

Now, if a stable entity were established, then, upon the exclusion of succession and simultaneity therein, the exclusion of its capacity for causal efficiency would be established— just as, in a certain locus, the absence of a *śiṃśapā* tree follows from the absence of trees.
Otherwise, if the locus as a factual basis were not established, where could the absence of the *śiṃśapā* be perceived?
Nor is that [subject] established, because it is precisely what one intends to negate.
Even if it were admitted to be established, its rejection would not be logical, since you have accepted that the subject (*dharmin*) is established by its own nature;
consequently, this reason—“because of existence” and so forth—is also inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it occurs in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*).
This is not so;
for we do not independently employ this non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
What then? We merely employ it to bring about an undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) for the opponent.

If you accept their stable nature, then you must also not accept their capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), because the presence of succession and simultaneity— which pervade that capacity— is absent therein;
for when the pervader is absent, the pervaded cannot possibly remain,
otherwise the relationship of pervader and pervaded between the two would not exist at all.

Consequently, since the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) has ceased, their existence (*satva*) also cannot be admitted, because existence is defined by the capacity for causal efficiency;
by this means, their non-existence alone is established.

Furthermore, in the case of a dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), it is not necessary that a real entity (*vastubhūta*) as a substratum (*dharmin*) be relied upon, because what is intended to be proven there is merely the cessation of the probans (*sādhana*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) ceases.

And this [relationship] is understood from the mere statement—"in the absence of the pervader, the pervaded also does not exist"—in a general sense, even without the inclusion of a specific substratum (*dharmī*), provided that the relationship of pervasion between the two properties existing as the pervaded and the pervader has been established;

just as it is said, "In the absence of a tree, there is no *śiṃśapā*. As it has been stated: "Therefore, in the case of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), a locus is not necessarily required here;
for its [the pervader's] absence implies the absence of that [the pervaded], even by such a statement."
Thus [ends] 392,
He demonstrates that it is not logical for a stable entity to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) sequentially, beginning with the words "The effects," and so forth:
"For effects are delayed due to the absence of their causes."
When the efficient cause is present, by what could their delay be caused?
(395) For an effect does not come into being or cease to be according to its own will; rather, its existence or non-existence conforms to the presence or absence of its cause.
