In this regard, if that entity were stable and of a single nature, and thus remained at all times as the cause for all effects, then why would all those effects—which require nothing more than its mere existence—not arise all at once, such that they would instead occur in a sequence?
"Delay" means procrastination;
by means of that, even his subsequent task would be accomplished beforehand.
The meaning is that because the cause possesses unimpeded capacity, it is like the desired effect;
thus [the author] anticipates the opponent's reply with the words "But even so," and so forth.
Moreover, there exist successive auxiliary causes for that which is permanent,
depending upon which it produces the collection of effects in a sequential manner.
(396) Even though a stable entity is present at all times, its auxiliary causes nevertheless come together with it in succession.
Therefore, [the opponent] argues that "in dependence upon that [auxiliary], it will produce its effects sequentially";
to this, [the author] replies with the words beginning "sādhu" (well said).
This may be true; however, do they become its auxiliaries by being causes of its suitable form, or by performing a single purpose?
If they were causes of its suitable form, then that entity would be produced by them.
And that [nature] is impossible to produce, because its own essential nature remains as it is at that time.
Or, if its essential nature were produced, its eternity would be lost.
Therefore, if this excellence is distinct [from the entity], how can it be the agent? 398–399.

For no auxiliary cause whatsoever is possible for that which is eternal; to explain: an auxiliary cause would have to exist either by imparting an excellence (*atiśaya*), as for instance the earth and other factors are auxiliaries to a seed by imparting specific states such as swelling;
or by performing a single purposeful action together, as for instance color and other factors are to the eye in the mere act of opening [the eyes] to see a form.
Of these, the first alternative is not tenable.

For instance, this excellence (*atiśaya*) being imparted to it by its auxiliary causes must either be non-different from its own nature, or different, or both, or neither—these are the four positions as stated by the Ājīvikas. Among these, the first position is not tenable; because, like the entity's own nature, it would be eternally present due to its non-distinction from it, and since what already exists cannot be produced, or else, if it were produced, it would follow that the entity itself is produced just like that excellence, and consequently, its permanence would be lost.
Now, if the second position is held, then because the effect arises solely from the excellence [of the auxiliary factors], it follows that the entity is not the agent;
"this" refers to the eternal object.
He clarifies this very point with the verse beginning "tasmin sati" and so forth:
"For when that exists, there is the arising of effects; because of its absence, there is non-arising. Thus, it alone is established as the cause. (400)
"In that" means "when there is an excess";
"thus" [is the meaning].
Because it follows the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with that [object],
[the author] anticipates the opponent's response right here with the words "But even so" (*athāpi*) and so forth:
"Nevertheless, because of its connection with that [object], it indeed possesses the status of a cause."
What relationship is desired between those two? It cannot be identity (*tādātmya*), because there is no non-distinction [between them].
Nor can it be origination from that (*tadutpatti*), because that would entail simultaneity; and consequently, there would be the arising of effects simultaneously. (401–402)
"Teneti" means "exceedingly";
"tasyāpi" means "of that also."
He provides the answer with the words "What connection can there be for that which is eternal," and so forth;
the meaning is: what connection [could there be]?—none at all.

For the relation is indeed of only two kinds: identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*). In this case, it cannot be characterized by identity, because difference has been admitted; nor can it be characterized by origination from that, because the [effect] arises solely from its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*).

If, therefore, it is admitted that [the effect] arises from those successive excellences (*atiśaya*), then, because the excellences are produced solely by that [cause], they would arise all at once; and consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of all effects arising simultaneously,
since the cause possessing those excellences would be present at all times.
In that case as well, if there were dependence on another, an infinite regress would result.
Therefore, an effect cannot be produced even once from that [cause] alone, because there is no connection [between them].

Now, if it is argued that even in that case, because the production of excellence depends upon auxiliary causes, the effects do not occur simultaneously due to the gradual production of excellence—that would be incorrect; for in this way, there would be an infinite regress.

For instance—even in that case, the status of being a "cooperative cause" (sahakārin) must be asserted by virtue of its producing another excellence (atiśaya). Since that excellence is distinct [from the entity], the relationship between them is unestablished; if it were produced [by the entity], there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of its being produced all at once. If, in that case as well, there is a dependence on further cooperative causes, then this very same inquiry recurs, resulting in an infinite regress (anavasthā). Consequently, the relationship of the entity with the excellence would never be established, and since that is unestablished, the effect would not arise from it; rather, the effect arises from the excellence alone.

If the relation is inherence (*samavāya*), that too is considered in this way: is that which is held to be the inherent cause (*samavāyin*) of it [the effect] something that provides assistance to it? 404.
Or else, if the first alternative— that it is not so— is accepted, then that very production [of the effect] has already been refuted immediately prior. Furthermore,
its connection with the excellence (atiśaya) cannot be characterized as "arising from that" (tadutpatti).

What then? It is characterized by inherence (*samavāya*) in that [substratum], because that excellence inheres in that eternal substratum. Showing that this is incorrect, he says: "In that case too," and so forth, ending with "or not so."

The connection is that "it is not intended to be an inherent property (samavāyin) because it is not a benefactor (upakārī) to that [substance]. In that regard, according to the first position, since the benefit is non-different from the object being benefited, that very relationship characterized by its production would have to be accepted;
and that has already been refuted immediately above.
404 405 Now, if the second position is held, then, due to the absence of any distinction, everything would be inherent in everything.

He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "anye'pi" and so forth: "If it is not considered that this [entity] is a benefactor to that [inherence], then all other entities as well would likewise be inherent, because there is no distinction. (406)
"It is just so," because it is not distinct [from the object] due to its lack of efficacy, like the desired object itself.

With reference to both the positions of "both" and "neither," he says: "Because the conceptual alternatives of difference and non-difference are each individually negated, the dual nature of that excellence belonging to the entity becomes excluded. (407)
By the very refutation of each individual alternative, the alternative consisting of both is also refuted, because there exists no alternative consisting of both apart from those two.

Furthermore, since the abandonment or acceptance of one form is inseparable from the acceptance or abandonment of the other form, it is illogical for a real entity to possess the nature of being both [existent and non-existent] or neither; for it is not possible for affirmation and negation, which are mutually contradictory, to apply to a single thing at the same time, as that would entail the loss of its unity.
And this has been established in the examination of the person (*pudgala*) and so forth; he demonstrates that as follows:
"In the examinations of the person and so forth, because the two categories have been refuted, there is no excellence of a dual nature, nor is there one that is neither. (408)

Now, if the second position is adopted—that it is by virtue of performing a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*) that it possesses auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), as some have said: "It does not depend upon auxiliaries, nor is it the producer of the effect when separated from them; for its nature is established by its very essence (*nisargasiddha*) such that it is a producer only when all auxiliary causes are present, like the final cause (*antyahetu*), and not alone. Therefore, even though it exists, there is no consequence of the effect being produced at all times."
He demonstrates this as follows: "Now," and so forth:
"If the eternal [cause] does not depend upon auxiliary conditions, nevertheless, being devoid of them, it is not a productive agent, unlike the final cause. (409)
This is its own inherent nature; for it possesses causal efficiency only in the presence of those [auxiliaries]. Therefore, the effect does not occur at all times, even though that [nature] exists.
Not so.
This should be connected with the word "agent" (kāraka),
serving as a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) like the final cause;
or alternatively, it is connected with the subsequent term "agency" (kārakatva) as a similar example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
The suffix *vati* should also be applied after a word ending in the sixth case (*ṣaṣṭhyanta*), in the sense of "in the state of being that" (*tadbhāve*);
that is, even when there is the existence (*sadbhāve*) of that eternal category (*padārtha*).
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "Let it be so," and so forth.

"Let it be so; however, if that very nature which is considered to belong to it in the state of completeness is also held to exist in the state of incompleteness, then the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) would have to be eternal.

(411) Let this conceptualization stand; however, this must be examined here: Is that same nature which belongs to it in the state of completeness with its auxiliaries also present in the state of incompleteness, or is it something else? If it is the same, then it follows that the auxiliaries themselves must also be eternal.
He asks, "How so? and says: "Because when that which has a nature connected to them exists, those [others] also persist."
If it were otherwise, its incomplete form would lose its unity.
Furthermore, because of this mutual dependence, there can be no successive arising of effects.
The analysis of the compound is: "that whose nature is connected with those auxiliary causes."
"Of those too" means that,
like the dragging of the shackles when a man bound in shackles is being dragged, there is likewise a following along of those auxiliary causes.
For in this way, that very [entity] persists without abandoning its prior nature;

for if it does not abandon the nature connected with the auxiliary cause, then by the force of not abandoning the nature connected with that [auxiliary], there follows— by implication— the non-abandonment of the auxiliaries as well,
since being related necessarily depends upon the counter-correlate.
Otherwise, that very thing would not be its nature; as for the position that it is something else, he says "and if it were another," and so forth.

For if it is maintained that its form, when devoid of auxiliary causes, is something other [than its original nature], then there follows the undesirable consequence of the loss of its permanence, because the form is non-different from the entity itself.
Therefore, even when there is dependence upon auxiliary causes, it is not logical for stable entities to perform causal efficiency sequentially.

Nor does it occur simultaneously; this he demonstrates with the words, "And simultaneity is certainly not accepted," and so forth: "And simultaneity is certainly not accepted, because their effects are seen to perish and are seen to occur in succession. (413) Even by others, simultaneity of the effects of eternal entities is certainly not accepted.
For instance—these effects are described as belonging to eternal entities:

pleasure, pain, and so forth belong to the self; sounds belong to space; successive cognitions belong to the mind; gross objects arise from atoms through the sequence of dyads and so on; and all things produced belong to time, space, the Lord (Īśvara), and the like.
Furthermore, the sequential emergence of these is well-established through direct perception itself.
Thus, by accepting simultaneity, both contradiction with direct perception and contradiction with one's own tenets have been stated.
Now, demonstrating the contradiction with inference, he says: "All [cognitions] without exception," and so forth.
If that entity which consists of causal efficiency ceases after having performed all its effects simultaneously, then its momentary destruction is established.

To explain: there are two possible positions regarding whether, after performing all its effects at once, that nature of his which is capable of purposeful action (arthakriyā-samartha) ceases or rather persists.
In that regard, if the position is that [the entity] ceases, then its momentariness is established,
because there is the arising of different successive natures at every moment and the spontaneous destruction of each preceding nature.
If that same nature persists, it would produce the effect once again; how then can the capacity of that which is of a nature incapable of acting be admitted?
For, being devoid of all capacity, it is like a lotus in the sky.
"All non-existent things are non-momentary, because capacity is the defining characteristic of a real entity" (416).

Now, if the second alternative is adopted, then, while that nature of its capable self persists, it would have to produce the effect again, because it has not abandoned its previous form, just like its prior state;
consequently, the very same sequence would have occurred, and thus the assertion of simultaneity is contradicted by inference.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even if that [permanent entity] lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through either succession or simultaneity, nevertheless, its capacity (*sāmarthya*) certainly exists. To this he says: "Of that which has a nature incapable of acting," and so forth.
For the capacity of entities is established as the basis for the production of effects;
and how could that which performs no action whatsoever be capable?
Otherwise, why could one not establish the causal capacity even for things such as a sky-lotus?
One might argue: "Even if its capacity has ceased, its existence (*sattva*) has not ceased;
therefore, because the reason 'because of existence' (*sattvāt*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*," [the author] says: "Non-existent," and so forth.

For this alone is the defining characteristic of a real entity (*vastu*), namely, the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). If that [capacity] has ceased, how can the nature of being a real entity—whose very definition it is—subsist in those things?

Thus, it is established that space and other such things, which are intended to be non-momentary, are fit to be treated as non-existent, like the son of a barren woman, because they are devoid of the capacity for causal efficiency through either successive or simultaneous action. (415)
Now, if this nature of being a real entity (vastutva), characterized as causal efficiency (śakti), is not accepted,
then the definition of real entities as set forth by the opponents would have to be rejected.

Moreover, it might be argued: "If the definition of a real entity (*vastu*) were exclusively characterized by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), then all this [that follows] would be appropriate.
But if that is so, what else must be stated as the definition of a real entity?
For instance, the reason why non-reality (*avastutva*) is attributed to things such as a rabbit's horn is precisely the absence of the capacity for causal efficiency."

The meaning is that since existence and non-existence are defined by their mutual exclusion, it follows by implication that the very capacity for causal efficiency— which is the opposite of the definition of non-existence— is established as the definition of existence.

Here, he anticipates the opponent's reply: "If it is held that the connection with 'Being' (sattā) is the definition of things, that is not so, because [that connection] is unestablished due to [the non-existence of] inherence and the like; or else, how could one thing be the definition of another? (418)

For the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) is not the defining characteristic of a real entity (*vastu*); what then? It is the connection with existence (*sattā*), that is to say, inherence in existence (*sattāsamavāya*).
The remainder of the sentence is that it is not logical for that [causal efficiency] to be the defining characteristic of a real entity.

Because inherence (*samavāya*) and so forth are unestablished— the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) including existence (*sattā*)— if inherence and the rest were established, then inherence would be the defining characteristic of a real entity (*vastu*).
Since these two are the very subjects under discussion,

and because there exists the probative evidence (bādhaka-pramāṇa) that will be stated later— or rather, because of the aforementioned probative evidence itself— there is no establishment of either existence (sattā) or inherence (samavāya).
Since existence cannot be established as having a relationship with anything else— because it cannot be assisted by anything—
it has been stated that there can be no mutual relationship between two things that do not assist one another, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore,

it must be stated what the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is for those two— existence and inherence— as well as for the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*), if they are indeed real entities (*vastu*).

For existence (sattā) does not inhere in inherence (samavāya) or in the ultimate particulars (viśeṣas), nor does it inhere in existence itself; rather, according to the established doctrine, existence is that which causes the three categories—substance, quality, and action—to be existent. Therefore, this definition of a real entity (vastulakṣaṇa) is non-pervasive (avyāpin).
Granted that existence (*sattā*) and so forth may be established;
nevertheless, inherence in existence (*sattā-samavāya*) is not a suitable definition, because it is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*).
For one distinct entity cannot be the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of another distinct entity, such that the latter could serve as the definition of the former.

To explain: for one of dull intellect who does not understand the true nature of a thing, when its definition is being discussed, it is that very intrinsic nature (svabhāva) which, as perceived through its exclusion from something else, must be stated as the definition by which he determines that very thing to be the actual nature of the object. For example, earth is defined by its hardness;
and no other entity can be the nature of another entity, because that would entail the loss of their distinctness. Therefore, how could anything else serve as its definition?

Since the word *lakṣaṇa* has been introduced as denoting intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), some say: "What subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is there against the existence of such an entity which, even for an omniscient one, does not produce a cognition? For it is by means of such [an entity] that this pervasion (*vyāpti*) would be established through universal inclusion—that whatever exists is all momentary."
Nor does his omniscience suffer loss through not knowing that [unconditioned thing], because his scope is restricted solely to knowable objects;
for one would be non-omniscient only by failing to know a thing that is capable of being known, but that [unconditioned thing] is not knowable,
as it is incapable of producing cognition even when one strives to do so.

He replies to them with the words "And all," and so forth: "And every activity, such as the investigation of an object, is appropriate for one who seeks purposeful action and possesses an undisturbed mind, but not for one who is like a madman. (419)
Therefore, it is only for that which is useful to someone,
in some way, at some place, and at some time, that the establishment of its existence is logical;
and it is precisely the momentariness of such an object that is being proven.
Pervasion (*vyāpti*), which involves the inclusion of all cases, is stated to reside in that very [locus].
For this entire investigation into the existence or non-existence of an object—that is, of any mere thing—is undertaken by one who seeks causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and not out of mere habit;
otherwise, one would be a madman.

Therefore, for a discerning person, it is only with respect to that collection of objects which serves some purposeful function—either directly or indirectly—for certain seekers of utility, at a particular place and time, that a determination of reality is appropriate;
not otherwise, because there would be no basis [for such a determination] and it would be purposeless. This is the sense.
By the inclusion of the word "etc. (ādi), the investigation of specific objects such as fire, water, and so forth is understood.

Furthermore, regarding that which is well-established among those who act with foresight—that only that which is capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*) is a real entity—it is precisely that nature, namely the nature of being capable of purposeful action, whose momentariness we establish.
Since this is intended as the reason (*hetu*) characterized by the capacity for purposeful action, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*);
for the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of such a reason with the probandum is established through a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāra*).

For that pervasion of the reason which is demonstrated in a general manner, without making a distinction between the subject (pakṣa) and the similar instances (sapakṣa), is the pervasion that encompasses all cases (sarvopasaṃhārā vyāptiḥ).

Now, as to why the status of being a real entity (*vastutva*) is not accepted even for that which is devoid of the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*), he says "niḥśeṣa... and so forth:
"But that which is devoid of all capacities, resembling the son of a barren woman..."

Even the mind of the Omniscient One never becomes a cause for this [unconditioned]. For no such thing is ever produced there, since its form as an effect and so forth is not observed; therefore, the wise do not establish the existence of anything that lacks a causal basis.

No purpose whatsoever is served by establishing momentariness in that regard; furthermore, any objection raised therein is fruitless—even with respect to the mind of an omniscient being. (424) "Even [in the case] of the mind of an omniscient one."
The word "also" (api) implies not only [the perception] of a moment of the same kind, but also of effects such as the holding of water;
for it says "from the non-perception of the effect's form and so forth.
Here, "effect" (kārya) refers to its result; "form" (rūpa) refers to its intrinsic nature (svabhāva); and by the word "and so forth" (ādi), its location, time, and specific state are included.
The meaning is that for such an entity, there is no distinction whatsoever from things like a hare’s horn;
nor is there any purpose served for one seeking causal efficiency by proving momentariness in such a non-existent thing,
because it is incapable of either attaining what is beneficial or avoiding what is harmful, whether perceived or unperceived.
As it has been said: "What is the use of investigations for those seeking causal efficacy regarding that which is incapable of such efficacy?
What is the use of a lustful woman examining whether a eunuch is handsome or ugly?"

Therefore, the objection raised by the opponent—asking, "How is it understood that this is momentary? and so forth—is entirely futile, because the proponent does not intend to prove [the subject] as being momentary. 422–423.

Now, [the author] demonstrates that the definition of a real entity (*vastu-lakṣaṇa*) as "the capacity for causal efficiency" (*arthakriyā-sāmarthya*) is also incorrect because it is over-extensive (*ativyāpitva*): "But surely," and so forth—"But surely, even sky-lotuses and the like possess the capacity for causal efficiency."
Nor do these exist as real entities by virtue of being the cause of their own cognition.

For instance, things such as "sky-lotuses" are not capable of performing a causal function characterized by the production of cognitions such as "sky-lotus, sky-lotus," and yet they do not exist in an ultimate sense; therefore, this definition of existence as "capacity" is over-extensive (*ativyāpin*).
Regarding this, he states the rebuttal: "It is indeed without an objective basis," and so forth.

This cognition—which arises solely from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of verbal expressions regarding such things as a sky-lotus—proceeds even though it is entirely without an objective basis. (426)

The causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) of things such as the sky-lotus is unestablished, because those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) arise solely through the maturation of their own habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and are therefore without an objective basis (*nirālambana*).
Now, he states what constitutes the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the production [of effects] from such things as the sky-lotus: "But if non-existence were the cause," and so forth.

If non-existence were the cause, then [the cognition] would arise continuously; for non-existence, being devoid of any specific qualities, never requires anything else. (427) That of which the sky-lotus and so forth are the cause is described as such; when that state exists—that is, when the condition of having the sky-lotus and so forth as its cause is present—the cognition of that sky-lotus and so forth would always occur—it would be produced—because its cause is eternally present and unimpaired.

Nor is it logical for that [cause], which cannot be assisted by others, to depend upon them, such that it might produce [the effect] only occasionally due to a deficiency of auxiliary factors; with the words "even in the case of momentary things," etc., he raises the objection regarding the view of Bhadanta Yogasena.
Even if entities are momentary, how indeed can there be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)?

For the initial auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) do not impart any excellence (*viśeṣa*) to one another. Since [the effect] is established in its entirety at the very moment of birth, it cannot arise later; for an entity does not exist prior to its birth.
If a particularity were to arise from that which is devoid of particularity, why would an effect not [also] arise?
Nor are those collections of auxiliary causes distinguished by anything else, for they are subject to the same logical inquiry; furthermore, there would be an infinite regress for you.
Since they do not perform causal efficiency either successively or simultaneously, their reliance on momentariness is therefore futile.
Likewise, when no excellence whatsoever is produced by auxiliary factors, [momentariness is likewise futile].
Then the continuum would have to be admitted as being always without distinction.
(432) If destruction were causeless, this [destruction] would exist at the very beginning; if its occurrence did not exist at the beginning, how could it exist at the end? (433)
If it is maintained that there is no cause for the destruction of entities other than their own causes, how can they be contradictory in some cases and not in others?
For he [the opponent] has said: "Even if entities are momentary, there is indeed a contradiction regarding their causal efficiency (arthakriyā) in terms of either succession or simultaneity."

Whether they are themselves capable or incapable: if they are capable, then they would not depend upon auxiliary causes, for it is not logical for that which is already capable to have any dependence;
yet if they are incapable, even so, their dependence on such causes is all the more illogical.

For instance: those factors that move within the first complex do not attain mutual distinction from one another, because in the states of having arisen or not yet arisen, they are neither benefactors nor beneficiaries due to their existence or non-existence;
and consequently, since they are undifferentiated in the first state, there could be no production of a subsequent distinct moment from them.
Furthermore, if a subsequent moment that is no different from those [preceding moments] were to arise, why would the effect not also arise?

Nor is it reasonable to say that they have arisen from a preceding complex (kalāpa) that is distinguished [from others], because there is likewise an absence of mutual distinction among the members included within that complex;
if a distinction were to arise for them from something else, there would be an infinite regress.
Thus, since there is no distinction [between the permanent and the momentary], how can an effect arise from an undifferentiated collection of causes?
If it were produced from something undifferentiated, everything would arise from everything;

and consequently, even though causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible through either succession or simultaneity, just as these [momentary things] exist as performers of causal efficiency, so too will eternal things exist. Therefore, your recourse to their momentariness is useless.
Therefore, the meaning is that the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Nor is it reasonable to say that the production of an effect will occur only when the continuum has reached a particular state and not at all times;
for, according to the principle already stated, there is no distinction produced by auxiliary causes, since the continuum remains entirely undifferentiated at all times.
Nor is it reasonable to say that a "continuum" (*santati*) is a particularity restricted solely to its own material cause (*svopādāna-kāraṇa*),
because this contradicts what is observed;
for instance, it is observed that the appearance or cessation of an effect depends on the presence or absence of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*).
Furthermore, if a particularity were dependent solely upon its own material cause, then it would follow that the cause would produce its effect independently of auxiliary conditions;
moreover, according to the principle already stated, since the continuum would always be without distinction,
the production of specific effects such as shards from jars and the like would be impossible.

If destruction, characterized by the cessation of the continuum of homogeneous moments, were causeless, then because it would be independent [of causes], it would have to occur even prior [to the existence of the entity];
if it does not occur at the beginning, it would not occur later either, since there is no difference from the prior state.

Furthermore, if one does not accept that for the destruction of entities there is another distinct continuum as a cause apart from their own causes, then how could fire and the like be the opposites of cold and the like? For it is not logical that something which performs no function can be an opposite, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for in this way, everything would absurdly follow as being the opposite of everything else.

Therefore, the application of non-apprehension by way of contradiction, as well as the formal establishment of [the prohibitions against] killing living beings and so forth, would be extremely difficult to accomplish; this is the intended meaning.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said," and so forth.
It is said: in the initial stage, these [causes] do not assist one another;
rather, they become co-operative causes through the performance of a single purposeful action.
Even though there is no mutual assistance, these are not indistinguishable from one another.
Arising from the power of their own material causes (*upādāna*), they produce the complex of parts (*kalāpa*) individually.
For it is indeed from that which is capable [of producing the effect] that the production of the effect occurs; yet this does not render the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) useless.
To explain: there are two kinds of auxiliary status—namely, by way of performing a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritā*) and by way of mutual assistance (*parasparopakāritā*).
In this regard, with respect to an immediate effect, there is only the performance of a single purposeful action, not mutual assistance,

because it is impossible to impart a distinction to [the cause] within a single moment due to its indivisibility. However, with respect to a mediated effect, since a subsequent distinguished moment arises from them through mutual influence, there is the nature of cooperation characterized by mutual assistance, because they produce the mediated effect through mutual assistance with respect to the continuum (*santāna*).

In that regard, although there is no mutual distinction among those factors occurring in the first stage, their state of cooperation is nonetheless entirely uncontradicted, because they perform a single purposeful action.

Nor are they indistinguishable with respect to the production of a subsequent moment characterized as an immediate successor, for each has arisen from its own preceding causes and conditions as being individually capable of producing such a collection of subsequent effects.

Those causes and conditions also arise from their own respective causes and conditions, and those [in turn] from others; since an infinite series of causes is thus accepted as being beginningless, even this infinite regress is not a fault.
Furthermore, although each possesses its own capacity, there is no pointlessness regarding the others, because they have arisen in that manner through the power of their own causes.
Nor is their separate existence possible, due to the absence of any such cause.
Nor [do they produce it] later, because of their momentariness;
that is to say, the individual producers of the aggregate are each capable of producing the aggregate existing in the second moment.

The mention of "its own material cause" (*svopādāna*) should be understood as being intended to negate the utility provided by auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) occurring at the first stage; it does not mean that some effect can arise from its material cause alone, because everything arises from a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), as it has been said: "Nothing arises from a single [cause]; everything arises from a causal complex."
From that time forward, whatever distinctions arose were produced by him.
Because they possess that nature as their inherent character (*prakṛti*), those [factors] are conducive to it.
From that point onward— that is, beginning from the time subsequent to the second moment—
they are produced by that.

Why are they produced by specific causes brought about by auxiliary factors? Because their nature is of that form—that is, those whose nature (prakṛti), or intrinsic character (svabhāva), consists in being produced by specific causes brought about by particular auxiliaries, are so described;
[this refers] to those things which are conducive to that [result].
The phrase "because it has that as its nature" (*tadrūpaprakṛtitvāt*) is to be connected [to the preceding].
In the expression "useful for that" (*tadupayoginam*), the word *ca* (and) is indicated elided; thus, the meaning becomes this:

since those particularities (*viśeṣa*) existing in the second moment—which are useful as causes for the effect existing in the third moment—possess a nature capable of producing an effect born from auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) that produce particularities, the particularities existing in the third and subsequent moments are produced by them.
He says— beginning with "niyata" and so forth— how this rule also applies to these [things]:
"In this world, entities possessing fixed and inconceivable powers [arise] at every moment."
They are not subject to questioning, just as the power to burn resides in fire.

(438) Indeed, the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities do not admit of being questioned, because their specific natures are brought about by a succession of their own causes and conditions. This is just like the burning capacity of fire; for these [entities] arise with distinct powers at every moment through the application of successive and antecedent conditions.
Therefore, even if they are perceived as having an identical form due to some similarity, their intrinsic nature remains indeed distinct.
Therefore, this [argument] that "only a certain thing is the cause of a certain thing, and not everything is the cause of everything" is trivial;
for the word *bhavanti* means "they arise."
Regarding what was also said— that if destruction were without a cause— he replies: "But that destruction which consists in the cessation of the continuum (*santāna*) has no cause," and so forth.
Even at its end, no [inherent] existence exists; likewise, birth is prevented.
Furthermore, the production of dissimilar shards and the like occurs only with a cause;
yet that too does not arise at the very beginning, because at that time the cause is non-existent.
For destruction is of two kinds: that consisting in the cessation of the continuum (*santānoccheda*), and that characterized by the production of a dissimilar continuum (*visadṛśasantānotpāda*).

In this regard, if it is said with reference to destruction in the form of the cessation of the continuum, that is incorrect; for there is no existence of that [destruction] even at its end, because it is devoid of any nature (*nīrūpatvāt*). Therefore, why is it asked, "How could it exist even at the end?
Since its existence at any time is not admitted, the consequence you draw regarding the presence or absence of its existence at the beginning and the end is entirely inconsistent.
Only this: birth—that is, origination—by way of the linking of a subsequent similar moment, is what is negated in that case;
for instance, the destruction of a jar or the like does not occur, meaning that very thing does not come to be.
However, nothing at all is affirmed therein.
Now, if the second type of destruction, characterized by the arising of a dissimilar moment, is intended, its lack of a cause is unproven;
for it is admitted that, as a real entity (*vastu*), it arises through the power of causes such as a hammer.
For this very reason, it does not arise at the beginning, because its own causes, such as the hammer, are absent at that time.
In order to establish the resolution of contradictions, he says: "It is of two kinds," and so forth.
Momentary entities are of two kinds: some, such as fire and the like, are causes of the diminution of cold and so forth; others are not of that nature.
However, people who have not perceived the true reality imagine a contradiction [between these].

Even in the case of the relationship between cause and effect, which was mentioned first, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator occurs in many ways; however, this relationship of things is not at all real.
For that very reason, it is also said that there is "the apprehension of contradiction."

For some entities are causes of the diminution of certain others through a sequence of arising with increasingly slower moments—for example, fire and the like are causes of cold and the like; others are not so, meaning they are not causes of diminution—for example, those same fires and the like are not causes of the diminution of smoke and the like. In this regard, although the causal relationship exists in the first-mentioned causes of diminution, the world—its light of knowledge being obscured by the cataract of ignorance—mistakes them for being contradictory.
The phrase "in various ways" refers to distinctions such as fire being the opposite of cold, wind of a lamp, and light of darkness;

however, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there is no relationship of sublated and sublator between entities whatsoever. This is because that which exists is established in its entirety, and it is impossible to effect a change in its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, given the dilemma of whether such a change is distinct from or non-distinct from the entity itself, in either case its production is impossible.
Since even a non-existent thing, by virtue of its very lack of reality, cannot produce anything, the contradictory is ineffective in both ways.

For this very reason, the Teacher stated that the cognition of contradiction arises because there is an absence [of the effect] when another [contradictory] is present, despite the cause being complete.
The meaning is that "the cognition of contradiction" refers to the determination of contradiction, but not to an ontological contradiction.
The word *api* has the sense of *ca* (and), and it should be understood as following immediately after the word *eva*, with its grammatical function shifted.

With the words "But surely... and so forth, [the author] raises an objection from the perspective of Jaimini and others, namely that the thesis of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):
"But surely, when the operation of the senses is present, there arises a recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in the form 'this is that very same thing,' which is unshakable and uncontradicted. (444)
Consequently, this sublation by perception (pratyakṣabādha) becomes unavoidable in all reasons adduced for the purpose of establishing momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga). To explain:

immediately following the operation of the sense organs, there arises with respect to mountains, bodies, thunderbolts, and so forth, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called recognition (pratyabhijñā), in the form "this is that very same thing," which negates the momentary destruction of entities.

Although recognition is indeed observed in the case of nails, hair, grass, and so forth that have grown back, nevertheless, there is no lack of validity in the two recognitions concerning diamonds and the like, because their objects are not sublated;
for this very reason, it is said: "unshakable" means "unsublated."

The point is this: just because a cognition of hair produced by eyes impaired by darkness is not found to be valid, it is not logical for one with clear vision to declare that even an ocular cognition produced by clear eyes—which has real hair as its object—is invalid.
In that regard, he states its nature as being free from doubt by means of its unshakability, since there is an absence of such doubt as "Is this the same [person] or another?"
By the term "unsublated" (abādhita), non-erroneousness is indicated.
He refutes this with the words "Certainly not" and so forth:

"Indeed, recognition cannot be established as perception, because its object is an indescribable nature of a thing, yet it is both associated with verbal expression and free from verbal expression. (446)
Furthermore, recognition is erroneous; it is distinct from each individual perception because it functions by determining non-difference even with respect to things that possess different forms.

In this regard, its status as perception is first of all unestablished; for since the characteristic of being a real entity (vastutva) lacks concomitance, it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (*samaya*) for it.
The cognition grasping that [object] is, as it were, a mental verbalization; for it is impossible to grasp an object whose relation [to a word] has been apprehended by conjoining it with a word.
Therefore, being a perception, it must necessarily be free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), because its object is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
And because it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is non-erroneous;

therefore, the experts declare that this definition of perception—which conforms to the logical principle that "each [instance of] perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous"—is established.

Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not free from conceptual construction, because it is experienced in the form of internal verbalization (*antarjalpa*), such as "this is that very same thing."
Nor is it non-erroneous, because it functions by determining non-difference among things that are actually different.

He asks, "How so? and says: "If this [cognition] were to have as its object a form previously prepared, then it would indeed arise previously, because it exists for that purpose, just like the previous cognition. (448)

For if this [subsequent cognition] had as its object the thing already previously perceived, then it would have been produced and desired at that very time, because its causal conditions would be complete insofar as they have that [previous object] as their object, just like the previous cognition; for "tādarthya" means that which has that as its object—
namely, that previously known entity or thing being its object— and the state of having that as its object is "tādarthya."
And it is not thus; he states the reversal of the reductio (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*) as follows:
"And it is not thus; therefore, this is not considered to be the grasper of that object."
Because it arises at the same time as that cognition, like the cognition of another object;
and because it functions toward a differentiated form through the determination of non-difference, this [cognition] remains erroneous, like the cognition of a magical ball. || 449-450 ||

The formal arguments (*prayoga*) are as follows: If something does not occur even when a certain factor is present in its entirety, it does not have that factor as its object. For example, auditory consciousness does not arise with respect to color even when color is present in its entirety; likewise, recognition does not occur at the time of perceiving a diamond (*vajra*) and so forth, even when they are present in their entirety. This is because the pervading property (*vyāpaka*) is not perceived.

Thus, if the diamond and so forth were eternal and independent of other factors, recognition having them as its object would necessarily have occurred previously, since its causes would be unimpaired. Yet it does not occur; therefore, its impermanence is established.

Furthermore, because activity proceeds by determining non-difference among things that are actually different—just like the cognition of a magical sphere—this [cognition] is an error; thus, this [argument] remains entirely valid.
For this very reason, the claim that its object is uncontradicted is also unestablished, since its object is contradicted by the very same reason that proves the aforementioned erroneous nature.

Furthermore, its validity does not exist because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, just as in the case of memory; demonstrating this, he says: "That which has been accomplished," and so forth.
Furthermore, since it operates upon an object for which the action has already been accomplished— like memory and so forth—
it is not logical for this [recollection] to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it lacks the sense of being an instrument (*karaṇa*).
For that alone which is the most excellent instrument for the accomplishment of the act of cognition is called the "most effective factor" (*sādhakatama*) and the "means of valid cognition."

Furthermore, if recognition were to have as its object a thing already grasped by a prior means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, since it would not be the most effective instrument (*asādhakatama*) for an object for which the act of cognition has already been accomplished, how could it possibly attain the status of a *pramāṇa*?
Otherwise, even memory would possess the status of a *pramāṇa*;
moreover, being one whose status as a *pramāṇa* has not yet been established, it cannot serve as a sublater (*bādhaka*), as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

It might be argued: "Let it be that this [recognition] has no independent validity; nevertheless, by taking as its object the same entity as before, it certainly sublates momentariness. This is incorrect. For it does not have the preceding object as its domain in an ultimate sense, because it is a conceptual construction (*mānasa-jalpa*). Rather, although its actual object is something else entirely, it arises through the power of delusion as a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object previously perceived. Thus, it is called "having the previously perceived object as its domain" only by virtue of that determination. Therefore, how could the refutation of momentariness be established on the basis of this recognition, which is inherently erroneous?
With the words "present" and so forth, he points out the lack of proof for the charge of grasping what has already been grasped according to the view of Kumārila:
"For existence at the present time was not apprehended by the previous cognition."
If there is a distinction in this [recognition] that does not exist in memory, it is as follows:
memory arises with respect to merely what was previously cognized; however, this recognition—"This is that very same thing"—is something additional. (452–453)

For he says: "Indeed, the present existence of the object was not apprehended by the previous perception, because that [previous perception] did not arise with the form of grasping [the object] as 'this is that very same thing.
Therefore, there is a distinction between this recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) and memory.
To explain how [there is a distinction], he says: "The previous," and so forth.
For recollection proceeds by grasping only the form of a previous cognition as "that";
recognition, however, grasps an additional objective form as "this," and is thus distinct from—and superior to—recollection; this is the meaning of "distinguished."
Therefore, having sublated both doubt and error, recognition attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Regarding the question "Why do those two invalidate it?", he states the reason: "Because they are non-existent once [the object] is known.
Since doubt and error are both non-existent once [the object] is known, recognition (pratyabhijñā) certainly attains the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by subverting them. || 454 ||
Because those two do not exist when the object is known, it is like coldness in a place enveloped by a mass of thick, blazing flames.

One might object: "Just as even an object established by inference—such as the dark complexion of a son and so forth—may later be sublated by perception and thus undergo a change in nature, so too here, even if the permanence of an object is established through recognition, its change in nature is nonetheless established because its successive effects are subsequently proven by inference to be sequential. Therefore, how can momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*) be sublated? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even though known by others," and so on:
"Even though an object has been known by others [through inference], it may turn out to be otherwise through direct perception."
But when [an object] is already apprehended by perception, there is no possibility for another [means of knowledge], such as inference and the like, to arise.
(455) "By others" means by inference and so forth.
For example, [the argument] "He must indeed be dark-skinned because he is his son, like his currently visible son," and so forth—this would be otherwise by means of perception (*pratyakṣa*).

That is to say, it would be otherwise by means of perception acting as the instrument; "otherwise" means that it would be contrary to the form established by means of inference (*anumāna*) and other sources of valid cognition.
"Avaruddha" means "objectified"; it does not mean that there is the possibility of its [the effect's] arising from anything other [than the cause].
The meaning is that it is not possible for inference and other means of cognition, being other than direct perception, to arise as sublaters [of it].
To the question "Why?", he says: "For who," and so forth.
For who, once a matter has been firmly determined by the superior authority of perception, would subsequently determine its opposite through other, weaker means?
Indeed, it is logical that a matter established by inference should be set aside by direct perception.
Because that [scriptural testimony] is the eldest of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
inference and the others do not seek to effect a subversion of what is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since they are weaker than the firm [perception].
Being free from doubt and error, "error" refers to being otherwise than it truly is.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely), etc.:
"But surely, if you maintain that present non-existence is distinct [from past existence]..."
"In that case, the difference [between the two] has been established by you yourself.

Is that present existence which is the object of recognition different from the existence previously grasped by perception, or is it that very same [existence]? If it is different, then since the difference has been established by your own words, you would be abandoning your own position; for us, however, this results in the proof of our desired conclusion."
Even if existence is non-different [from the object], how could it be apprehended by a prior cognition?
For if that [existence] were not apprehended, it would follow that the object itself is not perceived.

Now, if the position is that [the object] is not different [from its nature], then how could it be that it was not apprehended by the preceding cognition, such that one might say, "It was not apprehended by the preceding cognition"?

For it cannot be argued: "Just as the momentariness of sound and so forth, though non-different from the existence [of those things], is said to be unapprehended even when that existence is apprehended, so too will this be the case"—that is incorrect.
For it is not established that, even when the subject (*dharmin*)— sound— is apprehended, its non-different nature, momentariness, remains unapprehended; rather,
it is said that although it is apprehended, it is "unascertained" due to the absence of a cause for the arising of ascertainment,
since ascertainment does not arise from mere experience alone.
Because that [inference] depends on factors such as the subject's desire to know, repeated practice, and excellence [of the means],
this is not possible for you, since even the preceding perception possesses the nature of a determinate judgment (*vyavasāya*).
And when that object-nature is being ascertained, its present existence—which is non-different from it—is necessarily ascertained as well.
For if that were not ascertained, it would follow that the very nature of the object is also unascertained, since it is non-different from that [existence] which is itself unascertained.
As for those who say that the validity of recognition (pratyabhijñāna) is based on the determination of a doubtful object, that too has been refuted by this very argument.

Furthermore, there is no determination here of the existence of a doubtful object, because doubt persists due to the observation of recognition even when similar successive moments arise, as in the case of [the illusion of] hair and the like.
Regarding what was stated, "Even if an object is known by others," and so forth, he says: "And by perception," etc.

Furthermore, if there were sublation by perception regarding the domain of inference and other means of knowledge, then inference and the rest would not be valid means of cognition because of that sublation, just like the cognitions of one suffering from ophthalmia and so forth.

(459) For any inference and the like—such as "because he is your son"—for which sublation by perception might occur within its own domain or object, it possesses no validity at all; for, since its object is being sublated, there is an absence of correspondence with reality, just like the cognition of one with ophthalmia.
What was stated—that even an object known by other means of cognition might be otherwise through perception—is entirely inconsistent, because it is impossible.
Furthermore, demonstrating that the claim regarding the primacy of perception is likewise unreal, he says: "And in the case of its correspondence with the object," and so forth.
Since the capacity to correspond with the object is equal [in both cases], why is there such hostility toward this [scripture]?
In the absence of that [correspondence], however, inference and the other means of knowledge would not be valid at all.
For this alone is the validity of the means of knowledge: namely, the capacity to cognize the object.
If that [quality] is accepted for all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then by what means would this direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) possess primacy?

Furthermore, one might argue: "Only direct perception possesses correspondence with the object (*arthasaṃvādakatva*), not inference (*anumāna*) and the rest. To this he says: "In the absence of that," and so forth.
That is to say, in the absence of that—namely, correspondence with the object and so on—inference and the other means of valid cognition would not be valid cognitions at all.
Since the conventional usage of "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) is based on its non-contradiction with the object, and since that [non-contradiction] exists here [in the case of inference],
[the author] raises the objection regarding the means of valid cognition stated by Bhāvivikta, beginning with the words "nanvanena" and so forth.
But surely, by this inference, the universal concomitance (vyāpti) in all reasons is sublated, or else there is a destruction of the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā) which includes all cases.
To the question "What is that inference?", he says: "The intended," and so forth.

The cognition that arises with respect to a specific object such as the sun or moon intended [by the speaker] has, moreover, as its object the sun and so forth as connected to that very time; for, insofar as it does not have the earth as its object, it is designated as "cognition thereof" (i.e., cognition of the sun). 462.
For example, the first cognition has as its object the moon, sun, and so forth at that specific time.

As it has been said: "The cognitions of the moon, sun, planets, constellations, and so on, which have become the subjects of dispute, have as their objects precisely the moon, sun, planets, stars, and so on, delimited by the time of the intended cognition of Devadatta and others; because, while not being perceived as connected with the earth, they are denotable by the words 'cognition of the moon, sun, planets, constellations, and so on,' just like the cognition of the stars and so on belonging to Devadatta occurring at the first moment."
The phrase "having as its object the intended sun, moon, and so forth" means having as its object luminous substances (*taijasadravya*);

the qualification "while not being perceived as connected with the earth" is for the purpose of avoiding a logical deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to cognitions whose objects are the sun and so forth as they appear in paintings and the like.
"Param" means other than that; the meaning is "at a time other than that."
462 463 This is another authority belonging to him alone.

Those things which are the substrata of universals such as "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth, those which are the substrata of those [universals], and those specific cognitions (*prajñānaviśeṣa*) having them as their objects—namely perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, memory, recognition, the cognition of established facts, doubt, error, subsequent determination (*anuvyavasāya*), dreaming, and dreamless sleep—all these do not perish immediately after acquiring their own existence. This is because they possess the properties of being knowable (*jñeyatva*), being cognizable (*prameyatva*), being nameable (*abhidheyatva*), being either existent or non-existent, being delimited by a cognition whose object is knowable and distinct from both existent and non-existent, being neither graspable nor ungraspable with respect to its object, being neither expressible nor non-expressible, and being nameable by a sound produced through conjunction and disjunction of substances belonging to the same or different classes, just like prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the other types of absence.

In this context, "form and so forth" (rūpādayaḥ) are the substrata of universals such as "form-ness" (rūpatva); and the "substrata of those" (tadāśrayāḥ) are the substrata of those form and so forth. What are they? They are pots and the like. "Vision of the perfected ones" (siddhadarśanam) is the cognition of a yogin. The remainder has already been explained. Being either existent or non-existent means existence or non-existence; since there is no object of knowledge distinct from the existent and the non-existent, there is no cognition having that as its object. And because of its very non-existence, it is established that it cannot be delimited by that [cognition].

Thus, because there is an absence of any apprehension of an object that cannot be apprehended, its state of being unapprehendable is established. Furthermore, that which has an expressible object is "expressible"; therefore, for that which is not expressible by any denoter, its lack of expressibility is established precisely because it lacks any meaning. Substances of the same genus include the lower lip, teeth, and so forth, due to the commonality of being produced (*kṛtakatva*). Those of a different genus include space (*ākāśa*) and the like. From the mutual conjunction and disjunction of these [substances], a primary sound is produced; and from that, through a causal series, a resultant sound reaches the path of hearing. It is by means of this [sound] that [the word] possesses expressibility.
For their process is as follows: the first sound indeed has its origin in conjunction and disjunction; from that sound, other sounds manifest according to the analogy of the *kadamba* flower cluster.
Among these, only that which reaches the region of space within the ear-cavity is perceived, and not the others.
He demonstrates this very collection of proofs with the verse beginning, "All [qualities] such as color-form (*rūpa*) have their substrata," and so forth.
All those things which are the substrata of "form-ness" (rūpatva) and so forth, as well as their common substrata, and whatever cognitions arise having them as their objects—
these do not perish immediately after their production.
"By reason of being knowable and being nameable, like a sky-lotus.
(465) The mention of "knowability" and "nameability" is illustrative;
other reasons as well should be understood [in this context].
*Khe* means in the sky; *aravindam* means the sky-lotus (*ākāśakamala*). 464–465.

Uddyotakara, however, says: "The cognitions occurring at non-simultaneous times regarding a subject of dispute have a single object, because, while there is a non-deviating coreferentiality with that [object], they are denoted by the same word, like the various cognitions of many persons regarding a single moment of the present."

In this context, "non-deviating" (*avyutthāyi*) means that which has the nature (*śīla*) of not deviating—that is, not becoming otherwise—due to the force of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). The "co-referentiality with those cognitions" (*tat-pratyaya-sāmānādhikaraṇya*) refers to the co-referentiality of those cognitions, such as the cognition of a jar. Thus, it is described as "that which is non-deviating and which possesses co-referentiality with those cognitions," meaning "when there is uncontradicted co-referentiality.
Furthermore, this qualification is intended to avoid the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) by [cognitions] such as those of a lamp.
And the state of being denotable by the same word— as in "Caitra’s cognition, Caitra’s cognition," and so forth—
is what this [text] demonstrates: "Those cognitions which are the objects of dispute and which occur in succession," and so on.
It is proclaimed that all of them also have a single object as their domain;

for, since they are established with a common expression based on a single, uncontradicted substratum, it is just as there are not various kinds of cognitions regarding a single present moment. (466–467)

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "proclamation" refers to the thesis; "having a single substratum" means grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); and "unsublated" means that which lacks sublation; thus, it is the state of having a single substratum together with that lack of sublation.
466 467 Here, he provides the rebuttal beginning with "by that which is to be proven" (sādhyena), etc.
First of all, in the case of the first reason, the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) is deficient with respect to the probandum (*sādhya*);
for not every object, by virtue of being a cause, exists at the same time as its own cognition.
(468) "In the case of the first reason" means:

Regarding the statement "because it is designated as the cognition of that," even the initial cognition of the moon and so forth does not have the moon and so forth as its object delimited by its own time,
because only that which serves as the cause [of the cognition] can be its object.
Furthermore, it cannot be simultaneous, because the relationship of cause and effect would be untenable;

as it has been said: "Because that which is non-existent lacks capacity beforehand, and because it is of no use afterwards, all causes must exist prior [to their effects]; therefore, an object does not exist simultaneously with its own cognition."

With the words beginning "yadā" (when), he demonstrates that even when the reason is qualified by the condition "while not being perceived as connected with the earth," it remains inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
since words such as "sun" and so forth arise merely from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
In the case of lamps and the like, [the reason] is shown to be inconclusive by those cognitions [of them].

Regarding the second set of reasons as well, since the subject (*dharmin*) such as "universal" (*jāti*) and so forth does not exist, and since momentariness is not desired [for it], he shows that proving the absence of that [momentariness] therein would result in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) with the words "of universal, etc. (*jātyādeḥ*).
Because universals and the like lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), momentariness is certainly not desired for them.
The proof stated for the purpose of establishing the non-existence of that [momentary destruction] is futile.

(470) By the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of the substrata of that [destruction], such as form and the pot, as well as the cognitions having them as their objects; for these too are indeed non-existent when characterized by the aforementioned qualifications. Therefore, the proof that was stated for the sake of establishing the absence of that momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitā*) in those [substrata] is useless, because there is no dispute regarding it—this is the sense.
Even here, no subtle scrutiny has been made;
if such were to be performed, then a vast web of faults would descend upon this [position].

For instance, this reason (*sādhana*) stated as "being either existent or non-existent" is unestablished (*asiddha*) both in the subject of the thesis (*dharmin*) and in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), because the word "either" (*anyatara*) has its object in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). And conceptual construction occurs only when there is a possibility of multiple things, not in the case of a single thing.
Furthermore, the coexistence of both existence and non-existence is not possible in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*),
because, being of the nature of a real entity (*vastu*), only its existence is possible;
nor is such a coexistence possible in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*).

Since it is possible for that [non-existence] to be merely non-existent due to its being a non-entity, the reason (hetu) possesses a redundant qualification. To explain: even the formulation "because it is denotable by words" is not appropriate here, since the status of being a word is already established simply by the mention of "denotability."
Furthermore, the qualification by means of terms such as "of the same class" (*samānajātīya*) is utterly trivial;
likewise, it should be understood that any other qualification of the reason (*hetu*) is likewise useless.
Moreover, all these reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Because no subverting proof (bādhakapramāṇa) has been shown for these [reasons] in the case of the opposite of the probandum (sādhyaviparyaya),
and this will indeed be explained later.

Regarding what was stated, "those which are the objects of dispute," and so forth, he says in response: "The state of being expressible by the same word" applies even to cognitions such as those of a lamp; therefore, this reason is inconclusive (vyabhicārin). || 471 ||

Regarding the phrase "lamp-cognition" (*dīpajñāna*): since one observes the application of a common term even for cognitions of lamps and so forth that have distinct objects, this reason—"because it is denotable by a word denoting that which is the object of the cognition of a lamp and so forth"—is fallacious (*vyabhicārī*) due to its presence in heterogeneous instances.
Alternatively, the reading may be with an interrogative intonation (*kākvā*):
"Therefore, because it exists in those [distinct objects], does this reason not become fallacious for you? No, rather, it certainly *does* become fallacious. This is the meaning.
"If there is grammatical coreferentiality," he says, raising the objection of the opponent's view: "If grammatical coreferentiality is assumed to be sublated in those cases."
Even in the case intended [by the opponent], why is this sublation not clearly perceived?

(472) The qualification of the reason—"provided there is co-referentiality with that cognition which does not undergo sublation"—was indeed made for the sake of avoiding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by cognitions such as those of a lamp; for the single-objectness of these cognitions of a lamp and so forth is sublated.
To explain: at that very moment, the lamp is perceived to have a long flame and a curved flame, and to be bright and even brighter.
The opponent’s thought is: "In that case, how can there be any deviation (vyabhicāra) of the reason?
To show that even this qualification is unestablished (asiddha), he says: "Even in the intended [case]," and so forth;
"why is sublation (bādhā) not observed even there, in the intended property to be proven (sādhyadharma)?"

For instance, even in the case of Caitra and others, a cognition arises that possesses a changing form through the distinctions of childhood, youth, adulthood, and so forth; likewise, in the case of mountains and the like, there is change through the distinctions of cold, heat, and so on. Therefore, their alteration is even more evident than in the case of a lamp or similar objects.
Otherwise, if that very same entity which was previously connected with cold were later connected with heat, then both cold and heat would have to be perceived in both states.
This is because it would follow that if the nature of the entity is connected to one [quality], then both [qualities] must necessarily exist whenever that entity exists.
This has already been largely explained by the analogy of pulling a man bound in shackles being equivalent to pulling the shackles themselves;
therefore, even with its qualification, the reason (*hetu*) remains unestablished (*asiddha*).

He also states the sublation by inference: "The cognitions under dispute do not have a single object as their domain, because they arise successively, like the cognitions of lightning, a lamp, and so forth. (473)

For there is a contradiction with occurring sequentially in cognitions that arise from a single object, because it is contradictory for that which has no difference in its effect to depend on other [conditions].

(474) The formal argument is as follows: whatever occurs sequentially does not have its complete cause always present, such as the cognitions of lightning, lamps, and so forth; and the cognitions under dispute occur sequentially. This is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Nor is the reason inconclusive, because it is impossible for that which has a single object and possesses its causes in their entirety to arise sequentially; nor can there be dependence on other causes, since a permanent entity cannot be assisted by them,
and dependence on that which provides no assistance is illogical due to the consequence of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Alternatively, if there were assistance [rendered], it would entail the consequence of the loss of eternality; this has been discussed hundreds of times.

And he demonstrates that in all these arguments, the reasons are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because there is no subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary case (*vipakṣa*), by stating "doubtful" and so forth:
"In all these reasons, there is a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*), because no subverting proof has been shown for those [reasons] that exist in the contrary case. (475)
Thus ends the examination of the permanence of entities; it is easily understood.
Thus concludes the examination of the permanence of entities.
Now, for the purpose of establishing the basis for the determination of the relationship between actions and their fruits, the author begins with an objection, saying "momentary," and so forth.
If every entity is touched by momentary impermanence, then how can there be the relationship between action and its fruit, or the principle of cause and effect?
(476) The mention of "momentary impermanence" is for the purpose of excluding impermanence that persists over a duration of time.

Momentary impermanence (*kṣaṇikānityatā*) is the impermanence of things that exist for only a moment; if you assert that the entire range of entities is permeated—that is, overcome—by this, then how could these well-known connections between actions and their fruits, as recognized in both the world and the treatises, be established?

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), those bases for objections imagined by the foolish—such as the means of valid cognition that apprehends cause and effect, recognition based on experience, the desire for another object when one object is seen, bondage and liberation, recollection, determination preceded by doubt, searching for what was buried by oneself, and the cessation of curiosity regarding an object already seen—are included.

The point is that a proposition (*pratijñā*) does not achieve proof if it contradicts what is well-known in the world or in the scriptures; thus, there is the fault of contradicting what has been accepted and what is commonly recognized.
For it is well-known in the world that the very person by whom an action such as a virtuous deed was performed is the one who experiences its fruit;
indeed, it is not established in common experience that when a virtuous or other action has been performed by Devadatta, Yajñadatta experiences its desirable or undesirable fruit.
Nor is this stated in the scriptures, as it is said: "Who else shall experience the fruit of the action performed by this very person?"
And this [position] contradicts the doctrine of momentariness,

because, in the absence of a single agent who appropriates the fruit of karma, it would entail the fallacies of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "That which," and so forth.
That moment which is conceived as the agent of wholesome [actions] and the like does not persist at all at the time when the fruit is produced. (477)
The moment that is described as the experiencer at the time of the production of the fruit has not performed the action at all, because it did not exist previously. Thus,
there is no appropriation of a single agent for both the action and its fruit.

[The doctrine of momentariness] entails the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done; it is deeply attached [to its own position] yet extremely contradictory. For that [momentary entity] does not persist at all, since it is ceased immediately after its arising.
"Because they are not appropriated by a single agent" means that those two—the action and its fruit—are not grasped by one and the same agent.

Consequently, because the agent is not connected with the fruit, there is the "destruction of what was done" (*kṛtanāśa*); and because one who is not the agent is joined with the fruit, there is the "acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*).
The meaning is that it is "extremely contradictory" because such a thing is not seen in either worldly convention or the treatises.

Thus, having for the moment accepted [the existence of] causal activity (*pravṛtti*), the consequence of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) has been stated.
Now, he demonstrates that activity itself is not possible by presenting the opinion of Kumārila, beginning with the words "nairātmya" and so forth:
"But in the position of the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmyavāda*), one understands even beforehand:
'Because of my destruction, the fruit would not exist; or it might belong to someone other than me. (480)
Thus, a discerning person desiring a result would not engage at all in the undertaking of auspicious or inauspicious actions, for the result remains far off.
Indeed, if the momentariness of all phenomena is accepted, then selflessness itself must be accepted.
Because everything is dependent on causes and thus lacks independence, a discerning person, before engaging in an action, understands—determines—what that [cause] is;
he says: "By my own destruction," and so forth.
