"Since my non-existence follows my destruction, there would be no fruit for me at the time of its production because of my absence;

yet, if the fruit were to exist, it would belong to another moment distinct from me. Knowing this, even the engagement of a discerning person is impossible, let alone a fruit produced by an action preceded by such engagement, for that remains utterly impossible.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the connection between action and its fruit is not tenable.

Now, demonstrating the impossibility of the relation between cause and effect according to the view of Kumārila himself, he says: "Neither the future nor the past entity is capable of performing an action; even the present one does not persist for such a duration of time. (482)
The meaning is that having arisen, it does not persist for as long as the time required to accomplish its effect, because of its momentariness (kṣaṇikatva). 482
He provides the justification for the passage beginning with "not the future," in due order, stating: "For that which has not yet attained its own nature," and so forth.
For an entity that has not yet attained its own nature is not fit to be an auxiliary to another; nor is that which has perished, nor is its [mere] persistence capable of performing a function. (483)

Furthermore, if the destruction of the preceding moment is conceived as being without any continuity (*niranvaya*), then the arising of the subsequent [moment] is not tenable because it would lack a cause.

For that which is called "future" is defined as having not yet attained its own nature; and that which has not attained its own nature is non-existent. That which is non-existent is devoid of all causal capacity (*sāmarthya*); and how can that which is devoid of all causal capacity be fit to become a factor for another—that is to say, how can it assume the state of being a cause with respect to another? || 484 ||

The connection [of the argument] is as follows: since causal status is admitted only for that which is capable, even that which has perished cannot serve as a factor for another because it is devoid of all capacity;
nor, moreover, does a presently existing thing have a "standing" such that it would be capable of performing an action—that is, producing an effect.
Furthermore— if it is postulated that the preceding moment perishes without leaving any trace (niranvaya), then the subsequent moment could not arise due to the absence of a cause.

It might be argued that just as the lowering and raising of the two ends of a balance scale occur simultaneously, so too the destruction of the cause and the arising of the effect are intended to be simultaneous; thus, since it is accepted that the effect arises from a present cause that has not yet perished, its arising will not be without a cause. To this, he says: "Even if there were simultaneity of destruction and arising," and so forth.
Even if there were simultaneity of destruction and arising, there would be no mutual dependence [between them] as cause and effect, because the operation of one does not assist the other. (485)

Even if the equality of destruction and arising is postulated, there can be no relationship of cause and effect between destruction and arising, nor between those two [entities] that possess them; for such a thing is impossible, because they are mutually independent.
To the question, "How is there independence? he says: "Because it does not assist in its operation.
This means that the effect is not assisted—that is, not benefited—by the operation of that [destruction] or of that which possesses it (the entity undergoing destruction).

For destruction, being devoid of form (*nīrūpa*), lacks any activity; furthermore, even for that entity which is considered a cause, there is an absence of activity because it is not present at the time the effect exists.

(485) It might be argued: "The relationship of cause and effect will exist through mere immediate succession (*ānantarya*) even without an activity. To this he says: "And that which is being born," and so forth.
Just as fragrance and other qualities, though arising when the form of a jar perishes, are not accepted as its effects, so too it is with other forms.

(486) If it were the case that whatever arises immediately after something else must be its effect, then— since fragrance and the like arise from within that very collection [of qualities] possessing moments of form of the same genus immediately after a moment of form belonging to the configuration of a jar and so forth— that fragrance would also have to be its effect.
And even though this [subsequent form] occurs immediately after [the preceding form], it is not accepted as its effect;

for there is no mutual relationship of cause and effect among derived material forms (*bhautika*) as there is among the primary elements (*bhūta*), because they belong to distinct continua—so the opponent thinks—and thus other forms as well. Therefore, subsequent moments of form belonging to the same class must not be grasped as the effects of a [preceding] form merely on account of their immediate succession, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—this is the intended meaning.

Having thus demonstrated that mere immediate succession (*ānantaryamātra*) cannot be the basis for establishing the status of being a cause, he shows his own position by way of a conclusion: "Therefore," and so forth.
Therefore, that alone is the cause of an effect whose activity is observed prior to the production of that effect; it is not mere immediate succession. (487)
But it is not merely immediate succession;
rather, it is based on the established relationship between cause and effect—this is the remainder of the sense.
Showing the very same point in brief, he says: "This is the summary," and so forth.

This is the summary: if the production of an effect were to arise from a cause that has perished, then because that which is destroyed is inexpressible (anupākhyatva), this [effect] would be without a cause. || 488 ||
And since multiple moments could arise from that which has not perished within its own kind,
how would the momentariness of entities not be contradicted at that time?
Herein, there are two possible alternatives.

The effect must arise either from a cause that has perished or from one that has not perished, for there exists no entity that is neither perished nor unperished. In this regard, the first position is not tenable; since that which has perished is non-existent, if one were to accept production from it, it would follow that the effect is causeless.
Consequently, it is not tenable that existence and so forth are eternal;

nor is the second [alternative] possible, because since entities persist for multiple moments, there would be the undesirable consequence of their momentariness being lost— how then could this not be contradictory?
The meaning is that it is indeed contradicted;

for instance, an entity first arises, then exerts activity, then, having produced its effect, subsequently perishes. In this way, the presence of a single entity across multiple moments would result in a contradiction of momentariness.

Having thus established the impossibility of the relationship between cause and effect, he says the following— beginning with "momentary" and so forth— in order to demonstrate the impossibility of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that could apprehend it:
"If a jar or the like were momentary, it would not be perceived by the eye."

For things that have perished are not perceived, just like objects that have long since passed away. Even the causal relationship between entities is not established through perception and non-perception, because the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of those things is not perceived.

For the causal relationship is established through perception and non-perception; however, since entities are momentary, they do not persist at the time of their own cognition and are therefore simply unperceivable, because a causal relationship cannot occur between things that exist simultaneously.
Consequently, perception and non-perception are simply absent.

Since non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is itself a specific form of perception (*pratyakṣa-viśeṣa*) by virtue of its nature as the apprehension of an object that is not mixed with anything else, it is impossible for that [non-apprehension] to exist in the absence of the apprehension of the object; how then could the causal relation be established through perception and non-apprehension? (490)

"Let it be granted that there is apprehension of an object; nevertheless, because there is no single persisting agent who connects the preceding and succeeding moments, their relationship is not established. Demonstrating this, he says: "Or who," and so forth:
"Or who, being established as an agent, could connect the sequential progression?"
When this [object] is seen, that [cognition] is seen; however, it is not perceived when this is not seen.
"Gati" means apprehension, and since this apprehension occurs in a sequence, it is called "sequential apprehension."
Who connects them—that is, who synthesizes them?
No one at all.

For if someone, upon perceiving this fire, were to perceive smoke and so forth, and then, upon its non-perception, were not to perceive those [effects], and if such a sequential process were thus connected by way of a single agent, then the establishment of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) would occur; but according to your view, there is no such connector, and therefore the causal relation cannot be established. This is the meaning.
Now, demonstrating the impossibility of recognition, he says: "In things that are subject to momentary destruction," and so forth;
and recognition is difficult to establish in the case of entities that perish in each moment.
For an object seen by one person is not recognized by others.

Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the synthesis (*ghaṭana*) of two perceptions—the prior and the subsequent—based on their having a single object and a single knower, in the form: "That very same object which was previously seen by me is now being seen.
And this [recognition] is not possible if all things are subject to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅgitva*).
Because there is no single entity that is both the knower and the object known,
for Viṣṇumitra does not recognize an object seen by Devadatta; the mention of "either one" is intended as an illustration.
It should also be understood that no other object is recognized [in the act of recognition].

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even when there is difference—as in the case of hair, nails, and so forth that have been cut and grown back again—recognition will still occur due to similarity. Anticipating this, he says: "Due to similarity," and so forth.

Recognition may arise due to similarity even in the case of distinct things such as strands of hair, provided there exists a single cognizer; however, if there were a duality [of cognizers], it would be without basis. Furthermore, if no single entity exists that performs the act of synthesis (pratisandhāna), [recognition is impossible].
When a form is seen, there arises desire and so forth; how could that same [desire] occur with respect to tastes and other objects?
For if there were a single knower, then, by virtue of that unifying subject, there would be recognition based on similarity even when the objects known are different.
But in the case of "dual difference"—where "dual difference" means the difference between both the knower and the object known—recognition would be entirely without foundation.

Furthermore—if there were no single person who serves as the one who links [past and future], then how could it be that upon seeing the form of a citron fruit or the like, there arises a desire preceded by the recollection of its taste and other qualities which are invariably concomitant with that form, and an inclination toward its consumption?
For otherwise, the desire and so forth of one person would not arise from the sight of something seen by another.
(Verse 494)
Showing that even bondage and liberation are not attained [by the moment], he says: "Bound by the shackles of passion and so forth," and so on; another moment exists within the prison of existence.
"One who is unbound is liberated"—this [notion] is not understood.

For one moment is bound by passion and so forth, while another is liberated; this is not understood—that is to say, it is not possible—[as stated in the verse] "the protector from existence" (bhavavāraka).
Existence (*bhava*) is cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*); that itself is the "cage"—the prison.
Showing that effort for the sake of liberation is futile because liberation does not exist, he says: "For there is no liberation," and so forth.
For liberation is never possible for one who is bound, because [the bound] would undergo absolute destruction; therefore, the effort of those seeking liberation is futile.
(497) Now, one might argue: "Liberation will belong to one who is not bound at all; what contradiction is there in this? To this, he says: "Liberation," and so forth.

It is observed that one who attains liberation is seen to have been bound by shackles and the like; yet it is also observed that one who is unbound attains liberation—such a thing is not contradicted by experience.
For it is both commonly recognized and observed in the world that he alone who was bound is the one who is liberated.

However, the proposition that there is liberation for one who is not bound is sublated by worldly consensus and by direct perception; thus, the meaning is that the proposition contradicts direct perception.
(498) He also states the sublation by inference, beginning with "residing in a single locus," and so forth.

These two—bondage and liberation—have a single substratum because they exist in such a manner; therefore, like their worldly counterparts, everything is established most beautifully. (499) The formal argument is as follows: those which are bondage and liberation have a single substratum, just like worldly bondage and liberation; and these two, characterized as the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and their dissociation (*tadvisaṃyoga*), which are the subjects of dispute, are indeed bondage and liberation. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
"Likewise, because of abiding" means because of abiding in the nature of bondage and liberation; that is to say, because they consist of the forms of bondage and liberation.
"Those two" refers to those [two].

And thus, since bondage and liberation are established for a single substrate, the self, the connection with the fruits of all actions and so forth remains most excellent— that is to say, it is established in a most beautiful manner—
because the aforementioned defects are absent.
"By this very [reasoning]" means that in this very manner, there is the impossibility of memory and so forth.
Because there is no single substratum among things that perish moment by moment,
and because there is no single agent,
one must understand the impossibility of the previously mentioned phenomena: memory, certainty, searching for what was hidden by oneself, and so forth.
Even in that case, if there were a difference of substratum, it would entail contradictions with what is observed and so forth;
for when Caitra— the experiencer— is in doubt, or is desirous of depositing [the object], Maitra’s recollection, certainty, inference, curiosity, cessation [of inquiry], and so on, are not possible.
To this, he replies with the words "In this regard, it is said," and so forth:
"In this regard, it is said that when the status of all causes and effects is established, these [phenomena] are indeed proven to be unimpeded even in the absence of a self. (501)

For even though there is selflessness (*nairātmya*) in all things, this established order of the relationship between action and its fruit and so forth is brought about by the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇatā*). And since the causal relation exists, everything is entirely consistent; thus, nothing is lost. It might be argued: "That very specific restriction of the causal relation is not possible without a self (*ātman*. To this he says: "Just as... and so forth.
Just as the fixed capacity of a seed and so forth toward a sprout and so forth exists even in the absence of a persisting self, so too is the state of things in the internal domain.

For just as the fixed capacity of a seed and so forth toward a sprout and so forth occurs even without a self acting as an internal controller, so it will be with respect to internal entities as well.
For seeds and the like are not presided over by a self as the locus of experience in the manner of the body;
otherwise, the argument that "this living body is not soulless, because it possesses breath and so forth"—lest it follow that it would lack these—would not be tenable.
For only if breath and the like were seen to cease upon the cessation of the self in the case of a jar or similar object could the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the reason be established.
If, however, even a jar or the like were to possess a self (sātmakatva), then how could this reason be "negative-only" (vyatirekī)?
[The phrase] "even in the absence of an associated self" means even in the absence of some associated essential nature (svabhāva).
What, then, is this "stability"? He says: "Indirectly or directly," and so forth;
for something possesses power either indirectly or directly in some respect.

Consequently, the relationship between actions, their fruits, and so forth, is logically established. (503) For just as the determination of cause and effect is fixed in the external world, so too is it within this internal aggregate of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*). Due to the restriction of causal potency, from a specific virtuous or non-virtuous action alone, a determined result—whether desirable or undesirable—manifests through a succession of moments. From the experience of form and other objects comes memory; from deliberation comes ascertainment; from establishing [a premise] comes investigation; for one who desires, there is the sight of the object; and from that, the cessation of curiosity—all of this is entirely consistent.

For recollection and the like are not established for the Buddhist as being the concomitants of a single substantial entity; rather, they are merely this cognition, as it has been said: "Action exists and its fruit exists, but an agent is not found who casts off these aggregates and takes up other aggregates, except for the conventional designation of phenomena."
In this regard, this is the conventional designation of phenomena (*dharmasaṅketa*): namely, "when this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "action, fruit, and so forth," there is the inclusion of memory and other such factors.
The relationship, however, is that of the produced and the producer (*janyajanakabhāva*).

504. If this is so, how then is it stated in the world and in the treatises with reference to various individuals, such as: "This very person performed the action; who else shall experience its result? To this he says: "The establishment of agency and so forth," etc.; the establishment of agency and so forth is intended by way of the unity of the continuum (*santāna*).
That which is superimposed by conceptual construction is not accepted as a factor for the establishment of reality.

(504) People, whose light of knowledge is impaired by a dense mass of the darkness of ignorance, set aside investigations into identity, difference, non-existence, and so forth regarding the self; instead, they determine the continuity of mental formations—which possess forms determined by specific causes and effects—to be a single unity, and thus engage in worldly discourse such as "I am that very person who acts," and they proceed toward liberation.

And it may be argued that, out of deference to those [beings'] conceit, the Blessed Tathāgatas—desiring to protect the people to be trained from falling into the abyss of the view of annihilationism—demonstrate the unity of the continuum and establish [attributes] such as agency; and that from such an establishment, the thing itself is established. To this he says: "That is not a factor," and so forth.

For it is not possible to establish reality by virtue of the attachment of foolish people who have fallen into conventional truth and whose minds are turned away from the investigation of reality, because that attachment is sublated by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) established through selflessness and momentary destruction.

Anticipating the objection of an opponent who, believing that the example is unestablished because the "separation from a persisting self" is not proven in the case of seeds and so forth, [the author] says: "In the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya), that very same [relation] would be the causal relation," and so on.
In the absence of positive concomitance, that very same [relation] would be the causal relation.
Just as a specific [cognition] is connected with those arising in another continuum, so too is it here.
Now, the causal relationship between seeds, sprouts, and so forth is observed to be fixed; in that case, there is not even the slightest subtle part that possesses a nature of persistence.
"Concomitance" (anvaya) means "following after" (anugama); the remainder [of the sense] is "of some intrinsic nature" (svabhāva).

It might be argued: "There is indeed a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) even in the case of seeds and the like, as stated by Uddyotakara: 'In that case as well, those parts of the seed, having abandoned their previous configuration (*vyūha*), attain another configuration; and upon attaining this other configuration, the earth-element, being moistened by the water-element and cooked by an internal fire-element, produces a substance consisting of sap (*rasadravya*); that sap, together with the previous parts, attains the state of a sprout and so forth.'"
To the question, "How then can it be said that there is not even a subtle part [of the cause] therein? he says: "Of earth and the rest," and so forth.

If earth and the rest were not distinct [from one another], then no difference would be logical among seeds, sprouts, creepers, and so on, because of their being a single essence; therefore, it is established that [the effect] is without persistence (niranvaya).

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the existence or non-existence of karma, its fruits, and so forth, once the relationship of cause and effect has been established, enough with others making further efforts regarding what that effect might be. This is what is meant: This is what is being said: [the opponent's effort is redundant].

If earth and the other elements, while existing in a subsequent configuration, persist without having abandoned their prior intrinsic natures, then it would not be possible for them to abandon their former arrangement and undergo the acquisition of another arrangement; because of that identity with the former state, they would remain as before, and consequently, no mutual distinction between seeds, sprouts, and so forth would be established.

If a difference among sprouts and so forth is admitted on the grounds that they possess a single nature, then, since there must necessarily be an abandonment of their prior nature, one must admit the abandonment of the previous configuration of the earth and other elements and the attainment of another configuration;
otherwise, as it has been stated, there would be no difference at all.
Furthermore, since things arise with distinct and successive natures, from what could there be a persisting entity?

And thus, when the relationship of cause and effect is established in this way, everything—including the connection between actions and their fruits—is rendered coherent; whereas if it is refuted, it falls apart. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the existence of actions, fruits, and so forth, an effort must be made by others to establish the relationship of cause and effect—meaning, by the superior Buddhists who follow the highest philosophical vision.

And for the sake of establishing their non-existence, opponents—that is, the *tīrthikas*—must exert effort to establish the non-existence of that very causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇatā*). The phrase "in the establishment of causal relationship" should be repeated twice; in one instance, the vowel *a* should be elided [to form *asiddhau*].

507 508 Regarding this, in order to dispel the two alternatives concerning "perished" and "not perished" formulated by the opponent, [the author] establishes the causal relationship— which is the root of all systematic arrangements— by stating, "To this it is replied," and so forth.
To this it is replied: for the effect is produced in the second moment, while in the first moment the cause has arisen and is as yet undestroyed;
yet, because of its momentariness, that effect does not exist at the time of the moment of the cause or at the moment of the effect itself.
Or rather, in the commentary, the effect is accomplished when that [cause] has ceased;
for it is not our position that the effect arises from a cause that has not perished, nor does this entail the consequence of simultaneity.

To explain: in the second moment, the effect is produced in dependence upon that very cause which, having attained its own existence through its causal status in the first moment, has not yet perished.

And that [effect], being produced in such a manner, arises from the cause precisely while it is not yet destroyed, because at the first moment the cause has not perished; furthermore, the cause does not persist until the time when the effect's existence occurs.
Because it does not persist due to its momentariness, even if there is continuity, it lacks causality at that time; for once the effect has been produced, it can no longer perform any function.
510 He demonstrates that very point of its being ineffective with the words "And not," etc.:
"And what has already arisen previously cannot be produced again by it."
Because its nature consists of unreal existence, there is no stability from birth to birth;
"no stability otherwise" means that otherwise, there would be no fixed order (niyama).
In other words, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
For if that which has already been produced were to be produced again, then, because there would be no distinction [from its prior state], it would follow that it must be produced yet again;
consequently, there would be an infinite series of births.
Furthermore, there would be no cessation of the activity of causes, and it would follow that even a cause is itself produced, since there is no distinction [between them].
Consequently, the established order that "this is the cause" and "this is the effect" would not exist.
Having concluded with the words "Therefore," etc., he demonstrates that the position of the proponent is faultless:
"Therefore, from that unperished cause existing in the first moment, the effect is produced; however, it is produced from the potent [cause] in the second moment itself. (512)
If the effect were to arise from what has already perished in the third moment or thereafter, it would follow that the effect arises from a cause that has been destroyed, as will be explained later.
Furthermore, if that [effect] were to arise in the first moment, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneity.

Furthermore, that [theory] is not tenable according to logic, just like the theory of simultaneous causality (*sahabhūhetu*). Moreover, the "perished alternative" is untenable precisely because it is not accepted. To explain: if it were accepted that the effect arises in the third moment and so forth—as is asserted by the Vaibhāṣikas, who maintain that "one past [moment] bestows [the fruit]"—then [that would be the case].
In that case, the production of an effect from a cause that has not perished would have to be accepted;
however, this position is not ours,
as it is devoid of logical justification.
Furthermore, the consequence of simultaneity might occasionally arise if the effect were held to exist in the very first moment— just as those Vaibhāṣikas maintain regarding the co-existent cause—
and this is untenable.
He asks "Why? and says: "Because of the non-existent," and so forth.

Since that which is non-existent lacks causal capacity prior [to its production], and since the effect can only arise when there is causal capacity, a clear simultaneity of cause and effect is contradicted. (515)
For a cause that produces an effect existing simultaneously with it would have to produce it either while being unarisen or while already arisen.
It cannot first be unarisen, because it does not exist prior to the arising of the effect,
and because that which is non-existent is devoid of all causal capacity.

If it is argued that when [the cause] has arisen, it will produce [the effect] because it possesses capacity, he replies: "Because the effect is impossible when there is capacity. For when its capacity exists in the state of having already arisen, the effect must likewise have arisen, being of the same nature as that [capacity]. In that case, where would its capacity find application?
Therefore, the acceptance of the simultaneity of cause and effect is contradicted by the means of valid cognition known as inference.
[Objection: Is it not the case that the relationship of cause and effect is indeed the relationship of object and agent, and that this is contradicted when they exist at different times?
For the relationship of object and agent is never observed between a jar and a potter when they are not simultaneous. To this, he says: "Not so," and so forth.
For an effect does not produce itself by grasping its cause with a pair of tongs, as it were, from which this simultaneity might arise;
nor is the fruit born by firmly embracing its material cause.
Just as a lover and his beloved might exist simultaneously, so too would the existence of these two [cause and effect] occur at once.

For if the cause were to operate toward the production of the effect according to the logic of grasping with tongs, or if the effect were to exert an activity toward its own birth by embracing its own cause—like a woman’s embrace—then their simultaneous existence would be a necessity.

However, this entire universe is indeed devoid of activity; for in reality, there is neither an agent nor an object of action, except as a conventional designation of dharma. This is the collective meaning.
"Nature" (prakṛti) means the cause.

517. If this is so, and if both effect and cause are indeed devoid of activity, then how is it that people say, "Fire produces smoke" or "Smoke arises depending upon fire"? To this he says: "Because of necessity," and so forth.
By necessity, because it arises from its own cause at the first moment,
that which is produced immediately after something else is said to "generate" that thing, even though the entity itself is devoid of activity during the presence of the second moment. (518)
[This refers to] those [words] which conform to conventions produced by mere intention to speak (vivakṣā).

Because of the specific restriction of the capacity of a cause—which arises from its own causes and conditions—whatever effect is produced from a certain cause that exists in the first moment, [that cause] is said to "produce" that effect, provided it has "proximity" (sannidhi), meaning its presence, in the second moment; this is the analysis of the compound.
The term "produces" is used as an illustration (upalakṣaṇa).
It should also be understood that [the effect] arises depending upon this or that;
who, then, are those who speak thus? and so forth.

The meaning is that it is the users of language themselves— who engage in linguistic practice according to conventions arising from the intention to speak independently of external objects— who say this.
Now, one might object: "How can that which, having arisen, does not enter into an activity for the sake of producing a specific effect, be a cause? To this he says: "Apart from birth," and so forth.
What result could there be here from an activity occurring at a time distinct from birth? Existence itself is the activity, since it is when that existence is present that the effect arises. (520)

Since the effect is already accomplished immediately after the existence of the cause, the operation that occurs at a time subsequent to the birth of the effect is entirely ineffective with respect to that effect. For what is called the "operation" (vyāpāra) of a cause?

It is that immediately following which the effect attains its arising; and since the effect arises immediately after the existence of the cause, let existence itself be what is denoted by the word "operation. What is the use of postulating an operation distinct from birth?

520. If this is so, and there is no activity (*vyāpāra*) on the part of entities, how is it that this is taught—that the effect has a dependence upon the cause, and the cause has an activity toward the effect? He says: "That which is the rule of immediate succession (*ānantarya-niyama*), that alone is designated as 'dependence'."
The operation (*vyāpāra*) of a cause is its constant presence at the time of the arising of the effect.

For this alone is the dependence of the effect upon the cause, namely, that it occurs immediately after the latter; and for the cause as well, this alone is the operation toward the effect, namely, its constant proximity at the time of the effect's arising.

Furthermore, you must accept that the causal status of either an activity (*vyāpāra*) or an entity possessing activity (*vyāpārin*) with respect to an effect arises solely from the principle of "existence when that exists" (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*). For there is no means other than positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) for apprehending the relationship between cause and effect. This being so, why is the causal status not attributed even to the mere entity (*vastumātra*)? Indeed, it is not unestablished that the effect follows the positive and negative concomitance residing in the mere entity. Therefore, let that very mere entity be the cause; this shows that the effect’s conformity to the positive and negative concomitance residing in the mere entity is established, as expressed in the verse beginning with *tadbhāva* and so forth.

"Even an operation, merely because it arises when that [cause] exists, is postulated as a cause; or rather, let that which possesses it [the operation] be the cause. It is better to accept that very [entity] itself.
Regarding the word "postulated": [it means] imagined.
The meaning is as follows: whatever other operation—whether of the nature of both or neither—has been postulated by you, "possessing that" (*tadvān*) means possessing that operation;
the connection with the subject at hand is that such a thing attains the status of a cause solely on the basis of its being produced by that [operation] and producing that [effect].
The meaning is: let the mere entity itself—devoid of any distinct operation—be the cause.
"What excellence is there in that [activity] by which it is said to be 'preferable'? To this he says: "When an entity exists," and so forth.
For when an entity exists, the emergence of a sprout from a seed and so on are observed; however, no such thing is ever perceived to occur merely through the existence of an activity. (523)
"In the entity" (bhāve)—that is, in the mere entity, meaning when the seed and so forth are devoid of the entry of any other operation.

By this, it is shown that it is established that effects follow only the positive and negative concomitance residing in the entity itself, and not the positive and negative concomitance residing in an operation.

It might be argued: "Even if the conformity of the effect to the positive and negative concomitance residing in the operation is not established, nevertheless, that [operation] will still possess the status of being a cause. To this, he says: "adṛṣṭaśakteḥ... and so forth.
"Even if the unseen power (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*) is postulated as the cause, why is the causality of anything else not also accepted? Or what is its distinction from that [unseen power]? (524)

For if one were to thus postulate even an operation (*vyāpāra*) as the cause, another [operation] would also have to be postulated, since there is no distinction [between them] due to their having unseen powers (*adṛṣṭa-śakti*); consequently, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, another is not postulated because of a lack of basis (*nibandhana*), then let there be no postulation of an operation either, for the absence of a basis is equal in that case as well.

Furthermore, as for this operation (*vyāpāra*) which produces an effect, does it do so by entering into another operation, or rather by its mere existence? If it were by entering into another operation, then that other operation alone would be the cause, not the [original] operation. If that other operation is also considered a cause, the same objection applies;
for if its status as a cause were imagined to result from its entry into yet another operation, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, if the position is that [the cause produces the effect] by its mere existence (*sattāmātreṇa*), then even a thing (*padārtha*) would produce the effect by its mere existence alone, just like an operation (*vyāpāra*); thus, the postulation of an operation is useless. He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "And by another," etc.:
"And just as an operation is accepted as the cause of an effect even without anything else, why then are other things not also causes? (525)

For just as an operation is accepted as a cause for an effect such as a sprout even without another distinct operation, why are other entities not likewise accepted as causes while being devoid of any distinct operation?
Or perhaps it might be argued that the operation does not directly assist the effect.
What then? He says that it is indeed the entity (*bhāva*) itself that possesses activity: "Alternatively, the entity," and so forth...
The connection with the context is "it is accepted as a cause.

For even in your view, this [cause], while being an agent possessing activity, remains devoid of the entry of any further activity; thus, that very [case] will serve as the illustrative example—this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, he demonstrates that an entity has no activity apart from its existence, because such activity is not perceived when the object has reached the conditions for perception: "We do not perceive what is intended to be visible," and so forth. We indeed do not perceive it in this manner.
How then can we accept that as its basis for connection?
For you maintain that the operation (*vyāpāra*) is something perceptible, as Kumārila has stated: "The operation of which is perceived prior to the completion of the effect," and so forth.

Furthermore, that entity whose nature is the operation must be either distinct from the thing possessing the operation or non-distinct from it, since there is no other possible mode for a real entity; the alternatives of being both or neither are simply impossible.
If that [operation] were a distinct entity from the word-meaning, then the word-meaning would not attain the status of being a cause,
because causality would belong solely to the operation which is separate from it.
If it is argued that the word-meaning also possesses the status of being a cause by virtue of its connection with the operation;
For a relationship cannot be established between two things that do not mutually benefit one another;
otherwise, it might be argued that the operation is indeed assisted by the word-meaning.

That too is incorrect, for that [entity] has no further operation by which it might assist an operation; otherwise, due to an infinite regress of operations, since they would only connect with one another, a connection between an operation and the entity itself would never be established. If, on the other hand, it were the case that an entity assists an operation even without another operation, then why should the effect not likewise assist [the operation] through its mere existence, without an operation—thereby rendering superfluous the postulation of an operation as a distinct entity?
For there is no one who can obstruct that which, even in its effect, proceeds by means of its mere existence;

therefore, an operation (vyāpāra) that is a distinct entity is not logical. If, on the other hand, the position is that it is not a distinct entity, then it is established that existence itself is the operation.
Since it is the very nature of the entity itself that is denoted by the word "existence," the operation cannot be established as something distinct from birth. 527

Furthermore, just as cognition, while arising in the apprehension of an object, functions by its mere existence even though it is devoid of activity, so too will the causality of all entities exist without an operation occurring at a subsequent time; this is shown in the verse beginning with "buddheḥ":
"Just as for cognition, its very birth is not what constitutes its status as a means of valid knowledge."
In the same way, why is that causality not accepted in all entities?
For there is no operation of cognition distinct from its birth;

as Kumārila stated while explaining the purpose of the term "birth" (*janman*) in the sūtra—"When there is contact of a person’s sense organs with what is existent, the birth of cognition is perception"—he said, "The birth of cognition" [is used] to indicate that the cognition is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely as it is being born.
For the operation of causes is indeed observed to be distinct from their arising;
lest the same [distinction] apply to the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as well, "arising" is intended [here],
meaning its status as a cause.
That [word] "tat" refers to those for whom the cause is the birth of the instruments;
that state is their "tattva" (reality).
It might be argued that it is logical for an entity to possess activity, since cognition does not persist after its occurrence due to its momentariness; to this he says:
"For just as cognition is momentary, so too have other born things been proven to be likewise. Therefore, this world is devoid of activity. (529)
"Established" means that, as in the examination of the permanence of entities, momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) pervading all things has been established; therefore,
it is "just like that."
Just as in the case of cognition,
[it follows] from this, because of momentariness.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is momentary is devoid of any operation distinct from its birth, just like cognition; and it has already been established that seeds and other such things are momentary. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is that, since there is no persistence [of the cause] after its birth, an operation without a substratum is impossible. Therefore, it is established that the basis for determining the causal relationship is merely immediate succession (*ānantarya*), and not an operation.

Regarding what was stated, namely "the one being born [is perceived] along with odor and so forth," he says—"by way of continuity" (*prabandhavṛttyā*) and so on—in order to show that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even in that case:

"The mutual causality of odor and the rest is indeed accepted by us through their existence as a continuum; therefore, this [objection] which attempts to prove their causality does not contradict that [position]. (530)
For indeed, the state of being a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) among form, taste, and so forth, with respect to their mutual continuity, is precisely what is intended;

as it has been said: "Without the operation of potency, there is no other cause for taste itself," and "The movement of those [entities] belonging to past times is known through the mark of their effects."

[Objection: But surely, just as smoke sometimes occurs immediately after fire, it also occurs immediately after cows, horses, and so forth; how then is immediate succession not subject to deviation? [The author] says: "Even when occurring immediately after another," etc.;
even when occurring immediately after another, only a specific thing is the cause, not everything.
In the same way, this [principle] is equally established regarding permanent things as well.
For we do not say that mere immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is the basis for the apprehension of the causal relation; what then? That which is necessary (*niyata*).
To explain: when something occurs immediately after a specific thing, that [specific thing] is accepted as its cause.
Furthermore, smoke does not arise immediately after a cow or similar entities alone, because it exists even in the absence of a cow or such;
moreover, this objection applies equally to you who maintain the doctrine of permanence: why is it that smoke, though arising immediately after a cow or similar entities, is not their effect? (531)

Regarding this, another says: "If it is held that whatever is engaged in a particular effect is not its cause, then let it be accepted that whatever has a restricted existence in something is the cause of that thing. (532)
With the words beginning "In which," he states the rebuttal for his own position as well: 532.
Thus, first of all, the causal relationship between entities has been established even if they are momentary.
Now, in order to establish the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that realizes this, he says: "Existence and non-existence," and so forth:

"These two, existence and non-existence, are established through perception and non-perception, if it is held that an object is to be known by consciousness possessing an aspect (*sākāra-vijñāna*). (533)
When you maintain that an object is cognizable by a cognition devoid of form, this is equally perceived even in the case of [theories such as] momentariness and so forth;
for indeed, every single cognition arises from its own preceding causes.
The nature of cognition arises as having the form of time, portions, and so forth.
For just as the perception of permanent entities is established for you, so too will it be established for us regarding momentary ones;
for instance, when the perception of an object occurs, does it occur through a consciousness that possesses a mental image (*sākāra*), or one that is devoid of a mental image (*anākāra*)?

In that regard, if [cognition] possesses an aspect (*sākāra*), then the experience of the object by cognition is simply the experience of its own aspect; thus, there is no difference whatsoever between the positions of the object being stable or unstable. Alternatively, if it is without an aspect (*anākāra*), then too there is no difference;
for instance, that cognition arises from its own preceding causes in such a way that it perceives only the form and so forth that exist at the same time as itself, and nothing else.

Since that [cognition] has arisen as having the very nature of the awareness of that [object], there is no distinction whatsoever regarding whether the object is stable or unstable when cognition is admitted to have the inherent nature of cognizing form and so forth occurring at the same time.

Furthermore, you must necessarily admit that the nature of cognition in its apprehension of specific form and so forth occurring at the same time is produced solely by a prior cause; otherwise, even though they occur simultaneously, why would cognition determine only the form and so forth, and not the sense faculty?
And since that [capacity] is exactly the same even if things are momentary, this [objection] is trivial. 533–534.
With the words "sākāra" (having an aspect) and so forth, the opponent raises an objection regarding the two [positions]: "If consciousness has an aspect, would there not be a diversity of the mind?"
If there were no imprinting by the form [of the object], there would be no basis for proximity.
(536) If cognition possessed a form, then in the case of variegated carpets and the like, the cognition itself would have to be variegated.
Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity to possess manifoldness (*citratva*), as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If, on the other hand, it were formless (*anākāra*), then the determination that "this cognition has blue as its object and not yellow" could not be established;
for since there would be no distinction due to the uniform nature of consciousness (*bodharūpatā*) everywhere, there would be no basis for proximity (*pratyāsatti*).
He responds with the words beginning "By you also," [stating]: "When that [objection] must be stated by you as well, there is some reply to it."
"And whatever solution you have for this, that shall be ours as well.

This objection is common to both of us, because even you must necessarily accept one of the two positions—either with form (*sākāra*) or without form (*anākāra*)—otherwise, cognition that apprehends an object could not be established;
nor is there any other mode apart from these two positions."

Since that by which cognition will apprehend the object is such that it is not logical to challenge one side when both sides share the same fault, therefore whatever answer you have here shall also be ours.

For instance: in the case of the theory of images (*sākārapakṣa*), you must necessarily describe the answer that the images are unreal, or that they are non-different from a single cognition due to the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), even though there is a difference [between cognition and its image].

That very answer will be ours as well. Even in the case of the theory of no-images (*nirākārapakṣa*), one must describe that the nature of cognition—which makes specific objects known—is produced by the aforementioned cause;
this will then be our answer too, for us Buddhists who are proponents of imageless consciousness (*nirākāravijñānavādin*). Thus, this resolution is not to be challenged; such is the rebuttal.

Having thus established the means of valid cognition that apprehends the relationship between cause and effect, he says—"The destruction of what has been done," and so forth—in order to refute the faults of the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done: "The destruction of what has been done would indeed occur if [the cause] did not produce an effect."

Nor is it accepted that [the cause] is thus, because there is no causality in a continuous series (prabandha). Furthermore, there would be the arrival of what was not produced if an effect were ever to arise without its cause;
this is not so, because of the necessity of causal power.

For if, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), some agent or enjoyer were intended, then by accepting the momentary destruction of things, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the loss of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) and so forth. However, since this entire universe is merely a matter of conditioned causality (*pratyayatāmātra*), nothing is created by any agent, nor is anything enjoyed;
how, then, could the consequence of the loss of what has been done and so forth be applied?

Now, if it is argued that because the capacity to produce desired and undesired fruits— established by the volitions of prior wholesome actions and so forth— is lost, and because the fruit arises from a specific capacity not established by prior karma, there follows, respectively, the faults of the destruction of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*), that is incorrect. For there is no contradiction whatsoever between the continuity of the capacity established by prior karma and the doctrine of selflessness (*nairātmya*).

For instance: just as in the case of seeds sprinkled with the juice of lac and other substances, specific potencies (sāmarthya-viśeṣa) deposited by prior actions continue through the continuum (saṃtāna); from these, when they have reached maturity at a later time, a desirable or undesirable fruit arises.

Nor is it accepted that the production of a fruit occurs from a continuum that has not been infused with impressions (saṃskāra) by prior actions; therefore, how can the fault of "the acquisition of what was not done" (akṛtābhyāgama) apply?
Uddyotakara, however, says: because the mind is unstable, the infusion of impressions by actions is not possible.
That is incorrect;

for there is no such thing as "imprinting" (*vāsanā*) for that which is stable and has not abandoned its prior nature, whereas for that which is unstable, imprinting is simply the production of another distinct state of being.

Furthermore, as for what was stated in the treatise—that which is stable and neutral (avyākṛta) is "perfumable" (*vāsya*)—this is said with reference to stability in terms of continuity (*prabandha*).

For that which is subject to cessation (*ucchedin*), because it lacks presence at the time when its fruit is to be produced after a very long period, it cannot function as a cause; therefore, it is untenable for such a thing to serve as the substratum for the latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding the production of such a fruit. Thus, since this person has said something based on ignorance of the established tenets of others, his statement deserves to be disregarded.

Kumārila, however, says: "We do not claim that there is the loss of what has been done (*kṛtanāśa*) or the acquisition of what has not been done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) due to the destruction of an action performed by some agent, for in your view no agent exists at all. Rather, it is because you admit the destruction of an action and its fruit without any continuity (*niranvaya*) that the faults of the loss of what has been done and the acquisition of what has not been done follow as logical consequences."

Showing that, since such loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*) and acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*) are accepted [by us], it is not right to charge us with an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpādana*), he says: "By means of the conceptual distinction of momentary difference" (*kṣaṇabhedavikalpena*).

By means of the conceptual distinction of momentary difference, the objection regarding the destruction of moments and so forth is raised; however, nothing at all undesirable has been brought forward by the opponents. (540)

Because the preceding moment of karma perishes without leaving a trace, there is the loss of what was done (*kṛtanāśa*); and because a previously non-existent moment of the fruit arises, there is the acquisition of what was not done (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Thus, whatever objection is raised regarding the loss of what was done and so forth based on the conceptual distinction between moments is precisely what we accept;
for we shall demonstrate that there is no continuity whatsoever, even of the slightest portion of a real entity.
Regarding what was said—that a discerning person would not act at all—he replies with the verse beginning "ahīnasattva":

"For those whose courage and views are undiminished, the conceptualization of momentary difference does not lead to action in any way whatsoever due to the conceit of the unity of the continuum. (541)
But those who have fully awakened to reality, having understood the necessity of causes that perish moment by moment, undertake virtuous actions.

As for those who have not yet abandoned the innate and acquired views of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and so forth, they simply do not possess this conceptualization of the distinction between moments.

For instance—even those ordinary beings who are virtuous, having determined through reasoning and scripture that things are truly momentary and selfless, and thus having realized reality as it is, proceed with their activities while harboring the satisfaction that "we shall become happy" by conceiving the continuum as a unity; they too likewise understand the nature of dependent origination:

that from acts such as giving preceded by compassion and so forth, there arise in succession other and further momentary conditioned factors (saṃskāra) characterized by the welfare of oneself and others.
But they do not [act] out of injury and so forth; rather, having ascertained the specific determination of cause and effect, they engage in virtuous and other actions.
As it has been said: "As long as the loss of love for oneself does not completely perish, one remains neither at ease nor established in well-being while imposing suffering [upon others];
therefore, effort is made to eliminate false superimposition, even in the absence of an experiencer."
How the causal relationship and the means of valid cognition that apprehends it are established has already been demonstrated [in verses 541–542].
Regarding the statement that recognition is difficult to establish among entities that are subject to momentary destruction, he says: "Of only some," and so forth;
for only certain mental states possess a specific causal efficiency (kāryakāritā).
Therefore, memory and the other [mental functions] are everywhere established and uncontradicted.
Regarding the term "kāryakāryitā": that which has an effect is "kāryin," meaning a cause.
The state of being effect and cause is "effect-causality," meaning the relationship of cause and effect;
for in ultimate reality, there is no such thing as a rememberer or an experiencer.

The summary of the meaning is as follows: it is not the case that "only he by whom something was experienced remembers it"; rather, memory and so forth arise only in that continuum where the seed of memory and so on has been deposited through a powerful experience, due to the production of successive moments that are increasingly more distinguished. This is because the relationship between cause and effect is strictly determined;
as it has been said: "And the consequence of [someone else] remembering or experiencing [what another did] does not constitute a refutation."

Since memory arises regarding something previously experienced by a certain [cognition] that was not [previously] remembered, and since recognition and so forth are produced preceded by such recollection, there is no contradiction.

Furthermore, it is not established anywhere that recognition and so forth are based upon a single cognizer, such that it could be said, "But if there were a duality [of cognizers], there would be no basis [for them]. This is because difference is admitted everywhere solely on the basis of the relationship of cause and effect.

Regarding what was stated—that the establishment of bondage and liberation is untenable because [the self] is bound by the shackles of passion and so forth—he says in response: "And those which exist as cause and effect," and so on;
for in that context, ignorance and the rest are considered to exist as cause and effect.
Bondage is defined as that [state], and liberation is the purity of the intellect resulting from its removal.
(544) Indeed, for us, bondage and liberation are never established as residing in a single person, because no one who is being bound or being liberated is established.
Rather, the formative tendencies beginning with ignorance and ending with old age and death are conventionally designated as "bondage" because they are the causes for the arising of suffering.
And so it has been said: "In this way, there occurs the origination of this entire mass of suffering.
Furthermore, when those [factors] beginning with ignorance have ceased through the knowledge of reality, that stainlessness of the intellect is called liberation from bondage (*nirmukti-mukti*).
As it has been stated: "The mind itself, when permeated by the afflictions such as attachment and the rest, is indeed *saṃsāra*."
"That very [state] when freed from those [defilements] is called the end of existence.

(544) Furthermore, regarding what was stated as "having a single substratum" and so forth, he says— "The two are established as having a single substratum," etc.— demonstrating that even there, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
These two, bondage and liberation, are not established as having a single substratum, even in the worldly sense; for it is well known that everything is indeed momentary.

Since it has been proven that every entity perishes immediately after its arising, there is no established case anywhere of bondage and liberation having a single substratum; thus, the example is unestablished.
Having thus established his own position, he refutes the opposing position with the words "in every way" (*sarvathā*) and so forth:
"Because no excellence exists in any way, such [a nature] as this is contradicted in the self."
"Otherwise, the established order of agent, enjoyer, bondage, and so forth, as well as impermanence, would not exist.
(546) Thus concludes the examination of the connection between action and its fruit.

For if some bondage were produced for the self by afflictions such as passion (*rāga*), or some excellence (*atiśaya*) by means of cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, then there could be an established order of its bondage, liberation, and so on.

The sense is that, since there can be no production of any excellence (*atiśaya*) in that which is eternal, such an established order of bondage, liberation, and so forth— characterized by the fixed limits of cause and effect— is not possible for it, just as it is not for space. Otherwise,
if an excellence were produced in the self, then because that excellence would be identical with the self, the self itself, being non-different from that excellence, would likewise be impermanent.

Furthermore, it has been analyzed in a hundred ways that an excellence (*atiśaya*) residing in something else is not tenable because the relationship [between the agent and the excellence] is unestablished (see verse 546). Thus concludes the examination of the connection between action and its fruit.

The Examination of the Category of Substance: Now, in order to establish that [the self] is devoid of such adventitious attributes as quality, substance, action, genus, inherence, and so forth, the author introduces the examination of the six categories and says: "Of genus, etc. and so on.
"The lack of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) in genus and so forth, which was previously explained, is untenable;
for the six categories, beginning with substance, exist as ultimate realities.
Thus say the followers of Akṣapāda and Kaṇāda, relying solely on scripture.

"This negation of substance and so forth is stated in brief. (548) [Objection: Previously, in the "Examination of Enduring Entities," it was stated that because universals (*jāti*) and the like lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), momentary destruction is not at all accepted; thus, that previously demonstrated absence of intrinsic nature in universals and the like is incorrect. For the followers of Akṣapāda and others assert that the six categories (*padārtha*)—namely, substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—are ultimately real.
Because they are disciples of Akṣapāda, the Naiyāyikas are called Ākṣapādas;
however, the disciples of Kaṇāda are the Vaiśeṣikas, who are called Kāṇādas and are said to rely on scripture alone (āgamamātraka).
Those who possess only scripture devoid of reasoning are called "those who rely on mere scripture.
In this context, beginning with the words "earth and so forth," he first states the classification of substance (dravya) for the purpose of refuting it as a category:
"Substance is held to be ninefold, divided according to the distinctions of earth and the rest;
that which begins with earth is fourfold, and is twofold by way of being eternal or non-eternal. (549)
The sense is that it is indeed possible to state the refutation of [the categories] by means of their specific divisions once they have been analyzed.
The term "ninefold" is based on the Sūtra: "Earth, water, fire, air, ether, time, space, self, and mind."
In this context, the substance consisting of earth, water, fire, and air—this fourfold category—is of two types, distinguished as eternal and non-eternal.
(549) Demonstrating this very twofold nature, he says: "First, those whose nature consists of earth and so forth," and so on.
Those atoms which are accepted as being composed of earth and the other elements are impermanent; however, those things which are produced by them [the atoms] and so forth are perishable.
For earth and the other elements, when consisting of atoms, are eternal, because atoms are eternal.

Those [compounds] initiated by those [atoms] are impermanent, according to the logical principle that "that which has a cause is impermanent. Regarding the term "initiated by those" (*tadādyaiḥ*): those atoms are "the first" (*ādyāḥ*) among those [compounds] of which they are the beginning; thus, they are called *tadādyāḥ*.
The meaning is that space and the others are indeed eternal.
(550) In this regard, he says "therein," etc., in order to negate these four types of substance.

In this regard, the non-existence of those things in the form of eternal atoms has been established, because the momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) pervading all things without exception has been proven.

[Verse 551] In that context, as for these earth and other elements described as being in the form of eternal atoms, their non-existence in the form of eternity has indeed been established by proving the momentary destruction that extends across all things without remainder.

Whatever exists is all momentary, because for that which is non-momentary, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradicted by both [successive and simultaneous] action; thus, since existence—which is defined by that [causal efficiency]—is excluded, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been established.
(551) Here too, he states the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*): "In the case of permanence," and so forth.
If [the atoms] were eternal, all gross objects would indeed arise simultaneously;
for they have no dependence on conjunction and the like, since those [causes] are without distinction.

(552) If it is admitted that the atoms which are the causes of gross objects such as mountains are eternal, then it follows that their effects—the gross objects—would arise all at once, because their causes would be complete and unimpaired.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things whose complete causes are unobstructed arise all at once, just as many sprouts arise simultaneously when their complete causes are unobstructed; and gross entities, which are intended to be the effects of eternal atoms, have their complete causes unobstructed. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

If there were non-arising even when the complete causal complex is present, it would follow that there is never any arising at all, because there is no distinction [between the two states]; this constitutes a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
Now, it might be argued that three kinds of causes are accepted: the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), and the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*).
Among these, that in which the effect inheres is its inherent cause.

However, that which, while not being inherent [in the effect], attains the status of a cause is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), such as the conjunction of parts in the production of a composite substance.
But the remaining type of cause is the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth; this is their distinction.

Anticipating the objection that "the status of being a complete cause is unestablished because the required conjunction and other factors are absent, and therefore the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished," he says: "conjunction and so forth..."
For if some particular quality were imparted to atoms by means of conjunction and so forth, then they would depend upon it;
however, since atoms are eternal, no particular quality can be imparted to them by others.
Therefore, how could conjunction and the like be something upon which they must depend?
Furthermore, there is no simultaneous arising of gross things such as bodies and houses, because we observe that bodies and so forth arise sequentially;

therefore, the formal argument is the opposite: those which have sequential effects as their cause are eternal, just as seeds and the like—which produce sequential effects such as sprouts—are eternal; and atoms are likewise [sequential in their effects]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Aviddhakarṇa states a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the eternality of atoms: "That which is intended to be the producer of atoms does not possess the property of being real, because it is not an object of a means of valid cognition that establishes existence, like the horn of a donkey."
The term *saddharma* refers to the property (*dharma*) of that which exists (*sat*), meaning its existence; it has been approached or attained by that [atom], which means "it exists.
This is a negation of that [existence], meaning there is no cause for the production of atoms.

Demonstrating this very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) preceded by a doubt, he says: "If that which has reached the true dharma (*saddharma*) is not accepted as producing atoms, because it is not an object of a means of valid cognition whose purpose is the apprehension of what already exists" (verse 553).
The connection [of the words] is: "If it is not accepted that [the means of knowledge] produces atoms and conforms to the true nature of reality.

"Apprehension" (upalambha) is the perception of what exists; "attainment" (adhigama) is that which has this apprehension as its object or purpose—that is, the means of knowledge (pramāṇa) for which that is the goal.
The rest is easily understood.

By this, it has been demonstrated that the thesis asserting the impermanence of atoms is sublated by inference; for, according to the statement "that which exists and lacks a cause is permanent," the permanence of atoms is established by virtue of their being without a cause. (553)
With the words "Not because of non-establishment" and so forth, he states the non-establishment of the reason:
"Because the cause of the dyad (aṇuka) is not seen as being anything other than [the threads], such as the weaver;
for all cloth and the like consist of atoms. (554)

[Objection: Surely wehravers and the like are established as the causes of cloth and such things, not of atoms; so how can wehravers and the like be seen as the cause of atoms? [Reply: He says, "consisting of atoms," etc.;
the intention is that we shall establish this point later.

Furthermore, he demonstrates that the reason is inconclusive because there is no contradiction in the existence of objects remote in space, time, or nature, even when the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehend them are absent—stating "because of the absence of a cognition grasping an existent," and so forth:
"Or rather, existence is not established merely by the absence of a means of valid cognition that grasps an existent;
for when a means of valid cognition is withdrawn, there is no certainty regarding the non-existence of the object. (555)
The meaning is that there is no certainty regarding the non-existence of an object, just as in the case of [perceiving] a *piśāca* or similar entities.

Having thus refuted the causal substance, he speaks in order to refute the effect-substance: "But that whole (avayavin) produced from those [parts], which possesses distinct qualities and parts, is not perceived at all; therefore, it is not established, as it lacks any means of valid cognition. (556)
Qualities (*guṇa*) are color and so forth; parts (*avayava*) are threads and so forth. That which possesses their distinction—that is, their separation—is what is thus described.
Such a whole (*avayavin*), distinct from qualities and parts, is not perceived;

for a substance characterized as a cloth or the like, being a separate entity from its white and other qualities as well as from its parts such as threads, never appears in any visual or other cognition in its entirety.
Thus, since no substance existing as an entity distinct from its qualities is perceived here, the doctrine of the quality-possessor (*guṇin*) is refuted.

Furthermore, because no whole (*avayavin*) distinct from its parts is perceived, the doctrine of the part-possessor (*avayavin*) is also refuted by the following formal argument (*prayoga*): whatever meets the conditions for perceptibility and yet is not perceived in a certain place does not exist there, just as a jar or similar object is not found in a particular location when it is not being perceived. And neither a quality-possessor nor a whole—which are both asserted to be visible—is perceived in that very same place as something distinct from the qualities and the parts; therefore, [the whole is non-existent] due to the non-perception of its own nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because of the statement, "In the case of a large [object], there is perception due to its possessing multiple substances and due to color," since those two [substances and color] are intended to be visible.
With the words beginning with "But surely" (*nanu*), Uddyotakara, Bhāvivikta, and others raise the objection that the reason is unestablished.
Indeed, a crystal stone is seen when in contact with a colored substrate;
likewise, a crane and other such objects are seen even when their own form is not perceived.
This is also the case with a man concealed by a garment, even though his form and other attributes are not apprehended.
The cognition of a person is observed [as distinct from his qualities], just as the cognition of a cloth is [distinct] in the case of a dyed garment.

(558) Thus they say: "The possessor of qualities is indeed perceived as distinct from the qualities themselves, because it is perceived even when its qualities, such as color and so forth, are not perceived."
For instance, a crystal stone, while in proximity to an adjunct, is indeed perceived even when its own inherent white quality is not apprehended;
and at night, in a faint light, a crane and the like are indeed grasped even when their white color and so forth are not seen.

Similarly, in the case of a man whose body is covered by a floor-length bodice, although his dark complexion and other features are not perceived at that time, the cognition "this is a man, this is a man" certainly arises.

Even when a cloth dyed with astringent substances, saffron, or the like is not perceived in its own form because it is overwhelmed by the color of the dye, the cognition of "cloth" certainly still occurs.
Thus, it has first been demonstrated that the distinction between quality and the possessor of quality is established by direct perception itself;
now, demonstrating that it is also established by inference, he says: "Form and so forth," etc.—form and the other qualities are absolutely distinct from the blue lotus and the like.
Because of that exclusion, the horse is utterly distinct from Caitra and others, as well as from earth and so forth, and from form, smell, and the rest;
this is due to the difference between singular and plural designations, just like the distinction between the moon and the stars. (559–560)

The quality is distinct from the blue lotus and so forth, because by means of that [lotus]—as in the expression "the color and other qualities of the blue lotus"—it (the quality) is distinguished from that blue lotus and the rest.
Just as in the case of "Caitra’s horse," where the horse is distinguished from other owners by Caitra and is therefore distinct from him, there is another formal argument:

each of the substances—earth, water, fire, and air—is distinct from color, taste, smell, and touch, because they are the referents of singular and plural number respectively; just as in the case of "the moon" and "the stars."

For just as the singular "moon" and the plural "stars" are perceived as the basis for the distinction between the moon and the stars, so too here, the singular "earth" and the plural "color, taste, smell, and touch" [indicate a distinction];
this should be applied similarly to water and the other elements.
As for the distinctions among the stars, they are Puṣya and so forth.

Having thus established the difference between the quality and the possessor of the quality, he says "vibhinna" and so forth in order to establish the difference between the part and the whole: *vibhinnetyādi* (and so forth).

The thread and the cloth are distinct because they possess different makers, powers, and so forth, due to their association with contradictory properties, just like the distinction between a pillar and a jar.

(561) The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which have different makers, effects, times, and dimensions are distinct, such as pillars, jars, and the like; and the objects under investigation likewise have different makers, effects, times, and dimensions.
The reason is neither unestablished nor inconclusive;
for the mutual distinction between entities is based solely upon the superimposition of contradictory properties, as is the case with pillars and the like, and even between a whole and its parts.

To explain: the weaver woman is the agent of the threads, while the weaver is the agent of the cloth; the cloth is capable of performing functions such as warding off cold, whereas the threads are not. Furthermore, the threads exist at a prior time because they are perceived even before [the cloth], whereas the cloth exists at a subsequent time, occurring after the operations of the weaver and others. Moreover, the cloth possesses a certain magnitude in terms of its length and breadth which is not possessed by each individual thread; thus, there is a difference in dimension. Therefore, the meaning is that the logical reasons (hetus) are not inconclusive (anaikāntika). 561

Having thus established the difference between the parts and the whole through inference, he says the following—beginning with "In the absence of gross objects"—in order to establish it through direct perception as well:
"If gross objects were impossible, there would be no perception of trees and the like; for atoms are beyond the senses, and there could be no mention of 'atoms' [if they were not perceived]. (562)
For a very subtle object is described as such only in relation to a gross object;
but in the absence of any gross single object, in relation to what would its subtlety exist?
(563) For if the whole (avayavin) did not exist, there would be the consequence of no perception at all, because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses.
If the gross were non-existent, the designation "subtle" would not even occur;
why? He says: "For [the notion of subtle] is dependent upon a gross object," and so forth, which is easy to understand.
