But surely, crystals and the like are perceived in the form of red and other colors?
"And they do not possess that nature [of being momentary], because that would entail the destruction of their own position.

(564) He refutes this with the words "But surely" (*nanu*) and so forth: as for what was stated—that crystals and the like are perceived in their pure state even when their inherent qualities are not perceived—that is unproven;
for since that cognition is erroneous due to its lack of correspondence with reality, it has no [external] object.
For instance: when a hibiscus flower or similar object is placed nearby, the crystal is perceived as having a red or other color;
likewise, even cranes and others, though being white, are seen in a dark form—and yet they do not possess that nature, namely a red or such color, in reality.

Why? Because it would entail the destruction of your own position. For if their nature as such were real, then even when that specific form is not perceived, they would still be perceived; thus, the position you have just stated would be undermined.
One might argue: "Even a crystal or similar object is indeed perceived as distinct from its red or other colors. To this, he says: "tadrūpa... and so forth.

And no other nature distinct from that form is perceived; nor is it logical for them [the crystals] to be cognized by a cognition of another form, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For no other nature—no essence characterized as a crystal and so forth—is seen apart from that red and other forms, since only the red and other forms are actually perceived.
If it is argued that even crystals and the like, though not possessing that form, are perceived in the form of red and so forth, he says: "And not," etc.
For it is by virtue of its own form that the cognition's status as having a specific object is established;
if a cognition of one form were to have another object, [the rule would fail].
This being the case, even the cognition of form would have sound and other objects as its domain, since there is no distinction [between them].

Furthermore, showing that even if it were granted that a cognition of one form could have another object, your desired conclusion would still not be established, he says: "White and so forth are likewise."
"Likewise, it is also possible that white and other such qualities are cognized [independently];
therefore, this cognition is erroneous, like the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and so forth.
For instance, it could also be conceived that white and other qualities exist in that manner, devoid of any substance (guṇin) distinct from them, and appearing in the form of red and so on."
Consequently, the substratum possessing qualities (guṇin) is not established;
the word "ca" is used for emphasis and is displaced in its position, being intended to follow immediately after the words "śuklādayaḥ" (white, etc.),
as in the phrase "this is an error."
The ellipsis is "because it is not in accordance with reality" (566).
And as for what was said [in verse 567], beginning with "when the Person is within the *kañcuka*s," etc.
Even that [cognition] is not perception, because it is accompanied by verbal designation (*sābhijalpa*) and because its form is indistinct;

rather, this cognition is inferential, having as its object a person characterized merely as a collection of form and so forth. Thus, he shows that there is no establishment of a composite whole (*avayavin*)—in the verse beginning with *kañcuka*, etc.:
"Regarding a person situated within a garment, the cognition is indeed inferential."

"Because of the perception of the casing which is the arrangement of its cause. (567) That person is so described because he is the cause of an arrangement whose nature consists merely of an accumulation of form and so forth; that is, the arrangement which has him as its cause. The "arrangement" refers to a specific configuration belonging to that "casing"—thus it is so described. By this, it is demonstrated that the inferential cognition arises from a specific mark known as an effect (*kārya*).
Regarding what was said— that there is the cognition of "cloth" in a dyed cloth— he replies with the verse beginning "kaṣāya," etc.:
from lac, saffron, and so forth, another color arises in the cloth.

For, since the cloth is momentary, when its previous form—such as white—is destroyed, a new form and so forth arises solely through the power of a different causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Once that [new form] is apprehended by direct perception, there subsequently arises a conceptualizing reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśajñāna*)—such as "cloth, cloth"—which follows upon direct perception, which has the aggregate as its object, and which, though based on linguistic convention, is ultimately devoid of a real object. Thus, its status as direct perception is unestablished.
Nor is this an inference, because its object was already grasped by a previous perception and because it lacks the characteristics of a logical mark;
therefore, there is no obscured form present here.

This might be the case: if the unperceived white color and so forth do not exist at all in the cloth, how is it that it is perceived again in states such as after washing? To this he says: "Again," and so forth.
From that very same [prior] form, depending upon water and other factors, another form arises—such as whiteness from [the cloth], just as blackness arises from copper and the like. (569)

Just as when iron or other metals, having acquired a brilliant color and so forth through contact with fire, subsequently develop a dark color and so forth, in that same way, another color—such as white and so on—is produced; thus there is no contradiction.

(569) It might be asked: "How is this understood—that another color is produced, and not that the previous color, having been suppressed, was previously unperceived but is later perceived due to the cessation of its suppression? To this he says: "In the state of remaining as it was," and so forth.
But if the form remains in that same state, there can be no suppression by another, because its original nature, which was previously unsuppressed, persists.
The formal argument is: that which has not abandoned its un-suppressed intrinsic nature cannot be suppressed by another.

Just as in its previous state, the nature of that very form remains unrenounced and unoverpowered even in the state of being overpowered; thus, there is the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
If one accepts that its nature is renounced and overpowered, its distinctness from things such as color (*rūpa*) and blue lotuses (*indīvara*) is established.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the genitive case" (*ṣaṣṭhī*), etc., he says: 570. [Regarding the statement] "color and so forth [are distinct] from blue lotuses and so forth," he says: "The genitive case," and so on.
The use of the genitive case, distinctions in number, and so forth, arise solely from the speaker’s intention;
therefore, it is not logical to establish the true nature of things based on them.
(571) For if the application of the genitive and other such cases were established as corresponding to the actual state of things, then the establishment of those things would follow from that.

To the extent that these [constructions] arise merely from independent whim and do not depend on distinctions and so forth existing in external objects, how can the establishment of a real entity (*vastu*) proceed from them?

In this regard, there is the use of the genitive case, as in "the color and so forth *of* the cloth" (*paṭasya rūpādayaḥ*), and the difference in expression such as "the cloth *is* the color and so forth" (*paṭo rūpādayaḥ*);

by the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the locative case here, as in "the color and so forth *in* the cloth" (*paṭe rūpādayaḥ*), and the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*), as in "the state of being a cloth" (*paṭatvam*)—this is what is intended by the phrase "and so forth."
With the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*) and so forth, [the author] establishes the very point of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*):
for instance, the existence of the six [categories] is not admitted by others to be distinct [from their own nature].

Nor is a single group among them accepted as having any real referent. To explain: in cases such as "the existence of the six categories" or "the group of those six," the genitive case and so forth occur even though there is no actual difference [between the whole and its parts];
for you do not admit that existence and the like are anything other than the six categories themselves.
This is an illustrative example;
likewise, in cases such as *dārāḥ* (wife) and *sikatāḥ* (sand), we do not perceive a difference in meaning despite the presence of the plural number.
Furthermore, in the expression "one's own state is *svatvam*," no state (*bhāva*) distinct from the self is intended.
With the words "saṃjñāpaka" and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's reply:
"The reality [of an object] is held to reside within the domain of the means of valid cognition that makes it known."

If it is argued that "the existence of the six [categories] exists," then it follows that this existence must be something other than those six. The meaning is as follows: "existence" (astitva) is the state of being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes [an object] known; it is a distinct property (*dharmāntara*) consisting in being the object of a means of valid cognition that apprehends what is existent.
Therefore, there is no deviation [in the definition]. This is the intended sense.
To this, he states the following reply: "He [the opponent] falls into the consequence that there is something other than the six"—the word "category" (*padārtha*) is to be supplied as the remainder;
thus, a seventh category would result, and consequently, the commitment to only six categories would be lost. This is the sense.
If it is argued that there is no fault because [the number] is accepted, then how is it stated that there are "six categories"? To this he says: "These six..."

If it is argued that these six are declared to be the substrata (dharmin) and that the properties (dharma) are indeed intended to be distinct from them, then what kind of relationship is held by you to exist between that [substratum] and those [properties]? It cannot be conjunction (saṃyoga), nor any other [inherence], because such a restriction would be impossible in the case of substances.
Inherence exists, and no other relation has been accepted by the opponents.

Those entities which are of the nature of subjects (dharmin) are called the six categories; however, those which are of the nature of attributes (dharma) are indeed intended to be distinct from them. For instance, the text in the *Padārthapraveśaka* states: "Thus, this enumeration of subjects has been made without [explicitly mentioning] their attributes."
He provides the answer with the words beginning "Who is this? and so forth: "of that"—meaning of a property such as existence—and "by them"—meaning by the six categories.
What relationship exists by virtue of which this [property] becomes a property (*dharma*) of those [subjects]?
For, without a relationship, the state of being a property-possessor (*dharmī*) and a property (*dharma*) is not logical, because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For in that case, everything would be the property of everything; yet there is no relationship whatsoever with them.

To explain: relation is indeed of only two kinds, characterized as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and characterized as inherence (*samavāya*). Among these, it cannot first be of the nature of conjunction, because, being a quality (*guṇa*), it is restricted to substances (*dravya*) alone. Nor can it consist of inherence, because inherence is accepted as being unitary like existence (*bhāva*); and if there were a relation consisting of inherence by means of another inherence, a second inherence would have to be admitted.

If it is argued that the relationship between property and its substratum (dharma-dharmin-bhāva) will exist even without a [further] relation, he says: "In the case of the impossibility of a relation," and so forth.
And since a relationship between them is untenable, how could it be their property?
If it were merely because they produce it, then others would also be of that same nature.
For it has been stated that in this way there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, if it is argued that because Dharma is produced by those six categories, this Dharma is said to belong to them, then other things such as water and so forth would likewise— merely by virtue of the relationship characterized by being produced from them— be related to things like a bowl and the like. Consequently, the postulation of other specific relations called conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) in their case would be useless.
"Its existence as well" thus involves a distinct case-ending; and if there were another [existence] for that [existence], an infinite regress would result.
Furthermore, even granting that existence (*astitva*) is indeed a distinct entity (*dharmāntara*), there would still be a logical inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*);
for that [existence] itself certainly possesses existence because it is a real thing (*vastu*).
Consequently, how could there be a case-ending (*vibhakti*) based on a distinction (*vyatireka*) in that regard?
Now, if another existence is admitted even in that case, then there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā).
If it is argued that an infinite regress does not constitute a refutation because it is accepted [as such], he says: "Anyā... and so forth.

When another property is superimposed upon it, the status of being a substratum (dharmitā) is attained there; for this very reason, even substances and the like are accepted as having the status of a substratum.
Indeed, because of the successive superimposition of properties upon all things, they would all possess the status of a substratum.
Consequently, the claim that "these six are stated to be only *dharmis*" (subjects) is untenable, because there exist other *dharmis* besides the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*). This is the sense.
Furthermore, if it were argued that "only those which are of the nature of *dharmin* have been determined as being six," this too is entirely without substance;
for in such a case, there would be no mention of qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), universals (*sāmānya*), particularities (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*).

It is not that these have only the nature of a substratum (dharmin); rather, they also possess the nature of attributes (dharma), precisely because they are dependent upon a substance, and thus through this very fact,
other attributes may also inhere in them.

Another, however, says: "The existence of the six [categories] consists in their being accessible to a means of valid cognition that apprehends what exists; and accessibility is the consciousness whose object is the six categories, because when that [consciousness] exists, the linguistic usage of 'existent' proceeds. Likewise, knowability is produced by knowledge, and nameability is produced by naming."
Therefore, the genitive case is indeed based on distinction (*vyatireka*),
nor does this lead to an infinite regress, nor does it entail the consequence of a seventh category of existence;
thus, even that [objection] is merely a conceptual construction.

If their very essence as a self-nature consists precisely in being entities capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-samartha*), then there is no contradiction whatsoever if those very entities capable of causal efficiency are designated by means of an ablative case-ending (*vyatireka-vibhakti*)—such as "the existence of these"—when there is a desire to know merely the exclusion of other differences.

For even a nature that is non-different from that [object] may be mentally extracted from it and expressed as if it were different; this is entirely without contradiction, because words function according to mere intention, just like the conceptualization of qualities such as abundance or beauty in stories composed by invention.
As for the argument beginning with "vibhinnakartṛśaktyādeḥ" (due to the difference in agent, power, etc.), he says: "And from the first ones," and so forth.
If the difference of the cloth from its initial threads is being established, then the futility of the proof would be unavoidable;
for those other threads that have arisen have indeed reached a specific state.

If it is argued that there is a difference between the cloth and the threads existing in the initial state—which have not yet acquired the designation "cloth"—and which are occupied with specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), then what is being proven is already established.

This is because all entities are momentary; thus, even though the threads denoted by the word "cloth" are not distinct from the preceding threads (in terms of their nature), their production is admitted [as a new occurrence].

Now, if it is argued that the cloth's distinctness from those threads existing at the same time as the cloth is established, [the author] says "one" and so forth, demonstrating that in that case the reasons would be unestablished (*asiddha*).
In order to make known their utility for a single purpose, and with the desire to avoid the faults of prolixity, incapacity, and futility that would arise from separate mention,
there is conciseness in linguistic usage through complete expression. (581)

A cloth that possesses distinct properties such as the capacities and dimensions of its various makers cannot be established as being co-temporal with those [individual threads] upon which the speakers have projected a single verbal designation. (582–583)

If at that time a cloth were established as existing simultaneously with the threads yet distinct from them, then properties such as having a different agent from the threads could be established for it; however, this very cloth distinct from the threads is not established, since it is precisely the proof of their difference that is currently under discussion. Furthermore, the difference between things does not arise from a mere difference in name, such as "cloth" versus "threads," because another name is applied even when no other functional purpose is observed.

For instance: certain threads, having reached a specific state, become capable of performing a single purposeful action, such as removing cold, whereas others—which are produced by women [into garments]—do not.

In that context, a single term, "cloth," is applied by users to designate those specific threads that are useful for that single purposeful action, so that their usage may be non-confused even though there is no separate entity [apart from the threads].
To the question, "Why, then, is a single term applied? he says: "In the case of separate terms," and so forth.
If each [word] were denoted separately in the scripture, there would be the fault of prolixity (*gaurava*).

For instance, as many words as there are objects capable of accomplishing the single intended purpose would have to be employed; thus, there is the fault of prolixity. Furthermore, it is impossible to specify their unique, uncommon form; thus, there is the fault of incapacity (*aśakti*).

And when there is a designation by means of a conceptualized general form (*sāmānyākāra*), it is better to convey it through a single expression alone; for no fruit whatsoever is perceived from the effort of conveying it separately and repeatedly, which results in the fault of futility (*vaiphalyadoṣa*).
However, when the denotation is made as a whole, the merit is the economy of linguistic usage (*vyavahāralāghava*);
thus, when there is a desire to express all things collectively, the term "one speech" (*ekā vāk*) is used, just like the words *jagat*, *tribhuvana*, and *viśva*.
The meaning is that the word "cloth" (*paṭa*) refers to the verbal expression;

furthermore, the agent and the properties such as capacity and dimension are what is meant by those two [terms]. Having formed a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) with the word "distinct" (*vibhinna*) [applied to both], the suffix *matup* should then be applied.
Regarding what was stated, namely that "a gross object is impossible" and so forth, he says in response: "They are mutually supportive."
The supersensuous nature of atoms is unproven, because when they have reached a particular state, they become perceptible by the senses;
for one who holds the position that atoms are eternal, their supersensuousness would persist forever due to the absence of any change in them, whereas for us, they come together with one another.
And those atoms which are produced as mutually supporting one another do not possess supersensuousness, because they fall within the range of other [senses].
(584) "Mutually supporting" means being mutual auxiliaries.
With the words "blue and so forth," etc., he demonstrates that very fact of being within the range of the senses:
"The blue and so forth is the imagined, inherent form of the atoms."
And visual cognition and the like are experienced as having the appearance of blue and so forth.
[Objection: But surely atoms are held to be situated according to distinctions of direction such as priority and posteriority, yet they are not perceived in that form;
so how can these be objects of direct perception? To this he says: "By the distinction of priority and posteriority," and so on.

Even though these [cognitions] lack a defining characteristic due to the absence of a distinction between preceding and succeeding moments, nevertheless, their status as direct perception remains uncontradicted, as is the case with a beverage (*pānaka*) and the like.
(Verse 586) The compound *adhyakṣatābādhā* is analyzed as "the non-contradiction (*abādhā*) of the status of being direct perception (*adhyakṣatā*)" (*adhyakṣatāyā abādhā*).

The meaning is that this [cognition] is non-composite because it is not subject to sublation; thus, its status as direct perception remains uncontradicted, just as in the case of a beverage and the like.
For instance—in the case of fermented liquor, heated stones, or gold mixed with mercury—it is only the atoms that are perceived in that manner;

for there is no composite substance (*avayavidravya*) there, because heterogeneous substances do not originate a new substance. Nor, even if there were a difference from the atoms, could a conjunction be perceived there, because it would lack a perceptible substratum.

For where even one of the two conjoined entities is not perceived, conjunction itself is not perceived— just as, for example, the conjunction between a *piśāca* and a jar, or the conjunction between the solar orb and the points of space or direction. Furthermore, where all the conjoined entities are of the nature of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and are thus imperceptible, how could the conjunction residing therein be perceptible?
If this is so, and there is no certainty in any respect, how indeed can their status as direct perceptions (pratyakṣa) be logical? To this he says: "Of all," and so forth;
[this refers to] all things whatsoever, which consist of the nature of exclusion from everything else.
The same applies even in the case of perception; thus, there is no certainty regarding all aspects [of an object].
For even when an object is grasped by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) according to other systems of thought, there is no certainty regarding all its aspects.

To the extent that an aspect produced by the exclusion of other things (*arthāntaravyāvṛtti*) is not ascertained, to that extent it is established that the object is perceived [only in those aspects].

Because even when something is apprehended in all its aspects, if a determination of another mode does not arise, it is as if unapprehended due to its unsuitability for conventional discourse; therefore,
it is "just so."
"Just as that object was experienced" (verse 587).

Now, since the object is experienced by perception in its entirety because it is partless, why does a determination not occur in its entirety? To this he says: "Even though it is accessible to non-conceptual perception," and so forth.

Even though the defining characteristic of an object is partless and accessible only through non-conceptual perception, that which serves as the cause for the determination of its distinctions is what is cognized. (588) "Aksa" means that which arises from the *akṣa* (the sense organ); thus, it refers to sensory cognition.

The analysis of the compound is: "non-conceptualization" (*akalpanam*) and "the conceptualization of what does not exist" (*avidyamāna-kalpanam*), and that [is] "sensory" (*akṣam*). Therefore, even in that which is to be understood—that is, even in that which is to be understood by non-conceptual sensory cognition—the phrase "determination of its difference" (*yad-bheda-vyavasāya*) [applies].

Because differentiation (*bheda*) is exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), and the cause of the determination (*vyavasāya*)—that is, the certainty (*niścaya*) regarding that differentiation—is habituation (*abhyāsa*), proximity (*pratyāsatti*), the sharpness of the intellect regarding degrees of intensity (*tāratamya-buddhi-pāṭava*), and so forth;
for it is not mere experience alone that is the cause of certainty, but rather habituation and the rest as well.
Therefore, the meaning is that where these [factors] exist, certainty is produced.
And all of this has been stated while accepting the proof of atoms and the proof of the perceptibility of external objects.

However, for the Proponent of Cognition (*vijñānavādin*), no external object such as blue is established by perception, because even in the absence of an external object—as in dreams—one observes the appearance of such blue and so forth, which leads to doubt. Furthermore, since that form of blue is devoid of a nature that is either one or many, it consists of the appearance of a deluded cognition; nor are atoms established, because their unity cannot be proven when they are divided into spatial parts through their existence in prior and posterior positions.
Regarding that, how can it be said that atoms are perceived as having forms such as blue, or that their sequence is not perceived, due to the superimposition of another object caused by error?

(588) One might argue: "If the whole (*avayavin*) did not exist, then how could there be for one whose eyes are engaged the determination that 'this is a single mountain' with respect to many atoms? To this, he says: "Similar," and so forth.

Just as there is the delusion of unity in a lamp due to the arising of flames that are similar [to one another], so too is there the delusion of unity when there is the cognition of many subtle objects existing in immediate succession.

For instance, in the case of a lamp and the like, because of the occurrence of successive, similar flames in uninterrupted succession, a delusion of unity arises despite the actual difference; likewise, this delusion of unity results from the perception of many extremely subtle objects in uninterrupted succession. Thus, there is no fault.

If this is so, how can atoms be established as being perceptible when they are not perceived as distinct? To this he says: "If their perceptibility is not admitted because their distinction is not perceived," and so forth.

How is that [perceptibility] observed in the case of a lamp and the like? Or is the whole (avayavin) likewise enveloped [by its parts]? For if that which cannot be determined through distinction is not accepted as perceptible, then how is that perceptibility observed in a lamp and so forth, where the prior and posterior divisions are not perceived?
Or is the whole, even though not grasped through the distinction of its parts, accepted as such in terms of perceptibility? Thus, this [argument] is inconclusive.
With the words beginning "etāvat" (only this much), he instructs the opponent to raise an objection:
"Only this much might be the case here; how is it that there is no certainty regarding these [things]?"
It is understood that this is the form of the atoms of blue and so forth.
That too is not a valid reason, because cognition certainly does not have something beyond its range as its object,
nor can it have a single gross entity as its object, due to the contradiction between grossness and unity.
"Of these" refers to the atoms;
"that too" refers to that [same thing].

That which is uncharacterized due to the separation of atoms is causeless, because the apprehension of blue and so forth residing in atoms can arise from other [causes] as well. To explain: a proponent of external objects, being such, must certainly not accept that this cognition is without an object; otherwise, there would be nothing but the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*).

Furthermore, this object consisting of form and so forth, appearing in a gross form, must be either one or many. Even if it were one, it would have to be either composed of parts or not composed of parts.
In that regard, first of all, it is not logical for this [entity] to be of a dual nature, because it contradicts perception and other means of valid cognition.
He states what that contradiction is: "If the gross [object] were of a single nature," and so forth.
If the gross [object] were of a single nature, then when it is covered by even a mere fly’s foot, the whole would necessarily be covered, because there is no division [within it]. (593)
Furthermore, if there were a single part that was red, everything would become red, just like that [one] part;
or else, if contradictory properties were present, multiplicity would necessarily follow.

For if the gross object were one, then when one part is covered, the covering of the whole would result, and when one part is colored red, the coloring of the whole would result, because according to your view, there is no difference between the covered and the uncovered, or between the red and the non-red.
Furthermore, the superimposition of mutually contradictory properties upon a single entity is not tenable, as it would lead to an over-extension;
for in that case, the entire universe would become a single substance, and consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneous production and so forth.
Moreover, when one part is covered, the whole is not seen to be covered; thus, this contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Likewise, there is also contradiction with inference (anumānavirodha).

For instance: that which is superimposed with mutually contradictory properties cannot be one, just as a cow and a buffalo. A gross object, being of a perceptible and non-perceptible nature and thus superimposed with contradictory properties such as being covered and so forth, is [thereby shown to be many]. This is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi);
the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that everything would be one.
Uddyotakara, however, says: "Because there is no difference within a single entity, the application of all words [to it] would be untenable."
He raises an objection with the words "But this... and so forth:
"But surely, since it possesses a single nature, on what basis is the word 'all' used here?
For that [word] refers to multiple objects, yet the whole is not manifold in its essence. (595)

For instance—the word "all" (sarva) has multiple objects as its referent, yet the composite whole (avayavin) is not manifold; therefore, how can the word "all" be applied [to it], such that it would follow that "everything is covered"?
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning with "nanu" (but surely).
But surely, those things such as clothing, the body, and houses which are established through worldly convention, have been described by you as being wholes (*avayavin*).
[For example: "The entire garment is red," "all," "without exception," and likewise "the whole."
In this regard, everyone employs the expression "arisen from mere desire" (icchāmātrasaṃbhūta).
When there is such an intention to speak, we too describe it as follows:
"everything would be red," and so forth; for words have no fixed constraints.
For those very things well-known in the world, such as clothing, the body, and so forth, are conceived by you as being the "possessors of parts" (avayavin).
And in that regard, the application of the terms "whole" (sarva) and "part" (ekadeśa) is already well-established in the world;
thus, speakers say such things as, "the entire garment is red," and so on.

And when such an intention is present—that is, when there exists in the world the desire to communicate the redness and other qualities residing in objects such as a cloth that occupies an extensive space—we too, following common understanding (*pratīti*), employ words such as "all" (*sarva*) and so forth in order to demonstrate the contradiction for you.
Furthermore, this fault belongs only to you who accept the unity of a gross object, not to us; for we do not maintain the unity of a gross object. [596]

It might be argued: "This is not a fault for me either, because this designation of 'cloth' and so forth with respect to its constituent parts, such as the threads, is figurative and metaphorical; since it is based on their being the causes of that [cloth], the application of words such as 'all' will thus be possible."

If it is argued that the designation [of the cloth] is figurative (*bhākta*), then a distinction in speech (*vacobheda*) would result; yet there is no difference in the cognition (*buddhi*) regarding the two intended objects, whether they are taken as primary (*mukhya*) or secondary (*gauṇa*).

(599) If this were so—that is, if there were a distinction in speech such as the use of the plural number—as in "all these cloths are red," then such a distinction would necessarily follow at all times.
Furthermore, you do not accept the singular number when there are many [objects].

Now, it might be argued that the word "cloth" (*vastra*) and so forth applies to the parts by taking on the number belonging to the whole (*avayavin*), and thus functions while not abandoning the gender and number inherent in its own denotation;
showing that this too is incorrect, he says: "And not," and so forth.

For if this designation were figurative (bhākta), then there would arise a distinction or difference in the cognition regarding the primary and secondary meanings, characterized by a faltering movement [of the mind]. Yet, no such difference exists; for instance, in the case of the statement "all the cloth is red," such a cognition does not occur [that the whole is red while parts are not], nor is it the case that the cloth itself is red, but rather its constituent threads are red. Furthermore, by the word "and" (ca), it is indicated that you do not admit that the cloth is denoted by the word "all" (sarva), because it is a single entity. Therefore, how could the word "all"—devoid of words like "cloth"—apply to the parts by taking on their number?
Alternatively, "difference" (bheda) means manifoldness; that [difference] does not exist between these two things intended as the secondary and the primary.

For no distinct form is perceived between the threads and the cloth, as is the case with color, taste, and so forth. Furthermore, a relationship of secondary and primary cannot possibly exist between two things whose distinct forms are not perceived.
With the words "But surely... and so forth, he anticipates the rebuttal of Śaṅkarasvāmin:
"But surely, because conjunction does not pervade [its locus], redness does not apply to the whole, nor is the whole perceived as being covered. (600)

For he has said: "Redness" (rāga) is defined as the conjunction of a cloth with substances such as dye or saffron; and since conjunction is non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti), it follows that when one part [of the cloth] is dyed, redness does not occur throughout the whole, nor does the covering of one part of the body by garments and the like result in the covering of the whole.
He demonstrates that this is incorrect: "But surely, in a partless substance," and so forth;
for surely, in a partless substance, what could remain unpenetrated?
If its own nature [remains] in that state, then difference is established; or for that very reason, [if it does not remain so].
Therefore, existence in many locations is not established in a single [entity]; hence, the manifold nature of cloth and other things is proven to be distinct from atoms.

For if cloth and such were indeed a single substance, then what part of that impartite substance would remain unpenetrated by the dye and so forth, such that conjunction could be non-pervasive? If, on the other hand, you admit the persistence of an unpenetrated nature, then difference is thereby established by that very persistence; for it is impossible for there to be a single nature in that which is both pervaded and unpervaded due to their mutual contradiction. Furthermore, the occupation of a wider space by a single entity is not logical, because it lacks parts.
Otherwise, since all aquatic creatures, elephants, and so forth would be indistinguishable as being of one and the same nature, the distinction between the gross and the subtle would not obtain.

If it is argued that this distinction is caused by the initiation or non-initiation of fewer or more numerous parts, then let those very parts—arising in such and such numbers—be the basis for the arrangement of the gross and the subtle; what is the use of a "whole" (avayavin) initiated by them, given that its causal capacity is unobserved?

Moreover, even though there is a difference in the number of constituent parts (avayava), there is no mutual distinction among the composite wholes (avayavin) themselves because they are partless; for if such a distinction were to exist by which the differentiation between gross, subtle, and so forth would occur, then, since that distinction would be caused solely by the perception of the greater or lesser number of parts, it would follow that only the parts themselves are admitted [as real], as the conventional usage of "gross" and so on occurs precisely therein. Consequently, only the atom (aṇu) would be accepted as the object of perception, because nothing other than the gross or the subtle is ever perceived.

Furthermore, what is the meaning of the statement that "conjunction is non-pervasive" (*avyāpyavṛtti*)? If it means that it does not pervade the entire substance, that is incorrect, because it is accepted that a substance is not an object of the term "entirety" (*sarva*).
If, on the other hand, it means that it exists in one part of its substratum, that too is incorrect, because a [partless] substance has no parts.

If it is argued that [conjunction] resides in the constituent parts (avayava) that initiate that [whole], then, since the parts alone would be red, the form of the whole (avayavin) would be non-red; thus, the red and the non-red would be seen simultaneously.
Furthermore, as for that very constituent part which initiates it: if it has the same form as the whole, then the same objection applies, namely, that conjunction exists only partially within it.

If, on the other hand, it has the form of an atom (aṇu), then because atoms are beyond the senses (atīndriya), the conjunction residing in them would also be beyond the senses, and consequently, there would be no perception of the red.

It might be thought: "Just as in the case of the form of a finger, its perception is said to occur only upon the perception of its substratum, whereas the perception of conjunction does not occur only upon the perception of its substratum; therefore, it is called non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti). This is incorrect, for there is no perception of conjunction when its substratum is not perceived.

Just as in the case of the conjunction between a jar and a *piśāca*, and because passion (*rāga*) is also not perceived when its substratum is unperceived—since it is perceived only when its substratum is perceived—it too would thus be a pervasive occurrence (*vyāpyavṛtti*).

It might be argued: "Even when a substance inherent in other parts that are not colored is perceived, the passion consisting of conjunction is not perceived; therefore, it is not the case that this [passion] is perceived whenever its substratum is perceived. That too is incorrect.

For in this way, since the whole (*avayavin*) which inheres in both the dyed and the undyed [parts] is a single entity, it would follow that even when a part is dyed, the color would not be perceived by means of that part, because the color is not perceived despite the perception of its substratum (*āśraya*).
Furthermore, there is no means of apprehending the conjunction other than the perception of the substratum;
therefore, it cannot be of a single form.
The object,
though endowed with multiple forms, appears as consisting solely of an aggregation of atoms due to its capacity for manifestation,
since it is impossible for that which possesses constituent parts to be a single unity.

Therefore, it is established that jars and other such objects consist of atoms; thus, it is proven that the form [of the cognition] consists of blue and other atoms, because no other single-natured object is possible.
Regarding what was said—that there would be no mention of atoms—he replies: "But one who has not understood the reality of the object," and so forth;
"one who has not understood the reality of the object, however, conceives of the mass as a single [entity]."
The world, depending on that which is imagined, speaks here of an "atom" (paramāṇu).
Regarding the phrase "depending on that which is imagined": the analysis of the compound is "that which has its dependence upon that imagined [thread]."
603 He states another refutation: "Or this designation, being independent of a cause, remains fixed in such [a state]," and so forth.
Just as the word "Lord" (Īśvara) follows conventional usage even when applied to one who possesses no wealth,
so too is it [the case] with that which is partless and unobstructed.

Just as the term "Lord" (īśvara) is applied even to a pauper by virtue of convention, without any underlying cause such as actual sovereignty, so too is this term "atom" (aṇu); thus there is no fault.
In this way, it has been demonstrated in general that a single gross substance—whether composed of parts or not composed of parts—is not tenable.
Now, he states a specific refutation of that [entity] by which the whole (avayavin) is asserted to be commenced:
"The threads, hands, and so forth, do not at all inhere in a single whole, because they are multiple, just like mats, huts, houses, and so on. (605)

Alternatively, if the intended substance were not dependent upon multiple parts, then its existence would be untenable due to its oneness, like an atom; this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramā*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is manifold is not inherent in a single substance, just as many things such as mats and huts are not inherent in a single substance; and these [threads, hands, etc. are manifold. This is because of the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).

Alternatively: that which is one must reside in a single substance, just as a single atom; and the substance designated as a "whole" (avayavin) is indeed one. Thus, there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving what is incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi).
This is a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅgasādhana);
and in both applications, he states the subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) for the contrapositive: "The impossibility of [its] subsistence is the subverting proof."
The non-occurrence of the whole in its parts— that is, its non-establishment by means of valid cognitions— is the subverting proof in this case.
Furthermore, as to how there is a lack of logical connection, he says: "For that," and so forth.
For that [whole] would have to exist in another part either by means of the very same form that possesses its own single occurrence, or else by another; since there is no other possible way. (607)

In that case, its existence [in another part] is conceivable only through that very same [form], not otherwise; for it exists in those parts by being embraced by that [form], and not in any other way.

Thus there are two positions: either that substance, which is one, exists in other parts with the very same form as that which was embraced by one part, or else it exists with a different form. For in reality, there is no other alternative besides identity or difference.

In that regard, the first position is not tenable; since it is already encompassed by that very same constituent part, what opportunity would there be for it to exist in another constituent part at that very same time?
For otherwise, if it were to exist elsewhere as well, its existence in this intended substance would not be by way of its entire self (sarvātmanā).
This is because it possesses no other nature by which it could also exist elsewhere, for that would entail the undesirable consequence of the loss of its unity.
Establishing the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), he says: "Not at all," and so forth.
For just as an infant does not remain simultaneously in the laps of two different nurses, so too an object embraced by one thing cannot at that same time reside in another.
The formal argument (prayoga) is: whatever object is embraced by one entity does not, at that very moment, exist elsewhere.

Just as an infant held in the lap of one nurse does not occupy the lap of another nurse, so too a substance [occupied] by one part cannot occupy another; this is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
The statement of the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is that a substance would not thus resort to another.

He states the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaye*): "Because that which has a nature connected to it [the cause] exists even where that [cause] is not present, it would follow that it shares the same location as that [cause], and there would be identity due to the lack of distinction. (610)

If it were to exist by means of a different self in each [part], then a single entity existing in multiple locations could not be established, because a difference in nature constitutes a difference in the thing itself.

(611) For if a substance whose nature is connected to its intended parts were to exist in another part located in a different place, then those parts would occupy the same location; consequently, the parts would attain a state of oneness of self, that is, a single nature.
Why? Because of non-distinction—that is, because it exists in an undivided form;

for otherwise, if it were to exist in a divided form, it would not possess the property of being in a single location. Now, as for the second position—that it exists in one place by means of another nature—that too would not be established, since a single entity existing in multiple locations would be impossible, given that a different nature occurs elsewhere and because the difference between entities consists precisely in the difference of their natures.

611. But Uddyotakara says: "This is merely a designation of the locus, the supported, the property, and the substratum; [the statement] 'it exists in the parts as a whole' refers to what is called 'attainment' (prāpti), which is of the nature of inherence (samavāya) and characterized by the state of being supported. To this he replies: "If it is argued that its existence in them consists in having inherence as its essence," etc.
If it is argued that its existence in those [parts] consists in having inherence as its essence... then indeed [we reply]: ...

Even regarding that [position], this investigation rushes forward as if out of anger: "In such a mode of existence as this—which was just described—is it by means of the very same nature inherent in one part that it exists in the other parts, or by means of another? This investigation rushes forward as if unable to endure the web of defects fabricated by a dull-witted mind.

Thus, having first refuted the occurrence [of the whole] by not making the distinction between the whole and its parts, he now states the negation of occurrence by way of the method established through dependent designation (upādāya-prajñapti): "Or else," and so forth;
for if it were to occur in its entirety, multiplicity would follow as a logical consequence.
And it is not desired that [the substance] exists either partially or as a single [unit], nor does it exist anywhere at all.
(613) Sometimes that substance exists in its parts either in its entirety or by way of a part.

If it were to exist in its entirety, then it would follow that it has as many selves as there are parts; for unless there is a difference in its nature with respect to each individual part, it cannot exist in its entirety [in every part].
Since a function [of the whole] is impossible through a self that does not exist,

and since a function [must occur] by means of its entire self, it follows that the whole would be manifold— just like a water-lily and other objects situated simultaneously in multiple bowls and the like.
Alternatively, if the position is taken that it functions by means of a single part, then there would be an infinite regress regarding those parts.

For instance, those parts by which that substance exists in its constituent members are themselves its parts; it must likewise exist in them, and in the same way in others, leading to an infinite regress.

Anticipating the objection that "those parts by which it exists in the members are indeed its own self and not distinct entities, since there are no other parts apart from them, and thus there will be no infinite regress," he says: "nor is it one."
For if this were the case, there would be no single composite whole (*avayavin*), because it would be nothing more than a mere accumulation of parts;
and such being the case, let the object consist merely of the perceived collection of hands and so forth—what is the use of postulating other parts that are supposedly identical with its own self?
He states another fault as well: "And it is nowhere [perceived]."
The ellipsis is "it would reside" (vṛttaḥ syāt).
This is what is meant:
if the parts were each [identical to] the whole, then the whole would indeed reside in the part.
To the extent that the individual parts are not each the whole, it follows that they would lose their status as being "parts";
nor does another whole exist by way of its own nature— so how, indeed, could that [whole] be said to reside in the parts?
With the words "by way of independence" and so forth, he anticipates the rebuttal of Śaṅkarasvāmin:
"That proof which proceeds by way of independence or as a reductio ad absurdum..."
For truth indeed coheres with its own perception; however, a mode of existence—
whether in its entirety or in part— is nowhere observed, and because such a mode is impossible, neither substance nor anything else could exist.
Either this [inherence] is not excluded in some case where it is perceived, such as in a substance, or else,
if it is not perceived therein, the question regarding its difference is not appropriate.
At most, one could say that "subsistence does not exist," but even that is not [the case].
It is logical [to consider it] perception because it is established through direct experience by means of the cognition "this is here.
If that is not accepted as perception, then let some subverting argument be stated;
otherwise, even cognitions of form and so forth would not possess the status of perception.

For he says: "Whether established independently or by way of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), a proof is only tenable when it is itself perceived; otherwise, there would be the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatā*). Now, you have not perceived anywhere the occurrence of a single thing in many [locations] either in its entirety or in part, such that from the impossibility of that occurrence the composite substance (*avayavidravya*) would be non-existent. If, however, such an occurrence were perceived somewhere, then it would exist in substances and so forth just as it does there, and thus there would be no refutation. Furthermore, if such an occurrence were observed in some case, then in that very same manner it would also exist in substances and the like; therefore, there is no negation."

Now, if that subsistence (*vṛtti*) has not been perceived, then a question regarding its distinction—whether it exists in part or in its entirety—is not appropriate; for a negation of a particular attribute is only logical once the substratum (*dharmin*) is established. However, when the substratum itself is unestablished, then the negation of that very thing is superior. Therefore, one should simply say "there is no subsistence at all," rather than a negation of a particular [mode of] subsistence. But that is not correct, because the subsistence of the whole (*avayavin*) in its parts is established by perception itself.
To the question "By what kind of perception?", he says: "From the cognition 'this is here'."
The meaning is: "from such perception as 'this cloth and so forth exist here in these threads'.
Now, it might be argued that the perceptual nature of this cognition is unestablished; if that were the case, some subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) must be stated regarding this point.

If it were to be non-perceptual because there is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that sublates it, then even your own cognition of color-form and so forth would not be perceptual, for there is no distinction [between the two cases]. 614
618. He provides the rebuttal with the words "In this regard," and so forth:
"It has already been established, by way of non-difference, that there is no activity here."
"There is no cognition [of the relation] here as 'here,' because that form does not appear.
For, by the passage beginning "since it resides in only one," the occurrence of a single thing in many has already been refuted in a general sense.
Furthermore, as for the claim that the occurrence is established through perception itself on the basis of the cognition "this is here," that too is unworldly.

In this world, even a conceptual cognition does not function in the form "the horn is here [in the horn]" or "the cloth is here [in the threads]"; rather, it functions as "the horn is in the cow" or "the threads are in the cloth. Furthermore, in the perceptual consciousness, the form of the cloth or similar objects does not appear as something inherent in the threads and so forth, nor as something distinct from them.
Furthermore, when [the substrate] does not appear through discrimination, the cognition "this exists here" cannot arise;
for those who possess discrimination, the notion "water is here" does not occur when water is not appearing in a vessel or similar object.
Regarding what was stated—that a mode of existence (vṛtti) has never been observed either in its entirety or in part—he says: "By the words 'entirety' and 'part,' etc.
This meaning is illuminated by the words "entirety" and "part": "Does its existence occur through its lack of parts (nairantarya), or does it exist in some other way? (620)

Whether it be like a bilva fruit situated in a vessel or the like, or like Caitra and others seated upon many seats—by the word "entirety" (kṛtsna), is it meant that its partless essential nature exists in all its constituent parts with that same partlessness, as is observed in the case of a bilva fruit placed in a certain container? This is the meaning clarified by this term; or else, is it otherwise, such that the word "single part" (ekadeśa) clarifies that it is like Caitra and others observed when reclining upon many seats?

Whatever this may be, even that which was stated by Uddyotakara—"Since the application of the terms 'whole' (*kṛtsna*) and 'part' (*ekadeśa*) is impossible in a single composite whole (*avayavin*), this question is improper: does it exist by way of a part, or does it exist as a whole?

For 'the whole' indeed denotes the entirety, while 'a part' denotes something when there is multiplicity; thus, these two terms, 'whole' and 'part,' are untenable in relation to a single composite whole"—that too has been refuted by this very [argument].

And so, in common worldly usage, one indeed observes the application of the terms "entirety" (*kṛtsna*) and "part" (*ekadeśa*) with respect to things such as a foot, as in: "The entire foot rests in the bowl," or "It rests with one part.
Nor is it correct to say that this [usage] is merely figurative (*upacarita*), because—as was stated previously—it proceeds without faltering (*askhaladgati*).
Thus, the fourfold substance ending with air has been refuted;
as for that called "self," it was already rejected previously in the examination of the self.
Now, for the purpose of refuting space (*ākāśa*), time (*kāla*), direction (*diś*), and mind (*manas*), he says: "Dependent upon something," and so forth.
Sounds are dependent upon something because of reasons such as their perishability, like a jar or a lamp; and that [substratum] will indeed be space (*vyoma*). (622)

In this regard, the substance called space (*ākāśa*) is first established by the opponent: "The substance called space exists; it is eternal, unitary, and has sound as its inferential mark (*liṅga*) on earth. Sound is its mark because it is a quality (*guṇa*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever things are endowed with properties such as perishability and having an origin are dependent upon something, just like jars, lamps, and so forth. And these sounds are likewise [endowed with those properties]. Therefore, these sounds must be dependent upon something; that which is their substratum (*āśraya*) will, by implication, be the void—namely, space."

For this sound cannot logically be a quality of the four elements beginning with earth, because, while being perceptible, it does not originate from the qualities of its causes, because it does not persist as long as the substance [in which it resides] endures, and because it is perceived elsewhere than in its substratum;

for the qualities of tangible substances are observed to be the opposite of these stated properties, provided they are perceptible— the qualification "while being perceptible" is included to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to the qualities residing in atoms produced by heat (*pākaja*).

Because it is perceptible by the external sense organs, because it is graspable by other selves, and because it is perceived as distinct from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), sound is not a quality of the self;
for the qualities of the self, such as pleasure and so forth, are observed to have the opposite characteristics.
Furthermore, because it is graspable by the auditory organ, sound is not a quality of space, time, or the internal organ (manas).
Therefore, by the method of elimination, sound is the mark (liṅga) of space;

and that space, because its mark is the non-specific [universal] sound and there is no specific mark [to distinguish it], is one. It is a substance because its quality is perceived everywhere, because it possesses pervasive qualities, and because it is not dependent on anything else.
"Because it is uncreated, it is eternal"— this is the system of the opponents (verse 622).
With the words "the sun, etc.," he states the proof for [the existence of] time.
The cognition of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, is based on the distinction between actions and substances such as the sun and others, just like the perception of a jar; likewise,
this [cognition] arises from the perception of wrinkles, grey hair, roughness, movement, and so on.
Since the cause is of a different character, that is indeed what is intended by "time.
By the word "substance" (*dravya*), wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth are to be understood. [The argument is:

This cognition of priority, posteriority, and so on—expressed as "the father is prior," "the son is posterior," "simultaneously," "for a long time," "quickly," "is being done," "was done," and "will be done"—must be based upon a category of entity distinct from the substances such as the sun's motion, because it is of a different character from the cognition of wrinkles, grey hair, and the like, just like the cognition of a jar and other such objects.
That which is its cause is, by implication, time;

for instance, this cognition of priority and posteriority is not produced by space, because the cognition "he is prior" arises even with respect to an elder person situated in a direction other than one's own.

Likewise, even when a son is situated in the western direction, he is not designated as "western" [based on that location], nor is the designation produced by wrinkles, grey hair, and so forth, because the cognition [of those] is distinct from the cognition [of "son"]; nor is it produced by action, for the same reason— that the cognition [of action] is distinct from the cognition [of "son"].
And thus the Sūtra states: "The posterior, the prior, simultaneous, non-simultaneous, long, and short—these are the marks of time.
Therefore, properties such as eternity and unity should be understood to belong to this [time] just as they do to space.
624. To establish the [existence of] directions, he says: "From the cognitions of 'east,' 'west,' and so forth"—thus, direction itself is inferred from the cognitions of 'east,' 'west,' and so forth.
The inference of the mind is held to occur through the sequence of the arising of cognitions;
it depends upon causes distinct from the eye and other [senses], just as the successive apprehension of color and so forth occurs like that of a chariot and such.

Taking a corporeal substance as a limit, those ten notions which arise with respect to other corporeal substances alone—namely, "this is to the east," "to the south," "to the west," "to the north," "to the southeast," "to the southwest," "to the northwest," "to the northeast," "below," and "above"—that from which these arise is *diś* (space/direction).
And so says the Sūtra: "That from which [the notion] 'this is from here' arises is the mark (*liṅga*) of space."

Since these are specific cognitions, and it is not logical for specific cognitions to be accidental, nor can they depend on one another as corporeal substances—because that would result in the non-existence of both due to mutual dependence—it follows that, since no other cause is possible, these are the inferential marks (*liṅga*) of Space (*dik*). Furthermore, the qualities of this Space, such as unity and omnipresence, are to be understood as being the same as those of Time.
Nevertheless, although Space is one, it possesses a plurality of distinctions such as "East" and so forth, due to the differences in its effects.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: this cognition of priority, posteriority, and so forth, is based on a category distinct from corporeal substances, because it is of a different nature than the cognition of those [substances], like the cognition of pleasure and so forth.
Thus he states the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for the mind: "In succession," etc.

Even when there is the simultaneous presence of the contact between multiple sense organs and their objects, since the arising of cognitions is observed to occur in succession, there must exist another cause distinct from the sense organs and their objects, by whose presence or absence the arising or non-arising of cognition occurs.
Therefore, by means of the successive arising of cognitions—that is, through the production of knowledge—an inference regarding the mind is established.
Accordingly, the Sūtra states: "The non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark of the mind.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: this apprehension of color and other objects necessarily depends upon a cause distinct from the eye and other [senses], because it arises successively, just like [the movement of] a chariot and so forth.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "upāttādīti" (625–626).

Since sound is accepted as having its cause in the primary elements (mahābhūtas) such as those that are appropriated (*upātta*), it is already established that sounds are dependent upon them; thus, the first [reason] is not a valid proof.
If what is being proven for these sounds is merely their general state of being dependent, then the reason suffers from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

For instance: sounds are held to have as their causes the primary elements (mahābhūta), both those that are appropriated (upātta) and those that are not; and within those elements, the sounds are indeed dependent upon them as their effects, because their acquisition of self-nature is bound to them, since effects are dependent upon their causes.
"Appropriated" means taken possession of by mind and mental factors;
by the word "etcetera," the inclusion of being caused by unappropriated great elements is intended;
[the phrase refers to] "in those."
"In the appropriated great elements, etc."— the word "iti" means "therefore."

The meaning is that what was stated [in the verse] beginning with "In some cases, words are based on the primary [meaning]" (ādyam iti samāśritāḥ kvacic chabdāḥ) is not a valid proof, because it suffers from the fallacy of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).

Now, if it is intended to prove that these [qualities] possess a specific kind of dependence by virtue of being inherent in a substance that is formless, eternal, unitary, and all-pervading, then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because there is no corroborating example (*dṛṣṭānta*) endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhya*). This is shown in the verse beginning with "eka" and so forth: "But the inherence [of these qualities] in a single, all-pervading, and eternal ether is not established; for they lack positive concomitance (*anvaya*), since [the reason] applies [to the ether] simultaneously. (628)

The phrase "this is not established for them" is connected with what precedes; furthermore, he demonstrates that the thesis is contradicted by inference with the words: "because it would entail [the consequence of] non-succession and so forth."
The connection is as follows: it has been stated that their inherence in space (*nabhas*) is not established.

For if these [sounds] were inherent in the eternal, unitary substance of space, then—just like multiple sounds produced at once—all sounds, even those belonging to a different time, would exist at the very time they are intended, because their causes would be unimpaired and they would share a single substratum;
furthermore, it has already been demonstrated that an eternal entity does not depend upon anything else.
Nor is it logical for that which provides no assistance to be an inherent cause (*samavāyin*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Thus, there follows the consequence of [the world] being non-successive;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the consequences of [all] persons perceiving [simultaneously] and other such defects are also implied.

For the auditory organ consists of space, and space is one and the same; consequently, there would be hearing of all sounds reaching it. Indeed, because of its partless nature, such a restriction as "this is my own auditory organ" and "this is another's" is not logical.

It might be thought: "The ear-cavity (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*) conditioned by the unseen merit or demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) of that person is the auditory organ (*śrotra*) of only that portion of space delimited by it; for this very reason, the perception of sound does not occur through other apertures such as the mouth or nose, and it is precisely due to the impairment of that ear-cavity that deafness and the like are established.
This is indeed untenable, because since space is partless (*niraṃśa*), such a division is impossible.
Nor can imagined divisions of parts bring about, by virtue of superimposition, a causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that is accomplished only by the actual division of a real entity.
For water, even when metaphorically designated as "fire," does not actually burn or consume;
furthermore, if it is thought that this is because conjunction (saṃyoga) is said to be non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti) in one part of space,
this too has already been refuted.
Furthermore—the pot, the ear, the auditory canal, and so forth would also occupy the same location, because they are all in contact with the one undivided space;

for by that very nature of space with which one is conjoined, others are likewise conjoined. Consequently, other objects such as pots would also exist in the very location intended [for the ear], since they are conjoined with the space whose nature is already conjoined with them, just like a pot situated in that same place.

For this very reason, even sounds would possess spatial location; consequently, many faults such as the following would ensue: that the well-attested distinction between the positions of certain objects as being distant or near would be contradicted, and so forth.

(628) Furthermore, he demonstrates that for both time and space, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in a general sense, the lack of positive concomitance (*anvayāsiddhi*) of the reason in a specific sense, and the sublation of the thesis (*pratijñābādha*) by inference—starting with the words "viśiṣṭa" and so on.
The cognition of "prior," "posterior," and so forth, which is based on mental attention arising from specific conventions, does not derive from time nor from space;
for since these [time and space] possess a partless and unitary nature, the occurrence of priority, posteriority, and so on is impossible.
If it is argued that [the distinction] arises from the difference in the related objects (*saṃbandhibheda*), then surely those two [cognitions] would be fruitless.

The "specialized convention" (*viśiṣṭasamaya*) refers to the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) of "prior," "subsequent," and so forth, applied only to objects produced in a sequence of priority and posteriority. The "mental impression" (*manaskāra*) arising therefrom is "attention" (*ābhoga*); that which has this as its basis is described as such. For this very reason, there is no fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), because this cognition is based upon the linguistic convention regarding the specific object.

Therefore, indicating that if the mere cause is what is to be proven, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); whereas if it is proven with specific qualifications, there is sublation by inference (*anumānabādhā*) and the fault of lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*), as before; he shows that the reason is contradictory (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of what is intended—with the words "partless," etc., and "of those two," referring to space and time.
It is intended to prove that the cognition of priority, posteriority, and so forth is based upon a single, partless category known as space-time; however, this is not established.

For instance, an object becomes an object only by producing a cognition that conforms to its own form, and in a partless entity, distinctions such as priority and posteriority are impossible, whereby a cognition of priority and posteriority caused by those [distinctions] could arise.
Therefore, because it proves the opposite of what is desired, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*).
With the words "if [it is argued] due to the difference in relata," the author anticipates the opponent's reply:

"Now, if it is thought—that external and internal entities related to space and time, such as lamps, bodies, and so forth, possess priority and posteriority; therefore, this priority and posteriority belonging to their relata is designated as belonging to those two, space and time; thus, there is no contradiction in the reason"—this is the sense.
To this he states the following reply: "In that case, those two would indeed be fruitless.
For if it were conceived in this way, space and time would be rendered purposeless, because the effect intended to be accomplished by them would have already been produced by their very correlates.
For instance: time is accepted as the cause that produces the cognitions of prior and posterior moments, lava, nimeṣa, kāṣṭhā, kalā, muhūrta, day and night, fortnights, and so forth;
space is accepted as the cause for the determination of directions such as east and north;
yet this entire diversity does not exist within those two [time and space] in themselves.
Furthermore, since [the entity] exists within its various manifestations, the conceptual construction of it [as a separate entity] is entirely useless.

He demonstrates that even when the mind is the means of proof, if one proves merely a cause in general, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*): "The eye and so forth... and so on.
For we also accept a mind distinct from the eye and other [senses], namely that cognition which arises immediately after the six [cognitions] is the mind (*manas*). (631)
"But if the mind were eternal, cognitions would occur simultaneously;
therefore, the reason stated here results in the subversion of what you desire.

(632) He demonstrates the lack of concomitance (*ananvaya*), the contradiction of the thesis by inference (*anumānabādhā*), and the contradictory nature (*viruddhatā*) of the reason specifically regarding the proof of a single, eternal mind, beginning with the words "But if [the mind] were eternal" (*nitye tu*).

The term "that which effects the destruction of what is desired" refers to the proof that [the mind] depends on impermanent causes distinct from the eyes and other [senses]; otherwise, if it were to have permanent causes, its sequential arising would be contradicted because its causes would be unimpaired [and thus simultaneous].

And confirming that very same contradiction of the reason with a touch of irony, he says: "The Sugata... and so forth; [this is] for the sake of proving or disproving the mind as designated by the other Buddhists.
"I think this Sūtra was composed with a different form and a different intention.
(633) Thus concludes the examination of the category of substance (*dravyapadārtha*).

I consider it thus: for the sake of establishing or disproving the mind (*manas*) as desired by both the Buddhists and the non-Buddhists, this Sūtra states: "The non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark (*liṅga*) of the mind."
The collective meaning is that [the term] is formed by eliding the vowel *a* within one part [of the compound]. As for the meaning of the individual parts, it is stated as follows:
the analysis of the compound is "those [who are] Buddhists (*saugata*) and other non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*), and those two minds indicated by them."
For those two, respectively, there is success and failure, or failure accompanied by success; for that purpose, with that as the cause, he asks:
"How, moreover, does a single sūtra convey two contradictory meanings? and says: "sākāram," etc., meaning "that which exists together with an aspect (ākāra)."

The term *aliṅga* is an indication with the vowel *a* elided (*praśliṣṭākāra*) for the purpose of proving that the mind of another is not established [as a separate entity]; however, for the sake of establishing the mind according to the Buddhists, it is otherwise—the meaning is "with the letter *na*" (*an-akāra*).
To the question, "How can both having a form (*sākāratva*) and being without a form (*anakāratva*) be established for one and the same thing?", he says: "It is repeated" (*āvṛttam*).
"In that case, recurrence is logical"—this concludes the examination of substance as a category.
Thus ends the investigation of the category of substance.
The examination of the category of quality (*guṇa*) states the refutation of qualities and so forth: "By the refutation of substances," and so on;
by the refutation of substances, all those things dependent upon them are likewise refuted.
In that case, qualities, actions, and so forth are indeed discarded, as they are so regarded.
[Verse 634] Qualities, actions, and the rest, up to the particularities (*viśeṣa*), are discarded precisely by the negation of substances, because these depend upon them;
and in the absence of a substratum, it is logically impossible for dependent things to exist.
"Thus considered" means they are accepted as being either directly or indirectly dependent upon substance;
for instance, quality and action are intended to be directly dependent upon substance.
And thus the Sūtra states:
"That which subsists in a substance, possesses qualities, and is not a cause in conjunctions and disjunctions, being independent [of other causes], is the definition of a quality (guṇa).
And: "That which subsists in a single substance, is devoid of qualities, and is an independent cause in conjunctions and disjunctions is the definition of action (karman)."
"Residing in a single substance" means that it has its locus in a single substance;
however, some qualities reside in multiple substances, such as conjunction, disjunction, and so forth.

Furthermore, some universals and particulars reside only in substances, such as earthness (*pṛthivītva*) and the like, as well as qualityness (*guṇatva*) and actionness (*karmatva*), which reside in the categories of qualities and actions that are connected to substances. However, the great universal called "Being" (*sattā*) resides in the three categories beginning with substance.
Therefore, when substance has been refuted, qualities and the other categories are also refuted without any further effort.
It is thus shown that the fruit of the investigation of the remaining categories is already completed within the investigation of substance (dravya) itself.
[Objection: "In that case, the refutation of inherence (samavāya) must then be undertaken separately. To this, he says: "Where, of what? and so forth.
When the relatum has been discarded, where and for whom could there be inherence?
Nevertheless, this specific negation is stated once again.
For inherence is described as having the nature of subsisting in the five categories.

When the fivefold types of related entities, such as substance and so forth, have been discarded, where could there be inherence (samavāya) of anything? The meaning is that it belongs to nothing at all, nor in any place, because all bases and dependents have been refuted. In this regard, the specific negation of qualities (guṇas) is now stated.

In that regard, the Sūtra states: "Color, taste, smell, touch, number, dimension, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, cognitions, pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, and effort are qualities.
