By the word "and" (*ca*), heaviness, fluidity, viscidity, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), merit, demerit, and sound are also included.
Among these, color is perceptible by the eye and resides in earth, water, and fire.
Taste is that which is perceivable by the gustatory faculty; it functions in earth and water. Smell is that which is perceivable by the olfactory faculty; it functions in earth.
Touch is that which is perceivable by the tactile faculty; it functions in earth, water, fire, and air.
He states the negation of these first four, beginning with form and so forth: "In a large substance... and so on.

If it is maintained that blue and other colors exist as a single entity within a large substance, then when that [substance] is manifested by light passing through an aperture, why is its manifestation and perception not [also] seen? (636)
For it is only in a large substance that those qualities which are inherent therein attain the conditions for perception; therefore, he says "large.

Now, if it is maintained that in that substance there is only one partless [quality], such as blue and so forth, of four kinds, then even when a subtle light from a lamp or similar source passing through a crack in a keyhole illuminates the color blue and so on inherent in a larger substance like a jar situated inside a room, it would follow that there is illumination and perception of the entire color and other qualities existing throughout the whole substance, because of its being partless.
For a single entity has no parts by which there could be manifestation in one part [as occurs] with light through a hole; this is an illustrative example,
for if the fragrance were manifested in one part of the earth by water, it would follow that it must also be manifested and perceived in other parts.
If one were to touch a portion of a flame or taste a portion of a mango fruit, there would be a perception of that much of the touch and the taste inherent in that substance.
To the objection that this might indeed be the case for the manifestation and perception of the entirety of blue and so forth, he says: "And not," etc.

And it is not accepted that blue and so forth exist as divided by spatial location; since they are manifested at that time [as such], their division must therefore be atom-by-atom. (637) "At that time" means...
At that time,
by means of that light from the crevice.
Regarding the phrase "of that" (tasya):

if the blue and so forth were admitted to have an internal differentiation into atoms, then— by virtue of possessing atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*), like the substance of an atom of earth and so on— they would possess qualities (*guṇavattva*) and thus would be of the nature of a substance (*dravya-rūpatā*) alone, not a quality (*guṇatva*).
Furthermore, for those things which have become thus and are divided into atoms, there is a dispute over the name by applying the designation "quality" (guṇa).
Nor is it logical that they possess the status of a quality simply because they are dependent [on something],
since dependence is untenable for both the existent and the non-existent, and because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
For in that case, since a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) rests upon its constituent parts (*avayavadravya*), it too would become a quality (*guṇa*); this is the intended meaning.

(637) In this context, number (*saṅkhyā*), characterized by oneness (*ekatva*) and so forth, is the cause for the conventional usage of "one" and so on. Furthermore, it resides in a single substance (*ekadravyā*) and in multiple substances (*anekadravyā*). Among these, the number one resides in a single substance.
However, number such as duality (*dvitva*) and so forth resides in multiple substances (*anekadravyā*).

In that regard, one should understand that for number residing in a single substance (*ekadravyā*), its eternity and production are like those of color (*rūpa*) and other qualities belonging to water-atoms (*salilaparamāṇu*) and the like.

But for number residing in multiple substances: its production arises from unities accompanied by a cognition of multiple objects; its destruction results from the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), and in some cases, from the destruction of its substratum.

The opponent maintains that this twofold number is established both through direct perception itself and, because the cognition of specific distinctions depends on other causes, also through inference;
regarding this, he states its refutation: "Not having that form," and so forth.

Number does not appear in cognition as something distinct from elephants and the like that are excluded from what is not of that nature; nor is it accepted as being perceptible, for it does not exist at all.

Indeed, since number is not perceived apart from those elephants and so forth to which names such as "collection" (samuccaya) and the like have been applied—even though it would meet the conditions for perception—it is, like the horn of a hare, an object of conventional usage for what is non-existent.
For it is intended as something visible;

and thus says the Sūtra: "Number, dimension, separateness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and action are perceptible by the eye because of their inherence in substances possessing color. (VS 4.1.12)
Furthermore, demonstrating that number is not established through the cognition of specific qualities, he says:
"However, this cognition of 'one' and so forth regarding jars follows from the mental attention to a convention established by desire, just as it occurs in the case of cognitions and the like. (639)
Since they [substances] lack substantiality, there is no differentiating number whatsoever among them;
therefore, it is not at all logical for that cognition [of number] to be figurative (*bhākta*), because it is unerring (*askhalitatvataḥ*).

For just as in cases such as "one cognition" or "two cognitions," the notion of "one" and so forth occurs even in the absence of a [real] number, so too in the case of objects like jars which are unaccompanied, the cognition of "one" and so forth will arise following upon the mental attention (*manaskāra*) or application (*ābhoga*) toward the convention established by one's own will; thus, this [argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

For there is no number in those [qualities] such as knowledge and the rest, because they are not substances (*adravyatva*), and because number, being a quality (*guṇa*), is dependent upon a substance.

Now, if it is thought that this [application of number] to them is figurative (*gauṇa*)—that knowledge is "one" as if it were a single entity, and that the common property (*sādharmya*) here is its lack of assistance and so forth—[the author] says in response: "That knowledge... (*tajjñānam iti*).
Indeed, it is not appropriate to consider this knowledge as figurative (*bhākta*), because this cognition proceeds with an unerring course (*askhaladgati*).

For example, while the cognition "the Vāhīka is an ox" is erroneous—since he is like an ox but not an ox, due to the absence of a dewlap and so forth—this [cognition] does not err in such a way. It is as if it were one, such as knowledge and so on, yet it is not merely one;
rather, just as the cognition regarding jars and other objects is unerring, such is the case for knowledge and the rest as well.
It might be argued that this cognition is not described as being dependent upon similarity.

However, one might suspect that the cognition of "one" and so forth regarding these qualities, actions, and inherence occurs because of the oneness and other properties residing in the substance which serves as their substratum, due to their inhering in the same object; anticipating this objection, he says:
"If it is postulated that the cognition of 'one' regarding qualities and so forth arises from the oneness inherent in that substance, by virtue of inhering in the same object," (verse 641).
To this, he states the following reply: "Let it be so," and so forth.

Let it be that there is such a cognition of pervasion (or duality, etc. in a single cognition; however, what dependence does this have upon these [six categories] or upon the six categories and so forth as its cause? || 642 ||
This cognition is secondary (gauṇa) because it arises from inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*) and the like; thus, it is erroneous, just as the notion of fire in a boy [is erroneous].

For if this cognition were derived from a unity (*ekatva*) etc. inherent in that substance, then let it be granted that in a single cognition or in pleasure (*sukha*) etc., there is the cognition "one, one" due to their inherence in a single self-substance (*ātman*). However, [this does not apply to the case at hand].

But what is the cause for the cognition of "two," "three," "four," and so forth? For in that case, there is no duality or such residing in a single self (ātman) which could be the basis for such a statement as: "the six categories [are], pleasure and pain, desire and aversion, the fivefold action, generality is twofold—higher and lower—and there is one existence, and one inherence. What is the cause for this?
For in that case, there is no number inherent in a single object; therefore, because it is non-pervasive, this conceptualization also is not tenable.

Furthermore, whether you state that the cause is "inherence in a single object" (*ekārthasamavāya*) or some other factor imagined by your own intellect, even so, this cognition arising from "inherence in a single object" and the like would be figurative (*gauṇa*), because there is no other distinct entity [to serve as its primary referent]. Consequently, it would be subject to slippage (*skhalita*), just as the cognition of "fire" applied to a young boy is erroneous due to the absence of the grounds for its application; yet such is not the case. Therefore, the previously mentioned defect remains unrefuted.
With the words "gajādi" and so forth, [the author] raises an objection regarding the proof for establishing the number, as stated by Aviddhakarṇa.

Furthermore, the cognition of number is established as being distinct from the cognitions of elephants and so forth, because it arises from something other than those [objects], like the cognition of a blue cloth and the like.

For he (the opponent) says: "The cognition of number is based on a factor distinct from elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth, because it is different in character from the cognition of elephants and the like, just like the cognition of a blue cloth."

Regarding the phrase "arising from something other than that" (*tadanyotthā*): the analysis of the compound is as follows—*tadanya* means "other than that," namely other than elephants, horses, chariots, and so forth; *utthānam yasyāḥ* means "that from which [the cognition] arises.

He replies with the verse beginning "icchā" (desire), etc.: "In that case, the establishment of the desired [property] regarding cognition and so forth would occur either through the means of mental attention to a convention fashioned by desire, or by this very [term] 'number'. (645)

Since internal factors such as the mental application of convention (*saṅketamanaskāra*) and so forth, which are distinct from the elephant and other [external objects], are accepted as the causes [of the cognition], there is a proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhyataiva*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the recollection of convention (*saṅketasmaraṇa*) and others are included.

Now, if it is intended to prove that [the cognition] is based on an object distinct from the manifestation of convention (*saṅketābhoga*) and so forth, then [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); this he demonstrates by means of pointing out a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*): "In the case of cognition and so forth, it would exist by this very [reasoning] or by number (*saṅkhyā*)."

By this very reason—that is, by the argument "because it is distinct from the cognition thereof"—number would also apply [as a universal] even in cases such as "one cognition," "two cognitions," or "five actions"; for there too, the single or other cognitions are distinct from their own corresponding cognitions. Yet number does not so apply there. Therefore, the point is that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, regarding that number such as duality (*dvitva*) and so forth which resides in multiple substances—the production of which from unities accompanied by the cognition of multiplicity is described by you—he shows that this is without foundation: "And dependent upon cognition," and so forth.
If the production of number is described as being dependent upon cognition...
Why is it not accepted that the cognition of that [object] arises from the mere application of convention?

(646) The inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding the cognitions of oneness, duality, and so forth, as well as the cognitions of their universals and the relations between them.
"The cognition of that" refers to...
Why is it not accepted that the cognition of "two," "three," "four," and so forth regarding numerable objects arises merely through the application of convention?
For in this way, the causality of something whose capacity is unobserved would not have to be postulated; otherwise, there would be an infinite regress of causes.

Thus, since the presence of that [number] follows the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) with the existence of the enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi), it is that very cognition which is rightly to be postulated as the cause.
Otherwise, one would have to imagine that even deities cause purging upon encountering a *harītakī* fruit.

Furthermore, dualities (*dvitva*) and the like—which are intended to be perceived and which are distinct from the objects excluded by conjunction (*samuccaya*) and so forth—are neither observed nor logically consistent; for the occurrence of a single entity in many [substrata] has been refuted, and it will be demonstrated later that universals (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*) are also to be rejected. This is the underlying sense.
With the words beginning "mahat" (646), he states the refutation of dimension:
that which is called dimension is divided into categories such as "large," "long," and so forth.
Why is that [distinction] not considered to exist in the object itself, simply due to the difference in form?
Dimension (*parimāṇa*) is the cause for the conventional usage of measurement; it is fourfold: large, small, long, and short.
Among these, the large is of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.
The quality of extreme magnitude (paramamahattva) is eternal in ether, time, space, and the self;
it is non-eternal in substances such as triads (tryaṇuka).
Likewise, atomicity (aṇu) is also of two kinds: eternal and non-eternal.
The atom and the mind are eternally characterized by perfect sphericity;
the dyad alone is impermanent.

Even in large objects such as the *kuvala*, *āmalaka*, and *bilva* fruits, this conventional usage [of "large"] is merely figurative, in view of the absence of that [sphericity] in its highest degree.
For just as the magnitude (*mahat-parimāṇa*) in an *āmalaka* fruit is not the same as that in a *kuvala* fruit,
so it should be applied elsewhere as well.
In this regard, what is the distinction between the largeness and length existing in triads (*tryaṇuka*) and the like, and the minuteness and shortness existing in dyads (*dvyaṇuka*)?
It is said that in this regard there is a mutual distinction between largeness (*mahattva*) and length (*dīrghatva*),
because we observe a difference in linguistic usage, such as: "Let the long one be brought from among the large," and "Let the large one be brought from among the long."
The distinction between atomicity (*aṇutva*) and shortness (*hrasvatva*), however, is perceptible only to those yogins who perceive such things; this is the system of the opponents.

Furthermore, the opponent considers that [the categories] beginning with "the great" (*mahat*) are established as entities distinct from color and the other [sensory qualities], because they are apprehended by cognitions different from the cognitions of those [qualities], just like pleasure and so forth.

In this regard, if the intended meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is "because they are apprehended by a perceptual cognition distinct from the sensory cognitions whose objects are color and the rest," then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For, apart from the objects such as color-form (rūpa) existing in their respective states, no dimension (parimāṇa) such as "large" or "small" is perceived appearing in sensory cognition. Now,
if it is intended that the conceptual cognition which thinks "it is small," "it is large," and so forth, is what is meant by "cognition distinct from that [sensory] cognition"—
even so, the reason remains inconclusive (anaikāntika), because there is no subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against its presence in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
For this [cognition], in the ultimate sense, has no object of apprehension whatsoever, because it is conceptual (*sābhijalpa*).

It arises merely by determining "large" in accordance with a previously established convention, when those very forms and so forth—which possess a single orientation and the like—are perceived; this is done for the purpose of demonstrating the difference [of those forms] from other forms and so forth that lack such characteristics. Therefore, there is no establishment of a separate entity [such as "largeness"].
For this very reason, since there is nothing to be determined here apart from form and the rest, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is also unestablished (*asiddha*).

Furthermore, the thesis is contradicted by perception, because the "greatness" and so forth of the desired [atoms], though claimed to be perceptible, are not perceived apart from color-form (*rūpa*) and the like.

Therefore, why is that dimension (*parimāṇa*) not accepted as being identical with the object—such as color-form—when it occurs in a single direction toward that object, based on its distinction from the object as it is not manifested?
For in this way, the postulation of unseen and irrational categories would not have been made; this is what he shows by means of the particle *eva*.
For instance, when many forms and so forth are seen or touched as they extend toward a single direction, people employ the conventional expression "long";
and when something smaller arises in relation to that, they employ the expression "short.
The same logic should be applied to "large" and other such terms.
Just as there is a negation of form and so forth, the negation of the "great" (mahat) and other principles must be stated by means of the two alternatives of being one or many.

Furthermore, demonstrating that the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) of the reason is even more evident because it is observed to occur even in the absence of the probandum (sādhyābhāva), he says: "Long," and so forth.

Just as a long garland of palaces is perceived as something great, even though no such dimension is actually constructed there; if it is designated in that way because of its inherence in a single object— 648. If [it is argued] that it is designated thus through inherence in a single referent...
Neither magnitude nor length is intended to be the inherent property of the substratum [the palace].

For even in the absence of the magnitude and other qualities imagined by you, the production of cognitions such as "large" is experienced in the case of a row of palaces and the like; and it cannot be argued in this manner [that the cognition must have a real basis].

Wherever a quality called "length" (mālā) inheres in things such as palaces, there "largeness" (mahattva) and so forth also inhere; therefore, by virtue of inhering in the same object, that [palace] is designated as "long" and so on.
Showing that this too is contrary to one's own system, he says: "Not largeness," etc., ending with "in the substrata."
In the case of palaces,
the intended measure is half a *krośa*, one *krośa*, and so forth.
He asks why it does not exist and says: "And the palace is intended [to exist]."
The palace is held to be the quality of conjunction, which is immeasurable;
it has no further series, nor is it the substratum for metaphorical designation.
For instance, you maintain that the palace is a quality consisting of conjunction, not a composite substance, because it does not originate from substances of heterogeneous classes.
Furthermore, that quality (guṇa) cannot possess dimension (parimāṇa), because of the established tenet that qualities are themselves devoid of qualities.

Consequently, since qualities such as palaces and the like lack another quality called "a row" (mālā), the very expression "a row of palaces" would not exist; how then could there be distinctions such as "a large row" or "a short row"?
For instance—a garland is accepted as being of the nature of number, and since number is a quality (*guṇa*), it depends solely upon a substance (*dravya*) and not upon a quality.

Even when a garland is considered to be of the nature of a composite whole (*avayavin*), even then a substance can only have another substance as its substratum, not a quality; thus, it is not logical for a garland to have a temple as its substratum.
Now, suppose a garland is admitted to be of the nature of a universal (*jāti*).

Even so, because a universal (jāti) exists in its entirety in each individual substratum, even a single palace would be called a "garland," just like a tree—as it has been said: "If a house is a conjunction, then what would a garland of them be?
If it were a universal, then even a single house would be called a 'garland,' just like a tree."
Thus,

the impossibility of designations such as "one," "long," or "great" remains just as it was in the case of a garland; for there is an absence of qualities such as oneness in its substrata like palaces,
and because the intended length and so forth do not exist in the wooden beams and other components.
Furthermore, in the case of many rows of palaces, the derivative designation "row upon row" (mālāmālā) would not occur, because a genus cannot arise from what is not a genus—
as it has been said: "If there is a plurality of rows, how can that word [be applied] to a genus, since there is no genus [therein]?"
Therefore, it is not logical that there should be a basis for this metaphorical designation, nor that its substratum or locus should be so; the meaning is that such a basis is untenable.
Furthermore, this cognition of "largeness" and so forth with respect to garlands and the like is not one whose application falters;
therefore, it is not appropriate to regard it as merely figurative.

Indeed, a secondary (gauṇa) usage is not tenable if it is indistinguishable from the primary (mukhya) cognition, because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga). As it has been said: "In the case of a garland and the like, greatness and so forth are desired; and that which is figurative (aupacārika) is not [truly] figurative, because it is grasped by a cognition that is indistinguishable from the primary."
Thus, [verse 650]:

"In this regard, that by virtue of which a substance, even when conjoined, is separated as 'this is distinct from that'—that cause of separation is called distinctness (*pṛthaktva*). And it is a different entity from jars and the like, because it is apprehended by a cognition distinct from the cognition of those [objects]," such is the opponent's position, as explained previously.
Therefore, bearing in mind that here too the reason is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), just as in the case of dimension (*parimāṇa*), he says:

"The conventional usage of abstraction (*apoddhāra-vyavahṛti*), such as distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) and so forth, which is postulated from its cause—is it not considered to be based on a nature that is essentially different [from that cause]? (651)

For in this case as well, no distinct entity called "separateness" (pṛthaktva) appears in perceptual cognition apart from form and the other [sensory objects]; thus, its being grasped by a cognition distinct from that [perceptual] cognition is not established. For this very reason, since it is not perceived despite being intended to meet the conditions for perception, it is simply non-existent;
nor can its existence be established on the basis of a conceptual cognition such as "it is separate."

For those very entities, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, by virtue of abiding in their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), are perceived as having an essence that is excluded from both homogeneous and heterogeneous things; thus, they will serve as the basis for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of "separateness. Therefore, no separate entity [called "separateness"] is established. Consequently, regarding this conventional practice of abstraction—which is described as being caused by separateness—why is it not considered to reside in entities whose natures are distinguished from both similar and dissimilar classes?
The sense is that it is logical that it resides precisely in those [entities].
By this, the inconclusiveness of the reason is demonstrated;

the analysis of the compound is as follows: those whose self-nature (svabhāva) or essence is distinct are called "vibhinnātman"; these are the "bhāvas" (entities), and that which has its "niṣṭhā"—meaning its completion or culmination—in them [is the term being defined].

Showing that the presence of the reason (hetu) might even be observed in the counter-example of the probandum (sādhyavipakṣa), he says: "For [things] such as cognition, pleasure, and so forth are mutually distinct," and so on.
And other [qualities] likewise must be called "distinct" even without another [quality] being their constituent part.
For among qualities such as pleasure (*sukha*) and the like, there is no quality called "distinctness" (*pṛthaktva*), because qualities themselves are devoid of further qualities;
nevertheless, they are to be called "distinct" by virtue of their mutually exclusive natures.
Just as other factors serve as the instrumental causes for the linguistic usage of "removal" (*apoddhāra*) regarding that [substance],

so too will other things considered substances, such as jars and the like, exist even without another quality named "separateness" (*pṛthaktva*) distinct from themselves; nor is this cognition regarding them merely figurative, because it is indistinguishable from a primary cognition— this is the intended meaning.

Alternatively—demonstrating that the linguistic practice of abstraction (*apoddhāra*) is based on distinct categories of entities, he states the sublation of the proposition by inference through the following formal argument (*prayoga*): "Those things whose natures are mutually excluded do not have as their substratum a 'separateness' (*pṛthaktva*) distinct from themselves, just like pleasure and so forth;
and jars and so forth have natures that are mutually excluded. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

The impossibility of one [entity] residing in many, the non-establishment of a relation because *samavāya* (inherence) will be refuted, and the undesirable consequence that there would be no linguistic usage of it regarding pleasure and so forth, constitute the subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
In that regard, he says "yau... and so forth, for the purpose of refuting conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*).

The conjunction and disjunction which others postulate as the causes of the cognitions of "conjoined" and so forth, and which are restricted to substances, are useless. (653) According to the system of others, the causes of the notions of "conjoined" and "disjoined" regarding substances are, respectively, conjunction and disjunction; these have the nature of reaching and not reaching that which was previously unobtained, and they arise from the action of either one or both [of the objects], as well as from other conjunctions and disjunctions.
And this is merely a formal procedure;
there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever that establishes the real existence of these two. Therefore, these two arguments postulated by others are useless:

"Whatever has no means of valid cognition to establish it is not an object of the conventional usage of 'existent' for discerning people, such as the son of a barren woman; and for the opponents, there is no means of valid cognition establishing conjunction and disjunction"—this is an inference based on the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

By means of the verse beginning with "bījodaka... (seeds, water, earth, etc.), he raises the objection that the reason [adduced] is unestablished (*asiddha*), by pointing out the opinion of Udyotakara:
"Seeds, water, earth, and so forth, are always the producers of their effects."
It follows that [the self] is inactive because it is devoid of distinctions; however, due to the impossibility of conjunction,
it is understood that the field, seed, water, and so forth are dependent [on other factors],
since they constantly produce their own effects, like the staff, the wheel, and water.
That entity which is depended upon by them shall be conjunction;
and because it possesses qualifiers, it is understood to be indeed distinct [from its relata].
When it is said, "Bring the two conjoined things," one perceives the conjunction of those two.
For this [reason], it indeed brings about those two alone by excluding everything else.
For he says:
"If conjunction were not a distinct entity, then the field, the seed, and so forth, being indistinguishable [from one another], would always produce sprouts and the like; yet such is not the case."

Therefore, because effects are never produced from [mere] causes alone, the field and other factors are dependent upon other effects for the production of effects such as sprouts; just as the lump of clay, the staff, water, thread, and so forth, are dependent upon the potter and others in the making of a jar.
That which is thus depended upon is established as conjunction (*saṃyoga*).

Furthermore, that conjunction between two substances is established through direct perception itself as being a distinct entity from them, because it is perceived as a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇabhāva*).

For instance, when someone is told by another, "Bring the two substances that are conjoined," he brings only those two specific substances whose conjunction he perceives, and not just any substance; otherwise, he might bring anything at all. This same logic applies to the establishment of disjunction through its opposite.

By what cause does this distinction in cognition arise— that "this object is continuous" and "this object is discontinuous"? If those two [objects] do not exist here, then this distinction cannot exist here either.

Moreover, even when things are equally immediate, how could the distinction in cognition—namely, "this object is contiguous" and "this object is separated"—be logically possible if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) were not here distinct entities (*arthāntara*) within the object? For a specific cognition cannot possibly arise without a specific feature in the object, as that would lead to the absurd consequence of such a cognition occurring at all times and in all places.
And as for this cognition of separation which concludes [the perception] of contiguity...
This false cognition is of two kinds, even when occurring in the case of what is continuous.
And every false cognition conforms to a primary object;
that primary object must be stated here, for when it is stated, those two [the cause and the nature of the error] are established.

Furthermore, this cognition which arises for a person situated at a distance as a continuous perception of dhava and khadira trees, even though they are located very far apart; and that other cognition which arises regarding a row of cranes perched on the top of a tree, even though they are contiguous, as if they were separated—both of these are false cognitions because they function toward an object in a manner that does not correspond to its actual state. Moreover, a false cognition never arises anywhere without a prior experience of a primary (real) object.
For one who has not experienced the sight of a cow, the delusion "this is a cow" does not arise from seeing the object that is a gavaya;
therefore, some primary referent must necessarily be stated as the basis for this delusive cognition.
And when that is stated, those two—conjunction and disjunction—are established.
For apart from that, no other basis for this cognition can be established.
If this cognition "earring" arises [with respect to a man], what is its cause?
It does not arise from the state of being a man and an earring, because that would entail [the cognition] occurring at all times.
Furthermore, the negation of a thing perceived in one place is only logical in another place.
And since conjunction is observed, how can it be denied?
Therefore, [the distinction] such as "Caitra is without earrings" exists as a reality, because the application of negation and affirmation proceeds through such differentiation.
Furthermore, it must be stated on what basis this cognition, "Devadatta is wearing earrings," arises;

for it cannot arise based merely on the existence of the person and the earrings, because that would entail the undesirable consequence of such a cognition occurring at all times whenever Devadatta and the earrings are present.
Furthermore, it is observed that worldly linguistic usage proceeds by way of affirmation and negation only with respect to that whose existence has been perceived somewhere by someone;
if conjunction (*saṃyoga*) has never been perceived by you, how could there be such a differentiated usage as "Caitra is without earrings" or "Caitra has earrings"?

For instance, in the statement "Caitra is without earrings," it is not the earring that is negated, because its existence—projected through differences of space and time—is impossible to negate; nor is it Caitra, since he shares the same logical status [of being established]. Therefore, what is negated is the conjunction of Caitra with the earring.
Similarly, by the affirmative sentence "Caitra has earrings" as well, there is no affirmation of either Caitra or the earring, because both are already established.
By the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), it is understood that what is affirmed is precisely the hitherto unperceived conjunction.

Therefore, conjunction and the like do indeed exist as real entities, by virtue of which such distinct cognitions arise as the formulation of prohibitions—such as "Caitra is not wearing earrings"—and so forth;
the word "etcetera" includes the previously mentioned points, such as their being apprehended as qualifiers.
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said," and so forth.
It is said: Water and other factors are not indistinguishable by virtue of their momentariness;
even though they exist, they depend upon another state, such as the absence of obstruction.

(664) Regarding the claim that seeds and so forth would always produce their effects because they are indistinguishable, the lack of distinction among seeds and the like is unproven, since all things, being subject to momentary destruction, are productive only when they have reached specific states.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "the field, the seed, and so forth," he shows that even there, if one intends to prove merely the general fact of dependence, it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). He says, "Even when existent," and so on:

we ourselves indeed accept that seeds and the like, though existing, are capable of producing effects such as sprouts only by depending on other conditions such as the absence of obstruction; thus, there is *siddhasādhyatā*.
In that case, "where" refers to a particular location or state where obstructions and the like do not exist.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the counteraction of opposing conditions and so forth is intended;
the meaning is that in whichever other state there is no obstruction, no existence at a distant location, no resistance by an opposing factor, or any such impediment to the production of the effect.
Furthermore, since a state is not distinct from its own nature (*svabhāva*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*) as a separate entity is not established.

Now, if you intend to prove dependence upon another category of entity called "conjunction" (saṃyoga) as favored by you, then the reason is inconclusive because its positive concomitance (anvaya) with such a property is unestablished, and the example is devoid of the probandum (sādhyavikala); this is the sense. One might ask: "How is this understood—that earth and other elements depend on a specific change of state (*avasthāntara-viśeṣa*) as the cause for producing effects such as sprouts, and not rather on a conjunction that is a distinct entity (arthāntarabhūta), such that if you were to prove mere dependence in general, you would be proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In mere conjunction," and so forth.

If water and the other elements were dependent solely upon conjunction, then the effect would arise immediately after the conjunction, or it would never arise at all. (665) For if they were dependent solely upon conjunction, then the production of the effect, such as a sprout, from earth and the other elements would necessarily occur at the very first moment of their meeting, because the cause would be complete thereafter just as it was before.
Furthermore, if [the effect] does not arise upon the first encounter, it follows that it would never arise later either,
because the state of being an incomplete cause remains indistinguishable from the previous non-productive state.
Moreover, it is not logical for earth and the other elements to depend on a conjunction that provides no assistance, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Nor is it logical for conjunctions to be occasional, because their causes— earth and the other elements— are eternally present.
If it is argued that even in the production of that conjunction, earth and the others are held to depend upon action (*karman*) and so forth, [that is not the case].
In that case as well, the objection is equally applicable;
for instance, if one asks, "Why does that [past] action not produce [its result]? what could be said in response?
If you say, "Because of the absence of the impelling cause," then one must ask, "Why is that [impelling cause] absent? Thus, if one accepts an eternal cause, the same objection applies everywhere.

However, for one for whom every entity is indeed impermanent, there is no consequence of all things arising simultaneously, because the succession of causes is beginningless; this is due to the dependence of subsequent effects upon preceding causes,
and because all of them are absent at once due to the simultaneous deficiency of their respective causes.

Therefore, in your own view, it follows that earth and the other elements would always be the cause for the production of effects such as sprouts; thus, it is established that earth and the others do not depend on conjunction as a distinct entity.
As for what was said regarding "because of the presence of qualifications" and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "the state of having reached [conjunction]," etc.
For when a particular state has been reached, these two things— being produced in immediate succession— are perceived by him as such; for conjunction,
which is a distinct entity from the conjoined objects, does not enter the range of the perceiver’s vision, such that he would grasp the substance as qualified by it upon seeing that [conjunction].

What then? Those two entities that arise in a continuous state, distinguished from those that previously existed in a state with an interval between them, are precisely what is denoted by the word "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*), because the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) has been established as referring to a specific state. Therefore, when one perceives two such entities that have become the objects of the word "conjunction," it is these alone that one brings, and no others; for a discerning person does not act on the basis of a word regarding an object that has not been made known by that word.

Regarding what was stated as "without interval" and so forth, he says: "Separated or otherwise produced, it serves as the cause for cognitions with or without intervals, just like a house, the Vindhya, and the Himalaya mountains. (667)

The collective meaning is as follows: since it is precisely another object arising in that manner which serves as the basis for the distinction in cognition, this [argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
In that context, the connection is that an object which has arisen as separated becomes the cause of the cognition of an interval (*sāntara-buddhi*).
"Otherwise" means...
The connection is with the phrase "that which has arisen without interruption"; "like a house, the Vindhya, and the Himalaya" serves as an illustration for these two respectively, as appropriate.

For, according to your own view, there is no further conjunction that serves as the basis for the cognition of "non-interval" between two houses produced without interval and which are themselves of the nature of conjunction; nor is there, for those same two houses produced with an interval, a disjunction that serves as the cause for the cognition of "interval," because it has already been stated that qualities are devoid of qualities.

Indeed, even in the case of the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains, disjunction is not the cause of the cognition of an interval, since by convention, disjunction is a non-attainment preceded by attainment.
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "And this cognition which [occurs] at intervals," he says: "False," and so forth;
not every false cognition follows the primary object.
Some [cognition] arises even without dependence on similarity due to an internal disturbance,
just as the perception of two moons occurs for one whose mind is directed elsewhere;
or else, the primary cause here is that which has arisen in an uninterrupted stream.
The claim that "all false cognition arises from the apprehension of similarity" is unproven;
for we observe that some [false cognitions] arise even without depending on similarity, solely through a defect of the sense organ.

For example, even when one's mind is occupied with a conceptual thought directed elsewhere, there arises before one a cognition of two moons—clearly manifest and permeated by the form of two moons—which, though produced by a defect of the sense organ caused by ophthalmia (*timira*), is entirely unstained by the blemish of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). This occurs merely through the appearance [of two moons] despite the presence of only a single moon.
By the phrase "of one whose mind has gone elsewhere," he demonstrates that the cognition of two moons is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*);

for in a non-conceptual mind there is no grasping of similarity, since such a mind consists of the determination of the identity between objects seen previously and subsequently, and thus takes the form of a verbal association with an object previously experienced.

Alternatively, let it be granted that the previous false cognition conforms to the primary object; nevertheless, he shows that even so, your desired conclusion is not established—with the words "or [the object] produced as uninterrupted, etc.
By the inclusion of the word "etc.," an object produced as interrupted is also included.

For that very object, whether arising as interrupted or uninterrupted, exists primarily as that which is first designated by distinct names such as "vibhakta" (distinct) for the sake of activity directed toward the exclusion of what is not of its own kind; thus, your desired conclusion is not established.
Regarding what was stated, "This cognition that 'it is Kuṇḍalī' and so forth," he says there: "Kuṇḍalī," etc.
This cognition "he is wearing earrings" arises only with respect to Caitra and the earrings during their specific states of being joined, just like the conjunction [itself].

For just as the conjunction between Caitra and the earrings arises only when they have reached a particular state and not at all times, so too this cognition "he is wearing earrings," being dependent upon a specific state, why should it not arise only then and not at all times?
Those two, Caitra and the earring, for whom a particular state has arisen, are described as such.
Regarding what was stated elsewhere— that "of a thing previously observed," and so forth— he replies with the verse beginning "that excellence of state," and so on.
Such a specific state, observed elsewhere, is denied in cases such as "there is no earring in Caitra," because conjunction is not perceived by you [the opponent].

That cognition which has been described as being based on a particular state is negated when that state—having reached the conditions for perception—is not apprehended in another state; however, this does not apply to the conjunction imagined by you, since it never appears in any cognition as distinct from the objects conjoined.
Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (asiddha).

It might be argued: "Even if no proof-establishing means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) has arisen for us regarding conjunction, what subverting means of valid cognition do you have? To this he says: "Not from that which is intended by others," and so forth.
The cognition of a "joined" object does not arise from conjunction with something else that is intended [as the relatum],
just as the cognition of "joined" in the case of palaces and the like arises through the cognition of being joined;
or else, because it arises when multiple objects are present.
Just as cognitions have as their objects multiple threads and so forth that are already distinct,
so too these two types of valid cognition (pramā) should be described accordingly even when there is a distinction [between the object and its parts].
Furthermore, the subverting argument is that it is not logical for a single entity to reside in many [locations].

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is a cognition of conjunction (*saṃyuktabuddhi*) arises solely with respect to specific entities that do not possess the "conjunction" postulated by you; for example, the cognition "two palaces are joined" and so forth. And this [cognition] "Caitra is wearing an earring" and so forth is a cognition of conjunction. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Alternatively: that which arises when multiple entities are brought together arises solely with respect to those multiple entities devoid of the "conjunction" postulated by you; for example, the cognitions whose objects are multiple threads situated at a distance from one another. And this cognition of being joined is likewise. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). [End of] "the cognition of being joined."
The meaning is that it is the cognition of being conjoined (*saṃyukta*).
These same two means of proof should be stated for the negation of disjunction (*vibhāga*):

because it is a cognition of being divided (*vibhakta*), or because its arising depends upon the non-proximity of multiple objects, the cognition of disjunction in respect to rams and the like is based solely on specific objects that lack the disjunction postulated by opponents; just as, for example, a cognition whose objects are two rams situated at a great distance, or one whose objects are the Vindhya and Himalaya mountains.

Now, what is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) for the reason, by which the suspicion of the reason’s occurrence in the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is removed? To this he says: "Of one," and so forth.

Just as the existence of one thing in many places is not logical, so too has this been elaborated upon in the refutation of the composite whole (*avayavin*) through the passage beginning with "by that very form which possesses existence in one [place]," and thus it is not elaborated here again.
673–674 He states the refutation of priority and posteriority, beginning with the words "priority, posteriority," and so forth.

Furthermore, that "remoteness" and "proximity" which are postulated as the causes for designations such as "prior" and "posterior," and which depend upon space and time as their limits, do not exist [as real entities],
just as blue and other colors [are not distinct from the cognition of them] because they are established as occurring in a temporal sequence.
Even when other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are excluded, they are described in that same way; so too are others.

Since the designations and cognitions "this is remote" and "this is proximate" arise, remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*) are established respectively as the causes for the conceptualizations of "remote" and "proximate.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the corresponding cognition (*pratyaya*) is included.

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: This cognition of "farther" and "nearer" is based on an object distinct from the jar and so forth, because it is of a different character than the cognition of those [objects], like the cognition of pleasure and so forth.

For instance, when two physical bodies are situated in the same direction, the application of the cognitions "farther" and "nearer" is neither based on direction nor on time. This is because, even at a single point in time, such cognitions arise through the distinction between a youth and an elder who are present and conjoined with indefinite directions and locations; for the distinction [in cognition] occurs despite the lack of distinction in that [direction or time]. This is the intended meaning.
And no other basis for this cognition can be stated;
therefore, it is established that "priority" and "posteriority" are that which serves as the basis for this [cognition],
and not that which is dependent on space and time.
The meaning is that [the cognition] does not have as its limit objects that are conjoined with or proximate or remote from the spatial and temporal locations (*dikkālapradeśa*).
For, by the terms "space" (*dik*) and "time" (*kāla*), there is an indication through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) of those things conjoined with the spatial and temporal locations;
thus, indeed, it has been described by the opponent that both of these—remoteness (*paratva*) and proximity (*aparatva*)—are twofold: produced by space and produced by time.
In that regard, the production of spatial [qualities] occurs as follows:

when two objects are situated in the same direction, an observer takes one as the proximate limit and forms the cognition "this is remote compared to that" with respect to the substratum of priority (*paratva*); then, depending on that cognition, priority arises from conjunction with a more distant spatial region.

Furthermore, taking the remote object as the limit, the cognition "this is proximate compared to that" arises with respect to the substratum of posteriority (*aparatva*); depending on that cognition, posteriority arises from conjunction with a nearer spatial region.

This is the process of production for those [qualities] produced by time. To explain: between two persons, a youth and an elder, who exist at the present time and are conjoined with indefinite directions and locations, there is one observer who, based on the presence of wrinkles, grey hair, grown beard, and so forth, infers the great number of sunrises and sunsets that have occurred for the elder. Taking the youth as the limit (*avadhi*), a cognition of remoteness (*viprakṛṣṭā buddhi*) arises toward the elder; depending upon that cognition, and from conjunction with a further portion of time, the production of "remoteness" (*paratva*) occurs.

Taking an elder as the limit, for one whose youthfulness is inferred by the growth of his beard and so forth, there arises the notion of proximity toward a younger person—in whom the smallness of the sun’s rising and setting [cycles] has been inferred. With respect to that [notion], another [quality] arises from conjunction with another point in time;

thus, he shows that this proof for priority and posteriority is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the reason (*hetu*) also occurs in the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣe*). He explains: "Just as blue and other forms," etc.;
"existence" (*bhāva*) means arising, and "establishment" (*vyavasthiti*) is accompanied by that; the analysis of the compound is "the establishment of existence in a sequence."

This is what is meant: just as in the case of blue and other colors, the temporal distinction is established through a sequence of production due to the limiting condition of time (*kālopādhi*), and not due to the limiting condition of a quality (*guṇopādhi*); yet, even though there is no quality characterized as "priority" (*paratva*) or "posteriority" (*aparatva*), the designations "prior blue" and "subsequent blue" occur because qualities themselves are devoid of qualities—why is this not accepted in the case of jars and other objects as well?

By this, he demonstrates that if one merely intends to prove here that [the designation] has a cause distinct from the object itself, then the logical reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it occurs even in the opposite of the property to be proved (*sādhyaviparyaya*).

Now, if it is intended to prove that this cognition is based on a specific quality caused by the categories of eternal space and time, then there is an absence of an example and the thesis is contradicted by inference.

For it can be argued as follows: "Whatever is a cognition of 'prior' and 'posterior' is based on an arrangement of sequential production produced solely by objects devoid of the qualities imagined by others, because it is a cognition of 'prior' and 'posterior,' just like the cognition of 'prior' and 'posterior' regarding color and so forth; and this [cognition] regarding jars and so forth is a cognition of 'prior' and 'posterior'—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*)."

If it is argued that this cognition of "priority" and so forth with respect to blue and other qualities is merely metaphorical due to their inherence in the same substrate, and therefore the reason is inconclusive; and that because priority and the like are accepted as being causes for blue and the rest through a traditional succession, the example is devoid of the property to be proven— this is not so, for it has already been refuted that metaphorical status is tenable because the cognition occurs without faltering,
and furthermore, since those two [priority and posteriority] are not perceived even in their own substrates, a cognition based on their power is not logical.

Therefore, how could that [priority and posteriority] be based upon form and so forth, or how could it be imagined in relation to pleasure and so forth occurring at earlier or later times? For there is no inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*) in those cases.

Furthermore, since space and time have already been refuted and thus do not exist, priority and posteriority—which are caused by them—also do not exist; so whence can there be any suspicion of them being the cause?
By which reason the probans would become inconclusive?

Furthermore, for you [the Vaiśeṣikas], there are no spatial or temporal parts (*pradeśa*) from whose conjunction—accompanied by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*)—the production of "priority" (*paratva*) and so forth could occur, because those two [space and time] are unitary in nature and partless.

Nor is it logical to assume a figurative distinction of parts that conforms to causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), since such efficiency is dependent upon the actual nature of the thing, and what is figurative is unreal. Thus, there is no inconclusiveness.
Furthermore, as before, the unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) of the opponent's reason (*hetu*) must be stated.
With the words "Number," and so forth, he raises the objection of the opponent's proof for the category of qualities such as number under discussion:
"If it is your view that all [qualities] beginning with number and conjunction are not distinct from the substance, because they function as its delimiters, just like a staff and the like. (677)

The description of these [qualities] as conventional entities (saṃvṛtisat) establishes what is desired; however, they cannot be defined as being either identical to or different from reality, because they exist only conventionally.

All these aforementioned qualities, such as number and so forth, are not non-different from the substance, because they serve as the cause for the exclusion (vyavaccheda) of that substance. For whatever is the cause of the exclusion of something is not non-different from it, just as a staff and the like are not non-different from Devadatta.
In this case, if the probandum is merely the negation of non-difference from the substance, there is the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*),
because it is accepted that all things existing conventionally (*saṃvṛtisat*) are non-entities and are therefore inexpressible as being either identical to or different from [the substance].
With the words "Now, therefore" (*atha*) and so forth, he anticipates the response of Aviddhakarṇa:
"Now, the indefinability (*anirvacanīyatva*) of the aggregate (*samūha*) and so forth is being negated."
Because they possess a fixed nature, like color, sound, taste, and so forth.

He said: "The specific states of the collection and the continuum are not inexpressible in terms of being either identical to or different from [their constituents], because they are endowed with specific properties, just like color, taste, and so forth."
He refutes this with the passage beginning "by way of being devoid of intrinsic nature" (niḥsvabhāvatayā):

"By virtue of its being devoid of intrinsic nature, its properties are not established as determinate in reality, like a lotus in the sky; rather, they are merely superimposed by conceptual construction. (680)
In that very case, [the reason] is inconclusive because of [examples such as] the sky-lotus and so forth;
for non-difference and difference are established only with respect to real entities.
(681) For if the reason intended is "having a nature that is ultimately restricted," then the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*).
For it is not established that for the Buddhists, things such as continua (*saṃtāna*), which are conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*), possess ultimately real, fixed properties (*niyatadharma*).

If, on the other hand, the reason (*hetu*) is stated in a general sense, then even for things like sky-lotuses, there certainly exist imagined fixed properties such as non-existence and incorporeality; thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) when stated in that manner.

The meaning is that this has been stated by setting aside those properties that, while conceptually constructed, lack any real basis in commonality. Furthermore, this reason is inconclusive because non-difference (abheda), which is non-otherness, and difference (vyatireka), which is otherness, are established only in relation to real entities (vastu) and not elsewhere.

Furthermore, since continua and the like do not exist as real entities because they exist only as designations (*prajñaptisattva*), how can their identity with or difference from a real entity be established?

Thus, it has been demonstrated that in the first formal argument, if the probandum is merely the negation of the non-distinctness of number and so forth from the substance, one falls into the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
If it is thus argued that number and the like are distinct from substance,
then the reason is unestablished in its substratum (āśrayāsiddha), because number and the like themselves are unestablished.

Now, it might be argued: "It is not merely the negation of non-distinction that is being established; rather, since two negations imply an affirmation, the two negations establish precisely the non-distinction from substance.
Anticipating this with the words "of number and so forth," [the author] refutes it with the words "unestablished in its locus" and so on: "In this way, [it is not] non-distinct from substance."

What then? The meaning is "of those that are distinct" (vyatirekiṇaḥ). He demonstrates that very non-establishment of the substratum, such as number and so forth, with the words beginning "from the collection" (samuccayādi).
But that which is distinct from aggregation and so forth is simply a substance (*dravya*) that is described in such a way;
and thus, the distinction [of the substance] from its own nature would be established as being precluded.
"Is described in such a way" means...
One might argue that distinctions such as "one," "two," or "many" are established even for things that consist of substance; to this he replies with the words "from its own nature," etc.
For there is no distinction of a thing from its own nature, because that would entail the consequence of the thing being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
"Contradicted" means mutually opposed;
for difference and non-difference are contradictory when existing simultaneously in one place, because they are defined by their mutual exclusion.
Thus, first, the qualities ending with "otherness" (paratva) have been refuted.
As for those beginning with cognition (buddhi) and ending with effort (prayatna), which are accepted as qualities of the self because they reside in it,
they should be understood as refuted by the very refutation of the self.
Furthermore, it is not logical for the self to be their substratum; for instance, the self could be their substratum either as the cause of their production or as the cause of their persistence.
It cannot be as the cause of their production, because that would entail the constant production of pleasure and so forth, since the causes would always be complete.
Moreover, it has been discussed hundreds of times that there can be no dependence on auxiliary factors for that which cannot have any excellence imparted to it by others.
Furthermore, an eternal entity lacks the capacity to produce an effect, because such capacity is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity,

and it has already been established that for an eternal entity, purposeful activity (arthakriyā) is incompatible with both succession and simultaneity. Nor is it logical [to posit an eternal cause] as the cause of persistence, because persistence is not distinct in nature from the persisting entity itself.
If that were its cause, it would simply be stated that it has a "stationary" cause;
however, that has just been refuted.
Furthermore, since that stationary entity possesses a completely established essential nature, no cause for it is possible.

Because that [agent] does nothing for it, even though the abiding remains present despite the distinction; since no benefit has been conferred by him upon the abiding— which is a separate entity— because he merely produces it, how could that which renders no assistance be its substratum?
Nor is it logical that this [entity] is a benefactor by producing a stability related to that [permanent entity], because such a relationship is unestablished;
nor is it logical for it to be a cause with respect to stability, as it has already been stated that the capacity of a permanent entity to act in any way whatsoever is impossible.
Furthermore, this entity being established must either have an unstable nature or a stable nature;
if it has an unstable form, how could it be established by another,
since that would entail the consequence of its losing its own nature?

Now, even if its nature were stable, the sustainer (*sthāpaka*) would still be entirely ineffective, because its stability is established by its own very nature; furthermore, as for those entities that possess form (*mūrta*), one might indeed postulate a substratum (*āśraya*) as a preventer of their downward motion. However, as for these [mental states] such as pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, since they are formless (*amūrta*), there is no downward motion; thus, what could the substratum do for them? Moreover, it is impossible for either an existent or a non-existent thing to serve as a substratum, because both are devoid of dependence and are essentially indefinable (*anupākhyatva*).

The point is that, in this way, since it is not established that pleasure and the other [qualities] are dependent on anything else as appropriate, there is no such thing as a "quality" (guṇa). Furthermore, the intellect (buddhi) is accepted by others to have the nature of cognition (jñāna), as it has been said: "Intellect, apprehension, and knowledge are synonymous."
And even for such a cognition, its nature as self-cognized is not accepted by the opponents; rather, it is held to be cognizable only by another cognition.
Furthermore, since such a cognition—like color and so forth—is not established by itself, its very status as a cognition is untenable, as he will demonstrate.
It is also accepted that pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, and effort are of the nature of non-cognition;
this too will be refuted in the examination of the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Considering that heaviness, fluidity, and viscidity should be negated just like color and the other qualities, [the author], without explicitly negating those, states the negation of *saṃskāra* (disposition): "That which is called velocity," and so forth.

The threefold *saṃskāra*—namely, that termed velocity (*vega*), that known as mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and that characterized as elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*)—as it has been taught, does not hold up in its entirety. (684)
Because all things are momentary, no action whatsoever exists that could serve as the cause for a continuum known as "impulse" (*vega*).
There are three kinds of formative forces (*saṃskāra*): impulse, mental impression (*bhāvanā*), and elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*).
Among these, that which is called *vega* (velocity) arises from an action dependent upon specific effort or impact within five corporeal substances—earth, water, fire, air, and mind.
It is the cause of a continuous series of actions in a fixed direction and is opposed by conjunction with a substance possessing touch;
for instance, in the case of arrows and the like, it is caused precisely by a specific action generated by a specific effort.
Because it prevents one from falling during the interval [after death], its existence is established as being inferred from the effects of such determined actions and so forth;
however, in the case of branches and the like, [the movement] arises from action produced by the impact of a clod of earth,
whereas that which is termed *bhāvanā* is a quality (*guṇa*) of the self (*ātman*).

That which is called "born of knowledge" (*jñānaja*) and "the cause of knowledge" (*jñānahetu*) is established as existing because its presence is inferred from the effects of memory and recognition regarding things seen, heard, or experienced;

however, *sthitasthāpaka* (elasticity) is a quality of corporeal substances. It is that which restores its own substrate—characterized by a dense arrangement of parts and persisting over time—to its former state exactly as it was, even when altered by effort;
for example, a palm leaf or similar object that has been folded for a long time returns to its original position once it is unfolded and released.
In bows, branches, horns, tusks, and so forth, as well as in cloths and other objects that have been bent or twisted, its entire activity is indeed perceived;
thus, it is threefold.
In this regard, the effect called "connection with action" (karmasaṃbandha) attributed to that which is termed "impetus" (vega) is unestablished,

because momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga), which pervades the entire range of categories of entities, has been proven. Consequently, since all things cease to exist immediately after acquiring their own nature, there is no action whatsoever of which this [impetus] could be the cause of a continuous series (prabandha).

Furthermore, even if it is intended that the "continuum of activity" (*kriyā-prabandha*) is simply the arising of entities as they are perceived while abandoning the location of their own material cause (*svopādāna-deśa*), there is still the fault of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). This is because it is the preceding causes and conditions themselves that are inferred from the continuum of such activities constituting the nature of those entities as they arise in various ways; it is not the aforementioned *saṃskāra* (latent impression), since no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with it has been established anywhere.

Furthermore, if the non-falling of arrows and the like were due to the power of such an impression (*saṃskāra*), then they would never fall at all, because the velocity—which is the cause for obstructing their falling—would remain present everywhere. Consequently, how could this falling that is observed to occur suddenly in the case of an arrow traveling through an undifferentiated space be explained?

Nor can it be argued that the falling occurs because the power of the velocity is destroyed by contact with material things such as air; for if that were so, the consequence would be that the arrow would fall even before reaching its destination, since the contact with air, which is opposed to that velocity, exists everywhere.
Now, it might be argued that because the velocity (vega) is absolutely stronger, it overcomes even the opposing conjunction with air and carries the arrow to another location.
If this were so, by what means would its strength be diminished by a subsequent [conjunction] such that it would not carry it even to a very distant place?
For it is observed everywhere that an arrow falling in mid-course occurs even while moving across the expanse of space where the conjunction with air is uniform.

Furthermore, it is impossible to claim that the velocity [of the arrow] is different later on; for otherwise, there would be no cause for its production, since in all cases the inherent cause—the arrow and so forth—is indeed without distinction.
Nor is it reasonable to assert that the cause called "action" (karma) becomes distinguished later, because that too is subject to the same objection.

Alternatively, even if there were a difference [in the subsequent velocity], since there is no cause for the destruction of the preceding velocity, it would remain in that very same state; thus, the arrow would never fall.

Furthermore, it has already been stated that conjunction with air cannot be the cause of its destruction, as that would entail the arrow falling prematurely, because air is present everywhere without distinction, and thus its conjunction is likewise indistinguishable throughout. Therefore, this [argument] is trivial.

685. He states the refutation of that which is called "cultivation" (bhāvanā): "But that which is called cultivation," and so forth; "but that which is called cultivation is a mental impression (saṃskāra) consisting of a latent tendency (vāsanā)."
If it is argued that this [memory] is not a quality of the self, then it is logical, because that [self] has been refuted.
(686) For if, on the basis of effects such as memory, one were to establish merely a general "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*), then that would be proving what is already established;
for a cultivation consisting of a capacity deposited by a prior experience, which is essentially identical with the mind itself, is indeed accepted as the cause of memory and so forth.

If it is intended to prove that what is commonly known as "impression" (*vāsanā*) is actually a mental state (*bhāvanā*) whose intrinsic nature is a quality of the self (*ātma-guṇa-svabhāva*), then, because a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between such [a quality] and memory and so forth is not established anywhere, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and the thesis (*pratijñā*) is sublated by inference (*anumāna-bādhā*).

Since the self (*ātman*), which is the substratum of that [impression], has been previously refuted and is therefore non-existent, its non-existence is also established. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which are dependent upon something else do not maintain their existence when that [substratum] is absent, just as a painting does not exist in the absence of a wall or similar surface. Furthermore, according to the opponent's own view, the impression (*saṃskāra*) is dependent upon the self. Thus, because there is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*), the desired conclusion is not established, since that self has already been refuted.

Therefore, it is logical that the *saṃskāra* (mental impression) consists solely of the latent trace (*vāsanā*) of the mind and is not a quality of a self (*ātman*); this is the result of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The sense is that while one [the former] is established by a means of valid cognition, the other [the latter] is the opposite.

He states the refutation of the third [position] as well: "But that which has the nature of *sthitasthāpaka* (the sustainer of duration) is not tenable because of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
Since a persisting object is impossible, if it were to exist, its stability would arise solely from its own nature. (687)
To explain: regarding the object that he causes to remain stationary, there are two possible positions—either he himself is inherently unstable, or he is inherently stable.
If he is inherently unstable, then since he ceases to exist after a single moment, for whom would he be a stabilizer?

If, on the other hand, it is the second position—that he exists (is real)—then because objects that already exist possess that very nature [of stability], namely, the state of remaining without falling away from their form, what is the use of postulating a stabilizer who performs no function at all? The same refutation as before should be stated here.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even though all things are momentary, their efficacy is said to consist in their abiding for a single moment and their persistence through a continuous series; to this he replies with the verse beginning "But for a single moment," etc.:
"But abiding for a single moment arises from its own cause alone."
And due to the influence of each preceding moment, there is a continuous succession [of moments].
(688) Those things, being produced from their own causes alone, are established as lasting for only a single moment;

for their "stability" is said to consist solely in the acquisition of their own nature, and not in the maintenance of their own form at a later time once their existence has been acquired, because that which is inherently unstable cannot persist at a later time.

Alternatively, if it were to remain stable, there would be the consequence that it could never cease, because it would be no different afterward than before; furthermore, this would entail that it lacks that specific nature [of change].

Since the production of each subsequent effect is brought about by the capacity of each preceding cause, even in the case of a continuous series (*prabandha*), the efficacy of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is not established.
[The opponent objects: "In that case, let this [cause] be the stabilizer of that which is non-momentary. To this he replies: "Not otherwise," and so forth.
Since this [entity] does not arise in any other way, for whom would it be a stabilizer? Therefore, [it is not].
Nor can its causality be observed; it might be either a *saṃskāra* (impression) or something else.
Furthermore, this quality (*guṇa*) is held to be a stabilizer for things like cloth only after they have already arisen;
thus, what is called a "quality" or a "saṃskāra" is in every respect impossible [in this context].

For it has already been stated that since that which is non-momentary cannot undergo change, its persistence is due to itself alone; therefore, what could such a thing do for it so as to be its "stayer"?
Furthermore, one might argue: "Let it not be a stayer; rather, let it be the producer of the moment itself. To this he says: "And not of this," and so forth.

For the determination of the reality of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) is dependent upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And apart from well-known causes, the causality of this [alleged stayer] in relation to cloth and the like has not been seen—that is, ascertained—either through perception and non-perception, or through the exclusion of the effect (as in the case of the eye and other sense organs), by which means its status as a cause could be conventionally established.

Now, if the causality of even that which has unperceived efficacy (*adṛṣṭasāmarthya*) is postulated, then it follows as a consequence that either a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) or something else— such as the cry of a parrot or a crane— must be postulated as the cause of production; for there is no distinction whatsoever based on having unperceived power by which you would find satisfaction in postulating [causality] for one thing alone, such as a latent impression, whose capacity remains undetermined.

Furthermore, this [soul] is not accepted by you as the cause of production; rather, it is held to be a quality that stabilizes things such as cloth after they have already been produced. And in that regard, its inefficacy has already been described.
This refutation was stated only by granting, for the sake of argument, that it is the cause of production.
The sense is that, at some point, someone might even transgress the boundaries of their own system and conceive [the matter] in this way;
he concludes previously with the words "of the qualities, the refinements, and the names," etc.
690 He states the refutation of the characteristics and qualities of dharma and adharma, beginning with the words "the mind," etc.,
because the [nature of] the mind, its conjunction, and the self have already been established in detail previously.
That which is endowed with the characteristics stated by others is not established as *adṛṣṭa*.
[In the examination of the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*):
*Adṛṣṭa* is a quality of the self (*ātman*) that bestows the fruit upon the agent, arises from the conjunction of the self and the mind (*ātma-manaḥ-saṃyoga*), and is opposed by its own effect.
And that [unseen force] is of two kinds, distinguished as dharma and adharma.
Among these, dharma is the cause of what is pleasant, beneficial, and liberation for the agent;
