whereas adharma is the cause of what is unpleasant, harmful, and transgression—such is the definition of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) as stated by others.

Since the self (*ātman*), the mind (*manas*), and that which is considered their cause—their conjunction (*tadyoga*)—have already been refuted, it is established that [the object] is non-existent due to the very absence of a cause.

As for sound (*śabda*), which is asserted to be a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇa*), it has already been rejected previously by such arguments as "because it would entail the lack of succession" (*akramādyāpatita*); therefore, no further refutation of it is stated here.
Thus concludes the examination of the category of quality.
Now, for the purpose of refuting the category of action, he says "momentary," and so forth.

In entities that perish moment by moment, actions such as upward throwing and so forth are impossible; for once an entity has perished at the place where it was born, it is impossible for it to reach anything else.
[This is because] the Sūtra states: "Actions are upward throwing, downward throwing, contraction, expansion, and locomotion. (NS 1.1.7)

Among these, *utkṣepaṇa* (upward throwing) is that action which arises as the cause of conjunction and disjunction with respect to the upper and lower regions— for example, when an action is produced in a limb of the body or in a corporeal substance connected to it, such as a clod of earth, by virtue of effort or other causes, such that it is the cause of conjunction with points of space defined by the upper direction and the cause of disjunction from those delimited by the lower direction; the action that has the opposite effect regarding conjunction and disjunction is called *avakṣepaṇa* (downward throwing).

Contraction (*ākuñcana*) is the cause of curvature in a straight substance, as it has been stated: when there is disjunction of the distal parts, such as the fingers, of a straight substance like an arm from their respective conjoined entities such as space, and there is conjunction with the proximal regions such as the shoulder, that action by which the whole characterized as the arm becomes curved is contraction.
Conversely, when conjunction and disjunction arise in the opposite manner, that action by which the whole becomes straight is expansion (*prasāraṇa*).
That which is the cause of conjunction and disjunction with objects such as jars located in indefinite directions and regions is *gamana* (motion).
Action is of four kinds, beginning with upward throwing (*utkṣepaṇa*). [The other three] are causes of conjunction and disjunction with space and so forth located in definite directions and regions;
however, *gamana* produces conjunctions and disjunctions with regions in all directions, that is, with indefinite directions.
For this very reason, only five types of action are possible, since whirling, flowing, and so forth are included within "going.
Furthermore, this fivefold action is established as having its existence inferred from the effects of conjunction and disjunction occurring in corporeal substances.
The specific conjunctions and disjunctions of everything constitute its common effect; therefore, its existence is established through its effects.

Likewise, it is established through perception, as it has been stated: "Number, dimensions, distinctness, conjunction, disjunction, priority, posteriority, and action are perceptible by the eye because they inhere in substances possessing color."
Thus, this system of others has been stated in brief.
In this regard, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*) have already been refuted, their effect is unestablished (*asiddha*).

If it is argued that conjunction and disjunction—characterized merely by arising in immediate succession—are stated as the reason because they are the effects [of motion], even so, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Because such an action is not established as being concomitant with those two in any instance, the reason is also contradictory (*viruddha*) due to its pervasion by the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*). Furthermore,

if the mere existence of a cause is what is to be proven, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), since air and other elements are accepted as causes of such conjunction and disjunction.

Furthermore, when a specific property is to be proven, even the thesis itself is sublated by inference; for instance, regarding the occurrence of action in an entity, whether it be momentary or non-momentary— it cannot belong to that which is momentary, because it perishes at the very place of its birth, since destruction precludes the possibility of reaching another location.
The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: Whatever perishes in a particular location does not reach another location subsequent to that time, just like a lamp or similar objects;
and all entities under discussion perish in the very location of their birth. This is an observation of a property incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi).
Showing that the reason is not inconclusive, he says: "Birth," and so forth.
For others have asserted that the time of action is a time distinct from birth, even in the case of objects such as lamps, which are accepted to perish very rapidly. (693)

Those things whose destruction is desired to be even more rapid are likewise [subject to this rule]; for even in the case of a lamp and the like, which are admitted to perish after an extremely brief time, activity occurs only at a time subsequent to their birth, because such a thing, by virtue of persisting for six moments, is not momentary (akṣaṇika).
To the question "How so?", he says: "For instance," and so forth.
For instance: contact with the cause, the manifestation of the universal, then motion in its own constituent parts, and immediately after that, disjunction. (694)
There is the destruction of the conjunction, and from that follows the dissolution of the substance;
thus, even in the case of an object such as a lamp, its duration is held to be exactly six moments.
To explain: first, there occurs the moment of connection with its own cause.

Thereafter follows the time of the manifestation of its own [specific and] general properties; then the time of the action of the parts; immediately after that, the time of the disjunction of the parts; then the destruction of the conjunctions of the parts that constitute it; and finally, the destruction of the substance. Thus, even for an object such as a lamp, a duration of exactly six moments is accepted. Therefore, since there is no entity whatsoever that possesses motion and is momentary, for all things that possess activity, the activity occurs only at a time subsequent to their birth;
nor is the reason unestablished, because nothing else can be proven to be momentary.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even if we indeed accept the momentariness of entities..."
Nevertheless, he asks why the action does not occur precisely at the time of their birth—and answers with the verse beginning "paścima" (the western):
"When separation from the western location and conjunction with the eastern location are possible, the mover, or another, is conceived as the substratum of all action. (696)
That which occupies a moment of existence is never of a mobile nature;
for it is impossible for such a thing to undergo a transition to another location, even by the measure of a single atom.

For only that which can effect a separation from a posterior location and a conjunction with a location situated in front becomes a "goer," or else it serves as the locus for extension and so forth; nothing else is so, such as space and the like.

Furthermore, there is no delay for those things that exist for only a single moment, by which they might abandon a previous location and subsequently occupy another; because at the very time of their existence they are overcome by cessation, they are incapable of traversing to another place.
Therefore, it is also not logical for action to occur at the time of birth.
Nor can it exist at the two limits—the preceding and the succeeding moments—because at those times it is non-existent (anupākhyatva).

Therefore, for that which does not exist even for a single moment, let alone the possibility of traversing a distant location, there is not even the movement across a space the size of a single atom; how, then, can there be action in that which is momentary?
He demonstrates that it is not the case for the non-momentary either, with the words beginning "But if there were stability," and so forth.
If, however, the entity were stable, then all activities such as movement and so forth would be utterly impossible, especially since its nature remains unchanged across all states.
For that which is always of a single form is called non-momentary; in such a case, the occurrence of action is absolutely impossible, because, like space, it is forever devoid of distinction.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That which is always without distinction cannot possess activity, just like space; and that which is held to be non-momentary is always a thing without distinction. This is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*).

Anticipating the objection that even if a non-momentary thing is indeed without distinction, it might nonetheless possess activity because its very nature (*prakṛti*) consists of being a mover and so forth—and thus the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*)—he says "yadi" and so on.
If that [entity] were by its very nature of the form of a goer and so forth, then motion and the rest would exist at all times; thus, it could not remain motionless for even a single moment.
For, even in the absence of motion and the rest, these [qualities] would necessarily still belong to it.
Because their previous form has not been abandoned, just as at the time of the arising of motion and so forth.

(700) For if these [beings] such as Devadatta and others were intended to be momentary by nature, being endowed with motion, upward throwing, and so on, then they would never remain stationary, because they would always possess the nature of a mover and so forth.

Consequently, even when motion and so forth are absent for this Devadatta and others—that is, even during a state of stillness—those [actions], namely motion and so forth, would follow [as being present].
Because it does not abandon its prior nature, just as at the time of the arising of motion and so forth.
Furthermore, if that [entity] were by its very nature in the form of coming and so forth, then non-coming and the rest would exist at all times; it would not possess even a single moment of movement.
This is because, even when motion and such occur, it remains essentially immobile.
Because it has not abandoned its prior nature, it is like time, which is characterized by immobility.
(702) Now, if, out of fear of this fault, its state of being a non-goer and so forth is accepted,
then, being of a single uniform nature like space, there would always be non-going and the rest.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), upward throwing and the other [five types of action] are included;

consequently, even when motion and the rest are present, it follows that the substance must remain immobile, because it has not abandoned its nature as non-motion, just as in a state of immobility there is no vibration— that is, action—
and yet one says "it possesses vibration," meaning it possesses action.
The suffix *vati* is applied after the locative case-ending [of the word] "niścalātmakakāla" (time whose nature is immovable).

Furthermore, it might be argued: "It does not have a single nature; rather, because it possesses both natures—as the goer and the act of going—the aforementioned fault does not follow, and the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But if," and so forth.
"But if this goer were at one time one way and again otherwise, there would be a state of difference due to the association with mutually distinct selves. (703)
In the phrase "ekadā ca," the particle *ca* (and) is displaced; it should be understood as following the word *punaḥ* (again),
meaning "and again"— that is to say, "otherwise."
For in this way, because of the imposition of contradictory properties such as being a goer and a non-goer, there would follow the loss of its unity.
Therefore, demonstrating that its momentariness is thereby established, he says: "They are absolutely distinct," and so forth.
It is determined that those two selves are absolutely distinct,
because they possess contradictory attributes, like a moving object and a stationary object.
(704) "Those two" refers to...
The meaning is that [the two states] existing in the conditions of moving and non-moving are like moving and non-moving objects,
such as a creeper and a mountain.

Having thus established that the proposition is sublated by inference, he now states [the following] while also establishing that it is sublated by direct perception: "That which is intended to be perceptible, namely action, is not distinct from the substance," and so forth.
Even that [action] is not seen, nor is its existence logically tenable.

(705) Whatever, being characterized by perceptibility, is not perceived, enters into the conventional usage of "non-existent" for those who investigate; for example, a cloth not being perceived in a certain place. Action is not perceived apart from the entities such as color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth; this is a non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
For action is never observed appearing in sensory cognition as something distinct from color-form and the rest when they arise occupying another location.

Furthermore, this cognition that arises associated with verbal expression—such as "lifting up" or "lowering down"—is not perception because it is accompanied by conceptualization (*sābhijalpatvāt*). Nor is it logical for this [cognition] to arise from the experience of the category of action (*karmapadārtha*), since we observe that [the cognition] arises precisely from form (*rūpa*) and so forth as they manifest in various ways. This is because [the cognition] functions through a determination (*adhyavasāya*) directed toward those very [objects] according to linguistic convention;
and this has just been established immediately prior, on the grounds that motion and so forth do not exist in either permanent or impermanent things.
Therefore, what was stated—that action is established by perception itself—is unproven (*asiddha*).
Concluding the very point already stated, he says: "Whether unstable or stable, in this way, motion and so forth are impossible," and so on.
"Because of the impossibility of attaining disjunction from the former and the other regions.
Regarding the word "thus": it is because [the opponent's position] has been refuted by the aforementioned perception and inference; hence, "because of the impossibility of attaining disjunction."

The connection is to be understood respectively as: "because division [of the atom] is impossible by its prior location," and "because reaching [a new location] is impossible by its subsequent location.
(706) If this is so, then how does the worldly convention of "motion" occur? To this he says: "In another location," and so forth.
"But because of the perception [of an object] in another location, there arises the illusion of motion due to the continuous arising of similar and yet distinct entities, like a lamp.
(707) Thus ends the examination of the category of action (*karma*).
Regarding the phrase "of similar and subsequent entities" (*samānāparavastūnām*):
the analytical explanation (*vigraha*) should be made as "those which are both similar and subsequent," and then "those which are such entities.

Because of the perception of the occurrence of the birth of those similar and subsequent entities—which is their arising in immediate succession by abandoning the location of their own material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*)—there arises the cognition that "this very thing is moving," just as a lamp being carried by someone becomes the cause for the cognition that it is "going to another place."
For it is not the very same lamp that moves to another location,
since it is held to endure for six moments;
indeed, it is the very nature of an entity— devoid of prior and posterior limits— that is designated as "birth."
Therefore, its perception is indeed logical;

or alternatively, this [word] "janmanaḥ" ends in the ablative case, and the connection is as follows: because of the continuous arising of similar and subsequent entities, there is perception in another location.
Thus ends the examination of the category of action (karma) and the general examination.

With the words "In substances, etc. and so forth, he begins the refutation of universals (sāmānya) and particulars (viśeṣa): "When substances and the rest have been negated, the universals (jātis) are also rejected; for all those [universals] are postulated as subsisting in the three categories [of substance, quality, and action]. (708)
"Universals" refers to generalities;
and since these reside in the three categories consisting of substance, quality, and action, they are discarded by the very refutation of those [three categories].
For there can be no existence anywhere for things that are dependent (āśrita) without a substratum (āśraya), as that would entail the consequence of their being non-dependent.

The mention of "generality" (jāti) is illustrative; particulars (viśeṣas) are also intended to be dependent because they reside in ultimate substances, and thus they too are discarded by the very refutation of the substratum.

Nevertheless, wishing to state a specific refutation once again—and because it is impossible to refute that whose essential nature is not known—he first demonstrates the essential nature of the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), saying "In that regard," and so forth:
"In this context, this universal (*jāti*) is accepted by others as being twofold: [first] the universal alone, called 'Being' (*sattā*), because of its persistence across all things. (709)

Substance-ness and the like are called both "generality" and "particularity," because they serve as the cause for a cognition that persists across their own substrates and because they differentiate their own substrates from all things of different classes. (710)
Therefore, it is established that they alone are the causes of the cognition of exclusion.

In this regard, the universal (sāmānya) is of two kinds: the higher and the lower. The higher is called "Being" (sattā); and because it is the cause solely of the inclusive cognition (anuvṛttipratyaya) with respect to all three—substance, quality, and action—it is a universal alone and not a particular (viśeṣa).

Furthermore, there are [universals] characterized as "substance-ness," "action-ness," and so forth. Because they are the cause of the cognition of continuity among their own substrata, such as substances and the like, they are called "universals" (*sāmānya*). And because they serve as the cause for the cognition of exclusion from heterogeneous things by qualifying their own substrata, even while being universals, they are designated as "particulars" (*viśeṣa*). For instance, regarding this cognition of exclusion that arises with respect to qualities and so forth—such as "it is not a substance" or "it is without quality"—the causality for this belongs exclusively to these [universals] such as "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) and "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*), and to nothing else; for there exists no other [universal] such as "non-substance-ness" (*adravyatva*).

The point is that, due to the difference in perspective (*apekṣābheda*), the status of a single entity as both a universal (*sāmānya*) and a particular (*viśeṣa*) is by no means contradictory. 709–710.
He states the definition of particulars (*viśeṣa*): "Only particulars," and so forth;
however, some particulars are indeed the causes of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) alone.
Those ultimate particularities (*viśeṣas*) which reside in eternal substances have been described [above].

Some maintain that these are indeed only particulars and not universals (*sāmānyas*), because they are merely exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*); the meaning is that they are the cause solely of the cognition of exclusion.
To the question "What, then, are these?", he says: "eternal," and so forth.
And thus it has been stated: "Particularities (viśeṣas) are those that reside in eternal substances";
[the phrase] "residing in eternal substances" means...

Among the atoms, space, time, direction, self, and mind, [the qualities] are called "final" (*antyāḥ*) because they exist in these; for atoms constitute the limit of both the destruction and the origination of the world, while liberated selves and liberated minds represent the ultimate limit of *saṃsāra*. Thus, because they are most clearly perceived within them, they are said to be "final."
Furthermore, their occurrence is in all eternal substances, beginning with atoms;
for this very reason, they are called "ultimate" (antyāḥ) because they reside in eternal substances. Thus, both [terms] are employed.
In that regard, they are called "particularities" (viśeṣāḥ) because, by being the cause of mutually exclusive cognitions, they distinguish their own substrata from others.
Furthermore, from what source are these [atoms] established? To this he says: "By whose power," and so forth;
by whose power the cognitions of yogins arise regarding atoms and the like.
"This one is distinct from that one"—thus do people rely on each [object] individually. (713)

For just as in the case of people like us, a cognition regarding cows and the like—which is distinct from the cognition of horses and so forth—is observed to be caused by the configuration (*ākṛti*), quality (*guṇa*), action (*kriyā*), and conjunction of parts (*avayava-saṃyoga*), such as respectively: "it is a cow," "it is white," "it moves swiftly," "it has a thick hump," and "it has a large bell"; likewise, for yogins who are superior to us, since no other cause is possible, that power by which there arises in each [atom] a distinct cognition of the form "this is different from that" regarding eternal atoms that are identical in configuration, quality, and action, as well as liberated selves and internal organs (*manas*), and by which there arises the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) "this is that very same one" despite the distance of space and time—those ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*), whose existence is inferred from the specific cognitions of yogins, are thus established.
And these [universals], each residing in its respective substratum, are established for yogins through direct perception itself.
Now, as to how the universals (*jāti*) are established, he says: "Through direct perception," and so forth.
However, universals such as "existence" (sattva) and "cowness" (gotva) are established through direct perception,
because cognitions such as "existent" arise whenever the operation of the sense organs is present.
It is established that whatever arises following the positive and negative concomitance of something must arise from that very thing.

Furthermore, since the production of cognitions such as "existent" with respect to substances and so forth conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) residing within the sense organs, why should it not receive the designation of being "produced by the senses," just like other sensory cognitions? Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Demonstrating their existence through inference as well, he says: "By inference... and so forth.
Their existence is also understood through the power of inference, because the cognition of their specificities arises from another cause. (715) "The cognition of specificities" means...

The opponent considers the following to be a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason): "A cognition whose form is distinct from the entity such as substance (*dravya*) must arise from another cause; that is, its existence or production (*bhāva-utpāda*) is due to another cause. Whatever cognition has a form distinct from a given entity arises from another cause distinct from that entity, just as the cognition of 'red' and so forth regarding cloth, leather, or woolen blankets [arises from dyes etc.]. And this cognition of 'existent' (*sat*) and so forth regarding substances and the like is likewise. Thus he argues.

He demonstrates this very point regarding the purpose of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by presenting the arguments composed by Bhāvivikta and others, beginning with the words "In the case of cows and so forth":
"The specific cognitions of the words 'cow' and so forth [arise] with respect to cows, elephants, and so forth."
Words such as "cow" have as their objects entities distinct from the convention, the form, the individual, and so forth; for,

while they refer to cows and the like, they are different from the words and cognitions [denoting those conventions, etc.], just as in the case of the cognitions and words "with calf" and "with goad" applied to those very same animals.

The qualification [of the definition] and the statement of its essential nature are provided as an illustration by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), because there is deviation [from the definition] in the case of cognitions such as that of a hare's horn.
Furthermore, the cognition that persists across cows and other individuals is distinct from the individual bodies themselves.
Because it is a qualifier, it arises like the cognition of "blue" and so forth.

(719) Furthermore, "cowness" is a distinct entity from both the essence of the cow and the non-cow, because it is the object of a different cognition, just like color, touch, and so on; and because it is said to belong to that [cow], just as Caitra belongs to a horse. (720)

Regarding this, Bhāvivikta stated: "The specific designations and cognitions of 'cow' and so forth with respect to cows, horses, buffaloes, boars, elephants, and the like, are based on other causes that are associated with and conformable to a nature distinct from convention, configuration, the individual body (*piṇḍa*), and so on.

This is because, while having cows and the like as their objects, they are designations and cognitions distinct from the designations and cognitions of the nature of the individual body and so forth; just like the specific designations and cognitions such as 'the cow with its calf,' 'the buffalo burdened by a load,' 'the boar with a dart,' and 'the elephant with a goad' applied to those very same cows and others."
By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), it is established that the specific designations and cognitions regarding the nature of lumps of clay and so forth,
as well as those other causes, are "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like. In this context,
"designation" (*abhidhāna*) means the word (*śabda*), and "cognition" (*prajñāna*) means the conceptualization (*pratyaya*), which is to say, knowledge (*jñāna*).

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *samaya* means convention (*saṅketa*), *ākṛti* means configuration (*saṃsthāna*), *piṇḍa* means substance (*dravya*), and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth is intended. Those things whose own nature is distinct from these [convention, configuration, substance, etc. are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) corresponding to their respective designations and cognitions; those other causes which are related [to the object] are the "basis" (*nibandhana*) for them—this is the analytical explanation (*vigraha*). Alternatively, the analysis should be performed thus: they are both distinct from convention and so forth, and they are related to their own nature in accordance with the designations and cognitions such as "existent" (*sat*) and so on.
The remainder is as before;
"proclamation" is the formal declaration.

Because there is a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to cognitions such as "the horn of a hare," the qualification "while having the cow and so forth as its object" is added in order to avoid that.

The analysis of the compound is: "that whose nature (*tattva*) consists in those [cognitions] which possess designations and cognitions distinct from the designations and cognitions of the essential nature of the individual body (*piṇḍa*) and so forth.
By way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*), [the counter-examples] are the specific designations and cognitions of the essential nature of the individual body and so forth.
For in that case, since there is an absence of any other cause for the [cognition] apart from the individual body (*piṇḍa*) and so forth, the aforementioned reason is also absent.

However, Uddyotakara says: "The recurring cognition regarding cows and the like arises from a cause distinct from the individual body and so forth, because it is a qualifying cognition, like the cognition of blue and the like;

likewise, 'cowness' (*gotva*) is an entity different from the cow, because it is the object of a distinct cognition, like color, touch, and so forth; and because it is the object of a designation such as 'its,' just as one designates Caitra's horse as distinct from Caitra."
He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "In cows, etc.," which is easy to understand.
He refutes [the objection] with the verse beginning "asāram" (it is essence-less): "This effect is essence-less; it is merely a description of its process."
But no means of valid cognition exists here that makes that known.

For cognitions such as "existent" and so forth, which occur immediately after the functioning of the sense organs, are not established [as perceiving a universal]; rather, they arise from the application of linguistic convention.
Regarding the statement that because of the presence of the operation of the sense faculties, cognitions such as "existent" and so forth are dependent upon the sense faculties:

if the intended meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is "because they arise immediately after the operation of the sense faculties," then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), because [such cognitions] are mediated by the recollection of the application of linguistic conventions (*saṃketa*) and other factors, due to their being conceptual (*savikalpa*).

And it cannot be argued that, in the absence of a single underlying entity, how could entities whose natures are mutually exclusive serve—even indirectly—as the basis for a cognition of a non-differentiated form? Anticipating this objection, he says "just as," etc.:
"Just as [the use of] *dhātrī*, *abhaya*, and so forth, in the curing of various diseases..."
Power is perceived either individually or collectively, even though there is diversity among them.
There exists no single "universal" (sāmānya) possessing that power within them,
because the alleviation of disease is observed to vary according to distinctions such as being slow or quick.

There is no excellence whatsoever in a universal due to differences such as field and so forth, because it is eternal and uniform; however, such excellence exists in the case of earth and other substances.
Thus, even though there is absolute difference, some things possess restricted potencies.
They become the cause of a uniform conceptual cognition (*pratyavamarśa*) and so forth, and nothing else does.

For instance, just as myrobalan fruits (*āmalaka*) and the like—though their individual forms are mutually and utterly distinct—are each, whether individually or collectively, endowed with the capacity to dispel various kinds of diseases even without a recurring commonality (*anugāmin*); for it is not tenable to say that a universal (*sāmānya*) alone performs such purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) there, since no universal exists among them that is capable of accomplishing those diverse purposeful actions.

If that were the case, then this observed capacity of certain individuals—such as nurses and others—to pacify diseases quickly or slowly at certain times and places would not exist, because a universal is of a single uniform nature.
Nor is it logical to claim that the universal itself, having acquired excellence through specific refinements such as the field, milk, or irrigation, produces these diverse causal functions;
for since it is eternal and its modifications cannot be imparted by others, no excellence whatsoever can arise from differences in the field and so forth, owing to its uniform nature.

However, that excellence of impermanent things such as nurses and the like varies according to the differences in their substrates (kṣetra) and other factors; therefore, they alone possess the capacity to pacify diseases and so forth.

Consequently, other entities such as jars and the like will likewise—by virtue of arising from their own causes and conditions in such a manner—be by their very nature the causes for a uniform conceptual reflection (*pratyavamarśa*) and so on; thus there is no fault.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "uniform conceptual reflection and so forth," the inclusion of the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as holding water, is intended.

But how, then, is it established that these [words] are separated by convention, mental effort, and so forth? To this he says: "In the case of the word 'existent' (*sat*)," and so on, when there is the intention to express its utility for the mere effect.
An agreement is made regarding them, or according to one's own preference for another [object].
(727) For the purpose of employing various specific functions, such as carrying or milking, users establish linguistic conventions like the word "cow" and so forth. (728)
These cognitions of "existent" and so forth are observed to arise from the mental attention to those conventions, and not immediately after the operation of the sense faculties.
For if there were no production of cognitions such as "existent" for those who have not grasped the convention, otherwise, the establishment of conventions would be rendered useless.

Therefore, when those who establish conventions apply the verbal designation "existent" (*sat*) after having reflected upon that non-difference which is established solely by the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) as determined by a single uniform mental apprehension— [in that case, the cognition of "existent" and so forth arises] either with respect to that [capacity],
or else with respect to another [verbal designation],
namely the word "entity" (*vastu*).

In the same way, it should be understood that even from the specific hearing of words such as "cow," a convention (*saṃketa*) is established when there is a desire to know the specific capacities for carrying loads and so forth.

Consequently, at the time of usage following the establishment of the convention, even when cows and the like are perceived, there occurs first the mental application (*ābhoga*) of the previously made convention, then the recollection of that name, and subsequently the arising of the cognition of "existence" (*sat*) and so forth; this sequence is indeed clearly observed.
However, in some cases, due to extreme familiarity and the extremely rapid production of these stages, the sequence is not discerned.
However, those whose practice is sluggish do indeed perceive that [object] very clearly; thus he concludes:

"Therefore, because it is obstructed by the manifestation of the convention (*samaya*) and so forth, and because it does not arise directly, their status as perception (*pratyakṣatva*) is unestablished. Furthermore, it is not logical for that which arises through a mediated succession (*pāramparya*) to be considered perception, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, showing that because it is based on tradition (*smārta*), the cognition of "being" (*sat*) and so forth is improperly considered direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), like other traditional memories (*smṛti*), he says: "Without verbalization," and so forth.
First, consciousness indeed arises in a non-verbal form; from that comes the engagement with conventional symbols, and from that, memory; and from that, those [subsequent cognitions].

(730) Because a convention cannot be established for a specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), and because one conceptualizes after having seen [it], first of all, a cognition dependent on the sense organs arises which has the specific particular of the object as its domain and is devoid of association with verbal expression.

Thereafter, regarding that very object which has been perceived, there arise—immediately following that, and according to the occasion—cognitions such as "existent" and so forth, which have as their object the thing perceived and consist in the determination of it; since they express that very perceived object, how could these cognitions not attain the status of being memories?
For this reason also—as from the determination of what was perceived—[they are memories].
"Those" refers to the cognitions of existence and so forth.
But why is this sequence of the arising of cognitions not observed? To this he says: "Elsewhere," and so forth:
"For one whose mind has gone elsewhere, there is the perception of the mere object; from that very [perception], [the subsequent cognition] proceeds by means of the exclusion of all adjuncts. (731)

Since those cognitions of "existent" and so forth arise according to this sequence, for that very reason—in another case, when the mind has gone elsewhere toward a different object, and one sees an object situated before oneself with a distracted mind—the perception of the mere object devoid of all adjuncts occurs first, because the mental attention (manaskāra) toward the conventional designation of the object present before one has not yet arisen.

Otherwise, if every cognition were accompanied by verbal expression (*sābhijalpa*), how could one whose mind is directed elsewhere perceive the object situated before them as being empty of all adjuncts?
For two expressions are not experienced simultaneously at one and the same time;
thus, it is unestablished that [the cognition] directly follows the positive and negative concomitance residing in the sense organ.
Regarding what was stated there concerning "cows and so forth," he says: "In the case of the reason," and so on.

Even if the first [reason] is present, it is futile; for it is precisely intended that those [cognitions] are produced by the application of convention (*samaya*). That which is associated with them possesses positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). (732)

If it is being proved in general that these [cognitions] are based solely on some other cause that is a corresponding correlate (*anurūpa-saṃsargin*), then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For the very apprehension of the convention (*saṅketa*) regarding "cow" and so forth is the corresponding correlate for the cognition and designation of "cow" and so forth. To explain: when that [apprehension of the convention] exists, [the cognitions] occur, even when there is a mental attention (*manaskāra*) toward a different class; and when it does not exist, they do not occur.

Therefore, that alone is established as their cause, possessing positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), because they strictly follow its own positive and negative concomitance. Consequently, the effort of employing this logical reason is futile.
If that [example] were excluded from the subject class (pakṣa), the illustration would be devoid of the property to be proven (sādhya).
It is not so; for those causes, such as the goad and so forth, are directly like external things.

Indeed, there is no operation of designations or conceptual constructions regarding the "speaking of the wicked" (*khalabhaṇa*), for its entire nature transcends the range of speech; such is its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). (734) Now, if one includes this mental attention to convention within the very category [of the subject] and seeks to prove that these [conceptualizations] are based on a connection with a concomitant called a "universal" (*sāmānya*)—which is distinct from that [subject], eternal, unitary, and pervasive—then the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*); for a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with anything of such a kind has never been established.

Furthermore, these things such as the calf and the goad, which were described as being the causes for the naming and cognition of the cow and so forth, are not established as such causes. For those [particulars] that have attained their own specific nature (*svalakṣaṇa*) do not possess the capacity to be direct causes for naming and cognition, because the specific nature has a form that transcends the domain of all speech and conceptual construction. Therefore, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

Moreover, if one were to postulate causality through a mediated succession (*pāramparya*), it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since everything is present everywhere as a cause through some mediated sequence.
If this is so, how then does the world determine external things such as the goad and so forth to be the cause? To this he says: "Antarmātra... and so on.
"But they rely upon that which is conventional (sāṃvṛta), which has ascended to the level of the internal alone."
One engages with things such as a goad that are determined to be external forms.

Regarding this: first, it has been stated that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the substratum for the conventional designation (*prajñapti*) of a goad and so forth, is not touched by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*).

As for that which is conventional (*sāṃvṛta*), because its nature is fashioned by the artisan of imagination, it is established solely within the internal [mind] and is not external. However, due to the lack of discernment between the perceived object and the conceptual construction, people, regarding that form as if it were external, rush toward it as if it were an external entity. Therefore, the status of being an external form is not established for goads and the like.
The phrase "relying on the goad and so forth" is to be connected with the preceding [statement].
The meaning is that, relying on a conventional goad and so forth—which has ascended into the internal measure (antarmātrā) and is determined as an external form—one proceeds toward the external.
"Internal measure" refers to the intellect (buddhi).
And as for the qualification "provided that it has cows and so forth as its object," that too is entirely improper; showing that this is because there is nothing to be excluded, he says:
"The absence of activity, quality, and designation is also described as the reason," and so on.

The qualification "of the cognition of non-existence" is purposeless. (736) That too is incorrect; for if it were a cause, it would possess substantiality, and by virtue of its causal power, the cognition of non-existence would apply without distinction even to existence and other categories. (737)
Even though you describe the very absence of action, quality, and designation as the cause for the cognition of non-existence,
that too is incorrect; thus, [the following] is the explanation of why the absence of action and so forth cannot serve as a cause.

For instance—the capacity to produce an effect is precisely what is called "causality," and that capacity is necessarily grounded in a real entity (*vastu*), since being a real entity is defined by that very characteristic.

If even a non-entity (*abhāva*) were to be endowed with such a capacity, how could it not then attain the status of a real entity? Since being a real entity depends solely upon this [capacity], it would consequently abandon its very nature as a non-entity.
Furthermore, because non-existence consists in the departure from the intrinsic nature of a real entity—

if the absence of action, quality, and designation were the cause for the cognition of non-existence, then the cognition of non-existence would also apply to [the categories of] existence (*sattā*) and so forth, since there is no difference therein regarding the absence of action, quality, and designation, just as in the case of a rabbit's horn and the like. (736)
Showing that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "As for 'dissimilarity,' dissimilarity is unestablished, because there is the cognition of a mass, shape, and so forth."
Therefore, this reason is unestablished even for those who know that [the universal].

For in the cognitions of cows and so forth, there is no other object to be determined apart from the individual bodies and such, by virtue of which these cognitions would be distinct from the cognitions of those [individuals].
Demonstrating that the thesis is contradicted by inference, he says: "The inclusive cognition," and so forth.
"Because the inclusive cognition has the manifestation of individual words, whereas the universal is described as being devoid of the forms of phonemes, shapes, and syllables. (739)

This is what is meant: you seek to establish that for the following cognitions there exists a cause distinct from the individual [letters] and the like, which serves as their objective support (*ālambana*); however, this is untenable, because such a thing does not appear [in cognition], and because there appears instead something characterized differently, namely the phonemes, shapes, and so forth.

For instance: you describe the universal such as "cowness" (gotva) as being entirely devoid of color, shape, and the form of syllables; yet cognition is experienced as accompanied by the appearance of color and so forth. How, then, could its objective support (ālambana) be something devoid of color and the rest? For it is not logical that a cognition having one form should have an objective support of a different nature, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever cognition has the appearance of an object distinct from [another] does not apprehend that [other] object; for example, the cognition of sound does not apprehend form. And the continuous cognition (*anvayī pratyaya*) has the appearance of color (*varṇa*) and other qualities distinct from the universal (*jāti*). Thus, by the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), it is established that the word possesses the manifestation of both the individual sound (*śabdavyakti*) and the individual [object].

"Sound" refers to the designation such as "cow" and so forth; "individual" (*vyakti*) consists of color and shape; the manifestation of these two belongs to it, hence it is "possessing that" (*tadvān*).

Regarding the syllables—such as the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and *visarjanīya*—Śaṅkarasvāmin, however, has said: "Even universals such as 'blueness' (*nīlatva*) have the very form of blue and so forth; otherwise, there would be no recurring cognition in the form 'this is blue. Therefore, since the reason [adduced by the opponent] is unestablished (*asiddha*), there is no sublation by inference."
To this, he says: "Even if the universal... and so forth.
Even if the universal were of the nature of blue and so on, what difference would there be between it and a quality?
Furthermore, a single blue or other color is not perceived as something that persists [through multiple instances]. || 740 ||
If this [universal], though appearing, is not perceived through discrimination,
then how could the cognition and the word apply to the individual by its power?
(741) This cognition of the universal is indeed of a determinate nature, according to the opponents.
And since non-apprehension would otherwise result, it is logical that there is no lack of perception [of the universal].
This being the case, a distinction between qualities such as blue and the universals such as blueness would not be established, because there is no difference in their form.
It might be thought that a quality such as blue is not something that persists [as a universal].

But since a universal (sāmānya) is that which follows after individuals existing in different places and times, [the opponent] says that there is a difference in form: "And it is not unitary and pervasive," and so forth.
For no other [entity] distinct from qualities such as blue—a [universal] such as "blueness" (nīlatva) that follows after and is pervasive of the forms of blue and so on—is observed to appear;
this is because in direct perception (adhyakṣa), only a single, unique blue and so forth appears.

Nor does a second [quality], such as blueness and so forth, appear in the conceptualizing mind, because it determines (adhyavasāya) exactly what has been perceived [by the senses]. One might argue that this is just like your own [position]: just as momentariness, though appearing, is not discerned by the dull-witted through differentiation, so too is this universal. That too is incorrect.

Thus, what has been described—that by the power of perceiving that [universal], non-differentiated cognition and verbal expression arise even with respect to distinct individuals—is not tenable. For a cognition of the qualified object does not arise when the qualifier is not perceived; just as the notion "one who possesses a staff" (daṇḍin) does not occur when the staff is not perceived, so it would be in this case as well.
This is because you describe particulars as being, by their very nature, beyond the scope of words and cognitions.

Furthermore, how can a cognizer who apprehends those various particulars—whose bodies are by nature excluded from the objects of cognition and verbal expression—by the power of perceiving a commonality, not be considered a perceiver of that very [commonality]?

Moreover, it is appropriate for one for whom perception is exclusively non-conceptual to say that "even though it appears, it is not perceived," because perception is defined as the operation of a determinate cognition (*niścaya*). But for you, whose position is that all perception is indeed conceptual, such non-perception is untenable, as it would entail the consequence of total non-apprehension.

For this indeed is the comprehension of their own objects by determinations: namely, that very act of determining them. If they do not determine [the object], it follows that they do not apprehend it at all.

Even if one were to grant the establishment of a distinct entity other than blue and so forth, your desired conclusion would not be established, because the object you intend to prove is sublated by inference, and thus the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished. Demonstrating this, he says: "Even if [it is] established," and so on:
"Even if it is established that there is another cause, the universal (*sāmānya*) is not established."
It follows [the object] as one, and it is distinct from non-duration because of its sequential arising.
"Distinct from non-duration" means distinct from impermanence; that is to say, it is permanent.
Why is it not established? [The answer is: because they arise sequentially;
the remainder of the sentence is "of the denotations and cognitions of 'cow' and so forth.

For if these were caused by such a universal property (*sāmānya-dharma*), then they would not arise sequentially; rather, since their causes would be complete, they would arise simultaneously, like multiple objects that arise at once.
For that which cannot be assisted by others has no dependence whatsoever.
Now, having granted the establishment of the reason, he states the deviation [of the reason] with the words: "the word *padārtha*."
What other cause does the word "padārtha" (category) depend upon among the six [categories],
such that the cognition "it exists" persists even with respect to existence (*sattā*) and the others?
For there is no further property called "padārthatva" (categoriness) within the six categories by virtue of which the recurring cognition "this is a category, this is a category" could occur.

Likewise, existence (*sattā*) does not reside in universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), or inherence (*samavāya*), such that there would be a cognition of "it exists" regarding them; for existence is established only in substances (*dravya*), qualities (*guṇa*), and motions (*karman*).

Since it is the position of our opponents that the designation [of "existence"] regarding substances and so forth is based solely on the universal, no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is alleged on that account.

It might be argued that even in that case, there exists the property of being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends existence and so forth; therefore, this designation here too is caused by something else, and thus there is indeed no deviation. To this he says: "If [the cognition] is caused by another property," and so on: "If the cognition of 'existence' in that case were also caused by another property, then, because of the consequence of an infinite regress due to that other property also requiring a cause, it would follow that there is no subject (dharmin) at all. (745)
Therefore, this reason is held by them to be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*);
nor has its pervasion (*vyāpti*) been established through a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāra*).

Even if it were admitted that [the cognition] is caused by another property (*dharma*), the fault of inconclusiveness remains exactly as it was; for even in that case, there exists the notion of "existence" regarding this property, namely: "there is a real property."
In that case as well, if another property were admitted, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress;

furthermore, since those other properties would also serve as the substrata for yet other properties, they too would necessarily become subjects (*dharmin*). Consequently, the restriction to the number six—that only six categories are subjects—would no longer hold.

Now, if, out of fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), one does not resort to another property (*dharmāntara*), then the reason (*hetu*) would be rendered inconclusive (*vyabhicāritā*) by those cognitions which operate upon these objects or upon properties such as existence (*sattā*). Or, even if its inconclusiveness due to being too common (*sādhāraṇānaikāntikatā*) were avoided, by what means would its "doubtful negative concomitance" (*saṃdigdhavyatirekitā*) be refuted? To this he says: "And not because of a universal application," etc. "Universal application" (*sarvopasaṃhāra*) refers to the demonstration of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the probandum across all subjects (*dharmī*).

It might be argued that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed appropriate here; for in the absence of another cause, how could the difference between the cognitions of those objects be established? Indeed, there is no difference among many cognitions even when they have a single object. If such a difference were to exist, then even the cognitions of color, taste, and so forth would not be established as having distinct objects, because the determination of a difference in objects is produced by the difference in cognitions.
But this too is incorrect.

Indeed, it is not logically tenable from the perspective of ultimate reality that a cognition of a universal has the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity as its object, because a cognition permeated by verbal expression does not take the specific characteristic as its object. Rather, since there is an exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of that single entity from this and that [other thing], conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and denoters (*vācaka*)—which are of manifold varieties—proceed with respect to that entity by way of the experience of that entity, according to the habituation of convention, even in the absence of a universal. If this were so, what contradiction would there be? It is for this reason that the lack of pervasion (*vyāptyabhāva*) is stated.
Regarding what was stated, namely that [the universal] "subsists" in cows and so forth, he says: "Immediately after that," and so on.

Immediately following that, the proof for [the existence of] a universal (sāmānya) which was proposed by this very [opponent] has been refuted by this same [argument]. In that case, [objections such as] the establishment of what is already accepted (iṣṭasiddhi) and so forth apply equally. "By this same" means by the very refutation of the reason just mentioned.
In that case as well, the fault is equal;
for in this instance too, the [alleged] establishment of the desired conclusion and so forth are identical.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the lack of the probandum in the example, the unestablished nature of the reason, its deviation, and so on are included.
He states another form of deviation as well: "In the case of cooks and so forth," etc.;
that is, in the case of cooks and so forth, a specific cognition arises.
Furthermore, the cognition of non-existence regarding non-existent things would not occur without a single underlying common factor (anugāmin).

Therefore, because of these aforementioned cases— such as forms created by mere desire, or those that have perished or not yet arisen— the reason [proffered] is inconclusive (anaikāntika) with respect to all of them.
For in those cases, there is no single, recurring cause—such as "cook-ness" or "reader-ness"—by which the recurring cognition "cook," "reader," and so forth could arise.

Likewise, regarding the four types of non-existence, such as prior non-existence and the rest, how could there be a recurring cognition of "non-existence, non-existence"? For even here, there is no universal (sāmānya), because a universal must reside in a real entity (vastu).

Furthermore, in the case of figures like Candrāpīḍa created by the power of imagination, or white palaces and the like constructed in the sky, or in those who have perished or not yet been born, such as Mahāsammata, Śaṅkha, and others—how could the cognition [of them] occur without a single recurring factor?
For even there, no universal exists, because it depends upon the individual instance.
With the words "not in the case of cooks, etc. and so forth, he establishes the cognition regarding cooks and the like:

"There is no basis whatsoever for the cognitions of 'cook' and so on; if it is argued that there is action [as the basis], then surely that action differs with each individual, just as [the individuals] do. (750)

If there were no persisting entity (anvayin) among distinct things, a persisting cognition would not be logical; therefore, a single universal (sāmānya) that conforms to all individuals is accepted. Furthermore, if a cause is postulated that is devoid of any connection to action (karma), [it is untenable].
In that case, why are the individual instances themselves not accepted as its causes?
Furthermore, the cognition of "cook" and so forth would not occur with respect to one whose action has ceased;
for the opponents do not accept that the action is always present there, just as they do not accept the universal (jāti) to be so.
If the cognition and the term "cook" and so forth are applied to those individuals by taking past or future action as the basis, that is not a valid reason, because [the action] is non-existent.
For it is not tenable to say that the cognition regarding cooks and the like is based on their action.

Since you also admit that this action is distinct for each individual—on the grounds that a recurring cognition (*anvayī pratyaya*) is not possible among distinct things without a single unifying factor—you postulate a universal (*sāmānya*) that pervades all individuals.

If, however, an action could be the cause of a non-different designation and cognition even while being devoid of such recurrence (*anvaya*), then why this aversion toward individuals? Why reject them and instead postulate a universal as the cause of that [cognition]?

Furthermore, if the cognition [of "cook" and so forth] regarding cooks and the like were based on action, then the cognition "cook" would not occur in one who has ceased acting and is not currently performing cooking.
For you do not accept that action is always present—like a universal (jāti)—such that the cognition would persist even when the action has stopped.

Indeed, whatever is based on something cannot exist in the absence of that thing; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga), whereby everything would be based on everything.

Nor is it logical that past or future karma should be the basis for its conditions, because that which is past and so forth does not exist, and it is impossible for what is non-existent to function as a cause. 750–751.

Śaṅkarasvāmī said: "The recurring cognition of 'cook' and so forth arises from the connection with an action that is linked to the genus of that action; therefore, even when the action has ceased, the cognition of 'cook' and so forth is to be understood as resulting from the indication of the permanent cause by means of that action. He demonstrates this [with the verse beginning] "If [the cognition is] due to the connection with an action... and so on: "If the cognition [of 'cook'] were due to the connection with an action related to the genus of action-ness (kriyātvajāti)..."
"And even when the action has perished, [the cognition occurs] because of the perception of the constant cause by means of that [action].
(755) "By that" refers to the action.
The genus "action-ness" (kriyātva-jāti) is the permanent cause;
[the author] refutes this with the words beginning with "na tu" (but not).
But when the action has perished, even if it were characterized there, that eternal genus which is to be grasped does not exist, because it has ceased from its own substratum.
Its own substratum is the action; [for] the genus "action-ness" is that very action itself.

For there is no apprehension or persistence of a universal (jāti) in isolation from the apprehension of its substratum, because that would entail the consequence of it being non-dependent. It might be argued: "Since the universal has been characterized at one time, even when the action has ceased, the cognition based upon it continues to function with respect to its substratum. To this, he says: "The staff," and so forth.

For indeed, the cognition of "one who possesses a staff" (daṇḍin) and so forth does not occur with respect to those individuals belonging to the class of staff-bearers and the like at a time when they are separated from that staff.
(757) Even so, there exists another universal (jāti), namely "cook-ness" (pācakatva) and the like.
Even in the case of a newly born [entity], there would arise the cognition of "cook" and so forth due to that connection; otherwise, it would be like the cognition of "existent" and so on.
If you say that [the quality] is inherent, then it would not exist there even later, as there is no difference [in the circumstances].

Because of the deficiency in the nature of that which is connected to them, this inherence (*samavāya*) does not exist between those two; likewise, how could it exist later when there is identity (*tādātmya*)?

For if it were so, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for even when Devadatta and others have abandoned their staffs, the cognition "he has a staff" or "he has an earring" would not occur simply because the class of staffs and so forth was perceived at one time.

Nor is it correct to claim that a universal such as "cook-ness" (pācakatva-jāti) exists here [in the newborn] as well; for since the universal would already be present even in one just born, the cognition of him as a "cook" and so forth would necessarily follow.

It might be argued: "Just as the cognition 'it exists'—though based on the universal of existence (sattā)—does not occur at all times, so too the universal, though inhering in a particular substrate, will not occur at all times. Therefore, in the state of being just born, the universal will simply not inhere.
[The term] "inhering" is illustrative; it should be understood that [the universal] is likewise not manifested.

If that were the case, then that [universal] would never be inherent in it; for instance—first of all, because of the deficiency in the nature of being related to those two, namely the universal and the substance, there is no inherence of the universal; and even later, since that deficiency remains exactly as it was, how could it be inherent? For, according to your view, the substance is not momentary, such that it might subsequently become qualified in that way.
"Inhering in those two" refers to the genus and the substance.
Regarding "identity" (tādātmya): it refers to the state where the previous form characterized by defects has not been abandoned.
Furthermore, showing that there is a fault even if one accepts that the substance is impermanent, he says: "If indeed," and so forth.
If indeed the individual manifestation (vyakti), being unstable, were to acquire excellence, then the deficient nature of the universal (jāti) would never cease. (761)

If it is argued that while an individual (*vyakti*) acquires excellence later due to its instability, the universal (*jāti*), being stable, possesses a nature that is not deficient in its inherence (*samavāya*) even after [the production of the individual], just as it did before—how then could it ever truly inhere [in a new individual] later?

Nor can it be said that the universal exists at all times with a nature that is non-deficient in its inherence in a substance that comes into existence at a later time; for if that were so, it would follow that the substance itself is eternal, since the universal, whose very nature is connected to it, would exist eternally.
Indeed, in the absence of a second related entity, it is not logical for there to be a non-deficiency in the nature of being connected to that [entity].
With the words "cooking and so forth," etc., he anticipates the rebuttal formulated by Uddyotakara:
"And cooking and such actions are considered to have a primary instrument (sādhana)."
Regarding the phrase "the cook and so forth," that predominance exists even among other cooks.
For he [the opponent] says: "This is said because of a failure to understand the meaning of the reason:
just as words such as 'cook' are recurring (anuvṛtta) yet there is no universal (sāmānya) called 'cook-ness,' so too are there recurring cognitions with respect to cows and the like."

The meaning of the reason "because specific cognitions are not without cause" is that a cognition distinct from the cognition of the individual object arises from another cause; it does not mean, however, that every inclusive cognition (anuvṛttipratyaya) arises solely from a universal (sāmānya).

This being so, that which is the primary instrument (*sādhana*) for the action of cooking is denoted by the word "cook" (*pācaka*); and since this primacy exists even in another cook, there is no fault [in the application of the term].
He refutes this with the passage beginning "This so-called predominance," etc.:
"What indeed is this so-called predominance? It is not power, because of the lack of logical connection."
For this very reason, neither substance, action, quality, nor selfhood can be postulated [as the universal].
What is this so-called "predominance"? If it is power (*śakti*), that is incorrect, because power is restricted to each respective substratum and thus lacks connection with other individuals.
Nor is it the essence or intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of substances and the like; for independence (*svātantrya*) likewise lacks such connection.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), a desired property (*dharma*) distinct from the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) is understood.

Furthermore, regarding the statement that "production [occurs] from another cause," which was said to have this meaning, it has already been refuted: if one proves in a general sense that "there exists some other cause," there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the application of convention (*saṅketamanaptkāra*) is accepted as being the cause. However, if [the cause] is specified, there is a lack of positive concomitance (*anvayavaikalya*) and deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to cognitions such as "cook" (*pācaka*).

He concludes with the verse beginning with "tad" (that): "The cognition regarding [terms] such as 'cook' consists in determining a mere form that is distinguished from what is heterogeneous to it, and it depends upon various linguistic conventions. (764)
Therefore, words and cognitions do not function toward a distinction [of objects] except according to convention, unless there is a single underlying [entity] that persists.
That is to say: for that reason, since no other cause can be discerned, the cognitions of "cook" and so forth would not be possible [if such an entity did not exist].

Therefore, even with respect to distinct objects such as cooks, there arises a conceptual cognition (*śemuṣī*)—an intellect—in the form "cook, cook," which, according to convention, determines a mere object excluded from those of a different class; this occurs because the exclusion of the dissimilar is present everywhere.

For this very reason, even in the case of cows and so forth, cognitions and words will function according to convention to determine a non-different form, even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*); thus, the logical reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
With the words "And likewise," and so forth, [the author] establishes that there is a cognition of non-existence regarding non-existence.

And thus, the cognition of non-existence is not contradictory in the case of non-existent things, nor is a recurring verbal expression contradictory, because both follow from the application of a convention for that which lacks [real] referents.

For this alone is the pervasive basis of a universal cognition, namely, the mental engagement with a convention; otherwise, by what means would the recurring cognition and verbal expression "non-existence" in the case of non-existent things not be contradictory? Indeed, there is no genus (*jāti*) here, because a genus must inhere in a real entity.
Regarding the question "Why is there no contradiction?", he states the reason: "Because those two follow from a convention regarding an object that does not exist.

That convention in which an object such as a genus (*jāti*) and so forth is non-existent is described as such; because of the following—that is, the concomitance (*anvaya*)—of those two, namely sound and cognition (or word and cognition), this means that they conform to the presence and absence of the mere convention.
With the words "of the jar," etc., [the author] anticipates the response of Śaṅkarasvāmin:
"This is the prior non-existence of the jar; this is the destruction of the jar."
The intellect perceives only those entities that have that [form] as their limiting adjunct (upādhi).
If it is argued that its recurrence everywhere is due solely to the universal residing in the adjuncts, this is not so, because there is a difference [in nature] based on their respective substrata.
The cognition "jar" and so forth is logically consistent as being inclusive of those [particulars],
but the notion that "this is non-existence" is of a different character;
for a cognition such as "cow" or "horse" is not held to arise by virtue of [an underlying] existence (*sattā*).
"A single universal must be postulated as the basis for the uniformity of all means of proof.

For he [the opponent] says: "Indeed, among those absences, no cognitions are observed that are devoid of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). What then? Everywhere, a cognition of absence—such as 'the prior absence of the jar' or 'the posterior absence of the jar'—depends upon absences that have a real entity as their limiting adjunct.
Therefore, in every case, the recurrence of that cognition is due solely to the universal residing in the limiting adjunct; thus, there is no deviation [in the logical reason]."
The connection [of the word] "tasyāḥ" (of that) is with "dhiyaḥ" (of the cognition), because it is the subject under discussion;
he refutes this with the words beginning "naivam" (not so).

The analysis of the compound is "that which is accompanied by dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) and is not based on that" (*atadāśraya*); or it may be a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*).
The meaning is that [the objection] is in no way tenable, both because of the dissimilarity and because of the lack of basis in that.

Regarding that, he provides a detailed justification for the phrase "due to their distinctness" (*vailakṣaṇyāt*), beginning with "the jar," and so forth: Cognitions of different forms cannot be based on a single limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), because if all common effects were accomplished by that one alone, it would follow that the postulation of multiple universals (*sāmānya*) is useless. Therefore, let cognitions such as "jar" arise by virtue of universals such as "jarness" (*ghaṭatva*); but how could cognitions such as "non-existence," which are utterly distinct from those, be reasonably based upon them? For a cognition of "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like does not arise by virtue of [the universal] "existence" (*sattā*).

But Bhāvivikta says: "It is not accepted that in every case the cognition conforms to its cause; for instance, the number 'plurality' inherent in elephants, horses, dhava trees, khadira trees, and so forth, is the cause of the cognitions of 'army,' 'forest,' and the like; whereas the conjunction of heterogeneous substances is the cause of the cognitions of 'beverage,' 'sour gruel,' and so forth. Otherwise, there would arise the cognition: 'many [things] are conjoined.'"
Having raised this objection with the words "If that [cognition] is not according to its cause" and so forth, he provides the rebuttal with the words "If it were so" and so forth:
"If cognition in all cases is not held to correspond to its cause, then for cognitions such as 'army' and the like, number and so forth must be accepted as the basis. (771)
If this is so, why is this cognition— which follows the manifestation of distinctions established by conventions fashioned by desire— not accepted as being directed toward these very particulars?
(772) "This" refers to...
The cognition of a universal is the convention; its distinction is the particular.

"What, then, is the excellence here by virtue of which this is said? To this he replies: "When there is knowledge of difference... and so forth; for it is when there is knowledge of difference that there arises the desire to establish a convention. From that...
Her production is from that, her hearing is from that, her enjoyment is from that, and her cognition is from that.
(773) Through both positive and negative concomitance, this alone is determined to be the efficient cause; regarding other [causes], there would be an infinite regress. (774)

The causal relation is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance; and that [relation] is ascertained with respect to the cognition of a universal, which consists merely in the application of a convention fashioned by intention.

To explain: first of all, an experiential cognition (*anubhava-jñāna*) arises whose object is a particularity (*bheda*). Once that has arisen, the desire to establish a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) is born. From that desire follows the performance—that is, the making—of that convention. Then, at the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), there occurs the hearing—that is, the audition—of that very [word]. Following this hearing, there arises a mental application (*ābhoga*) directed toward the object of the convention as it was heard. And from that mental application, through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of those very particulars, the cognition "this is a jar" and so forth comes into being, because of the resulting engagement with those particulars.
From the cowherds down to the common folk, it is determined that only these many factors are the causes of this cognition;

however, if one were to postulate a universal (*sāmānya*) whose causal capacity is unobserved as a cause, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For even after postulating that [universal], why should another factor not also be postulated, since it is equal in having its capacity unobserved?
In that very context, he states the reinforcement:
"For [only] a corresponding associate would exist," and so forth; thus, there is the postulation of another purpose.
But regarding the distinctness of cognitions, this much alone is better accepted:
for in this case, it is better to postulate a restriction of capacity, which is established through positive and negative concomitance among those whose powers are known.

For instance, while you were determining a cause called an "objective support" (ālambana) corresponding to universal cognitions (*sāmānyabuddhi*), you postulated a universal for a multitude of distinct individuals. If even that postulated universal produces cognitions of other forms, then this much alone would be better: namely, that only that which has been described as having a perceived efficacy should be postulated.
For in this way, the postulation of an unperceived object would not have been made.

Furthermore, when asked how a non-different universal can produce distinct cognitions, one must necessarily say this: that there is a specific restriction of power (*śakti-pratiniyama*) among entities such that even a single thing is capable of generating cognitions of multiple forms.

If this is so, then rather than postulating a regulating power for the universal, one should simply postulate it for the particulars themselves—since their powers are already known and their capacities are certain;
for in this way, one would not be acting in contradiction to experience.

It might be argued that the causal capacity of the universal (sāmānya) is also certainly established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka); to this he says: "anvaya... and so forth.
Furthermore, positive concomitance (anvaya) is not found in universals because they never exist;
nor is negative concomitance (vyatireka) possible for eternal entities.
(777) Since cognitions such as "always existing" never arise [in relation to them], it is not logical that these [cognitions] should follow the positive concomitance residing in them.

For if these [particulars] were to conform to the universal, then, since the universal exists at all times, why would they not exist at all times? Indeed, the universal has no dependence on anything else, because it cannot have any particularity imparted to it by others; therefore, these [particulars] do not conform to the positive concomitance residing in that [universal].

Nor do these [cognitions] conform to its negative concomitance (*vyatirekānuvidhāna*); for instance, when these cognitions such as "existent" (*sat*) do not arise, one cannot say that the absence of the universal (*sāmānya*) is the cause there, because since eternal things persist at all times, their negative concomitance is impossible.
