For, in the ultimate sense, it is the thing (*vastu*) alone that is grasped by words and cognitions; therefore, because the nature of a thing is directly communicated by words through affirmation and negation, the view of those who maintain that the meaning of a word is an affirmation (*vidhi*) is that affirmation alone is the word-meaning.
For the proponents of Apoha, however, there is in reality no objective nature of things that constitutes the denotation of words;

for every verbal cognition is indeed erroneous, since it functions by determining a non-differentiated form with respect to objects that are actually distinct. Yet, where there is an indirect connection with a real entity, there is correspondence with the object despite the cognition's error—such is their view.

In this regard, that non-different form which is superimposed upon objects by the conceptualizing intellect is called "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoḍha*) because it arises through the force of experiencing objects as excluded from others, because it manifests itself as being excluded from others, because it is determined as one with the object excluded from others by those who are deluded, and because its fruit is the comprehension of an object excluded from others.
Thus, it is well known that exclusion (*apoha*) is the meaning of a word.
To this, the proponents of positive affirmation (*vidhivādin*) raise an objection:

If, for you, the adjuncts—namely substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence—which serve as qualifiers and causes for verbal cognition, do not exist in reality, then how is it that in the world there proceed designations and cognitions such as "the man with a staff," which are caused by adjuncts such as substance and the rest?

For instance: in common worldly usage, the cognition and verbal expression "one with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) or "one with horns" (*viṣāṇī*) are well known to have substance (*dravya*) as their limiting adjunct (*upādhi*); "white" or "black" have quality (*guṇa*) as their adjunct; "he moves" or "he wanders" have action (*karman*) as their cause; "it exists" or "it is found" have existence (*sattā*) as the basis for their application; "cow," "horse," or "elephant" have genus and species (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*) as their adjuncts; and "the cloth is here in these threads" occurs by virtue of inherence (*samavāya*).
Therefore, in the absence of these [categories] such as substance and the rest, the cognitions and verbal expressions such as "one with a staff" would be without an object.
The word "etc. (*ādi*) is connected to each [of the preceding examples].
By that [term], there is the inclusion of each individual cognition and verbal expression belonging to the same class, such as "umbrella-bearing" or "horned";
however, the ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣas*) are perceivable by yogins alone, and thus they are not included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).
Furthermore, these two [the universal and the particular] cannot be without a cause, because it would follow that they would function everywhere, at all times, and without distinction.
Furthermore, there is no occurrence of these two without distinction;

therefore, the opponent's formal argument is as follows: "Substance and the rest exist, because their occurrences are mutually unmixed. Whatever has mutually unmixed occurrences is based on a real cause, just like the cognitions of the ear and other senses; and the word-cognitions such as 'the man with a staff' (daṇḍin) have unmixed occurrences. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

The subverting proof [against the opponent's position] is that if there were signlessness (animittatva) without distinction in all cases, it would follow as an undesirable consequence that [cognition] would arise everywhere.
He provides the following rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said":
"It is said that there is no object whatsoever for these cognitions and verbal expressions; rather, the seed residing within the internal dimension alone is their basis. (869)

In this regard, if it is intended to prove that these [cognitions] possess a cause (*sanimittatva*) primarily by means of an external object that serves as their objective domain (*viṣaya*), then the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because there is no subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the opposite of the thesis.
Alternatively, if it is intended that they possess a cause by virtue of some cause whatsoever, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

For we indeed accept that the awakening of the latent impressions of internal discourse (*antarjalpa-vāsanā*) is their cause; however, it is not an objective domain, because the preceding verbal cognition, being erroneous, lacks an objective domain.
"Residing within the measure" means residing in consciousness; that is to say, it refers to the latent impression (*vāsanā*).
Corroborating this very point with scripture, he says: "Of whatever [word]," and so forth.
For whatever object is expressed by whichever word, that [object] is not found [to exist as such]; for that is indeed the true nature (*dharmatā*) of things. (870)
"Whichever object"—
whether it be a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), a universal (*sāmānya*), or the like— that indeed is the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
That is *prakṛti*—that is to say, the fact that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things transcends all paths of speech, as it has been said:
"By whatever name each phenomenon is expressed, that [phenomenon] is not found therein; for that is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena."

If it is asked, "What is the proof for the fact that verbal cognition is erroneous and lacks a real object? we have already stated the proof here: because it functions by determining non-difference among things that are actually different, this entire verbal cognition is erroneous.

For instance, whatever cognition takes one thing to be what it is not is erroneous, such as the cognition of water in a mirage; and this verbal cognition likewise determines non-difference among objects that are distinct. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, this [cognition] does not have a real entity as its object in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*), by virtue of which the reason [of the argument] might be considered unestablished (*asiddha*); for that [universal] has already been refuted at length. Or, let there be a universal; even so, if it were an entity distinct from the particulars (*bheda*), then the determination of non-difference among things that are different would be nothing but an illusion. For it is not logical that things should be identical through something else [distinct from them]; they could only be said to "possess" it [the universal]. Even if the universal were not a distinct entity, then in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) the entire universe would be a single entity alone, and thus the cognition of a universal therein would be nothing but an illusion.
A cognition of a universal does not have a single real entity as its object, because such a cognition is preceded by the apprehension of differences;
and once its erroneous nature is established, its lack of an objective referent is also established,
since there is no object that imparts its own form to the cognition and thereby satisfies the definition of an objective support (*ālambana*).
Alternatively—their lack of an object is established in another way:
for that alone which is the conventionally agreed-upon referent of words is their proper object, and nothing else, because [otherwise] there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
And since no convention exists for these [words] with respect to any real entity (*vastu*) in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), it follows that cognitions and words are without objects.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which have not had a convention established for them in relation to a particular object do not, in the ultimate sense, denote that object; just as, for example, the word "horse" does not denote an individual possessing a dewlap and so forth when no convention has been established for it. And all words have not had conventions established for them in relation to every object.
This is because the property of being a denoter is pervaded by the property of having a convention established, and that [pervading property] is absent here.
Furthermore, this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Demonstrating this, he says: "Since," and so forth.

For the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the universal (*jāti*), its connection (*tadyoga*), the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*), as well as the form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*), do not truly fit the meaning of a word in reality. (871) For instance, when an object for which a convention has been grasped is established as the meaning of a word, there are these alternatives: is it established as the particular characteristic, or the universal, or its connection—that is, the relation with that universal—or the possessor of the universal, or the form of the cognition of the referent? These are the conceptual options.
In that regard, since the occurrence of conventions is impossible in all [entities], the statement "in reality" indicates that he does not negate conventional word-meanings; therefore,
there is no contradiction with his own words.
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with one's own statement in the thesis;
for it is impossible to demonstrate that these things, such as the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), are not the referents of words without first communicating them by means of words.

And by demonstrating the particular characteristic and so forth through words with the desire to communicate that [fact], one would necessarily be admitting that they are indeed the referents of words.
Furthermore, since that very same [position] is negated by its own proposition (*pratijñā*), there is a contradiction with one’s own words (*svavacanavyāghāta*).

By this, what was stated by Uddyotakara—that if words were non-expressive, there would be a contradiction between the proposition and the reason—is also refuted. For we do not deny the existence of word-meanings altogether, as that is recognized even by cowherds; rather, what is negated is the property of "reality" (*tāttvikatva*) which is superimposed upon them by others.
But it is not so for the substratum (dharmin).

Regarding that, since the impossibility of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has already been demonstrated, he states "In that [case]," and so forth, in order to establish that it is not the referent of words.

In that regard, first of all, the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not communicated by words, because it lacks continuity across the time of the convention, the time of usage, and the time of attainment.
"It is not communicated by words" means:
The meaning is that there is an absence of convention (*saṅketa*) therein.

To the question "How is there an absence of convention?", he says: "By the absence of pervasion," and so forth; because of the separation from the pervasion—that is, the encompassing—of that time which is obtained or reached through convention and linguistic usage.
The ellipsis "there is no convention regarding that particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) is to be supplied.

This is what is meant: a convention is indeed established for the sake of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), not out of mere whim. Therefore, it is only with respect to that which possesses the quality of pervading the time of both the convention and its subsequent usage that a convention is appropriate for speakers, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, a particular characteristic does not possess the quality of pervading the time of both the convention and its subsequent usage.
Therefore, there is no convention regarding that [particular].
Why, then, is it impossible for a particular (svalakṣaṇa) to pervade the time of the convention and the time of practical usage? To this he says: "The natures of the individuals," and so forth.
These [particulars], whose nature is that of individuals, do not follow one another in their mutual form,
due to differences in place, time, action, capacity, appearance, and so forth. Therefore, the object perceived at the time of the convention is not seen during practical usage.
Nor can one who has not grasped the convention [be awakened] by a word, as in the case of others.

For specific individuals such as brindled cows (*sāvaleyādayaḥ*) have forms that are mutually and absolutely excluded from one another due to differences in location and so forth; these do not interpenetrate one another.
Therefore, for a person who has established a linguistic convention regarding one [individual], there would be no practical usage (*vyavahāra*) with respect to others.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "reflection and so forth," there is the inclusion of color, shape, specific states, and the like.

The point is that since no conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is observed [in those cases], there is an absence of linguistic convention (*samaya*) regarding them; therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
And showing that there is no lack of certainty (anaikāntikatva), he says: "Nor [is it] unapprehended," and so forth.
That in which a convention (*saṅketa*) has been apprehended is "thus"; one in whom a convention has not been apprehended is "unapprehended-conventional" (*agṛhītasaṅketa*), meaning "as if other."
From the word "dhvani," meaning "like an object of a different class."
This is what is meant: if a word were to convey an object for which no convention has been established, then even the word "cow" would convey a horse,
and the act of establishing conventions would be rendered purposeless.
Therefore, the occurrence of an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and thus the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.

This very reason—*because it has not been established by convention* (*akṛtasamayatvāt*)—was indicated by the Master Dignāga in the statement: "A genus-word (*jātiśabda*) is not the denoter of particulars (*bheda*), because of their infinity (*ānantya*).
For by the phrase "because of their infinity," the impossibility of establishing a convention is precisely demonstrated.

By this, what was stated by Uddyotakara—"If you take words as the subject (*pakṣa*), then because 'infinitude' (*ānantya*) is a property of real entities (*vastudharma*), the reason is misplaced (*vyadhikaraṇa*);

if, on the other hand, only the particulars (*bheda*) are made the subject, then there is no example possessing either positive or negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and thus infinitude is not a valid reason"—is refuted. Furthermore, he himself said: "This fault applies to one for whom particulars are denoted by words without qualifications; but for us, substances, qualities, and actions are denoted as qualified by existence (*sattā*) and so forth."
For instance: wherever one perceives a universal such as "existence" (sattā) and so forth, there one employs a word such as "existent" (sat);

and since the universal such as existence is indeed one and the same, it is possible to establish a linguistic convention (*samaya*) regarding the particulars characterized by that universal; therefore, infinity [of particulars] is not an obstacle.
This is incorrect, for it has already been established that a real entity (*vastubhūta*) such as existence, whether distinct or non-distinct from those particulars, does not exist.

Or, let there be a universal; even so, since multiple universals can coexist within a single particular, the application of words such as "existent" (*sat*) and so forth would not serve to distinguish them without confusion.
Furthermore, the author of the convention (*samayakāra*) would not be able to indicate particulars by means of existence and so forth without first presenting existence and the rest through language;
nor is there any application of words like "existence" to things for which no convention has been established.
Consequently, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

Even if it were argued that the cognizer himself, through the observation of linguistic usage and by means of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), understands the convention (*samaya*) for words such as "existent" and so forth—
that too is incorrect.
For no one perceives a linguistic usage that encompasses every particular without exception;

and if it is argued that— having perceived a repeated usage with respect to particulars possessing existence and so forth on one occasion— one comes to apply that same designation even to unperceived members of that class, we say no,
because they have not been perceived.
For a convention is not possible regarding infinite particulars that are unperceived and divided by the distinctions of past and future, because this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
If it is argued that one indeed understands them by grasping them through a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*),
then it follows that the application of words has as its object only those things superimposed by conceptual construction, and not particulars in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*).

For since the past and the future are non-existent and thus not present, the conceptual cognition arising with respect to them is entirely without an object; as it has been stated, they are therefore simply non-existent. Consequently, how could a convention established therein be a real entity in the ultimate sense? Enough of this prolixity. Since the reason exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory; thus it is established that words do not have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object.

It might be argued that for entities such as the Himalayas and so forth, because they possess a stable and uniform nature, no distinction based on differences of place, time, and so on is possible; therefore, since they pervade the time of the convention and its subsequent usage, a linguistic convention (*samaya*) is possible with respect to them. Consequently, the reason [adduced] would be unestablished with respect to one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddhatā*). To this, he says: "The Himalayas and so forth," etc.
Even those things such as the Himalayas and so forth, which appear to be non-different in terms of space, time, and other attributes— in them, atoms have been proven to be distinct and momentary.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), mountains like Malaya and others are included.
For these [entities] have the nature of being an accumulation of many atoms; therefore, there is no convention that encompasses all their parts.

Furthermore, since it has been established that they perish immediately after arising, there is no persistence of the nature observed at the time of the convention during the times of practical usage (*vyavahāra*). Thus, the reason (*hetu*) is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

Thus far, it has been demonstrated that a convention (samaya) is impossible because linguistic usage is untenable with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which would lead to the consequence of the convention being useless.
Now, demonstrating that it is impossible precisely because it cannot be produced, he says: "It is impossible," and so forth.
It is impossible to conceive of a convention for this [object], whether it has arisen or not yet arisen.
A convention regarding what has not yet arisen is not tenable as something real, like a horse's horn.
Nor is it possible when [the object] has arisen, because of the recollection of words previously grasped.

How indeed can a convention (*samaya*) be made there when [the object] has long since passed? (877) All entities have been previously established as perishing immediately after their arising; regarding these, a convention being made would have to be made either for those that have not yet arisen or for those that have already arisen. In that regard, first of all, a convention is not logically tenable for things that have not yet arisen, because, being non-existent, they lack the characteristics of any description whatsoever and thus cannot function as a substratum.
The inclusion of the term "real" (bhāvika) is for the purpose of excluding conventional [entities].

Therefore, even in the case of a son or the like who has not yet been born, there is no contradiction with what is perceived, because such [conventional entities] have as their object things constructed by conceptualization (vikalpa) and are thus unreal,
like a horse's horn.

The suffix *vati* is not applied to a word ending in the locative case (*saptamyanta*), nor is it logical for a convention (*samaya*) to be established regarding what has already arisen. To explain: when that [object] has been perceived, and when the recollection of its distinct name—which is preceded by that perception—has occurred, then the convention must be made, and not otherwise, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Consequently, at the time of recollecting the distinct name, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has long since ceased due to its momentary destruction. Thus, just as with something unborn, no real convention exists even regarding what has been born, because both [the object and the name] are absent at the time the convention is being formed.

For instance, even at the time of the experience itself, the particular (svalakṣaṇa), being momentary, does not possess a present existence by virtue of being the cause of that [experience]; how much less, then, will it exist at the time when the recollection arises—following after the experience—which consists in the enjoyment of non-difference?

Now, it might be argued: "An agreement will be made at a moment occurring at the time of the formal act, which is of that same class and produced by the power of its capacity. To this, he says: "And whoever else," and so forth;
"and whoever else [is] of that same class [produced] by the power of that [capacity] at that time..."
In that case, there is no mental application (*ābhoga*) toward the convention, nor is similarity conceptualized.

(878) Even though at the time of establishing a convention another moment exists in proximity, nevertheless, because mental application toward it is impossible, a convention is not tenable. For no one, while establishing a convention after perceiving a horse and beginning with the recollection of its name, would apply the convention "horse" to a cow or other animal present at that time which has not been made an object of mental application.

Now, it might be argued: "Since there is similarity among all the unique characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of moments, one will establish a convention by determining them as a unity. To this he says: "And similarity is conceptualized.

For similarity is indeed superimposed by a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpabuddhi*); and when that [similarity] is communicated by means of words, the unique characteristic itself would remain inexpressible.
Thus, in this way, the establishment of a convention regarding the unique characteristic is not possible.

Nor can it be the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the sound itself; for the author of the convention applies a distinct name to the object only as it is presented by memory, and memory is not able to present an expression exactly as it was experienced in reality, because that [original experience] has long since ceased.

Furthermore, there is no memory regarding that which one currently utters, because it was not previously experienced; nor is it possible for memory to present what has not been made an object of its own cognition.

Therefore, that which is established by memory and being synthesized is, by virtue of being constructed by conceptualization (*vikalpa*), nothing but a non-particular (*asvalakṣaṇa*); thus, there can be no convention (*samaya*) regarding a particular.
Consequently, it is established that the particular is inexpressible (*avyapadeśya*).

Right here, in order to establish that the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible, he states another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): "The cognition of heat and so forth, which arises from the sounds of names and the like, does not appear clearly, just like the sensory cognition of those [very] objects. (879)

For just as the sensory cognition whose object is a thing such as heat is experienced with a clear manifestation, it is not so [experienced] when arising from words such as "heat. Indeed, those whose eyes, tongues, or noses are impaired do not experience the color, taste, and so forth of a citron or similar fruit upon hearing the word for it, in the way that those with unimpaired eyes and other senses experience them through sensory cognition.
As it has been said: "The one who is burned perceives the burning from contact with fire in one way;
the meaning of 'burning' is manifested by the word 'burning' in another way."

Thus, "like the sensory cognition of that object" (*tadarthendriyabuddhivat*) is the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); the analysis of the compound is: "that which has that object, and it is a sensory cognition."

Even if that [external object] does not exist in that manner, why then would the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the word not be its object? To this he says: "It is not its," and so forth—"It is not a fitting connection for that word, nor is it produced by it."

When a cognition exists, an object appears; just as when there is a cognition of form, taste [does not appear]. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which does not manifest in a cognition produced by something is not the object of that [cognition], just as taste is not [the object] in a cognition produced by form. And the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not manifest in a verbal cognition; this is a non-apprehension of the establishing factor (*sthāpakānupalabdhi*).
Here, the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) is the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

For instance—the capacity of a word to generate a cognition having that [object] as its content is alone called its "denotative power" (vācakatva), and nothing else. Furthermore, it is not logical for a cognition to have a certain object as its content if it is devoid of that object's form, because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Nor does a single entity possess two forms, such as a distinct and an indistinct one, by which it could be said that words denote the very indistinct form inherent in the object itself.
Because duality is contradictory in a single entity, and because it establishes mutually contradictory natures for those existing at different times;
however, the Naiyāyikas state that the referent of a word (*padārtha*) consists of the individual (*vyakti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), and the genus (*jāti*).

The meaning of a word is *padārtha*, which is to say the meaning of a term (*śabdārtha*). In this context, by the term "individual" (*vyakti*), substances, qualities, and specific actions are denoted; thus, the Sūtra states: "An individual is that which is the substratum of specific qualities and is corporeal."

The meaning of this is stated first according to the opinion of the author of the Vārttika: that which is distinguished is a "distinction" (*viśeṣa*). A distinction from qualities is a "quality-distinction" (*guṇaviśe�ṣa*), by which action is denoted. Furthermore, the term *guṇaviśeṣa* is presented here using the grammatical device of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of two identical words); thus, the category of quality (*guṇapadārtha*) is grasped. These qualities are also distinctions, hence they are "quality-distinctions. The inclusion of the word "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) is for the purpose of excluding generic form (*ākṛti*).

For instance, the configuration (*ākṛti*) is a particular kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) by its very nature, and conjunction is included within the category of quality (*guṇa*). Consequently, if the term "particular" (*viśeṣa*) were not employed, the configuration would also be apprehended [by the word "substance"];
however, its inclusion within the individual (*vyakti*) is not intended, because it is mentioned separately as a distinct term.
By the term "substratum" (*āśraya*), a substance (*dravya*) is denoted; the meaning is that the substance is the substratum of those specific qualities—that which serves as their locus.

In the Sūtra, the instruction is given by omitting the word *tat* (that); the analysis (*vigraha*) should be made as follows: "particular qualities" (*guṇaviśeṣāḥ*) means particular qualities and particular qualities [repeated]; "the substratum of those particular qualities" (*guṇaviśeṣāśrayaḥ*) means particular qualities and their substratum. This is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*), and the neuter gender is used because gender depends upon worldly convention.
Therefore, the meaning is this: that which is the substratum of particular qualities is called both "individual" (*vyakti*) and "form" (*mūrti*).

In this context, when the word *mūrti* refers to a substance (*dravya*), it should be understood as having its derivation based on the locus (*adhikaraṇasādhana*); [thus,] "that in which the parts coalesce" is *mūrti*. But when it refers to qualities such as color (*rūpa*) and so forth, it has its derivation based on the agent (*kartṛsādhana*); [thus,] "those which coalesce—that is, inhere—in the substance," namely color and the rest, are *mūrti*.

However, the word *vyakti*, when referring to a substance, has its derivation based on the object (*karmasādhana*), whereas when referring to color and the rest, it has its derivation based on the instrument (*karaṇasādhana*).

According to the opinion of the author of the Bhāṣya, however, the meaning of the sūtra as it is heard is this: it is his view that substance alone is the substratum of specific qualities, and it is the individual (*vyakti*) and the corporeal form (*mūrti*).

As it has been stated: "That substance is the substratum, as the case may be, of specific qualities such as color, taste, smell, touch, gravity, fluidity, density, and mental impressions, as well as of non-pervasive specific dimensions; it is called 'corporeal' (*mūrti*) because its parts are congealed (*mūrcchita*).
By the word "form" (*ākṛti*), the conjunction of the limbs of living beings, such as the hands and so forth, and their further parts, such as the fingers and so forth, is denoted.
And so says the Sūtra: "The configuration (ākṛti) is that which expresses the genus and its marks.

The commentary on this states: "One should know that configuration by which the genus and the marks of the genus are expressed; and that [configuration] is nothing other than the fixed arrangement (vyūha) of the parts of individual beings and of their various component parts. By the word "arrangement" (vyūha), a particular kind of conjunction (saṃyoga-viśeṣa) is meant.
By the inclusion of the term "fixed" (*niyata*), artificial conjunctions are excluded.

In this context, the "marks of the genus" (*jāti-liṅga*) are the limbs of living beings, such as the head, hands, and so forth; for by means of these, the genus characterized as "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like is indicated.
However, sometimes the genus is manifested directly through the configuration (*ākṛti*); that is, when cowness is manifested upon seeing the specific arrangement of the head, hands, and other parts.

Sometimes it refers to the class-characteristics (*jāti-liṅga*): when the universal such as "cowness" (*gotva*) is manifested by individual parts such as horns, whose own constituent arrangements are revealed, then the configuration (*ākṛti*) serves to manifest that universal and its characteristics.
By the term "universal" (*jāti*), that entity called a "commonality" (*sāmānya*) is expressed, which is the cause for the production of a single denotation and cognition through a single word.
And thus the Sūtra states: "A genus (*jāti*) consists in the production of a common [cognition]"; the meaning is that a genus is the cause for the arising of a common cognition.

In this regard, showing that by this very same [argument] used to refute the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as the referent of a word, the status of both the individual (*vyakti*) and the configuration (*ākṛti*) as the referent of a word must also be understood as refuted, he says: "By this very [method]," and so forth;
by this very method, there is the refutation of the individual and the configuration.
Since others also maintain that even for those two [the universal and the particular], it is precisely their nature as specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is intended;
the intention is that the refutation of the "universal" (*jāti*) will come later,
which is why it is called "refutation."
The phrase "as the referent of a word" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
He asks, "Why? and says: "Because they consist of nothing but specific individualities (svalakṣaṇa)," and so forth;
[the word] "of those two" refers to the word and its referent.

The meaning is this: since no linguistic convention (*samaya*) has been established for the particular (*vyakti*), the configuration (*ākṛti*), or the unique characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), they are all equally not the referents of words; therefore, the reason "because no convention has been established" is neither unestablished (*asiddha*) nor inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore—individuality (*vyakti*) is characterized by substance, quality, particularity, and action, while form (*ākṛti*) consists of conjunction; and since these [categories], such as substance and the rest, have already been refuted, he demonstrates that for this reason as well, it is not tenable for these two to be the referents of words due to their non-existence: "Since the refutation of substance and so forth, as well as their conjunctions, has already been stated, the establishment of those two as the referents of words is not ultimately valid. (882)

Having thus established the impossibility of linguistic convention (*samaya*) with respect to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), he now states the following, establishing the impossibility of convention with respect to the three [categories] beginning with the universal (*jāti*): "Because the universal and the relation have already been refuted at length previously, the other three types of word-meanings are not postulated as being immediate. (883)

The meaning is as follows: "immediate" refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); the universal (*jāti*) is that which is associated with it, and the possessor of the universal (*jātimat*) is that which possesses that association. Since both the universal and its association are absent, the possessor of the universal is likewise impossible, because its designation is produced by those two, and the possessor is essentially identical to the specific characteristic; thus, the fault inherent in that position remains exactly the same.
Kātyāyana [holds] that the meaning of a word is the universal (*jāti*); Vyāḍi [holds] it is the substance (*dravya*); and Pāṇini [holds] it is both.

But even this is refuted by the very same [argument], because the universal is untenable and the substance consists of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), such that the faults inherent in those respective positions do not cease.

Summing up, he says: "Regarding that which is called the 'referent' (padārtha) consisting of the individual, the configuration, and the genus, that is impossible, because all of them are devoid of intrinsic nature (nīrūpatā). (884)
"Therefore" means "for that reason," [namely] "the absence of form."
The absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatā),
the form of cognition, and that which resides within cognition do not follow after an external object or another cognition.
Furthermore, that [mental image] which does not produce the intended object cannot truly be said to be the [referent].

For the form of the cognition exists in identity with the cognition itself; thus, like the nature of that cognition, it does not follow after another cognition or the object to be communicated. Consequently, because it does not persist through the time of the convention, the time of usage, and the time of attainment, no linguistic agreement (*samaya*) is possible there either, just as in the case of the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*). Or, even if it were to persist through the time of usage, it would still not be logical for users to establish a linguistic agreement regarding it.

For instance—thinking, "Perhaps a person seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), having recognized from this word objects capable of purposeful action, will engage with them," speakers apply denotative terms; it is not out of mere whim. And this form of conceptual cognition (*vikalpabuddhyākāra*) is not able to accomplish for its seeker the intended effect, such as the removal of cold, because even when that experience arises, the [external object] is absent.
Therefore, since there is no linguistic convention (*samaya*) regarding that [conceptual form], the reason—"because no convention has been made"—is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

It might be argued: "There are other word-meanings such as 'existence' (astitva) and so forth; therefore, since a convention (*samaya*) is possible regarding those, the reason is simply unestablished (*asiddha*). To this he says:
"Those others who explain the word-meaning otherwise than [the threefold division]," and so on—that is, those others who propound word-meanings such as 'existence' and so forth in a different manner.
They too have already been refuted by these [arguments]; nevertheless, it is stated again:
"by these" means by the refutations of the referents of words such as "specific characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth.
The meaning is that these are included within the specific characteristics (svalakṣaṇa) and so forth.
To show what those meanings of "is" (astyartha) and so on are, he says: "The meaning of 'is'... and so forth.

"The meaning 'it exists' (astyartha) is the defining characteristic of that which is to be conveyed by all words; they say this is common to words such as 'cow' and those like 'the unseen force' (apūrva), 'deity' (devatā), and 'heaven' (svarga). The word "iti" is displaced in its sequence and is connected immediately after "astyartha";
thus, the meaning is as follows: that which is perceived as the meaning "it exists" is the defining characteristic of the signified object (pratyāyya) of all words.

The meaning is as follows: "The definition of the word-meaning" refers to that which is signified by words such as "cow" when objects like cows are the referents; they say that this is equal to *apūrva*, the deity, and heaven—that is, they say it is equal to the word-meanings of *apūrva* and so forth.

For just as words such as "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) do not instill any specific form of an object within cognitions—wherein only this much is understood, namely, that there exist certain objects to which words like "unprecedented" are applied—so too is it the same with words like "cow" whose referents are perceived;
for from them also, one understands only this: "there exists some object denoted by the word 'cow' or the like, which is connected with the universal *gotva* (cowness).
As for the apprehension of a specific form that arises for some people in that regard, that occurs due to the force of their own philosophical tenets.
Showing the meanings of words included by the word "etcetera" (ādi), he says: "The aggregate," and so forth:
"Either the aggregate is the denoted object, or it is a collection without conceptual differentiation."
Or rather, some maintain that the referent of a word is a non-existent association (saṃsarga).

Some say that words such as "Brāhmaṇa" denote a collection of austerity, birth, learning, and so forth, without the use of either disjunction (vikalpa) or conjunction (samuccaya), just as words such as "forest" denote dhava trees and others. For instance, when "forest" is uttered, there is no cognition through disjunction such as "is it a dhava, or a khadira, or a palāśa? nor is there a cognition through conjunction such as "it is a dhava, and a khadira, and a palāśa. Rather, the dhava trees and others are cognized collectively.
Similarly, when the word "brāhmaṇa" is uttered, there arises no cognition of either austerity (*tapas*), caste (*jāti*), or learning (*śruta*), nor of "austerity, caste, and learning" individually;
rather, austerity and the others are perceived as a collective whole, distinguished from other related entities.

In that context, *vikalpa* (option) is the determination of one specific member among many non-restricted members of a collection; whereas *samuccaya* (conjunction) is the determination of the distinct natures of several restricted factors being simultaneously connected to a single [subject].
That for which both conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) and synthesis (*samuccaya*) do not exist is described as such.

Others, however, maintain that the relation of substances and so forth with respect to forms not determined by [categories] such as "substanceness" (*dravyatva*) is the word-meaning; and because that relation is unreal due to the unreality of its relata as word-meanings, it is called "unreal.
Alternatively, because austerity, learning, and so forth appear as a unity like the color black (*mecakavarṇa*), their mutual connection is itself unreal.
For these [atoms], whether individually or collectively, are not perceived in their own form; rather, like a firebrand-wheel (*alātacakra*), their aggregate appears having transcended its own nature.
Thus, that which is real despite having unreal adjuncts (*upādhi*) is the basis for verbal designation.
Or rather, the word itself, having attained the state of being expressed (*abhijalpatva*), becomes the denotable object (*vācyatā*).
Others, however, say: "That which is real despite having unreal adjuncts (*upādhi*) is the meaning of a word.

In that regard, the unreal adjuncts—the particularities such as bracelets, rings, and so forth—which belong to that reality, namely the universal essence of gold and the like which persists through all its differences—that reality is what has unreal adjuncts.
"Based on words" means that which serves as the ground for the application of a word, i.e., the denotable object;
others, however, say that the word itself, having attained the state of conceptual representation (*abhijalpa*), is the meaning of the word.
Regarding this, he asks: "What is this 'discursive talk' (abhijalpa)? and says:
"When, through the connection 'this is that,' the form [of the object] is unified... and so forth.

They call that sound "abhijalpa" when it is [unified] with its object. (890) The settling of the object within the word—namely, the connection "the word itself is the object" or "this is that"—is the basis for this; therefore, when the form of the word becomes unified with the object, they call that word, which has assumed the form of the object, "abhijalpa.

Others, however, maintain that the meaning of a word is the very form mounted upon the intellect, which has an external object as its domain, is grasped as an external object, and is manifested as having the nature of the intellect. He demonstrates this [with the verse beginning] "Or else," and so forth:
"Or else, that object which is the domain of the intellect, based upon an external thing, and which is known as an 'external thing'—this is held by some to be the meaning of a word. (891)
"An object of cognition" means revolving within the cognition; that is to say, residing in the cognition,
being based on an external object.

That which has for its basis an external object— whether existent or non-existent— that serves as a support like a written sign or mark, and which proceeds to manifest its own nature, is "based on an external object.
This means that it arises in the form of a cognition known as "this is an external object," and is subsequently determined as being external.

For instance: as long as the form of the cognition, which has not yet been projected onto external objects, is apprehended through the contemplation of its true nature as being merely the form of cognition itself, so long its status as the meaning of a word is not determined. This is because there is an absence of connection with any specific action;

for actions such as "bring the cow" or "eat the fuel-cake" are not possible in respect to such a purely mental form. And since it is an object capable of connection with action that is denoted by words, that [form] apprehended as the mere form of cognition is not the meaning of a word.

But when it is projected onto an external object, then the cognizer, being mistaken regarding its externality, conceives of that [mental form] as having the capacity to accomplish an action; thus, it becomes the meaning of the word.

Now, what is the distinction between this view and the position of the proponent of *apoha*? For even by the proponent of *apoha*, it is indeed stated that the form of the cognition, grasped as having an external nature, is the meaning of the word—as it has been said: "Furthermore, because there is the apprehension of the exclusion of others through the attribution of that [external] form."

The claim that "the meaning of a word is the object, and that [object] is indeed the same [as the mental form]" is not contradictory; however, this is not so, because this proponent of the theory of the mental form (buddhyākāravādin) maintains that the meaning of a word is, in the ultimate sense, the mental form— which is non-erroneous with respect to the external object, possesses an objective referent, and is superimposed upon substances and other categories that are ultimately real.

Now, [the opponent] maintains that [cognition] is without a real object (*nirālambana*), erroneous because it functions by determining non-difference among things that are actually different, and that it is based upon mutual difference (*itarētara-bheda*). However, if one accepts what we say— that "all this false appearance is the apprehension of objects as having a single nature,
and its seed is mutual difference, for which purpose the designation exists"— then [our position holds].
Thus, in that case, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established;
and as he will say later: "If its seed is mutual difference, then this is our position."

Furthermore, for the proponent of apoha (*apohavādin*), nothing whatsoever is accepted as the denotatum of words from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), whether it be the form of a cognition (*buddhyākāra*) or something else.

For instance, that alone which appears in a verbal cognition (*śābda-pratyaya*) by way of being determined (*vyavasīyamāna*) is the meaning of a word; and the form of a cognition is not determined by a verbal cognition. What then? It is only the external object (*bāhya-vastu*), which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākārin*).

Nor is an external object determined by that [cognition] in terms of ultimate reality, because it is not determined according to its true nature, and because it is not the true nature according to how it is determined;
therefore, the referent of a word is merely superimposed.
And that which is superimposed is nothing at all; thus, nothing is denoted by words in terms of actual existence.
Furthermore, as for what was said—that "the meaning of a word is that very object"—this refers only to an object superimposed [upon consciousness].
However, for the proponent of the form of cognition (*buddhyākāravādin*), it is the form of cognition itself that is intended as the ultimate denotable object; thus, there is a great difference.

But others say that, due to habituation, a word is a cause for intuition (*pratibhā*) and not a conveyor of external objects; he demonstrates this [point] with the verse beginning "due to habituation":
"In brief, every word is a cause for intuition through habituation, just as it conveys meaning to children and to animals. (892)
The repeated observation of a word's application toward a particular object is *abhyāsa* (repetition).
*Pratibhā* (intuition) is the wisdom conducive to the comprehension of an action as delimited by its specific means;
it is produced by a word accompanied by the repeated observation of its usage.
That [understanding] differs for every sentence and for every person;
however, because that division of it is immeasurable due to the infinity of linguistic usage, it cannot be fully formulated. Therefore, he says: "And for children and for animals," and so forth.
For just as the striking with a goad and other such actions become causes for intuition (*pratibhā*) when they are performed for the sake of making elephants and others understand a meaning.

Likewise, all words such as "tree" and so forth, which are accepted as having referents, become causes for the synthesis of mere intuition (pratibhā) according to habituation, but they do not directly convey an external object; for otherwise, how could the various conflicting scriptural traditions and literary compositions of invented stories manifest distinct categories of objects constructed by one's own conceptualization?

He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "In that regard" (tatra): "In that case, is this denotable object 'existent' intended to be the particular (svalakṣaṇa), or a universal (jāti), or a connection (yoga), or something else, or perhaps a reflection (pratibimbaka) of the cognition? (893)

These aforementioned defects apply even when the mere sense of "existence" (asty-artha) is what is to be expressed; in that case, linguistic usage based on differentiation is not possible. (894) If the sense of "existence" is held to have the nature of the previously mentioned specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) and so forth, [then the aforementioned faults follow].
In that case, the previously mentioned fault would follow;

furthermore, because the meaning of the word "exists" has an undetermined specific form, if only that were conveyed by words, there would be no conventional usage based on distinctions such as "cow," "gavaya," or "elephant," since those distinctions would not be conveyed by the words.

With the words "gotva" and so forth, [the author] anticipates the opponent's reply: "It would arise from the cognition of the mere existence of the object as qualified by the word 'cowness' (*gotva*)."
"But that [distinction] is due to the non-apprehension of differences such as 'horn-shaped' or 'blue' and so forth.

(Verse 895) This might be argued: "Because the mere existence of an object qualified by the word and the universal 'cowness'—devoid of distinctions such as being brindled—is understood from the word 'cow,' there will be a linguistic usage based on that distinction."

If this is so, then how can it be maintained that the meaning of a word is the mere existence [of an object], given that specific particulars such as "cow" and so forth are indeed what are being communicated? Anticipating this objection, the opponent offers a rebuttal: "Because specific features such as horns are not manifested—that is, are not cognized—from the word," it was said, "there is some object that is communicated. However, there is no fault [in our position], because it is not the case that the qualifiers *gotva* (cowness) and so forth are not cognized by the words *gotva* and so forth.
He replies with the words "But surely in this way," and so forth:

"But surely, in this case, there would be the denotation of both the object possessing those [qualities] and of the differences; and if that were so, the fault already mentioned would apply there, yet no other object is perceived. (896)
If it is held that what is expressed is the mere object qualified by "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth, then the denotation of the object as possessing that [universal] would have to be admitted.
In that case, since the universal and its inherence (*samavāya*) have been refuted, the object possessing it is impossible; thus the previously mentioned fault remains.

Furthermore, because the object possessing that [universal] consists of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), the same difficulties as before necessarily follow: the impossibility of establishing a linguistic convention (*asaṃketatva*), the lack of communicability (*avyavahāryatva*), and the consequence of an indistinct appearance (*aspaṣṭāvabhāsa*).
If it is argued that there exists an object distinct from the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, he says: "No other object exists and is perceived.
When examined, no object distinct from the particular characteristic and so forth enters the range of the intellect.
He states the fault in the position that [the word] denotes a collection: "Even in the denotation of a collection," and so forth.
Even in the denotation of a collection, the denotation of distinct universals (jāti) is evident, because austerity, genus, action, and so on, are denoted in their totality. || 897 ||

In the position that the word denotes the aggregate (*samudāya*), it is even more clearly admitted that there is a denotation of both the universal (*jāti*) and the particulars (*bheda*), such as austerity (*tapas*) and so forth; thus, all the defects that arise in the position of denoting each individual [member] occur simultaneously in the case of denoting the aggregate.
Regarding the two positions beginning with "or even if they are unreal" (*asatyo vāpi*), he states the defect: "nirdhāritā... and so forth.

However, the relation of substances and so forth, whose own natures have been determined, occurs through conjunction (*yoga*); and as for that universal (*sāmānya*) which is real, it was already refuted previously [in verse 897],
because the meaning of a word is untenable in the form of particulars, universals, and so on.
It is not logical for the form of a word to be unified with its object. This verbal discourse exists only within the mind due to the distinction between the external [object] and its connection;
therefore, what difference is there between this and the immediately preceding position that cognition consists of discrete moments?
The view that the form of cognition (*buddhyākāra*) is the meaning of a word has already been refuted, because that which is non-different from cognition lacks pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*).

This is because, as previously established in the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*), [the relation] characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*) was rejected; and because, in the examination of the Sāṅkhya, a real universal (*sāmānya*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇa*) that is non-different [from its substratum] was rejected, while even a universal that is different [from its substratum] was refuted in the examination of the six categories. Therefore, neither an unreal conjunction nor an unreal universal based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) can be the denotable object.

Regarding the position of *abhijalpa* (conceptual identification), he says: if some object of a word were possible, then there might be an identification with it; however, since it has already been established that an object of a word in the form of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth is impossible, how could there be an identification with that? Furthermore, this *abhijalpa* exists only within the intellect—for instance, because a difference between external word and object is established through their being grasped by different sense organs and so forth, any real unification of the two is indeed improper. Therefore, the unification is logical only for the word and object existing within the intellect, due to their residing in a single cognition.

For it is thus: the essence of the word (*śabdātmā*), having assumed the form of the referent (*abhidheyākāra*) while its own verbal nature has vanished, revolving within the intellect (*buddhi*), internalizes the object through its division according to its own inherent form; this is called "internal discourse" (*abhijalpa*).
And it is logical that this is merely a form residing within the intellect itself, not something external, because the external [object] is by all means of a nature entirely distinct from it.
Consequently, what difference is there between this and the previously mentioned position regarding the meaning of the word as being the intellect? None at all.
In both cases, the meaning is strictly Buddhist;
however, this much alone differs: that the word and its object are identified as one.
But the fault remains exactly the same: how can that which is non-different from cognition proceed to become a separate object?
He demonstrates that very point with the words beginning "Even the form of the cognition," etc.
900–901 He states the fault in the position that [the meaning] is produced by intuition (pratibhā):

Furthermore, if intuition (*pratibhā*)— which is also a word-meaning— has external objects as its domain, how could there be diverse intuitions regarding an external object that is fixed in a single nature? (902) Or, if these [intuitions] are without an object because they exist merely as mental impressions (*vāsanā*), [then...]
How could there be either practice or activity regarding external objects?

(903) If you maintain that [cognition] occurs with respect to its own form through the mental resolve (*adhimokṣa*) upon an external appearance, then it follows that the object of a word is unreal, because one acts [toward it] through delusion. (904)
Nor is it logical that it [cognition] be seedless, for that would lead to an over-extension in all cases.
If you claim that its seed is the mutual difference [between objects], then this is our own position.

(905) If intuition were, in the ultimate sense, directed toward external objects, then diverse intuitions could not arise among those who abide by conflicting conventions regarding a single object, such as sound, because it is impossible for a single thing to possess multiple natures.

If, then, [words] have no objects, it would follow that activity and comprehension regarding an object do not occur, because the word does not have that as its object. Alternatively, if those activities and comprehensions occur through an error consisting in the determination of an object within one's own internal reflection—which is not the actual object—then it follows that the meaning of a word is erroneous. Furthermore, the seed or cause of that error must be stated; otherwise, if an error were to arise without a seed, it would occur everywhere and at all times.

If, on the other hand, the very mutual difference between entities is accepted as the seed of this [cognition], then you are merely proving our own position; thus, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
904–905 Now, he states a refutation that applies equally to all these positions, beginning with "yadi vā" (or if...).

Alternatively, if all of this were momentary, or if it were not so [i.e., not momentary], then in the case of momentariness there would be no connection (*anvaya*), and sequential cognition would not otherwise be possible. (906) Is all of this—the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the universal (*jāti*), and so forth—momentary or non-momentary? Regarding that, in the first position, because there is no possibility of the connection at the time of linguistic usage of what was perceived at the time of the convention, there can be no linguistic agreement (*samaya*) with respect to that.

Furthermore, in the case of non-momentariness, since there can be no successive existence from what is not successive, it would follow that there is an absence of successive cognition regarding the objects of words;
"otherwise" means in the case of non-momentariness.
906 But others say: "The word leads one to infer the intention to speak the meaning," as it has been stated: "Inference of the intention to speak does not exist apart from the word."
To this, he says: "By this very [argument]," and so forth.
By this very [reasoning], the intention [of the speaker] (*vivakṣā*) is also refuted as being cognizable through words;
for if the meaning of a word is impossible, where could such an intention be, and where could there be an audition [of the word]? (907)

If it is maintained that ultimate intention (*vivakṣā*) pertains to objects that are ultimately real word-meanings, that is unestablished; for no word-meaning whatsoever, such as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), is possible.

Therefore, there is no ultimate intention regarding any object, because a recurring object (*anvayin artha*) does not exist, nor is there any word that expresses it. Thus he says: "Or where is the scripture? (*kva vā śrutiḥ*).

The Śruti [states]: "Sound is [intended] in the sense of 'intention to speak' (vivakṣā), not in the sense of 'that which is to be conveyed' (pratipādyā). It follows that the operation of the Śruti toward an external object distinct from the sound does not occur, because it has not been so enjoined, just like any other unrelated meaning."

Now, if it is thought that there is a similarity between the object such as form (*rūpa*) which revolves within the speaker’s intention and the external object, and that because of this similarity, activity toward the unexpressed external object will occur—as in the case of twins—then he says: "How could there be activity [of the word] toward what is not expressed by the word, on account of similarity?
(sārūpyācca). How indeed can there be an operation of the hearing [of the word] toward that which is not denoted?
By this, [the view that the word] has a name such as "similarity" (*sārūpya*) and so forth is refuted.

This being the case, activity toward the external object would never be possible; for even when a word is uttered that refers to something else intended by the speaker—as in the case of twins—activity might occur [toward the wrong object].

Even the Vaibhāṣika who maintains that there is a dissociated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*) called "name" (*nāman*), which has sound as its object, and which is called a "sign" (*nimitta*) in the form of a mark of the object—that too should be seen as refuted by this very [argument].

For instance: if that name and so forth were momentary (*kṣaṇika*), then there would be no logical connection (*anvaya*); if it were non-momentary (*akṣaṇikatva*), there would be the impossibility of successive cognitions; and there would follow the consequence of an absence of activity toward external objects. Furthermore, because of the lack of similarity (*sārūpya*), [the cognition] would not occur at all times. Thus, every refutation stated above applies entirely and without exception. Or rather, [it is refuted] "by this"—[meaning] by what was just said.

According to the possibility [of refutation], by means of the critique of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, it should likewise be stated here: "For the nature of names and the like, which does not partake of anything else, cannot be the object of convention; thus, for that which is non-existent (*asat*), expressibility is in no way possible."
Thus,
as stated in verse 908: "If words illuminate an object that has merely ascended into the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), it would follow that they do not apply to external reality."
Anticipating an objection from the opponent here, he says:
"If [it is argued that] the activity of one who determines an external object as having a form conjoined with the intention to speak (and inference), then that is simply our own position again. (909)

The intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) resides in the continuum of the speaker, and the inference of that very intention occurs in the continuum of the listener. Thus, "connected with those two"—meaning linked to the intention and its inference—is the sense of "appearing as that. For the speaker and the listener, who determine that form as being external, activity toward an external object will occur here. This is what is meant: although in ultimate reality there is only the experience of one's own appearance, the speaker forms such a determination: "I am conveying an external object itself to this person."
The listener also thinks in this way: "This person is presenting only something external to me.
Therefore, like the vision of two moons by two people suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*), all this verbal convention (*śābda-vyavahāra*) is [illusory].
If this is so, you have fallen into our own position; thus, your argument is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Since [the reason] had previously been introduced by way of "intuition" (*pratibhā*), he says "again" (*punar*) for this reason:
it has thus been established that the reason "because no convention (*samaya*) was made" is not unestablished (*asiddha*);
as for its being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) or contradictory (*viruddha*), these have already been refuted.
Therefore, it is established that words function through the exclusion [of others] as previously described.

(909) Here, an opponent—whose mind is deceived by hearing the word "exclusion" (apoha) and who does not understand the intended nature of exclusion—raises an objection regarding the contradiction between the thesis and its own implication, saying: "But how can you say that a word functions through the exclusion of others?"
But how can it be said by you that a word effects the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), when in this [cognition] no mere negation is perceived?
Rather, from words such as "cow," "gavaya," "elephant," and "tree," [a positive entity is understood].
The verbal cognition proceeds by way of determining a positive form (vidhirūpa).

[Regarding the phrase] "the word effects the exclusion of others" (anyāpohakṛcchabda), the word *iti* is to be supplied; the meaning is: "How is it stated that 'the word effects the exclusion of others'?"
Why is it not the denotable object? He says: "It is merely a negation," and so forth.
It is claimed that "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is intended as nothing more than a mere negation; however, in this verbal appearance, a mere negation is not apprehended.
Rather, the verbal cognition is observed to function precisely through the determination of a positive entity-form.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which does not appear in verbal cognition to be the meaning of a word, because that would lead to over-extension;
therefore, there is a contradiction with experience regarding the thesis.
911. With the three verses beginning with "yadi gaur," [the author] raises the objection regarding the contradiction of cognition and so forth according to the opinion of Bhāmaha:
"If this word 'go' were [to exist], then this word would have its purpose fulfilled in the exclusion of others..."

Let another sound be observed as the producer of the cognition of "cow" regarding the object "cow. (912) If the word "cow" were intended solely for the purpose of conveying the exclusion of others (*anyavyavaccheda*), then, since its function would be fulfilled therein alone, no cognition of the object possessing a dewlap and so forth would arise from the word "cow. Consequently, one would have to search for yet another sound to produce the cognition of "cow" directed toward the object possessing a dewlap and so forth.

It might be argued that since two cognitions are produced by a single word "cow" (*go*), no other sound (*dhvani*) need be sought; to this he says: "But not so," and so forth. "But surely words have cognition as their fruit; yet how can there be two fruits for one [word]—namely, the cognition of an exception and the cognition of a rule? (913) [Note: The provided text contains a corrupted segment regarding the correction table, which has been omitted from the translation.]
Those for whom the result is knowledge consisting of both the domain of injunction and the domain of prohibition are described as such.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "And not for one [word]," and so forth.
For it is not the case that a single word, whether performing an injunction or a prohibition, has a result characterized by two simultaneous cognitions.

The word "is perceived" is to be supplied as the ellipsis; moreover, it is not logical that the result should be a cognition consisting of both negation and affirmation, which are mutually contradictory.
With the words beginning with "prāk," he states the reason for the accumulation [of conceptualization]:
"Prior to this, there would be the cognition 'it is not a cow' for one who hears the word 'cow,' which is why the sound 'cow' is employed for the purpose of negating the non-cow. (914)

Furthermore, if the exclusion of the non-cow (*ago-nivṛtti*) were primarily expressed by the word "cow" (*go-śabda*), then immediately after hearing the word "cow," the hearer's first cognition would be "it is not a cow. For that alone is established as the meaning of a word from which a cognition arises directly and without mediation; yet, no cognition of the exclusion of the non-cow arises without such mediation.
Because it would follow that the cognition of "cow" could not arise, and because it would follow that the cow would be understood even before [the negation], apoha is not the meaning of a word.
With the words "the exclusion of the non-cow," etc., he points out the flaw in the proposition according to the view of Kumārila.

"By those who have accepted that the commonality (*sāmānya*) to be expressed is the cessation of suffering (*agonivṛtti*), it has been clearly stated by this very statement that what is expressed—namely, 'cowness' (*gotva*)—is indeed a real entity (*vastu*).

For he [the opponent] says this: "The commonality characterized as *apoha*, when designated as the object of expression, is sometimes expressed as having the nature of an exclusion-by-implication (*paryudāsa-lakṣaṇa*) or as having the nature of a simple negation (*prasajya-lakṣaṇa*)."

In that regard, in the first alternative, there is the fault of the thesis consisting in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For we maintain that the universal called "cowness" (*gotva*) is what is denoted by the word "cow," whereas you, by asserting that the universal characterized as the exclusion of non-cows (*agonivṛtti*) is expressed by the word "cow," are merely expressing that very same thing under a different name; thus, the dispute is over nothing more than a name. Now, he explains how that very same thing is expressed by a different term with the words beginning "consisting of the nature of another entity" (*bhāvāntarātmaka*).
Since every non-existence is established as being of the nature of another existence, let it be stated what that existence is which consists in the exclusion of horses and the like.
(916) For this reason, because every kind of non-existence— characterized as prior non-existence and so forth— is established as being of the nature of another existence.

And as it has been said: "That which does not exist in milk, such as curd and the like, is called prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*); the non-existence of milk in curd is characterized as non-existence through destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*);
and the absence of a horse and so forth in a cow is called mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*)."
The parts of the head that are sunken and devoid of growth or hardness—such as [the absence] in the form of a hare's horn and so forth—are called absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
These distinctions cannot belong to a non-entity; therefore, this [non-existence] possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastutā*).
Thus, by this it is demonstrated that milk and the like, being non-existent in the form of curds and so forth, receive designations such as "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva) and the rest;

since it is thus established that non-existence has the nature of another positive entity (bhāvāntarātmaka), you must state: what is this non-existence intended by you which has the nature of the exclusion of horses and other things?
It might be thought: "What is there to say here? This [object] is simply the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the cow and so forth. To this, he says:
"[It is] not accepted [by you], for the particular (*viśeṣa*), being of an uncommon nature, is beyond conceptualization" (*neṣṭo'sādhāraṇātmā vo viśeṣo nirvikalpanāt*).

And likewise, because it would follow that the brindled cow and others would not be universals (sāmānya), therefore that form which is fully established in each of all [individual cows] must be the cause of the cognition "cow"; and such a thing exists. (917–918)

As for that unique particularity which consists in the exclusion of horses and the like, why is it not accepted by you? He says: because it is free from conceptual construction (*nirvikalpa*), since in that state all conceptual constructions have subsided.
The universal (*sāmānya*) alone is held to be the object of conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), whereas the unique particular (*asādhāraṇa-artha*) is not the object of any conceptual cognition.
As it has been said: "The form cognized by itself (*svasaṃvedya*) and inexpressible (*anirdeśya*) is the object of the sense-faculties.
The reason for its being a particular is its unique nature; the meaning is that it is a particular by virtue of having a unique nature.
Having thus stated this without distinction, he now states this very same point specifically: "And likewise," etc.

Just as you do not accept that the unique particular (*asādhāraṇa-viśeṣa*), which consists in the exclusion of horses and so forth, is the denotation of the word "cow" (*go-śabda*), so too [the opponent's position] does not accept that the entity (*bhāva*) consisting in the exclusion of horses and so forth is the denotation of words such as "Śābaleya"; here too, the phrase "is not accepted" carries over.
Why? It is said: "Because it would entail the consequence of [the universal] being non-common.
If that were accepted, then the universal would not be denotable by words, because it would lack anvaya (concomitance).

Since, for this reason, an entity consisting of the exclusion of horses and so forth cannot be established as something unique (asādhāraṇa), therefore the cognition of "cow" is based on that which is fully present in each individual instance, such as the brindled cow and others, among all members of the same class.

And since that very universal called "cowness" (gotva) is merely designated by the term "exclusion of the non-cow" (ago'poha)— it being nothing more than a different name for it— there is the fault of the thesis consisting in proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).
Now, regarding the position that [the universal] has the characteristic of a simple negation (*prasajya-lakṣaṇa*), he says:

"And if the word and its object are conceived as having the nature of a mere negation," and so forth. If it is assumed that the word and its referent consist solely of the form of a negation, [then the following ensues].
"Emptiness would be of another kind, denotable by the word 'non-existence' (919).

That is to say, the word "non-existence" is a term denoting non-existence characterized by the exclusion of the non-cow (*agopoha*); what is denoted by that word would be an emptiness of external objects, because of the denial of the nature of real entities.

That which was previously proposed by you at the time of introducing the doctrine of *vijñaptimātra*— and which was refuted by us— is here again stated under the guise of *apoha*, during this discussion on the meaning of words, because it repudiates an object established by common experience. (919)
And then he states what the fault would be: "In that case," and so forth.

In that [cognition], there would be the apprehension of a portion of the self by the cognitions of horses and the like; therefore, the claim that the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is the denotable meaning is accepted in vain. 920

When that emptiness is the object of expression, verbal cognitions such as those of "horse" and so forth would result in grasping only their own internal mental components (*ātmāṃśa*), because they do not grasp the actual nature of external objects.
To the question, "What is the fault in this being the case? he says: "In that case," and so forth.
This being the situation, the status of *apoha* as the expressed meaning would be accepted in vain.
The meaning is that since the object of a word would then necessarily be a positive form of the mental aspect (*buddhyākāra*)— which does not depend upon an external referent—
this would contradict the very thesis [of the proponent] by violating their own accepted tenet.

He demonstrates this very point with the verse beginning "sāmānyam" and so forth: "The universal (*sāmānya*)—that is, the form of the object (*vasturūpa*)—will be the meaning of the word as it appears to the cognition; [this is] conceptually constructed (*prakalpita*). (921)
The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: the form of the cognition itself, which is the nature of the real entity (*vastu*), will be the universal (*sāmānya*) that is the referent of the word.

It might be argued: "Even though that cognition has that as its objective support (*ālambana*), it proceeds with a form excluded from cognitions of dissimilar things such as cows; therefore, the conceptualization of apoha is indeed logical. To this, he says: "the nature of the real entity," and so forth.

And that cognition which arises with respect to the objects of words has the form of a real entity; in those cases, the object itself would be conceived as the denotable [meaning], being a cognition that does not exclude [others].
"Having the form of a real entity" means that it results in a positive form.
"That cognition" refers to the cognition of horses and so forth, which lacks an objective basis (*anālambana*) regarding the referents of words.
In the case of horses and so forth that have been determined [as such], it is the object itself,
consisting of the nature of the cognition that determines the individual forms of horses and so forth.
He demonstrates the result of the restriction: "that which has no exclusion by the intellect" (*buddhyanapohakam*).
That object of expression, which is of the nature of the intellect, wherein no exclusion (*apoha*) exists, is so described;
it is that which has no exclusion by the intellect.
The meaning is that it is devoid of the exclusion of another cognition;

or alternatively, "apohaka" means that which excludes, and "anapohaka" means that which does not exclude; thus the compound "buddhyanapohaka" means that which does not exclude a cognition—this is what is being stated.
Although a cognition is distinguished from another cognition, nevertheless, it does not arise as having the determination of the exclusion of other cognitions;
