rather, it arises as having the form of an affirmation (*vidhirūpa*) with respect to objects such as horses and the like. Therefore, it is logical to postulate that the denotable object is indeed a real entity (*vastu*) in the form of an affirmation, and not an exclusion (*apoha*), because one cognition does not exclude another cognition.

Furthermore, this *apoha* which has been postulated by you as the meaning of a word is intended to be the meaning of a word abstracted from a sentence; however, the meaning of a sentence is characterized solely as *pratibhā* (intuition), as it has been said: "This meaning of a word is distinguished [from the sentence] through abstraction;
this meaning of the sentence, called *pratibhā*, is produced first by that [sentence]."
To this it is replied: "Even though [it does not exist]," and so forth (*asatyapi ca* etc.).
[The sentence-meaning is characterized as intuition (*pratibhā*); that is,] even if an external object does not exist, the sentence-meaning is intuition (*pratibhā*). Just as:
The word-meaning (*padārtha*) would likewise be exactly so; why then is *apoha* postulated?

(923) Just as you describe the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*)—despite the fact that an external object does not exist as the denotation of a word—as being characterized solely by *pratibhā* (intuition), and not characterized by *apoha*, so too the word-meaning should be characterized solely by *pratibhā*, just like the sentence-meaning. Thus, why is *apoha* postulated as the nature of the word-meaning?
The sense is that both the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning should simply be of a positive (*vidhi*) nature.

It might be argued that because there is an exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of one intuition (*pratibhā*) from another intuition of a different class, apoha is therefore postulated; to this he says: "From another cognition," etc.—"And the exclusion from another cognition is not perceived in the cognition."
"And because it consists merely in the production of its own nature, [cognition] which terminates in a positive form does not bear another aspect.
(924) If it is argued that although this [other aspect] is not perceived, it nevertheless exists, he says: "Because it consists merely in the production of its own nature," and so forth.
Even though there is a differentiation of one cognition from another cognition, nevertheless, there is no operation of words with respect to that [differentiation].

For instance: when this cognition arises from a word, it is not observed to bear any part understood from the word that consists of the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of other cognitions, distinct from its own production as a positive form (*svarūpa*). What then? The meaning is that it arises precisely as one whose determination is of a positive nature (*vidhirūpāvasāyin*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for a portion of a real object (*vastvaṃśa*) understood from a word to be the word-meaning, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, the sense is that the proposition is contradicted by direct experience (*pratītibādhitatva*).

Furthermore, by means of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), he says "those which express distinct universals" (*bhinna-sāmānya-vacanāḥ*) and so forth, demonstrating that [the opponent's position] is indeed sublated by perception and other means of valid cognition:
"Those which express distinct universals and those which express particulars..."
If exclusion (*apoha*) were the denotable object, then all terms would become synonyms.

(925) For those words which denote distinct universals, such as "cow" and "horse," and those which denote particulars, such as "Śābaleya" and so forth, would all result in being synonyms for you, because there is no difference in their referent, just like the words "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and "peda" (*pādapa*). (925)
Why, then, is a difference in meaning not possible? He says: "Because they are mixed," and so forth.

Since that [exclusion] is devoid of the conceptual constructions of unity and plurality, and because the natures of things (*ātman*) are non-entities, there is no difference whatsoever among the exclusions (*apoha*). (926)

For conceptual constructions such as being mixed (*saṃsṛṣṭatva*), unity, and plurality are possible only with respect to real entities (*vastu*), not with respect to non-entities (*avastu*). Since exclusions (*apoha*) are non-entities, it is not logical for them to have conceptual constructions such as mutual mixing; so how can their mutual distinction be established?
(926) Now, if their distinction is admitted, then it follows that they must necessarily be real entities. This is what [the author] shows with the words "Or if... and so forth.

Alternatively, because it is subject to differentiation, [it would be like] a non-common portion of an entity and a non-entity; and if it were a non-entity, then because there would be no plurality, it would not escape being a synonym.
"Entity" is the statement of the thesis to be proven.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which are mutually distinct are real entities (*vastu*), such as particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); and exclusions (*apoha*) are mutually distinct; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Consequently, it is established that if something is a real entity, it must be a positive affirmation (*vidhi*) alone as the meaning of a word.
By this, it is stated that the thesis is contradicted by inference (*anumāna-bādhita*).

Now, if it is admitted that exclusions (*apoha*) lack any real objective basis (*avastutva*), then, because there would be no plurality [among them], the consequence of their being synonyms (*paryāyatva*) follows as before; this is an absolute certainty.
(927) Here, the opponent anticipates a rebuttal from the Buddhist, beginning with "But surely... (*nanu ca*) and so forth.

But surely, the distinction of the exclusion (*apoha*) will be established through the distinction of the horses and so forth, as it has been said: "The meanings [of words] are distinct due to the difference in what is to be excluded (*apohya*); they are dull in the comprehension of the distinction of their own referents.

Consequently, even if there is no intrinsic distinction [in the exclusion itself], once a distinction is established for the exclusion—which consists in the exclusion of non-cows and the like—due to the distinction of the excluded objects such as horses, they will not be synonyms.
With the words "no distinction," etc., the opponent states a refutation:
"No distinction arises for that [apoha] either from itself or from another.
(928) There is no distinction—that is, no plurality—of that apoha from itself, because it has the single flavor of non-existence.
Even if it were to exist through another, it would be merely conceptual and not ultimately real;
for it is not logical that a distinction which does not exist inherently could possibly arise from something else.
Why is this not logical? He says: "For even those things that are associated... and so forth.

"For even the substrates that are associated do not differentiate [the object] in terms of its form; therefore, the idea that 'it would be differentiated by the excluded objects (apohyas), which are external,' is a mere fabrication. (929)

For instance: the related things—the correlates such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others—are internal bases; yet, they are unable to differentiate that *apoha* by way of its form—that is, by its intrinsic nature—because it is accepted that a single *apoha*, characterized as the exclusion of the non-cow, applies to all [individuals] such as the brindled cow and so forth. How then could it be differentiated by external things to be excluded, such as horses?
For that whose internal object is not a differentiator will certainly not have an external one;
otherwise, the status of being "external" would be forfeited.
Therefore, he mocks [the opponent] by saying that this conceptual construction is excessive:
"If that is so, then the internal bases themselves, as the correlates, will not be the differentiators. To this, he says: "In the same way," and so forth.
In the same way, a distinction in this [universal] based on a distinction in its substrata is also not tenable;

for even in the case of a real entity, a distinction is not admitted merely through a distinction in its relata. How much less so could that which is unreal, unconnected, and undifferentiated be excluded?
(a)ta evā The correction table does not display the parentheses in the error *anavāptaviśeṣāṃśaṃ ya (ddhima)*. The correction table displays the error as *yadvimatya*. *yatkimapyanirūpitam* || 931.
*asyeti* refers to *apohasya*.
He asks, "Why is it not tenable? and says: "For indeed," and so forth.

Let us set aside for a moment the claim that a non-entity does not differ based on the difference of its relata; for since it lacks intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), even in the case of an entity, as long as a difference is not perceived due to the difference of its relata, [the entity itself] does not truly differ.

For instance, a single entity such as Devadatta, when connected simultaneously or successively with multiple seats and so forth, is perceived as not having acquired any difference [between those states]. How much more so, then, the case of that which is a non-entity (avastu) consisting of the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti)? Precisely because it is a non-entity, it is unconnected—that is, unrelated—to anything, and because it is a non-entity, it is not excluded from other heterogeneous things.
For this very reason, since its specific aspects have not been apprehended, how could such a thing acquire difference even through the difference of its correlates?

Furthermore— let it be granted that there is indeed a distinction based on the difference between related entities; nevertheless, for you who do not admit a real, positive universal (*vastubhūta-sāmānya*), that very related entity which serves as the locus of exclusion (*apoha*) cannot be established.
He demonstrates that the differentiation of the latter is conceived through the differentiation of the former: "Nor can [it be] unestablished," and so forth.
No one at all is able to know cow and other things as having the nature of an object of exclusion (*apoha*) when their similarity is unestablished. // 932 //

The point is this: if a real similarity (*sārūpya*) among cows and other such things were established, then their status as the substratum for the exclusion (*apoha*) of horses and so forth would be proven without distinction; it could not be otherwise. Therefore, one who wishes these [terms] to have exclusion as their object must necessarily admit similarity; that very thing, being a real universal (*sāmānya*), will be the denotation of words. Thus, the conceptualization of *apoha* is entirely useless. Here, the word "object" (*viṣaya*) signifies a substratum (*āśraya*), as in the expression "fish have water as their object. (Verse 932)

He demonstrates that even for those who postulate differentiation based on the difference between excluded objects (*apohya*), that [differentiation] cannot be established without a real, positive universal (*vastubhūta-sāmānya*)—as shown in the verse beginning with "Even the excluded objects... (933):
"Even the excluded objects, such as horses and the like, cannot be determined without the presence of a single common property; thus, their exclusion (*apoha*) is not established."

For if there were some single, recurring property common to all individual horses and so forth, then all of them could be excluded without distinction by words such as "cow" and the like; but this is not the case otherwise, because their specific differences would remain unapprehended. Furthermore, if one were to admit a common property, the conceptualization of *apoha* (exclusion) would be redundant. Therefore, for these reasons, *apoha* is not established.
Moreover, you yourselves maintain that exclusion (apoha) is established solely by means of words and logical marks (liṅga);
yet, it is not logical for those words and logical marks to function without a real entity (vastubhūta) as a universal (sāmānya).
Therefore, by what [means] could exclusion be established? This is what he demonstrates with the verse beginning "And not through positive concomitance" (na cānvaya...).

Furthermore, the operation of words and logical marks is not devoid of positive concomitance (*anvaya*); nor is there exclusion (*apoha*) without those two; and there is no positive concomitance in that which is unique (*asādhāraṇa*).
[Verse 934] "Devoid of positive concomitance" means...
The meaning is "without positive concomitance" (anvaya);
that is, without those two— namely, word and logical mark— there is no exclusion (apoha).

If it is argued that the word "is understood" (*gamyata*) is to be supplied [to the verse], and that the operation of words and logical marks will be carried out by establishing a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, he replies: "And there is no concomitance in the unique particular.
The specific characteristic is unique and does not partake of anything else; how, then, could there be a concomitance with it?
Thus, in this way, if there were a conceptualization of apoha, the very operation of words and logical marks would not be possible.

Or, even if such an operation were to occur, it shows that the accepted validity (*prāmāṇya*) of these two would be lost—this is what is indicated by the verse beginning with "And apoha... and so forth.
Furthermore, since exclusion (*apoha*) is not established, where could concomitance (*sāhacarya*) be stated?

And when that [concomitance] is not perceived, there would be no validity for those two [word and logical mark]. Validity belongs to words and logical marks only when they do not deviate from the object to be conveyed; yet you maintain that the object to be conveyed is exclusion, and because it is of the nature of a non-entity, it is unestablished due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
And then, if it is asked: "In what object should the concomitance—that is, the non-deviation—of word and logical mark be stated?
What is the use of stating it?", he says: "In that," and so forth;
"in that" refers to...
"In their concomitance" refers to those two: the word and the inferential mark (liṅga).

The point is that validity is characterized by non-contradiction (avisaṃvāda). Now, it might be argued that even without having grasped the concomitance (sādharmya) between word and logical mark (liṅga) and their respective objects, these two will convey their own meanings merely through the non-perception of anything heterogeneous; to this he says: "And not by mere non-perception," and so forth.
Nor can there be comprehension from those two by mere non-perception alone;

for since everything is unperceived [in that sense], comprehension would not be distinguished [from error]. The inclusion of the word "mere" (mātra) is for the purpose of excluding the perception of positive concomitance (anvaya).
He asks, "Why would it not be so? and replies with the words beginning "in all cases" (*sarvatraiva*).
"In all cases" means in the case of the similar (*sajātīya*), the dissimilar (*vijātīya*), and its own object (*svārtha*).
Consequently, the cognition—the conceptual determination (*pratyaya*)—that "this is for its own sake" and "this is for the sake of another" would not be distinguished.
It would not convey even its own meaning, because [the relationship] is not perceived there either, just as it is not in the case of another's meaning; this is the sense.
As for the reading "somewhere *pratyāyya*," in that case, the object to be conveyed (*pratyāyya*), which is the denoted meaning (*abhidheya-artha*), is not distinguished—that is, it does not differ.

Thus, since it would entail the undesirable consequence of abandoning the accepted validity of the operation of words and logical marks, it is not tenable that exclusion (apoha) is the meaning of a word.

Regarding what was stated previously—"nor is there a similarity [of the object] with that which is unestablished," etc.—the opponent anticipates a reply: "Now, even though [it does not exist]," and so forth.

Now, even in the absence of similarity (*sārūpya*), if there were to be a conceptualization of exclusion (*apoha*), why is this "exclusion of the non-cow" (*ago'poha*) not conceived for both the cow and the horse?

(937) If the conceptualization of the exclusion of the non-cow were to occur among brindled cows (*śābaleya*) and others even without similarity, then why would it not be applied to the cow and the horse as well? For there is no distinction [between these cases].
Because the rule beginning with "gavāśvaprabhṛtīni ca" has been forgotten, the Brahmin said "of the cow and the horse.
He demonstrates that very same lack of distinction [in the following]: "and from a *śābaleya*," and so forth.
The difference from a brindled cow is the same for both a black cow and a horse;
if no other universal is accepted, then where could the exclusion of the non-cow (ago'poha) operate?—where could the exclusion of the non-cow operate? (938)

Just as [the term] does not apply to a horse because of its difference from a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow), so too it would not apply to a *bāhuleya* (a black cow) either, since that too possesses a difference from it; this same logic should be applied to the *śābaleya* and others as well, because the difference is indistinguishable in all cases. (938)

Moreover, demonstrating that just as it is not logical for words to have an object-referent in the case of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth due to the impossibility of linguistic convention (*samaya*), the same applies to exclusion (*apoha*), he says: "By the senses," and so on.
"Even by the senses, the exclusion of the non-cow (*ago'poha*) is not first apprehended; nor does the operation of a word [occur] elsewhere. Having seen what, then, could that word be applied? (939)

For it is one who has himself ascertained the object who establishes a convention when making that convention; yet exclusion (*apoha*) is not initially determined by the sense faculties—at a time prior to the period of linguistic usage, which means at the time of establishing the relationship between a name and the named.
The point is that exclusion is a non-entity (*avastu*), whereas the sense faculties have only real entities (*vastu*) as their objects.

It might be argued that a word will be employed after one has perceived a particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) excluded from others; to this he says: "Not elsewhere," etc., meaning not elsewhere than in the exclusion of others (anyāpoha). 939
If it is argued that "let there be no determination of exclusion by the sense-faculties; it will occur through inference," he says: "By what was stated before," and so forth.
By the aforementioned sequence of arguments, even inference does not exist here; for the experience of its [inference's] relationship is likewise not at all possible. || 940 ||

In this regard, the previously mentioned argument— "nor is there an operation of words or logical marks devoid of positive concomitance" (*na cānvayavinirmuktā pravṛttiḥ śabdaliṅgayoḥ*), and so forth—
also applies to the experience of the relation;
the phrase "together with the word" (*śabdena saha*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
By the word "also" (api), he shows that not only do the previously mentioned [faults] such as dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) and so forth fail to obtain;
"by that" (*tena*) means for that reason.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that the reason "because no convention has been established" is inconclusive,
since it is admitted that words function even with respect to an exclusion (*apoha*) despite the absence of a convention.
Furthermore, demonstrating that a convention is impossible regarding exclusion (*apoha*), he says: "The state of being denotable by the word 'non-cow'...

and so forth. [The phrase] "the state of being denotable by the word 'non-cow' and the state of being understood" is intended. But how is it that [exclusion] is not seen where the word "cow" occurs at the moment of experiencing the connection? (941)
"Indeed, you ought to explain how it is that horses and the like are not denoted by the word 'cow'—that is, how it is understood by you that they are not denoted by the word 'cow'?
To this, the Buddhist replies: "It is not seen where... and so forth, referring to the moment of experiencing the relationship [between word and object].
The meaning is: "at the time of the comprehension of the convention.
With the words beginning with "from one," the opponent states a refutation.

For from one [individual], indeed... [the list of corrections shows this error as *ekasmānnahi* without a space]. "Whatever is other than a single mass of a cow (*gopiṇḍa*) and so forth would all be the object of exclusion (*apohya*); thus, there is no denotability of a universal (*sāmānya*). (942) For if it were not accepted that the word "cow" applies to anything other than that which was perceived at the time of the experience of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), then everything other than that single cow-mass—such as a *śābaleya* cow—which was made the object of the convention, including a *bāhuleya* cow and the like, would also have to be excluded by the word "cow."
Consequently, the claim that the universal (*sāmānya*) is the denotable object would not be established.

Furthermore, showing that because of the consequence of the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) regarding the exclusion (*apoha*), he says: "And [if] established," and so forth.
If a cow were established [as a positive entity] and then excluded by "non-cow," and that [non-cow] were essentially the negation of a cow,

then that which is negated by the negative particle (*nañ*) must be stated as being the cow itself. If that [cow] were essentially the exclusion of the non-cow, there would be a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).

If the positive entity (*bhāva*) is already established, then the conceptualization of exclusion (*apoha*) is futile. (944) The cognition of a "cow" occurs through the exclusion of the "non-cow. Now, that non-cow consists in the negation of the cow; therefore, in the expression "non-cow," one must state what the referent of the latter term is, which would be negated by the negative particle (*nañ*) in the phrase "not a cow.
For it is impossible to effect the negation of something whose own nature (*svarūpa*) is not known.
Furthermore, it might be asked: "What is there to say here? Is this 'cow' essentially the exclusion of non-cows? To this he says: "And that," and so forth;
"that" refers to the cow.

For in this way, because the cow has the nature of being the exclusion of the non-cow (*agoparihāra*), its cognition occurs only by means of the cognition of the non-cow; and since the non-cow consists of the negation of the cow, its cognition occurs only by means of the cognition of the cow. Thus, the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) becomes very clearly evident. Now, it might be argued: "The cow that is negated by the word 'non-cow' is established as having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) for the sake of the *apoha*—that is, for the sake of establishing the *apoha* characterized by the exclusion of the non-cow. Therefore, there will be no mutual dependence. To this, he says: "If it were established," and so forth.

If this is so, then the conceptualization of apoha—that the meaning of every word is exclusion—is futile, because there exists a word-meaning in the form of a positive injunction (vidhi). Therefore, some word-meaning in the form of a positive injunction must be established and accepted; for if that is not accepted, the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) is unavoidable.
Concluding that very point regarding mutual dependence, he says: "When the cow is not established," and so forth:
"But when the cow is not established, the non-cow does not exist; and in its absence, how can there be a cow?"
Furthermore, there is no relationship such as that between locus and located between two absences;
thus, "the absence of that" [refers to] the absence of a cow.

The teacher Diṅnāga stated, for the sake of establishing the relationship between the qualified and the qualifier, that "words such as 'blue lotus' denote objects as distinguished by the exclusion of other objects," and so forth.
Showing that this is incorrect, [the author] says: "Not [a relation of] locus and located," and so on.
For it is only logical to say that something is qualified by another when some real (vāstava) connection between them is established.

Furthermore, since the blue lotus and the non-blue lotus are of the nature of negations—consisting respectively in the exclusion of the non-blue lotus and the non-lotus—a relationship such as that of locus and located cannot possibly exist between them, because they lack positive form (*nīrūpatvāt*).
By the use of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), one includes other relationships such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and inherence in a single substratum (*ekārthasamavāya*).
Moreover, in the absence of a real relationship, it is not logical to have a cognition of something qualified by that [relationship], as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, it might be argued: "It is not our intention that there is a specific exclusion of non-lotuses (*anutpala*) by means of the exclusion of non-blue (*anīla*) and so forth, such that this fault would arise;
rather, it is the very object itself, excluded from both the non-blue and the non-lotus, that is established as such."

The intended meaning here is that a thing qualified by the exclusion of other objects is expressed by the word; therefore, he says: "And the unique entity is not apprehended as possessing apoha," and so forth—nor can a relationship be postulated between a real entity and a non-entity. (946)

The intended meaning is that because the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is inexpressible, the faults inherent in that position would necessarily follow. Even if one were to admit that the unique entity is indeed cognizable, [the author] demonstrates that its being qualified by the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) is not established, stating "How else... and so forth.

Apoha is a non-entity (*avastu*), whereas the unique entity is a real thing (*vastu*); and a relationship between a non-entity and a real thing is not tenable, because such a relationship must have two real entities as its substrata.

946 Furthermore—even granting that a relation exists, it is still shown that it is not logical for exclusion (apoha) to function as a qualifier: "By its mere existence in its own nature," and so forth;
nothing can be a qualifier by virtue of its own essential existence alone.
That by which the qualificand is colored through one's own cognition is the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa).
For blue and so forth do not become qualifiers of lotuses and the like merely by their existence;
rather, that which, being known, colors the qualificand through a cognition colored by its own form, is called a qualifier.
He demonstrates that this method is not possible in the case of exclusion (apoha) with the words "And also not," etc.:
"Nor is there an awakening to exclusion produced from words such as 'horse' and so forth."
In this context, the cognition of the qualified object is intended, and it does not occur when the qualifier is unknown.

For the exclusion (apoha) is not determined by the cognition of a horse or similar things; rather, it is the real entity itself that is so determined. Consequently, since the apprehension of exclusion is impossible through that [cognition], the horse or other such objects are not colored by their own cognition [of exclusion].
It might be argued that exclusion (apoha), even if unknown, will serve as a qualifier; to this he says: "viśeṣya... and so forth.
For a cognition of the qualified object does not arise when the qualifier has not been apprehended;
thus, it is said to be "that whose qualifier is not known."

"Let it be granted that there is the cognition of exclusion (apoha); nevertheless, since the object does not possess a cognition of that form, it is improper for that [exclusion] to be its qualifier. Demonstrating this, he says: "And a qualifier cannot make something of one nature appear otherwise," and so forth.
A cognition cannot make an object of one nature appear as something of a different nature.
And how could that [object] be called a qualifier with respect to a cognition of a different nature?
For every qualifier is observed to produce a cognition of the qualified that conforms to its own form;
a qualifier of one nature does not produce a cognition of a different nature regarding the qualified.
For a blue lotus does not produce the cognition "it is red," nor does a staff produce the cognition "it is a earring";
nor, in this case, does a verbal cognition arise as colored by the absence of horses and so forth—what then? It is one that determines the form of a positive entity.

It might be argued that even a cognition that produces something of a different nature is called a "qualifier"; to this he says: "And how could it be of a different nature," and so forth—"of a different nature" means not conforming to the qualifier.
He states what the fault would be if that were so: "But otherwise," and so forth.
"But otherwise, if the conceptualization of a qualifier were to apply even to the qualified object, then in that case, anything whatsoever could be accepted as a qualifier. (950)

Now, if you argue that the conceptualization of a qualifier would still occur even when the particular (viśeṣa) is established otherwise because it does not conform to its qualifier, then in that case, everything such as "blue" and so forth would become a qualifier for everything, and consequently, there would be a lack of fixed order.
To this, he says: "That which is cognized through non-existence," etc., [meaning] that even by means of exclusion (apoha), the object to be qualified is colored by one's own cognition.
Furthermore, in a qualified object whose nature is cognizable through non-existence, there is no reality;
therefore, for you, there is no real entity that is expressed as qualified by exclusion (apoha).

(951) "Non-existence" (abhāva) is exclusion (apoha). That which is cognized through such exclusion—due to its identity with it—is "cognizable through non-existence" (abhāvagamya). A thing whose form or intrinsic nature (svabhāva) is thus cognizable through non-existence is described as such.
If the cognition of an entity were by way of its non-existence, then it would not be an entity at all, because existence and non-existence are contradictory.
Concluding the present topic, he says: "qualified," and so forth (verse 951).

It might be argued: "The operation of words and logical marks (*liṅga*) is observed only with respect to an object that is excluded from others, not with respect to one devoid of exclusion (*apoha*); therefore, it is said that exclusion is conveyed by words and logical marks, but not because they convey a mere negation (*prasajya*). Consequently, none of the aforementioned contradictions regarding cognition and so forth will arise. Anticipating this, he says: "Even if," and so on. "Even if the operation of words and logical marks is not possible with respect to an object devoid of exclusion, nevertheless, the cognition [produced by them] relies upon the real entity (*vastu*) for its apprehension. (952)

Even if that object is indeed excluded from others, nevertheless, the cognition arising from a word or a logical mark (*liṅga*), while being produced with respect to it, does not take as its objective support that exclusion of others, even though it exists; what then? It rushes toward a specific part of the object itself, because of its attachment to that very part.

That part of the object which is determined by either a verbal or an inferential cognition is alone its object, not that which is not determined, even if it exists. For the fragrance and other qualities of the *mālatī* flower are not established as the denotable meaning of the word "mālatī" merely by virtue of their existence.
Nor is this [position] tenable—that words and logical marks function with respect to an object that is excluded from others; he demonstrates this with the words "And not," etc.:
"And a unique particular (asādhāraṇa) does not revolve in the intellect, nor is its apprehension tenable because it is free from conceptual construction. (953)

For, according to your view, an entity excluded from others must be a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is indeed non-common; yet it is your position that such a thing does not appear in a cognition produced by words or logical marks,
because it is apprehended only by non-conceptual cognition,
whereas cognition produced by words and logical marks has the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

Furthermore, even if it were admitted that this [cognition] has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, that too does not accord with reason; showing this, he says: "And also not," and so forth.

For an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) entity is not to be apprehended by a cognition produced from words or logical marks (*liṅga*), because in that [entity], all conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have completely subsided.
To explain: a conceptual construction proceeds only through contact with qualifiers such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, and not by grasping the pure entity itself.

Now, it might be argued that even though a unique object is not apprehended by means of a word, it is said to be "qualified" through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*). To this, he says: "And [the claim] that the qualified is not apprehended by a word," and so forth; that the qualified is not apprehended by a word is sheer audacity.
Therefore, a universal must be accepted as the object of both cognition and words.
(954) Establishing the reality of the universal by means of another argument as well, he says: "When," and so forth.
When [the universal] is not denotable by words, then because it is not denotable, there can be no exclusion (*apoha*) of the individuals.
In that case, the universal would be excluded, and by its exclusion, the reality of the individuals would follow. (955) Since individuals— whose nature consists of unique,
particular entities— are inexpressible, they cannot be the objects of exclusion, because it is impossible to negate that which has not been mentioned.
The meaning is that the universal would have to be excluded because it is the denotable object [of the word].

It might be argued: "Even if a universal (*sāmānya*) were indeed excluded (*apohya*), how could its status as a real entity (*vastutva*) be established? To this, he says: "There is no state of being excluded," and so forth.
"There is no state of being excluded for non-entities (*abhāva*), because there is no exclusion of a non-existence from [another] non-existence.
Therefore, the exclusion of other exclusions is manifested [only] by means of a universal that is a real entity. (956)
Regarding the phrase "of absences" (abhāvānām):
if it were the case that exclusions (apohas) possess the nature of real entities (vastutva), they would indeed be [real] things.
He states the proof for this: "Because of the avoidance of non-existence and existence.
This means because of the abandonment of the nature of non-existence by those [entities] that are non-existent.

What is meant is this: if the objects of exclusion (*apohya*) were themselves exclusions (*apoha*), then their nature as non-existence would be negated; and upon that negation, the nature of non-existence would be abandoned by those very non-existences.
Consequently, some maintain that because non-entities characterized as apoha would abandon their nature as non-existence, they would necessarily become real entities;
others, however, say: "due to the avoidance of the non-existence of non-existences," which means because there is no non-existence of non-existences.

For it is not logical that exclusions (apohas), which are by nature non-existent, should themselves be the objects of exclusion, because negation has as its object a real entity; therefore, it is determined that when the exclusion of one [term], such as "cow," occurs in relation to another exclusion, such as "horse," it is necessarily an exclusion of that which has become a universal.
Therefore, it is established that because it is the object of exclusion (*apohya*), the universal (*sāmānya*) is a real entity (*vastu*).
Furthermore, there must be either mutual distinction or non-distinction among exclusions; regarding the first position, he states the fault as follows: "And of the non-existence... and so forth.
And if the non-existence of non-existence were distinct from it, it would indeed be an existence; if not, the consequence of its being white follows for you. (957) [Explanation:
"Of non-existence" means of that which is denoted by the word *agau* (non-cow); "the non-existence" refers to the object denoted by the word *go* (cow).

If it [the non-existent] were something different from that previously mentioned absence— meaning it were other than it— then it would necessarily be an existent (bhāva), because an existent consists solely in the cessation of non-existence.
If, on the other hand, it were not different, then even a cow would result in being a non-cow for you, since identity is understood through such non-difference.

It might be argued: "By words such as 'cow' and 'horse,' it is only the specific individualities (*svalakṣaṇa*), which are mutually excluded, that are negated (*apohya*), not absences (*abhāva*). Therefore, the consequence that they would be real entities by virtue of being negatable is not undesirable. To this, he says: "Even though," and so forth.
Even though in other words there might be the state of being a negatable entity (*vastu-apohyatā*):
However, for the word "existent" (*sat*), no distinct object of exclusion (*apohya*) is admitted other than that which is called non-existence (*abhāva*).

(958) Although in the case of words other than "existent," such as "cow" and so forth, the status of being an object of exclusion is established for real entities like mountains and the like, for the word "existent," there is no object of exclusion other than that which is called non-existence; the meaning is that non-existence itself is the object of exclusion, because the word "existent" functions by way of excluding the linguistic usage of the non-existent (*asad-vyavahāra*).
958 Then he states what the fault would be: "In that case, even for that which is non-existent... and so forth;
"In that case, the status of being an entity would belong even to that which is non-existent, and thus there would be a great difficulty."
If that [exclusion] is not established, neither existence nor non-existence exists; for it is said: "Neither existence nor non-existence is established" (959).
As before, by avoiding both presence and absence, if there were an exclusion of the non-existent (*asat*), it would result in the very status of being a real entity (*vastutva*).

Consequently, for the proponent of Apoha, the status of being a real entity would follow even for the non-existent, which contradicts their own fundamental tenets. Alas, what a great calamity has befallen!
If it is argued that even non-existence (abhāva) must be a real entity (vastu), he says: "In the case of its non-establishment," and so forth.

If that non-existence were not established, the existence (sattā) of no entity whatsoever could be established, because according to your own view, the definition of an entity is established through the exclusion of non-existence.

Furthermore, if that non-existence were itself something to be excluded (*apohya*), it would follow that it possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastu*); consequently, its own essential nature would be unestablished, and thus even non-existence (*asattā*) cannot be established. This is because non-existence consists in the exclusion of existence (*sattā-vyavaccheda*), and existence, according to the manner previously described, is impossible [in the case of non-existence].

As was stated before: "It would be differentiated by the external things to be excluded," and so forth; and as was also stated: "Because exclusions (*apoha*) are not real entities, there can be no differentiation among them," and so forth.

Regarding this, some Buddhists offer a rebuttal: "Indeed, the differentiation of exclusions (*apoha*) does not arise from the differentiation of the objects to be excluded, nor from the differentiation of their substrata; rather, due to the continuity of various latencies (*vāsanā*) for conceptual constructions of unreal objects that have operated since beginningless time, exclusions—which are in reality devoid of objects—are superimposed upon external, differentiated objects by cognitions that, though lacking real objects, appear as if they were apprehending distinct objects. These exclusions, thus superimposed by those [cognitions], appear as if they were differentiated while being [in fact] non-differentiated. Therefore, through the differentiation of the latencies, exclusions will possess both differentiation and the nature of existence. To this, he replies with the words "And yet not... and so forth.

Nor can the diversity or even the positive nature of exclusions (apohas) be postulated based on a difference in mental impressions (vāsanā), for such [a causal relationship] is not admitted in the case of a non-entity; indeed,
it is not thought that there can be a mental impression in regard to a non-entity.
It has been thoroughly established in the investigation of the Vijñānavāda that there is no cognition whatsoever that is without an object;
therefore, since conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) involving unreal objects are impossible, how could the latent predisposition (*vāsanā*) deposited by them come to be?
For [the object] is non-existent.

The meaning is this: since there is no object that serves as a basis, and because consciousness cannot exist without an object, there is an absence of the consciousness that deposits latencies (*vāsanā*); how, then, can there be a latency?
Consequently, due to the absence of latencies, how could there be a distinction among exclusions (*apoha*) produced by latencies, or how could they possess a real nature? This is the intended sense.
Having thus refuted the exclusion (apoha) intended as the denoted object, he speaks in order to refute that which is intended as the denoter, beginning with "by you" and so forth:
"By you, even a difference between words caused by that [exclusion] is not obtained;
for a word that is not common [to others] is not a denoter, because it has never been perceived before. (961)
In that regard, when a universal (*sāmānya*) consisting in the exclusion of other words (*śabdāntarāpoha*) is postulated,

just as [the distinction between] expressive words is not postulated because it lacks the nature of a real entity, so too is the mutual distinction between the signified and the signifier not postulated. (962)
And it has already been established that there is no distinction [among words] based on the distinction between their respective objects of exclusion (apohya).

The "distinction of words" refers to the mutual difference among words— both those denoting distinct universals and those denoting particulars— and this [distinction of words] is the cause [of the distinction in their referents].
That which has as its cause (nimitta) either a difference in latent impressions (*vāsanā*) or a difference in the exclusion of referents (*vācyāpoha*) is "caused by that" (*tannimitta*). [Objection:

But surely the difference between words is already well-established through perception itself, due to the difference in their causes and the superposition of contradictory properties; to this he says: "For it is not unique," and so forth.
For this is said with reference to the word as a signifier (*vācaka*), and the unique sound (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is the object of auditory cognition is not a signifier.

He asks "Why? and replies: "Because it was not seen previously. For that word which persists until the time of linguistic usage was not perceived at the earlier time of the convention; and that which *was* perceived has long since ceased to exist, so no linguistic usage can be made with it. Nor is it logical to employ for usage that which was not perceived at the time of the convention, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) cannot be the signifier.

There is indeed a dispute on this point even for you yourselves, as it has been stated: "The specific nature of an object or a word is not accepted as being the denoted or the denoter, because that was never perceived before; rather, it is the universal (sāmānya) that will be taught."

Thus, because the expression is made with reference to the denotative word, there is no fault. This being the case, if it is postulated that the exclusion of other words (*śabdāntarāpoha*) is the denotative word-universal (*śabdasāmānya*), just as the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*) is the object-universal (*arthasāmānya*), then— in exactly the same way, by the previously stated method beginning with "the unity and plurality of the conjoined," and so forth— the mutual distinction among the exclusions of words (*śabdāpoha*) does not hold, just as it does not hold for the exclusions of the denotable objects (*vācyāpoha*).

Because they lack form (*nīrūpatva*), just as a mutual distinction between denoters does not cohere, so too a mutual distinction between the denoted and the denoter is not postulated, due to their being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
To the objection that "there will be a distinction [between them] by way of the distinction of their respective exclusions (*apohya*)," he says: "Nor even... and so forth.

And just as difference is not conceptualized even due to the difference among the objects to be excluded (*apohya*), so too it has been established by the passage beginning with "there is no particularity (*viśeṣa*) inherent in that [exclusion] itself" (vv.
Thus, having demonstrated that the thesis is contradicted by what has been accepted through perception,

[the author] now says— "It is not cognized," etc., providing a proof with the desire to set forth the faults such as the contradiction of what has been accepted by demonstrating the consequence of the absence of the relationship between signifier and signified.
There would be no relationship of signifier and signified between the two exclusions (*apoha*), because they are non-entities,
just as in the world there is none between a sky-flower and a hare’s horn in your own view.

Since those two which are non-entities possess the relationship of signifier and signified— just like a sky-flower and a hare’s horn— and yet the denoted and denoting exclusions would both be non-entities, this constitutes the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

[Objection: "But surely, because the absence of rain is perceived from the absence of clouds, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*. To this, he says: "If one were to say it is inconclusive upon seeing the absence of rain and the absence of clouds," and so forth. That is to say, if one were to claim it is inconclusive based on observing the non-existence of rain and the non-existence of clouds.
In my position, it is indeed a vast thing; but how could this be so in your position?
[Verse 965] Regarding "the non-existence of rain and clouds"—that is, their non-being, meaning their absence—since the designation has the state of being (bhāva) as its primary sense.

Having observed those two— the subject and the predicate under discussion— if the Buddhist were to state the reason "because it is a non-entity" [to prove that the absence of rain and clouds is not a probans], that too is incorrect; because, in my position, there exists here too a real entity consisting of space and light devoid of those [clouds and rain] in this application regarding the absence of rain and clouds, since it has been established that non-existence is a real entity.
But for you, the Buddhist, even this [is problematic]: from what [source] does this relationship of the signified and the signifier exist between the absence of rain and the absence of clouds?
The word "api" (even/also) is out of its proper order; it is to be connected immediately after "ada" (this).
By that, the meaning becomes as follows:

Not only is it not tenable for you that there is a relationship of signifier and signified (*gamyagamakatva*) between two exclusions (*apoha*) that have become the subject of dispute, but this relationship of signifier and signified between the absence of rain and the absence of clouds is likewise untenable.

Furthermore, regarding that which you describe as the capacity of words and logical marks (*śabda-liṅga*)—which are subordinate in their positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and primary in their negative exclusion (*vyatireka*)—to convey their own objects; and regarding the fact that [a word] is not observed in the referent of another word, yet is observed even in a portion of its own referent.

It has been described that the ease of establishing a relationship [between word and object] exists in verbal testimony (*śruti*) and that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*), and so forth; however, this is not tenable if one accepts the theory of exclusion (*apoha*). Demonstrating this, he says: "And if the meaning of a word is not accepted as having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*)," and so on.

If the meaning of a word is not accepted as being of a positive nature, then even its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would not exist, for that [negative concomitance] is preceded by it [the positive form]. (966)
The phrase "preceded by that" means preceded by the injunction; the sense is that it is preceded by the injunction because negation (vyatireka) is characterized by the cessation of the injunction.

Furthermore—this denial of what is well-known in the world, namely the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣyabhāva*) and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in words such as "blue lotus," follows from the theory of exclusion (*apohavāda*).

And as for this which is said—for the sake of establishing that qualifier-qualified relationship and coreferentiality: "Because their objects of exclusion differ, [words] have different referents; they are dull [in themselves] regarding the comprehension of the difference between their own objects."

Because they produce a single, non-different effect in one instance, they stand in the relation of qualifier and qualified; yet there is a distinction because each requires only its own specific form, and thus it is not abandoned by its own universal,
nor is it grasped [as such], since doubt arises when there is equality, and these two [words] have a single referent.
Showing that this [position] is untenable, he says:
"If it is here accepted that the denotable object is mere exclusion (apoha) alone," and so forth.
In words such as "blue lotus," which denote a variegated object, there is no establishment of either the qualifier-qualified relationship or grammatical coreferentiality;
for when "non-blue" is excluded, there is no exclusion of "non-lotus. (967–968)

Nor does the other [the qualifier] exist there [in the word]; therefore, the relation of qualified and qualifier does not belong to the two words, nor could it belong to them independently of their denotable objects.
(969) Previously, the relation of qualified and qualifier between the two objects themselves was already refuted.
Now, since this [distinction] is being refuted even in the case of two words, there is no tautology.

In that context, the state of mutual exclusion is the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*), and that is established only within a sentence, as in "a blue lotus" (*nīlam utpalam*);
likewise, it also occurs between terms in different grammatical cases, as in "the king's man" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*) and so forth.

Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is the occurrence of two words, applied to distinct causes (or meanings), in reference to a single object; and this is established precisely within the compound formation (*vṛtti*), as in the case of "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*). Regarding that co-referentiality and so forth found in words such as "blue lotus," which denote a variegated (*śabala*) meaning—the claim that the meaning is variegated—that is not established. For the meaning is diverse (*citra*), as it has been said: "For that is neither merely blue, nor is it merely a lotus."
To the question, "Why does [the argument] 'because it denotes a collection' not constitute a proof? he says: "For not," and so forth;
because when non-blue is excluded, there is no exclusion of non-lotus.
In this context— "in the absence of non-lotuses"—
the other [term] is "nīlavyudāsaḥ" (exclusion of the blue); however, in some places, there is a reading with the feminine gender as "itarā."
It should be understood in relation to the term "falling away" (*cyuti*);
the other— meaning "non-blue falling away"—
has no relationship of container and contained between these two, because they lack form (*nīrūpatvāt*), so to speak.
Furthermore, it has been stated that in the absence of a relation, the status of qualifier and qualified is not tenable due to the fallacy of over-extension;
by this, it is implied that in your view, there is no denotation of a variegated object at all, because all words would denote only non-existence.
Therefore, the relationship between qualifier and qualified is not logical.

It might be argued: "Let there be no relation of qualifier and qualified between the two objects; why, then, should it not exist between the two words that denote them? To this he replies with the words "of the two words," and so forth: For the relation of qualifier and qualified is only metaphorically attributed to the two words denoting those objects by way of the objects themselves. Since that [relation] is impossible in the case of the object, how could its attribution occur even in the case of the denoting word? (967)
Refuting grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), he says: "And as for grammatical coreferentiality... (968–969).

Furthermore, there can be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between two exclusions (*apoha*) because they are distinct; if it were claimed that such coreferentiality exists by virtue of their objects, what kind of "residing" (*ādheyatā*) could there be for those two? Coreferentiality occurs only when there is a subsistence in a single object.

Furthermore, it is not possible for the words "blue" and "lotus" to function with respect to a single referent, because the two exclusions (*apoha*) denoted by them—which consist in the exclusion of the non-blue and the non-lotus respectively—are distinct.
For it has been stated by you yourselves: "They have different referents because their objects of exclusion (*apohya*) are different."

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: words such as "blue lotus" are not the objects of the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because they have different referents, like the words "pot" and "cloth. Now, it might be argued that since the exclusion of non-lotuses (*anutpalavyudāsa*) exists in the very same place where the exclusion of non-blues (*anīlavyudāsa*) also resides, the two exclusions (*apoha*) denoted by the words "blue" and "lotus" both subsist in a single object; therefore, coreferentiality is attributed to the words themselves by means of their objects. To this, he says: "And [not] by way of the object," and so forth. That... [is as follows].

Regarding the phrase "the coreferentiality of those two": no real substratum-ness (ādheyatā) is possible for the exclusions of the non-blue and the non-lotus, because that which lacks form cannot reside anywhere, just as in the case of the son of a barren woman; such is the intended meaning.

Furthermore—let it be granted that those two [existence and non-existence] may indeed be the properties to be contained within objects such as the blue lotus; nevertheless, he shows that even though they exist, they are not conveyed by words, with the words beginning "And not" (na ca), etc.:
"And a unique particular (*asādhāraṇa-vastu*) is not apprehended, nor does anything else exist for you."
Of what use is the identity of two words when that very object is not being apprehended?
(971) For it has already been stated that the unique object itself, such as a "blue lotus," is not apprehended by the word, because all conceptual constructions have ceased with respect to it.

Consequently, when that foundational object is unknown, how can the relation of being contained (*tadādheyatā*) within the two exclusions (*apoha*) which serve as its locus be grasped? The point is that the apprehension of a property (*dharma*) is necessarily dependent upon the apprehension of its substratum (*dharmin*).

Furthermore, it might be argued that there exists another substratum for those two, distinct from the uncommon object, and therefore this fault does not apply; to this, he says: "And another," and so forth.
"Those" refers to yours.

One might argue: "Even if identity of referent is not understood, it nevertheless remains established by the actual state of things. To this he says: "Not being understood," and so forth; "identity of referent" means grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
The phrase "where is it of use? means "nowhere," because even that which exists is not a factor in verbal discourse if it is unknown.

971. Now, it might be argued: "If only the exclusion (vyāvṛtti) were expressed by the word, then this fault would indeed arise; however, since the object possessing the exclusion is what is denoted, there is certainly co-referentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya), because two words conditioned by two different exclusions both apply to a single object that possesses the exclusion. To this, he says: "Now, moreover... and so forth, [meaning] "if it is asserted that the object possessing the exclusion of others is what is denoted."
Even in that case, because it is dependent upon another, pervasion by the word is difficult to obtain.

(972) "Even in that case" means that even when a thing possessing exclusion (*apoha*) is accepted as the denotable object, the pervasion—that is, the implication—of non-blue and other particulars such as blue lotuses by words such as "blue" is difficult to obtain. For what reason? Because the word "blue" and so on are dependent; for that [word] expresses the object as possessing that [quality], with the exclusion being subordinate, and not directly.

Furthermore, because there is no direct denotation [of those other qualities], there is no implication of the distinctions residing therein; just as, for example, the word "sweet" does not imply white and so forth.

Although, according to the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), white and the like are indeed distinct from sweet and the like, nevertheless, a word has the capacity to imply only those distinctions that reside in the object directly expressed by it, and not those that reside in an object expressed through dependence on another. This is the intended meaning.

Furthermore, since words such as "blue" do not imply the specific differences contained within that [universal], lotuses and the like would not be its particulars; and if they were not its particulars, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) would not be possible.

Thus, it is shown that the objection you stated against the position that [the word denotes] merely the possessor of the universal—namely, that "the word is not a denoter of the possessor because it is not independent"—is equally applicable to the position that [the word denotes] merely that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).

To explain: if the meaning of a word were merely that which possesses a universal (*jātimanmātra*), then the word "existent" (*sat*) would denote a substance with the nature of the universal as a subordinate element, but not directly; consequently, because it would not imply the specific differences such as "pot" and so forth residing within that substance, it was stated that there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) due to the absence of those differences. That same objection applies equally to the position that the meaning is merely that which possesses exclusion (*vyāvṛttimanmātra*). For even there, the word "existent" denotes a substance with exclusion as a subordinate element, but not directly; thus, the failure to imply the specific differences residing therein is exactly the same in this case as well. What difference is there here between [the positions] "universal" (*jāti*) versus "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*), or "possessor of a universal" (*jātimat*) versus "possessor of exclusion" (*vyāvṛttimat*)? He states another fault: "liṅga... and so forth.
Furthermore, no connection with gender, number, and so forth exists for the exclusion (apoha); nor does it exist by way of the individual instance (vyakti), because that [instance] is inexpressible.

(973) "Genders" refers to femininity, masculinity, and neuter; "numbers" refers to singularity, duality, and plurality; and by the inclusion of "and so forth," the connection with action, time, and other factors is encompassed.

There is no connection between these [logical marks, etc. and apoha, because apoha is a non-entity (avastu), whereas these are properties of real entities (vastudharma). Furthermore, it is impossible for a word to denote an object that is devoid of its logical mark and other such features;
therefore, the meaning of the proposition is that it would entail a contradiction with actual cognition (pratītibādhā). This is the intended sense.

Furthermore, it might be argued that because the individual (vyakti), which serves as the substratum for exclusion (vyāvṛtti), is a real entity (vastu), it possesses a connection with gender, number, and so forth; and by means of this [individual], exclusion (apoha) is also established. To this, he says: "And of the individual," etc. For that individual, being non-conceptual (nirvikalpa), cannot be designated through a connection with gender, number, and so on; therefore, how could the establishment of that [exclusion] in relation to exclusion be accomplished by means of it?
Demonstrating that both the exclusion (*apoha*) and the linguistic convention (*śabdārthavyavasthā*) lack pervasiveness, he says: "In verbal forms," and so forth:
"In verbal forms, the exclusion of another is not perceived; for there exists no negatable object there in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*). (974)

Regarding verbs—namely, words ending in verbal suffixes (*tiṅanta*) such as *pacati* (he cooks) and *gacchati* (he goes), which have action as their primary meaning—no exclusion of another is understood. Why? He says: "For it is not of the nature of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*)," and so forth.

Just as in the case of nouns ending in nominal suffixes (*subanta*), such as the word "jar" (*ghaṭa*), there exists a negandum of the nature of a relative negation in the form of a completed entity such as "non-jar," it is not so in the case of "he cooks" and the like; for no completed counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) whatsoever is perceived.

It might be argued: "Let there be no negation in the form of a paryudāsa (exclusion); rather, a negation in the form of a prasajya (absolute negation), such as 'he does not cook,' will serve as the object of negation for [the affirmation] 'he cooks. To this he says: "For even when saying 'not not,'" and so forth.
For even when "not not" is uttered, it is the negation itself that is being negated;
however, the act of cooking remains unnegated, persisting in its own essential nature. (975)
Furthermore, in this case, the cognition of [the action] as something to be accomplished (sādhya), as well as the representation of it as "past" and so forth,
would result in being groundless, because the exclusion (apoha) is already established.
Even when one says "he does not cook," only the negation of the prasajya-pratiṣedha itself would be expressed.
And so, he states what the fault would be: "Since 'he cooks' is not prohibited," and so forth.

Because the two negations have as their object the affirmation, the phrase "he cooks" remains in its very own form, which is essentially affirmative; thus, affirmation alone would be the meaning of the word.
Furthermore, in this case of "he cooks" and so on, the state of being an action-in-progress (sādhyatva) is perceived.

An action whose some parts are accomplished and some are unaccomplished—such an action, consisting of sequential parts, is the object of the cognition of being "to-be-accomplished" (*sādhya*); furthermore, in expressions such as "it has been" or "it will be," there is a perception of specific temporal distinctions such as past and so forth.
However, such possibilities as being "to-be-accomplished" do not exist for *apoha*, because it is already accomplished and consists solely of the nature of non-existence.

Therefore, under the view that the meaning of a word is *apoha*, the cognition of being an object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) and the cognition of "past" (*bhūta*) and so forth would result in being without a basis; thus, there is a contradiction with experience (*pratītibādhā*).
The phrase "the representation of 'past' and so forth" means that the determination of "past" and so forth constitutes the cognition (*pratyaya*).
Furthermore, demonstrating that [the opponent's position] is non-pervasive, he shows the contradiction with experience itself, beginning with the words "In the case of injunctions, etc. (vidhyādau).
In a mass of meanings such as injunctions (*vidhi*) and the like, there is no determination of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Furthermore, when a negative particle (*nañ*) is joined with another negative particle, what kind of exclusion could possibly result?
Since particles such as *ca* (and) have no connection with the negative particle at all, there is no exclusion there either.
Furthermore, the exclusion of others (anyanivṛtti) cannot be designated as the meaning of a sentence.

In words such as "non-exclusion of others" (ananyāpoha), the denotable object itself cannot be determined; how much less, then, can there be an object of exclusion for words such as "knowable" (prameya) or "cognizable" (jñeya)? || 978–979 ||

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), invitations, summons, and so forth are included. There is no determination—that is, no apprehension—of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), which is the exclusion of other things (*anyavyavaccheda*).
The sense is that the reason for this is precisely what was stated previously: that in such cases, there exists nothing to be negated in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*).
What kind of exclusion could there be when a negative particle (*nañ*) is joined with another negative particle, as in "Devadatta does not not cook"?

There is no such thing as a double negation, because it is merely the contact with a positive injunction; furthermore, particles (*nipāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and prepositions (*karmapravacanīya*) are accepted as being words (*pada*), yet they have no connection with the negative particle *nañ* because they do not denote substantial entities (*asattvavacana*).

For instance, just as in cases such as "non-pot" (*aghaṭa*), when words like "pot" (*ghaṭa*) are connected with the negative particle (*nañ*), another object such as a cloth (*paṭa*) is apprehended; thus, by means of that exclusion, the meaning of the word "pot" devoid of the negative particle is determined. However, there is no such connection of the particles *ca* and so forth with the negative particle in expressions like "not *ca*" (*nacca*).
Nor is it logical for there to be an exclusion (*apohana*) by a negative particle that is not so connected.
Therefore, there is no exclusion in the case of *ca* and the other particles.
The meaning is that there is an absence of exclusion (apoha).

Furthermore, the meaning of a sentence is held to be a single variegated form, like a mottled color; therefore, the exclusion of others cannot be designated therein, because no counter-correlate (pratiyogin) with a fully established form is perceived.

Furthermore, that exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) in the form of the exclusion of non-Caitra and so forth—which is described here [in the case of] "Caitra, bring the cow" and the like by means of grasping the individual parts (*avayava-parigraha*)—would be merely the meaning of a word (*padārtha*), not the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*), because it is impossible to analyze a sentence in this way as being composed of parts. Thus, the established system of the meaning of words would be non-pervasive (*avyāpinī*). Moreover, in expressions such as "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) or "non-exclusion of others" (*ananyāpoha*), no denotable object other than a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) can be determined—that is, it is not perceived.

For instance: it is not merely the form of an exclusion (*apoha*) that is understood as the denoted object, because through a double negation there is a determination of only a positive entity (*vidhi*).
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), synonyms such as "exclusion from others" (*ananyavyāvṛtti*) and "differentiation from others" (*ananyavyavaccheda*) are included. [Objection:
But is this not redundant, since it is already covered by the rule "when a negative particle is joined with another negative particle"?
This is true;

however, it is stated again for the purpose of making it known that even by the very statement of one who maintains that "the meaning of a word is the exclusion of others" (anyāpoha), a positive injunction (vidhi) is intended.

For instance, in the case of the word "exclusion-of-others," the object to be excluded is the meaning of the word "non-exclusion-of-others," and that is not perceived as anything other than a positive injunction.

Furthermore, regarding those words such as "the cognizable" (*prameya*), "the knowable" (*jñeya*), and "the denotable" (*abhidheya*), there is nothing whatsoever that can be excluded (*apohya*), because everything possesses the very nature of being cognizable and so forth.

For instance, whatever is imagined to be excluded by these terms, when it is apprehended in the form of an exclusion, remains nothing other than having the nature of the "knowable" and so on; for it is impossible to exclude that which has not been made an object of cognition.
Consequently, because these [exclusions] lack a real object, the established system is non-pervasive. 977–978.

But was it not stated in the *Hetumukha* that, having postulated the "unknowable" (*ajñeya*) as a conceptual construct, inference regarding the "knowable" (*jñeya*) proceeds by means of its exclusion?
How then can there be a lack of pervasion (*avyāpitva*) in the determination of the meaning of words? To this, he says: "Having excluded," and so forth.
And in the conceptualization of what is to be excluded (apohya), it is better to assume the real entity itself;
furthermore, because the form of cognition is denied, no internal object is denoted.
Nor is there even the status of being "excluded" for that [internal object]; therefore, exclusion (apoha) is not established in them.
"The referent of words such as 'thus' (evam) and so forth cannot be defined by means of exclusion (apoha).

If even all that is knowable is conceived as its object of exclusion by virtue of being knowable, then it would be better to conceive the very thing itself—precisely in its positive form—as the word-meaning, since that is what is determined by worldly convention.
For in this way, neither the superimposition of the unperceived nor the denial of the perceived object would be committed; such is the intended meaning."
For this very reason, it was said that "this is better.

However, for those who say that the object of all words is nothing other than the reflection of a conceptual construction (*vikalpapratibimbaka*), and that it is this very thing which is called "denoted" and "excluded," he says the following in response: "And because the form of cognition is negated," and so forth.

Cognition is formless, while the external object possesses form; moreover, that [object], being connected with external space, is clearly perceived. Thus, we have refuted the existence of a form within cognition. Therefore, since an internal form mounted upon the intellect does not exist, it is illogical for words to denote such a thing. Furthermore, it is not logical for that internal object to be the referent of exclusion (*apoha*), precisely because of its non-existence.
Thus it is said: "among those [internal forms]."
Furthermore, in words such as "the object of cognition" (*prameya*) and so forth,

even for those words like "thus" (*evam*) or "in this way" (*ittham*), no object of exclusion (*apohya*) is perceived, because there is an absence of any counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) in the form of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*).
One might then argue that there exists a negandum in the form of a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), such as "not thus" (*naivam*), and so on.

This is not so; what has been stated here is as follows: even here, in the instruction "it is not not thus," there is a negation of a negation; however, that which is "thus" remains unnegated in its own essential nature, and thus the very same principle mentioned previously applies. 980
981 All of this has been set forth as stated by Kumārila; now, beginning with the words "Of the word 'all'," [the author] raises the objection against Apoha stated by Uddyotakara:
"And what object is conceived as the excluded referent (*vyavacchedya*) of the word 'all'?"
For there would be nothing whatsoever that is not a universal name for which [the exclusion] could be negated.

If it is argued that "one" and so forth are non-universals, then the exclusion of the object (arthāpoha) follows as a consequence; for the parts have been refuted, and the whole is not desired as something distinct from its parts.
Thus, regarding the meaning of a collective term, because the individuals [composing it] are excluded and because nothing else is desired, all such terms would result in being meaningless.
This applies even to words like "two" and so forth, which are intended here as referring to a collection.

By the negation of one and so forth, such [entities] would not exist. (985) Furthermore, as for that exclusion (*apoha*) which is said to be the meaning of the word "cow"—is it an entity or a non-entity? If it is an entity, is it a cow or a non-cow? (986)

If [you argue] that "non-cow" does not exist, this dispute concerns a matter characterized by a positive injunction. If a non-cow were the denotation of the word "cow," it would demonstrate an extraordinary skill regarding the meaning of words! Furthermore, this [position of yours] is not tenable as a mere negation, because [positive acts such as] commands and the like would be impossible.
For no one indeed understands non-existence from the word "cow.
He [the opponent] says:
"It is incorrect that exclusion (apoha) is the meaning of a word, because it is not all-pervasive."

Where there is a duality of categories, one is understood through the negation of the other—as in the word "cow," where the cow is understood and the non-cow is negated. However, this is not the case with every word;
for there is nothing such as "non-all" that could be excluded by the word "all."
Now, if you think that "one" and so forth—which are not the whole—are excluded by the word "all," that is not correct, because it would entail the fault of negating its own meaning.

For in this way, the word "all," functioning by excluding "one" and so forth, would become meaningless; since the limbs are prohibited, and there is no admission of a "possessor of limbs" (the whole) distinct from the limbs.
By the word *aṅga*, a single part (*ekadeśa*) is expressed.

In this way, all collective terms (*samudāya-śabda*), when functioning as negations of a part, would result in being meaningless, because no collection other than its constituents is admitted. Furthermore, since words such as "two" and so on denote a collection of objects, if one were to negate "one" and so forth, there would be nothing for them to collect; thus they would be meaningless. He demonstrates this by saying: "they would not be of such a kind."

The meaning is that those [entities] which are the objects of a collective synthesis (samuccaya) would not be of such a nature. Furthermore, as for this "exclusion of the non-cow" (*agovyavaccheda*)—the meaning of the word "cow" defined as "that which is not a non-cow"—is that a positive entity (*bhāva*) or a negative absence (*abhāva*)? If it is a positive entity, is it a cow or a non-cow?
If it is a cow, there is no dispute.
Now, if [you claim] it is "non-cow," then the meaning of the word "cow" would be "non-cow"—this is an extraordinary skill in understanding the meaning of words!
Or if [you claim] it is "absence," that is not tenable, because it is not an object of either the command or the comprehension;
for upon hearing the word, neither a command nor a comprehension could occur with respect to an absence.
He demonstrates this as follows: "Even this non-existence is not tenable," and so forth.

*Praiṣaṇa* means *praiṣa* (an injunction); it is the application [of a word] by the speaker for the sake of the listener. This is a property of the speaker, while *sampratipatti* (comprehension) is a property of the listener.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), all positive properties such as carrying, milking, and so forth are included;
furthermore, the meaning of a word is understood through cognition, and no one understands non-existence from the word "cow.

Furthermore, since exclusion (*apoha*) is of the nature of an action, its object must be stated. In this regard, concerning the exclusion expressed as "it is not a cow," is this exclusion of the cow or of the non-cow?
If the cow is the object, how can there be the absence of a cow in the cow itself?

If the non-cow is the object, how can there be a cognition of one thing based on an exclusion whose object is something else? For when a *khadira* tree is being cut, the cutting does not occur in a *palāśa* tree.
Now, regarding the negation of "non-cow" in relation to a cow—as in "a non-cow is not a cow"—by what means was "non-cowness" previously suggested such that it must now be negated?
Considering that the first two alternatives here are irrelevant, [the author], demonstrating only the third alternative, says: "A non-cow is not a cow," etc.
