Why is the meaning of the word "a non-cow is not a cow" accepted as *apoha* (exclusion)?
For by whom has "non-cowness" been attached [to the cow], such that it must be excluded?

(989) Furthermore, as for this exclusion of the non-cow (*agovyāvṛtti*) which is said to be the meaning of the word in the case of the cow—is it accepted as being distinct from the cow or non-distinct? (990)
Whether it be distinct [from the substance], or dependent upon it, or perhaps independent;
if it were dependent, it would follow that it is a quality (guṇa), and therefore it could not be denoted as a substance.
Consequently, by the word "cow" (gaur), there would be the expression of a mere quality.

There would be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [between "cow" and "goes"], but one does not say, "The cow goes," or "The cow stands. (992) Now, if this object were entirely without a substratum, what would it be by virtue of which it is designated as "the cow" for the purpose of negation, such that one says, "the non-cow"? (993)
Moreover, if this "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is held by you to be non-different [from the cow], then it follows that this is simply the cow itself; what more has been said than that?
(Verse 994) The word *ca* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*).
And for what reason do you say that the meaning of the word "cow" is defined by the exclusion (*apoha*) of "non-cow"? This is the sense of the sentence.
Why, then, should this not be stated? He says: "By whom," and so forth; furthermore, *apoha* is untenable because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is impossible.
For instance: Is this "exclusion of the non-cow" (*agorapoha*) in the cow distinct from the cow, or is it non-distinct? If it is distinct, is it dependent (*āśrita*) or independent (*anāśrita*)?

If it is dependent, then by virtue of being dependent, it follows that it is a quality (*guṇa*); consequently, the word "cow" would denote only a quality and not the non-cow, and thus grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "the cow stands" or "the cow walks" would not be possible.
If, on the other hand, it is independent, then for what reason would there be a genitive case in the expression "the exclusion of the non-cow"? (i.e., why "of the non-cow"?)
Now, if it were non-different [from the cow], then that would simply be the cow itself; thus, nothing at all would have been accomplished.
This exclusion (apoha), which corresponds to each individual manifestation, may be either one or many.
If it were one, then being connected with many cows, it would simply be "cowness" itself.

Even if it were manifold, its infinity would be associated with it just as it is with individual objects; therefore, its denotability is not applicable in the same way as that of distinct particulars.
Furthermore, it must be stated whether this exclusion (apoha) is one or many with respect to each object.
If it were one, then it would be nothing other than the universal "cowness" (gotva) related to multiple individual cows;
if, on the other hand, it were many, then— due to its infinity like that of the individuals— it could not be designated, and thus it would simply be inexpressible.
And is this "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) intended to be denotable or undenotable? Even if it is denotable, is it so by way of a positive form or through the negation of another? 997.
If this [universal] were denotable by way of its positive nature, then the view of exclusivity would have to be abandoned;
for it has been described that the meaning of a word consists everywhere in the exclusion of others.
Now, if the exclusion (apoha) itself is denoted through the setting aside of other exclusions, [then...]
In each such case, if there were a desire [to apply another exclusion], an infinite regress would result. Moreover, if this *apoha* is held by you to be truly inexpressible,
then your own statement that "the word effects the exclusion of others" (*anyāpohakṛcchabda*) would be contradicted.
Furthermore, you must first be asked this: is apoha denotable or undenotable?

If it is denotable, is it denoted by way of a positive form (*vidhirūpa*) or by way of the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*)? In that regard, if it were by way of a positive form, then the word-meaning would not be exclusively "the exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*). Thus, [your thesis] that "the word-meaning is the exclusion of others" is not absolute.

If, on the other hand, the position is that it is "by means of the exclusion of others," then there would be an infinite regress (*avyavasthā*), because that exclusion of others would have to be expressed by another exclusion of others, and that too by yet another.
Alternatively, if it is "inexpressible," then the claim that "a word effects the exclusion (*apoha*) of the meaning of other words" would be contradicted.

All of this has been stated and presented by Uddyotakara. Regarding that, Ācārya Dignāga stated: "Because the substratum is undifferentiated everywhere, because it is not subject to destruction, and because it is fully present in its entirety, the properties of a universal (*jāti*)—characterized respectively by unity, eternity, and individual pervasion—reside in *apoha* alone. Therefore, even on account of the excellence of qualities, it is correct that the meaning of a word is precisely the exclusion of other objects (*arthāntarāpoha*).

Anticipating this objection, Kumārila, in his concluding summary, says: "Moreover, [the properties of] unity, eternity, and individual inherence... and so forth, referring to those things which possess the state of being inherent.
When [the mind] operates upon exclusions (*apoha*) that are devoid of any positive designation, what further "thread" could there be to produce a "cloth"?

Therefore, only in those words where there is a connection with the negative particle (*nañ*) would there be a portion consisting of the exclusion of others; elsewhere, only its own nature is understood. (1001–1002)
"In those very words where there is a connection with the negative particle (*nañ*), such as in 'an edible village pig' and so forth,
it is [the negation] of its own self."
In other cases, where the negative particle is absent, the very nature [of the thing] is characterized as an injunction.

1001 1002 Having thus raised the opponent's objection according to its primary points, he begins the refutation with the words "because of the lack of understanding of the exclusion of others" (*anyāpohāparijñānāt*), and so forth.
Because they do not fully understand the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), these people of wrong views, being self-satisfied and ruined, are evil-natured and destroy others as well.
For instance, exclusion (apoha) is of two kinds: by way of relative negation (paryudāsa) and absolute negation (niṣedha).
Exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is also twofold, based on the distinction between that which has the nature of cognition and that which has the nature of an object.
"By way of exclusion and negation" means:
[it is] characterized as exclusion because of exclusion, and as absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) because of negation.
"Due to the distinction between the nature of cognition and the nature of the object" means due to the distinction between the nature of cognition and the nature of the object.

In this context, the "nature of cognition" refers to the appearance in cognition which is determined as having a single, uniform form that persists across objects; the "nature of the object" refers to the intrinsic nature of the object, namely the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the object as excluded from what is heterogeneous.
The compound "vibhāga" (division) is a [tatpuruṣa] compound meaning "the distinction between these two.
In this regard, showing the nature of the essence of cognition (buddhi), he says: "The causes of a single reflective awareness," and so forth.
Those objects which were previously stated to be the causes of a single reflective awareness—such as fearlessness and the like—are by their very nature distinct from others. (1005)
"Depending upon those [mental impressions], that reflection of an object which appears in cognition—
even though it lacks the nature of the object in its conceptualizing aspect— is determined to be 'objects' themselves. (Verse 1006) "As before," [it was said].

In the previous examination of the universal (*sāmānya*), it was stated in the passage beginning with "just as the *dhātrī*, *abhaya*, and so forth," and therein it was said: "Just as many things such as the *harītakī* produce the effect characterized by the alleviation of fever and the like even without a single common universal,

so too will objects such as the brindled cow (*sāvaleyādi*) be the causes of a uniform reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) by their very nature, even while existing as distinct entities, without a real, ontological universal."
"Equal to *abhayā* and so forth" means they are similar to *harītakī* and the like;
their equality consists in their performing the same purposeful function.

The connection [of the sentence] is as follows: "depending on those" means depending upon those objects that have the same purpose, such as fearlessness and so forth; having made them the cause, the conceptual cognition (*vikalpaka-jñāna*) which arises by the power of experiencing them—in that [cognition], the reflection of the object (*arthapratibimbaka*), which is the appearance of the object (*arthābhāsa*), shines forth as if identical with the object itself; in that [reflection], the term "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is applied. Thus ends the section on "conceptualizing."
"In conceptual" means "possessing conceptualization";
and this [term] is in grammatical apposition with "cognition," [as implied by the phrase] "even in the absence of being the nature of the object."
Even though the nature of external objects does not exist,
it is "ascertained," meaning it is determined through conceptual construction.
Now, as to how there is this designation "its exclusion" (*tasyāpoha*), he says: "From another appearance," and so forth.

Because it is distinct from other appearances, and because it serves as the cause for attaining a real entity excluded from others, there is also a movement toward that entity by way of the [conceptual] object which is not [directly] connected [to the particular].
That result, which is the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), is excluded from what is of a different class.
Or, because of the determination [of the object] as being identical with that [exclusion],
this designation "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) is stated for it based on a valid ground;
its name "exclusion" (apoha) is given due to four reasons.
It is primarily called *apoha* because it manifests itself as distinct from other manifestations superimposed by other conceptual constructions;
this is based on the etymological derivation that "it is excluded" (*apohyate*) or "exclusion from others" (*anyasmād apohaḥ*), i.e., "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).
However, it is used figuratively in three ways.

(1) Either because the properties of the effect are superimposed upon the cause—as it is said: "by way of being the cause for the attainment of the object excluded from others"—or (2) because the properties of the cause are metaphorically attributed to the effect; this he demonstrates by saying: "even by way of reaching an unconnected object.
"Unconnected" (*aśliṣṭa*) means not related to anything else, that is to say, excluded from others.
That very object is the means (*upāya*), because through the power of experiencing it, such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises;

and because it is determined (*adhyavasita*) by deluded cognizers as being one with the referent of the exclusion of dissimilar things (*vijātīyāpoha*). This is the fourth cause. He shows this with the words "vijātīya" etc., [referring to] "of this" (*asya*).

The term *sanibandhanā* means that it exists together with its basis (*nibandhana*), namely, the fourfold [basis] already mentioned— such as the distinction from other appearances— which belongs to the reflection of the object mounted upon the conceptualizing intellect (*vikalpabuddhi*). Thus, it is "with a basis."
Showing the essential nature of apoha as having the object itself as its essence, he says: "Even in the case of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)," and so forth.

The connection with the subject at hand is as follows: even in the case of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) which is its cause, this designation "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is stated to be well-founded because of the existence of the exclusion of other [things].
Regarding that, he states the reason: "because of the existence of the exclusion of other [things]."

"From another," meaning from that which is of a different class (*vijātīya*); "separation" (*viśleṣa*) means exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*); "because of its existence" means because of the presence of that separation from what is of a different class.
By this, it is stated that, primarily, the designation "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) applies to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself.
He demonstrates the essential nature of apoha, characterized as a non-presuppositional negation (prasajyapratiṣedha), with the words beginning "prasajya":
"And a non-presuppositional negation is [the case where] 'this cow is not a non-cow'."
This exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is indeed understood with extreme clarity.

Having thus established the threefold nature of apoha, he says—beginning with "In that case, this..."—while applying it to the subject at hand, the meaning of words: "In that case, this first [type of] apoha is conveyed by words."
Because cognition that determines external objects arises from words,
the first [cognition] consists of a reflection of the object as it has been described.
Regarding this, he states the reason: "of that which determines an external object," and so forth.

For whatever indeed appears in verbal cognition is appropriately the meaning of the word; however, in this case, there is no determination of a non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), nor is there an appearance of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as in sensory cognition. What then? A verbal cognition arises solely as one that determines an external object.

Therefore, that very reflection of the object is appropriately the meaning of the word, because it appears directly in verbal cognition by way of having that [reflection] as its nature, and not anything else—this is the sense.

Furthermore, he demonstrates that the well-known relationship between a word and its object, characterized as the signifier-signified relation (*vācyavācakabhāva*), does not exist apart from the cause-and-effect relationship; rather, it is essentially of the nature of cause and effect: "In the arising of a cognition [bearing] a reflection of that form, and from the word... and so forth.

This relationship between the signified and the signifier (*vācyavācakabhāva*) arises as having the nature of cause and effect (*hetuphalātmaka*). That is to say, when the production or arising from a word occurs for that reflection—which is of such a nature (defined by the characteristic of having an externalized form superimposed upon it)—that relationship, when examined, is found to consist solely of the relation of cause and effect.

For instance—the echo is called the "designator" (*vācaka*) because it generates a reflection, and that reflection is the "designated" (*vācya*) because it is produced by the sound. Therefore, what was stated—that "mere negation does not appear here in verbal cognition"—is inconsistent; the point is that mere negation is not accepted as the meaning of a word.

Thus far, it has been shown that exclusion (*apoha*) characterized as a reflected image (*pratibimba*) is the primary meaning of a word, because it is directly produced by words. Now, demonstrating that even for the remaining two types of exclusion, their status as the word-meaning is figurative and thus not contradictory, he says: "Directly," and so forth.
When this [reflected image] is established as the direct form, even the non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) is understood by implication. (1013)

When there is a relation [of exclusion] such that "this is not its own nature" or "this is the nature of another," the comprehension of an object as excluded from other things occurs by implication (arthāt) alone;
therefore, this too is figuratively designated as the word's own meaning (svārtha).
But this twofold apoha is not said to be directly verbal [in nature].
"And thus" means by way of being produced.
Furthermore, demonstrating why a *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) is understood through implication, he says: "It is not its nature.
This is because the nature (*ātman*) of that reflection of a cow or the like is not the nature—that is, the intrinsic essence (*svabhāva*)—of another reflection such as a horse or the like.

Having thus established that the denotation of a word is secondary (*gauṇa*) due to the necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatayā*) with the understanding of exclusion characterized as absolute negation, he now establishes this for the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as well, saying: "When there is a relation," and so forth.

In that regard, the connection of a word with a real entity is an indirect bond characterized by the relation of cause and effect. First, there is the experience of the object as it actually exists; from that, the desire to speak arises; from that, the movement of the palate and other vocal organs; and from that, the word. When such a succession constitutes the connection of the word with external objects such as fire, then, given that connection, there occurs the comprehension of the object—even though it is excluded from things of a different class—by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Therefore, both types of non-presuppositional negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) and exclusion (*apoha*), which consists in a real entity differentiated from others, are figuratively designated as "this" as the meaning of a word,
while [the other type] has the specifically characterized particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its nature.
By the word "also" (api), the nature of the prasajya [negation] is likewise [indicated].

Regarding what was said by Uddyotakara concerning the teacher Diṅnāga: "If the exclusion (apoha) of a word is not the denoted object—that is, if the exclusion of the word 'non-cow' is not the thing to be expressed—then its own meaning must be stated apart from the denoted object. Or, if that [exclusion] itself is its own meaning, even so it is contradictory; for it is said that a word expresses by performing the exclusion of the meanings of other words within its own meaning. For at that time, the meaning of this statement becomes: "It is called 'expressing' because it expresses [its own meaning]."

Demonstrating that this was stated due to a failure to understand the meaning of the sentence, he establishes that there is no contradiction with the Master’s own words: "By excluding other objects," and so forth; that [statement] is not contradictory, for it means that the scripture expresses its own object while effecting the exclusion of other objects. (1016)

For it has been established that even the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is, by way of metaphorical designation, the word's own referent (*svārtha*). Therefore, when a word produces—that is, generates—an exclusion (*apoha*) consisting of a reflection that is excluded from other reflections, which constitutes the exclusion of other objects within that own referent consisting of the particular characteristic, it is said to "denote" it; this statement of the Teacher (Dharmakīrti) is not contradictory. With the words beginning "bāhyārtha," etc., [the author] explains this very statement of the Teacher.
By determining an external object, it produces a reflection through which it is designated as "this";
however, this [cognition] does not touch the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) that possesses differentiation.
Apart from the mere portion consisting of that [mental image], it has no other act of denoting.
This is the Master’s intention:
that for a word, no function of denoting an external object is possible other than the production of a conceptual reflection (*vikalpapratibimba*) which determines an external object.

Because all phenomena are devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*), the scripture (*śruti*) is said to express its own meaning by producing a conceptual reflection that functions through the determination of an external object; however,
it does not touch upon a distinct particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— excluded from both similar and dissimilar classes— because such a thing is beyond its capacity to act.
The phrase "beyond the mere measure" means that there is no other act of denotation (*abhidhā*) for the Veda apart from its capacity to produce such a reflection.
Having thus stated the nature of apoha, he now begins to refute the objections raised by others.
Regarding what was said—"If the word 'cow' [is applied]," and so forth—he replies with the words "And of that," etc.
And when that reflection moves, its separation from others is understood by implication, because it does not possess the nature of anything else.

(1019) For the word produces only the cognition of a cow; however, the exclusion of others is understood through implication, not directly from the word, because that reflection of a cow is devoid of the nature of any other appearance. Otherwise, there would be no apprehension of it as having a determinate form.
Therefore, no other sound need be sought as the producer of the cognition of a cow,
since the cognition of a cow is produced by that very word "cow" alone.

Regarding the objection that "words have knowledge as their fruit," he says: "Like the sentence regarding eating by day," and so forth. This [word] also has two fruits, both directly and through its capacity, because there is no positive concomitance (anvaya) that is devoid of negative concomitance (avyatireka). 1020.

For example, in the sentence "Devadatta is fat because he does not eat during the day," the explicit expression of its own meaning is the prohibition of eating during the day; however, the injunction to eat at night is what is understood, not explicitly. In the same way, for a word such as "cow" which conveys a positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the direct result is the cognition of that concomitance, whereas the understanding of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) arises through implication.
He states the reason for this: "Because," and so forth;
because there is no positive concomitance of an injunction that is devoid of negative concomitance.
What then? It is precisely that which is non-deviant in its exclusion of dissimilar instances; for there is no possibility of anything whatsoever that is not excluded from the dissimilar.
Therefore, it is entirely consistent for a single word to have two results.
He asks "Why? and says: "Because sound does not produce these two directly," and so forth.
The expression of its own meaning and the exclusion of another thing—

(1021) if it were intended that a single word simultaneously produces two results for one [object], namely the cognition of affirmation and negation, then there would be a contradiction. However, if— as in the case of the sentence regarding eating by day— it is accepted that one result is direct while the other is obtained through implication (*sāmarthya*), then there is no contradiction.
Furthermore, what was stated previously regarding the cognition "it is not a cow" and so forth is also refuted,
because it is not accepted [by us].
For we do not maintain that the word "cow" directly expresses the negation of non-cows;
rather, it has been demonstrated that this occurs through implication (sāmarthyāt).
Regarding what was stated—that the exclusion of the non-cow (*agotva-nivṛtti*) is the universal (*sāmānya*), and so forth—he says: "Such a manifestation," and so on.

Such a manifestation is accepted as the universal, *gotva* (cowness), because it is determined as being identical across all [individuals], such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others. || 1022 ||
"Such [an object]" means that which is superimposed as an external form and ascended upon the intellect;
here he states the justification with the words "everywhere," and so forth.
Because there is a determination of the form "cow, cow" with identical uniformity in all cases such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) and others, that [form] is called their universal (*sāmānya*).

He shows that its status as an external object is also designated only by virtue of the cognition of deluded perceivers, and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), by stating: "and because of the determination [of it] as a real thing."
And because it is determined as "a real object," it is also called a "real object";
for that cognition, being erroneous, arises instantly from its own seed.

[Objection: Now, if at some time a primary real entity in the form of a universal were perceived as residing in an external object, then, through the perception of similarity, an error regarding a universal might occur there; however, since a primary object is impossible, that very error of yours regarding a universal is untenable. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For it arises instantly," and so forth.

"Instantly"—this cognition has arisen from an internal disturbance (*antar-upaplava*), without depending on the perception of common characteristics (*sāmānya-darśana*) and so forth, just like the cognition of two moons and the like.
For not all errors arise solely from the perception of similarity; rather, they also arise from internal disturbances. Thus, there is no fault.
Showing that, therefore, the fault of proving what is already established does not occur, he says: "And that very [exclusion] is called the word-meaning in the form of that," and so forth.
And because it is determined through such an error as being a commonality and a real entity;
that very form of the cognition, superimposed as something external, is called "exclusion" (apoha), the "meaning of a word," and a "commonality" (sāmānya) consisting of an external object.
He states the reason for this here: "because it is determined through such an error."
The reason why [the object] is both the referent of a word and of the nature of apoha has already been stated: because a cognition that determines an external object arises from a word,
and because it is distinct from other appearances, and so forth.
Why, then, does that [universal] not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality? He says: "The universal," and so forth;
for its having the nature of a real universal entity is not tenable as something ultimately real (*bhāvika*).
For how could that which is non-different in nature from cognition proceed to become a different object?

(1025) In ultimate reality, this [universal] is not distinct from cognition; therefore, how could it become a different object, by virtue of which that universal of objects would exist as a real entity?
As it has been said: "And how could that which is non-distinct from knowledge proceed to become a different object?"

Therefore, the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) does not occur; for you do not accept that the universal called "cowness" (*gotva*), which is the form of cognition, is of an unreal nature. What then? You have postulated an external, unitary, and recurring, ultimate universal such as cowness residing in individual cows like the brindled one (*śābaleya*). Thus, there is no fault of proving the already established—this is the sense. As for what was said regarding its being "of the nature of a mere negation," etc., since that is not accepted [by us], there is no fault.
Regarding what was stated—"And in that [cognition], the cognitions of horses and so forth," and so on—he says: "Even though," and so forth.
Even though this form is not distinct from the nature of the cognition, nevertheless its status as an external object is determined by those who are deluded. (1026)
This is easily understood.
Regarding what was stated— that the word-meaning is independent of the object-meaning— he says "of that," and so forth.

It does not follow that such [conceptual cognition] is independent of objects, because it arises from a causal lineage originating therein; furthermore, it has been established that it lacks substantial reality in its own nature.

For when there is a connection to a real entity through a causal lineage, even though it is an erroneous conceptualization—like the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel—it is not independent of external objects.

Therefore, the claim that cognition is independent of external objects—as stated in the passage beginning "And that cognition has the nature of a real entity"—is unestablished. To this, he replies with the words "By that," and so forth:

although that cognition has the nature of a real entity, it has been demonstrated by the passage beginning "That is not its own nature, nor the nature of another" that it lacks the status of a real entity in terms of that external self or the self of another cognition.
The point is that it is unestablished [to claim] that "the exclusion of one cognition by another is not understood" by that [cognition], because it is understood through implication (sāmarthya).
Regarding the statement "even when an external object does not exist," he says: "consisting of a reflection," and so forth.

Exclusion (*apoha*) consisting of a reflection arises even from a word; this very thing, called intuition (*pratibhā*), is for us the meaning of the word as well. (1028) For just as exclusion consisting of a reflection, called intuition, has been described by us as the external object in the case of the sentence-meaning, so too is it the word-meaning.

Since exclusion (*apoha*) consisting of a reflection (*pratibimba*) arises even from a word (*pada*), this very exclusion consisting of a reflection is considered by us to be the meaning of the word (*padārtha*) as well—not only the external object or the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*); this is the sense of the word "also" (*api*).
Therefore, because there is no disagreement [on this point], a censure is not appropriate; such is the intention.
Regarding the claim that "the exclusion from other cognitions is not perceived by the cognition itself," he says: "Because it consists merely in the production of its own nature," and so forth.
Indeed, because it consists merely in the production of its own nature, it does not bear any other part; therefore, the exclusion from other cognitions is perceived by the cognition. (1029)

For precisely because that cognition does not bear any part other than the mere production of its own nature, it is therefore—by virtue of being established in its own intrinsic being—that the exclusion of one cognition from another is perceived. Otherwise, if it were bearing the form of something else, how could it be perceived as excluded from that?
Thus, [the exclusion] occurs through the non-apprehension of the nature of an object distinct from itself.
Regarding the passage beginning with "words denoting distinct universals," he says: "Just as... and so forth;
just as for that which does not exist, there is no ultimate distinction.
Non-difference is likewise [non-existent]; therefore, there would be synonymy.

For just as it is said that because exclusion (*apoha*) lacks intrinsic nature and has no existing form, there is no mutual difference between them, so too is non-difference [non-existent]. Thus, in the absence of any distinct objects, how can the consequence of synonymy be urged?
Clarifying this very point, he says: "For non-difference is the state of having a single form. [Objection: But how can there be that [single form] in things that are formless? [Response:
If the object were a single unity, then its various synonyms would necessarily become its denoters. (1031)

If it is argued: "Even if there is no single form (*ekarūpatva*) among things that lack form (*nīrūpa*), why should synonymy (*paryāyatā*) not still occur? he replies with the verse beginning *ekatve 'rthasya* (1031). It might be thought: "Even if there is indeed no real (*bhāvataḥ*) single form among formless things, there is nevertheless a conceptual (*kālpānika*) one; therefore, the consequence of synonymy is entirely appropriate. To this he replies with the verse beginning *rūpābhāve 'pi*.
"And even in the absence of a [real] form, oneness is constructed by conceptualization;
just as so too is difference. Therefore, how could there be synonymy from that?
(1032) "Even in the absence of a form" means:
The meaning is: "even though there is an absence of intrinsic nature" (svabhāva).
If this is so, how is the distinction between synonymous and non-synonymous words established? To this he says: "In reality, however," and so forth.
In reality, however, words are neither synonyms nor non-synonyms; for it has been explained that there is no single external object denoted by them, nor is there a plurality.
(1033) For if, from the perspective of ultimate reality, there were some denotable entity—whether distinct or non-distinct—that belonged to words, then they would either be non-synonyms or synonyms.

To the extent that it has been described—by means of [the categories] the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), the genus (*jāti*), its connection (*tadyoga*), and the possessor of the genus (*jātimat*), and so forth—that there is nothing whatsoever to be expressed by these [words], [one might ask]: "In that case, how is the systematic arrangement of synonyms and so forth established? To this, he says: "But rather... and so on.
However, even if many [entities] are observed to perform a single function, a single word is applied there by superimposing a single property upon them.

In this regard, even in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*), the basis for establishing the status of a word as a "universal term" is this: that many [entities] possess the capacity to produce a single effect.

For by their very nature, some entities, even though many, perform a single purposeful action; in order to demonstrate their capacity for that single purposeful action, a single term is applied by speakers through the superimposition of a single form for the sake of brevity.

For example, among many [qualities] such as color and so forth, which are capable of performing the single purposeful action characterized by fetching honey, water, and the like, the term "jar" is applied.
But how, in the absence of a single following [cause], is it logical for there to be a single auditory perception among many? To this he says: "In the case of the eye, etc. and so forth.
Just as in some cases, such as with the eye and other [senses], there is a single result, namely the cognition of form; |||
If someone were to apply a verbal designation (*śruti*) [to a group of things] even without a single accompanying universal (*anugāmin*), [it would be possible].

For the application of words to objects is dependent solely upon one’s own will; for instance, regarding the eye, visible form, light, and mental attention—which have the single result of visual consciousness—if someone, by the force of their will, were to apply a verbal designation such as "universal" (*sāmānya*) even without a single accompanying universal, who could possibly prevent them?
Indeed, among those [factors] such as the eye and so forth, there exists no single universal called "the state of being a producer of visual consciousness."
For you also maintain that universals (*sāmānya*), particulars (*viśeṣa*), and inherence (*samavāya*) are producers of visual consciousness;
yet, universals and inherence do not exist within those [particulars], because a universal is devoid of further universals, and because inherence lacks a second inherence.

Now, one might object: how can a jar or the like be said to perform a single function, given that its effects—such as holding water—and the cognition apprehending it are indeed differentiated by the distinctness of their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*)? To this, he says: "And of jars, etc.
and so forth; the effect of jars and the like is the holding of water and so on.
And although that cognition which has those [objects] as its domain is distinct— even though it is twofold—
it is called "one" because it is the cause of a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*).
Nevertheless, by virtue of being the cause of that [cognition], the objects are non-different.

Although that effect differs due to the difference in their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, the effect known as cognition is said to be "one" because it is the cause of a reflective awareness (*parāmarśajñāna*) that determines a single object. And because they serve as the causes of that cognition, the objects—characterized by the fetching of honey, water, and so forth, as well as by individual instances such as jars—are also said to be "non-different. He demonstrates this: "Nevertheless, because they are the cause of that [cognition], the objects are said to be non-different";
here, the word "are said" (*ucyante*), which was in the context [of the previous sentence] in the plural form, is connected [to the current subject] through a change of grammatical number.
The word "api" (also/even), being displaced in its order, is connected immediately after the word "arthāḥ" (objects);
by this, the capacity to perform a single purposeful action is indeed established.
But surely, in this way, an infinite regress would result?
For instance: that reflective cognition (pratyavamarśa-pratyaya) itself is differentiated by the differentiation of its own particulars (svalakṣaṇa), and thus its unity is unestablished.
Consequently, for one who pursues a further single-form effect of reflective cognition in order to establish its unity, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā).
And because of this lack of a settled single effect, the application of a single linguistic term (eka-śruti) to anything would never be established.
This is not so;
for we do not assert the unity of the reflective cognition (pratyavamarśapratyaya) on the basis of its having a single effect.
What then? On the basis of its determining a single object. Therefore, there will be no infinite regress.
Since it is established by its very nature that all reflective cognitions (*pratyavamarśa-pratyaya*) possess the determination of a single object, the following meaning results:

because they are the cause of a single-form reflective cognition, the effect known as "cognition" is said to be one; and because they are the cause of that [cognition], objects such as jars and the like also partake of the designation of unity.
Concluding that even without a real entity as a universal, things such as jars are established as being denotable by general terms, he says: "In that case," and so forth.
In this regard, words such as "jar" and so forth, which are said to be general expressions, are the single causes for a reflection that is excluded from those of a different class.
Showing that even with respect to a single object, the application of multiple unmixed words occurs even without a universal-particular (*sāmānya-viśeṣa*), he says: "In that way," and so forth.

Likewise, because it performs multiple functions, that which is one is spoken of as if it were many; this is conceptually constructed based on its manifold exclusion (*parāvṛtti*) from things that do not perform those functions.
Even though something is inherently one, by virtue of entering into various causal complexes (*sāmagrī*), it comes to perform multiple purposeful actions.

In that regard, even without a distinction of properties such as a real universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth, many designations are applied through the superimposition of multiple properties due to the multiplicity of distinctions among entities that do not produce those [specific] effects.
(1039) He provides an example for this, beginning with "Just as... and so forth.

Just as resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is also [said to be] visible (*sanidarśana*), or as sound is known to arise immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarajñāta*), or as sound is inaudible (*aśrāvaṇa*);
form is called "resistant" because it acts as an obstacle to the arising of another in its own location.
The illustration is: visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*). Because it produces that [consciousness], it exists together with it; thus, it is "with demonstration" (*sanidarśana*).
He states a second example as well, beginning with "effort" (*prayatna*):
for just as sound, though being one, is said to be "known after effort" because it is the result of knowledge following effort.
And because it is the fruit of auditory cognition, it is "audible" (*śrāvaṇa*);
for "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) is indeed "audition" (*śruti*), which is to say auditory cognition; that which exists as manifested therein is "audible."
Alternatively, it is "auditory" (*śrāvaṇa*) because it is grasped by hearing.

Thus, it has been shown that even in the case of a single [object], multiple designations are applied through the distinction of its non-causes; now, he shows that in some cases a designation is applied even through the distinction of its non-causes, beginning with the words "through the distinction of its non-causes," etc.
In some cases, a word is applied by way of excluding its cause;
for example, the word "sound" [is used] as "arising from effort," or "honey" as "bhrāmara" (bee-honey).
Regarding "bhrāmara":
[The term] "made by bees" excludes honey produced by small insects and the like;
thus, the difference in scriptural designations for a single entity has been shown based on the distinction between such non-causal and causal categories.

Now, desiring to demonstrate that the application of a word to a particular object occurs merely through the exclusion of its effects and causes—even in the absence of a universal—he says: "Because of the distinction from its effects and causes, a word is here applied to something; for example, 'color is not audible,' or 'lightning is not produced by effort. (1042)
From those [things] which have the aforementioned effect and cause as their nature—that is, from those things that possess such characteristics—there is a separation, meaning an exclusion.
What, then, is this "hearing" (śruti)? He says: "non-hearable" (aśrāvaṇa), and so forth.
Just as form is said to be "inaudible" by way of excluding sound, which is the result of auditory cognition,
so too lightning is designated as "not produced by effort" by way of excluding objects such as pots, which have effort as their cause.

Having thus demonstrated that even in the absence of a real entity such as a universal (*sāmānya*), the application of words through differentiation is based solely on exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), he states the following to show that there is no consequence of synonymy: "By means of [the phrase] beginning with 'thus'... and so forth.
"Exclusions are postulated as being based on distinct objects through various subdivisions; likewise, the linguistic expressions (*śruti*) are grounded in those [exclusions]. (1043)
Therefore, for us, words that denote distinct objects according to convention function through differentiation and are not synonyms.
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), words denoting specific states such as "child" and so forth, as well as words such as "selflessness" (nairātmya) and the like, are included.

"Based on distinct objects" (*vibhinnārthanibandhanā*) means those exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) for which the basis (*nibandhana*) is an object (*artha*) that is distinct—that is, excluded—from this or that; they are described as such.
Thus it is said.
Just like the exclusion itself,
they are "based upon that," meaning they are based upon the excluded object.
The "śrutis" are words, because they are the cause for the comprehension of such objects through a serial process.

It might be argued: "Let it be that these [terms] are not synonyms, since their difference in meaning is merely conceptualized; however, how can the establishment of their denoting a universal or a particular be proven without actual universals and particulars? To this, he says: "Many and few," and so forth.
Because their objects are extensive or limited, and because they lead to the inference of that [exclusion],
it is not contradictory for these [words] to express both the universal and the particular.
For the word "tree" produces a reflected image that leads to the inference of the mere exclusion of non-trees with respect to all [trees], such as the *dhava*, *khadira*, and *palāśa*.
Therefore, because its scope is manifold, the denotable object of this [word "tree"] is said to be a universal (*sāmānya*);

however, because the word "dhava" and so forth produces a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that determines only a few specific trees by excluding others such as the *khadira*, its denotable object is said to be a particular (*viśeṣa*).
Regarding the objection beginning with "But [if there were] no difference in the excluded objects," etc., he says: "And those," and so forth.
Those exclusions (vyāvṛttayaḥ) of objects, being constructed by mere conceptualization, do not differ in reality according to the difference in the excluded objects or their substrates. (1046)

For if the distinction between exclusions (apoha) were intended to be real based on the distinction between the objects to be excluded or the distinction between their substrates, then this objection would apply; however, since these exclusions— which are based on the distinctions between similar and dissimilar entities— are differentiated only through conceptual construction and not in reality,
[the author] shows that they appear as distinct from the entity only by virtue of conceptual construction and not in reality, stating "tāsāṃ hi" and so forth.
For their external form is imagined and not real; moreover, difference and non-difference are established in reality only with respect to an actual entity.
[The author] asks, "Why is it not real? and replies with the words "difference and non-difference," etc. (v. 1047).
1047 However, from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is conceptual constructions themselves that are differentiated; this is shown by the verse beginning with "svabījāneka... and so forth.
Due to the power of conventions regarding objects that are distinct from their own seeds,
conceptual constructions (vikalpas) arise as differentiated, determining those very forms;
yet they do not attain a single nature, nor are they divided into fragments.

Objects consist of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), yet this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) floats over them. The analysis of the compound is as follows: its own seed is the predisposition (*vāsanā*) for conceptual constructions of wind and so forth, as well as the object distinguished from many [others] and the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*); the "power" (*śakti*) of these is their capacity. It is from that [capacity] that conceptual constructions—which determine an object excluded from many heterogeneous things—are differentiated, but not the objects themselves.

For instance: trees such as the *dhava* and others do not attain a single identity by way of a universal form such as "treeness," nor are they divided into fragments by way of distinctions in properties such as momentariness;
rather, it is only conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that flows in such a manner, but not the actual object (*artha*).
As it has been said: "Ultimate objects are neither conjoined nor divided in themselves."
"Form is both one and many; [this notion] regarding them is a delusion of the intellect.
Regarding what was stated—"Nor [is it possible] for those whose similarity is unestablished," and so forth—he replies: "Even in the absence of the persistence of a single property," and so on;
"even in the absence of the persistence of a single property, [cognitions] have as their objects the exclusion (apoha) of that which is to be excluded."
They are understood through their distinctness by means of different conceptual determinations (pratyavamarśa).
The analysis [of the compound] is: "those to be excluded (apohya) and those that are the objects of exclusion (apoha-gocara).
In this context, horses and so forth are the things to be excluded, because the word "cow" functions by excluding them.

Individuals such as the *śābaleya* (the brindled cow) have exclusion (*apoha*) as their objective domain; since the exclusion of the non-cow has them as its object, even if there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of a single universal form among them, nevertheless, those which are the causes of a non-differentiated reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) possess well-known similarity, while those that are the opposite are the opposite.

It might be argued: "How can distinct objects be established as the causes of that very single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśa*) without a single universal? To this he says: "For in a single unifying cognition... and so forth.
For it has been demonstrated that, although they possess difference by their very nature, only certain things are useful for a single unifying cognition, while others are not. (1051)

This has been established in the *Sāmānyaparīkṣā*: just as a nurse and other such entities perform a single purposeful action even without a universal (*sāmānya*), so too certain distinct entities will serve as the causes for a reflective judgment (*pratyavamarśa*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "nor [is it] devoid of positive concomitance" (*nacānvayavinirmukta*), he says: "not having that nature" (*atadrūpa*), and so forth.
The particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is the mere thing (*vastumātra*) excluded from what does not possess its form;
thus, this positive concomitance (*anvaya*) being established through effort is not contradictory.

(1052) Even though a universal (*sāmānya*) as a real entity does not exist, nevertheless, positive concomitance being established by means of the mere particular characteristic itself—which is excluded from heterogeneous classes—is not contradictory.
How so? He says: "In which," and so forth;
for in that [which is under discussion], there exists a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) distinct from smoke.
In that [locus], even though it is not fire, there exists a specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is excluded from non-fire.
Just as in a kitchen, such a thing exists here which is differentiated from non-smoke;
therefore, a specific individuality differentiated from non-fire exists here.
"In which" refers to the location where this [object] exists;
"and here its own-characteristic is distinct from smoke" is the demonstration of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

By the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, he demonstrates the presentation of the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*); or rather, he shows that even when the five-membered syllogism is formulated through positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), it serves as a demonstration of the [logical] possibility.
And this was stated regarding the effect-reason (*kāryahetu*); now, regarding the essential-nature reason (*svabhāvahetu*), he says: "of that which is non-existent," and so forth.
That which is distinct from non-existent things such as a human horn,
and which, like a cognition or a lamp, is excluded from everything— even from the permanent—
is of a non-existent nature; and thus this particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of sound and so forth is likewise [non-existent].
In this way, through the distinction thus specified, there is indeed a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) by means of this [reason]:

whatever particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is excluded from the non-existent is, because it lacks that nature, also excluded from everything permanent—just like cognitions, lamps, and so forth;
and such is this particular characteristic of sound and the rest, as it does not have the nature of the non-existent.

Therefore, by this reasoning, since it does not touch upon specific particulars (*viśeṣa*), the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) being established with respect to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is not contradictory; and this has been demonstrated as the positive concomitance of the reason "because of existence" (*sattvāt*).

If it is thus the case that the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is by means of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) alone, how then is inference established as having the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object? To this he says: "And that very same [specific characteristic] is proclaimed as having its distinctions unexpressed," and so forth.
That very same [specific characteristic], when its internal distinctions are not intended to be expressed, is what is designated [as the general characteristic].
Nor is there anything else [to be excluded] because it is not undesired as a universal characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa).

For that very particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), when its internal distinctions are not intended to be expressed, is called the "universal characteristic. It is a "universal characteristic" because it is characterized—that is, determined—by means of a generality, which is to say, by not attending to its specific differences.
The phrase "there is nothing further" refers to what is asserted by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), because that is not accepted [by us],
as it has been said: "Because that very [object] is apprehended through both its own form and the form of another, two types of objects of cognition (meyadvaya) are maintained."

Likewise, it has been stated elsewhere: "The inferential mark (liṅga) is said to have the universal as its object because it relies solely on a thing that is excluded from what is not of that nature, since [the mark] does not reside in particularities."
Therefore, the concomitance of the mark (liṅga) and the word is also stated by means of the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa) alone;

nor do we determine the absence of the mark in the counter-example (vipakṣa) merely through non-observation—what then?—but rather through a specific kind of non-perception (anupalambha). This is the intended meaning.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "the difference from Sābaleya," he says: "In the case of a difference from the offspring of Śabalā, [that difference] is equal for both Bāhuleya and the horse."
"Does the nature of 'cowness' (gotva) exist there [in the individual] by excluding the horse?

1058 Indeed, you ought to explain this: even though the difference between a *sābaleya* and a *bāhuleya* is equal, why is it that the nature of 'cowness' exists only in those individuals such as the *sābaleya*, and not in the horse?

It might be argued: "What is there to say here? For it is only the *sābaleya* cow and others that are capable of manifesting that universal 'cowness' (*gotva*), not horses and the like; therefore, it resides only in them and not elsewhere. Nor is this objection appropriate: 'Why is only that *sābaleya* and so forth capable of manifesting it?'—because this is a restriction based on the specific nature (*svabhāva*) of things. Indeed, the nature of things does not admit of questioning, since the restriction of their distinct natures is produced by their own causal series. To this, he replies: "In its manifestation," and so forth.

If it is maintained that "that very [cognition] itself is capable of manifesting it," then even in the case of a similar reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*), that [cognition] alone is capable, not the horse.
(1059) Regarding the word "tasya" ("of that"):
That very thing is the "cowness" of the brindled cow and others, but it is not the horse.

If this is so, even though there is a difference [between individuals], our position—that the spotted cow and others alone, and not the horse, are capable of producing a uniform conceptual reflection even in the absence of a universal—is not contradicted at all.
To the question, "What follows from that?", he says: "tādṛk" (of such a kind), and so forth.
And where such a reflective awareness exists regarding a given object,

there the exclusion of the non-cow (*ago'poha*) of the cow-universal (*gojāti*) proceeds, even in the absence [of a real universal]. (1060) Where, in an object such as a brindled cow (*sābaleya*), such a reflective awareness— the cognition "cow, cow"— arises.
In that very case, even though a real entity consisting of the genus "cow" does not exist, the exclusion of the non-cow (*agopoha*), which is of the nature of a reflection, proceeds.
(1060) Showing that what was stated [by the opponent] beginning with "by the sense organs," etc., is unestablished, he says: "And that which is distinct from the non-cow," etc.
An object that is not distinct from the cow is determined by the senses;
however, the superimposed reflection is understood through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*).
Having perceived this, a person employs a word for it.
Furthermore, his experience of the relationship [between word and object] is clearly established by that very fact.
In this regard, the exclusion (*apoha*) consisting of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is indeed apprehended by the sense organs;

as for the exclusion whose nature is the reflection of its own object, it is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), because it is ultimately of the nature of cognition.
The particle *ca* (and) serves to aggregate unmentioned meanings;

by this, it is shown that through implication (*sāmarthyāt*), even the nature of exclusion as a negation (*prasajya-ātman*) is indeed understood, such that it is demonstrated that "it is not that [object] itself, but rather the other-nature.

Therefore, having perceived this very *apoha* in the form of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, the word is employed by people in the world, but not a universal (*sāmānya*) that exists as a real entity (*vastubhūta*), because that [universal] does not exist and does not appear [in cognition].

And only by seeing that very [object] for which a word is employed by the world is its relationship with that object understood, and not by any other, because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Regarding what was asked—"And how, moreover, is there the state of being denotable by the word 'non-cow'?"—he says here: "In such a thing," and so forth.
That is to say, where there is no such reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) regarding an object, the state of being denotable by the word 'non-cow' is clearly understood therein. || 1063 ||
Regarding what was stated—"and once established, the non-cow would be excluded," and so forth—he replies: "Cows and non-cows... and so on.
Cows and non-cows are well-established through distinct conceptual cognitions;
however, the word alone is unestablished and is employed according to one's whim. (1064)
For the apprehension of one thing does not depend upon another distinct entity for its cognition;
this [charge of] mutual dependence is therefore groundless in this case.
Indeed, entities such as cows and the like, by producing distinct conceptual reflections (pratyavamarśa) through their own nature, are correctly determined in their differentiation.

Regarding these [entities], for the sake of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*), users employ words as they please, even when [the relationship] is not established [by nature]. For instance: if the apprehension of the form of a distinct entity required the grasping of another category (*anyapadārtha*) for its comprehension, then there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). However, since a distinct entity is perceived even without the grasping of another, and once it is established through differentiation as the cause for the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of a distinct form, a convention such as "cow" or "non-cow" is applied at will; thus, how could there be mutual dependence in this cognition?
For the sake of wealth,
Regarding what was stated—that there is no relation of locus and located, and so forth—he replies: "Even though its external reality is unknowable," and so on.

"Even though its external reality is unknowable, this cognition of a word, due to an intense cognitive distortion (*upaplava*), determines its own internal manifestation as having an external form. (1066)
This much is accomplished by words; words do not even touch the object itself, nor is any object qualified by exclusion (apoha) denoted by them.
For, in the ultimate sense, no object qualified by exclusion is denoted by words.

Since it has been established that no object whatsoever is touched by words because of the absence of causal totality (*sāmagryabhāva*) anywhere, for instance, verbal cognition—though having as its object nothing external—arises by determining its own reflection, its own form, as being an external object; it does not, in the ultimate sense, touch the intrinsic nature of a real entity, because it does not determine [the object] according to its true reality.

1067. If this is so, how is it that the Master stated: "Words such as 'blue lotus' express objects qualified by the exclusion of other objects"? To this, he says: "By the exclusion of other objects... and so forth; as for what was further stated: "They express [objects] as qualified by the exclusion of other objects."
This meaning was intended there by the author of the *Lakṣaṇa*.
To the question, "What is this intended meaning? he says: "By way of mutual difference," and so forth;
those entities which [exist] through mutual difference by means of a cause or an instrument.

Distinct, unmixed with things of different classes, and ascertained—such are the sounds produced by trees and the like. Because they produce a cognition that superimposes their own nature [upon the object], this constitutes the negation of [the existence of] universals and the like. || 1069-1070 ||
For there are two kinds of objects: the external and that which is mounted upon the intellect.

Among these, in the case of the external object, there is no denotation by words in an ultimate sense; rather, it is said metaphorically that "words express objects" simply because they produce conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that determine those objects.
And the purpose of this metaphor is the refutation of the theory that words denote universals (*jāti*). This is the overall meaning.
The meaning of the individual parts is now stated: "by way of being different from one another" (*anyānyatvena*) means difference from another, that is, exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*).
By that "being different from one another"—whether as a logical reason (*hetu*) or as an instrument (*karaṇa*)—entities such as trees are distinguished, that is, determined;
the sense is that they are determined as excluded from others.
By this, the meaning of the instrumental case in the word *nivṛttyā* in the phrase "distinguished by the exclusion of other objects" (*arthāntaranivṛttiviśiṣṭa*) has been explained;
*dhvani* means "sound."

But as for that object which has ascended into the intellect (*buddhi*), he shows that it is denoted by words primarily (*mukhyataḥ*) alone: "In the intellect," and so forth; those which evolve within the intellect, these he calls "internal" (*abhyantara*).
And their distinction by way of exclusion has been stated immediately following this;
[this refers to] the resonance "this" (ayam).
Now, he explains how their being qualified by the exclusion of other objects is to be understood, stating "and by exclusion," etc.,
immediately followed by "by way of mutual difference," etc.; for even those objects established in the intellect are presented as being distinguished from others.

[Objection: But if no part of the object at all is communicated by the word, then how was it stated by the Teacher that "a certain portion of the object is understood through the exclusion of other objects"? To this he says: "By the exclusion of other objects," and so forth;
[it means] that of that object, [a portion] is understood through the exclusion of other objects.
"That which is called a 'part' is precisely that reflection.

[Objection: But since a reflection is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), how can it be established as a part of a real entity? To this, he says: "Because it relies on the perception of a real object excluded from other objects," and so forth.
And there, a portion of the object that has been superimposed upon it is designated [as the reflection].

(1073) Because it arrives by way of the perception of an object that excludes other things (*arthāntaraparāvṛtta*), and because that very thing—being excluded from other things—is superimposed as identical [to the object] by those who are deluded, that very reflection is figuratively designated as a "portion" of the object.
Applying the meaning of the instrumental case here as "by means of the exclusion of other objects" (*arthāntaraparāvṛttyā*), he says:

"The meaning of 'cause' (*hetvartha*) and the meaning of 'instrument' (*karaṇārtha*) are as before; therefore, if a thing were not different from what belongs to another class, it would not be so [distinct]. (1074)

"As before" means that just as it was shown in the passage "they do not state [the object] as qualified by the exclusion of other referents" by means of the phrase "as being other than others," etc., so too should it be applied here; this is the meaning.
Alternatively, he demonstrates that this instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) everywhere indicates a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇā*), [expressing] "by means of that very self."

Now, one might object: "The exclusion of other sublaters is a property residing in the external object; how can that serve as either a cause (*hetubhāva*) or an instrument (*karaṇabhāva*) for the apprehension of a reflection? To this he says: "If the object were not excluded from things of a different class," and so forth.

For if the object were not excluded from heterogeneous entities, then it would not be determined as having the nature of a reflection through its identity as an object excluded from the heterogeneous; therefore, it is logical that the exclusion from other mirrors serves as both the cause and the instrument. This is the intended meaning. 1074
Regarding the passage beginning with "And one form should not make another different; cognition is the qualifier," he says:
"The exclusion of the non-cow is otherness, and that resides in its own self.
Even when there is a statement of difference, it is merely the absence [of the other] that does not cease. (1075)
Even when it functions as a qualifier, the cognition of the real entity is not lost;

for this qualifier is constructed by conceptual thought (kalpanā), even though there is no actual difference [between the entity and its qualities]. Therefore, having extracted that property (dharma), it is established as if it possessed a distinct identity.
For by that [exclusion], a qualification indeed arises for it, just as in the case of a staff and so forth.

(1077) If the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*) were intended as a positive entity (*bhāvarūpā*) serving as a qualification of the object, then all these objections would be valid. However, since the exclusion of others is taken as a qualification precisely as the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the object itself, the cognition of the qualified object necessarily conforms to the qualification. For instance, when the "exclusion of the non-cow" is expressed as "cow," it is of the same nature as the cow's difference from horses and other things; it is not something else.

And therefore, although this exclusion of the non-cow (*agonivṛtti*) is designated as "cow" by way of distinction when there is a desire to know merely the rejection of other differences, nevertheless, in the ultimate sense, that [exclusion] resides only within the essence of that cow, just like "otherness. For what is called "otherness" is not something other than the object itself; rather, it is that very thing.
Otherwise, that object would not be established as distinct from that other thing.
Consequently, even though the exclusion of others functions as a qualifier, the cognition of the real entity as the qualified object certainly arises.

It might be argued: "In the world, a qualifier is indeed well known to be distinct from the qualified, as for example a staff is [distinct] from a man; yet exclusion (vyāvṛtti) is non-distinct from the entity. Therefore, how is it logical for that [exclusion] to be its qualifier? To this he says: "Conceptual construction," and so forth.

In the ultimate sense, it is not logical for anything to be a qualifier of anything else, because that which provides no assistance cannot function as a qualifier. Furthermore, if one were to admit that it does provide assistance, then since the cause does not persist at the time the effect arises, the relationship of qualifier and qualified between two things existing at non-simultaneous times is untenable. On the other hand, if they were to exist simultaneously, then because both would be fully established in their entirety at that very moment, there could be no mutual assistance; thus, the relationship of qualifier and qualified is likewise untenable.
Therefore, since all entities abide in their own respective natures and are like iron rods [standing independently], their conjunction is merely a product of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).

Thus, although in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*) there is no difference between the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and that which possesses it (*tadvat*), nevertheless, by relying on the difference constructed by conceptualization, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇa-bhāva*) will come to be.

And as for what was stated— "When [it is said] 'the cognition'... [and] "Since they are not denotable by words, individuals are not excluded," and so forth— the correction table shows no space for the error.
Regarding this, he says: "The appearance," and so forth.

Those who contemplate reality say that the appearance is the meaning of a word; however, the world, not knowing the distinction between the perceived and the conceptualized, considers it to be external. (1078)
Therefore, by virtue of this determination, it has been established that in reality only individuals are denotable, and there is nothing denotable for words; thus,
the claim that "individuals are not denotable" is unproven.

To explain: that which we have described as the inexpressibility of individuals (*vyakti*) pertains to the investigation of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), and not even to conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*). However, it is well known—even from the perspective of the unexamined—that it is precisely the individuals that are expressible according to convention; thus, the reason [you provide] is unestablished (*asiddha*). [The term] "the perceptible" (*dṛśya*) refers to the external particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); [the term] "the conceptualizable" (*kalpa*) refers to the appearance (*pratibhāsa*) that revolves within conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*). Now, if ultimate inexpressibility is being adduced as the reason, then since the exclusion (*apohyatva*) of individuals is also not accepted ultimately, this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). This is what [the author] shows with the words beginning "In reality... (*tattvataśca*).
With the words "In this way" (*ittham*) and so forth, he concludes that the reason (*hetu*) is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*).
And thus, because individuals are denotable by words, they possess the quality of being excluded (*apohyatā*);
however, for the universal (*sāmānya*), there is no exclusion, nor does it possess substantiality even if it were excluded.
As it has been said: "In that case, the universal is not what is excluded; and from its exclusion [of others], it would follow that it is a real entity. (1080)

Thus, he demonstrates that even in that case, the reason "because it is to be excluded" (*apohyatvāt*) is both unestablished (*asiddha*) and inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), by means of the passage beginning with "of the universal" (*sāmānyasya*),
since it has already been established that exclusion (*apoha*) belongs only to individual instances (*vyakti*).

The meaning is that even in the case of an exclusion (apoha), there is no status as a real entity, because there is an absence of a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the reason when the opposite of the probandum is asserted.
Regarding what was stated, namely that "non-entities cannot be excluded" and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "Not a non-entity," etc.:

"For in this way, a non-entity is not excluded [by the thought] 'this is a non-entity'; rather, since a positive entity (bhāva) does not have that [non-entity] as its nature, it is precisely that [positive entity] which is intended to be excluded. (1081)
If one were to say "non-existence is not non-existence," then non-existence would not be excluded in such a way that its nature as non-existence would be abandoned.
What, then, is the case?

That which is existence, because it has a positive form, stands distinguished from the form of non-existence; therefore, by implication, it is intended that this [existence] is what is to be excluded by non-existence.
Clarifying this very point, he says: "That which is called 'name'... and so forth; for that which is not of the nature of something is indeed said to be its *apoha*.
An entity is not of the nature of non-existence; and if that [non-existence] is excluded, there is no substantiality.
"If that is excluded" means that when there is such an exclusion of that very non-existence, substantiality does not result.

Here, clarifying the very point of inconclusiveness by demonstrating examples established for both sides, he says: "The state of being produced by primordial matter (prakṛti), God (īśa), and so forth," and so on;
when it is urged that things are not produced by primordial matter, God, and so forth.

For an entity is not established as being produced by primordial matter (prakṛti), God (īśvara), or other such causes. To explain: even you Mīmāṃsakas do not accept that entities are created by primordial matter, God, time, and so forth;

and just as an entity does not thereby become a real thing even when such production is denied, so too there will be no attainment of reality for a non-entity (abhāva) even if it is the object of exclusion (apohya). Thus, [your argument] is inconclusive (anekānta).
Regarding what was stated— "In that case, there would be the great difficulty that even a non-existent thing possesses the nature of a real entity"—

he shows that this too has been refuted by the very same demonstration of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), as indicated by the passage beginning with "Therefore, not even of a non-existent... and so forth.
Therefore, even for that which is non-existent, there is no status of being an entity; thus, there is no difficulty whatsoever in establishing it.
Furthermore, existence exists only when that [non-existence] is established, and that non-existence itself is thereby established.
Regarding the point that "if that is not established, existence does not exist, nor does non-existence," he says: "And when that is established, existence exists," and so forth.

Even when that non-existence is established in the manner described, the existence of the entity is nonetheless established, because it is established as being situated within its own intrinsic nature; and that very establishment of non-existence in the manner described is what is recognized as "non-being. This has already been addressed in this very context, on the grounds that the refutation applies equally to both cases.
Now, he states the rebuttal in its proper sequence;
regarding what was said there, namely, "the non-existence of non-existence," and so forth, he says: "not being a cow," and so on.

The exclusion of the non-cow is held to be the cow itself as something possessing distinct characteristics; therefore, this [cow] is indeed a positive entity (bhāva), and thus the consequence of it being a non-cow does not apply.
If it is argued that "it is indeed a positive entity," this is not an instance of establishing an undesirable conclusion, because it is actually desired.

For instance: the horse and so forth, which are non-cow by nature, are held to be distinct from the cow only as a specific positive entity (*bhāva-viśeṣa-rūpa*), not as consisting of a negation (*abhāvātman*). Therefore, it must be a positive entity;
and since the distinction of the cow from the non-cow is accepted, there is no consequence that the cow would lack the nature of being a cow.

Regarding what was stated—"for that [cognition] is not held to exist with respect to a non-entity"—he says "it exists even with respect to a non-entity," etc., demonstrating that this is unproven and inconclusive:

"It exists even with respect to a non-entity; there is a latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by the mind alone, as in the case of things fashioned from various distinctions of conceptual construction. (1086)

Furthermore, based on the difference in latent impressions (vāsanā), both differentiation and the nature of existence are attributed to exclusions (apoha), just as they are in things constructed by conceptualization. [Objection:
It is unproven that the mind has non-entities as its object.
For instance—the mind indeed functions by superimposing the form of an object produced from a limited sphere of experience;

and that [mind] certainly deposits a latent impression (*vāsanā*) in the immediately succeeding consciousness for the sake of producing a subsequent conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of a similar kind, from which, once again, by virtue of the maturation of the continuum (*saṃtāna*), upon encountering an awakening condition, a mind of precisely that same nature arises. Just so, even for exclusions (*apoha*), mutual differentiation and the state of being real will occur through the power of conceptual construction; thus, [your argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
The meaning of the individual parts, however, has not been analyzed separately because it is easily understood.
Regarding what you have stated—that no distinction in words caused by that [exclusion] is found—he replies with the verse beginning "of whatever kind," etc.:
"Just as this exclusion of other objects has been established as the denotable meaning, let it be understood that the exclusion of other words is exactly of that same kind. (1088)
As for the phrase "of such a kind," it refers to that which consists of a reflection;
and its distinction from another reflection is indeed perceived most clearly.
Therefore, the sense is that everything stated at length [in the opponent's argument] is entirely inconsistent.
Regarding the refutation of the formulation beginning with "there would be no relationship of indicator and indicated," he says: "The entity," and so forth.
