Because they are determined as real entities (*vastu*), it is not established that the two types of exclusion (*apoha*) are non-entities; this is so on the conventional path, while on the ultimate level, it proves what is desired [by the opponent].

(1089) If "because they are non-entities" is stated as a general reason, then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*); for since the two exclusions—the signified and the signifier—which consist of mental reflections, are determined by the deluded as external entities, they indeed possess conventional reality.

Now, if the reason is stated by relying on ultimate non-substantiality, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); for we do not, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), accept anything as either the signified (*vācya*) or the signifier (*vācaka*).
He demonstrates this very point with the verse beginning "na vācyam" and so forth:
"In the ultimate sense, there is nothing whatsoever that is either the expressed or the expresser among entities subject to momentary destruction, because they lack pervasiveness. (1090)

"Due to the lack of pervasiveness" means that because of momentariness, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) lacks pervasion over the time required for convention and linguistic usage; this is the meaning.
It might be argued: "We do not deny a real relationship between the signifier and the signified."

Rather, by relying on the fact that both *apoha* and [the object] are ultimately non-entities (*avastu*), it is only their conventional status as the signified and the signifier (*gamyagamakatva*) that is negated, not their real existence (*bhāvika*). Therefore, there will be neither the fault of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhatā*) nor the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) in the thesis. For if both were assumed to be either merely conventional or ultimately real, these two faults would indeed arise; thus, he says: "And that relation of signified and signifier... and so forth.
Even if that conventional relationship of signifier and signified is denied on the grounds of relying upon the ultimate unreality of cessation and origination,
nevertheless, the fault of inconclusiveness remains unavoidable.
"By means of objects constructed by conceptual thought (vikalpa) and the words that denote them.

(1092) This being the case, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika); for although objects such as Mahāśvetā and the like, which are constructed by conceptual thought, and the words that denote them, lack substantial reality (vastutva) from the perspective of ultimate truth (paramārtha), a conventional relationship between the signified and the signifier (vācyavācakabhāva) is nevertheless observed.
He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "by means of objects constructed by conceptual thought," and so forth.
It might be argued: even in those cases, such as Mahāśvetā and others, the universal (sāmānya) exists in the ultimate sense as both the denoted and the denoter.
Anticipating the objection that, therefore, there is no deviation [of the reason] by those [examples], he says: "For indeed... and so forth.

For they possess no universal (*sāmānya*) to be denoted, nor do they have a denoter for it; nor does the word’s capacity to denote consist in its own-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is subject to momentary destruction. (1093)

Since the universal has been refuted in detail in the "Examination of the Universal" (*Sāmānyaparīkṣā*), there exists neither a denoted object nor a denoting word that is a universal among those [particulars]; thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to that universal.
In the phrase "the denoter" (*vācakam*), the word "universal" (*sāmānya*) is also connected with the subject under discussion.

One might argue: "Even if there is no real entity (*vastubhūta*) as the denoted (*vācya*) there, the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of words such as 'Mahāśvetā' certainly exists as the denoter. To this he replies: "The word does not possess the nature of being a denoter," and so forth.

Since it has been established that momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) pervades all categories of entities, the specific individuality of a word cannot be a denoter; because of its momentariness, it is impossible for it to be the object of a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*).
And it has been demonstrated that [the object] does not persist until the time of practical usage;
therefore, he concludes with the words "tasmāt" (therefore) and so forth.
Therefore, those two—the reflection and so forth—must be accepted as conventional;
in them, the presence of that [inference] without deviation remains unavoidable.
(1094) "The two" refers to...

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the expressed, the expresser, the reflection, and so forth," he demonstrates that even if one accepts that cognition is formless (*nirākāra-jñāna*), one must necessarily admit some other specific internal factor belonging to the cognition itself, which takes the form of determining an object where there is no actual object. He indicates this with the words "in those"— that is,
in objects constructed by conceptual construction (*kalpanā*).
The word "tad" means "therefore" or "because of that," [referring to] the fact that the reason is inconclusive.
Regarding the statement, "And by whom the word-meaning as a positive form is not accepted," he says: "And [the word-meaning] as a positive form," and so forth. That is to say:
"And by whom the word-meaning as a positive form is not accepted."
For the mind arises bearing that [object's] appearance, as it determines the object from the word.

When words denote their own objects, there is an exclusion of other things by implication; this connection is also a negative concomitance (vyatireka), for that [exclusion] is preceded by that [denotation]. (1095–1096)
For it is not that we do not accept the word-meaning as having a positive form (vidhirūpa) in every respect, such that you would be attributing an undesired consequence to us;
rather, because a cognition arises from a word that determines an object, the word-meaning is indeed accepted as conventionally having a positive form.
However, in reality, there is nothing at all that is denotable by words; thus, what is being negated is a word-meaning that is ultimately real and positive in form.

Since the meaning of a word is accepted as being conventional and having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*), when it expresses its own object in a positive form, the exclusion of others (*anyavyatireka*) is understood through implication; thus, it is entirely logical that exclusion is preceded by affirmation.

This might be the case if the meaning of a word were admitted to be of a positive (vidhi) nature; how then is it that the author of the definition stated in the *Hetumukha* that "there is no possibility of a positive [referent]"? To this he says: "There is no possibility," and so forth.

There is said to be no possibility of a positive referent because universals (*sāmānya*) and the like are impossible, and because words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have real entities (*vastu*) as their objects. (1097)

Since the denoted [object], such as the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and the denoter are ultimately non-existent, and since words and conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) have no object in reality from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), the Master stated that affirmation (*vidhi*) is impossible when relying on ultimate truth; thus there is no contradiction.
Regarding the statement "the denotability of mere exclusion (*apoha*)," etc., he says: "In the case of 'blue lotus,' etc. [1097]

From words such as "blue lotus" (*nīlotpala*), only a single reflection is apprehended—one that is excluded from what is non-blue and non-lotus. (1098) The word "blue lotus" expresses a reflection that possesses both forms: the aspect of the object (*arthākāra*) which is exclusively excluded from the non-blue and the non-lotus; it does not denote a mere absence (*abhāvamātra*). Therefore, by virtue of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), words like "blue lotus" indeed possess the capacity to express a real object. Consequently, in accordance with that [determination], grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is perfectly justified.

Regarding what was said—"Now, it is asserted that the object denoted is a thing possessing the exclusion of others (anyāpohavat)"—to this he replies: "But not 'possessing the exclusion of others,' etc. That is to say:
we do not maintain that the denoted object is a thing possessing the exclusion of others.

Since exclusion from what is other does not exist apart from that [entity] itself, for us there is no exclusion other than it. This fault of dependence, which applies to a universal (*jāti*), is not applicable here; for when the meaning of a word is stated as "pure," it is not distinct [from the entity]. (1099–1100)

Therefore, when the meaning of a word is *apoha*, the establishment of the relationship between qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyatva*) and grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not contradicted.

(1101) For if exclusion were something other than the excluded entity itself, then the faults previously mentioned regarding the view that [exclusion] possesses [the entity] would follow; however, for us, there is no exclusion other than the entity excluded from others. Rather, it is the excluded entity itself that is expressed in such a manner when there is a desire to know merely the rejection of other distinctions.

Thus, it was stated that when the genus (*jāti*) is primarily denoted, because the possessor of that genus (*tadvat*) is expressed only through dependence (*pāratantryeṇa*), there is no implication of the distinctions residing within it; consequently, the undesirable consequence follows that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth with it would be impossible. However, this [consequence] does not apply to the position of Apoha, because the possessor of the exclusion of others (*anyāpohavat*) is not what is being denoted.
He demonstrates this [point] with the words: "This fault of dependence on that," and so forth.
The word "that" refers to...
Therefore,
when the definition of the word-meaning as "exclusion" (apoha) was proclaimed by the teacher Diṅnāga, who possessed pure intelligence, it was stated that [this meaning] is "pure" (avadāta).
Regarding this, he states the reason: "Because of non-separateness" (*apṛthaktvataḥ*).
This means that because the word-meaning, characterized as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), is not separate from—that is, is not distinct from—the object-entity excluded from others;
[this applies to] the relation of qualifier and qualified, and so forth.
Easy to understand.
And showing how [the use of] grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth is not contradictory, he says: "From the mere [word]," and so on;
that is, from the mere word "blue" and so forth, a qualified reflection [arises].
The [cognition] proceeds by wavering among the cuckoo, the blue lotus, the bee, and so forth; then,
by the exclusion (apoha) of the cuckoo, the collyrium, and others, it is again established as having a specific object through the word "indīvara" (blue lotus), being thus definitively determined.
Thus, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth remain uncontradicted;
however, for the opposing school, the systematic establishment of all these [linguistic phenomena] is extremely difficult to maintain.

To explain: when "blue" is uttered, there arises a conceptual reflection whose form is subject to doubt regarding bees, cuckoos, collyrium, and other things that are distinct from yellow and the like, yet which are determined as being other objects.

That [object] is understood as having a determined nature when it is established by means of the word "lotus" (*utpala*) with respect to a thing that is excluded from non-lotuses and differentiated from cuckoos and so forth.

Therefore, because there exists a relationship of the excluded and the excluder (*vyavacchedya-vyavacchedaka-bhāva*) between the words "blue" and "lotus" in relation to the aforementioned mental reflections (*buddhi-pratibimba*), their status as qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) is not contradictory.

Alternatively, since both words convey a single object consisting of a mental reflection excluded from both the non-blue and the non-lotus, they possess grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) by virtue of functioning toward a single referent; such is the collective meaning.
The meaning of the individual components is now stated: "floating" means lacking a firm foundation, that is to say, being of the nature of doubt;
and the word *pika* is a synonym for the cuckoo (*kokila*).
The remainder is easily understood.

One might argue that even in our own position, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth are not at all contradictory; therefore, he says: "But in the opponent's position," and so on, ending with "that systematic arrangement."
The establishment of its grammatical coreferentiality and so forth is "the establishment thereof" (tadvyavasthā).
To explain how it is difficult to establish, he says: "For instance," and so forth.
For instance, by means of a single word, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is expressed in every respect.

And if that [universal] has already been expressed in such a manner, why would there be a cognition of another particular (bheda), for which purpose another word would be employed here? In reality, if it were not [already] expressed in every respect, it would follow that it is manifold. (1105–1106)

In the view of those who maintain that the meaning of words consists solely in injunctions (*vidhi*), once the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a blue lotus and so forth has been denoted by the single word "blue" alone, there can be no ignorance regarding other particulars—such as whether it is a lotus or perhaps collyrium—because that object would have been communicated in its entirety.

Furthermore, for a single person at one time, there is a contradiction between being known and being unknown with respect to a single thing. He demonstrates this [with the question]: "Why is there no cognition of the distinctions?"
*Amati* is knowledge that is contemptible; it is *mati* (cognition) that is flawed,
meaning it consists of doubt and error.

And thus, because there is an absence of doubt and error, he shows that neither the desire for the employment of other words such as "lotus" (*utpala*) nor the desire of the speaker arises; this is shown by the passage beginning with "for the sake of which," where "for the sake of which" means "for the sake of the cessation of which misconception."

Now, it might be argued: "That entity was expressed by [the word] only in part, not in its entirety; therefore, another word must indeed be sought to express its other intrinsic natures. To this, he says: "In every way," and so forth.
For a single entity does not possess parts such that there could be an expression of it by means of a part, because unity and plurality are characterized by mutual exclusion.
Consequently, as many parts as you may propose, you have merely established as many distinct entities; thus, neither a single entity nor a manifold one is established.

It might be argued: "In this case, it is not a substance that is denoted by the word *nīla* (blue); what then? It is either the quality called 'blue' or the universal 'blueness' inherent in it. Likewise, by the word *utpala* (lotus), only the universal 'lotus-ness' is expressed, not the substance. Therefore, because they denote different objects, it is indeed appropriate for the word *utpala* to require another word [to complete the sense]. To this, he says: "The universal of blueness," and so forth.

If the universal "blue" or even the quality "blue" is apprehended by the word "blue," then the universal belonging to other blue lotuses must be determined through the auditory perception of the word "lotus.
This being the case, because of the difference between the two [universals], they are like the words "bakula" and "lotus."
Grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth are all the more untenable.
[Regarding the compound] "another blue-lotus universal" (*anyendīvarajāti*):
it is a compound consisting of "another" (*anyā*) and "blue-lotus universal" (*indīvarajāti*).
"vyavaseyā" means that which is to be determined;
"utpala-śruteḥ" is a word ending in the ablative case.

In this view, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is even more untenable; for, just as with the words "bakula" and "utpala," the words "blue" and "utpala" do not apply to a single object, since it is not the case that "the bakula is the utpala. (1107)

It might be argued: "Even though the word *nīla* denotes a specific universal (*jāti*) and quality (*guṇa*), nevertheless, by means of those two, it also denotes the substance (*dravya*) connected with that blue quality and its universal; likewise, the word *utpala* also denotes that very same substance by means of its universal.

Therefore, because it is possible for these two to function with respect to a single object, there will be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), but not between the words *bakula* and *utpala*. To this, he says: "By means of the quality and its universal," and so forth.
If a substance connected with a quality and its genus is what is expressed by the word "blue," then the mention of the word "lotus" would be redundant;
for that very same thing which is connected with those two [the quality and the genus] is also possessed of the genus "lotus."

Since it has already been stated there by the word "blue" (*nīla*) alone that [the object] is connected to both the quality called blue and its universal called blueness (*nīlatva*), the mention of "lotus" (*utpala*) would be redundant; such is the analysis of the compound. Thus, the mention of "lotus" would be purposeless.
Since that substance has already been established by the word "blue" itself,
he demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "by those two," and so forth;
"by those two" means:

It might be argued that this is due to the quality (*guṇa*) and its universal (*jāti*): although the word "blue" denotes a substance (*dravya*) possessing that quality and its universal, nevertheless, because it is observed to apply to multiple objects, a cognition of a determinate form does not arise in the cognizer regarding the object "lotus," since even cuckoos and other things are blue;
therefore, the employment of the word "lotus" is indeed purposeful, as it serves to exclude doubt regarding other objects.
This is stated incorrectly because of a failure to understand the subject matter at hand;

for in this context, the relevant point is that under the view that the word-meaning is a positive injunction (*vidhi*), grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth would not be possible.

Furthermore, if the word "lotus" (*utpala*) functions solely to exclude doubt and does not bring about the cognition of a substance, then the positive injunction could not be the word-meaning, since the word "lotus" would only convey the exclusion of a form superimposed by error.

This which is being stated is mutually contradictory: on the one hand, it is said that the word "blue" denotes a substance such as a blue lotus; yet, on the other hand, it is claimed that no certain cognition arises in the cognizer regarding that [substance].
For it is not logical that something in which doubt arises should be the meaning of a word, since that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor can doubt find any room in a thing that has already been made the object of a certain cognition.
This might be argued:

"Even if there is no co-occurrence (*vṛtti*) of the words 'blue' and 'lotus' in a single object, there is nevertheless a co-occurrence of their referents—the quality [blueness] and the universal [lotusness]—in a single substance;
therefore, their grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) will occur by way of their referents. This is incorrect, because it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

In this way, there would also be grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "color" (*rūpa*) and "taste" (*rasa*), because their respective objects—color and taste—subsist in a single substance such as earth; furthermore, the cognition whose object is a single referent, such as "the blue lotus," would not arise, because the two [words] would denote separately the quality and the universal that are each inherent in a single substance. And since there is no coreferentiality between two words when a cognition having a single referent does not arise, enough of this prolixity. (1109)

It might be argued: "The very object that is connected with the quality blue and its universal is not what is denoted by the word 'lotus' (*utpala*); rather, it is something else. Thus, the hearing of the word 'lotus' will not be redundant. To this, he says: "From that which is connected with the quality and its universal," and so forth; [the object] possessing the universal of lotus is other than that which is connected with the quality and its universal.
"If the two words 'blue' and 'lotus' were to have different substrata"—
the word "if" serves as a restriction;
that is, "were they to have different substrata."
The meaning is that [the two words] would have different substrates (vyadhikaraṇa).

1111 Now, it might be argued: "Even though that very same substance is denoted by the word 'blue' (*nīla*), and that very same thing is also denoted by the word 'lotus' (*utpala*), nevertheless, the word 'blue' does not denote the substance by way of its form as being related to the universal of lotus-ness; rather, it denotes it precisely by way of its form as being related to the quality of blueness and its universal. Therefore, when the term 'lotus' is employed to denote this substance's form as being related to the universal of lotus-ness, it will not be redundant. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the passage beginning "Now, [regarding] lotus-ness," and so forth.
Now, the word "blue" would not denote a substance connected with a quality and its genus by way of having a form related to "lotus-ness. This is the connection [of the sentence]:
"Now, the word 'blue' would not denote a substance connected with a quality and its genus by way of having a form related to 'lotus-ness. (1112)
Granted that the form of the possessor of the lotus-ness may be of a nature other than that [lotus],
yet that which is connected with "lotus-ness" is indeed connected with both of those.
"That which is expressed by the word 'blue' is made the object here by verbal cognition in its entirety; it has no parts, for the word 'lotus' does not produce a different meaning.
This is incorrect.

For the nature of being related to the lotus-genus (*utpalajāti*) is not something other than the nature of being related to the quality blue (*nīlaguṇa*) and its genus; for if it were, then when the nature of being related to "blue-lotus" and so forth is denoted, the nature of being related to the lotus-genus would not be denoted of the substance.

Since, however, both natures of being related [to the two qualifiers] are non-different from the single substance, those two [natures] are likewise one and the same. Thus, it is incorrect to claim that when one form is denoted, the other form is not denoted.

Furthermore, let us grant for the sake of argument: let it be that the nature related to "lotus-ness" is indeed distinct from the nature related to "blue" and its universal. Even so, the verbal expression "lotus" would still be entirely redundant;
for that very partless entity which is connected with the universal "lotus-ness" is the same one that is connected with these two—the quality "blue" and its universal—and nothing else.

And since that [lotus] is partless, it is denoted in its entirety by the word "blue" alone and made an object of the verbal cognition consisting of ascertainment; thus, what other unexpressed nature of it remains for which the word "lotus" might be meaningful?

Uddyotakara, however, says: "In regard to a partless entity, this conceptual distinction—that it is apprehended in its entirety and not in part—does not apply, because the word 'all' (sarva) has multiple things as its object, whereas the word 'one' (eka) functions by way of parts.
Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the words "And if not," and so forth:
"And if there is no conceptualization of 'entirety' or 'part' in that which is devoid of differentiation..."
This is not due to a lack of understanding of the sentence-meaning; for this is what is intended here:
by the very first word, that [object] is revealed in its entirety.
No aspect of the self is omitted; it is expressed exactly as it is.
"Free from division" means in the case of an entity that is partless;
"the conceptualization of the alternatives of totality and division" [is thus addressed].

The conceptualization that [the word] makes its object either "in its entirety" (*sarvātmanā*) or "by way of a single part" (*ekadeśena*)—that is, through the distinction between totality and partiality—is stated due to a lack of understanding of the meaning of the sentence. For instance, the intended meaning of the statement "it is illuminated in its entirety by the very first word 'blue'" is as follows: the thing is expressed exactly as it is; no aspect of its nature is abandoned such that the word "lotus" would have to function to express it, because that thing is partless (*niraṃśatvāt*). Therefore, this is merely a quibble of words (*vākchalam*).

Just as the word "utpala" [lotus] would thus be meaningless, so too the employment of other words such as "impermanent" (anitya) and so forth would result in being meaningless. Since their employment exists, they would merely be synonyms, like the words "taru" and "pādapa" [both meaning tree]. Making this extension [of the argument], he says: "By this very [reasoning]," and so forth.
In this very manner, the utterance of other words there would not be fruitful; in their expression, they would certainly be synonyms.
(1117) "Utterance" means...
The application [of the term] is stated as "in speech," meaning in utterance.

As it has been said: "Otherwise, if a single object were pervaded by one word or by a single cognition, there would be no further scope for other [words or cognitions], and thus they would become synonyms. (1117)

It might be argued: "Even in your position, when a single object has been denoted by one word, why does it not follow that there is an absence of doubt and error regarding other distinctions, and why does it not follow that other words would fail to function? To this he says: "But for us," and so forth.
"But for us, an external object is not denoted by a word; nor is it held that cognition has an external object as its domain. (1118)
For, since they have made it their object with their entire being,
after the cognition of the word, there [in that case] synonymy will follow.
(1119) "By those two" means...
"Beyond the cognition of the word" means at a subsequent time.

Now, one might ask: why does the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) not constitute a fault when the referent of a word is conventional (*sāṃvṛta*)? To this, he says: "But the reflection," and so forth.
The reflection, however, is produced by the word only in a sequential manner;
yet it appears as a unity and as something external due to delusion.
Grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and other such relations exist in accordance with that reflection.
But in the ultimate sense, these words are considered to be without an object.

For, by the word "blue" (*nīla*), there is first produced a conceptual reflection (*vikalpapratibimbaka*) which is excluded from non-blue objects, which floats over lotuses and so forth, which does not exclude them, and which is determined as having an external form. Then, by the hearing of the word "lotus" (*utpala*), that very same [reflection] is produced as excluded from non-lotuses, with the nature of a single superimposed external entity. Thus, in this sequence, a mistaken conceptual reflection is produced which is excluded from both the non-blue and the non-lotus, and which is determined as a single external form. In accordance with that [reflection], conventional co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth are indeed logical.
But why is it not tenable from the perspective of ultimate reality? He says: "From the perspective of ultimate reality," and so forth.
Regarding what was stated—that "there is no connection of gender, number, and so forth with the exclusion (apoha)"—he says here: "As for the connection with gender, number, and so forth...
This connection with gender, number, and so forth does not belong even to individual entities;
it is caused by conventions fashioned by human will and is certainly not real.

The status of these [features]— gender, number, and so forth— as real properties of things (*vastu-dharmatva*) is unestablished, because they arise solely from conventions fashioned by independent whim;
this applies to individuals as well, as indicated by the word "also" (*api*), which includes the exclusion (*apoha*) as well.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That which does not conform to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of another thing is not a property (*dharma*) of that thing, just as coldness is not a property of fire; and gender, number, and so forth do not, in reality, conform to the positive and negative concomitance [of the object]. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
To show that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "The bank (*taṭaḥ*), the bank (*taṭī*)," and so on.
"Taṭaḥ," "taṭī," and "taṭam"— this threefold gender-distinction does not belong to the object itself,
because all cognitions of it appear as variegated (śabala).

For if the gender were a property that apprehends the actual thing (*vastu*), then, since the words associated with the three genders— *taṭaḥ*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*— would apply to a single entity called a riverbank (*taṭa*), it would follow that a single thing possesses three forms.
Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity to possess the three natures known as female, male, and neuter, because that would entail the loss of its unity.
If things possessed of contradictory properties were nonetheless one, then the entire universe would be a single entity;
consequently, it would follow that all things arise and perish simultaneously.

Furthermore: since it is observed that for every single thing, the three genders are apprehended either by a single word or by another word, it follows that all cognitions directed toward such objects must have a variegated appearance (*śabalābhāsatā*), like a multi-colored gem (*mecakādiratna*).

Now, it might be argued: "Even though all things possess the three genders, those cognitions will appear only as the specific form intended to be expressed by the speaker, due to the influence of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*); thus they will not have a variegated appearance. To this, he says: "Or, if [the cognition] follows the intention," and so forth.

Or, if they were to follow the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), they would not have that [external object] as their referent; by virtue of that [intention], they would be of a single form, yet the object is not of a single form.
(1124) Or, if they were to follow the speaker's intention—[the word "of cognitions" (*cetasām*) is to be supplied as the subject].

For if it is admitted that cognitions become uniform in form by the power of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), then those cognitions would not have as their object a thing consisting of three natures, because they would be devoid of the forms of those [three natures], just as visual consciousness does not have sound as its object by virtue of that [intention].
Thus, it is by the power of the speaker's intention.

Even for one who thinks that the established arrangement of femininity, masculinity, and neuter-ness is as previously stated with respect to dissolution, production, and persistence, [the author] says "persistence," etc., demonstrating that this too is not tenable:
"The establishment of gender is dependent upon persistence, production, and dissolution."
"If there were [a basis for gender], it would follow that there is no distinction between genders" (verse 1125).
The break in the verse occurs after "yadi syāt.

For if the establishment of gender (*liṅgasthiti*)—that is, the determination of gender—is based on [qualities] such as stability (*sthiti*), then all things would possess all three genders without distinction, like the word *taṭa* or a chain; this is because stability and the other qualities exist everywhere, just as they do in the case of a riverbank (*taṭa*).
Otherwise, even in cases such as *taṭas*, *taṭī*, and *taṭam*, there would be no three genders, because there is no distinction [between them];
therefore, over-extension (*ativyāpti*) is a defect of the definition.
Showing that [the definition] is non-pervasive because of the observation of deviation, he says: "Non-existence," and so forth.

Regarding that which is called non-existence (*abhāva*), the state of being indefinable (*nirupākhyatva*), or emptiness (*tucchatā*), what kind of connection with persistence and so forth could be imagined for things that are non-existent? (1126)

For even in the absence of duration and the other [characteristics], in the case of non-existent forms such as a hare's horn, one observes the cognition of the three genders through words such as *abhāva* (non-existence), *nirupākhya* (the indefinable), and *tucchatā* (insubstantiality); therefore, this grammatical rule regarding gender is not universal.
Their arising is considered birth (*prasava*), and their destruction is considered dissolution (*saṃstyāna*).
The very nature of entities is designated as "stability.
In that case, since there is no destruction within arising, how can it be called "origination"?
Furthermore, since there is no stability possessing the form of a self, how can it be sung as "birth"? (1127–1128)
In the case of contraction (*saṃstyāna*), there is neither duality nor anything else; how then can it be designated as "disappearance," "destruction," or even "vanishing"?
Furthermore, in the case of persistence (*sthiti*), by what cause are "persistence" and "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) spoken of?
Furthermore, their form would be undifferentiated, resulting in a single gender.
For this reason as well, [the theory] is non-pervasive, because we observe the application of words endowed with all three genders to each of those very states—subsistence and so forth.
To illustrate: *prasava* is called production (*utpāda*), *saṃstyāna* is destruction (*vināśa*), and the essential nature itself is subsistence (*sthiti*).

In that case, since there is an absence of persistence (*sthiti*) and withdrawal (*saṃstyāna*) during manifestation (*prasava*), how could terms such as "arising" (*utpāda*), "origination" (*utpatti*), or "birth" (*janman*)—which possess feminine and neuter genders—be applicable?

Likewise, since there is an absence of manifestation and persistence during withdrawal, how could it be designated by words such as "disappearance" (*tirobhāva*), "destruction" (*vināśa*), or "vanishing" (*tirobhavana*)?
Furthermore, by the use of the word "also" (*api*), he demonstrates how even "withdrawal" (*saṃstyāna*) cannot be designated by its own specific term.

Likewise, since contraction (*saṃstyāna*) and production (*prasava*) are impossible while [a thing] remains in a state of stability (*sthiti*), it must be stated for what reason that stability is expressed by such words as "having the nature of stability" (*sthitisvabhāva*).

Furthermore, if it were argued that because these states—stability and the rest—are mutually inseparable in form, each one of them will possess the capacity for the three genders, [the author] says: "Or if they are inseparable," and so forth.
For if their forms were mutually inseparable, then there would be only one gender in the ultimate sense, not three genders.

1130 But another says: "The particular universals, such as femininity and so forth, are like [the universals] such as cowness. To him, he replies: "If these, such as femininity and so forth, are considered to be like cowness and so forth," and so on.
If these [qualities] such as femininity are held to be like cowness and the like...
By the refutation of the universal (sāmānya), those [categories] of that kind are already discarded;

for since universals and particulars were previously refuted in the "Examination of the Universal" (Sāmānyaparīkṣā), it is a definition of the impossible, because such properties as femininity and so forth are impossible.

Furthermore, he demonstrates that the definition is too narrow (*avyāpitā*) because we observe the application of words with feminine, masculine, and neuter genders—such as *jāti*, *bhāva*, and *sāmānya*—even in the absence of another subordinate universal (*sāmānyaviśeṣa*) within those very same universals and particulars:
"Whether it be 'universal' (*jāti*), 'being' (*bhāva*), or 'commonality' (*sāmānya*), these are accepted among them; however, further universals are not applicable to universals. (1132)
It is not logical for universals to possess further universals,
because it is an established tenet that universals are devoid of further universals;
and this has been stated on the basis of the Vaiśeṣika tenets.

However, when grammarians (vaiyākaraṇas) postulate further universals (sāmānya) within [already established] universals—as it has been said: "Even when a word denotes a universal of meaning, all words denote universals, because all word-meanings are established as being characterized by their functional activity (vyāpāra).
For the system of universals observed in other treatises need not necessarily be accepted by grammarians."
For universals (jāti) have their forms inferred from the operation of denotation and cognition, as well as from the effects [of linguistic usage]; indeed, there is no fixed limit to them.

Therefore, because a universal existing as the substratum of a genus is established through the observation of the effect enjoined [by words], this scriptural statement "universals" (jātayaḥ) serves as its basis;
that is to say, they are defined by their operation, meaning their characteristics are determined through the operation of denotation and cognition.
The refutation just mentioned applies to those [arguments] as well by way of rejecting the universal; thus, such [objections] are already discarded.
(1132) And he states this common refutation: "Non-existence," and so forth.
How could [terms] such as "non-existence" (*abhāva*), "indefinability" (*nirupākhyatva*), or "insubstantiality" (*tucchatā*) be merely conventional?
For that reason, this establishment of the three genders occurs.

Indeed, there is no universal (*jāti*) in non-existent things such as a hare's horn, because a universal is a property of real entities; therefore, the application of words like "non-existence" to them would not otherwise be possible.
Therefore, the fixed status of logical marks is not all-pervasive;
thus, it is established that this arrangement of the three types of logical marks arises solely from conventions fashioned by human will.
Showing that even number does not follow the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) inherent in the object itself, he says: "Number, too," and so forth.

For number, too, is merely conventional and is postulated by the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), even when there is a distinction between difference and non-difference, as in the cases of "wife" (*dārāḥ*) and "forest" (*vipina*). || 1134 ||
Number, too, is merely conventional and not real, because it is constructed through the force of intention even when no real distinction exists— as in the case of "wife" (dārāḥ) and so forth;
therefore, the reason [adduced] is not unestablished.

For instance—the numbers such as plurality and singularity do not have the nature of difference and non-difference residing in the object itself; for in cases such as *dārāḥ* (wife), *sikatāḥ* (sand), and *varṣāḥ* (rainy season), the number of plurality occurs even though there is no actual difference in the object.

Likewise, in cases such as *vanam* (forest), *tribhuvanam* (the three worlds), *jagat* (the world), and *ṣaṇṇagarī* (the six cities), the number of singularity is designated for the object even though there is no non-difference.
Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Nor is it inconclusive, because that would entail the absurd consequence that everything is every dharma;
nor is it contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa).
With the words beginning with "nanu" (now then), he raises an objection regarding the unestablished nature of the reason according to the view of Kumārila:
"Now, if a word such as 'dārāḥ' (wife/wives) is applied to both the individual and the genus, it functions by taking on the number of either the individual or its constituent parts. (1135)
Furthermore, the word "forest" (vana) expresses either many individuals qualified by a specific number of the genus, or it expresses the genus as residing in many individuals. He says this:
the word "wife" (dārā) and others are sometimes applied to the genus and sometimes to the individual.

In that regard, when [the word] is applied to the genus (*jāti*), it functions by taking up the number belonging to the individual (*vyakti*); and since the individuals are many women, when it is used for the individual, it functions by taking up the plurality of the parts of that individual, such as the hands and feet. However, by the word "forest" (*vana*), distinct individuals—such as mango, khadira, and palāśa trees—are conveyed as qualified by the number belonging to the genus "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) inherent in them. Therefore, the singular number in "forest" occurs because it denotes a substance qualified by the singular number belonging to the genus.

Alternatively—the universal (*jāti*) itself, which resides in individual entities such as *dhava* trees, is what is expressed by the word "forest" (*vana*); therefore, the singular number is used, because the universal is a single entity.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely):
"But surely, by this rule, every single statement is destroyed; if there is no intention to speak [of anything else], let that very [intention] be its basis. (1137)
By this aforementioned method, everything—the singular number in "tree" (*vṛkṣa*) and so forth—is refuted—that is, abolished—because this same principle applies equally everywhere;
for here too, one could indeed say: "In that case, if [the word] 'tree' and so forth is applied to both the individual (*vyakti*) and the universal (*jāti*," and so on.

Now, if it is thought that in other cases—such as with trees and the like—there is no intention to express the number of the individual or its parts, then in that case, number would not follow the actual presence of the underlying relation (*anvaya*) and so forth, because number follows only the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), according to positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, let that very same intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) be the basis for this plural number in cases such as *dārāḥ* (wife/wives), since even in the absence of actual plurality, a single entity may be intended to be expressed as many; therefore, the reason [adduced] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
As for what was stated—that the word "forest" (*vana*) expresses an individual qualified by a genus and a specific number—to that he replies with the verse beginning "of the genus" (*jāteḥ*), etc.

There is no number belonging to the universal (jāti), nor can things qualified by it [be numbered] through a connection with that which is connected [to the universal], even if such a connection were possible. For the universal possesses no number, since it resides only in substances.

Now, if this Vaiśeṣika method is not accepted, then how could the individual entities such as *dhava* trees be established as qualified by that number, whether it resides in the existence (*bhāva*) or in the number itself?
It might be argued that they are established through a connection with a connection, or through a connection with that [number].

To explain: when number is distinct from the universal (jāti), then the individual entities such as *dhava* trees are qualified by that [number] through a mediated connection (*pāramparyeṇa*), because the individuals are connected to the universal which is itself connected to the number one; but when number is non-distinct from the universal, then they are qualified by it through a direct connection. Therefore, they are established as being qualified by the number of the universal.
He offers a rebuttal with the words "If this were so," and so forth.

If it were argued thus: "Even a single tree may be called a 'forest,' for even many [trees] are so designated solely through their relation; and that [relation] exists here as well" (1139)—if the application of the word 'forest' to individual trees such as the *dhava* occurs either through a relation with a related thing or through a relation itself, then even a single tree might be called a 'forest,' because the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is present.

For instance—even many *dhava* trees and others are called a "forest" solely due to their connection with a genus (*jāti*) and a number, and not for any other reason; yet since that same connection exists even in a single tree, why should it not be called so?
Or rather, regarding the statement "the genus residing in many individuals," he says: "residing in many individuals," and so forth.

And that [cognition] which rests upon many individuals would likewise reside in even a single one, because the cause for it is the same; thus, the cognition of a "forest" would arise even in that case.
For even on this view, there would be the designation "forest" for even a single tree.

For instance: that very universal (*jāti*) which is denoted by the word "forest" as residing in many individuals (*vyakti*), is established even in a single individual such as a *dhava* tree; and since the cause for that cognition of "forest" is identical everywhere, why would the cognition of "forest" not occur even with respect to a single tree?
With the words "by means of positive and negative concomitance" and so forth, he concludes the discussion on causality:

"Therefore, by means of positive and negative concomitance, this restriction regarding words such as 'one' and so on arises from the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), not from the object itself, because of the latter's variability. (1141)
"Because of its deviation from that" means because of the deviation of that object.

Regarding the statement that "no connection with gender, number, and so forth exists for the exclusion (apoha)," the author addresses what is indicated by the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), namely the connection with action, time, and so on, by saying "action," etc.
Even the connection with action, time, and so forth has already been refuted;
therefore, these [grammatical categories] are merely conventional (*sāṃketika*) and do not exist even in individual entities (*vyakti*).

Since the connection with action and so forth has already been refuted by the negation of categories such as "time for action" (*karmakāla*) and the like, it is improper to claim that even these possess the nature of real entities (*vastudharma*).
Those which exist in convention (*saṅketa*) are conventional (*sāṅketika*).

Or, let it be granted that these [exclusions] are properties of real entities (*vastudharma*); nevertheless, because exclusion characterized as a reflection (*pratibimba*) is determined by those under delusion to be the form of an external individual (*bāhyavyakti*), there will—by virtue of this conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*)—be a connection with gender, number, and so forth, mediated through the individual. Thus, he demonstrates that what was stated—"Since the individual is inexpressible, that [exclusion] exists [as such] even by way of it"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and unestablished (*asiddha*) from the perspective of conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*). This is shown in the passage beginning "by the determination of the form of the individual":
"Or if exclusion is said to be expressed by the determination of the form of the individual..."
Its connection with tallness and so forth exists by way of the individual;
"it is called *apoha* by means of the word"— this is the ellipsis.
The word "tat" means "therefore," and "asya" means "of this."
Regarding the statement "In the case of verbs, there is no [exclusion] of anything else," etc., he says: "For the purpose of establishing [the word] in its intended [referent]," and so forth.
A word is employed by speakers for the purpose of directing the intellect toward a desired object;
therefore, the exclusion of what is undesired is established by implication alone.

[Objection: It is not established that the exclusion of others is not perceived in the case of verbs (ākhyāta). For instance, when a certain object is sought to be known, a word is employed by those engaged in linguistic communication to direct the listener’s intellect toward it, not out of mere whim. Thus, when the intended meaning is understood, the exclusion of the unintended is indeed perceived through the very power of that expression.
Because the desirable and the undesirable are of the nature of mutual exclusion, [the opponent] might argue that "everything is indeed desirable. To this, he says: "Everything indeed," and so forth.
Everything indeed cannot be intended [by a word], because that would result in the lack of restriction regarding all objects;
therefore, the exclusion [of other meanings] by words such as "that" (*tat*) and so forth is perfectly clear.

(1145) If everything were indeed intended, then a specific word-meaning would not be established, and consequently, the listener's engagement with a particular object through a word—by way of excluding certain other objects—would not occur. Therefore, it is untenable to say that "everything is intended."
Therefore, the exclusion of what is not intended [by the speaker] follows by implication from words such as "he cooks" (pacati); this is indeed understood quite clearly.
With the words "For instance" (tathāhi) and so forth, [the author] demonstrates that very exclusion of the unintended which is apprehended through implication.
For instance, when it is said "he cooks," it is understood that he does not remain indifferent, nor does he eat, play, or the like; thus, the exclusion of other [actions] is apprehended.
Therefore, there is both this state of indifference and another distinct action.
If whatever is intended is necessarily of the nature of exclusion (*paryudāsa*),

then for the expression "he cooks," there exists an exclusion consisting of the negation of other actions, such as being indifferent, eating, playing, and so forth. Therefore, what was stated— that "there is no object of negation in the form of an exclusion"— is unestablished,
because there is indeed an exclusion that consists of *paryudāsa*.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which consists of exclusion (paryudāsa) and that which is to be excluded (apohya).
The connection is as follows: for whatever [object] is intended as determinate, there exists for each of them something to be excluded that consists of the exclusion of indifference and so forth.
And as for what was said: "One who cooks remains unprevented, abiding in his very own nature."

In this regard, demonstrating the contradiction with his own words for the opponent, he says: "The statement 'he cooks,' etc., and the claim that 'it remains in its own nature without being negated'—this sentence of yours is mutually contradictory. (1148)
"This negation of another form exists by its own nature alone;
otherwise, the restrictive particle [eva] employed would be meaningless. (1149) But how is this mutually contradictory? He says: "This negation of another form," and so forth.

By the restriction expressed in the phrase "it exists by way of the very nature of the meaning of 'he cooks' (*pacati*)," which shows the form as it has been manifested, it is demonstrated that the self-abiding of "he cooks" occurs through the negation of any other form;
otherwise, this very restriction you have employed—namely, "by way of its own nature alone"—would be purposeless, because there would be nothing to be excluded.
Regarding what was stated— "and here there is the cognition of being something to be accomplished," and so forth— he replies with "the state of being established," and so on:
"What kind of state of being established can there be for an exclusion (*apoha*) that is devoid of any designation?"
There is no production whatsoever of things such as a sky-lotus.
If it is argued that it appears as a "real entity" because of the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) that it is one, then what follows from that?
Is its possession of properties identical to those of real entities thereby established? (1150–1151)

If you have grasped *apoha* as being of an indefinable nature (*nirupākhyasvabhāva*), how can it be said that "it is established" (*niṣpannatvāt*)? For there is no establishment whatsoever of things such as a sky-lotus, since they are characterized by the absence of all definitions. To this [objection], one might say: "Even though this *apoha* is ultimately indefinable, nevertheless, because it has been determined as having the form of an external object by deluded perceivers, this *apoha* appears as if it were definable.
To this, he replies: "What follows from that? (*tataḥ kim iti*)?
If it is indeed the case that this [apoha] appears as having a positive designation (*sopākhyatva*), even so, what here has occurred that is favorable to the subject at hand?
To this, the opponent replies: "Its similarity of properties with real entities (*vastu*) is understood.

By this, just as a real entity is perceived as having a perfected form (*niṣpannarūpa*), so too apoha, being manifested through its similarity of properties with real entities, is perceived as if it were perfected; thus, the statement "because of its perfection" is established.

If this is so, since you yourself have demonstrated the cause for the cognition of "being an object to be accomplished" (*sādhyatva*) as well as for the cognition of "past" (*bhūta*) and so forth, it should not be said that these [cognitions] would result in being causeless. Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Therefore, the cognition of being an object to be accomplished... and so on.

Therefore, the cognition of being an object to be accomplished (sādhya), as well as the conceptualization [of it] as "thus" (*tathā*) and so forth, follows as a consequence because it shares the same form as real entities; thus, it has those [entities] as its cause.
Regarding the phrase "it has those as its cause":

Regarding what was stated— that because [positive entities] share the same nature as real things (*vastu*), there is no determination of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) within the mass of objects such as injunctions (*vidhi*) and so forth— he replies with the verse beginning "In injunctions, etc. (*vidhyādau*).

In the case of a mass of meanings such as affirmation (*vidhi*) and so forth, non-existence (*nāstitā*) and the like are negated by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), but not by the word itself—that which is not intended to be expressed.

Since the meaning of affirmation and so forth exists as being excluded from negation and the like, when that [affirmation] is understood, non-existence and so forth—which are not intended to be expressed—are negated by implication. Thus, even here, the determination of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) certainly occurs.

Regarding the statement "and also when a negative particle is joined with a negative particle," he says: "And also when a negative particle is joined with a negative particle, such an exclusion (apoha) would occur," and so forth.
When those four [conditions] are present, such as it is that is perceived;

for when there is a connection with a negative particle (*nañ*), the meaning of the negative particle is understood as the affirmation of something, and by a third negative particle, its absence is established. (1154–1155)
When another [word] is employed for the purpose of negating that [fourth], and when it is intended [as such], it makes known the exclusion of the others by means of that [negation].
Thus, there is the existence of this tetrad.

To the question, "In the presence of the fourfold negative (nañ), what kind of thing is cognized?", he says: "In connection with the negative," and so forth; here, the word *artha* is to be construed with the word *vidhi*.
"His separation" means the negation of that injunction;
"another for his negation" refers to the same.
The meaning is that it serves as a negation of that which was presented by the third "nañ" (negation) and is devoid of affirmation;
"turīya" means the fourth.

Because the suffix *yat* is prescribed in the sense of completion by the rule "caturasthayatāvādyakṣaralopaśca," the phrase "tasmin vivakṣite" means "when that fourth [negative particle] is employed."
By the fourth [word], "tena," it is made known that there is the exclusion of another by means of the negative particle (*nañ*).
Because, by means of the exclusion of the negation expressed by the third negative particle, there is the presentation of an object in the form of a positive reflection.
1156 Clarifying this very point by means of an illustration, he says: "It is not that he does not cook," and so forth;
for when it is said, "It is not that he is not cooking," it is understood that "he is cooking."
For by the third [word], the connection with indifference and so forth is understood.
But in the fourth, that [agent] is determined to be distinct from those [states], as in "he cooks.
Therefore, in this case, the exclusion of other [possibilities] is equal to that of an injunctive sentence.
"This is distinct from that" means it is distinct from indifference and so forth; thus,
there is a cessation of other [notions] equal to that of an injunctive statement.

Just as in an injunctive sentence such as "he cooks" (*pacati*), the cessation of indifference is intended by implication, so too it is established that in the case of the second *nañ* as well, its exclusion [of the action] occurs;
however, the example of four *nañ*s is given for the sake of clarity. (1157)
To the objection that even particles such as *ca* (and) cannot be joined with the negative particle *nañ*, he says: "Conjunction and so forth," etc.
Whatever meaning, such as conjunction (*samuccaya*), is intended by *ca* and other such particles—
By that [negation], there would be the exclusion of other things such as alternative meanings (*vikalpa*) and so forth.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of the following: for the particle *vā*, the meaning is "alternative"; for the particle *api*, it is "possibility," "conjunction," "permission," and so on; for the particle *tu*, it is "qualification"; and for the particle *eva*, it is "restriction.
This is what is meant by "of others than that."
Therefore, by that [word] "ca" and so forth, there is no other [function], such as conjunction (samuccaya) and the like.
To the objection that the exclusion of others cannot be designated within the meaning of a sentence, he says: "In the meaning of a sentence," and so forth.
The exclusion of others is indeed well-known in the meaning of a sentence; for it is said that the meaning of a sentence is simply certain word-meanings combined together. (1160)

And those things which are of a different class from them are clearly to be excluded; these very same [exclusions] constitute the meaning of the sentence as well, for there is indeed nothing else that exists apart from them. (1161) "Together" [is the term].
The meaning is that they are connected to one another by way of the relationship of cause and effect;
"of them" refers to those entities (padārthas).

Now, one might object: "The word-meaning (*padārtha*) is one thing, while the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*) is another; how then can it be said that those very things which are to be excluded from the word-meanings are also the things to be excluded from the sentence-meaning? To this he replies: "There is no such thing other than them. The point is that there exists no sentence-meaning distinct from the word-meanings that is either partless, variegated in nature, or resembling a mottled color, because such a thing, even if it met the conditions for perception, is not perceived. (1160)
1161 Clarifying this very point by means of an illustration, he says: "Caitra," etc.; that is, when the meaning of a sentence such as "Caitra, bring the cow" has been understood.
The exclusion (apoha) of other agents, objects, and so forth is understood by implication.

For in this sentence, no object other than the referents of words such as "Caitra" appears in the cognition; rather, when the meaning of "Caitra" is apprehended, the exclusion of non-Caitras and so forth is understood through the force of logical necessity (sāmarthya).
Otherwise, if the exclusion of other agents and so forth were not intended, then the mention of Caitra and others would be entirely purposeless;
consequently, no one would utter anything at all, and the world would be utterly devoid of activity.
Regarding the point that in words such as "exclusion of others" (ananyāpoha), the denotable object is not determined, he says: "In 'exclusion of others' and so forth... [Verse 1163].

In words such as "exclusion of others," no positive entity (vidhi) is apprehended, as was previously established by the refutation of universals (jāti) and the like, which are favored by our opponents.

For here, the word-meaning in the form of an affirmation characterized by universals (*jāti*) and so forth, as intended by you, is not determined from the perspective of ultimate reality; this is because such universals and the like have already been refuted at length previously, in the examination of the universal (*sāmānya*) and other sections.
What, then, is determined? To this he says: "But rather," and so forth.
However, from this [positive] determination, a conceptual construction arises; subsequently, when there is the negation of the word-meaning as apoha, the cognition arises.

(1164) If it is maintained that the cognition arises upon the negation of the word-meaning as apoha, then the word-meaning as apoha should not be accepted, because it has been negated. To this, he says: "But that [cognition], being of such a kind, is non-correspondent."
But that [cognition] is non-corroborative because it lacks a connection to such a real object;
therefore, not all verbal cognitions determine a real thing.
(1165) "That" refers to...
A term such as "exclusion of others" (*ananyāpoha*) is "non-corroborative" (*asaṃvādaka*);
it is non-corroborative because it does not correspond [to reality], or because no correspondence exists for it.

Why? Because of the loss of connection with a real entity (*vastu*), for there is no such connection with a real entity as previously described, since the existence of a real entity characterized by genus (*jāti*) and so forth has already been refuted. If this is so, how then does the cognition of the exclusion (*apoha*) as the word-meaning arise from words such as "exclusion" (*ananyāpoha*)? To this he says: "Not [derived] from words" (*na śābdāḥ*).

For indeed, certain verbal cognitions arise as being intent upon unreal objects precisely because they originate from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the habitual practice of false conceptualization; therefore, the existence or non-existence of things is not established by virtue of them.

Regarding what was stated [in verse 1164], beginning with "the object of knowledge (*prameya*), the knowable (*jñeya*), the word (*śabda*)," and so forth, he says: "The object of knowledge," etc. (verse 1165).

Regarding words such as "knowable" (*prameya*) and "cognizable" (*jñeya*), for which thing is there nothing to be excluded? Indeed, these are not employed by discerning persons in isolation or out of context.

(1166) It is stated that for which word, such as "knowable," there is no object to be excluded? If this is said with reference to the word "knowable" and so forth when it stands alone—that is, outside of a sentence and devoid of connection with other words—then it is a case of proving what is already established, because a word used in isolation is meaningless precisely due to its lack of usage.
He demonstrates this: for it is not "mere" (kevala) in the sense of being "unseasonable" (akāṇḍa);
"mere" (kevala) means devoid of any other word.
Regarding the term "unseasonably" (*akāṇḍe*):

since discerning persons employ words for the sake of favoring their audience and not out of mere habit, and because a favor— characterized by the removal of doubt or error— cannot be rendered for a listener merely by [the word] being existent.

For instance—if the communicator were to dispel the doubt and error that have arisen in the listener regarding some matter and produce an indubitable cognition, only then would he have performed a favor for others;
and such a favor cannot be accomplished by the mere utterance [of the words].

Therefore, because it benefits the listener by removing doubt and the like and by producing certainty, the employment of words is purposeful; thus he shows that this [word] is employed only when situated within a sentence—beginning with "But" (kintu) and so forth: "But when there is the possibility of doubt or error for someone regarding something, it is employed by the wise for the sake of removing those. (1167)
Because it produces a cognition free from doubt and error,
that very [speech] employed by them is experienced as successful.
1168 *Āreka* means doubt (*saṃśaya*).
"Of someone" refers to the listener;
"in some [place]" refers to the object.
"For the sake of their cessation" means for the sake of the cessation of those two, namely doubt and error;
"by that" [refers to the aforementioned means].
By the phrase "by them," it is meant "by those who are discerning," beginning with the term "the knowable" (jñeya).

Alternatively, [the author] shows that it is unestablished when the words "the knowable" and so forth are taken as they stand within the sentence itself, by stating: "That which therein... (yattatra).
Whatever is regarded there as a ground for suspicion by those of dull intellect is precisely what is refuted by him; otherwise, his utterance would be fruitless.
For if he were not suspecting something, why would he ask?
Or how could one of sound mind utter a word that does not produce a mental impression (*saṃskāra*)?

For in that case, by means of words such as "knowable" (*prameya*) situated within a sentence, exactly that which is suspected by those of dull intellect—the inert-minded—is excluded; therefore, this claim that there is nothing to be excluded by words such as "knowable" is unestablished. Otherwise...

If the meaning were that [the scripture] would not remove what is suspected by those of dull intellect, this might be so; however, it is not the case that nothing is suspected by the listener. To this he says, "For something indeed," and so forth.
For if the listener did not have doubt regarding any object, why would he depend upon instruction from another? Indeed, one asks another for the sake of certainty; otherwise, one would be insane.

It might be argued: "Even if there is indeed a ground for doubt on the part of the listener, nevertheless, that [doubt] is certainly not removed by that word. To this he says: *atatsaṃskārakam* and so forth.

The refinement (*saṃskāra*) characterized by the removal of the listener's ignorance and so forth is "that-refinement" (*tatsaṃskāra*). That word in which such a refinement does not exist is "non-effecting-that-refinement" (*atatsaṃskāraka*).
The suffix *ka* is applied here according to the rule *śeṣād vibhāṣā*.
How can one who speaks thus be a communicator possessing a sound mind?
The meaning is that [the proponent] would indeed be like one who is insane,
because words are employed solely for the purpose of refining the understanding of the listener.

Regarding this, in which statement does that point of doubt for the dull-witted lie which is here being refuted? He says: "That which is said to be 'form and so forth, cognizable by visual cognition and the like,'" and so on.
For this which has been superimposed by that [person] is indeed refuted by someone else.
By the word "by that," it is meant by the statement: "form and so forth are cognizable by visual cognition and the like."
To the question "What is that which is superimposed?", he says: "Not by that alone which is dependent on the eye," and so forth;
it is not only by that [cognition] dependent on the eye that form, such as blue and so on, is perceived.
However,
as for that which has been superimposed by those of dull intellect— namely, the claim that "the form of blue and so forth is cognized even by a single, eternal consciousness residing in the ear"—
that is refuted by this statement: "form is to be cognized by visual consciousness."

The meaning is that form is to be cognized only by the consciousness dependent on the eye, and not by the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth; [this is stated] because of the delusion that [forms] are to be cognized as having such characteristics as momentariness. 1172. In the case of the delusion, [they are] to be cognized in the form of momentariness and so forth.
Are these phenomena (dharmas) to be known by the cognition of the Omniscient One?
Are even non-existents—those which do not produce a cognition—to be known? The term "knowable" (vijñeya) is stated in order to dispel such delusions as these. 1173–1174.

In this way, are all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) to be known in the form of momentariness and so forth, or not? Or rather, are they to be grasped by the mind of an omniscient one, or not? For regarding those non-entities (*abhāva*), characterized by the absence of all description, which do not even produce cognition—as to whether they are "knowable," when such a doubt arises, this is said: all phenomena are to be known in the form of momentariness and so forth, and they are to be known by the cognition of an omniscient one; as for non-entities being "knowable," what is negated here is that superimposed form of knowability and the like upon phenomena by way of non-momentariness and so forth. (1173)
How can it be refuted by mere words? To this he says: "tādṛk" and so forth;
for those [entities] possess such knowability because of the proof of their momentariness and other properties.

Even non-existence is to be known as conventional because it is established by this [cognition] through its nature as "such-and-such," since it is proven by valid cognition in the form of momentariness and so forth. (1175)
Now, as to how the knowability of non-existence is established, he says: "It is known," and so forth;
"by this self" means by that which has the nature of non-existence.

The meaning is that even non-entities possess the status of being objects of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) because they are established in some way by the intellect; otherwise, there would be no conventional discourse regarding them at all.

Now, one might object: in the context of the inquiry, "Are words objects of cognition (*prameya*) or not?", when the term "objects of cognition" is employed, even for a listener who is unaware of the specific topic under discussion, a conceptual cognition arises regarding sounds and so forth in the form of a mental projection simply upon hearing the word "objects of cognition" alone. If, therefore, the isolated word has no meaning at all, how can there be a comprehension of meaning? To this he replies: "Having seen that the words 'object of cognition' (*prameya*), 'knowable' (*jñeya*), and so forth, serve as the cause for comprehension only when situated within a sentence, [one understands them] even at other times. (1176)
The cognition that arises regarding a solitary [word] amidst various fluctuating objects occurs in accordance with its sentence;
and such a cognition certainly exists even from words such as "jar" and the like. (1177)
Therefore, words such as "pot" (ghaṭa) are equal to sounds such as "knowable" (jñeya).

This is the collective meaning here: there is no comprehension of an object from the hearing of an isolated word alone; rather, for one whose intellect is captivated by the similarity to a meaningful word previously perceived within sentences, there arises the misconception of comprehending an object from the hearing of an isolated word. For instance, in whichever sentences the listener has previously perceived the word *prameya* (knowable), it is precisely regarding those objects that this cognition arises—it is unstable in its referent and takes the form of a mere floating impression.
And this is equally true for words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*) and so forth;

for instance, when the context is "Should water be brought by a jar or by the hollowed palms? and the word "by a jar" is used, a person who is unaware of the context will have a cognition—based on the preceding sentences—that possesses expectancy regarding as many meanings as have been seen in which sentences the word "by a jar" was used, precisely in accordance with those prior sentences.

Therefore, he shows that just as words expressing praise (*arthavāda*) denote specific meanings, so too do words such as "object of knowledge" (*prameya*) and so forth—hence the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).

Regarding what was stated in the passage beginning with "and in the conceptualization of the excluded (apohya)," he says: "And in the conceptualization of the excluded, it would be better to conceptualize the entity itself"—this [objection] is contradicted by what has been taught, because there is necessarily an exclusion of others. (1179)
"Only the entity itself is conceptualized therein, for it is precisely that which is intended to be expressed;
therefore, there is an exclusion of what is not intended to be expressed, but not of everything intended to be expressed.
(1180) "Only the entity itself," and so forth.

Indeed, it is only a real entity (*vastu*) that is imagined by us to be the meaning of a word by virtue of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), provided that it is what is intended to be expressed (*vivakṣita*). Since it is not a non-entity (*avastu*), when that [entity] is cognized, the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of what is not intended to be expressed is necessarily understood through the force of implication; thus, the established system of the meaning of words is not non-pervasive (*avyāpinī*).

And it was with reference to precisely that point which is a ground for doubt for one of dull intellect that the Teacher stated: "Having made the unknowable (*ajñeya*) a conceptual construct, inference [operates] upon the knowable (*jñeya*) by means of its exclusion."
Regarding the passage beginning with "Because of the negation of the form of cognition" (jñānākāraniṣedhāt), he says: "The form of cognition," and so forth.
However, the negation of the form of cognition is not possible because it is self-cognizable;
for there exists a manifold superimposition that is without an external object.
There is indeed a certain fixed [aspect] residing within the cognition itself with respect to each respective object.
And that very intrinsic nature (svabhāva) must necessarily be admitted;

it is precisely what we have called the "aspect" (ākāra), the "reflection" (pratibimba), the "appearance as that" (tadābhatā), the "impression" (ullekha), and the "manifestation" (pratibhāsa)—the difference in terminology is of no consequence. (1182–1183)
"It cannot be done"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
How is the self-cognizability of the form of cognition established? To this he says: "For it exists," and so forth.

In dreams and similar states, it is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*), as clear as the understanding of even a cowherd, that cognition is independent of an external object, being superimposing (*āropaka*) and assuming the form of an object even in its absence.
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that an object situated in another place or time is perceived in that [present] form, because that object lacks such a form.
Nor is it logical for one thing to be perceived through the form of another, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, you must necessarily admit some specific quality residing in the cognition itself that is produced by the object, by virtue of which— despite the equality of all cognitions in their nature as awareness— the cognition is distinguished through a division such that there is an experience of blue alone with respect to each particular object, and not of yellow. And once that is admitted, it follows by implication that cognition must indeed possess a form (*sākāra*),
because apart from a form, no other distinct intrinsic nature can be determined.

Therefore, since you have expressed that very same thing by the term "specific intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*), whereas we have used terms such as "aspect" (*ākāra*) or "mental image" (*ullekha*), there is merely a dispute over names. 1181–1182.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of words such as 'thus' (*evam*) and so forth," he says: "Of words such as 'thus,' etc."— that is,
for words such as "thus" and so on, there exists [the counter-correlate] "not thus" and so forth.
"That which is to be excluded" is clearly defined as having another mode [of being].

(1184) Thus, when that which is superimposed as "not thus" is excluded by words such as "thus," it is indeed most clearly understood; therefore, there is no lack of pervasion in the determination of the meaning of words.
Thus has the refutation stated by Kumārila been answered; now that which was stated by Udyotakara is being answered.
Regarding what he said—"What object is conceived as being excluded by the word 'all'?"—he replies with the words beginning "And when brought into common usage," and so forth.
And since even the word "all" (*sarva*) is brought forward in common usage, it possesses something to be excluded; and its meaning here is intended to be this "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*).
