Here too, just as with words such as "knowable" (*jñeya*), the word "all" is never used in isolation but is always employed within a sentence; therefore, that which is a ground for doubt for the dull-witted mind is precisely what must be negated.
"Intended to be expressed" means desired to be expressed.
He states what that intended meaning is: "All phenomena," and so forth.
All phenomena are selfless, or all persons have passed away; in that context, a sense of totality is understood, while some particular portion is excluded. (1186)
To the question "Which portion is excluded here?", he says:

"Only some"—only certain external things such as jars and so forth are accepted as being devoid of self; and thus the delusion that someone might have regarding [the existence of] motion is removed. (1187)
Regarding the objection beginning with "If [it is argued] that 'one and so forth is not all,'" and so on, he replies with "And the negation of all parts," and so forth:
"And the negation of all parts is certainly not intended in that context;
this would result in the negation of its own meaning (svārthāpoha), therefore it is stated out of ignorance. (1188)

For if the negation of every single member [of the compound] were intended when the word "all" (sarva) occurs in the sentence brought forward in common usage, then the exclusion of its own meaning (svārthāpoha) would follow as a consequence. However, since only that which is suspected by one of dull intellect is negated, how can the fault of subverting its own meaning arise? The same should be said regarding words such as "and so forth" (ādi). 1188
Regarding what was asked—"Is it an entity or a non-entity? and so forth—he says: "It is not an entity," and so on.
In reality, apoha is neither an entity nor a non-entity; it is characterized by neither difference nor identity; it is neither dependent nor independent; and it is neither one nor many. (1189)
To the question "Why is it not an entity?", he says: "In that way, it does not exist," and so forth.
It does not exist in reality in the manner in which it is determined; therefore, it is neither an entity nor a non-entity, because it is apprehended as a real thing. || 1190 ||

This [object] is determined by the deluded as having an external form, yet it does not exist in that manner; therefore, because it lacks the nature of an external form, it is not a positive entity (*bhāva*).
To the question, "Why then is it not a non-entity (*abhāva*)?", he says: "And it is not a non-entity, because it is determined as a real thing.
Since it is shown to have an external form, it cannot be said that it is absolutely a non-entity.
1190 Now, as to why [the relationship] does not consist of characteristics such as difference and identity, he says: "Difference, non-difference, and so forth," etc.
All [notions] such as difference and non-difference are established as existing in reality (*vastusat*).

And since the referent of a word is devoid of intrinsic nature, these [distinctions]—such as difference and non-difference, or by the word "and so forth," dependence and the like—are without a foundation. For these properties do not belong to real entities; how then could they find a footing in the *apoha*, whose form is fashioned by the artistry of conceptual construction?

As for what was said—that because exclusion (*apoha*) is of the nature of an action, its object must be stated—that is unproven; for the exclusion denoted by the word consists of a mental reflection (*pratibimba*), and since that reflection has the form of an external object as determined by conceptualization (*adhyavasita*), it is not a mere negation.

For this very reason, the two alternatives—"is it the object of 'cow' or the object of 'non-cow'?"—are untenable, because it is determined precisely as having the cow as its object, and thus as being of a positive nature (*vidhirūpa*).

Regarding what was said—"For by whom has 'non-cowness' been attached to the cow, such that it must be excluded by this [word]?"—to that he replies: "And the word directly effects the exclusion of other objects for us," and so forth.
The word directly effects for us the exclusion of other objects.
But when its own meaning has been expressed, that [negation] is understood through implication (sāmarthya).
It has been demonstrated in detail that it is not the case that "that nature is the nature of another"; therefore, this [objection] is raised here by one who is ignorant of the opponent's position.
"For by what has 'non-cowness' been attached [to the word], such that it is excluded by this [word] 'cow'?
It is not the case that this is excluded by the word through direct confrontation.

For if the word were to convey the exclusion of others as its primary meaning, then this [objection] would hold; however, the word first of all produces the aforementioned reflection of the object, and the exclusion is understood only by implication once that [reflection] is grasped. Thus, this which has been stated is merely something said out of ignorance of the established doctrine (siddhānta); such is the summary of the meaning.
The remainder is easily understood.
The alternative views regarding exclusion (*vyatireka*) and so forth have already been refuted.
Regarding what was stated—"Is this exclusion (*apoha*) the denotable object? and so on—he replies with the words "By which one," etc.

By which word is the expressibility of exclusion (apoha) being questioned— is it by this [word "exclusion"] or by a word such as "jar"? This is in the investigation of whether the meaning of a word is an exclusion or a positive injunction (vidhi).
"That which appears as 'exclusion' (apoha) is precisely what is thus cognized. For this cognition directly apprehends that the reflection is the meaning of the word;
however, the negation of [realities such as] universals and so forth is understood through the force of implication.
And words such as "jar" or "tree" express that very same reflection; because they produce it, they directly [denote it], yet they exclude what is other than the object.
Therefore, there is no fault regarding affirmation (vidhi), nor does any undesirable consequence follow.
The fault of the position that [the exclusion] is not expressible does not apply to us, because we do not accept that [position].

(1199) In this regard, if the alternative concerning whether "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is what is expressed is raised with reference to the word "exclusion of others," then since it is accepted that this [exclusion] is expressed by that word precisely in a positive form (*vidhirūpa*), it is not logical to charge us with an undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*). For instance, when the discussion is underway as to whether the meaning of a word is a positive entity or the exclusion of others, and it is stated that "the exclusion of others is the meaning of the word," there arises in the cognizer a cognition that determines the exclusion of others characterized as a reflected image (*pratibimba*) as previously described.
However, by implication, there is a negation of the word-meaning in its positive form.

Now, with respect to words such as "jar" (*ghaṭa*), even there, the exclusion (*apoha*) characterized as a reflection is produced directly by those words "jar" and so forth; it is conveyed by them in a positive form, while the understanding of the cessation of others occurs through the force of implication (*sāmarthya*). Thus, there is no undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*), nor is there the fault of lack of systematicity (*avyavasthā-doṣa*).

He shows that because the exclusion of others is understood through implication (*sāmarthya*), it is merely a restatement (*anuvādyatva*); and since the position that [the universal] is inexpressible (*avācya*) has not been accepted, there is no opportunity for the faults arising from that position to emerge—thus he says: "But as for the fault in the position that it is inexpressible... (vv. 1195–1196).
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "oneness and permanence," he says:
"Oneness, permanence, and so forth are imagined, not real;
therefore, making a joke about this indicates great scholarship. (1200)

For if the description of oneness and so forth were made from the perspective of ultimate reality (*pāramārthika*), then it would indeed be a cause for laughter on your part. However, since this was described by the Teacher as merely conceptual (*kālpnika*) in accordance with the perception of delusion, how could it possibly become a cause for laughter for the wise? Rather, one who refutes while failing to understand the intended meaning of the entities becomes an object of extreme ridicule for the wise.
Therefore, regarding the statement "in those very words where there is a connection with the negative particle," etc., he says: "By the force of the restriction," and so forth.
"By the force of the restriction, even the exclusion of others (anyāpoha) is understood; it is the self-nature itself that is understood, since otherwise the restriction would be fruitless. (1201)

It is not only where there is a connection with the negative particle (*nañ*) that the aspect of the exclusion of others (*anyanivṛtti*) is understood; for even where there is no connection with the negative particle, it is indeed understood. This has been established by your own words when you made the restriction that "only its own nature (*svātman*) is understood.
Otherwise, the restriction would be entirely meaningless.
For it is most clearly determined that wherever only its own nature is understood, the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) is also understood by the force of that very restriction.
With the words "In that case, for whom... and so forth, the opponent raises the very point that the determination of the word-meaning as apoha lacks universal applicability:
"For whom, then, even an external object is not accepted as existing otherwise [than it appears]."
By that [reasoning], what exclusion (*apoha*) is said to be expressed by words such as "the son of a barren woman"?

For instance, in the case of a word like "the son of a barren woman," there exists no external object such as a son—which would serve as the locus of exclusion (*apohāśraya*)—that is differentiated from others. What, then, is said to be the basis for the exclusion that is its denotation? Indeed, the exclusion must necessarily have a real entity as its locus, because it is not distinct from the object excluded from others.
He refutes [the objection] with the words "due to the absence of form" and so forth:
"Because non-existent things lack form, words that denote universals and the like are not even to be suspected [of denoting them]; they are established as indicators of mere appearance alone. (1203)

Since non-entities such as the son of a barren woman lack any form of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), words referring to them cannot be suspected of denoting universals (*jāti*) and the like. For while one might suspect that words functioning with respect to real entities (*vastu*) have either a [real] form as their denotation or a reflection (*pratibimba*) as their denotation, since a non-entity is defined precisely by its distinction from a real entity, how could there possibly be a suspicion that words functioning with respect to it have a real entity as their object?
Therefore, the objectlessness of words is even more evident; since they produce nothing but a reflection, this is certainly understood, and thus there is no ground for such a suspicion.
He demonstrates this very point with the verse beginning "artha" and so forth:
[it is] constructed solely from the latent impressions (vāsanā) arising from verbal discourse that is empty of objects.
Whatever reflection appears is expressed by words;
"by words" means by such words as "the son of a barren woman" and so forth.

Furthermore, in order to establish that those words which have real entities as their objects denote merely a mental reflection (*pratibimba*), he states the proof, beginning with "tanmātra": "These words, which directly illuminate that alone, are accompanied by doubt."

Because they depend upon convention, like words that denote imagined objects. (1205) Those things which depend upon convention are indicators of nothing more than the reflected images of conceptual constructions produced solely by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) left by empty talk devoid of real objects; for example, words such as "son of a barren woman" denote imagined objects and depend upon convention. And the words under dispute, such as "pot" and so forth, are accompanied by doubt and depend upon convention. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Having thus established his own position, he states the following as a proof for the refutation of the opposing position: "Those sounds which establish the formulation of distinctions and so forth accepted by others are not [authoritative] themselves; therefore, they should be understood to be just like that. (1206)

"Differentiation" (bheda) refers to the specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa); by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the inclusion of genus (jāti) and other categories is intended. "From that" means because it is dependent upon convention (saṅketa).
"In that very same way" means like the expression of an imagined object.
Avoiding the charge of inconclusiveness regarding both reasons, he says: "The impossibility of convention," and so forth.
For the impossibility of convention regarding difference and the rest has already been established previously;
and as for their fruitlessness, there is no doubt regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of those two reasons. (1207)

Because it is impossible to establish a convention [for such things] and because they are not shared by anything else— as has been previously established regarding the impossibility of convention and the futility of convention in the case of specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth—
it follows that for these two reasons, there is no doubt regarding their exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*).
With the words "But surely" (nanu) and so forth, the opponent raises the charge of inconclusiveness regarding the first reason:
"But surely, even on the theory of exclusion (apoha), how is the establishment of a linguistic convention possible?"
And how could there be success for that [cognition], since it is not established for both?
For the cognition of the speaker and the listener is not mutually perceived;
nor is that [cognition] seen at the time of the convention, yet it is observed during the actual usage.

Just as there is an impossibility and futility of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) regarding specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the like, so too is it the same in the case of the theory of exclusion (*apoha*). Consequently, since no convention has been established, it is also not logical for words to illuminate that [exclusion] alone; thus, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
And how could its efficacy (*sāphalya*) possibly be possible?—this is the remainder of the sense.
Regarding the phrase "of that," [the author] asks:
"But how is it that a convention is impossible there? and replies: "For that is established only for two."
The word *hi* indicates the reason (*hetu*);
for that apoha consisting of a reflection is not established as one for both the speaker and the listener, who are the respective objects of the linguistic convention.
Why is this? He says: "For [it is] not cognition," and so forth.
The knowledge of those with limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) is indeed to be personally realized within themselves (*pratyātmasaṃvedanīya*);
for one person of limited vision cannot perceive the knowledge belonging to another.
Furthermore, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), the exclusion (*apoha*) characterized by the nature of a reflection is not distinct from cognition itself.
Furthermore, since neither the speaker nor the listener has established any single object as the referent of the convention, where could the convention be made or grasped?
For a speaker is not able to establish a convention regarding an unestablished entity, nor can a listener grasp it, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
To explain: the reflection of an object mounted upon the listener's own cognition, which the listener perceives, is not experienced by the speaker.

And that which is perceived as crooked is not [perceived] by the auditory faculty, because each [cognition] experiences only its own respective manifestation. Furthermore, demonstrating its lack of purpose, he says: "In convention," and so forth.

That reflection or crookedness which was experienced by the auditory faculty at the time of the convention is not experienced at the time of practical usage, because, due to its momentary perishability, it has long since ceased to exist.
Furthermore, that which is experienced at the time of linguistic usage was not perceived at the time of the convention,
because at that time something entirely different was being experienced;
nor is it logical for there to be usage for one thing when the convention was made for another, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "of each its own," and so forth.

Even though it exists in the cognition of its own respective manifestation, it functions in the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an external object, since it is equal for both [the cognizer and the object].

For, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), even the form of cognition is not intended as the denotable object (*vācyatā*) of words, such that the impossibility of convention (*saṅketa*) therein would be urged; because this entire verbal transaction (*śābdo vyavahāraḥ*) is held to be erroneous—following one's own internal appearance (*svapratibhāsa*)—just like the vision of two moons by two people suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). It arises merely as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) determining an object from words, due solely to the awakening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of ideation devoid of an actual object.
That reflection of words is called the "denotable" (*vācya*) because it is produced [by them], but not because it is actually denotable.

For although, in ultimate reality, the speaker and the listener each experience only their own respective manifestation, nevertheless—just as in the case of two people with ophthalmia—the seed of error being identical, both the speaker and the listener possess an equally identical determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding an external object.
Nevertheless, the speaker has this conceit (*abhimāna*): "The very same object that I perceive, he perceives."
The same should be applied to the listener as well.

If it is asked, "How is it that this determination of a single object is mutually known by these two, the speaker and the listener?"—even if, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is not known, nevertheless, because the seed of error is identical, this conventional transaction exists as a mere delusion according to one's own mental appearance, like the case of two people with ophthalmia; this has already been explained. Therefore, the establishment of linguistic convention based on the determination of a single object is indeed logically consistent.
Here he states an illustration: "For just as one whose eyes are afflicted by cataracts speaks of two moons," and so forth.
"Likewise, all verbal usage is considered to be for one equal to oneself.
Regarding "for one equal to oneself," the meaning is: for another person who is like oneself, that is, for another who suffers from the same visual disorder (timira).
And he shows that the convention is not purposeless: "and its pervasiveness," meaning that this pervasiveness of it is intended as being based on conceptual determination (*adhyavasāyika*).
"For these cognitions produced by words are false appearances" (1212).
Thus ends the examination of the word-meaning.

Furthermore, the pervasion of the conventional usage over the time of the convention is accepted only by virtue of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the reflection of the object as determined by both the speaker and the hearer, not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*); for even at the time of conventional usage, the speaker and the hearer have the conceit of identity between the two objects perceived at earlier and later times.
Now, he asks why this is not accepted from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), stating: "Because they appear falsely," and so forth.
This concludes the examination of words and their meanings.
Regarding the examination of the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*):
there are four types of divergent views held by opponents concerning the nature, the result, the object, and the number of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

In order to clearly demonstrate the definition of the means of valid cognition by refuting those views, and to establish that "the two means of valid cognition are determined by their association with clear definitions," he says: "Direct perception," and so forth.
The perception and inference that others have stated for the sake of establishing the *upādhi* (limiting condition) are not established as having such characteristics; for such is their nature.
(1213) "For the sake of establishing the *upādhi*" means...
"By others," namely by the Vaiśeṣikas and so forth, for the purpose of establishing [categories] such as quality, substance, action, genus, and inherence.
"Thus" refers to what is about to be said [verse 1213].

In this regard, there is a disagreement concerning the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*), namely that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of perception is either conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or has the nature of non-cognition (*ajñāna*), such as the visual faculty and so forth. To refute that [view] and state its definition, he says: "Perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). Perception is free from conceptual construction; conceptual construction is a cognition associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpinī pratītiḥ*), because it consists in the cause of designation (*klṛpti-hetutva*), and not [the sensory faculty]. (Verse 1214)

In that context, having restated that cognition is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*), its status as perception (*pratyakṣatva*) is prescribed; for in every case, it is the definiendum (*lakṣya*) that is being prescribed—
as in the example, "That which trembles is the *aśvattha* tree," where the object of definition here is perception.
Since it is precisely the definition of "tall" that is under discussion here—
and not the definition of "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous," which might lead one to think that this [definition] is being enjoined—

furthermore, because the nature of cognition is obtained by implication through the negation of conceptual construction (just as when one says, "Let a cow without its calf be brought," the cow-nature is understood by the negation of the calf), the word "cognition" (*jñāna*) was not explicitly stated.

What, then, is the intended meaning of "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*) here? He states that perception is cognition from which [conceptual construction] has been removed; thus, conceptual construction is "cognition associated with verbal expression. Now, is that [definition] consisting of being the cause of conceptualization (*klṛpti*), etc., as Śaṅkarasvāmin and others have extensively criticized it, to be accepted or not? He says: "but not that consisting of being the cause of conceptualization, etc."; the word "is accepted" is to be supplied.
By that, it is meant that the defects which others have alleged against that basis do not apply at all, precisely because one does not accept their position.

It should be understood that "postulation," "designation," and "being the cause thereof" refer to universals (*jāti*) and so forth; for there is no designation without the distinction of universals and the like.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), one should include *vitarka* and *vicāra*—which are the causes of the coarseness and subtlety of the mind through its association with words—as well as the conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper, and other such factors.
“Expression” (abhilāpa) means a denotative word, and that [word] has a universal form (sāmānyākāra); that which appears [to cognition] as possessing such [a form] is so described.
But from what is such a cognition established? To this he says: “The object of a word,” and so forth.
That [cognition] which, in the form of "tree" and so forth, is capable of connecting word and meaning, arises as if accompanied by verbal expression even when words are not actually employed.
(Verse 1215) The connection is: "that which, in the form of 'tree' and so forth, [arises] even when words are not employed."
Alternatively—the connection is that by the former [statement], [it was shown that conceptualization] is capable of joining word and object in forms such as "tree" and so forth;
by this [latter statement], he demonstrates the establishment of conceptualization through direct perception itself, because conceptual construction is established for all living beings.
For it is shown that this [habitual tendency] is indeed established as the cause of such activity even from childhood:

"Because of the continuity of the latent impressions of the cultivation of the meanings of past names and objects, even one just born becomes proficient in activity through connection with that [tendency]. (1216)

Past existence means past birth; therein, the cultivation of name and object (*nāmārthabhāvanā*) is the repeated practice of word and meaning. The latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by that is its capacity; the continuity or persistence of that exists even in an infant.

Therefore, even for him, there occurs a conceptual cognition (*pratīti*) associated with verbal expression, through the connection with which he becomes skillful—that is, adept—in the performance of activities characterized by smiling, crying, sucking the breast, joy, and so forth.
Consequently, by this effect, the aforementioned conceptualization is indeed inferred even in the case of an infant.
As it has been said: "In this world, the procedure for action (*itikartavyatā*) relies entirely upon words;

even a child understands it through impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited previously. Furthermore, that [procedure] arises for them as if manifesting externally an object that exists internally within the measure of time (*mātrā*), distinguished by sounds in the form of phonemes (*akṣara*) that have coalesced with Being (*san*); by means of this, they subsequently become proficient in grasping conventions (*saṅketa*).

With the words "cintā" (thought) and so forth, he further states the establishment of conceptualization through direct perception: "And that which is clearly experienced at the time of thinking, imagining, and so forth..."
"Like something permeated by sounds, it cannot be denied.
With the words "tasyāśca" (and of that), he states its establishment even through the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of the effect known as verbal usage:
"And through the determination of that [universal], the status of word and object is established as erroneous."
Because it is impossible for anything else [to exist], if this [conceptual construction] were non-existent, then even such a thing would not be possible.

(1218) Since the previous masters have refuted the reality of the established relationship between word and object and have determined it to be an error, if this conceptual construction were non-existent, then that established relationship between word and object—even one that is erroneous—would not be possible; for that relationship is established only by virtue of the intention behind it.

Furthermore, since it has been demonstrated that other external factors, such as specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth, are unfit to be the denotable objects [of words], [one might object]:

"But surely others do not describe conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) merely as a cognition associated with verbal expression; rather, they also describe it as being capable of connection with universals (*jāti*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), and so on."

To the question "Why is that [conceptual construction] not apprehended?", he says: "Others understand conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) as that which is capable of being associated with universals (*jāti*) and so forth; however, because universals and the like have been refuted and because they are not perceived, such [a construction] is not tenable. (1219)
The phrase "because of non-perception" is to be connected with "of genus and so forth";
and this refutation has been stated while provisionally accepting the existence of genus and the rest.
With the words "of genus and so forth," and so on, he supports that very point of non-perception: because genus and so forth are not perceived, their connection [with the object] does not appear.
"And how can a connection [of the universal] with its object be established, as in the case of milk and water?
(1220). Regarding the phrase "as in the case of milk and water":

just as it is impossible to effect a separation of milk and water once they have been mixed because they do not appear distinctly, so too—even though universals and the like exist—because they do not appear distinct from their substratum, it is impossible [to establish a connection] with that substratum; this is the meaning.

If, then, conceptualization (*kalpanā*) as the association with universals (*jāti*) and so forth is indeed not logical, how is it that the author of the definition stated: "Conceptualization is the association with names, universals, and so forth"? He replies: [The phrase] beginning with "to be abandoned" (*heya*) and so forth is stated by way of two [types of] mention in order to explain the objects of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted.

This conceptualization (kalpanā) is declared to be of two kinds, established as "other" and "self. Among these, conceptualization consisting of the association with universals (jāti) and so forth is to be abandoned, being established by others; conceptualization consisting of the association with names is to be adopted, being established by oneself. To show this, both types of conceptualization have been specified. How is this understood? He says: "Because of the mention of the pair"—because the name and the universals and so forth constitute the group of "name, universal, etc.," and their association is thus stated as two categories. Otherwise, it would have had to be stated either as "association with name, etc. or simply as "association with universal, etc."
This is not an exhaustive enumeration, for otherwise it would follow that the word "etcetera" (ādi) would be redundant.

Now, one might object: conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a property of cognition; therefore, what is under discussion here—given the context of direct perception—is precisely the demonstration of its absence, not the demonstration of the absence of properties belonging to the object.

Anticipating the objection that "the connection of names, universals, and so forth with their possessors is a property residing in the object and not in the cognition; therefore, the author of the definition is stating something irrelevant," he says: "And this connection of names and so forth...
This connection of names and so forth proceeds by immediately implying its own cause [the cognition]; thus, it is not a statement of something irrelevant. (1222)
"Immediately following"—that is, the immediate cause (*nimitta*), which is its [the cognition's] reason.
That, moreover, is a cognition (*pratīti*) permeated by verbal expression (*abhilāpa*);

and because it arises in the form of a synthesis (*anusamdhāna*) of two things, it is designated as "joining" (*yojanā*). However, no one at all joins anything, because all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*).

Its projection occurs by way of two modes; that [connection] from which it arises is so described. Because it makes [the meaning] understood, the *bahuvrīhi* compound is used even when there is a lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).
Alternatively, [the term "cause" may be applied] by metaphorically attributing the effect to the cause;
yet there is no further purpose for this metaphorical usage than to reveal the nature of that which produces a specific effect as distinct from other causes.

Alternatively, he shows that there is no fault [in the definition] by forming the compound *yojanā* as "that by which something is joined" (*yojyate 'nayā*), and thus indicating that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is specified as being precisely that which is expressive (*abhilāpinī*). He says: "Name, genus, and so forth," etc.
That conceptual construction (*kalpanā*)—which is a cognition (*pratīti*)—is so described because all names, genera, and so forth are joined (*yojyante*) by it; it is called "expressive. (1223)
With the words "Or rather" (*yadvā*) and so forth, he states another solution:
"Or rather, it is simply the conceptual construction established in our own system that is presented;
for the connection is made by construing [the text] as 'in every case, an object associated with a name is expressed. (1224)

If this is so, how is this passage from the Master’s *Vṛtti* to be interpreted? It runs as follows: "In the case of arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), an object qualified by a name is expressed, such as ‘Ḍittha’; in the case of genus-words (*jātiśabda*), by the genus, as ‘cow’; in the case of quality-words (*guṇaśabda*), by the quality, as ‘white’; in the case of action-words (*kriyāśabda*), by the action, as ‘cook’; and in the case of substance-words (*dravyaśabda*), by the substance, as ‘staff-bearer’ or ‘horned one.

For by this passage, it is clearly demonstrated that even an object joined with qualifiers such as a genus is expressed as something distinct [from the qualifier]; therefore, he says: "In all cases," and so forth.
The phrase "in all cases" refers even to words such as those denoting genus (*jāti*) and so forth;

what is meant is this: just as when arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*) are employed, an object qualified by a name is expressed, so too in the case of words denoting genus and so forth, such as "cow" (*go*), an object qualified by a name is expressed—this is to be applied throughout the entire treatise.
How, then, should this other instrumental ending in "by genus," "by quality," "by action," or "by substance" be construed? He says: "But by those... and so forth;
for it is through them, expressed by the instrumental case, that [the word] attains its meaningfulness.
This [name] establishes its meaning as "this is such-and-such" by means of the genus (*jāti*) and so forth.

(Verse 1225) An object qualified by the name through the genus acting as the instrument is expressed as "cow"; likewise [it is expressed] by means of qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth. In this way, those [categories] such as the genus attain their purpose through their connection with the name via the instrumental case-ending. If this is so, one might ask: how is the connection to be understood in the rule *nāmajātyādiyojanā*? He says: "of the name, by the genus and so forth"—the word "connection" (*yojanā*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.
By the phrase "this very [conceptualization]," he points specifically to the conceptualization obtained through the sense of the compound:

"the joining with universals and so forth" (*jātyādiyojanā*) means the joining of a name with universals and so forth; thus, the meaning of this compound is established as "this joining of a name with universals and so forth" (*nāmajātyādiyojanā*). This is the intended sense.

Anticipating the objection that, if this were so, the established rule would be non-comprehensive because of the absence of bases for application such as genus (*jāti*) in arbitrary words (*yadṛcchāśabda*), he says: "Because of the existence of the genus denoted by the arbitrary word," and so on. This means that it is not [non-comprehensive] because of the presence of the genus which is the object denoted by the arbitrary word.
One should consider that there is no lack of pervasion [in this definition], though there is a separate mention [of these words] because they are well-known.

This is what is meant: even those words such as "Ḍittha" and so forth, which are recognized as arbitrary (yadṛcchā) names, persist from birth until the moment of death; being unable to convey an object that is distinguished by unique particulars changing at every moment, they take as their denotatum a universal (jāti) inherent in the object as delimited by the boundaries of a long duration of time.

Otherwise, how could words—which are established as having for their objects specific portions of an entity delimited by the differences between states such as childhood—convey an entity that also possesses the distinctions imposed by states such as old age?

Even for those who hold the view that the body is not momentary but rather persists through time, it is nonetheless established that the substance is different in each distinct state, due either to the connection with diminishing parts over time or to the actual loss of parts.

Even when transformation is observed, that entity which is connected to a particular state is what is intended by the word; therefore, if it were to resort to another state, that very same entity would not be denoted by that word. Just as the word "milk," whose denotative power is fixed upon milk, does not apply to curd, so too [the word] would not apply to another state even in the case of the body. Thus, a universal (*jāti*) must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, even if the universal were not a real entity, the systematic application of words would remain non-pervasive.

For instance: those very same particulars, when their distinctions are not intended to be expressed, are taken as the "universal" (sāmānya) and are thus designated everywhere by words denoting a genus (*jāti*). Therefore, the author of the *Lakṣaṇa* has specified that arbitrary words (*yadṛcchā-śabda*) are distinct from genus-words. He says, "But because of common usage" (*prasiddhes tu*):

for in the world, words such as "cow" (*go*) and so forth are recognized as genus-words, whereas words such as "Citrāṅgada" and so forth are recognized as proper names; hence the separate mention [of the latter]. Now, with the words beginning with "nanu," the opponent raises an objection.
"But surely, because it expresses the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), a genus-word (jāti-śabda) is merely a word of intention (vivakṣā-śabda),
since it is dependent upon the speaker's intention.
[The author] replies with the verse beginning "True" (satyam).
"It is true that this has been said by one learned in logic for the sake of conforming to worldly convention;
for only this much of a word has entered the path of common usage.
(1228) "For only this much" means:
"It is of five kinds, through the distinction of words for genus, quality, action, substance, and [proper] name.

(1228) Now, if it is intended that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) established by one's own school alone is meant, why then did the Teacher later describe the conceptual construction established by his own school separately with this passage: "But others say that a qualified object is expressed by words which are themselves devoid of meaning"? To this he says: "But those [genus and so forth]..."
However, those [factors] such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth do not exist here as separate entities as they do in common worldly usage;
it is for the purpose of establishing this that the passage beginning with "others, however" (*anye tu*) has been described.

What is meant is this: genus and the rest do not exist as ultimate realities (*pāramārthika*) distinct from individual manifestations (*vyakti*) such as the brindled cow; rather, they are conventional (*sāṃvṛta*). It was for the sake of demonstrating this point that the author of the definition stated this, and not to show some other separate conceptual construction.
"Others" refers to the Buddhists;
"by those devoid of objects" means by those [cognitions] which lack external referents.
The meaning of the Master’s text is that [exclusion] is the object of words which are independent of genus and so forth, and which have exclusion alone as their domain.

Showing that this conceptual cognition (*kalpanā*) which expresses [its object] is not only accepted by us, but must necessarily be accepted by others as well—otherwise the world would be entirely non-functional—he says: "Even those who rely on conceptualization consisting in the association with universals (*jāti*) and so forth, must necessarily accept a cognition that is expressive. (1230)

Otherwise, because there would be no connection [between them], and because two entities—just like two things joined by a logical reason—would be perceived as independent, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) itself could not be postulated.
Or else, consequently, this entire universe would become something subject to conventional usage (*vyavahārya*). // 1231 //
This [object] is considered to be the basis of linguistic usage when it is conjoined with forms such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth.
(1232) The conjunction with genus and so forth is invariably concomitant with the conjunction of words;
thus, the statement "it is called such" becomes fruitful. (1233)

Even regarding the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) accepted by others as the association of genus, quality, action, and substance, conceptual construction is nothing other than the association with a name.

For in that case, an object delimited by genus and so forth is apprehended as qualified by the name itself; otherwise, since there would be no association—as in the case of apprehending multiple objects independently—how could there be conceptual construction? Consequently, the world would be mute.
For this very reason, even when seeing a man equipped with a staff, one does not associate him as "staff-bearer" until one recalls the specific name.

Precisely because all mental construction (*yojanā*) is pervaded by the association with words, it is for this very reason that in expressions such as "cow," an object qualified by the teacher’s [accepted] universal (*jāti*) is said to be "denoted.
Otherwise, in the absence of a name, how could there be the question "what is denoted?"—
since the act of denotation (*abhidhāna-kriyā*) is a property of words.
With the words "Therefore" (tasmāt) and so forth, he concludes the establishment of conceptual construction (kalpanā):
"Therefore, for all proponents established in their respective systems..."
"This conceptual construction (kalpanā), which is free from dispute, should be established without effort; this is my view.

[Verse 1234] He states the intention of the author of the *lakṣaṇa* (definition) as he points out that conceptual construction is twofold in nature—that is, having the form of accomplishment (*siddhi*)—by saying "having grasped all this," namely, the description of name, genus, and so forth.
In this context, he has thus employed the two views of himself and others;
having stated, "The difference for us from those [others] is precisely this," he then uttered the subsequent sentence beginning with "But others... and so forth.

The connection is as follows: "He composed" [the work] which describes the objects of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, which occurs without the application of genus (*jāti*) and so forth, and without the application of names (*nāman*), and which was previously described as the "description of names, genus, and so forth."
The presentation of one's own and others' views is for the purpose of explaining what is to be rejected and what is to be adopted.
He asks, "How then is the *Nyāyamukha* treatise to be interpreted? and says: "In this way," and so forth. The *Nyāyamukha* treatise is to be explained by means of this direction:
because of the connection with the word "cognition" (*jñāna*), it is "understanding" (*pratīti*) that is indicated therein. (1237)

In this regard, the *Nyāyamukha* text states: "That cognition which, through the metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of non-difference between the qualifier and the designator regarding the form of the object and so forth, is free from conceptual construction (*avikalpaka*), and which operates in relation to each sense organ (*akṣam akṣam prati*), is perception (*pratyakṣa*). Here, the "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*) refers to the genus (*jāti*) and so on; the "designator" (*abhidhāyaka*) refers to the name (*nāman*). The metaphorical attribution of non-difference between these two—the genus and so forth, and the possessor of the genus, as well as the name and the bearer of the name—is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). Even in cases where there is apprehension through distinction, such as "this is its cowness" or "this is its name," conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is indeed admitted.

Now, it might be objected: "Was it not stated that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a cognition that follows in succession? How then can the aforementioned conceptual construction be obtained [from the definition]? To this he says: "Because of its connection with the word 'cognition' (*jñāna*). What is meant by this is as follows: by demonstrating that cognition itself is perception through its contrast with conceptual construction, he has shown that conceptual construction is a property of cognition.

And thus the meaning is as follows: that cognition which is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*) through the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of non-difference from names and so forth is perception (*pratyakṣa*); however, that cognition which is not non-conceptual in that way is not perception because it consists of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). By implication, it is established that "conceptual construction" is a cognition associated with verbal expression (*abhilāpinī pratīti*), as defined by its opposition to perception; in this manner, the inclusion of the views of others and our own is demonstrated. Alternatively, he shows that the Teacher has merely provided a description of his own position by saying "or rather" (*yadvā*), and so forth.
Alternatively, "differentiation" (*bheda*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) by which a word effects the exclusion of others;
and by this [qualifier], it effects the delimitation (*vyavaccheda*) of universals (*jāti*) and so forth.
"Differentiation" (*bheda*), "qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*), and "exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti*) have the same meaning.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that which expresses it [the universal], but not those of genus (*jāti*) and so forth; this is the metaphorical attribution of non-difference to that [universal].

Now, if conceptualization (*kalpanā*) is a cognition associated with verbal expression, then it is the subject (*dharmin*). However, there is no possibility of one subject being [predicated] of another subject, such that its negation could be made as a property (*dharma*) of that [other subject]; thus, [your statement] expresses something unrelated.

Likewise, if perception is "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*), how is it that it is expressed by the word "perception"? Thinking that the meaning of "free from conceptual construction" is indeed an inexpressible object, others such as Bharga and Bhāradvāja raise this objection.
[The author], connecting [the response] by stating that all of this has already been refuted, says: "And thus, having the nature of cognition," and so forth.
That which is thus considered to be conceptual construction has, in this way, the nature of being cognized.

And the negation of identity [between perception and its conceptual content] is described as being established by perception itself. (1239) Even though it is denotable by words such as "perception" (*adhyakṣa*) and so forth at that time, this does not contradict the absence of conceptual construction (*kalpanāviraha*) in perception; for that denotability by words is not [the essence of] perception. (1240)

Otherwise, form, smell, and so forth would possess conceptual content; therefore, this position held by others of dull intellect has no foundation whatsoever. (1241) If [it is argued that] "perception" is denoted by the word *pratyakṣa*, [then...]
How is it understood that [perception] is free from conceptual construction? How is it improper?
By this passage—"That in which this conceptual construction does not exist is perception"—the author of the definition establishes the negation of identity (*tādātmya-pratiṣedha*).

The meaning is that such knowledge—which consists of conceptual construction—does not exist; it does not, however, mean a negation of the substratum (*ādheya*). First of all, this is not a valid objection.

The second [objection] is likewise not a valid objection, because the meaning of "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) has been explained as meaning "not denotable by words" (*anabhidheyārtha*).
What then? The meaning is "non-conceptual.

Even though non-conceptual cognition is designated by a word in accordance with conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), nevertheless, it will not become conceptual in the same way that color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth do; thus, this [objection] is of no consequence.
It might be argued: "Let it be so that the conceptual construction is as described;
however, how is it established that [perception] is free from conceptual construction? To this he says: "Perception," and so forth.
"Perception is free from conceptual construction, as it is experienced with extreme clarity;
for even when the mind is attached elsewhere, there is still the perception of blue and so forth by means of the sense faculties.
By this, he demonstrates that the absence of conceptual construction is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) as a form of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

It might be argued that this very conceptual construction (vikalpa), while distracted by another object, perceives the blue and so forth situated before one; to this he says: "Not that very [construction]," and so on.
For it is not that very conceptual construction which perceives that object.
Because it would abandon the expression of past objects and so forth, and because it would result in the application of their names [to the present].

(1244) For if that very conceptual construction were to apprehend that object, then it would apply the name of that very blue thing and so forth by abandoning the expression of past objects and so forth;
for it has been stated that this is because one does not perceive the association of two expressions in a single [object], and thus it would abandon the expression of the past and so forth.

The name of that which has become manifest is "that name"; its "connection" (ghaṭanā)—that is, its application (yojanā)—is its "attainment" (āpti), meaning its acquisition (prāpti) or, in other words, its occurrence (prasaṅga).

It might be thought: "In that case, why is it not understood that at that time another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) indeed apprehends that object? To this he says: "At that time, that name," and so forth.

At that time, there is no other conceptual construction associated with that name; for [otherwise] there would be a simultaneous perception of two [objects], which is neither observed nor desired. (1245)

By this, he states the contradiction with direct perception and the contradiction with one's own tenets regarding the thesis of two simultaneous conceptualizations; "of the two" refers to the two conceptualizations—this is the ellipsis.
He concludes with the verse beginning "vikalpaka": Therefore, conceptual cognition is experienced as coexisting with [sensory] knowledge;
thus, it is clear that this sensory consciousness is free from conceptual construction. (1246)
The opponent might argue that it is unproven that [cognitions] arise simultaneously with conceptual construction; anticipating this objection, he says:
"If it is thought that cognitions arise only in succession, then the misconception of their simultaneous occurrence is due to their rapid operation, like a whirling firebrand. (1247)
If they arise sequentially, how is it that they are perceived simultaneously? To this he says: "But the conceit of simultaneous existence...

Just as with a firebrand (*alāta*), as when a firebrand is whirled rapidly, there arises from the conjunction of those perceptions a single cognition in the form of a circle; likewise, due to the rapid production of cognitions, there is the conceit of their simultaneous existence.

Alternatively—the word "firebrand" (alāta) refers, by metaphorical attribution (upacāra), to the cognitions whose objects are that [firebrand], namely the cognitions regarding the subject (the knower);
the suffix -vatī is used as before.
"No," he says, rejecting the prima facie view;
for at that time, no conceptual construction associated with the mental impression of the object facing [the mind] exists as a visible thing— this is what was stated in verse 1248.
He thinks as follows: "The establishment of simultaneous occurrence is not the subject under discussion here;

rather, what is intended is the absence of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in cognition. And that [absence] is established by the non-apprehension of a conceptualization associated with the name of an object—even when the mind is directed elsewhere—at the time of experiencing an object present before one, provided such a conceptualization meets the conditions for apprehension. Therefore, no refutation has been stated here."
For instance, even if [the two] are indeed perceived sequentially within cognition, yet conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is not so perceived, there is no contradiction with the subject at hand.
Furthermore, demonstrating that this misconception of simultaneous occurrence is not an error, he says: "Error," and so forth.

Error, the conceit thereof, and its manifestation are continuous; therefore, the simultaneity of the object and the cognition is clearly established. (1249) The word "error" (*bhrānti*) is to be connected with the subject under discussion, namely, that it is not [the case].
The analysis of the compound *tadabhimāna* is "the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding that"—namely, the conceit regarding the simultaneous existence [of the two].

The status of something as an error is established by the force of a subverting means of valid cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*); however, there is no such subverting cognition here, by which it could be an error.

How is it that [the object] does not exist? He says: "And that manifest [object] is continuous. The word "that" refers to the cognition of an object present before one; it is clearly experienced simultaneously with a mind that is not attached to another intervening object.
If such a cognition of an object is called perception (*pratyakṣa*), how can there be any delusion?

Showing that there is not only no proof whatsoever for establishing the erroneous nature of simultaneous occurrence, but rather there is evidence to the contrary, he says: "In the case of watching a dancer," and so forth;
"everything is perceived simultaneously during such states as watching a dancer."
Even when there is a great interval between them, that [cognition] is an error due to its rapid occurrence.
(1250) Since cognitions of a creeper, a palmyra tree, and so forth proceed with extreme swiftness, why does the conceit of their occurring simultaneously not likewise apply here? (1251)
And when the mental construction is pure, no sequence would be discerned;
for the rapid operation of all cognitions is such that they appear to endure for a long time.
Therefore, there would be no perception of sequence in any object whatsoever.
The appearance of simultaneous apprehension would be like the cognition of sound and so forth.
(1253) Even though each individual cognition is separated by five other cognitions, it appears as if uninterrupted during states such as watching a dancer;

for instance, at the very moment one beholds the dancer, one simultaneously hears the sound of music and the like, tastes the flavor of camphor and the like, smells the fragrance of flowers placed in the nostrils, feels the touch of the breeze from a fan and the like, and thinks of giving garments, ornaments, and so on.

Furthermore, if—due to the force of rapid production—an illusion of the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions arises even when there is a great interval between them, then in cases such as *latā*, *tāla*, *sara*, and *rasa*, because each cognition is separated by only one [intervening] moment, the hearing of the phonemes would proceed with extreme swiftness, resulting in the appearance of the phonemes as being simultaneous.
Consequently, when words such as *sara* and *rasa* are heard, there would be no distinction in their audition nor any distinction in the comprehension of their meanings.

Furthermore: when a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consisting of the reflection upon various objects of knowledge arises, uninterrupted by heterogeneous sensory cognitions such as those of the eye, there is a rapid occurrence; thus, no determination of succession would be possible.

Moreover, since all cognitions are momentary and do not persist for long, they possess a rapid occurrence; consequently, the perception of any object would not appear as successive, just like the cognition of sound and other [sensory] objects.
Just like the perception of sound and so forth during the state of watching a dancer.
Showing that the example "like a fire-brand" (alātavad) is deficient in the probandum (*sādhyavikala*), he says: "Even in the case of a fire-brand," and so forth.
Even in the case of a firebrand, the illusion of a wheel arises all at once,
not from the synthesis of successive visual perceptions, because it appears with perfect clarity.
For indeed, synthesis is performed by memory alone, and not [by direct perception].
Because an object that has already passed away cannot be apprehended by vision;
and because its object is not clearly manifest due to having perished, it follows that this appearance of a wheel would not be clearly manifest. (1255–1256)

For this is not a mental error that arises by joining together successive perceptions; rather, it is a single, simultaneous sensory error in the form of a wheel produced by the power of a specific causal complex (*sāmagrī*). This is because it possesses a vivid appearance (*vispaṣṭapratibhāsatva*);

indeed, it is not logical for that which is bound to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) to have a vivid appearance. To explain: such a synthesis is performed by memory alone, not by sensory cognition, because the latter, arising through the power of the presence of an object, lacks the capacity to grasp a past thing.
Furthermore, the object of this memory is not clearly manifest; why? Because it has perished.
Therefore, since there would be the consequence of it appearing unclearly, this is not a mental error;
rather, it is born of the sense faculties. Thus, the illustrative example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).

Having thus established the absence of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) in cognition through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), he now establishes it through inference (*anumāna*) with the words "And if," and so forth: "And if, moreover, for whatever entity there exists no cause for the establishment of its specific form, that [entity] is not determined as such by the wise. (1257)

Just as a white horse (*karka*), which lacks a dewlap and other [characteristics], does not exist in the form of a cow, so too there is no apprehension of an object qualified by qualifiers in the case of conceptual cognition;
for such conceptual existence depends upon the presence of the sense organs.
The counter-example consists of the brindled cow and so forth; otherwise, there would be an over-extension.
Nor is the reason unestablished, because [the opponent] denies the existence of universals and the like;
and since there is no determination of difference, such a qualification does not exist. (1259–1260)

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That which lacks a cause for its being established in a certain form is not so established by discerning practitioners; for example, a white horse (*karka*), which lacks the collection of dewlaps and other features that serve as the cause for the designation "cow," does not exist as a cow.

And in the case of perception—which arises by the power of its uncommon object, such as blue—it lacks the cause for being established as a conceptual state (*savikalpaka-bhāva*), namely, the apprehension of an object qualified by qualifiers. This is a non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).

By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyeṇa*), [the counter-argument is as follows]: there would follow the undesirable consequence that all things would be established in every respect by [a single cause], such as *śābaleya* and *bāhuleya* cattle; furthermore, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the establisher would act without foresight (*aprekṣāpūrvakāritā*). This is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). The summary meaning is this: *karkaḥ* means a white horse.
The phrase "of genus and so forth" implies "of the qualifier.
Showing that even if genus and so forth were real entities, they would nonetheless not be unestablished (asiddha), he says: "and because they are not perceived as distinct."
The phrase "from form and so forth" (*rūpādeḥ*) is to be supplied as the object intended to be qualified (*viśeṣya*).

[The opponent objects: "Even if there is indeed no discernment by way of difference, why does it not nonetheless function as a qualifier? To this he says: "And it is not the case that what is undiscerned through difference... [is a qualifier].
Therefore, because the apprehension of an object qualified by a qualifier does not exist, this reason is not unestablished (asiddha).

It might be argued: "Let it be that universals (jāti) and so forth do not serve as qualifiers; however, the very nature of the word itself will be the qualifier. To this, he says: "Even the name," and so forth.
Even the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a word is not at all its designator;
for it has already been refuted that a specific characteristic can be either the denoted or the denoter.
Therefore, only that which is superimposed (*adhyāropita*) is accepted as the denoted and the denoter.
And perception apprehends an object that has not been superimposed [by conceptual construction].

(1262) This is because [perception] exists when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) exists, and it is absent when that is absent; furthermore, when there is an obstruction or the like, that [perception] also undergoes exclusion.

(1263) For there is no linguistic convention regarding the particular characteristic, nor regarding the particular characteristic of a word, because neither of these persists at the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra*).
Furthermore, there is no nature of a word other than its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*);
nor can an object that has not been conventionally designated (*asaṃketita*) be joined with a word, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*);
nor does conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occur without the joining of a word.
Therefore, the relationship between the signifier and the signified is merely superimposed and not ultimate.

[An objection might be raised: "In that case, perception, by apprehending an object that is itself superimposed, would become conceptual (savikalpaka). To this, he says: "not superimposed," and so forth, ending with "due to its absence."
The connection is "also because of its absence";
that is to say, because of the absence of that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), there is also the absence of that perception (*pratyakṣa*) due to its absence.
To the question "When is there an absence of the particular characteristic?", he says: "due to intervention (*vyavadhāna*) and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), distance of place, time, and so forth are meant.
With the words "incapable of convention" (*aśakyasamaya*) and so forth, he states yet another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*):
for the nature of blue and other [objects] does not partake of anything else, and is thus incapable of conventional designation.
Therefore, their cognition is not associated with verbal expression.

Regarding the question—"How is it that the nature (ātman)—the essence—of blue and so forth is 'inexpressible' (aśakyasamaya), meaning incapable of linguistic convention?"—the author states the reason: "Because it is not shared by others" (ananyabhāk).
"Ananyabhāk" means uncommon— that is to say, not present at the time of linguistic usage—
since convention exists for the purpose of linguistic usage; therefore, there is no linguistic convention (śabda-saṅketa) regarding this [particular].

Furthermore—this convention (samaya) occurs with respect to that which has been made an object, not with respect to that which has not been made an object. First of all, perception does not make the blue and so forth its object while it is as yet unarisen; nor can it, once arisen, apply a verbal designation by taking up that designation.

Since [the object] is momentary at the time of its arising and at the time of grasping the designation, the perception is no longer in relation to the object; thus, by what means and where could there be an application? For this reason also, the nature of the blue and so forth cannot be subject to convention.
Because blue and so forth are not associated with verbal expression,
they are not permeated by linguistic designation.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) therein is as follows: whatever has not grasped a convention (*samaya*) regarding a certain object cannot be conceptual (*savikalpaka*) with respect to that object; for example, visual consciousness is not conceptual with respect to odor. And since perception has not grasped a convention regarding the nature of blue and so forth, this is the apprehension of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalambha*).
With the words beginning "But surely" (*nanu*), [the author] raises the objection that the first reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) according to the view of Sumati the Digambara.
[Objection: Granted that names and so forth may not be the qualifiers grasped by it;

nevertheless, the unestablished nature (asiddhatā) of the reason does not cease at all, because [the reason] consists in the non-apprehension of [the object] in a form excluded from other things. (1265) If [this is your view]:
Either there would be the apprehension of the mere object, or there would be no apprehension at all, as in the case of a jar.

(1266) If there is no apprehension of the jar in its form as distinguished from other jars, then there would either be the apprehension of the mere jar or indeed no apprehension of the jar at all. (1267)
For he describes every entity as having a dual nature consisting of both the universal and the particular; and the universal is of two kinds:
that which is delimited by a particular, such as "cowness" (gotva) and so forth, and that which is undelimited, such as "existence" (sattā) and "reality" (vastutva).

In this regard, that which is undifferentiated and of a single form is the object of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), which consists of mere observation (*ālocanāmātra*); the other, however, is the object of conceptual perception (*savikalpaka*). This is his [Prabhākara’s] system.
Kumārila, however, describes non-conceptual observational cognition as having the particular characteristic of the individual (*vyakti-svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

However, conceptual perception has a universal as its object; regarding that, for the purpose of examining the view of those such as Kumārila who maintain that perception is mere sensory intuition (*ālocanāmātra*),
the proponent of that [position] should be asked this:
Is that object standing before the sense-faculty apprehended as qualified by its own nature—which is impossible for any other object—or not? If he should say "no," [the opponent asks: "No?"

To this it is replied: If "non-apprehension" means non-apprehension of an object in a form distinguished from other objects—that is, if one intends a certain object and there is another object distinct from it, and one maintains that the object is not apprehended as qualified by that nature (or *svabhāva*) which belongs to the intended object but does not exist in the other object—then there must be either the apprehension of that object alone, meaning the apprehension of that very object which is exclusive to itself and devoid of any nature that could belong to another object;
or else, if even that is not apprehended, then there would simply be non-apprehension.

The example "as in the case of a jar" has been stated; he explains it with another verse beginning with *ghaṭāntara* and so forth: If that jar were not perceived by way of a form that does not exist in the jar delimited [by others], then there would either be the apprehension of the jar in its mere generality—that is, the apprehension of the mere jar as undifferentiated by any particular such as silver, copper, or the like—or else, if even the mere jar is not apprehended, then there would be no apprehension of anything at all, even of what is intended; thus, there would be a total non-apprehension of the jar.

In this case as well, since there is no apprehension of the specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) in the object of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*), it follows as a necessary conclusion that there would either be an apprehension of the mere object (*arthamātra*) or no apprehension at all.
1267 Now, regarding the first position, he says here: "If it is thought that [the cognition] apprehends through its existence as distinguished from other objects of apprehension..."
[The sensory cognition] would be conceptual, like the cognition of a tree and so forth.

(1268) If it is intended that sensory cognition grasps an object qualified by a nature that is impossible elsewhere, then it follows that it is conceptual, because it grasps an object qualified by some specific form, just like the cognition "this is a tree" and so forth. (1268)

It might be thought: "There is no such thing as a mere object (*artha-mātra*) which is apprehended as qualified by its own nature; rather, that very qualified form which you and I consider to be the particular (*viśeṣa*) is what exists and is apprehended. To this he says: "A particular untouched by the universal does not exist at all"—meaning that no particular exists that is not touched by the universal.
"If it is [perceived] during apprehension, then it is not perceived because it is indistinct due to its being a manifestation.

(1269) Here, "mere" (*mātra*) refers to the universal (*sāmānya*), which is designated as "existence" (*sattā*). There exists no particular (*viśeṣa*) whatsoever that could be perceived independently of that [universal].

Regarding this, the following might be argued: "Even if that universal exists according to your view, it is not touched upon at the time of apprehension. To this he says: "If it is [perceived] during apprehension, then it is not perceived because it is indistinct due to its being a manifestation."

If, at the time of apprehension, that universal called "existence" (sattā) is not touched by sensory cognition and only the particular is grasped, then that particular being grasped would be devoid of existence, lacking the nature called "existence," and thus would become essence-less (niḥsvabhāva). Consequently, it could not be an object of sensory cognition because it is "without existence"—that is, because its state of being has departed—just like a flower in the sky.
"It is a rash assertion to claim that cognition whose object is qualified is not conceptual construction;
for without a connection with a qualifier, the state of being qualified is impossible.

This is the conclusion: therefore, it is a rash assertion on the part of you who accept [this view] while contradicting the means of valid cognition, that there is no cognition whose object is qualified that is not conceptual construction.
He states the proof for this very point: "Not by means of a qualifier," and so forth.
The meaning is that one does not possess [the staff] without a connection with the staff; likewise, even that which is qualified is not tenable without a connection with a qualifier.
Therefore, the apprehension of the connection with a qualifier is conceptual (savikalpaka).

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: "Cognition having a qualified object, which has no other locus [than its own], is conceptual (savikalpaka), because it has a qualified object, like the cognition 'this is a cloth' and so forth.
He refutes this with the words beginning "sajātīya" (of the same class).
Cognition is held to have a qualified object because it apprehends an object excluded from both similar and dissimilar things, not because of a connection with a qualifier.

(Verse 1271) Herein, if the meaning of the reason "because it has a qualified object" is "due to a connection with a distinct qualifier," then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). For instance, for the Buddhist, there is no such thing as a "qualifier."

By what means could there be a cognition of a qualified object through the apprehension of a relation between them? Rather, it is because of the apprehension of the mere object as excluded from things of its own class and from those of other classes—that the cognition is considered to have a qualified object.
How then is there such a designation as "its qualifiedness" or "the state of being qualified by this," which implies a distinction? To this he says: "Difference," and so forth.
For difference has been said to be "distinctness" (*vaiśiṣṭya*), not the connection with a qualifier;
even when one says "it is distinct," it is not perceived as being permeated by that verbal expression [of the qualifier].
(Verse 1272) Difference is the exclusion from those of the same class and those of different classes.

And that [exclusion] is not other than the excluded entity; for it is the entity itself that is so designated when there is a desire to know it in its mere nature, by means of the rejection of other differences. One might object: "If the apprehension of an object as distinct from things of a different and the same class necessarily occurs, then the apprehension must be conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because it proceeds with the form 'this is distinct. Otherwise, how could it have that as its object? For if it were to proceed with a different form, it would not be logical for it to have that as its object, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even [the cognition] 'it is distinct,' etc."
To the question, "How then is it designated as 'different'?", he says: "In that which is distinct from its own nature and all other things without exception," and so forth.

But when that [object] has been grasped, a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises in the same way. When an object is grasped as distinct—that is, as excluded—from all other entities whatsoever by its own nature, then, because there is the manifestation of a unique form such as blue, a conceptual construction subsequently arises which determines the difference; it is accompanied by the recollection of the form of a word and expresses "it is distinct. If, however, that [object] were not of the nature of verbal expression, nor had a reality whose essence was conjoined with it, then even if it were grasped while being associated with names such as "distinct" or "non-distinct," it would not truly be grasped as such.

Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*). (1273) Now, if the meaning of the reason "because it has a qualified object" is taken on the grounds that it is qualified by virtue of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), even then, the reason is not non-ambiguous (*anaikāntika*) by itself; showing this, he says: "viśeṣaṇa... and so forth.
The universal is held by others to be unqualified by attributes and apprehended by non-conceptual cognition; therefore, in this regard as well, the case is the same [for us].
For the universal indeed has two forms: that which is qualified by attributes and that which is unqualified.

In that regard, that which has an undifferentiated form is intended to be graspable by non-conceptual cognition; even there— in the case of the universal— this quality of being graspable by non-conceptual cognition is the same.
To the question "How so?", he says: "For by means of the particular," and so forth;
for that universal is understood through the particular.
Therefore, it follows that the consciousness which apprehends that [universal] is conceptual (savikalpaka).
For that which is distinguished—that is, excluded—from this particular is perceived as the universal;
otherwise, it would not be a universal at all, since it would not be excluded from it.
Furthermore, the cognition that grasps this universal—which is itself excluded from particulars—would necessarily be conceptual (*savikalpaka*), because its object is qualified;
yet it is not so according to your own view.
Therefore, [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by virtue of itself.

Here, it is said that Sumati himself, having raised this doubt, refuted the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason in a general sense; he demonstrates that very point with the words beginning "nirviśeṣam":
"If difference is apprehended without distinction, it is called a universal (*sāmānya*)."
Therefore, it is not tenable for the universal to be qualified by the particular.

(1276) For there exists no universal whatsoever whose nature is distinct from the particulars, such that—being apprehended as qualified by its own nature—it could become the object of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka-vijñāna*). Rather, it is the particulars themselves, when apprehended without their specific differences and perceived independently of their restricted individual natures, that are called the "universal"; that is to say, they are what is denoted by the word "universal."
And furthermore, how could there be a distinction of the universal from that particular, by virtue of which the cognition grasping it would be conceptual?
To the question, "In that case, how is there a non-confused determination of the universal and the particular? he says: "Because of the disparity," and so forth.
It is said that these very things, being perceived through their states of dissimilarity and similarity,
establish the existence of universals and particulars within themselves.
