For it is these same distinct entities, when perceived as either similar or dissimilar, which— by sequentially undergoing the status of being the designator and the designated for the terms "universal" and "particular"— establish the distinction between the objects of the conventional usage of universals and particulars.
He refutes [the objection] with the verse beginning "This state of inequality and equality... [stating]:
"If this state of inequality and equality is held to be differentiated,"
The particularity of the universal remains exactly as it was in its specific state.
Or, if this [universal] is indeed undivided, how can there be an unmixed state?
For there is no other possibility for their existence than by not excluding one another.
"Differentiated" means unmixed;
that is to say, the universal is one thing and the particular is another.
The statement that "the universal is distinguished by way of the particular" is merely an illustration;
likewise, the particular is also distinguished by way of the universal,
because both are clearly differentiated through their mutual distinction of intrinsic nature.
"Unmixed abiding" means being unmixed;

as that very Sumati stated: "A particular (viśeṣa) is directly perceived only when permeated by the nature of universals such as existence, and not otherwise. Therefore, it is logical that the form of the qualified object (viśeṣya) consists precisely in its having a qualified object [as its domain]. Furthermore, since a universal can be directly perceived independently of all particulars, it is not contradictory for it to be the object of non-conceptual [perception]."
If it is argued that this non-confused state would not exist, and that neither a distinct nor a non-distinct [nature] is intended, he says: "Mutually... and so forth.
Because for those things characterized by a state of mutual exclusion, the negation of one nature is inseparable from the affirmation of the other, there is no third category.
Furthermore, demonstrating that the claim "differences are apprehended without distinction" is mutually contradictory, he says: "Apart from the nature of the particular," and so forth.
Apart from the nature of the specific particularity (*viśeṣātman*), there is no other characteristic of difference.
If one does not touch that very nature, how can it be said that there is a perception of those [particulars]?
And even if one touches that nature, [how could there be perception] of those things distinguished by other differences?
"The cognition that has arisen regarding these [particulars] is conceptual" (1281).

For there is no "distinction" (*viśeṣa*) other than the particulars themselves; and if that distinction is not touched upon by a cognition that grasps the universal (*sāmānya*), how could the particulars be grasped by it? The point is that since they are not distinct from an ungrasped nature, they too remain ungrasped.

Now, if it is held that [the particulars] are apprehended, then upon the contact with their form—that is, upon the apprehension involving contact with the form of difference—the particular is also necessarily apprehended because it is non-different from what is apprehended, just like the apprehended nature itself. Thus, in these particulars, the cognition intended to have the universal as its object would result in being conceptual (vikalpaka).

Furthermore: even if it were granted that the universal (*sāmānya*) is not distinct from the particular (*viśeṣa*) because it is non-different from it, nevertheless, it is certainly distinct from such things as a hare’s horn, which are non-entities (*nirupākhyā*); thus, it would have to be graspable by conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), yet it is not so. Therefore, showing that [the reason] is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "And from a non-entity... and so forth. "And from a non-entity, the universal is perceived as a particular; therefore, according to you, that too would be graspable by conceptual cognition. (1282)

If that which is non-existent is not qualified by it, then what is the difference [between them]? If it is of the same nature as that, then why is its qualification by it not admitted? (1283) It might be argued: since the universal does not exist, neither can a particular nor a similarity be possible.

For instance—it is postulated that non-existence (*abhāva*) is that which is nothing at all; yet such a thing is neither specifically qualified nor even equal [to anything else] in a general sense, because that would entail its being a positive entity (*bhāva*). To explain: if that void were generally qualified, it too would necessarily be a real entity (*vastu*), for a nature termed "particularity" (*viśeṣa*) cannot belong to a non-entity. And without a nature termed "particularity," it is impossible to speak of something as "qualified."
Nor can it be equal, because that would entail its being a real entity;
for a non-entity cannot possess a form identical to anything else, and without an identical form, equality is not logical, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, taking the universal (*sāmānya*) as a void limit, neither equality nor distinction is tenable.
For instance: whatever serves as a limit (avadhi) such that something else is equal or superior to it, that limit itself is seen to be either equal or unequal [to that other thing].
For if that limit were not seen as equal or unequal by it, then the other thing possessing the limit would likewise not be seen as equal or unequal. (1282)

Furthermore, there is no such thing as "non-existence" (abhāva) that is distinct from existence (bhāva); rather, it is existence itself that is called "non-existence" when it does not become another form of existence. Therefore, how could it possess any specific qualification (vaiśiṣṭya)? Sumati has stated all of this, and taking up his point, [the author] says: "This very non-essentiality of the object," and so forth.
Indeed, even for a real entity (vastu), this specific qualification is nothing other than its lack of identity with that [other thing].
And since the universal is not of the nature of non-existence, why is it not qualified by that [particular]?
Therefore, whatever cognition arises with respect to the particular (svalakṣaṇa), having as its object that which transcends the path of words, all of that is non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka).

For indeed, that which constitutes the distinction of a non-entity from the side of an entity is nothing other than the negation of its reality; it is simply its not having that nature, which is to say, a difference in definition.
And this is exactly the same for a universal as it is for a non-entity such as a rabbit's horn.

For instance: non-existent things such as a hare’s horn are characterized by the absence of all causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), whereas a universal (*sāmānya*) is not accepted as being thus; therefore, its distinction from that [non-existence] is clear.

Consequently, even if it were distinguished from non-existence, there would be no consequence of it being a real entity (*vastu*); thus, this [objection] is trivial. As for what was said—"Non-existence (*abhāva*) is not something entirely different," etc.—in that regard, he has failed to analyze the very meaning of his own statement.

For instance, when it is stated that "an entity itself does not become another entity," a distinction of that [entity] from other entities is thereby expressed; since this involves the mention of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it is merely the manifestation of blindness. Enough of this digression.
Thus, with the words "therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth, the conclusion regarding the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is reached.

By presenting the view of the followers of Kumārila through the passage beginning with "For there is a cognition of mere observation" (ālocanājñāna), [the author] raises the objection that the reason in the formal argument beginning with "for whatever has no cause for the establishment of its own form" is unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddhatva*).
For there exists an initial non-conceptualizing awareness (*ālocanājñāna*),
which is like the cognition of infants, the mute, and others, arising from the pure object itself;
at that time, neither the particular (*viśeṣa*) nor the universal (*sāmānya*) is experienced.
However, it is the individual (vyakti) itself that is determined as the substratum of those two.
Furthermore, the cognition by which the object is subsequently determined through its properties such as genus (jāti) and so forth is also accepted as being of the nature of perception (pratyakṣa).

To explain: all perception is made the subject (*pakṣa*). In that case, regarding every locus (*dharmin*) called "perception," there is no apprehension of an object qualified by qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) as the cause for the establishment of conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*); thus, this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*), because in perceptions other than initial sensory awareness (*ālocanājñāna*), the apprehension of an object qualified by qualifiers such as universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth does indeed exist.

Alternatively, if the reason is stated by making initial sensory awareness itself the subject, then it is considered to be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). [The opponent replies:
"[It is] like the cognition of infants, the mute, and so forth."
It is similar to the cognition of an infant and similar to the cognition of a mute person; by the word "etcetera" (ādi), those who have fainted are included.
The similarity consists merely in the absence of specific verbal expression.
Furthermore, the purity of the object is due to its being devoid of the two types of universals;
this very point he clarifies with the second verse beginning with "not a particular" (*na viśeṣa*), where "particular" (*viśeṣa*) refers to...
Subordinate universals such as "cowness" (gotva) and the like are called *sāmānya*,
while the "great universal" (*mahāsāmānya*) consists of "reality" (vastutva) and the like.
By the phrase "the substratum of those two," the pure object (*vastu*) is shown;

then, by the words "beyond that" (*tataḥ param*) and so forth, he makes manifest that very same fallacy of the reason being unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddhatā*). This is indicated by the words "beyond that."

It should be understood that the cognition by which an object is subsequently determined through qualifiers such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, following the apprehension of the pure object itself, is also accepted as perception (*pratyakṣa*).
By the phrase "through genus and so forth," he demonstrates the apprehension of an object qualified by its qualifiers;
and by this, it is stated that the reason [adduced by the opponent]—namely, the capacity to apprehend an object not previously apprehended—is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Even when there is conceptualization again and again, whatever realization may arise, all of that is accepted as direct perception (pratyakṣa) in accordance with its connection [to the object].
"Again and again" means...
"In the third moment and so forth, for as long as" means "for as long as it is a realization of an object not previously realized"; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"According to its connection" means according to the connection of that sense organ (akṣa).

It might be argued: "If the object endowed with all its properties such as universals (*jāti*) and so forth does not appear at the time of the first operation of the sense organ, then it should likewise not appear at a later time, since there is no difference [in the circumstances]. To this he says: "For those who have merely entered," and so on.
Indeed, it is not understood that objects do not appear to the senses simply because they have merely entered into inner chambers and the like from the heat [outside]. (1290)
The phrase "from heat" should be construed with "as soon as they have entered the luminous state."
By means of an interrogative intonation (*kāku*), he shows that [objects] are not perceived by the sense faculties; rather, on the contrary, they are indeed perceived.
Having thus established the illustration, he says—beginning with "Just as"—in order to apply it to the subject of the illustration:
"Just as [people], having first known [an object] by its mere appearance, subsequently awaken to it in its true nature, so too [do they awaken] to the phenomena of birth and so forth. (1291)

Just as one first perceives a mere appearance within the inner chamber and subsequently knows it specifically as "blue" and so forth, so too, having first known [the object] by way of its essential nature (*svarūpa*), one will later possess direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by way of properties such as genus (*jāti*) and the like; thus there is no fault.

If that is so, then if the validity of every successive apprehension after the initial discerning cognition (*ālocanājñāna*) were to constitute direct perception, then suppose someone, having discerned something with the discerning cognition, subsequently closes his eyes and conceptualizes it by way of properties such as genus; since there would be a new apprehension for him, that too would have to be considered direct perception. To this he says: "But if," and so forth.

If, however, after having perceived [an object], someone were to close their eyes and conceptualize it, that [cognition] would not be perception, because it does not follow from the connection [with the object]. (1292) "Having perceived" (ālocya)— *Note: This verse is part of a discussion on the nature of perception (*pratyakṣa*) versus conceptualization (*vikalpa*). It argues that for a cognition to be considered direct perception, it must be immediate to the object; mere mental construction after the fact lacks the necessary causal link.*
In the act of visual perception, having known [the object],
the connection is that one should close the eyes.
"Because it does not follow from a connection [with the object]" means that it does not arise by way of a connection with the senses;
as was stated by that same Kumārila: "Thus, although the path is equally one of mere conceptual construction, where there is a following of the fruit of the connection with the senses..."
"Its perceptibility is such that it is well-known in the world even without this definition";
[the author] replies to this with the verse beginning with "tad" (that).
That is incorrect; for if that cognition is directed toward the particular (svalakṣaṇa), it remains unassociated with verbal expression even when grasping universals (jāti) and so forth.
Thus, it has already been established previously that this particular is indeed inexpressible.

In that [perception], the cognition is necessarily non-conceptual (nirvikalpaka), even when there is the grasping of universals (jāti) and so forth. The word "even" (api) is used in the sense of admission.

First of all, since universals and the like have already been refuted, they do not exist at all; how then could there be validity in their apprehension? Or, let them be granted to exist for the sake of argument; nevertheless, in their apprehension, just like the initial sensory perception (ālocanājñāna), the subsequent cognitions must be non-conceptual because their object is the particular characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). This is because it is admitted that universals and the like are not distinct from the particular characteristic—this is the intended meaning.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which apprehends the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), just like sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*); and the cognition intended as subsequent direct perception (*uttarapratyakṣa*) apprehends the particular characteristic. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), and it is a proof by reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*). Furthermore, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the reason, because it has already been established in the previous section on "Exclusion of Others" (*anyāpoha*) that this particular characteristic is indeed inexpressible;
nor is there any contradictoriness (*viruddhatā*), since the reason exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
It might be argued that the reason is unestablished because it has only the universal (jāti) as its object; to this he says: "jātimātra... and so forth.
If there were apprehension of the genus alone, there would be an absolute distinction from the qualifier;
however, this is not accepted by the opponents as it has been stated. (1295) "An absolute distinction from the qualifier" means...
The word "from the qualified" (*viśeṣyāt*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied];
and since this is not accepted by others,
there is an absolute difference between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*).
He asks, "How is it not desired? and says: "As has been stated," with the words "by that very [means]" being the ellipsis.
He asks, "What is that? and says:
"If indeed the qualifier were absolutely distinct from the qualificand, then how could it produce in the qualificand a cognition corresponding to itself? (1296)
Since a distinction is also admitted in a certain sense, he says "absolutely" (*ekāntataḥ*) to clarify this;
for instance: genus and so forth are held by him to have a nature that is both distinct and non-distinct [from the individual], being neither absolutely distinct nor absolutely non-distinct.
And thus he says: "Because there is a difference in cognition, it does not follow that color and the other [sensory objects] are one."

Furthermore, it has been stated that "oneness and manifoldness are accepted due to the distinction between existence (*sattā*) and form (*rūpa*) and so forth"; for it is said that "the distinctness of the universal (*jāti*) and so forth from the individual (*vyakti*) does not indeed exist."
"Otherness" (anyatva) [is] "conformable to itself," meaning it is colored by the nature of its own qualifier.
The meaning is that a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is so called because it causes the qualified (*viśeṇya*) to be apprehended as colored by itself; otherwise, its status as a qualifier would be untenable.
As it has been said: "That by which the qualified is colored through its own cognition is the qualifier.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Since [the cognition] has both as its object by virtue of having both the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its objects, it is unproven that subsequent cognitions have the particular alone as their object. To this he says: "Of the particular and universal natures," and so forth: "A single cognition is not capable of cognizing both the particular and universal natures; for if it were otherwise, there would be conceptualization (*savikalpa*), and indeed, the former [cognition] would not be distinct from the latter. (1297)

It is not logical for a single cognition to be the knower of both the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). To explain: that single cognition must be either conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). In the case of its being conceptual—that is, when it possesses conceptualization—it does not attain the "cognition" (*vit*) of the aforementioned particular characteristic; otherwise, there would be a contradiction.
In the view that [cognition] is non-conceptual, there would be no awareness (*vit*)— that is, no cognition— of "the other," namely, the universal nature (*sāmānyātman*).
Thus far, it has been established that if other cognitions have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, they would necessarily be non-conceptual (*avikalpa*).

Now, even granting for the sake of argument that they are conceptual (*savikalpa*), [the author] says "ekāntena" and so forth, demonstrating that their status as valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*) is not tenable because they apprehend what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*).
If it is argued that because there is no absolute difference [between the universal and the individual], the first [cognition] has already apprehended [the object] through the universal and so forth,
then the subsequent [cognition] would be equal to a recollective cognition, since it merely apprehends an object already known.
For instance, it is not accepted at all that the universal and so forth are absolutely different from the individual.
As it has been said: "Indeed, there is no posteriority of genus (*jāti*) and so forth from the individual (*vyakti*).

Therefore, since the genus and so forth are apprehended by the very first act of sensory perception (*ālocanājñāna*), the subsequent cognition that ascertains the attributes such as genus is necessarily invalid, because it apprehends an object already apprehended, like a memory-cognition (*smārtajñāna*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition apprehends what has already been apprehended is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like memory; and the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) following upon perception apprehends what has already been apprehended. This is the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

In this regard, if the meaning of the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is apprehended through the exclusion of the object of superimposition," then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). Alternatively, if the meaning of the reason is "because it is apprehended in some way or another," then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to inference. Demonstrating this, he says: "When there is an apprehension in the form of various indistinct universals," and so forth.
If it is argued that there is no such thing as a determined object, [we reply] that determination is indeed successive (uttarottara).
(1299) Just as inference has as its object the exclusion of superimposition (samāropavyavaccheda), so too does determination have as its object the exclusion of superimposition. (1300)

For instance: first, it is apprehended by indeterminate perception (*ālocanājñāna*) in its unmanifest form, not in a determinate form; however, each subsequent determination is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its object is the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*), just like inference.

Just as when a subject (*dharmin*) such as sound has been grasped by perception, the determination of impermanence through [the reason] "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) constitutes a valid means of knowledge, so too will this determination have the exclusion of superimposition as its object.
For you yourself have no dispute on this point: that determination has the exclusion of superimposition as its object.

As it has been said: "Because of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator between the mind of certainty and the mind of superimposition, it is understood that its activity occurs when there is the removal of superimposition."
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "No," and so forth.

Inference does not possess the status of a valid means of cognition by virtue of having the elimination of superimposition as its object; for if that were so, it would follow that even memory would be a valid means of cognition,
since it too prevents the arising of superimposition immediately following perception.
As for the inferential knowledge you accept as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), that does not exist for you [in this case].
For in instances such as "the white cow is moving," no superimposition (*samāropa*) is experienced following the perception, which could then be negated.

The validity of inference consists in the exclusion of a superimposition that has already arisen, and not merely in the exclusion of the object of a superimposition; for otherwise, it would follow that even memory is valid. Furthermore, there is no warding off of an arisen superimposition by a conceptual construction such as "the cow is white and moving," which occurs immediately after that perception, because in the interval no superimposition has arisen. If it is asked how it is that no [superimposition] has arisen, he says: "the cow," and so forth.

For a conceptual construction does not arise without being cognized; thus, by the non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehension, the non-arising of superimposition is established.

1303 Thus far, all this has been stated while provisionally accepting [the existence of] universals (jāti) and so forth; now, however, demonstrating that universals and the like do not exist at all from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha), and therefore how perception can possess conceptualization (savikalpatā) by having them as its objects, he says:
"In reality," and so on—"Universals and the like do not exist as being identical to, different from, or both."
That conceptual cognition which would attain the status of perception [is impossible],

because of the non-existence of a positive concomitance (anvaya), because of the difference [between particulars], because of the non-appearance of them as distinct, and because of the mutual exclusion between otherness and identity. (1304–1305)
For universals (*jāti*) and the like may be, in some cases, non-different from individuals, or different, or of a dual nature being both different and non-different.
First, the initial position is not tenable because of the absence of persistence (*anvaya*); that is, due to the lack of continuity.
For a form that persists through multiple entities is called a universal (*sāmānya*), and individuals do not thus interpenetrate one another such that they themselves could constitute the universal.

Alternatively, if there were a mutual pervasion (*anvāveśa*), it would follow that everything has become a single form alone, which results in the non-existence of the universal itself, since that [universal] must have multiple substrata.

Nor is the second position tenable—that [the universal appears as one despite its many substrata]—because it does not appear as distinct from the particulars; "from the particulars" means from the individual manifestations (*vyakti*).

And that which does not appear [to cognition] cannot become an object of direct perception, as it has been said: "Particulars do not follow along [with one another], and nothing else that follows along appears;
and since [the universal] is not distinct from the cognition, how could it become a different object?"

Thus, the third position is also not tenable: because the two positions of "otherness" and "identity" exist through mutual exclusion; for when two things are defined by their existence through mutual exclusion, the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other.
Alternatively, since "otherness" and "thatness" are established through mutual exclusion, because the determination of one occurs through the exclusion of the nature of the other,
there is no connection with a third category.

Now, if perception is indeed non-conceptual, how can there be worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) by means of it? For instance, if one determines, "This is a means to pleasure" and "This is a cause of suffering," then one proceeds toward the attainment of the former and the avoidance of the latter.
Furthermore, it would follow that there could be no transaction involving inference and the object of inference.
For instance— at the time of inference, the subject (*dharmin*) or the property (*dharma*) must necessarily be apprehended as ascertained by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
yet that cannot be ascertained and apprehended by perception, because perception is non-ascertaining in nature, nor can it be done by inference, due to the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Since there would be no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would follow that all worldly transactional activity (*vyavahāra*) is abolished.

Therefore, against one who might object that this claim of non-conceptuality is sublated by inference because of the operation of inferential and other types of transactional activity based on a logical mark (*liṅga*), he says: "Even non-conceptual [cognition]," and so forth;
even non-conceptual cognition possesses the power to produce conceptualization.
Therefore, by means of that [conceptualization], it becomes a constituent part of all conventional discourse.
Regarding the phrase "by means of that":
even non-conceptual [perception] becomes a constituent part of all conventional discourse as a cause for ascertainment through the medium of conceptualization.

For instance: although perception (*pratyakṣa*) is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), it arises by delimiting an object such as fire—which is excluded from both homogeneous and heterogeneous classes—by way of the production of a manifestation in its own form.

And because it grasps an entity established in a specific form and conforms to the form of the entity as excluded from heterogeneous things, it brings about affirmation and negation regarding that very entity: "This is fire, not that [which is] a cluster of flowers and so forth.
Although these two conceptualizations are not in direct correspondence with the object due to their being mediated, their validity is not denied.

Because activity proceeds through the determination of identity between the perceived object and the conceptual construction, there is no attainment of the true nature of the thing as it has not yet been apprehended;
for this very reason, because it is the cause of two types of conceptual construction, it also functions as the basis for indicating the absence of a third possibility.

To explain: when something is active toward a certain object, it determines that object because it appears as such; and because nothing other than that is perceived therein, it thereby excludes everything else.
Furthermore, by establishing that all entities are divided into two classes—namely, the perceived and what is other than it—it indicates the absence of any other alternative;

for if this were so, then since [properties] such as impermanence are already grasped by perception itself within the substratum (dharmin) such as sound, the inferential conceptualization (*anumāna-vikalpa*) operating therein would not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
This is not a fault.

Even when perception has arisen, only that aspect in which it generates a determinative cognition (*vyavasāya*) is fit for practical activity (*vyavahāra*) and is said to be "apprehended. However, in a case where—due to the influence of a cause of error—the perception is unable to generate a determinative cognition because of the onset of superimposition (*samāropa*), that object, despite being apprehended, is as if unapprehended due to its unsuitability for practical activity. In such a case, the validity of inference belongs to it as it proceeds to exclude the superimposition already set in motion; it does not belong to the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising immediately after perception, because that lacks the exclusion of the superimposition already set in motion.
But what is the reason that, even when an experience arises regarding the nature of an object as distinct from everything else, a corresponding certain recollection does not likewise occur?
It is said:
because it depends on other causes; for a certainty does not arise merely because something has been experienced.
Because that [recognition] depends on other causes such as the desire for practice and proficiency,
just as when one sees the father approaching— even though he is not distinct from the teacher— one determines, "My father is coming," and not "The teacher is coming.

In this context, [the author] shows what Bhāvivikta and others argue—who, by means of the production of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), refute its being a factor in worldly transaction (*vyavahārāṅgatva*)—in the passage beginning with "not non-conceptual" (*nāvikalpam*): "Not non-conceptual, nor capable in regard to conceptual construction, because of the difference in objects; and because it is non-conceptual, like the cognition of color-form (*rūpa*) etc., and like the eye etc.

(1307) Sensory perception (*indriyajñāna*) is not the cause of conceptual mental perception (*savikalpakamanovijñāna*), because their objects are different, just like the cognitions of color-form, touch, and so forth; and because it is non-conceptual, just like the eye and other sense organs.

Regarding the reason "because it differentiates objects," the example is "like the cognition of form and so forth"; regarding the reason "because it is non-conceptual," however, the example is "like the eye and so forth.
[The author] states the refutation with the words beginning "tad atra" (in this case):

Therefore, there is no contradiction here between these two [reasons] and [the possibility of] conceptual construction (vikalpa), nor is their object different, because they both result in the ascertainment of that same object.
Furthermore, both reasons are inconclusive (anaikāntika), since no contradiction has been demonstrated between the two reasons and the opposite of the probandum (sādhyaviparyaya).

By the phrase "nor is the object of these two [reasons] different," he states that even though conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) possesses an object, the reason "due to a difference in objects" is unestablished (*asiddha*).

However, showing that from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha) conceptual construction (vikalpa) is without an object, and is therefore even more unestablished at that time as well, he says: "In reality, however," and so forth:
"In reality, conceptual construction proceeds without a basis."
There is no object whatsoever for it that could be differentiated [from it].
By the phrase "form, sound, and so forth," he states that the example "like the cognition of form and so forth" is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*);
for there is indeed a mutual causality among the cognitions of form, sound, and so on.
Therefore, this example cited is one in which the probandum is unestablished;
for among cognitions of form, sound, and so forth, there exists a state of causality by way of their being mutual immediately preceding conditions (*samanantara-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, by demonstrating the presence of this reason—"due to the difference in objects"—in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), he states its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*): "In the case of the cognitions of fire, smoke, and so forth... and so on.
Even a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is clearly observed in this [reason], because of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) between the cognitions of fire, smoke, and so forth. (1311)
Regarding the phrase "in this case," with respect to the reason "due to the difference in objects":

just as the cognition of a mark such as smoke is the cause for the cognition of the possessor of the mark (liṅgin) such as fire even when there is a difference in objects, so too will it be here; thus, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Having thus established that perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*), he states the purpose of including the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*): "The hair-net," and so forth;
this was composed for the sake of excluding cognitions such as those of a hair-net.
The inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" is because that [cognition] is not accepted as valid cognition due to its being erroneous.
Here, "non-erroneous" should be understood in the sense of non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāditva*), and not by way of having an aspect corresponding to the object as it exists in reality;

for otherwise, since the object is not established according to the Yogācāra view, the definition of perception intended by relying on both systems would suffer from the fault of being too narrow (*avyāpti*).

Non-contradiction (*avisamvāditva*) consists in the capacity to bring about an object capable of performing the intended purposeful action (*abhimatārthakriyāsamartha*), but it does not consist in actual attainment, because obstacles and the like may occur. If this is so, one might ask: "Let there be only the inclusion of the term 'non-erroneous' (*abhrānta*); what is the use of including the term 'free from conceptual construction' (*kalpanāpoḍha*)? To this, we say: no.
Because it would follow that even inferential conceptualization is perception; thus,
some say that this too is mental [perception].
"Even that [cognition] is mental"—this is not so, because it arises from the state of the sense organ;
for its modification is observed when that [organ] is modified, and [it occurs] like the delusion of a snake and so forth even when the impairment of the sense organ has not ceased. || 1313 ||
"One should turn back from the delusion of the mind because [the object] appears clearly;
therefore, it is not proper for them to include the term 'non-delusive' (abhrānta)," such is their intention.

Now, one might object: "Granted that it is mental cognition; nevertheless, the inclusion of the term 'non-erroneous' (*abhrānta*) must still be made. For this [definition] was not begun merely to establish the definition of perception for sensory cognition alone; rather, it is intended for mental cognition as well, such as the cognition of yogis. And in that regard, even dream-cognition possesses non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpatva*) because it has a clear manifestation, yet it lacks non-erroneousness. Therefore, it is indeed appropriate to include the term 'non-erroneous' in order to exclude that. This is true.

However, since sensory error is also possible, this position of theirs is incorrect; therefore, in order to demonstrate that [the cognition] is born of the senses, he says: "This is not so," and so forth.

Because it occurs when the sense organs are present, and because a modification characterized by impairment is perceived when there is a modification of the sense organ characterized by injury, this cognition of a mass of hair and so forth is born of the senses, just like other sensory cognitions. Furthermore, if it were a mental error, then it would cease solely due to the cause of that mental error, even if the impairment of the sense organ had not ceased.
The example "like the delusion of a snake and so forth" implies another undesirable consequence: that there would be no clear manifestation [of the object].
For a cognition permeated by conceptual construction cannot have a clear manifestation of the object, since it functions solely through the delineation of a universal (sāmānya).
With the words "tadbhāva" and so forth, he anticipates the objection raised by an opponent.

The state of being conditioned by that [object] is not directly established [as a probans], for it is deviant; yet, in an indirect sense, it is established because of its concomitance with that memory-cognition.
Likewise, the state of being modified by a modification of that [object] exists even in those things produced through a succession.
In the world, this is clearly observed in cases such as mules and the like;
all mental delusions cease through investigation.
Thus, there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of cognitions of general entities (*bhāvasāmānya*).

These [cognitions] do not, by their very nature, operate with respect to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a real entity; if it is argued that their cessation occurs in that manner, then the same applies to the case of two moons and so forth. If it is argued that there is no cessation of existence, then the same holds true for cognitions of universals (*sāmānya*).

For those who are devoted to the doctrines of Īśvara and other such delusions, there is no cessation of their errors even upon hearing millions of arguments; on the contrary, those dull-witted ones further declare, "These are not valid arguments at all. (1319–1320)

In this regard, if "being produced by that very thing" (*tadbhāvabhāvitva*) in a direct sense is the reason (*hetu*), then the reason is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*). For it is not established for the opponent that error arises directly from the sense faculties, since that [direct production] is precisely what remains to be proven. If, on the other hand, "being produced by that very thing" in a general sense is the reason, then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because such production exists even in the case of memory-cognition, which constitutes a counter-example (*vipakṣa*), due to its occurrence through a mediated sequence (*pāramparya*). Furthermore, as for the fact of "changing in accordance with the change of that," that too is unestablished in a direct sense; and even if it were accepted in a mediated sense, it would still remain inconclusive.

Since a mule born from a donkey and a mare exhibits the form of a donkey—even though there is an intervention by stages such as the *kalala*—it is subsequently seen that it is a transformation of the donkey; therefore, direct production [from the cause] is not established by this.
Furthermore, regarding the claim that mental error ceases through investigation, there is also inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) due to cognitions of the generality of existence (*bhāvasāmānya*).

For even for you who understand the non-existence of a universal (*sāmānya*) through reasoning, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form of "existence" or "universal" does not cease with respect to entities such as jars.

Now, if you think that when one investigates by means of reasoning, these cognitions of universals indeed cease with respect to the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) in this manner— that they do not engage with it— then this too is no answer;
for even cognitions such as that of two moons cease precisely in this manner when one investigates by means of reasoning, in that they do not engage with the particular characteristic.
If it is argued that they do not become mental merely by that much,
because their existence does not cease, then that is the same for universal-cognitions;
for their intrinsic nature also does not cease.
He refutes this with the verse beginning "tadbhāvabhāvitā" (the state of being produced by that): "The state of being produced by that is not directly established for one whose mind is non-erroneous;
nor is an intervention established, for nothing is perceived in between. (1321)
Even one whose mind is attached to another object perceives two moons and so forth without interruption; therefore, there is no arising through a causal succession.
This is because it is possible to withdraw the cognitions of entities and their universals.
Cessation is indeed possible even for the intellect of the Lord by His own will;

it is not unestablished, but rather already established. Why? Because no obstruction is established by the non-erroneous cognition of a single moon, since that which is to be perceived is not perceived in the interval.
He clarifies this very point with the words "for another purpose" (*anyārtha*) and so forth;
it should be connected with the phrase "the non-interruption of the double moon and so forth.
For this very reason, there is also no deviation regarding the fact that [the cognition] undergoes modification when that [object] undergoes modification.
For even that [cognition] is not obstructed in such a way that there would be a deviation [from the rule] by means of cases like the *vegasara* (a type of horse);
for even in the case of cognitions of general entities (*bhāva-sāmānya*), when one effects the withdrawal of desire, cessation indeed occurs.
However, the withdrawal of cognitions such as those of a net of hair (*keśoṇḍraka*) through desire is not possible; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).
If it is argued that even sensory cognition ceases when the eyes are closed by the will, such cessation occurring by the power of the will—[we reply:
no, for visual consciousness does not cease immediately upon the cessation of the will;
what then?

The closing of the eyes occurs by the power of volition; consequently, when the eye has ceased [its activity], that visual cognition ceases. However, mental error ceases directly by the power of volition; thus, they are not the same. This is to be understood as follows: since an object is indeed seen even when the eye is directed toward it, though one does not wish to see it, therefore volition does not have direct efficacy regarding the cognition of the eyes and other senses.
Even though cognitions such as that of a yellow conch are erroneous, they possess the status of valid cognition.

Others explain [the definition] as "non-contradiction with purposeful action" (arthakriyā'visaṃvāda). However, some even among our own school do not accept the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta),
because they maintain that even erroneous cognitions, such as the perception of a yellow conch shell and the like, are indeed direct perception (pratyakṣa).

For it is thus: that [cognition] is not inference because it is not produced from a logical mark (liṅga), yet it is a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa) because it is non-contradictory; for this very reason, the Teacher Diṅnāga did not include the term "non-erroneous" (abhrānta) in his definition.

Because [the teacher] has pointed out the fallacious perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) by means of such terms as "error," "conventional reality," "ignorance," and "inference," the Master’s intended definition is simply: "non-erroneous and free from conceptual construction" (*avisaṃvādikalpanāpoḍha*). As for the phrase "accompanied by *timira*," this word *timira* is a synonym for ignorance (*ajñāna*), just as in the expression "it destroys the *timira* of the dull-witted."
"Taimira" means "occurring in darkness," which signifies being deceptive;
he refutes this with the words beginning "That is not so."
In that case, there is no attainment of causal efficiency (arthakriyā) corresponding to the determined form; otherwise, an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would follow.
Furthermore, even in the cognition appearing as hair-tufts and the like, there is a state of correspondence (saṃvāda).
Therefore, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) is difficult to avoid for [cognitions] such as that of light.
For validity arises through two modes: either non-contradiction with the appearance (*yathāpratibhāsamavisaṃvāda*) or non-contradiction with the determination (*yathādhyavasāyam*).
In this case, there is no non-contradiction with the appearance, because the yellow appears, yet that which is as it appears is not attained.

Nor is there non-contradiction (avisaṃvāda) according to the way [the object] is determined (adhyavasāya), because it is precisely the yellow [object] that is determined as possessing a specific causal efficiency (arthakriyā), yet no such causal efficiency of that form is actually attained.
Furthermore, validity cannot be established even by non-contradiction with respect to an object not so determined, because that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga);
for even in the case of the cognition of [illusory] hairs and the like, there is the attainment of light and so forth, which were not so determined.
1325–1326 Now, if you think: "Even though the color (*varṇa*) as determined is not obtained, the shape (*saṃsthāna*) is indeed obtained," to this he says: "Not color," and so forth.
Furthermore, a shape distinct from color is not logically possible;
for there is no correspondence admitted between the manifest color and [the perceived shape].
(1327) This is easily understood.
1327 With the words "If [one considers] the form," etc., he states the cumulative argument:
If validity is postulated while disregarding the form [of the cognition],...

"How could all that has been stated—such as 'for the determination of an object is of that same nature because of its non-contradiction with purposeful action' (1328)—not be contradicted? Therefore, the possibility of such correspondence arises from the cause that is the maturation of latent impressions (vāsanā). (1329)

For validity cannot be postulated merely on the basis of non-contradiction with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) while disregarding the mental aspect (*ākāra*), because that would entail the consequence that the objective form itself lacks validity; thus,
"having that form" means having the nature of an appearance residing within the cognition.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he shows that this contradicts the statement of the Teacher (*ācāryīya vacana*) and so forth, namely: "For in whatever way the form of an object is presented—as white and so on—in that very form is that object cognized.

However, it should be understood that the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*) arises from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) solely through the maturation of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the prior experience of the object. In the case of the cognition of a yellow conch, the cause for the maturation of the latent impression is the white conch itself; it is through its predominance (*ādhipatya*) that such maturation occurs.
That non-contradiction whose origination arises from the cause of the maturation of latent predispositions (vāsanā) is so described.
He explains how pleasure and so forth are perceived through direct perception by saying "mental," etc.:
the same reasoning that establishes the non-conceptual nature of sensory and mental consciousnesses is what establishes the non-conceptual nature of pleasure and so forth. (1330)
Regarding the principle that [mental cognition] cannot have a convention [attached to it],

although this principle was not explicitly stated for mental cognition, nevertheless, the same principle that applies to sensory perception— namely, its incapacity for convention— is equally applicable to it as well.

Alternatively, the cognition of a yogi here is mental; and since that will be explained later, no definition of mental [perception] has been provided here because it is well-known from the established tenets (siddhānta).

Furthermore, the fact that it is not sublated by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has already been demonstrated by the Teacher himself, and thus it is not being demonstrated here—this is the intended meaning.
With the words "they are non-cognizers" and so forth, he raises the objection of the Vaiśeṣika school:
"How indeed can they, being non-cognizers even of another, possess self-awareness?"
If these [objects] were to be cognized by a consciousness residing in the same object,
then they would not only fail to be self-cognizing; that is to say, they would also not be of the nature of cognition, as they would not be the cognizers of even an external object.
Their established doctrine is that [objects] are known by means of a cognition inhering in a single self;
he refutes this with the words beginning "without interval" (*nairantarya*).

For when external objects are perceived in uninterrupted succession, why is pleasure and so forth not experienced continuously at that time? It is because it is held that what is to be experienced is by the mental consciousness alone, and not by [the sensory] mind.

If it is argued that its existence at that time [is established] because of the description of successive births, and that it is simultaneous birth itself that is not accepted—not its duration—then we reply:
no, for its duration is refuted by the proof of momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga). || 1333-1334 ||
If it is argued that there is a single simultaneous delusion due to rapid occurrence, that too has been refuted;

for a vivid manifestation would not occur within the scope of memory. Furthermore, if that delusion is postulated as having the form of pleasure, pain, and so forth—[the list of corrections displays this error as *śātā śātā* with a space, whereas it should be *sātāsātādirūpā*]—then [it follows that the object is not external].
At that time, the existence of pleasure and the other [feelings] would be characterized by their mere presence [in the object].
Furthermore, when yogis perceive pleasure and so forth through direct perception, they too would become afflicted, because their experience would be identical [to that of others]. (1336–1337)
For you, the very existence of suffering within oneself is not the experience;
rather, it is the cognition having that as its object. And such a cognition exists in the mental continuum of another.
This is equally true in the case of the inference of another's suffering; for instance: [text continues]
"Inference is described as having an object, but not as being without a domain.
(1339) By this, he states that the thesis is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa-viruddhatā*).

When pleasure and so forth are experienced at the same time as a cognition that has an external object as its support (*ālambana*), by which single cognition residing in the same substratum would they be known? Not by that very same visual or other sensory cognition which has an external object as its support, because that [sensory cognition] has an external object as its support; and because pleasure and so forth, being internally cognized, are held to be known only by a mental consciousness (*mānasa-cetas*).
Furthermore, at that time, the existence of a mental consciousness is impossible, for it is accepted that cognitions arise only in succession.
Even if it were argued that only the arising of cognitions is accepted as occurring in succession and not their duration,
this is incorrect.

Since the momentariness of all living beings has been established, even that illusion of simultaneity which arises through rapid succession has already been refuted. Furthermore, a clear manifestation in the form of pleasure and pain would not be possible, because it is accepted that when pleasure and the like are objects of conceptual construction, they are cognized only by the mental consciousness (*mānasa-cetas*).
Furthermore, because that [conceptual cognition] is conceptual,
it does not possess the appearance of a clear object;
for we maintain that only that which is produced by sensory cognition— assisted by its own object and the immediately succeeding object— is accepted as perception.

Moreover, if pleasure and the like were objects of apprehension, they would appear as discrete entities, just like blue and other such objects; yet there is no perception of a form such as "pleasure" that is distinct from cognition.
If it is argued that the apprehension of the form of pleasure and so forth as non-different from cognition is an illusion, [we reply:]...
In that case, the existence of pleasure and so forth is established as being of the nature of self-cognition,
because pleasure and so forth are characterized solely by the form of being pleasant and so on;
and if that nature is established for cognition, then pleasure and so forth are established as having the intrinsic nature of cognition.
However, since [objects] distinct [from consciousness] are unestablished, error is unestablished;
therefore, "pleasurable" (sātā) is favorable, while its opposite is "unpleasurable" (aśātā). By the word "etcetera" (ādi), equanimity (upekṣā) is included.
Furthermore, if it is not accepted that the very existence of pleasure and so forth—characterized by their arising within one's own continuum—is itself their experience, [then the following applies].
However, when the cognition of that object arises for yogins who perceive the pleasure and so forth of another, their state would be identical to that of the person experiencing it;
yet one should not say that their state is not identical because they exist in a different mental continuum (*saṃtāna*),
for it is not accepted that their [cognition] follows as something residing within its own continuum.
What then?
It is the arising of a cognition having that as its object;
and since that [arising] exists even for those who apprehend another's mental continuum, the same undesirable consequence follows.

Now, if both [the self and the cognition] are admitted as the cause of the experience of pleasure and so forth, then, since they are experienced as residing within one's own continuum (*svasantāna*), the self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of pleasure and so forth is established. For it is precisely by being of the nature of self-cognition that "residing in one's own continuum" serves as the cause and the differentiator from those residing in another's continuum; provided, that is, that they are of the nature of self-awareness. To the question, "How then can there be such a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) for those, such as the Mīmāṃsakas, for whom yogins are not established? he says: "By others," and so forth.
For, unlike for the Buddhists, for others [i.e., non-Buddhists], inference is not ultimately devoid of an object;
consequently, when inferring the suffering of another, the inferer would likewise experience that same suffering.

Pleasure and so forth are understood precisely as pleasure, pain, and the like, but they are not understood as being "cognition" itself; therefore, that [pleasure] is not cognition, unlike a jar or other such objects. 1340.
Śaṅkarasvāmin says: "Pleasure and the like do not have cognition as their intrinsic nature, because they are not designated as 'cognition,' just like a jar and so forth.
With the words "If it were thus," etc., he states the refutation.
If that were so, then even regarding the cognition "this is knowledge," we would have no understanding; consequently, in that case as well, the state of being "non-knowledge" would follow.

(1341) If, due to a difference in convention, there were a difference in intrinsic nature, then it would follow for you that when someone were to establish the convention "this is non-knowledge" even with respect to a cognition, the designation "knowledge" would not exist in the mind, and thus even that cognition would become "non-knowledge."

It is evident [that consciousness is self-luminous] because its nature is luminosity; if it were not so, the same consequence would follow for pleasure, pain, and the like—why then is all this not [admitted as such]?
1342. [If you say that pleasure and pain are not luminous,] is it not the case that all of this [consciousness] is likewise [not luminous]? What is the difference?

We shall explain the cognition of the yogi, which arises from the cultivation of the true nature of reality, is free from conceptual construction and error, and is fully purified by the means of accomplishment (sādhana).
Now, since cognition, being luminous by nature, is clearly experienced, it cannot possibly be non-cognition; and this same principle applies equally to pleasure and other such states as well.
And because this very reason is inconclusive (vyabhicārī), this [objection] is of no consequence;
we shall explain [this] in the *Sarvajñasiddhi*.
1342–1343 To refute misconceptions regarding the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), he says: "The object," and so forth.

In this context, the apprehension of the object is held to be the fruit of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), or else self-awareness [is the fruit]; whereas the means of valid cognition itself is either similarity of form (sārūpya) or even fitness (yogyatā).
When the external object is the object of knowledge, the apprehension of the object is the fruit of the means of valid cognition, while similarity of form is the means of valid cognition.
Even though self-awareness exists, because this [object] manifests according to its form,
when the object of cognition is the nature of the cognition itself, self-awareness is the result; the means of cognition (pramāṇa) is fitness (yogyatā), which,
by taking into account the perceived state of possessing an operation, is that very same fitness belonging to the cognition itself.

Since it is by means of that [cognition] alone which one perceives the self and not jars and other objects, cognition is characterized as the illuminator of the self precisely through its fitness (*yogyatā*) acting as the instrument; thus, fitness possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to self-awareness. As it has been said: "In that case too, because they possess the nature of experience, those [objects] are fit for the awareness of their own selves. That fitness is the means of cognition, the self is the object of cognition, and self-awareness is the result.
Thus, with the words "1344.
*chedana*," and so forth, he anticipates the objection raised by the followers of Kumārila.

"If it is argued that just as there is no cutting of a *palāśa* tree when an axe has reached a *svadira* tree, so too in the world there is no identity between the axe and the act of cutting [if they were distinct]," (1345) [this was] said by the Buddhist against one who maintains that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) are distinct: "If a distinction between the means of valid cognition and its result is admitted, then the means of valid cognition and its result would have different objects."
And this is not tenable;
for when an axe or similar tool is employed for cutting, the cut does not occur in a *palāśa* tree when the *khadira* tree has been reached.
Therefore, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its fruit (*phala*) have the same object, they are non-different.

Regarding this, Kumārila stated: "He who, desiring the identity of object, asserts that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the result (*phala*), contradicts the worldly distinction between the goal and the instrument;
just as when an axe reaches the *khadira* tree for the purpose of cutting, the cut does not occur in a *palāśa* tree."
In the same way, in the world, there is no identity between the axe and its act of cutting;
thus,
"cutting" (chedana) is that by which something is cut.
1345. He states the reply beginning with "No" (na):
"The establishment of the probandum and the probans does not occur by virtue of being the basis for a fixed determination."

But in a cognition that is formless, that [distinction of] configuration is indeed not tenable. (1346) The determination of the comprehension of objects—such as that "the awareness has blue as its locus and not yellow"—has as its sole basis the conformity of the cognition to the object (*arthasārūpya*), and nothing else. Thus, the distinction between the means and the end, or the established and the establisher, is based on the relationship of the determined and the determiner, not on the relationship of producer and produced; for there exists no ultimate relationship of agent, instrument, and so forth, since all phenomena are devoid of activity due to their momentariness. Indeed, when cognition arises bearing the form of the object, it appears as if it were performing an activity, as if it were delimiting the object.

This very activity of attaining the object is the function of cognition, and not merely its state of being invariably concomitant; for it is not the case that sprouts and the like— which are invariably concomitant with seeds and so forth— do not exist [as effects],
such that cognition alone would be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Therefore, by way of establishing that cognition possessing an aspect (*sākāra*) alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and not that which is aspectless (*nirākāra*), its validity is demonstrated;
and this establishment is to be understood through the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) obtained subsequent to that [direct perception].
Therefore, with the words "imagined," and so forth, he states that there is no contradiction with worldly convention:

"Therefore, a distinction exists as something imagined, like that between a bow and its arrow; however, this [distinction] based on the relationship of producer and produced is not accepted here. (1347)

"Just as in the case of the bow and so forth"— meaning that just as one says "the bow pierces," "he pierces with the bow," or "the arrow, having issued from the bow, pierces," and thus the various roles such as agency attributed to the single bow are not contradictory, so it is here as well. (1347)
And when a joint is being split by an axe or similar tool, it is said that the cutting enters [the object]; therefore, unity is established there.

Furthermore, when the cutting of a tree or the like by an axe is examined, it remains characterized precisely as an entry into the substance to be cut. And since this entry is a property inherent in the axe itself, there is in reality an identity with the cutting; thus, there is no contradiction.
By the words "in the case of a settled rule" and so forth, he shows this:
once a settled rule has been established, it may indeed be postulated even otherwise.
The rule regarding the arrangement [of the means and result] is stated by way of the relationship between that which is produced and that which produces.

(1349) Just as Kumārila established the distinction between the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) through the relationship of producer and produced in his passage beginning with "because it has the result of determination" (*paricchedaphalatvāt*), so too for us there is no contradiction;

as was stated by the Master: "In that case as well, the metaphorical designation of 'perception' (*pratyakṣatva-upacāra*) is not contradictory even with respect to the eyes and other such causes, because they are the causes thereof."

We say this much: at the outset, the arrangement of the means and the object of proof must necessarily be established by means of a systematic distinction; for it is not logical for activity to proceed with a fixed restriction according to the distinction of objects without first establishing a distinction between cognitions. And since the basis for establishing a distinction between cognitions is precisely their similarity (*sārūpya*), it follows by implication that similarity is the most effective instrument of proof (*sādhakatama*). Furthermore, it is because of similarity alone that cognition is an instigator of action, and it is as an instigator that its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is determined by one who desires to act—not out of mere whim.

As it has been said: "For every discerning person seeks both valid and invalid means of cognition for the sake of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, only that aspect by which a cognition possesses the capacity to prompt activity must be demonstrated. Furthermore, when the relationship between the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is established not through the relation of producer and produced, the aspect that prompts activity is understood as "conformity" (*sārūpya*). Consequently, establishing the means of cognition by way of its production would be entirely fruitless. For this very reason, the Teacher, considering that establishing the means of cognition through this [production] is not a factor for initiating activity, resorted to a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).
Once that established order has arisen, let it be conceived as the relationship between producer and produced even in another way;
even so, there is no fault at all.

With the words beginning "pariccheda" (ascertainment), he demonstrates that very establishment of the result according to the Kaumārila school: "For it is held that the immediately preceding [cognition] which has functioned as the ascertainment of the object is the cause; however, in the case of cognition as the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the subsequent [result] is the fruit. (1350)
If it is argued that [cognition] has self-awareness as its fruit, this is not tenable because of the negation [of external objects];
furthermore, if the means of cognition (*māna*) possesses the form of the object, the consequence follows that there would be a difference between the object and the result.
(Verse 1351) "Of what has occurred... [is the beginning of the commentary].
The meaning is "of the eye and so forth which have begun to function";
the "supreme fruit" is characterized by the cognition of avoidance, acquisition, and indifference.
This further point was stated by Kumārila himself: "Because self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is denied, its status as the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is untenable.
Furthermore, if the objective form (*viṣayākāra*) were the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would follow that the means of valid cognition and its fruit have different objects;
for instance, the objective form has the external object as its domain, whereas self-awareness has the nature of the cognition itself as its object."
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "All," etc. (1350–1351):
It cannot be denied on the grounds that it would lead to the consequence of [the cognition of] everything;
nor is there any difference in meaning here, for self-cognition is considered to be the cognition of an object.

Since "for one who has no perception of the apprehension itself, the seeing of the object is not established," self-cognition cannot be denied, as that would lead to the consequence that all objects are imperceptible.

Nor is it logical to claim that there would be the consequence of having different objects of cognition; for self-cognition is also accepted as being the cognition of the object because it is its effect,
yet it is not so by virtue of being identical with it—
self-cognition, however, arises from its conformity to that [object], and thus there is no contradiction.
By the words "svātiriktā" and so forth, Śaṅkarasvāmī provides the following proof:
"The means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) performs an action distinct from itself, because it is a causal factor (kāraka)."
If it is argued that [the self] is like an axe or similar tools, then it would be purposeless;
for according to the logic already stated, there is no other fruit [of such tools], nor is their status as "agents" established, since we intend by "agent" the sense of being a producer. (1353–1354)
If there is an intention to express [the reason] as "being an establisher," there is no contradiction whatsoever;
therefore, the reason is inconclusive because no contradiction has been demonstrated. [The argument is:
"A means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) performs an action distinct from itself, because it is a causal factor (kāraka), like an axe or similar tools. || 1355 ||

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "it is fruitless" (vaiphalyam), etc., because it is fruitless due to the fault of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā); for another produced result has already been stated by [the author] in the passage beginning with "ascertainment" (pariccheda).
The word "hi" (for) indicates the reason;
as for the example "like an axe and so forth," it is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because it has been established that oneness exists together with the act of cutting.

Furthermore, regarding the reason "because of being an agent" (*kārakatvāt*), if one intends to mean the relationship between producer and produced, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), since [the opponent] maintains that [the cause] is intended solely as a sustainer (*sthāpakatva*).
Even if one intends to express that the means of proof establishes [the object], it is inconclusive because there is no contradiction;
and if one intends to express it in a general sense, it is likewise inconclusive because no contradiction has been demonstrated.

Now, if cognition were to possess the form of the object, then the correspondence with the object (*sārūpya*) would constitute its validity; however, this is not the case, because cognition is established as having an identical form and identical nature to the apprehended object, yet it is not actually so, since it belongs to a different category from the apprehended object, just like color and taste. To this, he says: "The apprehended," and so forth.
If it is argued that cognition cannot possibly possess a form common to the object of apprehension because it is a different category [from the object], like taste and color,
then we have explained all of this in accordance with logic.
This and other points are clear in the discernment of the grasped and the grasper.
Since we follow the logic of the Vijñānavāda, this is precisely what we accept; thus, nothing is lost.
For instance, whatever unclear refutation of the grasped has been stated by you—

However, this clear means for the discernment of the graspable is now stated by us: "graspable" refers to the object of perception; "grasping" is attachment to it; and its "discernment" is its removal. (1356)
"What is that clear means of proof? To this he says: "In every respect," and so forth.
For if there were identity in every respect, cognition would become non-cognition.
If similarity were based on sharing even a single aspect, then everything would be a cognizer of everything.
Since cognition also excludes as many heterogeneous things as the object does, this constitutes similarity in its entirety;
however, the exclusion of only a few objects constitutes partial similarity.
To the question, "How then was the validity [of cognition] stated to consist in its similarity to the object?", he says: "But," and so forth.
However, the possibility of similarity exists in the doctrine that external objects truly exist.
This has been elucidated in order to show that [the object] must necessarily be admitted [to exist].

For, in the view that cognition possesses a manifestation, even though the mind is distinct from the apprehended object, there may still be a figurative perception [of the object] because the reflection possesses the same form as it.
"But for one who maintains that consciousness is not the receptacle of the similarity to the object— which is what is desired—
this very mode of external perception does not exist at all. (1361) Thus ends the examination of the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

"Sa" refers to the form in which the possibility of similarity [with the object] arises, or the appearance; that is, the conformity with the object (viṣayasārūpya). That which possesses this is "nirbhāsi" (that which appears).
"From the object of apprehension" means from the external object;
"of the reflection" [is the meaning].
"Because the form of cognition possesses that same nature" means because it has similarity to the object.
"Bhākta" means figurative;
it is a metaphorical designation for "knowing."
The word "of the object" (*arthasya*) is to be supplied as the remainder; it is the "receptacle"—that is, the basis.

As for the misconception regarding the object: since the existence of a universal as a real entity has been refuted, and since it has been shown by implication that perception—which is accepted as having a real thing as its object—has no object other than the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*), this misconception has not been refuted separately.

As for those who say that this definition of perception is indeed improper—arguing that a definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is formulated so that, by being characterized by that form, others might act upon it, and not out of mere whim; and further arguing that in the world there exists no capacity to prompt or dissuade action even in that which is characterized by being "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and so forth—that is incorrect.

For it is not possible to establish the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things according to one's own will, such that a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) could be formulated otherwise; rather, experts formulate definitions by restating the very nature of things as they actually exist, with the desire to communicate well-known specific characteristics. For example, [they define] the hardness (*kharatva*) of earth;
otherwise, it would be flawed by the defect of impossibility.
Furthermore, there exists no other defining characteristic for perception besides its being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and being non-erroneous (*abhrānta*).
For instance, it must necessarily be admitted as non-erroneous because it is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and it is free from conceptual construction because its object is the direct particular (*svalakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, since it has been established that because a unique particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) cannot be the object of a linguistic convention, its cognition is non-linguistic (*anabhijalpatva*),
therefore the wise declare that its definition is strictly in accordance with logic;
and yet, from this definition, the engagement and withdrawal of discerning persons do not fail to occur.

For instance: having determined that the cognition of universals such as "pot-lifting" and "number," as well as the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and likewise the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and so forth—which is postulated by others to be perception—is respectively either conceptual (*savikalpaka*) or erroneous, they turn away from the insistence on the reality of number and other such properties postulated as the objects of those cognitions;
and having concluded that only that which is demonstrable—the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) such as blue—is the real entity, they proceed toward that.
Furthermore, it has already been stated previously how even non-conceptual perception possesses the capacity to prompt action.

If this is so, then it would be proper to formulate only "freedom from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍhatva*) as the single definition, and not "non-erroneousness" (*abhrānta*). For instance, that very form which is established prior to activity is what ought to be set forth as the definition for those desiring to act; that which is unestablished is not suitable, as it is equivalent to non-existence.

Furthermore, the determination of non-erroneousness does not exist prior to the correspondence with causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). For those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśana*) are not able to know the truthfulness of a cognition without first apprehending its effect; this is because for them, the power of an object is always inferable from its effect, and because truthfulness is characterized by the capacity to bring about the attainment of the object as it was presented. Moreover, there is no utility in determining truthfulness at a later time, since activity would not occur again thereafter.
This objection is not tenable;

for it has been stated that the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) must necessarily be included in the definition, lest there be the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), which would result in the erroneous cognitions of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍraka*) and the like also being considered valid.
Furthermore, the argument that limited vision (*arvāgdarśitva*) is the cause for the lack of certainty prior to action is itself inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
For what obstacle is there here such that those who perceive only the immediate range (arvāgdarśin) must not ascertain any capacity whatsoever?
For if this were so, it would follow that they could ascertain nothing at all;
