consequently, their very lack of consciousness would be established.

To whatever extent even young animals, through the power of habituation, possess mental modifications arising from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of past knowledge of living beings, they are indeed observed to avoid precipices and the like and to grasp their mother's teats and such, having determined—even prior to actual activity—that "this is a means to pleasure" and "this is not a means to pleasure.

For thus, even for those whose minds are overwhelmed by desire, grief, fear, and so forth, and who therefore cultivate what is non-existent, the capacity of habituation to produce a cognition with a vivid appearance is clearly perceived, independent of the recollection of similarities and other such factors.
However, where there is no repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), their capacity can only be inferred from its effect, but not everywhere.
By this, the ascertainment of signs such as smoke is also explained;

for even there, because smoke and so forth—which are the effects of those [causes]—are by nature mutually and absolutely distinct in their own-being, and because the ascertainment of that distinction depends on causes such as repeated practice, the possibility of ascertaining the sign exists. Therefore, there is no rejection of inference.
But surely, if there is no initial engagement, practice cannot be established; therefore, it must be explained how that very engagement comes about.
It is said: from doubt.
If it is asked, "How can perception, which is a cause of doubt, possess validity in that regard? [the reply is:
"And how can that which is a cause of certainty possess validity?
If you say it is because it produces a determinate cognition (*avasāya*) and thereby prompts the seeker to act toward that object," [then the same applies to the former].
This is equally true for the cause of doubt as well:

although in that case there is a determinate cognition (*vyavasāya*) contrary to the form of the object as it is being perceived, nevertheless, perception does not function as an instigator by way of that [contrary] form, because what is determined in that way is not desired;
nor does it function as a deterrent, because the seeker is prompted to act by means of the cause that is the determinate cognition of the desired object as it is being perceived.

Otherwise, it would follow that a person seeking an object would neither engage with nor withdraw from perception, which is the cause of doubt; yet this is not the case. Rather, for those who seek an object and for whom the occurrence of misfortune is improbable, the engagement driven by that very seeking is more powerful.
In this respect, there is no difference whatsoever between this [perception] and perception as a cause of certainty.

However, where there is exclusively a cause for determining a form that is contrary to the object as it is perceived, or where there is a failure to produce any determination at all, it is correct to say that it is non-valid (*aprāmāṇya*) precisely because it does not lead the seeker of the object to act in any way; this is not the case elsewhere. Enough of this.
Thus concludes the examination of the definition of direct perception;
[now begins] the examination of inference.

Now he states the definition of inference (anumāna): "Inference is held to be twofold through the division into that for oneself and that for others; inference for oneself is the perception of an object to be inferred from a mark possessing the three characteristics. (1362)
The statement of the three-featured logical mark (liṅga) is further said to be for the sake of others;
however, a meaning possessing only one or two of these features is considered a fallacious mark (liṅgābhāsa).
Inference is of two kinds, distinguished as being for oneself (svārtha) and for others (parārtha).

In that regard, inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) should be understood as consisting of the cognition whose object is the thing to be inferred, arising from a three-featured mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) characterized by presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), presence in similar instances (*sapakṣasattva*), and complete exclusion from all dissimilar instances (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*). Inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), however, should be seen as consisting of the verbal statement that illuminates the aforementioned three-featured mark. Now, he asks: "What is the definition of a fallacious inference (*anumānābhāsa*) that has not been stated? and replies with the verse beginning "each one," etc.

"Sound is eternal because it is produced, because it is corporeal, and because it is immeasurable"—these are each of a single form, because they respectively possess only the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), its existence in the similar class (*sapakṣasattva*), and its exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*). In that regard, those of a dual form are as follows: "Sound is non-eternal because it is visible, because it is audible, and because it is incorporeal," since these respectively lack the existence in the subject, existence in the similar class, and exclusion from the dissimilar class.
As it has been said: "Sound is eternal because it is produced, because it is corporeal, and because it is immeasurable."
"By virtue of being formless and inaudible, it is impermanent; and by virtue of not being visible to the eye. (1362)
With the words "otherwise" (anyathā) and so forth, he raises the objection representing the view of Pātrasvāmin:
"Indeed, when [the probans] is impossible otherwise, its status as a valid reason is observed."
Therefore, even that which possesses the three aspects [of the reason] is not [a valid reason] when it is absent; thus, those with three characteristics are impotent.
For he (Dignāga) said:
"Only the state of being otherwise impossible is a sound reason, but not one possessing the three characteristics."

For instance, if the condition of "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathānupapannatva*) were absent, even the three-featured [reason], such as "being his son," would not be seen to possess the status of a valid reason; therefore, those who claim that reasons have three characteristics are impotent— that is, unattached— to this point, namely, "otherwise."
The meaning is that "inseparability from the probandum" (sādhyena vinā'nupapannatva) refers to the presence of the reason (hetu) only where the probandum exists.

With the words "otherwise" (anyathā) and so forth, he establishes the reason as having the single defining characteristic of "inseparability from the probandum otherwise," by demonstrating in detail both positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka).
That which possesses the property of being otherwise impossible (*anyathānupapannatva*) is accepted as the logical reason (*hetu*).
Such an object has a single characteristic, or it does not have four characteristics.
That which possesses the single characteristic of being otherwise impossible is "one-characteristic" (*ekalakṣaṇaka*).
That alone is accepted as the reason by worldly people or by investigators, and no other;

however, since the three characteristics such as "being a property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatva) are implied by this very [reason] through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), it may also be considered as possessing four characteristics.

Nor indeed is it characterized by four marks; for it is logical that it may sometimes have one mark, two marks, or even three marks. Since "the impossibility of being otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*) is the single mark, it is designated as having "one mark. Considering both "establishment among similar instances" (*sajātīyasiddhatā*) together with "the impossibility of being otherwise," and "exclusion from dissimilar instances" (*vijātīyavyāvṛtti*), it is said to have "two marks. Having "the impossibility of being otherwise," "presence in similar instances," and "exclusion from the opposite of the probandum" (*sādhyavipakṣa*), it is said to have "three marks. However, a reason is not intended to be "three-marked" merely through its connection with the three characteristics such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*).

Because it is untenable for that [subject] to be the cause with respect to right cognition (samyagjñāna) [1365]; or rather, due to its predominance, it is designated by the single characteristic of "otherwise-untenability" (anyathānupapatti) alone, and not by [the other three conditions] such as "being a property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatva), because those are subordinate and thus ineffective. Demonstrating this, he says: "Just as," and so forth.

Just as in the world, one who has three sons is called "one who has an only son" because that one son is a good son, so too should it be seen here. [Objection: But surely, due to the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), only that which possesses the three-fold form is a valid reason (*sahetu*); for this reason, he says "inseparable," etc., [stating] that being a good reason is logical.

The relation of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) is never found in [logical reasons] possessing the three forms; rather, it is observed only in those reasons that have "impossibility otherwise" (*anyathā-asambhava*) as their sole constituent factor.
(1367) Those for whom "impossibility otherwise" is the single constituent factor are so described; they are the "reasons having impossibility otherwise as their sole constituent factor."
With the words "otherwise" and so forth, he concludes the very point already stated:
"Only that which possesses the property of being otherwise impossible [to occur] has the status of a logical reason."

Let both examples exist or not; for they are not the cause [of proof]. Where there is the condition of "inexplicability otherwise" (anyathānupapannatva), what is the use of the three [characteristics]? Where there is the condition of "inexplicability otherwise," what is the use of the three? (1368–1369)
The two examples,
characterized by similarity and dissimilarity, are not the cause.

Immediately after the phrase "where the occurrence of the probandum is otherwise impossible" (sādhyapratipatter anyathānupapannatvaṃ yatra), the reading of the half-verse beginning with "otherwise impossible" (nānyathānupapanna) should be inserted.
Demonstrating the absence of an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) in the three-fold [reason], he says: "He is dark-skinned because he is his son, just as other sons are seen to be dark-skinned."
Thus, a reason possessing three characteristics does not function for the sake of certain determination.
Therein, with the words "one characteristic" and so forth, he demonstrates through an elaborate series of examples that the capacity belongs to a reason possessing only one characteristic:
"In that regard, a reason with one characteristic is devoid of the two types of examples."
Existence and non-existence are, in some sense, of the nature of existence,
because they are apprehended in some sense.
Here, there exist no external examples— whether based on similarity or dissimilarity— neither in the form of formal arguments nor as objective entities.
Since the entire aggregate of entities, consisting of both existence and non-existence, has been made the subject (*pakṣa*),
and since there is nothing else apart from that,
this [reason] possesses only a single characteristic: the impossibility of its existence otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) and the absence of negative concomitance (*avyatireka*).
"In some way" means by some mode such as "knowability" (jñeyatva) and so forth;
"consisting of existence" means being of the nature of the existent (sat).
In this case as well, the phrase "in some way" (kathañcit) should be connected;
thus the meaning becomes: because they are apprehended in some way, they possess the nature of existence in some way.
Now he states examples of the two-featured reason:
"The moon-marked one is not non-moon because it is designated as being the moon"—this is called another [type of] two-featured reason. (1372)
"This sensation of mine is caused by a falling insect," so it is determined,
because its arising is obtained through contact with that falling insect.
(1373) The eye is always possessed of an extraordinary power for the purpose of apprehending form.
Or else, because they are being applied to that [subject], or because of the observation of that [subject]:
if the self, the pot, and so forth, are in some way non-existent in nature, then they are in some way unperceivable, like the horn of a donkey. || 1374–1375 ||
In some way, even things such as the self or the horns of a hare are perceived in some manner, just like the self, a jar, and so forth;
or else, it is understood that "your [property] is also there in the house."

From hearing the word "your father" here in this house, [the existence of your father is inferred] solely through the impossibility of its being otherwise (anyathānupapatti). Furthermore, it is observed that even in the case of things such as words and lamps, there is a capacity to indicate [an object], despite the absence of their being properties of the subject (apakṣadharma).
Therefore, let for us the reason (*hetu*) consisting of a single characteristic be the means of comprehension by virtue of its primacy;

what is the use of other [characteristics] such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharma*), which are merely imagined in vain? (1379) Either "the hare-marked one (*śaśin*) is not non-moon" is the thesis (*pakṣa*), or else "the hare-marked one is the moon" is the thesis. The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it is designated as 'moon' through conventional usage well-known in the world," or "because it is pointed out as being the moon. By way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), [the example is] a clod of earth and so forth.

And this other [example] is said to have two characteristics: "This pain of mine is caused by a falling insect. This means that its arising—its production—is obtained through the contact of a falling insect, that is, a moth (*pataṅga*).
Furthermore, in the compound word *anyapadārtha* (the meaning of another word), a general sense is intended here; therefore, the feminine suffix *ṭāp* does not occur.

The eye possesses the most efficient power for grasping existing visible form, because, provided it is unimpaired, it is employed as an instrument by a person acting with foresight when there is a desire to see form; or else, because of the observation that it delimits visible form—
whereas the ear and other senses function differently.
In this case, since form (*rūpa*) is absent in all three [types of] reasons, and because there is an absence of a similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), there is a twofold nature [of the reason]:
"The self, a jar, and so forth, are in some way non-existent by nature, because they are in some way unperceived, like a donkey's horn."

In this case, there exists no instance of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), such as a jar or the like, because every aggregate consisting of entities is somehow asserted to have the nature of non-existence; furthermore, non-existence has been presented as the instance of similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
And there is no third category apart from existence and non-existence wherein the exclusion of the probans could be pointed out following the exclusion of the probandum.
Alternatively, [one might argue that] things such as a donkey’s horn possess existence in some respect, because they are perceived in some respect, like the self or a jar;

here too, the absence of a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta) should be applied by the same reasoning as before. Or: "This house has your father as its occupant, because the sound of your father's voice is heard."

In this regard, it is said that because there is no similar instance (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), the reason has only two characteristics. For example, words, lamps, and so forth are observed to be indicators—just like the mark of smoke—even in the absence of the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Indeed, words, lamps, and the like are not properties residing in the object such as a jar; nevertheless, the object is cognized from the word and so forth. Thus, the reason possesses two characteristics: the absence of a counter-example (*vipakṣābhāva*) and the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapannatva*). 1372
1379. He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "That" (*tad*): Is this definition of the reason (*hetu*) understood in a general sense?
Alternatively, [the invariable concomitance] might exist either in the subject (*dharmin*) whose specific nature is sought to be known, or in the example (*nidarśana*).

In that regard, the invariable concomitance of the reason (*hetu*) with the probandum (*sādhya*) would have to be either in a general sense, by virtue of including the specific subject, or in a specific sense, by virtue of including the specific subject.

Even if it were in a specific sense, there are only these possible alternatives: it would have to exist either in the subject that is the locus of the probandum whose specific nature is sought to be known, or in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*). Such are the positions that can be conceived.
Regarding that, he states the fault in the first position: "If, by means of a generality," and so forth; [the meaning is:
if it were thus when that [reason] has been understood through a generality with respect to the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).

The existence of the reason would be revealed, but it would not bring about the establishment of what is intended [to be proven]. For visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) is not seen to be an indicator of impermanence with respect to the subject (*dharmin*), namely sound, merely by virtue of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) in the absence of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). Thus, the first position is untenable;
it does not bring about the establishment of what is intended.
The meaning is that it would not achieve the intended proof regarding the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "For example" (*tadyathā*).

For example, just as the non-deviation of "visibility" [from impermanence] is established in a general sense through its destruction, yet that [visibility] is not a means of proving it in the case of sound;
if it is argued that its existence in the subject (dharmin) is being demonstrated, then that being the case—
That very threefold nature is established even in your own system;
and "that" refers to its being visible to the eye.
"Of that" refers to the proof— the means of cognition— of destruction.
Now, if it is argued that the aforementioned fault shall not occur, and thus the existence of that reason in the subject (*sādhyadharmin*) is indeed resorted to,
then in this case, that very same threefold nature (*trirūpatva*) which constitutes the definition of a reason in our own system has also come into being within your own view.
He asks, "How so? and says:
"For it is by the impossibility otherwise (*anyathānupapatti*) that positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are understood."
Because it exists in that subject (dharmin), there is the reliance upon its being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva).

The positive concomitance (anvaya) is its presence in the similar instances (sapakṣa); the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is its absence from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa). "Reliance" (saṃśraya) means taking recourse to; that is to say, its inclusion.
By the phrase "by the teachers," he demonstrates that there is no contradiction with their own view;
for the teachers have also specified such a definition in brief: "The property of the subject (grāhyadharma) which is pervaded by a portion of that [property] is the logical reason (hetu). (1385)
"Property of the apprehended" (*grāhyadharma*) means the property of the apprehended subject (*sādhyadharmin*), that is to say, the "property of the locus" (*pakṣadharma*). 1385
Now, he states the second position:

"Now, this definition of the reason is understood from some means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as residing in the subject (dharmin) itself; therefore, there is no non-establishment [of the reason], but the same does not hold for the probandum (sādhya). (1386)
For if the probandum is not apprehended, there can be no certainty regarding the reason either;
therefore, the reason is useless because the probandum is established by something else.
Furthermore, there would be the fault of mutual dependence in the ascertainment of both the reason and the probandum.

"When both [the reason and the probandum] are unestablished for one of the two [parties], and the other is also not ascertained... (1388). Now, if it is argued that the very definition of a logical reason (*hetu*) is its inseparable connection with the probandum (*sādhya*) specifically within the subject (*dharmin*), as it has been said: "Others accept the status of a reason for that which is not seen without the probandum in the example; but for me, [it is accepted] for that which cannot exist without it in the subject."
And because of the Śābaras' [reliance on] presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) and the Bhikṣus' [reliance on] inference,
our inference is said to be something entirely different, like Narasiṃha,
with respect to the subject (dharmin).
The meaning is: that which, by its very nature, cannot exist in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) without this property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*).

If that is the case, then since the reason is established in the subject of the thesis as being inseparably connected with the property to be proven by the very same means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the property to be proven is also established by that same means; thus, the reason is redundant.

Now, if the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established, then the reason (*hetu*) is likewise not established; because the definition of a reason is its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitā*) with the probandum in the subject (*dharmin*), and that invariable concomitance is not established when the probandum is unestablished—thus the reason is unestablished. If it is argued that the reason is established once the probandum is established through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since invariable concomitance is necessarily dependent on the establishment of both, then what is the use of the reason at that point? For the probandum has already been established. Furthermore, if one were to attempt to ascertain the probandum from the reason, there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "Of the two," and so forth.

The establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is preceded by the establishment of the reason (*hetu*), because the reason exists for that purpose; yet the establishment of the reason—which is characterized by its inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the probandum—is itself preceded by the establishment of the probandum. Thus, it is evident that there is a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*).
He states the third position: "Even in the case of an illustration."
Even if that [pervasion] were established in the illustrative example (*nidarśana*), there would be no cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) regarding the subject (*dharmin*).
For its pervasion is not ascertained by means of a universal induction (*sarvopasaṃhāra*).
"In the illustrative example" means: in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*), which is distinct from the subject possessing the property to be proved (*sādhyadharmin*).
"In its establishment" means in the establishment of the reason (*hetu*).

This is what is being said: if it is maintained that the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of the reason exists only elsewhere—in the example-subject (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*)—and not through a universal inclusion together with the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*), then how could there be a cognition of the probandum (*sādhya*) from the reason in the subject of the thesis?
And how could it not be so? He says: "Not indeed," etc.
(verse 1389). With the words "He who too," etc., he now refutes the examples.
As for this reason stated here— "because of some kind of apprehension"— it is indeed fruitless, because there is no object of doubt whatsoever.
This reason stated as "because of some kind of apprehension" is useless, since there is no subject that is in doubt.
The meaning is "because it would be a proven object of proof" (siddhasādhyatvāt);
for an already established object is not desired as the subject of a reason;
what then?
It is doubtful; for instance, because a reason is stated when there is doubt,
even that which is established as if it were separate is simply not a locus for the reason, since the probandum is already established.
Now, it might be argued: "In this case as well, there exists a subject for the reason that is indeed doubtful. To this, he says: "Of an entity," and so forth;
for the identity of an entity with its own nature is ascertained by everyone.
How is its being established in some way [proven]? Why is it stated thus?

(1391) Since the fact that an entity has the nature of existence in some way is already ascertained by everyone, why do you state it thus—that an entity has the nature of existence in some way—and [why speak of] "that nature"?

The statement that "an entity has existence as its nature" is merely an illustration; for even a non-entity (abhāva) certainly possesses existence as its nature in some way—for instance, in the form of being an object of cognition (*prameya*). Thus, the logical reason (*hetu*) is redundant.

Now, since this is not established for the Sāṃkhyas and others, he states that it is being proven: "In the doctrine of the identity of all things (*sarvabhāvaikya*), even so, [the distinction exists] due to the difference between modifications (*vikāra*), self-nature (*ātman*), and so forth."
By some [means], the state of being luminous by nature is fully manifested by the self.
Even those who rely on the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) residing in all things,
they too rely on qualifiers such as "in reality" (tattvataḥ) and so forth.

The doctrine of the unity of all existents belongs to the Sāṅkhya; in that doctrine, it is precisely by those Sāṅkhyas themselves that its nature is revealed through some essence or intrinsic nature. To explain how this is so, he says: "by means of the distinction between the nature of transformation and so forth. Here, "the nature of transformation" refers to the essential character of transformation.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), those who hold that primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is unmixed and has the nature of pleasure, pain, and so on, as well as the *puruṣas* which are distinct from one another and from primordial matter— namely, the Mādhyamikas— are included.

They too have relied upon the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) of all phenomena as being qualified by the term "in reality" (*tattvataḥ*), and not because they accept [the existence of] seeing, arising, and so forth in every respect; for that reason,
it is said "in reality."
By "logically" (*nyāyataḥ*),

the inclusion of "ultimately" (*paramārthataḥ*) and so forth is implied through the word "etcetera" (*ādi*); and this must necessarily be accepted by everyone, for it is certain that every entity possesses, in some sense, the nature of existence.
Otherwise, its being apprehended in some way would not be established.
If the object of dispute (*vyavahāra*) were that which is to be proven (*sādhya*), then an example would be well-established.
Otherwise, if this is not accepted, even this reason—"because it is perceived in some way"—is not established;
for the fault of the reason known as "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhyatā*) was stated previously.

Now, if it is argued that while [the reason] was previously stated as unestablished (*asiddha*), the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is being proven, then a well-known example (*nidarśana*)—in which such usage has been established before—is possible; thus, [the reason] would indeed possess the three characteristics (*trirūpa*).
Otherwise, in the absence of an example, even that conventional usage would not be established.
1394 He states the refutation regarding the second application: "In 'candra' etc.,
the state of being designated as the moon also persists in the similar instance (sapakṣa)."
In some cases, [the term] "māṇavaka" refers to a young boy, or perhaps to camphor, silver, and so forth;
whereas "māṇavaka" [in another sense] refers to a man.

Now, one might object: "If a three-featured reason (*trirūpa-hetu*) is indeed possible for proving that [the moon] is the moon, then why did the Teacher state that there is an absence of inference for a person who asserts that the hare-marked one is not the moon, when that person speaks to the world in order to prove its moonhood? For he said: 'Even where there is an absence of inference due to the reason being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatva*), [the subject] is set aside by a contradictory meaning established through verbal convention (*śābdaprasiddha*), as in: "The hare-marked one is not the moon, because it exists. By this passage, [he stated] that this is not a valid thesis (*pakṣa*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "In the proof of moonhood..."

In the case of a reason for proving "moon-ness," there would be the fallacy of being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇatā*) if it were based on the nature of a real entity and excluded from what is commonly recognized.
"Based on the nature of a real entity" means... [1396]

In this case, the "uniqueness" (asādhāraṇatva) is stated with respect to a proof that conforms to the actual existence or non-existence of a real entity; however, it does not apply to a reason characterized by conventional renown (*prasiddhi*),
because such a reason conforms to mere intention and thus possesses positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Since this person is mistaken and denies all conventional consensus, it is impossible to establish his "moon-ness" by means of a definition based on common renown (*prasiddhi-lakṣaṇa*);

nor is there any other logical mark (*liṅga*) functioning through the force of real entities (*vastu-bala-pravṛtta*) by which moon-ness could be established in the hare-marked one (*śaśin*), because designations such as "moon" follow mere whim and thus do not constitute the properties of real entities. Therefore, for him, an inference without an example has been stated, as it was said: "Not accepting the moon-ness of the hare-marked one, what kind of cognition does he desire?"

Thus, that [reason] is considered to be "without an example" (*adṛṣṭānta*) and "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) with respect to it; in some readings, the text says "proving it is not the moon" (*acandrasādhana*),
and there the connection is "in that very case" (*tatraivaṃ*).

When the reason "the hare-marked one is not the moon because it exists" (sattvāt) has been stated by the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*), the teacher has declared that the "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇatā*) of the respondent (*uttarapakṣavādin*) who proceeds against him to prove its status as the moon is the cause for the absence of inference. This was stated in the passage beginning with "where there is an absence of inference due to uniqueness," etc., referring to relying on a logical mark (*liṅga*) that functions through the force of reality rather than through conventional renown (*prasiddhi*).
Regarding the third reason as well, he says: "falling," etc. (1396).
No distinction is observed between [the pain] produced by a falling insect and that which arises from contact with a falling insect; thus,
no distinction is observed.

The reason is merely a part of the meaning of the thesis; for instance, here the fact of being caused by a specific insect is intended as the probandum (*sādhya*) regarding the sensation, and that very same thing is stated as the reason (*hetu*) in different words. Thus, there is no distinction between the reason and the thesis.

1397 Now, [the opponent] might think: "When the qualification 'of that which is falling' is not employed, and instead the general reason 'because it has attained its arising' is stated, then there is no fallacy of being a part of the meaning of the thesis. To this he says: "Of that which is falling," etc.;
for the effect of "that which is falling" is certainly a qualification of the reason.
Otherwise, the charge of inconstancy (vyabhicāritva) would result as unavoidable. To prevent inconstancy due to the sensation produced by another insect, a qualification must be applied. (1398)

As for the conventional usage of "being an effect," if that [usage] has been forgotten, it can be established as having the three characteristics [of a logical reason] provided there is a previously established instance;

(1399) for if the conventional usage of cause and effect is being established for someone who has forgotten it, then the reason would possess the three characteristics, since instances such as fire and smoke— which have well-known causal relations— exist as examples.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the eye and form," he says: "of the eye," and so forth;
first of all, the existence of the eye as a substratum (dharmin) is unascertained.

"And its proof is not tenable, because of the consequence of [fallacies] such as unestablishedness (asiddhi). The word "and" (ca) is to be construed with the preceding clause. The phrase "its proof is not tenable" constitutes the division of the sentence.
By the word "such as" (ādi) in "unestablishedness and so forth," the fallacies of deviation (vyabhicāra) and contradiction (virodha) are included.
When existence (*sattā*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), every logical reason (*hetu*) fails to escape three defects;

namely: if the reason is a property of an existent (*bhāva-dharma*), it is unestablished (*asiddha*); if it is a property of both, it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); and if it is a property of a non-existent (*abhāva-dharma*), it is contradictory (*viruddha*).
As it has been said: "There is no property of an existent that is unestablished, while that which relies on both is deviant."
If existence (*sattā*) is something distinct from the property (*dharma*) and the entity (*bhāva*), how can that existence be proven? Furthermore,

if it is argued that what is being proven in the subject (*dharmin*), namely the eye, is the capacity to produce visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), even then, since "capacity" (*śakti*) and "existence" (*sattā*) are synonyms, proving that [capacity] would entail proving existence itself.

Even if there were a distinction [between the two], because that [distinction] is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it would be unestablished; thus, the reason (*hetu*) would be unestablished due to its lack of a locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).
Likewise, this [reason] "because of the apprehension of color" (*rūpagrahaṇāt*) should also be understood as unestablished, because it does not possess the property of the subject (*apakṣadharma*).
How, then, is the existence of the sense-faculties such as the eye established even for you? To this he says: "But," and so forth.
"But even when visible form and the other [objects] are present, visual cognition does not sometimes arise; therefore, it is understood that the object alone is not the cause. (1401)
The phrase "at times" refers to the state when the eyes are closed;

for we do not establish the eye as such by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), but rather, since the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of cognition is observed with respect to certain forms and so forth while they exist, it is established that this cognition requires another cause and cannot arise from those [forms] alone. Thus, that very cognition is the subject (*dharmin*), and there is no fault such as the unestablished nature of the reason (*asiddhi*).
That which is the other cause is designated as "the eye";
however, the conventional usage of distinctions is based upon established tenets.

It might be argued: "Let it be that, according to the principle stated, consciousness possesses the status of a subject (*dharmin*); nevertheless, the reason (*hetu*) remains twofold. To this he says: "By its own causes... [The verse continues:
"...and since sprouts and the like, which arise as determined by their own causes, exist within that very example, the dissimilarity (*vailakṣaṇya*) is thus perfectly evident. (1402)
"Dependent on its own cause" means that whose arising is bound to a cause;

such things as sprouts, which have an origin dependent upon their own causes, are observed to be occasional, and thus they serve as the examples. In this manner, the formal argument (*prayoga*) should be constructed as follows:

Those things which occur only occasionally in the presence of something else do not arise from that alone, but rather depend upon other causes; for example, although earth and other factors are present, sprouts and the like exhibit positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) based on the presence or absence of the seed; likewise, although color-form and other objects are present, visual cognition occurs only occasionally depending on whether the eyes are closed or open. This is an "observation of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*) in the case of negation, whereas in the case of affirmation, it is a "reason consisting in essential nature" (*svabhāvahetu*).
Regarding the phrase "in some way" (*kathaṃcit*) and so forth, he says: "In some way" (*kathaṃcit*);

and when proving that [things] have a non-existent nature in some way, as in the case of jars and the like, the futility of the reason and its lack of established presence (*aprasiddhi*) are seen, just as before. (1403)

Here too, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the non-existence of jars and other such things is established in some manner. If it is argued that it is not established, then this reason (*hetu*)—namely, "because they are not perceived"—is itself not established; thus, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). This refutation should be stated as before, just as it was stated regarding the reason for proving that [the self] has the nature of existence.

Regarding what was said—that because of the absence of a counter-example (vipakṣa), there is no example based on difference (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta)—he replies: "And here too," and so forth. "And here too there is a clear illustration by way of difference: for that very nature of theirs becomes the counter-example. (1404)

Even when proving that things possess the nature of existence (*sadātmatva*), there is the establishment of what is already accepted and the non-establishment [of the reason] in the case of soulless things (*nirātmasu*), as well as the presence of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) in exactly the same way.

When the nature of existence is intended for jars and so forth in the very form in which they are perceived, then that very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of theirs would indeed serve as the example of dissimilarity.

Since the reason— namely, non-apprehensibility— is absent in that intrinsic nature, the same [faults], such as the establishment of what is already accepted (*iṣṭasiddhi*), apply equally here in the formulation "in the case of being selfless" (*nirātmasu*).

Regarding the phrase "the attainment of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) in absences": the attainment of dissimilarity—characterized by the absence of the probandum (sādhya)—through the absence of the probans (sādhana) is the pervasion (vyāpti);
it is exactly so.
Because of the impossibility of a difference in nature [between the subject and the example].

Regarding the passage beginning with "tvadīya" (your), he says: "Even that connection with the father which is established for the house from the hearing of the word 'father'—in that case, the reason possessing the three characteristics is manifest. (1406)
In some cases, a voice previously perceived as being connected to a specific person would have its causal basis rendered difficult to maintain if that person were not experienced beforehand.
(1407) "Of that" refers to this.
If there were no experience elsewhere in some other location of that which is connected to the father, the reason would be unestablished (asiddha).
By the verse beginning with "yasmin" (in which), he demonstrates that very same threefold nature:
"In that [subject] where it was previously perceived and also not perceived, whether it be positive concomitance (anvaya) or negative concomitance (vyatireka), it is clearly seen therein. (1408)

A word, however, makes an object known in no way whatsoever as something external, because there is an absence of impossibility [otherwise]; rather, it is an indicator of a distinct [cognitive] form. And when that [distinct form] is what is being communicated, the difference [from the external object] is extremely clear.
For a word is not employed unless there is the presence of a desire to speak [something].
A lamp, however, is not an indicator [of objects] such as blue by virtue of being a logical mark (liṅga);
rather, it is so described because it produces that which is capable of generating cognition.
When [the reason] is of the nature of an indicator (*jñāpaka*) or a mark (*liṅga*), the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth is considered;
otherwise, why is this not also urged in the case of the eyes and other [senses]?
Furthermore, even by way of "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), the quality of being visible (*cākṣuṣatva*) is not a prover.
Because they lack the property of being present in the subject (*pakṣadharma*), those [reasons] possessing only one characteristic are impotent.
For those stated as having a single form, a dual form is observed;
and for those stated with a dual form, a triple form arises through the presence of the property in the subject.

If it is argued that [the word] implies [its object] solely through *anyathānupapatti* (otherwise-unaccountability), we say no; for in the case of sound and so forth, even though [visibility] is desired [of them], such unaccountability does not exist. Regarding sound, its state of being otherwise-unaccountable with respect to an external object is unestablished; therefore, it lacks the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*) for that [external object], because its occurrence depends solely on mere intention (*icchā*). If, however, it is with respect to an object existing within the intellect (*buddhiparivartin*) that [unaccountability is claimed], then the three characteristics (*trailakṣaṇya*) are indeed present, just as they are for smoke. This is because when the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*) is absent, the word is not employed; thus, by being an effect of that [desire], it is accepted as an indicator of the fire [of the speaker's intention], just like smoke—but not in the capacity of a denoter (*vācaka*).
A lamp, however, like smoke, is not intended as an indicator by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*).
What then?

It is conventionally established as an indicator by producing jars and other objects capable of generating cognition, but not by virtue of being a logical mark; therefore, any consideration regarding its "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth—as if it were a logical mark—is entirely improper.
Otherwise, one would have to point out that the eye and other [sense organs] also possess the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth.
The phrase "otherwise" and so on concludes the present topic:

since visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*), although invariably concomitant with impermanence, does not prove impermanence in the case of sound; and since the property of being a characteristic of the subject must necessarily be relied upon in all cases, therefore, for those reasons stated as having a single form by relying on the property of being a characteristic of the subject, the possession of two forms is necessary; and for those stated as having two forms, the possession of three forms is necessary. For this very reason, logical reasons characterized by only a single feature—namely, the property of being a characteristic of the subject—are impotent.

Nor should it be said that because the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth are implied solely by the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*), they do not possess the status of a definition independently; for you yourself have stated that "otherwise-unaccountability" exists even without the property of being a feature of the subject. Furthermore, you have said: "Even in the case of things such as words, lamps, and so forth, where there is no status as a feature of the subject, the capacity to indicate [the probandum] is observed through 'otherwise-unaccountability' alone.

Moreover, in the case of visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*), although impermanence is otherwise-unaccountable, that [visibility] is not a feature of the subject; thus, [your position] is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding what was stated—"He is dark-skinned because he is his son"—this [argument] does not provide certainty even though it possesses the three characteristics (*trilakṣaṇa*). To this, he says: "tatputra... and so forth.

Because the reasons such as "being his son" possess a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar class (*sandigdhavyatireka*), the presence of the three characteristics is not established; for there is no contradiction with the heterogeneous class, since there is no contradiction in the case of one who might be his son yet not be dark-complexioned. Thus, because its exclusion from the opposite side is doubtful, this [reason] does not possess the three characteristics, and the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).

It might be argued: "If there were a difference in the effect while the cause remains non-different, then indeed there would be a contradiction, as it would follow that the effect is causeless. To this, he says: "Action," and so forth.
In every respect, and especially so, a deviation from the norm is possible for causes such as karma, diet, and so forth, even in the case of his being that person's son.
For this [son] is neither the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) nor the effect (kārya) of the visible [father], nor is he simply the non-perception of the visible.
Nor is there non-deviation for anything distinct from that [complex].

Since a change of state—such as being fair-skinned and so forth—is possible due to specific virtuous and other types of karma, as well as differences in conditions such as food and temperature, how could there be a contradiction? For the distinction in causes is established.

Furthermore, the argument "because he is his son" is not a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), as is the case with "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). For "being produced" has no other reality apart from impermanence; however, it is not the case that "being his son" lacks another essential nature, since the designation "his son" is made in relation to someone who consists of the five aggregates of appropriation (*pañcopādānaskandha*). Nor is it a reason based on effect (*kāryahetu*), because the causal relationship between them is unestablished.

Nor can it be established through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), because that pertains to positive affirmation (*vidhi*) and because there is no contradiction [between the two]. Thus, the absence of colors other than black is not established; nor is there any other inferential mark (*liṅga*) distinct from this, since there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) elsewhere.

And there can be no capacity for proof without a necessary connection, because that would lead to over-extension; therefore, this is neither a valid reason nor does it possess the three characteristics—how, then, could there be non-deviation?
Non-perception of the perceptible is non-apprehension of that which has met the conditions for apprehension.
With the words "But surely... and so forth, he states the defect of the definition, namely its lack of pervasiveness (avyāpitā):
"But surely, non-deviation is observed in other [cognitions] as well."
Just as the blooming of night-lotuses and the swelling of the ocean are the signs of the moon's rising, so too, from the presence of sunlight,
the existence of shadows on the opposite sides is perceived.
In the darkness, when a firebrand is seen, smoke is perceived from afar; and from the rising of the Kṛttikās, the proximity of Rohiṇī is inferred.
Just as, from the rising of the moon, there is an inference of the blooming of night-lilies and the swelling of the ocean.

By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inference of the blooming of lotuses from sunrise; the inference of shadow on the far side of mountains and such from the presence of sunlight; likewise, the perception of smoke upon seeing a half-burnt piece of wood—a firebrand—from afar in the darkness; and similarly, the proximity of the Rohiṇī constellation is perceived from the rising of the Kṛttikā constellation, since it is well known that the constellations rise in the very order they are recited, beginning with Aśvinī.

And yet, all of this is not included within the three types of logical reasons (hetu). Why, then, is it said that [the definition] does not fail [to apply] to anything other than those [three]? (1419)
To this, he states the following reply: "In this regard," and so forth.
Therefore, in this case, all other qualities such as cognition and so forth are considered by those who possess inference to have arisen at the same time as that [quality] of the causal factor;
for it is from such a cause that the establishment of the effect occurs.
And if no connection were possible, there would be [the absurdity of] everything being the cause [of everything].
For what reason? Because those things such as awakening—and the blooming of night-lotuses and so forth—which have arisen or been produced, [would otherwise arise from anything].
Of what specific nature are they?

"Simultaneous with those"—meaning they are simultaneous with the rising of the moon, the heat of the sun, and fire. They are considered to be inferred from such a causal property—that is, from a specific cause. What is meant is this: whatever is the cause of the rising of the moon and so forth, which arise at the same time as the blooming of the night-lotuses (*kumuda*) and other phenomena, that very same [cause] functions as the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*) for the blooming of the night-lotuses and the like. Thus, while those [phenomena] such as the rising of the moon infer their own corresponding cause, they also infer by implication (*arthāt*) the simultaneous occurrences such as the blooming of the night-lotuses; however, they do not do so directly. Therefore, this type of inference is included within the category of the "effect as a reason" (*kāryahetu*).

And this must necessarily be understood: if [signs] were to convey [their objects] solely through non-obstruction, then they would convey anything at all, since they would be indistinguishable in their state of being unobstructed.
Therefore, even in this case, an obstruction must be stated, and that [obstruction] is precisely characterized by the aforementioned relationship of cause and effect.
1422 1423 Then, he asks: what is the obstruction to the rising of Kṛttikā when Rohiṇī is near? He says: "By the wind," and so forth.
That very specific wind which is the cause for the rising of the Kṛttikās is indeed, through its continuity, the cause for the proximity of Rohiṇī;
therefore, the cognition of the cause's property is considered to be the cognition of that [effect]. (1424)
The cognition of that [wind] is independent; there is no other [cognition] here whatsoever.
Here too, because it depends on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there is an inference of the property of the cause, namely, that it is wind (*prabhañjana*).

As it has been said: "The cognition of an existing thing, such as its own nature and so forth, based on its dependence upon a single causal complex, occurs through the inference of the properties of the cause, just like [the inference of] the transformation of fuel by means of smoke."
Now, as for the transition from the reflection to the original object, that has no inclusion anywhere, because the reflection is not a real entity.
Therefore, suspecting that the definition is not all-encompassing, he says: "And from the mark," and so forth.

From the mark known as the reflection, an inference proceeds which has the original object (*bimba*) as its domain; this is logical because it is distinct from [inference] arising from a mark that is an effect (*kāryaliṅga*). || 1426 ||
With the words "together in one place," etc., he anticipates the objection of the challenger:
"Since two things cannot exist together in one place, there is no reflection of a real entity;
therefore, how can its status as an effect be logical if it is ultimately real? (1427)
The reason for its lack of substantial reality is that two things cannot exist together in one place.

For in the very same location where the form of a mirror is seen, the reflection is also seen; yet there can be no coexistence of two forms in a single location because they possess resistance (*sapratighatva*). Therefore, the simultaneous existence of two forms in one place is impossible, and thus this [reflection] is an illusion.
Alternatively: "Because two things do not exist together in one place"—of which two?
Of the surface of the mirror and the reflection of the moon.
The surface of the mirror exists in one place, while the reflection of the moon is seen inside it in another, like water in a well;
since that which arises in one location is perceived in another,
there is no such thing as a reflection that possesses any real substantial existence.
However, such is the power of that causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that it appears in that way; for the distinctions in the capacities of phenomena (*dharma*) are indeed inconceivable. (1427)
He refutes this with the verse beginning "mūrta" (the embodied):
"Even if this reflected image, being material, lacks substantial reality, how could the consciousness that appears as its likeness be non-substantial? (1428)

And here, it is precisely that [cognition] which is intended as the effect serving as the logical mark (*liṅga*), for it proceeds without any external support by virtue of its sovereignty over the original object (*bimba*).
(1429) In this context, what is intended as the logical mark is cognition itself existing in such a state as an effect; it is not an external entity called a reflection.

How is it that the statement of the three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) was previously described as being for the sake of another (*parārtha*), yet now the statements of the proposition (*pakṣa*), conclusion (*nigamana*), and application (*upanaya*) are also proclaimed by others to be inference for the sake of another?
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "The statement of the thesis," and so forth.
Even by others, the statement of the thesis and the other members are described as being for the sake of another;
however, because it is not a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*), the thesis is useless. (1430)
He replies with the words "asādhana" and so forth:

*siddhi* (establishment) is the means of proof (*sādhana*), that is to say, the comprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya*). That which is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of it—that is, its cause—is the "constituent part of the means of proof. The negation of that is "not being a constituent part of the means of proof.
Therefore, because it is not a constituent part of the means of proof, it is useless and should not be employed; this is the meaning.

"Useless"—if explained as "not being a cause," it would constitute a part of the meaning of the proposition itself (1430). To the question, "How is it not a member of the proof? he says: "Because of the lack of connection," and so forth.
Because it lacks a [logical] connection, that [inference] is not directly capable of establishing the object; nor is it appropriate [to do so] indirectly, because it indicates what is unconnected.
This is because it merely points out the subject matter of the property to be proven (sādhya) and the proving property (sādhana).
If this [statement] possessing the form of an example is accepted as a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*),

then surely there is a deviation (*vyabhicāritā*) here due to statements such as "concession" (*abhyanujñā*). Furthermore, it would be useless in cases where the object [of the thesis] is already demonstrated.
However, the indication of the unattached [probandum] follows from the very statement of the probandum itself.

What is meant is this: because there is no relationship between words and their objects, the [thesis-statement] is not directly useful; nor is it indirectly useful like the statement of a reason, because it does not indicate that which is attached [to the proof], as has been said:
"They made that statement of the thesis for the purpose of communicating the intention."
The production of doubt is what is brought about; therefore, it is not a direct means of proof for the probandum,
nor is it sufficient even as an indirect one, because it merely states the [probandum] itself.

Some hold the view that the proposition (*pratijñā*), although not constituting a formal member (*anavayava*) of the syllogism, should nevertheless be employed like the example-member (*dṛṣṭāntapada*), for the purpose of indicating the objects of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the proving property (*sādhana*).
This is because, according to the statement "the two remaining forms are shown by the example" (*dṛṣṭāntena pradarśyate*),
the example-member— even though it is a separate non-member— is employed solely for the purpose of demonstrating the two forms distinct from the property residing in the subject (*pakṣadharma*).

He replies to them with the sentence beginning "dṛṣṭānta" (the example), which is a statement of permission: "Do this: prove that sound is impermanent. By the word "etcetera," statements of command and entreaty are included.

Even for such a statement, there might be an instruction for the purpose of indicating its formal application; for without even these [elements], the commencement of a proof could not possibly occur out of nowhere. [Objection:
It is fruitless, because the object to be proven is understood even without it.

For instance: when it is stated merely that "whatever is produced is impermanent, and sound is produced," the cognition that "sound is impermanent" arises even without the explicit statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*).

In that case, how is the formal arrangement of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) and so forth established? For it is said: "A thing that is similar by virtue of the general property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is called the similar instance (*sapakṣa*)," and "the absence of that [property], which has been established, is the dissimilar instance (*asapakṣa*)."

For if there were no statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*), then even the three-fold character (*trairūpya*)—which is dependent upon that [proposition] and based upon its reliance on similar instances (*sapakṣa*)—would not exist; thus, everything would be incomplete and disordered.
To this, he replies with the words beginning "no" (*na*).
There is no conceptual differentiation of the similar class (*sapakṣa*) and so forth at the time of stating the proof;
however, they are divided in the treatises in that manner for the sake of conventional usage.

For instance, even a commoner who has not mastered the conventions of the similar class and so forth, upon being told merely "where there is smoke, there is fire, and here there is smoke," understands the positive and negative concomitance and indeed realizes the presence of fire, even without the convention of the similar class and so forth. Therefore, at the time of establishing the proof, there is no formal arrangement of the similar class and so forth.
To the question, "Where, then, does the conventional usage of 'similar instance' (sapakṣa) and so forth occur?", he says: "In the treatise" (śāstre tu).
Alternatively, he demonstrates that even at the time of stating the proof (sādhana), establishing those [distinctions] is not contradictory, by saying "the subject" (prakṛta) and so forth.

Even that [establishment] is not contradictory, as it relies upon the subject matter at hand; for the proponent does not state the proof for the opponent right at the beginning of the section. (1436) Even though there is no employment of the thesis (*pratijñā*) at the time of stating the proof, nevertheless, that formal arrangement being made by relying upon the subject matter at hand—the locus of the property to be proven—is certainly not contradictory.

Nor should it be said that at the time of the proof (sādhana), the very subject under discussion (*prakṛta*) does not exist; for this is not so, because even for the opponent—the proponent of the formal statement of the thesis (*pratijñāprayoga*)—the proponent states the proof all of a sudden, that is, out of context (*akāṇḍa*). [The opponent might argue: "Granted that the subject (*dharmin*) whose specific nature is desired to be known is the subject under discussion, nevertheless, how can this rule being established be performed by relying upon that subject under discussion? To this he says: "The desired to be known... (*jijñāsita*) and so forth.
For "presence in the subject" (pakṣadharmatā) consists in its occurring in that which possesses the specific quality sought to be known;
the "similar instance" (sapakṣa) is so called because of its similarity to that [subject], and the "dissimilar instance" (vipakṣa) because of the absence of that [quality].
This is easily understood.
The definition of the application (*upanaya*) is: "The application is the conclusion regarding the subject of proof, either as 'it is so' or 'it is not so,' depending on the example.

Regarding this, the venerable teacher Dignāga established that the statement of the application is not a means of proof (*sādhana*), because it merely illuminates the meaning of the reason already stated, like a second statement of the reason. To this, Bhāvivikta and others said, in order to show the non-establishment of the reason: "Indeed, the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is not illuminated by the statement of the reason occurring immediately after the thesis, because that statement expresses only the cause [of the inference]."
"Sound is impermanent because it is produced. Now, if one asks whether that "being produced" exists or does not exist in sound, its existence is understood from the application (*upanaya*).

Alternatively, the application serves for the purpose of reflection (*pratibimbana*): previously, by the statement of the reason (*hetu*), "being produced" was indicated in sound without qualification; therefore, by the application, the reflection of that "being produced"—which has been shown in the example to have an inseparable connection (*avinābhāvitva*) with the probandum—is demonstrated through the mind [of the listener], as in: "And so, sound is produced. Thus, because it highlights a specific distinction, it is not a mere repetition.

Here he says: "And if the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth are not stated, because the reason (*kāraṇa*) is not stated, the statement of the application (*upanaya*), which ought to be made, does not serve to establish the existence [of the probandum]. (1438)

Since the mere existence [of the probans] was stated previously and its pervasion is subsequently revealed, the intended object is fully established; therefore, the "reflection" (pratibimbaka) is useless for the purpose of establishing existence. (1439) "For the sake of establishing existence."
The remainder [of the sentence] is "in the locus of the reason" (*hetordharmiṇi*).

This is the meaning here: since the employment of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has been refuted by the aforementioned method, there is no such thing as the statement of a reason, such as "being produced," occurring immediately after it;
and consequently, the statement of the application (*upanaya*), which must precede the statement of the reason, should certainly not be made.

Now, if the statement of the application (*upanaya*) is made for the purpose of establishing the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), then another result for the statement of the reason (*kāraṇa*) must be stated.
To this, one might say that the very demonstration of its being a reason is the result;
but that is not so.
What is the purpose of establishing that very [property] when it has already been shown that the proof of the probandum (*sādhyasiddhi*) occurs even otherwise?
Therefore, apart from the demonstration of the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), no other fruit for the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*) can be asserted.

Consequently, once the property of being a feature of the subject has been established by that very first statement of the reason, the application (*upanaya*) employed to demonstrate that same thing most clearly reveals its own redundant nature; so how could there be any lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) regarding the reason?

The reflection [of the reason] is also entirely useless; for, since the mere property of the subject (pakṣadharma) has already been stated by the statement of the reason, and its pervasion (vyāpti) with the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) has been declared, the intended object is fully established. Thus, what is being said clearly constitutes a redundancy. Therefore, how could there be any lack of proof (asiddhatā) regarding the reason here?
In this context, the definition of the conclusion (*nigamana*) is: "The restatement of the proposition (*pratijñā*) following the statement of the reason (*hetu*).

In such formulations as "therefore, [sound] is impermanent," the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*) indicates the efficacy of the reason as established by the example. That which constitutes a restatement of the meaning of the proposition is the conclusion.

It is called a conclusion because by means of it the proposition, the reason, the example, and the application are brought together (*nigamyante*), supported, and connected as having a single purpose.

In this regard, there is not even the employment of the formal proposition (*pratijñā*); how much less, then, can there be a conclusion (*nigamana*) consisting of its restatement? Therefore, the conclusion is not a member of the proof (*sādhana*). On this point, the venerable teacher Diṅnāga stated: "The conclusion is not a means of proof precisely because it is a mere repetition.

To this, Uddyotakara and others reply: "There is no redundancy here, because the proposition is the statement of what is to be proven (*sādhya*), whereas the conclusion is the statement of what has been established (*siddha*)."
Furthermore, there is no establishment [of the conclusion] without the conclusion (*nigamana*).

For instance, without it, even if the other members are stated, the doubt as to whether "sound is impermanent" does not cease; therefore, in order to remove that doubt, the conclusion must be stated separately.
To this, he says: "The three-fold," and so forth.

Since the proof is established by the very power of the demonstration of the three-fold reason, there is no suspicion of the contrary; therefore, the conclusion (nigamana) is useless. (1440) When "being produced" is ascertained in the subject (dharmin), namely sound, as being invariably concomitant with "impermanence," how can there be any suspicion of its contrary, namely permanence? For it is not fitting for a person of sound mind to suspect coldness in a physical object whose nature is definitively ascertained to be pervaded by a mass of blazing flames.
Nor does it cease from that [fault] merely by means of a conclusion (nigamana) that is devoid of logical justification.
However, Aviddhakarṇa says: "A single meaning is not established by means of scattered statements."

To this, he replies: "In order to establish the connection, the conclusion (nigamana) must be stated separately"—to which it is said: "By means of connected [statements]," meaning that a single meaning is established by statements that are indeed connected.
Therefore, a separate conclusion (*nigamana*) need not be stated for the sake of establishing the connection [between the members of the syllogism].

Once the connection between the reason and the probandum—characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination therefrom (*tadutpatti*)—has been established, that single intended object is demonstrated through the force of the statements regarding the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), which are themselves connected by way of their meaning.

Thus, although these statements are scattered, they are nonetheless interconnected through the synthesis of a single meaning; therefore, a separate conclusion need not be stated to establish that connection.
Some explain that inference is of two kinds,
based on the distinction between that which perceives the particular (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*) and that which perceives the universal (*sāmānyaparidṛṣṭa*).
"Some" refers to Kumārila and others;
for they describe inference as being of two kinds: that based on specific observation (viśeṣatodṛṣṭa) and that based on general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).
Regarding that, he states which one is the "inference from specific observation" (*viśeṣatodṛṣṭa*): "The relation between two specific [things] has been perceived by direct perception," and so forth.
When a person who has formed a cognition of cow-dung fuel, its specific location, and so forth,
goes to that very place at another time and perceives that same fire again and again, it is [due to] his previous cognition. (1443–1444)
Its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises from the cognition of an object whose existence was previously doubted;

and this is what Vindhyavāsin has written regarding "inference based on the perception of particulars" (*viśeṣadṛṣṭa*), when one must state that fire and smoke are distinct entities within the scope of inference by generality (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). (1445)
"Because it moves with absolute certainty, the sun is called *sāmānyadṛṣṭa*.

(1446) This is the meaning: previously, having perceived a particular fire and a particular smoke in a specific location through direct perception, one who has subsequently traveled far away, upon seeing that same particular smoke again and again, infers that very same fire previously apprehended; this is inference based on the observation of particulars (*viśeṣatodṛṣṭam anumānam*), because its object is a particularity previously grasped through direct perception.
Nor is it invalid because it apprehends what has already been apprehended; for there exists an additional element, namely the removal of doubt as to whether the fire remains or has ceased.
This is the summary meaning (*piṇḍārtha*).
Now the meaning of the individual parts (*avayavārtha*) is stated: "the connection perceived through direct perception" (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasaṃbandham*).
What is the connection here?

Śabarasvāmin states the definition of inference: "Inference is the cognition of one part, which is not in contact with the senses, based on the perception of another part by one who knows the relationship [between them]."

That [inference] is of two kinds: that based on a relationship perceived through direct observation (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*) and that based on a relationship observed through generalization (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭasambandha*).
An example of inference based on a relationship perceived through direct observation is the cognition of the form of fire from the sight of the form of smoke.

An example of inference based on a relationship observed through generalization is the recollection of the motion of the sun after having perceived that Devadatta’s arrival at another location is preceded by his movement.

In this regard, Kumārila, desiring to explain inference based on a relationship perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*), says "perceived through direct perception," and so forth.
The connection [of the words] is as follows: "They describe inference as that which has its relationship perceived through direct perception.
This is because in the immediately preceding verse, the subject under discussion was "they describe it thus" (*evaṃ pracakṣate*).
Regarding the phrase "of which two":

it refers to those very specific instances of fire and smoke that have become the objects [of cognition], for which the notion of "cow-dung fuel" has been produced by a person—that is, generated with the thought, "These two, fire and smoke, originate from cow-dung fuel"—and likewise for which the notion of a specific location such as a mountain has been formed—that is, with the thought, "These two, fire and smoke, are situated in this specific location such as a mountain. The analysis of the compound is as follows: "those two whose fuel is cow-dung" are *gomayendhanau*; "those two whose location is that [place]" are *taddeśau*; and the two together form the compound *gomayendhanataddeśau*. (The term *gomayendhana* means "having cow-dung as its fuel," and *taddeśa* means "having that place as its location.")

Those two specific features are the beginning of those other specific fires, such as those in forests of *sarja*, *sarala*, and *sallakī* trees; [the compound] "in those" (*teṣu*) refers to things like cow-dung fuel and specific locations, and the compound is formed by splitting the locative case (*saptamī-yoga-vibhāga*).

When the cognizer who has produced—that is, brought about—such indirect cognition (*matir apratyakṣā*) perceives that very same fire at a later time through that very same mark (*liṅga*), such as smoke, while situated in that same location...
The connection is with the phrase "again and again.

In that case, the status of that cognition as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatā*)—meaning it constitutes a distinct means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*)—is derived from its being a perception (*pratyakṣātmaka*) compared to the previous cognition.
Alternatively, the connection is that one cognizes that very same fire based on the previous cognition acting as the cause.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: "that whose existence is being doubted" refers to a thing about which one wonders whether fire exists or whether it has ceased; "that and that thing" means the object itself; and "the cognition of that" is the full analysis.

This is what was stated by Vindhyavāsin as inference based on a perceived relationship seen through direct perception (*pratyakṣadṛṣṭasambandha*), specifically termed "inference based on what is seen in particular" (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭam anumānam*).
Now he states [the definition of] "inference based on what is seen in general" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*): "Fire, smoke," and so forth.
For the author of the Bhāṣya has cited the recollection of the sun’s motion based on its arrival at another location as an example of inference from general observation (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa).

In this regard, the following objection arises: "Indeed, when an inference is made based on a common property between another fire and another smoke, then there certainly exists an inference 'seen through generality' (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) regarding fire and smoke; why then did the author of the Bhāṣya set aside fire and smoke—which are proximate because they revolve within the mind—and instead cite only the sun as an example of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*? Anticipating this objection, Kumārila, explaining the intention of the Bhāṣyakāra, says: "Regarding another fire and another smoke... [etc.]

Regarding inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*): although fire and smoke should have been cited as examples for this type of inference, the author of the Bhāṣya instead provides the example of the sun. This is because the movement of the sun is never perceived at any time; thus, he considers that in the case of the sun’s movement, only inference based on general observation is possible, and not inference based on specific observation (*viśeṣatodṛṣṭa*). Thinking to demonstrate a distinct domain [for each type of inference], he cites the sun alone as the example, and not fire and smoke, because there is no inference based on general observation in the case of the latter.
He states the refutation with the words "tadatra" and so forth:
"In this case, because the all-pervasive momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) has been established, inference is not possible for that very same [subject] as it existed previously. (1447)
If that unity is merely imagined through the desire to express the oneness of the continuum, it has no real existence whatsoever, nor does its substantiality possess any ontological reality.
(1448) [Regarding the term] "all-pervading":
If it is argued that, although momentariness exists, there is oneness due to the unity of the continuum for all pervasive entities such as fire and smoke, he replies: "It is imagined.
In that case, oneness is merely imagined and not ultimate; for from the perspective of ultimate reality, nothing whatsoever has any persistence.

Consequently, it would be illogical to say "by that very [cognition] situated in that place," nor could there be reality for what is merely imagined; thus, the statement "because of the cognition of an object whose existence is being doubted" would be incoherent.

Furthermore, it might be argued that the "seen through particulars" was explained by relying on a unity merely superimposed by conceptual construction, rather than one that is real. To this he says: "And not," etc.;
for you do not admit that there is knowledge devoid of an object.
And if it were a conceptualized object, it would clearly be devoid of a real referent.

(1449) One might argue: "Even though the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) is perishable, the universal (*jāti*) exists as imperishable; therefore, there will be a real unity, and it will not be devoid of a referent. To this, he says: "Even when the form of the manifestation perishes... and so forth.
Even upon the destruction of the form of the manifestation, the generic configuration (*ākṛti*) of those two [the manifestation and the universal] certainly persists.
If [the universal] does not exist because of the attainment of momentary destruction, then for what reason have you stated this rule:
"The relationship is perceived by direct perception only between those two specific individuals"? (1450–1451)

Having once perceived [an object] through inference, why is a subsequent inference of that very same object not accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? For what distinction is there from the previous one?
