If it is argued that this is not a valid means of knowledge because it apprehends an object already known, [we reply: ...

Why is it not observed that the former [case] is also similar to the Smārta [tradition], since it serves to remove the doubt that arises in the interval? If you argue that there is an excess [of elements] there, is this not equally the case here as well? (1453–1454)

Therefore, this perception of the universal (sāmānya) is free from further expectancy, as it effects the removal of doubt regarding whether [a thing] exists or does not exist; for that [universal] alone is what [is perceived]. Ākṛti = jāti (genus).

If [the opponent accepts] "yadi" as a concession, since the opponent desires the identity of the universal and the individual, how could the persistence of the universal be possible upon the destruction of the individual? Otherwise, because their acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema) would be distinct, one would have to admit an absolute difference between the two; such is the state of affairs.
This is merely a concessionary argument (*abhyupagamavāda*);
for since the universal (*jāti*) has already been refuted in detail on one occasion, how could it possibly exist?
Even if it were to exist—*bhāve 'pi*.
Furthermore, even for that [inference], momentary destruction follows, because momentary destruction has been established as all-pervasive.

Moreover, when one determines again by means of that very same mark (liṅga) the very same fire already determined by inference, why is that not described as "seen through particular observation" (viśeṣato-dṛṣṭa), such that the qualification "seen through direct perception" (pratyakṣato-dṛṣṭa) is desired?
If it is argued that [the Veda is authoritative] because it causes one to realize an object already realized, [we reply:
no,
for this is equally true even in the case of what is perceived by direct perception.
If it is argued that there is an additional element in the case of what is perceived by direct perception (pratyakṣa)—namely, the removal of doubts occurring in the interval—that is not so;
for the same additional element exists even in the case of what is seen through inference (anumāna).

Therefore, in all cases regarding entities that perish moment by moment, the inference is based solely on what is observed in a general sense (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa), and not on what is observed in a specific sense (viśeṣato dṛṣṭa).
"However, some of evil vision, while attempting to convey their intended meaning through these words, declare that inference is not a valid means of knowledge.
(1456) "Some" refers to...
Bārhaspatya and others [refute] by means of these [arguments], namely those of the form: "Inference is not a valid means of knowledge."
By this, he states the contradiction with his own words;

for instance, by one who speaks in order to communicate his own intention to another, thinking that "intention is understood from a statement or a logical mark" (liṅga), the validity of inference is demonstrated; yet, by saying "that is not a means of valid cognition," that very [validity] is denied. Thus, there is a mutual contradiction.
This refutation will be made explicit later.

Because it is preceded by a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics, inference for oneself (svārthānumāna) is not tenable as a means of valid cognition, since it produces false knowledge that destroys what is desired, just like [the cognition produced by] a [faulty] reason. 1457.

Even if existence is not [itself] an inference, the three-fold character (trairūpya) of the logical mark (liṅga)—unlike its two-fold character—is not the cause of inferential cognition; therefore, there is no inference [from it].
This is because [existence] would contradict inference and because it would establish contradictory [conclusions].
Furthermore, because it is possible [to find] everywhere, there is the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).

In that regard, first of all, the Cārvākas put forward this proof: "Inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*) is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is preceded by a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*), like false cognition.

And: "The eyes and other [senses] exist for the sake of another (*parārtha*), because they are composite (*saṅghātatva*), like the parts of a bed, a seat, or the like. This [latter inference], which indeed subverts what is desired [by the opponent], is a false cognition because it possesses the three characteristics; for that which is produced from a mark possessing the three characteristics is [itself] such [a false cognition].
Furthermore, the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) is not the cause of inference, because it exists even in cases that are not inference, just like the two-fold character (*dvairūpya*).

Moreover, in every proof, there is the possibility of a contradiction with inference, as follows: "The property intended to be proved (*sādhyadharma*) is not a qualifier of the subject (*dharmin*), because it is a part of this [subject-object] aggregate, just like the essential nature of the subject itself."

For by this [argument], all inference has been rendered non-inferential; moreover, whenever an inference is made, there is the possibility of "contradictions regarding specific qualities" (*viśeṣaviruddha*). For example, when it is argued, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a pot," someone might raise a contradiction regarding a specific quality, saying: "Just as this reason establishes impermanence, so too does it establish the absence of being a quality of space (*ākāśaguṇatvābhāva*)," and so forth.

And in every case, the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) is possible; for example, when it has been stated, "Sound is non-eternal because it is produced, like a jar," someone might state a non-erroneous contradictory: "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*). Such an elaboration of examples is to be found in the *Tattvaṭīkā*.
Likewise, Bhartṛhari said:
"Because the powers of entities differ according to the variations of state, place, and time, their establishment through inference is extremely difficult. (1460)
Even for this [cognition], whose power is already known, that power is obstructed with respect to various purposeful actions upon its connection with specific substances.
(1461) Even an object inferred with effort by skillful inferents...
Others, being more proficient, establish the matter quite differently:
(1462) "The capacities of entities differ according to differences in state, place, and time;

therefore, it is not possible to determine their existence through inference. For one cannot apprehend it through inference in this way: 'Devadatta is incapable of carrying a load, because he is Devadatta, like Devadatta in his childhood state.'"
For here, because a difference in power (*śakti*) is possible due to a difference in state (*avasthā*), there is an inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāra*).

Likewise, a difference in taste, potency, and post-digestive effect (*rasa-vīrya-vipāka*) is observed among the *āmalakī*, the date palm (*kharjūra*), and others due to a difference in location (*deśa*); in that case, it cannot be established that "all *āmalakī* fruits are astringent," on the grounds that they are like the *āmalakī* currently being experienced.
Similarly, a difference such as coldness or heat occurs in the water of wells and so forth due to a difference in time (*kāla*); in that case, one cannot reach the certainty that "all water is cold."
In such passages as these,
the genitive case in "of states" (*avasthānām*) is used in relation to the phrase "due to the difference of state, place, and time" (*avasthā-deśa-kālānām iti bhedāt*);
whereas the genitive in "of entities" (*bhāvānām*) is used in relation to conventional usage (*prasiddhi*).

Likewise, the capacity for burning that belongs to fire—which is ascertained in respect to grass and the like—is obstructed when it encounters a mass of clouds; yet one cannot infer in that very case: "The mass of clouds is burned by fire because it is composed of earth, just like grass and the like.
Similarly, it is undesirable that an object established in one way by one person should be established in another way by another person who is even more proficient.
Inference for the sake of others, however, is not a means of valid cognition with respect to the speaker.
On account of the restatement, one does not personally realize the object through that [restatement].
Even with respect to the listener, this [cognition] arises as having its own object;
for what difference is there between a cognition rooted in hearing and one rooted in seeing?
Speech is not an inference for others with respect to the listener, because it is a cause of cognition within the listener’s own continuum and because it makes [the object] known;
furthermore, unlike a sense faculty, it does not directly manifest the inferable object. (1465)
Therefore, this [inference] is not like the cognition of the relation of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva).

(1466) Now, if it is argued that its "being for the sake of another" (parārthatva) is in view of the exclusion of others (paravyāvṛtti), that too is incorrect, because it would follow that even [cognition] directed toward one's own object would be for the sake of another. (1467)
Another, however, says: "Inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from the perspective of the speaker because it is a restatement (*anuvāda*);

but from the perspective of the listener, it is indeed for one's own sake (*svārtha*). For what difference is there between one who understands that object through the door of hearing and one who does so through the door of seeing?
Just as when the visual faculty is active, there is no designation of it as being 'for the sake of another,' so too let there be no such designation for the activity of the auditory faculty either."
Vision— the sense organ of sight—
is so called because it is by means of this that consciousness perceives.

In the same way, speech is not a *parārthānumāna* (inference for others) with respect to the cognition [of the listener], because it is either the cause of the cognition occurring in the continuum of the listener, or because it is an indicator (*jñāpaka*), just like a sense faculty;
thus, the two reasons are stated by means of a conjunction: "being the cause of the cognition in the listener's continuum" and "being an indicator."
The phrase "as in the case of the sense organ" is an indication of an illustration;

this is another formal argument: speech does not constitute inference for others from the perspective of the listener, because it does not directly manifest the object of inference, just like the cognition of the relationship of invariable concomitance (avinābhāva). Therefore [it is not inference for others].
Because it does not directly illuminate the object of inference;

since it lacks direct illumination of the object of inference, therefore, unlike the cognition of the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), speech does not possess validity with respect to the auditory organ—this is the meaning of the sentence.

*Avinābhāva* is the [connection] of the probans (*sādhana*) with the probandum (*sādhya*); the analysis of the compound is: "the cognition of that mark (*liṅga*) which has that very [connection] with the probandum."

Now, if it is argued that it is called "for the sake of another" (parārtha) with reference to the activity of another, even so it is incorrect; for there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of even one's own purpose being "for the sake of another," since "otherness" (paratva) is relative, like the near and far shores (pārāvāra).
He refutes [the opponent's position] with the verse beginning "trirūpaliṅga" (1467):
"Surely, the state of being preceded by a three-featured logical mark is the defining characteristic of correspondence."
And since validity has tallakṣaṇa (the characteristic of non-discrepancy) as its definition, why is that being negated?

Regarding that, in the first formulation, he states the contradictory nature of the reason "because it is preceded by a three-featured mark" (*trirūpaliṅgapūrvatvāt*), considering that "tallakṣaṇa" indicates the state of being non-discrepant (*saṃvāditva*).

Since the cognition produced from a logical mark (liṅga) possessing the three characteristics is indirectly connected to the real object, it is non-deceptive, just like perception. As it has been said: "In this way, because the cognitions of the mark and the bearer of the mark are indirectly connected to the real object, they do not deceive, even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [object]."
Thus,
its characteristic is this: namely,
the characteristic of non-contradiction.
As it has been said: "Valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge.
For even in the case of perception, one who maintains its validity cannot point to any other basis for establishing its status as valid cognition except for non-contradiction;

and since that [non-contradiction] exists even in that which is produced by a three-featured logical mark (liṅga), why is its validity denied on the grounds of non-contradiction simply because it is preceded by a three-featured logical mark?
By this, the contradiction between the probandum and the probans is stated by implication;

for instance: where there is the state of being preceded by a three-featured mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), there is non-discrepancy (*avisaṃvāditva*); where there is non-discrepancy, there is validity (*prāmāṇya*). And since validity and invalidity are characterized by mutual exclusion, a contradictory reason (*viruddho hetuḥ*) has been indicated by the force of the argument.
With the words "false cognition" (*mithyājñāna*) and so forth, he states that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).
False cognition is common [to both sides] with respect to the opponent's position;
it is described as a cognition produced by that which destroys what is desired, not in an ultimate sense. (1469)

For, in accordance with the actual state of things, that cognition is determined to be non-contradictory; therefore, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) precisely because it contradicts what the proponent desires.
Consequently, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory, and there is also the lack of the property to be proven (*asādhyatā*) in the example.
In this very manner, the reason [adduced] in the second case is unestablished (asiddha).

For that [cognition] is indeed a valid means of knowledge because it establishes the opposite of what the proponent desires; otherwise, if invalidity were established for everything at all times in relation to some other object of proof, then even perception would fall into the same predicament.
It was called "false cognition" only with respect to the opponent's position, not according to the actual state of things.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *pūrvasya* means "of the first proponent," and *pakṣaḥ* means "the position"; thus, *pūrvapakṣaḥ* (the prima facie view) is the dependence upon that [position].

For, with respect to the intention of one who maintains that the eyes and other sense organs have as their sole purpose an object toward which no excellence can be added (*anādheyātiśaya*), it is called "false cognition" (*mithyājñāna*), because the eyes and other organs are established as being the causes of impermanent and manifold cognitions and so forth.

"Contradiction" (viruddhatā) [is a fallacy] because the state of being preceded by a three-featured logical mark (trirūpaliṅgapūrvatva) is never present in what is not a means of valid cognition (apramāṇa),
whereas in a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it is indeed present in the produced cognition that brings about the sublation of the intended object.
But surely, when formulating a proof that contradicts the Lokāyata, the example is not established at all;

for the opponent does not accept that cognition produced by [defective causes] which subverts what is desired is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and an example that is unestablished for either party cannot serve as such.

However, according to the principle that "only that which expresses what is certain for both parties constitutes proof or refutation," it is said: although validity (*prāmāṇya*) is not explicitly accepted here by the opponent through words, nevertheless, non-contradiction (*asaṃvāditva*) is indeed accepted because it cannot be denied; and since he accepts that, by the force of the circumstances, he must also accept validity as a matter of fact. Thus, a contradiction is pointed out by the very nature of the power of things (*vastubala*), and not merely in accordance with the opponent's own admission.
Alternatively, it is called "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it indicates a contradictory reason (*hetu*).

In this regard, the contradictory reason (*viruddha-hetu*) is as follows: "That which is non-discrepant is a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); and the cognition produced by a three-featured mark (*trirūpa-liṅga*) is non-discrepant. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*). It is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because that would entail the consequence of [the object] being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*) and lacking a cause. It is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because that would entail the consequence of direct perception itself being invalid. Nor is it [unproven] due to the probandum (*sādhya*) being unestablished.
"There is no probandum here" means it is "unprovable"; the state of being so is "unprovability," which is to say, "the absence of a probandum.
This refers to the second [type of fallacy].
Nor is there a lack of proof for the reason in such cases as "the three-fold nature" and so forth,
because [that reason] is absent nowhere at all in what is not an inference.
"By this very [method]" refers to the principle beginning with "the three-fold mark" (*trirūpaliṅga*), and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of the contradiction by inference" (anumānavirodhasya), he states the rebuttal: "that which has identity" (yattādātmya), and so forth.
Logicians declare that only that which is ascertained through a relationship of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*) is a valid means of proof for establishing [a conclusion].
In such a means of proof, there is no contradiction with inference or other such fallacies.
Indeed, that [contradiction] cannot occur anywhere without both internal presence and the cause;
two mutually contradictory properties are not compatible in a single entity. Therefore, there is no such thing as a "non-erroneous contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*).
"Of such a kind" refers to [the logical reason] being bound by identity (*tādātmya*) and origination from that (*tadutpatti*), [respectively] through the nature (*ātman*) and the cause (*hetu*).

Without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and without cause (*kāraṇa*), that mark (*liṅga*) would not exist respectively, because it would follow that there is a lack of intrinsic nature and a lack of causality.

As it has been said: "The property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), which is intended [to be proved], is not a qualifier of the locus (*dharmin*). In that case, if the property to be proven were not a qualifier of the locus, then the aggregate itself would not exist; consequently, the reason "because it is a part of that aggregate" would be unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, as for what was said—that in every inference there is the possibility of reasons contradictory to the particular (*viśeṣaviruddha*)—that is incorrect.

Since a reason is considered "contradictory" (*viruddha*) because it proves the opposite of what is to be proven (*sādhya*), and since a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is not intended to be proven in the domain of inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta-anumāna*), a "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*) is not possible;
for that would entail the presence of two mutually contradictory properties in a single substratum (*dharmin*).

Regarding what was stated in the passage beginning with "of states, places, and times," he says: "And for those whose characteristics have been mastered, when there is a correct determination of the logical mark (liṅga), it is the occurrence of inference; otherwise, it is not called inference. (1475)
Since the potencies of entities differ according to the variations of state, place, and time,
it is therefore not at all difficult to establish them through inference.
Even an object that has been inferred with great effort by skillful inferents—
It cannot be established otherwise by others, even by those more proficient.

A logical mark (*liṅga*) that is well-ascertained is accepted as a means of cognition, not one that is doubtful; for smoke, when doubted as being steam or the like, does not lead to the certain cognition of fire.
If it is asked, "How is the ascertainment of the logical mark itself achieved? [the answer follows].
Just as for those who know [the distinction] regarding gems, forms, and so forth, through practice;
for indeed, those who have practiced the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those [objects] distinguish smoke and the like from vapor and the like.
Moreover, even those who act without having properly discriminated [the mark] certainly encounter fire;

therefore, since a well-discriminated logical mark (*liṅga*) does not deviate [from its object], the establishment of things distinguished by differences such as their states is not difficult to achieve,
nor can an object definitively ascertained from a well-discriminated mark be made otherwise.

Indeed, once fire has been inferred from smoke that is well-ascertained, its being otherwise cannot be established, because it is impossible for a single entity to possess two contradictory natures. As for what was said—that Devadatta is incapable of carrying a burden—and so forth, as well as the claim that a mass of clouds is burned by fire—these do not constitute a valid logical mark (*liṅga*) at all, because they lack the three required characteristics (*trairūpya*). For the exclusion of a reason from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) cannot be established by mere non-perception.
As it has been said: "The absence [of the reason] from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) does not follow merely from its non-observation;
rather, the necessity of inseparable connection (avinābhāva-niyama) arises from the restrictive relationship of identity (tādātmya) or causality (tadutpatti)."

As it has been said: "The rule of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) is established either by the relation of cause and effect or by an essential nature (svabhāva) as a regulator; it is not [established] by non-observation, nor by observation.
And in this case, there exists neither the relation of identity (tādātmya) nor the relation of origination (tadutpatti).

It might be argued: "How is it that a well-ascertained logical mark (*liṅga*) does not deviate? For there is no reasoning (*yukti*) for this. To this he says: "For [it is] not the nature (*svabhāva*)," and so forth.

For neither a nature nor an effect exists apart from its own nature or its cause, because [otherwise] they would fall into the state of being without a basis for their distinction; and without those two, there is no inference. (1478)

For there are only two kinds of logical marks (*liṅga*), namely: essential nature (*svabhāva*) and effect (*kārya*). Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), moreover, is included within essential nature. Furthermore, these two types of logical marks cannot possibly exist without a subject possessing those marks (*liṅgin*)—namely, one called "essential nature" or "cause"—by which there might be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Why is there no convergence? He says: because of the attainment of both difference and causelessness—the attainment of these two, namely difference (*bheda*) and causelessness (*animittatā*).

For [in the case of] an essential reason (*svabhāva-hetu*), difference results in the absence of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāvatā*); for an effect-reason (*kārya-hetu*), causelessness results in being without a cause (*nirhetukatva*). Furthermore, no other logical mark (*liṅga*) is accepted apart from essential nature and effect, because otherwise, due to the lack of a necessary connection (*apratibandha*), an inseparable relation (*avinābhāva*) would be impossible; thus, those two [essential nature and effect] are indispensable.
This [term] ending in the dual number refers to both intrinsic nature and effect.
Regarding what was stated—that inference for others (parārthānumāna) is a means of valid cognition—he says: "Because the statement of the three-featured mark... and so forth.

That which was described as being inference for others is so called from the perspective of the listener, because it serves to indicate [the object] clearly through the statement of the three-featured mark. (1479)

Thus, the nature of inference is accepted here as being both secondary (gauṇa) and conventional (sāṅketika), by virtue of its indicating that which is already connected [to the probans]; therefore, there is no over-extension [of the definition].
If inference were not a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), then your own contradiction would be rendered fruitless.
Indeed, no discourse whatsoever conveys the speaker’s intention [directly].

As for what was stated regarding the fact that speech is an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), that is in relation to the listener; therefore, the defect arising from the absence [of inference] in relation to the speaker does not apply.

Furthermore, even in relation to the listener, it is called an "inference" either because it indicates a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*)—and thus is a cause of inference in a figurative sense—or by virtue of linguistic convention (*samaya*).
Since the designation "inference" (anumāna) is applied specifically to that which indicates a connection (*saktasaṃsūcaka*),

there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)— such as the undesirable consequence that the sense organ or the cognition of the relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva-sambandha-jñāna*) would also be considered inference for others (*parārthānumāna*)— because those two lack the quality of indicating a connection.
For this very reason, this [inference] is distinguished from the primary consciousness (*saṃvid*) which is rooted in perception (*darśanamūla*).

For instance: the direct cognition of a mark (*liṅga*) such as smoke occurs through visual perception, not through auditory cognition; for by the latter, only the word itself is directly grasped. And the word is not a mark of the external object in the same way that smoke is, because no necessary connection is established between the word—being dependent upon the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*)—and the external object. It is described as "for the sake of others" (*parārtha*) only insofar as it indicates that mark such as smoke, since, by virtue of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises that determines [the object] in that way with respect to the external thing. However, when the intention is what is to be understood, it is "for one's own sake" (*svārtha*) from the perspective of the hearer.
For instance: because it is an effect of that [intention], the word is held to be an indicator of the speaker's intention— just as smoke [indicates fire]— but not by virtue of being a denoter,
since knowledge [of the object] is not apprehended from it.
The statement "verbal expression is fruitless" means that inference is not a valid means of knowledge;
for indeed, there is no one to be instructed who, upon hearing those words, would understand the speaker's intention.
By this, he states the contradiction with his own words;
and this has already been explained previously.

Puraṃdara said: "Inference that is well-known in the world is indeed accepted even by the Cārvākas; however, that which is called inference by some while overstepping the worldly path is what is being rejected."
Anticipating this objection and refuting it, he says: "If the worldly [sign] is accepted... and so forth.

If it is argued that the worldly sign is intended, and not that which is postulated by others, [we reply]: Surely even the world understands the cause and so forth from the effect and so forth. (1482)
In reality, however, that very same thing has been sufficiently stated by the proponents of logic as well:
"What is it that you yourself have abandoned when [the object] is already admitted by the world? (1483).
[Objection: "But surely the world [also admits it]..."
The connection is that "one understands the cause and so forth";
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of the effect and so forth," the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is included.
Likewise, in the phrase "the cause and so forth" (*hetvādi*), it is also the essential nature that is included.
The plural number, however, is used because of the diversity of individual instances.

That very sign (*liṅga*) which, being constrained by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), leads one to understand the object of worldly experience—that alone has been described as the "sign" by us. If that is admitted, what would be abandoned such that there could be a denial of its status as inference?

Now, it might be argued: "We do not accept any inference at all; rather, our opponent accepts it as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, because he accepts it, my statement does not become futile. To this, he replies with the verse beginning "By that which is not a valid means of knowledge" (*apramāṇena*): "And what does the opponent understand by means of this which is not a valid means of knowledge?"
And what kind of cognition could this be that is produced by something non-authoritative?

Furthermore, from where has this certainty arisen—that the other person has accepted that as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? For another's acceptance is not perceptible (*pratyakṣa*), nor do you possess any other means of valid cognition by which such a certainty might occur.
Even granting that such a certainty exists, what does it matter that the other person is convinced by that non-authoritative [cognition] accepted by the other? This is certainly no calamity.

Now, one might think: "Just as a sword is snatched from an enemy's hand and that very same enemy is struck down by it, so too, having accepted that very thing which the opponent has admitted to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the opponent is refuted. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Established by what is not a valid means of knowledge" (*apramāṇakṛta*). This is what is meant: if, out of delusion, the opponent has accepted something that is actually not a valid means of knowledge as being a valid means of knowledge, how can the production of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) for the other person be effected by that which is not a valid means of knowledge? For a valid means of knowledge has correct knowledge as its fruit.
For it is not the case that by taking up just any cutting instrument, thinking "it is a sword," one is able to cut another; thus, the analogy is not equivalent.
(1484) Aviddhakarṇa says in the *Tattvaṭīkā*: "Now, why should the opponent be convinced by means of a proof? For only that which is established for both parties can serve as a means of conviction."

This is incorrect because inference consists of speech and is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the speaker; nevertheless, the speaker establishes [the matter] for another by means of it, since the effort is for the sake of communicating to another,
and there is no necessity for it to be established for both parties.
He raises this doubt with the words "If inference," etc.:

"If inference were a means of valid cognition, it would not reveal [its object] through the speaker's verbal expression; therefore, just as that [inference] is, so too would this [verbal testimony] be. (1485)

Because it does not illuminate an unknown object, that [cognition] is held to be non-valid; it is not [non-valid] because of the speaker’s incapacity, nor is your [position] so, by way of indicating [the speaker]. Thus ends the examination of inference (anumānaparīkṣā).
"This" is the speaker;
"by that" [is the referent].

He states the refutation by means of the words beginning with "ajñāta" (unknown), which consist of speech: for it is not intended that speech lacks authority because it indicates [its object] in dependence upon a speaker; rather, [it lacks authority] because it does not reveal an unknown object.
This [scripture] indeed possesses the quality of indicating the speaker who composed it; however, your inference does not indicate the speaker who composed it— thus these two cases are not equal,
for otherwise [your inference] would be established for both parties alike.
Therefore, it is logical that a means of valid cognition not deviating from that principle is appropriate for everyone, just like direct perception; this is the correct conclusion.
Thus concludes the examination of inference,
the examination of other means of valid cognition, and the investigation of verbal testimony.
Now, in order to establish the restriction to two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and to address the disagreement regarding their number, he says: "But surely," and so forth.

But surely, because other means of valid cognition such as verbal testimony (*śabda*) and others are possible, for what reason has the definition been stated for only two means of valid cognition? (1487)

By this [verse], he states the fault that the definition of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is too narrow, as well as the futility of the restriction to "two" in the phrase "ascertained by the two types of valid cognition" (1487).
He then refutes [this objection] with the words beginning "It is said" (*ucyate*).

It is said: no means of valid cognition other than the two [perception and inference] is tenable, because it lacks the defining characteristics of a means of valid cognition; and even if such characteristics were present, it would be included herein [within those two], as indicated by the phrase "because of being included therein" (antargamāt). 1488.
Regarding the phrase "because of being included therein":

Regarding these very two means of valid cognition, this is what is meant: there is no characteristic of a valid cognition other than these two that consists in non-contradiction; and since it is included within these very two, no separate means of valid cognition is mentioned.
In this regard, he demonstrates these two points: how other [means of knowledge] lack validity, or if they do possess validity, how they are included herein.

Regarding this, other [schools] have accepted other means of knowledge (pramāṇa) called verbal testimony (śabda), analogy (upamāna), presumption (arthāpatti), non-existence (abhāva), reasoning (yukti), non-perception (anupalabdhi), possibility (sambhava), tradition (aitihya), intuition (pratibhā), fame (khyāti), and renown (prakhyāti).
Among these, concerning verbal testimony, he says: "From the cognition of words," and so forth.
Others have declared that verbal cognition (*śābda*) is the knowledge of an imperceptible object (*parokṣārtha*) arising from the knowledge of a word;
and that [knowledge] arises from a sentence that is either authorless (*akartṛka*) or spoken by a trustworthy person (*pratyayin*).
And this, they say, is certainly not perception (*adhyakṣa*), because its object is imperceptible.
Nor is inference possible, because it lacks the defining characteristics [of a valid reason].
For it is well-established that the subject (dharmin) qualified by a property (dharma) is the possessor of the mark (liṅgin);
and as long as there is no such object [for the reason], there can be no inference.

In this regard, Śabarasvāmin states the definition of verbal cognition (*śābda*): "Verbal [cognition] is the knowledge of an object not in contact [with the senses] arising from the knowledge of a word.

That cognition which arises at a time subsequent to the apprehension of the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) of a word, concerning an object that is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), is considered to have come from the word; thus, it is the means of valid verbal cognition (*śābdapramāṇa*).
And that is of two kinds.
This [cognition] produced by words that are not of human origin and that produced by the speech of a trustworthy person is distinct from perception because its object is beyond the senses;
nor is it inference, because it lacks the three characteristics [of the logical mark].

For instance—the subject (dharmin) qualified by the property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is accepted as the object of inference (anumeya), neither the subject alone nor the property alone; and as long as the mark (liṅga) is not determined as having that subject as its locus—that is, as long as there is no determination of its being a property of the subject (pakṣadharmatva)—the operation of inference is not possible, meaning that until such determination occurs, there is no inference.
He asks: why is that very determination of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) not [considered sufficient]? He says: "And whoever... (*yaśca*).

And that very thing which is postulated here as the subject (*dharmin*) is its object of cognition (*prameya*); for as long as that [subject] is not determined, there can be no determination of its being a property (*dharmatva*).

Furthermore, that which is postulated here in verbal cognition (*śābda*) as the subject, such as a tree and so forth, is itself the object of cognition, because it is precisely that which is to be established.

In this context, it is only the property (*dharma*) that is the object of cognition, not the property-possessor (*dharmī*) as qualified by that property; for as long as that property-possessor is not determined—that is, not ascertained—how can its being a property of that [subject] be ascertained? (1492)

If that [subject] were already apprehended prior to the property-of-the-subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), what would be the point of subsequently knowing the property-of-the-subject and so forth, such that there could be the status of inference? Furthermore—if this subject (*dharmin*) were known prior to the ascertainment of its being a property of the subject, then the effort to ascertain the property-of-the-subject and so on would be fruitless; for every exertion is for the sake of understanding the subject. If that has already been understood, what now is the use of the labor of defining the property-of-the-subject and the rest?
And this has been stated even while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]:
the word is not a property (*dharma*) of the subject (*dharmin*), such as a tree, because it is perceived in the location of the speaker. (1493)

Thus, first, the absence of the property of being a predicate of the subject (pakṣadharmatva) has been demonstrated; now, demonstrating the absence of positive concomitance (anvaya), he says: "And there is no positive concomitance," and so forth.
"And there is no positive concomitance of the word with the object of cognition (prameya); for the capacity to be concomitant is perceived in all things by means of their functional activity. (1494)
It is "ascertained" (nirūpyate) in the sense that it is determined by means of an operation.
"By way of real existence," that is, by way of being;
what is meant is this: only that which exists can be a concomitant, not that which does not exist.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Where," and so forth.
Where there is smoke, there is clearly a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with the existence of fire; however, it is not certain in the same way that where there is a word, there is an object. (1495)
"Where there is smoke, fire is necessarily present"; therefore, this fire is a concomitant of smoke. But the word does not have such a concomitance with its object.
Demonstrating how it is not so, he says: "Not at all," and so forth.

It cannot be said that it [the word] does not exist in that place or at that time; for if it were argued that this is due to its being eternal and all-pervading, then that would apply equally to all words.
Consequently, because it is perceived everywhere and because its absence is never apprehended, [it must be present everywhere].
It would follow that all words convey every possible object.
For there is no existence of an object in a place occupied by a word;
to illustrate: the word "piṇḍakhajūra" (a type of date) is heard in places such as Pāṭaliputra, yet the piṇḍakhajūra does not exist in that location.

Likewise, at the time of the word, the object does not necessarily exist; for while words such as "Dilīpa" or "Mahāsammeta" are present, their objects are past or future. How, then, can there be a concomitance of the word with the object? Now, it might be argued: because words are eternal, they persist at all times; thus, there is no difference in time between the word and its object. Nor is there a difference in location, because, being all-pervasive, they abide in all places. Therefore, due to their eternity and omnipresence, there is a concomitance of words [with their objects].
In that case, since that eternal omnipresence is equal in all words, it would follow that the denotation of a specific object by a specific word is not possible;
rather,
every single object would be denotable by any word whatsoever, because every word is observed everywhere— in all places and at all times— together with every object.
The negative concomitance (vyatireka)— the absence of the probans where there is an absence of the probandum—
is not apprehended, because it is not perceived.
Precisely because of its eternal omnipresence.
"Therefore, verbal cognition, like perception, would not be inference, because it lacks the three characteristics [of a logical reason] and because it excludes such an object [as that of inference].
Having concluded with "therefore," he demonstrates the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
"Verbal cognition is not inference" is the statement of the thesis (*sādhya*); "because it lacks the three characteristics [of a valid reason]" is the logical reason (*hetu*);
"like perception" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"Because of the avoidance of such an object" is the justification for the reason;

that is to say, because it is devoid of—that is, lacking—an object such as the subject (dharmin) qualified by a property (dharma), which is the object of an inference arising from a mark (liṅga) such as smoke.

Granted that it may be distinct from inference because it lacks the three characteristics [of a valid reason], how then is this verbal testimony authoritative? To this he says: "From the statement 'Agnihotra'... and so forth.
Because the production of unshakable knowledge arises from the statement regarding the Agnihotra and other such rites, its status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be denied. (1499)
Because it is free from doubt and error, it is unshakable and immovable;
because there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like perception and the other [means of knowledge].
Thus, Śabarasvāmin said: "And from the statement 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice,' it is not understood with uncertainty as to whether heaven exists or does not exist."

Furthermore, this [cognition] which is understood with certainty cannot be false. For that is a false cognition which, having arisen, is subsequently sublated by the thought "this is not so. But this [Vedic cognition] does not vary across different places, times, or persons; therefore, it is non-erroneous.
As for worldly speech, if it comes from a trustworthy person or concerns an object within the range of the senses, it is indeed non-erroneous.

However, if it comes from an untrustworthy person or concerns a supersensuous object, it is invalid as it originates from human intellect, for it is impossible for a mere human being to know such things.
By the words beginning with "therein" (tatra), he states the defect of the definition— namely its impossibility— in regard to this first verbal definition,
"from a sentence that has no author," for the possibility and the meaning [of such a sentence] are inconsistent.
Therefore, the first definition of verbal testimony has been declared impossible;
for there is no possibility whatsoever of a sentence being without an author, since the all-pervasive doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has already been established,
or [will be established] by the reasoning to be stated hereafter.

Even if its existence were possible, its meaningfulness could not be established; therefore, because it is impossible for this imperceptible object to be known from an authorless statement, the definition of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is untenable.
To the question, "How is it that there is no authorless sentence? he says: "Because [the speaker] is capable," and so forth.
Because the nature of being either capable or incapable would persist at all times, the cognition resulting from that [nature] would either always occur or never occur at any time.

In this regard, there are two alternatives: the sentence would either be inherently incapable of producing knowledge, or it would be capable of producing knowledge at some time and incapable at others.
In the first case, because it follows that potent nature, the cognition resulting from it would necessarily occur at all times.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) for this is as follows: whatever has unimpeded capacity regarding a particular effect must necessarily produce it, just as the final causal complex (*sāmagrī*) does; and since the non-human sentence has unimpeded capacity for generating cognition at all times, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Alternatively: whatever has its causes complete must necessarily come into being, just as a sprout with complete causes does; and since the cognition resulting from the non-human sentence has its causes complete, this is a reason based on essential nature.

Even in the second case, because that incapable nature would persist at all times, consciousness would never arise when that [nature] is present, just as a sprout does not arise when its causes are deficient.
To the question, "How is it that [the cognition] being possessed of an object is not consistent? he says: "Because of hatred," and so forth.
Just as defects such as hatred and delusion are known to be causes of falsity,
so too are qualities such as compassion and wisdom known to be causes of truth;
yet, in the absence of a person who is their substratum, neither of these two can possibly exist.
Therefore, it follows that there would be pointlessness in a word that does not depend on a person.
For meaningfulness occurs in two ways: either by having a non-erroneous meaning or by having an erroneous meaning, since there is no third category.
And it is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that the causes of these two forms of meaningfulness are, respectively, excellence (*guṇa*) and defect (*doṣa*).

For instance: just as a person overwhelmed by defects such as passion is seen to be a speaker of falsehood, so too one endowed with qualities such as compassion is seen to be a speaker of truth. And the person is the substratum for those two—the quality and the defect—which are the causes of truthfulness and falsity. Consequently, upon the cessation of the person, there is the cessation of the quality and the defect; and upon the cessation of the quality and the defect, there is also the absence of truthfulness and falsity. In the absence of these, since no other alternative is possible, it follows that a non-human (apauruṣeya) word would be purposeless due to the absence of its cause.
For it is not logical for an effect to arise without a cause, as that would entail the consequence of its being causeless;
consequently, there would be no restriction regarding place, time, substance, and so forth.
This should be understood as a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum).
Otherwise, if one were to establish [the Veda] independently, there would be a contradiction with what is perceived;

for instance, the comprehension of meaning from such sentences as "One desiring heaven should perform the Agnihotra sacrifice" is indeed observed, and what is perceived cannot be denied. Furthermore, since the lack of an author is not established for both parties, the logical reason (hetu) would be unproven (asiddha).
In a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅgasādhana), however, both [reasons] are faultless;
for instance, if the Veda is accepted as being of non-human origin, then its lack of purpose must be accepted,
because of the absence of a person who could provide it with meaning.
Nor is it purposeless; therefore, by way of an incidental argument, it is demonstrated that [the Veda] must indeed be of human origin.

In order to support this very *prasaṅgasādhana*, [the author], demonstrating the absence of contradiction with observed reality, speaks while raising an objection, beginning with the words "artha... and so forth:
"If it is argued that [the meaning] does not follow from the cognition of the object, [we reply] that this [meaning] would arise from the commentary (*vyākhyāna*);
for a person is seen to be independent when explaining a meaning according to his own will. (1504)
If its capacity to illuminate the real nature of things were inherent by its very nature,
then even one who has not learned the linguistic convention would have comprehension of the meaning from it.
A lamp, which is inherently an illuminator, does not depend upon a convention.
And because there is a difference in time [between the convention and the perception], there is a transition to a different object.
For even when a convention exists, a lamp does not illuminate smell, taste, and so forth; nor is it possible for that [lamp] to possess such a capacity.
The connection is with the phrase "if not, it would be purposeless"; the underlying sense is that, consequently, there would be a contradiction with perceived reality regarding the thesis.

It would indeed be a contradiction of observed fact if the comprehension of meaning from the Veda itself were to arise independently of instruction; for this comprehension of meaning arises equally from the side of the commentator, and not from the Veda alone, independent of convention.
To illustrate: a Mīmāṃsaka or others are seen explaining the meaning of the Veda according to their own will, and it is not logical that an inherent meaning should conform to human desire.
In this regard, it might be argued: "A person does not describe an unprecedented object according to their own whim;
rather, that which is inherently established is what is revealed by the person. Therefore, there is indeed a contradiction with observed reality.

If this is so, then if the Veda possesses an inherent capacity to illuminate an existing state of affairs, it would follow that even one who is ignorant of linguistic convention would derive an understanding of the meaning from that Vedic sentence.
If it is argued that the Veda is a cause for the comprehension of meaning only when dependent upon convention (*saṅketa*) and not by itself, that is not so;
for lamps and the like, which are by nature causes for the comprehension of objects, do not depend upon convention.

Otherwise, the convention alone would possess the capacity for the cognition of meaning through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and not an inherent relationship (*svābhāvika-sambandha*). Furthermore, even if one grants that the cognition of meaning arises with the assistance of convention, there remains a fault; thus he says "from the convention" (*samaya*) and so forth: if there exists another convention (*samayāntara*)—that is, a convention composed by the authors of etymological treatises (*niruktakāra*) and others, distinct from the convention established by the Mīmāṃsakas—then it would follow that from that word, a cognition of a different meaning than the intended one would occur.
For a lamp is not capable of illuminating things that are not its objects of illumination, such as odor or taste, merely by virtue of convention.

Granting that a word may indeed function toward another object through the force of convention, he demonstrates nevertheless that its validity is not established: "In order to cognize"—if a word functions even toward another object by the force of human desire, then, due to this confusion (*saṅkara*), that power to illuminate the actual state of affairs cannot be determined; how, then, could there be comprehension of the intended object from it?
Alternatively, it is explained in another way:
that power of the word-nature (*prakṛti*) which illuminates the actual meaning may, at times, be restricted to a single meaning or restricted to multiple meanings; these are the two positions.
Regarding that, he states the fault in the position of restriction to a single meaning: "the existence of [the need for] another convention" (*samayāntarabhāva*).
Regarding the second [point] as well, he says: "That capacity cannot be known," because of the confusion (sāṅkarya); such is the sense.
As it has been stated: "If words were restricted to a single meaning, there would be no comprehension of another meaning."
"When there is a connection with multiple meanings, there is the possibility of the manifestation of contradictory [meanings]. (1504)

Having thus demonstrated that the first definition of verbal testimony is untenable, [the author] states "Therefore," etc., showing by way of conclusion that the reason—"because it produces unshakable knowledge"—is unestablished (*asiddha*):
"Therefore, since the cognition of an object is impossible [in that way], how could it possess unshakability?
That [cognition], however, is rightly understood as being conventional (*sāmayika*); it does not differ from the speech of a person. (1508)
Those who know logic do not perceive any distinction between these two;
however, for those Vedic scholars who are ignorant of the path of logic, this [conviction] is unshakable.
When, according to the reasoning already stated, the very cognition of meaning is impossible if there is no authorship by a person, then how can that [cognition] be unshakable?

Furthermore, it has been previously established by the passage beginning with "this [meaning] would arise from the explanation," that this cognition of meaning which is perceived from a Vedic sentence is necessarily conventional (*sāṅketika*).
For this reason as well, it is logical that this is indeed conventional,
because a Vedic sentence does not differ from human speech— that is, it does not transcend the nature of human speech.
The point is that this does not differ from human speech;
as to why this is so, he says: "by those who know the logic," and so forth, regarding "those two."
He mocks the Vedic scholars, saying that since both Vedic and human compositions can be produced by persons in every respect, there is no distinction whatsoever between the Vedic and the worldly.

In the second [definition] as well, regarding the definition of verbal testimony (*śābda*) stated as "that which is uttered by a trustworthy person" (*pratyayitodita*), he states the fault of the definition, namely its impossibility (*asambhavita*), with the words beginning "āpta... and so forth.

Because an authoritative person (āpta) is not accepted [by them], even the second definition of verbal testimony is not tenable; or, if one were to accept it, he would remain undetermined as being "this very person. (1510) Since the Mīmāṃsakas do not admit the existence of persons whose defects have been eliminated, an authoritative person is simply not accepted; thus, how could there be validity for his word?
"It is not fit" means it is not logical,
that is to say, it is impossible.

Furthermore, if an authoritative person (āpta) is accepted, then even when such an authority is sought, he cannot be definitively identified as "this is that very person" through a finger-pointing method (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*). Thus, he is effectively non-existent [for the purpose of establishing certainty].
For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for ascertaining the specific virtues or defects of others, because those qualities are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).

Moreover, since physical and verbal behaviors can be performed intentionally even with ulterior motives, how can the authority of their words be established? This is because those who perceive only what is near (*arvāgdarśin*) cannot determine them without confusion.
Generally, it is observed that conviction regarding something is derived from its statement;
if that [conviction] arises from trust, then the statement serves the purpose of bringing about the understanding of what is beyond the senses. 1511.
It is not otherwise, for even one who was previously unreliable may become reliable due to the absence of [defects];

indeed, there is no rule that because he is unerring in one instance, he must be so in all instances. (1512) Alternatively, it might be argued: "We accept as 'trustworthy' (pratyayita) that person whose words are seen to produce conviction in the majority of cases, even though his defects have not been eliminated—not one whose defects are entirely destroyed. Therefore, the word of such a trustworthy person is accepted; thus, in the definition of verbal testimony (*śābda*), the charge of impossibility does not apply."
This too is incorrect;

for it is not logical that the necessity of things being so everywhere follows from the mere observation of non-contradiction in one instance, because deviation is still possible; otherwise, there would be no definition of what constitutes a deviant [reason].

Having thus specifically demonstrated that the two-fold definition of verbal testimony is flawed, he states the general refutation: "What connection could there be between words and even external objects? and so forth.
One must establish those [conditions] by which these [cognitions] would possess the status of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Because they are apprehended by different sense organs and so forth, they do not have a single nature, nor do they arise from that [single cause];
and because of deviation, it is not logical for anything else to possess non-deviation.

Indeed, there exists no connection between words and the objects denoted by them—neither characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) nor characterized by origination from that (*tadutpatti*)—by virtue of which these words, in expressing those objects, would possess validity. In this regard, first of all, there is no connection characterized by identity, due to reasons such as being apprehended by different sense organs; therein, "apprehension by different sense organs" means apprehension by distinct sensory faculties.
For instance: sound is apprehended by the auditory faculty (*śrotra*), while the object is apprehended by the visual faculty and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the distinction between the causes of temporal, spatial, and phenomenal appearance is included.

However, Kumārila says: "The argument that [an object] is distinct because it is apprehended by different sense faculties is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for instance, when many people see a single form, the form would consequently have to be distinct because it is apprehended by different sense faculties."
Furthermore, it might be argued that because there is no difference in the genus (*jāti*) of the visual faculty, it must indeed be graspable by a single sense-faculty.

If that were so, then even though existence (*sattā*) is graspable by multiple sense-faculties, it would possess the property of being graspable by a non-differentiated sense-faculty due to the non-difference in the genus of the faculties; thus, its oneness would be established.
Therefore, the determination of the difference or non-difference of objects is based on the difference or non-difference of cognitions, not on the difference or non-difference of the sense-faculties.
And it is said: "That which is perceivable by multiple sense faculties does not attain distinctness;
otherwise, because it is perceivable by [faculties] residing in different bodies, there would be a distinction in form.
If you argue that there is no distinction due to the non-difference of the genus (*jāti*), then that is the same in the case of the sense faculties themselves."
"Therefore, because the cognition is identical, the sentient being is not different despite the difference in the sense faculties"—
this is incorrect, because the same logic applies even when proving a difference based on a difference in cognition.
For even here it can be argued as follows: the claim that "a difference in objects follows from a difference in cognitions" is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
To explain: when many people perceive a single form, there is indeed a difference in cognition because multiple visual consciousnesses arise;
yet, at that time, there is no difference in the form itself.
If unity is postulated for the visual consciousness because there is no difference in its genus (*jāti*), then it follows that form, taste, and so forth would also be one,
since their consciousness-genus is non-different even though there is a difference in their respective cognitions.
Consequently, the statement that "unity of form and the rest does not follow because their cognitions are different" would be contradicted.
Therefore, this is a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*).

Alternatively, even though there is a difference in specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), whatever kind of distinction in characteristics exists, the conventional usage of "difference" and "non-difference" well-known in the world is based on whether they serve as causes for a single or multiple conceptual reflections (*pratyavamarśa*); such distinctions and non-distinctions of cognition are thus adopted. This is all the same regarding the sense organ as well; so, enough with this digression.
Nor is there a relationship characterized by origination from that, because of deviation;
for [the cognition] occurs even in the absence of the object, arising merely from the speaker's intention.
Furthermore, there can be no non-deviation for anything else that lacks the relation of being produced from that [object], because that would lead to over-extension;
therefore, a word has no validity as a means of knowledge with respect to its denoted object.

1514. If this is so, why was it said: "Verbal cognition is not a separate means of valid knowledge from inference; for it expresses its own object through the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), just like [the mark] 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth"?
Anticipating this objection, he says "from words" and so forth, demonstrating how [the cognition of another's mind] is intended to be included within inference:
"From all words whatsoever, this intention to speak is inferred;
for its cause is ascertained through perception and non-perception. (1515)
The phrase "to all [authoritative persons]" refers even to those whose status as human authors is admitted;
and that intention is understood from their speech because it is the effect of that [intention].
It is not, however, by virtue of being denotable;
for, through positive and negative concomitance within one's own mental continuum, it is ascertained that the cause of words is the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*).
As for what was said—that "one speaks by means of the exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*)—therein, "speaking" (*bhāṣaṇa*) means manifesting or making known.

And its commentary is as follows: "It indicates [the object] through an exclusion connected with another meaning, just like 'being produced' (kṛtakatva) and so forth. This must necessarily be understood; otherwise, the example "just like being produced" would be devoid of the probans (*sādhanavikala*), for the verbal expression of "being produced" and the like is not possible, since that is a property of sound (*śabdadharmatva*).
Furthermore, because it speaks by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), the reason would be "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).
Now, even in the case of intention (*vivakṣā*), it is not appropriate for a word to possess validity (*prāmāṇya*).
For instance: validity does not reside in a specific intention to speak, because of deviation, since we observe a person under delusion uttering one sentence when intending something else;
nor does it reside in the general intention to speak, because that would be futile.
For the mere cognition of the speaker’s intention does not anywhere serve as a factor for practical activity (*vyavahāra*), because from that one cannot ascertain a specific object.
Anticipating this objection, [the author] states "of the deluded," etc., and thereby asserts the validity [of the word] with respect to the specific intention: "deluded and non-deluded," etc.
If it is observed that when one who is deluded intends to speak of one thing, the resulting sentence appears to be about something else,
then [the listener] would likewise not act upon this [speaker's] intention because of that commonality [of discrepancy].
Thus, the distinction between sentences uttered by the deluded and those uttered by the non-deluded is perfectly clear.
The wise discern the excellence of speech from its context and other such factors.

(1517) For one must necessarily admit a distinction between those [utterances] produced by the deluded and those produced by the non-deluded; otherwise, the difference in cause would not be a differentiator.
And that distinction, skilled persons certainly discern from the context and so forth.
The subject at hand—the context—is understood by the word "etc. (*ādi*) as including composure, a serene countenance, and so forth.

He asks, "How is it that there is indeed a distinction (*vailakṣaṇya*) in words? and answers: "By the distinction of the causes"—that is, the specific difference among them [the words] due to the distinction of their causes, and not otherwise.
They understand that this is a defect [of the person], but it does not belong to the mark (liṅga) itself.

Even in the case of smoke, whose nature is sometimes doubted, its status as a mark for fire would not exist even at the time of ascertainment, because it has been observed otherwise on other occasions. (1518–1519)
The meaning is "due to the difference in causes.
Therefore, an effect that has been properly discerned does not deviate from its cause; thus, there is indeed validity regarding the specific intention [of the speaker].
However, this fault belongs to those who do not perceive the distinction in those words which serve as the inferential marks (*liṅga*), and not to the inferential mark itself.
A logical mark (liṅga) is not accepted as a means of cognition by its mere existence; rather, it must be certain.
Therefore, this is a fault on the part of the cognizer.

For otherwise, since smoke—when being doubted as being vapor or the like—is not something other [than smoke], it would lack the capacity to produce cognition; consequently, even when it is certain, it would fail to function as a logical mark for the probandum, fire.

Furthermore, when this entire verbal convention is accepted as being purely erroneous—like the vision of two moons by two people suffering from ophthalmia, occurring solely in accordance with one's own internal appearances—then how could there be the consequence of invalidity based on pointing out a deviation regarding a particular intention (*vivakṣāviśeṣa*)? For in that case, ultimate validity is not admitted with respect to that particular intention.
Thus it has been said: "Its status as inference is indicated with reference to conventional designation, having placed it within the mind, and not with reference to ultimate reality."
Thus [ends] 1518,
Establishing validity even when the object of proof is the mere intention to speak (*vivakṣā-sāmānya*), he says: "Of those," and so forth:
"Even for them, there is no contradiction with the mere intention to speak, because inference exists as an absolute certainty for the sake of establishing [the presence of] life and so on. (1520)

For all of these, whether employed by those who are mistaken or non-mistaken, there is no contradiction in their being forms of inference based on the commonality of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), because of its absolute existence— that is, its non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). Furthermore,
it is not the case that teachings issue forth at will from walls and such, even from the presence of that person, like [jewels] from a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
One should not suspect a deviation [of the reason] on account of this admission;
for even there, the primary instrument is indeed the intention to speak, since the activity of speech occurs therein solely by the force of the latent impressions deposited by previous resolve.

For instance: even when one who has thoroughly mastered a text is engaged in activities such as speaking or walking at the time of beginning a lesson or the like, he still conceives of something else;

for the prior intention (*pūrvasamīhā*) is indeed their cause. Otherwise, one might have to point out the fallibility (*vyabhicāritva*) of smoke and other such marks simply because smoke is perceived in a cowherd’s water-clock (*gopālaghaṭikā*) and the like.
Therefore, in every case, there is no possibility of fallibility when the effect is taken as a mark in consideration of place, time, and so forth; thus, its existence is absolute.
Nor is there futility, because the activity undertaken for the sake of establishing breathing and so forth can be fruitful;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), causes such as defects in the instruments of knowledge are included.

Granted that the word possesses validity with respect to the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), even so, what here is the subject (*dharmin*), what is the probandum (*sādhya*), and how is the relationship established, such that—by virtue of the presence of the three characteristics (*trairūpya*)—it would be included within inference and not constitute a separate means of valid cognition? To this he says:
"In the case of the intention to speak"—for when the intention to speak is the object to be known, the possession of the three characteristics is indeed quite clear.
That [intention] is to be proven as residing in the person, who is the substratum possessing the property, because it is established by the effect, namely the speech:
"This person possesses the desire to express the meaning of the word 'tree', because he is the user of the word 'vṛkṣa', just as I was in previous states. (1521–1522)

Where a speaker is perceived, the person is the locus (*dharmin*) and the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) is the property to be proven (*sādhya*); and in that case, the relationship [between the intention and the sound] is already established within one's own continuum.
However, where no speaker is perceived, the locus is the location (*pradeśa*) qualified by a person, which is the property to be proven.
For instance, even a location certainly possesses the quality of being a cause of sound.
Because one hears different kinds of sounds in places such as mountain caves.
Therefore, where the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) and so forth of words is rejected by others as being external, we do not at all accept their validity there;
however, where this [validity] is accepted by them, it is clearly present there in its three-fold form.
But when the intention to speak is the probandum, the three characteristics [of the reason] are revealed.
This being the case, verbal cognition would possess the nature of inference— just like smoke and so forth—
because it is accompanied by the three features and because its object exists in such a manner.
Thus concludes the investigation of verbal testimony.

With the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*) and so forth, [the author] states that if the probandum is the status of verbal testimony as inference in relation to external objects, then the reason "by being devoid of the three characteristics" (*trairūpyarahitatvena*) is futile;
however, with the words "where... (*yatra*) and so forth, he states its lack of establishment (*asiddhatā*) in view of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*).
Because the three-fold nature of the word with respect to that [object] has been demonstrated.
Thus concludes the investigation of verbal testimony; now follows the investigation of analogy.
Concerning comparison (*upamāna*), he says: "Of what kind? and so forth.
When a forest-dweller is asked by city-dwellers, "What is a gavaya like?", he speaks the sentence: "As is a cow, so is a gavaya. (1526)

In this regard, its status as an analogy (*upamāna*) is well-known; however, in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, because it is not excluded from scripture (*āgama*), it is described quite differently. When one is asked, "What is a *gavaya* like?", the statement, "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*,"—it is this statement that is known as an analogy among the elder Naiyāyikas.

In the *Śābara-bhāṣya*, however, Śabarasvāmin, considering that such comparison (*upamāna*) is already included within verbal testimony (*śabda*) and thus it is not logical for it to be a separate means of knowledge, described a different kind of comparison with the following passage:
"Comparison also produces a cognition regarding an object not present [to the senses] by way of similarity,
just as the sight of a *gavaya* [produces] the recollection of a cow."
Desiring to explain this very point, he says: "Having seen a cow," and so forth.
When, having seen a cow in the forest, he subsequently beholds a gavaya that possesses many common features and has a rounded neck,
his cognition of the gavaya at that time consists merely of the apprehension of its form.
Furthermore, even that which is specifically conceptual is indeed perception;
such as [the cognition] "this animal has a form similar to a cow.
When the operation of the sense organs is present, this kind of perception of a genus (jāti) is accepted.

Having previously seen a cow and subsequently gone to the forest, when one sees a *gavaya*—which is characterized by possessing many commonalities of parts (*bhūyo’vayavasāmānyabhājam*), meaning it possesses numerous commonalities of its constituent parts—and which has a rounded neck (*vartulakaṇṭhakam*), meaning it is devoid of a dewlap—at that time, first of all, there arises a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perceptual awareness (*ālocanājñāna*) which grasps only the essential nature of the *gavaya*; this is indeed perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, that which arises in the specific form of conceptualizing (*viśeṣeṇa vikalpayat*) that "this animal is similar to a cow" is also indeed perception, because it arises through the operation of the sense organs (*akṣavyāpāreṇa*). (1528)

It might be argued that, by the force of memory, it is only a non-existent similarity that arises through conceptualization and not through the operation of the senses; anticipating this objection, he says: "In that case, although... and so forth.
In this regard, although that cognition arises after recollecting the cow,
it would nonetheless be within the range of the senses because of its presence residing in the gavaya.
Even though that cognition which grasps the similarity is preceded by memory, nevertheless, because the similarity is present by virtue of its location in the gavaya, it is an object of the senses.
Proximity (*sannidhi*)— that is, the state of being present—
is the reason for proximity because it resides in the *gavaya*;
since the similarity resides in the *gavaya*, therefore its proximity [to the cow] exists.

Now, one might object: "Since similarity resides in two things, how is it logical for its apprehension to occur in a single place, such as the gavaya? To this he says: "Like a universal," and so forth;
for similarity, like a universal, is fully present in each individual instance.
Since that [similarity] is perceived even when the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is not seen—
because it exists as something common to both— it is "possessing a universal" (*sāmānyavat*).

Although similarity resides in two things, nevertheless, because it is considered to be fully present in each individual thing possessing the universal, it is indeed perceived in one place alone due to its presence there, even when the counter-correlate, such as a cow, is not seen.

This might be argued: "If similarity were a real entity (*vastu*), it would be perceived; however, its very status as a real entity is not established. To this he says: "And the reality of similarity," and so forth—namely, that the reality of similarity cannot be denied.
That [similarity] is the connection with many common parts belonging to another class.

(1533) The relation characterized by the inherence of many common parts—such as horns and so forth—of cows and the like within a single individual of another class, such as the *gavaya*, is similarity.
Furthermore, a relation is not absolutely distinct from its relata, because otherwise there would follow the undesirable consequence that there would be no cognition of the relation and so forth.
The term "of another genus" (*jātyantara*) is employed in order to indicate that there is no similarity because of the existence of commonality in all parts among those of the same genus.
Now, demonstrating the essential nature of analogy (*upamāna*), he says: "In that [analogy]... (1533).
Within that very same state of affairs, the cognition that arises in the form, "This cow is similar to that animal," is analogy (*upamā*).
That cognition which is produced regarding an imperceptible cow, having the form "The cow is similar to this visible animal," is the means of valid knowledge known as analogy (*upamāna*).
Showing its object of cognition (prameya), he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
Therefore, that which is remembered would be qualified by similarity.
The object of cognition (*prameya*) for analogy (*upamāna*) is either similarity (*sād�riśya*) or that which is based upon it.

Since analogy possesses the characteristics as previously described, therefore, that which is remembered—such as a cow—as qualified by its similarity to a *gavaya* and so forth, is the object of cognition for analogy;
or else, it is simply the similarity itself as residing in the cow and so forth.

"But surely, similarity has been perceived through perception, and the cow has already been made an object of cognition through memory; what further additional object of knowledge (*prameya*) remains, such that by the apprehension of it the validity of analogy (*upamāna*) would be established? To this he says: "When the similarity has been understood through perception and the cow has been remembered... (*pratyakṣeṇāvabuddhe ca sādṛśye ca gavi smṛte*).
