Because the [cow] qualified by similarity is not established through any other means, analogy (*upamā*) possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). (1536) Even though the similarity has been grasped by perception and the cow has been made an object of memory, nevertheless, since the cow-individual as qualified by similarity is not established through any other means— neither perception nor memory— analogy is authoritative for the cognition of that [qualified object].
1536 On this very point, he states an illustration: "Even when [the object] is perceived"— that is, just as even when a place is perceived and fire is being remembered...
Inference is not invalid simply because its object is already distinguished [from others];

just as in the case of a locus such as a specific spot, even though that locus is perceived and fire is grasped through memory, inference is not invalid—indeed, it is valid precisely because its object is the specific spot as qualified by fire—so too it is with analogy. (1537)

Now, it might be argued: "Let comparison (upamāna) be a means of valid cognition; how then is it a distinct means of valid cognition from perception and the others? To this he says: "Not so," for at that time, the status of being a direct perception (pratyakṣatā) is not established for the cognition, because it is devoid of the operation of the connection between the sense organ and its object. (1538)
Furthermore, because the three characteristics [of a logical reason] are not established, it cannot be an inference;
for here, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth are not possible in any way.
(For the similarity residing in the cow previously [perceived] is not grasped as a property.)
And that which is being apprehended in a gavaya cannot be an inferential mark for cows.
First of all, it is not reasonable to regard it as perception, because it does not arise from the contact of a sense organ with its object;
nor is it inference, because the three characteristics [of the logical reason] are absent.

To explain: here, either similarity is postulated as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), or the gavaya and so forth which are actually perceived. Regarding that similarity, if it is postulated as the logical mark (*liṅga*), there are two alternatives: it would have to be conceived as residing in the cow, or as residing in the gavaya.
In this regard, similarity residing in the object of cognition (the cow) cannot be the logical mark, because it has not been apprehended prior to the perception of the gavaya;
and it is not logical for that which is unapprehended to serve as a logical mark, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

[The opponent might argue: "In that case, similarity existing in the cow will be the inferential mark (*liṅga*), because it has been apprehended there [in the cow]. To this he says: "And that which is being apprehended in the *gavaya* is not an inferent of the cows, because it belongs to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*), like the blackness of a crow.

[Objection: "In that case, since [the similarity] has been apprehended in the cow after seeing the *gavaya*, this will serve as a logical mark (*liṅga*) residing therein. [Reply: He says—"The proposition" (*pratijñā*);
because it is a part of the meaning of the proposition itself, what resides in the cow cannot be a logical mark.
Furthermore, because it lacks a necessary connection, the gavaya cannot function as a mark (liṅga) for the cow.
Since similarity is the object of cognition, it is not logical for that very similarity to be the mark.
To the objection that "in that case, the gavaya itself will be the mark," he says: "The gavaya... [verse 1541].
In this case as well, because they reside in different substrata (*vyadhikaraṇatva*), the gavaya cannot function as a logical mark (*liṅga*).
[Objection: "In that case, let there be no validity for comparison (*upamāna*. To this, he says: "And it is not invalid," and so forth.
And that cognition is not invalid because it reveals an object not previously known,
since prior to seeing the gavaya, its similarity [to the cow] was not apprehended;
for previously, the cow had not been perceived as qualified by similarity to a gavaya.

It might be argued that it is logical for there to be validity [in perception] because there is the manifestation of a cow as a limiting condition (*upādhi*) of similarity to what was previously unknown;
[the author] refutes this with the verse beginning "prameya" (1542).
Since there is no objective entity (prameya-vastu) [to which it could correspond], its status as a means of valid cognition (mānatā) is not intended;
for if similarity consists in the connection with many common parts (avayava-sāmānya),
then since universals (sāmānyas) have been refuted, how can there be a plurality (bhūyastā) among them?
If there exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes that [universal], then there is indeed a connection with those [means].

Furthermore, the reality of the universal and its being graspable by perception [are established] because it is an object of knowledge other than non-existence, just like a unique particular (*asādhāraṇavastu*).

If it is argued that comparison (*upamāna*) is not a means of valid cognition because its object of cognition does not exist— just as there is no means of valid cognition other than the six accepted ones— and that therefore there is no object of cognition consisting of similarity (*sādṛśya*) characterized by the connection with many common parts, and thus the reason [for its existence] is unestablished (*asiddha*), we say:
that is not so.

Since universals have been refuted in the "Examination of Universals" (*Sāmānyaparīkṣā*), there is no plurality among them, nor is there any connection with them; thus, the reason (*hetu*) cannot be considered unestablished (*asiddha*).
One might argue: "There certainly exists a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes universals; therefore, the reason is indeed unestablished."
In this regard, the proof is as follows: "The universal (*sāmānya*) is a real entity (*vastu*), and it is likewise graspable by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)," is the pair of propositions;

"because it is a cognizable object other than non-existence" (*abhāvānyaprameyatvāt*) is the reason, meaning that its nature is to be a cognizable object other than the cognizable object that is non-existence.
The example is "like a unique object";
this is the definition of being a unique object.
1544–1545 He states the refutation with the words beginning "abhāva" (non-existence), etc.:

For those proponents who maintain that the object [of cognition] is a universal (sāmānya) subsumed under the category of non-existence, there is a lack of proof regarding the first probandum, and furthermore, in both propositions, the reason is a part of the very meaning of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*). Regarding the term "universal object" (*sāmānyārtha*), the word "object" (*artha*) here refers to the cognizable (*prameya*). Since the Buddhists, who assert that the universal is devoid of intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), claim that the universal is other than non-existence, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Furthermore, in the first case of the probandum—the definition of a real entity (*vastu*)—there is the fallacy of being a part of the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).

For instance: "That which is other than non-existence is a real entity," because the definition of existence (*bhāva*) consists in the exclusion of non-existence (*abhāvavyavaccheda*); thus, that very [exclusion] is presented as the reason (*hetu*) by means of a different word, and it is also the very same thing that is the probandum (*sādhya*). Therefore, there is the fallacy of being a part of the meaning of the proposition.
Furthermore—comparison (*upamāna*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because its nature is that of memory (*smṛti*), just like any other instance of memory.
Demonstrating that it has the nature of memory in this context, he says: "In this way," and so forth.
However, it is logical in this case that certain parts of the gavaya are the cause of a cognition identical [to that produced] by the parts of the cow's form.
Thus, when he sees the gavaya there, a memory arises in him.
Since the parts of the form of a cow have been seen many times before, for this very reason our cognition does not arise through similarity with that [cow] in the case of a horse and so forth;
otherwise, what difference would there be when a gavaya is seen? (1548–1549)

By their very nature, even in the absence of a real entity called "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), certain parts of the *gavaya* are the causes of conceptual cognitions involving a common reflective judgment (*tulyapratyavamarśavikalpa*) together with the parts belonging to the cow. There is no distinct entity named "similarity" other than those parts which are the causes of the common reflective judgment, because no entity other than them appears in the cognition. Therefore, upon seeing a *gavaya*, there arises in regard to the parts of the cow a cognition that is essentially a form of memory, produced by the force of repeated observation; it does not, however, grasp a real entity called "similarity."
Otherwise, since there is also a connection with many common parts in horses and other animals, why would a cognition not arise regarding them upon seeing a gavaya, just as it does regarding a cow?
For there is no distinction here, as similarity exists in both cases; "otherwise" refers to this.

If they were not seen repeatedly, this fault would indeed arise regarding their status as memory; however, this fault does not apply because memory occurs only with respect to that which has been previously seen repeatedly,
owing to the restricted nature of the causes that awaken memory.

It might be argued: "Let it be that memory exists; nevertheless, why is memory itself not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? To this he says: "Because it reveals an object already known," and so forth. Therefore, this [memory] is not a means of valid cognition; how, then, could there be the status of another means of valid cognition [in it]? (1550)
"This" refers to memory.
Having conceded that similarity is a real entity (*vastu*) according to the opponent's own view, he states the invalidity of comparison (*upamāna*): "Or let it be," and so forth.
Or let similarity be a real entity; however, like a universal (*sāmānya*), it is already perceived in front [of one] even when the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), such as a cow, is not seen. (1551)

And thus, its nature as a form of recollection does not cease in any way; for while similarity exists in the cow by its mere presence, it has not been definitively determined in this manner: "the similarity [of the cow] is with the gavaya. (1552)

But comparison (upamāna) cognizes the dissimilarity [of the object] from that [memory]. (1553) Let it be granted that similarity is a real entity and, like a universal (sāmānya), is fully present in its entirety; nevertheless, when a cow standing before one is being grasped by perception prior to the sight of a gavaya, that similarity—being non-different from it—is also already grasped as standing before one, just like the very nature of the cow. Otherwise, its non-difference would not be established.
Furthermore, because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) since it takes the form of memory.
However, it might be argued: "Previously, similarity was indeed apprehended in its mere existence; however, it was not apprehended in this specific form—that 'this cow is similar to this gavaya.
But comparison (*upamāna*) cognizes it in this very aspect; therefore, its nature as memory is unproven."
Regarding this, he says: "If indeed," and so forth:
"Even if it was not previously grasped by its name, it was nevertheless grasped by its very own nature, which is designated as its self. (1554)
Even if the cow-substance, as qualified by the name "similarity to a gavaya," was not apprehended prior to the sight of the gavaya, it was indeed apprehended in its own nature;
that is to say, its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) was apprehended.
To the question "What is that nature?", he says: "That which is designated as its self."
That which is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that cow-substance is designated as its "self" (*ātman*);
by means of that—that is to say, by that essential nature characterized as its own intrinsic being—it is apprehended.
If it is indeed apprehended, then what of it? He says: "Not name, not form," and so forth.

Name and form do not constitute the reality of things, for if they were, then even those who have fully realized the true nature of the self would remain ignorant [of that reality] when name and form are not apprehended. || 1555 ||

Indeed, the name is not the very nature of things, such that if that name were not apprehended prior [to the object], there would be no apprehension of the object even though it has been grasped; furthermore, for one who maintains that perception is determinate in nature, it is not at all reasonable to say that "it has not been apprehended.

If the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were established by this much alone, there would be no limit to the number of such means; for they could be [established] as means of valid cognition in other ways as well.
Furthermore, if one were to postulate another means of valid cognition based on the mere fragment of knowledge that "this is similar to that," it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
"Perception, inference, verbal testimony along with analogy, presumptive testimony, and non-existence— these six are the means of establishing what is to be proven";
thus there would be no limit to the number of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Showing this very same over-extension (atiprasaṅga), he says: "In the perception of a row of trees, etc."—
that is, because of the perception of a single tree within the sight of a row of trees and so forth.
The certainty that "this is that same [tree]" arises from the cognition of a second tree;
it must rely on another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it does not depend on similarity and so forth.
If you argue that this is not so because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, then the same [objection] applies to analogical cognition (upamāna) as well.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of rows of ants and the like is intended.
At the time of seeing a row of trees and so forth, upon the perception of the first tree, the certain cognition "this is the first tree" does not arise;
however, when the second tree is perceived, the certain cognition that arises regarding the first tree—"this is the first tree"—would have to be a distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara).
Why?
Because it does not depend on similarity;
since it does not depend on similarity, this is not comparison (*upamāna*).
It is not perception because it does not depend on the operation of the senses;
it is not inference because it does not depend on a logical mark (liṅga);
and it is not verbal testimony because it is independent of words.
It is not presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because it does not depend on a perceived or heard fact that would otherwise be inexplicable;
nor is it non-existence (*abhāva*), because it does not depend on the cessation of a means of knowledge or its object.
Likewise: "This was before that," "this is after that," "this is long," "this is short," "this is large."
If it is argued that in such cognitions as these, the consequence of non-validity (*apramā*) would follow,
and that this [cognition] is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it is a memory (*smṛti*) consisting of the apprehension of what has already been apprehended;
The same [charge] of apprehending what has already been apprehended applies to analogies as well;
the plural number in the phrase "in analogies" is used because of the multiplicity of individual instances.
And upon the perception of a gavaya, one proceeds toward [the exclusion of] horses and the like.
Is that cognition of dissimilarity not another means of valid cognition?
If you say it is not because it is included within non-apprehension (*abhāva*), it is not so, because it has a positive entity as its objective support.
Or, if it were merely a case of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), the same would apply to cognitions of similarity. (vv. 1559–1560)

Furthermore: just as the cognition of similarity in a cow arising from the sight of a gavaya is established as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), why should the cognition of dissimilarity in a horse or other animals arising from the sight of a gavaya not likewise be established as a distinct means of valid cognition?
If it is argued that it is not a distinct means of valid cognition because it is included within the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva*), this is not tenable.
Why?
Because it has existence as its objective support,
since non-existence has non-existence as its object.

It might be argued: "Dissimilarity is indeed the absence of similarity; therefore, it is certainly included within [the category of] non-existence. To this he replies with the verse beginning "anyonya" (mutual), etc.:

"If, while mutual non-existence exists, an object of cognition (*prameya*) consisting of non-existence is established, then such an object of cognition is equal—that is, identical—to those [cases] where there is the cognition of similarity, which are intended as analogies (*upamāna*)."
To the question "How so?", he says: "Of similarity," and so forth.
For just as the distinction of similarity is cognized there, so too is the distinction of all commonalities of parts understood.

(1561) Just as the distinction from similarity is perceived there in the cognition of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), so too in the cognition of similarity (*sādharmya*) the absence of all commonalities of parts is apprehended; thus, it would be included within non-existence (*abhāva*), just like the cognition of dissimilarity.
He states the proof for this very point: "Furthermore," and so forth;
that by which the connection with the generalities of many parts is apprehended.
If there were a connection with the commonality of all parts, the consequence would be that it [the object] would be the reality itself.
The phrase "by which" (*yena*) is an explanation of the cause;
by which—that is, because—in the cognition of similarity, a connection with the commonality of many parts is perceived.
However, there is no connection with the commonality of all parts; therefore, even in this case, there is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
Otherwise, if there were a connection with the commonality of all parts, it would follow that the essence of that [cow], namely cowness (*gotva*), would belong to the *gavaya*.

Some maintain that analogy (*upamā*) is the cognition of the connection between a name and its referent, occurring when one who has heard the statement of extension perceives an object possessing a similar meaning.
(Verse 1563) "By some" refers to this view.
The Naiyāyikas state the definition of comparison (*upamāna*) as follows: "Comparison is the means of establishing that which is to be established through well-known similarity.

That which has well-known similarity is the *gavaya*, whose similarity with the well-known [cow] is established; by relying upon it—that is, having recourse to it—the establishment (*sādhana*), meaning the proof, of that which is to be established—the relationship between a name and the object named—is comparison.

For indeed, this very meaning—that analogy (*upamāna*) is the comprehension of the relationship between a name and its referent arising from the knowledge of similarity which depends upon a memory produced by a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) instilled by traditional scripture (*āgama*)—has been stated by others in a different manner: the sentence of instruction "the *gavaya* is like a cow" is the scripture; the quality called a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is that which is instilled by it; and the knowledge of similarity that arises depending upon the memory of the meaning of that instructional sentence, triggered by the sight of a *gavaya* in the forest, is what has been so described. "Name" (*samākhyā*) means a designation, that is to say, a word.

The meaning is identical [to the previous definition], namely that analogy (*upamāna*) is the cognition of the relationship between that [object] and its corresponding object. (1563) He states the refutation with the words "In that case as well" (*tatrāpi*), etc.:
Even in that case, the unconfused comprehension of the connection with the name occurs only at the time of hearing that extended application statement (atideśavākya), provided it is [heard];
thus, because it apprehends an object already grasped, it does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Just as in the case of recollection, [comparison] lacks the status of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) because it is devoid of the function of an instrument (*karaṇa*).

In that regard, since the comprehension of the relationship between the name and the named has already arisen at the time of hearing the analogical statement (*atideśavākya*), what arises subsequently would be a grasping of what has already been grasped; thus, like recollection, it would not possess the status of a pramāṇa. One might object: "There is no contradiction here in that it both grasps what has been grasped and yet possesses the status of a pramāṇa. To this he says: "because it is devoid of the function of an instrument."
The meaning of "instrument" (karaṇa) is the state of being the most effective means (sādhakatamatva), by virtue of its engagement with an action that has not yet been accomplished.

It might be argued: "Previously, the cognition of the connection with the name had not arisen at all; therefore, because it would be grasping what has already been grasped, the reason [you provide] is unestablished. To this he says: "Now, that [cognition]...
Now, even if that [cognition] had not arisen, how could one then apprehend [the object], thinking, "This is that very thing whose name was heard by me"? (1566)

If the comprehension of the connection with the name had not previously arisen, then the cognition in the form "This is that gavaya for which the name was heard by me before" would not have occurred. On this very point, he states the justification: "For instance," and so forth.

For instance, when one perceives a gavaya without having heard its name, no one is able to know that "this is the name he heard for it. However, Aviddhakarṇa says: "One understands [the object] in a general way through scripture (āgama), but the understanding of its specific particulars is through analogy (upamāna)."

Therefore, he anticipates that view: "If [the person] has employed comparison"—if, having employed comparison, one perceives the relationship by means of apprehending similarity through its specific object. || 1568 ||
He is so described because he possesses an appropriate analogy and a statement of extension (atideśavākya).
He explains the meaning of this very point with the second verse, beginning with "For from scripture... (āgamād dhi).
For he knows that connection through scripture as having a general scope;
however, he understands it as having a specific object by means of analogy. (1569) The specific object is the gavaya.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely):
"But surely, elsewhere [it is not the case that] there is no cognition of the relationship of the name."
For its comprehension of another object is not tenable due to the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga). The word "not" (na) is to be connected with the word "is tenable" (yujyate).

That is to say, once the connection of a name with one [object] has been understood, it is not logical for that same name to be understood as referring to a different object, because that would lead to an over-extension.
Showing this very same over-extension (atiprasaṅga), he says: "Not indeed"—
for when the name of Citrāṅgada is uttered, no one [else] [is perceived].
After some time, one perceives that sound in the one wearing the beautiful crown;
therefore, that which was previously known by him through conceptual reflection as an external object, designated by the name "universal" (sāmānya), [is actually internal].
Even upon perceiving a gavaya, one who does not know the distinction between the perceived object and its mental construction understands it as such, yet conceives of it as being external.
(1573) Aṅgada— a type of ornament known as a bracelet.
He who possesses a variegated armlet (*citrāṅgada*) is thus described;
for when someone is called "Devadatta" because he has a variegated armlet, another person at a later time does not apply that word *citrāṅgada* to Yajñadatta, who possesses a beautiful crown.
A *kiriṭa* is a diadem; he who possesses that which is both beautiful and a diadem is thus described.

Therefore, to avoid an over-extension [of the definition], it is only in that object which is superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and grasped by a cognition that determines it as an external object—that name or designation (*saṃjñā*) is apprehended; even when a *gavaya* is perceived, that name is understood in reference to that very [conceptual construct], and not to the external particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) called *gavaya*.
And it is precisely this conceptual reflection (*vikalpapratibimbaka*) that is conventionally designated as the "universal" (*sāmānya*).
Since that [external object] imagined by him has been refuted, how then can there be the conceit of an external particular (svalakṣaṇa)? To this he says: "The visible," and so forth.
Now, he asks: "What contradiction is there in the application of words and so forth to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? He says: "In this way," and so on:

"In this way, it must be understood that conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and verbal expressions (*dhvani*), which have the specific characteristic as their object, have also been refuted in detail. (1574)

Since it has been refuted in detail in the *Śabdārthaparīkṣā* that words and conceptual constructions have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, therefore the referent of a word is merely superimposed by conceptual construction;
even though [the particular] is their object, there occurs only inference.
And its being produced from a mark possessing the three characteristics is understood as follows:
"That which is similar to a cow is the object of the term 'gavaya'," just like the mental image of a gavaya present at the time of grasping the convention. (1575–1576)
Or, let it be granted that those conceptual words have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object;
even so, because they are included within inference itself, analogy (*upamāna*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Anticipating the objection—"How can this [analogy] be included in inference without being produced from a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*)?"—the author states "trirūpa... and so forth, in order to demonstrate that it is indeed produced from a mark possessing the three characteristics.

The reason (*hetu*) is "having a resemblance to a cow"; the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is "being within the range of the auditory perception of the word *gavaya*"; the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is the mentally present *gavaya* appearing in conceptual cognition at the time of grasping the linguistic convention; and the subject (*dharmin*) is the *gavaya* currently being perceived. (1575)
It might be argued: "At the time of establishing the convention, 'the gavaya is like a cow,' the gavaya has not yet ascended into the mind;
therefore, the example is unestablished. To this, he says: "Even though present in the mind," and so forth.
Even if he were a Buddhist, if he were not in that state [of perception], at what point would this convention be established? And how could this be similar to a cow?
Not only is it not within the range of the eye, such is also the meaning of the word.

If nothing conforming to the similarity with a cow were to appear in the cognition, then on what basis would the convention "this is similar to a cow" be established? Yet, such a convention is indeed established; therefore, one must admit that some form conforming to the similarity with a cow, residing within the cognition, appears at the time of the convention.

(1577) Thus, having first accepted the relation between word and object as the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for analogy (*upamāna*), it has been demonstrated that this [analogy] lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*) because it apprehends what has already been apprehended and because it is subsumed under inference (*anumāna*).

Now, there exists no other relation distinct from the two related entities (*sambandhin*), and those two related entities have not been apprehended by any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: at the time of the convention (*samaya*), the word was apprehended by auditory cognition, and subsequently the *gavaya* standing before one was apprehended by the eye; what further object of knowledge (*prameya*) remains, by virtue of which the validity of analogy (*upamāna*) might be established?
Demonstrating this, he says: "There is no relation... and so forth;
it has already been proven that there is no relation distinct from the related entities.
Long before, at the time [of hearing], the sound was grasped by the auditory consciousness;
and now this animal standing in front is seen by the eye.
Since these two have been cognized separately, their conjunction is not a valid means of knowledge (pramā). || 1578–1579 ||

"Because it apprehends what has already been apprehended, the cognition of the connection with that name—just like [the memory of] fragrance and sweetness—does not transcend the nature of recollection.
(Verse 1580) By this, he states its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) because it grasps what has already been grasped; [this is] established.

In the examination of the category of quality (*guṇa*), it might be argued: "Even if the two related entities are perceived separately by the cognitions of the auditory organ and so forth, and their connection is established through comparison, then comparison (*upamāna*) would possess validity (*prāmāṇya*) on account of that connection. To this he says: "separately," etc., "like fragrance, sweetness, and so forth."
The suffix *vati* is used in the sense of the locative case (*saptamy-arthe*).

The meaning is as follows: just as in cases such as "this object being experienced is sweet" or "it is fragrant," the cognition consisting of the grasping of a connection [between a name and its referent] regarding the object is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so too this [cognition under discussion] ought not to be one either.

Therefore (*tat*), the cognition of the application of a name—the knowledge of the relationship with a designation (*saṃjñā*)—does not transcend the nature of recollection (*smārttatām*), according to the principle already stated.

It might be argued: "The connection with a name is not established anywhere by way of similarity; rather, it is observed to be made by directly pointing out the named object, as in 'this is a cow,' and not when the object is beyond the senses. To this he says: "And the cognitions of the application of names, produced by infinite means, arise even without depending on similarity, as in the case of kings and so forth" (verse 1581).
"Samākhyā-yoga-saṃvidah" refers to the cognitions of the relationship between names and [their] referents regarding [beings] such as Narapā and others.

In order to demonstrate that very quality of being produced by infinite means in the case of kings and others, he states an illustration beginning with "sitātapatra" (the white umbrella), and so forth.
"The king, whose feet are covered by the white parasol, stands in their midst"—this is what is said according to the specific instruction.
When he is seen at a later time, the notion arises that "he has that [royal] name. (1582)
At that time, it becomes another means of valid cognition (*apramā*), because it does not depend upon similarity (*sādharmya*) and so forth.
For example, someone says to another: "Go on this business to your brother; see the lord of men (*narādhipati*) as he goes along with many men mounted on elephants and horses.
He replies: "Which among them is the lord of men?"
He says: "The one whose feet are covered by the white parasol and who possesses the rays of the sun—among them is the lord of men.

Having received that instruction and gone there, upon seeing the king distinguished by those aforementioned characteristics, the cognition arises: "This is that very person named the lord of men. According to your own view, this too would result in yet another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
Why?
Because it does not depend on similarity and so forth,
this [author] demonstrates by this [statement] that it is not included within the six means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

Aviddhakarṇa, however, maintains that there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and that there is no object of cognition (*prameya*) other than the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). To refute this, [the author] provides the following proof: perception (*pratyakṣa*) is accompanied by another means of valid cognition distinct from inference (*anumāna*), because it is a means of valid cognition, just like inference;
or, inference is accompanied by another means of valid cognition distinct from perception, because it is a means of valid cognition, just like perception.

Likewise, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is accompanied by another object of cognition distinct from the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because it is an object of cognition, just like the universal characteristic; or, the universal characteristic is accompanied by another object of cognition distinct from the particular characteristic, because it is an object of cognition, just like the particular characteristic. This very point he states with the word "other" (*anya*).

Another [proponent] establishes the existence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) through the power of inference: "Perception is conjoined with another means of valid cognition distinct from inference, because it is a means of valid cognition, just like inference;
and inference is likewise [conjoined with another means of valid cognition]. (1584)
In this way, this reason is not unimpeded, because it reveals a contradiction [with your own tenets].
Furthermore, in this very manner, your position regarding the fourfold nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be undermined.
Whatever response you have for that [objection] will serve as the response here as well.
Thus ends the investigation of the analogy;
"connected" (saṅgata) means related, that is to say, accompanied by a second [entity].
This should be understood as an illustration that also serves to establish other objects of knowledge.

Because the subverting proof (bādhaka) against the presence of the reason in the counter-example of the probandum has not been demonstrated, no necessary connection (pratibandha) between the probandum and the probans has been shown; thus, all reasons are inconclusive (anaikāntika), since their exclusion from the counter-example is doubtful. Furthermore, the restriction of the number of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) to four—namely, perception, inference, comparison, and verbal testimony—would be contradicted, because by this very same method other means of valid cognition would exist.

For instance, one could state the following: "Perception is accompanied by another means of valid cognition distinct from inference, comparison, and verbal testimony, because it is a means of valid cognition, just like inference."

Furthermore, that which is asserted as the threefold nature of the objects of cognition—namely, the universal (*sāmānya*), the particular (*viśeṣa*), and that which possesses both the universal and the particular (*sāmānyaviśeṣavān*)—would also be contradicted, because it is possible to establish other objects of cognition by that very same method.
Whatever solution you have for this will also serve for us; therefore, enough of this prolixity.
1585–1586 Thus concludes the investigation of analogy.

The Examination of Presumption (Arthāpatti). With reference to presumption, he says: "That object which is known through the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and cannot exist otherwise... and so forth.
It postulates another unseen [factor]; this is what is cited as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Where an object determined by the six means of valid cognition—namely perception, inference, comparison, verbal testimony, presumptive testimony, and non-apprehension—with respect to place, time, and so forth, is otherwise inexplicable, such that "if this kind of object did not exist," the conceptual construction regarding an imperceptible object is cited as the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony.
As Śabarasvāmin has stated: "When a perceived or heard fact is not otherwise possible, there is the postulation of an unseen [fact];
for example, when Devadatta is alive, his absence from the house leads to the postulation of his being outside."
"Seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) means cognized by the five means of valid cognition other than verbal testimony; "heard" (*śruta*) means cognized by the means of valid cognition that is verbal testimony.

Regarding this, he states the examples for presumption (*arthāpatti*) preceded by each of the six means of valid cognition in their respective order, beginning with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*), and so forth.

In that regard, from the burning [of fuel] known through direct perception, the power of burning in fire is inferred; and from the movement of the sun, its possession of that power [to move] is inferred. The powers of all entities are established by the presumption based on their effects.
And those [powers] are understood as unprecedented, even without the apprehension of a [prior] relationship.
Among these, presumption based on perception (*arthāpatti*) is as follows: having perceived burning through direct perception, one postulates the power of burning in fire.
That based on inference is as follows: having inferred the movement of the sun from its arrival at another location, one postulates its possession of the power of movement.
Since the capacities of all things are always established through the presumption based on their effects,
this presumption (arthāpatti) is sometimes preceded by perception itself— when, having perceived the effect through perception, one understands the capacity of the cause. However,
when the capacity of the cause is understood after the effect has been cognized through inference or other means, then the presumption based on the effect is preceded by inference and so forth.
Those [cognitions] are so described because their means of proof is the "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti) of the effect.
Nor can it be said that the causal capacity has already been apprehended previously; for those capacities are always understood as something new.
Therefore, since there is no apprehension of an object already apprehended, validity indeed exists.

In this regard, one might think that these powers are inferable through their effects as logical marks (*liṅga*), and not cognizable by the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). To this he says: "Because they are understood apart from the apprehension of a relation" (v.
1588); since they are understood without the apprehension of a relation, they are therefore not inferable.
Demonstrating precisely this absence of the apprehension of a relation, he says: "And not..."—
that is, neither a prior relation nor any other [relation] is apprehended now.
For in this context, the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) must exist together with their effects.

However, the relationship of these potencies with their effects has not been apprehended prior to the time of inference—unlike fire and smoke in a kitchen or similar places—because they are beyond the reach of the senses.
By this, the absence of positive concomitance is stated.
Nor is the relation apprehended now at the time of inference, precisely because it is beyond the senses;
by this, the absence of the property in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is stated, for it is illogical that the effect should be a property of the potencies residing in their causes.

Alternatively, in the case where the capacities of the ear and so forth are the subject, whatever reason is employed, all of it results in being unestablished in its locus (āśrayāsiddha) because the locus itself is unestablished.

Furthermore, when the powers residing in the auditory organ and so forth are made the subject of the argument, then whatever reason is employed to establish those powers within the subject of the auditory power and so on would all be *āśrayāsiddha* (unestablished in its locus), because the powers that constitute the locus are themselves unestablished.
Therefore, all powers established through the presumption based on the necessity of an effect (*kāryārthāpatti*) are not inferable.
Upon hearing such statements as, "Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day," the resulting cognition of his eating at night is called *śrutārthāpatti* (presumption based on what is heard).

In this regard, presumption preceded by verbal testimony (*śābdapramāṇa*) is as follows: from hearing a statement such as, "Fat Devadatta, who has not undergone any medicinal treatment, does not eat during the day," one postulates the meaning that he eats at night.

It might be thought: "The meaning 'he eats at night' is understood from this very sentence, 'The fat Devadatta does not eat by day'; therefore, [the author] says: 'And the referent of words such as "night" is not [understood]'—meaning that the referent of words such as 'night' is not apprehended within the sentence concerning the day."
There is neither a connection nor a distinction between the daytime and other such objects and the act of eating at night, by virtue of which that sentence could be the means of conveying it;
furthermore, because [the words] are occupied with another meaning, there can be no assumption of a second meaning. (1593–1594)
Therefore, this [sentence] is understood through another sentence present in the mind;

thus, even though it is not part of the [physical] scripture, that sentence which is so understood must have its means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) stated among perception and the other [means of knowledge]. || 1595 ||
When a sentence has not been uttered, perception is certainly not admitted [as the means of knowledge].
Nor is it inference; for this [sentence] has never been seen together with an example [that could serve as a basis for inference].
If, however, you maintain that it functions as a logical mark (liṅga) even when no relationship [between the sentence and its meaning] has been perceived— || 1596–1597 ||
By the mere utterance of that [word], the comprehension of the entire sentence occurs;
because it is devoid of [external] relations, nothing else distinguishes it.
For the meaning of a sentence is indeed twofold: namely, conjunction (*saṃsarga*) and exclusion (*bheda*).

In this context, *saṃsarga* (association) is either the non-differentiation of entities from one another, like milk and water, or their existence in a state of mutual exclusion through the relationship of the excluded and the excluder; alternatively, it is the fixed relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).
Exclusion (*bheda*) is the differentiation from what is of a different class;
this sentence-meaning, though of two kinds, is not possible here.
For instance, the meaning of "eating at night" is not a form of connection between the meanings of the words *divā* and so forth—namely, "by day" and so on—because they are absolutely distinct.
Nor is it of the nature of a difference (*bheda*), because words such as "by day" do not function by way of excluding "night" and so forth.

Now, if it is thought that the sentence "he eats by day" has a second, distinct meaning—namely, "he eats at night"—the author says: "because it is exhausted by another meaning. Since the sentence is already fully utilized in the negation of eating by day and so forth, it is not capable of simultaneously establishing another matter, such as eating at night; therefore, there is no postulation of a second meaning.

Therefore, he shows the non-verbal nature [of this meaning] by stating that the meaning of this other sentence— "he eats at night"— is based on what is present in the mind (*buddhisthena*), even though it is not derived from scripture (*anāgamikatvepi*).
Even if it is not verbal,
since the absence of verbal status has been established by the aforementioned reasoning,
one must state the means of valid cognition that apprehends that sentence which is understood as "he eats at night."
The sense is that since this would have to be one of the means of valid cognition such as perception and so forth,
and yet it is not any of those,
it follows that this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition.
Refuting the claim that this [inference] is one of the means of valid cognition such as perception and so forth, he says: "But not," and so on.
In that regard, it is not logical for the statement regarding eating at night—which has not been uttered—to be considered perception, because it is not being heard;
nor can it be considered inference, because there is no [established] relationship [between the sign and the object].
For instance: this statement regarding eating at night has never been observed in conjunction with that statement regarding daytime [eating], whereby a relationship [of concomitance] could exist;
nor is there any other indicative mark (liṅga).
Nevertheless, one might argue that even if the relationship is unperceived, this will still function as an indicative mark; to this he says: "If... (yadīti).

For if that which has an unestablished connection were to possess the status of a logical mark (*liṅga*), then from the utterance of the first sentence there would be comprehension of all sentences; why then [would there not be comprehension] of the sentence regarding eating at night alone?
Because, being devoid of a [specific] connection, the sentence regarding eating at night is no different from any other sentence.
Because there is an absence of a [logical] connection, every sentence is, in effect, indistinguishable from any other. 1593–1594.

He states [the type of inference] preceded by analogy (*upamāna*)—beginning with "gavaya," etc.—[as follows]: the capacity to be apprehended by the cognition of that cow which has been analogized through a *gavaya*...

It is apprehended through the capacity produced by the power of analogy. (Verse 1599) That specific capacity of the cow-individual—which has been compared by means of a gavaya and is to be grasped by the analogical cognition—is measured by that presumptive reasoning (*arthāpatti*) which arises from the power of analogy.
He states the [inference] preceded by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*): "The denotation (*abhidhā*) would not be established otherwise," etc.
Having understood the expressive capacity [of the word] through presumptive testimony, because there is no other way to account for it, [one understands the universal]. (1600)
The certainty regarding the eternity of the word is established by yet another *arthāpatti* (presumption):
for that which is non-eternal cannot possess the continuity of conventional usage based on linguistic convention; this is the designation [of the reason].
(1601) *Abhidhānam-abhidhā*.

The meaning is as follows: since the communication of meaning would not be established for a word otherwise—that is, without its expressive power—one must understand (i.e., realize) this power of indication; and because there is no other recourse for that power of indication except for the eternity of the word, the certainty of the word's eternity is established by yet another *arthāpatti*.
To explain how expression would not be established without eternity, he says: "For [if it were] non-eternal," and so forth.
For instance— if that which was perceived at the time of the convention were not to persist at the time of linguistic usage,
then the making of the convention would be entirely purposeless,
since its purpose is for the sake of usage.

Furthermore, because the relationship with the word that functions at the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) has not been previously grasped; or else— as stated in the phrase "because it has no other recourse" (*tadananyagati*)—

it is because there is a determination of non-difference (*avyatireka*) from the word perceived at the time of the convention (*saṅketa*), since the word existing at the time of usage has no other source of origin than that.
To the question, "How is there certainty regarding non-difference? he says: "For that which is impermanent," and so forth.

He states the presumption based on non-existence (*abhāvapūrvikārthāpatti*) as follows: "The establishment of Caitra’s presence outside the house, which is described here, [proceeds] from the house as qualified by the absence of Caitra determined through the non-operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*). (1602)
One should cite that other type of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) which arises from non-existence;
for it is distinct from inference (*anumāna*), because the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and other such factors are not its constituent parts.
[It operates] regarding an object qualified by an external location, or regarding a location qualified by that [object].

How can that absence of perception regarding the object of knowledge (prameya) be a property of the subject (pakṣadharma)? Furthermore, in this case, the absence from the house of one who is alive is postulated as the property of the subject;
yet, that cognition [of his absence] does not arise without first cognizing his existence outside.

However, that "absence from the house" which is pure and devoid of [the cognition of] existence is not a prover [of Caitra's being outside], because it is observed even in the case of those who are dead, since it pertains to external exclusion. That absence of Caitra which is determined and ascertained through the non-operation (nivṛtti) of means of valid cognition such as perception, and by which the house is qualified—as in the statement "Caitra is not here in the house"—the establishment of his being outside (bahirbhāva), namely the certainty that "Caitra exists outside," while Caitra is alive, has been described here in the *Bhāṣya* by Śabarasvāmin; this is cited as an illustration to indicate other types of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). This is the meaning.
For example: when Devadatta is alive, the postulation of his being outside based on his non-perception at home—this is an illustration of presumption (arthāpatti) preceded by non-existence (abhāva).
Since logicians generally maintain that this is a form of inference (anumāna), the author states "pakṣa" and so forth in order to refute that view.

Since its members, such as the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), are neither a constituent part nor a cause of this [cognition], it is therefore entirely distinct from inference, just like perception. For instance: when the object of cognition is either Caitra or another person qualified by an external location, or an external location qualified by Caitra or another person—in either of these two types of objects—the absence of Caitra or that other person in the house, being located in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇa*), how could it be a property of the subject?
The intended meaning is that it certainly could not be.

Furthermore, when the absence from the house is conceived as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), there are two alternatives: either that absence from the house belonging to Devadatta while he is alive is what is conceived, or [the absence] in a general sense.
Regarding the first alternative, he states the fault with the words beginning "of one who is living," etc., ending with "the cognition of that."
Regarding that—the cognition (saṃvitti), which is the certainty, of the living Devadatta—that does not arise without having ascertained Devadatta’s existence outside [the house].
By this, he points out that the reason is either unestablished (*asiddha*) or, if it were established, it would be a case of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Furthermore, in the second alternative, he shows that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the absence of Devadatta and others from their houses is observed even when they are dead; thus he says: "But the absence from the house..."
"Existence" refers to the state of being alive.
Thus, presumption (*arthāpatti*) is of six kinds;
among these, by four [types] the capacity (*śakti*) is the object of knowledge (*prameya*), by one the eternity of the word, and by the other an external substance.
With the words beginning with "therein," he states the refutation: first of all, the definition here is untenable;

for instance, the postulation of an unperceived [entity] is based on the premise that an object consisting of what is seen, heard, and so forth would otherwise be inexplicable without that unperceived [entity].
To this, the following is examined.
Is a relationship between that unseen [object] and some perceived or heard object ever observed, or not?
If it is observed, there follows the consequence of its being an inference (*anumāna*), because it relies on the perception of a relationship as its means.
If, however, it is not established, then one must also postulate non-burning power for fire, just like its burning power, since there is no distinction in terms of the relationship being unobserved.
If it is argued that combustibility is not to be postulated because fire has never been observed together with non-combustibility,
then in that case, combustibility itself should not be postulated either, since it too has never been observed in any instance together with [non-combustibility].
Therefore, once a relationship is established, it is logical to postulate the second related term upon seeing one related term that is invariably concomitant with it.
And if it were conceived in this way, because it would have the perception of a relationship as its means, it would be included within inference itself.
Furthermore, the examples provided there are also incorrect.

Regarding the claim that "the capacity of an object already established through perception and other means is cognized by means of the four types of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)," he states a general refutation: "In that case, apart from the capacity," and so forth.

In that regard, there is no such thing as "power" (śakti) over and above the capable [entity] which could be understood through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); for the capable entity is indeed directly perceived (pratyakṣa).

Since power is not something distinct from the object itself, and that capable thing is directly perceived, [presumptive testimony] is not a means of valid cognition because it would merely be grasping what has already been grasped.
The mention of "perception" (adhyakṣa) is an elliptical indication [of other means of knowledge].
With the words "of burning and so forth," he states a specific refutation of the example of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) preceded by perception.
But that which is observed as the cause of burning and so forth— fire and the like— is,
beyond doubt and without error, nothing other than power (*śakti*). For it is precisely through that [power] that there is utility toward effects that are distinct [from the cause].
An entity would be devoid of agency if there were no distinction in its cognitive application (upayoga).
For the definition of capacity (śakti) is that very nature which is capable of causal efficiency (arthakriyā); and this entity, being of such a nature, is determined through direct perception.
"Without doubt and without error"—this is an adverbial phrase.

Now, if a separate power (*śakti*) is admitted, then since it is the power alone that is effective regarding the effects, the entity itself would become a non-agent; consequently, the consequence follows that it is not a real thing (*avastutva*), because the definition of a real thing is its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).

Now, if it is argued that utility must be admitted so as to avoid the consequence of [the entity] being a non-entity, then, when that utility is admitted, that power is not distinct. Why is it not distinct?
Because that very nature—which is the capacity for causal efficiency—is itself the power; there is no other definition of power.

As for the designation of "the power of an entity" as if it were distinct [from the entity], that is said of the entity itself in such a way when there is a desire to know only that [power], by excluding other differences. 1608–1609.
It might be argued that the definition of power (*śakti*) is not the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*); what then?
It says "other," etc., to show that it is indeed something else.
There is no means of valid cognition whatsoever for the establishment of a characteristic of "otherness";
nor is there any purpose served by knowing it, since its effect is established from its form alone.

(1611) There is no means of valid cognition for the establishment of another characteristic, namely "capacity," which could—by means of that valid cognition—distinguish this capacity from non-existence, which is characterized by the absence of all functional power.

And there is no purpose whatsoever for those seeking causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in knowing such a thing as it is; for causal efficiency is established from the very nature of the entity that is useful, as it has been said: "What is the use of investigations for that which is capable of causal efficiency? [They are] for the sake of that [efficiency]."
What is the point of examining the beauty or ugliness of a eunuch for a woman in love?
If it is argued that another definition of capacity is to be understood through presumptive testimony based on the necessity of an effect (*kāryārthāpatti*), [we reply: 1611. [This is not so.]
This [definition] does not hold, because it would result in the effect being something other than what it is in reality.

(1612) It might be argued: "There is indeed another definition of power (*śakti*), namely: that form which is always to be inferred from the impossibility of the effect otherwise—that is power. To say that the definition of power is its being inferable from the effect is not correct.
Why?
Because the effect occurs otherwise—
that is, even without a distinct power, the effect is established.

He asks, "How so? and replies: "For this comes from that entity. Since this effect arises—that is, is produced—from an entity (bhāva), namely a thing (padārtha), therefore the existence of the effect is possible even otherwise; why then postulate a separate power (śakti)?
For fire, being directly perceived as distinct from water and other substances, is capable of burning and so forth; what need is there for any other capacity?
Clarifying this very point, he says: "Water and so forth," etc.
If that power is not absolutely distinct, then it too must possess a dual nature;
yet this cannot be due to contradiction, since its non-difference [from the substance] is also directly perceived.
It might be argued: "This fault would indeed arise if we were to assert that power is absolutely distinct from the entity;
what then? We hold it to be of a dual nature, being both distinct and non-distinct. But this too is not tenable.
He asks, "Why? and says: because of contradiction.

If it is distinct, how can it be non-distinct at that very same time? Or if it is non-distinct, how can it be distinct? This is a contradiction, namely, the simultaneous perception in a single substratum of two properties whose definitions consist in mutual exclusion.
Indeed, this is what constitutes difference: that it does not have the nature of the other, as has already been explained.

Let it be granted that the power possesses a dual nature; nevertheless, that power, being of a dual nature, is indeed perceptible. This is because the non-difference of the power from the object is observed, and not an absolute difference such that it would be imperceptible.
Consequently, the claim that power is eternally inferable solely through its effects would be contradicted.
Furthermore, since its status as perception is established, the exclusion of its being an object of inference does not cause us any harm;

for it is precisely because of this that we do not seek to infer it in this context. Moreover, regarding the exclusion of the inferability of capacity—which was asserted in such statements as "the capacities of all entities are established through the presumption based on their effects"—that does not cause us any harm.

Why? Because we do not accept inference (*anumāna*) with respect to this object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since inference consists in the cognition of an imperceptible object (*parokṣārtha*); by this, he states that [the object] would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Regarding what was stated—"and in the case of the faculties of hearing and so forth"—he says here: "But those... and so on.

However, as for those entities such as the faculty of hearing which are not within the range of perception, their very existence is understood through an inferential mark (*liṅga*) characterized as a capacity (*śakti*). (1616)

But was it not previously established that existence (*sattā*) is indeed what is being proved? How then can it be said that "existence is understood"? To this he replies with the verse beginning "by another cause," etc.:

"For that cognition of sound and so forth depends upon other causes; even when [the object] exists, it does not arise because of the absence of its specific cause, just like a sprout and the like. (1617)

Existence is not established directly; rather, what is established is the dependence of the subject—the cognition of hearing and so forth—upon another cause. This is because, even when other causes of that [cognition], such as mental attention (*manaskāra*), are present, the cognition of hearing and so forth may still be absent.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: if something occurs only occasionally despite the presence of a certain condition, it depends upon another cause; for example, a sprout occurs only occasionally despite the presence of earth and other factors. Likewise, the cognition of hearing occurs only occasionally despite the presence of mental attention and so forth. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

When it has been established that [the existence of the sense organs] depends on other causes, it is said that their existence is understood in this manner—that those other causes are well-known as the ear and so forth—and not by direct perception; thus there is no fault. Regarding what was stated—"from the movement of the sun, which is inferred"—he says: "the material cause," and so forth.

And since the birth [of the flame] occurs in a location not identical to that of its substrate, it is perceived as continuous due to the sun’s extension across different locations, like a flame and so forth;
otherwise, this would not occur for something of a stable nature.
"But its power to reach another location has been refuted by another [argument].

(1619) By this, he states its inclusion within inference; for instance: whatever is observed to reach another location, that arises by abandoning the location of its own material cause, as in the case of a flame reaching another location; and the sun likewise reaches another location—this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).

Nor is this [reason] inconclusive, because for an entity that is stable in nature and of a single form, this attainment of another location is not logical; for it would involve neither abandoning its previously determined nature in the former location, nor—if such abandonment were to occur—would there simply be the arising of something entirely new.
This alone is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).

It might be argued: "This instance of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) has been cited regarding a capacity that is already established, not regarding its origination; therefore, how can it be said that this arthāpatti is included within inference? To this he says: "But capacity [as a distinct entity] has been refuted. (vv. 1618–1619)
Regarding the example of presumptive testimony based on what is heard (*śrutārthāpatti*), [the opponent] says: "Fat," and so forth.

There is no certainty regarding the meaning of the statement, "He is fat and does not eat during the day," because a person might speak otherwise due to the influence of hatred, delusion, and so forth. (1620)
By this, he states that the fact of being preceded by verbal testimony (*śābdapramāṇa*) is unestablished.
It might be argued: "Indeed, it is not the case that the implication of another sentence is made in dependence upon the comprehension of a meaning from a [given] sentence."
What then?
He says that this is established by perception alone, independent of the comprehension of an object: "by that which is independent of the comprehension of an object."
If another sentence with a meaningful content were to be implied by [the first] sentence independently of the comprehension of meaning, then there would be an implication of other statements.

(1621) A "sentence independent of the comprehension of meaning" (*arthagatyanapekṣa*) is one that does not depend on the understanding of sense; if, by such a mere sentence alone, another sentence possessing a meaningful content were implied, then there would be an implication of other statements—meaning that an implication of even another sentence entirely different from the statement regarding eating at night would result.
Because it would lack distinction due to being devoid of a relationship,
if it were to imply a meaning through a necessary connection with a real entity, then that same fault would apply upon depending on the comprehension of that meaning.

With the words beginning with "atha" (now), he raises an objection regarding the opponent's intention: "Now, if it is held that the comprehension of the object in that case occurs by way of an approach [to the word], or if the comprehension of the object arises from another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), let it be so. (1622)

Now, lest there be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), one might argue that, according to the principle of following the actual state of affairs, the understanding of the meaning is intended here in the form of another’s assent, because the other speaker has been accepted as a reliable authority (*āpta*);
or else, that the knowledge [of the fact] arises from another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such as perception, as in the case of "Devadatta is fat and does not eat during the day.
To this, he replies with the words beginning "Let it be," and so forth.

Let the understanding of the matter of eating at night follow from that—namely, from the fatness qualified by the absence of eating during the day—and not from another sentence present in the mind; for if this were so, it would be included within inference itself and would not constitute a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). This is the intended meaning.
Demonstrating that very inclusion, he says: "The night," and so forth.

A person associated with eating at night is understood to be desired [as the subject], because of his fatness despite the absence of eating during the day, just like anyone else [who eats at night]. (1623)
The "intended" (iṣṭa) refers to the specific person under consideration, characterized by eating at night;
the "reason" (hetu) is "because of fatness despite the absence of [other] food";
and the "example" (dṛṣṭānta) is "like other persons."
And this is a reason based on an effect (kāryahetu).
To the question, "How is the causal relationship established here?", he says: "In eating," and so forth.
Since fatness when there is eating is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there is a cognition of the [cause] from the thing that is actually connected to it.

Because the causal relationship between fatness and eating is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance— just as in the case of fire and smoke— it is logical that there is a cognition of the real thing, namely eating, from the effect, namely fatness, due to their connection.
However, it is not logical for one sentence to produce the cognition of another sentence that is not connected to it, because this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
To demonstrate this very same over-extension, he says: "sarvasambandha... and so forth.
For how could a sentence, which is devoid of all connection, be cognized through a single sentence? Otherwise, everything would be cognized from it.
(1625) How indeed could a sentence—devoid of, that is, lacking, every connection characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*)—be cognized?

Otherwise, if even that which is devoid of all relations were perceived, then everything— such as jars and the like— would be perceived from any single object, such as a jar; but this is not the case.
Therefore, comprehension must be admitted to arise from that necessary connection;
thus, with the words "for instance," [the author] supports the very point regarding the over-extension of the argument.
For if there were no relationship, or if the relationship existed but were not ascertained,
this sentence being understood would result in being invalid (*apramāṇaka*).
"If the relationship exists" is the accepted position.
First of all, there is no relation whatsoever between one sentence and another sentence; even if a relation exists, if it is not ascertained, it is as good as non-existent.

Consequently, that which is understood when the relation is unascertained would lack a valid means of knowledge—it would be a cognition without a basis. And if cognition were without a basis, the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that everything could be cognized from everything would be unavoidable.
With the words "of that which is connected," etc., he anticipates the opponent's objection:
"If it were not by royal decree that the validity of what is connected is established, how could the validity of perception exist without a connection? (1627)
Regarding this, the opponent says: "If you claim that validity belongs only to that which is related [to its object], then this is merely a royal decree; there is no reasoning here at all.
For instance, if 'the validity of what is related' were not a royal decree, then how could one say that perception possesses validity without connection—that is, without a relation? (1627)
To this he states the following reply: "But surely... [Nanu...].
Surely, if [an object] were cognizable despite being unrelated, why would there not be cognition of anything else as well?
Indeed, when devoid of a relationship, no distinction whatsoever is observed. (1628)
The status of being a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*) is established even in the case of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) solely on account of its connection [to the object].
For validity consists in correspondence (*saṃvāda*), and that arises from the object itself through the attainment of its own nature. [Objection:

"If something unrelated were to be cognized, then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) because there would be no distinction [between what is related and what is not]. To this, you have provided no answer."
As for what was said—that how can perception possess validity without a [logical] connection—that too is entirely inconsistent;
for indeed, no one accepts the validity of perception without a connection.
What then?

Validity is established even in the case of perception (*pratyakṣa*) solely through its connection [to the object]. To provide the justification for this here, he says: "For correspondence," and so forth.
Correspondence is the capacity to bring about the attainment of the object; it is validity.
Furthermore, how could that correspondence with perception be logically established by necessity unless the [perception] were to derive its own existence from that object?
To address the question, "What fault would there be otherwise? he says: "Because it is not its cause" (ataddhetoh).
It is not logical for that [scriptural] agreement to occur if it is not its cause or if it is causeless;
otherwise, there would necessarily be an agreement among all [such texts]. || 1630 ||
That object is the "cause" (hetu) of which [perception]; it is thus described. That which does not have that as its cause is "not having that as its cause" (ataddhetu), meaning it has another cause.

Therefore, from perception that does not have that as its cause—or from that which lacks a cause altogether due to the deficiency of all causes—there could not necessarily be a correspondence with that [object], namely, a correspondence with the object (arthasaṃvāda).
What then?
The same undesirable consequence applies here as well: that there would have to be a correspondence among all objects—that is, among every single object.

Alternatively, the author explains that the positive statement—"Fat Devadatta does not eat during the day"—while inferring its own specific cause, namely the intention [to speak], through the inference of a property of the reason (*hetudharma*), implies by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) the negative statement "he eats at night," just as smoke implies a transformation of fuel; however, this is not done directly. To demonstrate this, he says: "By this... and so forth:
"By this [statement], the intention appearing as a second sentence is inferred; and from the positive statement, the understanding of the negative [corollary] is held to occur. (1631)
"By this" means by the inference of the property of the reason (*hetudharma*), and not directly;
for from the positive statement (*anvayavākya*) such an intention is understood, in which the negative statement (*vyatirekavākya*) also appears.

Otherwise, if eating at night were not intended [by the speaker], and if the mere prohibition of eating were what was desired to be conveyed, then one would have simply said, "Devadatta does not eat," rather than stating the negative implication as "he is fat, [but] by day."
Regarding the understanding of the negative statement "the cow which is compared to a gavaya," he says: "of the comparison" (upamāyāḥ).

Since the validity of analogy (*upamā*) has been refuted in detail, the validity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), which arises from it, is likewise precluded. Even if analogy were valid, nevertheless, since presumptive testimony preceded by analogy would be grasping what has already been grasped, its separate validity is not tenable; for there is no distinct object of cognition (*prameya*) characterized as a capacity (*śakti*). Demonstrating this, he says: "Upamāna... and so forth.

In the case of the means of valid cognition known as analogy (*upamāna*), it is held that "cowness" (*gotva*) is its objective support (*ālambana*); and that which is supported by its own existence is considered to be the producer of its own cognition.
What need is there, then, for another power (*śakti*) here, for the sake of which [power] one would have to look elsewhere?
The validity of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) depends upon analogy (upamāna),
for its purpose is that which serves to bring about the cognition of capacity.
The remainder is easily understood.

Regarding the passage beginning with "abhidhānānyathā," he states that the example of an *arthāpatti* preceded by another *arthāpatti* is inconclusive: "Even in the absence of non-difference, the communication of meaning by words is not contradicted, just as the cause consisting of hand-gestures, tremors, and so forth [conveys meaning]. (1635)

For just as it is not contradictory for impermanent things such as the shaking of hands or the winking of eyes to convey meaning, so too it is certainly not contradictory for words even when they lack non-difference [from their referents]; thus, this example is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
In that context, "otherness" (*anyatva*) is impermanence (*anityatva*), while "non-otherness" (*ananyatva*) is the absence of otherness—that is to say, permanence (*nityatva*). (1635)

But was it not said that "what is impermanent does not participate in the continuity of conventional usage based on linguistic convention"? To this, he replies: "Because it is the cause of a uniform reflective awareness (tulyapratyavamarśa), just as words possess the capacity to convey meaning through their instability, so too is [their usage] not contradictory. (1636)

Although there is no continuity among particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) because they are momentary, nevertheless, certain particular characteristics, by their very nature, become causes—through a succession of moments—for a delusive reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśajñāna*) that has a non-differentiated form; being grasped as a unity, they become signifiers by virtue of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), just as, for example, a flickering flame becomes a signifier [of its object]. This is the remainder [of the sense].

1636. Regarding the example "just as shaking," the opponent, pointing out its lack of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*), says: "Indeed, those actions which are seen residing in perceptible substances... and so forth.

Their eternality is accepted [by us] on the basis of recognition, just as the eternality of phonemes (varṇa) is accepted by us through recognition. Thus, since the same applies to actions such as those of the hands, the example is not devoid of the property to be proven (sādhya), namely impermanence; therefore, there is indeed no deviation (avyabhicāra).

1637. If this is so, then since [sounds] are eternal, why is their perception not constant through actions such as those of the hand? To this he says: "Due to the absence of manifestors... and so forth; because of the absence of manifestors, there is a continuous non-perception of these [sounds].
"That which is the producer for you is itself considered the manifester of these [actions].
(1638) [The word] "āsām" refers to the actions.
