The opponent’s intention is as follows: "Just as for you there is no eternal perception because of the absence of a producer, so too for us there is none because of the absence of a manifestor; thus, the refutation is the same. (1638)
He refutes this with the words "Not so," and so forth: "It is not so;
for if the capacity were unimpeded, that cognition would occur continuously; but when it is separated from that [capacity], it would never occur at all. (1639)
Consequently, it is the manifestors (*vyañjaka*) of those [actions] that come together, not their causes;

as for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), its validity regarding permanence has already been refuted earlier. (1640) Herein there are two possible alternatives: those actions which are held to be manifested must either be inherently capable of producing cognition or not.
In that case, since capacity exists, one would necessarily obtain knowledge of them constantly— that is, eternally—
because that capable nature is eternal and thus unobstructed by anything;
for it is impossible to obstruct that which cannot have any excellence added to it without first producing a specific modification.
If, on the other hand, they lack capacity, then in the absence of that—that is, in the absence of capacity—that cognition could not arise at all; so what is the capacity of the manifestor?
Therefore, since those actions are held to be eternal, causes conceived as manifestors do not in any way cohere with them.
However, in the case of impermanent things, it is logical that a previously non-existent nature arises from a manifestor; thus, manifestors are appropriate for those [impermanent things].
Regarding what was stated—that their eternity is accepted as being like that of [the phonemes] on account of recognition—he replies:
"Recognition"—when eternity is the probandum, recognition is put forward as the reason; however, that [recognition] was previously refuted in the examination of the permanence of entities.

Regarding what was stated— "from the qualification of Caitra’s absence as determined by the non-existence of a means of valid cognition"— he says here: "But from Caitra’s absence in the house, his existence outside is not tenable," and so forth.
Because the suspicion of death can also be accounted for in another way;

if the absence from home while one is alive were intended to establish one's existence outside by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), this would not be the case, since there is no certainty even in that regard. (1641–1642)
For one who does not see Caitra in the house, being a person of limited vision, no means of valid cognition whatsoever exists regarding his connection with life;
"otherwise also" [is the case].
"The absence of Caitra in the house is established only through his being outside";
by this, he points out the inconclusiveness [of the reason].
Now, it is not mere absence that is stated here as the reason in this example of presumption (*arthāpatti*), but rather the absence from the house of the living Devadatta.
This is not correct;
why?
Because even in that case, since there is doubt regarding Devadatta’s being alive, the reason would be unestablished due to doubt (*saṃdigdhāsiddhatā*).

He states the reason for this uncertainty: "In the house," meaning that for one who perceives only what is proximate, there is indeed doubt because of the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determines the living state of that Caitra.

1642–1643 Now, it might be argued: "Even if the means of valid cognition consisting of perception does not exist for one of limited vision regarding Caitra’s being alive, inference and the other means certainly do exist. To this, he says: "Now," and so forth.
Now, when his being alive is ascertained through verbal testimony and other means,
and his absence from home is also ascertained, then this [non-apprehension] possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Regarding the phrase "through verbal testimony and other means":

The sound uttered by him is heard, or at that time a trustworthy person, though hidden behind a wall or such, says while performing austerities, "Caitra is alive. Furthermore, from non-existence—that is, from the form of the cessation of means of knowledge such as perception—and when there is the ascertainment of Caitra’s absence in his house, the absence of Caitra qualified by his being alive is established; thus, this presumption (arthāpatti) arising from non-existence would indeed possess the status of a valid means of knowledge.
He replies with the verse beginning "Even then" (tadāpi):
"Even then, the fact of being unconnected with the house is ascertained through the perception of non-perception;
therefore, in that case, the existence outside is determined solely from the inferential mark (liṅga). || 1645 ||

For a man who is not associated with the house is certainly seen as being outside, like a person standing at the door observed by those stationed within the courtyard of the home. Even an adversary becomes one who has entered the interior of the house in this regard.
"Therefore, this presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) does not differ from inference. Thus concludes the examination of presumptive testimony;
by this, he states its inclusion within inference.

For instance: Caitra is the subject (dharmin) here; his being outside is the probandum (sādhya); the reason (hetu) is his non-connection with the house despite being alive; a person standing in the courtyard of the house is the similar example (sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta);
but one who is inside the house is the dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
"Sadana" means a house;
the pervasion [of the reason] is ascertained by these two examples alone,
and thus the logical reason (hetu) is not unestablished (asiddha).
Since his absence from home is first established through the non-perception of what is perceptible, whereas his being alive is established only by the opponent’s admission,
the reason is in fact doubtful from the perspective of ultimate reality; for there is no means of valid cognition that definitively establishes his state of being alive.
But has it not already been stated that sound and so forth exist?

If that is the case, then since the living state is ascertained by the very same means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes sound and so forth, the existence of the person outside [the body] is thereby established; what, then, is the purpose of resorting to presumptive testimony (arthāpatti)?
Therefore, [this is accepted] on the basis of the opponent's own admission.
Having accepted the established reason, it has been demonstrated that presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) is included within inference. 1645–1646.
Thus concludes the examination of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); now follows the investigation of non-existence (abhāva).

With reference to non-existence (abhāva), he says: "Where the five means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) do not arise with respect to the nature of an object for the purpose of cognizing the existence of that object, there is the status of non-existence as a means of valid cognition. (1648)

In this regard, the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that existence and non-existence— the positive and negative characteristics— are both real entities, and that every object possesses a dual nature consisting of both existent and non-existent aspects.

Now, since an entity is established as being composed of both existent and non-existent aspects, for what reason does the pentad of means of valid cognition, ending with presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), fail to arise with respect to that aspect of the entity which is called the "non-existent" portion?
For the purpose of awakening the aspect of existence within the real entity— that is, for the purpose of awakening the existent portion of the entity—
therein, regarding the non-existent portion as the object of cognition (*prameya*), non-existence functions as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By this, only its object is indicated, but not its own nature.

To the question, "What then is its nature?", he says: "The non-arising of perception and so forth," etc.; the non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge is held to be the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*).
That [absence] is either the non-modification of the self or the cognition of another object.
The non-arising of the means of knowledge, beginning with perception and ending with presumption (arthāpatti), is accepted as "the absence of a means of knowledge" (pramāṇābhāva);
this is a genitive tatpuruṣa compound or a karmadhāraya compound.
In some versions, the reading is "abhāvaḥ pramāṇe";
in that case, the locative case is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*), and the singular number is used for the genus (*jātāvekavacana*).
The meaning is that among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), non-existence (*abhāva*) is a means of valid cognition.

As Śabarasvāmin has stated: "Non-existence (abhāva) is also the absence of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇābhāva), regarding an object that is not in contact [with the senses], such as 'it does not exist'. Now, what is this "non-arising" (anutpatti)? He says: "It is either the non-modification (apariṇāma) of the self (ātman) or a cognition (vijñāna) directed toward another object.

This refers to the non-arising of perception and the other means of knowledge; it is called the substance of the self (ātmadravya) in its state of equilibrium (sāmyāvasthā), which has not been modified into the form of a cognition of an object such as a jar, which is intended to be negated.
Or [is it] the cognition of a ground as distinct from a jar and so forth?
(1649) But surely, "non-existence" is said to be the absence of a real entity.

How can this [absence] be a real entity? For it might be suspected that a real entity cannot be a separation. Anticipating this, he states the following while establishing the reality of absence: "Because of the absence of valid cognition" (pramābhāvāt);
and from the absence of valid cognition regarding entities, their non-existence is apprehended;
moreover, this is divided fourfold according to the distinctions of prior absence (prāgabhāva) and so forth. || 1650 ||

If non-existence (*abhāva*) were not a real entity (*vastu*), then, because it would be devoid of all causal efficiency (*sāmarthya*), there could be no cognition of non-existence; furthermore, the fourfold division of non-existence—into prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth—would not exist. But this is not the case. Therefore, since the cognition of non-existence cannot otherwise be accounted for, and since the worldly linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) involving its fourfold division cannot otherwise be explained, non-existence must be a real entity.
Some maintain that these two arguments constitute the means of valid cognition known as presumption (*arthāpatti*);
others, however, describe the statement "and it is divided fourfold" as an inference (*anumāna*).
And they establish this through the following formal argument: non-existence is a real entity (vastu), because it is differentiated, like a jar or other such things.
Furthermore, explaining how its differentiation is fourfold, he says: "In milk, curd," and so forth.
That which does not exist in milk, such as curd and the like, is conceived as antecedent non-existence (prāgabhāva);
the non-existence of milk in curd is characterized as destructive non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva).
And that which is the absence of a horse and so forth in a cow is called mutual non-existence (anyonyābhāva).
It does not possess the form of another, and therefore its non-existence exists by way of its own nature.
The parts of a head that are sunken and devoid of growth and hardness are intended as "absolute non-existence" (atyantābhāva) in the form of a rabbit’s horn and the like. (1652–1653)

Furthermore, this worldly convention regarding the distinction between causes and effects would not exist if non-existence were not differentiated by [the four types of] prior non-existence and so forth. That which is perceived in the world as "the effect characterized by curd or a jar does not exist in its cause, such as milk or clay," is called prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
If prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) did not exist, then the effect such as curd would indeed arise from milk and so forth;
likewise, that which is the absence of what is called "milk" in the curd is posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*),
otherwise milk would indeed remain in the curd.
The absence of a thing such as a cow within another thing such as a horse is called mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*).
This is because that cow and so forth lacks the nature of another, such as the essence of a horse; therefore, the mutual non-existence of those two is asserted.
Otherwise, if mutual non-existence did not exist, horses and the like would indeed be present within cows and the like.

The parts of a rabbit's head, being devoid of depression, growth, and hardness, and being absolutely non-existent in the form of horns and the like, are called absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).
Although in this case, according to the actual state of things, it is a mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), it is nevertheless called absolute non-existence based on common worldly usage;
for generally in the world, the conventional treatment of mutual non-existence occurs through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), as in: "This is a cow, not a horse."
If absolute non-existence did not exist, it would not be the case that "this is not the horn of a rabbit," for then the horn would indeed exist on the rabbit;
as Kumārila has said: "Curd would exist in milk, milk in curd, and a cloth in a jar."

If this [scripture] were not authoritative, then there would be no horn on a rabbit, no consciousness in earth and the other elements, no form in the self, no smell in water, no taste in fire, nor those two [smell and taste] along with form in air, nor those three [form, taste, and smell] together with touch in space.
Thus, in that context: consciousness is the self (ātman),
and form (mūrti) is solidity (kāṭhinya).
Together with form,
those two— smell and taste— would exist in the wind along with touch, being accompanied by form.

Those [qualities]—form, taste, and smell—together with touch, would exist in the void (vyoman)—that is, in space—and furthermore, there would be no worldly transaction based on the distinction between causes and so forth if non-existence were not differentiated by its divisions such as prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and the rest;

for example, one who desires curd takes milk as the material cause, but one who desires milk does not take curd as the material cause; likewise, one who desires a cow does not take a horse, nor does one who desires a horse take a cow.
Thus, conventional usage proceeds through such distinctions as cause and so forth.
Furthermore, even if this [entity] has indeed undergone a fourfold division, why must it nevertheless exist as a real entity? To this he says: "And not of a non-entity," and so forth.
And these distinctions cannot belong to a non-entity; therefore, this [non-entity] possesses the nature of a real entity.
The non-existence of effects and so forth is that which is the existence of causes and so forth.
For a distinction of a non-entity is not logical, because it must have a real entity as its substratum.
Therefore, [the author] asks: "What kind of entity is non-existence (abhāva), and what is its nature as an entity? He replies: "Of effects and so forth.

The very existence of a cause, such as milk, is itself the non-existence of the effect, such as curd; and the very existence of an effect, such as curd, is itself the non-existence of the cause, such as milk. This is the nature of non-existence as an entity.

Furthermore, demonstrating its status as a real entity through inference, he says: "Or else," and so forth—"since it itself is the object of apprehension by the cognitions of inclusion and exclusion."

Therefore, like a cow or other such things, non-existence should be understood as a real entity because it is an object of cognition; this is the thesis. The two reasons are: "because it is apprehended by both inclusive and exclusive cognitions" and "because it is an object of cognition"; the example is "like a cow or other such things. (Verse 1656)

In that regard, the inclusive cognition (*anuvṛttibuddhi*) is the uniform notion "this is non-existence, this is non-existence" regarding all four types; the exclusive cognition (*vyāvṛttibuddhi*) is the notion characterized by distinctions such as "this is prior non-existence, not non-existence through destruction. Regarding this, three kinds of non-existence have been described by Kumārila.

The first [type of non-existence] is the non-modification (apariṇāma) of the self; the second is the cognition of the specific qualities of another object, because of the statement that "it is either the non-modification of the self or the cognition of another thing"; the third consists merely in the cessation of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa-nivṛtti-mātra), because of the statement that "the cognition produced by the three-fold [cause] is what is intended as inference, and dependence upon a cause does not apply at all to that which is of the nature of non-arising. Regarding this third type of non-existence, having raised an objection, he offers a rebuttal, saying: "If it is non-existence, how can it be a means of knowledge?"
If [you ask] how non-existence can be a means of knowledge (*māna*), what kind of object of knowledge (*prameya*) is there in this case?
For just as the object of knowledge is indeed non-existence, so too should the means of knowledge be accepted as such.
(1657) Now, it may be asked: "How can non-existence, characterized by the non-arising of perception, be a means of valid cognition?"
To this it is replied: as for what constitutes the object of cognition (*prameya*) here— if you say that the object of cognition is of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*),
then let it be accepted that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be exactly as the object of cognition is.
Why, then, is it said: "How can non-existence be a means of knowledge? For it is not logical that a definition [alone] constitutes a means of valid cognition"?

Let it be that non-existence (abhāva) possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (prāmāṇya); however, how is its distinction from perception (pratyakṣa) and the other [means of knowledge] established? To this he says:

"Because it is denoted by the word 'non-existence'... and so forth. Non-existence is indeed distinct from perception and the others among the means of valid cognition, just as it is distinct from the objects of cognition (prameya) that are non-existent. (1658)

Alternatively, non-existence (abhāva) is measured by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that conforms to its own nature, because it is an object of cognition (prameya), just like existence (bhāva); therefore, it is distinct from that which has the nature of existence.

The non-existence of the means of valid cognition such as perception is itself a means of valid cognition distinct from perception and the others, because it is denoted by the word "non-existence," just like the non-existence of an object of cognition.

Alternatively—the subject (*dharmin*) is the object of cognition called "non-existence" (*abhāva*); its property to be proven (*sādhya*) is the state of being an object of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) corresponding to itself; the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is an object of cognition" (*prameyatvāt*); and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is an object of cognition called "existence" (*bhāva*).
And that which is the means of valid cognition corresponding to itself is established as being other than perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the rest, which consist of existence.
1659. He provides the rebuttal with the words "In this regard," etc.:
"In this matter, the transformation of that which possesses eternal existence has been refuted."
"The existence of its opposite [non-existence] as something occasional is not tenable.
(1660) By this, he states the impossibility of the first definition, "the non-modification of the self.
For, by way of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), "non-modification" is intended as a definition that is the opposite of modification and is occasional.
For otherwise, if an occasional [state] were not intended by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), then there would always be the cognition of the existence of the entity;

and such non-transformation as described is impossible for the self, because transformation has been refuted for that which possesses eternal existence (*nityasattva*). Therefore, how could there be recourse to its opposite, non-transformation, by way of exclusion? In this context, *sattva* means the self (*ātman*), and it is called *nityasattva* because it is both eternal and existent.
Or alternatively: that which has eternal existence—that is, existence (sattā)—is so described; in other words, it is "eternal.
Thus, there is the existence of its opposite.
The opposite of that transformation is non-transformation; it is not logical for that [non-transformation] to be occasional.
Rather, it must exist at all times, because the self is one and eternally of a single nature.
Now, it might be thought: non-transformation is not an entity consisting of the opposite of transformation;
rather, it consists merely of the negation of transformation.
Therefore, it is not the case that the definition is impossible. To this, he says: "If its mere negation," and so forth.
If what is intended here is merely the negation of that [non-existence], then its existence as a real entity would be understood at all times, because that [negation] does not exclude it. || 1661 ||
The negation or rejection of that transformation is itself "mere-ness" (tanmātra); that which has this very [negation] as its essence or nature is called "non-transformative.
Because this non-transformative state, whose essence is negation, is eternally of a single form, there is an absence of transformation in the self.
Having conceded the point by saying "let it be so," he states the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpitā*) as a defect of the definition:
"Or let there be no transformation for this [self]; even so, there is inconstancy (*vyabhicāritā*)."
Because even when that [consciousness] exists during states such as sleep or fainting, the object is still possible;

and because when other cognitions are present, nothing else is seen apart from them—if it is argued that this [consciousness] is intended to exist in the form of the cognition of a jar and so forth, [we reply: 1662–1663.
What distinction was stated then between this second position and that which you indicated as two alternative positions,
[namely] that "it is subject to deviation"? (1664)

By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "fainting, etc.," states such as being obstructed or having one's back turned are included; [the fault of] over-extension applies even when those states are present.

Even though the substance of the self exists in an untransformed state, when there is the presence of another cognition distinct from the cognition whose object is the thing (such as a jar), it is precisely the cognition of the space devoid of the jar and so forth that is intended as the "untransformed" state,
because it is not transformed into the form of the cognition of the jar and so forth.
"Of him" means of the self;
"this" refers to that [self].
If it were thus non-modification, then no distinction would have been stated between this [view] and the second position— that consciousness [arises] from another object;
consequently, the presentation of two positions would be purposeless.
With the words "in another object," etc., he states the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāritā*) regarding the second definition of non-existence:

"If cognition occurs with respect to another object, then the non-existence of everything—even that which is imperceptible—would be understood, by relying on that second [definition] of non-existence. (1665)
"Even of that which is invisible" means even of that which is remote in terms of place, time, or intrinsic nature; "the absence of a second" [is established].
Or, regarding the cognition of another object,
when that which possesses a form equally capable [of being perceived] is present along with other causes [of cognition].
If it is argued that non-existence is perceived when there is no cognition of anything other than that [object], then it might further be said:
"It is not intended that the non-existence of everything unperceived is what is to be proven;
what then?"
"Of that which has a form possessing a corresponding capacity"—that is, that which has a form (yogyatā) corresponding to that perceived [locus] such as a place devoid of a jar or the like;
this means "of that which has reached the conditions for perception.
"The cognition of another thing distinct from it" refers to the cognition of a place devoid of a jar or the like.
He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "śakya" (1666): "Non-existence belongs only to that perception which has the appearance of an object capable of being seen."
This being so, she may be described as unerring for [the cognition of] others, but not otherwise.
(1667) How is a cognition that has arisen regarding another object known?
If it is held that cognition is considered imperceptible and is known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), (1668) [then...]
Since that [non-existence] is also essentially of the nature of knowledge, from where would its own apprehension come?

If it were said to be established by another presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result. (1669) This applies equally to the non-existence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the non-existence of the object of cognition (*prameya*).
If that were the case, how would an entity not be included within direct perception?

[The compound] "śakyadarśanavastvābha" is a *karmadhāraya* meaning: that which has the appearance (*ābhā*) of a thing capable of being seen—that is, a thing that has reached the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), and which is also direct perception; [it applies] to such things, and not to others.

Because inference and the other means of knowledge have as their object only that which is imperceptible, and there is no cessation of that which is imperceptible— being remote in terms of space, time, or intrinsic nature— even when those [means of knowledge] themselves cease to function.
Therefore, their cessation would be fallible,
and consequently, the inclusion of the term "etcetera" (ādi) in the phrase "non-arising of perception and so forth" would be meaningless.
Furthermore, it must necessarily be admitted that if the cognition of another object were determinate, it would thereby establish the absence of the counter-positive.

Otherwise, if non-existence were established from that [cognition] by its mere existence, it would follow that non-existence would be established for every person even from a cognition produced in relation to a single individual. In that case, how could that very cognition—which has arisen regarding an object other than that [intended one]—be known at all by that Mīmāṃsaka who maintains that cognition is imperceptible? It could not be known at all.
The connection with the subject at hand is: "if it is known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).
As it has been stated: "Since cognition is not established when its object is unknown, that cognition is inferred from the mark (*liṅga*) which is the knowledge of the object."

For here, the term *liṅga* (logical mark) denotes that which is otherwise inexplicable (*anyathānupapatti*); the meaning is that from that which is otherwise inexplicable, the object is known— that is to say, it is inferred, or rather, it is cognized as validly established (*pramīyate*).
If that is the case, then since that presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also of the nature of a cognition, it must be explained from where its own source is derived.
If you say it is from another presumption, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Furthermore, if the reality (*vastutva*) of non-existence (*abhāva*) is admitted, then just as the absence of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāva*) is a real entity, so too is the absence of an object of knowledge (*prameyābhāva*); therefore, why is non-existence not admitted to be simply perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) on account of its being a real entity?
By which [reason] another distinct means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara), called non-existence (abhāva), would have to be postulated for the sake of attaining that [non-existence].
With the words "of the effects and so forth," and so on, he establishes that [these] are indeed included within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For the non-existence of effects and so forth is indeed an existence [consisting] of the cause and so forth; and that, having a nature distinct from others, is apprehended by perception itself.

Thus it has been said: "The non-existence of effects and so forth is indeed the existence of the cause and so forth. And that existence of the cause and so forth, having a nature distinct from others—that is, a nature distinct from the effect and so forth—is simply perception. What other object of cognition (*prameya*) could there be for non-existence, such that there would need to be another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That for which there exists no object of cognition (*prameya*) distinct from [another] is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) from that [other], just like a seventh means of valid cognition; and for non-existence (*abhāva*), there is no object of cognition distinct from the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*). This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
(1671) Here, the opponent, raising the objection that the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), says: "In its own nature," and so forth.
In an entity that is eternally composed of both existence and non-existence by virtue of its own nature and the nature of others,
some aspect is known by some people at some time.
And when a portion of a positive entity is apprehended, the operation of perception and other means of knowledge occurs.
The operation [of cognition] occurs toward the aspect of non-existence when its non-arising is intended to be grasped.

(1673) If the object of knowledge were of a single nature, then there would be an absence of the object of knowledge; however, since an entity consists of both natures—being existent and non-existent respectively through its own-form and other-forms—while that entity consisting of both natures remains, a certain form—that is, its own-nature—is known by certain means of valid cognition, but not everything by all means. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "perception," etc.

When the positive aspect (*bhāvāṃśa*) is apprehended, then the operation belongs to the five means of cognition beginning with perception, not to the non-existence (*abhāva*). When the negative aspect (*abhāvāṃśa*) is intended to be apprehended, the operation belongs to their non-arising—that is to say, the non-existence [of those means] consisting in the non-arising of perception and the others.

The reason would be unestablished if a single entity could possess a dual nature; however, since it is contradictory for a single thing to have a dual nature, [the author], demonstrating this, says: "The very intrinsic nature," and so forth.

"Indeed, the very intrinsic nature of things is held to be excluded [from others]; and this [nature] exists as that [excluded] essence, and it is perceived by direct perception through that very essence. (1674)

A thing is not excluded from another thing by means of the other's form; rather, it is by its own form. Therefore, it is the very form—the very nature—of things that is perceived as excluded from other things, because they abide in their own respective natures.
And insofar as a thing is excluded by that [own] essence, that thing is indeed existent, not non-existent.
And this object is perceived as having an essence excluded from others; thus, there is no apprehension of a second form.

(1674) Thus far, the proposition that [reality] possesses a dual nature has been shown to be contradicted by perception. Now, demonstrating that it is also contradicted by inference, he says: "Arthakriyā... (functional efficacy).
That which is capable of causal efficiency is called "existent," and anything other than that is called "non-existent.
Since these two are contradictory, their coexistence in a single locus is not logical.
[Objection: If it is argued that [a thing] is capable with respect to its own effect but incapable with respect to another... [1675]
Indeed, this duality of form does not exist at all within a single entity.
If it is maintained that one [form] is entirely incapable of performing the function of the other, then two distinct entities would result; therefore, there is no duality of form for a single thing.

"That which performs a purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*) is existent, such as the form (*rūpa*) intended as existent; and that which does not perform a purposeful action is intended as non-existent"—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, two things that are mutually contradictory cannot be perceived simultaneously in a single entity, just as in the case of shade and sunlight, or cold and heat. Since the forms of existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory, [the opponent] raises the objection that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) regarding its own probandum, by means of the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

For instance—that very same single entity is capable of performing a causal function (arthakriyā) that it is itself to accomplish, but is incapable of performing a causal function to be accomplished by another; therefore, the reason characterized as "the capacity for causal efficacy" is unestablished (asiddha), because a thing's status as possessing causal efficacy is not established in relation to a causal function to be accomplished by another.
Furthermore, there is no mutual contradiction between the forms of existence and non-existence, due to the difference in their respective points of reference (apekṣā).

For instance: it is called "existent" with reference to the causal efficiency (arthakriyā) to be accomplished by itself, but it is called "non-existent" with reference to that which is to be accomplished by another. However, if it were called "non-existent" while referring only to its own [specific] accomplishment, there would be a mutual contradiction. To this, he states the resolution: "But indeed, that very same thing"—namely, that very nature of the entity which is capable regarding its own accomplishment is the same that is incapable regarding the accomplishment of another; it is not something else.
For a thing does not become different merely because of a difference in its relations,
since it is partless; such is the case here.
Therefore,
for that reason, there is no duality of form in a single entity.
Now, [the author] says "it is indeed another" to show that the form which is incapable of performing one purposeful action is indeed different, and not that very same [form].

In that case, you have merely established two distinct entities: that which is capable of causal efficiency is one thing, and that which is incapable is the second; you have not, however, demonstrated that a single entity possesses both natures.
1677 He states the refutation regarding the third definition of non-existence, which consists merely in the cessation of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa): "And of non-existence," etc.,
provided that the reality of non-existence has been previously accepted.
Furthermore, for what purpose is its formlessness (nīrūpatā) described?
It was previously accepted [as such] because of the statement that it is either the non-modification (apariṇāma) of the self, or consciousness, or another entity.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, "Its formlessness [is established] in this way, and thus its status as a means of valid cognition (*māna*) should also be accepted," the intended meaning— which will be explained later— is that it is not logical for that which is formless to possess the status of a means of valid cognition (*prāmāṇya*), because a means of valid cognition is characterized by the apprehension of an object.
Showing that very intention, he says: "Of the formless," and so forth.

For if the formless [cognition] were to lose its nature as cognition, its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) would not be tenable; for that [status] is characterized by the consciousness of the object of cognition (*prameya*). (1679)
This is the formal argument:

that which does not have the nature of the apprehension of an object of cognition is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as a jar or similar objects; and non-existence (*abhāva*) is devoid of the apprehension of an object of cognition. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

1679. It might be argued: "The eye and other [senses] do not have the nature of the apprehension of the object of cognition (*prameya-adhigati-rūpa*), yet they are called 'means of valid cognition' (*pramāṇa*) because they are the causes of the apprehension of the object of cognition; likewise, non-existence (*abhāva*) would also be so. To show that this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "Because it is the cause of that," and so forth.
If it is called a "means of valid cognition" because it is the cause of that [apprehension], like the eye and so on...
A thing devoid of form can never possibly possess the status of being a cause. Furthermore, how can that non-existence be apprehended as distinct from the nature of cognition?
If it is argued that it is known through the very absence of a valid cognition directed toward it, then there would be an infinite regress.

If non-existence were to be understood from the absence of a means of valid cognition due to the absence of an object, and from the absence of an object due to the absence of a means of valid cognition, there would be a mutual dependence.
Therefore, that which is the perception of one thing is itself called the non-perception of the other.
And that independent establishment [of consciousness] exists by its very nature because it is non-inert;

nor is it appropriate to assume it metaphorically on the grounds that it is the cause of valid cognition, since for that which is formless— characterized by the absence of all causal capacity— it is not logical for causality to be possible,
and if it were possible, it would entail the loss of its formlessness.
Because that [non-existence] would be indistinguishable [from existence], and because it would follow that consciousness would never cease while it exists;

furthermore, as was stated previously, it is not logical for that which is unestablished to be a means of cognition due to the risk of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, it must be explained how that non-existence is established. It cannot be established by itself, for if it were, it would follow that the absence of an object of knowledge (*prameyābhāva*) is also established by itself;

consequently, the conceptualization of non-existence would be useless, since its purpose is to establish the absence of the object of knowledge, and that absence of the object of knowledge would be established by itself just like the absence of a means of cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*).

Nor is its establishment through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), because since that [object] is distinct from the nature of cognition, how could it be apprehended by self-awareness, given that self-awareness perceives only the nature of cognition itself?

If, on the other hand, its establishment were through another means—namely, the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) directed toward it—then how is the establishment of that very absence of a means of valid cognition regarding that object achieved? If that too were established through something else, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

As it has been said: "The non-existence of an object is understood through non-perception; the non-existence of that perception [in turn] must be understood by another means, leading to an infinite regress. Now, lest there be such an infinite regress, one might accept that its establishment follows from the absence of an object of cognition (*prameya*).
This being the case, a circularity (itaretarāśrayatva) results;

for instance, the establishment of the absence of the means of knowledge follows from the absence of the object to be known (prameya), and the establishment of that [absence of the means] results in the establishment of the absence of the object to be known. Thus, the fault of circularity enters here most clearly; it is like the case where the eyeball enters while the pupil comes out.

Therefore, the non-apprehension of one thing is simply the apprehension of another; thus, there is no separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence" (abhāva) apart from perception (pratyakṣa).
It might be argued: "How is that very apprehension of one thing established? In that case too, the same difficulty as with non-existence would arise. To this he says: "And that," etc.
That perception of one thing is established by itself independently, not through anything else; therefore, there is no consequence of an infinite regress (anavasthā).
Why?
Because by its own nature—that is, by its very constitution—it is non-inert, meaning it has the nature of light;
nor does [the definition] over-extend to other things merely by virtue of their existence, because they do not possess that nature.
Now, he asks: "What is the aversion to the establishment of cognition through another? and says:
"Of cognition," etc.—the establishment of cognition from another [source] occurs either from a logical mark (*liṅga*) or even from another cognition.
Alternatively, if it were otherwise impossible [to establish the probans], then in every respect its occurrence would be non-existent.
If each of the three interrogations were possible, then for you there would be many endless and proliferating regressions here. (1684–1685)
Therefore, because only one [object] among those of equal capacity is perceived,
the fitness for the determination of non-existence in others is understood.
When any single [object] is cognized, the sky is understood to be devoid of the moon.
And how can the absence of all sound be ascertained in any particular case?

(1687) Some maintain that cognition is apprehended through an inferential mark (*liṅga*), and that this mark is either the knowledge of an object, or an action, or the sense-object, or the manifest object, and so forth.

Others maintain that cognition is perceived by a subsequent cognition (*buddhyantara-pratyakṣa*), and not as having the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvid-rūpa*), because of the contradiction between being the agent and the object with respect to itself.

Some [hold that it is established] through the impossibility of the known object otherwise: if cognition did not exist, the known object would not be established, because its nature is inherently insentient (*jaḍa*).
Thus, three positions have been stated.

Regarding the interrogation of each of those three—namely the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth—as to how that mark and so on are themselves established, if they were to be established, many infinite regressions (*anavasthiti*) would ensue.

For instance—that triad of the mark (*liṅga*) and so forth is unestablished if cognition itself is unestablished; therefore, its establishment must also be sought through something else. If one were to resort to yet another mark and so forth in that case as well, there would be the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) due to questioning at every step.

Therefore, from the perception of one [thing], the non-existence of others is cognized. When a negation is to be made regarding a particular place and time, the negation must be applied only to those things whose nature is equally capable of being perceived (*tulyayogyātman*), because it is impossible to negate others there.

However, when identity (*tādātmya*) is negated, the negation of everything must be understood as occurring, because everything is established as being "other than that" (*tadanyatva*). This is on the grounds that "it is not of that nature, but of another nature. Now, when one determines the absence of the moon in the sky, at that time there is no perception of anything else there, such that it could be said that "the absence of the other is established through the perception of one. For in ultimate reality (*paramārthatas*), there is no such thing as "space" (*ākāśa*) which could be seen as distinct from the moon.

Even that entity which others imagine to be real is beyond the reach of the senses. Furthermore, regarding the ascertainment of the absence of sound in a certain location, it must be asked: from the perception of what does this arise? It cannot be said to be from the perception of the patch of ground, because that [ground] and the sound do not share an identical state of perceptibility. For instance, the patch of ground is visible (*cākṣuṣa*), whereas sound is audible (*śrāvaṇa*). And it is accepted that mutual difference exists between two things that possess an identical state of perceptibility, according to the statement: "The mutual difference of two things associated with a single cognition consists in their not being mutually dependent."

Nor should it be said that [time exists] because of the perception of time; for there is no time distinct from external objects that could be perceived, and even that which is accepted by others as its constituent parts is beyond the senses. (1684)

He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "prakāśa" (illumination): "The perceiver considers that very mass of light and darkness to be space (*vyoma*), because there is neither existence nor perception of anything else. (1688)

Even the distinction from all [other] sounds is understood from the perception of the effect; and that [perception] is established ultimately through the self-awareness (*svavedana*) of other cognitions. (Verse 1689) "Of the aggregate" (*rāśeḥ*).
The connection is with the phrase "in consciousness" (*saṃvittau*).
For the perceiver perceives that very mass of light and darkness as "space," and nothing else;
for instance, by day or by night, one perceives it as being like sapphire or like a mass of clouds.
Furthermore, for the imagined space, there exists no color, shape, or the like other than that [mass of light and darkness]; thus,
because space as imagined by others does not exist apart from the mass of light and darkness, it is non-existent.
Since it is indeed beyond the senses, even the absence of all other sounds is understood through the non-apprehension of the effect, namely auditory cognition;

and that non-apprehension is established by the perception of other cognitions, such as those of the eye and so forth. Thus, here too, there certainly exists a single apprehension characterized by the perception of another cognition.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the existence of the cause is not pervaded by the existence of the effect, such that the cessation of that existence of the effect would necessarily cause the cessation of the former?
For causes do not necessarily become effective [or possess their purpose]. [Response:

We do not say that every existence of a cause is pervaded by the existence of the effect; rather, it is only a specific kind—characterized by unimpeded capacity—that is pervaded. It is only of that [specific kind] that negation is made here, not of every [cause].

For instance—even where the non-existence of a jar is established through the perception of a mere location—that too is simply the "non-perception of an effect," namely the non-perception of the perception of the jar;
because it is only the absence of a jar that meets the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) that is being proved, not the absence of every [object].
And what is it that meets the conditions for perceptibility?

That very thing which possesses unobstructed capacity—that specific nature (*svabhāva*) characterized by perceptibility which has been described as "whatever is a [perceptible] nature is necessarily perceived"—is indeed directly perceived.

Otherwise, even in this case, the existence of the jar would not be pervaded by the perception of the jar; and consequently, since the absence of that which does not pervade does not entail the absence of that which is not pervaded, the non-existence of the jar would not be established.

Therefore, every non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) should ultimately be regarded as nothing other than the non-apprehension of an effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), which serves as the basis for the conventional designation of non-existence.
With the words beginning "ittham" (thus), he states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason "because it is denotable by the word 'non-existence'":
"And thus, since its nature as a real entity (*vastu-rūpatva*) is established, [the cognition] whose essence is the means of knowledge of non-existence..."
Even when [the non-existent] is included [within the categories], its denotability by the word "non-existence" (abhāva) remains uncontradicted.
This is because, as stated in the passage beginning with "In this way, that which is the perception of one is said to be the perception of another," and so forth.

The phrase "even though it is included [within perception], it is not contradicted" means that even though non-existence (abhāva) is included within perception, its being denotable by the word "non-existence" is not contradictory.
By this, he states that the reason (hetu) is excluded from the counter-example (vipakṣa).

Or, regarding the claim that "non-existence is measured by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) corresponding to itself," this is a case of proving what is already established, for such correspondence indeed exists. 1691.
Thus ends the investigation of non-existence:
such is its conformity;
non-existence is the non-apprehension characterized by the apprehension of something else.

Furthermore, as for what some object: "Surely a cognition that has the mere absence of an entity as its objective support cannot be included within perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other [means of valid cognition], because it has the mere absence of an entity as its support, whereas perception and the others have real entities as their objects;

yet this [cognition] is not invalid, because it is non-discrepant (*avisaṃvādin*), for you who maintain that things undergo destruction without residue do not deny the absence of an entity"—this too has been answered by the foregoing.
It is not by that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that mere non-existence (*abhāvamātra*), devoid of qualifiers such as place and time, is apprehended;
rather, it is apprehended precisely with its qualifiers in the form: "In a certain place and so forth, a jar or the like does not exist."

And since that [cognition] occurs precisely through the capacity to apprehend the location and so forth in their isolated state, it does not possess a separate validity (*prāmāṇya*) of its own; for one conceptualizes the isolated location and so forth exactly as they were apprehended by perception.

Alternatively, even if there were an apprehension of a non-existence devoid of qualifiers, it would not be logical for the cognition grasping it to have validity, because its object is not a real entity (*avastu*).
Furthermore, the investigation into valid cognition for those seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is grounded in real entities; therefore, this [argument of yours] is trivial.
1691 Thus concludes the investigation into non-existence;
the investigation into the non-apprehension through reasoning.
With reference to reasoning (*yukti*) and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), he says: "When this exists, that necessarily comes to be; when it does not exist, that does not come to be.
Therefore, from this [cause], that [effect] necessarily arises; this is what is called "reasoning" (*yukti*). (1692)
The sage Caraka states that this [non-apprehension] is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*),
for it is not inference because no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*) can be found here.
By whatever apprehension an object is known, through the absence of that [apprehension], [the non-existence of the object is established].
Its non-existence is understood; this is considered its non-apprehension (anupalabdhi).
This too is a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), because it does not depend upon examples and so forth;
for even in the case of an example, non-existence is established by this very [means].

The realization that something is an effect because it exists only when another thing exists is a form of reasoning (*yukti*). Since this [realization] involves conceptual construction (*savikalpaka*), it is not direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); nor is it inference (*anumāna*), because there is no corroborating example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For even an example would require the realization of its being an effect based on the very fact that it exists only when the other exists; thus, one would have to seek another example for that as well, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, Caraka—the physician—states that this is indeed a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*):
likewise, the cognition of non-existence through the cessation of perception is non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
If this [analogy] were also a distinct means of valid cognition, the same reasoning as for inference (yukti) must be sought.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "kārya" (1694–1695).

The apprehension of both causal relation and non-existence is not restricted [to separate means], because in this case there is no distinction between the probandum and the probans. (1696) The compound *kāryakāraṇatābhāvapratipattiḥ* is analyzed as follows: "causal relation" (*kāryakāraṇatā*) and "non-existence" (*abhāva*) constitute "causal relation and non-existence" (*kāryakāraṇatābhāvau*); the apprehension (*pratipatti*) of these two is the compound. In that context, the apprehension of causal relation is by means of reasoning (*yukti*), and the apprehension of non-existence is by means of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*); thus they are connected respectively.
In this case,

whether it be a formal argument (*yukta*) or non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), even in these two types of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*).
To the question "How so?", he says: "tadbhāva... and so forth.
Apart from the state of being contingent upon that [cause], no other causal relationship is observed; apart from the non-perception of what is perceptible, no other non-existence is cognized. (1697)

In that case, there is no distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*). To explain: the probans is "occurrence when that occurs" (*tadbhāvabhāvitā*), while the probandum is "the state of being cause and effect" (*kāryakāraṇatā*); yet no distinction is perceived between these two, because they are synonyms, like the words *taru* and *pādapa*.

Furthermore, even in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), there is no distinction; for if what is intended is merely the cessation of perception, then since that is unestablished, the same faults as before, such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*), must be stated.
If, on the other hand, non-perception is simply the perception of something else, then it is included within the very category of "non-perception of the perceptible" (*dṛśyānupalabdhi*).

And by this [reasoning], non-existence is not being proven, because that is established by perception itself; for this very reason, he says: "leaving aside the non-perception of the perceptible," and so forth. (1697)
Now, if it is thought that the absence of the relation of cause and effect is not being proven with respect to the navel, but rather the absence of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), then he says:
"In the proof of the capacity for the conventional usage of its existence," etc.
At the time of the convention, the object known [by that term] exists as an illustration. (1698)
Thus concludes the investigation into reasoning and non-apprehension.

Regarding those two—the existence of cause and effect and their absence—the term "the state of that" (*tadbhāva*) refers to the conventional usage concerning them; that is, the practice characterized by the application of cognition and verbal designation. It is the fitness for such practice that is being established here.

And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things whose nature is invariably perceived immediately after the operation of a certain [agent] are fit for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of being its effect; for example, jars and the like, whose natures are experienced immediately after the operations of a potter and so forth at the time of their convention (*saṃketa*). And likewise, sounds have a nature that is invariably perceived immediately after the operations of the palate and other [articulatory organs]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Likewise, even in the case of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), when the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) [of absence] is to be proven, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: those things which are intended to have reached the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) and are not perceived in certain locations are fit for the conventional usage of their absence; for example, the head of a rabbit and the like are fit for the conventional usage of the absence of horns. And there is the non-perception of the categories such as the "Universal" (*sāmānya*)—which are intended by others to have reached the conditions for perception—in the brindled cow and other individuals that are accepted as their substrata. This is the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).

Because there is the perception of brindled cows and the like as distinct from that [universal], the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*); nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because manifestation will be refuted later, and because the conventional usage of "non-existence" is based solely on this much; nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Thus ends the investigation of non-perception through reasoning.
Regarding the investigation of possibility (*sambhava*):
in this context, "possibility" refers by implication (*lakṣaṇayā*) to a collection; and when the collection is understood, the members of that collection are understood.
For example: when the existence of a thousand is known, there is the cognition of the existence of a hundred and so forth.
Regarding this, he states the following objection—that this is not inference because of the absence of an illustrative instance (dṛṣṭānta)—beginning with the words "samudāya" and so on.
The constituents of a collection are the causes for establishing that collection;
the cognition of the possibility of a hundred and so forth arises from a thousand as an effect-sign (*kāryaliṅga*).
Thus ends the investigation of possibility (*sambhava*).

Since there is no aggregate distinct from its constituent members, and therefore the constituents themselves are the cause for the establishment of the aggregate, the cognition that a hundred and so forth arise from a thousand is produced solely from the mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅgaja*).
Thus concludes the investigation of possibility (*sambhavavicāra*).
Consideration of Tradition and Other [Means of Knowledge]:

Others, however, maintain that tradition (*aitihya*) and so forth are distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Among these, tradition is a succession of reports whose original speaker is not specified, such as: "A yakṣa dwells here in this banyan tree."
*Pratibhā* is knowledge that is independent of specific place and time, sudden, and indicative of what exists or does not exist;
for example, it occurs to a young girl, "Today my brother will come," and since that indeed happens exactly so, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding this, he states the refutation: "Tradition, intuition," and so forth.

Because tradition, intuition, and the like are for the most part subject to deviation, it is not possible for such things to possess the status of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). || 1700 ||
This is the investigation of tradition (aitihya) and so forth;
by the word "and so forth" (ādi), recognition (pratyabhijñā) and the like are included,
since these too have been accepted as valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) by certain others.
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*):
since even that which occurs within a dream is sometimes seen to be true, it would [absurdly] follow that it constitutes a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).
This concludes the investigation of tradition (aitihya) and so forth.
Having thus refuted other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in detail, he says "Or rather," etc., while refuting them in brief:
"Or rather, this effort is being made in the wrong place, since..."
The object is established as being of exactly two kinds: perceptible and imperceptible.
For indeed, the object is twofold: direct and indirect.
But surely there is yet another [category], namely that which is both perceptible and imperceptible, neither perceptible nor imperceptible? To this he says: "Both," etc.
For that other [category] consisting of both or neither is not at all tenable; for in a single cognition, action and non-action are contradictory in one and the same thing. (1702)

For an object that directly produces knowledge is called "perceptible" (pratyakṣa), whereas that which is the opposite of what has been described is considered "non-perceptible" (parokṣa) by the wise.
First of all, verbal testimony, analogy, and the like do not have the first type of object as their domain.
Because it would be included within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), memory would be rendered useless;
or, even if its object were beyond the senses (*parokṣa*), how could it be the object of all [cognitions] unless this [object] were directly perceived, like a perceptible thing? (1704–1705)
Even if cognition occurs by depending on another [object], is that [cognition] connected to it or not? Is there an appearance of distinction or not?
If it arises from something unconnected, the consequence of a lack of determinacy follows.
Furthermore, pervasion is not established if there were an appearance of difference [between the subject and the property].
As long as cognition has an imperceptible object, relies upon a connected entity, and does not apprehend its difference, that cognition is clearly inference. (1707–1708)
Thus concludes the examination of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

For it is not logical that a single entity should possess a convergence of multiple mutually contradictory properties, as this would entail the loss of its unity. To explain: an object is called "perceptible" (*pratyakṣa*) when it is the direct cause of a specific cognition that determines an object exactly as it was apprehended, without the mediation of a sign (*liṅga*) or the like.
And by defining it in this way, it is established that cognitions such as "sound is momentary" do not have a perceptible object.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a single entity to possess both activity and non-activity in one and the same respect, such that it would have the nature of being both perceptible and imperceptible based on its producing or not producing cognition.
Nor is it logical for it to have neither nature, because the negation of one nature in a thing is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other nature.

However, there is no contradiction between activity and non-activity when they pertain to multiple things in relation to a single object; for example, color and taste [are active] toward visual cognition, and likewise, a single thing may be active toward multiple objects, as color is [active] toward both visual and auditory cognitions. It is for this reason that he said, "of a single thing, in one place."
Therefore, there are only two kinds of objects;

in that regard, the validity of verbal testimony and the other means of knowledge must apply either to a perceptible object or to an imperceptible one—thus there are two positions. It cannot be the first case [the perceptible], because [verbal testimony] would then be included within perception, since its object-domain would be non-different from that of perception.

Now, if after an object has been apprehended through perception, it is apprehended by those [other means] once again, he says: "Or there would be futility, because it would be the grasping of what is already grasped, leading to the consequence of invalidity, just like memory.

Regarding the second position as well, that remote object, being the object [of inference], must either be perceived directly or indirectly through dependence on another; therein, it cannot be direct, because that would entail its non-remoteness (non-inferentiality), like a perceptible object.

For this very reason, it is called "indirect" (*parokṣa*), because it does not produce cognition directly. If it were to produce cognition directly, one would have to ask: how could it be called "indirect"?

Furthermore, regarding the apprehension of an indirect object, four possible positions arise: [the cognition] may arise from something connected or from something unconnected; and it may appear as a distinction (*bhedābhāsa*) or appear as non-distinction (*abhedābhāsa*).
As for the appearance as a distinction—for example, the cognition of a specific fire, such as one produced from grass or leaves, arising from the generality of smoke (*dhūmasāmānya*).
If there were an appearance of non-difference— as when smoke leads to the determination of fire alone as excluded from heterogeneous things—

there would be instability in cognition due to the lack of a necessary connection, whereby anything could be understood from anything at all. Alternatively, if there were an appearance of difference, then the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason by the probandum would not be established, because a concomitance (*anvaya*) with a particular instance is impossible.
Consequently, it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Alternatively, if it is an appearance of non-difference, then its inclusion is within inference itself; demonstrating this, he says: "Regarding an object that is beyond the senses," and so forth, ending with "not apprehending its difference."
If it is devoid of the appearance of difference and determines the mere object as excluded from those of a different class—
just as the cognition of mere fire from smoke— then such [cognition] is clearly inference, because it has the perception of a relation as its means, like the cognition of fire from smoke.
Thus concludes the examination of other means of valid cognition; [this is] the examination of the doctrine of manifoldness (syādvāda).
In order to establish that [the entity] is not mixed with the nature of another even by the slightest part, he begins with an objection, saying "But surely" (nanu) and so forth:

"But surely, if an object consists of multiple natures, just like a variegated gem, then what contradiction could there be for [the categories of] Being and the rest being [simultaneously] present by their very nature? (1709)
As it has been said: "That which is capable of causal efficiency is called 'existent,' and anything else is called 'non-existent';
a coexistence of these two in a single locus is not tenable due to their contradiction."
In this regard, the *ahrīka*s (Nirgranthas) and others object:

"Every entity indeed possesses a manifold nature consisting of both the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), just like a gem that reflects variegated colors. Therefore, how can there be a contradiction between existence (*sat*) and the other properties, such that it is said: 'There is no co-inherence in one place,' and so forth?
By the word 'and so forth' (*ādiśabda*), [properties such as] action and non-action, unity and plurality, and so on are included."

Although this objection has already been refuted by the passage beginning with "But surely that [is the same]," it is stated again here either to provide a detailed exposition or to present another argument.

In that regard, in order to prove that [the object] consists of both the universal and the particular, the shameless one (the opponent) states two formal arguments in sequence, beginning with: "Existence... (bhāva iti).
An entity that is not distinct from another entity does not differ from a sky-flower.
If it were devoid of non-distinctness, it could not be established as different from them.

(1710) Suppose there is some intended object, such as a jar; if that entity, the jar, were non-distinct from another entity, such as a cloth—that is, if it were excluded from it—then it would have no distinction from a sky-flower, because it would be excluded from all other entities whatsoever. And for something excluded from other entities, no other possibility exists except that of being a sky-flower.

Therefore, by one who accepts that this entity is not equal to a sky-flower, it must be admitted that its being a "real entity" (vastutva) is a generality (sāmānya) consisting in its equality with other entities. Thus, its nature as a generality is established. If it is asked, "In that case, how is its nature as a particular (viśeṣa) established?"—it is said in reply: "If it were devoid of inequality [from others], it could not be established as distinct from them. That is to say, if that very entity, such as a jar, were devoid of that inequality which it possesses relative to another entity such as a cloth—that is, if it were not unequal to that jar.

In that case, the cognition "this is a jar" and "this is a cloth" would not establish that the jar and so forth are distinct from words and the like; yet they are indeed distinct, as if from their own intrinsic nature.
Therefore, the fact that they consist of particularity (viśeṣa) is also established.
With the words "In every way" (*sarvathā*) and so forth, he extensively supports the meaning of these very two syllogisms:
for even if one intends this entity to be unequal in every respect, [the following holds].
The nature of being an entity is necessarily forfeited by another entity.
For when an entity has ceased to exist, what other possible state can be perceived for it, except non-existence, like a lotus in the sky? || 1711–1712 ||
Therefore, by one who desires that this entity not be equivalent to a sky-flower, the universal called "substantiality" (vastutva) must be admitted as its similarity to other things.
Otherwise, [the author] states another argument for proving that it possesses the nature of a universal, beginning with the words "for that cognition would not exist," and so forth.
Otherwise, why is it that this cognition does not occur with respect to crows’ beaks and the like,
but is restricted solely to [real] entities?
If you say this restriction is due to similarity (*sārūpya*), then for us, that very thing is the universal (*sāmānya*).
The power that conforms to intrinsic nature has been described by this very [argument].
Therefore, absolute difference does not at all hold for anything;
for every thing is differentiated from others only by way of its own objective form.
"Otherwise" means:

if an entity (*bhāva*) were not similar to other entities, then one must state the reason why the identical cognition "this is an entity, this is an entity" arises with respect to jars and the like, but not with respect to things such as a crow's teeth. If you say that similarity (*sārūpya*) is the cause, then it is established that this very thing is the universal (*sāmānya*), for similarity is a synonym for the universal.

If you argue that there is a persisting power (*śakti*) residing only in jars and the like, and not in things such as a crow's teeth, and therefore this power inherent in their own nature (*svabhāva*) is the cause; [we reply:]...
That [universal] too has been described by this very same principle of similarity;
that is to say, the response here is the same as in the case of similarity,
because it would follow that it itself would possess the nature of a universal.
Therefore, it is established that all things, such as pots and the like, are mutually non-different in their nature as real entities. 1714–1715.
To establish the distinction [between the two], he says:
"If that which is devoid of dissimilarity from the objects taken as limits," and so forth.

That entity would not be different from those [parts], for its non-difference from them would be like its own nature (tadātman). Indeed, a difference in form (*vairūpya*) is defined as being distinct from their essential nature; yet to claim that this difference in form is both [distinct] and not distinct is a mutual contradiction.

Therefore, by one who accepts the difference of objects in some way, their dissimilarity must also be accepted; hence, they possess the nature of particulars (*viśeṣātmatā*). (1719) [From those that have been made the limits...]

If a jar or the like were devoid of dissimilarity (*vairūpya*) from other objects such as a cloth, then, due to non-difference, that jar would not be distinct from those cloths; for it would follow that they are non-different, just like its own essential nature (*ātmasvarūpa*). To explain: the very essence of the jar and so forth that is distinct from the cloth and others is indeed what is called "dissimilarity," and nothing else.

Consequently, to say that there is no difference between the jar and others despite the existence of dissimilarity is a contradiction of one's own words, because "difference" (*bheda*) and "dissimilarity" (*vairūpya*) are synonyms.

Having thus established that [reality] consists of both the universal and the particular, he says the following to demonstrate that these two—the universal and the particular—are the causes of linguistic usage without being confused: "This entity is indeed of a single nature;
this very entity, though of a single nature, is held to possess manifold forms, and these [forms] exist as objects of apprehension by the cognitions of inclusion and exclusion. (1720)
These [latter] are proclaimed as "universals" (sāmānya) because they are inclusive;
however, the others are designated as "particulars" (viśeṣa) because they are exclusive.

Herein lies the ultimate truth: like a multi-colored gem, a single entity possesses multiple forms; and among those forms, some are apprehended by inclusive cognitions, while others are apprehended by exclusive cognitions.

In this regard, those things which are apprehended by a cognition of conformity are proclaimed as "universals" (sāmānya) because of their conformity; whereas those others which are apprehended by a cognition of exclusion are postulated as "particulars" (viśeṣa) because of their exclusion. Therein, the cognition of conformity has a non-differentiated form such as "existence, existence," and so forth; the cognition of exclusion has a differentiated form such as "this is a jar, not a cloth," and so forth.
To this he provides a rebuttal, beginning with "If they were mutually identical in nature," and so forth:
"If the universal and the particular were mutually identical in nature..."
In reality, this confusion does not occur; thus, a dual nature is not tenable.
Even if these two lack each other's intrinsic nature, multiplicity would follow; and even in such a state, a dual nature is not established. (1722–1723)
In this regard, there are two positions: is that which is the universal (*sāmānya*) itself the particular (*viśeṣa*), or rather, is the universal one thing and the particular another?
Regarding the first position, if the universal and the particular were mutually identical in nature, there would be confusion (*saṅkara*);

consequently, due to the absence of any distinction such as "this is the universal" and "this is the particular," it would not be logically tenable for a single entity to possess a dual nature in ultimate reality.

Now, if the second position is adopted on the grounds that there must be no confusion (*sāṅkarya*) between the two, then even if their mutual absence of essential nature (*parasparāsvabhāvatva*) is admitted, a plurality—that is, a difference in essential nature (*svabhāvabheda*)—between the universal and the particular necessarily follows.

For this non-confusion between the two would only occur if there were a plurality between them; and even if such a state of affairs exists—that is, even if there is plurality—it would merely result in two distinct entities, and thus it is not logical for a single entity to possess a dual nature.

Now, it might be argued: "Even if there is indeed a mutual distinction between the universal (*sāmānya*) and the particular (*viśeṣa*), nevertheless the entity consisting of both the universal and the particular is itself non-different.
This, however, is mutually contradictory;

for instance, if the non-difference of the universal and the particular from a single entity is admitted, how could a mutual distinction between their own natures be established? Because, given their non-difference from one [entity], they would necessarily follow as being non-different from each other as well, just like the nature of that single entity.

Furthermore, if the mutual distinction between the universal and the particular is admitted, a single entity non-different from them would not be established; for, being non-different from those two, that which is intended as one would result in duality, just like the nature of the universal and the particular themselves.
Therefore, the claim that "one thing consists of both" is mutually contradictory. 1722
With the words "Even though," and so forth, he raises the objection of Sumati:
"Even though there is a single nature, a distinction of properties is established here."

And there is no contradiction in the coexistence of difference [and identity], just as in the case of the potencies of causal factors. Furthermore, it is not the case that what is observed is untenable; for even when there is identity between the universal and the particular, the adherence to worldly practice based on their difference is observed.
