How can they accept— or indeed how could they admit— that the states are non-different from the entity itself?
For the states do not exist without having first come into being, and having come into being, they perish.
And yet, an entity is not accepted as being such [i.e., momentary], because its existence at all times is admitted;
therefore, how could those [states]—being non-existent before they come into being and perishing after they have arisen—be logically identical with that [entity]?
They certainly cannot.
Because their acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are distinct;

for otherwise, since they would be identical in nature to it, there would follow the consequence that these [states] also exist eternally, just like the intrinsic nature of a thing (*vastu-svabhāva*), due to their non-difference from it. Or else, there would follow the consequence that the thing itself does not exist prior to its manifestation and so forth, just like the specific form of the states themselves.

Granted that there may be a conceptualization of distinct states, even so, the superimposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*) has not been avoided at all. To explain: in the middle state, does the entity act by its own nature (*svarūpa*) or by the nature of another? If it acts by its own nature, then since that very same nature exists in the other two conditions—the past and the future—how could this agent-nature undergo both activity and the cessation of activity?
If, on the other hand, it acts by the nature of another, then it would follow that it is a non-agent once again, which leads to the undesirable consequence of its being a non-entity.
Thus, first of all, it is not logical that the very same entity, such as fire, exists in both past and future states.

Suppose, then, that it is something else; in this case, one might argue that there is no fault of the confusion of mutually contradictory properties—such as activity and non-activity—in a single locus, because the entities are distinct.

However, that entity which is fit for effects such as burning and cooking, namely fire and so forth, would arise having previously not existed, and would perish after having existed; thus, there would be a contradiction with the doctrine of eternal existence, due to the absence of any underlying persistence (*anvaya*).

It might be argued: "Even though a thing arises having not previously been capable of causal efficiency, and perishes after having existed, nevertheless, in its past and future states, the entity continues to exist as something incapable of causal efficiency; therefore, there is no contradiction with the acceptance of its eternal existence. To this, he says: "That very same [entity]..."
"That alone is a real entity which is capable of causal efficiency;
and that [efficiency] does not exist in those two [the past and the future]. Since it does not exist, the production of an effect from them is impossible.
(Verse 1821) "That alone" refers to...
"Capable of causal efficiency in those two" refers to the past and future states.
That which exists [as such] is unfit for causal efficiency.

Now, it might be argued: "The capacity for producing an effect is indeed admitted even in the past homogeneous cause (*sabhāgahetu*) and others; therefore, the claim that 'an effect cannot arise from that' is unproven. To this he replies: "And the past entity, because it comes into being after not having existed, clearly becomes present, just like other [present] things; and it is also characterized by occasional occurrence (*kādācitkatā*). (1822)
If there were no cause, an entity would either always exist or never exist, as it would not depend on anything else;
moreover, an object is said to be "present" when its existence is restricted by a cause.
This is considered by others to be the distinction [of a present thing] from cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and other such states.

And the conditioned nature (*saṃskṛtatva*) of form and the other aggregates arises from their connection with birth (*jāti*), duration (*sthiti*), and so forth. In that regard, it is said that "birth" is the producer of this [entity]; yet, as a producer, it is neither different nor non-different from that form which has not yet been born. (1824–1825)
First, an excellence that is non-different from that [entity] cannot be produced,
because it exists even prior to its manifestation, just as it does after manifestation. On the other hand,
an excellence that is different does not exist, because there would be no connection due to their distinctness.
Furthermore, there would be the consequence of the non-existence of the effect [prior to its production], because it is non-existent beforehand.

Moreover, regarding its alteration, persistence, or destruction, these very same faults concerning aging and so forth follow from the alternatives of its being either different or non-different [from its prior state]. (1827–1828)
"Like anything else" means like the present time, which is not a subject of dispute;
"also because of its occasional nature" means likewise.

The connection is that "the present [entity] follows the same logic as others. Nor is this reason devoid of positive concomitance (*ananvaya*); for instance, whatever object is produced by causes and conditions is called "present," and whatever is occasional must necessarily have causes and conditions as its source. This is because for that which is causeless, there are only two possibilities: either it exists at all times or it does not exist at all, since it would not depend on anything else. Therefore, whatever is occasional necessarily has its existence produced by causes and conditions; and whatever has its existence produced by causes and conditions is necessarily present. Thus it is established.
Furthermore, there is a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between being present and being occasional;
moreover, if the past and future existed substantially (*dravyataḥ*), it would follow that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are eternal.
Consequently, no distinction would obtain between form (*rūpa*) and the other aggregates on one hand, and analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and so forth on the other.

Now, others hold the view that because form and so forth possess the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*), they are conditioned, whereas space and so forth are not; thus, form and so forth are distinct from cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*) and the like. This is incorrect. For instance, these four are the characteristics of the conditioned: birth (*jāti*), aging (*jarā*), duration (*sthiti*), and impermanence (*anityatā*).
In this regard, it is accepted that their functions consist of such things as producing: birth produces, duration stabilizes, aging causes decay, and impermanence brings about destruction.

In this regard, what specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) does *jāti* produce such that it is called the "producer" (*janikā*) of form (*rūpa*) and so forth? Is this distinction produced by it something distinct (*para*)—that is, separate—from that form and so forth, or is it non-distinct (*apara*)—that is, not separate? These are the two alternatives.

First of all, it cannot be non-distinct; because that distinction would have been already accomplished even prior to the operation of the *jāti*, it would be impossible to bring about, just as it is after its accomplishment.
For it is not logical for that which is already accomplished to undergo further action, as that would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Nor is an excellence (*atiśaya*) produced as something distinct; for if it were distinct, a relationship such that "this excellence belongs to this form and so forth" could not be established.
To explain: the relationship cannot be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), because their distinctness is admitted;
nor can it be admitted [as identity], because that would entail the previously mentioned logical faults.
Nor can the relationship be characterized by "arising from that" (tadutpatti), because arising occurs only from the universal (jāti) itself;
nor is there any other relation, since relations such as that of container and contained are included within "arising from that.

If, on the other hand, "arising from that" were admitted, then since the particular arises solely from that [the universal], it would follow that the particular arises eternally; thus, what service would the universal perform?

If it is argued that [the cause] produces [the effect] by depending on the genus (*jāti*), this is not so; for dependence upon a genus that provides no assistance is illogical, as it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Alternatively, if there is assistance, then upon considering whether that assistance possesses excellence or is distinct [from the entity], there follows the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Therefore, a relation is established only when there is a distinction [between the terms].
Furthermore—since that excellence did not previously exist, one would have to admit the doctrine of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*).

Likewise, when aging effects alteration, stability effects persistence, and impermanence effects destruction, whatever faults arise from the dilemma of whether these [alterations and so forth] are different or non-different from the original entity must be stated to apply to aging and the others just as they do to "birth" (*jāti*). (Verse 1822)
These [factors], such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth, initiate their own effects by means of a nature consisting in a restriction of capacity; yet that very form exists both before and after.
And since the form of capacity exists [at all times], why do they not initiate [their effects] at that time?
At the commencement of its own corresponding activity, there is the state of being unlimited in time (amitādhvatā).

Furthermore, as for the fact that universals (*jāti*) and so forth are held to initiate their own effects due to a restriction of their capable nature (*samartha-svabhāva*), since that capable nature of theirs exists at all times, it follows that they would always be initiating their own effects.
Nor can there be a deficiency in causes and conditions, because those too are eternally present.

Consequently, because birth and other factors would perform their own functions, such as production, during both past and future states, it would follow that there is an infinite number of temporal paths within even a single path.
Furthermore, are entities such as the past and so forth momentary or not? If the former, then for those two [past and future], that same state of having immeasurable time-periods follows;
for the very moment that arises therein becomes the present.
That which, having arisen, has perished is the past; that which is yet to be is the future.
(1832) Furthermore, there are two positions: whether the past and future are momentary (*kṣaṇika*) or not momentary.
In that regard, if the first position holds—that they are momentary—then the very same [fault of] having infinite time-periods (*adhvan*) follows.
He demonstrates that very [moment] which is called "the moment" (kṣaṇa) in verses 1831–1832.

Moreover, if they were non-momentary, your established doctrine would be contradicted; for in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), it is proclaimed that "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary.
(1833) Now, if the position is that they are non-momentary, this results in a contradiction with the established doctrine—by which "established doctrine" (*kṛtānta*) is meant the *siddhānta*.

For it is the established tenet that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary (1833). There is also sublation by reasoning: if they exist, they must necessarily be subject to momentary destruction.
For here, an obstruction [to the opponent's position] has been established as if it were present.
Furthermore—not only is there a contradiction with our own tenets, but there is also a contradiction with authoritative scripture (māna) regarding the proposition;
for instance, by the rule that "whatever exists is momentary, just like the present, and since the past and future exist, they too must follow as being subject to momentary destruction."

But previously—in the section on momentary destruction—it was established that this reason is invariable (*apratibaddha*); thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). To explain: the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is the definition of existence (*sattva*). Since causal efficiency is incompatible with a non-momentary entity by virtue of its contradiction with both successive and simultaneous action, the cessation of causal efficiency entails the cessation of existence, which is defined by it; thus, existence is excluded from the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*).
These past and future [entities] must either be capable of causal efficiency or not; if they possess the reality of capacity, they would be present, like anything other than them.
But if they lack the state of being present, they are devoid of all power.
It would follow that [past and future things] are non-existent, like a sky-lotus and the like.

(1836) Furthermore, all unconditioned things such as space are subject to the same objection; since they are postulated as being non-conclusive [regarding the proof of existence], they too cannot be the basis [for establishing the existence of past and future things]. (1837)
The capacity for restricted purposeful action in entities arises from conditions;
if there were no cause, everything would be applicable everywhere simultaneously. The production of the capacity for restricted purposeful action is fashioned by conditions.
There is no other characteristic for an entity that is present than this [characteristic of existence].
And since that [characteristic] exists unimpaired for you in the past and future entities as well, why does the state of being present not follow for them too? (1839–1840)
Furthermore: regarding these past and future [entities], there are two alternatives—they must either be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) or not.

If they are capable, then, given the existence of that capability, they would necessarily follow as being present, just like the present which is beyond dispute. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is capable of causal efficiency is present, just like the undisputed present; and the past and so forth are capable of causal efficiency. This is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) based on a reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Nor is this [reason] inconclusive, because if presentness were excluded, it would follow that all things past and future are devoid of all capacity, like a sky-lotus;

the formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: those which are not present are not capable of anything whatsoever, just like a sky-lotus; and since past things and so forth are not present, there is a non-perception of the pervader (vyāpakānupalabdhi).

Nor is there an inconclusiveness due to the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) factors—space, analytical cessation, and non-analytical cessation—for these too are included within the subject of the proposition (pakṣa).
Therefore, there is no basis for the hypothesis of inconclusiveness;

for it must be admitted that this capacity of entities for specific causal efficiency arises from conditions. Otherwise, if it were causeless, then in the absence of a determining cause, the specific capacities of entities would not exist, and consequently, everything would be applicable to every effect.

Therefore, since it is not logical for there to be a restriction of capacity in unproduced things such as space and so forth, there is no basis for the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) based on them. Nor is there the fallacy of the reason’s presence in a doubtful counter-example (*saṃdigdhavipakṣavṛttitā*) in the first argument; because that which is produced by causes and conditions—the power inherent in a restricted causal efficiency—is precisely the definition of the present. And since this complete definition of "presentness" exists even in the past and so forth, why would the status of being "present" not follow [for them] as well, given the absence of any other determining factor? (1835)
One thousand eight hundred and thirty-six, one thousand eight hundred and thirty-seven, one thousand eight hundred and thirty-eight.
Therefore, this effort toward union with heaven or liberation is fruitless.
Indeed, no fruit whatsoever to be accomplished through effort (*īhā*) is observed here.

Furthermore—for one for whom the past and the future exist substantially (*dravyataḥ*), the fruit also exists eternally; thus, effort aimed at attaining heaven (*svarga*) or liberation (*apavarga*) would be fruitless, because there is no fruit whatsoever to be accomplished by effort. In that case, what efficacy could there be for effort characterized by vows (*vrata*), observances (*niyama*), and so forth?
If it is argued that there is capacity for production,
then it is established that production occurs by coming into being after not having been;
or, if that [production] also exists [already], then what has capacity now, and for what?

If it is argued that [the cause] possesses the capacity to bring [the effect] into the present, what is this so-called "bringing into the present"? Is it the drawing [of the effect] from another location?
In that case, it follows that the entity is eternal, because it exists at all times.
Since formless entities such as sensation (*vedanā*) and the rest are inactive, how could there be an attraction?
And it is established that this very attraction comes into being after having not existed before.

Heaven is the summit of Mount Sumeru and so forth; apavarga is liberation. The attainment of these two is their conjunction (*saṃsarga*); the effort toward that consists of vows, observances, and the like.
Now, if it is not admitted that they possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-śakti*), [then...]
If this is so, then for this very reason their non-existence follows, like a flower in the sky. Alternatively, if the second position is adopted— that they are incapable of causal efficiency— then,
for that very reason of being devoid of causal efficiency, their non-existence follows, like a flower in the sky.
Since non-existence is characterized by the absence of all causal capacity (sarvasāmarthya-viveka),

having thus stated the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establishes the non-existence of past and future things, he says "the reasons," etc., in order to refute the means of valid cognition that establishes their existence.
The reasons, which are properties of an entity (*bhāvadharma*), do not share in the status of being established when [the subject] is unestablished;
or else, they are contradictory because they subvert the locus (*dharmin*) due to the establishment of its present existence.

(1843) For the previously mentioned reasons—such as "because of being included within the time-periods" (*adhvasaṃgṛhītatva*) and so forth—are unestablished in their substratum (*āśrayāsiddha*), since the locus, such as the past and so on, is itself unestablished.
As it has been said: "A property of an entity does not exist when [the entity] is unestablished.

Even if they were established, nevertheless, because their existence in the present is established, these reasons are contradictory (*viruddha*), as they prove a nature contrary to the actual character of the property.

How, then, is it taught that past and future forms and so forth are included within the time periods? For a rabbit’s horn, being absolutely non-existent, is not established as either past or future. To this he says: "Having been," and so forth. That form which, having existed, has ceased, is declared to be the past;
that which is to be, provided there is a completeness of conditions, is the future. (1844)
However, it has been established that if [the object] were a sentient being (*sattva*), the status of being present would necessarily follow;
for the mere state of existing is the definition of that which is present. This is easily understood.
If that is so, how then is the existence of form, sensation, and so forth taught? To this he says: "The state of being form and so forth," and so on.

Having superimposed upon this [present entity] its past state, which consisted of form and so forth, as well as its future state, it is described as such; however, this is not so in terms of its actual existence.
(1846) "That state" refers to that condition.
Regarding that state [of consciousness], he asks: "If it is thus dependent on two, how then was consciousness said to have a single basis? He replies: "In dependence upon a dyad."
Regarding what was stated by the Seer of Reality—that consciousness arises dependent upon a dyad—that teaching was intended with reference to the mind that possesses an object.

For consciousness is indeed twofold: that which has an objective support (*sālambana*) and that which does not (*anālambana*). It was with reference to that which has an objective support that the Blessed One taught the doctrine of consciousness having a dual basis.
1847. Now, as to how it is determined that even cognition exists without an objective support (*nirālambana*), he says: "Of the cognitions of an eternal God and so forth," etc.;
for indeed, there is no objective support whatsoever for the cognitions of an eternal God and the like.
"Because of the separation of those [cognitions] from the forms of dharmas such as sounds and names.
(1848) By the word "etcetera," imagined entities such as *pradhāna* and time are included.
He states that it should not be thought that these cognitions have sounds and so forth as their objective supports, saying: "sounds, names, etcetera," and so on.

The form (*ākāra*) of that [object], such as God (*īśvara*) and so forth—characterized by eternality, being the cause of all things, and so on—which is determined (*adhyavasīyate*) by that cognition, is the form with which the word or name is dissociated; this refers to a specific dissociated formation (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-viśeṣa*), or, by the word "and so forth" (*ādiśabdena*), to the cause (*nimitta*) and other such factors accepted by others, whose nature consists of the reflection of the object (*arthapratibimbaka*) and so on. (1848)

If, then, consciousness exists even without an object, how is it designated as "knowledge"? For it is said that "that which cognizes is consciousness"; and if there is no object to be known, what would constitute consciousness? To this he replies: "By virtue of the mere accompaniment of awareness. It is called "consciousness" by virtue of the mere accompaniment of awareness; and this [designation] is attributed to it because its nature is non-inert, due to its luminosity. (1849)
If it is argued that even the following of awakening is not possible without awakening, he says: "And that"— that is, the following of awakening— "of this"— of consciousness.

What is being said? That which is its non-inert nature is designated as "the nature of consciousness" because it possesses the nature of light—like light existing in the sky—due to the absence of any other object to be illumined and the lack of any other illumination.
(1849) And how can that which has transcended action bestow a fruit? To this, he says: "It is the cause of maturation," and so forth.
The ripening cause (*vipāka-hetu*) is not accepted as yielding its fruit once it has passed away;

rather, the fruit is held to arise from the continuum of consciousness (*vijñāna-prabandha*) which has been perfumed (*vāsita*). Perfumed means that which has been produced as capable of generating a fruit through a successive series.

If this is so, how was it said by the Blessed One: "There is that karma which has been exhausted, ceased, and transformed"? He says: "With reference to that very [impression]"—that is, with reference to that very impression (*vāsanā*) within the continuum of the mind (*cetaḥ-santati*).
"It is taught that 'karma exists' by way of figurative usage (*bhaktyā*), as if it were the destruction of the root.
Regarding "by way of figurative usage" (*bhaktyā*), this means by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāreṇa*).

Just as when a continuous stream of results such as gold produced from a primary substance exists, that primary substance is said to be "unperished" even though it has perished, so too is karma [said to exist].
To the question, "What is the purpose of this teaching by way of metaphorical designation? he says: "[It is] to prevent the view of annihilation."
And thus has this been revealed by the Teacher for the sake of destroying the view of annihilationism;
otherwise, how could the teaching in the *Śūnyatā-sūtra* be interpreted?

When it is said that "past karma does not exist," the disciples might conclude that even the capacity to produce a fruit—which was deposited by past karma through a continuous succession—is non-existent; thus they would fall into the view of annihilationism. Therefore, the Blessed One stated, "Karma exists."

Otherwise, if the past existed by way of its own intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), how would one interpret the teaching in the *Paramārtha-śūnyatā-sūtra*: "The eye, when arising, does not come from anywhere; when ceasing, it does not go to any accumulation"? For it says, "the eye, having not been, comes to be; and having been, it passes away.
If you argue that "having not been" means "not having been in the present time," [that is not so].
Since the entities of the time-periods are not different from the things themselves, those very things are the time-periods because they are described as existing in such a state;
furthermore, if it were to come into being after not having existed within its own self, then it would be established that the future eye does not exist.

Furthermore, if conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) were to exist eternally, there would be an absence of cause and effect, and consequently, an absence of the truths of suffering and its origin. Due to that absence, there would also be an absence of the truths of cessation and the path. Thus, because of the non-existence of the four noble truths, thorough knowledge, abandonment, realization, and cultivation would not be possible. And because of their absence, there would be no persons (*pudgala*) abiding in the fruits or those entering toward them; thus, the entire teaching (*pravacana*) would be nullified. Therefore, the conceptualization of a collection of entities such as the past and so forth is not tenable.
Regarding the question of how yogins possess distinct knowledge of the past and the future, he says: "By way of succession," and so forth.
Yogins discern that form which constitutes the causal relationship of the present, whether it be mediated through a succession or immediate;
they subsequently follow it with minds accompanied by conceptual construction.
Although pure mundane cognitions do not have reality as their object,
teachings concerning the past and the future proceed by relying upon that continuum— the actual existence of its causes and effects in the past, and their future occurrence.
The teachings of the Tathāgata, whose stream of cognition is free from the entire web of conceptual construction, proceed entirely without effort. (1856) Thus ends the Examination of the Three Times.
With respect to past objects, it has attained the state of being an effect; with respect to future objects, it attains the state of being a cause—
by those whose nature follows conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), meaning by those who possess conceptualization (*savikalpa*).
"In reality, by means of non-objects" means that because cognitions accompanied by conceptual constructions (*abhilāpa*) do not take the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object;
"therefore" (*tat*) means for that reason.
The teachings concerning the past and so forth, which rely upon the actual and future continuity of cause and effect, proceed for yogins who are not yet purified;
however, for the Blessed One, the Tathāgata, even pure mundane knowledge does not exist, because he is eternally in meditative equipoise due to the abandonment of all ignorance,
and because conceptual construction has ignorance as its very nature.
As it has been said: "Since this conceptual construction itself has taken on the nature of ignorance, it proceeds by superimposing its own form as if it were an external object.

Therefore, for one who has attained a physical existence resembling a wish-fulfilling gem through the power of the previously accumulated equipment of merit and gnosis, the teachings proceed spontaneously, without effort.
Thus ends the Examination of the Three Times and the Examination of the Materialists.
In order to establish that [reality] is without beginning or end, he says, beginning with an objection: "If," and so forth:
"If no persisting entity whatsoever exists here, then there would be no other world, because of the non-existence of one who goes to the other world. (1857)
"Some" refers to the self (*ātman*) and so forth.

Among these, because the self has already been refuted previously, it lacks persistence precisely due to its non-existence. As for consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the other [aggregates], because they are momentary and because continuity (*anvaya*) has been refuted in the "Examination of the Three Times," there is no continuity.

But [an opponent might argue] that the body and so forth will be the transmigrators to the next world; to this he says: "The body," etc.—since the body, intellect, sense-faculties, and so on, perish at every moment.
It is not logical that there is a world beyond, nor is another [self] admitted.
Therefore, just as fermented acids, wine, and so forth arise from specific elements (*bhūta-viśeṣa*), so too does cognition arise or is manifested from those very same [elements]. (1858–1859)
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), feeling, perception, and mental formations are included;
no other [entity] is admitted, such as a self (ātman).
This is understood as a mere conformity to the Lokāyata position;
for his sūtra states: "Because there is no one who goes to the next world, there is no next world," and furthermore:
"Earth, water, fire, and air—these are the four principles (tattvas); from these arises consciousness."

Regarding this, some commentators explain that consciousness arises from them, while others say it is manifested; therefore, he states the two positions: "It is born, or else it is manifested," as in the case of sourness in sugarcane.
The power to produce intoxication;
by the word "etcetera" (ādi), the capacity to produce fainting and so forth is included.

1859. [Objection: It is well known that consciousness arises in dependence upon the eye and other sense organs as well as objects such as visible forms; so how can it be said that consciousness arises from those [elements] alone? To this he says: "A particular configuration" (*sanniveśaviśeṣa*).
And it is in a particular configuration of earth and the other elements that [the sense organ] is established.
This designation of "body," "senses," and so forth is [merely conventional]; indeed, no other reality exists.
And thus their Sūtra states: "The designation 'object' and 'sense-faculty' applies to the collection of those [elements].
For there are no senses or the like apart from the primary elements (mahābhūta), since they are designated as such based solely on specific configurations of those elements.
Furthermore, there is no such thing as "configuration" (saṃsthāna) that is distinct from the things possessing configuration;
and these four great elements are established by direct perception,
nor is there any other reality apart from them established by direct perception.
Furthermore, there exists no means of valid cognition other than direct perception by which the establishment of another world and so forth could occur;
nor is there a causal relationship between two states of consciousness that are the subjects of dispute.
Because they reside in different bodies, [these cognitions] are like the cognitions of a cow and a horse.

(1861) Or rather, these cognitions are not considered to be produced by the intended cognition, because they possess the nature of cognition, just like cognitions connected to another continuum. (1862)

Furthermore—if the mind residing in a past body were the cause of the mind of the first birth, and the mind at death were the cause of the future mind, then, because the continuity of the mind would never cease, one might postulate a "next world. However, as for those two minds—the first of which is the subject of dispute—there is no relationship of cause and effect between them, because they reside in different bodies, just like the cognitions residing in a cow and a horse.

Alternatively—the cognitions belonging to a birth-series (*janmabuddhi*) are the subjects (*dharmin*); the probandum (*sādhya*) is the negation of their being produced by the final consciousness residing in a past body; "because it is a cognition" (*jñānatvāt*) is the general reason (*hetu*); and the cognitions residing in another continuum (*anyasantānavartinī*) are the illustrative examples (*nidarśana*). The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: if something is a cognition, it is not produced by that intended final cognition residing in a past body, because it is a cognition, just like a cognition residing in another continuum.

Furthermore, these cognitions existing within the intended body are of the nature of knowledge; thus, there is the perception of a property pervaded by its opposite (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). This is because the state of being knowledge (*jñānatva*) is pervaded by that which is opposed to being produced by the cognition of the intended [body] (i.e., being produced by a cognition other than that).
Thus, the negation of a past birth has been established;
now, for the sake of negating a future birth, he says: "The mind of one with attachment," and so forth—"the mind at death possessed of attachment does not effect a connection with another mind."
By virtue of being a consciousness at death, [the mind] of one free from afflictions is like this:

just as the dying mind of one possessed of passion does not link to another subsequent mind because it is a dying mind, like the final mind of an Arhat—this is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi). "Like this for one free from afflictions" means: * **Thesis (pakṣa):** The dying mind of one free from afflictions does not link to another subsequent mind. * **Reason (hetu):** Because it is a dying mind. * **Example (dṛṣṭānta):** Like the final mind of an Arhat. This is an inference based on the perception of that which is incompatible with the pervader. Just as the dying mind of one possessed of passion lacks the capacity to link to a subsequent mind due to its nature as a dying mind, so too is the case for one free from afflictions. The reason is established because the state of being free from afflictions is incompatible with the arising of further existence; thus, the pervader (the capacity to link to a subsequent mind) is absent, and its incompatible counterpart (the state of being free from afflictions) is present. Therefore, the conclusion follows.
Regarding the knowledge of death (maraṇajñāna) [verse 1863], he asks: "From where, then, does the arising of the mind occur? and answers: "From the body alone," and so forth.
"Therefore, it is logical that knowledge arises from the body itself, which is presided over by the prāṇa and apāna [vital breaths] and so forth; this has been declared by Kambalāśvatara.
(1864) And likewise, the Sūtra says: "From the body itself."
Regarding the statement "as declared by Kambala and Aśvatara" (verse 1864):

[An objection is raised: "But even when the body has not yet been produced—in states such as the *kalala* and so forth—consciousness certainly exists, albeit in a state of fainting (*mūrcchita*). Since that consciousness is established as being produced by a preceding consciousness belonging to a different body, how can there be the restriction that [it arises] 'from the body alone'? To this, he says: "In the *kalala* and so forth," and so on.
To claim that consciousness exists during the stages such as the *kalala* is reckless;
for since the sense faculties have not yet arisen, no object can be apprehended therein.
Furthermore, it is not logical for cognition to have any form other than the apprehension of an object.
Therefore, its existence is not tenable even in states such as fainting (mūrchā).
Nor does the cognition persist at that time in the form of a potentiality (śakti),
for since potentialities lack a substratum, their persistence is not logically possible.
If the self, which is the substratum of cognition, does not exist, then the body alone must be its locus;
yet, when the body eventually ceases to exist, what would be the support for the functioning of cognition?

(1868) For the sense-faculties and their objects are the causes for the arising of consciousness, since cognition consists in the apprehension of objects; and since the sense-faculties and objects are absent during the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*, how could consciousness—which is their effect—exist then? Thus, by the non-perception of its causes, the absence of consciousness in states such as fainting is established; this is the general meaning.

Nor is it reasonable to imagine that consciousness exists at that time in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*), because the self (*ātman*) postulated by the Naiyāyikas and others—which would serve as its substratum—or the continuum of consciousness (*vijñāna-prabandha*) do not exist then. Furthermore, a potentiality without a substratum is not tenable; therefore, by implication, the body alone must be the substratum at that time.

Since there is no other self that serves as the substratum for cognition—whether it be a continuum of consciousness (*vijñāna-prabandha*) whose nature is the substratum of cognition, or a self (*ātman*)—because such a thing does not exist at that time, then at the end, in the state of death, when the body which is the support has ceased, how could cognition remain without a support? Thus, the non-existence of future births is established. (1865)
One thousand eight hundred and sixty-six, one thousand eight hundred and sixty-seven, one thousand eight hundred and sixty-eight.
If another body is observed that relies upon a different physical frame produced immediately after the previous one, how is it understood that [the self] exists? Furthermore,
[the continuity of consciousness] proceeding in a different body is like the minds of elephants, horses, and so forth.

How could that consciousness be bound to a single continuum? Therefore, one must accept some transmigrating person who is the single substratum of cognition and is without beginning or end; otherwise, there would be utter nihilism. || 1870–1871 ||
Now, it might be argued that mental activity will occur by depending on the body of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), which arises immediately after death; but this is incorrect,
for no other body is observed arising immediately after death,
and it is not logical to ascertain the existence of something that has not been observed.

Because that [intermediate state] would be an object of the convention of non-existence, it is not logical for a consciousness existing within a single continuum to take refuge in another body; for this would entail the loss of its connection to a single continuum, just like the minds of an elephant and a horse.

The formal argument is as follows: whatever consciousness functions in different bodies is not connected to a single continuum, just like the minds of an elephant and a horse; and the minds of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and the death-state (*maraṇabhava*) function in different bodies. Thus, there is the undesirable consequence of perceiving something that contradicts the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalambha*).
But this is not the case; therefore, there is a reversal [of the reason].

That which is connected to a single continuum does not function in a different body, just as the mind of an elephant does not depend upon the body of a horse. And since the mind of a living being is connected to a single continuum, this is an "observation of the pervaded by the contradictory" (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
This is because being connected to a single continuum is pervaded by functioning within a non-different body, which is the opposite of functioning within a different body.
The conclusion begins with the word "one" (eka).
"Origin" (ādi) means birth, and "end" (nidhana) means destruction. That which has neither origin nor end is "without beginning or end" (anādinidhana).
"Nara" refers to the Self (ātman).
Alternatively, by the phrase "nāstikatā para," this sūtra indicates that because there is no one who goes to the next world (paralokin), there is an absence of a next world (paraloka). 1869–1870.
1871 He replies with the words "In this regard," and so forth:
"In this matter, this very world is the 'other world'; no other whatsoever exists."

A certain state of the continuum of the primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (tadādeya), such as cognition (jñāna) and so forth, which possesses a fixed limit, is what is designated [as a "person"]; and of that [continuum], which is without beginning or end, there are the designations "subsequent," "prior," and "here. || 1872–1873 ||
Just as those who are attached to the pleasure of what is merely seen imagine that the next world consists of another place and so forth, so too do we speak here [of the nature of that world].
If, however, a next world distinct from that is being denied, [then our position remains].
In that case, the means of proof would be futile, since there is dispute regarding its non-existence.
Now, because the continuum is not a real entity, the occurrence of another state is impossible;
how then could the world or another [being] established therein be real? (1875–1876)

Indeed, by the word "continuum" (saṃtati), those moments which constitute the continuum are indicated in their totality for the sake of brevity, just as [the term] "forest" [indicates its constituent trees].

In this regard, what is this so-called "other world" (paraloka) that you seek to negate? Is it something other than the four aggregates (skandhas), such as consciousness and the rest, which stand in a causal relationship as material cause and effect; or is it simply those very [aggregates]?
First of all, the first position is not tenable, because it is not accepted [by us].

For there is no "other world" here that exists apart from the continuum of consciousness and so forth, which stands in the relationship of material cause and its effect, such that it could be accepted as existing.
What then?

Of that continuum of cognition and so forth, which is beginningless and endless, it is merely a certain limited state defined by boundaries such as a hundred years or the like that is designated as "the next world" or "this world. Just as you, out of attachment to whatever pleasure is perceived, designate a certain range of sensory objects—such as another place—as "the next world," so too has it been said: "A person is only as much as is within the range of the senses; likewise, another place, another time, or another state is repeatedly called 'the next world'."

If, however, the negation of a "next world" (paraloka) that is distinct from the continuum of consciousness and so forth existing in a cause-and-effect relationship is being made, then the proof is futile because it establishes what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*), since such a [substantially real] next world is not admitted [by us]. [Objection: But since the continuum (*santati*) is not a real entity (*avastu*), any specific state (*avasthāviśeṣa*) established within it must also be non-real. Consequently, this "next world" established as a specific state within that continuum would also not be ultimately real (*apāramārthika*).
[Response: This is not a fault.

By the word "continuum" (*santati*), the moments themselves, which are the actual entities (*vastu-bhūta*) that constitute the continuum, are manifested collectively and simultaneously for the sake of linguistic convenience, just as the *dhava* trees and others are denoted by the word "forest. (1872–1873)
One thousand eight hundred seventy-four,
one thousand eight hundred seventy-five,
one thousand eight hundred seventy-six.

How then was it previously stated, in the context of the discussion on how activity [arises] from the continuum as if from a person (*santānin*), that the continuum is not a real entity? To this he says: "Because it is conceived as a unity," and so forth;
it is considered to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) because it is conceptualized as a single entity.
It cannot be described as being either identical to or different from [the self], like a row of lotuses in the sky.

Furthermore, how could that [continuum]—which is beginningless and endless—not attain established proof, if this mind were considered to be the primordial [entity] existing without a cause? (1878–1879)
Whether it arises from an eternal cause, or is eternal by its own nature, or is produced solely from the elements (*bhūta*), or else is born merely from another cognition—
the initial consciousness at conception and so forth cannot be without a cause; for it is not logical that it should be causeless.
Existence occurs only occasionally; otherwise, it would exist in every way at all times.

Nor is it created by eternal entities such as the mind, time, space, the Lord (Īśvara), or the self (ātman), because that would entail its existence at all times, which contradicts the fact of its non-existence [at other times].
To claim that consciousness is a single entity with a permanent nature is a rash assertion,
for the distinctness of mental states such as those involving form, sound, and so forth, is clearly perceived. Furthermore,
its arising does not proceed from the elements— earth, fire, water, and the rest.
Alternatively, [if it were] the manifestation of all minds, there would be the consequence of their simultaneity.
(1884) For that quartet of elements is held by others to be of a stable nature; moreover, dependence upon auxiliary causes in the case of a stable entity has already been refuted. (1885)

However, that continuum which is conceived as a unity is considered to be non-substantial because it cannot be described as either identical to or different from [its constituent moments]—like a row of sky-lotuses. We do not establish the existence of the next world (*paraloka*) on the basis of a particular state of that [continuum].

Rather, if the negation of this very continuum of consciousness and so forth—which is designated as the "next world"—is what is being asserted, then the negation of the next world cannot be accomplished by way of negating its essential nature, because what is perceived cannot be denied.
What then?
By means of negating the attributes of being beginningless and endless,
how could this [mind] not be established as beginningless and endless?

If that mind which is considered to be the beginning were thought to be without a cause, or produced from a cause such as an eternal Lord of Consciousness, or else inherently eternal, or produced from the mere elements (*bhūta-mātra*), or caused by a cognition existing in another continuum— these are the five positions.

For if the preceding mind itself were caused by each successive preceding cognition existing within its own continuum, then the mental continuum would indeed be beginningless and not otherwise; it is with this intention that these positions are presented.
Among them, the first position is not tenable because it entails the consequence of eternal existence and so forth.
For entities become occasional only through dependence [on causes], and that which is causeless does not depend on anything at all—why then would it ever cease?
Nor is the second position tenable for this very reason: because it would entail eternal existence.

For the non-existence of effects is due to the deficiency of their causes; therefore, one must explain why that which possesses its causes in their entirety should not come into being. Nor is the third position tenable. Why? Because of the absence of that—that is, because there is an absence of perpetual existence.
By the words beginning with "one," he demonstrates that very absence [of the cause];
by this, he states the contradiction of the proposition with direct perception; and by the words beginning with "the earth," he refutes the fourth position.
Regarding the earth— the same fault applies here as in the position that the earth arises from causes such as an eternal God; for the four great elements are held by others to be eternal,

and it is not tenable to claim that production from an eternal entity occurs through a sequence dependent on auxiliary causes, since it has already been thoroughly demonstrated that an eternal entity does not depend upon an auxiliary cause that provides no benefit.
One thousand eight hundred and eighty-one;
one thousand eight hundred and eighty-two;
one thousand eight hundred and eighty-three.
1884–1885: Now, even by others this [world] is asserted to be strictly momentary.
If this is so, how is it that your own accepted position regarding them is not contradicted? [The opponent replies:
Let it be contradicted if you wish; however, it is accepted as logical that all things are determined to be momentary by all lines of reasoning. (1886–1887)

Now, if these four great elements are accepted as momentary by the other Cārvākas out of fear of the aforementioned defects, the intention is that even then, there remains only a defect. For instance: first of all, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for establishing a causal relationship between the intellect and the body, by which the opponent’s conventional usage could be established. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: where there is no means of valid cognition for establishing the existence of something, a discerning person should not employ a conventional usage regarding it; just as one does not employ the convention of "cold" with respect to fire.

Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish a causal relationship between the intellect and the body; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Nor is the reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*); for the causal relationship is established by perception and non-perception, and that is determined only through specific positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), not merely by observation and non-observation.

In that context, when it is necessary to determine an effect through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), one must rely on the principle that "when those [causes] are perceived, that which previously met the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) and was unperceived is now perceived. Otherwise, if one were not to require that it was previously unperceived while meeting the conditions for perception, then it might be suspected that the effect existed there even before [the causes], or that it had moved from another location;
consequently, the status of walls and other such things as being the causes of the [effect's] prior non-existence would not be negated.
However, when non-perception of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*) is demonstrated, that [doubt] is refuted,
because in that case there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of it;
thus, first of all, the certainty of the effect is established through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).

Even when determining an effect through negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), one must rely on the principle that "when all other capable causes for that effect are present, [the effect] does not occur in the absence of this one alone. Otherwise, if one merely demonstrates that it does not occur in its absence, its causal capacity would remain doubtful, because other things capable of producing it might also be absent. Consequently, one could even suspect the following: "There is some other capable factor there; the effect ceased due to its absence, and as for the fact that the effect is observed to cease when this particular thing ceases, that is merely a coincidental concurrence."
Just as the *piṇḍakharjūra* (date palm), which grows in regions where marriage with one's mother is customary, does not exist in other regions where such marriage is absent,
so too [the cause] must be qualified by the term "when capable" (*samartheṣu*).
For it is only in this way that its status as a cause is determined, since its absence alone follows the absence [of the effect].
For the absence of that which provides no assistance is not followed by anything else, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the relationship of cause and effect is perceived without doubt, and not otherwise;
yet such a positive or negative concomitance is not established for body and mind.

To explain: first of all, it is impossible to establish a certainty of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between one's own body and the mind, because from the time of conception until the emergence of consciousness, there is no perception of the body alone; for there is no perception [of the body] without the mind.

Furthermore, in the case of another's body as well, the mind does not fall within the range of perception (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇaprāpta*); thus, there is no apprehension of priority and posteriority, and consequently, no certainty of positive concomitance.
Nor is there a certainty regarding negative concomitance (*vyatireka*);

for even in that case, it is not possible to know the absence of one's own cognition through the absence of one's own body, because [the self] is entirely non-existent [to the other]. Nor can the absence of a cognition related to another's body be ascertained through the absence of that other's body.

Because that cognition possesses the characteristic of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatva*), there remains doubt regarding its distinction from the body even when the body has ceased; for this very reason, one cannot ascertain its distinction from the body in the case of walls and the like, despite the absence of a body,
since there too one doubts whether it exists due to its possessing the characteristic of non-apprehension.

Furthermore, it is not logical to determine non-existence merely from the non-perception of effects such as movement; for causes do not necessarily possess their effects. Moreover, since the cause of that [non-perception]—namely, the specific appropriation of a body characterized by craving and error—is absent, there arises a doubt as to whether the absence of cognition in that wall or similar object is due to the lack of its own cause, or rather due to its being distinct from a body.
Therefore, the reason is neither unestablished (*asiddha*) nor contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).
Nor is it inconclusive, for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) and would entail the loss of your status as a discerning person (prekṣāvat).

If it is asked, "What subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) is there then against the claim that the body is not the cause of the Buddha's cognition?", we reply: there certainly is such a proof. Thus, he will demonstrate the proof in the passage beginning with "the independent mental cognition" (svatantrā mānasī buddhiḥ), regarding the point that the body is not the cause of mental cognition.
Since its sovereignty over the linking of another body establishes that it is not dependent on the body, the existence of the next world is proven.

Furthermore, one must consider the following alternatives: let the body be the cause of mental cognition—is it a single composite whole (*avayavin*), or is it multiple, consisting of an aggregate of atoms? Or is it with sense organs, or without sense organs? Is it the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) or the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*)? Among these, it is first of all not logical for it to be a single composite whole, because such a thing has already been refuted.

Furthermore, it would entail the undesirable consequence of losing its nature as being composed of the four great elements (*caturmahābhūta*); for it is not logical for a single entity to possess a fourfold intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as that would result in the abolition of all conventional usage regarding multiplicity.
Nor should it be accepted as being composed of an accumulation of multiple atoms (*paramāṇu*).
And those atoms would have to be either causes individually or collectively.

It cannot be [produced] by each [cause] individually, because that would entail the consequence that a conceptualization arises for every single atom, just as a sprout arises from each individual seed.

Nor can it be produced by them collectively, because even if a single part such as the nose were missing, it would follow that no mental cognition could arise; this is just as a sprout does not arise when any one of the factors such as earth is absent.

For an effect that is dependent upon a causal complex (sāmagrī) does not occur in the absence of any one of its members, otherwise there would be the consequence of losing its very nature as being dependent on that complex.
Now, if all [factors] present are indeed causes of consciousness,
then there ought to be a distinction between that produced by a body with deficient limbs and that produced by a body with complete limbs, because of the difference in their causes;
otherwise, the difference in the effect would be without a cause.
When one who was previously possessed of all unimpaired faculties subsequently acquires impaired faculties, there is no specific distinction in the mental cognition (*manomati*),
because the refinement resulting from hearing and so forth continues at that time precisely as it was unimpaired.
Furthermore, the mental cognition existing in the bodies of elephants and other such beings would result in being superior, whereas human cognition would not.
Those who possess human birth with a small body are of dull intellect, whereas those with large bodies are of sharp intellect;
for we observe that when there is a decrease or increase in the cause, there is a corresponding decrease or increase in the effect.
Indeed, it is not logical for something to be the effect of another if it does not vary according to the variation of that [cause], as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Furthermore, because it would follow that the diversity of effects is causeless,
the position that [the mind] possesses the sense faculties is also untenable;
for in that case, would the mental cognition arise from each sense faculty individually, or from them all collectively?
It cannot be [the case that the mind] is each of these individually, because even when one sense organ is lost, the mental cognition remains unimpaired;
for instance, even when the functional organs and so forth are afflicted by diseases such as paralysis, the mental intellect experiences its own existence as unchanged, single, and unimpaired.

Furthermore, it is not logical that something which does not undergo modification despite the modification of another should be the effect of that other, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Furthermore, [if it were produced from the object alone], it would follow that it grasps only specific objects like visual consciousness and other sensory cognitions, that it is non-conceptual, and that its activity depends upon the presence of the object; this is because its cause would not be distinct [from sensory cognition].
Moreover, there is the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that multiple conceptualizations would arise simultaneously.
Nor is the position that it arises from the totality [of object and sense-organ] tenable, because it would follow that [the cognition] would be absent even when a single sense-organ is missing.

Nor is the position tenable that [the body] is not a sense-faculty (*anindriya*), for if it were so, then even hands and other limbs separated from the corpse would entail being causes [of cognition].
If it is held that a specific [conditioned] entity is the cause, then it must be accepted as being precisely endowed with a sense-faculty (*sendriya*).
Indeed, it cannot be shown that there is any distinct entity other than the sense-faculties (*sendriya*), nor is the position tenable that [the self] is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*).

For instance, that which is established as the specific cause by way of being the material cause is precisely that which—by constantly presenting its own existence—is a benefactor to the nature that follows all the particularities residing in the effect; and without whose undergoing of modification the effect could not be modified.

Just as each preceding collection of clay is the material cause (*upādāna*) for each succeeding collection designated as a "pot," for this very reason, whoever wishes to transform something transforms it only by modifying its material cause, and not otherwise;
for as long as the preceding material cause possesses unimpeded capacity, it is impossible for anyone to obstruct the arising of the succeeding effect.

Just as, in the case of a subsequent effect such as a jar that is about to arise, one cannot bring about a transformation [of the cause] without first producing a capable moment by way of not obstructing its prior clay-nature; and in every instance of the production of a transformation, this is precisely the sequence: namely, the production of a moment that takes up another [moment] which is incapable [of the previous state]. Otherwise, nothing directly contradictory would be possible.

For if it were possible, the effect itself would undergo modification directly, just as the cause undergoes modification; it would not do so solely by means of the modification of its material cause (*upādāna*).
However, in the case of a lamp, when a modification is produced in its light existing in another location through an intervening obstruction, the lamp is not the direct material cause of that light.
What then?
Each preceding moment of light is obstructed by the covering because it induces a transformation characterized by the production of a subsequent moment that is incapable [of emitting light].
Furthermore, that object with reference to which something is modified is not its material cause (*upādāna*); for example, when a cow is modified with reference to a *gavaya*.

And yet, without modifying the body, the mind and cognition are made the material cause of modifications characterized by dejection and so forth through the performance of undesirable actions and the like; thus, there is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

[Objection: But surely, when the body undergoes modifications such as nourishment due to food and digestion, a modification of the mental cognition characterized by passion and so forth is indeed observed.
Even if it is indeed observed [to be so], what of it?
For the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*) by this much alone;
for what is intended here is merely this: that which can undergo transformation even while the other remains untransformed cannot be its material cause (*upādāna*).

Furthermore, it is observed that in certain states, through the performance of undesirable acts and the like, a modification of the intellect occurs even without bringing about a modification of the body; how then can the reason [of your argument] be considered unestablished?

Nor is it logical to conclude that the intellect has the body as its material cause (*upādāna*) merely because it occasionally conforms to such modifications of the body, for this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For in that case, the external object would also have to be considered a material cause of the intellect.

For instance, even by the power of seeing loathsome objects such as the blood of a tiger, a mental transformation characterized by delusion and the like certainly arises in someone of timid mind; yet, on that account alone, that mental cognition does not become dependent upon the body.

Furthermore, since we observe physical transformations when the mind is afflicted by discursive thoughts such as desire and grief, it would follow [absurdly] that the body is also the material cause of those mental states. However, it is logical that only that which invariably and directly conforms to the modification of another is the material cause of that other;
and a transformation characterized by passion and the like does not invariably arise from the nourishment of the body.
Because it is impossible for someone who possesses analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyāna*)— even if their body is well-nourished— to [act in such a way],
and because one observes excessive passion and so forth even in a person whose body is utterly wasted, or in some animal whose physical dimensions are diminished; and furthermore,
it is not logical that something which occurs even in the absence of another thing should be the effect of that other, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor can passion and the like arise directly from the body, because they are mediated by improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanasikāra*) and other factors;
for instance, when there is nourishment of the body, there occurs within it the experience of pleasure and so forth produced by objects characterized as desirable.

In that regard, for one who possesses a self and a body, when there is pleasure and so forth, or the means thereto, the mind is pervaded by the misconceptions [of permanence] and so on; then arises the conceptualization of "this is beneficial" or "this is harmful" to me, which is the desire to assist or counteract the self. From that, there occurs satisfaction, dejection, and so forth, and from those, the production of determinations (*adhyavasāya*) regarding objects such as pleasure and so on. This is indeed established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*): because passion and the like are observed only when satisfaction and the like occur, and they are not observed even when nourishment and the like are present if those [mental states] do not occur. Therefore, nourishment and the like are not the direct cause of the modification of mental cognition.
And for this very reason, since it does not provide direct assistance, it is established that the body is not even a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*) for that [desire].

This is because earth and other factors are well-known to be cooperative causes only when they assist directly in the production of sprouts and the like; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, passion and the rest proceed only from the awakening of a preceding seed of their own kind.

However, for some who lack the practice of analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyāna*), factors such as bodily nourishment and the period of youth become causes for the awakening of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Or, let it be granted that the body is a direct benefactor to the mental cognition (*manomati*) which proceeds from its own material cause (*upādāna*);
even so, it is not established that the cessation of that cognition follows upon the cessation of the body.

Just as the cessation of fire does not entail the cessation of a jar or similar objects because they proceed from their own respective material causes, there is no undesirable consequence (aniṣṭāpatti);
nor is the reason inconclusive (anaikāntika), for that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga);
nor is it contradictory (viruddha), since it exists in the similar instances (sapakṣa).

Therefore, it is established that the body is neither the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) nor the auxiliary cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*); rather, it must be that the mental cognition arises solely from each preceding cognition. This might be argued: those two things for which there is a rule of coexistence are related as material cause and its effect (*upādānopādeya-bhūta*), just like a lamp and its light.

And since there is a rule of co-existence between the body and mental consciousness, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason); however, this reason is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*),
because it is accepted that in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), mental cognition exists even in the absence of a body.
Nor is the desired conclusion established, because it would entail that mental cognition is also the material cause (*upādāna*) of the body;
furthermore, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
since coexistence is possible even due to a difference in causes.

Just as in the case of fire and the melting of copper—for instance, copper, acting in conjunction with fire, initiates fluidity, but not by itself; so too here, the material cause of the body, such as the *kalala* stage, acting in conjunction with mental consciousness, initiates the subsequent body. Therefore, their coexistence does not arise from a relationship of material cause and effect (*upādāna-upādeya-bhāva*); thus, [the reason] is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, it might be argued: although at a later time mental cognition arises from each preceding cognition, nevertheless, that which exists at the very first moment must have the body as its material cause; therefore, the proof of beginninglessness is not established.
This is incorrect;

for it has already been established that there is no valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove this hypothesis, and if you argue that there is likewise no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), we reply: no.
There certainly exists a subverting argument (bādhaka), as follows:

if the mental cognition (manodhī), having arisen once from the body, were subsequently to arise from its own kind (sajātīya), then at all subsequent times it would arise only from preceding mental cognitions, and not from heterogeneous cognitions such as those of the eye and so forth; for smoke, having once arisen from fire, does not subsequently arise from another heterogeneous source, nor is mental cognition experienced at a later time as arising solely from a mental cognition.
Rather,
[the sequence] arises from indeterminate immediate conditions;

and whatever has been perceived as attaining its first arising from a certain [cause], it cannot possibly arise from something other than that, because that would entail the consequence of being causeless.

Alternatively, it is experienced that mental cognition (*manodhī*) arises immediately after the determinate cognitions of the eye and other senses; therefore, it is established that it occurs even in the absence of specific [sensory] cognitions. Furthermore, if the body were the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of mental cognition only at the initial moment and not at subsequent times, then why would it not function independently of the body? For it is not reasonable for it to have any dependence on a body that provides no assistance.
If it is argued that even for one whose cognition is preceded by another cognition, why does it not proceed alone? [We reply:
It indeed does not proceed, as in the case of the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
If that which possesses desire for a corresponding object exists in dependence upon it, then this is not at all a valid objection; however,
if it is subsequently admitted that the body also provides assistance, then there follows the undesirable consequence of the production of a manifold series of cognitions,
because the body— which serves as the material cause (*upādāna*) for other cognitions— would remain present as a producer in its unimpaired state.

For instance: whatever consciousness arises from the body, that very thing produces another distinct and separate consciousness; thus, for a single living being, immeasurable streams of consciousness would be produced at every moment.
Yet such an experience does not occur.
Furthermore, it might be argued that at a later time, the body is not intended to have a separate efficacy as a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).
What then?

It is false to claim that the body is not required for its operation, on the grounds that the mental consciousness—which proceeds in a continuous stream from its own material cause—receives assistance from the body because the latter acts as a cooperative condition (*sahakārin*) toward the production of each successive effect; therefore, it does not operate independently of the body.
For that which is well-known as the producer of something in a certain manner does not produce it otherwise, because there is no difference [in its nature].

Thus, for example, light and so forth, having been experienced as a producer by way of being an objective support (*ālambana*) for unimpaired visual consciousness, do not subsequently become producers of it in any other way—as it has been said: "Indeed, production is not something other than the state of being an object; such is the definition of being an object."
For form and the other [sensory objects] are not otherwise directly beneficial to consciousness;
otherwise, there would be no determination of the difference or non-difference in the nature of an effect as produced by its cause, because it would not conform to the benefit conferred upon it,
and consequently, the consequence of being causeless would follow.
Furthermore, you have not apprehended any other form of material causality (upādānatva) for the body at the initial moment, apart from its being a direct producer of consciousness;
what then?
It is simply its status as a direct auxiliary cause (sākṣādupakāritva).
Since that [body] exists even at a later time, why should it not be the material cause?
Or, if it were something else [that is the cause], then let there be nothing [as the cause] even previously, since there is no difference [in its status] afterwards.

Nor can it be argued that the body itself, acting as a cooperative condition for the preceding cognition, will serve as the material cause for each subsequent cognition, because the status of being a material cause has already been refuted in detail previously.
Because it would follow that even the cognition of the first birth must be preceded by another cognition;

for this very reason, this refutation of the Teacher applies all the more strongly even to the position that the elements are impermanent, as he said: "If a cognition produced once from the body were restricted by its own kind..."
If it is argued that the cessation of the body occurs only when it has become capable [of functioning] through something else, from where does that [capacity] arise?
Therefore, the beginninglessness of the mind and the intellect is established;
or rather, all cognition whatsoever is established as being beginningless without distinction.
To explain: an initial cognition must be either a sensory cognition (*akṣabuddhi*) or a mental cognition (*manobuddhi*).

It cannot be the first position, because in those who are asleep, unconscious, or whose minds are otherwise engaged, sensory cognition does not arise despite the presence of the sense-faculties, due to the absence of a corresponding mental attention (*anuguṇamanaskāra*).
Therefore, the sense-faculty alone is not the cause of sensory cognition.
Rather, it is determined that [the arising] depends upon a specific mental attention (*manaskāra*),
because the relationship between cause and effect is to be understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Furthermore, whatever is ascertained as arising first from something else cannot arise first from anything other than that [specific cause], for that would entail the fallacy of being without a cause (*ahetukatva*).
Just as smoke arises from a fireless source, the visual cognition that first arises depends upon a corresponding mental attention;
therefore, it is established that the sense organ alone is never its sole cause.
Otherwise, the undesirable consequence of causelessness (*nirhetukatva*) would follow as a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
Nor is the position that it is mental cognition (*manobuddhi*);
for that does not function independently with respect to an object not perceived by the sense organs, since that would entail the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth.
Or, if it were to arise, it must be stated whether it is conceptual (*savikalpika*) or non-conceptual (*avikalpika*).
In this regard, the first position is not tenable;

for indeed, every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that arises functions as being permeated by the form of a denotative word (*bodhaka-śabda*), because it is constantly experienced as having the form of internal speech (*antarjalpa*).

Furthermore, regarding this appearance of the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form of a denotative word, it must arise either by virtue of the apprehension of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), or because the nature of the word—which is essentially denotative—is a property of the cognition itself (just as its cognitive nature is), or because of the grasping of the word and its object.
Among these alternatives, the first position—that it arises from the apprehension of convention—is not tenable, because the convention was not previously apprehended.
Nor is the second position tenable.

To explain: the nature of sound is twofold, consisting of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). Among these, as for that which is the particular characteristic, because it is experienced as being non-expressive and as the form of [pure] cognition, it does not constitute the conceptual nature (*savikalpakatva*) of knowledge. Nor is this a property residing within the self of knowledge, because it appears as an external form like blue and other objects;
otherwise, even blue and the rest would be properties of knowledge, as there would be no distinction.
Consequently, the universe would consist of consciousness alone, and not be of the nature of a transformation of the elements.

Now, [the opponent objects]: "In the view that cognition possesses an aspect (*sākāra-jñāna*), the mode such as blue is indeed an attribute residing within the cognition itself, yet it appears as an external form; so why is it said that because it appears as an external form, it is not an attribute of the cognition's own self?
This is true.
However, because cognition appears in such a way due to being colored by an external object, it is established that this [aspect] belongs to the external object itself, rather than to the cognition.
What then?
It belongs to the external object alone.
Because that [particular] belongs to it (the word) as its own nature in that very [particular],
