whereas in cognition it is adventitious, being produced by the imposition of an object;
therefore, the essence of the word is neither of the nature of a particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as the denoter, nor is it a property of the essence of cognition.
Although the universal (sāmānyalakṣaṇa) is indeed denotative, it nevertheless does not constitute a property of the nature of cognition;
for it is applied to that which is apprehended by the ear as an external, other-specific individual (para-śabda-svalakṣaṇa), and not to the nature of cognition itself.
Indeed, a universal residing in one thing cannot be applied to another, as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga) within cognition.
For in this way, the nature of "cowness" (gotva) would have to be applied even to horses and the like;
yet, when the substratum (dharmin)— the specific individuality (svalakṣaṇa) of the word— is not apprehended, its property consisting of the expressive [word-form] cannot be applied,
because properties, being dependent upon their substrata, are not apprehended independently.
Nor can a subject (*dharmī*) whose nature is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) be apprehended by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),
because the latter has the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) as its object.
Therefore, it is established that conceptual constructions arise from the awakening of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) deposited by beginningless experience of particular characteristics.

Nor is the position that [conceptual construction arises] from the apprehension of the word and its object tenable; for words do not exist in the object, nor are they identical with it, because otherwise it would follow that even one who has not learned the linguistic convention would have cognition [of the object], and because it would follow that there could be no application of words to objects according to one's will.
Furthermore, although the object does not differ in its nature as impermanent and so forth, conceptual construction does not simultaneously construct all its aspects.
Since conceptual construction arises precisely by grasping a single, specific form through the exclusion of other forms,
a cause must be stated for this conceptualization of a single form;
and nothing other than repeated practice can be stated as that cause, as is the case with conceptualizations such as a corpse and so forth.

Furthermore, since conceptual cognition functions by the force of prior habituation, it is established that conceptual cognition is beginningless. Now, if the position is taken that it is non-conceptual, then a conceptual cognition would never arise;
for, according to the aforementioned principle, it could only arise at a later time through the power of linguistic convention. If this is argued, [we reply: no.
For one who abides in non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), there is no possibility of establishing a linguistic convention (*saṅketa*), because it is impossible to do so.
For instance, as long as neither the generality of words (*śabda-sāmānya*) nor the generality of objects (*artha-sāmānya*) appears in the intellect, a convention cannot be established;
and yet, a generality does not appear within conceptual cognition (*vikalpa-vijñāna*).
Furthermore, that which appears as a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)— neither upon it nor by means of it is a convention (*saṅketa*) established,
because such convention serves the purpose of practical activity (*vyavahāra*).

Moreover, since the particular characteristic perceived at the time of establishing the convention cannot possibly exist at the time of practical activity, one must necessarily admit the existence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) prior to the establishment of the convention regarding the particular characteristic.
And since that [cognition] cannot be established without repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), its beginninglessness (*anāditā*) is proven. Furthermore,

if it is not admitted that the cognition occurring in the first birth arises from the continuity of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by practice in previous births, then how could a newborn infant— even one belonging to the animal realm— possess the determinative judgment (*vyavasāya*) that "this is a means to pleasure" or "this is a cause of pain," by virtue of which it seeks the breast and other such things that are means to pleasure?
Not obtaining that [object], he begins to weep; and having obtained it, his weeping suddenly ceases as he performs actions such as eating.
For he has never experienced that the breast and so forth are the cause for allaying the pain of hunger, nor has he experienced that falling from a precipice and so forth are causes of injury.

By virtue of which even a newborn infant of a monkey or other species, fearing death due to the suffering arising from falling down a precipice, clings intensely to its mother’s breast and avoids places such as cliffs;

for it is not the case that one invariably desires to abandon or acquire objects whose fruits as means to the desirable or undesirable have never been experienced—lest this lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Furthermore, the analogy of iron moving toward a magnet is also untenable, for that movement is not causeless, as that would entail the consequence of it occurring at all times.

Alternatively, if it possesses a cause, then just as its cause—the magnet—is pointed out as being established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), so too a cause for this practice of rejection and acquisition must be conceived;
yet no such cause can be pointed out other than habituation (*abhyāsa*).

Therefore, this worldly activity of children, characterized by the acceptance of the desirable and the rejection of the undesirable, is produced solely by prior habituation; thus, the intention is that the beginninglessness of the intellect (*buddhi*) is established.

And thus, he will state common objections in the passages beginning with "an independent mental [cognition]" and "furthermore, in the case of suckling at the breast," and so forth; so enough of this prolixity.
Moreover—for those Cārvākas who accept momentariness—their own admission, that is, their own tenet, is contradicted: namely, the admission that the elements are eternal is contradicted.
If, out of devotion to justice, you possess impartiality even toward your own side, [then...]
Let this supreme principle be accepted: that the elements themselves do not exist.

(1888) Now, if momentariness is accepted because it is supported by reasoning, then let the system of Vijñaptimātratā (Cognition-Only) be accepted as the superior one; for in that case as well, the reason for acceptance—namely, its being supported by reasoning—is the same. (1888)

He asks "How so? and replies: "They do not have the nature of a composite whole (avayavin), nor is their being of the nature of atoms (aṇu) logical; for it will be stated that [the existence] of atoms is impossible. (1889)
"Of these" refers to the great elements;
"it will be explained."
Immediately following this, in the *Bahirarthaparīkṣā* (Examination of External Objects), verse 1889, he asks:
"If the elements do not exist at all, how then do they appear? and answers with the words beginning, "Their forms are not external realities," and so forth.
Due to the maturation of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*), things that do not have an external reality appear within consciousness, as in dreams and the like, and not from anything else.
(1890) "From anything else" means:

To the extent that [earth and so forth] are external to consciousness, how then do the conventional usages of "earth" and so on occur in both the world and the treatises? To this he says: "Of consciousness alone," and so forth.
Relying solely upon the manifestation of consciousness, this [world] is conceptualized as being like a dream or an illusion; it is not these four great elements.
[Objection: If the elements do not exist, then what is the cause of cognition? To this he says: "Of that which is other than that," and so forth.

It is not logical for anything other than that [object] to be the cause of the appearance of its semblance; rather, it is a previously arisen cognition that possesses the appearance of a real object which would produce a subsequent one.
Regarding the phrase "of anything other than that":

Therefore, it has been established that the initial consciousness does not arise from the four primary elements alone as something distinct from consciousness; now, in order to refute the position that [subsequent] produced consciousness arises solely from another consciousness, he says: "In another continuum," and so forth.
If the consciousness of another continuum is held to be its cause,
then is it its material cause (*upādāna*) or its auxiliary cause (*sahakārin*)? If it is intended to be the material cause, [then consider] the continuum of knowledge in the case of a son.
There would be a transmission of specific refinements such as learning from one's parents;
for this is the nature of the material cause and its product,
which is established and determined through positive and negative concomitance within one's own continuum.

If one postulates the status of a cooperative cause (*sahakāritva*) for that which has arisen through the power of its own material cause (*upādāna*), there would be no contradiction regarding the mind of another continuum (*santānāntara*).

That is to say, the mind belonging to another continuum—such as that of a mother or father—would have to be either a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) or a cooperative cause (*sahakāri-kāraṇa*). It cannot first be a material cause, because it would follow that even in the cognitive continuum of a son, the specific impressions (*saṃskāra*) derived from what was heard by the mother and father and so forth would not arise; just as [the impressions] of the parents themselves do not arise in their own subsequent cognitions.
Because in subsequent moments there is a conformity to the conditioning factors (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding moment,
the relationship between the material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) is thus established;
for this is ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) within one's own continuum (*svasantāna*).

Now, suppose it is thought: "Just as when one lamp produces another lamp, the subsequent lamp does not arise as qualified by the refinement (saṃskāra) of the preceding lamp characterized by its grossness and so forth; rather, there is the production of a mere lamp devoid of such refinement. However, that other lamp possesses a distinction from other lamps due to its own wick, oil, and so on—just as an object [is distinguished] from the cognition of it.
This is not so, because the refinement of a lamp and the like establishes a continuous stream (santāna) even within its own substratum.
Because that [lamp] is unstable;
for instance, when its fuel is exhausted, the non-existence of that very lamp is observed,
whereas the cultivation (*saṃskāra*) resulting from hearing and so forth is not thus unstable, since it persists for a long time.

Therefore, it is not logical for mere cognition, being devoid of mental cultivation (*saṃskāra*), to arise like a lamp or similar objects. Furthermore, in the case of a lamp and so forth, the distinction and non-distinction are merely conceptualized based on the production of a greater or smaller accumulation of atoms; however, there is no distinction or non-distinction therein belonging to the nature of a single entity. But here, within the very same nature of a single entity, there is distinction due to the cultivation of learning and so forth as it exists in the mother’s cognition, while there is non-distinction as it exists in the son’s cognition—what could possibly instruct one regarding this?

Furthermore, this undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) is stated regarding [the lamp] being the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa); however, one lamp is not the material cause of another lamp because they belong to different continua (saṃtāna). Thus, this [objection] is trivial.
Moreover, for those beings born from moisture (saṃsveda-jāti) who have no mother at all, how could their cognition be produced by the consciousness of another? Enough with this digression.
Now, if the position is that it is a cooperative cause (sahakāri-kāraṇa), then you are merely proving what is already established (siddha-sādhyatā).

1896. Therefore, he provides the proof for establishing beginninglessness:
"Therefore, the initial cognition therein arises from the power of its own material cause."

[The argument is: Because of reasons such as being consciousness (*vijñānatva*), [the first moment of mind] is like the present mind. (1897) The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever entity has the nature of the four aggregates (*skandha*)—consciousness, sensation, perception, and mental formations—is produced by the power of its own material cause (*upādāna*), because it possesses the nature of consciousness and so forth; just as those same four aggregates in states such as youth [are produced by their own material causes]. And the collection of the first moment of mind and so forth in the initial birth has the nature of consciousness and so forth. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
In this context, the mention of "initial consciousness" (*ādivijñāna*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all the aggregates.
Feeling and the other [mental factors] are also to be included.
He states the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the reason when its opposite of the probandum is established, beginning with "by another cause," etc. (verse 1897).
Because other causes have been refuted and the state of causelessness has been established, it follows that this determinate property would not belong to it otherwise.

(1898) Since other [proposed causes]—such as the eternal mind (*manas*), time (*kāla*), space (*diś*), and the Lord (*īśa*)—have already been refuted, and since its own material cause (*svopādāna*) is not admitted, there would be causelessness; consequently, this determinate property characterized by being consciousness and so forth would not exist.
Since an accidental intrinsic nature cannot be restricted due to the absence of a determining factor, it is impossible for it to be specifically determined;

therefore, the impossibility of specific dharmas such as consciousness arising without a cause serves as a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), as does the impossibility of their occasional occurrence.

Having thus established the past birth, he states the following as a means of proof to establish the future one as well: "The consciousness at the moment of death [is capable of giving rise to its own effect], because it belongs to one possessed of passion and is associated with attachment, just like the preceding consciousness. (1899)

Whatever mind is possessed of passion (*sarāga*) is capable of giving rise to another subsequent mind that takes it as its own material cause (*upādāna*), because it is possessed of passion, like a mind in a previous state; and the dying mind is possessed of passion—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*); for whatever mind is devoid of the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to the enjoyment of objects and so forth, all such minds are indeed possessed of passion, because they are devoid of the antidote, like a mind intent on sexual pleasure.

Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since the arising of a mind is caused by this much alone; thus, the impossibility of the complete causal conditions [for a new birth] serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
1899 This very point he demonstrates with the words "in whatever form," etc.: "In whatever form consciousness, producing [its effect], is determined..."
"Carrying that [nature] both before and after, why is it not a causal agent?
'Carrying that' refers to its own form— that is to say, its essential nature."
With the words "1900.
Regarding the opposing position," and so forth, he raises the objection that both examples in the two formal arguments (prayoga) are deficient in the probandum (sādhyavikalatā), stating:
"And in the opposing position, the established conclusion is that such cognition arises from the body alone."
How then are the two examples established as being endowed with the property to be proven?
Surely, the causality of the body has already been refuted, because [the body] cannot be simultaneous with the mind, and because there is no additional [cause].
Since it is determined that consciousness—such as memory, desire, and so forth—is cultivated by means of mental states like focused application (*ābhoga*) and virtue (*śubha*), it cannot be denied;
for a decrease and an increase are observed in cognitions based on their preceding states. (1903)
(1904) Due to the decrease or increase in the specific practice of learning, arts, and so forth;

(1905) however, when mental attention (*manaskāra*) is deficient, because there is no apprehension of another object to be known, it cannot even be said that cognition functions as a cause for cognition.
The reason "because it functions within a distinct body" is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For what kind of functioning could there be for an immaterial consciousness that does not fall [into a physical state] within bodies?

To explain: the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) consists in [the mind's] arising from its own material cause (*upādāna*) and its capacity to bring about the emergence of its own effect (*upādeya*).

Furthermore, for one who holds the view that consciousness arises eternally from the body alone, no example endowed with the aforementioned property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is established anywhere. How, then, can these two examples—"like the present mind" and "like the preceding consciousness"—be adduced?
This is not a fault, because the causality of the body has already been refuted by the argument that it would lead to the consequence of [multiple] cognitions occurring simultaneously.
Because there is no additional auxiliary cause (sahakārikāraṇa) to be depended upon, and because dependence is logically impossible for that which is eternal;
whereas in the case of the non-eternal, the previously mentioned refutations as well as the present one apply.

Furthermore, it is not tenable for something established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) to be rendered unestablished merely by way of a formal admission (abhyupagama), as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga); and thus, nothing would ever serve as a proof for anything.
As it has been said: "Not all [faults] are a refutation because they are undesired.
Furthermore, when a memory arises immediately after a mind of aesthetic enjoyment (*ābhoga-citta*) and is well-ascertained, then passion (*rāga*) arises from a mind of beauty and so forth.

For instance, passion arises in those possessed by desire who contemplate the beautiful, thinking: "She is lovely," "She is young," "She has a slender waist," "She has a beautiful face," and so on. Likewise, hatred arises in one who thinks: "He has wronged me," "He will wrong me," or "He is wronging me now"; since this is ascertained, how can it be denied, especially by one who maintains that perception alone is the source of knowledge?

Likewise, it is observed that the excellence or deficiency of subsequent cognitions results from the excellence or deficiency of the specific practice of learning, arts, and so forth, which preceded them; similarly, it is observed that due to distraction toward another object, there is a failure to grasp that [intended] object because of a deficiency in mental attention (*manaskāra*). Thus, the fact that cognition is the cause of cognition is beyond dispute because it is consistent with reason, whereas this is not the case for the elements (*bhūta*), as that would contradict reason.
For this very reason, the demonstration that cognition is the cause of cognition [is established].

In the first argument beginning with "the relation of cause and effect," the reason—that [the mind] resides in different bodies—is unestablished (*asiddha*). To explain: if "residing" is intended in the sense of the relationship between a support and that which is supported, then this is even more unestablished for the mind, which by its very nature does not fall, in relation to bodies; for even if a causal relationship exists, the mind, being formless, possesses the property of not falling, and it is not logical for that which has the property of not falling to have a support, as such a support would be ineffective. (1900)

Then, what does [the earth] do to be the support for water and so forth? He says: "It may be," and so on.
It may be the support for water and so forth by way of preventing their falling; but as for minds that have no motion, what is the use of supports? (1907)
If it is postulated here that "subsistence" (vṛtti) consists in identity (tādātmya), that too is untenable; for it is not logical for your cognition to be of the nature of the body.

Since that which is corporeal—such as the primary elements (prakṛti) and so forth—is produced by abandoning the location of its own material cause (upādāna), its substratum (ādhāra) is established through the obstruction of its movement, because [the substratum] is the cause of production at the location of the material cause.
However, it is not possible to establish such a relation for that which is formless.

If you intend the relation to be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), even that is not established; for it is not reasonable for one who is intent upon external objects to assert that consciousness is of the nature of the body.

But for me, who maintains the doctrine of consciousness-only (vijñānavāda), it is logical that the body has the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) as its intrinsic nature; this is the intended meaning. 1907–1908.
He asks why this is not tenable and says: "In the case of identity," and so forth.
For if there were identity, then just as the body is clearly perceived by others, why would the mind characterized by passion, hatred, and so on, not likewise be perceived? (1909)
The mind is known only by itself, whereas the body is perceived by both oneself and others;
thus, these two are distinct from one another, like an actor and the stage upon which he performs.
For if the body were grasped by others, it would follow that their passions and so forth are also grasped, since [the body and the mind] would be non-different.
Nor is there an inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to the power of the Brahmin [the priest], because that power is imperceptible at that time;

however, consciousness is not imperceptible, for otherwise it would follow that even the self could not be apprehended. Furthermore, those two which are respectively ascertained by both parties and ascertained by one party alone are distinct, like the experience of the stomach and the performance of a dancer; and the body and consciousness are respectively ascertained by both and by one. This is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
"By oneself alone" means by one's own self.
But from the perspective of non-dual knowledge (advayajñāna), this reason is not established,
because each respective manifestation is cognized [by itself], like [the vision] of one suffering from ophthalmia.
If it is observed that the mind perishes immediately after its arising in a continuous stream, why is momentariness not accepted for the body, given its identity with that [mind]?

(1912) If this were so, the refutation of the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātra*) being carried out by this very reason would be unavoidable; therefore, he says: "This reason is not established."
The reason is subject to the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatā*);
for instance, the fact that both [the object and its cognition] are ascertained is not established for the Vijñānavādin, because he always experiences only his own internal manifestation,
just like two people with ophthalmia seeing two moons.
Furthermore, at the time of cognizing an object of a different character, the mind—which arises continuously and perishes immediately thereafter—is clearly perceived;
consequently, if it were admitted that the body possesses such a nature, the undesirable consequence of its momentariness would follow.

Thus, first of all, a relationship characterized by identity is not established; suppose, then, that the relationship is characterized by origination from that (tadutpatti). And that origination from it would have to occur either by way of a support, as in the case of visual consciousness and its support, the eye, etc., because of the non-deviation [of the former] from the latter; or else, as in the case of smoke, which does not deviate from fire.
Thus, in this case, both types of occurrence are unestablished;
for instance, mental cognition does not depend upon the body in the same way that sensory cognition does, because it is not invariably and directly affected by the modifications of the latter;
nor is it invariably concomitant with it, since its existence is admitted even in the absence of a body in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

Nevertheless, even while conceding the established nature of the reason, he states its inconclusiveness: "Because it arises based on that, or because it is non-deviant from that; if its occurrence therein were admitted, even so there would be inconclusiveness. (1913)
Even cognition in its prior state, though existing within a body that perishes moment by moment, certainly effects a continuous reconnection [of karmic results].
If there were no distinctness therein due to the fact of belonging to a single continuum, [then this would be impossible].

Nor can there be a difference [between two cognitions] simply because they belong to a single continuum (ekasantāna). To explain: since there is no contradiction between the linking of another cognition and a cognition functioning within a body—even though it functions in a different body—the reason [that the body is different] is inconclusive (anaikāntika), just as the consciousness existing in the state prior to the moment of death certainly links with the consciousness occurring in the state of being alive, despite functioning in a different body, because the body is momentary (kṣaṇika).

If it is argued that the body is non-different [in the case of rebirth] due to belonging to a single continuum, and thus it is assumed that the cognition functions in a non-different body, then the same applies to the intermediate state body (antarābhāvikadeha).

For instance: this body in the next world is merely a specific state within the continuum of the body characterized by the five sense-bases (pañcāyatana), just like the difference between the states of childhood and old age.

Furthermore, in the second formal argument, the reason "because it is cognition" is clearly inconclusive (anaikāntika), as no subverting proof has been presented against the opposite of the probandum; thus, it was not explicitly mentioned [as a flaw].
Regarding the third application, beginning with "the knowledge of death with attachment" (sarāgamaraṇajñāna) for the years 1914–1915, he says: "of one whose outflows are exhausted," and so forth.
How is it considered that the consciousness of one whose outflows are exhausted (kṣīṇāsrava) does not undergo reconnection?
If you say it is because of the established tenets (kṛtānta) of others, it is not so, because those [tenets] do not accept [the means of valid cognition].
That which has no reconnection with another mind is "non-reconnecting" (asandhāna).
By this, he states that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is unestablished for at least one of the parties in the example;
for instance, from where is it established for the Cārvāka that the death-consciousness of Arhats does not link to another consciousness?

Even if it were argued that it is recited in the Buddhist school’s own established doctrine (*siddhānta*)—"Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, I know no further existence beyond this"—therefore, the non-linking is established.

This is incorrect: since the opponent's own tenet is not accepted as authoritative, how could the Materialist (Lokāyata) reach a certainty based on that which is accepted as non-authoritative? For if he did, it would follow that he must also have certainty regarding the existence of another world (*paraloka*). If you say that this [non-existence] is understood from some other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then why was that very thing not stated as the proof? Why was something that lacks probative force and merely indicates stupidity put forward? For it is not the case that because it is not a proof for someone else, it should not be mentioned. (1916)

Even by resorting to his own established tenets (*siddhānta*), [the author] says "those wise ones here," etc., demonstrating that for certain Buddhists, the example is not established as being endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*):
"Those wise ones here who declare that the Jinas possess non-abiding nirvana (*apratiṣṭhitanirvṛti*) and that the two vehicles culminate in that very vehicle. (1917)
And for them, even when relying on the tenets accepted by the opponent, the example would be unestablished with respect to the probandum-property (sādhyadharma) in this case. (1918) iha iti.
In the teaching of the Sugata,
there are certain wise ones who are Mahāyānists— namely, the Mādhyamikas.
For they declare that the non-abiding of the Buddhas is nirvāṇa,
because of their non-abiding in both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa;
and they declare that the vehicles of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas culminate in the single vehicle of the Buddha.
Because of the statement: "This vehicle of knowledge is indeed one alone, namely, the Mahāyāna. (1917–1918)

Having thus stated the fault of the example, he states the fault of the probans (*sādhana*), namely its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*): "And because no subverting argument (*bādhaka*) has been stated.

Because no subverting argument has been stated, there is a doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*); that is, there is a lack of invariable concomitance (*vyabhicāritā*) due to the possibility of the existence of a heterogeneous instance (*vijātīya*). || 1919 ||
"Because no subverting [reason] has been stated" is the reason for the fallacy of "doubtful negative concomitance" (*sandigdhavyatirekitva*);
however, the phrase beginning with "being suspected" (*śaṅkyamāna*) and so forth refers to "deviation" (*vyabhicāritā*), namely,
the existence of [the reason] in the dissimilar class (*vijātīyasadbhāva*).
Of what? It is understood that the question is "for what reason? And the analysis of the compound is: "this suspected existence of a heterogeneous [cause]."
Nor is the consequence of [the absurdity of] death a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), because in ultimate reality there is no such thing as a self or anything else that dies; rather,

it is merely when a dissimilar continuum arises that, due to the cessation of a particular state designated as a specific class (*nikāya-sabhāga*) in the world and in the treatises, such conventional usage occurs.
Regarding the statement that it is reckless to claim that consciousness exists during the embryonic stages such as the *kalala*, he says: "In the *kalala* and so forth," etc.
It is not reckless to say that consciousness exists in the *kalala* and so forth;
for even though the sense faculties have not yet developed, why should cognition not exist there? (1920)
The claim that "all cognition arises from the power of the sense-faculties and their objects" is perceived as a rash assertion, because in dreams and similar states, that cognition occurs otherwise;
furthermore, its form is determined to be different from the actual object.
Therefore, its existence is established even in states such as fainting.

(1922) If all cognition were known only by the power of the sense-faculties and their objects, that would be a rash claim; for in states such as dreaming, mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) manifesting blue and other colors is experienced even when the eye and other sense-faculties are absent and even without an object such as a visible form.
Nor can it be said that the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) is its support at that time, because it manifests as blue and so forth.
Furthermore, since body-consciousness has tangible objects as its domain,
it is incorrect to say that all consciousness consists in the apprehension of an object;
therefore, the existence of consciousness even during states such as fainting is not contradicted.

Furthermore, it might be argued that while the subsistence of consciousness in the form of a potentiality (*śakti*) is not contradictory, its subsistence in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*) is contradictory. To this he says: "Nor even...
Nor indeed does the intellect subsist in such a way by way of a potentiality; rather, at that time, the subsistence of cognitions is held to be by way of their own essential nature alone. (1923)
And from where does your certainty come that there is no mind in states such as sleep or fainting?

If you say it is because of the absence of sensation, then from where has that [absence] been established? (1924) If such a certainty were to arise for you in those states, [it would require a means of knowledge].
"If one thinks, 'I do not know the mind,' then the existence of a mind is established.
[Objection: If it is thought that consciousness exists during these states, why is there no memory of them, such as the forms [experienced] upon waking? (1925–1926)
That [memory] would be entirely without cause, because of the impossibility of proficiency and so forth;
thus, memory would not arise, as in the case of the mind of a newborn infant.
(1927) For if there were some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) establishing that the mind does not exist during states such as sleep or fainting, then there would be a contradiction.
If it is argued that the non-apprehension of self-cognition exists as a determining means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we reply: no;
for from what is the non-apprehension of self-cognition established?
Indeed, in that state, there is no ascertainment of the absence of cognition.
And if, during those states of fainting, you maintain the certainty that "I do not perceive the mind," then by that very certainty thus established, the existence of the mind is proven.
Furthermore, it might be argued: if the mind were present during states such as sleep and so forth, why would there be no recollection for a person who has awakened?
By the word "and so forth" (ādi), one includes those who have recovered from a faint or those whose intoxication has subsided.
Therefore, this non-remembrance is not a ground for establishing the non-existence of what was experienced;

for if remembrance occurred merely by the fact that something was experienced, then such a conclusion might hold. However, even when there has been experience, remembrance does not occur due to a deficiency in acuity, repetition, desire, and so forth—just as in the case of the mind experienced during the state of being newly born and the like.
If, even though existence [of the object] is established for you, there is still doubt because recollection does not occur, he replies by challenging this with the words "If it is so," and so forth.
If this is so, how is its existence in these states determined?
It is understood from the very reason previously described.
Furthermore, if it is not admitted that the mind exists in states such as dreaming or fainting...
In that case, there would either be death at the time of birth, or else an absolute absence of death.
Mental cognition is independent because it does not depend on the eyes and other sense organs; it functions solely by the power of its own material cause, as in the case of dreams and the like.
"Of this" refers to consciousness;
"in these" refers to [the sense bases].

Regarding the states such as sleep and so forth, the reason previously described applies: the initial cognition of a person who has awakened arises from the power of its own material cause (svopādāna), because it is a cognition, like the recollective and other cognitions that occur immediately after an act of attention (ābhoga).
Nor is this reason inconclusive (anaikāntika), since the necessary connection (pratibandha) has already been established by the prior refutation of any other cause.

Furthermore— if the mind (*citta*) were not present during states such as deep sleep, then death itself would occur. Now, if it is maintained that consciousness arises again in that body— which has become such [as described] and from which consciousness has departed root and branch— then, if its arising there is admitted, the consequence follows that death does not exist, because even for one who is dead, the re-arising of consciousness would result, since the mind and intellect alone possess the capacity to link to another birth, just like one who has awakened from sleep.
And so it has been said: "The [moments of] cutting, reconnecting, detachment, loss, and attainment are held to occur only in the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Therefore, demonstrating that the cognition of the mind (*manobuddhi*) relies solely upon a preceding cognition, he says: "Independent," and so forth.
Independence, meaning the state of being non-dependent, is the reason:

this mental cognition (manobuddhi) always arises solely from its own material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa), because it does not depend on other causes such as the eyes that are distinct from its own material cause, just as in the state of dreaming.
he refutes the unestablished nature of the reason (asiddhatā) by means of the word "tathāhi" (for instance/so it is).
For instance, conceptual constructions do not depend upon the sense organs and their objects,
because they occur even in the absence of the operation of those [senses], as in the case of [mental constructs such as] a sky-lotus and the like.
"Even in the absence of the operation of those" means...
The meaning is: "even when those two—the sense faculty and the object—are not functioning.
For it is not logical that something which exists even in the absence of another's activity should be the cause of that other, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

It might be argued: "Let it be that the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of a sky-lotus and the like is independent of sense-faculties and objects, since it occurs even in their absence; however, how can the conceptual construction 'this is blue' which arises when the eye is directed toward an object present before one, such as something blue, be independent of sense-faculties and objects, so that the reason [of yours] would not be unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to a portion of the subject? To this, he says: "Of those two," and so forth.

Even when those two [the object and its cognition] are absent, whatever conceptual construction regarding the past and so forth arises is determined to be exactly equal [to an illusion], due to its coloring by an unreal object.
Because it appears as the referent of a word, the nature of a real entity does not appear.
"In regard to conceptual constructions"— all of this has indeed been established in detail.
"Of those two" refers to the sense faculty and the object.

That conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of an object such as space, for which there is an appearance (*nirbhāsa*) that is empty (*śūnya*) and colored (*uparāga*) by a non-existent object (*asadartha*), is "colored by a non-existent object.
The meaning is that this [conceptualization of the Buddha] is also similar to that, being likewise devoid of an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*).
How so?

For every conceptual construction (vikalpa), because it functions through the articulation of words, manifests as the object of a word; and that which manifests as the object of a word does not manifest the nature of a real entity (vasturūpa), because a word does not function with respect to the nature of a real entity, since the word has not been conventionally established for that [nature]. This has been explained in detail in the *Śabdārthaparīkṣā*.

Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), the reason is not contradictory (*viruddha*); nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because if it did not arise from its own material cause (*svopādāna*), it would follow that it is causeless.

Anticipating the objection that "it cannot be causeless because it depends upon the body," he says: "In states such as numbness (*prasuptikā*), even when there is a physical alteration... and so forth.

There is no alteration of the mental cognition; therefore, this [cognition] does not depend upon it. For even when the body undergoes modification due to afflictions such as paralysis, there is no modification of the mental cognition; thus, this mental cognition does not depend on the body. Whatever is not necessarily and directly modified by the modification of something else is not dependent upon that thing—just as a horse, which is not modified by the modification of a cow, is not dependent on it. And since the mental cognition is not necessarily and directly modified by the modification of the body during states such as paralysis, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
With the words "svalpīyasī" and so forth, he demonstrates that being dependent on something is pervaded by being subject to modification through the modifications of that very thing:

for even when there is a very slight modification of the eye or other sense organs, such as [the onset of] cataracts (timira), the cognition dependent on the eye and other organs arises indeed as something modified. (1935)
Even upon the destruction of that body, the intellect (buddhi), which has the mind as its substrate, continues to exist by the power of its own material cause (upādāna) without contradiction.
And since there is no absence of that [intellect] here, which is all-pervading, it is established that cognition (buddhi) does not depend on the body.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in the fact that [the self] will not cease even upon the cessation of the body;
for when something does not depend on another, its cessation does not necessarily entail the cessation of that other thing,
just as, for example, the cessation of a cow does not necessarily entail the cessation of a gavaya.
And it is not the case that the body is the substratum of mental cognition; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader.

Regarding what was stated in the two verses beginning with "ending at death" and "the body arising immediately after death," he says: "Even the mind and intellect alone," and so forth: "Even if the mind and intellect alone are thus non-contradictory [with respect to rebirth], we do not exert ourselves to prove the existence of another body beyond that. (1937)
Nor can this [existence] be denied, because it persists even when not perceived, just as a person with weak vision does not perceive thin smoke and the like.

(1938) The intention here is this: the next world is what is intended to be proven here; and how could that not be established? It would be established if consciousness were proven to be beginningless and endless.

This is merely a specific state of this very [mental continuum] designated as the "other world," and not something distinct for each individual body; for even in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), where there is an absence of a body, the other world is nevertheless accepted.

If that mental continuum is established as being without beginning or end, then our "other world" is established. Therefore, we make no effort to establish a separate body, as such an endeavor would be fruitless.
Nor can its negation be established by mere non-perception;

for such non-perception might occur even while that body exists, due to a deficiency in one's mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and so forth, as in the case of a person with weak vision regarding a particular species. Indeed, we say it is like the non-perception of thin smoke; thus, negation is not established by mere non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*).
For instance, a subsequent existence (*uttarabhava*) is described as being visible to those of the same class who possess pure divine faculties.

For this very reason, there is no rejection of the subtle body (*ativāhika-śarīra*) postulated by the Sāṅkhyas; for even the body of a previous existence would not be perceived due to spatial distance, either because it has arisen in a very distant place or because of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*), like the bodies of *piśācas* and the like.
Even if there were no such distance, it would be impossible for one of limited vision to ascertain that "this very living being has become a moth" or some other state.
Like one whose body has been transformed through the application of medicine possessing inconceivable power.

How, then, are cognitions that have different substrates said to be connected to a single continuum? To this he says: "Even though they rest on different bodies"—that is, even though they rest on different bodies—they are connected to a single continuum like a stream, because they conform to its specific characteristics, as was the case with the preceding cognition. (1939)
Moreover, even newborn infants engage in desire for nursing the breast and so forth, and experience aversion toward injury;
this [desire and aversion] is inferred from such effects as crying and nursing the breast.
And all that consists of conceptual construction, and that is accompanied by the association with names.
"By way of conforming to its particularities" means that the cognitions of this life conform to those particularities of the cognition belonging to another birth.
And so it has been said: "Through the yoga of practice, auspicious and inauspicious actions become habitual for persons;
thus, without effort and without instruction, they act in another birth as if in a dream.

Regarding this, what was stated by the Cārvāka—that because the bodies of this world and the next are distinct, the minds residing within them cannot belong to a single continuum, and so forth—[is refuted].

"The first consciousness at conception and so forth does not belong to the same continuum as that which is the subject of dispute, because its body is different, like the consciousnesses of buffaloes, boars, and so on"—
this [argument] is refuted by the following: moreover, the next world is established from this very point as well.

To explain: whatever is a conceptual construction (vikalpa) is preceded by the practice of verbal experience, because it is a conceptual construction, like the conceptual constructions occurring in stages such as youth;

and this conceptual construction of newborns—the desire for suckling at the breast and so forth—is indeed a conceptual construction. This is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu), and the reason is not unestablished with respect to its locus (āśrayāsiddha).

Since this [behavior]—such as crying and suckling at the breast—is established through the activity of newborns who possess the desire for suckling and so forth, it is proven that this is a property [of consciousness].
For it is not logical that crying, suckling at the breast, and the like could occur in one who is devoid of conceptualization in the form of attachment, aversion, or non-aversion;
nor is it unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*). Thus he demonstrates: "And all that is of the nature of conceptualization."
That— consisting of the desire to suckle at the breast and so forth—
is entirely of the nature of conceptual construction (vikalpātmā), because it is experienced as having the form of longing and the like, which is the very essence of conceptual construction.
Showing that it is also not inconclusive, he says: "And that which is accompanied by a name" refers to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Because every conceptual construction (vikalpa) proceeds by means of a verbal articulation and is thus associated with a name,

and because that association with a name is not possible for a conceptual construction without the prior habituation to linguistic convention (saṅketa)— as has been established by us in detail previously [in verse 1939].
Furthermore,
even if it were granted that attachment to names is preceded by repeated practice, nevertheless, this does not serve as a means to achieve the desired goal.
What then?

He says that it is precisely the prior practice in this world that establishes the opposite [of what you claim]: "Neither name nor form," and so forth—"In this birth, neither name nor form exists for them; and in the absence of another existence, their cessation would follow as a logical consequence. (1942)
This is what is meant:
the practice of worldly people in this life is subverted by the cognition of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for those who have just been born;

and it is not logical that a reason (*hetu*) whose probandum (*pratijñārtha*) is being subverted should be considered contradictory (*viruddha*), according to the principle that "a reason is contradictory only when there is no subversion."
"Name-and-form" (*nāmarūpa*) means the form of name— the expressive nature— which, though revolving within the intellect, is superimposed upon external sounds and upon those [objects] as well.
"The destruction of those that have just arisen" means the destruction of those [desires] such as longing and so forth; that is "their destruction."

With the words beginning "tannāma" (its name), he concludes the meaning of the aforementioned proof: "This [result] arises through the power of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by the repeated practice of praising its name."
Because they have the nature of conceptual construction, they are like conceptual constructions at present;
"tad" means "therefore."
With the words beginning "yannāma," he demonstrates the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*):
that which is born from the ripening of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced by the repeated practice of familiarity with names.

For them, conceptual construction (vikalpa) proceeds; that is what constitutes their "other existence" (bhavāntara). [The compound] *nāmasaṃstavābhyāsa* means: *nāmnaḥ* is "of the word"; *saṃstavaḥ* is "familiarity," which is to say "experience"; its *abhyāsaḥ* is "repeated production.

The compound *yannāmasaṃbhavābhyāse* is formed by the rule of splitting the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*) using the locative case (*saptamī*). Thus, it means "in whichever existence there is the repeated production of the occurrence of names."

The latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by that [action] undergoes maturation (*paripāka*), which is the acquisition of functional activity (*vṛttilābha*) for the production of an effect corresponding to itself; "born from that" is the etymological derivation (*vyutpattikrama*) of the term "those who are newly born" (*sadyojātānām*).
With the words "1944.

By the power of the practice of names," etc., he raises the objection of a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) put forward by another: "If their [activity] proceeds solely by the power of the practice of names..."
Why then are the words of eloquent speakers not as clear, or why is their memory not so?
(1945) If the activity of conceptual construction proceeds from the habituation of previous conventions, then it would follow that even an infant should remember those previous conventions;
for the persistence of habituation is not logically possible without memory.
Furthermore, there would be the consequence of a continuous flow of clear speech activity, as if among eloquent orators;
consequently, the formulation of linguistic conventions would be rendered useless,
yet such is not the case.

Therefore, because there is an absence of recollection and because clear speech does not function, the state of being preceded by prior practice is contradictory. Thus, by means of a *prasaṅga-viparyaya* (the reversal of the reductio ad absurdum) and by way of refuting the essential nature of the property (*dharma-svarūpa*), he states the flaw in the thesis (*pratijñā-doṣa*) with the verse beginning "paṭīyasā" (1945).
Furthermore, in this *prasaṅga-viparyaya*, he states that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Due to a powerful impairment and because they are distracted by the process of maturation,
this functioning of these [mental states] would not occur, as in the case of the stages of a *sannipāta* (a derangement of the humors).
For prior habituation is not always pervaded by recollection and so forth, such that it would cause recollection and the like to proceed.

Or, even upon the cessation of that [dream], it would continue as long as the persistence of prior habituation remains, yet there would be no recollection; just as in the state of a medical complication (*sannipāta*),
so too in a dream, there is a persistence of prior habituation but no recollection.
The mention of the "conjunction" (sannipāta) is illustrative;
it is "more potent" because of its dwelling within the womb.
"Due to the confusion of maturation" means that there is a confusion regarding the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*),
which consists in their failing to function in accordance with the specific distinctions of place, time, intrinsic nature, and so forth, as they were originally experienced.
In this regard, that which was stated by the Cārvāka— that the recollection of past births is unproven because everyone who has come from the same village possesses such recollection—
is thereby refuted by this [argument].

For instance— even when all have arrived from the same village, not everyone remembers what occurred there; among them, those who are of dull intellect certainly become ones whose memory has been stolen.

With the words "svalpīyān api" (even the slightest) and so forth [in verse 1946], he states that the reason is unestablished with respect to a portion of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*) in the case of the reversal of the reductio (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*).
"But for those great-souled ones (*mahātman*), not even the slightest impairment is heard; their words are clearly articulated, and that memory is distinct.
(1947) "Of the great-souled ones" means:
Regarding those possessed of merit (puṇyavatām),
he states another argument for the establishment of the next world once again, beginning with the words "attachment, aversion, and so forth."
Furthermore, these [afflictions] such as attachment and aversion, which become intense through the practice of habituation,
are established by means of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). Those which occur for the first time here [in this life] are devoid of prior habituation.
What is the cause for their birth if there were no other existence?
For their birth does not occur merely through the presence of an object, since they do not arise even when that object is present if analytical cessation exists.
And because their predominance is observed upon the cessation of analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyā*), due to the increase of error even regarding objects that have perished or not yet arisen;
[and] because one superimposes qualities such as being pure, belonging to oneself, and permanent upon women and so forth. (Verse 1951)
Passions such as attachment do not arise because objects possess that [passionate] nature;

rather, even those occurring here [in this life] proceed without such external objects, due to the power of similar habitual practice, just like subsequent instances of attachment and so forth. (1952–1953)

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: The proficiency regarding passion, hatred, envy, intoxication, pride, and so forth, as well as wisdom, compassion, loving-kindness, and so forth, is preceded by practice. This is because, as observed in this very life, the proficiency of a person possessing sharp or dull qualities as described is seen to arise through the power of practice; and furthermore, there exists in some person even in this life a proficiency regarding those various [qualities] despite the absence of practice in this world. This is a reason based on the effect (*kāryahetu*), since the causal relationship has been established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); thus, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

Therefore he says: "Because they are ascertained through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the reason [that they arise] from the practice of another life is contradictory. If this is argued, we reply: no, for it is incorrect to prove that they are preceded by the practice of another life on the grounds that "those first-arising intense passions (*rāga* etc. are devoid of practice in this life."

Nor is it logical for them to be causeless, because that would entail their eternal existence and so forth; therefore, if there were no other life, what would be the cause for the arising—i.e., the production—of these potent factors such as passion and the rest?
Consequently, it is established that practice in another life is indeed the cause, and thus the next world exists.

The object is not the cause [of the arising of passion and so forth], because even when an object is present, passion and the like do not arise at times when there is the presence of analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) on the foul (*aśubha*) and so forth. Analytical reflection is the wisdom that takes the foul and so forth as its object and serves as the antidote to passion and the like;
since we observe the arising of passion and the like even in the absence of such an object, it is not logical that their existence depends upon the object.

For instance, even with respect to objects that are past or future, when a person’s error regarding increased pleasure and so forth arises through the power of conceptual construction (*saṅkalpa*), it is observed that those [afflictions] such as attachment become powerful once analytical discernment (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) has ceased.

Indeed, it is not logical for something to be the cause of another if there is no positive or negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) between the presence or absence of the one and the presence or absence of the other; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For this reason as well, the activity of the afflictions does not proceed by virtue of an objective support (*ālambana*).

For instance: if they were to proceed exactly according to their objective support (*ālambana*), then they would proceed by the power of that objective support, just as the cognition of blue and so forth does; however, they do not proceed in this way.
Rather, superimposing aspects such as "belonging to oneself," "permanent," and "pleasurable" even though these have never been experienced, they proceed toward women and other objects;
yet the objects themselves do not possess such forms as "pure" and so forth.
Furthermore, it is not logical that whatever is devoid of a particular form can be its objective support (*ālambana*), for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, because they have superimposed objects as their domain, attachment and the other afflictions are without an objective support.
Consequently, it is established that even those attachments and so forth which arise here in this life for the first time proceed by the force of the practice of their own kind from previous lives.
One thousand nine hundred and fifty-one,
one thousand nine hundred and fifty-two,
one thousand nine hundred and fifty-three.

If, then, objects are not the cause, how is it that attachment and other such states are seen to arise when an object is encountered? To this he says: "But upon the encounter with an object," and so forth.
However, upon the encounter with an object, there arises the occurrence of pleasure, pain, and so on;
therefore, these are born from the maturation of homogeneous latent impressions (*vāsanā*). (1954)

Afflictions such as attachment and aversion belong to those who hate analytical discernment and are subject to improper mental formations; they arise according to one's own power. However, objects themselves are not at all the direct causes of attachment, aversion, and the like.
For in that case, there would be only one affliction for all [beings], just as there is for the one who possesses the realization [of it].

This is the sequence: when an object presents itself, pleasure born of the senses arises; from that pleasure, provided there is no deficiency in analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyāna*), there occurs the ripening of the latencies (*vāsanā*) previously deposited by passion and so forth in those who abide in improper mental attention (*ayoniśomanaskāra*) characterized by the misconceptions of a self and so on; from that, the afflictions such as passion proceed. Thus, objects are not the direct cause.
It might be argued: "This is merely a description of one's own established doctrine, and there is no reasoning here at all. To this he says: "One," and so forth;
"one" means having a single form.
"In that [context]" means "in that object";
"of that" refers to...
"Just like the cognition of an object" means possessing the form that grasps blue and so forth.
Furthermore, affliction does not arise there in a single form;
for instance, with respect to the same female form, one person experiences passion, another hatred, and another envy—the manifestation of multiple forms is thus observed. (1954)
It might be argued that the initial passion and so forth in this life do not arise from prior practice [in a previous life].
What then?

It is said that it is through observing the conduct of others, such as sexual intercourse, or through hearing from others: "by perceiving the behavior of others" and so forth, or "by hearing from others."
Nor does this behavior belong to them, because deviation is observed;
"behavior" (vṛtti) means, in effect, the conduct of others.
With the words "not seen," etc., he demonstrates that very same fallacy:
"Boars, deer, and other animals, though they have neither seen nor heard of such events, certainly undergo transformation upon contact with the movement of their own kind. (1958)

"Vṛttānta" refers to the practice of sexual intercourse and so forth; those such as female pigs and others who possess a similar or corresponding mode of existence (*gati*) are so designated, and "contact" (*saṃparka*) with them means physical union.
"Corruption" means perversion;
that is to say, the practice of sexual intercourse.
In 1958, qualities such as wisdom, ethical discipline, and compassion, which are unaccustomed to cyclic existence,
function spontaneously and not like pride and the other afflictions. 1959.
This must necessarily be understood: that the spontaneous activity of passion and the like occurs solely through the power of habituation.

For instance, those qualities such as wisdom and ethical discipline, which are unaccustomed to cyclic existence and have not been practiced within it, do not function spontaneously or effortlessly, unlike intoxication and the like; this is an example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).
Intoxication is pride; otherwise, like intoxication and so forth, even wisdom and the other [faculties] would function by their own natural impulse.

Some say that passion arises from phlegm (*śleṣman*), hatred from bile (*pitta*), and delusion from wind (*vāta*); to this he replies with the verse beginning "By the influence of phlegm, etc."— that their emergence does not occur through the power of phlegm and the other humors.
Because deviation is perceived in every respect, as before;
therefore, since these [cognitions] which occur at the beginning are preceded by practice, that very other life is established, and thus the nihilist is defeated. (1960–1961)

In that context, "balāsa" refers to phlegm (*śleṣman*), as previously stated; just as deviation regarding sense objects was explained by such arguments as: "Even when there is the presence of analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyāna*), [the affliction] does not arise [if that reflection is absent]," and so forth.
Furthermore: through the increase and decrease of phlegm (*śleṣman*) and the other humors, there occur the increase and decrease of passion (*rāga*) and the rest.
Now, it is not logical for something to be the effect of another if its variation does not follow from the variation of that [cause], because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Likewise, intense hatred is observed even in one of a phlegmatic nature, but not intense passion; conversely, one of a bilious nature (*pittaprakṛti*) is observed to have intense passion, but not intense hatred and so forth. Thus, a confusion of causes and effects is seen.
Furthermore, it is not logical that something which exists without another should have that other as its cause;

for one is seen to be full of passion in a certain state, yet in that very same state one may be full of hatred. Therefore, because of this deviation as well, passion and the like do not have phlegm and the like as their properties.
"Therefore" is the conclusion.

Regarding the phrase "yadabhyāsapūrvakāḥ": the analysis of the compound is as follows—"yadabhyāsaḥ" means that in which there is practice; those for whom that [practice] is the preceding cause (pūrvaka) are "yadabhyāsapūrvakāḥ. (1960)
In verse 1961, beginning with "ihatyā," he anticipates an objection from another:
if it is to be proven that [the Veda] is preceded by study here [in this world], there would be sublation by what is perceived and what is accepted.
If [the reason] refers to being the cause of another existence, the example is devoid of the probandum (sādhya).
However, if the probandum is stated without qualification, this reason is contradictory (viruddha),
because it likewise excludes the fact that [the practice] has as its cause habituation in another existence.

In this regard, the following objection arises: Is it to be proven that those [afflictions] occurring for the first time are preceded by practice in this life, or that they are preceded by practice in a future life, or simply that they are preceded by practice in general? If that [general fact] were established, then by implication, the desired conclusion—that they are preceded by practice in a future life—would be established. Thus, there are three positions. Among them, regarding the first position: there is subversion of both what is observed and what is accepted. For it is not observed that afflictions such as attachment, when occurring for the first time, are preceded by practice in this life; nor is this accepted by the proponent of a future world. Thus, there is subversion of both the observed and the accepted.

In the second position as well, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), for there exists no instance anywhere of a materialist (*lokāyata*) whose activity is preceded by practice regarding the next world. In the third position too, the logical reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because, just like the example, it proves the absence of that which is intended—the state of being preceded by practice in another life. 1962
he provides a rebuttal with the words "sāmānyenaiva" and so forth: "The probandum is indeed in a general sense, and there is no contradiction of the reason."
"For there is no contradiction with it by which one could turn it back.
(1964) Thus, in this examination of the Lokāyata, it is precisely the third position that is intended here; nor is there a contradictory nature in the reason. Why?

For there is no contradiction whatsoever between this state of passion and so forth being preceded by practice in another existence and its being preceded by practice in a future world, such that it would preclude the latter.
Moreover, the distinction between "this world" and "the next world" is merely a conventional designation based on a difference in states.
Since beginninglessness is established by this method— just as there are distinctions such as childhood and youth— one should not be dogmatic about this [point that it is "like the opponent"].
(The list of corrections does not display parentheses.)
Thus ends the examination of the Lokāyata,
which is the examination of external objects.

The opponent [prativivādi] states: "It is like a reflection" (*pratibimbādisannibham*); this is the proof (*pramiti*). Now, in order to establish this qualification of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-viśeṣaṇa*), the Vijñānavādin presents the following.

In this regard, the doctrine of the Buddhist Vijñānavādins is that this triple world is nothing but representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*). Furthermore, that consciousness is infinite and impure due to the distinctions between the mental continua of individual beings for those who have not realized reality; yet it is pure for those who have abandoned their afflictions. It arises as something dissolving moment by moment for all living creatures, and is not a single, unchanging entity as the proponents of the Upaniṣads maintain.

In this system, the state of representation-only is asserted through these two aspects: because when there is an absence of an external object of apprehension—such as the nature of earth and so forth—there is also an absence of the status of being an apprehender.

Or, even if another mental continuum exists, because it is devoid of the characteristics of apprehended object and apprehending subject, the formal argument (*prayoga*) therein is as follows: whatever is cognition is devoid of the duality of apprehended and apprehender, because it is cognition, like the cognition of a reflection; and this cognition of healthy eyes and so forth, which is the subject of dispute, is indeed cognition. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), and one should not consider this reason to be non-pervasive (*avyāpti*).

To explain: first of all, no external object such as earth and so forth exists as its [the cognition's] apprehended object, because such an object is devoid of a nature that is either unitary or manifold.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not possess a nature that is either unitary or manifold is not apprehended as an existent by a discerning person, just like a sky-lotus; and the earth and other entities postulated by opponents are devoid of a nature that is either unitary or manifold. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Since existence is pervaded by both unity and plurality due to the absence of a third category, the impossibility of a relationship between the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the opposite case; thus, the immediately preceding reason is neither inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) nor contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

Here, pointing out that this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), and demonstrating the contradiction with perception and other means of knowledge regarding the proposition (*pratijñā*) stated as, "Let this supreme principle be accepted: that the primary elements (*bhūta*) themselves do not exist," the opponent speaks in order to demonstrate the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the first reason, beginning with: "If, apart from cognition...
[verse 1965]: "If the fourfold set of primary elements does not exist apart from cognition, then why is this appearing so clearly and distinctly? (1965)
If, even when such an appearance occurs, you admit its non-existence, then what proof could you have for the existence of the mind itself?
By the term "discontinuous," he demonstrates the establishment of an object of cognition distinct from consciousness; by the term "clearly," however, he indicates its perceptibility.
Confirming this very point by way of a further application, he says: "Of him who thus," and so forth (verses 1965–1966).
He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "bhāsamāna" (while appearing), etc.:
"While appearing, what is the nature of this external object that manifests?
Is it of the nature of atoms, or rather characterized as a composite whole? (1967)
The form of atoms is not perceived at all, because there is no perception of a cognition that appears as multiple partless forms;
for atoms would have to appear as devoid of any distinction of parts.
Otherwise, they could not possess perceptibility, because they do not impart their own form [to the cognition].

In that regard, the object established by perception, being external, must be one of the following alternatives: either it is multiple and non-different from atoms, or it is a single composite whole (*avayavin*) composed of them, or it is a gross entity not so composed.
Among these, the first alternative is not tenable, because no cognition is perceived that grasps multiple partless atoms as having corporeal form.

Because cognition is always experienced as having only a gross form, and because those [atoms] are not perceived within that cognition—this being an uncompounded application of the locative case—the following is the logical argument: that which does not appear with its own form in a cognition regarded as direct perception (pratyakṣa) cannot be apprehended as being directly perceived, just like a lotus in the sky; and multiple material atoms do not appear in a cognition regarded as direct perception that grasps a gross form. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Since perception is pervaded by the appearance of the aspect of a self, he states the following—beginning with "vyapeta" (verse 1967)—in order to demonstrate that very pervasion: "vyapeta... and so forth.

1168 1969 Now, it might be argued that because of the established tenet that [atoms] arise and perish only when aggregated, there is no appearance of individual atoms; as the Venerable Śubhagupta has stated: "Individual atoms have no possibility of existence either independently or non-independently."
To show that for this reason as well, atoms do not appear individually, he says: "Even by way of association... and so forth. This [objection] is not a valid response.
Even through their association with literary works, they shine by their very own nature;

they do not abandon their partless form, provided that these [entities] do not exist in such states [of limitation]. If their nature were to possess a limit of diminution, it would not belong to them.
How indeed could those [elements], being material, not become immaterial like sensation and so forth?
Regarding "in those states," it means in those combined conditions.

Furthermore: if atoms are partless, then it must be admitted that they are not corporeal; thus, he states a contradiction with his own proposition in the passage beginning with "labdhāpacaya... (having reached the limit of diminution).

That form or nature by which [the atom] has reached the limit of diminution is so described. This is what is meant: if they do not possess a nature that diminishes through the division of diminishing parts—that is to say, if they are partless—then they cannot be established as corporeal, like sensation and so forth, because there would be no distinction [between them].
With the words "equal" (tulya) and so forth, [the author] anticipates the rebuttal of Bhadanta Śubhagupta from the years 1970–1971.

Just as there is the delusion of permanence due to the arising of subsequent moments similar [to the preceding], so too, if there is the perception of an uninterrupted series of homogeneous [objects], there is the delusion of grossness.

(1972) For he says: "Just as for one who is deceived by the arising of successive similar moments, there arises the delusion of permanence regarding sound and the like even though they are perceived directly, so too, when there is the simultaneous perception of atoms that are adjacent in space and homogeneous, there occurs a mental delusion that they are 'gross'."
And thus, because there is no cognition of multiple partless forms, the reason is unestablished;
[the author] states the refutation with the words "by the power of its own operation," etc., as follows: "by the power of its own operation alone."
If perception were to produce [the cognition] solely by the power of its own operation,

how could those entities— such as the "subsequent reflective cognition" (parāmarśavijñāna) and the fact that "entities are momentary"— be objects of direct perception established through valid means of knowledge? (1973)
If atoms are understood to be such [partless entities], how then are yellow, white, and so forth perceived?

For that which consists of an accumulation of subtle [atoms] is not initially visible to the eye because of its grossness, like a mountain and the like; if it is argued that here too there is an inference regarding their totality and non-totality—[we reply: 1974–1975.
For grossness is indeed a property of a real entity, and it is not established in either of the two [proposed] subjects;
for there is no gross composite (avayavin), nor are atoms of such a nature. Now, if it is argued that the form existing through spatial extension is what is thus described:
Nevertheless, there is doubt because [the object] appears as a form manifested by erroneous cognition.
If it were not so due to its unreality, then— provided that its distinction [from error] has not been established—
what excellence would this [cognition] possess, unless it be the correspondence with the result?

Even when there is a correspondence with a cognition that manifests the effect, it is indeed stated [in the commentary] that this is due to the restriction of capacity as the cause; however, that [correspondence] could otherwise be possible.
By the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*), he shows that [the cognition] is independent of the operation of logical marks (*liṅga*) or scripture (*āgama*).

For instance—although perception arises without distinction, it is only that aspect in which it generates a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) corresponding to the apprehended form that is accepted as "perceived" due to its fitness for practical activity (*vyavahāra*); however, in that aspect where it does not generate such awareness, even though it was apprehended, it is as if unapprehended.
Consequently, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).

For, in the phrase "because of the non-perception of the cognition," the intended meaning is "because [the object] does not appear in the cognition—which is regarded as perception—that serves as the cause for reflective awareness."
As for what was said—that this notion of "grossness" is merely a mental delusion—that too is incorrect.
For instance, the determination of something as a delusion can only occur once its opposite has been established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
