just as the apprehension of permanence is established as an error because momentariness has been established by valid cognition.

Furthermore, atoms are not established by such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because they themselves are currently under investigation. Nor is this delusion of grossness mental, because it appears with clarity;
and it is not logical for that which is bound to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) to have a clear form, since the form of a universal (*sāmānya*) is inherently indistinct.
Furthermore, conceptual construction would not be possible without a universal form.
To this it might be replied: "Just like impermanence and so forth, atoms too are indeed established by means of valid cognition."

To explain: whatever is gross (*sthūla*) is composed of an accumulation of subtle elements (*sūkṣma*), just as mountains and the like; and the first visually perceptible substance possessing parts (*avayavidravya*) is gross. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
The inclusion of the term "visually perceptible" (*cākṣuṣa*) is for the purpose of excluding non-visually perceptible things such as dyads (*dvyaṇuka*).

In this regard, if the reason "because of grossness" is stated by relying upon ultimate grossness as a property of real entities (*vastudharma*), then grossness is not established for the proponent in either of the two subjects—the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) or the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*). Consequently, the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*) and the example would lack the probans (*sādhanavikala*).

Now, if that form which appears as a spatial extension, which is delightful only so long as it is not investigated, and which is well-known even to cowherds and others, is called "gross" because of its bulkiness, then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since such an appearing form exists even in erroneous cognitions like dreams, despite the absence of an accumulation of atoms.

Now, if the qualification "provided it is non-erroneous" (*abhrāntatve sati*) is introduced, then so long as the distinction—that is, the difference—of the form of cognition from healthy eyes and so forth from the form of cognition in dreams and the like has not been established against the Proponent of Cognition-only (*vijñānavādin*), non-erroneousness is not established anywhere; thus, even the qualification would be unestablished.

It might be argued: "There certainly is a distinction between cognition from healthy eyes and so forth and cognition from dreams and the like, by virtue of the correspondence with causal efficacy (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*).
To this we ask: what indeed is this so-called "correspondence with causal efficacy"?

If the attainment of an external object is meant, that is not established, because the non-existence of an external object is precisely what is being presented as the thesis to be proven. If, on the other hand, "correspondence with causal efficiency" (arthakriyā-saṃvāda) is simply the cognition appearing as the intended causal efficiency, then this could occur otherwise even without an external object as its objective support. Thus, the reason remains inconclusive (anaikāntika). To explain how it could occur otherwise, he says: "Because of the restriction of capacity [inherent] in the cause."
Because of the restriction of the specific capacity of the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*),
only a certain immediately preceding condition is capable of producing a certain consciousness, and not every [condition] produces every [consciousness],
just as you maintain regarding external objects; therefore, the restriction is established from that very fact.
With the verse beginning "Equal," etc., he points out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason "because of non-perception" according to the view of Sumati the Digambara:
"When a form that is equal is perceived, that which is unequal is not perceived at all."
If atoms possess a dual nature, then what is not logically established?

Since every entity consists of the nature of both the universal and the particular, atoms are traditionally held to be of two forms, by virtue of having both similar and dissimilar essential natures. (1980–1981)

In that case, whatever form is common is the object of sensory cognition; therefore, cognition having a single form is possible only with respect to atoms. However, whatever form is uncommon is held to be the object of yogic perception.
Thus, some of poor intellect imagine this confusedly.
For he (the author) has said this: because all categories possess the nature of both the universal and the particular, atoms are of two forms, by way of both similar and dissimilar aspects.
Among these, that form which is common is perceived by the sense organs, not the uncommon one.
Consequently, since a single uniform cognition is not contradictory in relation to atoms, it follows that atoms are established by direct perception; thus,
[the opponent's position] is confused and lacks a firm foundation.
Because there is an absence of even a single definitively determined form.
But has it not already been stated that the entity has a dual nature, which is a determined form? True, it was stated; however, showing that what was stated is incorrect, he says:

For how indeed could two forms be logical for a single entity? In that case, two entities would result, due to their having distinct forms from one another. But if they were of a mutually identical nature, then that duality of form would be contradicted.
And a distinction would be perceived by the sense organs, such as the eye, and so forth.

For instance, because one thing is distinct from another due to its two forms, it follows that there must be two separate entities; since there is only the existence of each of those two distinct forms individually, it cannot be said that a single entity possesses two forms.

Alternatively, since two forms are not distinct from a single entity, the two forms must be identical to one another, just like the nature of that single entity; how then could one thing possess two forms?
Furthermore, because the particular form is not distinct from the universal form, it would follow that the particular form must be perceived [by the senses].
Consequently, this unmixed distinction would not be established—that the common form is the object of sensory cognition, while the uncommon form is held to be the object of yogic perception.

Furthermore, 1984–1985: Not only is it mutually contradictory that "one [thing] has two forms," but this is even more contradictory—that which shows one thing to consist of two mutually opposed forms—as expressed in the passage beginning with "paraspara... and so forth.
"How could that which is of a mutually contradictory nature be of a single form?
For instance, since the similar and dissimilar forms are characterized by mutual exclusion, how could they be a single entity consisting of those two?
With these words, beginning with "saṃvitteśca" (and because of consciousness), he raises the objection based on the view of Kumārila.
Furthermore, it is impossible for contradictory cognitions to exist even in a single [entity].
If it were not of a single form, it would not be one; thus, this was not spoken by the Lord.
Indeed, that [object] must be accepted exactly as it is perceived.
For he said: "The claim that mutually contradictory forms cannot exist within a single object is not true;
why?
Because of consciousness."

For instance—it is not a command of kings that a single entity must exist in only one form; rather, whatever is perceived in a certain way must be accepted as being exactly so, because the determination of an object is based upon cognition.
And it is observed that cognition occurs in both single and multiple forms, due to distinctions such as existence, color, and so forth.
Therefore, it is established in that very manner.
He refutes that with the words beginning "That is not so" (tanna):
"That is not so, because even for what is non-existent there is cognition, as in the case of the yellow color of a conch-shell;
moreover, since there is no association with contradictory properties, there is no other definition of difference. (1988)
This being the case, no cognition whatsoever would be erroneous, and there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all conventional usage based on distinctions.
Alternatively, if the erroneous nature of some cognitions were due to their being sublated,
then how could multiple cognitions of a single object— which are themselves subject to sublation— not be erroneous?
Thus, since atoms are established neither through direct perception nor through inference, there is no contradiction with direct perception regarding the thesis that denies external objects,
nor is the reason unestablished.
Now, the opponent, raising the objection that the reason "because of being devoid of a nature that is either one or many" is of doubtful unestablished status (sandigdhāsiddha), says:

"Let it be that there is no establishment of atoms by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and let there be doubt; but how could there be certainty regarding their non-existence for those who are discerning? (1989)

He refutes [the opponent's view] with the verse beginning "conjoined" (saṃyuktam), etc.: "The form of an atom situated in the middle [of a cluster], which faces a single atom, is conjoined [with it], situated in a distant place, and established in contiguity. (1990)
If that very same atom is postulated as facing toward another atom, then the accumulation of mountains and the like would not be possible.
If, however, it is maintained that the form facing toward another atom is different [from its other sides], [then the objection does not apply].
How indeed could a single atom exist under such circumstances?

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is devoid of a nature that is either one or many is fit for the conventional designation of "non-existent," just like a lotus in the sky; and atoms postulated by the opponent are devoid of a nature that is either one or many. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), and it should not be thought that this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For instance, the oneness of atoms is first of all unestablished, because in things such as mountains, which possess an accumulated form, there exists a distinction of spatial parts (*digbhāga*).

By demonstrating that very distinction of spatial parts through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the accumulation of mountains and the like, he states the negation of their oneness as follows: "Whether conjoined or situated at a distance," and so forth.

Regarding this, some say that atoms join with one another; others say that they always remain with intervals between them and do not touch; while still others say that when there is no interval, it is merely designated as "touching. Now, in all three of these positions, if the atom situated in the middle and surrounded by many others were not to have distinct spatial divisions according to the directions (digbhāgabhedo), then there could be no accumulation [of matter], just as there is none in the collection of mind and mental factors (cittacaittādikalāpa), because it would lack constituent parts (anaṃśatvāt).

To explain: if the central atom were to face another atom with the very same aspect by which it faces one atom, then there would be the undesirable consequence that all the surrounding atoms occupy the same location; thus, no accumulation [of matter] would be possible. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever has a nature facing an atom of a single form must occupy the same location, just like the atom situated in the eastern direction relative to that very [central atom], or like a building situated in front of another building facing the same temple. And all the surrounding atoms have a nature facing an atom of a single form; this is therefore a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Therefore, there would be no accumulation [of atoms].
If, on the other hand, it faces [another atom] by means of a different aspect, then because the distinction of spatial directions exists, it cannot attain oneness, just like a jar or similar objects.

But Bhaṭṭa Śubhagupta says: "Just as for that which has a single nature, excluded from non-existent things, substances, and so forth, a plurality of universals is not postulated as being real, so too here, because atoms exist in a manifold [spatial] manner, their plurality is postulated, but not in an ultimate sense."

For instance: there is no such category as "direction" (dik-padārtha) imagined by Kaṇāda and others; because it would possess a single nature, the manifold cognitions of "east," "west," and so forth, would not arise. Rather, it is merely atoms situated in a sequence of priority and posteriority that are denoted by the word "direction. Consequently, the argument that "it possesses distinctions of spatial divisions" (dig-bhāga-bheda-vattvāt) would merely state that it is surrounded by many [atoms], and not that it is composed of parts (sāvayavatva). This [objection] is incorrect.

For instance: because atoms, like the mind, are partless (*niravayava*), they do not possess upper or lower parts in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*); therefore, there could be no surrounding by many [atoms] at all, just as in the case of the mind and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

Consequently, since the surrounding atoms would lack existence in the ultimate sense, how could there be a state of being situated in the midst of many by way of them, through which a spatial multiplicity might be imagined?
If, on the other hand, there were surrounding by many even in the absence of upper and lower parts in the ultimate sense, then the same would apply to the mind and its mental factors as well.
Furthermore, like atoms, mental states and so forth would also have to occupy a location; otherwise, even atoms would not occupy a location.
Consequently, there could be no aggregation [of atoms], just as there is none for mental states and so forth—this is the inevitable conclusion.

It might be argued: "Just as there is a temporal contiguity between the present moment of consciousness and the past and future moments of consciousness, yet the present moment of consciousness has no parts like a *kalā* or a *muhūrta*, so too atoms, even when surrounded by many others, will not possess spatial divisibility.
This is incorrect;
for in reality, there is no true contiguity between the present moment of consciousness and its predecessors and successors, because at that time those two [past and future moments] do not exist.

Furthermore, it is not logical for there to be a real temporal sequence (paurvāparya) with that which is non-existent; rather, the existence of the preceding and succeeding moments is merely conceptualized and projected by way of the fact that two coexistent things cannot stand in a cause-and-effect relationship. This is like the existence [imputed] to what was previously non-existent and what will later be non-existent. Nor, in this way, can a spatial sequence be conceptually imputed to atoms, because that would entail the impossibility of their aggregation (pracaya).
Moreover, it is not reasonable for entities to be without a cause, as that would entail their eternal existence and so forth.
Even for one who has realized the conventional nature of entities, it must necessarily be accepted that all entities possess causes;

and since they possess causes, it is not logical for cause and effect to be simultaneous, nor can the cause exist prior to the arising of the effect, because the cause would lack efficacy due to its non-existence [at that time].
Furthermore, since a cause is of no use once the effect has already arisen, the prior existence of all causes must necessarily be admitted;
as it has been said: "Because that which is non-existent lacks capacity beforehand, and because it is of no use afterwards."
The priority of all causes is [established] by their own cognition; therefore, the object does not exist [independently].

Thus, even though all entities are partless according to logic, the temporal priority and posteriority established by time exists as a matter of fact; however, it is objected: "How could spatial priority and posteriority exist if there were no possession of parts?

Now, if spatial priority and posteriority were to exist even in the absence of parts, then it would also apply to the mind and mental factors (*citta-caittasika*), since there is no distinction [between them and material things in that regard]. This has already been stated.
If it is argued that there is a distinction based on corporeality (*mūrttatva*), we say no; for that very point is unproven.

In the absence of having parts (*sāvayavatva*), what is merely called "corporeality" would be nothing more than a synonym for "having parts," and thus there is no other distinction whatsoever. This [objection] is trivial.

Therefore, since all entities possess a sequence of priority and posteriority established by time according to logic, that further, additional sequence of priority and posteriority established by space which belongs to some [entity] is not possible without its having parts; thus it was rightly said:
"For that which has a division of spatial directions, unity is not tenable. Enough with this elaboration.

On this point, some say: "In that case, let there be minute spatial regions (*pradeśa*) which constitute atoms (*paramāṇu*); even if one further postulates parts for those, the minuteness will belong once again to those very regions. If there is thus simply an infinite regress, it cannot be established that atoms have a merely conceptual existence (*prajñaptisattva*) by means of the consequence of their having parts."
Furthermore, even if they exist as mere designations (*prajñaptisat*), one must nonetheless necessarily admit a basis for that designation;
and that which serves as the basis for the designation will itself be the atom.
Alternatively, if it is being proven that atoms do not exist at all, even so, the reason (*hetu*) "due to the distinction of directional parts" (*digbhāgabhedāt*) remains unestablished (*asiddha*).
For things that are absolutely non-existent, such as the horn of a donkey, do not possess distinctions of spatial directions like the east and so forth;
nor is this a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) argument, because the distinction of spatial directions is not admitted [by the opponent].
To this, he provides the following rebuttal, beginning with "apeta... and so on.

Furthermore, regarding that atom which is asserted by others to be devoid of any division of parts—it is precisely concerning such a thing that this investigation has been undertaken; therefore, it is not the case that an undesirable consequence cannot arise from it.
This is because they [the opponents] accept that the very parts [of the atom] possess the nature of atoms.

In that case, their own thesis would necessarily fall into contradiction. Furthermore, because this is a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) argument, there is no problem here of the locus being unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*);
for it is by the force of the "connection" (*yoga*) and other properties accepted by the opponent that identity is indeed negated.
Thus, in all these positions, that [atom] cannot logically be a single entity; since unity is unestablished, it is also impossible for it to have a manifold nature.
Therefore, for the wise, the atom is fit to be determined as non-existent.
Because it is empty of a nature that is either one or many, like a sky-lotus.
(1997) For the proponent of atoms must necessarily admit some entity with a finalized form as being an atom;
otherwise, due to infinite regress and the resulting lack of a determined form, he would himself have established its total indefinability.
Consequently, it would be the opponent’s own desired conclusion that would have been established;

therefore, when an investigation is conducted regarding that very thing which has been definitively established and determined by you as being atomic, without resorting to the alternative of infinite regress, how could there be an infinite regress? There would be an infinite regress only if, through that infinite regress, a contradiction of your own accepted position were created;
however, nothing undesirable has been brought about for the opponent.
Since the opponent's desired conclusion is established by this much alone, this is indeed a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum);
nor is the reason (*hetu*) unestablished.

For the opponent has accepted that atoms possess conjunction (*saṃyuktatva*), contiguity (*nairantarya*), and being surrounded by many [atoms] with intervals; otherwise, how could there be cognition? Consequently, even if the distinction of spatial parts (*digbhāgabheda*) is not explicitly accepted in words, it nonetheless follows by the force of accepting properties such as conjunction and the rest.

For it has been stated that, in the absence of distinctions such as upper and lower parts, the three positions regarding conjunction and so forth are not tenable, just as in the case of consciousness and the like.
Furthermore, as for the claim that one must necessarily admit a substratum (*upādāna*) for the designation of an atom, and that this very substratum will be the atom itself—herein lies the truth:

the maturation of latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) deposited through hearing and reflecting upon false treatises is the basis for the delusion of atoms, appearing as motes of dust in a window beam and similar phenomena.

For it is not logical that the very same thing which serves as the basis for its designation should also be the cause [of that designation], because it would follow that it lacks the status of a conceptual construct (*aprajñapti-sattva*). Otherwise, if the self were the cause for the designation "self," then the aggregates (*skandhas*) would not be the cause;
consequently, there could be no negation of the self, just as there is none of the atom (*aṇu*). Thus, in this way, the oneness of atoms remains unestablished.
Because that [cognition] consists of doubt regarding that [object], the reason for establishing the conventional usage of the non-existence of atoms is not unestablished (asiddha). 1993–1994.
Having thus established that the external object is devoid of a manifold nature, he now says "and because of the impossibility of an atom," etc., in order to establish its lack of a unitary nature:
"And because of the impossibility of an atom, the composite whole does not exist, since it is accepted by others to be composed of atoms. (1998)

Even for those who maintain that a gross object is not composed of atoms, that [gross object] is likewise untenable as a single entity because it is divided according to its spatial directions, just like an atom; for if one part were moved by the hand or otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the movement of the whole.
Since this has been clearly and repeatedly threshed out, no separate refutation of it is stated here.

Thus, in establishing the non-transactional status of external objects through the formal argument beginning with "that which does not possess a nature of being either one or many," the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Consequently, the non-existent status of external things such as earth—which are the apprehended objects—is established. Since that [apprehended object] is unestablished, the status of consciousness as an apprehender (*grāhakatva*), which is conceptually constructed in dependence upon it, also does not exist; thus, the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is established. (1998) Having thus demonstrated representation-only due to the impossibility of an object, he now says "without appearance," etc., demonstrating it further by way of the absence of the characteristics of apprehended and apprehender.

Cognition cognizes [an object] as being without appearance, with appearance, or even with the appearance of something else; yet cognition never [cognizes] an external object in any way whatsoever. (1999) It is not tenable for the external to be grasped by a cognition that is formless, nor by one that possesses a form, nor by one that has a form other than the form of the object; and there is no other mode [of apprehension]. Therefore, it is established that cognition is always self-cognizing (*ātmasaṃvedana*), even if an external continuum of another exists; thus, the state of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) is proven.

Some maintain that even a cognition possessing one form can be the perceiver of an object possessing another form; for instance, it is claimed that even a cognition having a yellow form apprehends a white conch-shell.

As Kumārila has said: "In all cases, the external object is the objective support (*ālambana*), though its nature may differ in terms of place and time, whether it occurs in the same birth or a different one, and at the present time or at another time."
Thus, this third alternative has been raised as a doubt.

[Verse 1999] Now, one might ask: "Why do these conceptual constructions, such as 'non-appearance' and so forth, not apply even in the case of self-cognition? To this, he says: "Consciousness," and so on.
Consciousness arises as something distinct from insentient forms;

this very non-insentience is its self-awareness. For self-cognition is not intended here in the sense of being an apprehending subject; rather, it is by itself—by its own nature as luminosity, like light existing in the expanse of the sky.
Now, why is it not accepted as having the nature of the grasped and the grasper? He says: "By way of the relation between action and agent," and so forth;
however, its self-cognition does not occur by way of the relation between action and agent.

Since it is impossible for a single entity that lacks parts to possess a threefold nature, its self-awareness is indeed logical because it consists of the nature of consciousness; however, how can there be awareness of another, namely an object-nature, by means of that [consciousness]? (2001–2002)
The threefold nature [of cognition]— by way of the distinction between the object of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even for an external object, there will be cognition just as there is self-cognition, without the relationship of apprehended and apprehender; to this he says: "For its form is not [the form] of another," and so forth.
For its form does not belong to another such that, upon the cognition of that [other], the former would be cognized, because things are distinct in terms of ultimate reality. (2003)

Even if a single form such as "existence" (sat) is postulated among entities by way of the exclusion of "non-existence" (asat) and so forth, nevertheless, for the sake of explaining that [form], he says "in ultimate reality" (paramārthataḥ)—meaning that from the perspective of ultimate reality, there is no unity at all because of [the entities'] difference.

It might be argued: "Even if the external object is indeed different from cognition, it will nonetheless be cognizable, just like cognition itself. To this he replies with the words beginning "by virtue of having the nature of awareness" (bodharūpatayā), and so forth.
Since it arises in the form of cognition, it is indeed logical that knowledge is what is perceived;
however, how could an object—which is not cognition—be perceived when it has arisen?
(2004) Having thus established self-cognition, he now says "nirbhāsī" and so forth, demonstrating how it is illogical for an external object to be perceived by a cognition that lacks its form.

But in the view that cognition is luminous (*nirbhāsijñāna*), although there is a difference between the two in reality, there may still be a figurative (*bhākta*) perception [of the object] because the reflection possesses the same form as it.
This is so even for one who does not accept that cognition is colored by the form of the object.
This mode [of cognition] does not exist at all for that external sensation;
[it applies only] to the reflection, that is, to the form of the cognition.
"Because of that nature" means figuratively, due to similarity.
"This one is also non-primary"; thus,
it is designated as "non-primary" because it is fashioned through resemblance to that [primary state].

"Furthermore, it might be argued: just as a sword cuts an elephant and the like, or just as fire burns what is combustible, and yet these [instruments] such as the sword do not possess the form of the elephant and so forth, in the same way, cognition—even if it does not assume the form of the object—will determine the object. This is the doubt raised by the words "it might be thought," etc.

It might be thought: "Just as swords, fire, and so forth perform cutting, burning, and the like upon elephants, fuel, and other objects—even though they do not possess the same nature [as those objects]—so it is in this case.
Here, the genitive case in *dantidāhyādeḥ* is used in relation to *chedadāhādīn*.
By the word "existence" (*asti*), this knowledge is indicated; and by the word "etc. (*ādi*), things such as lamps—which serve as illuminators for blue and other objects—are included.
he provides the answer beginning with "tad idam" (this, then):
"This is inconsistent because those [causes] are the causes of such an origination."
Such perfected beings (siddhas) exist, yet knowledge is not likewise productive [of its object]. (2008)

For swords and the like are well known as burners and cutters precisely because they are the producers of elephants and other objects; that is to say, when struck by the edge of a sword or similar weapon, elephants are produced with their joints severed. Likewise, through contact with fire, fuel takes on the form of charcoal and so forth. Similarly, jars and other objects also become capable of generating cognition by virtue of light. However, no such benefit is conferred upon the object by the cognition; rather, it is by the object itself that consciousness is clearly produced. How, then, could that which is thus ineffective be its knower?

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to postulate that the very fact of being an effect of that [object] constitutes the cognition's status as its cognizer; for otherwise, one might as well conclude that it is the cognizer of the eye and other [senses].

However, the Venerable Śubhagupta says: "Cognition apprehends the object even without assuming the form of the object, because its nature consists in the determination of that [object]; therefore, one should not raise the doubt: 'How does it determine? In what manner does it determine?'"
And it is said: "How can that [object] be somehow the grasper? If that consciousness has the characteristic of discerning that [object], then there is no room for doubt as to how or what it might be.
To this, he says: "Because it has the characteristic of discerning that," and so forth.
The nature of consciousness as a discernment is only tenable if a discernment in the form of cognition could possibly exist for the object of apprehension;
otherwise, it is clear that consciousness is merely of the nature of discernment [without an object]. (2009)
And it has not been stated that the cognition of an object occurs in this manner.
For all this would be possible only if it were established that [cognition] consists in the determination of an object distinct [from itself]; but that very point is not established.
To explain: cognition does not determine [an object] by its mere existence, because that would entail the consequence of determining everything.

Nor can it be by virtue of being its effect, for that would entail the consequence that the eye and other sense organs would also be the cognizer. Furthermore, it is not accepted that cognition possesses a form (sākāratā), such that the cognizer could be non-different from the object due to sharing its nature.
Therefore, if the determination of the object were of the nature of cognition, then cognition would indeed consist in the determination of the object.
Otherwise, how could it be clearly stated that cognition has the nature of the determination of an object?

Consequently, since there is no distinction between the determination of the object and the cognition itself, the identity of the two would be established, and thus the doctrine of *vijñaptimātratā* (consciousness-only) would be proven.

To this, [the opponent] might say: "There is some specific quality belonging to this [cognition] by which it determines the object alone, yet it cannot be pointed out as 'this'. To this he replies: "And the perception of the object has not been pointed out in this way."
The word *viśeṣaḥ* is the distinction; [the correction list displays this error as *viśeṣa* without a visarga]. As for the remainder (*śe�ṣaḥ*):
although it is impossible to point out every unique entity in its entirety, nevertheless, it is indeed described by way of conventional designation (*udbhāvanā-saṃvṛtti*).
Otherwise, one would not even be able to speak of the distinctions of form (*rūpa*) and so forth.
If it is not clearly and undeniably specified that cognition is the awareness of an object in its unascertained form,
then the claim that entities are well-established when established in an uncharacterized form is merely a trifle.

[Objection: It might be argued that if the object to be determined does not exist, for whom would this determination belong? [Reply: He says: "To whom does that determination belong? and so forth; [the phrase] "to whom does that determination belong" does not admit of further questioning.
That [self-luminosity] is its very nature, just as continuity is the nature of pleasure and so forth.
(2011) For that [luminosity] itself is called its "determination" because its nature is manifestation;

just as continuity is [the nature] of pleasure and so forth. Indeed, it does not become something other than that [pleasure] merely because of the use of a distinct grammatical case, such as "of pleasure," nor is that continuity [separate from it].

Therefore, although there is a designation such as "the determination of blue" or "of yellow," which appears as if it were distinct, nevertheless, that [determination] is simply the intrinsic nature [of cognition] itself; it is described in that way because it manifests in the form of blue and so forth, since cognition has the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).
Now, what is this meaning of "self-awareness" by virtue of which it is so described? To this he says: "Its own form," and so forth.
"For the cognition of its own nature, it does not depend on another cognizer, nor is this [nature] unknown; such is the meaning of self-awareness.
With the verse beginning "vyāpṛtam" (engaged), Kumārila raises an objection regarding the point that "for the cognition of its own nature, it does not depend on another."
For knowledge, being occupied with the cognition of an object, does not reach its own self;
therefore, even though it is luminous, it awaits something else for its own awareness.
He (the opponent) says: "Even if knowledge is of the nature of light, nevertheless, it requires another for the illumination of itself."
But it does not itself reach— that is, attain— the self, because its activity is occupied solely with the illumination of objects;
for it is not logical that something engaged in one place should, without abandoning that, be active in another place at the same time.
Anticipating the objection that there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of a lamp, he states another alternative: "Or rather, such luminosity" and so forth.
Such luminosity consists in the experience of an object;
however, since this [lamp] lacks the experience of itself, it is not a manifestor of itself. (2014)
But if it does not have the nature of self-illumination, how can its status as an illuminator of external objects be established? To this he says: "When there is illumination," and so forth.
Just as the status of being an illuminator is observed in the case of the eyes and other senses with respect to form and other objects, so too will it be in this case as well. (2015)

Just as the status of the eye and other [senses] as illuminators of objects such as form is established even though they lack self-illumination, so too will it be in this case regarding cognition. One might ask: "Why does [cognition] abandon its own internal nature and illuminate only the external? To this he says: "The state of being an illuminator," and so forth.
The capacity to illuminate exists with respect to external objects, but not with respect to itself because of a lack of power;
yet, the power of all entities is not to be questioned in this manner.
(2016) He asks why there is no power for self-illumination, and answers: "And the power of all entities," and so forth.
As it has been said: "Fire burns, but space does not; who here is to be questioned? (2016). He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning with "But surely... and so forth.
But surely, the cognition of an object is designated as nothing other than knowledge itself; when that [cognition] is the very nature of [knowledge], what other operation could there be?
(2017) As for what was said—that [knowledge] is "engaged" in the cognition of the object—that is inconsistent, for the cognition of the object is not something other than knowledge.
For instance, "cognition," "apprehension," "awareness of an object," and "representation"—these synonyms denote nothing other than knowledge itself.

And when that awareness of the object is of the very nature of that [knowledge]—that is, when it is of the nature of knowledge—what other operation, distinct from its own nature, could there be for knowledge consisting of the perception of the object, by virtue of which one could say it is "operating" upon the awareness of the object?
Nor is it logical for an operation to exist within the self [of the agent].

[Objection: It might be argued: "How is it established that the cognition of an object has the nature of knowledge itself, such that 'knowledge' and 'cognition of the object' are synonyms? To this, [the author] says: "The experience of the object is its form," and so forth.
If the experience of the object is its form, and that [form] consists of knowledge...
It is logical that cognition has the nature of experiencing that object, yet that [nature] does not exist [in the case of self-cognition].
For if it were to have the nature of experience intrinsically, there would be the undesirable consequence of abandoning the accepted [object];
thus, even if it had the nature of experience, the cognition of the object would not be established. (2018–2019)
The experience of an object must necessarily be admitted as its form or intrinsic nature;
otherwise, how could cognition operate upon it?
For it is not logical for anything to exercise an operation toward that which does not exist, such as a rabbit’s horn.

Furthermore, if that nature consisting of the experience of the object were non-different from cognition, then that which was stated regarding cognition—that its being of the nature of an experience of the object is such that "its luminosity is of the nature of an experience of the object"—would be tenable. One might think that perhaps the opponent, when pressed, would even admit that cognition is non-different from the experience of the object; therefore, he says: "And that does not exist," meaning that the experience's non-difference from cognition does not exist.

The "accepted position" (upeta-artha) is the admission that cognition is characterized by a lack of self-awareness; there would follow the undesirable consequence of abandoning this [position] if one were to admit that cognition is not distinct from the experience of an object, because that would entail the consequence of self-awareness. To this, he says: "But for that [cognition], [it is known] from itself," and so forth, meaning: the luminosity of cognition is not intended to be due to its being of the nature of the experience of an object, but rather solely due to its being of the nature of experience itself.

Although that cognition has arisen as nothing but the nature of experience itself, and not as the nature of the experience of an object, nevertheless, the cognition of an object could not be established through such distinctions as "this is the cognition of blue" and "not of yellow."
He explains why [the goal] would not be accomplished in 2019: "For there is no basis for proximity in that case," and so forth;
for in that case, there exists no basis for proximity belonging to another.
Just as, in the position of those who maintain that consciousness possesses aspects (sākāra-vijñāna-pakṣa), there is the reflection of the object;
[this is] "of the other," namely, of the proponent of aspectless consciousness (anākāra-jñāna-vādin).
Regarding the view that "the external object possesses a form while cognition is formless," or that "such luminosity consists in the experience of the object," he says: "By nature," and so forth.
If, because it is by nature insentient, there is no self-awareness for this [consciousness],
then, due to the absence of the cognition of itself, its awareness of other objects would likewise be [absent].

(2021) If consciousness, being insentient in nature, does not cognize itself, then, since it is not directly perceived *per se*, the experience of objects would also have to be accepted as not being directly perceived.
It might be argued: "If indeed cognition (*jñāna*) is not perceived, why should the experience of the object (*arthānubhava*) also be unperceived?
For it is not the case that because color (*rūpa*) is unperceived, sound (*śabda*) must also be unperceived. To this, he says: "The so-called experience of the object," and so forth.
What is called the "experience of an object" is designated as nothing other than cognition itself;
if that [cognition] were of the nature of non-apprehension, what other apprehension could there be for it?
For we do not determine any other form for cognition apart from the experience of the object.

If we do not determine our own words as being distinct [from others], yet engage in discourse based on a conviction regarding that [other] nature, we would deceive both ourselves and others. Since the form of that cognition is unestablished, what other established nature could there be for the experience of that object? None whatsoever.
Furthermore, it might be argued that its establishment will occur through another cognition; to this he says: "By another cognition," and so forth.
If that object were experienced by another cognition while its own experience [of itself] remains unestablished, when indeed would it ever become established? (2023)

If [it is argued that] it is unestablished when there arises the cognition of that cognition, but established in the self-awareness [of that cognition] and in the awareness of another, then this is a well-spoken [refutation]: because of the establishment [of the first] and the non-establishment [of the second]. 2024.
[This refers to] the establishment of the cognition and the non-establishment [of its object].
It is not logical to say that an object is "manifest" when its manifestation is itself unestablished;

for instance, first of all, there is no establishment of the object even at the time of its own experience, because the experience—whose very nature is the manifestation of that object—is itself unestablished at that time. It must be stated: when will its establishment occur?

If it is argued that its establishment will occur at the moment the cognition of the cognition of the object arises—that is, at the time of the production of the cognition of the cognition of the object—then [the following applies].
This is an excellent statement:
for how indeed can that which is not established at the time of one's own experience be established at the time of another's experience? (2023)

"May [the proof] succeed in 2024, provided that there is no infinite regress; however, showing that such a regress is unavoidable, he says: 'If there were experience of that [second cognition] as well,' and so forth.
If the experience of that [second cognition] is not established, then the first [cognition] is also unestablished."
In that case, if another consciousness were to arise [to cognize it], an infinite regress would result;
"of that" refers to the second consciousness, which is the cognition of the cognition of the object.
"Of the first" means that the experience of the object is unestablished.
"It has no establishment," thus it is unestablished; its state is "unestablishedness" (asiddhatā).

Furthermore, if the experience [of a cognition] is admitted to occur through another cognition, then in that case as well, a memory certainly arises regarding that other cognition, such as: "The cognition of my cognition has arisen. For that too, an experience by yet another must be asserted, for a memory is not possible with respect to what has not been experienced. Therefore, it must be explained who, having no other task, produces this series of cognitions.
First of all, it is not the object [of the visual consciousness], because that is the domain of the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);
nor are they the sense faculty and light, because those two are utilized only in the case of visual consciousness;
nor is it without a cause, because that would entail its constant existence and so forth.
If it is argued that "that very preceding cognition produces each subsequent cognition," he says: "In the transition to another object, etc.
In such a case, there would be no transition to another object, yet that transition is observed.
Furthermore, in the transition to another object, that which is the final [cognition] must arise either from itself or from something else. (2026)
If that [final cognition] were not established, then all [cognitions] would likewise be unestablished;
consequently, total blindness would result for the entire world.
However, if the final cognition is established by itself, then the establishment of the others is certainly secured as well.
Because they possess the nature of cognition; otherwise, these would not have the nature of cognition, like a jar or similar objects.

(2028) For in that case, the transition to another object would not occur. To explain: each preceding cognition stands as the object for each succeeding cognition and is proximate to it by virtue of being its material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*). How then could [the mind] abandon such an internal factor and grasp an external object?
Nor is the object capable of obstructing that [succession], even though it is present, because it is an external factor.
If, on the other hand, even an external factor were to obstruct it, then no one would ever experience memory;
for there is no state in which an object is not present,
and thus memory itself would be cut off due to the absence of prior experience.

Furthermore—since those conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding the past and so forth arise even in the absence of the presence of an object, and because there would be no cause for their cessation, they would persist in a succession of conceptualizations until the end of *saṃsāra*; thus, no one would ever have the thought of an actual object.
Even if one were to grant that the transition to another object is impossible, it must still be explained by what that other cognition would be experienced.
Now, it might be argued: "That very subsequent cognition, which apprehends another object, grasps both the preceding cognition and the object. This is incorrect;

for instance, when a cognition apprehending form arises immediately after a cognition of sound, then because the cognition of sound appears in that cognition apprehending form, the appearance of the sound—which had already become established [in the mind] at that time—would also necessarily follow.

Even for one who maintains that cognition is formless (*nirākāra-jñāna*), it is not logical for the grasper of that [object] to be apprehended without the apprehension of the object itself; for it is not reasonable to apprehend the possessor of a staff (*daṇḍin*) without apprehending the staff. Thus, sound would appear even in visual cognition which grasps visible form, and likewise, in the case of conceptual cognition having *a* and other letters as its objects, two verbal expressions would occur in a single [cognition] according to the aforementioned principle.

For instance: when one reflects on the phoneme *a* immediately after reflecting on the phoneme *i*, then that cognition reflecting on the *a* would also reflect on the *i* as its own apprehender; thus, it follows that the expression of *i*, which is mounted upon its own cognition, would appear within the cognition expressing *a*.
Furthermore, every object would appear twice: because it appears at the time of its own cognition [and again later].
Since such an appearance does not occur, it is incorrect to claim that both are apprehended by a subsequent cognition.
Furthermore, one might argue: "Let it be that the final cognition is not experienced and not remembered; what fault would there be? To this he replies: "The transition to another object-domain.

Since self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is not admitted, there is no establishment [of the final cognition] by itself; nor is there establishment by another, because of the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). When that final [cognition] is unestablished, the preceding one is also unestablished, because its apprehension is not perceived. Consequently, the object too is unestablished; thus, nothing would ever be perceived, and the entire world would fall into blindness.

Now, if it is admitted that the final cognition is established by itself through self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) out of fear of the aforementioned defects, then, for the same reason, since all cognitions are indistinguishable in their nature as knowledge, let this application [of the argument] be made regarding self-awareness: whatever is a cognition does not depend on the operation of anything else for its own awareness, because it is a cognition, like the final cognition; and the cognition under dispute is indeed a cognition—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). For otherwise, if it were not established by itself, it would, like a jar or other objects, be of an insentient nature, and thus its very status as a cognition would be lost; such is the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*).
He states how a fixed distinction is observed when there is the quality of being an illuminator: "Producing cognition," and so forth.

When producing cognition regarding a form, the eye is considered its illuminator; however, because cognition is itself of the nature of awareness (*avabodha*), what comparison can there be between it and that [eye]? (2029)
The eye is said to be the illuminator of form because it generates a consciousness whose object is form;
however, consciousness does nothing to the form, since it merely makes known that which already exists as form.
And it is not logical for something to be an illuminator without performing some action, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
Therefore, analogy is similarity. 2029

With the verse beginning "That which is the cognition," etc., he provides a proof for one who maintains that cognition is formless (*nirākāra-jñāna-vādin*), in order to establish the non-difference between the cognition and the forms such as blue;
"Whatever is the cognition of something must certainly be the cognition of that [object];
therefore, that [form] is not distinct from it, or it does not differ from it. (2030)
Just as the self-nature of the cognition of blue, or like a second moon, this is the experience of the cognition of blue because it is the experience of the form of blue.
Whatever is the experience of something, that alone is necessarily the experience of that thing, and nothing else; therefore—from that which is denoted by the first "whatever" (yad).
That which is expressed by the word "second" is made entirely non-different;
or else, by way of reversal, non-difference is what is to be proven.
This is what is meant:
that which is not cognized as distinct from something else is non-different from it, just as the cognition of blue is non-different from its own nature,
or as the second moon appearing in the visual perception of one with cataracts is non-different from the [actual] moon.
"This is the cognition of blue" is the application of the property to the subject; here,
the subject consists of the blue form and its cognition,
and their non-difference is the property to be proven.

The reason—the rule of simultaneous perception as it has been stated—is precisely what is intended as the meaning of the reason in the Master’s formal argument beginning with "because of the rule of simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*).
Regarding this, the Venerable Śubhagupta says: "This reason is contradictory, because in common usage the word 'simultaneous' (*saha*) never occurs without another [thing]."
Therefore, this reason— "if there is simultaneous cognition"— is contradictory;
thus, this [objection] is incorrect.

That whose existence is restricted solely to the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is a contradictory reason (viruddha-hetu). This [reason] is not restricted solely to the dissimilar instance, because it exists in the similar instance (sapakṣa) as well;
for instance, in the world there is the conceit of the simultaneous perception of two moons, yet in ultimate reality (paramārthataḥ) there is no difference between them.

Moreover, just as people say "together" upon perceiving two moons simultaneously, so too here, although the form is not distinct from the cognition, the word "together" is employed based on a conceptualized difference, having treated the form—which appears as if external—as a second entity.

For not all linguistic usage conforms precisely to the actual state of things; thus, by the mere use of the word "together," there would be no actual difference in the logical mark (liṅga) that is tied to the real object, which would otherwise render the reason contradictory (viruddha).

Again, he himself says: "If the word 'together' (saha) means 'identical in object,' then the reason is unestablished (asiddha). For instance, in the spectacles of actors, the moon, or wrestlers, there is not apprehension of blue and so forth by one [person] alone;
nor is there apprehension of both the blue and its apprehension by one alone.
To explain: even when there is the apprehension of blue, there is no apprehension of those other apprehensions belonging to other mental continua."
And since all moments of consciousness of living beings are perceived by the Omniscient One, how could "perception by one [person] alone" be established?
Furthermore, the restriction to perception by one is established only if there is a negation of perception by others;
however, a negation of perception by others is impossible, because affirmation and negation are inapplicable to that which is remote by its very nature (*svabhāvaviprakṛṣṭa*).

Now, if the word "simultaneously" (*saha*) is intended to mean "at the same time," then the reason is in every respect inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because of the mind cognizable by a Buddha and its mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

For instance, it is well known that although there is a rule of simultaneous perception between the mind of another continuum (*santāna*) which is cognizable by the Blessed Buddha and the Buddha’s own knowledge, there is nonetheless a difference (*nānātva*) between them; likewise, even though mental states and their factors are perceived simultaneously, they are not one and the same. Therefore, the reason is inconclusive—all of this is incorrect.
For the intended meaning here is not that "single apprehension" refers to apprehension by only one [cognizer];
rather,
it means that the apprehension of the cognition and the object is mutually one and the same, and not separate.
For the very apprehension of cognition is the apprehension of the object of cognition, and the very apprehension of the object of cognition is the apprehension of cognition;

that is to say, in performances such as those of actors, the moon, or wrestlers, there is no apprehension of cognition whatsoever that does not also apprehend the object of cognition, nor is there any apprehension of the object of cognition that does not also apprehend the cognition. How, then, can there be the charge of "unestablished" (asiddha) [reason], or even the charge of "doubtfully unestablished" (saṃdigdhāsiddha)?
For instance—the opponent who maintains the existence of external objects has also admitted that the very self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of a cognition is itself the [cognition] of the object.

Therefore, the fault of being unestablished (*asiddhatā-doṣa*) which was stated by conceptualizing "single apprehension" (*ekopalambha*) as the apprehension of one and the same thing, should be seen as refuted precisely because that position is not accepted.
Furthermore, the moments of consciousness existing in another continuum are not determined by the mind of the Blessed Buddha.

Because that Blessed One is free from all obscurations and devoid of the stain of the grasped and the grasper, as it has been said: "For him there is no object to be grasped, nor is there grasping by him; he is empty even of being graspable by another cognition"—thus his sovereignty, consisting in the unimpaired establishment [of reality], exists merely by way of predominance.

As it has been said: "The activity for the sake of others proceeds continuously and effortlessly, being established by previous vows; because he accomplishes all purposes, he is accepted as omniscient.

This will be stated later, and therefore the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Now, one might object: "But did not the Master Dharmakīrti, while presenting the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by saying 'if it is argued that the object is the cause of cognition, such that its apprehension occurs first and the self-awareness (*saṃvedana*) afterwards,' show here that the word 'together' (*saha*) signifies simultaneity (*ekakāla*) and not identity (*abheda*)? For when simultaneity is intended, it is appropriate for the opponent to point out a difference in time, but not when there is identity. If this is argued, we say no.

Since temporal difference is pervaded by substantial difference, the demonstration of temporal difference is all the more appropriate for the purpose of establishing non-identity through perception, because the pervaded does not deviate from the pervader.

Nor is the reason inconclusive on account of the mind cognizable by a Buddha; for in that case, there is no restriction to a single perception, since that mind is experienced individually by each [of them].
For this very reason, the investigation into the reversal of their minds is likewise based on the fact that they each experience only their own self.

Alternatively, let it be that there is a perception of another's mind by the Blessed One’s mind; nevertheless, there is no lack of certainty [in our argument], because [the possibility of such] has been ruled out by necessity. For that in which even a difference in mutual apprehension is possible has been ruled out by necessity; however, this does not negate the multiplicity of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) through a distinction at the time of the continuum of those apprehensions.
Therefore, this is the meaning: for whatever [object] there is apprehension, that alone is its apprehension and nothing else.

However, the apprehension of the Blessed One’s cognition is not exclusively the apprehension of a mind belonging to another continuum, nor is the apprehension of a mind belonging to another continuum exclusively the apprehension of the Blessed One’s cognition; rather, it is also something else, because one perceives even one's own distinct mind.
For this very reason, there is no deviation [in the rule] regarding form and light.
Since light is perceived even by itself,

and since form is also perceived by certain specific living beings even when devoid of light, the reason is not inconclusive (anaikāntika), because its presence in the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) is impossible.

2031. It might be argued as follows: although the presence [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not certain, it is at least doubtful; therefore, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because its exclusion from the counter-example is doubtful.

For instance, even otherwise, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) is possible, since it is determined by the relationship between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*). This is because the very nature of cognition is that of a grasper, owing to its property of grasping an object, and the very nature of the object is that of being grasped by it. Furthermore, because these two depend upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*), they necessarily exist together.
Nor does it follow that the eyes and other [faculties] would likewise become objects [of cognition], despite the lack of distinction in their simultaneous arising; for they lack such a nature.

To explain: by means of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), a cognition is produced precisely in the form of a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object such as blue, and not in the form of a determination of the eye and so forth.
Furthermore, it is the blue and so on that is produced in the form determined by that cognition, and not the eye and so forth.
And it has been said: "There is no grasper other than cognition, apart from the visual objects;
therefore, the simultaneous awareness [of them] is not due to the non-difference of the blue object and its cognition.
Rather, the same causal complex that produced the preceding moment of the object produces the cognition."
"One should make it [the object] like the form of the world so that there may be simultaneous cognition"—
to this,
he replies: "Not of the nature of cognition," and so forth.
If the nature of cognition is not the supreme self (parātman), how can there be an awareness of the form of blue when cognizing the cognition of blue, if there is no non-difference between the two?

For it is not logical that there should be a rule of simultaneous perception for something distinct [from the cognition] without a necessary connection, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the cognition of something distinct here;
for instance, if there were an obstacle, it would have to be either identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*).
Identity is certainly not accepted by the opponent in this case, because that very thing is what remains to be proven (*sādhya*).
Nor is there simultaneous perception because of their arising together, since there can be no relationship of cause and effect between two things that exist simultaneously;
furthermore, this would entail the undesirable consequence that the eyes and other sense organs would also be perceived.

Nor does the relationship of object and subject arise merely through simultaneity due to the power of a preceding causal complex, for this would entail the undesirable consequence that the mind and mental factors, as well as the eyes and other organs, would be mutual objects and subjects of one another.

Nor is it correct to say that there is no over-extension because the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) produces [the cognition] in the form of a specific object and subject; for the very status of object and subject is what is currently under investigation and is therefore unestablished.

Indeed, the relation of object and subject is only logical once a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is established; yet it is precisely this necessary connection that is being investigated in the determination of the status of object and subject.
Furthermore, there is no other necessary connection apart from identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), by means of which the status of object and subject could be established.

Furthermore, it has been examined that the relationship between object and subject cannot be justified by way of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*); therefore, there is no co-apprehension whatsoever of a distinct [object]. Consequently, how could the reason (*hetu*) be characterized by a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*)? (2032) He states the second proof for establishing the existence of mental forms (*sākāratā*): "This is cognition," and so forth.
All this is cognition, and it does not have an external object as its domain;
for cognition [of blue] is self-cognition, just like [the cognition of] the self.

Whatever is cognition, that is not an object distinct from knowledge, just like self-cognition; and this [cognition] has the form of blue and so forth. This is the perception of a pervader of the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*).
Because consciousness is pervaded by the state of having no object other [than itself], which is the opposite of having another object as its domain,
[the author] says "primarily the object," etc., in order to establish that very pervasion.
Primarily, it does not grasp the object because it is established in its own intrinsic nature,
and secondarily, it does not do so figuratively because it is devoid of the coloring of the object's form. Like a pure crystal, it remains unstained by the forms of objects.
This is the proof directed against those who maintain that cognition is an object of sensation (*vedana*).

Since all phenomena (*dharma*) are devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*), in the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), there is no apprehension of anything by anything. Rather, consciousness (*vijñāna*), appearing in such a manner due to its luminous nature (*prakāśarūpatā*), is said to be the grasper of itself; yet it is not logically tenable for knowledge to be the primary grasper of an external object, because all entities are established within their own respective intrinsic natures (*svasvabhāva*). For that which is the nature of one thing cannot also be the nature of another.

It might be argued as follows: "The self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of cognition is not intended to be of the same primary nature as that of the object; rather, the cognizability of an object consists simply in its being the producer of a cognition that bears its own appearance. Consequently, if primary cognition were adduced as the reason (*hetu*), then the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*). Even if it were [adduced] on the grounds of a commonality in being denotable by the word 'cognition' in some sense, even so, the desired conclusion would not be established from such a thing. For the possession of horns is not established for gavayas and the like merely because they share the commonality of the word 'go' (cow)."

Now, if—on the basis of a subject (*dharmin*) consisting of blue or other forms as mounted upon cognition—the two-fold reason is intended according to the position of "cognition with form" (*sākārajñāna*), then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). As it has been said: "And in the position of cognition with form, that which appears therein is the object of cognition;
and if its non-difference [from cognition] is what is to be proven, then there would be the proof of what is already established."

Anticipating this objection from the Venerable Śubhagupta, he says: "By means of the coloring of the object's form," and so forth. The "coloring of the object's form" (*arthākāroparāga*) refers to that which is both the form of the object (*arthākāra*)—meaning similar to the object—and the coloring (*uparāga*), which is to say, the manifestation (*nirbhāsa*).
This is what is meant by "this."

Since this twofold proof is directed against the proponent of formless cognition (*nirākāravādin*), there is no proving of what is already established, nor is there any awareness of anything else even by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*), because the basis for such a metaphorical designation is absent.

Thus, it has first been established that cognition without an appearance does not cognize an external object; now, establishing this by resorting to the second position—that it is with an appearance—he says: "Let it be then," and so forth:
"Let it be then that cognition, possessing similarity [to the object], is the cognizer of the external."
Since that [external form] is also entirely untenable, the status of the knower as possessing a form is not logical.
For a real form is not tenable, because the determination of an object would have to depend upon it;
nor could an object be cognized by means of a false form, since such [a false form] exists even in erroneous cognition.
If it is asked how there can be falsity for those [cognitions] that possess forms, he says: "Because of being non-different from cognition," and so forth;
because they are not distinct from cognition, there could not be a multiplicity of forms.
Consequently, by virtue of that [form], there can be no establishment of the cognition of an object;
for since the form is not distinct from the cognition, the cognition itself would become manifold.
Otherwise, how could the oneness of these two be conceived? (2037–2038)

In the perception of a variegated carpet, because the forms are not distinct from the single cognition, they cannot possess multiplicity, just as the nature of the cognition itself does not; likewise, because the cognition is not distinct from the forms, it too would result in being manifold.

However, those who maintain that even cognitions of the same kind arise simultaneously in variegated carpets and the like, being as numerous as the forms themselves—just like the simultaneous arising of heterogeneous cognitions of color-forms, sounds, and so forth.
Furthermore, since the consequence would be that what is already established is being proven,
just as many forms such as blue and so forth are perceived in a multicolored carpet,

so too in a single form such as white, there are many forms consisting of near, middle, and far parts; thus, even in that case, the cognition whose nature consists of those [parts] would result in having a manifold nature.
If it is argued that this is indeed accepted,
then it must now be stated what constitutes a single cognition;
for if it is claimed that it has as its object an impartite atom, [that too is untenable].
This is contrary to experience;
for nowhere is anything appearing as partless and atomic observed in cognition,
nor is it logical that immaterial things should have a spatial arrangement characterized by priority and posteriority.

If, for the sake of establishing its reality, the postulation of multiple cognitions were to be considered valid, then how could the forms (ākāras) be real when the manifestation of spatial extension is unreal? For no form of the cognition of blue or other objects is perceived apart from the manifestation of blue and so forth as situated in spatial extension;
therefore, the postulation of multiple cognitions is indeed futile.
2037–2038 He states another refutation, beginning with "sarvātmanā" and so forth.
If there were identity in every respect, then cognition would be non-cognition and so forth;
if there were similarity in some respect, then everything would be a cognizer of everything.
(2039) "Non-cognition" means having an insentient nature.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [states such as] freedom from attachment and freedom from aversion are included.
(2039) Relying on this third alternative position—that it appears as something else—he says: "Even though it has another form," and so forth.
How can even a cognition having one form be the knower of something else?
Otherwise, everything would be cognizable by everyone, and the cause would not be the restricting factor.

(2040) Furthermore, it might be argued that whatever cognition is produced by a particular [object], that alone should be its cognizer; therefore, everything will not be cognizable by everyone. To this, he says: "And the cause is not the restricting factor."
The meaning is that it would follow that even the eyes and other sense organs would be objects of cognition.
With the words "Just as... and so forth, he anticipates the rebuttal of the Venerable Śubhagupta.
"Just as your cognition is, in reality, formless (*nirākāra*), yet perceives all unreal forms as real—if that were so [then our position would hold].

For he said: 'Just as for you Vijñānavādins, cognition is held to be ultimately formless, like the purity of the elements, gold, or space—according to the statement that "cognition is desired to be pure"—and yet it perceives those forms; in the same way, it [perceives] the external as well.'"
2041 Here he says: "It is unique," and so forth;
this very nature of mind and mental factors is indeed unique.
Therefore, for others, perception is in no way primary.
Based on dependence upon the same causal complex, or the relationship of cause and effect and so forth, the perception of what has already come into being may indeed be considered figurative.
But for an entity that is formless (nīrūpya), there is no dependence on a single causal complex, nor is there any other [cause]; therefore, it has not even a figurative cognition.
For that which has not come into being possesses no primary cognition.

For instance, that very form which is luminous by nature, unique, the locus of the *ahaṃkāra*, and manifests in the form of pleasure and so forth— that alone is the primary consciousness (*saṃvedana*) of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*), as it constitutes their very essence. Therefore, for others who are distinct from this knowing self and possess unreal forms, such primary consciousness is not tenable, precisely because they are unreal.
Nor is it figurative, because there is an absence of any basis for such metaphorical application;

for instance, dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*), the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), and— by the word "etcetera"— similarity (*sārūpya*), these would be the grounds for metaphorical usage,
yet none of these exist for that which is non-existent.
And there is no other basis for metaphorical designation;
rather, solely through the power of ignorance, a mistaken cognition arises that presents a non-existent form, even though it has no objective referent.

If it is argued that "in that case, that very error will serve as the basis for the metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) when there is a cognition of an unreal aspect," to this he says: "Or rather," and so forth.
Alternatively, it is designated as "knowing" a non-existent form due to error; for it does not know it in its true nature, since that [cognition] is indeed without an object.
Even by you, if consciousness were the knower of such [an object], [it would be so only through error].
"Due to error, it is said that the manifest is pervasive and devoid of an object for you.
Regarding this, "that" refers to the cognition described as having an unreal form as its object.
For instance—in ultimate reality, there is no unreal aspect that can be known; for if its knowability were accepted through affirmation, it would follow that it is actually real.

Furthermore, he himself says: "Why does the reflection not occur even regarding a Buddhist consciousness— that it has an aspect, that it is aspectless, that it is simultaneous, or that it arises from what is non-simultaneous?"

Just as the consideration is made that it is not logical for an object to be apprehended by a cognition possessing a form (sākāra) and so forth, why is such a consideration not likewise applied regarding the apprehension of an object by the knowledge of the Blessed One? To this he says: "Possessing a form" and so on—"Whether it possesses a form or is formless, it is not logical for one thing to be the knower of another"; thus, even in the case of Buddhist cognition, such a consideration does not proceed. (2047)

The Blessed One’s gnosis is not held to be a grasper of that [object], such that one would have to engage in this kind of reflection here; rather, it is accepted that because of his freedom from all obscurations, there is no conceptual construction of grasped and grasper.

Now, one might object: even if there is no external object to be grasped, nevertheless, another mind certainly exists within a different continuum; why then should that not be the object of the Blessed One’s cognition? To this, he says: "In the perception of another's passion and so forth... [Verse 2048]:

"If there were perception of another's passion and so forth, because of the arising of a similarity to that [object], the existence of obscuration would follow according to the view of those who maintain [only] perception. (2048)

For if the experience of passion and so forth existing in another’s continuum were [to be known] by another, it would be logical only through similarity (*sārūpya*) and not otherwise, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Consequently, if there were similarity in every respect, then even the Blessed One’s cognition would be impassioned;
this being the case, the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) would remain unabandoned, and thus the existence of an obscuration would follow.

Those who proceed by means of apprehension are "apprehensionists" (*upalambhika*); this refers to their view—or, alternatively, it means that when the Blessed One’s vision or gnosis is accepted as being non-apprehensive (*anupalambhika*). Even if there were partial conformity (*sārūpya*), nevertheless, because the dual aspect has not been abandoned, the existence of the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) follows, since [the cognition] is stained by the aspect of the apprehended object. For it is illogical for a single entity to possess two real forms; therefore, that [dual appearance] must necessarily be established as erroneous.
Furthermore, because even a small, faultless seed of delusion has not been abandoned, the Blessed One would remain one whose obscurations are not yet relinquished.
To the objection, "If he does not know anything at all, how then could he be omniscient?", he says: "Like a wish-fulfilling tree," and so forth.
Like a wish-fulfilling tree, though unmoved by the winds of all conceptual constructions, the Sage indeed brings about the fulfillment of the aims of the world.
Therefore, they say that even when he is not seen, the Jina is omniscient.
Because the performance of all the activities of an omniscient being occurs without effort (*anābhoga*), [it is called] "non-seeing.
Thus, "non-seeing" means that for him there is no seeing, that is, no perception (*upalambha*). Therefore, it is "non-seeing."
