Because they accomplish the welfare of the entire world without effort, according to their capacity and throughout the aeons, by the power of their former vows, they are called "Omniscient"; it is not due to the power of apprehension, for it is in every way impossible to apprehend any other intrinsic nature.

Having thus stated the means of valid cognition that negates external objects, [the author] says "of the cognition" (*dhiyaḥ*) and so forth, in order to adopt the proof for them as formulated by others:
"If the cognition has a form such as black and so on, how can that [external object] be its experience?"
If cognition consists of forms such as white and so forth, what evidence is there for an external object?
(2051) To explain: the establishment of an external object must occur either through perception or through inference, since any other existing means of valid cognition is included within these two.

In that regard, it cannot first be established by perception; for, does the apprehension of an object by a cognition regarded as perceptual occur through a formless [cognition] or through a formal one?
First of all, it cannot be by means of a formless [cognition], because there would be no basis for proximity;
as has been stated previously, if the cognition possesses a blue or other form, how could that cognition be the experience of that object? It could not be so at all.

Nor can it be by means of a cognition with a form; for, since only the single form residing in the cognition—such as blue—is perceived, the external object would necessarily be beyond perception (*parokṣa*) and not directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*).

For two blue things are never perceived [simultaneously] such that one is the reflection in cognition and the other is the object that deposits it; thus, this is not established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If it is argued, "Then let its establishment be through inference (*anumāna*)," [the response follows].
In this regard, the Venerable Śubhagupta offers the following proof:

"Whatever is a form of cognition, provided it is non-discrepant, is produced by another object of that same kind; for example, the subjective aspect [of cognition]. And this particular appearance of blue and so forth for one whose sense faculties are unimpaired is a form of cognition that is non-discrepant. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
He anticipates this objection with the words beginning "blue and so forth": *...nīlādītyādi...*

The appearance of blue and so forth is established as being born from a cause of a similar class by virtue of its being non-discrepant, just like cognition; [this is stated] "by virtue of its being non-discrepant. (2052)
The instrumental case here denotes a characteristic of the state thus attained (*itthaṃbhūtalakṣaṇa*).

By means of that nature of being an aspect of cognition—which is characterized by its correspondence and serves as the cause—the birth of the cognitive aspect from something of a similar class is established, just as in the case of consciousness;
that is to say, like the subjective aspect (*grāhakākāra*).
With the words "bāhyārtha" and so forth, he states the refutation:
"If either the reaching of an external object or its capacity for that is what is intended [as the definition of a valid cognition],"
For one who denies the existence of external objects, "conformity" is unestablished.

(2053) If conformity is intended to mean that a cognition is the cause for the determination of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), even so, this [definition] can apply even to a cognition that lacks an objective basis. (2054)

In this regard, if "consistency" (saṃvāditva)—meaning either the attainment of an external object or the capacity for that [attainment]—is intended as a qualification of the reason (*hetu*), then it is unestablished for the Proponent of Cognition-Only (*vijñaptimātravādin*) who denies external objects; thus, the reason is "unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*). Alternatively, if "consistency" is held to mean being the cause of a cognition that manifests as the desired purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), then the reason is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntika*), because its exclusion from the opposite case is doubtful due to the failure to demonstrate a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary.
This is because such consistency is not contradictory even in a cognition that lacks an objective basis (*nirālamba*).
In order to support the very absence of contradiction, he says: "Just as in the case of external water and so forth."
Just as the capacity and restriction of external water and other things are accepted, so too are these [capacities] in cognitions, because they are non-different from consciousness (saṃvid).
This [restriction] is also clearly evident through the appearance of inference, even though it is common [to both].

The form of fire and so forth is clearly manifest; it is not identical to that [formless] [object]. Furthermore, even though the appearance in inferential cognition lacks an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*), it possesses correspondence (*saṃvāditva*). Thus, because the existence of the contrary instance (*vipakṣa*) is certain, the reason—such as "being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatva*)—would be clearly an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*) due to its being over-exclusive (*asādhāraṇa*). To this, [the opponent] might say: "The lack of an objective basis for inferential conceptualization is unestablished. To this he replies: "The form of fire and so forth is clearly manifest," and so on.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is devoid of a particular form does not have that thing as its object; for example, a cognition of color does not have sound as its object. And inferential knowledge is devoid of external forms; thus, there is the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*);
for instance, that distinct form which belongs to fire and other such things is not identical to—that is, equal to—the form of inferential cognition, because the latter is indistinct.

Otherwise, just as an object appears in perceptual cognition according to its established form—distinguished by grass, leaves, and so forth—it would likewise appear in inferential cognition. However, setting aside its established form, the external object and the like appear in inference only as a general form that follows the signifier (*gamaka*).
Furthermore, it has been previously demonstrated that it is not logical for a single entity to possess two mutually contradictory forms consisting of both the universal and the particular.
Nor is the reason (*hetu*) contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Nor is it inconclusive, for that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

With the words "from such reasons as cognisability" and so forth, he anticipates the arguments of Uddyotakara: "If [the cognition] were distinct from the internal experience of another mind within one's own continuum, it would appear as separated by space due to the reasons of cognisability and the like. (2057)

He said: "That which appears as spatially distinct, such as blue and so forth, is different from internal experience because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), because it is impermanent (*anityatva*), because it is an effect (*kāryatva*), because it is a cognition (*pratyayatva*), and because it possesses a cause (*hetumattva*), just like the mind of another continuum (*santānāntaracitta*).
[Response: Even here, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāritva*) regarding the nature of this consciousness.
Nevertheless, [this applies] even to such things as the double moon perceived by those with diseased eyes;
here too, "even" refers to all the reasons [previously stated].

The fallacy of inconclusiveness (*vyabhicāritva*), that is, the lack of invariable concomitance (*anaikāntikatva*), exists even in internal experience because properties such as "knowability" (*prameyatva*) are present therein. For example, there is inconclusiveness with respect to the double moon and so forth appearing in the cognition of one suffering from ophthalmia;
however, the knowability of the double moon and such should be understood as being due to their being objects of conceptualizing cognitions (*vikalpaka-jñāna*) such as "this is a double moon."

Nor is there, with respect to that consciousness in which they appear, a non-attainment of the object; for as it has been said: "The non-attainment of the object by means of [the perception of] hair and so forth is not [an attainment]. (2058)
With the words "Otherwise," etc., he raises the objection regarding the non-establishment of the instance of deviation according to the view of Kumārila:
"If it is argued here that the object itself is external and is what is perceived, then surely this appearing form is not of the nature of that object. (2059)
And that [object], appearing in such a manner, is cognized by consciousness;
however, the intrinsic nature of the external object does not appear there in that way. How indeed could it be established as an object of cognition if it were not appearing?
And one knows that [object] as something else; thus, [the two claims] are mutually contradictory.

For this very reason, the self-cognizability of cognitions is difficult to establish, because we observe that there is a cognition of a manifestation that has become the self [of the cognition]. // 2061-2062 //
Therefore, this erroneous cognition does not conceptualize an object as it truly exists, but rather conceptualizes it otherwise; thus, it perceives itself [as such].

For he has said: "In this case, in cognitions such as that of a yellow conch or a double moon, it is precisely the external object—the conch and so forth—which is presented as the object of error and is apprehended in the form of yellow and so on."
To the objection that "therefore, deviation is not established," he says: "The form," and so forth.

This is the summary of the meaning here: it is logical that whatever form appears in a particular cognition is precisely what is cognized by it; for otherwise, every cognition would have everything as its object.
The state of being cognizable is pervaded by the state of appearing;

however, in a cognition having a yellow form (*pītākāra*), a white form (*śuklākāra*) does not appear, because that which is intended to be perceived is not apprehended. Thus, with the cessation of the pervader—the state of appearing—there follows the cessation of the pervaded—the state of being cognizable. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever form does not appear in a certain [cognition] is not cognizable therein, just as color (*rūpa*) is not [cognized] in the cognition of sound; and the form of a white conch-shell does not appear in a cognition having a yellow form. This is the non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
By the phrase "and he knows that," he points out a contradiction with his own words;
by the expression "for this very reason," he establishes self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) as a logical consequence.
By this, that which is desired by the followers of Jaimini—that "our cognition is not perceptible and is formless"—is refuted.

The conclusion begins with the words "Therefore" (*tasmāt*) and so forth; the connection is as follows: while [the cognition] is engaged in conceptualizing, it does not conceptualize the object itself as being otherwise. By this, he refutes what was stated by Kumārila.
With the words "atha" and so forth, [the author] states the very garland of proofs belonging to Kumārila himself.
Now, that form which is the grasper is distinct from that which is grasped,

because it is not perceived when that [object] is perceived, just like the grasper of taste and so forth. Likewise, the object is distinct from its grasper, since it is not perceived by one who is reflecting upon that [grasper].
It is not necessarily perceived [as a single entity], just like the perceiver of taste and so forth.
(2065) The two must be proven to be mutually distinct from each other, like taste and so forth;
or else, due to the lack of cognition of their identity, they are like the cognitions of different mental continua. (2066)
Cognition does not apprehend its own constituent part, because it arises from itself, just like its own causal capacity;
furthermore, there is a negation of its being an object of apprehension, for a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is devoid of duality.
Cognition belonging to Caitra makes known the apprehended portion of that cognition which has arisen from it.
Because it is cognition, [the self] cannot be produced in another body, just as [cognition is not so produced].

This cognition which grasps color (rūpa) is distinct from that color which is its object, because while that color is being cognized, this [cognition] is not cognized; just like the cognition that grasps taste (rasa) and so forth. Or alternatively: the object, such as color, is distinct from its own grasper, because when one reflects upon that grasper, it is not reflected upon, just like the grasper of taste and so forth.

Alternatively—the pair consisting of form and so forth, and that which perceives them, are mutually distinct, because when one is apprehended, the other is not apprehended; or because they are not known as a single unity, like taste and form, or like the minds of different continua;
or else, cognition does not perceive its own part, because it has arisen from [another] cognition.

And since the power of cognition is indeed called "latent impression" (*vāsanā*), the negation of cognition’s status as an object of apprehension must likewise be established, as follows: "A portion of cognition is not apprehended by cognition, because it is produced from cognition.

To the question of how an example endowed with the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is established in these two immediately preceding syllogisms, he says: "For a latent impression is devoid of both [subject and object]."

By way of the duality of the grasped and the grasper; or, another formulation: this cognition does not cognize that portion of a cognition arising from Caitra’s cognition, because it is a cognition, just like the cognition arising in another body such as Maitra’s with respect to that portion of a cognition arising from Caitra’s cognition.
2067–2068 He states the refutation with the words beginning "because they are not perceived separately," and so forth.
Because it has been demonstrated here that there is no prior perception of them as distinct,
[the opponent's position] is not established with respect to the range of arguments ending with the lack of knowledge of their uniformity (aikarūpya).
(2069) "Because of the non-distinct perception" means...

Because blue and the cognition thereof are necessarily perceived together, it is established that for one whose perception is not itself perceived, there can be no perception of the object; therefore, since the non-difference between blue and its cognition has been demonstrated through the proof of self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), the reasons [adduced by the opponent]—extending up to the "lack of knowledge of a single form"—are unestablished. (2069)

With the words "sabahiḥ" and so forth, the opponent sets forth an argument for [the existence of] the external: "Indeed, the cognition of the form of the object of apprehension occurs without the experience of an apprehending subject. (2070)

By this passage—"The external object possesses a form; it is perceived directly as connected with an external location"—the author of the Bhāṣya, Śabara, has demonstrated that the cognition of the apprehended object occurs even without the experience of the apprehending subject.
Consequently, the principle "because there is no cognition of the cognition" is established.
To the question, "How are the second and subsequent reasons established? he says: "I do not remember," and so forth;
they also remember that "no object whatsoever was apprehended by me at that time," as well as the arising of the apprehending cognition devoid of the form of the apprehended object. (2071)
Therefore, if there were non-difference [between the object and the cognition], there would be a recollection of the apprehended object as well;
however, it is only when there is a recollection of the apprehending subject that this [object] is grasped therein.
Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), the difference between the two is established.
And thus, these reasons are also well-established regarding the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin).

[Verse 2073] Even when there is no recollection of the apprehended object, a recollection of the apprehending subject is observed. If the apprehended object were absolutely non-different from that apprehending subject, then there would be a recollection of the apprehended object as well, just like the apprehending subject; yet such is not the case. Therefore, because they possess different fates (bhinnayogakṣema), the apprehended and the apprehender must be distinct.
To the objection that "there is indeed a recollection of the apprehended object as well," he says: "In the presence of the recollection of the apprehending subject," and so forth.
In that context,
at the time when the recollection of the grasper exists,
"this very one"— that is, the grasper alone— is perceived; the word "only" (eva) is placed out of its logical order [to emphasize] that the grasped object is not perceived.
"By means of positive and negative concomitance" refers to the presence and absence of the recollection of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject;
for instance, even when there is the recollection of the apprehending subject, there may be an absence of the recollection of the apprehended object.
He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "of one whose apprehension is unestablished," etc.:
"For one whose apprehension is unestablished, the cognition of an object is not established;
therefore, there is no awareness of the apprehended object apart from the experience of the apprehender. (2074)
He states the inconclusiveness of the claim that "this connection with an external object is perceived through direct perception" with the verse beginning *asvastha*:

"Likewise, what is seen by those with impaired eyes is observed as yellow and so forth; [though] it is cognized as extracted from the subjective portion, the other [object] is not so [cognized]. (2075)

The word "extracted" (*niṣkṛṣṭam*) marks the break [in the verse]. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) means that just as yellow and other colors, which are considered real, are perceived clearly as connected with external space, so too would they be observed even when perceived by one whose eyes are afflicted by jaundice and other such disorders.

If it is indeed so observed, what follows? He says: "And from the subjective portion, the object of cognition is not [separate]"—here, the word "separated" (*niṣkṛṣṭa*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis after "from the subjective portion."
"It is not [something] to be cognized"—this is the ellipsis;

by this, the following meaning is established: that yellow and so forth, as perceived by those with ophthalmia and the like, does not exist as a separate object of cognition extracted from the subjective aspect (*grāhakāṃśa*), and yet it is perceived as connected to external space; therefore, this [reasoning] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in the same way as the "other" [case].
By means of this mere appearance of distinct and clear [cognition], he establishes the equality of both cases, even regarding yellow and other colors that are considered real.

Regarding the point that "I do not remember anyone," he says: "And that memory, though its specific details are unperceived, pertains to an external form; however, it does not pertain to a form entirely distinct [from the object], because of the impossibility of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*) and other such factors. (2076)
By this, he states that the non-remembrance of the apprehended object when there is remembrance of the apprehending subject is unestablished.
It might be argued: if that memory pertains to the apprehended object, why is its specific character not perceived?
For one should remember that apprehended object exactly as it is—in all respects distinct from everything homogeneous and heterogeneous.

For in this way alone would that [cognition] have that as its object; otherwise, how could it, while not apprehending its difference from that, have that as its object? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Thus he says "from everything," etc.
What is meant is this:
conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not possess the capacity to apprehend an object exactly as it exists, because its domain is non-real (*avastu*).

Merely by the force of experiencing objects as they are, wherever there exist causes for determination such as desire and so forth, a mnemonic cognition (*smārta-pratyaya*) arises that determines the form of that [object].

In ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is entirely without an object, because it proceeds by determining what is not an object—the appearance within itself—to be an object; thus, every such [cognition] is born as nothing but an error.
However, the establishment of its object occurs through the power of that determination, not in ultimate reality.

Furthermore, the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the apprehended object does not exist even in the case of memory; rather, due to the absence of causes such as the proficiency of prior practice and the degree of proximity, its specific features remain unperceived, whereby it is distinguished from other instances of recollection.
(2076) One might ask: "How is it determined that the determination of the apprehended object exists here in memory? To this he says: "In what was grasped," and so forth.
If it were grasped [as an object], there could not be a recollection in this way;
nor is recollection experienced as being like a pure crystal.
This is because of the cognitions of a conch-shell as yellow and so forth, which serve as the reason for the latter two cases as well.
This direction [of argument] clearly applies to other proofs as well;

for if that memory were not to determine even the object of apprehension when its specific features are unobserved, then one would not proceed to reflect upon the object of apprehension even in a general form, such as "something was apprehended. Nor is the subject alone remembered with a form unmarked by the form of the object, appearing like a pure crystal.

Since it is said that "one remembers the arising of the apprehender as being devoid of the form of the apprehended," therefore, in the memory of that [apprehender], the non-remembrance of that [apprehended] is unestablished.

Furthermore, regarding these two final reasons—"because it arises from cognition" and "because it is a cognition"—the cognition of a yellow conch and the like, although it has arisen from a cognition, nevertheless apprehends its own part, the aspect of yellowness and so forth; and just as that [cognition], though itself a cognition, is the cognizer of the apprehended part of the cognition such as yellowness, so too is any other [cognition]. Thus, the two reasons are inconclusive (*vyabhicāritā*).

Furthermore, it has been established that the cognition of a yellow conch-shell and the like is without an external object; for this very reason, it has also been demonstrated that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is proven because one experiences the form of yellow and so forth residing within oneself.

"This is the direction" means that this is the general line of argument to be applied elsewhere as well—namely, as a method of refutation when an opponent puts forward arguments to establish the existence of external objects.

As for what has been stated by the opponent: "How is non-duality intended as the probandum? Since the appearing forms such as blue and so forth, as well as the nature of cognition, are established by experience, how can this [non-duality] be applied? If that were the case, it would result in the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of everything.
To this, it must be said:

there is no non-existence of everything, because external objects of apprehension, such as earth and so forth, which are distinct from [cognition] itself, do not exist by way of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇataḥ*).

However, because another continuum does not exist in the form of an object (*grāhya*), cognition is empty of the aspect of the object in relation to that [other continuum]. Furthermore, the agency of cognition—which is conceptually constructed by way of the definition "that which cognizes is cognition"—is also absent, and thus it is empty of the aspect of the subject (*grāhaka*). This is not, however, because even the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of cognition itself is absent, for there is no existence of anything whatsoever in any way.

Thus it has been said: "That which appears in cognition as blue, yellow, and so forth, as if external—that is real; therefore, in reality, there is no object of cognition (*vijñeya*) existing externally."

And that nature of being an agent which is attributed to consciousness in dependence upon that [object] is not real; therefore, even in non-dual consciousness (*saṃvid-advaya*), it is considered as "duality" (*dvaya*) when it is thus conceptualized. By doing so, this reading from the *Prajñāpāramitā* also becomes well-established: "Consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness, by way of the emptiness of characteristics."

2077–2078. Thus, having established the pervasion (vyāpti) of the reason with the probandum in the primary argument beginning with "whatever knowledge is [erroneous]," he concludes with the passage beginning "the subject of dispute" (vivādāspadam).
Therefore, the mind under dispute is non-dual because it is consciousness, due to its lack of being either an object of cognition or an agent, like a reflection.

(2079) By the qualification "under dispute," he means this: here, the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*) is the consciousness of healthy eyes and so forth, not every [consciousness]; however, the reason (*hetu*) is "because it is consciousness" in a general sense. Therefore, the reason does not suffer from the fallacy of being a mere part of the thesis (*pratijñārthaikadeśatā*).
The qualification "non-dual" is used because of the absence of both the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the agency (*kartṛtva*);
the intended meaning is that it is non-dual due to the lack of this dyad of object and agent, and not because of total non-existence,
as in the case of a reflection.

The cognition of the reflection is expressed by the word "reflection" through the metaphorical application of the term for the object to the subject; or rather, the suffix *vati* should be understood as following a locative case-ending, whereby cognition itself is obtained by implication as that which is contained [within the mirror]. Nor is the reason unestablished, because it is stated as an essential nature (*svabhāva*) by the exclusion of other differences, and not as the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*).
Nor is it contradictory, because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
With the words "But surely... and so forth, [the opponent] raises another objection regarding the example being devoid of the probandum (*sādhyavikala*).

But surely, even in the case of a reflection, cognition is held to have an objective support (*sālambana*), because when the visual rays are turned back, one perceives one's own face and so forth in that manner.

This is because the ocular rays, being struck by the surface of the mirror and the like, turn back and come into contact with one's own face and so forth; consequently, they become the cause for the perception of the face and other such objects in that way.
Therefore, it is from one's own face and so forth that there occurs a perception in the form of [the face] as it exists within the mirror and such;
consequently, it is established that the cognition of a reflection is devoid of the duality of the grasped and the grasper.

He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words "not by way of being face-to-face," and so forth: "It is not seen [by the eye] as being face-to-face; likewise, one's own face and so on are not perceived in that manner, because they are seen from different points of space according to the means of perception, just like any other object. (2081)

The connection is as follows: one does not perceive one's own face and so forth in that manner because one’s own face and so forth are not seen directly [by oneself], and because it is seen with distinctions of location, magnitude, color, and so on; thus, it is "not the perception of one's own face and so forth in that manner," just like any other external object.

This is said to be like the case of objects such as sound and so forth: (if) that cognition were the grasper of the face and other features, then it would grasp them exactly as they are situated; for it is not logical for a cognition having one form to have something else as its object, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For instance, one standing facing south and looking at the surface of a mirror sees one's own face facing north.

Likewise, on the surface of a very small mirror, even a large face is perceived as a small reflection; furthermore, it is seen as connected to the mirror's surface and as if deeply entered below it, yet the mirror's surface is not that thick, nor is the face or other parts connected to it in such a way. Similarly, in a lake of clear water, the reflections of trees and mountains standing on the bank are perceived with their branches and peaks turned downwards, yet they do not exist in that manner.

Therefore, the cognition of a reflection (*pratibimba-jñāna*) does not grasp one's own face and so forth, because it appears as something distinct from that [the face], just like the cognition of sound (*śabda-jñāna*). (2081) But the Venerable Śubhagupta says: "When [the thesis] 'being mere cognition' (*dhī-mātratva*) is to be established, the proof [adduced] such as 'being a cognition' (*jñānatva*)," etc.
Regarding the claim that "everything is said to be *śeṣavat* because it is not contradicted by anything of a different class," he says in response: "The nature of consciousness (*vijñānatva*), etc.
The nature of consciousness is luminosity (*prakāśatva*), and that [luminosity] finds no support in an object of apprehension (*grāhya*).
Because it is impossible for [cognition] to be without an appearance and so forth, its pervasion is thus ascertained.

We do not accept that the objective status of the apprehended aspect within the immediately subsequent cognition—which possesses the capacity [to know]—is ultimately real; therefore, [the object] is established as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
The establishment of representation-only (*vijñaptimātratā*) has been clarified by the wise;
we have followed its direction in this determination of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
(2084) Thus ends the Examination of External Objects.

For it has already been established through pervasion by means of the [arguments] beginning with "without appearance" (*anirbhāsa*) and "with appearance" (*sanirbhāsa*) that the reason is not inconclusive. This was stated by the venerable teacher Dignāga for the purpose of defining the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): "That which is the internal form of the object of cognition, yet appears as if external, is the object (*artha*), because it is of the nature of consciousness and also because it serves as its condition."
By this, the determination of the object within the apprehended aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*) has been established.

Furthermore, it was said: "Alternatively, through the transfer of potency (*śaktyarpaṇa*), even sequentially, that manifestation of the object produces a potency residing in consciousness and supported by consciousness for the sake of generating an effect corresponding to itself; thus there is no contradiction."
By this, its status as a cause is established, because it imparts a capacity to the immediately subsequent cognition for the production of an effect that conforms to itself;

yet, regarding this appearance, a refutation was stated by that same Venerable [Vasubandhu]: "Even if the apprehended portion (*grāhyāṃśa*) were the instrument of sensory cognition, because the cognition does not bear the likeness of that [portion], it is not its object, just as the sense organ is not. However...
To this, he replies with the words beginning "In the capacity" (*śaktau*), etc.;
[here] "in the capacity" and "in the immediately preceding cognition" (*jñāne*) are two locative case endings in grammatical apposition (*vyadhikaraṇa*).

Regarding the phrase "knowledge in the immediate [condition]," it means that in the *samanantara-pratyaya* known as the *ālaya*, that which is a power capable of producing the cognition of an appearance of such an object is not accepted as being ultimately real (*tāttvika*).

Since it has been established in detail by the Master that it is not tenable for something distinct from atoms and so forth to serve as an objective support (*ālambana*), and furthermore, lest there be a contradiction with common experience in the total negation of an objective support, he also addressed the contradiction with what is accepted [in scripture]: because of the statement in the Sūtra that "the four conditions are characterized as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), the immediate condition (*samanantara-hetu-pratyaya*), and the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*). Thus, in order to demonstrate non-contradiction, he explained how the objective condition intended in the Sūtra and in the world is of such a nature according to conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*), and not according to ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
But from the perspective of ultimate truth, all conditions whatsoever are indeed without objective support. 2082–2083.
2084. Thus ends the second part of the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, the Examination of External Objects.
In order to establish that "the examination of scripture" is independent and unattached to scripture, he says "others," and so forth:
"Others here, however, whose intellects are stained by ignorance, have declared..."
"This [world] is not tenable as being mind-only, because it contradicts scripture"—
so say the followers of Jaimini.
They say this: Injunction alone is the basis for the determination of dharma, adharma, and so forth; it stands as a common light for all living beings, like a universal eye.
Therefore, that alone must necessarily be resorted to as a means of valid knowledge by discerning persons seeking dharma, and nothing else, such as the words composed by human beings.
For instance, the speech of a person whose mind is overwhelmed by passion and other defects and by ignorance is not capable of making known supersensuous objects without error.

Therefore, dharma and so forth are not to be understood through those [ordinary] words, nor are they to be understood through the perception of one who sees only the immediate; for, being beyond the reach of the senses, they are absolutely imperceptible. To explain: dharma and adharma are characterized by their capacity to bring about desired and undesired objects respectively.
As it is stated in the Śābara Bhāṣya: "That alone which brings about the highest good (śreyas) is expressed by the word *dharma*.
How is this known?
Because people designate one who performs a sacrifice as 'righteous' (*dhārmika*)."
And whoever is the agent of something is designated by that [action], as in "cook" or "reaper";
therefore, it is he who unites a person with the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) who is expressed by the word *dharma*.
Thus, by this, it is established that *dharma* is the capacity of substances and so forth to accomplish a desired object.
For instance— the word *yāga* (sacrifice) denotes specific substances, qualities, and actions that are the means for attaining the highest good (*śreyas*),

and it has been shown therein that the term *dharma* applies to them; although those substances and so forth are perceptible in their own nature, they are not [perceptible] as the means to the highest good, and it is in that capacity (*tādrūpyeṇa*) that they are intended to be *dharma*, not merely in their own form.

As it has been said: "The highest good is indeed the pleasure of man; that is to be accomplished by means of substances, qualities, and actions characterized by Vedic injunctions. Therefore, dharma-ness resides only in these [means], and not in them by virtue of their being perceptible to the senses."
For their status as means to the highest good is always understood from the Veda;
and since their nature as dharma consists in that very character, they are therefore not within the scope of the senses.
And "by way of having that nature" means by way of being a means to the highest good (*śreyas*);
therefore, it is established that fitness (*yogyatā*) is *dharma*.
By contrast with dharma, it is clearly understood through implication that adharma is also capable of accomplishing undesirable ends;
moreover, one with limited vision (arvāgdarśana) is not able to perceive this capacity directly,
because it is always to be inferred from its effects.
As it has been said: "The potencies of all entities are established through the presumption based on their effects.
For otherwise, [the status of] being a person of limited vision would be lost;
nor is the perception of a yogi a means of knowing supersensuous objects, because it is a form of perception, just like other forms of perception.

Nor is inference appropriate for the apprehension of dharma and adharma, because it determines only those objects whose relationship [to the mark] is already known, whereas dharma is not of such a nature.
Nor is analogy capable of making dharma known; for analogy produces a cognition of similarity in respect to something not present to the senses.

Just as the sight of a gavaya [serves as the basis] for the recollection of a cow, so too there exists no perceived object similar to dharma through whose similarity its conceptualization might occur;
nor is presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) capable of bringing about the cognition of dharma and adharma.
To explain: presumption (*arthāpatti*) is the postulation of an unperceived object on the grounds that a perceived or heard object would otherwise be inexplicable;
however, no object whatsoever is inexplicable without *dharma*, such that its postulation would be necessary.

Furthermore, even non-existence (*abhāva*), which consists in the absence of a means of valid cognition, is capable of establishing the fact that "it does not exist," but it is not so in the case of a positive injunction (*vidhi*).

Therefore, if the *codanā* were unable to rescue dharma and adharma—which reside in the realm of non-existence—they would be swallowed by that very [non-existence]. Thus, dharma and so forth are defined by the *codanā*, not by the senses and other means; for the *codanā* alone is capable of making known such objects as the past, the present, the future, the subtle, the hidden, and the remote, whereas no other sense organ can do so. Consequently, the *codanā* must necessarily be accepted as the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
They say that *codanā* is a statement that impels one toward action or restrains one from it;
for example, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma" is impelling, while "One should not harm living beings" is restraining.
And the means for the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of that [Vedic injunction] is your thesis that the three realms are representation-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
That is not tenable;
why?
Because it contradicts scripture.
Because it is sublated by the Śruti— that is, the Veda—
since the Veda reveals the Agnihotra and other rites as being distinct from the mind,
and because [the Veda] itself exists independently of the mind.
The phrase "by way of mind-only" (*cittamātratayā*) is an illustration;
likewise, even the propositions of momentariness, selflessness, omniscience, detachment, and so forth, are indeed sublated,
because they persist by manifesting meanings that are contradictory to them.

It might be argued: "All of this would be sublated if its validity were established. To this he says: "For that is a means of valid cognition," meaning that it indeed stands as a means of valid cognition for everyone because it is not of human origin.
Since human utterances are understood to be false, [one might ask:
"How is it that this [Vedic word] is also called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), given that valid cognition is non-false knowledge? To this he says: "Because it is not produced by a person."

Because it is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), this formal argument (*prayoga*) establishes that [the Veda] is the cause of non-erroneous knowledge by means of the absence of the collection of defects such as passion (*rāga*), which are the causes of falsity: "Whatever is free from contact with defects that are causes of falsity is a cause of non-erroneous knowledge, just as the eye is when unafflicted by defects such as cataracts; and the Veda is free from contact with defects such as passion that are causes of falsity because it is not of human origin. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Avoiding the charge of inconclusiveness by means of a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*), he says: "Unreality" (*vaitathyam*).
For by this, he demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the probans;
that is to say: defects are the causes of falsity; wherever they reside, there alone do they bring about their own effect, falsity, and not elsewhere.

Since an effect cannot exist without a cause, or else it would follow that it is causeless, it is also not logical for something to be an effect of another if it exists independently of it, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the impossibility of a causal relationship between falsity (*mithyātva*) and defects (*doṣa*), and the consequence that falsity would be causeless, serve as a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the contrary position; thus, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: for that which lacks a particular cause does not exist there; just as smoke, whose cause is absent, does not exist [wherever it is not].
And the collection of defects such as delusion (*moha*), which is the cause of falsity, does not exist in the Veda. This is the non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).
Demonstrating that [the reason] is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "Defects exist," and so forth.

For it is suspected whether defects exist or do not exist in the case of what is spoken by a person; however, since there is no author for the Veda, for us there is no suspicion of defects whatsoever. (2087)

For defects (doṣas) reside in persons because they are their attributes; how then could they exist without their own substratum? Or, if they were to exist [without it], it would follow that they are non-resident (anāśrita).
For this is the nature of a resident attribute: that it conforms to its substratum.
And the person who is the substratum of the defects is the agent; since he has ceased [from activity] according to the Veda, whence can there be any suspicion of defects?
Those [reasons] that have perished—[is this not what is meant by "perished" (naṣṭa)?]—would also be subject to the fallacy of being unestablished due to doubt (saṃdigdhāsiddhatā).

This might be the case: how is the non-existence of the agent, who is the locus of faults, established? Therefore, he demonstrates that non-existence through the cessation of the five means of valid cognition (pramāṇa-pañcaka) that apprehend him, beginning with the words "The agent, for its part," and so forth.
First, it is maintained that the creator was never perceived at any time; having no previously observed relationship [with his effects], he is now [claimed to exist] based on ignorance alone.
Even though devoid of inferential proof, he is merely postulated to exist.
Scripture also does not establish that [the Veda], for there exists no "uncreated" scripture that is distinct from the "created" and the "non-created.
Since it is itself not a valid means of knowledge, the created [scripture] cannot be its communicator;
for even the words of Manu and others possess truth only because they were produced by him.
But how could one who is unrelated [to the Veda] and hostile to it be a speaker of truth?
Therefore, there exists no tradition among us regarding an author of the Veda, even if that author were someone else.
If anyone resembling an author of the Veda were seen at present, [then perhaps such an author might exist].
Then, by that very analogy, there would be an analogy even for the author [of the Veda].

(2092) If nothing whatsoever could be established as proven apart from the author of the Veda, then the author of the Veda would certainly be known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). (2093)
Indeed, there is nothing in the Veda that cannot be established without it;
for when this [non-existence] exists, many things such as authoritativeness and so forth fail to be proven.
Since it is inaccessible through the five means of knowledge, it is understood solely through non-apprehension (abhāva).
Therefore, this [author] is difficult to establish, because it is sublated by the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

First of all, an author of the Veda is not established through perception; for instance, it cannot be demonstrated by pointing him out specifically as "this is he," because he is not perceived at present. One must instead postulate that "there was an author"; yet, since he is unperceived, the claim that he existed at some time is without proof—this is the remainder of the argument.
Nor is it established through inference; thus he says: "With a previously unseen agent," and so forth.

The relationship characterized as that between the produced and the producer, which is currently asserted by those who revile the Veda with respect to the Veda, is caused by ignorance, because there is an absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that makes it known.
For no one is capable of apprehending a relationship between smoke and fire that has never been seen before.
Therefore, even though he is devoid of inference, that creator is postulated;

by the word "even" (api), it is indicated that he is not merely devoid of perception, but rather that verbal authority has also ceased to apply— this is expressed in the passage beginning with "āgamo 'pi" (verbal testimony as well).

Since there is nothing uncreated apart from the Veda, it cannot first be uncreated; nor can it be created, because that which is created is itself not a valid authority. To explain: if the scripture were created, its author would have to be some person such as Manu and others who are connected to the Veda.

Alternatively, it may have been composed by Manu, the Munis, and others who are unrelated to that [Veda]. With reference to the first position, he says: "Of the words of Manu and others," and so forth;
"by him alone" means by the Veda alone.
By this, he states the absence of intrinsic validity;
regarding the second position, he states its defect: "But [the person] is unrelated," meaning unrelated to the Veda, because he lacks authority therein.
"Composed by another" means composed by an unrelated person; [it refers to] the scripture concerning the author of the Veda— that is, that which establishes the existence of an author of the Veda.
He states the absence of an analogy with the words "one similar to the author of the Veda," and so forth;
he states the absence of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) with the words "without the author of the Veda"; [and he states] "it is known."
The six means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are printed below the letter ṭa; by that [means], it is delimited by the agent.
"Something" means that which has been cognized in this [cognition].
In the agentive case,
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "validity and so forth," it is meant that the establishment of dharma and other categories occurs precisely through non-existence (*abhāva*).
It is understood that "it does not exist" by means of the pramāṇa of non-existence,
because that [non-existence] is the object of negation;
or rather, it means that it is understood as "it does not exist" by way of the form of non-existence.
"Because of the absence of means of valid cognition,
and because it is sublated by the absence of means of valid cognition"— thus,
the non-existence of means of valid cognition is their cessation.
Since it is sublated by what is known as the means of valid cognition consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*),
it is established that there is no author of the Veda.

It might be argued as follows: "If the authority of the Veda is established by first proving its non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva), then alas, the authority of the Veda is rendered extrinsic (parataḥ). For indeed, the authority of the Veda is not cognized as long as its non-human origin has not been proven. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Aprāmāṇya... and so forth.
"The authorlessness of the Veda is desired for the purpose of removing its lack of authority; yet, because that [authorlessness] is a non-entity, it cannot be established by means of proofs.
By this, he says the following: "For we do not establish unestablished authority in a positive form."
What then?
Rather, the invalidity that has been attributed by another is negated;
and when the exception (apavāda) has been refuted, the general rule (utsarga), being itself uncontradicted, remains established by its own force.
Nor is authorlessness (*apauruṣeyatva*) being established, for by means of proving that, it would follow by implication that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
What then?
[It is not being established] because authorlessness is a non-entity (*avastu*), characterized merely as the negation of its presence.

2096. If it is not established [by others], how then is it established by itself? To this he says: "That which indeed," and so forth—that which a logician might state as a proof for its being of human origin.
By the refutation of that [opposing view], the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatā*) of the Veda is established.

(2097) Now, one might ask: even if the opposing position has been refuted, how can the establishment of one's own position be achieved for one who does not prove it through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), such that the proponents of the Veda would have their purpose fulfilled? To this he says: "For those two positions which are real entities," and so forth; for those two positions which are real entities, like *pradhāna* and atoms...
"By the non-establishment of one of these two, the other is not established by itself.

He explains this [regarding] "primordial matter (pradhāna) and atoms (paramāṇu)" with the words beginning "by the refutation of the state of being caused by primordial matter": even though the proof for the state of being caused by primordial matter has been refuted...
The world must be established as being composed of atoms by means of a different reason alone.

(Verse 2099) Even though the Vaiśeṣika has refuted the proof for the world having the *pradhāna* as its cause as presented by the Sāṅkhya, nevertheless, the world must still be established as being composed of atoms by means of a different reason; it will be the same here as well. (2099)
To this, he says: "For the sake of establishing the position of existence," and so forth.
Whatever proof (*sādhana*) is stated for the purpose of establishing the position of existence, when that is refuted, non-existence (*abhāva*) is established by itself. (2100)
Having refuted that which is asserted by opponents as the proof regarding the two limits—the prior and the posterior—the proponents of the Veda have accomplished their purpose.
The position of existence is human authorship; its cessation is the position of non-existence.

The meaning is that non-existence (*abhāva*) is established by itself, because for two things whose characteristics are defined by mutual exclusion, the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the affirmation of the other.

To illustrate: when the Buddhists set forth a proof to establish the two extremes of the Veda—namely, its production and its destruction at its prior and subsequent limits—the proponents of the Veda achieve their desired goal simply by refuting that proof; thus, they fulfill their purpose through the establishment of the Veda’s authorlessness, which is characterized by the absence of those two extremes. (2100)

[Objection: Even if that proof [of the Veda's authorship] has been refuted, the eternality of the Veda, which is of the nature of a positive injunction (*vidhi*), must still be established through a different effort. Therefore, how could the knowers of the Veda be considered to have achieved their purpose without establishing its eternality? To this he says: "Eternality is the very nature of the thing," and so forth.
[The meaning is: even for those who do not establish that eternality which is the very nature of the thing...
The accomplishment of that occurs spontaneously when the two opposing positions have been refuted.
(2102) The "two opposing positions" refers to the proof [of existence] at the two limits: the prior and the posterior.
He demonstrates how the eternity [of the Veda] is established by itself once the two preceding positions have been refuted: "The former limit of the Veda," and so forth.
The former limit of the Veda is characterized by being of human origin, while the latter is of the nature of destruction; indeed, the absence of these two is eternity. (2103)

Because permanence is characterized by the exclusion of both the prior and posterior limits, and because for two things characterized by mutual exclusion, the negation of one is necessarily concomitant with the existence of the other—as has been stated [in verse 2103]—if this is so, and if that absence is permanence, then it follows that permanence cannot be a property of a real entity (vastudharma). To this he says: "That which is not produced at the beginning..."
If it is held that the Veda is eternal because it is not created at the beginning and does not perish later, then that alone should be understood as its eternity;
for eternity is intended to consist precisely in being uncreated and indestructible.
And since these two consist of non-existence (abhāva), they do not require a means of their own proof.
By this, he demonstrates that for the Veda, which is a real entity (vastubhūta), this property [of being a means of knowledge] resides in its very nature.
Anticipating the opponent’s opportunity for objection—that if it is thus a real entity, then its eternality must necessarily follow—he says "the knowable" and so forth.
"Jñeya" means that which is to be known by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is to say, that which is to be established;
"tau ca" refers to non-creation and non-destruction.
The proof of its own nature is its "own proof" (svasādhana);

the point is that even for non-existence, there is no contradiction with being a real entity, and thus, despite having the characteristic of being uncreated and indestructible, it does not follow that eternality is a non-entity.

Thus, first of all, by the exclusion of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the consequent establishment of the absence of an author for the Veda, the reason—that it is free from the association with defects which are the causes of falsity—is not unestablished (*asiddha*). Nor is it contradictory (*viruddha*), because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*); nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because it is absent in the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). Thus, the validity of the Veda is established. Now, he begins in detail the refutation of the two arguments put forward by others to prove the invalidity of the Veda.

In this regard, there are these two means of proof: that which is perceptible by the senses and that which follows immediately after an effort; both of these are impermanent, just like a jar, and sound is likewise [of such a nature]. Thus, when the impermanence of sound is established through the general principle of the reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), the impermanence of the Veda is also established; consequently, by implication, its falsity will be proven—just as in the case of human speech—this is the intention of the opponent, such as the Buddhist.
Here, he demonstrates at length the sublation of the proposition (*pratijñābādhā*) by means of verbal testimony (*śābda*) and other pramāṇas.
First, he states the sublation by verbal testimony, beginning with the words "the meaning of the Vedic sentence," and so forth.
The thesis of one who asserts, on the basis of inference, that the meaning of Vedic statements is false, is overturned by the power of Vedic knowledge.
"Vedic" refers to that which has come from the Veda— such as, "From the Agnihotra sacrifice, heaven comes," and so forth.
By the force of that [perception], the [contrary] position is set aside, because it is sublated by it.

As it has been said: "And this [Vedic injunction] does not produce a doubtful cognition as to whether it exists or not; nor does there arise, at another time, in another person, in another place, or in another state, a subsequent cognition that 'this is false,' which would be a non-designatable [sublating] cognition. Furthermore, even if an inferential cognition should arise—based on seeing the subversion of other cognitions and concluding that subversion is established here as well—that too would be sublated when it is contradicted by this perception."
But [an objection is raised]: "How can there be the sublation of one by another when both are of equal strength?

Or, if there is indeed sublation despite their being of equal strength, why would it not also be sublated by inference? To this, he says: "And that [scriptural statement] is because it is equal to perception."
And because it is equal to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), that which is Vedic is more powerful;
it cannot be sublated by inference (*anumāna*) in any way whatsoever.
[To the question] "How then is inference sublated by that? he says: "Direct perception," and so forth.

Since the scripture itself is established as being more powerful when it is placed within the category of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), this constitutes a sublation (*bādhaka*) of inference (*anumāna*).

As it has been said: "The cognition arising from the words of the Veda is indeed direct perception; and inference that contradicts direct perception does not constitute a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)."
2108. How is it that scripture is more powerful than inference, such that it is equal to direct perception? He says: "Because it is independent of an example.
Because it is independent of an example and because it is free from defects, it possesses simplicity (lāghava).
Since scripture possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whereas inference does not possess such [status],
when there is doubt regarding a matter based on both scripture and inference, a definitive conclusion must be reached by that [scripture] alone, because scripture is more authoritative. (2109–2110)
In the phrase "in being a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇatve*), the locative case indicates the object with respect to parsimony (*lāghava*);
it does not refer to inference in that manner.
Because that [inference] depends upon an example and because defects exist therein,
it is indeed sublated by Vedic knowledge which is equal to perception.

[Objection: But surely, only that which is established for both parties can constitute a refutation. Since the Buddhist does not accept scripture as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)—given his restriction that there are only two such means—how can a contradiction be established against the Buddhist by means of the invalidity of scripture? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Even though the Veda makes its meaning known, [it is] 'not a valid means of knowledge for me,' etc. Even though the Veda makes its meaning known, [it is] "not a valid means of knowledge for me"—in this very way [the opponent argues]. Thus, even while the Veda conveys its own sense, it is rejected by the Buddhist on the grounds that it is not a valid authority for him. Therefore, since the Veda is not accepted as a means of knowledge by the Buddhist, it cannot serve as a basis for a refutation. This is the point.
It is not possible for a speaker of truth to declare something false merely out of hatred;
nor does it become invalid simply due to hatred or because it is disagreeable.
Furthermore, validity is not determined by either affection or approval. (2111–2112)
Moreover, even those who are hostile to the Veda do not utter anything that would constitute a reason for its lack of authority; were they to do so, they could not be considered speakers of truth.
[This is because] there are those constantly devoted to the duties of memorizing, studying, and explaining it.

How can that which is the cause of falsity, being unknown, be known by those who stand at a distance? For those who are experts in a particular field and whose interests are bound up with it are the ones authorized to know the merits and defects pertaining to that field. (2114–2115)
"But how can those wicked ones who hate Brahman and are cast far outside the Veda speak shamelessly about the merits and defects of the Veda?

(2116) He thinks as follows: "The establishment or non-establishment of a thing does not occur by mere wish; for if it were so, the validity of scripture would not be established merely by one's own acceptance. Rather, that which is established by the force of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is established for both parties. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the conviction arising from sentences such as 'the Agnihotra [is to be performed]' is more firmly grounded. Therefore, how can it be said that this is not a valid means of knowledge?"
The brief meaning is that this [position] of yours is a mere matter of words,
devoid of logical justification; "because it is not accepted" means it lacks the approval of the world— that is, it lacks worldly consensus.
The Śākyas and others are "distant" because they are excluded from the Veda and from such practices as its retention.

"Those for whom the purpose is bound to that" means: in that [Veda], the "purpose"—namely, the human goal characterized by sacrifice and so forth—is "bound," i.e., stated; those [who hold such a view] are the haters of Brahman.
Brahma is the knowledge that arises from the Vedas or is directed against those who hate the Vedas.

Alternatively: "Even if there were no sublation by scripture (*āgama*), nevertheless the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñārtha*) is indeed defective, because it is sublated by means of cognition such as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth. Demonstrating this, he says: "Furthermore," and so on.
Furthermore, since the permanence and omnipresence of sound are established by auditory recognition, who could determine its opposite?
(2117) By this, he states the sublation [of the opponent's view] through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

For instance: because it is recognized through direct perception as "this is that very same thing" at all times, its eternity is established by the direct perception known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*);
and because it is recognized in every location, its omnipresence (*vibhutva*) is also established. Who, then, would determine the opposite of eternity and omnipresence? No one at all.
The opposites of eternity and pervasiveness are non-eternity and non-omnipresence.
2117 He concludes with the word "therefore":
Therefore, indeed, there is oneness at all times and in all places.
That [identity], established by direct perception and recognition, sublates this [notion] at all times— namely, in the past, future, and present.
(2118) "At all times" means in the past, future, and present.
"Of this," [refers to] the inversion.

With the words "of the flame, etc.," he raises the objection that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is fallacious; [the opponent] says: "Even though flames and the like are momentary, there is recognition. If this is argued, it is not so; for in that case, what is recognized by us is the universal (*sāmānya*), which is indeed eternal. (2119)

However, in whatever respect a cognition of difference arises due to some limiting condition (*upādhi*), there can be no recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in that respect, as it has been determined by the cognition of difference.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of hair, nails, grass, and the like that have been cut and grown again, as well as waterfalls and so forth; for even in those cases, recognition exists, such as: "These are those very same hairs," "Those are those very same blades of grass," "That is the very same stream of the waterfall," and "That is the very same water of the river."
This is not the case;
for in that instance, the universal such as "fire-ness" (*tejastva*) is recognized, and since that is indeed accepted as eternal, how could there be any deviation [from the rule]?

Furthermore, that which is of the nature of an individual manifestation is indeed impermanent, yet it is not recognized [as such] through recognition; therefore, how can there be any deviation (vyabhicāra) in this respect,
namely in cases such as the degrees of intensity— milder, milder still, and so forth?
To the question, "How is it known that [the air] is characterized by some limiting adjunct (upādhi), such as slowness or upward movement? he says: "It is determined by the cognition of difference."
The meaning is that this is understood by one whose intellect is divided.

He states the sublation by means of inferences: "The cognitions of the individual instances of the word 'cow,' though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, either all have the same object or else they have various objects as their domain. (2121)
Because it arises as "cow," this word "cow" was manifested by yesterday's cognition of the word "cow," just as it is manifested today by the cognition produced now,
since both have the word "cow" as their object. (2122)
Either this [cognition] cognizes that [object], because of that cause, like a previous cognition;
or both [cognitions] would have a single object, like a single cognition;
or all cognitions of "cowness," though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, [would have a single object]. (2123–2124)

The cognitions produced by each individual utterance of the word "cow" must have as their object the same [word], because they are cognitions of the word "cow," just like a single cognition [of that word].
Alternatively, the word "cow" uttered yesterday still exists today,
because it is apprehended by the cognition of the word "cow," just like the word uttered today.
"The word 'cow' heard today was indeed heard by me yesterday as well;
for this very reason already stated, the word uttered yesterday—whether it be the sound itself or its denotative signifier—is stable and persists over a long period of time. (2126–2127)
Because it functions as a cognition of an object of knowledge that depends upon the experience of a relationship,

that which is such is observed to be stable, like the universal aspect of smoke (dhūmasāmānyabhāga). That which is unstable, however, is not a communicator [of meaning] that depends upon the knowledge of a relationship.
Because they have only a momentary cause, like the light of a lamp or a flash of lightning,
the position that sound is impermanent is therefore contradicted by all these firm and established inferences; consequently, it remains settled that sounds are eternal.

The cognitions regarding the individual instances of the word "cow," which are differentiated by the appearance of distinctions such as place, time, fast, medium, or slow [utterance], have a single object as their domain; they do not have multiple objects as their domain, because they arise while assuming the form "cow," just like a present cognition of a cow.
Alternatively: whatever cognition has the word "cow" as its object, that has the word "cow" as its object today, because it has the word "cow" as its object.

Today’s cognition of the word "cow" is a cognition of the word "cow" that had yesterday as its object, just like today's cognition of the word "cow" produced by a cow [actually present]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Alternatively: the subject (*dharmin*) is yesterday’s cognition of the word "cow"; the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is having yesterday’s word "cow" as its object; the reason (*hetu*) is "because it has the word 'cow' as its object"; and yesterday’s cognition of the word "cow" is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "iyam" (this):
"iyam" refers to that which is present today,
and "tam" (that) refers to...
The word "cow" perceived through the cognition of the word "cow" from yesterday is [the object] because of that cause,
namely, because it has the word "cow" as its object.

Alternatively: both the past and present cognitions have the same object, because they have the word "cow" as their object, just like the cognition of a single word "cow. The reason for this has not been explicitly stated because it is easily understood from the context.

Alternatively: all cognitions of "cowness" (gotva), though differentiated by distinctions of place and so forth, are produced by the single word "cow" because they are cognitions of cowness, just like the cognition of a single cow.

Previously, the cognitions were the subjects (*dharmin*) having the word "cow" as their object, and "having a single object" was the property to be proven (*sādhya*). Now, however, the cognitions having the universal "cowness" as their object are the subjects, and "being produced by the single word 'cow'" is the property to be proven; this is the distinction.
[The term] *hyastanoccāraṇa* means that its utterance occurred yesterday.
And this is the indication of the subject (*dharmin*);
"continuing even now" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); the rest is easily understood.
"A cow being heard [by the word] 'cow' even now" is the indication of the subject.
For its audibility even yesterday is the property to be proven (sādhyadharma),
because it follows from what was stated previously: [the reason] being cognizable by the cognition of the word "cow."
Alternatively—"Whatever word is expressive"—this is the indication of the subject (*dharmin*); "its possession of duration" is the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*);
and "because it functions toward the cognition of the object to be known in dependence upon the experience of its relation [to that object]" is the reason (*hetu*).

"Dependent upon the experience of a relationship" means it requires the experience of a relationship; that which is both "dependent upon the experience of a relationship" and "the operation of the cognition of the object to be known" is described as such.

Therefore, the object to be known (*jñeya*) is stable. By the qualification "existing for a long duration," he demonstrates through this attribute that what is intended here by "stability" is stability in terms of time, and not stability in terms of space, as in the case of a mountain or similar objects.

The example "like the portion that is smoke-in-general" is given because the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) cannot function as a logical mark (*liṅga*) due to its lack of concomitance; thus, only the general aspect (*sāmānyabhāga*) serves as the example.
The statement beginning with "but it is unstable," etc., is an exposition of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
"Because it has a cause that is contemporaneous":

"contemporaneous" (tādātvika) means pertaining to that time—something that follows the period of conventional usage; that which has such a cause, namely a relationship, is so described, and its state is "thatness" (tattva).
But surely, by this same line of reasoning, one could also assert the unity of jars and other such things;

for instance: all cognitions of individual jars, though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, must have a single object as their domain—or else they would not have various objects as their domain—because they arise with the thought "jar," just like a cognition of a jar produced at the present moment, and so on.
Anticipating the objection that "the oneness of jars and so forth is neither desired nor observed, therefore all these reasons are inconclusive," he says:
"In the case of the attainment of oneness of the jar and so forth, etc."— if [oneness] is intended as a genus (*jāti*), it is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
If one were to effect the merging of individuals in this manner,

then it must be stated that [the doctrine] contradicts what is observed, for the distinction between individuals is well-ascertained by all means of valid cognition, beginning with direct perception, which is the authority for all words.

If, by way of a reductio (*prasaṅga*), the oneness of jars and so forth is established in terms of their genus—that is, by way of the form of the genus—then that is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).
As it has been said: "For its part called 'genus' is eternal, while the other [part] is considered perishable.
Alternatively, if the oneness of the individual forms is established by way of a reductio, even then there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

The intention is this: since this proposition is sublated by perception and other means of valid cognition, all reasons (*hetu*) intended here are qualified by the condition that their objects must not be sublated; therefore, how could there be any deviation (*vyabhicāra*)?
"Contradiction with what is perceived" refers to the thesis; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
The rest is easy to understand.

Furthermore, he states the sublation of the thesis regarding the non-eternality of sound by means of inference (*anumāna*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). In this regard, the inference is as follows: those two things whose relationship is non-artificial are themselves non-artificial, just like space and atoms; and the relationship between a word and its object—which is designated as a "universal" (*jāti*)—is characterized by the nature of the signifier-signified (*vācya-vācaka-bhāva*), and is thus non-artificial. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāva-hetu*).
Warding off the charge of unestablished proof, he says: "And if it were artificial," and so forth.

"And if the relationship were artificial, because it would be abandoned upon the application of that [word], and because it would reside in only a single individual instance, it could not be universal. (2133)
Because of the confusion [caused by] the earthiness, substantiality, existence, and possession of a tail [of a cow],
the determination of "cowness" (gotva) would not occur without a multiplicity of applications [of the word].
Therefore, the word is uncreated and never perishes.

Because of the eternal connection with that which is eternal, like space or an atom. And it must be considered that if the connection were artificial, then because of the cessation of its application—that is, the destruction of the word's usage—the word itself would also be destroyed; thus, it would not be universal, meaning it would not persist through all usages.
Why? Because it resides in that single individual—that is, because it resides in a single cow-individual.

In this regard, there is an *arthāpatti* (presumption): when a universal is present in many individuals as well as in a single cow-individual standing before one, the cognition of "cowness" (*gotva*) alone, abstracted from the word "cow," is not possible without the word. To explain how this is so, he says: "earthen," and so forth.
This presumption (arthāpatti) is preceded by verbal testimony;
therefore, he concludes with the inference that "the word is non-artificial" by means of the term "eternal" (nityena).
Because of the meaning of the designation "birth" (jāti),
there is a constant connection at all times,
just as atoms [are connected] with eternal space (ākāśa).

Warding off the charge that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is inconclusive, he says: "And the word 'cow', when heard once, having as its object several universals present before it, does not attain the status of denoting its own specific meaning in isolation. (2136)
By means of numerous auditory perceptions, this [cognition] excludes life and so forth,
as well as the movement toward white and other colors, the possession of a dewlap, a tail, and so on,
and the individuals such as the brindled cow (śāvaleyādi) and the fragmentary object (khaṇḍādi), each according to its own specific basis.
The fact that [the word] expresses the extracted universal (gotva) is understood only after a long time.

As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "But indeed, when a word is eternal, having been uttered many times and previously heard in connection with various individual cows, it makes known its status as denoting the form (ākṛti) through positive and negative concomitance; therefore, for this reason also, it is eternal. Individual instances, however, have their own respective causes."
The meaning is that they are distinguished according to their respective [causes].
For their distinctness is the basis for the cognition of difference;
thus, those whose own distinctness is the basis for the cognition of difference are "those based on themselves" (*svanibandhanāḥ*).
The connection is with the word "avoiding.
It might be argued: "Even if it is indeed perceived after a long time, how is it established that the word exists at all times? To this he says: "For that duration," and so forth:
"If it remains stable for that duration, who will destroy it afterwards?"
Its perishability cannot be further inferred by any other reason.
Just as jars and the like are understood to perish through causes such as being cut by weapons or through decay, no such cause exists for sound.
"For that duration"—meaning for the duration of its production of its own distinct meaning.

Now, one might object: "Just as jars and other things, though stable for that duration, undergo destruction later due to hammers and the like, so too will it happen for sound. To this, he says: "It is possible for this," and so forth, [ending with] "furthermore" (*bhūyaḥ*).
