Furthermore, just as jars and other objects undergo destruction through being cut by weapons and the like, or through decay due to aging, no such cause exists for sound. Why? Because it is formless (*amūrta*), whereas jars and the like possess form (*mūrta*). This is the intended meaning.
As it has been said: "If the oneness of the jar and so forth were to result, then the proof of what is already established would be accepted by [the proponent of] the universal."

If, by this line of reasoning, one were to effect the attainment of oneness among individuals, then it would have to be stated that [the position] contradicts what is perceived and is opposed to all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);

this applies equally here as well. In the case of the attainment of oneness among *ga* and other [phonemes], everything must be stated as follows: since the universal (*jāti*) is accepted [by us], it would be a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*).

To explain: just as there are many individual instances of cows and the like due to differences in place, time, and speakers, so too are there many individual instances of phonemes such as *ga* and the like; and just as "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth are accepted as universals (*sāmānya*) residing in those individuals, so too is "phoneme-ness" (*gatva*) intended to be a universal. Anticipating this objection that everything is thus the same, he says: "Even though there is a difference in place, time, and speakers... and so on. [Verse 2141: Even though there is a difference in place, time, and speakers, the phoneme *ga* and the like are not differentiated, because in that regard the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is perfectly clear.

The intention is as follows: through perception known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the identity of individual instances (*vyakti*) is established; inference does not become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) when it contradicts perception, because perception is the eldest among all means of knowledge.

(2141) Now, one might object: "Since differences such as fast, medium, and slow are perceived, the difference between individual instances is indeed established; so how can it be said that recognition is perfectly clear? To this he replies: "For even when there is a difference in speed and so forth... (na hi drutādibhede 'pi...).

For even when there is a difference such as rapidity and so forth, another distinct and clear individual cow (*gavyakti*)— separated from other individual cows— is not perceived as being already established.
[Verse 2142] "Established" means...
"Unconceived" means interrupted; "divided" means distinct.
The meaning is that because the individual instance of the letter *ga* is unified through recognition, there is no other individual instance of the letter *ga*.

But surely, it is only the universal *gatva* (the nature of being the letter *ga*) that is recognized here, not the individual instance; so how can there be recognition of the individual? To this he says:

"The letter *ga*, etc."—an absolutely isolated substratum of *gatva* does not exist, because it cannot be defined by a cognition other than that of *ga*, just like the *gatva* postulated by others. (2143)

"Because it cannot be determined by a cognition other than that of the letter *ga*": *gānya* means "other than *ga*"; because it cannot be determined by a cognition directed toward that [other], it is ungraspable, like the *gatva* (the universal of *ga*-ness) postulated by others.
Because it is the established tenet of others that universals are devoid of further universals,
and because this [subject] is also a color, this [property] is to be proven.
Furthermore, this [sound] is to be proven [as impermanent] because it possesses color (varṇatva), just like the letter *kha* and others;
and since no counter-example (vyatireka) is observed, there is nothing seen here that could subvert [the argument].
The remainder of the sentence is "there is a negation of motion" (gatvaniṣedha).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) therein is as follows: "Whatever is a letter (*varṇa*), that is not the substratum of the universal 'g-ness' (*gatva*) in its most abstract form, just like the letter *kh* and so forth; and this letter *ga* is indeed a letter. This is an instance of the perception of a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), because the property of being a letter is indeed pervaded by what is contradictory to being the substratum of *gatva*.
Nor is there any contradiction with observed facts regarding the thesis here, as he says in the passage beginning with "of the negative concomitance" (*vyatirekasya*).
Vyatireka is difference;
dṛṣṭa is perception.

It might be argued: "For the Buddhist, this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For instance, the cognition of oneness is accepted as being based solely on the exclusion of others (*anyāpohana*), and not on a distinct property of 'going' (*gati*). Therefore, even if a distinct 'going' is refuted, oneness is not established for the phoneme by virtue of the cognition of oneness, because that [cognition] is based on the exclusion of others. Anticipating this objection, he says: "But let the nature of the phoneme, established for both parties, such as its eternity and so forth, be accepted exactly as it is desired in the case of a conceptualized entity, even though it is already established. (2145)
Because that [phoneme] is a single entity, a single cognition of the phoneme arises;
the existence of distinct cognitions occurs due to the difference in the manifestors.

Why, then, having abandoned the nature of the phoneme—which is established for both [parties]—are properties such as eternality, multiplicity, and pervasiveness attributed only to the imagined "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha)? This is because of the statement: "Because the properties of a universal (jāti) are established [therein]."

It is logical to postulate only that which is established for both [parties], for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of postulating something unobserved. Therefore, it is precisely because of the oneness of the phoneme (*varṇa*) that the cognition of its identity arises.
If this is so, how could there be cognitions of distinctions such as fast, medium, or slow? To this he says: "The cognition of distinctions," and so forth.
The manifesting agents are the conjunctions and disjunctions belonging to air.

Now, one might object: since air is not an object of the sense of hearing, its conjunctions and disjunctions are likewise not objects of the sense of hearing; how then can there be a perception of the manifested [sound] when the manifestor is unperceived? For it is not reasonable that a jar or the like, which is manifested by light, should be perceived when the light itself is not perceived. Thinking thus, the opponent raises the objection beginning with "nanu":
"Indeed, for one for whom both [the air and its qualities] are audible, there would have to be two cognitions."
"But since, according to you, [the phoneme] is beyond the senses, how can there be a cognition of distinctions through the sounds?

(2147) "Of whomsoever"—that is, for the Grammarians and others, the manifestor is sound (*dhvani*) consisting of resonance, and not that which consists of the conjunctions and disjunctions of air; for such a person, both the manifested and the manifestor are graspable by the ear, and thus there arises a twofold cognition: a single cognition and a cognition of distinction.

But for you, the Mīmāṃsaka, how could there be a cognition of specific distinctions through sounds (*nāda*) consisting of the conjunctions and disjunctions of air? Why? Because the sounds are beyond the senses (*atīndriya*); this is the remainder of the argument. (2147)
He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "nādena" and so forth:
"When sound is perceived by the auditory organ as refined by the resonance (nāda), some declare that there is a cognition of it through its association with that [resonance]. (2148)
"By means of its proximity" means by means of the proximity of the word; "of that" refers to the resonance (nāda).

"Perception"—some declare this to be "apprehension. Their view is that although the mere sound (*nāda*) is not apprehended by the ear, nevertheless, there is indeed apprehension of it when it is conjoined with the word (*śabda*); thus, they maintain that two distinct cognitions must necessarily arise.
By the phrase "or not at all," he establishes two views regarding the non-perception [of the phonemes]:

either there is no perception of them at all, or even if they are perceived, the cognition of the word arises by virtue of them, following the sequence of the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and it is through this that magnitude and so forth are apprehended. (2149)
"Of these" refers to those sounds,
which consist of the conjunctions and disjunctions of air.

He asks: "How can there be a cognition of the manifested (vyaṅgya) when its manifestor (vyañjaka) has not been grasped? He replies: "But the cognition of the word is by virtue of that," meaning it is by virtue of the sound (nāda), that is to say, by the mere existence of that [sound].

Granted that there is indeed the apprehension of the mere essential nature [of the sound], but how does the apprehension of specific qualities such as magnitude occur? To this he says: "Because it conforms to the latent impressions" (*saṃskārānukṛteḥ*), and so forth.

When a great latent impression is produced in the auditory organ by great sounds, then magnitude is perceived in the sound; when, however, it is small, then smallness is perceived. In this way, the distinction of degrees—greater or lesser—should also be applied according to the conformity to the latent impressions.

But surely, according to your view, this magnitude and so forth that is perceived resides only in the manifestor (*vyañjaka*) and not in the manifested (*vyaṅgya*). And since that [magnitude] is unperceived due to the non-perception of the manifestor, how could one superimpose upon the sound a magnitude and so forth residing in the manifestor without having first perceived it?

For there can be no superimposition of water and the like upon a mirage if they have not been made an object of perception. To this he says: "Sweet [is perceived] in the form of bitter," and so forth.
Just as those with deluded minds, due to a disorder of bile (pitta), perceive sweetness as bitter or white as yellow,
so too do those running at great speed or riding in a boat perceive stationary objects as moving. (2150)
They perceive mountains and the like through delusion, as do those who wander about them;
with eyes smeared by the fat of a frog, they perceive bamboos as snakes due to the smallness or greatness of the individual instances, and likewise [perceive] the universal residing therein.
Just as these [senses] perceive [objects] without grasping the cause [of the error],

so too will there be an illusion regarding the manifested [object] without having understood that which resides in the manifestor; just as, due to a defect of bile, one perceives an object such as sweetness in the form of bitterness without even apprehending the nature of the bile itself.
Just as people whose vision is disturbed by the rapid movement of a boat or by spinning perceive mountains and other objects as moving or spinning when they themselves are walking or turning;
and just as those whose eyes are smeared with the fat of a frog see bamboo poles in the form of serpents;

and just as, due to the smallness or largeness of the individual instances (*vyakti*), they apprehend the universal (*sāmānya*) residing in them—as the substratum of smallness and so forth—such that the great universal called "Being" (*sattā*) appears large, while "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like appear small.

Otherwise, since everything would be identical due to [the universal] being eternal and omnipresent, what could cause the smallness or greatness of a universal? Therefore, just as these [tastes] such as sweet are perceived in the form of bitter and so forth without the perception of the cause—such as bile—in the same way, there will be an illusion of greatness and so forth regarding sound even without perceiving the greatness and so forth residing in the manifestor; thus it is "without having understood."
The identity of agent is established in relation to the action of delusion; otherwise, however, the suffix -āp would not occur.

2152–2153 Now, how is it known that this cognition of shortness, largeness, and so forth regarding sound is due to external conditions (*paropādhi*), and not because of the actual existence of distinctions such as largeness and so on within the sound itself? To this he says: "The distinction of shortness and so on is intrinsic," and so forth.
However, a distinction such as shortness and so forth contradicts its eternity and other such qualities;
for how could that which exists at all times be itself measured by a *mātrā*?
Therefore, it is the pronunciation of it that should be understood as having the duration of a *mātrā*.
A phoneme (*varṇa*) is not itself composed of [temporal] measures (*mātrika*), whether it be two measures or three measures.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of distinctions such as long (*dīrgha*), protracted (*pluta*), acute (*udātta*), grave (*anudātta*), circumflex (*svarita*), and so forth;
[otherwise], this would contradict its eternity (*nityatva*) and other properties.
The meaning is that permanence is established by means of recognition (pratyabhijñā). 2154–2155.

With the words "nanu" and so forth, he raises an objection regarding the non-establishment of manifestation according to the view of another: "Indeed, the manifestation of a word by means of sounds is not tenable;
for that [manifestation] would have to occur either through the refinement of the word, or of the sense organ, or of both. (2156)

Therefore, if the sound were being refined there [in the ear], it would be perceived by everyone; for there can be no refinement in a single part of that which is partless and all-pervading. This manifestation of the sound, occurring through the conjunctions and disjunctions of the air, must arise either from the refinement of the sound itself, or from the refinement of the sense organ, or from the refinement of both—the sound and the sense organ.

In that regard, if sound were something to be refined (*saṃskriyate*), then being refined in one place such as Pāṭaliputra, it would be perceived by those situated in all places, because it would simultaneously be omnipresent (*sarvagata*).
Alternatively, if it were argued that only one part of it is refined and not the whole, he says: "of that which is partless" (*nirbhāgasya*).
For sound is indeed without parts (*niravayava*) due to its incorporeality (*amūrtatva*); how could there be a refinement of a partless entity through a single portion, even if it were omnipresent?
Furthermore, it might be argued that even for that which is partless, there will be a modification through differentiation due to the difference in its substrata; to this he says: "Nor also..."
Nor can there be a restriction of refinement based on a difference in substratum,
because sound is without a substratum, just like space, the self, and so forth.
Due to its omnipresence, sound is without a substratum, like space, the self, and so forth.

[Objection: "But surely, since sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), and qualities depend upon a possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), space exists as the substratum (*ādhāra*) of sound. To this he says: "Even so, space... and so forth;
even if space were the substratum there, [it is] being partless (*anavayava*).
There would be no refinement of a specific location, even though sound is perceived as a whole.
Since that ether is also partless, there can be no difference in refinement based on a difference in supporting locations.

Now, one might argue: "Even if ether is partless, nevertheless, due to the difference in its conjoined objects, ether—as delimited by the ear-canal and so forth—will be distinct, just like 'pot-ether' and the like. To this he replies: "even because sound is perceived as a whole."
The connection is that there would be no refinement (*saṃskāra*) of a specific location;
for the word is indeed perceived as an indivisible whole, and that perception would not occur if only one part of space were refined.
Concluding this very point with the question "How so?", he says: "For indeed," and so forth:
"Indeed, it is not possible for that which is established as a whole throughout the entirety of space to be perceived in its totality when only one part has been refined. (2160)
For sound, which exists pervading space, cannot be perceived in its entirety if it is refined by only one part [of that space].
He states the refutation regarding the position that the sense organ is what is refined, beginning with the words "In the position that the ear is space," and so forth.

Moreover, on the view that the auditory organ is space, because of its all-pervasiveness, there would be an equal reach [of the organ] even to sounds located at a distance; thus, it would follow that the cognition of sounds occurs here [simultaneously for all].
Furthermore, in this way, the auditory organ of all living beings would become one and the same.

Therefore, at the time of hearing one [sound], all of them would hear it. For those who hold the position that the auditory organ is space (*kha*), since space is a single entity and all-pervading (*vibhu*), its contact with all sounds is equal; consequently, even a sound situated at a distance would be perceived, and there would be a single auditory organ for all living beings.
Furthermore, when one person hears, then everyone else would hear as well, because the auditory organ is non-different;
and it must be stated that there is the fault that when one hears, all would not hear.

It might be argued as follows: "The auditory organ (*śrotra*) is space delimited by the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), which is conditioned by merit and demerit (*dharmādharmābhisaṃskṛta*). Therefore, since the auditory organ is established in that portion of space occupied by the ear-cavity, both of these faults—that the auditory organ would be equally reached [by all sounds] due to its omnipresence, and that there would be a single auditory organ for all living beings—are without foundation.
To this, he says: "Because it is partless" (*tasyānavayavatvāt*).

Furthermore, because it is partless, a region of space conditioned by merit and demerit cannot constitute the auditory faculty for the sake of establishing the two-fold distinction [of hearing and not hearing].
For, in the ultimate sense, there are no spatial parts to that which is partless.
By which any particular region of space would become the auditory organ;
there would be a twofold determination— the determination of inequality regarding reach (*prāpti*), and the determination of the multiplicity of auditory organs—
or else, a twofold determination regarding the perception and non-perception of sound.
Furthermore, an auditory organ once refined would perceive all sounds;
for an eye opened for a jar does not fail to perceive a cloth.

This very point must be considered: even in the case of the recollection of an object, there would be no distinction because the mental impression (saṃskāra) exists in the same location [as the auditory organ].
Furthermore, the auditory organ, once refined [by a single impression], would awaken—that is, cause one to perceive—all sounds at once.

Since that [auditory organ] is common to all sounds, and since those sounds, being all-pervasive (vibhu), occupy non-distinct locations suitable for perception, it might be argued that the auditory organ of the listener is refined specifically for the sake of perceiving that [particular] sound, such that it would cause the auditory organ to grasp only that sound and no other. To this, he says: "With regard to a jar," and so forth.
The meaning is that it is not the case that [the sound] is not perceived, but rather that it is indeed perceived, because the suitability of the location is the same.
To the question, "How can there be the perception of all sounds?", he says: "Because the embellishment (*saṃskāra*) exists in the same location and is without distinction.

For all sounds, being omnipresent (*vibhu*), exist in the same location within space (*ākāśa*); consequently, their embellishment is also entirely undifferentiated, and thus there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving all of them.
In some versions, the reading is "saṃskāro hy aviśeṣataḥ"; there, the word *hi* indicates a reason (*hetau*),
and *aviśeṣataḥ* is formed with the suffix *tasi* from the third case ending [of *aviśeṣa*] according to the rule beginning with *ādyādibhyaḥ*.

Consequently, this is the meaning: since the refinement (saṃskāra) of sounds has been performed without distinction, because they reside in the same location, it follows that there would be the apprehension of all sounds.

It might be argued: "Even if the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is non-specific, nevertheless, only that sound which is intended to be grasped by the auditory organ is perceived, and no other. To this, he replies with the verse beginning *sthiravāyu*: "And the refinement of this [sound], occurring through the removal of the obstructing steady air, would result in its perception in that location once the obstruction has ceased. (2166)

For wind is of two kinds: stable (*sthira*) and unstable (*asthira*). Among these, that which is stable remains covering sound like a dense darkness; and through the conjunctions and disjunctions produced by the air arising from the effort of the speaker, the removal of that stable air is effected by those very conjunctions and disjunctions. This alone is the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the sound, and not anything else such as the nourishment of its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because, being eternal, it is uniform in nature.
To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "It is seen," and so forth;
"it is seen" means [it is observed] in both worldly experience and the scriptures.
Just as, when darkness has been removed, there is indeed the perception of a jar or similar object situated in front—even if it is undesirable—because it is located in a suitable place;
as it has been said: "In that case, the sound would be perceived by everyone if it were being refined."
Thus, there is no fault here, because even a single word may be unrefined for one person and refined for another; as it is said:
"Just as a single woman is both a mother and a daughter due to a difference in perspective," so too, the states of being refined and unrefined are not established by the oneness of the word.
And if two states were admitted [for a single entity], it would either be known by all or not known at all.

(2167) Since the word is one, the two states of being refined (*saṃskṛta*) and unrefined (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot simultaneously obtain; because the state is non-different from the substratum of the state, the states themselves must also be one, just like the nature of the substratum. This is just as when a single woman is called both "mother" and "daughter."
In that case, only the word itself would be different, not the object; however,
here it is not merely the designation that is different, because the word persists without distinction in its fitness to be apprehended by all persons,
and consequently, there would be neither apprehension nor non-apprehension [of the object].
For it is not logical that the abandonment of a nature determined by causal efficiency should occur merely through a change in designation.

If it is argued that its nature is such that it is perceivable only by specific individuals, and thus perception and non-perception are not contradictory due to differences in human capacity, we say no;
for if an object has not been perceived by a person once, it will never be perceived by that person at all.
But this is not the case;

therefore, so that there may be no loss of its unity, one must accept that sound has only a single state, whether conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) or unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). To the question "What follows from that?", he says: "Since it is accepted as having a single state," and so forth.
2167 He states the fault in the position that both [the sense organ and the object] are embellished: "The faults already stated for each individually would apply to the embellishment of both."
Therefore, a manifestor of sound is not tenable in any way whatsoever.
(2168) The faults that were stated regarding the refinement of the sound individually and the refinement of the sense organ individually would likewise apply if there were a refinement of both;
thus he concludes with the word "therefore."
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "The answer," etc.:
the answer has been described by the author of the Bhāṣya as arising from the refinement of the auditory organ.
"And due to that difference [in the manifester], the difference in the heard sound is established for each individual listener.

As stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "Even for one who holds that [sounds] are manifested, this fault does not apply; for the conjunctions and disjunctions do not assist the ear-cavity when it is far away. Therefore, they are not perceived by that auditory organ which is at a distance."
"Due to its division"— that is, due to the division of the auditory organ (śrotra) as the ear-cavity (karṇaśaṣkulī),
there is a division of hearing— that is, a division of cognition. 2169
But how can there be a manifestation of one thing through the refinement of another? To this he says: "Just as in the case of a jar," and so forth.

Just as a lamp or similar object is accepted as the manifester of a jar and the like, so too sound would be [the manifester] precisely through the assistance of the eye when the auditory organ has been refined. (2170)

Just as a lamp or similar object, by assisting the eye, becomes the manifestor of a jar or other such things, so too sound, through the refinement of the auditory organ—that is, by means of the auditory organ’s refinement—will be the manifestor of the word-sound.

Now, it might be asked: "In what manner is the refinement of the auditory organ produced by sound, given that [the organ] is already established? To this he says: "And there is no objection to be raised here."

And there is no objection to be raised here as to "in what form does the refinement [occur]?", because this is the same even in the case of production; for in that case too, the capacity is beyond the senses.
(2171) "Because this is the same even in the case of production"—the word "objection" is to be supplied to complete the sense.

For even regarding the production of sound from its causes, the same objection applies; it can indeed be asked there as well: "In what form is the sound produced by the cause—whether that cause consists of the conjunctions and disjunctions of air, or something else? Since the power [of production] there is also beyond the senses, the objection is equal even in the case of the production of sounds; for just as the productive power of the causes of sound is imperceptible when sound is being produced, so too is it in the case of its manifestation. Thus, the objection is identical.
If it is asked how that power, which is beyond the senses, is to be inferred, he says: "Eternal," and so forth—
"Since power is eternally inferable from its effects, why is it being questioned?"
In that case, the only valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) understood is the mere fact of its occurring when that [cause] exists.
Whether it be a power to produce or a power to transform, in every respect, whatever power there may be, all of it is always to be inferred from its effect;
therefore, it does not deserve further questioning.

"What is that effect by which it [the capacity] is inferred? To this he says: "In its presence," and so forth. "In its presence" means when there is the presence of sound (*dhvani*). "Its manifestation" (*tadbhāvitā*) refers to the manifestation of the apprehension of the word-sound (*śabda*); that very thing is the proof for the capacity to manifest the word-sound therein.
The meaning is that the capacity is inferred through the effect, which is the apprehension of the word-sound.
By the inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*), the arising [of the object] is excluded;
he concludes with the words "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

Therefore, these manifestors appear by means of a power that is indeed beyond the senses, bestowing upon the sense-organ a power that is itself beyond the senses; thus they shine as the causes of manifestation.
Consequently, these sounds appear as the causes of manifestation by producing, through a power beyond the senses, a power in the auditory organ that is likewise beyond the senses.
The word "of sounds" (śabdānām) is to be supplied [to the verse].
Now, why are the *dhvanis* not understood as being merely the causes of production? To this he says: "Of those," and so forth.
However, for those who maintain that this sound is perceived by the ear without reaching it,
since non-attainment is equal [in all cases], there would be no distinction between the perception and non-perception of sounds located far or near.
(2174) In that case, the apprehension and non-apprehension of what is situated at a distance or nearby would be identical.

Furthermore, there would be neither a sequence nor the possibility of degrees such as intense or faint [in sound]. For those Buddhists who hold that sound is "produced without being reached" (*aprāptajāta*)— that is, it is grasped by the auditory organ while being produced without having reached it.

According to the established doctrine that the eye, ear, and mind do not reach their objects, and that sound has as its cause the primary elements (mahābhūtas) whether appropriated or unappropriated, it follows from their view that sounds situated at a distance, behind an obstruction, or nearby would all be equally unattainable by the ear. Consequently, for persons standing far away or nearby, there would be an equal lack of perception; the manner of perception for one nearby would be identical to that for one far away because there is no distinction [in the lack of contact]. Furthermore, there would be no sequential perception, such that those nearby perceive first and those far away perceive later.
Nor would there be a distinction in the intensity of the sounds, such as high, low, and so forth, whereby those situated nearby hear it intensely while those at a distance hear it faintly;
the same logic should be applied to the distinctions of degree as well.

Now, one might object: "Even for that Mīmāṃsaka for whom a sound already reached and not yet arisen is perceived by the auditory organ, why does this same undesirable consequence not apply to him as well? To demonstrate the distinction [between his view and ours], he begins with the words "Therefore," and so forth: "Therefore, even from the perspective of the Vedic scholar (śrotriya), let this conceptual construction be examined."
The air within the abdomen, struck by effort, undoubtedly moves; it moves, there is no doubt.
It conforms to the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other [articulatory organs], and because it possesses velocity, it necessarily persists for as long as that velocity lasts.
Due to its movement, conjunctions and disjunctions necessarily arise between it and the parts of the self, as well as with the still air.
Having reached the space within the ear, it imparts its power to each successive part of the auditory organ.
Since verbal cognition occurs even in the absence of that [external object], an unseen mental impression (*saṃskāra*) is postulated;
like the capacity for production, that too is nothing additional for us.
Likewise, its particularity would also arise from the apprehension of a particularity. (2179–2180)
The mention of the *śrotriya* is intended to demonstrate that he is not a mere logician;
and by this, he expresses the excellence of his own position through an indirect statement.
To the question "What is this conception?", he says: "Struck by effort," and so forth.

Effort (*prayatna*) is the operation of the articulatory organs such as the palate; impelled by that effort, the abdominal air (*vāyu*)—which has risen from the region of the navel, expanded in the chest, turned in the throat, and struck the head—emerges while moving through the mouth.
This very process is shown [by the passage] beginning with "it" (*sa*):
that air, as it exits, undergoes conjunctions and disjunctions with the palate and other parts.
And as he goes, he does not go as far as space; what then?
He goes as far as his momentum—that is to say, he goes exactly in accordance with whatever speed he possesses.
Why? Because of its velocity;

as that air moves, conjunctions and disjunctions necessarily arise between its own constituent parts and the still, stable air, and having reached the cavity of the ear, it imparts power to the sense of hearing.
In its presence—that is, when there exists conjunction and disjunction with air—the unseen refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ is postulated because sound is perceived;
just as you postulate that the production of a sound by other sounds or by articulated noises (*dhvani*) is unseen yet accepted as a capacity (*śakti*), so too is this refinement.

As it is stated in the Bhāṣya: "The parts [of air] set in motion by the impact, displacing the still air and other substances, produce conjunctions and disjunctions in all directions and persist as long as the momentum lasts; and because air is imperceptible, these conjunctions and disjunctions are not perceived, yet sound is perceived only while they have not ceased, not when they have ceased."

If this is so, then no distinction has been stated between the position of "manifestation" (*saṃskāra*) and the position of "origination" (*utpatti*); to this he says: "In that very way," and so forth.
That distinction—the distinction of manifestation—is established through the distinction in the apprehension of sound.
Consequently, for those standing at a distance or nearby, apprehension and non-apprehension do not occur equally, because the manifestation differs according to the difference in persons.
Regarding the question of how sound is not perceived when there is an obstruction such as a wall, he says: "A wall, etc. and so forth.
Even the obstruction by walls and such is possible for the wind, as is its impact upon the location of the ear by means of that intense movement;
and because of its sequential progression, it possesses the qualities of decay and velocity.
The intensity or dullness of the sequence of the *saṃskāra* (impression) is caused by such factors [as distance].

Even though sound is not subject to resistance (*pratighātin*), nevertheless, because the wind (*mātariśvan*) and the wall possess material form (*mūrttatva*) and are thus resistant, the sound does not reach the location of the ear; consequently, no *saṃskāra* of the auditory organ arises, and thus there is no hearing of what is obstructed.
For those, however, who hold that perception occurs without [the object] reaching [the sense organ], this very fault [of the obstruction] applies.

To the question, "In that case, how does the distinction of degrees—more intense, most intense, and so forth—of the auditory perception occur?", he says: "The striking against the location of the ear also...
The word "is appropriate" (*yujyate*), which is the subject under discussion, is to be applied everywhere;
[the phrase refers to] "the excellence of decay and velocity."
The connection is made by changing the case-ending (vibhaktivipariṇāma) as "they are joined with the perfections of perishability and the perfections of velocity.
Alternatively, the analysis (vigraha) is: "those which are both perishable and perfections of velocity.
Or else, it is a bahuvrīhi compound: "that wind which possesses perishable perfections of velocity."
And thus, the connection is that it is logical for the intensity and mildness of the sequence of impressions (*saṃskāra*) to have [the wind] as their cause;
the sequence of impressions is logical because that wind functions sequentially,
and its intensity is logical because it is endowed with the perfection of velocity.
Moreover, because it is subject to destruction even when authorized, the distinctions such as "more" and "most" should be applied by means of the word "etcetera.

[Objection: But surely, regarding the position that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is space (*ākāśa*), many faults in the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotrasaṃskāra*) were previously stated, beginning with "Because of its all-pervasiveness, the capacity for contact is equal," and so forth. So how is it that the author of the Commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*) later described [the theory] as resulting from the refinement of the auditory organ? [Response: He says: "The auditory organ is not necessarily space," and so on.
We do not necessarily accept that the auditory organ is space.
Furthermore, space is not partless, because that is denied by the Jainas and the Sāṅkhyas.

Therefore, the auditory organ must be either a specific portion of space or a distinct entity; it is established in each individual person as something known through presumptive testimony based on its effects.
It has been stated that the faults inherent in that position do not arise simply because it is not accepted;
and the connection [of the argument] is that space is not admitted to be partless.
Why?
Because of the refutation by the Jains and the Sāṅkhyas— since the partless ether (*vyoman*) has been rejected by the Jains (the Ārhatas) and the Sāṅkhyas,
the Mīmāṃsakas do not employ what is established in the tenets of others.
For whatever is established by reasoning is precisely what they accept; otherwise, their status as Mīmāṃsakas would be lost.
Therefore, there is no fault in accepting the ear as being of the nature of space (ākāśa), as is well-known to the Jains and Sāṅkhyas, or rather, as being a distinct entity.
That which is designated as the *karṇaśaṣkulī* (the ear-drum) is understood through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on the purpose of its function; that is,
it is understood through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the perception of sound.
Alternatively, demonstrating that there is no fault even under the view that the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is partless space (*ākāśa*), he says: "Even though," and so forth.
Although [the auditory organ] is all-pervading and unitary, nevertheless, it is only that person whose refinement of the resonance (*dhvani*) occurs in its substrate who perceives the sound.
(2185) Although it is all-pervading and unitary...
The word "ear" (*śrotra*) is to be understood as the subject;
nevertheless, that person in whose physical substrate—the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*)—the refinement (*saṃskṛti*) produced by the sounds occurs, only he perceives the sound, and no other.
By this, it is stated that the refinement belongs to the substrate itself, not to the auditory organ (*śrotra*).
The sense is that because that substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) differs for each individual person, the aforementioned fault does not follow.
(2185) He demonstrates that there is no fault even if the auditory organ (śrotra) is refined— “athāpi” (even so).

Moreover, even if there were a refinement of the sense organ (*indriya-saṃskāra*), the ear would not hear sound from a location other than its physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), because the concha of the ear would remain unrefined by that [refinement].
"Physical basis" (*adhiṣṭhāna*) refers to the concha of the ear (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*).

The refinement of the auditory organ occurs through the mediation of that [sound], not by itself; and because its physical basis is unrefined, the ear of those who are situated at a great distance, or whose minds are elsewhere, or who are asleep or unconscious, does not hear— that is to say,
one whose ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) is unrefined is described as such.
Regarding the phrase "adhiṣṭhānadeśataḥ," the suffix *tasi* is used in the sense of the locative case (saptamī).

Now, if sounds do indeed refine the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the location thereof, or the sense organ (*indriya*), why is it that those sounds whose existence is perceived only in certain places do not bring about the refinement of the sense organs and substrata of all living beings? To this, he says: "Because they have not reached the region of the ear," and so forth.

Because sound does not reach the region of the ear, there is no refinement of the auditory organ; therefore, the restriction of refinement is established by means of the distinction between the physical bases [of the organs]. (2187) Even if the sounds that effect the refinement of the bases were to refine the sense organs located in those same places...

Nevertheless, only when they have reached [their object] do they produce an embellishment (*saṃskāra*) in the object which possesses the capacity for such an embellishment, not when they have not reached it; therefore, there is no embellishment of the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth belonging to all persons.
Furthermore, the mention of "perception by the ear" (*śrotragrahaṇa*) is merely an illustration; even the embellishment of the substratum does not occur at all.

In some places, there is a reading: *aprāptakarṇadeśād vā* (or "because [the air] has not reached the region of the ear"). In that case, the previous solution was stated by relying on the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ (*śrotra*) through the medium of the refinement of its substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Now, however, even if the refinement of the auditory organ does not occur by way of the refinement of its substrate, there is still no fault; for only those air-currents that have reached the base of the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) are capable of refining the auditory organ, not those that have not reached it. It is for this reason that an alternative position is stated.
"From this" is the conclusion (2187).
With the words "But surely," etc., he anticipates the objection of the opponent regarding all three positions just mentioned.

Indeed, for one who maintains that there is a single sense-organ (*ekendriyavādin*), an organ that has received refinement (*saṃskāra*) in one substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) would have to be the perceiver in all bodies.

Since it is impossible for a single auditory organ to possess the two mutually contradictory properties of being refined and unrefined, [the opponent argues: because it is refined in one place and because it is non-different across all bodies, the auditory organ of even a deaf person would necessarily become a perceiver for the *ekendriyavādin*.
Consequently, there would be no established distinction among men such as deafness and so forth;
he offers a rebuttal to this with the verse beginning "puṃsām" (of men).
The production of cognition in persons is held to occur in specific regions of the body;
therefore, because it is located in a different place from the primary cause (the sound), the refinement of the auditory organ is deficient.

Although the selves of persons are omnipresent, the Mīmāṃsakas and others maintain that the production of cognition occurs only within bodies that are governed by merit and demerit (*dharma* and *adharma*).

Because the primary substratum, the body, occupies a different location—that is, they exist in distinct places—the refinement (*saṃskṛti*) of the auditory organ, even though it is all-pervading, is thus rendered ineffective; therefore, there is no occasion for the aforementioned defects in any case.
In this context, the reading is "that refinement" (*sātra saṃskṛtiḥ*).
In that context, the connection is that "that embellishment belongs to the auditory organ.
(2189) Now, one might object: since the self is all-pervading, the apprehension of sound everywhere would follow as an unavoidable consequence; to this, he says: "And even though it is partless..."
Furthermore, although our self is partless and perceives everything in its entirety, there is no fault in saying that it grasps [objects] only within the body;
for by this very reason, the established distribution of deafness and other such conditions is possible.
That very [object] is not to be enjoyed by another when it is governed by merit and demerit (dharma-adharma).
Just as one who, while still living there, is deposed from his lordship and no longer obtains enjoyment, so too a deaf person does not hear when others are listening. || 2191–2192 ||
This is what is meant:

even though this is so, nevertheless, the soul's apprehension of sound is limited solely by the body which is brought under control by merit (*dharma*) and other factors; therefore, there is no fault.

If it is asked: "But how can there be a distinction between the apprehension and non-apprehension, or the refinement and non-refinement, of the ear—which is part of the indivisible soul?"—[the answer follows].

Just as in the case of space— which, though partless, appears divided into "the space within a jar" and "the space within a pot" due to the differences among the objects with which it comes into contact— so too will it be here.

For this very reason, he demonstrates that the determination of deafness and other conditions occurs in the case of the all-pervading and partless auditory organ due to the differences among its associated objects.
(The phrase) "deafness, etc."— by this, that is,
by the reason consisting in the difference of the conjoined [substrata].

Even if those joined [to the sense organ] are indeed distinct, why is it that only a certain person becomes deaf? To this he says: "That very [organ] is not an object of experience. That very auditory organ does not become an object of experience for another person. Why? Because it is governed by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Clarifying this very point through an illustration, he says: "Just as there," and so forth.

Just as someone who is the owner of a village or the like, while still residing and being present in that very village, might be deposed from his ownership by the king and thus no longer receives the enjoyment of that same village; in the same way, a deaf person does not hear, even when another person elsewhere is hearing. 2190–2191.

But surely—since the triad of the auditory organ, sound, and space are all partless and all-pervasive, there can be no occurrence in a specific location; so how is the distinction between perception and non-perception, determined by their occurrence in a single location, obtained? To this he says: "Of the auditory organ, sound, and their substratum," and so forth.

Furthermore, the auditory organ, sound, and their substratum—the ether (*ākāśa*) being the substratum of sound—do not themselves possess parts, nor do they subsist in a single location; nevertheless, this [explanation] is not defective.
"Auditory organ, sound, and substratum" refers to the auditory organ, sound, and the ether which is the substratum of sound.
The name [of the whole] does not consist of its parts themselves;

however, since they exist as distinct conjoined entities, they are indeed present there figuratively. Thus he says "itself"—meaning that even so, this [whole] possesses such properties as being restricted to residing in specific locations and being perceived accordingly.
To the question "How so?", he says: "Of the manifestors," and so forth;
for the manifestors, namely the winds, possess distinct locations for their constituent parts.
And by that very [difference], the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is established according to the distinction of genus (*jāti*).

"Diverse" (*bhinna*) refers to those whose locations of parts (*avayavadeśa*) are designated as the substrata of the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*); their state is "the state of having diverse locations of parts. (Verse 2194)
And there is a difference in genus (jātibheda) due to the difference in the causal complex consisting of the palate and other [articulatory organs].
Now, it was argued that "once the auditory organ has been refined, it should perceive all sounds"; to this, he gives the following reply: "Impelled for another purpose," and so forth.
Just as the wind, impelled for one purpose, does not produce something else, so too that which is capable of refining one phoneme will not produce another. (2195)
"For the sake of another" means for the purpose of producing another phoneme; "capable of refining another phoneme" means capable of bringing about the modification of another phoneme.

The impression (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ which has the purpose of perceiving another phoneme is expressed by the term "impression of another phoneme," but it is not the impression of the phoneme itself, because the impression of the auditory organ is the subject under discussion; thus,
it will not produce another [phoneme].
The meaning is that one [sound] will not embellish another color (varṇa) by means of the embellishment of the auditory organ.
Alternatively, he asks why this restriction applies only to the winds, and says: "By others," and so forth.
Just as one phoneme is not produced by other articulations of the palate and so forth,
likewise, the projection of one sound (dhvani) is not carried out by those sounds that belong to another.
The intention is that, due to the differences in the articulations of the palate and so forth, the manifesting winds— the sounds (dhvanis)— are distinct.
The ellipsis "it is made [known] that the phoneme is not other" is to be supplied;
the "rejection" (kṣepa) of other sounds means their displacement (preraṇa).
There is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the phrase "by means of the contacts of the palate and so forth, which carry over into other sounds.
He concludes [the argument] with the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, based on the presumption of the effect regarding both production and manifestation, there would be an equal difference in capacity everywhere in relation to effort and the desire to speak.
(2197) The term "utpattyabhivyaktyoḥ" ends in the locative case.
Why is there an equal difference in the capacity of effort and the desire to speak with respect to both the production and the manifestation of sound?
Because it is understood through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the effect.
The meaning is that in both cases, the presumption based on the necessity of the effect (*kāryārthāpatti*) is operative.

Thus, having first accepted— respectively according to other philosophical systems and common worldly consensus— the auditory organ as being characterized by space (*ākāśa*) and the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), it has been argued that there is no fault in the manifestation of sound through the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that organ.

Now, relying on the definition of the directions (*dig*) as established in the Veda, and demonstrating that there is no fault in the manifestation of sound through the various refinements (*saṃskāra*) of that [direction acting as] the auditory organ (*śrotra*), he says: "Or rather," and so forth.

"Or rather, in accordance with the Veda, one should maintain the understanding that the auditory organ is the direction; for the Veda nowhere states that the auditory organ consists of space (*ākāśa*) or any other such element. (2198)

"For the quarters are the ear"—this is indeed stated regarding the [state of] dissolution; and that is a statement concerning the return to the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), just like [the statements] regarding the eye and so forth.
Thus ends the discussion on the notion that the quarters are the ear.
The meaning is that one must reach the certain conclusion that "the quarters are indeed the auditory organ.
To the question "How so? he says: "It is not of the nature of space.
If it is thus, and it is not stated even in the Veda that "the quarters are the auditory organ," then how is this obtained? To this he says: "The quarters are the auditory organ," and so forth.

Regarding the *prakṛtis*, which are the inherent natures, there are dissolutions (*pralayas*), meaning that at the time of destruction, the eyes and other senses of living beings dissolve into their respective *prakṛtis*. Concerning that dissolution, it is said in the Veda with reference to the sacrificial animal: "May his eye go to the sun; may his hearing go to the quarters."
Here too, the connection is with the word "gamayatāt";
the meaning of "gamayatāt" is that whatever has come from a certain place should go back there.

Therefore, although it is not explicitly stated in the Veda that "the ear is the quarters," nevertheless, by the force of the statement "May the quarters lead [the sacrifice] to the ear," it is indeed stated; he asks "How so? and replies with the words beginning "And that..."
And that statement, "the ear goes to the quarters," is intended to demonstrate the return of the ear to its source;
the meaning is that the ear, as the agent, should go to the quarters which constitute its source.
To the question "In what manner?", he says: "like the eye and so forth."
He explains this very point with the passage beginning "sūryam asya" and so forth.

"Just as the nature of light is declared by the statement, 'May his eye go to the sun,' so too is the ear of the nature of space. (2200) Just as the nature of light is declared by the sentence, "May his eye go to the sun"—where the word "of the eye" (*cakṣuṣaḥ*) is to be supplied—as the nature of space is declared by the sentence, "The ear is of the quarters" (*diśaḥ śrotram*). Such is the connection between the words to be made.
The meaning is that the cognition of the nature of fire is the state of being composed of fire.
Now, as to what kind of direction that is, he says: "Direction," and so forth.
And space is one and all-pervading, situated as far as the sky extends;
when delimited by the cavity of the ear, it becomes the sense of hearing, like a portion of space.
(2201) This is an elaboration of [space] being all-pervading: "situated as far as the sky extends."
If this were so, the distinction between those who are deaf and others would not be possible, because space is one; to this he says: "In the ear-cavity," etc.
Space is not the auditory organ in its entirety; rather, it is that which is delimited by the boundaries of the ear-structure (karṇaśaṣkulī).

[Objection: "But since it is partless, how can a division of parts be obtained for it? To this he says: "As much as... Whatever logic of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣika) there may be regarding the conceptualization of a portion of space, that same logic applies equally to a portion of direction; however, it is distinguished by scripture. (2202)
Just as there is a conceptualization of parts of space based on the distinction of its conjoined objects, so too will it be for the directions.
To the question, "What then is the distinction of this [theory of the directions] from the position that the ear is space? he says: "From scripture" (2202).
By this concluding summary, he indicates the established distinction regarding those who are deaf and so forth:
"Therefore, that portion of the substance of space which is governed by merit and demerit, delimited by the cavity of the ear, and is the auditory organ—that is what is refined. (2203)
Demonstrating that there is no fault even in the view that the impression belongs to the object, he says: "Even of the object...
Even if the impression belongs to the object, by that [impression] there is the embellishment of only one [object];
and because of the difference in capacity among men, it is not perceived by all. (2204)
As for what was said—"In that case, the word would be perceived by everyone if it were being refined"—there is no fault there;

why? Because of the difference in the capacities of men: since the refinement of the auditory organ differs according to the proximity or non-proximity of the air that refines the ear, there is a difference in capacity.

But surely, since sound is eternal and omnipresent, and thus indistinguishable with respect to all persons, how can there be both its apprehension and non-apprehension? To this he says: "Just as," and so forth—"Just as this [sound], even while being produced, is not perceived by everyone, because it occurs for all [persons] according to the distinctions of direction, place, and so on. (2205)
In the same way, the sound whose refinement (*saṃskṛti*) is produced by sounds situated near it is heard by that [person] alone, and not at all by those situated at a distance.
(2206) Now, how is it determined that the refinement of the object arises from the winds?
But it is not the case that [the sound] is merely the object; thus he says: "Because the production of sound has been refuted," and so forth.
Since [sound] cannot otherwise be accounted for, the arising of a specific refinement (saṃskṛti) from the articulated sounds (dhvani) is determined. // 2207 //
Since the all-pervasiveness and unity of sound are established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), there is no production of sound;
therefore, it is understood by implication that the production of a refinement (*saṃskāra*) arises from the articulated sounds (*dhvani*), but not the production of the sound itself.
But surely, as in the case of the seed and the sprout, the fact that words are the effects of sound is established by their occurring only when that [sound] exists (*tadbhāvabhāvitayā*).

Just as the sprouts and so forth are recognized to be the effects of seeds and the like because they are perceived only when those exist, so too words are perceived only when sound exists; why then should they not be its effects? For the designation of "effect" is based solely on this much. To this, he says: "by their occurring only when that exists," and so forth.

And in this case, the fact that [the cognition] arises when that [sound] exists is intended to be understood as indicating the existence of a capacity, just like the capacity of the auditory organ; for it is in the intellect that [the sound] is withdrawn.

For just as there is the perception of sound when the auditory organ exists, yet one does not infer from that fact of its arising when that exists a power of the auditory organ to *produce* sound, but rather a power of *perceiving* it; so too here, the fact that [the cognition] arises when those [articulations] exist would indicate merely the existence of a capacity regarding the articulations, but not a capacity to *generate* them. The point is that its connection is with capacity in general, and not with a specific kind of capacity.
Therefore, it has been demonstrated that this [reason] is inconclusive when a specific capacity is to be proven.

To the question, "How then is the specific capacity of the latent impression (saṃskāra) understood? he says: "For the intellect is withdrawn therein," because eternity is established by means of recognition (pratyabhijñā).

The meaning is this: by the principle of "inexplicability otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), the author of the Commentary has withdrawn the intellect from that specific latent impression (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*), but he does not infer the power of a latent impression merely from the fact that [the cognition] occurs when that [impression] exists.

(2208) Regarding what was stated concerning the position of dual impressions—that "the defects mentioned for each individually would apply to both being impressed"—he says here: "But in the case of the two-fold impression theory, those two defects are indeed futile."

But regarding the position that there are two types of *saṃskāra*, the two faults [previously mentioned] are indeed in vain; for since either one would be deficient, the sound would not be perceived by everyone.
The two faults which were previously stated for both positions are thus useless—meaningless.
He asks "How? and replies with "By which," etc.;
"by which" means "because."
Because of the deficiency of either the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotrasaṃskāra*) or the refinement of the object (*arthasaṃskāra*),
sound is not perceived;
for instance, even when there is a refinement of the sound, a deaf person does not grasp the sound due to the deficiency of the refinement of the auditory organ.
Even for one who is not deaf, there is non-perception of sound due to its non-manifestation;
the reading "the statement regarding the two defects is false" exists in some places,
and that is easily understood.
But surely, if sound is omnipresent, how is it that its multiplicity is perceived through spatial division, as in the case of a jar or similar objects?
For since it exists everywhere, it would be logical for it to be perceived everywhere in an undivided form.
Furthermore, for that which is omnipresent, distinctions such as being distant or near are not logical;
nor can it come from any particular location, because it abides everywhere;
nor is it logical for that which is eternal to possess distinctions of intrinsic nature such as being long, short, slow, or more or least intense.
Furthermore, a difference in time is not tenable;

therefore, because it is perceived as distinct through differences in place, time, and intrinsic nature, sound is established as being diverse and impermanent—like soldiers and so forth. Thus, how can it be said: "Since the production of sound has been refuted, its manifestation must otherwise be impossible; therefore, its birth from specific refinements [of the organ] due to articulated sounds (dhvanis) is determined"?
To this, he says: "In water and so forth," etc.;
just as even a single sun is seen as having many forms in water and other such media.
And since there is no difference in this [single object] simultaneously, let it be understood that the same applies to sound as well.
By this, I demonstrate the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason "being perceived in different locations."

[Objection: But surely, in the case of the sun, there exists a cause for the delusion of multiplicity in the form of the diversity of substrates such as water; however, here [in the case of sound], no cause for error is found, since the reason (hetu) is intended to be qualified by the condition "when no cause of error exists. Therefore, how can the reason be subject to deviation? To this he says: "Because it depends on the manifesting sounds" (*vyañjakadhvanyadhīnatvāt*). Because it depends on the manifesting sounds, it is perceived in that specific location; and yet, the sounds do not have the capacity to pervade the sky without interruption. // 2211 //
Because of this very nature of being interrupted, that [sound] is not perceived as all-pervading;
since sounds occupy different locations, the hearing of them is obstructed there.
Furthermore, because the intervening spaces are not filled, a break is perceived.
And because they occupy only a small portion [of space], there arises the notion that sound is also non-pervasive.
Due to their possession of motion and velocity, from whichever direction those [ear-cavities] come,
from that very direction the hearer perceives the sound as if it were approaching.
In this case as well, it is the same: the difference between the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*) is the cause of the illusion;
for the apprehension of the word depends upon the manifesting sounds—this is the remainder of the sentence.
"In that place" means in the place of the sound.
"That" refers to it.

Just as sound, such as a manifesting noise (*dhvani*), becomes the cause of the illusion of interruption and so forth regarding a word, [the author] says "and not... and so on, applying this principle,
beginning with the words "asau" (this).
"Sound" means "auditory perception"— the word "of sound" is to be understood as the ellipsis;
"therein" means in the location of space (ākāśa).
The state of having the internal space filled— this must be understood as being "by means of sounds" (dhvanibhiḥ);
and "of these" refers to those sounds.
They are called "sounds" (dhvanis) because they move toward [the object].
But is it not the case that even for the sun, which is a single entity, its perception as spatially divided is unestablished?
For instance, by means of the eye, distinct and separate reflections of the sun and so forth are perceived in each individual vessel,
but not the sun itself.

Anticipating the objection of an opponent who thinks, "But for you, who do not accept the reflection as a distinct entity, we see no cause whatsoever for the perception of multiple reflections," he says "He says," and so forth: "For what reason does [the reflection] appear separately in each vessel?"
"Different reflections are perceived simultaneously," so says the opponent.
*yugapat-tayā* means "simultaneously.
To this he states the following reply: "In this regard we say," and so forth.
Here we say that when the solar light, shining in the water, causes the visual light to proceed in the opposite direction [to its flow], || 2216 ||

The visual light, having its flow reversed by the solar light situated in the region of the clouds—which possesses the property of flowing downward—perceives the Sun, Āditya, as being situated in its own location;
since the Sun’s form is divided in manifold ways according to the vessel [of perception], how then can there be any plurality in Him?

(2217) The visual light, being driven back against its current by the solar light located in the region of the clouds and characterized by a downward-flowing nature, perceives the Sun, Āditya, as residing in His own place.

"Just as the vessel"—meaning, as long as it is the vessel, it appears as having a distinct form; therefore, how could there be multiplicity for this [consciousness]? It is not so, because the visual function is distinct; such is the sense.
Showing that it is precisely due to the functioning of the visual faculty that even what is non-different is perceived as if it were different, he says "īṣat" and so forth.
Just as when the eye is slightly closed by a finger,
even a single object is perceived as distinct due to the differentiation of the visual function, so it is for us.
(2218) "Slightly"— meaning just a little.
When the eye is pressed with a finger and closed, even a single object appears as many and distinct;
why is this? Because the functioning of the visual faculty is divided.
In the same way, for us, even a single word will be perceived as distinct; thus, there is no fault.
"But others," however,
means that others, desiring the emergence of a reflection, raise an objection here.
If that very [object] were perceived, why is it not seen above? Why, in wells and the like, is there no perception [of it] below the reflection?
And how could one facing east, while looking at a mirror, become one facing west? (2219–2220)

Thinking that the argument—"just as even the single sun is seen as having a manifold nature in water and other media"—is unproven because it is cited as a case where the reason deviates from its intended object, those who maintain that the reflection is a distinct entity raise this objection:
"If it is the very sun itself that is being seen, and not a reflection, then why is it not seen above?
For its perception would be such [as it actually is] only if it were grasping the form of the sun as situated in its own location."
Not otherwise;
for if it were otherwise, there would be an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, how could the sun and other objects situated far below in wells and such places be perceived?
If a reflection were not produced there,
then the sun and so forth would not be situated there in that manner; moreover, how could one facing east, while looking into a mirror, become facing west?
For at that time, his face is not seen to have turned toward his back. 2219–2220.
He provides the rebuttal with the verse beginning "apsūrya" (the sun in water), etc.:

"For those who see the sun in water, the eye always functions in two ways: one part directed upwards and the other downwards; therein, that which is illuminated by the upward rays [perceives the sun]. (2221)
Because the locus [of the eye] is not straight, the self does not reach the sun;
rather, though the sun is reached through a continuous series, one perceives it by means of a downward function.
Due to its identity with that [upward-moving series], one conceives of the upward movement as if it were downward.
"Therefore, the sun is perceived as being directly below [the observer], with a space between them.
(2223) He thinks as follows: if the sense-organ, having gone outside, were to perceive the sun, then it would follow that one sees it only when situated above, and not below;
however, it is maintained that this sense-organ is the perceiver only within the body, which is governed by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), and not when it is situated above.
As it has been said: "In that very context, if the sense-organ were to go outward to perceive an object, then this [consciousness] would indeed be the perceiver within the body; such is the sequence.
Thus, indeed, is the order.
For those who see both the water and the sun in a vessel of water, the single eye of those perceivers of the sun in the water functions in two parts, one upward and one downward.

Therein, the Self (the Puruṣa) does not perceive the sun illuminated by the upward part [of the visual organ], because the substratum is not straight—that is, because the substratum of the visual organ is not then situated in a straight line. However, the sun, as presented by its own solar light through the downward function which serves as the cause, is cognized by means of the [downward] function.

For indeed, it is said that the solar light imparts its brilliance to the visual faculty (*vṛtti*), the visual faculty to the eye, and the eye to the Self; such is this successive transmission from the luminous Sun. Regarding the phrase "the upward-tending solar light," who is it that perceives that Sun situated above as if it were below—that is, as if standing beneath it?
It is the Self.
Furthermore, the sun below is not something other [than the sun above]; why? Because of its oneness—that is, because that sun is non-different from the eye, according to others.
Therefore, by the very power of the eye's functioning just described, the sun is seen with an intervening space below in wells and the like.
Furthermore, due to the difference between vessels such as water and so forth, how could there otherwise be a perception [of them] without distinction? (2221)
As it was stated previously: "One looking into a mirror facing the east," and so forth.
Regarding this, he says: "In this way," and so forth.

Thus, perceiving the face as it is presented by the inward-turned function [of the sense organ] through its previously described mode of operation, one understands it to be "inward" due to delusion. || 2224 ||

It is said that first the visual rays go out, taking the face with them, as far as the location of the mirror and so forth; this is called the forward movement (*prāṅ-vṛtti*). Then, struck by the mirror and other such surfaces, they turn back and return to one's own face exactly as it is situated; this is the backward movement (*pratyag-vṛtti*).

In this regard, the forward-directed activity (prāṅmukhī vṛttiḥ) offers itself to the inward-directed activity (pratyagvṛttiḥ), and the inward-directed activity [offers itself] to the Self (ātman). Thereupon, the Self, perceiving that which is offered by the inward-directed activity, mistakenly thinks, "I shall go toward the face in an inward direction.
The point is that the very diversity of the visual activity is the seed of this delusion.
Having accepted the arising of a reflection as a solution, he says: "And even if it exists in multiple locations," and so forth.
Even though the reflection exists in many places, because it is apprehended by a single cognition, its multiplicity does not exist at all. (2225)
Even though the reflection is a distinct entity, there is no multiplicity among those reflections;
why?
Because they are accessible to a single cognition—that is, because they are delimited by a single cognition.
Likewise, because sound is apprehended by a single cognition, its unity is established. [Objection:
But why should there not be multiplicity for that which is perceived in different locations? [Reply: It shall not be so.

[Objection: But how can that distinctness which is established by the fact of being perceived in different locations be sublated by a single cognition? To this he says: "By difference of location," etc.
This distinctness [established] by difference of location is inferential; however, the cognition "it is that very same [object]" is perceptual, and as such, it is the sublater. || 2226 ||
The sense is that [it is] a sublater because direct perception is the eldest among all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Demonstrating that [the word] lacks validity because its being perceived as distinct due to differences in place and time is fallacious, he says: "By turn," and so forth.
Just as Devadatta, even while traveling through different locations one after another, would not be divided [into multiple persons], so too the word is not divided. // 2227 //
Likewise, it should be understood that the word does not differ in terms of place and time.
Thus, by way of deviation regarding place, the deviation of both has been stated;
now, by way of deviation regarding the difference in time, he states the deviation of both perceptions based on the difference in place and time,
beginning with the words "jñātaikatve" (when unity is known).

Just as a single object, once its unity is known, when seen again and again, is not different despite the difference in time, so too is sound not different despite the difference in location. (2228) One for whom unity is known through recognition is "one whose unity is known."
"Not by way of place" is an elliptical expression; likewise, [the entity] is not distinct even by way of time.
Since there is no contradiction, the demonstration of deviation in other cases is achieved by means of the deviation in a single instance.

With the words beginning "paryāyāt" (by way of succession), he raises the objection that the example is dissimilar: "If there is no contradiction by way of succession, let it be seen that [there is none] even by way of pervasiveness; for whatever property is established as being observed must be accepted by all. (2229)

For instance: although Devadatta is perceived at different places and times, there is no difference [in his identity]; in that case, "succession" (paryāya) serves as the cause of non-contradiction. But in the case of sound, there is nothing of the sort; therefore, there is a disparity between the example and the subject of the illustration.
To this, he states the cause of non-contradiction even here: "It should be seen also because of its all-pervasiveness"—the connection being that there is "non-contradiction."
With the word "also" (*api*), he points back to what was stated previously: "because the intervals between sounds have not been filled.
He asks, "Why is pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) accepted? and replies: "For the sake of establishing what is observed" (*dṛṣṭasiddhyai hi*).

That property which is appropriate for the purpose of establishing the perception of a single sound across distinct directions and locations is accepted precisely because it cannot be explained otherwise.

And in this regard, since the apprehension of sound at all times and in all places would not be established without its being eternal and omnipresent, its eternity and omnipresence are established through the impossibility of any other explanation (*anyathānupapatti*).
Then, demonstrating that even the property of being perceived through a difference in nature (*svabhāvabheda*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicāritā*), he says: "Just as in a large [space]," and so forth.

Just as the cognition of "greatness" arises in the sky when there is great earth, or the cognition of "smallness" when it is small, so too does the notion [of space] arise with respect to that which is absolutely uncreated.
Therefore, it is only here, in the application of words based on external adjuncts, that there is a delusion of the intellect.
Furthermore, coarseness and subtlety are not perceived as residing in the sound;
rather, that conceptualization of largeness and smallness [is actually] the intensity and dullness of the cognition.
And this [cognition] indeed occurs even when [an object] is illuminated by a great light, just as it does with a cloth.

When manifested weakly, [the sound] is always likewise weak even in the case of a jar and so forth; thus it is established that all properties such as length and so on belong to the *dhvani* (sound-current).

Herein lies the intended meaning: if the distinctions such as intensity (*tīvra*) and weakness (*manda*) residing in the word-sound (*śabda*) are adduced as the reason (*hetu*), then the reason is not proven (*asiddha*).
For how could one who maintains that sound is eternal assert that it possesses distinct intrinsic natures (svabhāva-bheda) based on external conditions?

If, on the other hand, it is argued that the cognition directed toward it— characterized by forms such as intense or faint— is the cause [of its perceived diversity], since such a cognition is not possible without a difference in intrinsic nature,
then the reason [adduced] is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Just as when a great mass of earth has been dug out, there arises in the sky—that is, in space—a cognition of its largeness and so forth based upon that [earth], even though largeness and such qualities do not exist in space by its own nature; likewise, in the case of sound—which is absolutely uncreated (akṛtrima)—this difference in cognition will arise due to the difference in the manifesting sounds (dhvani), even without any such difference in its own intrinsic nature.
He says this very thing in the passage beginning with "Therefore, in this case, thus," etc.
Now, if it is asked: "How is it known that this [difference] is due to an external condition (upādhi) and not due to the [sound] itself? he replies with the passage beginning with "And not," etc.

By this he says the following: one is deluded by superimposing the very intensity and dullness residing in the cognition onto the sound; however, there is no possibility of grossness and so forth existing in the sound itself, because its oneness is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

Furthermore, one might argue: "If such a difference in the nature of the object did not exist, how could it exist even for the cognition? To this he replies: "And that [cognition] is sharp," and so forth.

For just as in the case of a jar and other objects, even though there is no difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), a distinction in the cognition—such as clarity or dullness—occurs due to a distinction in the illumination; so too, in the case of sound, a distinction such as long and so forth will arise from a distinction in the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), even though there is no inherent difference in its own nature. Thus, there is no fault.
