Furthermore, demonstrating that the thesis of the impermanence of sound is contradicted by the fact that the expressive capacity of sound would otherwise be inexplicable, he says: "And not [is there] a connection with an unperceived object," and so forth.
A word does not become expressive unless its relationship with its object has been perceived; if it were otherwise, even a completely unprecedented word would manifest its own meaning.

This is an instance of presumption (arthāpatti) preceded by another presumption; for the capacity of a word to denote is established through the fact that verbal cognition would otherwise be inexplicable, and that very capacity is itself inexplicable without the eternity of the word—thus, this is a presumption based upon a prior presumption.
He explains this very point in detail: a word does not become expressive by its mere existence alone if its relationship [with its meaning] has not been grasped;

for if that were the case—if even a word whose relationship with its object has never been perceived were expressive—then even a word such as "cow," which is unprecedented and has never before been heard by inhabitants of the Coconut Island (Nālikera-dvīpa), would manifest its own meaning.

[Objection: But surely, since there is no dispute here among anyone, this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For no one accepts that a word whose relationship [to its meaning] is unknown is expressive;
however, how is it that this [word] is shown by this [proponent] to have a known relationship, given that it is eternal? To this, he says: "The perception of the relationship," and so forth.
Furthermore, the perception of a relationship is not possible for that which is impermanent;
if the establishment of the knowledge of a relationship is to occur, its persistence over time is certain.
Having placed both the word and the object before oneself, their relationship is established, and once established, it would be known at a later time.
However, because sound perishes as soon as it is uttered, this [position] is untenable; thus he says: "It is not possible for that which is impermanent.
Now, if it were to persist for that duration, then alas, its persistence at a later time would also be unavoidable, since there is no contradiction [in its continuing].
As it has been said: "Who will destroy this [entity] later, which remains stable for that duration? (2235).
Furthermore, it might be argued that it persists until the time of its connection [with a cause], and thereafter perishes of its own accord; to this he says: "In another," and so forth.
When the relationship [between word and object] is known in one case, another cannot be the communicator;
for when the relationship is known in the word "cow," the word "horse" is not its denoter.
(2236) "In another"—that which exists at the time of the convention.
The remainder is easily understood.
Now, [the author] anticipates the opponent's objection with the word "atha" (now/if).
Now, if it were the case that even another [person] could be an awakener by their very nature, then, in the absence of a restrictive cause, there would be no certainty as to who that person might be.
(2237) "Now, if it were the case that even another... refers to this.
If it is argued that a word existing at the time of application would be denotative by its very nature, just like a word existing at the time of convention, that is incorrect;
for without a basis, there can be no certainty that "this word is the denotator of this object. (2237)

But how can it be said that there is no certainty, when that very thing from which the cognition of an object arises is clearly ascertained by its own nature to be the indicator of that object? To this he says: "Since," and so forth.
"Since the cognition [arises] from this"—only when such a conventional usage is established might this be possible for listeners; however, it is not tenable for speakers. (2238)
It is true that for the listeners, this certainty may arise— that "this [word] conveys this meaning"— because the cognition of the object arises for them from it;
however, for the speakers, this is difficult to attain, for they do not themselves apprehend the meaning from that word, as they employ the word solely for the purpose of communicating to others.
How, then, can a certainty be possible for speakers?
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "Without having known," and so forth.
"Without knowing it, how could he intend to utter that sound at the very beginning?
If he knows it, then it must necessarily have been apprehended by him previously.

(2239) Thus, showing that this fault applies to the position of non-cognition, and that even in the position of cognition, its stability follows by necessity because it was certainly known previously, he says: "If he knows it," and so forth.

[Objection: But surely, just as light such as that of a lamp illuminates an object even though it is new, so too will a word convey its meaning. [Response: He says: "Because light is subordinate to perception";
because light is subordinate to perception, it is an illuminator despite its novelty.
And because similarity is not perceived, it is non-expressive even by way of that [similarity].
(Verse 2240) "Being a subsidiary to perception" means being a constituent part (*aṅga*) within perception;

by means of the refinement of its object or the refinement of the sense faculty, it attains the status of a constituent in perceptual cognition and thus becomes an illuminator, even if it is something newly arisen.
Because sound directly conveys supersensuous objects, it is not a factor of perception; therefore, there is a disparity [between the two].

Alternatively—that which is a factor of perception illuminates its object even without depending on a thorough knowledge of its relationship, as is the case with the eye and light, both of which are factors of perception.
Therefore, although it reveals even a novel [word], the word is not a factor in perception because its object is beyond the senses; this is the point of difference.
Now, one might argue that even a novel word will function as a signifier by following its similarity to a previous one; to this he says: "Because similarity is not perceived," and so forth.
For it is not logical that there be denotative capacity by way of similarity when that similarity is not perceived, because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, setting aside for a moment the perception of similarity, he says "Of which one... and so forth, demonstrating that similarity itself is impossible.

And on the basis of similarity to which single [word] could another be conceived as its denoter, when all preceding words are equal in that their connection [with the meaning] has never been perceived?
If it is argued that the one previously seen was meaningful, how could it have such a long duration [of existence]?
For that which is not perceived two or three times is not understood to possess meaning.

(2242) Indeed, once a single expressive word is established as meaningful, it might be assumed that another is likewise so because of its similarity to the first; however, that is not possible, since all words are already perceived as being connected with their respective meanings. Furthermore, one might argue: "That which was previously observed at the time of the convention is indeed meaningful, while the others will possess meaning through similarity. To this, he says: "From where does such a duration of time for that [word] come?"
Regarding that previously perceived word: how could it persist for so many moments, given that it perishes as soon as it is uttered?
If it is argued, "Even if it indeed perishes as soon as it is uttered, why should it not still possess meaning? [the author] says: "Twice, thrice," and so forth;
for the cognition of the relationship between a word and its meaning arises from repeated observation.

Now, if it is argued that [the word] becomes meaningful only when there is no apprehension of another word of the same class (*sajātīya*), he says that this is incorrect: "For those who have not perceived other words," and so forth.

It is a marvel that at that time, for those who have not previously perceived other words, this very [word] is meaningless, yet for others who have heard it, it becomes meaningful. For indeed, for those perceivers to whom another word is unfamiliar, it does not convey meaning at the time of hearing.

Since similarity, which is the basis for differentiation, is absent at that time, it is extraordinary to claim that the very same word— once its other meanings have been understood by those same perceivers— is the conveyor of meaning [for a new one];
for how indeed could action and non-action coexist in a single entity, being mutually contradictory?
Regarding the phrase "of those who have heard other [scriptures]": those cognizers whose hearing (*śruti*) has as its object words belonging to a different class are so described.

Thus, having first established the eternity of the word by the fact that its status as a signifier would otherwise be impossible, he now establishes it by the fact that the creation of a relationship [between word and meaning] would otherwise be impossible, saying: "First, without uttering the word... and so forth.
"First, the creation of a relationship is not possible without uttering the word;
nor is there any purpose for a relationship with a word that has perished once uttered. (2244)

Because it has perished due to its lack of connection, the first [utterance] is indeed useless; how could the subsequent one, which has not yet established a connection, be understood as having meaning? (2245) First there is the utterance, then the establishment of the connection, and then linguistic usage; how could such a sequence of usage occur for that which perishes as soon as it is uttered and thus lacks sequence?

Not only is it impossible to establish a connection with what has perished, nor is there any purpose served by it, because it does not persist through the time of linguistic usage and because a convention exists for the sake of such usage; he concludes this with the words "by that," and so forth.

That which lacks a relationship is "unrelated" (*asambandha*). Because of that [lack of relationship] and because it has perished, first of all, the word existing at the time of the convention is meaningless.
To the objection that "then the word existing at the time of usage will be meaningful," he says: "The latter," and so forth (verse 2244).

If, then, the sequential utterance and so forth of that which is non-sequential are untenable, let them occur simultaneously; thus he says: "The utterance of words," and so forth—[referring to] the worldly activities involving the utterance of words and the establishment of their relationships.
Since actions possess the nature of succession, who could ever perform them simultaneously?

(2246) The utterance of a word, the establishment of its relationship [with its meaning], and worldly linguistic usage—these three actions are by their very nature successive; they cannot be performed simultaneously.
And in the absence of simultaneity, the establishment of the relationship is untenable.
If one were to wait for a sequence [of cognitions], it would follow that the word is admitted to persist through a period of time;
"of those differentiated by place, time, and so forth" is the conclusion.
Because men who are separated by place, time, and other factors do not hear other words prior [to the convention], even a single word with an artificial relationship is not established.
Even when its relationship is being explained, this same objection would apply.
For there is no possibility of narration regarding things that have perished, those that are non-existent, or those in the present;
by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), states such as infancy, childhood, and so forth are included.
"Previously" (*pūrvam*)—means... [text continues].
This should be connected with the phrase "because another word is heard.
Regarding the words "perished," etc.:
"perished" means past; "non-existent" means future. Precisely because these two do not exist, it is impossible for there to be a communication of a relationship between them.
Even when it is present and being articulated, since it perishes immediately thereafter, how could there be such a duration of time? 2247–2248.
He demonstrates this very point with the verse beginning "arthavān" and so forth: "Which word is meaningful? Let it be stated whether it belongs to the hearer or the speaker;
for when a word has been previously heard, that [speaker] is not able to produce it. (2249)

First of all, he does not utter a meaningful [word]; nor would he utter something similar [to a meaningful word], for a word that is merely similar to a meaningful one is not applicable to the listener in that context.
Furthermore, because there is no apprehension of a meaningful [word], it is not itself meaningful.
At the time when the speaker becomes a listener, this very same consequence would follow.
For a speaker is not able to communicate to a listener a word previously heard, because that [word] has already ceased;
nor could he communicate as meaningful that which he is currently propounding.

Since no prior relationship has been established with that [word], this much might be conceivable—that it might express something similar—but even that is not possible; thus he says: "not similar to a meaningful word," and so forth.
For similarity with anything is not intended here; rather, it is with something that possesses meaning (*arthavat*). And that is untenable:

for if some word possessing meaning had been perceived by the listener previously, then similarity with it would be possible. However, since at the time of the prior convention there was no apprehension of anything possessing meaning, this [similarity] is not logical.
To the objection that "that which is being uttered will then be the one possessing meaning," he says: "And not that," and so forth.
And this [word], when being uttered, does not possess a meaning, because its relationship [to that meaning] has not been previously established;

this was stated by the passage beginning with "by the speaker" (*vaktuḥ*). Just as the speaker himself becomes a listener in turn, so too for him all these faults arise—the consequence that he does not utter a word possessing a meaning, and so forth.
By this, it is shown that for all speakers whatsoever, no word at all can possibly possess a meaning.
Therefore, he concludes:
"For this reason, the relationship between word and meaning must be accepted as indeed eternal; it is not logical for it to be conventional, because that is impossible in every respect. (2252)
With the words "not from itself" and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's prima facie argument:

"The expressive power of the signified and the signifier does not exist inherently; if there were mutual cognition between them for people, it would be due to convention, like the winking of an eye. (2253)
The expressive power of the signified and the signifier is not at all inherent to them respectively;
if so, how does cognition arise from a word? To this he says: "Cognition [arises] from convention," and so forth.

For whatever has a causal status that depends upon a convention regarding something, that [status] is not inherent to it, as in the case of the comprehension of a wink of the eye; and since the causal status of a word regarding comprehension depends upon convention, there is the perception of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
With the verse beginning "samaya" (2253), he refutes the detailed argument previously stated regarding the contradiction of the thesis of impermanence.
Is the convention (samaya) made for each individual person, or for each specific utterance, or was it established once at the beginning of the world by some single being?
Or does the relationship [between word and meaning] differ for each instance, or is it one and the same?
If [the word] were one, it could not be something produced; if it were different [in each instance], there would be a cognition of difference.

(2255) Regarding the convention that "this is its name," there are three alternatives: it might be established for the sake of communication either for each individual person, or for each individual utterance, or for each individual performance; or else, at the beginning of the world—at the time of the world's creation—it might be created once and for all, effortlessly, by some creator such as Īśvara. These are the three options.

Furthermore, if a relation between word and meaning were established, it would either be distinct for each individual being— or else, according to the second alternative, it would be one and the same;
in the latter case, like a universal (*jāti*), because it would follow across differences of place and time, it could not be something produced (*kṛtaka*).
The meaning is that it would necessarily be eternal.

Alternatively, if [the word] had a distinct intrinsic nature for each individual being, then a cognition of difference would arise for each being, because the difference in cognitions is based upon the difference in the objects of knowledge; yet, even when words such as "cow" are employed a hundred times, no cognition of difference occurs among those engaged in linguistic usage, since their usage proceeds precisely through the determination of non-difference.

Furthermore— [the author] says "of the cognitions of the speaker and the hearer" (vaktṛśrotṛdhiyoḥ), demonstrating that if the relation were distinct for each sentient being, there would necessarily be a cognition of difference [regarding that relation], and consequently, the cessation of worldly transaction (vyavahāra) would follow.

Because of the difference between the cognitions of the speaker and the listener, linguistic usage becomes impaired; for the relationship [of the word] in the speaker's mind is one thing, while that in the listener's mind is another.
(2256) "Because of the difference" means:
The phrase "of the object" (viṣayasya) is necessarily implied;

therefore, the meaning is as follows: since there is a difference between the objects that are the contents of the cognitions of the speaker and the listener, linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) would not occur through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of them as being a single object.
To the question "How so?", he says: "For [the object] of the speaker is other... and so forth.
Regarding what was stated— that the convention (samaya) pertains either to each individual person—
the author states the refutation here: "Of the hearer and the maker," and so forth.
Regarding the relationship between the speaker and the listener, whom can the speaker address?
For that which was previously perceived by him, he does not establish it for the listener; and that which he creates as something new has never before been established as a means of communication.
If it is argued that this is equally applicable to jars and the like, we say no, because of the well-established nature of the universal (sāmānya).

For although an individual whose causal capacity has been ascertained cannot be produced [anew], nor is its capacity for the effect determined in the case of one that is not being produced. (2258–2259)

Nevertheless, the capacity for pronunciation and so forth is established through the form (ākṛti), and that [form] has no beginning; therefore, the relationship [between word and meaning] is what possesses a beginning.
If it is further admitted that even for that [relationship] there is an eternal universal (sāmānya).
Nevertheless, our position is established; however, the possibility of two forms [of the relation] does not exist.
For the relation is indeed a capacity (*śakti*), and no difference in this [capacity] is perceived.
Since it is to be inferred from its effects, it conforms to the difference of those [effects]. (2261–2262)
And the postulation of the existence of a capacity is based on the impossibility of [the effect] occurring otherwise;
furthermore, when a purpose is accomplished by one [capacity], it is not desired to postulate many.
[Therefore,] he does not produce that for the listener.
Because that [object] has perished,
it does not establish what has been seen,
since it was not previously seen.
Regarding the phrase "even in the case of a jar and so forth," he raises the objection that the refutation is inconclusive by pointing out an over-extension of the argument:

the same undesirable consequence applies even to a jar and so forth; for instance, a jar seen to be capable of causal efficiency cannot be produced, because it has already been produced and then perished.
Furthermore, that which is produced now is not observed to be capable of causal efficiency because it has not yet been fully realized;
to this, he replies: "Not so, because of the established nature of the universal" (*na sāmānyaprasiddhitaḥ*), wherein "not so" (*na*) is the rejection of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).
Why?
Because the universal has been established;
the meaning is that its capacity is proven by means of that [universal].
Clarifying this very point, he says: "Even though," and so forth.

Even if a particular jar (*ghaṭavyakti*) whose capacity for fetching water and other such functions has been observed cannot be produced—because it has already been completed and then perished—even that which is present at this moment, its capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) has not yet been ascertained.

Nevertheless, how is it that the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) of every individual instance is established solely by means of the form (*ākṛti*]? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth;
"of that" refers to...
In some places, the reading is "and its beginning is not [found]" regarding the form (ākṛti);
this is its meaning: there is no beginning for that capacity for fetching water and so forth, because the form is eternal.

And because that [relation] is absolutely non-different from its substratum, as it has been said: "The distinctness of genus and so forth from the individual is not established; for us, even the relation [of denotation] must be beginningless by way of the form (*ākṛti*). If it is argued that this is so, he says "But the relation... and so forth, stating that this is incorrect.

Furthermore—if you also accept that the relation between word and meaning possesses an eternal universal (*nitya-sāmānya*), even so, our position that there exists an eternal entity is established; however, the word itself, which is the subject under discussion, remains unestablished. To this, he says: "But the occurrence of two forms is not possible.
There are two forms: the relation and its universal.
Only a single form is possible, but not a universal, because a universal must reside in multiple individuals, whereas a relation is unitary;
as to how the relation can be unitary, he says: "For it is indeed a power," and so forth.
There is no relation distinct from the powers;
if this is indeed the case, what follows? He says: "And difference," etc.—"difference" means non-identity.

He states the reason why it is not perceived: "For that," he says, "is always to be inferred from its effects," as it has been stated: "The potencies of all entities are established through the presumption based on their effects."

Then it follows that distinction in effect— meaning that without observing a distinction in effects, it is impossible to know a distinction in powers for the purpose of making known the distinction residing in the self— and yet,
in this case, there is no distinction in effect.

For instance—the effect of that [word] is its very cognition, and that [cognition] must have either the word as its object or the meaning as its object. It cannot be the former, because the word is always recognized as being the same; nor can it be the latter, for even when the word "cow" (*go*) and others are uttered a hundred times, no different kind of cognition arises.
He states the reinforcement: "Otherwise," and so forth.
For the capacity of the signifier and the signified is postulated precisely because the cognition of the meaning would otherwise be impossible;
and since the intended object is established by a single capacity alone, the postulation of multiple capacities is useless.
Nor can a difference in powers be inferred on the grounds of "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti), because that [reason] is capable of proving only the existence of power in general.

For this reason as well, the production of the relationship is untenable; therefore, demonstrating that the relationship is indeed eternal, he says: "And at the time of explaining the relationship," and so forth.
When a word such as "cow" is uttered, some understand the object through the cognition of the relationship, while others do not. (2264)
In that regard, if the relation did not exist, no one would comprehend any meaning;
yet if it did exist, there would be universal comprehension, which is not the case because some people lack its apprehension.

For instance, when it is said, "This cow must not be touched with the foot," some persons, having first ascertained the relationship between the signifier and the signified, understand the meaning only by means of that preceding relationship.
Others, however, whose connection [with their objects] is unknown, cognize only the word's own form and not its meaning;
in that case, if the connection were not a real entity, then every person— even one experienced in linguistic usage— would not determine the meaning,
for it is not logical that the existence and non-existence of a single thing should be mutually contradictory.
Therefore, the relationship is indeed eternally established.

Now, anticipating the objection— "If the relationship is eternally established, why is there not a comprehension of meaning for everyone at all times?"— the author provides a detailed refutation, saying "In its existence," etc., and with the word "not" (*na*), he averts that undesirable consequence.
Why?
Because it is not apprehended by some.
[The opponent asks: "Even if it is not perceived, why should it not produce its own effect?

For seeds and the like do not abandon their own function simply because they are situated within a hole in the ground or a pit. To this, [the author] replies: "Because it is a cognizer," and so forth.
For a signifier requires knowledge of its own nature;
therefore, even though it exists, it does not manifest [the object] if it is not apprehended.

(2266) Indeed, the property of a signifier is one thing, while that of a producer is another. A word, like smoke, is a signifier of an object, but unlike a seed and so forth, it is not a producer; thus there is no fault.
But surely, existence and non-existence are improper for a single thing because they are mutually contradictory; likewise, apprehension and non-apprehension would also be so.
If there is no contradiction between these two, then why this aversion toward existence and non-existence? To this, he says: "Of that which exists," and so forth.
Furthermore, it is observed that an existing object is sometimes not apprehended;
however, the existence of something absolutely non-existent cannot be established for anyone.
Moreover, the states of being existent and non-existent are contradictory and cannot coexist in a single entity.
Furthermore, the contradiction between being known and being unknown is not equal [to that of existence and non-existence].
For knowledge resides in a person; thus, due to the difference between persons, it is not contradictory.
And the knowledge residing in one person is not precluded by that [knowledge] belonging to another person.

The summary of the meaning is as follows: for the superimposition of mutually contradictory properties upon a single substratum (*dharmin*) is what constitutes a contradiction, but not when they reside in different substrata. Since apprehension and non-apprehension have different substrata due to the difference in persons [who experience them], they are not contradictory; however, existence and non-existence are not [non-contradictory] in this way, because they are intended to have a single substratum.

But surely, even on the view that there is apprehension and non-apprehension, by implication, existence and non-existence—which are mutually contradictory—must likewise occur within a single substratum;
for it is so: apprehension and non-apprehension are pervaded by the existence and non-existence of the object, since those two are dependent upon them.

Otherwise, one must state the reason why, between two persons standing in a location equally accessible, only one sees [an object] and not the other; having raised this doubt, he says: "The white [object] situated near both the blind and the non-blind is not perceived by the blind, yet it is perceived by the others; its existence or non-existence does not depend upon them. (2270)

For just as when a form is situated near both a blind person and one with unimpaired vision, only the latter perceives it while the former does not, yet for them there is neither existence nor non-existence of that white form; so it is with the relation as well.
To dispel the inquiry as to what the cause of this is, he states the justification: "Of capacity and incapacity," and so forth.
"Because of the difference between the capacity and incapacity of men, there is no contradiction in that case;

for indeed, there is no other cause for the non-perception [of an object] here than a connection [with a person]. He explains this as follows: "The mere existence of an object is not the cause of its perception; what then? It is the capacity residing in the person. Therefore, even when an object exists, its non-apprehension by a certain person due to a lack of capacity is not contradictory; thus, non-apprehension is not pervaded by the non-existence of the object."

If this were so, then even in the absence of a relationship, the apprehension or non-apprehension of an object would occur for persons due to the difference between their capacity and incapacity; thus, everything remains the same. To this he says: "For there is no other," and so forth.
The meaning is that the cognition of an object is preceded by the apprehension of the relationship;
the word "other" refers to the cause [of that cognition].
The genitive case here in "of perception" (darśanasya) is used in relation to the phrase "is the cause of the cognition of the word's meaning."
The ablative case ending in "sambandhāt" (from connection) here signifies dependence on another,
in this context of linguistic usage regarding words and their meanings.

Others, however, explain it as follows, describing it as a justification for the statement "there is no contradiction therein" due to the difference between the capacity and incapacity of men: "from connection" means from the capacity of the person;
"herein" refers to the white [substance].
Concluding the application of the example, he says: "In this very way," and so forth.
In this very way, the perception of conventional usage is equal to [the case of] the sense faculties.
Those who possess [this knowledge] understand the meaning from it, whereas others do not, like the blind.
"Vyavahāra" (conventional usage) is that by which one acts; it is the relationship between word and meaning.
Its "upalambhana" (apprehension) is its thorough comprehension.
That [consciousness] is dependent upon the sense-faculties;
for it is only those who possess a sense-faculty that perceive an object.
However, those who do not possess it do not perceive the object even when the object is present;
likewise, those who possess the thorough knowledge of the relationship understand the meaning from the word,
whereas those who do not possess it do not perceive it even though the relationship exists— thus, indeed, everything is the same.
It must be stated by whom this relation was first communicated to its creator. If it is argued that he communicated it to himself, no; for by that same logic, the same would apply to others as well.
If it is argued that for him it came from another, and for that other from yet another, then, since there is thus no beginning, it is shown that it is not created by anyone—at all, etc.

For all those who lack direct perception [of the relationship], the connection is established through its prior establishment; thus, there is no such thing as a beginning of the connection. (2273) That connection between word and meaning is preceded by the linguistic usage of elders, because it is a connection, just like a connection existing at the present time.
And the relation in question is the very relation that is the subject of dispute; thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

2273 Thus far, it has been demonstrated that a convention (*samaya*) is not possible for each individual person; now, responding to the claim that [the convention] pertains to each individual utterance, he says: "At each utterance," and so forth.
The production [of words] through repeated utterance is not tenable from the perspective of worldly convention;
for at the beginning of creation, no such action exists, as such a time is not admitted.
Indeed, it is maintained that the entire world has never been otherwise than it is now.

In the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), no dissolution known as ultimate reality is recognized. Alternatively, "dissolution" refers to night because all activities are withdrawn, while "day" is designated as creation because it brings forth all exertions.
Alternatively, dissolution (*pralaya*) may take the form of the destruction of a region or the destruction of a lineage;

however, we have no authoritative means of knowledge regarding a dissolution that consists in the total annihilation [of all things], because it is based on worldly convention (*vyavahāra*). (2277) Thus [it is said].
Because linguistic usage proceeds [in this way];
otherwise, linguistic usage would not occur because the relationship [between word and meaning] would not have been previously established. This concludes [the point].
Now, he states the rebuttal to what was said regarding "at the beginning of the world" and so forth: "And at the beginning of creation... and so on.
"Such" refers to that which is devoid of the relationship between word and meaning, consisting of creation and dissolution; "not such" refers to that which is otherwise.

Since there is an absence of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for that which consists of the total annihilation [of all things], how then is the conventional usage of "dissolution" (*pralaya*) and so forth established in the world? To this, he says: "There is no great dissolution," and so forth.
It is known as "ultimate" because it is understood by the world.
The intention is that while that which consists of the total annihilation [of the world] is merely imagined, it is not being refuted;
he demonstrates this very point with the words "or night," and so forth.
Then, as to why the ultimate [annihilation] is not accepted, he says: "But at the time of dissolution," and so forth.

Let it be granted that there is an ultimate dissolution (*pralaya*); nevertheless, since at that time there would be no creator such as Īśvara who possesses unimpaired impressions (*saṃskāra*) of memory, wisdom, and so forth, the establishment of a relationship [between words and their meanings] would not be tenable. Demonstrating this, he says: "And there is no one with undiminished memory," and so on; "no one with undiminished memory is the agent of creation and destruction."
A permanent entity such as Īśvara or the like, which one might suppose could establish a relationship,
is not tenable,
because such a thing has been refuted at length.
With the words "But surely," etc., he anticipates the opponent's objection:
"But surely, because the sequence is impermanent, the expressive word must be impermanent."
For a word (*pada*) is indeed accepted as the signifier, and the cognition of it depends upon sequence.

(2279) Indeed, a word is accepted as the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*), not as the *sphoṭa*; and because that [sequence] is dependent on human will, it is non-eternal. Consequently, the phonemes themselves would also result in being non-eternal, since the sequence is not distinct from the phonemes.
He asks, "How so? and says: "The word (*pada*), etc.

For instance, it is the word consisting of phonemes (*varṇa*) that is accepted as the signifier; because the cognition of a word is produced by the sequence of phonemes and not by a *sphoṭa*, and that sequence is of human origin.

He explains this very point: "The phonemes, because they are all-pervading, do not possess an inherent sequential occurrence; since sequence is an effect produced by impermanent sounds, it is therefore perishable. (2280)
Furthermore, its dependence on a person would arise from the power of his intention to speak;
consequently, the eternality of the phonemes (*varṇas*) maintained by you would be rendered fruitless.

For you Mīmāṃsakas, because the phonemes are all-pervading, there is no sequence produced by space, nor is there one produced by time, since they are eternal. Therefore, [the sequence] must be produced by the manifesting sounds (*dhvanis*).
The intended meaning is that because that [sequence] is impermanent, what is produced by it is also impermanent.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is produced by something impermanent is itself impermanent, just like a jar or similar objects; and the sequence of phonemes (*varṇakrama*) is produced by something impermanent. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

Furthermore, whatever arises by the power of a person’s intention to speak should be treated by a discerning person as being of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), just like the movement of hands, the winking of eyes, and so forth; and the sequence of phonemes arises by the power of a person’s will. This is also a reason based on essential nature.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even without a sequence, the phonemes themselves, as determined by the auditory organ, will be the conveyors of meaning; to this, he says: "And not," and so forth.
Furthermore, phonemes are not known to be expressive when devoid of sequence;
thus, it follows that the status of being a word belongs to the sequence itself. However, for those for whom the word is something distinct from the phonemes and devoid of sequence—
This postulation of the eternity of sound is meaningful only for them [the Mīmāṃsakas].
For it is not observed that phonemes alone, without a sequence, are the cause of the comprehension of meaning; therefore, a sequence must necessarily be admitted for them.
This being the case, it follows for you Mīmāṃsakas that the word-status and the expressive capacity belong to the sequence itself, and not to the phonemes in isolation.
Furthermore, because that sequence is impermanent, the expressive word would also be impermanent;
consequently, the postulation of the eternity of sound is futile.

For instance, it is the eternity of the expressive word that you seek to establish, not that of anything else; therefore, your proof for the eternity of isolated phonemes is irrelevant to the matter at hand.

Since that [phoneme] is not expressive, and since that which is expressive— namely the form of sequence— is not admitted to be eternal, every such effort is entirely fruitless. However, for those grammarians who maintain that the word called *sphoṭa*— which is partless and distinct from the phonemes— is the expressive unit, this postulation of the eternity of sound is meaningful.
Because that entity called *sphoṭa* is eternal.
Regarding this, he states the rebuttal: "First of all," and so forth—"First of all, it does not follow for us that the sequential order possesses the status of a word;
for this [order] is not observed to be an illuminator when it resides in a separate entity. (2284)

The meaning is as follows: *ānupūrva* (succession) is the nature of being successive; it does not follow that we [Buddhists] must accept that this mere succession possesses denotative power, because it is fallible (*vyabhicāritvāt*).
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "For not... and so forth, ending with "...based on another entity."
Nor is it accepted that the expressive [word] is merely preceded by the measurement of the substratum of the phonemes, such as gems and pearls; how so? He says: "This is a mere property."
"This [cognition] consists merely of the phonemes; no other entity is postulated for them.
Thus, when they are perceived in this way, the phonemes themselves would be the conveyors of meaning.
Regarding the phrase "no other entity": [it means that] there is no separate thing [apart from the phonemes].
The intention is that [the word] denotes [its object] independently;
for otherwise, there would be an ultimate distinction between the property and the property-possessor,
and that is not desired.
What, then, is the expressive [word]? He says: "In this way," and so forth.
"In this way" means by a specific sequence; this is what is being stated:

neither the mere sequence is expressive, nor that which has the phonemes as its substratum, nor the mere phonemes themselves. What then? It is the phonemes themselves, when accompanied by sequence, that are expressive.
Therefore, sequence does not possess primacy with respect to denotation; for when it is perceived as possessing that [denotative capacity], it is subordinate.
What then? It is the phonemes that possess it, since they are perceived as the substrata (dharmin); this is what has been demonstrated.

Regarding the two reasons stated—that [the Veda] is an effect because it possesses a temporal sequence (*anityadhvanikāryatvāt*)—he declares their lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) with the words "And not of the sequence," and so forth:
"Nor is there any 'effect-ness' (*kāryatva*) of the sequence, because it is adopted from what was previously established;
for no speaker adopts a sequence independently. (2286)

Just as it was stated by others regarding this [scripture], so too does another intend to speak it; therefore, its connection is beginningless, because it is adopted from what was previously established. (2287)
Because it adopts a sequence that is indeed fixed,
this very point is clarified by the words "The speaker does not," and so forth;
for like the relationship itself, the sequence is also beginningless.
He concludes with the words beginning "Therefore" (tena), etc.
Therefore, even though there is no absolute immutability, this "permanence" arises from conventional usage;
it is for this reason that we must diligently refute the independence of persons.
In the phrase "na iti," the genitive case is used for the agent (*kartṛ*) in connection with a verbal derivative (*kṛtya*).
Having done so, there is no fault [in the fact that] the prohibition of independence regarding sequence has been established;
therefore, even though this sequence lacks immutability (*kūṭasthatva*) like that of mountains and such, its eternality is to be understood from the linguistic usage of the elders alone.
By this, the eternality of the sequence is stated as being the eternality of usage, not the immutable eternality found in things such as mountains.
If this is so, why is the permanence of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-nityatva*) not accepted for the sequence of phonemes (*varṇa*) themselves? To this he says: "Even of phonemes...
That is to say, even for phonemes, [permanence] will not be established in this way, despite their non-eternality (*akauṭasthya*).
Since the [four] castes are eternal, the emergence of their sequential order arises from conventional usage (vyavahāra).
Just as the construction of jars and other objects occurs within eternal atoms, for in the absence of those [atoms], such a construction would be rootless and could not be perceived.
For even though phonemes possess non-eternal persistence due to their sequential nature, the linguistic practice of conveying meaning is established through the constancy of that practice.
To the question "How is it not established?", he says: "In the case of eternal [phonemes]," and so forth.

For if phonemes were eternal by virtue of being immutable (kūṭastha-nityatā), then, given the possibility of linguistic practice through a succession of persons, there would be the emergence of sequence—the acquisition of the self-nature of sequence—just as the construction of a jar or other objects originates from atoms.

In some places, the reading is "kramādayaḥ" (sequence, etc.); there, by the word "etc.," relations, recognition, and so forth are included. Now, he explains why composition is not possible for either [the phoneme or the atom] without their being eternal: "In the absence of that," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "the absence of that":

if both phonemes (*varṇa*) and atoms (*paramāṇu*) lack the state of being immutable and eternal, one might object that phonemes also possess subtle parts, just as atoms do which initiate the production of jars and other objects; as they say: "Phonemes also have parts that are a fourth [of their size]."
How then can the immutability and eternity of the phonemes (varṇas) be described?
This is not a fault;
for it has been established by the refutation of the *sphoṭa* that there are no constituent parts of phonemes.

Furthermore—if phonemes were not eternal by virtue of being immutable (kūṭastha-nityatā), then for all speakers there would be no such intention (*vivakṣā*) as "we are uttering words already uttered by another"; yet such an intention does occur. Therefore, demonstrating that this [intention] is not tenable without the eternity of phonemes, he says: "uttered by another," and so forth.
If your intention is certainly such that you say "I speak what has been spoken by another," then it follows that [the Veda] is eternal; and yet, you have no other evidence for this. (2291)

Now, one might object: "If the sequence of the phonemes *ga* and so forth is not ultimately eternal, nor are the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), nor the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs that impel them; and if [the agent] cannot produce those very things that impel the sounds, while those new ones he produces have never been seen to be impellers, then how can the phonemes, manifested in sequence, become the cause for the cognition of different meanings? Anticipating all this and providing the rebuttal, he says: "Just as by means of a genus (*jāti*), etc."—that is, just as the characterization of conventional usage for jars and the like occurs by means of a genus.
In the same way, [the existence of] sequence and so forth will be established by means of the universal (jāti).

Just as, although jars and the like are impermanent, their conventional usage is established by relying on a universal, so too will it be established for sequence and the like, even though they are impermanent.
He asks, "How is the characterization of conventional usage [established]? and says: "The universals (jāti) of the palate and so forth," and so on.
First, the universals of the palate and other [articulatory organs] are established in all persons;
the speaker, having characterized those sounds by means of them, emits them. (2293)

And their universals (jāti), which are the causes for the manifestation of sounds, operate as long as the phonemes (varṇa) persist, or else the individual manifestations (vyakti) associated with them do so.
For instance, the universals of the articulatory locations such as the palate are established in all persons because they reside in the palates and other locations that are common to all persons.

And the speaker, having perceived and determined the palate and other articulatory organs by means of those very universals (*jāti*) of the palate and so forth, subsequently emits—that is, impels—the manifesting winds, which are the sounds (*dhvani*).
This is according to the logical principle that "there is no cognition of a particular without its qualifier being apprehended.

Although those sounds are indeed impermanent, nevertheless, just like the universals of cow, horse, and so on, there exist as many universals as there are phonemes (*varṇa*); these very universals, acting in conjunction with the individual instances (*vyakti*), become the causes for the manifestation of the word-sound (*śabda*).

Alternatively— another position is that the manifestations of sound (*dhvani-vyakti*) themselves, accompanied by the universal (*jāti*), proceed toward the manifestation of the phonemes (*varṇa*) in accordance with them.

Now, one might object: even if there are distinct universals (*jāti*) for the sounds (*dhvani*), nevertheless, those sounds—even when characterized by their universals—are not capable of effecting the sequence of phoneme manifestation without a [temporal] sequence themselves. For instance, although they are differentiated by the difference of their universals, they possess no inherent sequence because they are partless; so how can there be a determination of sequence among the phonemes based on the sequence of the manifestors? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that regard," and so forth.

In that regard, the sequence of sounds would be preceded by the sequence of conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other articulators; and both [the sequence and the universal] are eternal by virtue of their universals (jāti).
Although the sequence of sounds is not inherent in them, nevertheless, it is the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs themselves that produce the sequence for them.

And since both the sequence of the conjunctions of the palate and so forth, and the sequence of the sounds (*dhvani*), are eternal by way of the universals (*jāti*) inherent in their own substrata, everything is consistent. [Objection:
But how can the eternity of a sequence—which is itself non-eternal—be characterized by means of a universal?
He says—"Just as... and so forth—in order to show how that which is thus characterized will become a constituent part of linguistic usage:

"Just as the parts of [actions such as] revolving are characterized by universals (jāti) and so on, and there is a sequential continuity, so too would it be for the palate and other [articulators], the sounds, and the phonemes. (2296)

Just as the sequential continuity of specific actions such as spinning and throwing—the word "etc. including ants and so forth—is characterized by their respective classes (bhāvajāti) and serves as a basis for linguistic usage; and just as, in this case too, the word "etc. includes the classes of ants and so forth, so too the sequential continuity of the palate and other articulators, sounds, and phonemes, characterized by the classes of the palate and so forth, results in linguistic usage. This is the connection [of the sentence].
The compound *tālvādidhvanivarṇabhāk* is analyzed as follows: *tālvādayaś ca dhvanayaś ca varṇāś ca* (palate and so forth, sounds, and phonemes); it is thus called "that which partakes in" these.

By this, it is stated that the sequence of the conjunction of the palate and so forth, characterized by its own genus (*svajāti*), is the cause for the exclusion of [mere] sound (*dhvani*). Furthermore, the sequence of sounds (*dhvanikrama*), which is preceded by the sequence of the conjunction and disjunction of the palate and so forth, and is characterized by its own genus, is the basis for the sequence of the manifestation of phonemes (*varṇa*). And that [sequence of phonemes] is the basis for the cognition of meaning; this is what is meant.

In some places, the reading is "parts" (bhāgāḥ); in that case, the connection is as follows: just as parts or portions of actions such as whirling, which possess a sequence and are characterized by their genus or by some other property, become the causes for conventional usage.

As some maintain that the persistence of the sequence residing in the palate and other [articulatory organs] is a factor in linguistic usage— reading "the recollection of the sequence" (*kramānusmṛti*) instead [of "persistence"]—
the construction there is as follows: just as the parts of [actions such as] whirling or pouring, characterized by universals and so forth, are recollected.

Thus, there will be a sequential recollection characterized by the universals (jāti) of the palate and so forth, which are the objects of the palate and so forth that possess the sounds and phonemes produced by the palate and so forth.

Alternatively, showing that the sequence of sounds is not produced by the order of conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and so forth, but rather is inherent (*svata eva*) because they possess parts, he says: "of the individuals" (*vyaktīnām*).
Or rather, it is precisely because of the subtlety of individual instances that the properties of the genus are determined;
and by virtue of that, even though the phonemes (*varṇa*) are all-pervasive, their sequential apprehension occurs through the [subtle] sounds (*dhvani*). (2297)

For those constituent parts which are initiatory and sequential are subtle; practical activity is not accomplished by means of them. Therefore, among those [parts], properties such as eternality, whose nature is that of a universal (*jāti*), are analyzed—that is, determined—as the causes for the manifestation of specific words.
To the question, "What is established by this?", he says: "By virtue of that," and so forth.
For even though the phonemes are all-pervading, they appear as if they possess a sequence due to the influence of the sequential sounds (dhvani).
With the words "In this way," etc., he concludes the subject at hand:
"In this manner, the phonemes, following all the qualities of sound which are established as eternal, would be the conveyors of the comprehension of different meanings. (2298)
The qualities of sound— such as sequence, intensity (or mildness), and spatial location—
are established as being eternal by way of their genus (*jāti*).
"Following along"— meaning persisting. 2298 Thus,

even if it is true that sequence and the like cannot exist in letters by their own nature due to their eternity and omnipresence, nevertheless, it has been demonstrated in detail that these [properties], residing in the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*), serve as a factor for the comprehension of meaning in the letters.

Now, showing another position—that these divisions conditioned by sound (dhvani), when perceived within the phonemes (varṇas), are indeed merely the means for comprehension even though they have ceased to exist—he says, beginning with "sequence" (ānupūrvī):
"And the sequence of phonemes, as well as those divisions of time known as short, long, and protracted, are understood to have sound as their limiting condition. (2299)
Those divisions of time for which sounds—the manifesting winds—are the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), acting as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), are described in that way.
Now, it may be objected: "But surely, for those who maintain the existence of time, it is accepted that time is one, all-pervading, and eternal."
As it has been said: "Some declare time to be a single, eternal, and all-pervading substance, like those things that possess the action of measurement apart from [any other] operation.
To the question, "How then is its division justified?", he says: "And time is one," and so forth.
Time is one, all-pervading, and eternal; though undivided, it is perceived as divided.
Like a phoneme, it is manifested by something in some particular object.
When it is manifested within phonemes, it serves as an auxiliary factor for communication.
However, because its own nature exists elsewhere as well, it is eternal.

(2301) Regarding the word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even though divided," it should be connected [to the other attributes] as "even though one," "even though eternal," and "even though all-pervading," since they form separate syntactical units.
To the question "How is it divided?", he says: "In all things, like the phonemes."

This is what is meant: just as even a single, eternal phoneme such as *ga* is perceived as divided according to distinctions of place and so forth when it is manifested in a particular location by a specific sound (*dhvani*), so too, although time pervades all objects, it is nevertheless apprehended as divided when it is manifested in a particular object by a specific action; however, when it is manifested in phonemes, it becomes a factor for the cognition of meaning.
If it is thus divided, how is its eternal omnipresence understood? To this he says: "Also elsewhere," and so forth.
Because it exists elsewhere as well—in things such as creepers and tender shoots—its eternity and omnipresence are established, just like existence (*sattā*).
The mention of "eternity" is illustrative.
Therefore, there exists no such property of words that is perishable.
Therefore, for those who maintain the eternity of phonemes, the word is eternally established.
With the words "Therefore" and so forth, there is a conclusion regarding the establishment of his own position, stating that it is of such a nature.

If, then, sequence and so forth are properties of time or properties of the manifesting sound (*dhvani*), and not ultimately properties of the phonemes (*varṇa*), how can they serve as a factor for their communication? For a property of one thing does not belong to another. To this, he says: "Even though it is a property of another," and so forth.

Even in the case of another's dharma, the status of being an auxiliary factor has been stated, as in the case of a horse’s speed and so forth; and regarding eternality, the validity of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) for all [scriptures] has been stated.
(2303) "Has been stated" [is the phrase].
By the statement "those who have boarded a boat and are traveling," and so forth,
the mention of those on a boat is indeed an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for all those on any vehicle,
just like the term "horse-speed" (*aśvaja-vādi*).

Just as the speed residing in a horse or similar animal becomes a factor for the attainment of another location by the men mounted upon it, and for the perception of movement in trees and the like, so too the sequence residing in the sound (dhvani) is a factor for the phoneme (varṇa) in the communication of meaning.

Having thus established in detail that the proposition of the non-eternality of words is sublated by the means of valid cognition known as presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), he says "In the case of eternality," etc., while concluding;
here, the word "therefore" (tasmāt) should be understood as the conclusion.

The phrase "of all" means that the eternity of the phoneme (*varṇa*) is established not only because the cognition of meaning would otherwise be impossible, but rather [it applies] to the palate and other articulators as well as to the sounds (*dhvani*), as stated in the Bhāṣya: "For if a sound perished as soon as it was uttered, another [sound] could not convey the meaning; therefore, it would not be uttered for the sake of others in a primary sense."
If, on the other hand, it has not perished, then it is logical that there is comprehension of the object because it has been perceived many times.
Thus, demonstrating that the thesis is also sublated by one's own words, by what is accepted, by scripture, and by common cognition, he says: "By one's own words," and so forth.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with one's own words and so forth in the proof of the non-eternality of sound;

for it is proclaimed that every proposition (*pratijñā*) is uttered for the sake of communicating the meaning to be proven. And it has already been established that this [proposition] does not express its own meaning as something non-eternal.
Therefore, because it conveys the intended meaning and is eternal, there is no sublation by scripture (*āgama*).
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of contradictions with what has been accepted (*abhyupeta*) and so forth is established as demonstrated.
And because a word does not become expressive through a connection with an unseen purpose, and so forth;
therefore, "arisen from the cognition of the object" means:
from the cognition of the object—that is, from the apprehension of the object—it is "arisen," meaning established; thus, "arisen from the cognition of the object."
That is to say, because [the word] possesses permanence, as established by the fact that the comprehension of meaning would otherwise be impossible.

He states the contradiction with what has been accepted: "(Regarding the phrase 'artha-abhidhāna... By establishing [the argument] while accepting the capacity for the expression of meaning, a person contradicts non-momentariness by means of what was previously accepted. (2306)
"By means of the capacities for the comprehension of meaning relied upon in each respective treatise, even by means of scripture (*āgama*), the non-momentariness of all proponents is not sublated.
(2307) [He states the sublation by scripture: "By means of the capacities for the comprehension of meaning," and so forth.
The supplement [to the sūtra] is: "Because the meaning of the proposition is sublated by those capacities of words which exist for the purpose of conveying meaning. (2306)

2307 He states the sublation by common experience (*pratītibādhā*) with the words "by all the world," etc.; and there is sublation by what is well-established for all the world, according to the manner previously described.
The contradiction with inference as well [is established] by the very same reason stated previously.
Since the non-difference of sound is determined through auditory recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*),
its contradiction with perception has already been demonstrated.
The direction previously mentioned— that is, as stated in the immediately preceding verse—
should rather be read as follows:
"by means of the capacities for the comprehension of meaning, which are determined by all the world."

Recalling the previously mentioned contradiction with inference and other means of knowledge— namely, that "the state of being subject to destruction contradicts the position of all proponents through worldly consensus"— he says: "There is also contradiction with inference," and so forth.

The previously mentioned reason is of various kinds: for instance, "the cognitions of the individual instances of the word 'cow,' though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, all have the same object, and do not have diverse objects,
because they arise as the thought 'cow,' just like a present cognition," and so on.
To say "all the more so" means:
furthermore, since the eternity and omnipresence of sound are established by auditory recognition, who could determine its opposite?
By this [it is shown],
Desiring to set forth certain remaining faults of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) as well as some faults of the reason (*hetudoṣa*), he says: "It must be stated," and so forth.

It must be stated: what kind of sound is this that is being proven to be perishable—is it composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), or is it material (*paudgala*), or is it a quality of space (*ākāśa*)? (2310)

Alternatively, [the word] may be distinct from the phonemes (varṇa), consisting of sound (nāda), having the nature of air, and being inexpressible; or it may be the sphoṭa, which consists of words and sentences, serving to exclude what is other than its own form.
Let these [theories] be subject to impermanence; for us, there is no permanence in them.
"Unestablished qualification" and "unestablished locus" constitute the fallacies of the reason (*hetu*).
(2312) He states the various conceptual alternatives regarding sound according to the different philosophical systems:
therein, sound is held by the Sāṃkhyas to be "three-constituted" (*triguṇa*) because its nature consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
The Digambaras call *pudgalas* atoms; this [doctrine] belongs to them, hence it is *paudgala*.
That is to say, it consists of that [sound];
for the followers of Kaṇāda maintain that the quality of space is distinct from color, while common people regard it as consisting of *nāda* (articulate sound).
As it is stated in the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya*: "Alternatively, in common usage, sound (*dhvani*) whose meaning is understood is called 'word' (*śabda*);
however, the authors of the *Śikṣās* say that [sound] is of the nature of air and non-expressive, as they state: 'The air assumes the form of sound.'"
The Grammarians (vaiyākaraṇa) maintain that there are both the word-sphoṭa (padasphoṭa) and the sentence-sphoṭa (vākyasphoṭa).
As they say: "In the intellect, whose seeds have been sown by the sounds (nāda) and which has reached full maturity through repetition, the Word (śabda) is apprehended together with the final sound."
Thus,
similarity (*sārūpya*)— that is, resemblance— is what is accepted by Vindhyavāsin;
whereas that which is accepted by the Buddhists as denotation is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), or the negation of the other.

In that regard, if the impermanence of things accepted by the Sāṅkhyas and others were thus being proven, then there would be the fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) known as "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhyatā*), because by the very statement [of the thesis], that which is already established is excluded; moreover,
such permanence is not what the Mīmāṃsakas intend to prove regarding sound.

Furthermore, with respect to us, there is the fallacy of the subject (*pakṣadoṣa*) known as "having an unestablished qualification" (*aprasiddhaviśeṣatva*), because the specific property-bearer (*dharmin*)— sound consisting of the three *guṇas* and so forth— is unestablished;
and there is the fallacy of the reason (*hetu*) known as "unestablished basis" (*āśrayāsiddhatā*),
because such a property-bearer is unestablished.
Now, if our proposed position were correct, then these two [properties] would themselves be merely words for you; that is, sound-ness (*śabdatva*) would likewise be so. (2313)
And that [universal] is impermanent for all [of us], which contradicts what is accepted as eternal;
for whatever universal is postulated here by anyone is held to be eternal.

Now, if this were our position—that we Mīmāṃsakas maintain that the letters themselves, such as the sound *ga*, are the word and that there is no distinct [entity] apart from them—then [the following would apply].

If that were the case, for a Buddhist and others, these two faults would follow: the fault of the proposition (*pratijñādoṣa*) consisting in the non-establishment of the qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣyatva*), and the fault of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) consisting in the non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).

If it is instead said to be "mere sound" (*śabdamātra*)—the remainder being "as the subject of the probandum" (*sādhyadharmitvena*)—then it follows that "your [Buddhist] universal of soundness (*śabdatvasāmānya*) is impermanent"; this must be supplied as the conclusion.

For instance: when all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) have been abandoned by means of the word "mere" (*mātra*), what else could remain as "mere sound" (*śabdamātra*) other than the universal (*sāmānya*)?
Therefore, by implication, you would be asserting that "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) itself is impermanent.
If it is argued, "Let it be so," [the author] says, "No"—for that [sound-ness] is held by everyone to be eternal, and so forth.
For even by the Buddhists who propound the theory of the exclusion of others (anyāpoha), it has been stated: "Because the properties of a genus are established.
By this, the fault of contradicting what has been accepted is stated;
he demonstrates that very point with the words beginning "whatever here," and so forth.

Whatever universal (*sāmānya*) has been established by any [proponent] according to their own tenets, all of that is held to be eternal by all disputants; otherwise, because of the arising of successive [particulars] just like the particulars themselves, it would fall within the category of particulars, and its very nature as a universal would be lost. (2313)

Thus, having first pointed out the fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) by means of an alternative regarding the property-bearer (*sādhyadharmin*), he now says "And impermanence," etc., wishing to point it out by means of an alternative regarding the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*):
"And impermanence (*anityatva*) is perishability; if it is said to be absolute..."

Consequently, our position would have an unestablished qualifier (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*). If it is argued that "being designated as non-eternal" is accepted in some way or another [as distinct] from the state of non-manifestation, then that [non-eternality] is indeed held to consist in manifestation itself. (2315–2316)

If that which is intended as the probandum—impermanence characterized by absolute, traceless destruction—is accepted, then for the Mīmāṃsakas, there is the fallacy of the subject (*pakṣadoṣa*) consisting in an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*).

For, just as for the followers of Kapila, the qualification of "traceless destruction" is unestablished for the Mīmāṃsakas; this is because even when jars and other objects disappear, they persist in the form of a latent potential (*śakti*).
For even in the case of a lamp and the like, it is held that its light particles, being subtle, move very rapidly from one place to another;
thus, if you intend to establish the designation "impermanent" in some such manner, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For instance, even in the case of eternal things, the designation "impermanent" is indeed accepted on the basis of their states of manifestation and non-manifestation.
Thus, the proposition that "sound is impermanent" has been refuted in detail; now, exposing the fault in the reason "because it is perceptible by the senses," he says: "Kevalaindriya... and so forth.

And when the reason (*hetu*) is conceived here as being "merely perceptible by the senses" (*kevalaindriyakatva*), a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is now perceived through the universal (*jāti*) that was previously established. Merely perceptible by the senses— that is, devoid of qualifiers such as "being an effect" and so forth— when such an unqualified reason exists, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the universal previously proven.
"Because the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is not established.

(2317) It might be argued: "Even if the negative concomitance is not established because the opponent accepts the existence of a universal (*jāti*), nevertheless, since the Buddhist and others do not accept a universal, it is indeed established for them; therefore, how can this be called 'inconclusive' (*anaikāntika*)? To this he says: "Unestablished," and so forth.

Just as a reason is not obtained by the opponent when the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is unestablished, so it is with positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). According to the principle that "only that which expresses what is certain for both [parties] is a proof or a refutation," just as a reason becomes defective when the property of the subject is unestablished for either one, so too it is certainly defective when either positive or negative concomitance is unestablished for either one.

The connection [of the words] is with the phrase "of the two, positive and negative concomitances, being unestablished," by means of a grammatical transformation (*vacanavipariṇāma*). [Objection: If only that which is established for both [parties] is a proof or a refutation, then how is it that you have asserted a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) against the Buddhist by means of a "fallacy" (*jāti*) that is unestablished for him? To this, he says: "In that case," and so forth.
In that case, even if the "universal" (jāti) were unestablished for the proponent of the proof, it would nonetheless remain a non-reason (*ahetu*) as long as it has not been refuted.
(2319) Even though the "universal" is not established as a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) for the Buddhist or other proponent of the proof, nevertheless, the doubt does not cease.
The meaning is that because it is impossible to refute that [objection], the reason consequently has a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar instances (saṃdigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttika).

Furthermore, he states another refutation of the probandum and the probans by means of an alternative conceptualization: "And [the inquiry] regarding 'being an effect' and 'being perceptible,' etc."—that is, the investigation as to what constitutes "being an effect" and "being perceptible," etc., is clearly evident in the cases of non-difference from individuals, difference, and the distinction between difference and non-difference. (2320)

In that regard, the fallacies of being unshared (*asādhāraṇa*), unestablished (*asiddha*), lacking a probandum (*sādhyahīna*), and having a defective similar instance (*sapakṣatākṣata*) should be stated according to the specific conceptualization, with reference to the proponent (*vādī*) or the opponent (*prativādī*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the property of impermanence (*anityatva*) is included.

In this regard, an investigation must be conducted as to the nature of "perceptibility by the senses" (*aindriyakatva*) and so forth: is it non-different from the individuals (*vyakti*), or is it distinct? Likewise, if it is held to be distinct, an inquiry must be made regarding those particulars (*bheda*): is that which is distinct from them variously different, or is it one and the same? In that case, if the position taken is non-distinction, the reason (*hetu*) of perceptibility by the senses would be "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*), because it is non-different from the individual; for, like the individual's own nature, it would lack concomitance with other individuals.

Even in the case of the position of difference (*vyatireka*), because the Mīmāṃsaka does not accept difference, it remains unestablished whether [the universal] is distinct or non-distinct with respect to each individual; thus, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For this very reason, the fault regarding the position of both difference and non-difference (*bhedābheda*) has not been stated, since that [position] would find its scope only if difference were established.
Even in the case where impermanence is treated as a negative concomitance (vyatireka), the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhya); that is to say, it is deficient in the probandum.

Even in the case where it is not a negative concomitance (avyatireka), the example is likewise deficient in the probandum, because one individual instance does not follow into or coexist with another individual instance.

2320–2321 Now, he states the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of this reason, "because it follows immediately after effort," with the words beginning "immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantaram*).
The cognition that arises immediately after an effort is a proof for being produced and impermanent;

yet even in that case, there is an inconclusiveness (anaikāntika) due to the three [factors]: cessation through deliberation (pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha), cessation not through deliberation (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha), and space (ākāśa), which are distinct from momentary things.
For the cessation of things through an act of intelligence is known as *pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*;
their cessation without an act of intelligence is by *apratisaṅkhyā*.
And both of these, because they are not subject to destruction, are held to be unconditioned (*akṛtaka*). (2323–2324)
For "being perceived immediately after an effort" is defined as "the state of being subsequent to an effort";

however, because this reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) even with respect to the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), it does not prove that what is produced is impermanent. To explain: the Buddhists maintain that there are three types of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) entities—cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), and space (*ākāśa*)—which are non-momentary, eternal, and distinct from momentary things.
Showing that this cause operates therein, he says: "preceded by cognition," and so forth.

That destruction of jars and the like which is preceded by cognition is *pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha* (cessation through deliberation); that which is not preceded by one's own cognition is *apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha* (cessation not through deliberation). This, indeed, is the Buddhist system according to them.
And those two [cessations] of jars and so forth are analytical and non-analytical cessation.
"Even though they are uncreated"— by the word "even," it is implied that they are also eternal.
And just as these two [space and nirvāṇa] possess the qualities of being unconditioned and eternal, so too...
Demonstrating, according to the very view of the opponent, how there is no occurrence [of destruction] in that cause, he says: "They say," and so forth.
They say: "Indeed, for you, destruction is established by its own nature as being causeless; for from the contact with fire, there arises a succession of embers from the wood. (2325)
Intrinsic destruction, however, is established solely upon birth;
it is subtle and unperceived because it occurs within a similar continuum.
But when a cause of a different character falls upon that similar continuum, [destruction becomes manifest]. || 2326 ||
At that time, the gross [entity] is manifested by an effect that is dissimilar [to its cause];
because a series dissimilar to it arises from the cause,
destruction— though not produced by that very [cause]— is clearly manifested.

The Buddhists say "it is so. But surely [it is observed that] wood is destroyed by fire and a jar by a staff; thus, causes of destruction are perceived. How then can this [destruction] be without a cause? To this he says: "For it happens," and so forth. For fire and the like are determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be the causes of other entities such as charcoal and the like, but not of destruction.

Since that [destruction] is established by its very nature, one might ask: "If destruction is indeed inherent, why is it not perceived even before the contact with fire and so forth? To this he says: "Subtle," and so on.
For the dull-witted, deceived by the production of successive similar moments, do not perceive [the subtle destruction].
However, because of the arising of a similar continuum, they imagine [the object] to be undestroyed;
for the cause, such as a mallet, is of a different nature,
and the effect, such as the potsherds, is of a different nature.
In this state, indeed, the grossness of destruction becomes manifest; therefore, with the words "by that," etc., the conclusion is made:
"a dissimilar continuum."
"Because it is of a different character from the cause"— this is a grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "by that very [cause]."
That which was indicated by the phrase "from which [it arises] by means of a cause" is connected with the subsequent term "is manifested."
