Pointing out that the reason (hetu) occurs in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa), he says: "That [sound], by means of the blow of a mallet," and so forth; it is that which follows immediately after the effort of striking with a mallet.
Because an uncreated cause would be seen to be fallible; therefore,
that cessation, being of two kinds, is said to be "immediately following the effort" such as the striking of a hammer when its cognition occurs immediately after the effort of striking with a hammer.
It was stated [in verse 2328] that "by three [reasons].
Having demonstrated the deviation [of the reason] with respect to two of them, he now says "ākāśam api" etc., demonstrating deviation even with respect to the third, namely space (ākāśa).
Even space, though eternal, is manifested when it is covered by earth and water through their removal by means of digging, cutting, and so forth;
likewise, when cognition is observed to follow immediately after an effort, [it is not produced but rather manifested].
Therefore, the reason stated there— that "the perception [of sound] occurs through the removal (apoha) of that [earth and so forth]"— is inconclusive;
for it refers to the removal of earth and other elements by means of their own sounds and other causes.
In this context,
the definition of sound is:
knowledge that arises immediately after an effort.
Having thus stated the faults of the reason (*hetu*), and desiring to state the faults of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), he says: "The similar instance (*sapakṣa*) also," and so forth.
Even the "similar instance" (sapakṣa) here is a conceptual construction; thus there is a lack of the probandum (sādhyahīnatā) regarding the literal meaning of the scripture.
Even in the position that the individual is what is indicated (lakṣaṇa), there is the dilemma of whether it is different from or non-different from the universal (jāti).
If it were different, the locus (dharmin) would not be established; if it were non-different, it would not be established for others [who do not accept that identity].
"Even though there is no distinction [between them], that entity is for me neither non-eternal nor eternal.

For its part designated as 'genus' (jāti) is held to be eternal, while the other is perishable; indeed, it has been previously established that a single entity possesses a variegated form. (2333–2334)
The similar instance (*sapakṣa*) is the example;
is that intended as the literal meaning of the word (*śrutyartha*) or as the individual (*vyakti*)?
If it is the literal meaning, then there is the fault of the example being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).
To explain: "śruti" means sound;

its "artha" is the denoted object, which is the universal such as "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva) and so forth. And since that [universal] is accepted as eternal by all theorists, there is no concomitance there with the property to be proven, namely impermanence.
In some places, the reading is *jātyartha*; in that case, a *karmadhāraya* compound should be formed,
and the meaning remains exactly the same.

Now, if the second alternative is accepted, even then one must consider whether that individual, which is intended as the example, is different from the universal or non-different from it; for if it were different,
then the subject of the example would be unestablished (*asiddha*) for the Mīmāṃsaka.

For the Mīmāṃsaka does not, like the Vaiśeṣika and others, maintain that the universal is absolutely distinct from the individual, as it has been said: "The existence of the universal and so forth as something separate from the individual is certainly not established. If, on the other hand, the position taken is that they are non-different, then for opponents such as the Buddhists, the property of the example (the *dṛṣṭāntadharmya*) remains unestablished.
For others do not consider the universal (*jāti*) to be non-different from the individual (*vyakti*).

Now, if the pot is adduced as an example by setting aside the dilemma of difference and non-difference, even then, for us, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*); demonstrating this, he says: "Even though there is no distinction," and so forth, [concluding with] "that."
He asks, "How is the entity 'jar' [constituted]? and says: "The part," and so forth; for of this entity 'jar,' the portion designated as the universal (jāti) is eternal.
But the other, known as the individual (vyakti), would be perishable—that is, subject to destruction.
To the objection, "How is it logical for a single entity to possess two mutually contradictory natures?", he says: "It has a variegated form," and so forth. (2332)
Furthermore, wishing to state the faults of the example by way of an analysis of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*), he says: "Impermanence," and so forth.

"If impermanence is conceptualized in this way such that destruction [without residue] is the probandum, then for me, the Mīmāṃsaka, there is the fallacy of the probandum being absent in the example; but in the other case, it belongs to you. This is the direction of the refutation. (2335) If impermanence is intended as the probandum characterized by destruction without residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*), then for me, the Mīmāṃsaka, there is the deficiency of the probandum in the example.
For we do not maintain the absolute annihilation of entities, since they persist in the form of potentiality (*śakti*).

Although "destruction" (*nāśa*) is a general term, it is understood from the context to refer to a specific sense characterized by destruction without residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*). Otherwise, how could the objection that the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*) be applicable?

[Objection: But has impermanence not already been analyzed by the passage beginning with, "If absolute perishability were meant by 'impermanence'..."? Why then is it analyzed yet again? [Response: True; however, that previous analysis was for the purpose of exposing a fault in the *pakṣa* (the thesis), whereas this present one is for the sake of the *dṛṣṭānta* (the example); this is the distinction. Now, if what is intended is not impermanence characterized by destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśa*), but rather another kind characterized by appearance and disappearance (*āvirbhāvatirobhāva*), then [the author] says: "In the other case... (*anyasyām*).
The connection is with "in impermanence"; it should be construed as "for you [there is] the fallacy of the absence of the probandum."
In that case as well, the word "of the example" is to be understood as the ellipsis;
for you Buddhists do not accept destruction with a persisting substrate (*sānvaya-vināśa*) as the Sāṃkhyas do.

Therefore, in your position, the example would be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). This path of refuting the proof for the non-eternality of sound has thus been explained to the wise; other matters should also be inferred and formulated by the learned themselves.
With the words "padārtha" and so forth, he anticipates the objection of the opponent:
"Even though the eternality of the relation between word and object has been established..."
Furthermore, the status of the Veda as a means of valid cognition regarding the meaning of sentences is not established here;
for, like the [grammatical] notions of *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*, the understanding [of sentence-meaning] arises from human convention.
Even though it is without any [intrinsic] basis, the meaning has been constructed by the ritualists (*yājñika*).
Furthermore, because it is a collection of words like other literary compositions, it is of human origin;
and since there is no authoritative person [to verify it], the Vedas lack the status of a valid means of knowledge.
For the meaning of a sentence consists in the injunction or prohibition of a specific action delimited by particular means of accomplishment.
In that case, the authority of the injunction (*codanā*) alone is valid, not that of the individual word-meanings;

therefore, when the authority of the Veda is to be established, the demonstration of the eternity of all three—the words, their meanings, and their relationship—is irrelevant to the subject at hand. Furthermore, whatever cognition of a sentence-meaning arises, it originates from convention (*saṅketa*), just as the cognition of "guṇa," "vṛddhi," and so forth arises from sentences such as *ādguṇaḥ*; and since the cognition of the meaning of the injunction-sentence is likewise produced, this constitutes a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
He demonstrates this very point with the words "from convention" (*samayāt*) and so forth;
the suffix *-vati* is used in the sense of the locative case, as in the expression "like *guṇa* and *vṛddhi*" (*guṇavṛddhyādivat*).
He provides the justification for this very point, beginning with "even without cause" (*niṣkāraṇo'pi*), and so forth:

It is conceivable that even though it is without cause—that is, without any basis—the ritualists (*yājñikaiḥ*) have, for the sake of their own livelihood alone, fabricated the meaning of Vedic statements such as "one desiring heaven should offer the *agnihotra*," based on their own unrestrained imagination.

Furthermore, whatever is of the nature of a composite is of human origin, just like stories such as plays or narratives; and the Veda is a collection of words—this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
And consequently, because it is of human origin, the Veda would be non-authoritative, like the speech of a man on a street;
if it is argued that it will nonetheless be authoritative despite being of human origin because it was composed by a reliable person (āpta), he says: "Nor is there a reliable person," and so forth.
He provides a rebuttal with the verse beginning "sambandha" and so forth.
The eternity of the Vedic sentences must be asserted according to the logic of the non-creation of linguistic relations;
for while such a notion might be possible regarding words like *vṛddhi* because they pertain to observed worldly usage,
this [notion of conventionality] is not tenable in the case of the Veda, since it is based on a conventional agreement.
For by whom has the connection between heaven and sacrifice, which is beyond the senses, been perceived?

(2340) The same logic that was stated regarding the non-creation of the relationship between words and their referents—namely, "To whom could a speaker turn when establishing a relationship for a listener, a maker, or one who does not make it?"—should also be asserted for the eternality of Vedic sentences.

To show the inconclusiveness [of the opponent's argument] in the claim that "the understanding of men arises from convention, just as [the application of] *guṇa* and *vṛddhi* [suffixes]," he says: "Because it consists of linguistic usage with perceptible objects," and so forth.

In cases such as *adeṅ* (Pāṇini 1.1.2), since the usage of terms like "guṇa" is observed with respect to a perceptible object, comprehension is indeed possible there by virtue of convention (*samaya*). However, this is not the case in the Veda, because since heaven (*svarga*) and the like are beyond the senses, it is impossible to establish a convention for them.

If this were so, then its futility would follow; to this he says: "And there is no futility for it," because the cognition of that meaning arises from it. Such a counter-argument must be stated regarding its being a composite [of phonemes]. (2341)
"All study of the Veda is preceded by study under a teacher, because it is designated as 'Vedic study,' just like one's current study. (2342) "Of that... [refers to this].

Regarding the proof that "the Veda is [non-eternal] because it is a composite," he says— "of the state of being a composite," etc.— showing that even this proof is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) by means of a counter-argument.

But surely, one could likewise say regarding the study of the *Mahābhārata*: "Whatever constitutes the study of the *Mahābhārata*, all of that is preceded by study under a teacher, just like the present-day [study]," and yet it cannot be established in this way.

Therefore, anticipating the objection that his counter-argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "Even in the case of the *Bhārata*... and so forth. [The verse reads: "In the case of the *Bhārata* as well, it would indeed be so; however, it is sublated by the tradition of its author.
But in the case of the Veda, there is no such tradition, and even that tradition which exists is based on mere explanatory passages (*arthavāda*). (2343)
The same objection might also apply to the *Bhārata*, but since Vyāsa is remembered there as its author, the intended meaning of the proposition is not sublated by that memory of an author;
however, in the case of the Veda, there is no such memory of an author— this is the remainder of the argument.

But surely, even in the Veda, an author is indeed remembered, as for example: "Agni and Āvaśvaka composed the Sāmans; the Sāman-singers [composed them] on Mount Kapotaka; the Aṅgirasas [composed] the Atharvans. To this he replies: "And that which is based upon an explanatory passage (arthavāda).
Even that memory of an author of the Veda is based upon an explanatory passage—an *arthavāda* being a statement whose purpose is to praise a meaning—and that of which it is the basis is so described.
For instance, in the expression "cakruḥ," the verb *karoti* does not have the sense of "doing" (performing);
rather, it has the sense of "remembering.
Thus, "cakruḥ" means "they remembered."
"How is this meaning determined? he asks, and says: "The past and future," etc.;
[this means] the past and future times are devoid of an author of the Veda.
Because they are temporal beings, just as in the world time is observed to be present [and not the creator],
it should be understood that Brahmā and others are not the creators of the sciences, due to reasons such as their being human, just like ordinary and extraordinary men. 2344–2345.
The two means of valid cognition are easy to understand.

Then, having concluded the entire subject matter under discussion with the words "tataśca" and so forth, he establishes the proof: "Therefore, let it be understood that the Vedic word is clearly non-false regarding its own meaning, because it does not depend on anything else, just like the cognition of a word-meaning from a word. (2346)

The cognition produced by that [Veda] is valid because it arises from an eternal sentence; just as the cognition whose object is the very nature of a sentence is valid, so too is the validity of the cognition generated by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*).
It is established as being like a cognition arising from the words of a reliable person (āpta),
because this cognition is not produced by the words of an unreliable person,
and it possesses no contradiction even when there is a difference in time, place, and so forth. (2348–2349)

Since both validity (*prāmāṇya*) and invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) are established within the Veda, even if an infinite succession of disciples and teachers is postulated, it serves to ensure its faultlessness. (Verse 2350) Whatever produces a cognition that does not depend on the mouth of an authorial agent is not false in that regard; for example, a word [produces a cognition] regarding its referent. Since a Vedic sentence produces a conviction regarding its own meaning without depending on the mouth of an authorial person, this is an "observation of the contrary of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Since falsity is pervaded by the quality of producing knowledge that depends upon a person acting as an agent,
its opposite— namely, independence from a speaker with respect to its own meaning— is established, just like the cognition of a word.
This is intended to demonstrate that words are the cause of non-contradictory cognition; it is not the case that the cognition of a word is intended as the illustrative example—
what then?

For in this case, the words themselves constitute the subject (*dharmin*) characterized by the nature of sound; and when their non-falsity is to be proven on the grounds that they serve as the cause for the arising of non-contradictory cognition, it is only appropriate that the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmin*) be of exactly that same nature.
Otherwise, the example would be deficient in respect to the property to be proven (*sādhyavaikalya*).

Likewise, there is another formal argument: "That cognition which is produced by an eternal sentence is correct because it is in accordance with reality, just like [the cognition] whose object is the nature of the sentence itself; and the certainty regarding the attainment of heaven and so forth from the Agnihotra and other rites is produced by an eternal sentence. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Since the eternality [of the Veda] has already been established in detail previously, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
The passage beginning with "codanā" has already been explained above.

Likewise, there are two further formal arguments (*prayoga*): That cognition which is produced by the speech of those who are not authoritative (*anāpta*) and not composed by them, yet remains free from contradiction regarding differences in place, time, person, and state—that is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like the cognition produced by the speech of an authoritative person (*āpta*). And this cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is likewise [free from contradiction]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*);
thus, the first reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), since the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) has been established in detail.

Nor does it apply to the second [alternative], as it has been stated: "From the injunction 'one desiring heaven should sacrifice,' it is not understood in a doubtful manner, such that one might wonder whether heaven exists or does not exist;
and this, being understood without doubt, cannot be false."

For that which, having arisen, is subsequently destroyed—thinking "this is not so"—is a false cognition; however, this [Vedic knowledge] does not undergo subversion at another time, in another state, or with respect to another person; therefore, it is non-erroneous.

Consequently, it is established that the Veda is a self-evident means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), like light, serving as the cause for the systematic arrangement of *dharma* and other categories, common to all the world.
Thus, it remains settled that the doctrine of "Mind-Only" (*cittamātra*) and so forth, as described by the Buddhists and others, is untenable.
Now, if the Veda is indeed intrinsically authoritative and common to all like light, why is it that certain people, such as the Buddhists and others, disagree with it?
Anticipating the objection that it is not logical for that [Veda] to be invalid with respect to them, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.

Therefore, just as with light, which is the eye for all people in the world, the obstruction experienced by others toward the Veda is indeed born of unrighteousness (adharma), like that of an owl. || 2351 ||

Just as, for instance, when the sun has dispelled the entire spread of darkness with its mass of exceedingly sharp rays and shines everywhere before the common eye of all people, the form of an owl or similar creature—whose eyes are too weak to perceive due to the obstruction of their own karma—does not enter the path of vision; even so, those such as the Śākyas, whose eyes of intellect are struck by the darkness of unrighteousness, meet only with repulsion despite the existence of the Veda, the sole eye of the entire world.
The word "kila" (it is said) indicates a lack of approval.
He clarifies that very point with the words "All this," and so forth:

"All this is merely the manifestation of false pride on the part of the twice-born; it has come about like the accidental letters bored by a woodworm, for not even a single well-spoken word belongs to them. (2352)
The phrase "like the woodworm's letter" means even by way of the maxim of the crow and the palm fruit (coincidence).
In this regard, concerning what was stated— that that which is free from the defects of causes of falsity is a cause of non-erroneous knowledge, and so forth— he says,
beginning with "Even though the agent is absent," in order to demonstrate the inconclusiveness [of the reason] while for the moment accepting that the reason is established:
"For even if the agent were absent, this [scripture] would certainly not attain the status of having true meaning."
Because of the deficiency of those causes and qualities, even in the absence of defects, this scripture is like that which has a false object.
(2353) Eṣā refers to the scripture.

Just as it is observed that one possessed of passion and other such defects speaks falsely, and thus through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) the defects are determined to be the causes of falsity in speech; likewise, it is observed that one endowed with qualities such as compassion speaks the truth, and thus qualities like compassion are the causes of truthfulness.

Consequently, by the removal of the cause, truthfulness would also be removed just as falsity is. Therefore, even if the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) were granted, truthfulness would not be established; hence, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
2353 Now, as to how the absence of qualities is ascertained, he says: "The qualities exist," and so forth;
it is suspected regarding human compositions whether qualities exist or do not exist.
"Therefore, futility results; for us, there is no suspicion of excellences at all.
(2354) This shows that whatever reason you have stated for the absence of defects is the very same reason for the absence of excellences, which are the cause of truthfulness. (2354)
Having concluded with the words "Therefore" and so forth, he demonstrates the consequence of the non-existence of both truth and falsity through the non-perception of their causes:
"Therefore, because there is no recourse to the causes of truth and falsity, and because of the absence of wisdom, compassion, and the lack thereof, that duality does not exist. (2355)
In this context, the connection is respectively as follows: wisdom and the like are the causes of truthfulness, while lack of compassion and the like are the causes of falsity;
"the two" refers to truthfulness and falsity.
He demonstrates what follows when duality is absent: "Futility," and so forth.
Therefore, futility is entailed, like the sentence "six cakes" and the like.
If meanings connected with action and its factors are indeed understood [from the Veda], this understanding would arise from the narration of human events, like the story of Urvaśī and others;
for even though the Veda lacks such purpose, it possesses that capacity by its very nature.
The Veda would result in meaninglessness, like the speech of a madman, such as "six cakes, ten pomegranates," and so forth. [Objection:
But surely for the Buddhist who seeks to prove the meaninglessness of the Veda, there would be a contradiction with perceived experience regarding his proposition;
for from the statement "heaven results from the Agnihotra," the comprehension of a meaning is directly experienced.
Anticipating the objection, "How can that [Veda] be refuted?", he eliminates the opponent's opportunity for speech with the words beginning "This... and so forth.

He thinks as follows: If the meaninglessness of the Veda were established independently, then there would be a contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñābādha*); however, this is merely a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum) being advanced, and in such a case, a contradiction of the thesis is impossible because there is no thesis being asserted therein.

Merely by means of the non-occurrence of a pervading property (*vyāpakadharmanivṛtti*), a contradiction in speech (*vacanavyāghāta*) is demonstrated through the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭāpatti*) for one who does not accept the non-occurrence of the pervaded (*vyāpyanivṛtti*);
nor is there any sublation by perception (*dṛṣṭabādha*).
For instance, this cognition might arise even from a meaningless Veda due to the influence of human interpretation.

Just as when a certain person, being ignorant of the fact that the Vedic statement "from the Agnihotra, heaven results" and so forth is explained by some as referring to the life stories of Bharata, Urvaśī, and others, nevertheless comes to understand that meaning from that very sentence, yet that sentence does not possess that meaning [in its primary sense]; in the same way, this comprehension of meaning could arise even from the Veda which is inherently meaningless. Therefore, how can there be a subversion of the proposition by perception?

Furthermore—let it be granted that there is indeed the cessation of the defect (doṣa) alone, which is the cause of falsity, and not of the excellence (guṇa); nevertheless, the inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) of the reason remains unavoidable. Demonstrating this, he says: "Even in the absence of defects," and so forth.
Even in the absence of defects, truthfulness is not established because of the existence of the other;
for there is also that which is called "meaninglessness. Therefore, there is another, supreme category.
(2358) For if there were no other category for words apart from truthfulness and falsity, then the presence of the second category would be necessarily concomitant with the absence of the first.

But when there is also a third category consisting of the useless (*anarthaka*), then the determination of truth cannot arise from the exclusion of falsity, because the other third category—the useless—has not been excluded.
Now, [if it is argued that] the capacity to produce the cognition of a true object exists inherently (*svataḥ*) and is established [in the means of knowledge].

The Veda is considered to be this [knowledge] which possesses a person (or is not dependent on a person), is free from desire, and has true meaning. If this were so, then that knowledge would occur at all times without interruption,
because its cause is eternally present, just as it is in the moment currently under consideration.

Or else, at the time of a single cognition, everything produced by it would become capable [of producing that cognition] by way of being its cause, just like the specific cognition intended [to be produced].

(2361) It might be argued: if it were admitted that truthfulness in the Veda is caused by qualities such as compassion, then, since those qualities reside in a person, when the person is removed, the qualities would also be removed; and consequently, just as falsity [is removed], truthfulness would likewise be removed.

Anticipating the opponent’s rebuttal—that because the Veda possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), it is by its very nature the cause of knowledge of true objects and not dependent on extrinsic qualities (*guṇa*), and therefore the reason [adduced against it] is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) nor does it entail the consequence of the Veda being purposeless—the author, while refuting this, says: "If that were so," and so forth.
The intention is that just as this Veda has meaningfulness by its very nature, so too might falsity be possible; thus, the reason remains indeed inconclusive.
And this he will state later:

"If [the Vedic sentences] were by their very nature causes of knowledge, then knowledge arising from them would occur at all times and simultaneously, because the cause would be unimpeded; how then could there not be the consequence of futility? The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whenever something has its cause unimpeded, it necessarily occurs at that time, just as the knowledge produced by sentences such as the *agnihotra* occurs at the moment intended for it; and the knowledge derived from all Vedic sentences has its cause unimpeded in every state [of existence]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
And regarding the position that [cognitions] arise simultaneously, he states another fault: "Thereafter," and so forth.
Thereafter, because of the exhaustion of its power to produce cognition, this Veda would not be eternal; or, if the power remains, cognition would arise again. (2362)

For instance: if the Veda, having produced all cognitions simultaneously, were thereafter to lose its power to produce cognition, then it would follow that it is subject to decay because of the exhaustion of that power which constitutes its very nature;

on the other hand, if it does not lose that power, then there is the consequence that cognitions would arise again at a later time. Thus, in no way can an eternal entity possess causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*).
Now, with the words "athāpi" and so forth, [the author] raises the objection that the reason—"that which has its causes complete"—is unestablished (*asiddha*):
"Nevertheless, it depends upon auxiliary factors such as explanations and the like;
and since those exist sequentially, that cognition is held to be sequential. (2363)
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "explanations, etc.," conventions and so forth are included;
and by "of these," it refers to those explanations and the rest.
He refutes this with the words "Not so," and so forth:
"It is not so; for what kind of dependence could there be on that which is already capable?"
If it is capable through that connection, then what [need] do you have for its permanence?

For indeed, one who is incapable would depend upon another; therefore, in the desire to produce a nature that is capable, there is no deficiency whatsoever in the nature of that which is already capable—so what kind of dependence could it possibly have?
Now, if it is accepted that what was previously incapable becomes capable later through the conjunction with auxiliary causes, then you must abandon all hope for the eternity of the Veda.
How so? He says: "Previously incapable," and so forth.
If that which was previously incapable is made capable again by them, then this [cognition] would follow as being human-made, because it depends upon a person;
for the capacity is not distinct [from the person]. This is the intended meaning.

If, however, there were a difference [between the Veda and its power], then because the relationship would be unestablished, it would follow that the Veda is not a causal agent; for it must be stated that the effect arises from the power alone.

As for the claim that "it is an auxiliary to knowledge," that Veda which serves as an auxiliary to knowledge is born from a human source, and the very nature of the Veda is born from a human source; and since that [nature] is non-different from the Veda, the Veda itself is likewise born.

Furthermore, showing that not only does the consequence of impermanence follow from dependence on another, but also that the postulation of its being authorless (apauruṣeya) becomes futile, he says: "For indeed," and so forth— "For this Veda, even if it were to remain [eternally], does not produce knowledge for us."
As long as it has not been illuminated by persons who act as lamps,
therefore the quality of being non-human (apauruṣeya) need not be postulated as the cause for knowledge of the actual state of things; for this knowledge proceeds from the explanation of a person.
Therefore, even if this authorlessness of the Veda were established, it would be useless;
for the knowledge that results from it—which is what is desired as its fruit—is dependent upon a person.
Thus, its authorlessness is postulated only for the sake of ensuring that the knowledge is true.
Moreover, even that postulation [of an eternal scripture] is not capable of producing knowledge of it independently of a person; thus, that postulation is futile.

Let persons themselves, as authoritative authors, be the cause of the knowledge of reality; what is the use now of this "authorlessness" (apauruṣeyatva), which merely presents itself as an established fact?

Now, [the opponent might argue: "Let there be no consequence of impermanence, and let the assumption of its being authorless not be rendered futile; therefore, we accept that the Veda is always capable. To show that in that case the same fault as before would follow, he says: "If it is capable," and so forth. "If this [Veda] is always capable, then what else does it require?
For when the sole cause is capable, knowledge must indeed arise from it for you. (2369)
It might be argued: "Even if there is dependence on persons, the quality of being authorless (*apauruṣeyatā*) is not rendered futile;
for it is only the meaning as it already exists that is revealed by persons, and nothing new is created. For if they were to create something new, their independence would have to be admitted."
Furthermore, being overwhelmed by passion and other afflictions, they compose scriptures with perverted meanings; by what could they be restrained?

Showing that this same collection of defects applies equally even when an explanation is made by persons, he says: "Independent," and so forth—"Independent persons here [compose] an explanation of the Veda according to their own whim."
Those who act [in this way] cannot be restrained by anyone at all.
Therefore, it is suspected that these people, being overwhelmed by defects such as delusion and pride, might even provide a contrary interpretation of the sacred scripture (śruti). (2370–2371)
Furthermore, no person is accepted as an independent knower of the meaning of the Veda—which concerns supersensible matters—who could then explain that Vedic meaning;

for his vision of supersensible matters occurs through his thorough knowledge of the Vedic meaning, not independently, while his thorough knowledge of the Vedic meaning cannot exist without his vision of supersensible matters. Thus, it clearly follows that there is a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Demonstrating this, he says: "Nor is there even a single human being who is an observer of the supersensible," and so forth.
For knowledge of the connection between heaven and sacrifices and so forth is certainly not without a scriptural injunction (acodana).
Since, according to you, there is no direct seer of supersensible objects, he who perceives through the eternal word (vacana) truly perceives. (2372–2373)
"Non-instruction" (acodana) refers to knowledge for which no instruction exists— that is to say, knowledge independent of instruction;
he states the reason for this with the words "because."
To explain how even this is so, he says: "By means of speech," and so forth.
That has been stated: therefore, there exists no direct perceiver of supersensuous objects;
rather, he who perceives by means of eternal speech, he truly perceives.
It might be argued that the Veda itself, without depending on human activity, will communicate its own meaning to this person.
He states that the consequence of mutual dependence does not arise: "The Veda," and so forth.
"The Veda, being devoid of intention, does not always express its meaning by itself; rather, it depends upon the human explanation, which is like a blind man's staff. (2374)

For the Veda does not, when first heard by one who is ignorant of its conventions, communicate its own meaning; what then does it do? To this he says: "Like a staff taken up by the blind," and so forth. The analysis of the compound is: that which is similar to a staff (*yaṣṭi*) taken up—that is, grasped—by the blind.
To the question, "What is the fault in its being dependent? he says:
"Being drawn by that [desire], it may fall even onto a wrong path," and so forth.
Therefore, it is not logical that the Veda is like light, nor that it has become like an eye;
"it" refers to the Veda.
Thinking "by her," one might fall even into a wrong path due to a masculine interpretation.
Because it reveals a contrary meaning,
that which was stated— "Therefore, one must not entertain any disagreement regarding the Veda, which, like light, is the sole eye for all the world"— is untenable.
With the words "And of that which is independent," etc., he concludes the subject at hand:
and when there is the production of consciousness by that which is independent, it is clear.
"Even its validity cannot be conceived, because it depends upon a person.
(2376) For it has been established that it is not logical for that which is [inherently] capable to produce knowledge by depending on a person.

Granted, let there be the production of knowledge even from that which is capable by depending on a person; nevertheless—the phraseological construction being "even though it produces knowledge by depending on a person, its validity is clearly not conceivable."
The word *api* is displaced; it should be understood immediately after the phrase "provided that it produces knowledge.
Clarifying the meaning of this very point, he says: "In accordance with the object," and so forth.

For validity is indeed established because [the scripture] is the cause of cognition according to reality; however, if it were dependent upon human interpretation, the conception of its being a means of valid cognition would not be sound. "The conception of its being a means of valid cognition would not be sound" means: [it would not be sound].
Furthermore, because it was previously established that he would fall even onto a wrong path while being dragged by her,
it follows that what was stated— "the Veda being established as a means of valid cognition, there is a succession of disciples and teachers"— is [contradicted].
Showing that it is incorrect to claim, "Even if an beginningless [tradition] is postulated, it is fit to be faultless," he says: "In this way," and so forth.

"In this way, since the Veda is not established as a means of valid cognition, even if a beginningless succession of pupils and teachers is postulated, it is not tenable for it to be free from fault. (2378)
Regarding the term "asthita," one should understand that there is an elision of the vowel *a*.
As for why it is not appropriate [to say otherwise], he says: because even a single [moment]...
Since not even a single person among them is considered to possess supersensuous vision, this [tradition], though conceived as beginningless, is therefore merely a succession of the blind.
(2379) If it has indeed become a succession of the blind, what follows? To this he says: "From one blind man to another," and so forth.
Just as a blind man led by another blind man certainly does not find the right path, so too the beginningless conceptualization regarding this [Veda] is fruitless.

As it is stated in the *Śābara-bhāṣya*: "In matters of this kind, the word of a human being does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge, just like the speech of blind men regarding specific forms."

Having thus stated the fault on the assumption that beginninglessness is established through the succession of disciples, he says "from another," etc., demonstrating that even this is not established:
"Manu, Vyāsa, and others were also knowers of the truth of the Veda from another [source]."
There is no means of valid cognition for the claim that this object was not composed by those very [authors], because it is absolutely beyond the senses.
"There is no means of valid cognition" is said because of its extreme transcendence.

It might be argued as follows: it is not because of being the cause of non-erroneous cognition that validity is desired on the basis of authorlessness; rather, [validity arises] from the eternal connection between word and meaning which possesses true referents. And this [connection] occurs when there is authorlessness. To this we reply: even in this case, [the reason] is indeed inconclusive.
For what is the reason for this restriction, that it must possess a true meaning because it is not of human origin?
Even granting that this may be so, he says the following to show that there is indeed a fault:
"Or let its authority arise merely from the eternal connection with a true meaning."
But no one can determine that yoga to be beyond the senses;
for since those objects are beyond the senses, the yoga residing therein is also beyond the senses, and all these men are by their very nature always lacking direct perception [of it].
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has truth as its object and is an eternal relation.

For an eternal relation is postulated; if this were not the cause for the cognition of meaning, then that postulation would be useless, since it possesses no other nature apart from being the generator of the cognition of meaning.
For the function of a relation consists solely in the production of the cognition of an object; how could that which does not perform this function be a relation?

Nor is this [relation] a cause for the cognition of an object by its mere existence; rather, it is so when it is known. Otherwise, cognition would arise from it even for one who has not grasped the convention [of the relation]. Furthermore, it is impossible for anyone to know it, because since the related entities such as heaven (*svarga*) are beyond the senses, the relation itself is likewise beyond the senses.
If it is argued that those who perceive supersensuous objects will know it, he says: "for those who do not see what is beyond the senses," and so forth.
As it has been said: "Therefore, there exists no direct seer of supersensuous objects;
he who sees through the eternal Word, he truly sees.
Thus, those who do not perceive with their own eyes are those who have not seen supersensuous objects.
If it is argued that the Śruti itself will make this known, he says: "This is mine," and so forth.
And he says: "This is my connection with the meaning," yet that Vedic revelation does not exist [in such a way].
Furthermore, a connection with meaning constructed by humans does not differ from [ordinary] human composition.

For the Person of the Veda (Vedapuruṣa)—being exceedingly compassionate, having a mind solely inclined toward merit, and devoted to the welfare of others—does not call out to these venerable Brahmins, saying, "Let this meaning of mine be grasped," and then, like a generous donor, personally hand over his own meaning to the Brahmins.
He says, "Then they will imagine it for themselves," beginning with the words *naraklṛpta* (2384),
and he demonstrates that very non-difference with the words *tadyathā* (2385), etc.

For example, just as the falsity of a human [statement] is suspected by people, why should that same suspicion not apply even to what is imagined [by them]? (2385) Surely one might think, "I shall understand the meaning without confusion"; yet the person who is the cause of confusion has been discarded. Just as words used by people themselves become confused, so too do the meanings devised by them—what difference is there in this case?
Thus, it may be suspected that there is a perversion.

It was previously established that, because the Veda lacks authority, the postulation of a succession of disciples and teachers is futile; now, even granting that it possesses authority by way of an eternal relationship, he demonstrates that in either case the postulation of a succession of disciples and teachers remains futile— beginning with the words "Even if authority were established," and so forth.

Therefore, even though the Veda remains authoritative, this beginningless succession of disciples and teachers, though imagined [as such], has become a "blind tradition" (andha-paramparā). Regarding what was said— "Could there not be doubt even regarding that which is imagined by men?"— the opponent here shows the impossibility of such doubt, starting with the words "But surely," etc.
Surely, a cognition regarding heaven and the like arises free from doubt and other defects,
just like the unshakable perceptual cognition produced by statements concerning the *agnihotra* sacrifice;
how then could the Veda, by producing such [a cognition], not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)?
For no one understands a doubtful meaning from this statement.
"Āreka" means doubt; by the word "ādi" (and so forth), error is included.

As it is stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya: "And from this injunction, 'One desiring heaven should sacrifice,' one does not understand anything doubtful—such as whether heaven exists or does not exist—and that which is understood with certainty cannot be false;
for that cognition which, having arisen, is subsequently destroyed by the realization 'this is not so' is a false cognition."
And this [scriptural teaching] does not undergo reversal in another place or at another time; therefore, it is non-false.

Otherwise, why would your mind—not even as you directly experience a massive mass of fire whose interior is blocked by a spreading profusion of bursting sparks—not be tossed about on the swing of doubt?

Consequently, not even a single means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) would exist for you; such is the intention of the opponent. The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: whatever cognition is free from doubt and error is an object of the conventional usage of "valid cognition" for discerning persons, just like the cognition that causes the determination of fire by one whose mind is unerring and who seeks its effects, such as burning or cooking; and the cognition arising from sentences such as "the Agnihotra [is to be performed]" is likewise free from doubt and error. This is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
[Otherwise, it] would have no basis.
The connection is with the word "pramāṇatām" (the state of being a means of valid cognition); [it refers to] "forming that [state]" as one's conviction.
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "Not so" (naivam), etc.
It is not so, because doubt arises [regarding them] just as it does regarding contradictory or irrelevant statements; for discerning people do not perceive any difference whatsoever among these.
Indeed, the ascertainment of existence or non-existence is not possible with respect to that which is beyond the senses.
If it is argued that certainty arises from the Vedic statement, why would it not arise from another [statement] of a different kind?
(2390) If the meaning of the reason is that a cognition free from doubt and the like arises for discerning persons from the Vedic statement, then the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For instance, just as there is equal doubt for discerning persons regarding the contrary statement "heaven does not result from the *agnihotra*," so too is there equal doubt regarding the statement "heaven results from the *agnihotra*. This is because, in the case of supersensible objects, there is no means of determining existence or non-existence, and because the correspondence with the actual state of affairs is unperceivable in both cases.
The suffix *vati* is applied to the word ending in the locative case (*viparītānyavākyavat*), meaning "like a contrary or other statement.
Now, it might be argued: "If certainty arises from the Vedic statement itself, what is the need to seek another cause? To this, he says: "Of a different kind," and so forth.
A conviction that determines a meaning contrary to the meaning of the Veda arises from "another," that is,
from a human source.
What is it that does not occur? It certainly does occur;

that is to say, in that case, even that [subsequent cognition] would be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because at that time there is no difference between the two, as neither is perceived to be sublated.

If it is argued that an unshakable conviction arises among discerning Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), and therefore the reason is not "unestablished" (*asiddha*), [the author] shows that even if it were so and the reason were not unestablished, its "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntikatā*) remains unavoidable: "Among the Vedic scholars... and so forth;
for this unshakable cognition indeed arises among the Vedic scholars.

For those whose intellects are overwhelmed by faith, that [certainty] is equal to that of others derived from other sources. For instance, an unshakable conviction arises in the minds of the Buddhists and others regarding the occurrence of suffering in states of woe resulting from sacrifices involving the slaughter of living beings. (2391–2392)

And no sublation of this cognition is observed at present, anywhere, or at any time; if it were to be suspected, that [possibility of sublation] would be equal even in the case of Vedic statements. (2393) That is so.
"Unshakable intelligence" refers to that of others, such as the Buddhists and so forth.
The phrase "from another" means that from this statement— that suffering arises from the misfortune based on the killing of living beings in sacrifice—
it demonstrates exactly this; the passage beginning with "for thus" and so forth is easy to understand.
Furthermore, he demonstrates the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the Veda’s lack of human authorship with the verse beginning *narecchā* and so forth:
"If the Veda were to reveal its own meaning by itself, independently of conventions dependent on human will, then it would be appropriate for it to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (2394)
For at that time, even when its own object is being misrepresented by those whose intellects are overwhelmed by defects such as delusion and pride, it does not abandon that object;
because it swiftly produces a cognition directed precisely toward that [object].
However, it is not accepted that this [word] illuminates a different object intended by persons.
For if there were dependence upon human desire, its illumination would not differ from that of human composition;
for its manifestation would then be dependent on that [desire], and thus it could even be erroneous.

The collective meaning is as follows: because of the autonomy of human desire, the Veda—which depends upon conventions governed by that [desire]—would not reveal its own intended meaning, as there would be no restriction on what it reveals. However, when the Veda conveys a meaning independently of that [human desire], it is then fit to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it generates the comprehension of its own meaning more swiftly than by disregarding human interpretation; for even when being interpreted otherwise, it does not abandon the revelation of its own meaning by its very nature, just like the eye and other sense organs.
The term *ākhyāyamāna* means "being interpreted."
*Aram* means quickly, that is to say, instantaneously.
Even that [convention] is inverted; it is merely human desire.

Granted that there may indeed be an inherent connection between words and their objects due to the Veda being non-human in origin, even so, your desired conclusion is not established; thus, demonstrating the inconclusiveness [of the reason], he says: "Moreover," and so forth.
Furthermore, just as the truthfulness of a non-human [text] is accepted as its natural state, why is its falsity not likewise suspected? (2398)
For it is indeed true that [the cognition] is true because it is the cause of the awakening to a true object by itself;
likewise, its being the cause of the awakening to falsity is also suspected to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
"Prākṛta" means existing in the *prakṛti* (nature); the meaning is "inherent."

Showing that one should simply accept the fact of being composed by an authoritative person (*pramāṇabhūtapuruṣa*) as the cause of the Veda’s validity, rather than its "uncreatedness" which indicates dullness, he says: "Furthermore," and so forth.
Furthermore, if you are indeed insistent that the Veda is a means of valid cognition,
then let effort be directed toward its having a faultless author and so forth;
for this [Veda] was composed by a faultless author and revealed by faultless revealers.
And it shines forth in this world as the means for knowing the true nature of reality;
by the word "and so forth" in the phrase "because it has a faultless author," the status of being a [reliable] expounder is included.

Now, [the author] asks: "How is the validity established even for that which has been explained by those free from faults? He says: "For those endowed with wisdom, compassion, and so forth," and so on;
for indeed, [the teachings] of those endowed with wisdom, compassion, and so forth are well-ascertained.
Even human speech is "true" when it is the cause of knowledge corresponding to reality.
As Śabarasvāmin has stated: "As for that which is worldly speech, if it comes from a trustworthy person or concerns an object of the senses, it is indeed non-false; thus, it is 'true speech'."
Furthermore, demonstrating that the quality of being non-human-made (*apauruṣeyatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "Not made by man," and so forth.
It is not the case that something produces knowledge of reality simply because it is not man-made;
for it is observed that forest fires and the like serve as causes even for false cognition.

Indeed, the error regarding objects does not arise solely from the imposition of human defects, since even forest fires and such, which are devoid of human agency, generate erroneous cognitions regarding blue lotuses and other things.
A forest fire is a fire that has occurred spontaneously through the friction of bamboo and other materials; this is to be understood here as the subject of deviation (vyabhicāra).

However, that fire which is produced by humans through the rubbing of fire-sticks and so forth cannot be considered non-human (apauruṣeya), because such a thing is impossible; therefore, the sense is that there is no deviation from the logical reason (hetu) in that case.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), mirages and so forth are included.
[The author] demonstrates that very fact of being the cause of false cognition with the words beginning "red," and so on.
For indeed, a red blue lotus is accepted [as existing] when there is light from fire;
if it is argued that fire and so forth [are not causes] because they are produced (*kṛtakatvāt*), then that reason is not tenable.
(2404) Furthermore, it might be said that we have not described "non-human authorship" (*apauruṣeyatva*) alone as the reason.
What then?

[The answer is that] "being uncreated" (*akṛtakatva*) is the qualification; or rather, the mention of "human origin" (*pauruṣeya*) is intended as an indication of being uncreated. Thus, anticipating the response of an opponent who thinks that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) due to fire caused by a forest conflagration—which is created—he says: "Of fire and so forth," etc.
Its cause— the cause of false cognition—
is refuted by the passage beginning with "Is it producedness? (verse 2404).
Or rather, is the artificiality of objects the very basis for false cognition?

For if this were so, smoke would not be a correct indicator of fire at all. A qualification is [valid] only when it excludes the reason from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*); otherwise, if one could obtain certainty through any qualification whatsoever applied to the reason, then there would be no inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika-hetu*) at all, since a qualification could easily be found everywhere by virtue of being bound to one's own will.

Furthermore, the qualification of "being uncreated" does not necessarily eliminate the Veda's status as a cause of false cognition; for instance, if it were established that being created is invariably a cause of false cognition, then its absence might occasionally eliminate that [falsity]. One might argue that this is indeed established; to this, he says: "For in this way," and so forth.
If being produced (*kṛtakatā*) were the basis for false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), then it would follow that non-producedness (*akṛtakatā*) is the cause of correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*).

This is because it is impossible for two mutually contradictory states, such as correct and false cognition, to have a single cause; for it is not logical that fire, which possesses the quality of hot touch, should be the cause of cold.
Consequently, smoke, by virtue of being produced, could not be the cause for the accurate perception of fire. (2405)
Furthermore, it might be argued that it was not established that being produced is the cause of false cognition alone and not of anything else;
rather,
what was intended was that in the case of false cognition, being produced is the sole basis and nothing else— thus, its having any other cause is what is being negated.
However, there is no negation of the fact that correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) has a produced cause (*kṛtaka-hetuka*);
nor is it intended that everything produced is, without distinction, a cause of false cognition (*mithyā-jñāna*),
such that— due to their mutual contradiction— correct and false cognitions would imply by necessity that what is the opposite of the produced is the cause of correct cognition.

However, because that which is produced (*kṛtaka*) is manifold, some things are causes of false cognition, such as jaundice (*kāmalā*) and the like, while others are causes of correct cognition, such as the unimpaired collection of sense-faculties and so forth.

Otherwise, since some produced thing like snow is observed to be a cause for the sensation of cold, one would have to postulate by implication a non-produced cause for the sensation of heat, which is contrary to cold;
yet this is not the case.

Therefore, since it has not been denied that a produced thing can serve as a cause for correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*), one might suspect that smoke indeed serves as the basis for correct cognition. Anticipating this, he says: "And thus, even though it is non-human... and so forth.
"And thus, even though it is non-human, the Veda stands as the basis for correct cognition; therefore, its postulation [as being human-made] is entirely in vain. (2406)

For if the state of being produced were the basis for both correctness and falsity, then that [state of being produced], upon its removal, would remove both false and correct cognition; thus, the Veda’s status as a cause of correct cognition would not be established by virtue of its being unproduced, because that [unproduced nature] is not the basis for it. Consequently, the qualification would be redundant, and the reason would remain inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Alternatively, it might be argued that by the phrase "by virtue of not being made by a person," the aforementioned reason—characterized by both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatirekin*)—is not indicated; rather, this is simply an application of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) alone.

For just as falsity—the opposite of the probandum—is pervaded by "being produced," which is the opposite of the reason, since falsity is observed only in human compositions; and thus, where there is present "not being produced"—which is contradictory to and excludes that which pervades falsity—then, through this contradiction, the pervader (falsity) is excluded by "not being produced," and consequently, the exclusion of the pervaded (falsity) is established by implication. Therefore, the conclusion that "what is not produced has a true object" follows by implication even without a positive concomitance (*anvaya*); hence, demonstrating the positive concomitance is redundant.
This is indeed true.
If the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the opposite [of the probandum] and the reason were established, it would be so;
however, it is not established.

For instance, if there were a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) regarding the reason in the case of the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyavipakṣa*), then there would be a pervasion between the two opposites; but that does not exist.
Nor is the non-existence [of something] established by mere non-perception, because of the possibility of deviation.
One might argue that since falsity is observed in the "produced" (kṛtaka), which is the opposite of the "unproduced" (akṛtaka), its absence in the unproduced is established by implication;
but this is incorrect.

For it is not possible to establish the absence of something in one place by observing it elsewhere; indeed, even a single property may be seen to pervade two contradictory [classes] through the observation of its pervader.

For instance, the single property of impermanence is seen to pervade both that which follows immediately upon effort and its opposite; yet, just because impermanence is not observed in that which follows immediately upon effort, it does not follow that it is absent in that which does not follow immediately upon effort.

Furthermore—if falsity were pervaded by "being produced" merely on the grounds that it has been observed in that case, then truthfulness would likewise be pervaded by it, since truthfulness too is observed in some human compositions; consequently, upon the cessation of "being produced," truthfulness would also cease just as falsity does, and thus the fact that [the Veda] possesses a true meaning would not be established by its being non-human. Enough of this.

Thus, having demonstrated at length the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the reason—"that which is free from the defects of causes for falsity"—which is implied by the phrase "because it is not made by man" (or "the uncreated"), or by "authorlessness" (*apauruṣeyatva*) as indicated by that [phrase], or by that very term itself; and desiring now to demonstrate its non-establishment (*asiddhatā*), he says in conclusion: "Therefore," and so forth. "Therefore, the proof of authorlessness, manifestation, and permanence, as well as the connection with eternal words and meanings, has been described in vain. (2407)
Even though that [object] exists, its status as a cause for knowledge of reality is not accepted; this has been explained in detail immediately above.
Therefore, we have no great concern with refuting this very point.

For who would prohibit that which is not useful to the subject at hand? "Apauruṣeyatva" (authorlessness), "vyakti" (manifestation), and "nityatva" (eternality)—this is the compound *apauruṣeyatvavyaktinityatvāni*. "Sādhana" means that by which something is established; it is a logical reason (*hetu*), as in the sense of "that by which [the probandum] is proven."
And that [reason] has been stated previously as being of various kinds;
"in that" refers to such qualities as being authorless (*apauruṣeya*).
"Of this [Veda]" means "it is accepted."
"It arises extensively" means in detail.
Regarding the phrase "the refutation of this":

since it has already been demonstrated that even if defects such as the lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) are raised, the intended object is not established, then raising those defects would be irrelevant to the subject at hand.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "yathārtha" and so forth:

for it is the status of scripture as the cause of knowledge that accords with reality which is the subject under discussion here; and it has already been established that this is proven even without [the scripture] being composed by a person. || 2410 ||
Regarding the term *āhopuruṣikā*:
here, a certain [matter] is stated in brief, so that those of subtle intellect may discern how the various destinies (*gati*) are dispersed by this [treatise]. (2411)
"One who has the conceit 'Oh, what a man I am! is an *ahopuruṣa*; the state of being such is *āhopuruṣikā*.
By the rule [Pāṇini 5.1.133] regarding the *manojñādi* group, the suffix *vuñ* is applied, and it refers specifically to conceit (*abhimāna*)."
Intellect (*dhī*) is itself vision (*dṛk*); because of their common nature, that [vision] is "vision. Those for whom the intellect-vision is subtle are described as such.
Regarding what was stated—"because it is inaccessible to the five [senses]," etc.—he says there: "of the means of valid cognition," and so forth.
"Even by the cessation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the object of cognition (*prameya*) does not cease,

because they [the means of cognition] do not possess the status of being a pervading cause (*vyāpaka-hetu*) with respect to it. By this, he demonstrates the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the fundamental reason (*mūla-hetu*).
For it is the pervader, whether as an essential nature (*svabhāva*) or a cause (*kāraṇa*), that, when being excluded, excludes the pervaded (*vyāpya*) or the effect (*kārya*),
because these two are restricted to it by way of identity (*tādātmya*) and origination (*tadutpatti*);
for if they were to occur even in the absence of that [pervader], their status as effect and pervaded would be untenable.

However, it is not possible for those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be either pervaders (*vyāpaka*) or causes (*hetu*) with respect to all objects. To explain: there is no pervasion by them because an object remote in space, time, or nature can exist even without a means of valid cognition; nor is the means of valid cognition the cause for that very reason, since the means of valid cognition itself is an effect of the object of cognition (*prameya*). Furthermore, an effect, when being negated, does not necessarily negate its mere cause, as such a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is observed.
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is neither a cause nor a pervader to be a negator, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, it is established that the absence of the mere means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is inconclusive (*vyabhicārī*) with respect to the absence of the mere object of valid cognition (*prameya*), which is the probandum. 2412

Clarifying that very same inconclusiveness by demonstrating its possibility in the counter-example (vipakṣa), he says: "Though unapproachable by those five," and so forth: "Even though the author of the Veda is not apprehended by those five [means of knowledge], he is not [thereby] understood to be non-existent, just as in the case of stories and the like whose authors are unknown. (2413)

The word "tat" means "therefore"; thus, the connection with the distant term is: "[He is] the agent," even though he is inaccessible [to the senses] through the five [means of knowledge], according to scripture (*śruti*).
Those stories and so forth for which an unconscious agent is stated are referred to as such;
subsequently, a *karmadhāraya* compound is formed with the word "story" (*ākhyāyikā*) and so on, and then the suffix *vati* is applied to the word ending in the genitive case.
Now, with the words "But even if," etc., he raises the objection that the reason is unestablished because it is subject to deviation:
"But even if their author were inferred on the grounds of their being meaningful or having distinct meanings, why could this not also be the case for the Veda? (2414)
Regarding the phrase "of these":
why is it that even from the hearing (*śruti*) of narratives (*ākhyāyikā*) and so forth, it is not likewise [the case]?

In the same way, why is an author not inferred for the Veda as well, on account of its possessing meaning and having distinct meanings? Since there is no difference [between the two cases], the lack of evidence [for an author] is unestablished.
Furthermore, there are two possible positions: either the cessation of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding all sentient beings, or the cessation [of such means] regarding oneself.

Showing that in the first position the reason (*hetu*) is "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*), and in the second it is "inconclusive" (*anaikāntikatā*), he says: "By all sentient beings," and so forth;
however, the fact of being unknowable by all sentient beings is at times doubtful.
For it may even be suspected that someone knows [the truth] through some measure of pride;

yet by that very fact, all living beings dwelling within the three worlds are clearly and entirely incapable of definitively ascertaining this [truth], for they are themselves unbounded in every respect. (2415–2416)
However, the fact that [the object] is not being perceived by oneself is inconclusive; for instance, the absence of that [object] is not ascertained by the mental constructs of other persons.
(2417) "This" [refers to the aforementioned].

By stating "it is not known by all beings that the Veda has an author," and so forth with the words "for instance" (*tathāhi*) and so on, [the author] supports the very point that [the reason] is inconclusive (*vyabhicāritā*) due to the mental constructs (*saṅkalpa*) of students and others belonging to other persons.
Regarding what was stated— that the agent is, for one thing, unperceived— he says "And the students... and so forth, in order to demonstrate the lack of proof for that claim.
The students of the Vedas are considered by direct perception to be their authors;
for they cannot logically be mere manifestors, since the manifestation of eternal things is impossible.
(2418) If it is accepted that no author whatsoever is observed, then because the students are indeed observed, the [reason] fails most clearly due to being unestablished (*asiddha*).

Now, if it is maintained that no original author (ādikartṛ) is observed, even then the reason remains "doubtful-unestablished" (saṃdigdhāsiddha), because it is possible that [an author] was seen by someone at some time. Furthermore, it might be argued that the reciters (adhyetāraḥ) are not established as authors; rather, they are manifesters (vyaktāraḥ). To this he says: "Not indeed," and so forth.
The word "they" refers to the students;
and how the manifestation of eternal things is impossible, he will demonstrate later.
If it is asked how even impermanent things such as a jar can be manifestors, [the answer is:
true;
in that case as well, no manifestor is possible.
If it is asked, "How then are lamps and the like perceived as manifestors? [the answer is:
for in that case, the lamp and so forth are indeed producers, since they produce a jar that is capable of generating consciousness.
In the world, something is recognized as a "manifestor" (vyañjaka) for the purpose of making known a specific generative nature;
however, no such manifestor is possible for the Veda, because its nature is unmanifest, unarisen, and devoid of prior or posterior states.

Granted that there may be a manifestor of the eternal; nevertheless, showing that this [manifestor] does not differ from a producer, he says: "Of those whose nature is perceptible, their emergence occurs upon its operation; if they existed even prior to that, perception would follow as a logical consequence. (2419)
Indeed, it is not logical for that which effects nothing to be a manifestor, because that would lead to an over-extension [of the term];
if it were to effect something, its status as a producer (janaka) would necessarily be admitted,
since the production of a produced particularity is characterized by the arising of a new intrinsic nature (svabhāvāntara).
Regarding the phrase "of those whose nature is perceivable":

it might be argued that even prior [to their manifestation], the Vedas existed with a perceivable nature; therefore, how could their existence be possible through the operation of those [causes]? To this, he says: "Of them," and so forth.
"Of them" refers to those Vedas whose nature is perceivable.
He establishes this with the verse beginning "tatkārya":

"The Veda is determined to be capable of producing its effects, such as linguistic usage and so forth, because it exists when that [Veda] is operative, just as a seed and the like [exist] when there is a sprout and so forth. (2420)

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever comes into being when there is the operation of X is fit to be designated by the conventional usage of "the effect of X," just as a sprout and the like, coming into being when there is the operation of a seed and so forth, is the effect of that [seed]. Since the Veda possesses a nature that is perceived when there is the operation of a reciter, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). "Conventional usage" (*vyavahāra*) refers to the performance characterized by rejection and acquisition;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of cognition and verbal designation is intended.
The reason is not unestablished, because it would follow that [the effect] would be perceived even prior [to its production];
nor is it inconclusive, because there is no other cause for the conventional usage of "effect.

Regarding what was stated, beginning with "the relationship of which has never been perceived before," he says: "Because they consist of a sequence of phonemes (*vyañjana*), like dramas, narratives (*ākhyāyikā*), and so forth, inference also understands the human authorship of the Vedas. (2421)

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: that which has the nature of a sequence of phonemes (vyañjana) is of human origin, such as plays, narratives, and the like; and the Veda has the nature of a sequence of phonemes. This is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
The reason is not unestablished (asiddha), because phonemes manifest only in a sequential order.
Showing that [the reason] is not inconclusive (anaikāntika), he says: "Otherwise," and so forth.
Otherwise, there would be no sequential form [of manifestation] due to [the word's] eternity and its pervasiveness;
nor is there a sequence of manifestation, because manifestation is impossible if [the word] is eternal. (2422)
"Otherwise" means that if it were not of human origin, but rather its eternity and omnipresence were described, then there would be no sequence.
For instance, a sequence produced by time— as in the case of a seed, sprout, and creeper— is not tenable here, because all [phonemes], being eternal, would exist simultaneously.

Nor is it [the case that the universal is perceived] due to spatial location, as in the case of a row of ants, because all [individuals], being omnipresent, abide in the same single spatial location of space;
nor is it due to manifestation, because manifestation is impossible for that which is eternal, since no excellence can be imparted to it.

Regarding what was stated—that even scripture (*āgama*) does not establish that [the self exists] because there is no such thing as "created" or "uncreated," and so forth—the author here replies: "Of scripture," etc.
Since the validity of scripture, of analogy (*upamā*), and of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) has already been refuted previously, it is not appropriate to introduce them here. (2423)
"Prohibited" refers to those [objections] in the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaparīkṣā*).

Regarding what was stated concerning scripture (*āgama*), analogy (*upamāna*), and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)— namely, "for the purpose of removing [the charge of] invalidity," and so forth.
To this, he says: "For the purpose of removing invalidity," and so forth.
That authorlessness of the Veda which is desired for the sake of removing its invalidity must also be established by means of proofs, because it is a real entity. (2424)
He explains how that [validity] can be an objective reality (vastutva), stating "from scripture" and so forth:
This independence of scripture is indeed accepted because it does not depend upon human activity;
and that [independence] is either a property residing in the object or an essential nature of the object of such a kind. (2425)

By the term "authorlessness" (*apauruṣeyatā*), the independence of the Veda is expressed; for it is used in connection with the sense that "the Veda is a means of valid knowledge precisely because it is independent of human activity. Otherwise, what excellence would be established merely by the negation of authorship?
And he shows that this non-authorship is a property of the thing (*vastudharma*) for those who hold that the distinction between property and property-bearer (*dharmadharmibheda*) is ultimate;

but in reality, it is simply the nature of the thing itself which is so designated when there is a desire to know it by excluding other distinctions. Thus he says: "or the essence of the thing," meaning "of such a kind."
Regarding the independent [argument] (svatantra) stated as "for the sake of establishing the position of existence," and so forth, he says in response: "The position of existence," and so forth.
To establish the side of existence, it is said: even when that proof has been refuted, non-existence does not establish itself;
for even when there is a proof for its existence, there would be no certainty of its existence.

But there is no certainty [of non-existence] based solely on the cessation of that [cognition], because even when means of knowledge have ceased, the non-existence of the object is not established. Therefore, for both [parties], the proof of the thesis would be limited to this much: "it does not exist. (2427–2428)

For when the means of proof (*sādhana*) employed for the sake of ascertaining a given object is refuted, there would merely be the absence of ascertainment regarding that object; however, this does not entail the cessation of the object itself, since it has been established that even upon the cessation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the object of cognition (*prameya*) does not cease—this being so because [the means of proof] is subject to the alternatives of being either a cause or a pervader. Thus it is said: "it is excluded."
When this has been cast [into the argument], it is appropriate to say only this much: "there is no establishment of the thesis for either side";
thus, the word *iti* should be supplied.
And that "it does not exist" should be understood immediately after this [statement].

Confirming this very point by means of an example, he says: "Not because of formlessness," meaning that it is not [the case] because of formlessness, just as sound [is not the probans], due to its deviation with respect to pleasure and so forth.
Even when this has been said, the perishability of sound is not established.

For instance, when a proponent of eternality, desiring to prove the substantial eternality of sound, employs the argument "Sound is eternal because it is incorporeal, like space," and the opponent refutes that proof of substantial eternality by stating, "It is not logical that sound is eternal because of its incorporeality, since [the reason] is inconclusive due to [the case of] pleasure and so forth," the impermanence of sound is certainly not thereby established. The same applies here; this is the sense.
The word "yathā" (just as) is to be understood as occurring out of its expected position.

The phrase "nityaḥ siddhyati" (it is established as eternal) should be supplied either immediately after "ukte 'pi" (even though stated) or immediately after "śabdaḥ" (sound), or it should be understood as an elliptical usage of a single part of the sentence, like the word "Bhīma" [standing for Bhīmasena].

As for what was said regarding the passage beginning with "of the prior and the posterior," namely "that which was stated by others as the proof for the two extremes of the prior and the posterior": [this refers to that very point].
Even when that [Vedic authority] is refuted, these proponents of the Veda remain unsuccessful;
"tat" means "therefore."
"Those who have not accomplished their aim," because their own position has not been established.
