Regarding what was stated— "eternalness is indeed intended [to be established] by way of being uncreated and indestructible," and so forth— he says in response:
"If eternalness is intended [to be established] by way of being uncreated and indestructible," and so on.
Since it is identical even in the case of that which is indefinable (nirupākhya) by virtue of being a mere negation,
eternal existence is not real, just as it is not real in the case of a sky-flower;
likewise, its authority is not established in the Veda either.

In this regard, there are two possible conceptualizations: is eternity intended by way of non-producedness and non-destruction in the form of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or in the form of relative exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? In the first case, because of the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to things such as a sky-lotus, the Veda’s possession of real, substantial eternity is not established;
for even though the production and destruction of a sky-lotus are negated, its possession of real, substantial eternity is not thereby established.
Likewise, since this is also the case with the Veda, the reason [adduced] is inconclusive;
consequently, its validity would be non-existent, just like that of a sky-flower.
Showing that [the reason] is also unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "Because of being produced," etc.;
even the negation of being produced and being perishable is not established.
Since it is stated that [the means of proof] has ceased, its permanence is not established; for "it" refers to that which has been refuted as having ceased.
Now, if the second position is held, then it should not have been said that "those two, being of the nature of non-existence, do not depend upon their own means of proof";
he demonstrates this with the words beginning "by those which consist of exclusion" (paryudāsātmakābhyām), and so forth.
If permanence is intended by means of these two [reasons] which consist of exclusion (paryudāsa), then those two depend upon their own proof because they consist of the nature of that [permanence].
That permanence which is of the nature of a real entity (vastu) cannot be established by those two.
When both of the two opposing positions have been refuted, that proof is established by itself; this is easily understood. (2435) [Note: This corresponds to verse 2434.]

Regarding what was stated [in verse 2434], "He who asserts the falsity of the meaning of Vedic statements by means of inference," and so forth, he replies with the words beginning "viniścitatrirūpa" (the three characteristics being ascertained), and so on.
"And regarding that proof which has been demonstrated as possessing the three well-ascertained characteristics,
even your father could never possibly refute it.
(2436) "Has been demonstrated" means...

In the examination of inference, that which arises from the logical marks (liṅga) of essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-perception (anupalambha) cannot be refuted, because it is dependent upon real entities (vastu);
nor can the alteration of the essential nature of a real entity be effected by anything, since such alteration is characterized by the production of a different essential nature.
Furthermore, by producing another intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nothing at all would have been done to that [original thing], because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Therefore, whatever object is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be sublated by anything; for otherwise, if that which conforms to the definition of valid cognition were subject to sublation, its very definition would be undermined, and due to a lack of confidence everywhere, that [cognition] would not be valid anywhere.
2436 This very point he demonstrates with the words "for it does not perish," and so forth:
"For that Person who is declared in the Veda as 'he does not perish,' and of this [Person]..."
The sublation [of the opponent's position] by means of inference has been clearly established regarding selflessness (nairātmya).

Furthermore, whatever else such as genus (jāti) and so forth was mentioned, that too has been proven to be sublated therein; and that inference, having its logical connection (pratibandha) made known, is the prior sublater. || 2437-2438 ||

Thus it is stated in the Veda; having introduced the subject with "This very one is the Self," they declare: "He is indestructible, for he is not destroyed. And it is further said: "Verily, this Self is indestructible, O Maitreyī, its nature is such that it is not subject to annihilation. "Not destroyed" means "indestructible," which signifies that it is eternal.
The word "are" is a term of address;

by the phrase "jāti and so forth," the inclusion of qualities (*guṇa*), substances (*dravya*), actions (*karman*), and so on is intended. Furthermore, how that *jāti* and so forth is sublated by valid cognition has been established in the "Examination of the Six Categories" (*Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*).
And that inference which subverts the self is also one whose necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been made known in the section on selflessness (Nairātmyādhikāra),

Now, one might object: "If that [Veda] is being established as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how can it be sublated here by me? Or, if even a means of valid cognition were to be sublated, why would inference not likewise be sublated by it?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Of that," and so forth—"Who, being a fool, would conceive of a sublation of that [inference], which is bound to the real nature of things (*vastu*)?"
Either by means of a mere word, which is insubstantial, or by means of a cognition arising from that [word]—
of that inference.
Since a word is based solely on the speaker’s intention, it has no necessary connection with the object to be known; therefore, it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that object.

Inference (*anumā*), however, arises by the power of a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is connected to the object through identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*); thus, it is connected to that real object and is alone the means of valid cognition. Consequently, it is this [inference] that serves as the sublater when it occurs in relation to that [object].

2439. Now, he demonstrates that if a word were a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to an object even when it is not connected [to it], then there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*): "even from the speech of a person."
Why do you not accept that even the cognition arising from the words of a human being regarding supersensible matters is equal to perception?

Why would there not be validity for the statement "heaven does not result from the Agnihotra sacrifice" as well, since there is no distinction between the two cases in terms of the absence of any obstruction [to truth]?
Showing that very same lack of distinction, he says: "Because of independence from examples," and so forth; "and because of non-perception, there is also an absence of defects."
If it is suspected that even this [Vedic cognition] is subject to sublation because it relies upon human beings,
then this suspicion does not cease even in the case of the Veda;
for its status as a cause of false cognition would be inherent in it.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even if no fault is perceived at that time, nevertheless, because [the Veda] rests upon a person, such a fault is possible. This applies equally to the Veda as well; for just as its truthfulness is considered natural, so too its falsity could be considered possible. Thus, there is no distinction whatsoever.

Regarding what was stated, "my [word] is not authoritative," and so forth, he demonstrates that this can indeed be asserted even regarding a human-authored statement such as "heaven does not result from the *agnihotra* sacrifice": "My [word] is not authoritative," etc.; even while a word conveys its meaning, it cannot be said by a person out of mere malice, nor can it be said by one who is virtuous. (2443)

The meaning of the sentence is this: the statement "Heaven does not result from the *agnihotra*" is a human utterance (*pauruṣeya-śabda*); even though it conveys a meaning, one cannot say, out of mere malice toward me, the Mīmāṃsaka, "This is not a means of valid knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
By this, he states that both human and non-human [utterances] are equally the basis for cognition regarding an object that is entirely beyond the senses (*atyanta-parokṣa*).
Consequently, since they are equal in being the basis for cognition, the claim that validity belongs only to the non-human [Veda] and not to the other is devoid of reason.
Nor can it be said that falsity is suspected only in those [scriptures] based on a person because defects reside in persons, but not in those that are non-personal (apauruṣeya),
for even in non-personal [scriptures], the possibility of being a cause for a cognition of false objects is conceivable.
He demonstrates this very point: "Thus, regarding things beyond the senses...

[The verse continues: "Thus, with respect to all words concerning supersensible matters, their relative strength and weakness are equal; why then, for what reason here, is there this partiality toward only one among them? (2444)
"All" refers to that which is produced by a person;
"in one place alone" means...
Regarding what was stated [in verse 2444], "Even for one who is hostile... and so forth, he says in response: "What has just been mentioned," and so on.
"The wise declare that the principle just mentioned is the cause for the Vedas' lack of authority; therefore, these [wise ones] would be speakers of truth.
Regarding the phrase "just mentioned":
"Because a word functions solely according to [the speaker's] intention and thus lacks any necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with the actual object," so say the wise— the Buddhists.

As stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "The cognition regarding the words of the Veda is indeed perceptual; and inference does not become a valid means of knowledge when it contradicts perception. Furthermore, as for that which was said—"For an injunction (*codanā*) is able to make known objects such as those past, present, future, subtle, hidden, and remote, whereas no other sense organ can do so"—all of this is refuted by this very [argument], because all of this is equally applicable even to a human statement.

Regarding what was stated concerning "retention, study, and exposition," and so forth, he says: "By those whose minds have been rendered dull by the meditation on the Veda produced by false attachment...
it is no wonder at all that the cause of falsehood remains unknown. (2446)
For no fault whatsoever is perceived by the Persians and others, who are devoted to such customs and are ever deceitful, regarding the marriage of their mothers and similar acts.

Furthermore, that study of the Veda has arisen from false attachment; thus, it is a compound of the third case (instrumental), meaning "rendered dull by that [study] taken together with" [false attachment].
And meditation (*ādhyāna*) consists of sequential reflection;
for, due to false attachment, one fails to perceive even an existing defect,
just as the Persians and others [fail to see the fault] regarding the marriage of their mothers and so forth— thus, there is nothing surprising in this.
Regarding what was stated, namely, "Furthermore, as for the permanence of sound," and so forth, he replies with the verse beginning "perception" (pratyakṣa), etc.
Perceptual recognition has already been refuted;
furthermore, because it is erroneous and conceptual, there can be no certainty regarding permanence [of sound] based upon it.

(2448) For the definition of perception is "free from conceptual construction and non-erroneous," and recognition is not free from conceptual construction, since it proceeds by delineating the form of a word in the manner: "This is that very same thing."
Nor is it non-erroneous, because it involves a synthesis of the identity between what was previously seen and what is presently occurring;

for that which was previously seen is not the very same thing that is seen later, since a sequential cognition cannot arise from a non-sequential cause. Indeed, an effect is characterized by its arising from something; if that which does not occasionally arise has its cause complete, why would the effects be delayed?
Furthermore, since that which is eternal cannot be assisted by anything else, no dependence upon other factors is possible;

therefore, the cognitions arising from it would have to occur simultaneously. The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: whenever something has its entire causal complex complete, it necessarily occurs at that time, just as visual cognition occurs when the full assembly of causes such as the eye and so forth is present.
Furthermore, the cognitions produced by words such as "cow" and so forth occur in all states due to causes that produce error; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Therefore, it has already been established in the previous examination of stable entities that recognition is not proven to be perception, because it is erroneous and conceptual (*savikalpaka*).

Furthermore, demonstrating that recognition is not established as occurring everywhere by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), he says: "And the cognition [of sound] mostly has an excluded form, because one observes: 'This was uttered by Śuka,' and 'This was uttered by Śārikā. (2449)
If you argue that this [perception] is due to the difference in manifestors (*vyañjaka*), we shall explain the refutation of manifestation (*vyakti*).
Furthermore, by this very logic of yours, all this would become one;
consequently, there would be no manifestor whatsoever, nor anything to be manifested (*vyaṅgya*).
For when [the object] is one and undivided, the conceptualization of difference is contradicted.
(2451) These words are of human origin, and these others are not made by humans;
even this distinction of yours would not exist if it were dependent upon recognition. (2452)

For when a sound is uttered by parrots, starlings, and the like, there arises a cognition that excludes one another based on the determination of distinct objects, such as "this was uttered by the starling" and "this [was uttered] by the parrot. Thus, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not established in all cases.

Furthermore, if it should be argued that this mutually exclusive cognition regarding the utterances of parrots and others arises due to the difference in the manifestors (*vyañjaka*), this too is untenable, because the existence of a manifestor will be refuted later.
He states this very point in the passage beginning with "So 'yam... (This is that...).
Furthermore, the cognition in the form "this is that" has an excluding nature;

moreover, if even an established difference among words is determined to be produced by the manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*) and not inherent (*svataḥ*), then there would be a lack of confidence in all cases. Bringing forward this over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says: "And for this very reason," and so forth.
If it is argued that "everything," meaning the entire universe, should be thus, he says: "Therefore, not," and so forth.
The conventional distinction based on difference—that "this is the manifestor" and "this is the manifested"—would not exist because there is no difference;

likewise, for you who rely solely on recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), the established distinction that "these are of human origin" and "these, such as *śaṃ no devīḥ*, are of non-human origin" could never exist, because there is no distinguishing feature.
With the words "Some... and so forth, the opponent demonstrates the distinction between Vedic and worldly [words]:
"Some [words] are indeed unitary because they are established through a sequence of manifestors; they are accepted as non-human (apauruṣeya), being endowed with a fixed sequence. (2453)

Because the sequence of the manifesting [articulations] is fixed by its established nature, certain [mantras] such as "śanno devīḥ" and others are perceived as having a strictly fixed order; therefore, it is established that those which possess a fixed order are non-human (apauruṣeya), while those contrary to them are, by implication, human (pauruṣeya).
[The author] refutes this with the words beginning "nanv ayam" (But this...).
[Objection: Surely this property of being produced by human effort (*pauruṣa*) belongs to the sequence of articulators such as the palate;
therefore, its reversal might also be possible at some time. [Response:
Its possession of a fixed sequence is unproven.

For instance: it is held [by the opponent] that this [order of the word] is due to the fixed sequence of the manifestors; yet that sequence of the manifestors—the palate and so forth—is not fixed, because its occurrence depends upon human will. Since human will is independent, as it has been said: "Where there is independence of will, what indeed can be called a restriction?

Consequently, regarding the claim that the sequence of "śaṃ no devīḥ" and so forth has always been exactly this way and will always be so, there is an absence of any authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish such a restriction; thus, it is possible that the sequence might sometimes be otherwise.

Regarding what was stated—that there is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) even though flames and the like are momentary—he replies: "The universal [property] such as 'fire-ness' (*tejastva*), etc. This universal has been refuted in detail.
In this regard, therefore, for us, the universal that is to be recognized is indeed eternal.
Showing that all of this can also be postulated in the case of phonemes (*varṇa*), he says: "In the case of phonemes," etc.;
[this recognition] is possible even in the case of perishing phonemes.

Those who consider the universal (*sāmānya*) to be what is recognized [through] re-cognition, or those who [consider it] specifically; however, in whatever aspect—such as fast, slow, and so forth—a cognition of difference (*bhedabuddhi*) arises, in that respect there can be no re-cognition. || 2457 ||
The universal is characterized by the exclusion of others (anyavyāvṛtti).

Regarding the passage beginning with "And the cognitions of the individual instances of the word 'cow' are differentiated by place, time, and so forth," he says: "But when the reasons are employed for the sake of establishing the oneness of the word" (*śabdaikatvaprasiddhyarthaṃ*).
Because it does not contradict heterogeneous [instances], the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not established.

Regarding those syllogisms of inference stated for the purpose of proving the oneness of sound, since no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been shown against the opposite of the reason, they are in every respect inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Regarding what was stated—"That which is of such a nature is seen to be stable, like the portion that is smoke in general"—the author, demonstrating that this example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), says: "The portion that is smoke in general... and so forth. [The portion that is smoke in general] is not... [it is already established]; thus, it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). (2459)

Only a real entity (*vastu*) that is excluded from heterogeneous things is called a universal (*sāmānya*) as a logical mark (*liṅga*), and not anything else; and since that [universal] is indeed impermanent, the example is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).

Regarding what was stated [previously], "in the case of the unity of the jar and so forth," he demonstrates that this same rebuttal applies equally to phonemes as well—starting with "of the *go* [cow], etc. and so on.
Even if oneness were to result for the word "cow" and so forth, the proof would be a *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) regarding the universal (*jāti*),
for the exclusion of what is not that form (*atadrūpaparāvṛtti*) is indeed non-different and merely conceptualized.
(2460) [If oneness were to result for individual instances (*vyakti*), there would be the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*).]

[Response: By means of the extensive application [of arguments] beginning with "Because the distinction between colors is determined through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth" (verse 2461), and "They are distinguished by place, time, and so forth," if the unity of the universal (*sāmānya*)—defined as the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*)—is being proven, then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). This is because we accept the unity of the universal, which is defined by the exclusion of what is not of that nature, on the basis of its determination by a single cognition (*ekabuddhy-adhyavasāya*) in all cases.

If, however, the unity of the individuals (*vyakti*), i.e., the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), is being proven, then the logical reasons (*hetu*) are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because their pervasion (*vyāpti*) is sublated by both direct perception and inference.

Regarding the phrase "by means of perception and so forth" (*ākṣādyaiḥ*): *ākṣa* refers to that which arises from the sense-faculties (*akṣa*), namely, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), inference (*anumāna*) is included.
The plural number is used with reference to the distinction between individual instances.
He asks, "How is difference known through direct perception? and replies with the verse beginning *yanmanojña*:

"Since the distinction between agreeable, disagreeable, and so forth is perceived directly, the difference [between cognitions] is established because cognitions occur in succession (like the case of Kumārī). (2462)

For cognitions of the individual instances of the word "cow," though differentiated by place, time, and so forth, do not have a single object, because they appear as distinct, just like [cognitions of] taste, color, and the like. Indeed, the appearance of distinctions such as *ṣaḍja* and so forth is determined by direct perception.
Nor is it like a manifestor [of sound], as that will be explained later.
Favorable is agreeable;
by the opposite, the reverse occurs.
He states the sublation [of the opponent's position] even through inference, beginning with the words "of cognitions" (*buddhīnām*), etc.;
the meaning of this will be clarified by the passage beginning with "those belonging to yesterday and today," etc.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognitions have distinct appearances, none of them have a single object, just like cognitions whose objects are taste, color, and so forth; and the cognitions of individual instances of the word "cow," which are distinguished by place, time, and other factors, have distinct appearances. This is an "observation of the contrary of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Warding off the charge that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "The ṣaḍja and so forth," etc. (vv. 2462–2463).
And because cognitions occur sequentially, their difference is established, as in the case of a young girl; providing the proof for this meaning, he says:
"Those of yesterday," and so forth—"all these cognitions of the word 'cow' from yesterday and today."

Those cognitions that arise sequentially do not have a single object, just like the cognitions of color, smell, and so forth. (2465) The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognitions are sequential do not have a single object, such as the sequential cognitions of taste, color, and so on; and these cognitions of the word "cow" from yesterday and today, which occur in succession, are likewise sequential. This is an observation of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
With the words "otherwise," etc., he refutes the inconclusiveness of both reasons:
otherwise, all cognitions would have a single object, and there would be a contradiction regarding their sequential occurrence, because the efficient cause is present. (2466)

Regarding the phrase "of all cognitions," this is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the reason "because of appearing as distinct" [which was used to prove] the undesirable consequence that cognitions of taste, form, and so forth would have mutually non-different objects.
Regarding the contradiction with sequential existence, which was stated in the verse beginning with "because of the occurrence in sequence" (24.66),
and concerning what was said about the relation being artificial and so forth, he says: "By its very nature," etc.

It has already been established previously that, by their very nature, there is a restriction of capacity among objects such that they produce a single unifying cognition (*ekapratyavamarśana*) despite their differences. Furthermore, because of this unifying cognition, [distinctions such as] the oneness of the word and so forth do not [apply].

The world considers the abundance of usage to belong to a single word; because it resides in multiple individuals, the relationship [between word and meaning] is established. Therefore, the word is universal, for it has attained oneness with respect to the individuals.
This is easy to understand.
2469 Now, as to why it is called "the world" (loka), he says: "In reality," and so forth.
In reality, however, no connection exists between a word and its object.
Therefore, because there is no production [of a real entity] from that [conceptual differentiation], it is superimposed by those who are deluded.
For this entire established system of word-meanings has already been explained in detail previously; it is entirely subverted because pervasion is impossible.

By the phrase "due to difference," he negates the relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*); and by the phrase "because it does not arise from that," he negates the relationship characterized by origination (*tadutpatti*).

There is no other relationship besides these two; nor is it logical for there to be a rule whereby a word conveys meaning without such a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Therefore, it has already been established in the previous discussion on the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) that the relationship between word and object is superimposed.

Therefore, pointing out the unestablished nature (*asiddhatva*) of both the reason and the example in such a formulation as "therefore, sound is non-artificial," he says: "The eternality of 'cowness' has been rejected, and the relation [between word and meaning] is also merely conceptualized;
even atoms, space, and so forth have been discarded—that [reason and example] do not exist in the case of the reason and the instance. (2472)
By the statement "the eternality of 'cowness' (gotva) has been discarded," he asserts the unestablished nature of the eternal;

by "the relation is also imagined," he asserts the unestablished nature of [the reason] "because of the relation"; and by "atoms, space, and so forth are also rejected," he asserts the unestablished nature of [the example] "like the dimension of space or an atom"—"discarded" (apāsta) meaning refuted in the *Ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*.
"No" is a negation;
"that" is used in the sense of "therefore.

Regarding the passage beginning with "present, multiple, common," etc., he says: "Let it be understood that the denotation of the extracted *gotva* (cowness) is achieved only after a long time, because it is determined by people who are deluded by its uniform appearance. (2473)
He asks, "How is its erroneous nature established? and says: "Because of its momentariness in reality," and so forth:
"Since this [entity] is not stable even for that duration because of its momentariness in reality, why is its continued existence even later desired? (2474)
Regarding the statement "as [there is] cutting by weapons and so forth," he says: "Even in the case of a jar, etc.
This also has been pointed out: that even in the case of a jar and the like, there is no cause whatsoever for its destruction; how then could such a thing exist in the case of sound? (2475)
Thus, this too has been demonstrated in the *Sthirabhāvaparīkṣā* (Examination of Stable Entities) by establishing that destruction is causeless.
The connection with the remote term "the cause of destruction" is as follows: "When there is no cause of destruction even in the case of a jar and so forth, how could there be one for sound?

By this, it is stated that [the argument] suffers from the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*) and that the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "of place, time, and the agents" (2475), he says: "the subversion," and so forth;
the subversion of recognition has been established previously.
Dharma is differentiated by the differences in place, time, and the performers [of the action].
(2476) Indeed, due to the distinctions of *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *pañcama*, and so forth, another distinct and clear manifestation of the cow is perceived through direct perception. (2477)
Nor is this establishment of difference justified by a difference in manifestors;
for it will be stated later that manifestation does not exist in eternal things.
(2478) This is easy to understand.

Regarding the formulation beginning with "the letter *ga* is absolutely," he states the fault of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*): "And distinct from the letter *ga*" and so forth.
Since a real universal (*gatva*) distinct from the letter *ga* is asserted [by the opponent], this fault of proving what is already established is unavoidable in the formal argument. (2479)
"It is not accepted" is to be connected with what will be stated later.

If it is argued that even for "g-ness," which consists of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), there is no such basis [as a universal], this is not so, because it would result in the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).
This is because there exists no phoneme *ga* that is distinct from the phoneme *a*.
"Of what substratum (dharmin) indeed is the property (dharma) 'the state of not being determinable by a cognition other [than that of the letter]'?

(2481) Now, it might be argued: "Even though the phoneme *ga* consists of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), its substratum does not exist"—thus, it is established in this manner so that there is no "proving what is already established" (*siddhasādhyatā*). For it is not the case that you do not accept that the letter *ga* and so forth are the locus of the exclusion of others. [To this, the author] refutes the prima facie position: "If it were established in this way, the reason (*hetu*) would result in being unestablished (*asiddha*)."
For instance: "Exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is not some distinct entity separate from the object itself as excluded from others;

rather, it is that very form of the individual phonemes such as *ga* which, by rejecting other internal distinctions of exclusion from heterogeneous classes, is designated by synonyms such as "exclusion of others," "other-exclusion," and so forth, when there is a desire to know that alone.

But if the non-existence of that very nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is what is to be proven, then for what subject would this reason—"because of the non-apprehension of a cognition of something other"—be a property? It would not be a property of anything at all.

Showing that the example "like the 'going' (gati) imagined by others" is also unestablished in its locus (*dharmyasiddha*), he says: "All inference, being real, requires something established for both parties, such as an example; therefore, by that [rule], the example suffers from the fault of the locus being unestablished. (2482)
By the word "etcetera" in the phrase "example, etcetera," the inclusion of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth is intended.
Furthermore, even if not explicitly stated by the proponent, that which is made the object of [his] intention is precisely what is accepted here.
Nor is it merely the state of being *ga* that you wish to establish;
rather,
by this means, you intend to demonstrate the oneness of the phoneme *ga*.

And showing that in this proposition a sublation by perception and other means of knowledge has already been stated, he says: "All this effort..."—all this effort of yours for the sake of establishing the oneness of the letter *ga* involves a sublation by perception that is difficult to avoid, as has been stated. (2483)
The word "this" (ayam) negates a substratum for a distinct [quality] such as "going," and by the word "and" (ca), the sublation by inference is included along with the sublation by perception.
"Arising" refers to that which was described [in verse 2483] as "agreeable," "disagreeable," and so forth.
Regarding what was stated in the passage beginning with "But [the object] established by both," he says: "The cognitions of the letter 'ga' belonging to yesterday and today... and so forth.
These cognitions of the letter 'ga', occurring sequentially, do not have a single object, just like the cognitions of taste, color, and so on. (2484)
Therefore, this single phoneme is not established as existing eternally in both [the speaker and the listener];
rather, its eternity is merely imagined for that which is constructed through exclusion (*apoha*).
This [eternity] is also connected to the word "udita" (arisen) by modifying the gender and case-ending.

Therefore, since the distinction between words has been refuted by both perception and inference, there is no single entity consisting of phonemes established for both [parties]. Thus, the eternality of the conceptualized "exclusion of others" (anyāpoha) alone is postulated, because unity is determined through a cognition of uniform reflective awareness.
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "perfected by the *nāda*," he says: "At the time of perceiving the sound," and so forth.
At the time of perceiving the sound, the air-currents residing at the extremity of the ear, which effect the refinement of the auditory organ (*śrotra*), are not perceived. (2486)
When a sound is perceived by the auditory organ as refined by resonance (nāda), its cognition through contact with that [resonance] is sublated by direct perception (pratyakṣa).

For if the air-currents that effect the refinement of the auditory organ were established by some means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), only then could it be said: "the auditory organ is refined by resonance."

And these [sounds] are not established; therefore, the notion that the cognition of that sound is perceptual due to its proximity to the word—that is, its proximity to the linguistic unit—is a basis for conceptual construction.
Regarding what was stated—that "sweet [taste] appears in the form of bitter," and so forth—he says: "In the form of bitter, yellow, and so on," etc.
Knowledge directed toward sweet and other tastes by way of forms such as bitter and yellow would be without an object, just as the cognition of a word [is without an external referent]. (2488)
By this, that which was stated—that "the cognition of the word [arises] by virtue of that [external object]"—is refuted;
for it is not logical that a formless cognition should have another thing as its object, as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Now, it might be argued: "Even if sound is not the object of that cognition, how can it be objectless? To this he says: "Because of the distinctions of fast, medium, and so forth," and so on.
For no sound other than those distinguished as fast, medium, and so forth appears;
and since a cognition of a certain form cannot be objectless when its object does not possess that form, how could this be? (2489)
For cognition arises through forms that are fast, medium, or slow; yet the word possesses no such fast form, because, being eternal and all-pervading, it is of a single uniform nature.
Nor is there any other object possessing a fast form that could appear [to consciousness].
Therefore, since there is no object corresponding to the form [of the cognition], this [cognition] is indeed devoid of an objective referent (*nirviṣaya*).

It might be argued: "That very same word, appearing in the form of fast [utterance] and so forth, as well as otherwise, will be its objective support (*ālambana*), just as it has been said: 'In all cases, the external is the objective support, though characterized by differences of place and time. To this, he replies: "And otherwise... (*anyathā ca*).
Otherwise, the statement that "one knows that very object" is contradictory;
for if there is a cognition of a different form, how indeed can that object be known?
Indeed, if consciousness is formless, then that external form must certainly belong to you [the object].
And since the external object is not of the same nature as that [cognition], how could it exist in such a way?
Even on the view that cognition possesses a form (sākāra-jñāna), when an appearance arises in the cognition in conformity with an external form, the object is said to be "known. (2491–2492)
In this case, cognition does not proceed in accordance with an external object;
therefore, it is established that all mind is devoid of an object and is erroneous. [Objection: This is contradictory.
Because reality and its opposite are characterized by mutual exclusion and thus cannot coexist in a single substratum;

furthermore, demonstrating that everything is indeed erroneous—being entirely devoid of an object whether in the position of formless cognition (*nirākāra*) or the position of cognition with form (*sākāra*)—he says: "In the case of the formless," and so forth.
For those who maintain that cognition is formless, it is the form of blue and so on residing in the object itself that is experienced.

Furthermore, since the object such as a conch-shell does not exist in the same way that the yellow color and so forth appear in a deluded cognition, its lack of being an object is indeed quite clear. Now, one might argue: "If the form of the yellow color and so forth does not reside in the object, then it must necessarily reside in the cognition; otherwise, if it were absent from both, how could it be experienced? And if it resides in the cognition, then how can you maintain that consciousness is formless? To this it must be said: [the response follows].
This is true;
however, this lack of an object for cognition is stated while accepting the position of those who maintain that cognition is formless (nirākāra).
As for one who maintains that cognition is formless, by him alone must the rebuttal to this [objection] be provided here.
Even in the view that cognition possesses a form (sākārajñāna), the experience of an object is established through the experience of a form whose nature resembles the object;
however, in an erroneous cognition, there is no experience of a form whose nature resembles the object, and thus it is indeed without an object.
Furthermore, regarding the apprehension of an object, there is no mode other than these two: having a form or being formless.
Therefore, it is established that all cognition is indeed erroneous and devoid of an object. 2490–2491.
Furthermore, showing that no cause for error is possible here, he says: "And there is no existence of a manifestor," and so forth.
Furthermore, the existence of a manifestor is not tenable, especially in the case of something eternal;
therefore, cognitions are not differentiated according to the refinement of that [manifestor] with respect to the sound (*dhvani*).

Indeed, it is the difference among manifestors that is described as the cause for the illusion of difference in the word-sound (*śabda*). However, there can be no manifestor of anything that is eternal, because such a manifestor would have no effect upon it. Nor is it logical for something to be a manifestor of that which it does not produce any specific change in, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle.
For in this way, anything whatsoever could be the manifestor of anything else;
therefore, it is not logical that there should be distinct cognitions regarding sound—the word—due to the embellishment of the manifestor.

Regarding what was stated—that just as a lamp and so forth are accepted as the manifesters of a jar and so forth—the author first introduces the meaning of the verse and then, refuting it with the second and subsequent verses, says: "For, just as [the lamp] restricts its power to the manifestation for the sake of perceiving a jar and so forth, so too the sound does not [restrict itself] to the ear for the perception of the word-sound. (2495)
If sound is inherently established as fit for apprehension by the auditory organ, why is it not apprehended even when that auditory organ is unrefined? [Response:
Apprehension would indeed occur because of the presence of the fit cause.
Just as at the time when a conditioned auditory organ exists, so it is for that [sound]. If it were not capable of being perceived then, how could it become so later?
And if it possesses the capacity [for perception] at that later time, the sound would have to be something else that has arisen.

Furthermore, even if knowledge does not arise from that [sound] by its own power, its production is nevertheless described as resulting from the hearing of refined [language] and so forth. (2499) Regarding this "ear refined by language," it must be stated: is sound by its very nature capable of producing a cognition of itself as its object, or is it incapable?
In the first case, there would be the undesirable consequence of perception occurring even before the refinement of the auditory organ;
this is precisely what [the author] states with the words "even when unrefined," etc.,
referring to "that."
"Of the word,
that" means "therefore."

The formal argument (prayoga), however, beginning with "if the cause is deficient," should be stated as before; furthermore, there follows the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the refinement of the auditory organ (śrotrasaṃskāra) would be useless.

If, on the other hand, the second position is held, then even the refinement of the auditory organ would not result in the perception of sound, because the sound would always be unfit [for perception];
therefore, in this position as well, the refinement of the auditory organ is indeed useless.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That which does not differ from a state incapable of producing a certain effect does not produce that effect; for example, *kodrava* grain [does not produce] a rice sprout. And even when the auditory organ is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), sound does not differ from its state of being incapable of producing cognition. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Nor is this reason (*hetu*) unestablished (*asiddha*); he demonstrates this by stating: "An entity" (*bhāva*) is that which possesses a connection with capability—that is, it is "endowed with capability" (*yogyatāyogī*).

Now, if the word *hi* were intended to be the cause for the production of cognition, then the dilemma regarding its suitability or unsuitability would apply to it; however, since it is the auditory organ (*śrotra*) alone that is held to be the cause for the perception of sound when it is refined, and not the sound itself, the aforementioned fault does not follow. Anticipating this, the author offers a rebuttal, saying: "Of the sound," and so forth.
In this way, sound would simply be ungraspable, because it would have no utility in that regard;
for there is indeed no distinction whatsoever between it and taste and the other [sensory objects].
For if this were so, then like taste and the rest, sound would not attain the status of being an object of knowledge due to its lack of utility.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not serve a function in a particular cognition is not an object of knowledge for that cognition; for example, taste and so forth are not objects of auditory cognition. And sound does not serve a function in auditory cognition. This is an instance of the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). It is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because if that which provides no assistance were to be an object of knowledge, there would be a lack of restriction, leading to the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even taste and so forth would be cognizable by auditory consciousness. 2500

But surely, because its own cause acts as a regulator, there will be no over-extension [of the principle]; for instance, that which arises from the conditioned auditory faculty, the immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), and so forth, arises specifically as the cognition of sound and not as the cognition of taste and so on, due to the specific determination of the causal capacity.

Moreover, even if one accepts that sound is a cause, one must necessarily accept a restriction regarding the specific causal capacity; for instance, when the objection is raised: "Even though all [causes] are equally causes, why is it that the cognition of sound consists only of the awareness of words, and not the awareness of the auditory faculty and so forth?"—the answer to this must be given solely by means of the restrictions on the causal capacities. Having considered all this and setting aside the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*), he says: "Or rather, it has the nature of the cognition of words," and so forth. That is to say: "This cognition, which indeed has the nature of the cognition of words, is produced by those [factors]—namely, the refined hearing and so forth—which do not depend upon the sound itself. (2501)
The word "nāma" (indeed) is used in the sense of admission;
and how this position is untenable will be demonstrated later by the passage beginning with "Who [is the agent] of cognition? and so forth, through such means as hearing the refined [teachings].
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) and others is intended.

Even if sound were not the cause [of the cognition], there would still be a fault; for instance, there are two alternatives: is this sound by its very nature (*prakṛtyā*) of the same essence as the cognition of it and its object, or is it not? Regarding the first alternative, he states the fault: "tajjñānajñeya... and so forth.
That which consists of both that cognition and its object follows along with whatever [word] it is;
thus, there would be a persistence of the word, and for you, there would also be a persistence of that cognition.
Otherwise, the cognition would not persist, yet it is that [cognition] which persists.
If [you claim] "that which is known by that [cognition] is the word," then there would be a contradiction for you.
For those two—the cognition and the object of cognition—are bound together as if by a chain;
since they exist as a single entity, the presence of the second follows from the first without deviation.

If sound were of the same nature as the cognition that knows it, then, like the form of the sound itself, that cognition would also be eternal at all times, because it would persist in accordance with the nature of its object.
For it is not the case that when Devadatta persists in his nature of being connected with a staff, the staff does not persist;
for they are bound together like a chain.
The word "hi" (for) has the sense of "because";

because the natures of the object of knowledge and the means of knowledge are bound together as if by a chain, it is established that when one nature exists, the existence of the second follows, due to their non-deviation.
"Let it be so; what is the fault? To this he says: "Conditioned," and so forth.

For it is precisely because [the cognition] is connected with the knowledge produced by hearing the refined [speech] that cognition is clearly implied even when there is no refinement of the auditory organ.
(2505) "For it is precisely because [the cognition] is connected with the knowledge produced by hearing the refined [speech]"— this is the meaning.
The word "the sound persists" (*śabdo 'nuvarttate*) is to be supplied as an ellipsis.

Since the sound, being connected with the cognition produced by the hearing of the refined [auditory organ], persists at all times, it follows that even for one whose auditory organ is not refined, the cognition of that [sound] would occur; therefore, the refinement of the auditory organ is useless. (2505)
He states the fault in the second position as well: "If that [word] were not of the nature of the object of knowledge... and so forth.
If the word is not of the nature of that [object], then like taste and so on, auditory cognition would not have the nature of cognizing it; such being the case. (2506)
This is clear.

And all of this has been stated while assuming that cognition, even though it does not assist that [object], has the nature of cognizing it; now, demonstrating that it is improper for cognition to have the nature of cognizing it in the absence of a relation, he says: "Or who... and so forth.
What indeed is the relationship between cognition and the word, such that it is desired [to be] of the nature of the understanding of that word? It cannot be identity, because they are distinct;
nor can it be "origination from that" (tadutpatti), because the word is not a producer [of the cognition].
If its production were governed by a fixed rule, then that [auditory organ] would have to exist at all times.

(2508) In this way, the cognition having that as its object would either always arise or never arise at all; since this dilemma stands, the postulation of an embellishment (*saṃskāra*) of the ear is useless. (2509)
For the restriction between entities is indeed twofold: identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), since there is no other [restriction] due to the absence of mutual assistance.
Furthermore, a relationship between that which is not assisted and that which does not assist is not logical, as it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Since neither of these two types of restriction exists between word and cognition, how could a cognition whose nature is the understanding of that [object] arise in the absence of such a restriction?
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Suppose it were argued that the nature of that cognition is established as the awareness of that [object] simply by the arising of its form, even without a connection;
this is incorrect.
Because the Mīmāṃsakas do not accept that cognition possesses a form (*sākāra-jñāna*), for they admit only formless cognition (*nirākāra-jñāna*).

Or, even if it were so, it would be illogical because it would entail the consequence that sound is beyond perception (*parokṣa*); for in that case, sound would indeed be imperceptible and not perceptual, and consequently, due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it, the very claim that "cognition has the form of that [sound]" could not be proven.
Nor is its establishment [as the object] possible through the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) of the effect, because we do not admit that it is the producer [of cognition].

This might be argued: "Even for the proponent of the theory of images (*sākāravādin*), for whom the object is indeed the producer, since the object is always imperceptible (*parokṣa*), how is it understood that the cognition possesses the form of the object? This is true.

However, this is the means [for establishing it]: that other cause, which is determined through the exclusion of the effect [of the sense organs], is ascertained by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) to be the differentiator of the blue and other forms within cognition.

For instance, since the eye, light, and mental attention are common to all cognitions, the differentiation of cognition into blue and so forth is not produced by them; rather, by implication, it is determined that this differentiation is produced by that other cause which was inferred through its exclusion. Therefore, because it is produced by that [other cause], it is established that this form is apprehended by the cognition.
But this [argument] is not even a valid means for you, because you do not admit that it [the self] is a cause.
It might be argued: "Since the eyes and other [senses] are also always imperceptible, how is their uniformity across all cognitions determined?
This is indeed true when considering the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*).

For that proponent of consciousness-only (vijñānavādin) describes the particularity of consciousness as being produced solely by the immediately preceding condition (samanantarapratyaya), just as in dreams and the like, and not as produced by an external object;
however, all this is said while assuming the existence of an external object.

Otherwise, this very point should be challenged: how could the existence of the external object be established even from the difference in the effects? Only the existence of a cause would be established, but not the external object; moreover, that cause might be internal, as in the case of dreams and so forth. Enough of this digression.
Furthermore, showing that even if the production [of cognition] by the word is admitted, there is still a fault, he says: "In its production," etc., beginning with "that."
He concludes with the words "tadutpattiḥ evam" and so forth, [referring] to the position that [the cause] is not a producer.
Thus, "one-sidedness" refers to the constant presence or absence of cognition characterized by existence or non-existence. (2507)

Thus far, having granted the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory faculty, it was stated that such refinement is useless by considering whether the object possesses a nature that is either productive or non-productive [of cognition]. Now, demonstrating that the refinement of the auditory faculty itself is not possible, he says: "For in the case of something occasional," and so forth.

For if the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) were occasional, then it would be reasonable to postulate a mental impression such that the occurrence of cognition happens only occasionally when that impression exists. Furthermore, this mental impression, characterized as a potency (*śakti*), is to be inferred from its effect, which is cognition.
Furthermore, that cognition must either be eternally existent or always coming into existence;
how indeed could it indicate an occasional refinement (*saṃskāra*)?
Therefore, the subsequent [explanation] regarding the refinement of the auditory organ has not been well-demonstrated.
For in this way, it is logical that consciousness, which is the effect of formative forces (*saṃskāra*), is occasional only if the formative force itself is occasional;
otherwise, while its cause remains eternally unimpaired, why would its effect occur only at certain times?

Showing that it is not logical for a modification (*saṃskāra*) to be occasional for an eternal auditory faculty (*śrotra*), he says: "And it is to be determined by the effect, which is cognition," and so forth.

For instance, a modification of the auditory faculty and the like, being determined by the effect that is cognition, would be a modification consisting of a power (*śakti*), since only power is determined by an effect. Furthermore, that power is indeed the very nature of the auditory faculty and is not distinct from it; otherwise, because the effect would arise [even without it], it would follow that the auditory faculty is not a cause, and because no relation would be established, if the power were present, the resulting cognition would always exist.
If, however, it were non-existent, then the cognition produced by it would never occur;

consequently, the occasional nature of cognition would not exist. Therefore, how could an occasional cognition indicate a refinement characterized as a capacity belonging to the auditory organ? It certainly could not.
Furthermore, even if one were to argue that the inherent capacity for the effect of cognition is not to be inferred;

What then? A previously non-existent, occasional capacity is produced in the auditory organ by the sounds; that very capacity is inferred from cognition. Therefore, he says—"A capacity is produced," etc.—that an occasional cognition is logically established as an indicator of that capacity: "If a capacity were produced in the auditory organ, or if it were non-different [from it], then its eternality would be lost, because of its being born [only occasionally]. (Verse 2513)
There are three possible positions: that the capacity (śakti) is identical with the auditory organ itself, or distinct from it, or both distinct and non-distinct.
In the first position, the auditory organ—even if it possesses a dual nature—would necessarily be impermanent, just like the nature of the capacity itself;
why? Because of its birth—that is, its production.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "It is not that we accept the non-difference of the auditory faculty from its power; rather, we hold that the power itself is non-different from the auditory faculty. Behold this, for it is the manifestation of great blindness!
For how could another [attribute] become distant at the very same moment as one's own nature is joined?

Since non-difference is characterized by the mutual interpenetration of their own-natures (*svabhāva*), it is quite absurd to claim that water, while existing at a distance from milk, does not experience its contact; therefore, this [objection] is trivial.
Let this position be granted; nevertheless, showing that it still entails a fault, he says: "And because of existence," etc.
Because it is not distinct from existence, even the conditioned would possess permanence; therefore, the cognition of entities would occur at all times. (2514)

Since the conditioning factor (*saṃskāra*) would also follow as being eternal, just like the nature of the entity itself due to their non-difference, there is this further fault; thus he says: "By that," and so forth (verse 2514).
He states the fault in the second position as well: "But in the case of difference... and so forth.
However, in the case of difference, its connection [to the ear] is not tenable;
furthermore, the ear would lack the status of being an instrument because cognition arises from the potency. (2515)

If it is admitted that the power is distinct from the entity [to which it belongs], then there could be no relationship such that "this is the power of that," because that which cannot be benefited lacks the capacity for dependence.
Nor does the auditory organ benefit the power, since it is accepted that only manifesters such as sound and so forth are the benefactors.

If, on the other hand, the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is also something that assists [the capacity], then there would be an infinite regress, since the capacity that assists the capacity must itself be non-different from the auditory faculty.
Consequently, because capacities alone would be linked in a series and the effect would arise from the capacity itself, the auditory faculty would be a non-producer;
and thus, the undesirable consequence follows that it is not a real entity (*avastu*).
Now, if it is admitted that the power which assists the [auditory] capacity is non-different from that capacity, then what is this aversion toward the non-difference of the primary capacity?

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of the constant production of the capacity, because its cause—the auditory organ—is eternal; and that which cannot be assisted has no dependence whatsoever upon auxiliary factors.

He states the third position: "Free from both difference and non-difference," and so forth; thus, a distinct alternative position is stated thereafter as being unrefuted by the refinement of the auditory organ. || 2516 ||
By this very [argument], the refinement (*saṃskṛti*) of both the object and the sense-organ must be rejected;
therefore, manifestation (*abhivyakti*) in the case of eternal [sounds] is entirely without foundation.
Consequently, [properties] such as long, short, and their sequence, which depend upon manifestation, [cannot exist].
Whatever things are analyzed, they are all likewise without a foundation;
this was stated in the examination of the person (*pudgala*) and so forth.
Because it is impossible for both affirmation and negation to apply to a single thing at one and the same time.

For instance, difference and non-difference are characterized by their existence through mutual exclusion, because the determination of one occurs precisely through the exclusion of the nature of the other. For when the nature of something is not determined without the exclusion of its own essence, that thing exists through the exclusion of the other—just as, for example, either of two things, existence and non-existence. And since those two are characterized by mutual exclusion, the negation of the nature of one is inseparable from the affirmation of the other; thus, by the force of the negation of "otherness," there is an affirmation of identity. Consequently, it is not logical to negate that [identity] at that very same time, because it would follow that "otherness" itself could not be negated. In this manner, the flaw in both positions must be stated.

By the phrase "by this very [means]," he concludes with the words "therefore" and so forth, by way of the two alternatives regarding the nature of being or not being fit for the production of knowledge according to its inherent character (*prakṛti*).
By the word "etc. in the phrase "kramādayaḥ" (the krama [readings] and so forth), the inclusion of the *pluta* (protracted) and *udātta* (acute) accents and others is intended.
Regarding those who maintain that this sound is perceived by the ear even though it has not reached it, and so forth, he says: "Even though there is a similarity in mere non-attainment," and so on;
for even if there is a similarity in mere non-attainment, there is no perception of everything [equally].
Because the restriction of capacity is established for iron by means of a magnet (2519):

although everything is equally unattained, nevertheless, due to the specific determination of the powers of entities, there is no apprehension of the previously mentioned object— that is, its grasping does not occur— just as the stone called a magnet, while attracting iron that is unattained, does not attract every unattained thing.

2519 By the words "the light of the magnet," etc., he raises the objection regarding the lack of proof for the example according to the view of Śaṅkarasvāmin: "If, even in that case, there is attraction through the reaching of the light of the magnet..."
[Objection: But how can it be understood that light exists if it is not perceived? [Response:

For he (the opponent) has stated that even in that case, the attraction of iron occurs solely by virtue of the penetration of the light of the magnet; otherwise, there would be an attraction of all pieces of iron situated in every location.

Although its light is not perceived like the light of a lamp, it is nevertheless inferable, because attraction is observed at a distance even when there is an obstruction (or, despite the lack of non-obstruction).
To this, he replies with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely), stating:
"It would not be visible"—thus, by means of non-perception (*anupalambha*), he negates the conventional usage of its existence.

Regarding the objection raised by way of a reductio (*prasaṅga*)—namely, that it would follow [absurdly] that iron situated in all places would be attracted—he says, in order to refute it, "Why is it not attracted? and so forth:
"Why does that light not attract wood and other such things?"
If it is argued that [the magnet] acts because its power is restricted [to specific objects], then this is the same even in the case of non-contact.

Even in the position that there is contact, the same undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) applies: why does that light of the magnet not attract all wood and other things that have come into contact with it?

If it is replied that there is no over-extension (atiprasaṅga) because the specific nature of things (padārtha-svabhāva) is restrictive, then in the case of non-contact as well, by what has the restricting nature of the thing been taken away, such that it is not accepted there? Therefore, the postulation of an invisible light is indeed useless.
Regarding what was stated— that in that case, the perception and non-perception by those situated far and near would be identical and there would be no sequence— he says "dūra" and so forth.
"By those situated at a distance, in the middle, or nearby, [the object] is perceived simultaneously,

immediately following the employment [of the word], because for all of them, it arises as a single class of cognition. (2522) Thus, the apprehension of succession is unestablished, since cognitions arise simultaneously immediately after the employment of the word."
Regarding what was said—that there can be no occurrence of intensity, dullness, and so forth—he replies: "By means of distinctions such as distant and near," and so on;
that is, just as [an object] is seen clearly or unclearly according to the distinction between being distant or near.
In the same way, there would be the perception of intensity, dullness, and so forth, even in the case of sound.

Just as form (rūpa), though not reaching [the sense organ] and being pervasive, is observed to be clear, distinct, or indistinct when it is perceived, so too in the case of sound—which is pervasive and perceived without [the sense organ] reaching it—there will be the experience of intensity, dullness, and so forth.
But surely, for the opponent, the non-reaching and perception of form is unestablished; how then can it be stated as an example?
This is not a fault;
for although it is not established by the mere word of another, nevertheless, that which is established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established for both parties.
But what is the means of valid cognition here? It is the simultaneous perception of objects both near and distant.

For that which possesses motion reaches what is near quickly and what is distant after a long time, just as Devadatta, traveling from one village to another, takes time; however, the simultaneous perception of both the tree branch and the moon is observed immediately upon the opening of the eyes. Therefore, it is understood that the eye functions without reaching its object (*aprāpyakārin*). Regarding this, Uddyotakara says: "Because cognitions arise so rapidly, the difference in time is not perceived; thus, this is a false impression, like the [simultaneous] piercing of a hundred lotus petals."

This is incorrect; for in this way, even in cases such as "saraḥ" and "rasaḥ," there would be no determination of sequence, since the rapidity of their arising is equal. Consequently, there would be no difference in perception, and since all cognitions arise rapidly, there would never be a perception of sequence. This has already been examined in detail; furthermore, he himself says: "If the eye were to function without reaching its object, then an obstruction such as a wall would have no efficacy, and thus the impossibility of obstruction [would follow].
Moreover, the non-perception of what is distant and the perception of what is near would not occur, because there would be no distinction [in the eye's relation to them]."
It might be argued: "Only that object which becomes an objective domain (*viṣaya*) of the eye is perceived, while that which does not become so is not perceived.
But this is not the case, because becoming an objective domain is impossible without a relation (*sambandha*).
"What is this so-called state of being an object apart from a relation? You merely say 'relation,' while I call it 'the state of being an object'; there is no difference whatsoever.
This is incorrect.
For us, the state of being an object is said to be the state of being a cause, not a [direct] relation.

To explain: a form (rūpa) or other object becomes what is called an "object" when it functions as a cooperative condition for the arising of visual consciousness; it does not become so by being conjoined with that consciousness.
And there are two kinds of meanings for the term "cooperation."

Or [the object] may be a benefit conferred upon another, as for example, the influence [exerted] by one situated in a room through its pervasion; or it may be the performance of a single purposeful action, as when one perceives a form merely by opening the eyes.
In both cases, the object is said to be simply a specific cause of consciousness, and not a related entity.
If it is argued that this very restriction to a specific cause would not exist in the absence of a relation:

Because specific determination is established through the power of its own causes, that [entity] arises from its own cause as precisely such [an entity], by virtue of which only a certain thing becomes a producer of cognition and not another; for all things possess distinct intrinsic natures due to the difference in their causes.
Furthermore, according to your view, even though the relation is equal, why is it that the eye perceives only form and not taste?

If it is argued that [the eye] does not perceive [taste] because there is no connection [between them], why indeed should that very connection not exist? Since the location is non-different, there is no restrictive cause here by which the eye follows only color (*rūpa*) and not taste (*rasa*), even though the latter exists in the same location; nor does it follow color that resides in an extremely distant location.
If it is argued that its own cause (*svahetu*) is the restrictor:

This same [objection] applies even to the position of non-attainment (*aprāpti*); therefore, enough with this elaboration. With the words "of those appearing as distinct," etc., he anticipates the opponent's objection.
If cognitions appearing as distinct have a single objective referent, how is this objection not equally applicable to those who maintain the existence of external objects?

(2524) [The opponent's intention is: How could cognitions appearing as distinct have a single object? For in that case, the cognitions of taste, form, and so forth would likewise have a single objective referent.

He states the rebuttal: "The same applies," and so forth, regarding cognitions of form—that is, even for cognitions whose objects are forms, this objection is equally applicable: how could there be a single objective referent for appearances that are distinct as clear and so forth due to differences such as distance and proximity?
And this is an objection raised by the proponents of external objects (bāhyārthavādins).

Those who describe the form as residing only in the object and not in the consciousness are the Vijñānavādins; for them, all consciousness is indeed devoid of an external object and is self-cognizing, arising as distinct precisely through the differences in its forms such as clarity and so forth—thus there is no objection against them.

As for those proponents of external objects (*bāhyārthavādins*) who hold the position that cognition possesses a form (*sākārajñāna*), since they do not admit a complete identity with the object in every respect, but rather a similarity in some respect, it is not contradictory for cognitions that appear as distinct to have a single object; thus, there is no objection against them either.

To the question, "What is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the perception of sound through contact, and what is the establishing proof (*sādhaka*) for its perception without contact? he says: "In the case of the position that there is perception through contact... and so forth.

For if there were perception through contact, then in the case of the sound of thunderclouds and the like, there would be no cognition of it as being discontinuous, just as there is none for the wax within the ear. (Verse 2525)
The phrase "like the feathers inside the ear" is a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) formed by the suffix *vati* added to a word ending in the genitive case.

Just as the continuous sound of a bird's wing that serves to relieve an itch in the ear is perceived, so too, since the sound of clouds and the like is grasped only when it has reached the region of the ear by spreading out according to the analogy of a *kadamba* flower bud, it follows that the perception [of distant and near sounds] would be identical.
Nor can it be said that this illusion of disjunction arises by virtue of its own causes, conjunction, inherence, or location,
because these are not perceived by the auditory organ;
for a cognition never arises that superimposes the form of an object that has not itself become an objective datum.
For visual consciousness does not superimpose the similarity of taste [upon the object].

Thus, having stated the proof that contradicts the apprehension [of the object] through contact, he states the proof for its apprehension without contact, beginning with the words "separated from that" (tadvicchinna).
Because it produces knowledge [of an object] even when separated from it, the ear—like the mind—must be non-contacting (*aprāpyakārin*); otherwise, it would be like the skin and other sense organs.
(Verse 2526) "That" refers to this.
Therefore,
"not otherwise, like the sense of touch and so forth" is an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta);
the meaning is that just as there is no perception through the separation [of parts] in the case of a sense organ such as the skin, so it would be here as well.
Having raised the objection that the example [of the eye] is deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*) by means of the passage beginning with "the mind also," he refutes it:
"Those who assert that the mind also acts by reaching [its object] do so only for a moment."
It is not logical that their consciousness should reside in a place far away [from the object].

In this regard, Uddyotakara, Kumārila, and others provide the following proof: "The eye and the ear function by reaching [their objects], because they are external sense organs, like the nose and so forth.
The inclusion of the term "external" is for the purpose of avoiding a deviation [in the inference] by the internal organ, the mind (*manas*).

Likewise, since it is an instrument (karaṇa) and does not perceive objects that are obstructed, like the sense of smell and so forth, the qualification "being an instrument" is added for the purpose of excluding [the mind], which is the object of cognition. Similarly, color and sound are perceived by external sense organs that function through contact (prāpyakārin), because they are objects of the external senses, just like odor and taste.

Likewise, regarding the cognition of form and sound, which have as their objective support objects grasped by external sense-faculties that function through contact (*prāpyakārin*), [the opponent argues] that they must have external sense-objects as their objective support because they are cognitions of smell and taste.
To this, he states the refutation beginning with "As for that," etc.:
"As for that proof of functioning through contact based on being an external sense-faculty..."
That [reason] is inconclusive because of its contradiction with something of a different class from the property in question; this is easily understood. (2528)
Therefore, regarding the passage beginning with "this is seen by those learned in the Vedas," he says: "Separated," and so forth.
Previously, they were separated from conjunction and disjunction; and because the wind is imperceptible, it is logical that [the sounds] are not non-distinct from it. (2529)
Therefore, because there is no distinction [in its nature], motion is not possible for it;
and because of the absence of momentum (*vega*), it does not persist as long as the momentum lasts. Thus, "previously" [is said].
To the objection that [conjunction and disjunction] might then be non-different from the six categories, he says: "Of air," and so forth.
For it is the very atoms of air, as they arise in states of being conjoined and disjoined, that are called conjunction and disjunction when they are non-different [from those atoms].
Furthermore, it is not logical for non-momentary entities to possess a nature of conjunction even sequentially, because they are of a single, unchanging form.
Regarding what was stated—"having reached the space of the ear," and so forth—he says:
"If [the sound], having reached the space of the ear, produces a capacity in the auditory organ, then why is there no perception of its movement, as in the case of a whip-lash? (2531)
"It is incorrect to say that the attention to sound obstructs the sensation [of pain], just as one who knows the blow of a whip or the wind [does not fail to feel them].
(2532) In this regard, there are two positions: either this wind might have a perceptible nature at some time, or...
Alternatively, [the air] may have an imperceptible nature.
In the first case, at the time of perceiving the sound, the movement of the air would also have to be perceived, just as the stroke of a whip is perceived.
Or, it might be argued that because two cognitions do not arise simultaneously, the attention to the sound—the perception of the sound—obstructs the sensation or perception of this air.
This is incorrect; for it is impossible to claim that one perceives the blow of a whip or an internal breeze at the same time as perceiving a sound.

For just as there would be an experience of an internal breeze produced by a fan or the like, and of the blow of a whip, at the moment of perceiving the sound, so too there should be a perception of the touch of the air reaching the region of the ear.
By this, he states that the thesis regarding the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
And it has been demonstrated that the illusion of simultaneous perception does not arise from the force of rapid production, because that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Granted that there may be an illusion of simultaneity caused by rapidity even when things occur in succession, nevertheless, he demonstrates that this is no answer at all because it is irrelevant to the present subject—starting with "From rapidity," etc.:
"The claim that there is an illusion of simultaneity despite sequential occurrence due to rapidity is of no consequence, for in every respect, air is not perceived here. (2533)
If it is argued that there is indeed an illusion of simultaneity due to the rapidity of the arising of cognitions, this might be so;
however, it cannot be the case that there is a total non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception.

For in this case, there is indeed no perception at all—whether by way of succession or simultaneity—of the air reaching the region of the ear. Therefore, the claim that this illusion of simultaneity in cognition is caused by rapidity is not a valid response.
The meaning is "vain.
