Now, with the words "But even if... and so forth, he states the second position.

Moreover, even if you describe wind as being beyond the senses, just as the followers of Kaṇāda do, by what means is its contact with the sense of touch established in your own commentary? (2534) [The followers of Kaṇāda] are the Vaiśeṣikas.
For them, air is inferred from sound;

the author of the Bhāṣya, Śabara, has also stated: "The conjunctions and disjunctions consisting of air are not perceived, even though they arise from the region of the ear-cavity of the imperceptible air. To this, he states the following objection: "What causes its contact with the sense of touch?"

*Spṛṣṭiḥ* means contact (*sparśaḥ*); its *āptiḥ* (attainment) is *prāptiḥ*, which is to say *prasaṅgaḥ* (an undesirable consequence). This is what is meant: how is it that this consequence of contact with air (*vāyu*), which has been raised by the author of the Bhāṣya, [occurs]? For instance, regarding those proponents of the *Śikṣā* who maintain that "air attains the state of sound," the author of the Bhāṣya said: "If sound were composed of air, it would have to be a particular configuration of air; however, we do not recognize the constituent parts of air as existing within the sound."
Just as a cloth is composed of threads,
yet it does not become [identical to them];
if it were so, we would perceive it through touch.
And we do not perceive the aerial parts residing in the sound;
having thus granted their supersensuousness, he states another fault with the words "Or let it be," and so forth.

Or let air be beyond the senses; however, for one who has attained that [state], there would be the perception of a tangible object that is neither hot nor cold, just as in the case of one who has reached [the state of] fire. (2535) "Tattadyoga" means conjunction with this or that particular wind; that which belongs to the triad of elements known as water, fire, and earth is described as such.
"Directed toward that," "attained to that," or "relying upon that"— in short, this is a compound with the second case ending according to the rule beginning with *dvitīyā-śrita* (Pāṇini 2.1.24),
and it stands in grammatical apposition with the word *spraṣṭavyasya* ("of the tangible").
There arises a feeling (*vit*)— namely, sensation (*vedanā*)— of that tangible object characterized by coldness, heat, or their absence,
just as in the case of another [object],
such as the air within the stomach which is held to be manifested by sound.
The suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the genitive case;

for example, as there is a cognition of the touch of cold and so forth belonging to the wind blowing with a mass of snow during the winter season, or as there is a cognition of the touch belonging to the breeze blowing during the summer season when all quarters of space are obstructed by the contact of the rays of the young sun, so too in this case, there would be a cognition of the touch of the wind existing at a time devoid of both cold and its opposite.

With the words "But even so" (*athāpi*), etc., [the author] anticipates the opponent's reply: "But even if there is no cognition because of its lack of connection with the ear-canal (*karṇaśaṣkulī*), how is it understood that [the sound] has reached the space of the ear (*karṇavyoman*)? (2536)

Therefore, this conception, which is based on the view of the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), is groundless and does not lead to the satisfaction of the wise; thus, it shines only among the Vedic scholars themselves. (Verse 2537) "Of that... [refers to the aforementioned].
The non-connection with wind is non-contact.
The connection is with the word "karṇaśuṣkulī" (the auditory canal); the rest is easily understood. 2536.

Regarding what was stated—"or else, in accordance with the Vedas," and so forth—he says, providing an extension (*atideśa*) by stating that "the refutation is the same" in that case: "Those who assert that space is partless... and so on; against those [who hold such a view], the arguments previously set forth apply.
The defects [previously mentioned] would be the same even if the auditory organ were a single, partless direction (dik).

(2538) Those defects previously stated regarding the position that the auditory organ consists of partless space—such as the futility of refinement (saṃskāra) and the impossibility of refinement—are equally applicable to the position that it is a direction; therefore, no separate refutation need be stated. (2538)
Regarding what was stated—"although it is all-pervading and one," and so forth—he says in response: "In the position that space is one and all-pervading," and so on.
"In the position that space is one and all-pervading, no division can be postulated;
for that space is indeed one alone, being both the substratum of the conditioned and something else. (2539)
The auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is of the nature of a single space; there is no such thing as an unconditioned ear-cavity (*śaṣkuli*).
Therefore, the restriction of its refinement (*saṃskāra*) is established through the distinction of its physical bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Consequently, when the sense organ has received refinement in one base, [it functions accordingly].
Let it be accepted that the production of cognition occurs in all locations [of the body] as its awakener;
let the production of cognition in men be accepted as occurring in the various regions of the body.
However, because space is a single entity, you do not admit a difference in location for the primary cause (pradhāna). ||2541–2542||
Furthermore, even if it is argued that our self, though partless, perceives everything in its entirety yet apprehends only the body, this position is still flawed;
for by this very same reasoning, the irregularity of deafness and other such conditions would also follow.
That very [unconditioned] cannot logically belong to another, for there is no distinction; furthermore, it does not have the unconditioned as its basis.
(2544) "Furthermore" means that it does not have the unconditioned as its support.
Indeed, this division is not logical for that which is partless, as it would entail the consequence of having parts.

However, if the division is merely conceptual, there is a contradiction regarding the occurrence or non-occurrence of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); for causal efficiencies do not conform to superimposed objects, because they are invariably tied to real entities.

Consequently, if a sense organ were refined upon one substrate and that [refinement] were of a cognizing nature, then—since that very same [organ] exists in its ultimate sense on other substrates as well—it would follow that it is refined and cognizing everywhere.

By this, everything that was stated [by the opponent], beginning with "in the bodily regions of persons," has been refuted; for he says [the following] to show that it is impossible for a single entity to have ultimate divisions: "of persons," etc., and "spatial separation from the primary matter" (*pradhāna-vaideśya*) means that the primary matter—that is, the body—is situated in a different location within space.
Even when this is stated, it is faulty because a single entity cannot be divided; thus,
there is no settled determination.
The absence of established order 2539 2540
2544 He demonstrates the lack of distinction itself: "For that which has not abandoned its prior form," and so forth;
for when no particularity arises, [the entity] has indeed not abandoned its prior form.
"How indeed could your ear be something not to be enjoyed by another?

(2545) Furthermore, it might be argued that because it is controlled by merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), there is indeed a distinction; to this he says: "Because of its permanence," and so forth.
Because of its permanence, it is independent, and thus it cannot be controlled by merit and demerit.
Furthermore, it would follow that the auditory organ is always the sky and is thus available for enjoyment by everyone.
Eternity is the reason for independence, and likewise for the lack of control [over it].
Now, he asks why there is no subjugation even of that which is independent, and says: "Dharma and Adharma," etc.
For space is never assisted by dharma and adharma, because it is eternal; and since it lacks the state of being an effect, what kind of subjugation could this be? (2547)

For it is said that by virtue of being independent (*anapekṣatva*), something is non-produced (*akārya*); and that which is non-produced cannot be brought under the control of anything, just like a rabbit's horn or [the state of] cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*). Since the auditory faculty (*śrotra*) is non-produced, this constitutes the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddhopalabdhi*). By the phrase "because of its permanence," he refutes the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the reason; and by the phrase "in the absence of being produced, what is this 'bringing under control'? he refutes its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*). 2547

[Objection: But surely the subjugation of even that which is not an effect is observed; for example, the ear, which was previously incapable of functioning, later becomes capable of functioning through the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth. Therefore, the reason [adduced] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). To this, he states the refutation:
"By the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, etc."—how could it become functional again by the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth?
Because of its eternity, it does not indeed acquire any distinction from those [mantras and herbs]. (2548)
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of scraping and so forth is intended;
the ellipsis to be supplied is: "how could this be [possible] if, even in that case, there were no state of being an effect (*kāryatā*)?"

[The opponent objects: "But surely, even for that which is unmodifiable, mastery [over it] will occur simply through the production of a particular state. To this he says: "Because of its eternity," and so forth (verse 2548). [The opponent replies: "In that case, since the locus is non-eternal, mastery over the eternal auditory faculty itself will occur by means of the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of that locus. To this he says: "But as for the locus," and so forth.
Even if the locus (adhiṣṭhāna) is impermanent, if momentary impermanence does not apply to it, then,
because an excellence of its own nature would be impossible, deafness and so forth would not be possible.
(2549) "Even if it is impermanent" means:

Because it perishes at a later time, even for that [entity], since it is of a single nature and thus like something eternal, the production of an excellence (*atiśaya*) is not possible; so how could there be any refinement (*saṃskāra*)?
(2549) Having granted the existence of such an excellence, he states the fault: "Or let it be," etc.

Or let there be some excellence (atiśaya) in that [organ]; however, such an excellence does not exist in space (vyoman), because it has no connection with a substratum, is eternal, and is independent.
Therefore, deafness and the like cannot be attributed to it even by way of that [space].
Even though the sky possesses parts, this [argument] is the same regarding its eternity;
"this" refers to the excellence [of the argument].

Even though [the quality] does not exist [in the ether], it will nevertheless belong to it due to its connection with its substratum; thus he says: "And not by the substratum," etc., referring to what was stated:

"The ether is not partless," etc. In that regard as well, if the eternity of the ether—which possesses parts—is admitted, then all the refutations that apply to the position of an eternal, partless ether apply equally here; this he extends by saying: "Of the ether," etc. (2550).
Regarding what was stated—"just as in that case, being [already] there," and so forth—he says in response: "even for one who exists in that very place," and so forth;
because of such ownership, there is likewise a removal [of the distinction].
If even that [self] does not possess momentariness, it is not logical [that he would lose his state].
For what excellence has arisen in him subsequently, by virtue of which he— having been deprived of his lordship— would not obtain enjoyment again?
This is easily understood.
Regarding what was stated—"for it is the manifesting winds... and so forth—he replies with "And when... and so on:

"And when such an embellishment (saṃskṛti) is not possible in either the auditory organ or the sound—due to the impossibility of an embellishment based on the alternatives of difference or non-difference. (2554)

For if the embellishment were distinct [from the auditory organ and the sound], neither the ear nor the sound would be embellished; furthermore, there would be no relationship whatsoever between the embellishment and those two.
Indeed, for that which is separate, the only possible relationship would be that of cause and effect.
And in that case, this [cognition] would exist at all times, because its cause is eternally present.
Even in the view that it is not a different entity [from the cause], it would likewise be eternal;
therefore, since it cannot be produced, it follows that cognition is eternal. || 2556-2557 ||

Therefore, a restriction of capacity for wind and so forth is not tenable, because when there is no connection with an object to be produced, capacity itself is also impossible. (2558) "When... [end of verse]
The meaning is "for which reason"; thus,
in the manner just described,
since there is no excellence (atiśaya) in that which is eternal, refinement (saṃskṛti) is simply not tenable.
The connection with what follows is that the restriction of capacity for wind and so forth is not tenable;
and demonstrating in detail how this refinement (saṃskṛti) is not tenable, he says "whether distinct or non-distinct," etc.
There are two possible positions: the refinement, as it occurs, must be either distinct or non-distinct from [the object], because no other mode is possible for a real entity.

In the first position, it follows that the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of both the auditory organ and the sound would be unestablished, because they produce a different object; for when a jar is produced, a cloth is not said to be refined, nor is a connection established between that refinement and those two [the ear and the sound], by means of which they might both be refined through the production of a refinement related to them.
To explain: since their difference is admitted, there is no relationship characterized by identity (*tādātmya*).

Furthermore, if a relation were to exist for that which is distinct [from the cause], it could only be characterized as the relation of cause and effect, since no other form of assistance is possible;
and if that causal relation were present, this impression (*saṃskāra*) would occur at all times, because its cause—the nature of the auditory organ and the sound—remains eternally present.
Regarding the second position as well, he states the fault with the words beginning "anarthāntara... and so forth.
"Like that" means like the nature of the ear and sound;
"this" refers to [the cognition].
Furthermore, since it is eternal, this impression (*saṃskāra*) is not produced by anything;
and if the arising of cognition from that impression were admitted, it would follow that cognition is eternal— this is the fault in [the theory of] eternality.
He concludes with the words "That is not so," etc.

With the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*) and so forth, he provides the proof for the non-eternality of sound: "Therefore, because manifestation is impossible, this cognition of sound is the result [of the production of the object], just like the cognition of the manifestation of a jar or similar objects, which is invariably concomitant with the production of the apprehended object. (2559)

Therefore, based on the presumption of an effect (*kāryārthāpatti*), the distinction in capacity regarding both production (*utpatti*) and manifestation (*abhivyakti*) would be the same everywhere in relation to effort and the desire to speak.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is occasional is produced by a cause that possesses origination, just like the cognition whose object is the manifestation of a jar; and the cognition of sound is occasional. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Because that [nature] is never perceived through cognition, the reason is not unestablished;
because manifestation has been refuted, it is not inconclusive; and because it exists in the similar class (sapakṣa), it is not contradictory.
The analysis of the compound *idamphala* is as follows: "this fruit" means that this fruit has the characteristic of being inseparable from the arising of the object to be grasped (*grāhya*);
the remainder is easily understood.
Since the refutation of the position that the ear is the quarters of space has already been stated previously, it is not repeated here.
Therefore, reminding one of that very same refutation mentioned previously, he says: "Whatever argument... and so forth:

"Whatever argument regarding the Kaṇabhuj [Vaiśeṣika] concerning the nature of a portion of space (*nabhobhāgatva*) may exist, all of it should be understood by the wise to apply equally to a portion of direction (*digbhāga*). (2561)

Regarding what was stated— "If there were embellishment of the object as well, then by that [perception] there would be the embellishment of only one [object]," and so forth— he says "of the object," etc.:
"Even if there were embellishment of the object, by that [perception] there would be the embellishment of only one."
Because [the object] has not perished and because of the restriction of capacity, there is no refinement of the object;
nor is it the case that by [refining] the object, there is a refinement of only one [of the two]. Therefore, this is not so.
Why? Because of its non-existence—that is, because the *saṃskāra* has been refuted;
for it was previously established that a *saṃskāra* is neither distinct nor non-distinct [from the object]. For this reason as well, there is no *saṃskāra* of the object.
Why? Because of the restriction of capacity, which will be explained; and the word "ca" (and) should be understood as having been omitted in the text.
Therefore, this is the meaning that results: [the restriction of capacity].
And because of the restriction of capacity, as will be explained hereafter, the refinement of the object is not tenable.
He demonstrates that very restriction of capacity with the words beginning "In the production of cognition," and so forth.
If it were incapable of producing cognition,
this word would never be perceived by anyone anywhere, because it would be of no use for that cognition.
But if it possesses the capacity to produce cognition, then [it would be perceived] by everyone, everywhere, and at all times.
This word would be understood because it exists as a cause of cognition. [Objection:
There are two possible positions regarding whether this word is by its very nature (prakṛtyā) unfit for the production of cognition at any time or not.
In the first position, it would never be understood by anyone.
In the second case as well, it would be cognized by everyone at all times, because its nature is uniform;
therefore, there is no efficacy for a mental impression (*saṃskāra*).

It might be argued that even a capable [cause] might sometimes fail to produce cognition due to the force of a contrary condition, while likewise, even an incapable [cause] might produce it once it has acquired capacity through auxiliary conditions; to this, he says: "For that," and so forth.
For whether it be capable or incapable, that [nature] which resides in the self by its very essence—
what opposing factor or auxiliary cause would be able to destroy that purpose?

Indeed, it is not logical for something to be an opposing factor or an auxiliary cause without either destroying or producing the intrinsic nature, as this would lead to an over-extension of the principle.
If one accepts the production of a partial destruction, there follows the undesirable consequence of the loss of permanence;
as it was said: "Just as when it is being produced," and so forth.
To this he replies: "And it is capable of producing cognition for some [persons]; therefore, while being produced, it is not apprehended by all. (2556)

Alternatively, if the refinement (*saṃskṛti*) of this [sound] occurs through the sounds produced by those situated nearby, then it is heard by them alone; how much more so by those situated at a distance? This fault does not apply to the theory of production (*utpattipakṣa*), because the sound is produced from its own cause as something capable of generating a specific cognition; therefore, it is not perceived by everyone at all times.

However, for one who holds that the word-sound itself is embellished (*saṃskriyate*), this very fault applies if such an embellishment is indeed possible; demonstrating this, he says "Or else" (*athavā*) and so forth.

Not only does the fault arise—that even a distant object would be perceived—if one accepts the capacity to produce cognition by means of the original nature (*prakṛti*) [of the sound], but there is a fault even in the theory of embellishment (*saṃskārapakṣa*). Therefore, another position is stated:
"But how much less so by those situated at a distance? (*na dūrasthaiḥ... kiṃ punar*).
The connection is "it is heard"; furthermore, he shows directly that it must indeed be heard. 2566
This very point is clarified by the passage beginning with "sāmīpye":
for even in the case of proximity, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is postulated as the cause.

Regarding the statement beginning with "Because the production of sound has been refuted" (verse 2568), he says: "From a specific refinement, etc."— if it is understood that the birth of a specific refinement arises from the sounds (dhvanis), even though they are situated at a distance, that refinement would be common to them all.
At that time, the production of sound cannot be refuted by anyone;
for that specific refinement [of the air] is not distinct from the sound,
and since it would otherwise follow that the sound itself is unknowable, the sound must also be produced.

If the embellishment (*saṃskṛti*) arises, then it would follow that the sound (*śabda*) also arises, because the sound is not distinct from that embellishment. Alternatively, if there were a distinction, then since cognition would arise from the embellishment alone, the sound would lack causal agency and would consequently follow as being non-cognizable.
Therefore, one must admit that the sound also arises.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "Just as for you, a sound is produced that is capable of generating a specific cognition, so too for us there will be a restriction of the latent impressions (saṃskāra); therefore, it is not perceived by those standing at a distance."
Regarding this, it is said: "And once refined," and so forth.
Furthermore, a word that has been refined never abandons its own nature, because of its connection with impermanence; and if it were perceived [as such], it would be perceived at all times. (2571)
Even if it were the case that [the object] is conditioned such that it is capable of producing a cognition occurring within the continuum of a specific person, there would still be a fault;
for instance: if it does not abandon its conditioned nature which is fit for producing the cognition, then it follows that that cognition would arise at all times;
if, however, it does abandon it, then it follows that it is impermanent.
Therefore, it must be admitted that [the effect] indeed arises from that.
Regarding what was stated— "But in the case of the two types of impressions," and so forth— he replies with "In the case of the two," and so on.
Even in the view that [the two] are conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*), it is true that there are two faults; however, there is no deficiency of either one, because of the persistence of the former.
According to the opinion of those for whom there is the position of origination, a deficiency of either one would be logical.
But this is not so in the position of those who maintain the existence of *saṃskāra* (potency/impression), because for them, the nature of that previously conditioned [entity] persists at all times.
With the words "For thus," etc., he demonstrates that very persistence.

For instance, the conditioned sounds of the auditory organ were not previously destroyed by their manifestors; otherwise, because of the occurrence of their destruction, there would follow the hearing of everything by everyone. (2573) [The phrase] "because of the occurrence of their destruction" means:
The meaning is that it would entail the consequence of impermanence;
otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the thesis, as all sacred scripture [would be undermined].
"Universal hearing" (*sarvaśruti*) means hearing at all times;

it does not have the analysis "hearing of everything," because that would be prohibited by the rule [Pāṇini 2.2.14] stating "and [a compound ending in] *karman* [is not formed with a word ending in *śravaṇa*]."

Furthermore, it might be argued that the auditory organ and the phonemes are refined such that they are suitable for hearing only by specific individuals; therefore, [the sound] is not heard by everyone.
If this were so, then those who are perceivers of other phonemes would not obtain the hearing of sound at all.

He demonstrates this very point with the verse beginning "niyata" and so forth: "If the auditory faculty and the phonemes are restricted and refined, then there would be no hearing of those phonemes by people of other castes. (2574)
The compound *niyatānāṃ puṃsāṃ śrutiyogyāḥ* is a genitive tatpuruṣa meaning "those who are fit to hear for restricted men.
Alternatively, the analysis (*vigraha*) is *anye ca te varṇaprapattāraḥ*, or "others who are seekers of the castes," or "seekers of other castes.

Furthermore, one might think: "There may be another refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the auditory organ and the sound that makes them suitable for the arising of the cognition of those other phonemes. Anticipating this objection, he refutes it with the verse beginning *tadvarṇa* and so forth:

"If the two [the ear and the sound] were refined again so as to be fit for the cognition of the person [hearing] those phonemes, then surely there would be hearing of those very same [phonemes] when those two persist. (2575)
The compound *te ca te varṇanarāśca* ("those and those who are both letters and persons") is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound.

Who, then, are they? "Letters" (*varṇa*) refers to those which are apprehended by other perceivers; "persons" (*nara*) refers to those among them who are the actual agents of apprehension. The compound *tadvijñānayogyau* ("capable with respect to the cognition of those") is a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound, meaning "capable with respect to the cognition of those two [letters and persons] alone."
"Of those two as well"— that is, of the previously conditioned ear and sound;
"of those two" refers to the previously mentioned phonemes and words.
This is what is meant:
later, when the phonemes beginning with *ka* are heard by others, they would likewise be heard by those who previously heard them,
because of the persistence of their prior nature.
Now, showing that if there were no persistence [of the same nature], it would follow that they are impermanent, he says: "In the case of exclusion," and so forth:
"If these auditory phonemes are entirely distinct [in each instance], how is it that they are not [perceived as the same]?"
Consequently, the hope for permanence regarding those [entities] is without foundation. (2576) This is easily understood.
Regarding what was stated—"Just as the one [sun], though so," and so forth—he replies with the verse beginning "In water, etc.":
"In water and such, this single sun is not seen as having a manifold nature, because all cognitions of its reflection remain without an objective basis. (2577)
For it has already been established without distinction that all erroneous cognition is devoid of an object;
nevertheless, he now establishes this specifically regarding cognitions of reflections, for both the positions of "with form" (*sākāra*) and "without form" (*nirākāra*).
With reference to the first position, he says: "They are without form," and so forth.
In your position as well, all cognitions are established as being devoid of form (*nirākāra*),
whereas the external object is admitted to possess form (*sākāra*). Furthermore, this reflection is observed as being situated within the water and other such media.

The sun and other celestial bodies existing in the vault of the sky do not abide in that manner [as they appear]. Why, then, does this very object appear thus? If it is argued that it is due to delusion (*bhrānti*), then for that very reason it is so; however, it is not clearly without a basis (*anālamba*), because it is devoid of an object possessing that form.
If the apprehension of that very [object] were otherwise, then this well-spoken statement would be otherwise; however, if it were so, everything would be a knower of everything.
If there were apprehension of that very [object], it would be seen as existing in that manner.
But if it were perceived as having another form, how could there be a perception of that [object]?
For even in the case of a cognition with a form, if that form is not distinct from the known object, it is not logical for the cognition to be its apprehender. (2582–2583)

For you, the Mīmāṃsaka, cognition is formless while the external object possesses form; therefore, that form which is seen within the water is not a form of cognition, because it is admitted that only the external object possesses form.
Nor is it admitted that this is a reflection (pratibimba) existing as a distinct entity, for that would entail the consequence that the sun itself is not perceived.
Nor does the sun enter into the water so that it might appear thus, since it resides in the region of space.

If it is argued that it appears as such through delusion (*bhrānti*), then in that case, the cognition would not have the sun as its objective support (*ālambana*), because that sun lacks a form within the water.

Consequently, it is established that since an object is devoid of the form in which it appears to a cognition, that cognition is without an objective support. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever does not possess the nature appearing in a particular cognition is not the object of that cognition, just as color-form (*rūpa*) is not the object of auditory cognition. And the sun does not possess the nature appearing in the cognition of the reflection; this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
The reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because the sun lacks a form existing within water;
nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*),
whereby anything whatsoever would become the object of perception for anyone.

Because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it is not contradictory (*viruddha*). Furthermore, if it were argued that it is indeed the same sun, but it is merely perceived otherwise due to a difference in location, and therefore the reason (*hetu*) is simply unestablished (*asiddha*),
then who other than you, a bold logician, could possibly assert that "it is that very same thing and yet otherwise"?

For instance, by the phrase "that very same [thing]," its positive identity is established; by the phrase "otherwise," its negation is expressed. How, then, could such mutually contradictory affirmation and negation be logical in a single entity at one and the same time?
If, however, that which is perceived otherwise were still that very same thing, then the entire universe would become one;
consequently, all things would arise and perish simultaneously, and all cognition would have only a single object.
Therefore, if this object were perceived exactly as it exists—with its distinctions of place, time, and so forth—then it would indeed be perceived as such; how then could there be a lack of proof?

Furthermore, even in the second case, the position that cognition possesses a form (*sākāra*), he demonstrates the lack of an external support for cognitions that are like reflections, beginning with the words "Even in the case of having a form" (*sākāre’pi*).

For in the view that cognition has a form, although there is the awareness of a form, an external object is said to be known because one experiences a form that is not distinct from the external object, and not because of an experience of a distinct form.
Otherwise, there would be an over-extension [of the definition];

moreover, in these cognitions of reflections, there is no experience of a form that is not distinct from the form of the sun. For otherwise, the cognitions of reflections would be indistinguishable from non-erroneous cognitions of the sun.
Regarding what was stated [in verse 2582]— "for those who see the sun in the waters, there is no sun," and so forth— he replies with the words beginning "through tradition" (pāramparya).
Let it be understood that what exists as handed down through tradition is perceived by the downward function [of speech],
yet even though it possesses an upward function, one considers it only as downward.
For if this sun were seen exactly as it actually stands, [there would be no such distinction].
It has been established that [the self] can be conceived as being awakened, and not otherwise; thus,
"it should be awakened" refers to the self.
"One who thinks" means one who considers the sun to have an upward course— that is, to be situated above.
This is what is meant by "the Self":

even if the Self perceives the sun situated above, which has been handed down through tradition, by means of its downward-turned function, why does it consider [itself] only as being below and not as being above?
For in this way alone is that very thing understood; if it were apprehended otherwise than as it actually exists, there would be an over-extension of the principle.

Regarding what was stated—"In this way, by the previously mentioned function, that which is presented by the inward-turning function," and so forth—he replies: "It is not thus; by that previously mentioned function, the inward-turning function is not presented."
One who is awakening, through delusion, understands the face as being the inward-facing [self].
Regarding this, he states the reason: "The cognition of a reflection," and so forth; that [cognition] does not have one's own face and so on as its objective support.
"Because it appears as something distinct from that, like the cognition of taste, sound, and so forth.
(2587) The expression "because it appears as something distinct from that" is a designation characterized by its state (*bhāvalakṣaṇa*).
The meaning is: "because it appears as something distinct from that.

This formulation is a *bahuvrīhi* compound: whatever cognition appears as distinct from something does not have that thing as its objective support (*ālambana*). For example, the cognition of taste and so forth does not have sound as its objective support, nor does the cognition of sound have taste as its objective support. And since cognitions of reflections appear as distinct from the face and so forth, this is an instance of the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
2587. Avoiding the charge of this [argument] being unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "In a very small [mirror], etc."—for indeed, what is very small appears in a mirror that is very small.
Furthermore, trees and other objects are perceived as being inverted when submerged in water;
likewise, the reflection does not face the same direction as the object in a mirror.
Moreover, this [reflection] appears as if situated within the water and so forth, whereas the original object remains at a distance.

Furthermore, the reflection is distinguished as gross, subtle, and so forth by conforming to its substrate (*āśraya*), whereas the original object (*bimba*) is not; therefore, the reason [adduced by the opponent] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
Even in a very small mirror, a large face appears as smaller, or even smaller still.

A tree or similar object submerged in water is perceived with its branches and so forth pointing downwards; likewise, a face is apprehended in water and other media as facing inward and situated at a distance, yet the original object (the *bimba*) does not exist in that manner.

Furthermore, due to the difference in the reflecting medium such as a sword, the reflection appears in forms characterized by distinctions like length and so on, whereas the original object does not possess such distinctions of length and the like. Thus, it is not unestablished that cognition manifests in a form distinct from [its object].
Avoiding the charge of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā), he says: "By means of a distinct appearance," and so forth.
If objects were cognized even by a manifestation that lacks their specific characteristics,
then every cognition of form, sound, and so forth would have all things as its object.
Furthermore, when the eye is slightly pressed with a finger, that which is seen—
Even though they are distinct, that error is likewise considered to be without an object. The subverting proof— that all cognition would result in having everything as its object—
which was stated in the passage beginning with "when slightly closed," etc., is also refuted by this very point, because that [cognition] too is without an object.
Regarding what was stated previously, beginning with "and in the case of existing in multiple locations," etc., he says there: "the arising of a reflection," and so forth.
However, the arising of a reflection has already been refuted here, because two material things cannot occupy the same place due to their mutual resistance.
Indeed, the substantial reality of a reflection was previously denied on the grounds that it is impossible for a material object to occupy the same location [as its original], and so forth. (2593)

"Let it be granted that the reflection is a real entity; nevertheless, its being apprehended by the same cognition [as the original] is unproven," showing this, he says: "Even if the reflection exists as occurring in multiple locations," and so forth.
On account of distinctions such as grossness and subtlety, unity does not exist at all.
(2594) By the word "etcetera," distinctions such as length and so forth are included.

Furthermore, it might be argued that even though there are distinctions such as grossness and the like, there is indeed a state of being accessible to a uniform cognition due to some commonality, such as blueness and so forth.
Even so, an ultimate identity is not established; it would only be a conceptual construct, and in that case, there is the fallacy of proving what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Furthermore, if an ultimate identity were to exist even when things are perceived as distinct by way of space and other factors, then let there be oneness between a Brahmin and a Caṇḍāla as well, due to their commonality of being human beings.
Likewise, by virtue of the commonality of "womanhood," your mother, your own wife, and your own mouth and anus would attain oneness due to their being composed of earth;
and if the entire universe were one because of its being a "real entity" (vastu), the consequence of simultaneous arising and destruction for everything would be unavoidable.

As for what was stated in the Bhāṣya—"Now, even if it were so, the simultaneous perception of a single existent entity in multiple locations is untenable"—[the author replies]: "Let the 'beloved of the gods' look at the sun; though it is one, it appears as if situated in many places... because of its distance, its location is not determined, and thus there is delusion; likewise, in the case of sound, there is a non-determination of its location due to delusion. To this, he says: "Of men," and so forth.
And this determination which arises in men, "The sun is situated above me," is certainly an error;
for all living beings [perceive] the very same sun. (2595)
They perceive [the sun] simultaneously, and never a second [sun];
because no second orb or sound exists here, and because it is seen and yet not seen [simultaneously], the sun is therefore determined to be one alone. (2596–2597)
Sound is by no means determined to be a single entity, because its multiplicity is observed both sequentially and simultaneously;
for when many speakers pronounce the phoneme *ga* and others at once, [its plurality is perceived]. (2598)
When they are applied [simultaneously], the distinction is clearly perceived.

Because the second solar disc—which has reached the conditions for perception—is not perceived, its non-existence is ascertained; thus, the oneness [of the sun] is established, and it is determined that the cognition "the sun is situated above me" is an error.
However, the oneness of the word is not established in such a way that its existence in different locations and so forth would be an error.
For if unity were established, then such a state of existing [as distinct] would be proven to be an illusion; however, that very unity is not established—thus, this argument is trivial.
[The word] "rāvam" is derived from "raveḥ" with the suffix -aṇ.
[Objection: But surely the oneness of sound is already established by the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). [Reply: He says, "But not so," and so forth;
the intention is that the invalidity of recognition has been demonstrated previously.
He demonstrates the establishment of plurality through simultaneity with the words, "For when," and so forth.
"Clearly" means because it appears through distinctions such as fast, medium, and slow [tempo].
Explaining it also by way of sequence, he says: "But in the case of its sequential application," and so forth;
for in its sequential application, it is not only [not established] by perception.

However, a distinction among cognitions is understood through their sequence, not solely by means of perception; for even then, there is an experience of a clearly manifest distinction due to the difference between [notes such as] *ṣaḍja* and so forth. Nor is this a distinction caused by a difference in the manifestors, since that has already been refuted previously.
"Also from the mark" (*liṅgāt*) means "also from inference" (*anumānataḥ*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whenever something does not occur, at that time its complete causal complex is not present; for example, visual consciousness does not arise in one who lacks the eye, even when the collection of conditions such as form, light, and mental attention is present. And at the time of the arising of the cognition of a single letter 'A' and so forth, the cognitions intended to occur subsequently do not arise. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Because the state of having unimpaired causal conditions is pervaded by the fact of coming into existence, and that [state] is absent here;
for if the probandum is the negation of the mere state of having unimpaired causal conditions in general, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
For even though an eternal sound may possess causal capacity, its non-arising at a later time due to a deficiency of auxiliary causes is indeed accepted by the opponent.

Now, if what is being proven is the negation of that state of having unimpaired causes which belongs to [an effect] due to a specific cause called sound, then the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*);
for visual consciousness does not fail to arise because of a deficiency in the cause that is sound.
What then?
This is not the case because of a deficiency of the eye.

The probandum is established in a general sense, and there is no fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). To explain: if it were possible for an eternal entity to depend upon another cause, then there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established;
however, that very possibility does not exist, because an eternal entity cannot be assisted by such a cause.
Indeed, only that which can be assisted (*upakārya*) may depend upon something that assists (*upakāraka*); otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle.

Therefore, if one accepts that a word which is independent [of other causes] is the cause [of cognition], then every cognition arising from it would possess its cause in its entirety and would thus occur at all times.
Conversely, if it does not occur, the absence of that cognition would indicate a deficiency in that very word. Thus, how could there be the fallacy of proving what is already established?

Furthermore, even when the deficiency of the cause is to be proven by way of a specific distinction, there is neither the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) nor the fallacy of the example being devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).

For this is the intended meaning here: that which does not occur even when something else is present cannot, according to you, be its cause; just as visual consciousness does not arise even when sound is present, and even when the specific nature of sounds such as the letter *ga* exists, the cognitions intended to be produced by them do not occur. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*). Here too, the impossibility of dependence for an eternal entity serves as the subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*) against the contrary position. Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) caused by seeds and the like situated in a granary, because it is impossible for them to be the primary cause with respect to the sprout. Enough of this elaboration.

Regarding what was stated previously—that [the perception of sound] depends upon the manifesting sounds (*dhvani*) and so forth—which, though already refuted in substance, is refuted once more by the author with the words "vyañjaka... and so on, desiring to demonstrate that this position remains flawed even if there were a manifestor for eternal things:
"And let its perception depend upon the manifesting sounds."
However, there must be a perception of that [object] in its actual state;
otherwise, this perception of it would not occur, because its true form would not be manifest.
For sound does not appear as something that pervades the entire expanse of space. (2601–2602)
Does the auditory perception conform to the fact that those sounds occupy different locations?
Or rather, would the manifested sound appear by its own nature alone, like a jar or other objects?
And all this has been stated as a mere analytical exposition, and the reason for it has also been explained.
The incapacity of manifestors and the impossibility of manifestation have already been established.
Furthermore, the notion that "this very same [entity] is perceived" has been previously refuted;
thus, the fact that it is differentiated by spatial distinction remains uncontradicted.
For if the apprehension of sound were dependent upon its manifestor, why would it not be apprehended as long as it remains pervading space?
Its apprehension would occur in that manner; otherwise, an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would follow, as has been explained previously.
Furthermore, sound is not apprehended as long as space exists.
Therefore, it is not logical for the hearing of a word to conform to the sound;
rather, it is logical that the hearing should conform to that very word which it hears.

And in this way, the word would be established through that hearing and not otherwise; consequently, it would manifest in its entirety, just like a jar or other objects—this is the summary of the meaning.
"Tad" means "therefore.
Regarding the passage beginning with "And just as one [moves] by way of succession," he says: "By way of succession," and so forth;
and whoever moves from a different location by way of succession—
It is established [that movement occurs] because of momentary destruction; otherwise, its motion would not be possible.
Since the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) continues without being separated from its former location, the attainment of another location is not logically tenable if that nature were stable.

For movement is simply the arising of an impermanent thing in another location, but not so for a permanent thing; because it is impossible for that which does not abandon its nature of abiding in one place to go to another location, and because if it were to abandon that nature, the consequence would be the loss of its permanence.
He demonstrates this very point with the words: "of that which is not separated from its previous location," and so forth.
As in the passage beginning "Just as when there is a great expanse [of water]," etc., he says: "Of the sky," and so forth.
Because space is devoid of any defining characteristic (*nirupākhyatva*), its manifestation cannot be conceived;
furthermore, because it is beyond the reach of the senses, this light is not actually in the sky, though it is perceived as such.

(2608) Since the substantial reality (*vastutva*) of space is unestablished, its manifestation is not logical; for its designation arises merely from the absence of tangible objects (*spraṣṭavyābhāvamātra*). Thus, when people do not perceive resistance in the dark, they say, "This is indeed space; there is nothing here."

Even for those who maintain that space (*ākāśa*) is a real entity, it is strictly beyond the senses; how, then, could there be a cognition of space? For this very reason, he says: "And because it is imperceptible.
If this is so, what is perceived when a pit is dug in the earth? He says: "It is light (*āloka*); it is thus."
Showing that even if space were a real entity, its manifestation would not be tenable, he says: "Furthermore," and so forth;
furthermore, manifestation is not tenable in space either, just as it is not in sound.
For knowledge is indeed a manifestation, and this would be eternal due to the constant presence of its cause.
Just as a manifestor is not possible in any way for a word, so too here, when there is a cognition of a word, the notion of an external adjunct is an error. (2609–2610)
Therefore, it is established that length and the other [phonetic qualities] are not properties of all sounds;
for those [qualities] would exist if sounds were the manifestors [of meaning], and that has been refuted.
"That would exist" refers to the aforementioned consequence.
Length and so forth are properties of the sound (dhvani),
and that [property] constitutes the manifesting nature (vyañjakatva) of those sounds.
Regarding what was stated—"nor is there a connection with an unperceived object," and so forth—he replies: "Even though these are absolutely distinct," and so on.
It has been discussed repeatedly before that even these words and their referents, though absolutely distinct, are capable of producing a uniform conceptual reflection (*pratyavamarśa*). (2612)

Therefore, a word whose connection to its object has been perceived does not become expressive through its own function; rather, it has been established that in reality, this [word] is not expressive. 2613.
This is the summary of the meaning here.
If you are establishing the consequence that there is an absence of a relationship between signifier and signified for ultimate meaning and word, then you are proving what is already established;

for instance, the status of universals (*jāti*), specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), and so forth as signifier and signified has been refuted at length in the "Examination of Words" (*Śabdaparīkṣā*).

Furthermore, even for that which is conventional (*sāṃvrta*), there is at that time an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*). For it has already been established in the investigation of *apoha* that certain objects, despite being absolutely distinct, by their very nature become the causes of a reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśajñāna*) of a single form, and thus bring about the conventional relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) between word and object.
Therefore, all this that is being said against the Buddhists who maintain that the meaning of a word is *apoha* merely flounders due to its extreme triviality.
2613 He states the justification for the capacity to denote [objects] from the perspective of conventional reality: "For these cognitions produced by words appear falsely," and so forth.
Indeed, these cognitions constructed by words possess a false appearance.
Because the relationship between the signified and the signifier is established for universals (*jāti*), specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*),

and so forth, those of uniform intellect— though these are in fact distinct in reality— regard the word "cow" as being one and the same due to that delusion, and thus engage in worldly transaction. (2614–2615)
Therefore, everything that has been stated by the twice-born who speaks much that is incoherent—putting forward a mere distinction of words—is without foundation.

For that form which is concealed by a conceptualizing cognition (*buddhi*) through its own appearance, because it does not manifest the object as it truly is, is called "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*); such a cognition is termed "concealment" (*saṃvṛti*). Whatever form is established by that [cognition] is said to be conventional.
That very thing is a conventional being and not an ultimate one, because it is non-existent and because all erroneous cognition is devoid of an object. 2614

Furthermore, it might be asked: "In the absence of ultimate identity, how do words bring about conventional usage characterized by affirmation and negation through the power of superimposition? To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.

For instance, hand-trembling and so forth do not possess oneness because they are distinguished by differences in cognition; moreover, their manifestation as a single entity has been refuted due to distinctions such as rapidity and slowness.
Furthermore, no single, persisting universal (sāmānya) is perceived therein.
And this [gesture] becomes a factor for understanding negation and so forth through convention;
by the word "etcetera" in the phrase "hand-waving etc.," the winking of the eyes and so forth are included;
and [it functions] through the distinction of being fast, slow, and so on.
The connection is with the phrase "due to a difference in cognition.
Furthermore, this difference consisting of rapidity and so forth is not produced by a manifestor, because manifestation has been refuted; thus, "its manifestation" refers to eternal manifestation.
Nor can it serve as a basis for linguistic convention by virtue of a universal (*sāmānya*), because such a universal is unestablished.
It is not logical for an unperceived universal to function as a basis for convention, as that would entail the occurrence of convention at all times. [Objection:
It might be a factor in the cognition of negation and so forth.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), injunctions, permissions, requests, and so forth are included. Their "comprehension"—that is, their cognition—is the "limb," meaning the cause; that [cause] consists of hand-movements and the like, and it follows that sound will likewise be such a [cause]. This is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Regarding what was stated— "Therefore, the relationship between word and meaning is said to be indeed eternal"— he says in response: "Directly," and so forth.

It has been stated that words do not directly convey [external objects] because they are devoid of any necessary connection with them; rather, these [words] are indicators of the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*). Indeed, there exists no real, ontological relationship whatsoever between a word and its object.

Whether it [the universal] be eternal or non-eternal, it is as follows: words do not denote an external object, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between them; this was previously explained during the examination of words (*śabdaparīkṣā*). Furthermore, for those who claim that words denote objects without such a connection, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If this is so, then what do they establish? He says: "These [words] indicate the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). They do not establish even the intention as a denotable object; rather, they indicate it by way of being a logical mark (*liṅga*). For this very reason, they are called "indicators" (*sūcakāḥ*).

For instance: from a word that has been uttered, a conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*) arises that determines the object, not the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*); and how can that which is not determined by means of a known word be the meaning of a word?
If this is so, what connection do these [words] have with the intention to speak, such that they might indicate it as a logical mark (*liṅga*)? To this he says: "Of that," and so forth.
For those [words] are ascertained through perception and non-perception as being the effects of that [intention]; thus, the causal relationship between them is clear.
(2620) Since words are ascertained within oneself as the effects of that intention to speak through perception and non-perception, the connection is indeed characterized by cause and effect.

"If that is the case, then the convention (samaya) is useless, because the causal relationship is ascertained by perception and non-perception alone. To this he says: "And the causal relationship... and so forth;
"and the causal relationship is ascertained by someone through convention," etc.
He would arrive at the intention [to speak] through words, like the movement of a hand.

He thinks as follows: although the causal relationship is ascertained with respect to intention in general, it cannot be ascertained with respect to a specific intention in another's continuum without convention (*samaya*); therefore, convention is established for the sake of ascertaining that. But how can this [specific intention] be ascertained even through convention?

For instance: if, at the time of establishing a convention (*samaya*), a specific intention of another were possible as a means of cognition, then that convention established therein would later, at the time of linguistic usage, become the cause for cognizing that specific intention.
However, such a means does not exist;

for a convention cannot be established without uttering a word. Consequently, if the specific intention were understood from that very word, there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*).

For instance: [an opponent might argue] that a word indicates a specific object by virtue of convention (*samaya*), yet convention cannot be established without the cognition of the specific and the non-specific; thus, there is clearly a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

This is not a fault, because when this entire verbal discourse is accepted as being solely in accordance with one's own internal appearance (*svapratibhāsa*)—due to its erroneous nature, like the discourse of two people with cataracts regarding two moons—then there is no room for such criticism.

Furthermore, it is not the case that in every instance the word alone is the cause for the cognition of a specific intention (*vivakṣāviśeṣa*); for otherwise, someone might establish a convention (*samaya*) by indicating a specific intention through direct pointing (*śṛṅgagrāhikayā*), context (*prakaraṇa*), and so forth, as well as by demonstrating a specific meaning. Thus, there is no fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Moreover, this objection applies equally to you, the proponent of injunction (*vidhivādin*): since the cognition of another person is not perceptible, how can there be certainty that the speaker and the listener have cognized the same object?
Furthermore, a convention (samaya) is not tenable without a certainty regarding the comprehension of a single object; whatever response you have to this point will also serve as mine.
It might be argued: "Since the word is not fixed to a specific intention (*vivakṣā*), how can its connection with that intention be determined by convention?
For a convention established here cannot make it signify another object, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This is not a fault;

for by the term "intention" (vivakṣā), what is intended here is that form of the object which, in ultimate reality, is not distinct from intention itself, being either non-transformed [into another] or existing as its own nature.
This is because, in the ultimate sense, it has the very nature of intention.

It is precisely this particular intention that is intended here, and the linguistic convention (samaya) applies to that alone, not to the unique particular (svalakṣaṇa); it is that very thing which is denoted by the word,
because from it arises a conceptual construction (vikalpa) bearing its form.
It has been stated that the mere intention (*vivakṣā*) itself is not denoted by the word (2621).

If this is so—if the relationship of the word is indeed characterized as one of cause and effect with the form of the object residing within the intention—then why do the teachers here and there speak of the "conventional" (*sāmayika*) or "convention" (*samaya*) as the relationship between word and meaning? To this he says: "Residing in the intention," and so forth.
This relationship of words, consisting of a causal connection with an object existing within the speaker's intention, arises when there is a convention (*samaya*).
Therefore, it is called "conventional" (*sāmayika*), and for that reason, [the meaning] is manifested by it.
The term *sāmayika* is said to refer to their relationship, but not in its primary sense.

When there is a convention (*samaya*) in the mind of the listener, [the word] arises or comes into being; thus it is *sāmayika*. Although the suffix *ṭhañ* is applied here according to the rule for words beginning with *adhyātma*, even though the root *bhū* is taken there as denoting existence (*sattā*), nevertheless, because in the ultimate sense there is no difference between existence and birth, that very thing is intended to be expressed as "coming into being" (*bhāva*).

Furthermore, the convention (*samaya*) does not exist within the continuum of the speaker; rather, it is called "convention" metaphorically because it illuminates [the object], since it cannot exist at that time due to its occurrence at a specific, distinct time.

2623. Now, if it has been stated that from the perspective of ultimate reality (paramārtha) there is no relation between entities, then how can there be the characteristic of cause and effect? To this he says: "By those which have become cause and effect," and so forth, ending with "those very [two]."

The two entities that constitute cause and effect are indeed distinct from one another; it is not a case of "causality" being a separate entity joined to them, but rather those very entities themselves are designated as such. 2624.
[These are] the two entities existing as cause and effect.
The phrase "tathodite" (when it has been stated thus) refers to [the passage] beginning with "kāryakāraṇatā" (the relation of cause and effect), for the sake of brevity. 2624.

If this is so, since those two [the word and its object] differ with each individual's application [of the convention], how can the speaker and the listener have a cognition of an undifferentiated relationship? For instance, it occurs to the speaker thus: "I am conveying that very same object by means of that very same word which was grasped by me at the time of the convention"; and likewise it occurs to the listener thus: "He is conveying this very same object by means of that very same [word]. Otherwise, how could there be linguistic communication between two people situated in different mental states? To this, he says: "And those... and so forth.
And since those [universals] are individually of a single nature, they are considered by the dull-witted to be pervaded by the time of convention and linguistic usage.
(2625) "By the dull-witted" means...
When it has gone, it is apprehended by those who are deluded.

That which is reached and pervaded by convention (*saṅketa*) and linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is thus described as "time" (*kāla*); its pervasion [is established] through the repetition of cause and effect in a uniform manner—this is the remainder of the sense. (2625)
Now, one might ask: why is a single, ultimate relation not accepted, such that only a conceptual one would be desired? To this he says: "But a single real relation," and so forth.
"But a single real relation is not at all tenable here; because objects are unmixed, there would be a lack of relation when there is difference. (2626)
A relation, if it were to exist, would have to be between things that are either distinct or non-distinct.
It cannot first be between distinct things, because all things remain established within their own selves and thus lack mutual commingling.
Even in the case of non-difference, since that entity is one and the same, with what could there be a conjunction, and for whom? Therefore, there would be a state of non-relation.

Regarding the refutation of the relationship characterized by convention (*samaya*), stated in the passage beginning with "Convention [is] for every person" and so forth, he says "Convention... etc., demonstrating that [the argument] proves what is already established:
"Convention is for every person and indeed for every utterance."

Thus and so forth has been stated by the opponent, who does not understand the position of the other side. For a convention (*samaya*) is not a primary relation between those two [the word and its object], because it is a property of humans;
rather, it is a relation in the sense that it is the indicator (*dyotaka*) of that [object]. (2627–2628)
Furthermore, others do not accept this [theory] at every utterance, because [the existence of] Īśvara and so forth has been refuted, and it was not created by Him at the beginning of creation.

For a "refutation" is defined as the occurrence of an undesired consequence; moreover, the Buddhist does not accept that the primary relationship between word and meaning is a convention (samaya), since that is a property of human beings.
And since that [position] has been refuted, there is no loss whatsoever to our desired conclusion;
furthermore, a property belonging to one thing cannot belong to another, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

As for what was said—that there are two positions, namely, that [the Veda] is produced at every recitation or that it was created at the beginning of the world—since we do not accept those positions, they are not subject to refutation.
Thus he says: "at every utterance," and so forth;
"this" refers to the convention (*samaya*).
The Buddhists [hold that it is] from another;
[the Naiyāyikas hold that it is] from God and so forth.
Of Īśvara, Brahmā, and so forth.
Regarding what was stated, "Or rather, there is a relation with each [individual]," etc., he says in response: "With each," etc.
That relation which exists with each [individual] appears distinct due to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*).
And a uniform reflective awareness is not contradicted even when there is difference.
The second position alone is correct here;

nor does it entail the consequence of a cognition of difference, because there is no contradiction in a uniform reflective awareness being the cause [of the cognition] despite the existence of difference.
Therefore, that which was stated—"if [the object] were distinct, there would be a cognition of difference"—is inconclusive.

One might object: "This momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) is not established for us; so how can it be said that [something] is distinct from momentary destruction? To this he replies with the words beginning "successively" (krameṇa).
And they say that the cognitions having that as their object clearly arise in succession; for otherwise, there would be no succession even for those [cognitions].
(2631) "Even for that" means...
They state the sequence of the relationship— the meaning is that they establish it—
with the thought that otherwise there would be no sequence for cognitions; such is the connection [of the words].
And this is the subverting proof regarding the contrary; the formal argument (prayoga) is to be understood as before.
Regarding the objection that "because of the difference between the cognitions of the speaker and the listener, linguistic convention (vyavahāra) becomes impaired," and so forth, he says:
"If a convention is established for many [terms] all at once, a distinct convention is not required, just as in the case of a single moment of blue and so forth. (2632)
There is no relation other than that of the speaker in the cognition, nor another distinct from that of the hearer;
and it is of a single form, since it persists for both. (2633) Furthermore, in order to establish the relation for the hearer, the speaker first enters into [the cognition of] that relation himself.
For it is precisely that which was previously perceived by him which he now brings about;
since his reflective cognition (pratyavamarśadhī) occurs in a single form, he therefore determines oneness even though the word and other factors are distinct. (2634–2635)

Just as a momentary instance such as blue does not undergo division even when perceived by many, so too the relationship will not be divided even when a convention is established by many; how much less so between two people?
This is because all are established in the same conceptual determination (*pratyavamarśa*).
Therefore, no relationship other than that [between the speaker and the listener] comes into being.
Regarding what was stated— "If it is argued that this is the same for jars and so forth, no, because the universal is already established," and so on— he replies there:
"In the case of jars and so forth" means that even in the case of jars and so forth, the universal has already been refuted.
For no form (*ākṛti*) is admitted that is distinct from the qualities of the elements;
nor is its capacity for holding water and so forth established by virtue of such a form, since those [qualities] are also eternal if they are non-different from the form. (2636–2637)
If [the power] were distinct [from the object], there would be the fault of [a lack of] relation; if it were produced from it, however, there would be impermanence.
Therefore, a power residing in the form [of the object] is not logical for [actions such as] fetching water and so forth.
Even if the power were distinct from the jar and other objects, these faults would certainly remain.
In that case, its effects, such as the retention of water and so forth, would necessarily follow as being eternal;
this has already been established in the "Examination of the Universal" (Sāmānyaparīkṣā).
Furthermore, he provides a refutation of this very point in brief, beginning with "Not indeed," etc.:

You, the Mīmāṃsaka, do not accept that a *jāti* (universal) exists as something distinct from the qualities—such as blackness and so forth—of the elements, such as the sun-born [fire] and others (or earth, water, and so forth).

Nor is it perceived, even though you claim it ought to be perceived. Furthermore, it is not tenable that it is non-distinct, because that would entail the consequence that those things, such as jars and the like, would also be eternal, just like the nature of their forms (*ākṛti*).

Furthermore, if it is admitted that [the universal] is distinct [from the individual], then there is the fault of the absence of a relation; for among distinct things, the only possible relation would be that characterized by origination from them (*tadutpatti*). Consequently, since such origination exists, the universal would result in being non-eternal, because it possesses the property of arising, like a jar.
(In some versions, the reading is "nityatā" [eternality];

in that case, the meaning is as follows: If the origination of jars and so forth from that universal is accepted, then the eternality of jars and so forth would follow, meaning that because the cause is eternally present, their production would necessarily be eternal.

In the position that it possesses the nature of both, the faults inherent in both positions would apply, and there would be the consequence of the loss of the unity of the entity, because a dual nature for a single thing is untenable; for in this way, those two would simply be stated as two distinct entities, not one single thing consisting of both natures.

It must be stated that these are the faults: the consequence of losing its status as a real entity if it belongs to neither category, and the impossibility of both affirmation and negation applying to a single thing.
The faults characterized by the non-establishment of the relationship [between cause and effect] and the resulting consequences of eternality and so forth,
as well as the further fault of the consequence that activities such as holding water would be eternal, [apply].
Regarding what was stated—that "the relation is indeed the capacity" (*śakti*) and so forth—he says: "And the capacity alone," etc. That is to say:
"The capacity alone is the relation, and its distinction is not admitted."
There would be a single power belonging to both word and object because they are non-different.
Even if they were different, there would be no relation whatsoever between that [power] and those two;
for if it were produced from them, it would lack permanence, and there is no other possibility for a real entity.
Nor is it "other," because,
as in the previous case, this would entail the logical fault of having the characteristics of being both or neither.
Regarding what was stated— "at the time of explaining the relationship," and so forth— he replies with "at the time of explaining the relationship," etc.:
"But when the word 'cow' or the like is uttered at the time of explaining the relationship..."
Some understand the object through the cognition of a relationship, while others do not;
for, according to the existence of a relationship, the object is manifested in whatever way it has been revealed.
However, if your [proposed] relationship were the case, everyone would grasp the object [simultaneously].
For you maintain that the relation is indeed a potency (*śakti*) that is eternal;
and is that [potency] restricted and unlimited in its production of the cognition of an object?
If it were restricted and unlimited, why would everyone not apprehend every object?

What is the cause for this even in the case of that which possesses a basis? If it is nature (*prakṛti*), then since it is so by itself, why does cognition proceed toward only one [object] there—given that before the grasping of the convention and upon its subsequent non-recollection, [the object] remains the same? (2645–2646)
For that capacity is established as being necessarily restricted to the production of that cognition; or else, if it is postulated that the capacity is restricted only when it is itself known—
if it were distinct as both known and unknown, its permanence would be lost.
But if there is identity, for what reason is this distinction described?

(2648) It would be logical that some perceive [the object] because such a relationship exists—namely, one characterized by the nature of cause and effect—since that [relationship] is established as producing a determinate cognition;
however, in your theory of the relationship, everything is untenable, as he shows with the words "your own" and so forth.

To explain: a relationship characterized by *śakti* (potency) is accepted; and that form which is generative is called *śakti*. Furthermore, it is held to have a single, eternal nature and is restricted to the production of the cognition of an object. Consequently, being restricted to the cognition of an object, is it held to be unlimited—meaning devoid of any limit in terms of persons—or is it not? These are the two alternatives. In the first case, there would follow the undesirable consequence that everyone would simultaneously and in every respect ascertain the object.

Even in the second case, a cause that determines the specific nature of producing a particular consciousness must be stated; for while it is logical that produced entities have their own causes and conditions as the determinants of their specific nature of producing particular effects, this is not the case for eternal things—this is the point.

It might be argued that even for eternal entities, their very nature (*prakṛti*) is such that they produce only specific effects and not everything, for natures do not admit of questioning. However, if this nature of theirs were intrinsic and independent of anything else, then prior to the apprehension of a convention, the cognition [of that object] would always arise for that very same specific cognizer who has forgotten the convention, because the fixed capacity to generate that cognition would be constantly present.

Now, it might be argued that because it is a signifier (*jñāpaka*), the power characterized as a relation (*sambandha-lakṣaṇā śakti*) produces cognition only when it is known, not when it is unknown; therefore, the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not arise.
This is incorrect, for if a mutual distinction between its known and unknown states is admitted, then its eternity is lost.

If, on the other hand, there is no difference [between the two], then the distinction between the two natures—the known and the unknown—is untenable; for it is not possible for a single entity, with respect to a single person, to possess two mutually contradictory natures, namely, being known and being unknown. (2642–2643)
Furthermore— thinking that the capacity for action could only be known if there were a means of practice, and that such a means itself is not possible— he asks, "Furthermore," and so forth.
Furthermore, by what means is the capacity [of words] held to be known?

If it is argued that it is through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), then because this principle applies here: one perceives directly (*pratyakṣeṇa*) the word, the elder, and the object denoted. (2649)
And one understands the listener's state of comprehension through inference based on their behavior;
furthermore, by the principle of "impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti), one perceives the capacity residing in both [the speaker and the listener].
Thus, they realize that the relationship [between word and meaning] is established by three means of valid cognition (tri-pramāṇaka) through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).

With the words "from presumptive testimony" (*arthāpatti*) and so forth, he first sets forth at length the opponent's rebuttal. To explain: this principle regarding the comprehension of the relationship was described by Kumārila as follows.
