First, one perceives through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) the word, the elder who utters the word, and the object which is the denotation; subsequently, one perceives—that is, ascertains—the listener's understanding by means of inference (*anumāna*) based on the mark (*liṅga*) characterized by purposeful action (*ceṣṭā*). By treating the instrument (*karaṇa*) as the causal factor (*kāraka*), the nature of the action as inference has been stated.
And thereafter, by means of presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), one cognizes the power residing in both— that is, the power residing in both word and meaning.

Since they are directly understood through presumptive testimony, it is said that "they are understood through presumptive testimony," and thus [the cognition] possesses three means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa).
He for whose realization there exist the three means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) characterized by perception, inference, and presumptive testimony is described as such. 2649–2650.
With the words "In quite another way," etc., he states the refutation:
"Because it is established in quite another way, the capacity cannot be understood."
"Because from a word based on convention, there arises an unconfused comprehension.
By this, he states that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since it has been demonstrated that comprehension is possible even without an eternal relation.

Showing that its postulation is not only improper due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish it, but also improper because it is contradicted by valid cognition, he says: "In the case of the eternality of capacity (*śakti*), however," and so forth.
"If capacity were eternal, it would not depend on anything such as convention (*saṃketa*); therefore, the comprehension of word-meanings would occur at all times. (2653)

Furthermore, if another capacity were present, the *dhvani* would not convey a different meaning— just as in the case of words such as *kālimā* or *ārya*— because the *dhvani* possesses a fixed power (*niyata-śakti*).
If it is maintained that there is only a single power intended for the illumination of multiple meanings, [then the following applies].
Or else, a single word would have to convey multiple meanings simultaneously.

(2655) The formal argument is as follows: Those words which reveal their objects by depending upon convention do not possess an eternal relation, such as the words *gāvī* and so forth; and the worldly and Vedic words such as *go* and so forth reveal their objects by depending upon convention. This is an "observation of the pervader of the contradictory" (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), because dependence is pervaded by the quality of possessing a non-eternal relation, which is the opposite of possessing an eternal relation.
And this proof will be presented later;
however, here only its pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.
For instance, words are held to be connected with a relation characterized as capacity (*śakti*), which is the cause for the comprehension of meaning, and which possesses an eternal connection.
Furthermore, since that capacity (*śakti*) is eternal and thus incapable of being assisted, it does not depend upon anything such as convention (*saṃketa*);
consequently, the comprehension of word-meanings resulting from it would occur at all times.

Moreover, is that capacity restricted to a single meaning or restricted to multiple meanings? Even regarding that, there are the following alternatives: in the case of restriction to multiple meanings, is the capacity that illuminates multiple meanings for a single word one and the same, or is it manifold?

In that regard, concerning the first position: when a different convention (*saṅketa*) is being established according to differences of place, time, and so forth, the observed capacity of a word or sound (*dhvani*) to convey a different meaning—as in the case of words such as *kali* and *mārya*, which respectively denote death and rain or calamity in the Dravidian and Āryan countries—that would not be possible, because its power is fixed, like the eye and other senses;
for the eye cannot, by virtue of convention, be directed toward the perception of taste and the like.
Even in the second position, there is the undesirable consequence that all persons would simultaneously comprehend the meaning of a word from a single sound;
he demonstrates this with the verse beginning "When the word is one," etc. (2653).
Right here, he states another fault: "And because of the capacity to illuminate the object," and so forth.
Furthermore, since the capacity to illuminate meaning is always established,
the understanding of that meaning— which is caused by it— would occur for everyone at all times.
If it is argued that this capacity is postulated as being dependent upon convention (*saṅketa*) in that regard, [the following applies].
Surely, that which is benefited would depend [on something else], but that [cognition] is unchanging and not something to be benefited.
"In that" refers to the comprehension of the object.
That power is immovable.
And this [permanence] is the reason for its being incapable of receiving assistance.
Even granting the dependence on convention, he states another fault: "And because the convention, which is the cause for illuminating the meaning, has its basis in humans... and so forth.
Even when produced by others, the possibility of falsity exists [in the Veda].

Thinking, "I must understand an object that is unmixed," you have rejected the person as the cause of confusion; yet, just as words employed by them in some cases become confused, why would the Vedic words—which are common to all objects—not become confused when they are applied to specific things by those men according to their own whims, since those persons lack knowledge of the true nature of reality?
For instance, convention arises from the power of desire, and since that desire operates with independence in those who do not know reality, by what could it be restrained?
Consequently, why would a convention—born of independent desire—be either arbitrary or hostile, such that it would avoid a contradictory meaning?
Having accepted the position that there is a capacity to illuminate multiple meanings, he states another fault: "The capacity to illuminate multiple meanings," and so forth.
"Indeed, let a single sound possess the capacity to illuminate multiple meanings; however, the objects such as the *agnihotra* sacrifice and others are not all applicable to every [sound]. (2659)
Since it is also possible for words to indicate meanings that are contrary to what is intended, your postulation of an eternal relationship between words and their meanings is pointless.

(2660) Even though words possess the capacity to convey various meanings, objects do not possess the capacity to perform all causal functions, because the relationship between cause and effect is strictly determined.
Otherwise, nothing would be either obstructive or non-obstructive;

consequently, when a specific object capable of purposeful action (arthakriyā) is intended to be communicated, how could it be established that the author of the convention applies a convention regarding only the desired object to a word that is common to all objects?
Therefore, because the possibility of falsity exists, the postulation of an eternal relationship is entirely useless.
Furthermore, demonstrating its lack of purpose once again, he says: "And in the case of convention," and so forth.
And when there is dependence upon convention, why is this relationship— characterized by eternal capacity— nurtured as being causeless?
For no [cause] whatsoever is observed for that which exists as an already established presence.
Apart from convention, there is no operation in the communication of meaning.

(2662) If the relationship were the cause of the cognition of meaning by its mere existence, then it would occur even for one who is ignorant of the convention; therefore, its dependence upon convention must necessarily be admitted.

Consequently, if convention itself is accepted as the cause of the cognition of meaning, why is another eternal relationship postulated which merely presents itself once established and serves as no cause at all?

For the function of a relation is precisely this: the production of the cognition of an object. If that is accomplished by convention (*samaya*), then what is the use of postulating another eternal relation?
Furthermore, it has been discussed hundreds of times that such a [permanent] entity, being incapable of having any excellence added to it, can have no dependence [on anything else].

Moreover, if one were to postulate a cause whose causal capacity is never observed, alas, why could one not postulate that "it is the deities who, upon reaching the *harītakī* fruit, cause purgation"?
With the words "For instance" (*tathā hi*) and so forth, he demonstrates that very same non-establishment of the operation of the relation.
For this linguistic usage is not observed without a convention;
therefore, the establishment of the relationship [between word and meaning] would result in an infinite regress.
Thus [it is said]: "Therefore..."
This succession is not for the sake of any purpose other than convention;
for if one were to postulate a causal efficacy for that which has not been observed to possess such power, there would be the fault of infinite regress.

For instance—even if a relation is postulated, why should another cause with an unobserved capacity not be postulated once again? Since there is no distinction in terms of having an unobserved capacity, this process would continue indefinitely, resulting in a great succession of undesirable consequences.

Having thus established the pervasion (vyāpti) of the subverting proof, he concludes the previously demonstrated inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva) of the presumption (arthāpatti) by means of the verse beginning with "narecchā" [human desire].
Even from a convention arising solely through mere human whim, linguistic usage is indeed possible; therefore, yoga is not established.
"Yoga is not established" means [it is not proven].
The word "eternal" (*nitya*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].

And by establishing it thus, he demonstrates that what was stated—namely, "because all those who lack direct perception [establish their views] based on the prior renown of their predecessors," and so forth—is stated in a manner that is mutually contradictory: "because it cannot be explained otherwise" (*anyathānupapatti*), and so on.
The impossibility of accounting for that linguistic usage otherwise is suspected;
however, since the connection (yoga) is beyond the senses, it is not apprehended by men.
This is because all [persons] lack direct knowledge [of it], due to its not having been established by each preceding generation.

If [it is argued that] "the connection is not established," why then is this [connection] postulated? For if all people were ignorant [of it], how could the establishment of the relationship occur through a succession of prior ignorance? Indeed, a chain of blind men is not capable of instructing others regarding specific forms, as stated in the Śābara Bhāṣya: "In matters of this kind, the word of a person does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge, just like the speech of blind men regarding specific forms."

It might be argued that all [ordinary people] are said to be ignorant because they do not perceive [the ultimate reality] directly, but not because they lack complete knowledge in every respect; for by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely the fact that verbal usage would otherwise be inexplicable, it is established that the elders of the past were indeed possessed of such knowledge.

This, however, is not so, because verbal usage could proceed even through a convention (*saṅketa*) other than that [of an eternal relationship]. This has not been definitively demonstrated; nevertheless, this remains doubtful: is this [relationship] eternal or is it non-eternal?
Therefore he says: "It is suspected," and so forth.

For instance, the existence of a mere relation is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), but not its specific nature, because a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) with that [specific nature] is not proven; this is the intended meaning.
Consequently, there is no difference between presumptive testimony and inference (*anumāna*).

It might be argued: "The capacity of the impermanent to cause the comprehension of meaning has not been observed, nor is it logical," as was previously established; therefore, by virtue of this incapacity, the permanent [word] is established.
To this we reply: this same argument applies equally to the permanent, and it remains unproven;
for instance:

It is the same that even for a permanent relation, the status of being a cause for the comprehension of meaning has never been observed. Since it is observed that gestures such as the movement of the hand function as communicators despite their impermanence, [your claim of] non-observation is unestablished;
therefore, [our] argument that it is illogical is likewise unestablished.

Furthermore, because it is contradictory for a permanent entity to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) either successively or simultaneously, that very [claim of permanence] is illogical—thus, this [objection] is trivial.
Having thus concluded that presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is inconclusive, he presents the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*): "Therefore, cows, horses, and so forth," and so on.
Therefore, words such as "cow" (go) and "horse" (aśva), being endowed with an eternal relationship [with their referents],
do not depend upon convention in the same way that words such as "gāvī" do.
(2667) "That" refers to this.
Therefore,
the connection is with the phrase "not [those] possessing an eternal relationship."
The formulation of the argument has already been shown [previously].

Now, one might object: since words such as *gāvī* and the like are grammatically incorrect (*asādhu*), their status as denoters (*vācaka*) is not accepted by the opponent; therefore, the example is unestablished (*asiddha*).

And so it has been stated by Kumārila: "When the word 'go' (cow) is established [as the correct term], the cognition of a cow that arises even from words such as 'gāvī'—which are produced due to the incapacity [of speakers] for that [correct term]—follows the original word.

This is its meaning: when the word 'go', which is the correct expressive term, exists, the cognition of a cow that occurs through the use of incorrect terms like 'gāvī' is said to arise; yet it does not arise from those [incorrect forms] themselves. What, then, is the source? It follows the primary, correct word 'go'.

The connection [in the phrase] "due to being produced by that incapacity" (*tadaśaktijakāritāt*) is one of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "gāvyādi" (words such as *gāvī*). When the word "go" (*gośabda*) is the correct [form], a person's inability to pronounce it is "that incapacity" (*tadaśakti*); the activity of the palate and other vocal organs arising from that is what is so described; and the word *gāvī* and others are "caused" (*kārita*) by that. Thus it has been stated by Bhartṛhari: "Just as a child being taught says 'avāśva' or 'ambāmba'... (the list of corrections shows this error as *avāśveti*).
That [correct form] is unmanifest to those who know it; therefore, through its manifestation, certainty arises.
Likewise, when a correct word ought to be used, if a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*) is employed instead, some meaning mediated by that correct word is inferred through it.
Therefore, he says this: "In the word 'cow' (go-śabda), etc."—
when the word 'cow' is present as a fit [object], [the cognition] arises from its being produced by that which is incapable [of producing it].
"The cognition of 'cow' even from words such as *gāvī* follows the original word [the correct form *go*].
To this, he replies with the verse beginning "That is not so," etc.:
"That is not so, because those who speak *śanakā* and other dialects do not understand the Sanskrit [word]."
How could there be a comprehension of meaning by following the root-words?
Therefore, a permanent relationship between word and meaning is not accepted; rather, it is logical that it is conventional, since that is possible in every respect.
The phrase "of Śanaka and others" includes fishermen and the like by the word "others," and includes barbarians and so forth.

For indeed, on the contrary, when the meaning is communicated to them by means of the refined (saṃskṛta) language itself, only confusion arises; therefore, it is not logical for the comprehension of the meaning to follow the original sounds. 2669–2670.

Regarding what was stated—"the dissolution (pralaya) may take the form of the destruction of a region or the destruction of a family," and so forth—he says: "deśotsāda... etc., meaning that which is the dissolution taking the form of the destruction of a region or the destruction of a family.
Or, that [Veda] which is desired by the Buddhas as being unimpeded might even be suspected [to be false] by Brahmā and others;
in such a Veda, any further cognition is considered to have its root destroyed, as are all erroneous conceptions arising from delusion, intoxication, and the like. (2671–2672)
"One might even suspect that the Veda has become something entirely different, having merely assumed the guise [of the original]," as long as no subverting evidence is revealed.
Thus he thinks.
We do not describe dissolution as consisting in the annihilation of sound, nor do we maintain that there is a beginningless Person who acts as the creator and destroyer;
rather, the entire world itself is beginningless.
Even linguistic usage proceeds as something established by conceptual constructions arising from beginningless latent predispositions.

However, this dissolution described by you in the form of the destruction of regions and so forth, as well as that which is characterized by the Buddhists as the *saṃvartanī* (destruction) by fire, water, and wind—which ultimately has the limits of the triple-thousand great thousandfold world-system (*trisāhasramahāsāhasralokadhātu*) below, reaching down to the wind-circle (*vāyumaṇḍala*), and above, extending respectively to the first, second, and third dhyānas—this [latter] is uncontradicted because it is not sublated by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Since it cannot be refuted even by Brahmā and others, it is suspected [to apply] even to the Veda. Therefore, in both these types of dissolution, the destruction of the Veda is possible, as is the possibility of its assuming a contrary meaning.

Thus, the suspicion that this Veda is something entirely different— having attained the state of being a mere semblance (*pratikañcukatā*) or a reflection (*tatpratibhāsatā*) of it— does not cease until you state a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*).
It might be argued that there indeed exists a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*);
for instance, at present, it is impossible for persons anywhere in any place to effect any alteration in the recitation or other aspects of the Veda.
Therefore, we conclude that it was so at other times as well and will be so in the future; anticipating this objection, he says: "If there were a desire to produce it otherwise," and so forth.
"Even if there were a desire to produce it otherwise, the sound would not proceed in that way, provided that such a desire arises in men and not otherwise. (2674)

One might suspect that this Veda is not of a nature where its text and meaning could be otherwise; however, if it were subject to activity according to one's own will, such a suspicion would not be dispelled. (2675) For if, even when the desire to alter it exists, the sound of the Veda did not proceed otherwise, and if the desire to alter it could not be produced, then the incapacity of a person to effect any alteration in the recitation and so forth of the Veda would be established.
Even in that case, it is not established for all men, because mere non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*),
and because we observe exceptional capacities among individuals;
for instance, the recitation of Vedic passages such as "śaṃ no devīrabhiṣṭaye" could be performed otherwise, or their meaning could be explained in a different way.
For instance, the Mīmāṃsakas, the authors of the Nirukta, and others are seen to explain the meaning of the Vedas in many different ways;
therefore, doubt is not dispelled.
Regarding what was stated—the description of the refutation beginning with "Nor is the sequence something produced" and so forth—he says: "Nor by all... and so on;
that is, the sequence is not accepted as established for all by all persons.

They also compose the sequence of words, sentences, and syllables independently; otherwise, some work would not be artificial for you, just like the Veda. Thus, even in the case of a mere collection of meaningless words, the status of being a human composition is destroyed. 2676–2677 The following is a list of the most important abbreviations used in "He intends to express it exactly as it was stated by others"—this lack of fixed rule (aniyati) is not like a [permanent] relationship; that is what is meant. Furthermore, "words," "sentences," and "syllables" were mentioned in that manner; the analysis [of the compound] should be understood as "the sequence of these."

The connection is: "even in the case of a mere book of nonsense, the activity [of composing it] is destroyed. A "book of nonsense" (*anarthagrantha*) is one whose subject matter (*artha*) does not exist; it is "nonsense" (*anartha*) like the sentence "ten pomegranates" (*daśa dāḍimāni*) and so forth, or it has a meaning contrary to the Vedas, like the tenets of the Buddhists and others. It is called such because it is both "nonsense" and a "book. By the word "mere" (*mātra*), he indicates pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The term *kṛti* means "instrument" (*karaṇa*),
as in the expression "so be it" (*tathā*) in the Vedas.
"Non-restriction" (aniyati) means lack of restriction;
that is to say, this restriction would not exist.
The word "tad" means "therefore.
Regarding what was said— "I speak those things spoken by another," and so forth— he says in response: "Those spoken by another," and so forth.

If one were to have such an intention as "I am speaking what was said by another," it would be due to a delusion consisting of a similar reflective awareness, just like [the perception of] a difference between actions.
(2679) "Just like [the perception of] a difference between actions" means:
By this [rule], the suffix *vati* is applied after a word ending in the seventh case;
through this, by demonstrating the possibility of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) for a single reflective awareness (*ekapratyavamarśa*), its inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) is stated.
It might be asked: "How is it established that this [perception] is an error? To this he says: "But those spoken by another... and so forth.
"But those [sounds] spoken by another are not [the same], because of their difference in pitch and other qualities;
nor is this a property of the manifestor, since it is perceived as being of the nature of the phoneme itself. (2680)
Therefore, since distinct colors are observed for each individual person, just as in the case of jars and other objects,
when such difference is perfectly clear, why is its mark denied?
[This refers to the phrase] "by means of accents and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "with [qualities] such as the acute accent" (*udāttādibhiḥ*), qualities such as fast, medium, and slow tempo are included;
nor is this a property of the manifestor (*vyañjaka*).
Why is it "beginning with vowels" (svarādi)?
Because that [vowel-group], beginning with vowels, is observed to have the nature of phonemes (varṇa).
The meaning is "because it is established. Regarding the phrase "its mark" (*taccihnam*):
the mark of that distinction of color is "its mark. By the words "why is that denied? For there is no other mark," [it is shown that] there is no other mark.
Regarding the passage beginning with "as in the case of jars and so forth by way of genus" (jātyā), he says: "prior [to that]," and so on.

And prior [to the production of the universal], the indication of the conventional usage of jars and so forth by means of the genus (*jāti*) is negated, because that [genus] does not exist and because it is incompatible with the individual (*vyakti*).
(2682) "Prior" refers to this.
In the "Examination of the Universal" (*sāmānyaparīkṣā*),
the phrase "by its non-existence" means by the non-existence of that universal (*jāti*).

Even if the universal exists, it is improper to characterize linguistic usage by means of that [universal], because there is no connection with the individual characterized as a jar or the like, since the universal cannot assist the individual.
Thus, he demonstrates that everything imagined by way of the universal is inconsistent: "Therefore, the universals of the palate and so forth... and so on.
Therefore, the universals (jāti) such as those of the palate and other articulatory organs are established as common to all men;
consequently, a speaker does not produce sounds by qualifying them with those [universals].
Regarding what was stated—“And their distinct universals are the causes for the manifestation of sounds,” and so forth—he replies: “That is not so,” and so on.

Therefore, those distinct universals (*jāti*) which are the causes for the manifestation of sounds do not persist as long as the phonemes (*varṇa*); nor do the individual instances (*vyakti*) associated with them [persist].
(2684) "That" refers to this.
Therefore,
regarding what was stated there— "the conjunction of the palate and so forth," etc.— he says in response: "In that case, the palate and so forth," etc.

Therefore, the sequence of sounds is preceded by the order of conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and other organs; and both [the sequence and the universal] are eternal by virtue of their respective universals (jāti).
As for what was stated, beginning with "just as in the case of whirling and so forth," he states there that the example is unestablished with the words "just as in the case of whirling and so forth."

Just as the parts of actions such as revolving are not characterized by a universal (jāti), and there is merely a succession [of parts], so too for us, the palate and other organs do not possess a universal that inheres in the sounds and phonemes;
this is because the existence of a universal has been refuted.
(Commentary) Regarding what was stated— "of the individuals alone," and so forth— he says in response: "Of the individuals also," and so forth.
Even for individuals, because of their subtlety, there is no determination of the properties of the genus;
therefore, even though the castes are all-pervasive, there is no perception of their sequence.
As it was said: "by virtue of that."
Regarding this, he says: "By virtue of that," etc.
As for what was stated previously, beginning with "the qualities of sound are eternal," etc., it is said in response: "That is not so," etc.

Therefore, the phonemes, following after all the qualities of the sound (*dhvani*) which are established as eternal, would not be the causes for the cognition of different meanings. (2688) Regarding what was stated— "And their distinct universals (*jāti*) are the causes for the manifestation of sounds," and so forth— he states the refutation of the universal (*jāti*), having provisionally accepted it, with the words "Furthermore," etc.

Furthermore: "The distinct universals (*jāti*) which are the causes for the manifestation of sounds proceed as far as the phonemes (*varṇa*), or else the individual manifestations (*vyakti*) associated with them [do so];
thus, because of the existence of these manifestors, there is a constant perception of sound. (2689)
Therefore, for you, even a sequence of phonemes whose nature consists of a sequence of individual instances is not logical.
This collection of particles should be understood as introducing a statement;
the word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason.

Therefore, this is the meaning: since the universals (*jāti*) remain as the causes for the manifestation of words, the perception of the word would consequently be eternal, because there is no sequence in its manifestation; thus, it is not logical that [the word] is of that nature [i.e., manifested], for it would be manifest at all times. 2689
From 2690 up to the commentary on verse 2706, many sentences have not been transcribed in the manuscript due to their absence;
only the space for completing the sentences has been provided.
Nor do we find another mirror by which we might complete [the text], nor is there an occasion here for completing the sentence through a consideration of what precedes and follows.

Since it is difficult to fill in the syntactical breakdown that occurs at every step merely by the power of one's intelligence, the author demonstrates this point here and there according to the available evidence;

therein, having accepted the relationship between the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*), he states the fault with the words beginning "of those whose forms consist in the relation to the individual," and so forth.
If there is a fixed determination of universals as having forms connected to individuals, then the eternality of the individuals themselves also follows as unavoidable.
Alternatively, if there is a fixed determination of individuals as having forms connected to universals [the same consequence follows].
Even for you who do not desire it, the impermanence of universals (jāti) would necessarily follow.

Because the relation resides in both [relata] and because the permanence of universals is admitted, it follows that the individuals, whose very nature consists in that relation, must also be permanent;
otherwise, the universals could not have that relation as their essential nature.

Likewise, because the impermanence of individuals is accepted, it follows that the universals (*jāti*), which consist in their very nature as relations to those [individuals], must also be impermanent.
Furthermore, if the individuals were to establish their impermanence by their own nature, it would follow that the universals related to them must also be impermanent;
otherwise, while one relatum remains intact, it would be illogical for the other to be deficient, as this would entail the loss of the very nature of the relation itself.
Warding off the aforementioned further objection, he says: "The manifestation is untenable," and so forth.
And since the impossibility of manifestation has already been established above,
those phonemes being thus extended would not be expressive; for [the cognition] "these are they" [would refer] to the end of the manifestation.
Regarding what was stated— that time is one, all-pervading, eternal, and so forth— he replies with the words "Time also," etc.:
Time also, being one, all-pervading, and eternal, has already been refuted.
Like color, it is not manifested by anything among all entities.

When it is manifested within the phonemes, it does not serve as a factor for communication because it is no different from other [manifested] things; furthermore, its eternity is established because of its existence elsewhere.

Therefore, the sequence of phonemes, as well as those divisions of time known as short, long, and protracted, are not logically possible as properties of the phonemes themselves, since they are merely adventitious adjuncts of the sound-current (dhvani). Consequently, there exists no such eternal property belonging to a word (pada) as you have described.

Therefore, for those who maintain that phonemes are impermanent, the impermanence of the word is established. (2697) Furthermore, even if it were another property, it would not be a constituent part [of the word], just like the speed of a horse and so forth, if one were to postulate here that the manifestation occurs through manifesting cognitions. (2698)
The phrase "precisely previously" refers to the examination of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārthaparīkṣā*);
[it means that] it is not manifested by anything whatsoever.
Because it is non-existent; and even if it were existent, because a manifestation of something eternal would be restricted [to a single instance],
and because of its non-distinction from others— *anyāviśeṣa* meaning "non-distinction from another" (*anyasmād aviśeṣaḥ*).

For instance: there is no object whatsoever that is not included within the nature of time as it is manifested in seeds, sprouts, creepers, and so forth; nor is there any difference in the nature of time as it is manifested in phonemes, because that single, eternal [time] exists elsewhere as well through its connection [with all things]. Therefore (tad iti), for this reason...
"It is not logical" because time does not exist; even if it did exist, its indivisibility has been accepted [by you]. Regarding this, he says "even in the case of another's property," and so forth.
The remainder is easily understood.
But regarding permanence, the presumption [of cognition] for all things has been refuted,
for it has been established that the nature of the cognition of an object belongs to impermanent things.
That which arises from the speaker's intention to express something, and which persists through a subsequent intention to express, [is not permanent].
The perception of that [final] phoneme arises immediately after the hearing of it;

having produced a cognition of the preceding phonemes, and not being heard too rapidly, it subsequently produces a memory within itself by depending upon the memory of those [preceding ones]. (2700–2701)

With respect to the cognitions that apprehend and give rise to them, this sequence— consisting of the state of being produced or the state of being a cause— is based on the person with regard to the phonemes.
Therefore, it is perfectly clear that the phonemes are distinct in every instance.
"Dama," "mada," "latā," "tāla," and so forth, according to the distinction of their sequence;
by such a sequence as this, these [words] establish the difference in meaning.
For this very reason, the postulation of *sphoṭa* here is also devoid of purpose.
Presumption (*arthāpatti*) has been refuted;
for, by the passage beginning with "from the trembling of the hand," etc., the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) and the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) have been described.

Even if [the phonemes] were eternal, they would not be considered identical, because the cognition is equal [only in appearance]. Furthermore, since each individual instance is distinct, the cause of the disturbance is that the phonemes are impermanent; thus, in cases such as *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*, it is logical that the basis for the difference in cognition is the [impermanence of the] sounds.

But they are not eternal, because they possess a uniform nature everywhere; nor is there any distinct entity (*vyakti*) other than them that exists in succession. Demonstrating all of this, he says: "Whosoever intends to speak of what... and so forth. This, first of all, is the general meaning (*samudāyārtha*) here.

In the continuum of the speaker, for each phoneme, the cognitions that give rise to them arise from the desire to speak (*vivakṣā*), being produced by preceding immediate conditions (*samanantarapratyaya*). And those [phonemes] directly produce successive cognitions of their own objects, acting as auxiliary causes for the successive apprehending cognitions in the continuum of the listener. Subsequently, they indirectly produce successive recollections of their respective objects.

Furthermore, with respect to those [phonemes] existing in the continuum of the speaker, their status as "produced" (*janya*) is in relation to the cognitions that give rise to them; or, with respect to those existing in the continuum of the listener, their status as "cause" (*hetu*) is in relation to [the subsequent cognitions]. That very [relation] constitutes their sequence (*ānupūrvī*).

Because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because the phonemes possess distinct intrinsic natures at every step—as in the case of *saraḥ* and *rasaḥ*—a difference in cognition is logically justified. However, this cannot be so for eternal [phonemes], because they are always and everywhere of a single uniform nature.
Nor is a sequence accepted as something distinct from those [phonemes].
The intention is that even if [the phoneme] were a different entity, its connection [to the speaker's intention] would not be established.
As for the meaning of the individual words: it is connected as "the phoneme arises.

In examples such as *sadā* or *sama*, the vowel *a* and so on follow the letter *s* and so on; [this arises] from another [intention] produced by the desire to express the letter *s*, which has become erroneous [due to the intervention of other factors]. Therefore, [it arises].
"Whatever intention (*vivakṣā*) there is for [producing] a *sa*-sound or the like, from that arises another subsequent intention; this is what is meant by "that which has arisen from that.
What is being said is this:

in the continuum of the speaker, whatever subsequent intention arises produced by the preceding intentions that give rise to each successive phoneme—from that [subsequent intention], whichever subsequent phoneme is produced, it brings about memory; this is the connection with what will be stated hereafter.

Thus, having first established that phonemes are produced [by the speaker] through the comprehension of the intention (*vivakṣā*) that gives rise to them—which resides in the continuum of the speaker—he now establishes their causality with respect to the cognition residing in the continuum of the hearer:
"of that" (*tasya*) refers back to what was previously specified as "the sound" (*ga*);
the connection is that "its hearing"—meaning its arising—occurs.
The term "immediately following" (*samanantaram*) means without any interval;
having thus established that [the object] is the cause for the knowledge of the hearer, he now establishes its status as the cause for memory.

"Preceded by" means that which has an arising (*udbhūtā*)— that is, a comprehension (*saṃvit* = *anubhava*)— of the knowledge (*vit* = *jñāna*) of the preceding phonemes; he is thus described as "one whose hearing is not too rapid."
Because the capacity for the production of memory exists in one who has rapid hearing,
each subsequent phoneme [is apprehended].

The compound *smṛtisamutthāpakagrāhiṇām* is a *dvandva* (copulative) consisting of "recollections" (*smṛti*)—meaning recollections of each preceding [letter] (with reference to that, i.e., by means of their cooperation)—and "graspers" (*grāhin*), where "recollection" refers to the recollection of its own respective object.

It is [the genitive plural] "of those phonemes" (*teṣāṃ varṇānām*). Alternatively, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (determinative) or *karmadhāraya* (appositional) compound formed by first joining "those which are both producers and graspers" (*samutthāpakagrāhīṇi*) and then [joining the result] with "of them" (*tatsamutthāpakagrāhīṇām*).

"Being produced in dependence upon those that originate it" [is the case for the phonemes], while "being a cause in dependence upon those consisting of the cognition of grasping, experience, and memory" [is the case for the word-meaning].

Having thus refuted this sequential order as something distinct [from the phonemes], and wishing to refute the *sphoṭa*—the essence of the word conceived by the Grammarians and others as a denoter distinct from the sounds—he says: "For this very reason," and so forth.
For that [sphoṭa] was indeed postulated by the grammarians for the sake of explaining the comprehension of meaning;
yet since the phonemes themselves possess that capacity, this postulation is purposeless.
Furthermore, because it is not perceived despite being perceptible, its non-existence is determined.

But if it were invisible, this [word-sound] could not function as an indicator, like a logical mark (*liṅga*). [The author] demonstrates this by saying "of that which is visible," etc.: for no eternal, partless essence of sound (*śabdātman*), distinct from the phonemes, is observed appearing in the auditory consciousness.
Since apprehension would [otherwise] result in the existence [of the object], its non-existence would instead be established;

furthermore, if the second alternative is taken, there are the following options: the logical reason (*hetu*) must be either a property of existence, a property of non-existence, or a property of both.
In the first case, the logical reason (*hetu*) would have to be either a property of the subject (*dharmin*) called *sphoṭa*, or a property of some other subject;

however, because that very subject called *sphoṭa* is unestablished (*asiddha*), a property of it cannot be the reason. Nor can a property of another subject be the reason, because it lacks the status of being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*).

Just as the property of being a "two-armed person" (bāhupada) is not even a non-existent property when proving the impermanence of a jar and so forth, because it would prove the opposite [of what is intended].
Nor can it possess both natures, because that would involve deviation;
for its establishment must occur either through an essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) or through an effect (*kāryahetu*).
The first position is not tenable, because that [nature] is beyond the senses; thus, its essential nature is unestablished.

Alternatively, if it were established, the effort expended in seeking [the reason] would be useless, since its essential nature is already established and the purpose of the exertion is precisely that.
Nor is the second position tenable, because a causal relationship with that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) cannot be established.

However, one might argue: "Just as the occasional nature of auditory and other cognitions establishes their dependence on other causes, and by implication establishes the existence of the sense organs such as the ear, so too here we shall take the cognition of meaning as the subject (*dharmin*). Even though the phonemes (*varṇa*) are identical, we shall postulate another cause called *sphoṭa* due to the difference in the cognition of meaning in cases such as 'sara' and 'rasa'. This also is incorrect.

Because the lack of distinction between phonemes (*varṇa*) is unestablished; for it has just been demonstrated that it is the phonemes themselves, as distinct in each word due to the difference between cause and effect, that are capable of producing the cognition of meaning, and thus there is no postulation of a [separate] entity.
This is the intended meaning: that such faults must be stated regarding the view that [the word] is inferable.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "This [self] is not an object of inference; what then? It is absolutely imperceptible. To this he says: "But if it were imperceptible, this [inference] would simply not exist"—just as a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is unknown cannot be a communicator of knowledge, so too would this [inference] be, because [the self] is unknown.
If it is claimed that its status as a cognizer is established because that cognition exists by its mere presence as a cause,
then it would have to be so at all times, just like the eye.
Even when there is no comprehension of the convention (*saṅketa*) and even when the phonemes (*varṇa*) have not been heard,
there is cognition regarding the objects to be expressed by them, due to the proximity of the capable cause.
For indeed, this [cognition] exists eternally, and it has no dependence whatsoever.
Nor is its manifestation [brought about] by sounds, conventions, or phonemes, because that is not observed.
For they say that manifestation is cognition; yet such cognition does not exist.
Therefore, the postulation of a manifestor for it is entirely purposeless.
Now, if it were the cause for the cognition of an object even when unknown— merely by its existence, like the sense organs such as the eye—
then the cognition arising from it would occur at all times;
likewise, that cognition arising from it would occur even without the apprehension of linguistic convention (*saṅketa*) and so forth.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "the convention" (*saṅketa*), and states the proof for that with "for instance" (*tathā hi*).

Now, it might be argued: "It is accepted that this [word] is the cause of the cognition of an object only when manifested by a convention, not by its mere existence; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not follow. To this, he says: "By sounds, conventions, and phonemes," and so forth.
"Because of non-perception" means because of non-apprehension and because it is intended to be invisible.
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "For this very knowledge... (2707–2708).
It might be argued: "The claim that 'what is appearing is not perceived' is unestablished."

For indeed, it is precisely in the intellect—in which the impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by each preceding phoneme have been repeatedly applied and have reached full maturity—that the partless word manifests. Thus he says: "By the sound," and so forth;
in the intellect, in which the seeds have been sown by the sound and which has reached maturity through repetition, the word appears together with the final articulation (*dhvani*). || 2711 ||
This too has been postulated by him here as being without a cause;
for even in that [cognition], no other word is perceived as appearing.
(2712) "Reverted"—that cognition in which the maturation of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) deposited by all previous cognitions has arisen is described thus.

The intention [of the phrase] "without a cause" (*nirnimitta*) is as follows: indeed, it is the phonemes themselves that are subsequently determined by a recollective synthetic cognition (*saṅkalanā-pratyaya*) according to how they were experienced.
For instance, after the perception of the final phoneme, we do not perceive any other partless essence of sound (*śabdātman*), nor does the speaker himself discern such a thing.

If it were only thus, thinking "it would be good for me," one whose mind is deluded by the desire for welfare dreams that at the very moment of the final cognition, the sound has reached its completion.

Thus, the refutation of the position that [the word] is eternal has been stated; now, he states a refutation common to both the eternal and non-eternal positions regarding the partless [word], beginning with "Let it be produced," etc.:
"Let it be produced or even manifested by sounds occurring in succession..."
Even for those who maintain that the *sphoṭa* is [manifested] by means of a sequence, their position is contradicted.

For neither the individual manifestation (*vyakti*) nor the universal (*jāti*) can logically be associated with a sequence, since they are partless and do not exist outside of their single nature; indeed, both would have to exist in every respect [simultaneously].
For some Vaibhāṣikas, by means of expressing the function of individual words, have accepted the sentence-sphoṭa as something produced because it is impermanent;
[they hold it to be] "partless" (*niraṃśaka*), meaning a reality devoid of constituent parts.

"Because of not being outside of a single form" means that since there is no existence apart from one form— whether known or unmanifest— the [universals and individuals] intended as both manifest and unmanifest would belong to everything.
Thus, both the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) would belong to all things.
And consequently, the employment of the remaining phonemes and so forth would be rendered useless. 2713–2714.
He states the refutation even regarding the position that [the word] has parts: "Even if it has parts...
Even if it has parts, just as phonemes are expressive in a sequential order, why should the parts of the *sphoṭa* not be likewise? Why are they postulated as something unseen? (2715)
For those parts of the sphoṭa must either be individually meaningless or meaningful.

In the first case, because they occur sequentially, there is the consequence that they would be non-expressive— just like the phonemes themselves— and their status as expressers would have to be merely imagined, since they lack that nature [of being expressers] despite appearing to possess it.

For instance: it is said that a sentence is a single meaningful entity, whereas its constituent parts are themselves meaningless; that [single] entity would have to be superimposed upon them through conceptual construction, like the quality of being a lion attributed to a young boy.

And if such a constructed denotative power is accepted, it is better that the very parts consisting of the phonemes (varṇas) be the denoters; why then should invisible parts of a *sphoṭa* be postulated?

If, on the other hand, they possess meaning, then the assumption of multiple [words] is purposeless; for it is said that a sentence is a form of speech whose meaning is complete. If each of its constituent parts were to possess meaning individually, then as many sentences would be produced as there are parts, and thus a single entity consisting of multiple parts could not be established.
Furthermore, it would follow that the meaning of the sentence would be understood upon the comprehension of just a single part.
As it has been stated: "Even if each [part] possesses meaning, the assumption of multiplicity is false."
And through the comprehension of a single constituent part, there would be the understanding of the meaning of the sentence.

Regarding what was stated—"For it is not logical that a universal and its individual manifestation should be manifested sequentially, since they are partless"—the author anticipates the opponent's rebuttal: "In the universal," and so forth; [the opponent argues:

"If the manifestation of the universal has already been accomplished by a single sound, one employs other phonemes simultaneously for the sake of ensuring the complete manifestation [of the individual]. (2716)
Since its nature is difficult to determine, it is made manifest once again by other phonemes belonging to the same class of articulation (samānavyaktika). || 2717 ||

Even if the universal (*jāti*) or the individual (*vyakti*) of the *sphoṭa* has been produced in its entirety by a single sound (*dhvani*), nevertheless, the employment of subsequent sounds is not useless, because their purpose is to bring about clear manifestation (*spaṣṭavyakti*). For just as a verse, though repeated again and again, becomes clearly manifest, yet no further distinction is added to it by that repetition beyond what was achieved by the first utterance; and yet the repetition is not useless—in the same way, here too, the subsequent sounds will not be useless. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "Since... (*yataḥ*), ending with "difficult to discern" (*duravadhārā*).
incapable of being determined 2716 2717
He refutes this with the words "of that very [one]" and so forth:
"Why does manifestation not recur again and again for either that very same [entity] or another? For, in this way, there is no distinction. (2718)
Now, as for the address "nanu": why is manifestation not produced by the repeated recitation of that very first articulated syllable, or of some other single syllable contained within it?
For once manifestation has been brought about by that [recitation], it cannot be said that it has not been brought about.

For instance, the successive utterances of each subsequent phoneme have as their sole fruit the repetition of that [first] manifestation, since all of them possess an identical capacity. And since that repetition can be accomplished by a single phoneme being repeated again and again, the utterance of the remaining phonemes would be useless.

Nor should it be accepted that the successive phonemes possess distinct capacities, because it is impossible to impart any further distinction to that which is partless; and since no further distinction can be produced, the postulation of distinct capacities would result in futility.

And showing that all this would be possible if manifestation were existent, but that very manifestation itself is not possible, he says: "The manifestation, consisting of the refinement of the object and the sense organ, is like the phoneme," and so forth.
This [manifestation] must also be refuted in the case of a cognition that appears as such;

the meaning is that just as in the case of syllables (*varṇa*), manifestation— in the form of the refinement of the object or the sense organ— was refuted through the dilemma of whether they possess a nature capable or incapable of generating cognition, so too should it be refuted here.
"Even in its appearance" means even in the appearance of the *sphoṭa*;
and this is a statement made on the basis of an accepted position (*abhyupagamavāda*).

This is what is meant: if indeed another essence of sound called *sphoṭa* were to appear as distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*), then its manifestation would be possible, since manifestation consists in being perceived;

however, it has already been explained previously that it does not so appear. Even granting that it might appear, manifestation is still not tenable in either case for something whose nature is inherently both perceptible and imperceptible.
Having concluded with the words "Therefore" and so forth, he demonstrates the sequence of the logical establishment that the comprehension of meaning occurs even without a *sphoṭa*:

"Therefore, prior to the perception [of the whole], that word which exists within the cognitions of the sequence—the cognition of all the phonemes taken together—is the cause of the cognition of the meaning. (2720)

Now, an objection is raised: "Since phonemes occur sequentially and are experienced only in sequence, and since recollection follows the manner of experience, how can a single recollective cognition appearing as all the phonemes together be possible without the *sphoṭa*? Furthermore, it is not logical for phonemes that are sequential to appear [simultaneously] when they are known non-sequentially. Anticipating this, he says: "For when the final phoneme is cognized... and so forth: "When the final phoneme is cognized, a recollection produced by all the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) arises simultaneously regarding all the phonemes. (2721)

He states this very point: first there is the direct experience (*anubhava*), and then, immediately following that, the recollections (*smaraṇa*) arise in sequence exactly according to the experience. Thereafter, at a later time, from those recollections, another collective cognition (*samuccaya-jñāna*) arises which is of the nature of memory and simultaneously determines all the phonemes, because it determines objects as they have been perceived.
He shows that this is well-known to all theorists and is not merely imagined by me, stating: "And in all... (verse 2721).

And in all these cases, for all theorists, a mental collective cognition (samuccaya-jñāna) is accepted regarding objects known sequentially, even though they exist in a temporal sequence. This is what [the verse] means. 2722.
Etad iti.
Regarding the knowledge of synthesis (samuccayajñāna) [verse 2722],
he shows that this must necessarily be accepted because it is supported by reasoning, stating "If not," and so forth.
If this were not admitted, then indeed the perception of a collection such as "one hundred" and so forth would never arise regarding things perceived sequentially.

For if every recollection arose only in sequence according to the original experience, then there could be no simultaneous conceptual construction of "one hundred" and so on with respect to hundreds and other numbers experienced in succession.
Furthermore, at the time of the arising of conceptual constructions such as "one hundred crores" and so forth, there would be no distinction [between them];
thus he concludes with the word "therefore."
Therefore, although there may be a sequential cognition of the phonemes by means of the ear and the mind, subsequently there would be a simultaneous recollection [of them].

(2724) If this were so, then the cognition of their collection alone would be the cause of the comprehension of the meaning, and not those phonemes themselves, because they have long since ceased to exist; and this is not tenable, because it is well-known even to children that the comprehension of meaning occurs immediately after the word. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Mounted upon that," and so forth.

Therefore, the phonemes mounted upon that [cognition] do not [directly] bring about the comprehension of the distant object; rather, it is from the word that the cognition arises, and for that reason it is so designated by worldly people.
(2725) "Mounted upon that" (*tadārūḍha*) means those which have ascended into that collective cognition (*samuccayajñāna*).
"By means of worldly [conventions]" (laukikaiḥ) is a formation of a secondary derivative (taddhita) in the sense of "belonging to oneself.

Anticipating the objection that even so, since those [past objects] have long since ceased to exist, they are absolutely non-existent; and thus, how could there be an ascent (or apprehension) of them? He says: "In a cognition possessing form," and so forth.
All this is logical only when cognition possesses a form;
for otherwise, how could those [objects] which have perished appear in memory? (2726)
He asks why it is not tenable in the case of a cognition devoid of form (nirākāra), and says: "Otherwise... and so forth.

Consequently, that which was described by Kumārila as a "cognition of the aggregate" (*samuccaya-jñāna*)—in the passage beginning with "for when the final letter is cognized," etc.—is tenable only in our own system, and not in the system of you Mīmāṃsakas who maintain the doctrine of formless cognition (*nirākāravāda*); this is what is being stated. (2726)
But surely this is also consistent for the Mīmāṃsakas; for according to their view, the phonemes (*varṇa*) do not perish, such that they would not appear.
Rather, they exist with their manifestations merely concealed. Anticipating this objection with the words "Now then" (*atha*) and so forth, he refutes it with the words "No" (*na*) and so forth.

Now, if those very same phonemes, having been previously experienced and subsequently having their manifestation obscured, were apprehended by a synthetic cognition (samuccayajñāna) as being merely remembered while remaining in their state [of existence], then that synthetic cognition would necessarily result in being clearly manifest, just like the cognition consisting of the experience of the self [at the time of perception]. (2727) For if those very phonemes, which existed previously as objects of experience, were later grasped by a synthetic cognition while their manifestation was obscured, then that synthetic cognition— like the cognition of one's own experience— would have to appear with clarity.

Furthermore, because the form resides externally and that [form] is of a single nature—if the individuals were concealed, how could they appear? For an individual has the very nature of being perceived.

Furthermore—[the author] shows that this [objection] would only hold if the persistence of the past were possible; however, since the past lacks persistence, its manifestation is not tenable: "And persistence has been refuted previously," and so forth. "If it persisted, there would be recollection at the very time of the cognition experiencing the phoneme, because of a single cause. (2728)

Regarding the word "previously," he states the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for this very point in the *Traikālyaparīkṣā*, beginning with the words "in its persistence" (*tatsthitau*), and so forth.
The subverting proof is the undesirable consequence that recollection would arise at the very time of the cognition experiencing the color,
because of having a single cause— that is, because of having an identical cause.

Here, the grammarians raise an objection: "If there is no single essence of speech called *sphoṭa*, then how is it that the cognition of the word 'cow' (*go*) arises with a single form? To this, he replies: "The phrase beginning with 'cow'...
[the fact] that there is a single cognition of 'cow' is certainly not denied by us."
And due to the identity of the object grasped by them, there would be the notion of oneness regarding the word.
"Ekamati" means that which has a single cognition; its state is "ekatva.
[The phrase] "due to the identity of the object grasped by them" refers to these two reasons.

"By that single cognition" (*tayā ekayā buddhyā*); "that which is to be grasped by it" (*tadgrāhya*) refers to the object; "having a single purpose" (*ekārtha*) means having a single utility; the compound *tadgrāhyaikārtha* is a *dvandva* (copulative) compound consisting of those two; the state of being those two is *tadgrāhyaikārthatā*. By these two [reasons], this is what is meant: because it is grasped by a single cognition and because it illuminates a single object such as one possessing a dewlap and so forth, the word "cow" (*go-śabda*) is said to be one.
And he shows that unity of cognition is not established in all cases: "Because of rapidity," etc.
Because of rapidity and because the difference is slight, that [unity of cognition] might occur in the case of the word "cow";
however, in the case of words such as "Devadatta," a clear distinction is perceived. (2730)
"Due to rapidity"— that is, due to quick pronunciation—
it has "little interval," meaning it has very little separation. Thus [it is said].

However, regarding the view that there is a single cognition [of the word] "Devadatta" and so forth, since the sounds (*dhvanayaḥ*) are perceived with much greater clarity and distinctness for each individual phoneme according to the Śākya method, the property of being a single cognition is unestablished in respect to one part of the subject (*pakṣaikadeśāsiddha*).
He provides the proof with the verse beginning "varṇotthā" and so forth:

"This cognition of the object arises from the phonemes, because it occurs immediately after the knowledge of them; for whatever [cognition] is such, it indeed arises from that, just as the cognition of fire arises from smoke and the like. (2731)

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever cognition arises immediately after a particular cognition is produced from that [preceding cognition] through a causal sequence, just as the cognition of a probandum such as fire arises from the cognition of a mark such as smoke;

and the cognition of an object occurs immediately after the cognition of a phoneme. This is an argument based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), wherein both the status of being an essential nature and the conventional usage of being an effect (*kāryatā*) are established here as the probandum.
By this, the distinction between the probandum and the probans [is established].
(2731) Anticipating the objection that this [reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "Not the phonemes," and so forth.

There exists no cognition of meaning that arises immediately after a cognition of a word-sound distinct from the phonemes; therefore, there is no other word-entity that is expressive. (2732) That is to say, there is no cognition appearing as a word-essence distinct from the phonemes arising immediately after such a cognition; rather, it is a cognition arising immediately after the cognition of the phonemes. Thus, the reason [adduced] is not unestablished (*asiddha*).
And by this, it is also shown that there is a conventional usage of non-existence based on the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility;
furthermore, showing that [the reason] is not inconclusive, he says: "Because it is an effect," and so forth.

For positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka), when ascertained in all cases, constitute the pervasion (vyāpti) which is the basis for the conventional usage of "being an effect" (kāryatā). Therefore, in this context, pervasion is ascertained.
The "basis for the conventional usage of being an effect" is the cause; what is that? It is positive and negative concomitance.

The relationship by way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists merely in the fact of following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that [cause]; nothing other than this is a factor for the conventional usage of "being an effect. Therefore, the impossibility of any other basis for the conventional usage of "being an effect" serves as the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and thus the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established.

It might be argued: "Let the sphoṭa not be the expressive agent; rather, the phonemes themselves, being eternal, will be the expressive agents, and their eternity is established through means of valid cognition such as perception. To this he says: "In the case of the impermanent," and so forth.
This refers to the demonstration of the expressive nature of the phonemes while they are indeed impermanent, once both recognition and inference have been refuted as proofs for their eternity. (2734)
Regarding "recognition and inference" (*pratyabhijñānumāne*),

there is a variant reading in some places as "recognition-inference" (*pratyabhijñānānumānam*); in that case, either a collective copulative compound (*samāhāra-dvandva*) should be understood— by the elision of the word *sahita*— or it is a descriptive determinative compound (*viśeṣaṇa-samāsa*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "contradiction with one's own statements and so forth," he says: "Of contradictions with one's own statements and so forth... and so on;
the objection was raised due to ignorance of these contradictions with one's own statements and the like.
But in the case of the position that [speech] is eternal, all those [faults] apply to you,
because it has been established that speech, being eternal, cannot be the manifestor [of meaning] due to its lack of sequence and so forth, and because it is not perceived as being eternal.
"All those" refers to contradictions with one's own statements and so forth;
"in sequence," and so on.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the Śruti and Smṛti are understood in their respective order;

for indeed, because [the Veda] is eternal, there is no sequence produced by time, nor is there one produced by space due to its omnipresence, nor is there one produced by manifestation because manifestation has already been refuted.
Likewise, it has been demonstrated in many ways that even in the production of knowledge, eternal things have no utility.
As it was said: "It must be stated which [of these] is the word," and so forth.
Regarding this, he says: "By means of the conceptualization of a difference in the substratum," and so forth.

That which is called the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) due to the conceptualization of a difference in the substratum [is not a fault], because the status of being a substratum belongs to that which appears [in cognition] due to ignorance of the definition of inference. (2737)
Whatever object, established through non-investigation, appears within cognition— even for those such as the Śanakas— that alone is declared to be the subject (*dharmin*).
Indeed, it is regarding that very [subject] that this dispute among proponents has arisen.
But regarding a subject (dharmin) constructed according to one’s own wish, there is no dispute for anyone.

That very subject which is established for both the proponent and the opponent by virtue of its appearance is the basis for dispute concerning specific properties; it is not one imagined according to one’s own whim, because there is no dispute regarding that. For no one is prevented from imagining a specific property in a subject constructed according to one’s own whim; thus [it is said] "as it appears."
This very point regarding that which appears is shown by the words "the object established through non-investigation," and so forth;
this is easy to understand.

Showing that when a subject (*dharmin*) is indicated without qualification, any conceptualization (*vikalpana*) regarding its specific qualities constitutes a "futile rejoinder" (*jātyuttara*), he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
Thus, conceptualizing a specific quality when [the subject] was indicated without qualification subverts the operation of all inference whatsoever. (2740)

The cognition produced by an injunction (*codanā*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is produced by causes free from defects; this [argument] is also analyzed as follows: "The understanding produced by an injunction connected with an eternal object is [valid]. (2741)

If this [cognition] is the subject (*pakṣa*), then for the opponent, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*). This is because it would follow that the basis is unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhi*). It was stated [earlier] that this [word] is eternal and is eternally connected with its object characterized by form; if the cognition produced by that [word] were the subject, then for the opponent, the reason remains unestablished.
(Verse 2742)
As it has been stated: "Impermanence (and) perishability," and so forth.
Regarding this, he says: "The state of being thus," and so forth.
"The state of being thus" is permanence; its opposite is impermanence.
For, when both the state of being thus and the absence of the state of being thus have ceased, what is it that is intended to remain? (2743)

The point is: if it is asked what state is intended [to belong] to that which abides, since the state is not distinct from the substratum of the state, then upon the cessation of the former, the latter necessarily ceases as well;
otherwise, how could it be logical for something that does not share the same fortune (yogakṣema) as another to possess its nature? This is the sense.
Regarding what was stated— "And if it were based on the sense-faculties alone," and so forth— he says in response:
"And if the reason is conceived here as being based on the sense-faculties alone," and so forth.
Because the universal (jāti) has already been refuted, no deviation [of the reason] is perceived;
"already" refers to the examination of the universal.

Even if there is no deviation [of the reason] from the genus, one might still suspect that it is inconclusive because its negative concomitance (vyatireka) is doubtful; anticipating this, the author states "svanirbhāsi" etc., demonstrating the necessary connection (pratibandha) of the reason, "being perceptible by the senses":
"That which is the cause of sensory cognition appearing as itself would be perceptible by the senses."

Furthermore, it has been established that causality does not exist in what is eternal. For an object is called "sensory" when it is the cause of sensory cognition which manifests its own appearance; and since it is proven that causal efficiency (arthakriyā) is incompatible with an eternal entity—whether occurring successively or simultaneously—the necessary connection (pratibandha) is established.
Regarding the argument beginning with "And it must be established in the case of being perceptible by the senses," etc., he says: "Of all [of them]," and so forth.
This nature of being a reason for such a meaning is well-established for all [reasons], even in the case of smoke and the like; otherwise, this dilemma would apply equally everywhere. (2746)
And it is described as "such" because its object is of this nature; that is, it is "such" in the sense of being agreeable only so long as it is not investigated.

Otherwise, one could likewise formulate a conceptual doubt even regarding smoke—for instance: "Is the smoke employed as a logical mark (liṅga) something perceived by the senses, or is it a transformation of consciousness, primordial matter (prakṛti), time, and so forth? Or is it a composite whole (avayavin) produced from atoms, or not produced at all? In such a conceptual doubt, there would be defects such as the failure of either side to establish its own position.
Regarding the statement that "knowledge immediately following effort is the proof for being produced and impermanent," he says:
"Knowledge immediately following effort... and so forth; [it means] that it does not initiate the production of an effect.
"Because for us, [things] such as analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*) are established as being conventional (*saṃvṛta*) due to their being obscured [by ignorance].

(2747) The connection is as follows: knowledge arising immediately after effort is itself the effect; therefore, the status of being the producer of that [effect] is not established for analytical cessation and the like.
For if, according to the Sautrāntika system, a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is raised by means of analytical cessation and so forth...

In that case, according to their own view, your argument for deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is not established, because for them, analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*) and so forth possess conventional existence (*saṃvṛtisat*).
Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is conventionally existent to be the producer of any effect, as that would entail the loss of its defining characteristic.

To explain: that which performs purposeful action (*arthakriyākārin*) is the ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), while anything other than that is conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*); such is the definition of the ultimately real and the conventionally real.

Alternatively, there is a deviation [from the rule] according to the Vaibhāṣika position; even there, he demonstrates that the kind of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyānirodha*) and so forth described by you as having the nature of destruction is not accepted by the Vaibhāṣikas—with the words "And not," etc.:
"And the two cessations are not admitted to have the nature of destruction, because they are associated with outflows (*sāsrava*)."
Pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha (cessation through deliberation) is that disjunction which occurs individually for each [defilement].
The other cessation, apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha (cessation not through deliberation), is the absolute prevention of arising.
Therefore, those who do not understand this established doctrine float about as mere vain conceited men.

Regarding the phrase "the two cessations," he explains what kind of things are intended by the two cessations— cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) and cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*)— by saying: "because [they are] with outflows (*sāsrava*)."

The distinction made with respect to defiled entities is attained through analytical wisdom (*pratisaṅkhyā*); therefore, it is called "cessation through analysis" (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*). Furthermore, this cessation is distinct from the substance that is bound [to the fetters]. For this very reason, it is said: "separately, separately," according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) that there are as many substances of disjunction (*visaṃyoga-dravya*) as there are substances of conjunction (*saṃyoga-dravya*).
On the other hand, "cessation not through analysis" (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is that dharma which constitutes an absolute obstacle to the arising of future dharmas and is distinct from disjunction.
And that is not obtained through analytical discernment;
rather, what is it?
It is due to the deficiency of conditions, and for this reason it is called "cessation not through analytical discernment" (apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha).

As it has been said: "Pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha is that disjunction [from defilements] which occurs individually; the other, apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha, is cessation that is the absolute prevention of arising."

Even if it were granted that non-existence and destruction do not have intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nevertheless there is no deviation [in the logical reason]; demonstrating this, he says: "Not from non-intrinsic nature," and so forth.

Neither non-existence nor self-destruction are produced immediately after an effort; rather, it is things such as the collection of potsherds and light that serve as the basis for such cognition immediately following an effort.
(2750) "Produced immediately after an effort" means...
The connection is "no," for what reason?
Because it is not its intrinsic nature.

For instance, destruction is merely the negation of the existence of a thing, and space is merely the absence of the tangible; therefore, both of these, being their own destructions, are devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). How, then, could there be for these two the property of following immediately after effort? Since it is only intrinsic nature that possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), [the opponent asks] what, then, is the basis for the cognition of destruction and so forth? To this he says: "shards," etc.;
"mass of light" means a collection of light.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the mass of darkness (tamas) is included.
As it has been stated: "Even though there is no distinction, that entity is neither impermanent nor permanent; such is my view," and so forth.
To this he replies: “Of a single... etc.”:
Because a single objective nature is excluded from having two forms, therefore a permanent entity called a ‘universal’ (jāti) is not tenable here in the case of a jar. (2751)
Regarding the passage beginning with "Impermanence is thus to be conceptualized," he says: "The mere rejection of the state of being as it was," and so forth.
The impermanence intended here is merely the negation of that state; in this regard, the lamp and such are clear examples of the probandum. || 2752 ||

Impermanence is intended as the probandum merely as the negation of remaining in that same state; in that case as well, the example of a lamp exists as being endowed with the probandum. Therefore, how can there be a deficiency of the probandum in the example?
With the words "of the flame, etc.," [the author] raises the objection—according to the view of others—that even examples such as a lamp lack the probandum.
Even flames and the like possess perishability; it is not unestablished. [Objection: But is it not unestablished?
For at every moment, light particles (*laghu*) move there to another location very quickly.
Indeed, in the region of the wick, a great amount of light remains concentrated.
In that case, as long as it moves forward (or upward), it is understood as "flame";
beyond that, what departs and goes forth would consist of light;
but what goes further than that cannot be discerned due to its subtlety.
For in that case, the parts of the flame and so forth travel to other locations very rapidly, rather than disintegrating at every moment.
2755 Now, he explains why they do not all spread simultaneously: "By the subsequent parts," and so forth;
when the path is obstructed by the subsequent parts, the preceding ones do not proceed.
Just as they are released from the subsequent [fire], so do those preceding [fires] proceed.
