(2756) Now, if they possess the nature of spreading, why do they not burn the grass, cotton, and so forth situated near them? To this he says: "Even upon transference," and so on;
even upon transference, the occurrence of these [fires] in the grass and so forth is not possible.
This is merely a conceptual construction because no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) has been stated [to support it].
The intended meaning is that these [causes] function only when in a state of aggregation, but not when in a scattered state.
He answers this with the words "tadetad" and so forth:
even if this conceptualization were accepted, the example would not be devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*).
For it has been stated that what is intended as the property to be proven—impermanence—is merely the negation of its remaining in the same state (*tādavasthya*).

Furthermore, that state of remaining as it is (tādavasthya) does not exist at all in the case of a lamp and so forth; therefore, how can there be the fault of the example being devoid of the probandum?
Nevertheless, [the author] states the fault even while granting this point, beginning with "Moreover" (kiñca).
Furthermore, for those whose power is unimpeded, this consequence— that burning would occur upon contact with grass, cotton, and so forth— does not cease, as before.
(Verse 2758) "Of those whose power is unimpeded" means...
The same applies to the parts of the flame and so forth,
because there is no difference from their state of aggregation.
Now, he demonstrates that if a distinction is admitted, then the undesirable consequence of the loss of its eternity is difficult to avoid— with the words beginning "Otherwise," etc.:
"Otherwise, what kind of eternal form would that [universality] have for you in relation to those [particulars]?"
When the distinction between that which has the nature of being capable and that which has the nature of being incapable is established, [the argument] is easily understood. (2759)

Regarding what was stated—that "the eternity of the sentence must be asserted on the grounds of the logic of the non-creation of the relationship"—to that he replies: "And of the relationship... and so forth.
Since the eternity of the relationship has already been refuted previously, the eternity of the sentence is not tenable on the grounds of the logic of the non-creation of the relationship. (2760)

Thinking that, according to your own view, even a sentence cannot possibly exist—that very thing whose permanence you seek to establish—one who examines the sentence says: "Of which [sentence]? and so forth:
"And of which sentence is permanence asserted—is it of that which consists merely of phonemes (*varṇa*), or of a sequence of phonemes that is distinct from them? (2761)
Is it that sometimes a sentence would be merely the phonemes themselves without distinction;
or rather—that the phonemes alone, arranged in a specific sequence, constitute the sentence;
or else—that the status of being a sentence belongs to something called *sphoṭa*, which is distinct from the phonemes? These are the three positions.
Regarding that, he states the fault in the first position: "Of phonemes," and so forth;
"there is no denotative capacity in phonemes devoid of sequence."
Therefore, such words do not belong to you [the Mīmāṃsakas], nor is there any sequential order among them.
Because they are all-pervading and eternal, no sequence of space or time is possible for them, unlike the case of written letters or the distinctions between fruits, flowers, and so forth.
If these [letters] were to possess an inherent sequence, the form "sara" would be possible,
but not "rasa" and so forth, because that would contradict the established order.
Furthermore, other letters such as the letter *ra* and so on are fixed and do not admit of any other sequence.
The phonemes arise from the wind, yet they are described as being eternal and unitary.
Otherwise, the recognition [of phonemes] which you yourself have stated as a proof for their eternity and unity would become fallacious, since it occurs even when there is difference.

Regarding the second position as well, he says: "Even a sequence does not exist for these [phonemes]. To explain: the sequence of entities is of only two kinds—either spatial, such as that of ants, written characters, and so forth; or temporal, such as that of the seed, sprout, stalk, flower, fruit, and so on. First of all, a spatial sequence is not possible for phonemes because of their pervasiveness. Since phonemes are omnipresent, it is not logical for a sequence based on spatial division to belong to something that exists by occupying all locations like space itself; for all [phonemes] reside in the same single location of space.
Nor is it produced by time, because all things, being eternal, would exist simultaneously.
Furthermore, the sequence must be either created by a person or inherent;
first of all, it is not accepted as being created by a person, because that would entail the consequence of the Veda having a human author.
If, on the other hand, [the sequence] were inherent (*svābhāvika*), then it would always be "sara" and never "rasa";

nor can it be accepted that the phonemes (*varṇa*) are distinct in every instance, because the permanence of phonemes is established through recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and it is precisely the negation of that [distinction] which is intended to be proven; otherwise, recognition would be fallacious.
Now, it might be argued that the sequence [of sounds] as they are manifested will then constitute the sentence; to this he says: "And not," and so forth.

Nor is the sequence of manifestations the sentence, because manifestation is denied in the case of what is eternal, and because [a sequence] lacks the fitness to constitute a sentence; therefore, its eternality is not tenable.
By the word "ca" (and), it is indicated that the sentence called *sphoṭa* is also not distinct from the phonemes.
The sense is that this has already been refuted by the Mīmāṃsakas themselves;
"because of the denial of the manifestation of an eternal [entity]" means because the manifestation of something eternal has been rejected.
Regarding what was stated— "because it is a linguistic convention concerning perceived objects," and so forth— he replies with the verse beginning "Just as *vṛddhi* and so on":
"Just as words such as *vṛddhi* have meanings fashioned by intention."
In the same way, words such as "heaven" and "sacrifice" are merely conceived;
for in works such as invented stories, dramas, and prose narratives, no eternal, real relationship between word and meaning is intended to exist.
Those for whom the meaning is fashioned by intention are so described;

"to be produced" (utpādyā) refers to those such as the *Mahāśvetā* and others, whose very form or nature consists of narratives that are themselves unprecedented and created by the person [the author].

In these works, such as dramas (*nāṭaka*) and prose romances (*ākhyāyikā*), a permanent relationship between word and meaning is not intended, characterized by [the powers of] direct denotation (*śakti*) or indication (*lakṣaṇā*). The point is that the same may be suspected regarding the Veda as well.
With the words "tatrāpi" and so forth, he raises the objection that the example is unestablished according to the opponent's view.

Even in that case, while the capacity (*śakti*) is eternal, the injunction (*niyoga*) is non-eternal; it is solely due to this [injunction] that error arises regarding the eternal capacity. Even there, in the case of stories and the like to be produced, the capacity is indeed accepted as eternal; however, the injunction which is performed by persons when the object does not exist is non-eternal, and it is solely due to this that a cognitive delusion occurs regarding the eternal capacity. Therefore, the example is unestablished.
He responds with the verse beginning "nanu" (But surely): "But surely, there is no external [object] there; for what object is the individual manifestation (vyakti) postulated?"
If it is suspected that [the object] is a conceptual reflection, then the same would be suspected regarding the Veda as well;
"external" means such things as Mahāśvetā and so forth.

Regarding what was stated—"By whom has the connection between heaven, sacrifice, and so forth, which is beyond the senses, been seen? and so on—to that he replies: "Who indeed can comprehend a potency whose connection with objects beyond the senses... and so forth.
Who indeed can comprehend a potency whose connection with objects beyond the senses [is established]?
Therefore, even the injunction (*niyoga*) in the Veda cannot be conceived as dependent on a human being.
Nor can its understanding come from the elders, for they too remain inherently ignorant by their own nature.
However, comprehension may be presumed to arise from an explanation that relies upon a person.
By this he says the following: you yourself have demonstrated by implication that whatever understanding of the meaning of the Veda arises, it arises solely from human-based explanations.

For instance: first of all, the power [of words] regarding supersensible objects is innate; therefore, with respect to a supersensible power, no human application of the word is possible, nor is its comprehension from elders possible, because they are all equally ignorant—just as the perception of a specific color cannot arise from the words of the blind.
Therefore, by virtue of this capacity, this comprehension of meaning is established solely through human explanation, as there is no other possible way.
With the words "nanu" and so forth, the opponent raises an objection:
"Is this inquiry not equally applicable to a scripture that is a human composition?
For one does not act upon it out of faith, nor even because of doubt regarding its meaning. (2774)
But surely this same objection applies equally to human-authored scriptures as well;

for instance, do contemporary people understand the meaning of the words of the Buddha and others—who were teachers beyond their perception—in accordance with the [original] intention, or rather the opposite?
He answers this with the passage beginning "not so," and so forth.
In this context,

the person [proceeds] regarding the reality of what is to be abandoned and so forth, along with its means, which is beneficial for human goals— whether that reality be composed by a person (*pauruṣeya*) or unperceived (*adṛṣṭa*). For instance,
it is precisely while adhering to logic (*nyāya*) that the wise followers of the Sugata proceed, and not merely on the basis of popular report (*pravāda*).

"By faith" means by a firm conviction born from reasoned reflection; that is to say, it refers to the certainty [arising] regarding an object established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since such firm conviction is only appropriate in the case of an object proven by valid cognition.
For otherwise, doubt would not have been transcended there,
or because of doubt regarding the object.

Regarding objects that are entirely beyond the senses, such as heaven, deities, and the *apūrva*—for instance, in the case of a human-authored statement, because it expresses the author's own intention, an unerring tradition is possible; thus, an uninterrupted tradition is rightly presumed through a lineage of hearers.
However, this is not the case with a non-human-authored [Vedic] text, because there is no instructor therein.

Furthermore, when a teacher speaks by means of action [or compassion] for the purpose of convincing the world, he does so by following the very conventions of the world; therefore, the establishment of that meaning could also arise from worldly renown. However, this is not the case for non-human [Vedic] texts, because there is no intention on the part of anyone therein.

If this is so, why do you not proceed on the basis of any scripture whatsoever, since doubt is equal in all cases? To refute this objection, he says: "When the object has been purified by perception and inference," and so forth.
For it is not the case that such self-evident cognition exists in the case of Vedic words, because [the conditions for it are absent].

Where the existence of the intended object is not contradicted by perception or inference, one who proceeds on that basis may be deemed praiseworthy even if there is doubt; but this is not so where the object is otherwise, because a doubt regarding an undesirable outcome has arisen due to the contradiction of perceived means of valid cognition.
To the objection that "if this is so, activity toward the Veda will likewise occur by this very same logic," he says: "For it is not the case... and so forth.
"Self-evident" (svayampratyaya) means that it is authoritative by itself;
therefore, it is not proper to engage with it after examining it through another means of valid cognition, as that would entail the consequence of its authority being extrinsic (parataḥ).
Furthermore, the purification of its objects is not possible;

for instance, the person (puruṣa) is taught in the Veda as one whose prior and subsequent forms have neither fallen away nor arisen, and who is both the agent of actions and the enjoyer of their fruits in succession— but this has been shown in the *Ātmaparīkṣā* to be untenable.
Likewise, the eternality of certain entities is recited, yet that too has been demonstrated as untenable in the "Examination of Stable Entities" (Sthirabhāvaparīkṣā).
Similarly, universals and the like, though not perceptible, are asserted to be perceptible; likewise, the sequential arising, abiding, and ceasing of entities, though impossible, have been specified.

Likewise, [the doctrine that] that which cannot have qualities added to it and which was previously a non-agent becomes a producer through dependence on another; likewise, that which is already accomplished remains by depending on another;
and likewise, that there is destruction even of that which is not an effect [arising] from a cause—much of this is found to contradict valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
How, then, could a discerning person engage with such a scripture?
Furthermore, Kumārila has stated another proof to establish the eternity of the relationship;

[the author] demonstrates that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to such things as dramas, which consist of narratives whose characters are produced— as in the verse beginning with "utpādya," etc.

Without considering that the dharma consists of narratives whose subjects are to be brought into being, others have described this [position] here as being equally incoherent. (2776) The analysis of the compound is as follows: it is a narrative (*kathā*) whose subject matter (*artha*) is to be brought into being (*utpādya*); thus it is called "one whose subject matter is to be brought into being" (*utpādyārthā*). And it is both that [narrative] and a story (*kathā*). Thus, the analysis is *utpādyārthā cāsau kathā ca*.

Regarding its nature as a dharma, he asks: "What is that described as having its meaning fashioned by desire? and answers with the verse beginning "the beginninglessness of word-meanings," and so forth.

Apart from the beginninglessness of words and their meanings, there can be no other cause for the beginninglessness of their relationship; therefore, in the Veda, no such thing as a [newly established] relationship exists.
(2777) This is because it is inferred that no relationship could be created due to the absence of any means [for doing so].
But let the inference regarding the non-communication [of the relationship] be contradicted by what is actually perceived.

(2778) The word has the nature of phonemes (*varṇa*), and its object is the universal (*sāmānya*); because these two are beginningless, their relationship—characterized as a capacity (*śakti*)—is also beginningless, since capacity is not distinct from the entity itself; this is the sense.
Thus, due to the absence of any means for creating a relationship, the non-creation of the relationship is inferred.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is devoid of the means for establishing a connection with something does not produce it; for example, a potter who lacks the collection of causes such as a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, water, and thread does not produce a jar. And all persons are devoid of the means for establishing a connection [with the listener]. This is an observation of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has been demonstrated that all persons lack such means, based on the reasoning: "To whom could a speaker resort in order to establish a connection between the listener and the act of speaking? and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that "if this were so, it would follow that there is an inference of the non-communication of the relationship just as there is of the cause," he says: "But the inference from non-communication...
and so forth; [the reason] "because the means for the inference of non-communication is lacking" is unestablished (asiddhi).
With the words "of the elders" and so forth, he demonstrates that very same lack of proof:
"And the understanding observed among the elders occurs again and again."
"Method" (upāya) means that its abandonment is not established with respect to comprehension.

This repeated observation of the elders’ cognition of the relationship is itself the method for explaining the relationship; for one is not able to explain it to another without having first understood it oneself. Thus, its abandonment [as a means] is not possible.
The loss of means refers to the failure with respect to comprehension,
that is, with respect to the understanding of the relationship.
With the words "For all this," etc., he states the refutation:
for all this would indeed be so, if there were a certain determination of the meaning of the Veda.
One who does not contradict even the elders would be established [as authoritative]; otherwise, there is a flaw.

(As it was said: "The beginninglessness of words and their objects," etc. In that regard, if by "beginninglessness" of words and objects you intend their eternity, that is unproven (*asiddha*), because the universal momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has already been demonstrated.

If, on the other hand, you mean the beginninglessness of the causal series, then there is the fallacy of the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and the contradictory (*viruddha*), because the relation is not distinct from its relata, and thus, like them, it would follow that the relation is non-eternal.

As for what was said regarding the absence of a means (*upāya*), that too is unproven; for it has been established that even though there is difference, certain objects are by their very nature capable of producing a single uniform conceptual determination (*ekākāra-pratyavamarśa*), just like the eyes and other sense organs.
Therefore, the intended meaning is that the cognition which determines a single object for both speaker and listener is itself the means for its own production.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "the understanding of elders is observed [to be based on words]," it has already been stated in this regard: "And there is no cognition of that from the elders, for they too remain ignorant by their own nature."
Otherwise, there would be a contradiction;

for if it is maintained that even those elders who themselves lack knowledge nevertheless apprehend the relationship, then there is a contradiction with what is perceived, just like a blind man's claim to see forms—this is the meaning. (2780)
Regarding what was stated—"such a proof must be asserted against the property of being a composite"—he says: "Established," etc.
Because [the pervasion] possesses a universal application that is already established, no counter-proof whatsoever is possible for a logical mark such as "being a composite. (2781)

That whose universal inclusion and pervasion (*sarvopasaṃhāravyāpti*) is established is described as such; its state is "thatness" (*tattva*). By this, he demonstrates that this [inference] proceeds by the force of real entities (*vastubala*), because for anything else, pervasion through universal inclusion is not established.

Furthermore, there is no possibility of a counter-argument (*pratisādhana*) against an inference proceeding by the force of real entities, because it is impossible to alter the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of things.
Nor is the occurrence of two mutually contradictory natures possible in a single locus, as that would entail the loss of its unity.
Showing that very establishment of pervasion through a universal synthesis, he says: "They are meaningful," and so forth;
they are meaningful, their objects are distinct, and they possess a specific sequential order.
Letters alone, when so designated as words, sentences, and collections, are thus described [as having meaning].
Since the possession of a meaningful, distinct, and specific sequential order is precluded if [the Veda] were of human origin, the pervasion [of the reason] remains unimpeded.
Thus, these [letters] are said to be "assembled" (*saṃhata*);
however, it was previously established that if letters were non-human in origin (*apauruṣeya*), all of this would be untenable; therefore, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is proven.

But is it not the case that the pervasion of this reason—"because it is denoted by the study of the Veda"—is also established through a universal synthesis? For instance, one might object: "An author of the Vedas is never perceived at any time. Anticipating this, he says: "The study of the Veda," and so forth.
If [the property] were merely the state of being expressible by Vedic study, there would be no such ascertainment of pervasion; rather, the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) would be doubtful.
Thus, in this proof, it is evident that [the reason] is characterized by a doubtful negative concomitance.
(2784) "But not so" means:
Just as, for example, in the case of "being a composite" (*saṅghātatva*),
the negative concomitance (*vyatirekitva*) of "being a composite" with the opposite of the probandum (*sādhyaviparyaya*) is not doubtful, whereas in this case, it is indeed doubtful.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "of such a kind" and so forth:
when it is established that the effect occurs in such a sequence and that humans lack the capacity [to produce it], this pervasion (vyāpti) cannot at all be ascertained here. || 2785 ||
When there is the direct perception of all human attributes, this certainty indeed arises, and it is possible for an omniscient being; such is the case.
|| 2786 || Such is the nature [of that certainty].

If it were certain that all men are incapable of producing such a sequence of phonemes—as in the injunction "one desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Agniṣṭoma"—then there would be certainty regarding the pervasion (vyāpti). However, [the author] shows that this very thing cannot be ascertained by anyone who is not omniscient, stating: "of all human attributes," and so forth, beginning with "and this."
Certainty 2785 2786

Now, one might object: since qualities of the Veda such as the teaching of dharma and its difficulty to recite are not observed in human compositions, the non-human origin of the Veda is simply inconceivable; so how could there be a state of "doubtful unestablishedness" (saṃdigdhāsiddhatā)? Anticipating this, he says: "It is conceivable," and so forth.
Indeed, the human origin of the Veda is clearly conceivable, given [the presence of] sexual misconduct, false actions, injury to living beings, and the speaking of untruths. (2787)
For qualities of the Veda, such as difficulty of pronunciation, lack of acute accentuation, obscurity, and unpleasantness to the ear, are indeed observed even in the words of atheists and others;
and whatever [miraculous effects] such as the removal of poison or prosperity are observed, [they are likewise seen elsewhere].
This is indeed true; it is observed even in the case of the mantras of Vainateya and others.

[The opponent] thinks thus: "Even if there is non-perception, since mere non-perception is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), the reason remains 'unproven due to doubt' (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*). For it is possible that at some time or place there might be persons who are the authors of such Vedic properties;
thus, mere non-perception is not established."
Since the teaching of sexual misconduct and other such things is observed even in the words of atheists and others,
[it follows that] "sexual misconduct" (*kāmamithyākriyā*) refers to *kāmamithyācāra*,
which is to say, approaching one's mother and so forth.

The instruction for that [rite] is as stated in the Gosava and other ceremonies: "The *upahā* drinks water, cuts grass, and approaches his mother or even a woman of a different lineage," and so forth; here, the term *upahā* refers to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*).

Regarding the instruction for the slaughter of living beings in the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) and other rites, as it has been stated: "Six hundred and sixty animals are bound on the middle day of the horse sacrifice, according to the scriptural injunction, [with the total] being less than three hundred and thirty animals."
Thus, untruth is false speech; this too has been taught as it was said: "O King, a lie joined with jest does not cause harm, nor among women, nor at the time of marriage."
"In cases of life-threatening danger or the seizure of all one's wealth, they say that five kinds of falsehoods are not sinful"—
this refers to these [offenses], such as sexual misconduct and so forth; "abhidhā" means naming or designation.
The connection is that the characteristics of the Vedas are observed even in the words of atheists and others.
The word "likewise" (*tathā*) functions as a conjunction. *Durbhaṇatva* means difficult to pronounce; *anudāttatva* means pleasantness; and *kliṣṭa* means interrupted or separated.

"Just as in the verse beginning with *ā mandrairindra haribhiryāhi mayūraromabhiḥ*, for here the particle *ā* in *ā mandraiḥ* is connected with the distant word *yāhi*; thus, it means *āyāhi* (come hither)."
Unsuitability for recitation (*aśravyatā*) refers to being unpleasant to the ear;
by the word "etc. (*ādi*), one includes the breaking of words (*padaviccheda*), protracted vowels (*pluta*), acute accents (*udātta*), and so forth.
[The phrase] "the prosperity resulting from the removal of poison" and so on...
The removal of poison is *bhūti*— meaning capacity or power (*prabhāva*);
alternatively, it is a compound of "the removal of poison" (*viṣāpagama*) and "prosperity" (*bhūti*),
where *bhūti* means manifestation, splendor, or sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), possession by spirits or grahas, subjugation, malevolent magic (abhicāra), and so forth are included;
"true" (satya) means non-contradictory.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "Vainateya and so forth," the inclusion of the mantra systems of the Buddhists and others is intended.
Regarding the statement "it would be so even in the case of the *Bhārata*," etc., he says: "Furthermore,
by this method, nothing whatsoever [is] of human origin."
For it is possible to infer even the Buddhist word in this way:
"The study of the Buddhist scripture mentioned first is preceded by the study of a similar [scripture], because it is designated as 'Buddhist study,' just like the present study."
If this is so, how then will that [teaching] of the Sugata be established? To this he says:
"Because its form is manifested by that," and so forth; and because it has a form manifested by that, it is called "his" (the Sugata's).
And even in that case, let the recollection of an author be based on the meaning [of the text] itself.
(2791) If it is argued that this is not accepted by others, then why is it not accepted when the reasoning is the same?
Let it be that this is not the position of the opponent; nevertheless, such a thing is suspected on the basis of logic. (2792)
That which has as its intrinsic nature (svabhāva) a form manifested by that Sugata is "thus" (tathā);
the state of being so is "reality" (tattva).
Even in that regard, the recollection of the Buddha as the agent can be explained as being based on a figurative eulogy (arthavāda).
For why, in this case as well, is the root *kṛ* not explained as having the sense of "remembering"?
It might be argued: "This is not accepted by the Buddhists, so how could it be established in this way? To this he says: "If the reasoning were equal, why would it not be accepted?
If this meaning were supported by logic, then why would the Buddhists not accept it? For it is not reasonable for a discerning person to reject a matter that is established by logic.
Even if a discerning Buddhist were not to accept this, we say that it is nevertheless logically entailed for you.
Strengthening this very point by means of that statement, he says: "And always," and so forth:
"And at all times, men for the most part speak untruth; just as there is no confidence in the present, so too there is none in the recounting of past events. (2793)
Thus, by this logic you have stated, no author is established anywhere, even when he speaks of his own composition in a work; therefore,
let this hope for the existence of non-human [authorship] be abandoned.
"For meanings contrary to the Vedic sense have indeed been propounded in them"—
this refers to what was just mentioned, beginning with "and always," and so forth.
It might be argued: "Let it be that all [scriptures] are of non-human origin. To this he says: "And therefore," and so forth.

The meaning is that, consequently, being of non-human origin would not establish the truthfulness of the subject matter, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the existence of the words of the Buddhists and others.

For instance: according to your own view, doctrines such as selflessness (*nairātmya*), which are contrary to the meaning of the Vedas and not established by valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇopapanna*), are taught in the words of the Buddhists and others; likewise, it is possible that even Vedic [doctrines] might be suspected [of being similarly unreliable].

Thus, the inconclusiveness [of the reason] has first been demonstrated; now, demonstrating its contradictory nature because it subverts what is intended, he says: "Moreover" (api ca), etc.—in this way, beginninglessness would indeed be established, but not a dependence on multiple [causes].
Therefore, if it were uncreated, then other scriptures would also be uncreated.

(2796) For it is intended to prove that this [Veda] is not of human origin, yet that is not established; what then is established? Only its beginninglessness, which is precisely what is undesired. One might argue: "If beginninglessness is established, then by implication its being uncreated is established as well, for it is not possible for something created to be beginningless. To this, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.
Therefore, because it is beginningless, whatever possesses the quality of being produced would also possess the linguistic usage of the Persians and others;
he demonstrates this very point with the words "For instance" (*tathāhi*), and so forth.
For instance, the linguistic conventions of the Persians and others depend upon others,
and the doctrine of the nihilists (*nāstika*) arises from the mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) of others.
[The phrase] "dependent upon others" means...
The meaning is that they function through the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of another person;
"arising from the refinement of another" (*parasaṃskārabhāvika*) means that for whom there exists an existence (*bhāva*) by means of the refinement of another, he is so described.

Or, it has the nature of coming into being through the mental processing of another; thus, it is "arising from the mental processing of another" (*parasaṃskārabhāvī*). Therefore, the suffix *ka* is applied in the sense of the base itself. For instance, even those philosophical systems whose conventions are fashioned by one's own intuition proceed precisely by the power of conceptualizing the meaning as it was heard [from others]; thus, their activity generally occurs solely through the force of another's mental processing, just like worldly transactions which function according to established views.
If it is argued, "Let there be the non-human origin (apauruṣeyatva) of all [scriptures]," he says: "Even if such a state of being uncreated were established," and so forth.
"Even if such a state of being uncreated were established, what benefit would that be for you? For this entire effort of yours is directed toward the cause of non-falsity. (2798)
Regarding such [a case] where the meaning may be false—
as in the statement "the past and future times," etc.— he says "because of being time," and so forth.

In the case of [properties] such as temporality and personhood, there is a doubt regarding the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), because— as before— the incapacity of humans to produce [such things] has not been established,
and because the manifestation [of a speaker] has already been refuted; therefore, let it be understood that the speaker is indeed the agent.
In both of those applications, it has been stated that the illustrative example (nidarśana) is devoid of the probandum (sādhya).

For, in establishing the incapacity of all men [to perceive supersensible objects], there exists a subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) against the reason; and since such a proof is not shown, the negative concomitance (vyatireka) of all reasons in the case of the opposite of the probandum remains doubtful. Thus, as before, there is inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā).
The example [of] "being devoid of the probandum" is like the proof for [the property of] being expressible by Vedic study;
that is to say, it is like the present time or like an ordinary man.
And then, regarding the passage beginning with "Therefore, you should go," he says "nara" and so forth.

Because it depends on the instructions of Nara and because it is a produced means of proof, there is no dependence on the speaker for its own object; nor is there [such dependence] for the subject and the example.
(2801) "For the subject and the example" means:
The meaning is: "in the subject of the thesis (sādhyadharmin) and in the subject of the example (dṛṣṭāntadharmin).
Regarding the passage beginning with "the cognition produced by that" (tatkṛtaḥ pratyaya), he says: "In [the case of] permanence, it does not exist," and so forth.

Furthermore, if the sentence were eternal, then the property of "arising from an eternal sentence" would clearly be unestablished for both the subject (*dharmin*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, the non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the injunction (*codanā*) remains uncertain.

The fault of being "doubtfully unestablished" (sandigdhāsiddhatā) applies to the latter reasons as well. Here too, as before, there is the non-establishment of the reason and the deficiency of the example regarding the property to be proven; the locative case [in the compound] refers to the fact that [the reason] arises from the statement concerning eternality.
The genitive in "of the sentence" (*vākyasya*) is a genitive of relation dependent on [the word] "eternality" (*nityatve*);
the genitive in "of that which arises from an eternal sentence" (*nityavākyodbhavatvasya*) is a genitive dependent on [the word] "unestablished" (*asiddhi*);
and [the genitive] in "in the latter ones" (*paścimeṣu*) [is likewise].
And [this applies] in cases such as "because it is produced by causes devoid of defects," etc.

Showing that these two reasons—"because it is produced by speech that is neither untrustworthy nor ill-composed" and "because it is free from sublation"—are certainly unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "And it is sublated," and so forth.
"And the Veda is clearly sublated once momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has been proven;
for [the Veda] is eternal in its own nature, and therefore the cognition produced by it is [erroneous], since [its object] has been created. (2804)
For it is stated in the Śruti that "the Puruṣa does not perish," and the refutation of that [position] has already been clearly set forth; thus, its lack of proof is evident.
For one for whom the difference of place, time, and person is as clear as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand...

In that case, this absence of sublation is determined by direct perception (pratyakṣa). The connection [of the words] is as follows: "First, it is eternal by its own nature" means "it is not sublated. This is what is being said.

For when momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*), which pervades all categories of existence, has been clearly established through inference proceeding by the power of logical reasons (*hetubala*), that Veda which is accepted as eternal is first sublated; thus, the mention of its "own nature" (*svarūpa*) is for the purpose of excluding its denotable content (*abhidheya*).
Therefore, the meaning is: how could a cognition produced by that [Veda] possibly arise?
It could not at all.

By this, he demonstrates that the reason "because it is produced by the speech of one who is unauthoritative and ill-prepared" is unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), and that the reason "because of the absence of sublation" is definitely unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpato'siddha*). He says: "For it does not decay," and so forth; for it is recited in the Veda: "This self is indeed indestructible; it does not decay; it is imperishable."
Regarding that person—the self—it was previously stated, in the proof of selflessness (*nairātmya-siddhi*), that there is a sublation;
therefore, its lack of establishment is certain.

Now, as for the objection: since it is said that "an injunction (*codanā*) is a statement that impels one to action," it follows that only a specific portion of the Veda is called an injunction, and not the entire Veda. However, it is the cognition produced by an injunction that has been made the subject of the thesis (*pakṣīkṛtā*).
Therefore, even if there is sublation of a Vedic text that has a different purpose, the reason—that there is no sublation of the *codanā* (the injunctive impetus)—is indeed established;
this is not a fault. By the term *codanā*, sometimes the entirety of a Vedic sentence is meant, and not always only that which is incitement to action;
otherwise, the sentence "One should not harm living beings" would not be a *codanā*, because it does not incite one to action.

Furthermore, that which was stated in the Bhāṣya—"In this context, both the beneficial and the harmful are indicated by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*)"—would also be contradicted; for an injunction does not impel one toward what is harmful, such that the harmful could be said to be indicated by it.

Moreover, regarding that other statement in the Bhāṣya—"Indeed, the cognition arising from a human-made word may sometimes be erroneous, but there is no means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for concluding that a Vedic statement is false"—if [the Veda] were subject to sublation even in its eternal aspect, then the possibility of sublation in the case of the injunction would be equally unavoidable.
For it has been stated by Kumārila: "And by establishing the absence of an author, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*hetutva*) will be proven.

Just as the sublation (*bādhā*) of Vedic statements concerning eternal entities such as the *puruṣa* is clearly observed even though they lack an author, so too in cases such as "Heaven results from the Agnihotra," the doubt [regarding sublation] is indeed difficult to ward off; thus, the aforementioned fallacy of being "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*) remains evident.

Therefore, turning back once more and further strengthening the point that [the reason] is doubtful and unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*), he says: "Like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand," and so forth;
"therein" means in another place, time, or person.

In this regard, that which was stated—"And this [scripture] does not vary in another place, at another time, or in another person; therefore, it is non-false"—is refuted by this [argument]. 2804–2805.
Regarding what was stated—"therefore, like light"—he says: "When the object whose form is not known by men," and so forth; "when that [object], being in darkness, remains as such."
The attachment of the dull-witted to the Veda is like that of the Persians toward their own customs;
and because they lack knowledge of its true meaning due to the influence of sinful tendencies, they likewise engage in the defilement of harming living beings and the like. (2807–2808)

"Form" (*rūpa*) means its own nature (*svarūpa*), and "meaning" (*artha*) means the denotable object (*abhidheya*). The analysis of the compound is: "those whose form and meaning are unknown to men. Among these, the form is unknown because it is impossible to determine through either self-ascertainment or ascertainment by another whether this is merely a phoneme (*varṇa*), or whether it is something else—a specific sequence of phonemes—or neither. The same lack of certainty regarding the meaning should be understood to apply here as well.
And then, when it has become darkness— because, due to the absence of certainty, it has become like a lack of light—
the "evil" is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) from the habitual practice of previous sins; its "outflow" (*niṣyanda*) is likewise the same.
Like the Persians,

Regarding what was stated at the outset—that those who seek dharma and adharma must necessarily rely upon *codanā* alone as the authoritative means of knowledge because they are discerning persons—the author replies: "With respect to dharma... and so forth.

Thus, the authority of *codanās* is not established with respect to dharma; it is not intrinsic (*svataḥ*), nor from others, because its meaning cannot be determined by those who are dull-witted. (2809)
The mention of "dharma" (virtue) is illustrative; "adharma" (non-virtue) is also to be understood.
If this is so, then what is the basis for the established distinction between dharma and the rest? To this he says: "Knowledge," and so forth.
"Therefore, let the person whose mass of internal darkness has been dispelled by the light of knowledge be designated as the teacher of the distinct meanings of the Vedas.
(2810) Thus ends the Examination of Revelation (*Śrutiparīkṣā*).
"Internal darkness" refers to afflicted and unafflicted ignorance; he by whom that mass of internal darkness has been dispelled and destroyed by the light of knowledge is so described.
"Of the secluded ones" means of those who are blameless—the wise (or pure)—that is to say, those who are unstained by the blemishes of animal slaughter, lust, improper conduct, and so forth.
The meaning is that it should be stated, "Let the instructor [of the Veda] be designated," for in this way, its postulated lack of human authorship (*apauruṣeyatva*) becomes meaningful;
otherwise, if its meaning were not understood, that very lack of human authorship would be utterly purposeless.

By this, the following is intended: this acceptance of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) which you maintain is not tenable without an omniscient being; therefore, such a being must necessarily be accepted, since it has been demonstrated that otherwise validity would remain unestablished in that regard. Consequently, let the supreme word spoken by him alone be the basis for Dharma and the like; what is the use of further postulating an authorless status (*apauruṣeyatva*) that is not supported by any means of valid cognition?

As for what was stated—that dharma and so forth are not accessible even through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of yogic perception—that too is faulty; the point is that the existence of the yogi will be established later by means of inference (2810).
Thus ends the examination of scripture (*śrutiparīkṣā*).

The examination of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) begins with the words "In this way" (*evam*) and so forth; by this, he further supports the independence of the Śruti from external constraints through another method,
once it has been established that the Vedas are of human origin (*pauruṣeya*).
Their intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is also effortlessly refuted [by this].

For instance, the followers of Jaimini (the Mīmāṃsakas), thinking that the validity of the Veda must be established, assert in general that all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are intrinsically valid, whereas invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

This is because, they claim, if validity were extrinsic, there would follow the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), which would result in the collapse of the distinction between what is a valid cognition and what is not.

To explain, four positions are possible: first, that both validity and invalidity are intrinsic (*svataḥ*); second, that both are extrinsic (*parataḥ*); third, that validity is extrinsic while invalidity is intrinsic; and fourth, the reverse of this. Among these, the first position is not tenable. To see why: would those two coexist in a single individual instance (*vyakti*), or in different instances? They cannot possibly exist in a single instance as properties characterized by mutual exclusion, such as validity and its opposite, because they are contradictory.

Nor can it be distinguished by the difference between individual instances, because in the absence of a restrictive cause and the impossibility of a determining factor, there would follow the consequence that the distinction between valid and invalid cognition could not be established without confusion.
For, since both would be independent, there could be no restriction such as "this alone is valid";

and because the difference between the two would be obscured by their commonality of sublation (*bādha*), and because no other means of determination is admitted, they could not be cognized separately, and thus the distinction that "this is valid" and "that is invalid" could not be established.

Nor is the second position tenable, because it would entail that cognition—which prior to [the determination] was devoid of both natures—is itself devoid of nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). For when validity and its opposite, which are defined by mutual exclusion, are absent, no other form can be ascertained for this [cognition]; thus, without doubt, it results in being indefinable (*anupākhyatva*).
And it has been said: "First of all, the two do not exist intrinsically due to contradiction, nor do they exist extrinsically."
For in this way, the absence of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāvatva) would necessarily follow for the very form of cognition.

If it were argued that there is no contradiction because of the distinction between individual instances of consciousness (vijñāna-vyakti-bheda), even so, since [consciousness] is independent of anything else, it cannot be determined where or what [the absence of nature] is not present. Thus, "kveti na nirūpyate" (it cannot be determined where).
Thus, the third position is also not tenable due to the fault of infinite regress;
for instance, validity cannot be expected from another source that is itself invalid, because that [other source] is inherently non-authoritative.

Nor can it be established by means of another valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that too would be subject to the same inquiry; if one seeks its validity from something else, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.
Consequently, for one who follows a succession of valid cognitions in order to establish even a single instance of valid cognition, an entire human lifespan would be consumed.
Therefore, since no other alternative is possible, it must be accepted that the validity of all valid cognitions is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), while invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: those things which are necessarily determined by the existence of something else do not depend on anything further in that regard; for example, space does not depend on anything else for its incorporeality (*amūrttatva*). And cognitions (*vijñāna*) and so forth, which are the subjects of dispute, are necessarily determined by the existence of their means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This is an "observation of the contrary of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Nor is this [reason] inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because a property that is impossible by itself cannot be produced by another, just as corporeality cannot be produced in space. As it has been said: "A power that does not exist by itself cannot be brought about by another. (2811)
Here, by means of the words "from themselves" (*svataḥ*) and so forth, [the author], considering the thesis-meaning to be insubstantial, begins the refutation by way of examining it:
"What meaning is intended by you for this statement: 'The validity of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is to be understood as being from themselves'? (2812)

To the question, "What is the intended meaning [of this]? the opponent replies: "In the cognition of the object of knowledge, etc."—the capacity for the cognition of the object of knowledge and so forth exists in them as inherent;
for a capacity that does not exist by itself cannot be produced by anything else. (2813)

If cognition (*jñāna*) is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then it possesses an inherent capacity for the apprehension of its object—that is, for the determination of the object of knowledge—because cognition has the nature of determining an object. Alternatively, if the eyes and so forth are the means of valid knowledge, then they possess that capacity for the production of true cognition. The phrase "by the word 'etcetera'" includes the idea that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) possesses an inherent capacity for the comprehension of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha*). Regarding this very point, the opponent first states the supporting argument, beginning with "nahi" and so forth.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Independence alone is the one [basis]," and so forth;
independence alone is the single foundation for validity.
For if dependence were admitted, that very validity would be destroyed;
thus [is stated] the establishment of validity.
For that very thing is validity,
because when the pervader ceases, the pervaded cannot remain.

It might be argued: "Let it be destroyed; what is the harm? To this he says: "For who," and so forth—"For who, indeed, would a proponent of logic (nyāyavādī) adopt a position that destroys its own foundation?"

By this very statement of his, even the means for its establishment is destroyed. [Verse 2815] Root-text: Validity (*prāmāṇya*) is that which is undermined by dependence, because dependence is contradictory to its pervader. For instance, validity is pervaded by independence; how then could it maintain its existence when dependence—which is contradictory to its own pervader—is present?
With the words beginning with "by which," he demonstrates the pervasion [of validity] by independence;
"by which" means "because of which.

He explains how it perishes: "For validity is established as dependent... For validity is not established anywhere as being independent; and what [means of knowledge], having an unstable cause, will establish the probandum? (2816)
"It would not be established," meaning there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
To the objection, "Let there be the fault of infinite regress," he says: "Not being established," and so forth.
A proponent whose reason is unstable and unascertained is described as such.

This is what is meant: for it is a known indicator that makes known the object to be pervaded, not by its mere existence. Therefore, how can a proponent who has not himself even understood [the matter] employ a proof for the sake of instructing another?

With the words "In this way," etc., he begins the refutation: "If the object is accepted in this manner, then surely it has already been established previously that the capacity of all things is non-distinct [from them]. (2817)
For that essential nature which is capable of performing its intended function is called a "capacity" (*śakti*).
If that [nature] were not of the nature of an existent entity (*bhāva*), then no entity could exist as a causal factor (*sakāraka*).

In this context, what is the intended meaning of the term "intrinsic" (*svābhāvikī*)? Is it "intrinsic" because it is eternal and thus causeless; or rather, even though it is non-eternal, it is "intrinsic" because it arises from its own causes at the very moment the essential nature of cognitions is produced, and is not subsequently imparted by another cause? Thus, there are two alternatives.
In this regard, the first alternative is not tenable; for instance, that [capacity] would have to be either distinct, non-distinct, both, or neither—thus there are four positions.

Among these, it cannot be the first, because the relationship [between the capacity and its locus] would be unestablished and it would follow that the entity itself lacks causal agency, and so forth. This is because it has been demonstrated many times that the capacity of all entities is indeed non-distinct from them.
Indicating this very point, he says: "Is desired," and so on.

For it is the capacity of its own nature that enables it to perform an action; and if that nature were devoid of the essence of existence (*bhāvātmatā*), that entity would not be an agent, which would consequently entail its lack of reality—this is the sense.

Now, if the position is that [the capacity] is non-distinct [from the object], then it could not be inherent; for since the object is impermanent—being produced by the power of causes—it follows as a logical consequence that the capacity, being non-distinct from it, must also be impermanent, as it too would be produced by the power of causes. Otherwise, there would be no identity [between them], because their acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) would be different.
He says this very thing: "And that such a power is impermanent," and so forth.
How can you maintain that such an impermanent power—the capacity of means of valid cognition—is inherent and produced by the force of its own causes? (2819)

Furthermore, demonstrating that because the capacities of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are not distinct from the cognitions themselves, it follows as an undesirable consequence that they must be either eternal or non-causal—just like the nature of the capacity itself—he says: "For if the capacity were intrinsic... and so forth.

"For if the capacity of the means of valid cognition were intrinsic, it would necessarily be either eternal or a cause; and since [the capacity] is identical with them, their eternity and causality would be certain. (2820)
And so, he states what the fault would be: "Always existing," and so forth.

"Alternatively, there would be constant existence or non-existence, because even in the absence of a cause, [the effect] would be independent; therefore, it is not logical for an effect dependent on that [cause] to be occasional. (2821)
Moreover, the nature and the effect of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas) are observed to be occasional; therefore, for you, their power is neither manifested nor inherent.
If they were causeless, there would be either constant existence or constant non-existence.
But since constant existence is already established even if not explicitly stated when [a thing] is eternal, it was not mentioned;
he states another reductio ad absurdum as well, beginning with "Therefore," etc., ending with "dependent on that."
By this [statement], the contradiction of the thesis with perception and inference has been shown as applicable;
for indeed, the occasional nature of the essential character of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established by perception itself.
It is also inferred from inference based on the sequence of effects; therefore, the acceptance of its permanence is clearly contradicted by both means of valid cognition.

With the words "of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānām*) and so forth, [the author] anticipates the opponent's means for resolving the two aforementioned undesirable consequences: "If the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of the means of valid cognition attains manifestation through manifestors, it then initiates its effect while depending upon other conditions. (2823)

For when the nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is manifested by its manifestors (*vyañjaka*), it is then perceived and nothing else; thus, even though it is eternal, there is no consequence of its being perceived at all times,

nor is there a consequence of the effect existing at all times, because it is admitted that [the means of cognition] initiates the effect only in dependence upon other causes, and not by itself alone.
The meaning is that, for this reason, the occasional nature of the effect arises from the presence or absence of other causal factors.
[The author] responds with the verse beginning "vyakti" (manifestation), etc.
If manifestation and dependence on other causes were separate [from the object], then for an eternal entity, there would be the constant perception of its forms and effects;
[this is because] "manifestation and dependence on other causes" refers to those two being dependent on other causes of manifestation.
For previously, in the examination of the Veda (*śruti-parīkṣā*), the permanence of manifestation (*vyakti*) was refuted in detail,
and it was established that dependence on other causes is illogical for that which cannot be assisted;
this applies to those effects which have that [manifestation] as their nature.
Regarding those means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), their "forms" (*rūpa*)— that is, their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*)—
are as stated; however, a dual nature is not tenable, because it would entail the faults inherent in both aforementioned positions due to contradiction and other defects.

Nor is there a "neither-nor" alternative; for since things that are defined by mutual exclusion entail the affirmation of the other when one is negated, it is not logical to negate what has just been affirmed at that very same moment, because affirmation and negation are contradictory in a single locus.
This point has not been explicitly stated here as the refutation is quite evident.
Now, having accepted the final three positions, he states the refutation:
"Whether it be distinctness or the nature of both," and so forth. Even so, that cognition would necessarily be eternal, for it is conjoined with an eternal power (śakti). (2825)
Separateness— the position of distinction;
the apprehension of both natures is illustrative, and the acceptance of the position of neither nature should also be understood.

Alternatively—even for that [negation], since its nature consists in the negation of both forms, it indeed possesses a dual nature; furthermore, in all three of these positions, because cognition is connected with an eternal power, it would follow that it is eternal. (2825)
He asks, "How so? and replies with the verse beginning "Otherwise, indeed," and so forth:
"Otherwise, it would not be eternal, because it lacks a constant uniformity; for at one time it is connected with the cognition of that [object], and not at another. (2826)
Otherwise, if cognition connected with power were impermanent, then the eternity of power would not be established;
why?
Because there would be no persistence of a single form.
The meaning is that there is an absence of conformity to a single nature. He demonstrates this very lack of uniformity with the words "at times," and so forth:

for if consciousness were impermanent, the capacity would possess two natures—one related to that cognition and one unrelated to it. And it is not logical for a single entity to possess two mutually contradictory natures, as that would entail the loss of its unity.
And because it would entail the abolition of the conventional usage of distinctions,
he addresses the second alternative, beginning with "Now," and so forth.
Now, [the opponent argues that] the capacity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) arises from their own causes,

and once they have arisen from their own causes, it is not further bestowed by others. With the verse beginning "tadatra" (2827), [the author] states the fault of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*), namely that it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Therefore, we have no dispute in this matter; for who could subsequently attribute a capacity to a partless entity that has already arisen from its own causes?
Indeed, it is only a form that is attributed by others at a later time.
Therefore, since that [power] is nothing other than the very nature of the entity itself, no self-nature of its own is taught for it.

For instance, because both types of entities—those with a stable nature and those with an unstable nature—are partless, they are not fully established [in a way that allows for change]; thus, at a later time, it is impossible for another cognition to deposit a power that constitutes their very self. If such a power were deposited, it would necessarily result in the production of a different entity altogether, rather than the deposition of a power that is identical to the entity's own nature.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that if one does not admit the power to be the very nature of the entity, it follows that the power would be non-productive (akāraka).

It might be argued: "Granted that there can be no conferring of power upon a partless entity at a later time, why should it not occur for an entity with parts? To this he says: "For [it would entail] the attachment of contradictory properties," and so forth.
For the connection with contradictory properties is said to be the differentiator of entities;
since [the entity] is not produced when that [property] is absent, it exists even in the case of potentiality.
"It exists" means: [it exists].
Regarding the consequence of contradictory properties (viruddhadharmaprasaṅga) [at verse 2830],
he states the specific refutation concerning an unstable entity, beginning with "sādhitā" and so forth.
And since it has been established that all things are momentary, nothing whatsoever possessing power is able to produce another cognition regarding them;
for they do not persist thereafter, by which [means] they... [could be perceived].
They might acquire their capacity for some particular result through other conditions;
"for some particular result" refers to the ascertainment of the object and so forth.
The rest is easily understood.
It might be argued: "If you have no dispute [with us], then how is it that you accept extrinsic validity (*parataḥprāmāṇya*)? To this he says: "But this much," and so forth.
"In this matter, these wise followers of the Sugata say this much:
even though this [validity] resides in some cognition, it cannot be known intrinsically (*svataḥ*). (2833)
"To be known" means to be determined;
"by itself" [means by its own nature].

This might be argued: since the capacity is not distinct from the nature of consciousness itself, which consists of mere experience and does not depend on corroboration by an effect occurring at a later time,
that capacity is indeed grasped whenever consciousness is grasped.
To the question, "How then can it not be understood?", he says: "yathāvasthita... and so forth:

"Who indeed, by virtue of being of the nature of experience alone, is capable of ascertaining the capacity [of cognition] to attain the understanding of an object to be known exactly as it exists, based on that experience alone? (2834)

"Bodha" is knowledge and "āpti" is attainment; "bodhāptī" refers to the knowledge and attainment of the object to be known exactly as it exists. Regarding that—that is, with respect to its object—the analysis of the compound is "the capacity [to produce them].
The term "from the solitary" (kevalāt) means from that which is independent of causes such as [knowledge of] relationships or the qualities of the means.
Why is it not the Lord? He says: "In the case of the non-authoritative," and so forth;
for by which [means] this perception of the mass of hair and so on occurs even when [the object] is non-authoritative.
The nature of experience exists in the perception of a mass of hair and the like— that is, in the perception of a tuft of hair and so forth— wherein a distinct form appears. (2835)

By this he says the following: although the incapacity has been experienced, it cannot yet be ascertained because of the similarity [of the cognition] to that which lacks validity, just like the potency of poison and the like;
for experience alone is not the cause of ascertainment, since it requires other factors such as repeated practice (*abhyāsa*).
Indeed, ascertainment occurs only in that aspect where no other quality is superimposed by the cause of error.
To the question, "From where, then, is that [validity] to be ascertained?", he says: "Therefore," and so forth;
therefore, either the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) or something else is required.
This knowledge of the purity of the cause is for the sake of certainty alone, and not for the purpose of producing [the cognition], like poison and so forth; or rather, it is something else. (2836)
The connection is that "nothing else is required for its production";
[this refers to] "of this" (asyāḥ).

The meaning is this: since certainty (*niścaya*) is based upon the capacity (*śakti*) which resides in the person (*puruṣa*), there is a requirement for dependence on other causes for the production of that certainty; however, this is not for the sake of producing the capacity itself, because the capacity is the substratum of that [certainty], and because the capacity is already established at the time of the simultaneous arising [of the cognition].
With the words "Just as," and so forth, he explains the example "like poison and the like":

"For just as in the case of poison, alcohol, and so on, because they are perceived as equal to other things and because their results do not appear immediately, there is no certain determination of their nature. (2837)

When the production of its result—such as fainting, perspiration, or delirium—is ascertained, identity is understood; likewise, in the case of cognition, there is an ascertainment of its capacity based on observing it to be equal to other [cognitions] that are not different from it. // 2838 // It is because of observing it to be the same as others.

Therefore, "something other than poison and so forth" refers to such things as *nāgarapānaka* (ginger drink) and the like; "similarity with that" means having the same form (*sārūpya*); the analysis of the compound is "the observation of that.
[The phrase] "due to the absence of immediate succession to the result" is analyzed as:
the result is fainting and so forth, and there is an absence of immediate succession to that.

The meaning is that there is no result immediately following [the action] because of the absence of a self; this is the ascertainment of the non-existence of a self, whereas [there is] despondency and so forth when there is no such ascertainment of a self.
"Tādātmya" means having the same nature as the poison and so forth;
it is the ascertainment of that [poison's] potency.
The certainty of attaining the realization of the objects of knowledge exactly as they exist.

Demonstrating the contradiction between his own words and his thesis, he says: "Furthermore," and so forth—"Moreover, you have stated that this validity, characterized as a capacity, is indeed beyond dispute and must be determined by another means of valid cognition. (2839)

"The potencies of all entities are established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) based on the necessity of their effects; thus, they are established by *arthāpatti*. How then are they not established by something else?"—as for the phrase "How then are they not established by something else?": [it means they are indeed established by something else].
The meaning is that it is indeed established [as a separate means of knowledge], because presumption (*arthāpatti*) is a distinct source of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding what was stated— that "that very [cognition] would perish"— he says "niṣpanna" and so forth, demonstrating its inconclusiveness:
"Of the validity that has been produced as a partless form from its own cause..."
Thus, in this way, there is no attainment of destruction [of certainty] because it depends upon something else.
Clarifying this very point, he says: "Not for the production of its own nature... and so forth;
another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not required for the accomplishment of its own nature.
However, that specific form is required for the sake of practical application (pratipatti).

It might be argued: "If you are establishing extrinsic validity (parataḥ-prāmāṇya) with respect to cognition, then for us as well, this is a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhyatā).

For instance, even cognition itself is accepted as being established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti); how much more so its validity, which consists in its capacity [to produce a successful result]?"

The claim that "in performing its own function, which is characterized by the ascertainment of the object, cognition does not depend on [another cognition], and therefore it is said to be self-evident," is incorrect;
for without the ascertainment of validity, the very ascertainment of its own object is impossible.

Furthermore, how can that which has been made the object of doubt and so forth be independent regarding its effect? Or, if there were dependence upon the apprehension by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), how would there not be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in one's own position? Thus, this [argument] is trivial.
With the words "Moreover" (*kiñca*) and so forth, he demonstrates the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the reason "because it is necessarily restricted to the existence of that."
Furthermore, in this way, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) would also follow as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*);
for that which does not exist intrinsically cannot arise from anything else.
Indeed, independence alone is the sole basis for invalidity.
Indeed, it is impossible to state [the capacity for non-contradiction] exhaustively from the outset;
however, just as the capacity for non-contradiction is ascertained from another source, so too is the capacity for contradiction.
Therefore, in every respect, these two are equal. (2844–2845)
Therefore, what excellence of validity is observed in its opposite [invalidity], such that it is held to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*) while invalidity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*)?
Likewise, regarding the capacity for correspondence (*saṃvāda*), it follows that certainty [arises] from something else.
"The two are equal" means that both valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) are the same,
because of the opposite [nature].
Even for one who, due to the lack of authority [in scripture],
maintains that the powers of things are neither innate because they are eternal, nor produced solely from their own causes because they do not depend on any other cause after having arisen;
What then?
Since powers arise from the very nature of things as having specific, determined forms, these powers possess the quality of being inherent.

For instance: whatever form exists within the causes themselves is precisely what is deposited by them in the effect. For example, when a jar is produced from shards, its color and other qualities are initiated through their own respective qualities; however, the power to fetch water and so forth is not deposited in the jar by them, because it does not exist in them, but rather that power manifests in the jar spontaneously. Likewise, in the case of cognition as well, the power to discern an object is not deposited in it by its causes—the sense organs and so forth—because it does not exist in them; rather, that power belongs to it spontaneously.
Therefore, the claim that "power is intrinsic" is merely his idle chatter;

for by this same logic, it would follow that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is also intrinsic. To explain: that [invalidity] too is characterized by the power to determine a contrary object, yet the eyes and other [senses] do not possess such a power.

Furthermore—if a form that does not exist in the self is not imparted by causes to the effect, then how is it that the sense organs and so forth impart to cognition a nature of form that does not exist in themselves, just as that [form] is imparted to consciousness even though it was non-existent? Why then would they not also impart the capacity to determine an object?
For there is nothing whatsoever to obstruct them in imparting that [capacity].

Furthermore—if, first of all, powers are admitted to be non-different from the entity, then, just like the nature of the entity itself, their own existence must be dependent upon causes; how then can they be considered inherent?

If, on the other hand, they are different, then they do not exist by themselves apart from the entity, and thus their connection with their own substratum is not established, because those [entities] would provide no assistance to them.
Nor is it logical for that which provides no assistance to be a substratum, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, if these [causes] were independent and signless (*animitta*), they would not depend on the restriction of place and time;
for instance, whatever depends on something else—whether it be dependent or independent—may cease to exist or not;
but as for that which proceeds independently and without dependence, why should it ever cease at any particular place or time?
Consequently, things would not possess their own specific capacities;
otherwise, everything would be applicable to everything.
However, others think: this statement—"all means of valid cognition [arise] from themselves," and so forth—is made on the basis of observing their effects.
For all entities, being already existent, are produced by causes due to the necessity of the arising of effects;
indeed, non-existent things such as sky-flowers can never be produced anywhere, nor can oil be produced from sand.
If production were of what is non-existent, then since there would be no distinction between one non-existent thing and another, everything would be produced everywhere at all times.
This is incorrect,
because it would entail the absurdity of the cause being purposeless; for according to your view, nothing is produced that is already non-existent.
Even if [the effect] already exists, because it is entirely free from all desire for action, there is nothing that must be done; for what could possibly act as its cause?
Thus, there follows the undesirable consequence of the absence of the relation between cause and effect.
If it is argued that manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is produced for that which already exists, we say no.

Because there is a contradiction in its being produced whether it exists or does not exist, for even in that case this pair of alternatives arises: is it produced while existing, or is it produced while non-existing?
Regarding the first position, it has been stated that production is untenable because there is no further excellence (atiśaya) [to be added].
In that case as well, if one resorts to manifestation, there is the consequence of an infinite regress;
nor is the second position tenable, because action is not admitted for what is non-existent,
or else, if it were admitted, it would follow that even an existent thing could be produced from what is non-existent.

Furthermore, would manifestation be produced as something distinct from the entity, or as non-distinct? If it were produced as something distinct, then nothing at all would have been done to the entity;
for when one thing is produced, another is not thereby produced, as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
If it is argued that manifestation is produced as something related to that [object], we say no; for since it cannot be assisted, its relation to that object is unestablished.
Or, if assistance is admitted, if that too were a distinct entity, it would lead to an infinite regress, and thus the relation would remain unestablished.
Even if [the manifestation] were not a distinct entity from the cause, it would follow that the causes are useless;

furthermore, since the manifestation—which has the nature of an assistance—would arise from the very existence of the substrate, it would follow that the manifestation is eternal, because the nature that is the cause of manifestation exists at all times.
Moreover, it has been demonstrated in many ways that dependence on another is not logical for that which cannot be assisted.
Now, if the position is taken that manifestation is produced as something non-different from the entity itself, that too is untenable because there is no excellence (atiśaya) [added].
For, to say that "that which is non-different is produced" amounts to saying that the very nature of the entity is being produced;
and since that [nature] exists [already] and is thus independent of all external conditions, its production is illogical—this is precisely what is being considered.
Furthermore— since there is no difference [between them], either the production of an entity that is non-existent would be like the manifestation [of what already exists],

or else, just as with the nature of an entity, it would follow that the manifestation itself must be produced as something already existent; and this too is not tenable, because there would be no excellence [in the result] and it would lead to an infinite regress, as has been stated.
Furthermore, if the operation of causes is admitted with respect to an existent object (*sad-artha*), it would follow that causes never cease their activity toward the production of the effect;
for what perceived object would cause the causes to desist?
If you say it is "the existence of the effect," no.
According to your view, because that [effect] exists even prior [to its production],
therefore it is produced from what is non-existent; for that which has a cause is not like a sky-flower or the like.
Because there is an absence of a cause capable of producing that [effect],
the restriction of the causal relationship will arise from the specific determination of the power of causes;
for it is not accepted that every entity is capable of producing everything.

Since the capacities of all entities are determined by a beginningless succession of their own causes, if it is argued that validity (*prāmāṇya*) is said to be "intrinsic" (*svataḥ*) because it cannot be produced by anything else when it is non-existent, then by this very same logic, invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) would also necessarily be intrinsic. Thus, this [position] is trivial. Furthermore, as for one who thinks that so-called validity is the capacity of a cognition to produce the determination of an object, and that since this capacity resides in a momentary cognition, it is non-existent intrinsically and cannot be produced—[this too is untenable].
