Because its activity is untenable at any of the three times:
for instance, it is certainly not produced prior to the arising of consciousness, because it is dependent;

indeed, it is not logical for that which is dependent to be produced in the absence of its substratum, just as a painting cannot exist in the absence of a wall, since that would entail the consequence of its being non-dependent.
Therefore, simultaneous production is also untenable because [the cause] is dependent;
for it is not possible for a wall and a painting— the support and the supported— to begin simultaneously,
nor can an action be performed after consciousness has already arisen, because of its momentariness.

Because there is no persistence for that duration of time, it is therefore said that the validity of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*). This is incorrect; for instance, as for what was stated—that validity is the capacity to produce the determination of an object—that is incoherent, because "determination of an object" is merely a synonym for "cognition."

Furthermore, it is not logical that a power residing in that very cognition should be the producer of that same cognition, because it would follow that [the power] is non-resident, and because the relationship of cause and effect is untenable between simultaneous entities.

As for what was said— that because [the power] is resident, it is neither produced simultaneously with nor prior to [the cognition]— that too is incorrect, since its status as "resident" is unestablished due to the lack of distinction [between them].

Indeed, it is the very intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an entity that performs a specific purposeful action; when there is a desire to know merely its existence, that [nature] is designated as "capacity" (*śakti*), not as a separate entity.

For if it were a separate entity, it would follow that the entity itself is non-productive, and the relationship between them would remain unestablished—this has been thoroughly analyzed in many ways.

Therefore, the power that constitutes the intrinsic nature of consciousness—because its acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*) are inseparable from those of consciousness—is like the very nature of consciousness itself; thus, it is not contradictory to say that it is produced even though it did not exist prior to the arising of consciousness.

Furthermore, it is entirely logical to say that it arises simultaneously with consciousness, because a phenomenon that constitutes the intrinsic nature shares the same acquisition and preservation as the entity itself.

Granted that power (śakti) may indeed be distinct from the entity (padārtha), nevertheless, its status as something "supported" (āśrita) is unestablished, because it is impossible for either an existent or a non-existent thing to be supported. To explain:
an existent thing does not depend on a support, because it is already fully accomplished in its entire nature and is therefore independent;
nor is it logical for a non-existent thing to have a support, because it can contribute nothing to it.
If it is argued that the Vindhya mountain exists because its existence is caused by the Himavat,
[we reply: no.
Since stability is not distinct from the sustainer,
it is the very nature of the sustainer itself that is expressed in that way by the exclusion of other differences;
and since the self of the sustainer is not produced by that basis [of stability], it is entirely ineffective.

Even if stability exists as something distinct from the stable entity, that which causes it to stand is entirely ineffective; for it produces a stability that is a separate entity, and nothing is produced for one thing by the production of another. Thus, in both cases, the sustainer is ineffective.

If it is argued that [duration] causes the stability related to that [entity], we say no; for, as in the case of the object to be established and the establisher, a relationship between the possessor of duration and duration itself is unestablished, and this leads to the consequence of infinite regress—a point already largely investigated.
Furthermore, if duration is accepted as a distinct entity that establishes the state of an object, then the destruction of no object whatsoever would ever occur.
Since the abiding [factor] that sustains [the entity] exists,
it cannot be said that destruction will occur through the power of a cause of destruction even while abiding is present;
for since that [cause of destruction] is likewise incapable of acting, its status as a destroyer is untenable.
For even in that case, this dilemma certainly arises: does the cause of destruction produce a destruction that is a distinct entity from the thing itself, or does it produce the thing itself?
It cannot be the latter, because the thing has already been established;
and if another [distinct] thing were produced, nothing would have been done to the original thing, as it would remain in its previous state.
It has been discussed at length in the *Sthirabhāvaparīkṣā* that because there is no destruction of an entity, a cause of destruction is ineffective;
furthermore: by its very nature, an entity must be either unstable or stable in its essence.

In that case, if an entity is produced from its own causes as being inherently unstable in nature, then once its nature is established, it cannot remain by itself; thus, both a cause of stability and a cause of destruction are ineffective for it.

Now, even if an entity (*bhāva*) is by nature stable, nevertheless, because its own nature cannot undergo alteration, there is no cause of destruction; and because it is itself stationary, there is no cause of stabilization. Thus, in both cases, the causes of stability and destruction are ineffective.

Furthermore, the position that [the entity] does not depend on anything non-existent is untenable, because since it lacks all intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the operations of being supported and acting as a support are impossible—just like a hare’s horn. Therefore, the dependence of power (*śakti*) is unestablished.

Alternatively, even if [the argument] were established, it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because form and other qualities are seen to arise simultaneously with the jar despite being dependent [upon it];
furthermore, this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the definition] applies even to invalid cognition,
for invalidity too is a capacity that produces the determination of a contrary object.
Furthermore, since the capacity residing in cognition does not arise even throughout the three periods of time, it would follow that invalidity, like validity, is intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
Moreover, if the capacity of cognition does not manifest even in the three periods of time, then cognition would result in being devoid of all efficacy.
For how could a property belong to something if that property does not arise for it even throughout the three periods of time? It would be like attributing material form to space.

Or from where was this most wonderful magical illusion learned by the powers (*śakti*), by which these [powers], although their existence has never been attained even in the three periods of time within consciousness, nevertheless experience a union with it?
If you say that they experience some great being because of its eternity, no.
Otherwise, it would follow that everything possesses those powers,

since there would be no regulating factor; for we do not perceive any cause or regulator for something independent to be connected with specific objects such that these [powers] belong to consciousness alone and not to anything else.

Furthermore, it has been stated that because there is no proximate cause, these [defilements] would accrue to everyone; nor is any basis for them logically tenable that is devoid of efficacy, since, due to their permanence, there is no specific nature (svabhāvaviśeṣa) to be produced. Enough of this prolixity.
Again, analyzing the meaning of the proposition in another way, he says: "From themselves," and so forth.

Because the validity of the means of knowledge is described as being from themselves (*svataḥ*), it is intended that their occurrence toward their own effects is also *svataḥ* for those things already produced. (2847)
This is what is meant:

now, by the phrase "intrinsic validity" (*svataḥprāmāṇyam*), the following sense is intended—the operation (*vṛtti*) of cognitions that have already arisen at a subsequent time, being intrinsic and independent of other causes; that is to say, their status as a cause (*hetubhāva*).
Therefore, the intention of the opponent is that there is no occasion for the aforementioned defects.

In that regard, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) do not depend upon a cause when performing their own function— whether it be the ascertainment of their own validity or the ascertainment of the object— in the performance of this function. 2847
To the question, "From where, then, does their dependence arise? he says: "For in the acquisition of their own nature," and so forth.
For it is accepted that entities depend upon causes for the acquisition of their own nature;
however, once they have acquired their own nature, they proceed toward their own effects by themselves alone. (2848)
Having established in general that entities depend upon other causes for their acquisition of self-nature, [the author] applies this principle to cognition as well, saying:
"Therefore, there is dependence only upon its own causes for the mere production [of cognitions]; this [dependence] is not for the sake of generating certainty regarding their own qualities. (2849)
The locative case in "svaguṇeṣu" (in their own qualities) is used in the sense of a locus (*adhārasaptamī*) with respect to the arising of certainty;

this is what is meant: when it comes to producing certainty regarding those intrinsic qualities of cognitions—such as their nature of non-erroneous awareness and their being produced from pure causes—there is no dependence upon other causes for these [qualities].
If this is so, how then do they function as causes in that regard? He says: "For in the production [of cognition]," and so forth;
for when independent [cognitions] arise, there is the ascertainment of the object for the sake of its validity.
The occurrence of those [cognitions], which are independent of their own causes, is like that of a jar or similar objects.

"Validity" (*prāmāṇya*) and "the object" (*artha*)—that is, the "object of cognition" (*prameya*)—constitute the "validity and the object. The connection [of the compound] is: "the production of the ascertainment of these two."
The determination of the object is said to depend upon initial perception (*ālocanā*),
because for others [the subsequent cognitions], it is of the nature of ascertainment by itself;
thus it is called "function" (*vṛtti*).
The meaning is "the state of being a cause.
With the words "a lump of clay," etc., he explains the example, [stating] "like a jar," and so forth.
A jar depends upon a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, and so forth for its birth;
however, it has no such dependence for the act of fetching water.
In this same way, intrinsic validity must necessarily exist at the very end [of the process].
"For if validity were dependent on another, an infinite regress would result.

(2852) Having thus established that there is no contradiction with the meaning of the thesis, he speaks—"and at the end, it must necessarily be so," etc.—in order to prove the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason "because [validity] is restricted to the existence of that" (*tadbhāvaniyatatvāt*).
The word "end" (*anta*) refers to...
The meaning is that "in the final knowledge";
"that" refers to validity (*prāmāṇya*).
He asks why this must necessarily be accepted at the end, and says: "Dependent on another," and so forth (verses 2851–2852).
He demonstrates this very point with the words "If [the validity] were intrinsic," and so forth:

"If validity were intrinsic, then since its establishment would depend on another means of valid cognition, and we were to desire the same for each subsequent one, we would never attain a final certainty. (2853)
Just as the initial cognition requires corroboration, so too must that corroboration itself be sought through further corroboration. (2854) Root-text:
"The initial cognition" refers to that which arises therein, the fundamental [cognition].
"In short, it is inherent in that [cognition];

for instance, extrinsic validity (*parataḥprāmāṇya*) might arise either from a cognition that accords with effective action (*arthakriyāsaṃvādajñāna*), or from the thorough knowledge of the excellence of its causes (*kāraṇaguṇaparijñāna*). Regarding these, showing first that the former position is not tenable, he says: 'Just as... (verse 2853).

Now, it might be argued that the validity of a cognition that accords with successful purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is accepted as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*), and therefore there will be no infinite regress. To this, he says: "If, however, for some [cognition]... and so forth; "If, however, the intrinsic validity of some [cognition] were accepted..."
For what reason would there be hostility toward the first [position] being such?

Regarding the second position as well, he states the fault of infinite regress: "If, in this way, the status of perception and other means of valid cognition were dependent upon qualities," and so forth.
If, in this manner, the validity of perception and the rest were dependent upon qualities...

Furthermore, qualities (guṇas) never exist without a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Therefore, for one who desires another means of valid cognition to determine those qualities, the validity of that [second] cognition would likewise depend upon qualities determined by yet another [means]. (2856–2857)
"Dependent on qualities" means that validity depends upon the thorough knowledge of the qualities of the cause.
The determination of their lack of validity means that they do not exist;
that is to say, they are unfit for the conventional usage of "existent."
"Of that too" means that for the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) which determines qualities,
[the determination of its own validity] depends on qualities determined by another [means of valid cognition].
The meaning is that validity depends upon the ascertainment of that quality which has been determined by another means of valid cognition.
Regarding this, he states an illustration: "Just as in the first case, so it is in others"—thus, as before, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Desiring such [a series] at every step, we would never attain a stable conclusion. || 2858 ||
If it is not accepted that the knowledge of qualities has its validity dependent upon those qualities,
then even the initial cognition of an object would not require the valid cognition of qualities.
Therefore, even after reflecting at great length, if validity is found to be intrinsic anywhere, [it must be so everywhere].
It must necessarily be admitted that validity resides in that very [first cognition] alone;
the meaning is that just as in the first cognition validity depends upon qualities determined by another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), so it is in other cases as well—
this is "as before."
Just as there is a determination of validity through correspondence, so too— in each respective case—
there is [determination] in each preceding cognition of excellence.

Now, if it is accepted that the validity of the cognition of excellences (*guṇajñāna*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) precisely out of fear of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), then what is this prejudice against the cognition of the object (*arthavijñāna*), such that its validity is held to be extrinsic (*parataḥ*) and not intrinsic? We do not perceive any reason for this. Therefore, it is like a bird that, failing to see the shore, must return to that very same place even after flying a great distance; enough with this ill-founded and perverse adherence to [the view of] extrinsic validity. This very point he demonstrates with the words "the cognition of excellences," and so forth.
"Dependent on qualities"— that is, it is so described because its validity depends upon the determination of those qualities.

It might be argued that there is a distinction between the cognition of correspondence and the cognition of excellence [of causes] on account of their being based on a fundamental cognition; therefore, the validity of those two is intrinsic, whereas it is not so for the first. To this, he says:
"The cognition of correspondence," and so forth—"By what superior factor are the cognition of correspondence and the cognition of excellence considered [to be more valid]?"
The dependence of the first upon that [subsequent cognition] will occur by virtue of its power.

Therefore, the status of being intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is established as the general rule (*autsargika*) everywhere; it is set aside only by the two [conditions]: the presence of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) and the knowledge of defects in the causes (*kāraṇa-doṣa-jñāna*).
Even if this [validity] were dependent on something else, an infinite regress would not follow;
for this [validity] is dependent upon a means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), yet that [means of cognition] is established as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
(2863) Now, if cognition is indeed intrinsically valid, then it follows that all cognitions would be valid. To this, he says: "Therefore," and so forth.

*Utsarga* means a general rule; that which pertains to it is *autsargika*. *Bādha* consists of the ascertainment of a different meaning [for the object] and the knowledge of the defectiveness of the cause; thus, there is sublation through the knowledge of the defectiveness of the cause.

But surely, since validity is established as the default state (*autsargika*), how can it ever be set aside? Furthermore, if invalidity were to be established by means of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-jñāna*) and the cognition of a defect in the cause (*kāraṇa-duṣṭatva-jñāna*), then that [invalidity], being established by those two, would be extrinsic (*parataḥ*). If it is argued that this is indeed accepted, then in that case, just as with validity, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) here as well. To this he says: "Dependent on another," etc.—there would be an infinite regress if invalidity were to arise from what is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*); however, invalidity is held to arise from a non-valid means of knowledge that is of a different class (*vijātīya*).
And since that [validity] is established by itself alone, how can there be an infinite regress?
He demonstrates this very point with the words "For a means of valid cognition," and so forth:
for a means of valid cognition is not established by another means of valid cognition.
For in that same way, invalidity is not established from what is itself invalid;
for when there is a commonality of origin and basis, no firm foundation is possible.
But that which belongs to a different class, having another cause, is firmly established upon a solid root.
The term "vijāteḥ" (of a different kind) is connected with the phrase "firmly rooted and established," which refers to this invalid cognition.
"Because it has another cause" is the statement of the reason (*hetunirdeśa*).
The analysis (*vigraha*) of the compound is: "that which has another cause characterized by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[This refers to the tree] being firmly established with deep roots.
*Dṛḍha* means that whose root-establishment is unshakable by defects such as infinite regress (*anavasthā*); its state is *tattva*. 2864–2865.

It might be argued that even if a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*) possesses intrinsic validity (*anapekṣya-prāmāṇya*), it is nevertheless only capable of establishing the invalidity of another cognition when it is itself perceived as being unsublated, and not otherwise. To this he says: "The subverting cognition, for its part... and so forth. The subverting cognition is the ascertainment of the object's difference [from what was previously perceived]; because its validity is independent, it sets aside the prior cognition. (2866)
"Apohate" means he rejects; that is to say, he refutes it by [establishing] its lack of validity as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It might be argued: "Even in the case of a sublating cognition, just as in the case of the first cognition, it is indeed possible for another sublation to occur immediately after that sublation; so how could the dependence on a further sublation have ceased there, such that there would be a certainty of its being sublated? To this he says: "In that case too," and so forth. "But even in that case, there might at some point be a need for a further exception for one who has conceived a doubt regarding the previous [cognition]; yet that too is removed by a slight [further] [cognition]. (2867)
In that context as well, "in some cases" refers to one who has conceived doubt regarding a subverting cognition characterized by the determination of a difference in meaning.
"Of the person, by the former" means by the first cognition.
"‘She too’ refers to one who relies on exceptions;
‘by a small [amount]’ means..."
The word "with effort" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
To explain how [the cognition] is sublated, he says: "another sublater," and so forth.

If, while searching for another [subsequent] sublater, yet another arises, then by the sublation of the intermediate one, the validity of the first alone is established. (2868) Now, if a thorough search is conducted with appropriate effort, [the following occurs].
Due to the absence of a root, it would not be known as a sublater of the sublater.
Therefore, because it is without exception, that very first [cognition] is sublated by the stronger one; thus, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is set aside.
Thus, one does not transcend this triad of investigative cognitions;
consequently, a sublater should not be suspected again by one for whom no sublation has arisen.

(2871) If, while that [second cognition] is being examined, yet another sublater of it arises, then because the middle one is sublated by the third, the first alone would be the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If, however, it does not arise because of the absence of its cause— the root— then, on the grounds that the first [cognition] is sublated by that very second, stronger one, its validity is set aside by it;
it does not prevail.
Who does not transgress?
The word "man" (pumān) is to be supplied as the subject.
Now, why does the third cognition not likewise require a sublater, just as the second cognition does, such that there would necessarily be a triad of cognitions for the investigator? To this he says:
"And therefore," etc.—[referring to] that cognizer for whom no sublater has arisen or been produced.

To the question "Why should this not be suspected? he says: "For he who, out of delusion, imagines an obstructing factor even when it has not arisen—he, being of a doubting nature in all worldly transactions, shall go to ruin. (2872)
"Kṣaya" means destruction, resulting from a fall from reality.
He supports this very point with the scriptural teaching beginning with "And so," etc.:
"And thus, O son of Kuntī, the state of being a doubting soul has been condemned by Vāsudeva: 'Neither this world nor the next exists for the doubting soul. (Gītā 4.40) [2873]
"By Vāsudeva" means by Viṣṇu;
"Kaunteya" refers to Arjuna, the offspring of Kuntī.

If this were so, then even in the first cognition, the suspicion of sublation would not arise; consequently, it would follow that all cognitions possess validity. Anticipating this objection, he says: "To whatever extent," and so forth—"to whatever extent a sublation is possible in a cognition, to that same extent [is the doubt]."
When something has been sought and not found within that very self,
one should not remain further speculating about that object with the thought, "It might perhaps exist at some time," by those knowers who desire their own [true] welfare.

In this regard—the meaning is that in whatever cognition (*mati*) a certain amount of sublation (*apavāda*) is possible, when that very sublation has been sought and yet has not arisen, then within that [cognition]—that is, in that cognition—it is understood that "it does not exist"; this is what must be supplied [to complete the sense].
Showing where and to what extent a refutation might be possible, he says: "Place," and so forth.
For those distinctions of place, time, person, and state which are established through conventional usage—these must be taken into account by one who seeks a refutation. (2876)
"Place, time, person, and state"—these are what was stated; "the distinctions of these" is the compound [meaning].

(2876) These various distinctions of place and so forth are obstructive only to certain things, not all of them to everything. Therefore, showing that one should not entertain doubts regarding all [factors] in every case, he says: "In a distant place," and so forth.
Due to being situated in a distant land, there might arise some suspicion regarding incorrect perception; in such a case, merely going near [the object] would suffice.
However, the limit for refutation does not depend on differences in time, person, or circumstances. (2877)
In that case, there exists dependence, as in the cognition of a mirage and the like.
"Suspicion of another" (anyāśaṅkā) means the suspicion of another thing, such as water.
"In some cases," such as with a mirage and the like,
means merely approaching [the object] from nearby.
The connection is with the phrase "the limit of sublation.
What is meant is this:

where distance alone can serve as the cause of error, there only the mere act of approaching is required to determine the presence or absence of a sublating cognition; one need not, however, wait for a lapse of time or other such factors.
In that regard, because it is the cause of non-delusion, he provides this illustration: "like the cognition of a mirage and so forth.
The cognition of a mirage and so forth refers to the delusion of water and the like regarding a shimmering heat haze and similar phenomena.
By the word "etcetera," one should understand such things as the perception of largeness in what is small, and likewise the perception of smallness in what is large or distant;
for in those cases, there can be no dependence on time and so forth for those who have approached nearby,
and the same applies to time and other factors.
Wherever it is possible for a specific thing alone to serve as the cause of error, one must rely on that very thing and not on anything else; this he demonstrates by means of an example.
Regarding that, he speaks with reference to a specific time: "In such darkness," and so forth.

In such a time of deep darkness, whatever doubt there may be regarding cows, horses, and the like, or whatever erroneous determination [arises], in that case, the limit is the appearance of light. (2879)
The time in which darkness is prevalent is described as such (saṅgatatamaḥ).
Regarding a specific kind of person, he says "tathā" and so forth.
For instance, in cases such as confusion regarding the moon or directions, or [errors in] the letters and accents of the Vedas, the determination of error occurs through questioning another person.

(2880) In the cognitions of those suffering from ophthalmia and the like, such as the perception of two moons, the ascertainment of error arises precisely from questioning another person; there is no dependence on time or other factors in that regard.
With reference to the distinction of states, he says: "By those whose faculties are impaired by passion, hatred, intoxication, madness, hunger, thirst, and so forth," and so on.
When an object is being known as something difficult to know, there is error due to the absence of that [knowledge].
(2881) "Due to the absence of that" means due to the absence of the state of passion and so forth.
By means of the phrase "debt and so forth," he demonstrates through worldly convention as well that, regarding the knowledge of an investigator, there is dependence on a third [person] alone:
"Even in the worldly transaction of debt and so forth, between two people disputing..."
There shall be one statement from the defendant and two statements from the plaintiff.
Out of fear of an infinite regress, no further statement shall be written down;
thereafter, the judge, the witnesses, and the members of the court shall deliver the verdict.
Thus, for all three types of knowledge, validity is held to be intrinsic in every case;
for this very reason, even the "threefold truth" of the gods is so designated.
Therefore, since both [the means and the result] are intrinsically valid, there is no infinite regress for either.
Thus, validity and invalidity are established according to their respective applications.

(2885) Furthermore—even if the validity of perception and the other [means of knowledge] were established extrinsically, but that of verbal testimony were not, even so, our position would still be proven.

For this entire undertaking has as its fruit the demonstration that the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And since the validity of verbal testimony as a means of knowledge is established as being intrinsic (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), the validity of the injunction is already proven; thus, thinking, "What need have we for the exertion of others to establish intrinsic validity?", he sets forth the intrinsic validity of verbal testimony, saying: "Whether it be eternal or composed by a reliable person, whatever sentence is ascertained by both the hearer and the speaker is not invalidated in the slightest. (2886)
Those who are teachers of knowledge and fellow students there, who ward off destruction, are capable of protecting such [a person].
Therefore, the statement is not vitiated by defects that are precluded by its merits.
Alternatively, in the absence of an author, those defects would be without a locus and thus could not exist.
For verbal cognition as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is of two kinds: that produced by an eternal sentence and that caused by a sentence composed by a reliable person (*āpta*).
In both of these cases, he demonstrates the faultlessness of the cause.

For instance: first, as for that which is an eternal (nitya) sentence, no defect arising from the listener or the speaker is possible, because it is perpetually preserved by teachers of knowledge, instructors, and students alike;
and as for that which is spoken by a reliable person (āpta), there, defects are precluded by qualities such as compassion and the like.
Demonstrating the faultlessness of the eternal word by way of another argument, he says: "Or rather," and so forth.
For defects such as passion and the like, being attributes of a person, reside only in an agent;
how could they persist in non-human (apauruṣeya) sentences once their substratum, the agent, has ceased to exist?
For then it would follow that [the quality] is non-dependent;
indeed, this is the nature of a dependent property: that it conforms to its substratum.

Now, one might object: "If the validity of the words of a trustworthy person (āptavākya) is accepted on the grounds that their defects are eliminated by [their] excellences (guṇas), then validity would have to be admitted as arising from excellences; consequently, an infinite regress (anavasthā) would occur here as well. Anticipating this objection, he says: "In that case," and so forth.

In that regard, two things are observed in the statement of a reliable person (āpta): the absence of defects and the presence of excellences (guṇas). And it has already been explained how validity arises from excellences; thus, because the speaker possesses excellences, there are no defects, as those [defects] have been excluded by them.
A statement is intrinsically valid and characterized by the absence of defects;
that pair whose nature consists of both the absence of defects and [the presence of] excellences is described as such,
and thus it has been stated.
Thus, by the passage beginning "If the status of perception and other means of valid cognition were dependent upon excellences," those [excellences] have been refuted; therefore,
they are "refuted by excellences."

The phrase "characterized by the absence of defects" means that the intention is that the qualities free from defects function solely in the negation of defects, and not in the conferral of validity. 2889

Now, anticipating the objection of an opponent that even if validity is accepted as resulting from the ascertainment of the absence of defects, there would still be an infinite regress, he says: "If the absence of defects... and so forth.
"If the absence of defects in the words of a reliable person (āpta) is understood from [the presence of] excellences (guṇas)..."
There would be that very same infinite regress following from the presence of excellences (guṇas). To explain:

the absence of defects (doṣābhāva) is to be ascertained through the thorough knowledge of excellences; and the validity of that thorough knowledge of excellences must again be determined by the absence of defects; there too, the absence of defects is to be known through excellences; and once again, it would be the same there as well—in this way, that very same infinite regress, which destroys all systematic order, remains as it was. (2891)
He provides a rebuttal with the words "This is not a fault," and so forth:
"This is not a fault, for at that time the knowledge of the qualities is not required as something being cognized; the qualities themselves are not what provide assistance there. (2892)
By their mere presence, all of them are capable of turning away defects;
while they exist, knowledge whose object is human defect does not arise.
(2893) "While they exist" means:
Regarding the qualities (guṇas):
If it is argued that validity is not produced because it is not brought about by [external causes], then what follows? To this he says: "And by defects...
Since validity is not sublated because it is not cognized as being affected by defects, and since it is established as being unsublated, it remains here too as self-evident (*svataḥ*). || 2894 ||
The connection is that "validity is not set aside.
Why?
Because it is not cognized; that is to say, because defects are absent due to being precluded by excellences, they simply do not exist and thus are not cognized.
"And established as not being set aside" means it is established because it has not been set aside; for when there is no exception to a general rule, it is established by its very nature,
and this is the case here as well.
The word "also" (api) implies that this applies not only to the words of a reliable person (*āptavākya*) but also to those that are authorless (*apauruṣeya*).
[Objection: Even if no defects are actually perceived in some human-authored statement, they are nevertheless possible, because such defects are inherent to it.

Furthermore, just as excellences (*guṇas*) are capable of excluding defects (*doṣas*) by their mere existence, so too are defects capable of excluding excellences. Why, then, is it said that "validity is not sublated because the defects are not perceived"? Anticipating this objection, he says: "The defects exist... and so forth.
In the case of human [speech], it is suspected whether defects exist or not;
however, in the Veda, since there is no author, for us there is no suspicion of defects whatsoever. (2895)

Therefore, that which is stated as the validity of the Veda due to its independence is established even more strongly as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*) in the case of what is composed by a reliable person (*āpta*).
Thus he thinks.

For it is not necessarily the case that we must establish the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of human speech; rather, this entire undertaking is for the sake of establishing the authority of the Veda. In that regard, even if human speech should turn out to lack authority, there is no harm whatsoever to the Veda, because its authority is established precisely due to the absence of any suspicion of defect. Thus, it is said [in the Bhāṣya] to be "independent" (*anapekṣatvāt*): "Therefore, it is a means of valid knowledge because of its independence; this being so, no other cognition or another person need be relied upon, for this is a self-evident cognition."

Furthermore—there are two possible positions: is activity toward an object already determined by another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) desired, or is it not? In that regard, if the second position—that it is not desired—is held, then he demonstrates that the authority of the Veda is established intrinsically (svataḥ) with the words beginning "The meaning of the Veda," and so forth.

The fact that the meaning of the Veda is at all times inconsistent with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is precisely what constitutes its status as a *pramāṇa*; otherwise, it would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
(Verse 2897) The "meaning of the Veda" refers to such statements as, "From the *agnihotra* sacrifice, heaven arises," and so forth.

"By other means of valid cognition" means by those other than the Veda, such as perception and so forth; "consistency" is the relationship through having a common object, and its negation is "inconsistency"—
[the phrase] "by that very [inconsistency]" refers to this.

If the position is that the activity of this Veda proceeds from non-attachment [to objects already known], then, since it would be apprehending what has already been apprehended (*gṛhītagrāhitva*), the cognition occurring at a later time would not attain the status of valid knowledge (*prāmāṇya*). Demonstrating this, he says: "Otherwise, it would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*)."

Otherwise—if it were maintained that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) functions even when its object has already been cognized by other means of valid cognition—then, because it would be illuminating an object already illuminated by another, it would be a mere restatement (*anuvāda*); consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) would follow that it lacks validity, like memory and so forth.

Therefore, whatever is a means of valid cognition does not depend upon connection with another means of valid cognition; thus, the point is that the self-validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) of every means of valid cognition is established.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "of another as well," and so forth:

"Even if another [cognition] were a means of valid cognition, association would not be the cause; for among cognitions of the same object, validity belongs to only one through the process of exclusion. (2898)
"Of others than the Veda as well, such as perception and so forth,
having the same object" means those that operate upon a single subject matter.
"Of one alone" refers to the first [statement],
because the others are merely restatements.
Nor is it logical for the validity of the first [cognition] to depend upon those subsequent cognitions, because they themselves lack validity since their objects have already been apprehended.

Anticipating the objection that "in places such as deep darkness, even an object already apprehended by the first cognition is indeed determined with greater clarity by successive valid cognitions during the state of bright light," he says: "Even where... and so forth.
Even where there might be a determination by subsequent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
it is certain that in that case as well, the object was not clearly ascertained by the preceding one.
The implication is that because the object of the preceding cognition was not ascertained, it lacks validity altogether.

Furthermore: if validity were to depend upon the connection with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*), then in that case, the validity of a cognition whose object has perished immediately after arising, as well as that of auditory perception, would not be established, because no other means of valid cognition operates regarding those objects. This is shown by the verse beginning with "sakṛt" (*once*):
"And there would be no validity regarding an object that has perished immediately after it arose."
And auditory cognition would not be a means of valid knowledge if it were unconnected with the eyes and other [senses].
"Unconnected with the eyes and other [senses]" means that it lacks a relationship by virtue of having the same object.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is independent of connection with another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is valid by itself (*svataḥ*), just like auditory cognition or a cognition that has arisen once and then perished regarding its object; and the cognition whose object is the meaning of the Veda is independent of connection with another means of valid cognition. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). [Verse 2900] With the words "auditory" and so forth, he raises the objection that the example is deficient in the probans (*sādhanavikala*): "If its validity [is established] because of its connection with another auditory cognition..."

In the Veda as well, [the validity] is established because of its connection with another cognition produced by it. However, for both [the Veda and other means of knowledge], there is no cognition produced by a different instrument; therefore, corroboration by a cognition produced by a different cause is not required.

For instance, even when a single sound is heard by many people, the validity of this auditory cognition is determined through its connection with another cognition produced by the sense of hearing; [the author] refutes [this objection] with the words "because of the connection with another cognition produced by that" (*tajjanya-vijñānāntara-saṅgateḥ*),
meaning because of the relation with another cognition produced by the Veda.
"Of both" refers to the auditory cognition and the cognition of the meaning of the Veda;

what is meant is this: in the statement "because of independence from connection with another means of knowledge," it is intended that "another means of knowledge" refers to that produced by a different instrument (*sādhana*), and not something to be accomplished by the same instrument. Therefore, because the reason is qualified, the sense is that the example is not deficient in its probans (*sādhana*).
"Corroboration by a cognition produced by another reason" (*hetvantarakṛtajñānasaṃvāda*) is explained as follows:

it is that which is both "produced by another reason" (*hetvantareṇa kṛtam*) and "cognition" (*jñānam*); thus it is so called. The analysis of the compound is: "corroboration" (*saṃvāda*) "of that" (*tasya*).

2902 Now, if it is intended that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*) merely by the occurrence of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to be established by the same means of proof, then [the opponent], considering this to be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), says: "Just as," and so forth— "just as, however,
there is a connection with another cognition dependent on the same sense-organ..."
Just as a cause has been established for perception, let it be stated likewise for the Veda.
[Objection: "A cause has been established" means that its validity arises from its connection with another auditory cognition. This is because of the statement [to that effect].
To the question of how this should be explained in the Veda, he says: "By a single sentence alone," and so forth;
for by a single sentence alone [is it established] across different places, times, and so on.
When there is correspondence with the object, no other cause need be sought.
Therefore, that cognition which has arisen firmly and does not contradict cognitions of other locations and so forth is undoubtedly a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).
"Firm" means being free from doubt and error;
"by means of cognitions of other places and so forth."
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the cognitions of other persons and so forth.
Showing that this reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), he says: "The validity of words and so forth is not to be proven by inference... and so on.

"The validity of words and so forth is not to be proven by inference; otherwise, let that [validity] of perception also not be proven by it, for there is no distinction [between them in being objects of proof]. (2906)
The sense is that the meaning of the Veda cannot first be established by perception, because it is beyond the reach of the senses;
nor can it be established by inference, as that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga) regarding words.

The word "of the Vaidikas" is the ellipsis [to be supplied], or the specific application [of the term] is understood from the context (2906). It might be argued: "This very thing is indeed accepted—that even perception has its validity established by inference. To this he says: "Of the means of valid cognition," and so forth.
If the validity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established by another [means],
then because that too must be established by yet another, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.
If, on the other hand, the validity of the establishing means were not established by another, [then the same would apply to the first].

Consequently, that [means of proof] would likewise be established for those things yet to be proven (sādhya). If, like perception, the validity of that inference were to be established by another inference, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā) regarding the thing to be proven.

Alternatively, if the validity of the means of proof called inference is not established by another, then the same [lack of establishment] would apply to the things to be proven, such as perception, because there is no distinction between them.
With the words beginning with "nanu," the Buddhist indeed supports the very point that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Now, perception and the other means of knowledge are not apprehended as being "means of knowledge" (pramāṇa) in this way;
and if they are not so apprehended, practical activity (vyavahāra) is not possible.

If there were no dependence on another means of knowledge for the means of knowledge themselves, then there would be no certainty regarding these perceptions and so forth that they are indeed means of knowledge.
Consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all worldly transactions;
he counters this with the argument beginning, "Because [the object] is apprehended by a means of valid cognition" (pramāṇaṃ grahaṇāt), and so forth.
Prior to its apprehension, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is established in its own nature and is independent; once its object has been cognized, it is then measured by others. (2910)

This is what is meant: although a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) may depend upon another means of valid cognition for the ascertainment of its own nature, nevertheless there is no cessation of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), because it is independent of other means of valid cognition with respect to the determination of the object. If the object is determined, then by that much alone all worldly transactions are completed; so what is the use of investigating whether there is ascertainment or non-ascertainment regarding its own nature, since this [investigation] has the purpose of ascertaining the object? This is the summary meaning. The meaning of the individual words is now stated: "prior to apprehension" means prior to the ascertainment that "this is a means of valid cognition."
"By its own nature" means by way of the determination of the object; "independent" [means independent of other causes].

The meaning is that [perception] does not depend upon another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) for the determination of its own object. Once its own object has been cognized—that is, ascertained—it is subsequently cognized by means of other pramāṇas such as inference (*anumāna*), as it has been said: "No one perceives a cognition with regard to an object that has not been known."

"But once it is known, one understands [the object] through inference" (2910). This might be the case: if the cognition itself is unknown, the determination of its own object would not be tenable, as it has been said: "For one whose perception is not itself perceived, the seeing of the object is not established. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And just as," etc.
Just as all objects are apprehended by the sense organs, such as the eye, even when they themselves are not known, so it is not with the means of valid cognition (pramāṇas).
Therefore, in this context, the state of being known (jñāyamānatva) is of no use for establishing validity.
Even the experience of objects is obtained from this very [consciousness] when it is unknown. (2912) This is easy to understand.

If this were so, one might suspect that by this same logic, even invalid cognition would follow as being valid in itself; anticipating this, he says: "Invalid cognition," and so forth—"For invalid cognition, moreover, stands as if it were a valid cognition with respect to its own object."

Its falsity cannot be apprehended without another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For that which is invalid appears as if it were valid; thus, it does not determine its own object by its mere existence. Therefore, its "falsity"—that is, its character of determining a false object—cannot be grasped without another pramāṇa; hence, it is established as being extrinsic (parataḥ).

But surely this is the same even in the case of a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*); for that too sometimes appears as if it were not a valid cognition with respect to its own object. To this he says: "For there is no alteration of the object," and so forth. For there is no alteration of the object as was previously apprehended, just as there is no [alteration] of its being such-and-such; likewise, in this case too, when there is an alteration, the cognition [arises] either from a defective cause. (2914)
And by that much alone, falsity is apprehended, not as having any other cause;
for it is at the very moment of its arising that this [cognition] is measured as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by the preceding one. (2915) Thus, by the former.
"Taken up by the immeasurable" means grasped.

The phrase "like thatness" (*tathātvavat*) is a dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). What is meant is this: just as thatness is apprehended by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), falsity is not apprehended by a means of valid cognition; thus, they are not equal.

For instance, a means of valid cognition is cognized as a "means of valid cognition" precisely at the moment of its arising, whereas a non-means of valid cognition is not [cognized] as a "non-means of valid cognition," because the former always appears as a means of valid cognition. This is the intended meaning.

With the words beginning with "tat," he concludes the argument regarding extrinsic invalidity (*parataḥ-aprāmāṇya*); alternatively, the connection is with the phrase "the cognition [arising] from a defective cause," and by that much alone.
Otherwise, this [objection] might arise through the cognition of existence and the cognition of a defective cause:

if the validity of these two cognitions were apprehended, then falsity would be apprehended by them; and if there were a dependence on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to apprehend their validity, there would be an infinite regress. Therefore, he says: "at the stage of its arising," and so forth.
The meaning is that "this" refers to the cognition of an object as otherwise and the cognition of a defective cause;
therefore, there is no infinite regress. This is the intended sense.

Regarding the proof stated by the Buddhists and others— that Vedic speech has false meaning because it is a statement, like the human statement "fire is cold"— he says "Therefore, even where... and so forth, demonstrating that this [reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Therefore, even in cases where falsity is demonstrated to others,
these two [points] must be stated there as well, and not merely a similarity of properties (sādharmya).
[This refers to the phrase] "even in cases where."
In the case of an injunction and so forth,
these two are the cognition of falsity and the cognition of a defective cause.
"Merely a similarity" means being equal [to a false statement] by virtue of being a sentence, etc., such as a human statement whose object is non-existent. 2916

Regarding the question "Why should it not be stated?", he provides the reasoning here with the verse beginning with "tatra": "In that regard, relying on some mere similarity to invalid cognition, the unwise seek to prove the falsity of all valid cognition. (2917)
For them, such a formulation of a means arises solely for their own destruction;
likewise, by means of a reflection, it appears as such even to another.
And because it has been refuted by that [reflection], it is a means that does not correspond to reality.
"Because its validity is not inherent, the Vedic injunction (codanā) is capable of being sublated.

(2919) The summary meaning is this: if something were invalid merely by virtue of sharing a common property with what is invalid, then it would follow that all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) are invalid; for one could indeed state a common property such as "being an entity" (vastutva) in every case.
To explain how [the opponent's argument] leads to self-destruction, he says: "It arises," and so forth.
"Of the other as well" refers to the Mīmāṃsaka;
"by means of a reflection" [is the method].

The meaning is that just as a reflection arises immediately after the original object, so too does a counter-argument (pratisādhana) arise for the Mīmāṃsaka immediately after the proof (sādhana) put forward by the Buddhist.

For instance, it can be stated as follows: "Vedic speech is not false, because it possesses the nature of being speech and so forth, just like the words of a person such as 'Fire is hot and luminous.'"

Because it has been refuted by such a counter-means of knowledge (*pratipramāṇa*)—that is, because it is contradicted—the argument presented by the Buddhists and others to prove the point that "the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) does not correspond to reality" is not capable of subverting the injunction. Why? Because of its status as a default means of knowledge (*autsargikapramāṇatvāt*).
That which has validity as its default state is so described; the state of being such is its "ness" (*tattva*).
(Verse 2917)

Regarding this, [the author] begins the refutation in due order, starting with the words "It is said here... and continuing from "And in the acquisition of their own nature by entities... and so forth.
To this it is replied: "But surely this systematic arrangement has a basis for those very things whose existence is admitted once they have arisen. [2920] "Has a basis" means...
The meaning is that [the agent] has the object as its locus, because an operation is impossible for that which is non-existent.
What, then, is this systematic arrangement? He says: "In the acquisition of their own nature," and so forth.
It is accepted that for jars and other things, there is a dependence on causes for the acquisition of their own nature;
however, once they have acquired their own nature, their engagement in their own effects occurs by themselves alone. (2921)
Now, he asks why this is not tenable even in the case of cognition, stating "But as for that... and so forth:

"But as for that cognition which you also accept as unstable immediately after its birth, what kind of activity could there be for it once it has ceased to exist after having acquired its own nature? (2922)
What kind of activity could there be for that which is non-existent?
None at all; the point is that because a non-existent thing is devoid of all causal capacity, it lacks existence.
Alternatively, even if it were existent, no activity could ever be established, because all entities are devoid of volitional effort (*nirīhatvāt*).
Furthermore, there is no effect for cognition in which it could be operative;
if it is argued that its nature consists in the determination of its own object, we say no.
If it is argued that because this [cognition] is a synonym for knowledge (*jñāna*), it "makes itself" its own object,
and thus its own function is the production of the ascertainment "this is a valid means of cognition" (*pramāṇa*), we say no;
for there is no certainty in some cases, and because error is observed.
By this, the contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition regarding the thesis here has also been established;

for, through the non-perception of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility—which consists in the perception of something else—the absence of activity in a non-existent thing is ascertained by perception.
Furthermore, it is established even by inference, due to its lack of form, like a sky-lotus.
By the phrase "this is also desired by you," he points out the contradiction with your own words;
he demonstrates this very point through the two verses beginning with "that same operation" (2922).

For the operation of causes is indeed observed to be distinct from their arising; lest the same be thought to apply to valid cognition as well, "arising" is specifically intended [as its defining characteristic].
Indeed, that [cognition] does not remain even for a moment, nor is it produced as something non-valid.

By which [cognition] one might subsequently operate toward the apprehension of an object, as in the case of the sense organs and so forth. For instance, Kumārila stated "operation" and so on in order to demonstrate the utility of the inclusion of the term "birth" (*janman*) in the aphorism: "When there is contact of a person’s sense organs with what is existent, the arising of cognition is perception. He did so for the purpose of establishing that the validity of cognition belongs to the cognition itself as it is being born.
He asks, "For what reason? and says, "Not indeed," and so forth;
"that" refers to cognition.
Now, with the words "athāpi" and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's reply.
Furthermore, if it is accepted that cognition is non-momentary and eternal,
this constitutes a contradiction of one's own tenets as well as a subversion by reasoning.
Likewise, elsewhere Kumārila has described cognitions as being both eternal and unitary.

As it has been said: "Because even cognitions possess the nature of consciousness, the Puruṣa is therefore held by us to be eternal and one; the diversity of cognitions, however, is based on [their] objects.
In this position as well, there is a contradiction with what has been accepted regarding the thesis, as well as a contradiction with inference.

For in this way, the momentariness of cognitions is accepted, as stated in the Bhāṣya: "For that [cognition] is momentary; it will not persist until the time of another cognition," and likewise from such statements as, "Indeed, it does not remain even for a single moment. Thus, there is also a contradiction with the authoritative teaching (*pravacana*).
2925 He demonstrates the contradiction by reasoning: "Established," and so forth;
for every entity has its momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) established in detail.
And since that which is eternal is not produced, what need has it for a cause?
(2926) He shows that the dependence on a cause is not logical if eternity is admitted—with the words "And since [it is] eternal," etc.:
for only that which is produced has a dependence on other causes, due to the desire to obtain its own existence; but what dependence can there be for that which, being eternal, is not to be produced?
2926. By the formulation of the argument beginning with "ataśca" (and therefore), he demonstrates precisely the sublation by inference (*anumāna-bādha*):
"And therefore, it can be stated that [the cognition] does not exist by itself."
"Subsequently, [the cognition] is non-existent with respect to its own effects, like a sky-lotus, due to its lack of form.
With the words "Or let it be," etc., he shows the sublation by perception and other means of knowledge while provisionally accepting non-momentariness:
"Or let the non-momentary cognition proceed by itself."
If [it is argued that the cognition] is for the sake of ascertaining its own validity, then why do doubt and so forth [arise]?
(2928) If it produces the ascertainment of its own validity by itself alone, then doubt and so forth regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would not occur;

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), error, contradiction preceded by that [error], contrary activity, the formulation of mutually contradictory definitions, and non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) are included.

Furthermore, because doubt and the like—which possess a form contrary to certainty—are experienced immediately after the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the absence of certainty is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) itself, just as the absence of a jar is established from the perception of a location devoid of it;
consequently, the thesis asserting their existence contradicts direct perception.

With the words beginning "prāmāṇya" (validity), he establishes the very contradiction regarding perception: "Since the ascertainment of validity there arises from that [perception] alone, once it has arisen, doubt and error find no footing. (2929)
"In that" refers to the ascertainment of validity.
Why are they said to be "without a locus"? He says: "Because of the relationship between the sublated and the sublator... and so forth.
For it is only when there is a distinction from superimposition that every certainty functions [with respect to its object]. (2930)
He asks, "Why is this so? and replies with the verse beginning *samāropa* and so forth:

For a certainty (*niścaya*), because its form is the opposite of superimposition (*samāropa*), does not attain its own stability without first setting aside its object; just as a hot touch [cannot coexist] with cold, how could there be the occurrence of error regarding an object already apprehended by that certainty?
Then, with the words beginning "tataśca," he also demonstrates the contradiction with his own statement:

"And therefore, for the sake of establishing the validity of the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (codanā), the argument regarding its arising from causes free from defects is pointless. (2931)

The state of being produced from a cause (*hetūtthabhāva*)—by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is included such [reasons] as being produced by speech that is not unauthoritative or ill-composed, and being free from sublation; for it is said:
"Cognition produced by Vedic injunction (*codanā*) is a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is free from defects..."
"Because it is produced by causes, like the cognition derived from signs, authoritative speech, or the senses;

likewise, because it is produced by speech not composed by an untrustworthy person and is free from sublation"—by stating this proof for the sake of establishing the validity of the cognition generated by the *codanā*, you have asserted that the determination of validity arises from an external means (*parataḥ*).
Yet, by asserting that "the validity of all means of knowledge is intrinsic" (*svataḥ*), you have denied that very point. Thus, there is a mutual contradiction between your statements.
With the words "Once established," etc., he anticipates the opponent's reply: "If intrinsic validity is established, then that [inference] serves to ward off exceptions."
Even if that [doubt] were accepted, it would still not be so, because such a doubt is impossible.
For that doubt persists only so long as certainty has not arisen; once that certainty has emerged, how indeed could this [doubt regarding] invalidity exist? (2932–2933)
By this means, an effort toward the cessation of that [doubt] would become meaningful;
for one who has ascertained the identity of a post does not suspect it to be otherwise.
(2934) Furthermore, it might be argued: "We do not state a proof for the sake of establishing the validity of the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction."
What then?
[If you say] it is for the purpose of negating the invalidity attributed there by another, that too is not tenable;
why? because such a doubt is impossible.

For it has been said: "Because of the relationship of the sublated and the sublator between the cognitions of certainty and superimposition. Therefore, since certainty has already arisen, from where does this suspicion of invalidity come, such that your effort in employing a proof for its removal would be fruitful?
To this, he provides an example: "In the case of a post," and so forth.
One who has ascertained "stump-ness" as being identical [to that object] is described in that way;
"otherness" refers to [the cognition of] "tree-ness," "person-ness," and so forth.
If this is so, how can the suspicion of invalidity be dispelled without the employment of a formal proof? To this he says: "yadrūpa... and so forth:
from whatever [means] the ascertainment of a certain form regarding a given object arises, from that very same source the suspicion of its opposite is averted. (2935)
"In which form there is certainty" means "certainty regarding that form"; "of the suspicion of its opposite" means "of the suspicion regarding a nature contrary to that form."
"From that very [source]" means from the ascertainment of its form.
Regarding this very point, he states an illustration: "Just as from smoke and so forth," and so on.
Just as when the existence of fire and the like is apprehended through signs such as smoke, the exclusion of its non-existence follows from that very same [apprehension]. || 2936 ||
The exclusion of its non-existence means the exclusion of the non-existence of fire and so forth.
He concludes with the words "apramāṇa" and so forth: "In this way, let it be accepted that the exclusion of non-authoritativeness occurs by itself;
therefore, a means of proof for the removal of non-authoritativeness is not logical. (2937)
Regarding this very point, he states the reason for the reinforcement: "If there were a suspicion regarding the two types of non-valid cognition," and so forth.
In that case, however, there would be no certainty regarding validity, because [the object] would have been apprehended by means of error. (2938)

By the verse beginning with "yaḥ" (2938), [the author] demonstrates the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving a pervasion by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), thereby establishing the very contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) regarding the two types of invalid cognition consisting of doubt and error.
That which is made an object by cognitions of doubt and error— like a post— is not, at that time, determined to have that [specific] nature.
Since the object made an object by doubt and error is pervaded by those two states which are opposed to certainty, there is no room for certainty regarding it.

By the verse beginning with "balibhuk" (the fire-eater), he demonstrates the contradiction with inference and the establishment of his own position, just as [it is done] by means of cognitions such as those concerning the fire-eater, smoke, causes, and defects.
The nature of a post, fire, invalidity, and so forth, is determined through other means [of cognition].

(2940) The formal argument is as follows: those things whose natures are made objects of doubt or error must have their true nature determined by something else, just like a post and the like; and the validity of certain cognitions is likewise made an object of doubt and error for some people. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Furthermore, the crow, smoke, and defects arising from causes, and so forth, have been described in that same manner.
The compound "pratyayāḥ" (conditions) refers to those [four]; and by these, the connection with the post and so forth is established respectively;
by this, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason is demonstrated.

Now, avoiding the charge of non-establishment (*asiddhi*) by teaching the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*), he says: "That which has become the object of doubt and error," and so forth. Thus...
Let the certainty regarding its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) be understood from another source;
"since" (*yad*) means "because."
"Of whom is it determined that [the object] has gone?"— the word "of what means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
For it has been demonstrated that the cognition produced by an injunction is subject to doubt and error;
"thus" means just as there is a subsequent ascertainment regarding a post or similar object.
With the words "tasya" and so forth, there is the presentation of the fruit of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇaphala).

As for what was stated—that once intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is established, that [cognition] serves to ward off exceptions—that is not tenable, because it has been demonstrated that such a doubt is impossible. Now, even granting that a formal argument (*sādhanaprayoga*) might be employed to remove the suspicion of invalidity, he says "And this... and so forth, showing that even such an argument is not tenable according to your own view.
And this is your position: "In whatever sentence there is the hearing of a negative particle, there alone is the exclusion of another; elsewhere, its own nature is understood.
And here [in our case], it is not the cognition produced by an injunction that is the means of valid knowledge.
"There is no employment of the negative particle (*nañ*) [in this case]; therefore, there is no exclusion of invalidity.

For you, who maintain that the meaning of words is positive injunction (*vidhi*), this is your position: only in a sentence where the negative particle is employed is the exclusion of another (*anyavyavaccheda*) perceived, whereas elsewhere it is only a positive injunction (*vidhi*).
However, in this probative statement beginning with 'not produced by a Vedic injunction' (*codanājanita*), there is no employment of the negative particle."
How, then, can the exclusion of invalidity be established by this?
Regarding what was said—"How then [can there be] doubt and so forth?"—he shows the meaning conveyed by the word "and so forth" (ādi) in that context: "Furthermore, etc.
Furthermore, if the validity of all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) were ascertained through itself alone (*svataḥ*), then why would there be a difference of opinion among proponents? (2944)
If the validity of all means of valid cognition were established intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then there would be no difference of opinion among proponents regarding the nature of that validity.
To explain how that [difference] is established, he says: "By which some," and so forth.

By some [ancient masters], the restriction that "some things arise from themselves alone" is stated; by others, it is held that there is no such restriction, [maintaining] that some things arise from themselves and some from other [causes].
(2945) Regarding the phrase "by some":
"By other Mīmāṃsakas" refers to the Buddhists.

Among these, some maintain that certain [cognitions] are intrinsically valid (*svataḥ-pramāṇa*), as follows: self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), the cognition of a yogi, the cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyā-jñāna*), inference, and perception resulting from practice (*abhyāsa-vat pratyakṣa*). For this latter is determined intrinsically because its causes of error have been dispelled by the power of practice.

Some, however, hold it to be extrinsic (*anyataḥ*), as for example: the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) which is the subject of dispute, and perception whose grounds for error have not yet been removed.

Because the knowledge of repeated practice and of causal efficacy has not yet been attained—if this were so, then according to your own view, there would be no dispute regarding inference and the like, since those would be intrinsically valid.

For instance: some maintain that inference arises from a logical mark possessing three characteristics, some that it is produced by a mark with two characteristics, and others that it originates from a mark with a single characteristic.

Furthermore, the formulation of definitions would be useless, and likewise, one need not establish the validity of that [system] toward the Lokāyata, since validity is ascertained intrinsically; this objection is the same [for both sides].
This is not a fault.

Since inference arises from the ascertainment of a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is constrained by identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), its non-deviation from the object is ascertained through its being produced by something indirectly connected to such a thing—even without corroboration by causal efficacy (*arthakriyāsaṃvāda*). Thus, its intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is asserted.

However, because the proponent does not fully understand the nature of the logical mark that is the cause of its production, they dispute with one another regarding inference while it is still unproduced, and not once it has been produced, for its nature and other characteristics are then ascertained.
For this very reason, the Teachers (Dignāga and Dharmakīrti) undertake in their definition nothing but the elucidation of the nature of the logical mark that is the cause of its production.
For how indeed could the production of inference occur from the ascertainment of the nature of a reversed logical mark?
As for the objection raised against the Lokāyata that one need not establish the validity of inference, that too is incorrect;
for we do not seek to prove the validity of inference.

What then? It is conventional usage (*vyavahāra*). To explain: the Lokāyata, deluded by hearing false treatises on reality, does not engage in that [conventional] usage even though he has established the validity of inference, unlike the Sāṅkhya. His usage, which is the subject, is established by demonstrating its object: "Whatever arises from something possesses the capacity to lead to the attainment of that thing, just as perception [leads to the attainment] of its own object; and this cognition of the inferable, having arisen from the inferable, arrives by way of the observation of a mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably connected to it. Thus, by stating the object of the convention, one engages in the linguistic agreement (*samaya*).
For in this way, he has established the conventional usage of "validity" for perception solely on the basis of its non-deviation from the object;

and what else is this non-deviation for it, if not its arising from that [object], as it has been said: "Because it does not exist when the object is absent, perception also possesses the status of a means of valid cognition."
Since two things are equal in being causes when they possess an interdependent nature,

this materialist (Lokāyata) proceeds in the same manner as the Sāṅkhya: although he determines that there is an absence of an elephant on the tip of a blade of grass, he fails to engage in the conventional usage of "absence" due to the delusion caused by his lack of study of the scriptures.

Furthermore, the validity of the cognition produced by an injunction (*codanā*) is not established, such that one could argue that its status as valid is here to be proven through the same application of inference as in other cases; for in that case, since the necessary invariable concomitance (*pratibandha*) is unestablished, it is validity itself that remains to be proven. Thus, the two cases are not the same. One might object: "Granted that there is a difference of opinion, why is it not tenable [to accept intrinsic validity] when validity is indeed intrinsic? To this, he says: "The dispute arises from delusion," and so forth.

"Since dispute arises from error, and that [error] is sublated by certainty, therefore those who ascertain reality would not dispute. (2946) By this, showing the establishment of the absence of certainty through the observation of dispute— which is the effect of an error contradicted by certainty— he demonstrates that the proposition of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) is contradicted by inference (*anumāna-viruddhatva*).
Furthermore, he demonstrates the perception of an effect that contradicts certainty, beginning with the words "from themselves" (*svataḥ*):
"If the validity of all means of valid cognition were determined from themselves..."
No one would be subject to deception through the operation of certainty.
For one who acts with the notion that what is not a valid means of knowledge is a valid means of knowledge is indeed deceived;
however, no one is deceived by the cognition of intrinsic validity, as this is the opposite [of error].

For non-conformity (visaṃvāda) is recognized as the effect of an error that is contrary to certainty; and this [non-conformity] would not occur if intrinsic validity were accepted, because by means of certainty, the cause of that [non-conformity], namely error, is removed.
On the contrary, [it occurs].
subject to contradiction 2947 2948

With the words "nanu" and so forth, the opponent objects: "But surely, does a cognition that has arisen without a means of valid knowledge (apramāṇa) incur any contradiction? For its certainty is held to be dependent on another, namely, a subverting cognition. (2949)
But one who acts on the basis of a valid means of knowledge does not encounter non-correspondence;
it is precisely for such a person that we maintain the determination of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*).
For non-correspondence occurs only for one who acts on the basis of what is not a valid means of knowledge.
Furthermore, it is indeed accepted that the ascertainment of that [first] means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) occurs through another;

moreover, there is no discrepancy for one who acts upon that which is a means of valid cognition, and it is precisely that [second cognition] whose intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is desired. Thus, how could the thesis of intrinsic validity be contradicted by inference?
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "nābhiprāya" (not by intention), etc.
This is not [the case] because of a failure to understand the intended meaning; for what is intended here is that,
in the determination of the validity of all means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*),
there is no such thing as a determination of intrinsic validity established by necessity.
By the force of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) is understood in that case;
for, without depending on the cognition of a defect arising from a cause that renders the object otherwise,
there is a determination of its lack of authority immediately following its birth.
The error of regarding what is not a valid means of knowledge as being a valid means of knowledge is not tenable;
