therefore, no one would ever act based on that [invalid cognition], because it lacks correspondence with reality.

What is intended here is this: if you accept that all valid means of knowledge possess intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), then you must have accepted that a valid means of knowledge is necessarily pervaded by the production of a certainty regarding its validity.

Consequently, wherever the ascertainment of validity—which pervades all means of knowledge—does not arise, there invalidity is established by implication, because validity and invalidity are mutually exclusive.

Thus, invalidity also follows of its own accord by implication, since it does not depend on the recognition of causes of non-conformity or defects; for invalidity is ascertained simply through the non-arising of the ascertainment of validity.
Furthermore, as for what was stated—that "the ascertainment of that [validity] is held to arise from a subsequent sublating cognition"—that is simply not tenable.

This being the case, since validity and its opposite would be ascertained immediately after the [cognition's] birth through the arising or non-arising of the ascertainment of validity, it would be impossible for any discerning person to act based on what is not valid; how, then, could there be the possibility of a discrepancy?
Thus, regarding the understanding of that [discrepancy]:
The meaning is: because there is a certainty regarding a state of non-correspondence [with reality].

These should be regarded as defects of the reason (*hetudoṣa*) alone, since they reveal the lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) of the reason by way of exposing defects in the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*); they are not, however, defects of the thesis itself.
For otherwise, since the thesis is not a constituent part of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), exposing its defects would constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the opponent.
Demonstrating the lack of proof for the example "like a jar" and so forth, he says: "And there exists no time for action distinct from the time of birth," and so on.
The example [given], namely "because jars and so forth are momentary," is unestablished (asiddha).

[Objection: But surely jars and so forth are indeed seen after their birth to perform purposeful actions, such as containing honey or water, without depending on a potter or other causes; how then can it be said that no time exists for them beyond their birth? To this he says: "teṣām" and so forth:
"For at a later time, those [jars] which do not depend on a potter and the like..."
Because it depends upon its own material cause and other factors, there is no self-initiated activity.
(2956) "Its own material cause" refers to each preceding moment of the same kind;
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the person who maintains it and other such factors is intended.

This is what is meant: at a later time, entirely different moments of existence such as a jar are seen to persist in dependence upon their own material causes and so forth; however, the continued existence of anything after its birth is not established, because all entities are momentary.
As for the passage beginning with "Just as the first cognition," he says "And not... and so forth.
Nor does an infinite regress result, because [the validity] relies on another means of cognition;
therefore, the determination of intrinsic validity occurs in the cognition of causal efficacy.
(Verse 2957) The opponent objects: (beginning with "But...")
"Surely, what excellence does that [subsequent cognition] possess over the preceding one,
such that it is not accepted as being dependent on another, just like the prior cognition?
He provides the rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said," and so forth.

It is said that validity is defined as correspondence with the object; and for that, there is no defining characteristic other than the cognition resulting from repeated purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Furthermore, a cognition manifesting purposeful action is clearly experienced.
And that [validity] is ascertained by a mind that reflects upon it as being produced solely by that [cause].
Therefore, because its own intrinsic validity is correctly determined, no further cognition of the attainment of purposeful action (arthakriyā) need be awaited.

And since that cognition which manifests the effect possesses the nature of valid knowledge (*jñāna-pramāṇa*), the determination of its validity follows from this very reason even in the first [cognition].
This is the summary of the meaning here: indeed, valid knowledge is defined as non-discrepant cognition (*avisaṃvādi-jñāna*).

From the statement that "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge," it follows that this non-contradiction is defined solely by causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), because the investigation into valid cognition has that as its purpose;
for a discerning person seeks what is either a valid or an invalid means of cognition for the sake of causal efficacy, not out of mere habit.

And that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is characterized by the arising of a cognition manifesting [effects] such as burning or cooking; for, precisely through its production, the expectation of one who has engaged in action seeking causal efficiency is satisfied.

Furthermore, that cognition of causal efficiency manifests of itself through the direct perception of self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), and because it is a clear experience, it is subsequently ascertained by the arising of a reflective cognition (*parāmarśajñāna*) in accordance with that experience; thus, it is established by itself. Moreover, no other fruit to be accomplished by it is desired by the person, such that there would be an infinite regress for one who pursues the arising of another subsequent cognition manifesting causal efficiency.

For instance, in the world, results such as prosperity or ruin are desired, and these are accomplished solely through the manifestation of cognitions consisting of pleasure, pain, and so forth; it is by this much alone that people, having attained satisfaction, desist. Therefore, its establishment is said to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*).
However, the validity of the preceding cognition—which serves as its cause—is not defined as the capacity to bring about that [result].

And since that capacity cannot be ascertained through non-repetition by those who do not know its effects, it is determined by the subsequent operation of the cognition of the effect; thus, the validity of the first [cognition] is said to be extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
Furthermore, avoiding the charge of infinite regress in another manner, he says: "In the first," and so forth.

For in the first case, regarding an object that is not a real entity, the second [type of cognition], which is characterized by correspondence with a real entity, would not arise, because its cause is impossible. This is because, for instance, in the case of an ashoka flower cluster and the like, there is no determination of it as fire.
A consciousness manifesting as burning or cooking never arises [from that which lacks such power].
Or, if it were to arise, it would follow that it is not of a different kind from fire,
because the defining characteristic of fire is simply its capacity for those effects.

For if the first cognition had operated upon a non-entity, then the subsequent cognition of the result would not have arisen at a later time due to the absence of its cause; for the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) is dependent upon a real entity.

Indeed, from a cognition that apprehends what is not fire—such as when one acts with the determination that it is fire toward an *aśoka* flower-cluster—the cognitions manifesting burning, cooking, and so forth, are not produced.

Or, if they were produced, then that [object] would simply be fire. Why? Because the defining characteristic of fire is precisely its being the cause for the production of effects such as burning and cooking.
The meaning is "of fire.
He concludes with the words beginning "Therefore" (tasmāt):
Therefore, as long as cognition appearing as purposeful action has not arisen...
"Thus, in the first [cognition], a doubt regarding its invalidity arises due to the cause of error.

[Objection: But surely the first cognition, like the cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyājñāna*), is produced directly by the object such as fire; so why is there a doubt regarding its invalidity in that case alone, and not in the subsequent one? Anticipating this objection, he says: 'Immediately thereafter,' etc.—'the non-perception of the result and the perception of similarity.'"
The dullness of the mother and so forth are the causes of error in this case;
however, once the cognition manifesting the effect has arisen, this [error] no longer exists,
because there is a direct perception of the activity bound to the actual object.

For in the first cognition there exists a cause of error; namely, the non-arising of a result characterized by burning and so forth immediately thereafter, the similarity to erroneous cognition, the dullness of the intellect, and—by the word "etcetera"—lack of respect, lack of practice, and so on. In the cognition of the result, however, no cause of error exists; therefore, its ascertainment occurs through itself alone (*svataḥ*).

Showing that even in the first cognition, where the cause of error has been dispelled by means of repeated practice and so forth, its validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), he says: "In the occurrence," and so on.

But when there is practice in the conduct [of meditation], a distinction is perceived from a cognition that does not have that as its object, even though the fruit of that [conduct] has not yet been attained in the first instance. (2969)

Just as for yogins, or for those who know [the nature of] gems, silver, and so forth, through the power of practice a cognition arises that is vividly manifest and has entirely eliminated the causes of error; likewise, in other cases as well, a cognition arising through the power of practice—being more vividly manifest and free from the suspicion of delusion—produces a subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśapratyaya*) that, by its uninterrupted determination of a commonality with its own class, is ascertained as excluded from what is heterogeneous and not its object. Thus, its validity is said to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*).

As for the one who thinks—that even when an activity has been repeated, the ascertainment of validity, characterized by the capacity to reach the object, occurs through inference alone because of the observation of a mark (liṅga) characterized by conformity [to the object], and thus the determination of validity is always extrinsic (*parataḥ*) and never intrinsic (*svataḥ*)—we do not understand that.
For it must be explained: from what does the ascertainment of the mark, characterized by unconfused conformity, itself arise?

If it is argued that this is due to repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), then in that case, if—by the power of practice—a non-confused similarity (*sārūpya*) common to members of the same class is determined through the exclusion of dissimilar forms because there is no cause for error, what is this aversion to its validity such that it would be claimed that even when experienced, it is not determined in the absence of a cause for error? Furthermore, what is this so-called "similarity"? If it is the nature of cognition (*bodharūpatā*), then since that exists even in false knowledge, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, if it is the appearance as having a red form that is [the probans], then since that exists in a cognition apprehending a cluster of *aśoka* flowers and the like, there is indeed a fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
Alternatively, if it is being an effect of an object such as fire, one must explain how that is ascertained;
for one who pursues another mark to establish that, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Now, it might be argued that by the power of habituation alone, that [cognition] is established through perception itself, even without following a logical mark (*liṅga*).

If that is so, then if such a capacity of habituation is admitted, why is it not also admitted that the ascertainment of [the object's] capacity occurs by the power of habituation alone, even without following a logical mark? Furthermore, if the fact that cognition is an effect of that [object] is established, then the pursuit of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is useless; for from the very determination that it is an effect of that, the capacity to bring about that object is established, just as in the case of inferential cognition.

Just as inferential knowledge possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) because it arises through the power of perceiving a mark (*liṅga*) that is connected to a real entity, and because it is determined to be indirectly the effect of that entity—and not by virtue of similarity (*sārūpya*), for otherwise there would be an infinite regress—so too here [in the case of perception] validity must be intrinsic. To explain: where the cognition of the probandum does not arise even when the presence of the reason in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is certain, the cognizer should then seek the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the instance (*dṛṣṭānta-dharmin*), as in the case of "being produced" and "impermanence."

In this case, however, since the capacity of cognition to lead to the attainment of its object is established precisely through the determination of that effect—namely, the ascertainment [of the object] by virtue of its non-deviation from that object—its "conformity" (tādrūpya) is not the inferential mark (liṅga).

If this is so, how is it that the Teacher, concerning the Lokāyata, said: "He indeed asserts that perception alone is a means of valid cognition, not inference"? [The answer is: Having observed the correspondence and non-correspondence of certain individuals in their activity, he would state its definition through pervasion (*vyāpti*) for the sake of ensuring that one who acts according to the instruction is not deceived. That is to say, what is established as such by way of similarity to what has been seen does not exceed the status of being inferable;
thus, there is no fault.
This was stated with reference to cognitions occurring in one's own or another's continuum that have objects not previously experienced.

Because of the statement, "except for those [cognitions] whose objects have been previously experienced," for otherwise, if validity were determined everywhere solely on the basis of similarity (*sārūpya*), then the prohibition "except for those whose objects have been previously experienced" would be purposeless.
Therefore, it is established that a cognition which arises when the causes of error have been dispelled by the force of repetition (*abhyāsa*) is valid intrinsically (*svataḥ*).
Regarding what was stated— that "just as the first cognition requires corroboration," and so forth— he replies with the verse beginning "vailakṣaṇya" (due to the non-perception of difference):
"But when there is no perception of difference, [the mind] is apprehensive of an object of a different class."
Without a cognition that manifests the object to be accomplished, there can be no ascertainment of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
Even though the status of being a pramāṇa exists in that [cognition], it cannot be ascertained;
it is cognized solely through a subsequent cognition of the first action. || 2970–2971 ||
Therefore, the first cognition depends upon its corroboration; yet, in that same manner, a further corroboration need not be sought through another corroboration.

For when validity, though experienced, cannot be ascertained due to the presence of causes for error, it is then determined by a subsequent cognition of successful purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*). Since a person’s desired objective is accomplished by that alone, their expectation is satisfied, and thus no further corroboration need be sought through another corroboration, just as was required in the case of the initial cognition.
Regarding the objection beginning with "If it is claimed for someone," he says: "Because of the absence of a cause of error," and so forth.
Since there is no cause of error, the first [cognition] possesses intrinsic validity; whereas hostility toward the second [cognition] arises because of the possibility of error in its absence. (2973)

But surely, a cognition whose capacity to reach a determined object is uncertain because its object is doubted and inseparably connected [with it], would not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like inference.

For instance, when there is doubt regarding the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) with the object in the case of inference, its validity is not accepted; likewise, it would not obtain [validity] in the case of perception either.
This is not a fault.
For perception is not accepted as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) because it reveals its object as being inseparable from itself like inference;
rather,
it is so accepted because it effects the determination of the object as it appears.
For instance—that which brings about the desired object for one seeking purposeful action (arthakriyā) is called a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

It does not become "that which causes attainment" by either moving the person to the location of the object, or by bringing the object to the location of the person; rather, it impels the person, and it does not impel that person by grasping them with its hand.
What then? It indicates the object of activity; and that indication is nothing other than the determination of the object as it appears.

Wherever there is doubt, there must necessarily be a determination of the appearing form, because without such determination, that doubt would be impossible; and since the operation of perception is completed by this much, a subsequent doubt regarding the invariable concomitance with the object does not obstruct the operation of perception. Thus, even when doubt arises, the validity of the perception remains intact.

That which arises as overcome by a determination of a form contrary to the object appearing before it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). For example, the cognition that apprehends a mirage is overcome by a determination of water; in that case, there is an absence of the operation of the aforementioned valid means of knowledge.

Furthermore, the cognition of yellow in a conch-shell and the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel are likewise invalid, because in those instances there is an absence of both the appearance and the determination corresponding to the actual object.
For the apprehension or non-apprehension of perception occurs by virtue of its appearance (*pratibhāsa*), and not merely by virtue of its non-contradiction with the object.

Furthermore, in this case, there is no appearance of an object as it exists in its own nature, place, and time; nor does that [object] remain identical across different places and times, because place and time are themselves differentiators of the nature of things.
Otherwise, the conventional usage of distinction would be annihilated.

Since inference, being conceptual in nature, has the universal as its object, its status as having a real entity as its object is not established by virtue of the appearance [of that entity], because the real entity does not appear;
rather,
it is established by virtue of ascertainment.
As it has been said: "How can that form which is not determined by determinations be their object?

Consequently, since inference—even when devoid of a semblance [of its object]—arises through the power of seeing an inseparable thing (*anantarīyakārtha*), its validity is due to its indirect connection with the real entity; therefore, a determination of the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) must necessarily be required therein.
"Otherwise, because inference could not arise," [it is argued]; thus, perception is not equal to inference.
Now, with the words "nanu" and so forth, the opponent raises the objection of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) given that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥprāmāṇya*).
But surely, if the validity of that cognition is not ascertained, how could a discerning person proceed toward it, since the desired object has not been attained?

For instance, for one who acts with prior deliberation, there must first be an ascertainment of validity for there to be activity; yet, if activity occurs, there is an ascertainment of validity. Because of this mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*), how could there be activity for a discerning person when the desired object is not ascertained?
He replies with the words "It is said," and so forth:
"O wise ones, he proceeds precisely by means of doubt."

Nor does the loss of its discernment follow in this case. (2975) For activity is of two kinds: that aimed at purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) and that aimed at the ascertainment of validity. Regarding these, it has been demonstrated how the first kind of activity occurs even when there is doubt, because perception prompts action merely by the determination of the object as it appears. Therefore, the loss of discernment does not follow under such circumstances; the intention is that activity is observed even when there is doubt about the object, as in the case of farmers and others.

Furthermore, it is not reasonable to claim that farmers and others who act with a determination regarding their means possess "deliberate action" (prekṣāpūrvakāritā), because a means is dependent upon its end; and in the absence of certainty regarding the end, certainty regarding the means is impossible.

Showing that the second course of action is even more appropriate when there is doubt regarding validity, he says: "Because of acting through doubt," and so forth. Since activity proceeds from doubt, the means for ascertaining its validity is certain; therefore, it is a means of knowledge even when doubt exists. (And that... 2976.

Since that person has ascertained that activity itself is the means toward the determination of validity by way of doubt, and since there is thus no doubt regarding the means, activity is indeed appropriate.
To explain how that status as a means was ascertained by him, he says: "In activity despite doubt," and so forth.
If my engagement [in an action] proceeds through doubt, and the attainment of the result occurs, then the certainty regarding its validity will indeed be known at that time.
It cannot be otherwise; therefore, such an objection here is not logical.
"Why does one abide in the means? For there is no other way. (2978) "For no one attains the goal without the means";
thus, even one who acts out of doubt does not forfeit their status as a discerning person. (2979)
"Even one acting out of doubt" means even one who has proceeded with doubt regarding validity;
the remainder is not analyzed because it is easily understood.

With the words "But surely... and so forth, the opponent demonstrates the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of the determination of validity based on the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), thereby supporting the very point of infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
"But surely, even in a dream, there exists a cognition that appears as purposeful action, yet it possesses no validity; nor does its cause—the first [cognition]—possess it. (2980)

The connection is as follows: "Because of that first [cognition]" means because it is the cause of the cognition of causal efficiency (*arthakriyājñāna*), it does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). (2980)
He refutes this with the words beginning "not so," and so forth: "It is not so;
for that state is indeed an illusion, as it is entirely devoid of external basis.
In those states, there exists no correspondence with an external object. (2981)
Furthermore, since [these states] have the nature of being self-cognized and are not distinct from mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*),
the distinction between the two states is clearly perceived by that [self-cognition].

(2982) If this objection is raised against a Buddhist who maintains the existence of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*), then it is shown by the first verse that [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For instance, that proponent of external objects (bāhyārthavādin) accepts validity based on correspondence with the object, not on correspondence with the cognition of purposeful action (arthakriyā). Furthermore, there is no correspondence with the object in dreams, because the entire dream state is illusory and thus all [cognitions therein] are non-discrepant [with their own nature]. Since all cognitions arise even without an external object, they are devoid of an objective referent (nirviṣaya). Therefore, the point is that since the definition of validity applies only to a cognition occurring in the waking state, it is not logical to claim a deviation (vyabhicāra) by means of this [dream-cognition].

Furthermore—cognitive awareness of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) in a dream is non-occurrence-based (*apravṛttaka*), unstable, and confused, whereas it is the opposite in the waking state; thus, if such [waking] cognition possesses validity, how can there be an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) based on dreams?
Now, if this is urged against the Yogācāra, even then it is irrelevant to the present topic;
for this definition of valid cognition belongs to the conventional level: "Valid cognition is non-discrepant knowledge."

In this context, non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*) is precisely the self-awareness of a cognition that manifests as purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), because when such [cognition] appears, people engage in worldly activity accordingly, and because the engagement with objects has that [cognition] as its purpose. Furthermore, that conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*) cognition occurs only in the waking state.
In that very world, because all conventional transactions are clung to as being ultimately real—
and not so in the state of dreaming— there is no deviation [of the reason] by the other [dream-cognition], since the qualification "while being a waking cognition" is not heard [in the argument].
It might be thought that there is a determination of its validity by means of something else.

"It follows that it would be an object of cognition (*prameyatva*); is this not indeed non-contradictory? (2983) This might be the objection: "If everything appears in its entirety [as being known] through another [cognition], how is this distinction determined? In that case, because it is being measured by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it would follow that it is an object of cognition (*prameya*). And it is not logical for a means of valid cognition itself to be an object of cognition, due to contradiction. The response to this is: "Is this not indeed non-contradictory? (nanvavirodhyadaḥ). This is the rebuttal.
The statement "it exists" is not contradictory, as it depends on different perspectives, just like the designations of cause and effect or father and son.
2983 He demonstrates this very point: "tadgrāhya" and so forth;
for its validity is proclaimed as being dependent upon the object to be grasped by it.
The establishment of its status as an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) occurs through its being understood by another [cognition].

And thus, due to a difference in perspective, the determination of the states of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) and being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*)—just like the relationship between cause and effect—is not contradictory. (2984–2985)

With respect to that object which is apprehended by that cognition, it is indeed the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and not the object of cognition (*prameya*); however, with respect to another establishing means of valid cognition, it is indeed the object of cognition and not the means of valid cognition. Thus, there is no fault of confusion, just as the terms "effect" and "cause" do not become confused due to the difference in their mutual dependence.
He concludes with the words beginning "evam" (thus):
"In this way, when the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is ascertained through the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*)."
"There is no infinite regress because further expectation has ceased"—this is established.

Regarding the phrase "because further expectation has ceased": the analysis of the compound is that it consists of "further" (*parā*) and "expectation" (*ākāṅkṣā*), meaning an expectation that is other [than the initial one].

Alternatively, *parākāṅkṣā* (extrinsic expectation) refers to the expectation directed toward something other than the [immediate] correspondence (*saṃvāda*). The compound is to be analyzed as "due to the cessation of that [expectation].

Furthermore, by the statement "valid cognition is non-contradictory knowledge," this definition is stated for that knowledge which is the cause for attaining a result characterized by the realization of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

Consequently, since the definition does not apply to the knowledge of the result itself, how could there be any room for the objection: "How is the validity of that [result-knowledge] determined?"—for such an objection would have no basis.
For instance, when it is defined that the seed is the cause of the sprout, how could a question arise among the wise as to how the sprout itself possesses the nature of a seed?

And just as the status of being a seed is understood from the observation of the sprout, so too the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is understood from the observation of its fruit, which is characterized by purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).
Furthermore, the fruit in that case is not apprehended by another means of valid cognition, for if it were, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would result.
Since the fruit, which is of the nature of knowledge, is established by its own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*),
and since error regarding the very nature of knowledge is impossible—
because if that were not ascertained, it would follow that self-awareness itself does not exist— this [objection] is trivial.

Now, having raised the prima facie objection regarding the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) in the determination of validity by means of the purity of the cause—starting with the verse beginning "Even when [the cognition] has arisen"—he refutes it with the verse beginning "In this case too. Even when a cognition has arisen, it is not yet definitively ascertained.

"As long as the purity of the cause has not been established by another means of valid cognition, even here the wise say there is no infinite regress; for that purity is recognized through a corroborating cognition that requires no further dependence. (2987–2988)
For when an object is proximate, the purity of the causes is understood without effort through the observation of the correspondence with the result; however,
when the object is remote, the cognition arising from those [causes] is valid knowledge (*pramā*).
Because it is produced by that [cause], this [cognition] has a proximate object as its domain, just as follows:
knowledge is indeed twofold—having a proximate object and having a remote object.
Among these, regarding that which has a proximate object, the determination of its validity does not arise from the ascertainment of the excellence of its causes.
What then?
[The certainty of validity arises] from a cognition that accords with purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

For in that case, it is not possible to ascertain the excellence of the causes as long as correctness is not determined through accord with purposeful action; therefore, once correctness is established, the subsequent ascertainment of the excellence of the causes is entirely irrelevant.

Furthermore, demonstrating that for knowledge whose object is remote, the ascertainment of its validity arises from the ascertainment of the excellence of its causes, he says: "In the case of the remote," and so forth.

For that knowledge which apprehends a golden conch and has a remote object, because it is produced by those [causes]—that is, because it is produced by pure causes—the ascertainment of its validity occurs just like the knowledge that apprehends a white conch with a proximate object.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is produced by pure causes is valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), just like the cognition apprehending a white conch-shell with respect to a proximate object; and this cognition appearing as a yellow-shaped conch-shell with respect to a remote object is produced by pure causes. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
But is not the reason unestablished?

For instance— the purity of the causes cannot be ascertained without correspondence with the object, because the sense organs are beyond the reach of the senses; and if there is dependence on correspondence with the object, then validity itself is already determined, making the ascertainment of the excellence of the causes entirely useless,
since that [ascertainment] occurs only after the determination of validity.

Now, it might be argued that at one time, having ascertained the possession of excellence through the correspondence with purposeful action (*arthakriyā-saṃvāda*) from a cognition whose object is proximate, one may later ascertain the possession of excellence—even for a cognition whose object is remote—without any further correspondence, because it has been ascertained at another time; therefore, the ascertainment of validity will occur.
This is incorrect, for it is not possible for entities that perish moment by moment to have an activity that is of a single, identical nature.

Anticipating all these objections—that because of the application of various successive conditions, there is a difference in capacity at every moment—he says: "By the attainment of the action to be accomplished as white," and so forth.

By the attainment of the action to be accomplished as white, just as when a conch shell is present before one, it is understood that the cognition arising from eyes affected by jaundice is not [perceiving the true color]. (2991)

Thus, when the purity of the cause has been established, that very cognition which arises at that moment regarding the yellow form in a conch made of gold attains the certainty of its validity (*prāmāṇya*) due to its production from a pure cause.
"Like the cognition of the white form in a conch-shell whose function has already been accomplished.

(2993) By this he means the following: We do not determine the validity of a cognition that occurs at a later time and concerns a remote object by means of the purity of its causes, such that the reason [in our argument] would be unestablished (*asiddha*), because distinct potencies arise through the application of various successive conditions at every moment.
What then? [The validity is determined] otherwise.

Precisely when the purity of the cause of a cognition apprehending a nearby object—such as that which grasps a white conch—is ascertained through the attainment of the purposeful action (arthakriyā) to be accomplished by its whiteness, at that very moment, the validity of the cognition of a golden conch situated in a distant place, which arises in the form of yellow, is determined on account of the complete purity of its causes;
for it is not possible for there to be a change in the causes in that same state, lest there be a discrepancy regarding the purposeful action of the cognition whose object is the nearby thing. (2991)
Showing that this is indeed accepted by you, the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsakas, he says: "Because of the non-affliction by hunger and so forth," and so on.
Because the author of the Bhāṣya has stated that there is no affliction by hunger and so forth, this [charge of] infinite regress is raised here out of delusion;
by this, the contradiction of the thesis with one's own words is also demonstrated.

For it has been stated by the author of the Bhāṣya: "When the mind or the sense organ is afflicted by hunger and the like, or when the external object is [afflicted] by subtlety and so forth, then there is false cognition (*mithyājñāna*); when they are unafflicted, there is right cognition (*samyagjñāna*). For the contact between the sense organ, the mind, and the object is the cause of cognition. In its absence, there is non-cognition; therefore, a defect residing therein is the cause of false cognition. Indeed, when [the causes] are defective, cognition becomes false, because we observe correct apprehension upon the removal of the defects."

If it is asked, "How is it that the absence of defects is understood? [the answer is: "If, while investigating with effort, we were to perceive a defect, then—due to the absence of any means of knowledge [to the contrary]—we would consider it to be free of defects.
By this passage, the author of the Bhāṣya has clearly stated that the ascertainment of validity arises from the knowledge of the purity of the causes;
otherwise, what would be shown by the phrase "while investigating with effort"?
And consequently, there is a contradiction of the thesis that validity is intrinsic (svataḥ-prāmāṇya).
As it was said: "By what [means] are the cognition of correspondence and the cognition of excellence considered superior? (2994)

Regarding that, what was previously stated concerned correspondence; now, concerning the knowledge of excellence (*guṇajñāna*), he says: "The validity of the first [cognition] is not apprehended due to the suspicion that it is produced by a defective cause; therefore, the knowledge of its purity is considered an additional factor. (2995)
"Validity belongs to the first" means that the status of being a valid means of knowledge pertains to the initial [cognition].
Regarding the knowledge of the meaning,
that [knowledge] is "first" because it arises prior to the knowledge of the purity of its causes.
Therefore,
with the words "Thus" (evam) and so forth [in verse 2995], he demonstrates that such activity is not faulty.
And thus, when the purity of the cause is ascertained through the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*),
it is logical that the [cognition] which does not perform purposeful action is not denotable [by the term "valid"].
(2996) "That which has not performed purposeful action" means...
That by which purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) has not been accomplished is so described;
"inexpressible" (*avācyā*) means that which is not to be spoken of, meaning it is beyond reproach.
He considers that this [determination of validity] is preceded by the ascertainment of validity (prāmāṇyaniścaya).

Therefore, regarding the statement beginning with "Thus, self-validity (svataḥpramāṇatva) is established as the general rule (autsargika) everywhere," he says: "If [validity were] from itself," and so forth.
If intrinsic validity is established as the general rule in all cases, it is set aside by the two [conditions]: the knowledge of a sublater and the knowledge of a defect in the cause.
In the absence of the knowledge of a sublater and the knowledge of a defect in the cause, there is validity.
And thus, for you, the ascertainment of its validity would have to be obtained from another [source].
For this non-existence is, in your view, a separate means of cognition called "non-apprehension" (abhāva), whereas in my view, it is an inference known as "non-perception" (anupalambha).
In this context, the first verse restates the opponent's position, while the second and subsequent verses provide the refutation:
for if validity were set aside by a sublating cognition or the like, then it would follow that the ascertainment of validity is admitted to occur due to the absence of such a sublating cognition;
consequently, validity would be declared to be extrinsic (*parataḥ*).
Since non-existence is also accepted as a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [one might object];
however, in our position, because it is subsumed within inference under the name "non-apprehension" (*anupalabdhi*), it is not a separate means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, since the general rule (*utsarga*) and the exception (*apavāda*) are not established as having words and their referents as their objects when conceived [conceptually], they have no authority whatsoever in the investigation of reality (*vastu*). This is because all things are established in their own respective intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*), and thus there is no conformity with any other intrinsic nature. Consequently, your mere presentation of these [rules] only reveals your ignorance regarding the proper scope of general rules and exceptions.

For instance, he shows that by the very same reasoning you have described, the opposite view—that there is both a general rule and an exception—can also be postulated: "By this very [reasoning]," and so forth.
By this very reasoning, even non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇya*) might be intrinsic (*svataḥ*);
for in that case as well, it can be argued that such is the underlying logic (*nyāya*). (3000)

Therefore, it is established that the non-validity of all [cognitions] is the general rule (*autsargika*), and it is set aside only by the absence of knowledge regarding sublation or the defectiveness of the cause. 3001.
Furthermore, as Kumārila stated: "Therefore, the validity of cognition is obtained by virtue of its nature as consciousness (*bodhātmakatva*)."

"It is set aside by the cognition of a defect arising from a cause that produces a change in the object's nature"— showing that it can indeed be stated even along this line of reasoning, he says: "In the same way,
by virtue of its being of the nature of consciousness, the non-validity of cognition is established," and so forth.

It is set aside by the knowledge of qualities arising from the cause of knowledge of the object as it truly is. (3002) If invalidity were dependent on something else, there would certainly be an infinite regress;
for this [invalidity] depends upon a means of valid cognition, yet that [means of valid cognition] is not established intrinsically. (3003)
The term *apramāṇatā* involves the elision (*praśleṣa*) of the vowel *a*;

and "knowledge according to the object" (*yathārthajñāna*) refers to knowledge that accords with the object and knowledge of the qualities arising from the cause (*hetūtthaguṇajñāna*), which is to say, knowledge of the qualities produced by the causal factors—this is a collective copulative compound (*samāhāradvandva*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "even though that [validity] is dependent on another," he says: "In invalidity," and so forth.
For this [is] non-authoritativeness,
and that [is] it.
The measure is 3002–3003.
To the question "How is it non-abiding?", he says: "For instance," and so forth.
For instance, you assert that validity arises from the absence of sublation;
yet the absence of sublation itself is accepted as another means of valid cognition known as "non-apprehension" (abhāva-pramāṇa). || 3004 ||
Since there is likewise an absence of sublation for that [cognition], its validity is asserted;
however, in such a case, no fixed rule regarding desire is found.
Regarding what was stated—"a sublating cognition," etc.—he says: "the state of being an independent means of valid cognition," etc.

Since the status of being an independent means of valid cognition (*anapekṣapramāṇatva*) is not established for a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*), it does not at all negate the preceding cognition. This is because its status as an independent means of valid cognition is unestablished, owing to its dependence upon the means of valid cognition known as non-existence (*abhāva*).
Now, with the words "athāpi" and so forth,
he further establishes the very point of infinite regress.
Moreover, if validity is accepted in some cases even without the absence of a sublater (*bādhaka*), then what is the reason for such hostility toward the same state in the first [cognition]?

(3007) If, out of fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), validity is accepted in some cases even without the absence of a sublater, then in that case, the absence of a sublater need not be required even for the first cognition.
And consequently, it would follow that all cognitions are valid.
As it was said: "In that case as well, there might be a dependence upon an exception," and so forth.
Regarding this, he says: "And this subverting cognition," and so forth.
This subverting cognition sets aside the prior knowledge because it possesses independent authority; if there were a doubt here, what could it be? (3008)

Furthermore, the possibility of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) that renders [the cognition] independent of other means of valid cognition (*anapekṣyapramāṇatva*) is suspected here; yet such a suspicion regarding a contradiction does not arise in the case of what is already ascertained. (3009) If the subverting cognition is one whose status as a valid means of knowledge is independent, then how could there be a suspicion of an exception (*apavāda*) with respect to it—such that it is said, "In that case too, there would be a dependence on an exception"? Consequently, this statement is mutually contradictory: that its status as a valid means of knowledge is independent, and yet a subverting factor is suspected therein.

For it is said that "independent" refers to that which is made the object of a certainty (*niścaya*); and where there is certainty, doubt (*āśaṅkā*) is impossible, because there exists a relationship of sublation between certainty and superimposition (*āropa*), and because doubt proceeds in the form of a superimposition by relying upon both parts [of a dichotomy].
Regarding the passage beginning with "then, by appropriate effort," he says: "In the view that validity is intrinsic" and so forth.

Even in the view that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), since [validity] is ascertained by its own inherent force (*svarasena*), why is effort exerted to establish the existence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*)? 3010
For instance, that in which no certainty of validity arises by its own force— even if it is ascertained here without effort— therein a sublater exists by implication.
Therefore, why is it said here that there are three cognitions for the investigator?
In that case, there is certainly no room for even a single [instance of error] by its own nature.
(3012) Furthermore, if doubt were to arise even when there is non-perception because of uncertainty, then non-perception would not be invariably concomitant with the absence of sublation. (3013)
This being the case, why have you been satisfied with these three?
For even when [the object] is not perceived, sublation might be suspected here just as before;
indeed, [doubt] does not cease until there is a correspondence with the result.
Since there is a suspicion of sublation regarding that [object], a restriction upon those three [means of knowledge] is fruitless.
Consequently, even when no sublation has yet arisen, one must again suspect a sublater; for the true nature of a thing never remains established through mere sophistry.

Knowledge that arises throughout one's entire life, which is free from any cause of sublation, yet appears as yellow in a white conch shell, does not constitute a valid means of cognition (pramāṇa). || 3017 ||

If the ascertainment of validity were intrinsic (*svataḥ*), then because validity would be pervaded by ascertainment, wherever there is a lack of ascertainment, invalidity would necessarily abide there; thus, the presence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) would be ascertained even without effort. Consequently, any effort for the sake of establishing its absence would be futile. Furthermore, in that case, there would not be even the possibility of requiring a single cognition of an investigator, let alone three; therefore, this which was stated is also inconsistent. He shows that these three cognitions of an investigator do not exceed [the required number] with the words beginning "Therefore," and so forth.

It might be argued: "The absence of a subverting factor cannot be ascertained by mere non-perception alone; for even if something exists, it may not be perceived due to being distant, subtle, or obstructed, and thus non-perception is not invariably concomitant with the absence of a subverting factor. Therefore, an effort must be made to establish the absence of a subverting factor."

If this is so, you must abandon the restriction of three cognitions for an investigator; for, just as in the case of the first cognition, a sublater may be suspected in other cases as well. Until the cognition of the result arises, by what means could the suspicion of sublation be removed, such that there would be a restriction to three? Indeed, for discerning people, the removal of suspicion is not appropriate through mere verbal assertion without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For the investigation of the means of valid cognition is based on the actual state of things; this is not a matter of sophistry (*chala*) being undertaken here, whereby one would examine merely a few instances of cognition.

If validity were established merely by the occurrence of the threefold cognition regarding an object, then alas, the cognition of those whose eyes are afflicted by jaundice throughout their lives— whose cognition arises only in the form of a yellow conch— would also be valid.

One might object: "If that [cognition] were invalid, why does no sublater arise after the examination of the three types of knowledge? Since it does not arise, one concludes that it does not exist. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Due to the absence of a cause for purification, a sublater would not arise; or due to some other cause, [it does not arise]; therefore, the doubt is not removed. (3018)
The cause of purification is the sprinkling of the juice of *droṇa* flowers and so forth;
due to the absence of that, or due to some other cause, the obstacle does not arise.

Just as for a person who has developed the illusion of water in a mass of mirages in a desert, the cognition appearing as a desert region devoid of the nature of water does not arise because he does not approach it;
thus, regarding the passage beginning with "for one might imagine" (utprekṣeta hi), he says: "it is indeed with a cause," and so forth.

Therefore, this suspicion exists only where there is a perception of purity through delusion; however, for the wise person, no suspicion would arise when seeing the correspondence [of cognition] with reality.
Such a person does not become one whose nature is doubt regarding all conventional transactions.
For his intellect is indeed free from doubt when he perceives purity and correspondence.
As for that dull-witted person who nevertheless entertains suspicion even here, I consider him to be censurable on account of his very nature of doubt.
It has been established that doubt is removed by both the purity of the cause and corroborative knowledge;
as for what was further stated, beginning with "And likewise by Vāsudeva," that merely reveals one's own reliance on partisan declarations of devotion (*bhaktivāda*), not the actual state of affairs.
For the determination of another’s nature cannot be known from mere words devoid of reasoning by a discerning person whose mind is alert.
To show that the statement of Vāsudeva is not contradictory because it is established by another related [text], he says "atrāpi" and so forth.

Here—in the demonstration of the correspondence with purity—regarding one such as you who raises a doubt, thinking that "even through a correspondence, a further correspondence must be sought in the same way," it is considered that the state of having a doubting mind was censured by the Unborn One, Viṣṇu.
Regarding the objection that might be raised concerning the passage beginning with "where [it] is conceived in the mind" (yatra sambhāvyate matāv), he says "place," and so forth.
When the determination of validity is conceived as being dependent on differences in place, time, and circumstances, then the ascertainment of validity from another source becomes manifest.
For instance, in the case of place, time, and so forth, [the absence of sublation] is well-ascertained.
"The determination of validity in prior cognitions occurs through another means of valid cognition" (3023).
By this, he demonstrates a contradiction with his own words;
for, if the determination of validity is conceived as depending on place, time, person, and circumstance, it is clearly stated that it is "extrinsic" (*parataḥ*).

Since the absence of sublation by other means of valid cognition regarding place, time, and so forth has been ascertained, how could the acceptance of the determination of validity in the first—the initial—cognition not be considered "extrinsic" (parataḥ)?

For the absence of sublation must necessarily be ascertained through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: if intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) were admitted, it would follow that all cognitions are valid; therefore, you must certainly state that intrinsic validity belongs only to that [cognition] where there is no sublation, and not to any other. Furthermore, that absence of sublation cannot be ascertained by mere non-perception (*anupalambha-mātra*), because of the possibility of error; rather, it must be ascertained through non-perception characterized by the impossibility of perception (*sāmarthya-anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta-anupalambha*), since only such non-perception is invariably concomitant (*vyāpta*) with the absence of sublation.

And since this non-apprehension of that which has reached the conditions for apprehensibility is not logically distinct from a corroborating cognition, it would follow that the determination of validity must be accepted as arising from a separate means of valid cognition (pramāṇāntara).

Regarding the phrase "debt and so forth" (ṛṇādīti) and so on, he says: "But that legal proceeding concerning debt and so forth which is capable of being expressed in three statements—that very kind of case, consisting of such a situation, is not to be cited as an example when establishing valid cognition. (3024)
In that case, the plaintiff and the defendant, though repeatedly recalling [the matter], do not obtain a clear perception of that object through subtle investigation.
Indeed, a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be established according to the actual state of things, and not through mere quibbling (chala). || 3025 ||
Therefore, this conventional usage [of debt and so forth] has been cited as being dissimilar to the subject at hand.

While the topic under discussion is the establishment of valid cognition— which is tied to the intrinsic nature of things— the citation of a deceptive form of usage such as debt and so forth, which is tied merely to conventions fashioned by mere whim, only reveals your ignorance of the subject matter.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The threefold truth of the gods," etc., he says: "The threefold truth," and so forth.

Even the threefold truth of the gods is not a cause for certain conviction; for if that [truth] were established as real by means of an initial [perception], it would not be established by subsequent [perceptions] either.
(3027) Regarding the phrase "by means of an initial":

If certainty does not arise from the first statement, then that certainty would certainly not arise from the two subsequent statements occurring at a later time, because there is no difference [between them].
He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "tadīyam" (his own), and so forth.
Since these two subsequent statements belong to that very same [opponent],
what distinction is there between them and the others in the absence of a valid means of cognition (*pratyaya*)?
(3028) "The subsequent" refers to the following.
In the absence of certainty regarding the non-existence of conditions that would arise at a later time.
The phrase "of the other two" means of those two that occur at a later time.

For if one were to speak falsely regarding one statement and a second, why would he not speak falsely regarding a third as well? Who then would be able to restrain him at that point, such that conviction could arise from the third?
Regarding the passage beginning with "Therefore, [if] intrinsic validity," he says "therefore" and so forth:
"Therefore, by the reasoning previously stated, there is an infinite regress even in your own position."
Therefore, validity and invalidity are established according to their respective applications.

The previously mentioned reasoning is as follows: namely, that you assert something to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because of the absence of sublation (*bādhaka*), yet this very absence of sublation is itself accepted as another distinct means of knowledge called "non-apprehension" (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), and so forth.
Regarding the passage beginning with "eternal and composed by a reliable authority," he says: "The sentence," and so forth; the eternality of the sentence has already been refuted by us in detail.
Furthermore, according to your tradition, there is no one who has completely exhausted all defects.
How, then, can one whose veil of ignorance is not yet exhausted be considered authoritative?
For it is possible that his speech might otherwise [be false] due to the presence of defects.

Previously, in the *Śrutiparīkṣā*, the notion of an eternal sentence was refuted in detail; therefore, since [the existence of such a sentence] is unestablished, how could there be any occasion for considering its intrinsic validity? Furthermore, since an "authoritative person" (*āpta*) is not admitted by [the opponent] himself, even a sentence composed by him remains unestablished. To explain: only one whose defects such as passion (*rāga*), which are the causes of falsehood, have been abandoned without remainder can properly be called an authoritative person. Otherwise, how could the status of being authoritative be established for one whose mind is overwhelmed by defects such as passion, which are the causes of falsehood?

Furthermore, you do not accept any person who has abandoned the entire web of afflictions, such that the word of an authoritative person (*āpta*) could serve as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for you.

Furthermore, even granting that there might be such a person as an authoritative one (āpta), he shows that his word remains nonetheless unestablished: "Even if [an authority] were born," and so forth.
Even if an authority were born, by whom could that multitude of his qualities be known, such that there might be a certain determination regarding a statement composed by an authority? (3032)
Even for one who perceives with a vision that transcends the senses and thus beholds the perfection of his qualities, what need would there be for the word of a trustworthy person?
For such a person, being independent of verbal testimony, realizes the object by himself.

Another person also does not understand the meaning from that [speech] due to a lack of recognition of the authoritative person (āpta). For it is not possible to determine, "This is the speech of such-and-such a person," without first identifying the authoritative person; nor is the identification of an authoritative person possible. To explain: even if one who has exhausted all defects without exception and perceives supersensuous objects identifies the speaker as authoritative, nevertheless, that person's speech is of no consequence at all. Since he himself perceives all objects directly, he does not act on the basis of their speech; therefore, for him, identifying them as authoritative is useless.

Furthermore, any other person of limited vision is not capable of ascertaining [the truth] with certainty; thus, they do not understand the meaning from that statement by themselves, because it remains uncertain.
Regarding the passage beginning with "those who are teachers of knowledge," he says: "In the doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*), because certainty arises intrinsically..."
Since destruction is impossible [for that which is self-established], for what purpose would there be a prevention?
[This follows] from the nature of certainty—that is, from the arising of certainty.
Otherwise, if certainty were not produced intrinsically (*svataḥ*), then the doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) would be abandoned.
Therefore, regarding the passage beginning with "or by those [faults] excluded by excellences," he says: "Indeed,
the statement is not at all corrupted by faults that have been set aside by excellences."
However, because the qualities [of the speaker] are not ascertained, it is impossible to determine that [the statement is authoritative].

Even if a statement possessing qualities is not corrupted by defects—since defects have been eliminated by the qualities—nevertheless, because the qualities residing in another's continuum are beyond the reach of the senses, it is impossible to ascertain that the statement possesses qualities when those qualities remain unascertained; nor can that which is unascertained be intrinsically valid (*svataḥpramāṇa*).
Alternatively, regarding the claim that defects would not exist due to the absence of an author, he says: "The sentence," and so forth.
The lack of an author for the sentence has already been refuted;
therefore, in the absence of an author, those defects cannot exist, as they would be without a locus. (3037)
"Much more so," as stated in the *Śrutiparīkṣā* (Examination of Scripture),
verse 3037.
Regarding that, concerning the statement "two are seen" and so forth because of what was taught there, he says:
"And the status of being a means of valid cognition [arises] from the excellences; this has been stated as it is logically appropriate.
Furthermore, when the excellences are not fully understood, the absence of defects is not perceived. (3038)

"It is not logical that a statement is valid by itself as characterized by the absence of defects, because the absence of defects cannot be known; for indeed, the absence [of something] is not a defining characteristic.
Thus it has been stated.

Regarding what was stated there by the wise, beginning with "the sentence is intrinsically authoritative and characterized by the absence of defects," that too is incorrect; for since excellences (*guṇas*) are beyond the reach of the senses, when they are not cognized, it is impossible to characterize the absence of defects—which consists in the presence of excellences.
He states this very point: "For the absence of defects is not a defining characteristic."

That by which something is characterized is a "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*); that which is not a characteristic is a "non-characteristic" (*alakṣaṇa*), meaning it does not serve as a secondary indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*).
The intended sense is that this is because [it] is not fully understood.
He shows that a characteristic cannot exist without being fully known: "For not," and so forth;
for indeed, when a staff is not fully known, people do not perceive [someone] as "staff-bearer."

The claim that "valid cognition is characterized by itself" is thus refuted. Since the absence of defects is established as having a determined nature through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) due to the absence of invalid cognition (apramā), it is logical that this is the definition of a statement; therefore, the establishment of validity is extrinsic (parataḥ).

Furthermore, even if the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*) were indeed the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), it would nonetheless still be a defect, because it entails a contradiction with one's own statement. For instance, if validity (*prāmāṇya*) is indicated by the absence of defects, then validity would clearly be extrinsic (*parataḥ*); consequently, the statement that "validity is intrinsic" (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) would be contradicted.

He clarifies this very point: if the absence of defects were ascertained by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) called "non-existence" (abhāva), then that [absence] could serve as a defining characteristic (lakṣaṇa); for it is impossible for what is unascertained to function as a defining characteristic. Furthermore, there exists no other means of valid cognition capable of ascertaining non-existence. Consequently, it would be stated even more clearly that validity is extrinsic (parataḥ), arising from the [means of cognition] known as non-existence.
Regarding what was stated— that knowledge whose object is human defects does not arise when those [defects] are present— he says "nṛdoṣa" and so forth:
knowledge whose object is human defects does indeed arise even while they are present.

"But even if there is an absence of faults, how can there be cognition [of it] when there is no knowledge of the excellences? (3042) Even if, while excellences are present, no cognition directed toward faults arises—because those excellences residing in another's continuum are beyond the reach of the senses and thus remain unknown—it would still be impossible to ascertain the absence of faults, since the absence of faults is of the nature of the presence of excellences. For indeed, the absence of a jar cannot be known if the location devoid of the jar is not itself known.
He demonstrates this very point with the verse beginning "hatred," and so forth:
"Hatred, delusion, and other defects are sublated by compassion, wisdom, and the like;
for if there were no certainty regarding compassion and the rest, how could their non-existence be established? (3043)
"Of these" refers to those faults.
Regarding this, Kumārila has stated: "At that time, however, the excellences (guṇas) do not operate by way of being themselves known;
rather, when the absence of defects (doṣābhāva) is to be cognized, they are helpful merely by their existence. This [view] is raised as an objection with the words beginning "tadā" (at that time).
At that time, however, the excellences (guṇas) do not function by way of being cognized;
rather, when the absence of defects (doṣābhāva) is to be known, they are helpful merely by their existence.
(3044) "Helpful" means...
With the words "If it were thus," and so forth, he provides the rebuttal against those who claim to be benefactors regarding the ascertainment of the absence of defects.
If, in this way, there were no doubt or a perverted cognition regarding whether faults exist in one who is esteemed as authoritative or whether they do not exist— [thinking] "they certainly exist"—
then for someone here, both that doubt and that perversion would indeed occur. (3045)

As long as this person is not understood to be the substratum of a multitude of qualities, [the absence of defects cannot be established]. (3046) If qualities were to function toward the ascertainment of the absence of defects merely by their existence, then no one would ever experience doubt or error regarding the absence of defects in a person recognized as authoritative (*āpta*), because such [doubt and error] would have been sublated by that ascertainment. But this is not the case; therefore, as long as the ascertainment of the possession of qualities does not arise, doubt and error concerning the absence of defects certainly persist. Thus, qualities do not function [to establish the absence of defects] by their mere existence.
Even if there is an absence of defects, if validity is ascertained intrinsically through ignorance [of those defects],
nevertheless, doubt would not arise regarding that speaker, just as it did previously.

Now, it might be argued: "Let there be no operation of the excellences (*guṇa*) for the sake of ascertaining the absence of defects (*doṣābhāva*); nevertheless, the ascertainment of validity (*prāmāṇya*) will arise from the very absence of defects, even if that absence is not itself ascertained. This too is incorrect, because—as in the previous case—there would follow the consequence of a lack of disagreement regarding the speaker's being accepted as authoritative (*āptasammata*).

For when the validity of his statement is ascertained *inherently* (*svataḥ*), it is not reasonable to have such thoughts regarding that speaker as "Is he a speaker of truth or not? or "Is he not at all [an authority]? By the term "disagreement" (*vimati*), doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyāsa*) are intended here.
Since "doubt" (*vimati*) is defined as a cognition of a contrary form (*viparītākārā mati*), it is possible for doubt to possess a contrary form because it rests upon both sides [of a proposition].

Furthermore, this other point which was stated by Kumārila: "Therefore, due to the absence of defects (*doṣa*) resulting from the presence of excellences (*guṇa*), there is an absence of those [defects]; and from that absence [of defects], [there is the absence of error]."

"The non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition is established by that [absence of defects], and thus the general rule remains unrefuted," and so forth; he shows that even this is indeed untenable when there is no certainty regarding the absence of defects, stating:
"Because of the non-cognition of the absence of defects, there is no existence of the two types of invalid cognition."
How is it cognized by which there might be a determination of validity?

(3048) Now, if validity is understood as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*) even when the non-existence of the two types of invalidity is not cognized, then there would be no disagreement [regarding this] as there was before. (3049)
For if knowledge were established as being free from the two types of sublation—namely doubt and error—then it would be a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*);
otherwise, how could a general rule (*utsarga*) apply to an object that is already overtaken by sublation?
Furthermore, since doubt and error are caused by defects (*doṣa*), it is not logical to determine their absence unless there is a determination of the absence of those defects.
The non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition means the non-existence of doubt and error.
He shows that very doubt: "Is his word authoritative? and so forth—"Is his word authoritative, or is it non-authoritative, or else this [other thing]?"
"Non-measurement [of validity] alone [is required] for all, because validity is ascertained intrinsically.

(3050) Thus, it has been demonstrated that it is not logical for the absence of defects and so forth to function as factors for the ascertainment of validity by their mere existence; now, demonstrating in detail these two points—that if there were a requirement for ascertainment regarding them, validity would be extrinsic and an infinite regress would result—the author says: "In the case of the absence of defects," and so forth, referring to all three: the absence of defects, the absence of non-validity, and the presence of excellences.
Therefore, cognition must necessarily be admitted as a certainty.

For it has been established that in the absence of defects, in the absence of the two types of invalid cognition, and regarding the presence of excellences, cognition—specifically that which is called "certainty"—must necessarily be admitted; otherwise, the determination of validity would be impossible.
If it is indeed admitted [that there is a means of knowledge], then what follows? To this he says: "That," and so forth;
it is thus conceptualized as being either invalid or valid.
How could that which is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) be a factor for the determination of the object as it truly is?

(3052) This aforementioned cognition regarding all three [stages] is accepted as a factor for validity; however, there are two possibilities: is it non-valid (*apramāṇa*) or is it valid (*pramāṇa*)? If the first alternative holds, then it cannot be a factor for the determination of validity, because it is itself non-valid.
For a witness who is apprehended as being unreliable does not become a factor for certainty in a legal proceeding; thus,
if validity were established extrinsically, the ascertainment of that validity [would likewise depend on another].
Or how is it understood that this cognition possesses the nature of valid knowledge?
If you say, "Because there is an absence of a subverting cognition," then the same problem recurs here once again: is that [subverting cognition] itself valid or not? (3053–3054)
Now, if the second position is held, then there would follow the consequence that the validity of that intended cognition depends upon something else, leading to the fault of infinite regress;
and desiring to demonstrate that very infinite regress, he asks: "How indeed...
and so forth, [referring to] "that too."
The absence of a subverting cognition (bādhakapratyayābhāva).
To explain how this same fault persists here as well, he says: "If validity... and so forth.

If the validity of the subject at hand were established through something else (*parataḥ*), then how could that which is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*) be the cause of a cognition that accords with reality? (3055)

It must be considered by what means the validity of this [cognition] is also understood; otherwise, the undesirable consequence follows that it would be established merely because no subverting cognition exists. (3056) This is easily understood.
"Of this too" refers to the absence of a subverting cognition (bādhakapratyaya).

Furthermore— if, by the reasoning demonstrated in the passage beginning "Therefore, from the absence of defects [in the causes] there is validity," validity were determined in all cases, then validity would have to be accepted as extrinsic (*parataḥ*) even previously, and there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
He shows this with the words beginning "Therefore."

Therefore, from the [presence of] excellences (guṇa) follows the absence of defects (doṣa); from that absence follows the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition; by this, the general rule (utsarga) remains unrefuted.
If validity is thus ascertained in all cases, then it is so here as well.
The multitude of faults previously mentioned would follow, as well as the consequence of infinite regress (3058). Regarding the phrase "previously mentioned":

since qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth residing in another continuum are beyond the senses of one with limited vision, they cannot be ascertained; consequently, the absence of faults (*doṣābhāva*) is also unascertained, and thus the non-existence of the two [other] means of knowledge remains unascertained as well. Therefore, validity could not be established on the basis of qualities and the like. Furthermore, if those [qualities] were to assist by their mere existence, then there would be no disagreement [regarding the validity of cognition]; such is the multitude of faults that would apply in every case.

Furthermore—regarding that which was stated as a factor for certainty in the form of validity, namely, "the absence of defects due to the presence of excellences" (*guṇa*) and so forth, consisting of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition and the absence of defects: is this pair intended as a mere absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), or rather as having the nature of a relative negation (*paryudāsa*)? Such is the twofold conceptual possibility.
He states the fault in the first position: "If the absence of defects... and so forth.
If this negation—"the existence of valid cognition consists in the absence of defects"—were to be postulated in isolation, its establishment would not be possible at all. (3059)
Its establishment through the non-perception of its absence is not tenable,
nor is it logical on account of the fault of infinite regress;
for if one intends a mere non-presuppositional negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), then its establishment would be impossible.
For instance, its establishment must occur either through itself or through another;
if it occurs through itself, it would do so either by virtue of being self-luminous or by producing a certainty;
if it occurs through another, it would do so either through perception or through non-perception—these are the possible positions.
First of all, its establishment through self-luminosity is not tenable, because that [non-existence] is not a real entity, whereas self-luminosity is a property of real entities;
for it is knowledge alone that is established by self-awareness through its nature of self-luminosity,
but not non-existence, which is characterized merely as the negation of the intrinsic nature of a thing.
Nor is its establishment through itself achieved by producing a certainty,
because non-existence is characterized by the absence of all causal capacity, making it impossible for it to be a producer;
for if it were a producer, it would follow that it possesses the nature of a real entity (*vastu*).

Since it cannot admit any additional excellence (*atiśaya*), it is independent of auxiliary causes; and because the effect, which arises from that [nature] alone, would result in being incessant, its establishment through perception (*upalambha*) by another is not possible. Why? Because of its non-existence—that is, because its nature is non-being (*abhāva*), whereas perception has existence as its object.
Nor can it be established through non-perception (*anupalambha*), for that would lead to the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

For in that case, since non-apprehension itself consists in the absence [of apprehension], how could it be established? Regarding this as well, the inquiry as to whether it is established by itself or by another certainly applies;
it cannot be by itself, because that would entail the aforementioned fault, nor can it be by another, because of the fault of infinite regress.
He demonstrates that very infinite regress with the words: "The non-existence of both defects and invalidity," and so forth.

The non-existence of defects and the two types of invalid cognition is understood through non-apprehension; however, the non-existence of that apprehension would have to be known by another [means], leading to an infinite regress. (3061) The compound is analyzed as follows: "defects" (*doṣa*), "the two types of invalid cognition" (*apramādvaya*), and "the non-existence of those two" (*tayoḥ asattā*). Thus, it refers to the non-existence of both defects and the two forms of invalid cognition.
Regarding the second [type of negation], that which consists of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), he states the fault: "If that [negation] consists of exclusion," and so forth;
"if that [negation] consists of exclusion, because of the perception of something else distinct from it."
The non-cognition of the absence of defects would consist in the cognition of qualities; furthermore,

it would follow that its nature is the cognition of the intended valid cognition, as well as the cognition of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition and that which is distinct from them.
If the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition is known either through its own nature or by exclusion, from where does your certainty arise that the remaining one is valid cognition?
