If you say it is through "the impossibility otherwise" (anyathānupapatti), then surely it must be established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti).
Or rather, such certainty might arise from another source through inference.

For the absence of defects, by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), would essentially consist of the presence of excellences; consequently, the cognition of that [absence] would also result in being of the nature of a cognition of excellences, which is not desired, because of the statement: "And excellences do not function as something being cognized."

Even the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition (*apramāṇa*), according to the view of relative negation (*paryudāsa*), remains essentially of the nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, the knowledge of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition would also result in being of the very nature of the intended knowledge of valid cognition. Therefore, it is not tenable to say that "by that [knowledge], the presumption (*utsarga*) of validity is not sublated," because such a connection is difficult to maintain.

To explain: since that very [knowledge] is determined to be valid cognition, the statement that "its validity is determined" would involve a relationship of cause and effect (*hetu-hetumadbhāva*), which results in a poorly constructed sentence-meaning due to the lack of distinction between the two.

Furthermore, because there is a distinction between cause and effect, that which is distinct from them—the cognition of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition (apramāṇa) as distinct from the thorough knowledge of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa)—would follow [as the result].
Nor is it logical for that [result] to be distinct from [the cause] in the sense of being a mere exclusion (paryudāsa).

Having accepted the establishment of the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition through the statement beginning with "when the non-existence of the two types of invalid cognition is known," he demonstrates extrinsic validity (parataḥprāmāṇya) according to the opponent's own view, by means of the principle of "inexplicability otherwise" (anyathānupapatti).
Because there is no other possible alternative, the intrinsic validity of any cognition other than those characterized by doubt or error must be admitted.
Demonstrating that the reasoning stated in the passage beginning with "therefore, from the qualities" (tasmād guṇebhyaḥ) is inconclusive, he says: "And for that very reason," and so forth.
And for that very same reason, it can be stated that invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) also follows inherently (*svataḥ*), because this [same logic] is clearly applicable there as well:
"Therefore, from defects (*doṣa*) comes the absence of excellences (*guṇa*); from their absence... [3066]
Because of that, the non-existence of the form of a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) remains unrefuted as a general rule (utsarga).
Since this state of being a general rule is constructed solely by the speaker's intention,
it can be clearly expressed even in the case of what is not a means of valid cognition, just like the term "means of cognition" (māna).
Since the validity of cognition is established by its very nature of being non-sublated,
it is set aside only by the knowledge of qualities arising from causes that produce knowledge of the object as it truly is.
Furthermore, because the qualities themselves are not being cognized, invalidity is not set aside.
And that too is established by itself as something not subject to sublation;
this is what is meant by "this."
To the question "What can be said about that?", he says: "Therefore," and so forth;
the suffix *vati* is added to the word ending in the locative case, *mānava*.
"That too" refers to invalidity;
the rest is easily understood.
Regarding the question of whether faults exist or do not exist, and so forth, he says: "Faults," etc.
Whether defects exist or not is doubted in the case of human compositions;
however, since an author is established even for the Veda, the doubt regarding defects is not absent for us.

(3071) Since the author of the Veda has been proven in the *Śrutiparīkṣā*, the claim that there is no author is unestablished. Therefore, for us who are discerning people, the doubt regarding defects in the Veda is not non-existent; rather, it certainly exists.
3071 Therefore, regarding the statement "because of independence," he says "therefore" and so forth:
"Therefore, because of its independence, the authority of the Veda is asserted."
That is unproven, because that [Veda] also depends upon an author;
"that also" refers to the Veda.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In the case of the meaning of the Vedas, by other means of valid cognition," he says: "If there is a corroborative cognition... and so forth.
That is: if there is a corroborative cognition, or else the purity of the cause.
Because doubt arises, there is no certainty regarding the authority of the Veda at that time.

(3073) If both of these—the cognition that accords with purposeful action and the cognition of the purity of its causes—are not accepted as the grounds for determining authority in the case of the Veda, then, due to the deficiency of the causes for certainty, the determination of authority in the Veda cannot be attained; for an effect is impossible without its cause.
Regarding the point that "even for another [cognition] there is validity," he says: "Even for another," and so forth.
Even when another [cognition] possesses validity, such a connection alone is postulated as the cause, because the ascertainment is based upon that. (3074)
"It is precisely thus"— that is,
characterized by the thorough knowledge of the quality of correspondence—

and here the fault of infinite regress has already been refuted; therefore, the claim that "whatever is a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) does not depend on connection with another means of valid cognition" is inconclusive (anaikāntika), because another means of valid cognition is required for the sake of ascertainment.
He demonstrates this very point with the words "For when [the means of knowledge] is established," and so forth:
"For when its status as a means of valid cognition (pramāṇatva) is established, certainty is produced by this [cognition]."

However, its status as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not produced by this [subsequent cognition] as something previously non-existent. By this, the following argument is also refuted: "Even where there might be a determination by successive means of cognition," and so forth; for when the validity of one [cognition] is ascertained through another, the status of that prior cognition as a means of cognition—characterized by its capacity to reach the object—is not lost.
Regarding the objection that "there would be no validity of cognition with respect to an object that has arisen and perished at once," he says: "sakṛt" and so forth;
even in the case of an object that has arisen and perished at once, there would indeed be validity of cognition.

Even when [the object] is not ascertained, that [cognition] certainly exists; and ascertainment also arises according to the sequence previously described. Thus, it possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (mānatā).
Demonstrating the very sequence already mentioned, he says: "If, because of the purity of the cause," and so forth;
that is, if there is a certainty consisting of the knowledge of the purity of the cause and so on, then...

If the purposeful action (arthakriyā) characterized by bathing and so forth has been attained, or if there is a repeated practice that is independent of the arising of a result, then— provided there is no separation from all the necessary means— there is the ascertainment of valid cognition (pramāṇa).
However, in the absence of all such means, there is no determination of valid cognition.

Therefore, although validity exists in that [cognition], it is not ascertained; being as if non-existent, it is designated as "not existing at all. (3079) And if the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) has been attained...
Then, the phrase "the certainty arises from that" is to be connected with the subject under discussion.

Now, an objection is raised: since the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*) has a different object, it is not logical for the validity of the preceding cognition to be established by it.

For instance, because a composite substance (*avayavidravya*) is impossible, visual cognition directed toward water grasps only color (*rūpa*), whereas the cognition of purposeful action such as bathing has only touch (*sparśa*) as its domain. How, then, could a cognition based on one object verify the validity of a cognition whose object is different? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This is not a fault.

Because two objects existing within a single continuum are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāva*), even a cognition having one object as its support will establish the validity of the cognition of the other object;
for those two—visible form and tactile sensation—do not exist in isolation from one another, since they depend upon the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatvāt*).

In this regard, since the initial cognition is observed to function toward an object even when it is not the actual object, one does not need to depend on a subsequent cognition that grasps the touch—which is invariably concomitant with that [color]—for the production of certainty.

[Objection: Even so, because all things are momentary, the touch that is invariably concomitant with the form grasped by the prior cognition is not made an object by the activity of the subsequent cognition; how, then, can certainty arise from it?
[Response: This is not a fault.

Regarding subsequent moments of form and so forth, if there is a desire for an objective causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) that is not distinct from the moments of form and so forth grasped by the preceding cognition, they are designated as a single unity because they share an identical *yogakṣema* (commonality of acquisition and preservation).
For those of limited vision do not conduct their worldly transactions based on momentary entities.

Alternatively, since the object of the subsequent cognition is invariably concomitant with the object—such as form—that was delimited by the preceding cognition, it stands in a causal relationship to it; thus, even though a distinction exists, the resulting ascertainment (*niścaya*) is not contradicted.
Regarding what was stated—"the auditory cognition would be invalid," and so forth—he replies with the verse beginning "of the auditory cognition":
The connection of the auditory cognition with [other cognitions] such as that of the eye is clearly more intimate;
for color, sound, and the rest exist depending upon a single causal complex (sāmagrī). (3080)
Because they are inseparable from one another and function as mutual causes within a continuum, their relationship certainly exists; this is thus perfectly clear.
For even the cognitions of those [objects] arise by way of that [relationship], like the transformation of smoke and fuel.

"The auditory cognition would be the means of valid knowledge [for that object], because it is connected with the cognition of other [objects]. (3082) The lack of connection with the other cognitions, such as those of the eye and so forth, is not established at all;

for instance, because the sound of a lute and its related qualities such as color are dependent upon the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there certainly exists between them a relationship characterized by mutual inseparability, just like the relationship between smoke and the transformation of fuel.

And when considering the operation of a continuous series (*prabandha*), each preceding group serves as the cause for each subsequent one; thus, there indeed exists a relationship characterized by direct causality. Consequently, even the cognitions that apprehend those [sounds] possess a connection through that indirect succession.
Therefore, auditory cognition is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it possesses the aforementioned relationship with other cognitions such as those of the eye and so forth.

For instance, when a person who hears the sound of a lute (*vīṇā*) or similar instrument from a distance and, desiring it, develops a doubt due to its similarity to the sound of a flute (*veṇu*) or other instruments, he acts; and upon seeing the form of the lute, the previously arisen doubt—namely, "Is this the sound of a lute, or is it the sound of a flute, song, and so forth?"—is dispelled.

Furthermore, in a place where one who has acted upon hearing the echo of a drum (*mṛdaṅga*) or similar instrument does not obtain the intended object, he realizes its lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) due to that discrepancy (*visaṃvāda*).
Regarding the statement, "But for both [of us], there is no cognition produced by another means of proof," and so forth, he says: "By another means of proof," etc.
But this cognition produced by another means of proof is determined [to be valid];
therefore, its correspondence with knowledge produced by another cause is desired. (3083) "This" refers to the cognition.

Regarding the [objection] that "it apprehends the form of the lute and so forth," as in the passage beginning "just as this connection with another cognition dependent on the sense organ," he says "in this way" and so forth.
Thus, in the case of perception, the conjunction of various cognitions dependent on different sense-faculties is established as the cause; however, this is not observed in the case of the Veda.
"This is not observed" means: [it is not seen].
The connection with another cognition depends on various sense faculties;
how then can this [connection] be established as the cause for perception? To this he says: "For instance," and so forth.
For instance, first there arises a visual cognition of water, which appears as drinking, bathing, and so forth; subsequently, there arises another [cognition] based on the tongue and the body.
"Visual" (akṣija) means...
The meaning of "the highest" is that visual consciousness has form as its object; it occurs at a subsequent time. 3085
Regarding the passage beginning with "For by a single sentence alone," he says: "Even by a single [sentence]," and so forth.
However, even by a single sentence, agreement with the facts cannot be obtained across different places, times, and persons, because doubt arises in every case. (3086)
"It is heard in the scriptures that 'from the Agnihotra sacrifice, heaven results'— this is equally [subject to doubt],

for when devoid of the factor of certainty, it is merely the croaking of words. By this, he states that there is a lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) regarding the correspondence with reality (*arthasaṃvāda*).

For instance, from the sentence "Heaven results from the Agnihotra," doubt certainly arises for a discerning person because there is no cause for certainty; thus, there is no establishment of correspondence regarding place, time, and so forth.
Showing that agreement is not found everywhere among other men either, he says: "In heaven and so forth," etc.
"Even among Brahmins, a difference of opinion regarding heaven and so forth is observed; therefore, no agreement on the matter is found here among men and others. (3088)

For instance—the authors of the *Nirukta* and others describe heaven (*svarga*) as a specific location such as the summit of Mount Sumeru, the abode of a particular being who surpasses humans, a locus of superhuman bliss, and enriched with various implements;
the Mīmāṃsakas maintain that heaven is simply a particular state of joy for human beings themselves;
and even regarding sacrifice (*yāga*), a disagreement is observed.
For it is heard that in ancient times, sacrificers offered an animal made of flour;
however, by others who were evil-minded and merciless, it was described that the animal is indeed a specific living being.
Therefore, he says that what has arisen is firm: "In knowledge produced by an injunction," and so forth.
Firmness was previously set aside regarding knowledge produced by an injunction, because the existence of its object in that way is doubtful due to its similarity to other things. (3089)
The phrase "previously" refers to the examination of scripture [in the *Śrutiparīkṣā*], where it was stated that [the object] is similar to other [cognitions].

Because it is equal to the cognition produced by human statements such as "heaven does not result from the *agnihotra* sacrifice" (3089). Furthermore, this is merely words on your part; for [the author] shows that the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*) does not fail to correspond with respect to place and so forth, in the verse beginning with "by those who are not all-seeing."
"How can this be determined by Brahmins who do not perceive everything—that the cognition produced by *codanā* is in agreement with all things?
Regarding the statement beginning with "And it cannot be established by inference," he says: "Determined," and so forth.
The validity of even perception is established by means of the inference stated with certainty;
because it is produced from pure causes, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like anything else.

For a *prasanga* (reductio ad absurdum) is defined as the occurrence of an undesirable consequence, and it is not the case that the establishment of the validity of perception through inference is undesired, such that a *prasanga* could be leveled against it.

Just as the validity of perception is established by means of inference, so it was previously stated; he now recalls that very point: "Because it is produced from pure causes, it is a valid means of knowledge, like anything other than those [invalid cognitions]."

Regarding the statement, "Just as perception grasps a proximate object," and "by which other means the validity of the means of valid cognition is established," and so forth, he says: "Of everything," and so on.
Furthermore, the validity of everything need not be established by means of another instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
because it has already been proven that there is no error in the cognition of causal efficacy (*arthakriyājñāna*).
Just as there is no error in the cognition of causal efficacy, so it was previously established by the passage beginning with "agreement with the object" (*vastusaṃvāda*).
Therefore, because validity is established through corroboration by a cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*), there is no infinite regress.
He demonstrates that this is likewise not the case when [validity] is established by inference as well, beginning with the words "the self" (*ātman*) and so forth.
And even when an inference arises from the evidence known as "self" (svabhāva) and "effect" (kārya), because their non-deviation is certain, there is no error whatsoever.
(3093) The analysis of the compound is: "that which has the name 'self' and 'effect' as its evidence. Thus it was stated.
That logical mark (*liṅga*) which is certain and non-deviant is described as such.

This is what is meant: inference, which arises by the power of the ascertainment of a logical mark called "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) or "effect" (*kārya*) that is constrained by the relations of identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*), is intrinsically a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because there is no cause for error; thus, there is no infinite regress (3093).
Regarding the passage beginning with "If [it were] not established by another," he says: "In some cases," and so forth.

However, in some instances, an error arising through the power of various causes of delusion is dispelled by this [means], because in that case there is no certainty [regarding the object]. || 3094 ||

Because of the absence of causes for ascertainment such as repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), error may arise in some initial perceptions; thus, its validity cannot be established by itself. Regarding the statement, "A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established in its own nature prior to its apprehension," and so forth, he says: "Unmanifested," etc.

An object does not become established as manifest by way of an unmanifest manifestation, just as in the case of another's perception; therefore, it must be accepted that knowledge is known [by itself].
(3095) That object whose manifestation is unmanifest is described as such.
Knowledge must necessarily be known, for if it were unknown, it would follow that everything is unknown; indeed,
knowledge is said to be nothing other than the manifestation of an object, and if that manifestation were imperceptible, it would follow that the object itself is also imperceptible.

For example, regarding an object that is the referent of a cognition occurring in another person's continuum, because its manifestation is unmanifest, the formal argument is as follows: whatever object has an unmanifest manifestation is not perceptible to that [person], just as an object perceived by a perception occurring in one person's continuum is not perceptible to another. And the cognition under dispute, which belongs to someone, has an unmanifest manifestation; thus, there is the apprehension of a factor incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Nor is the reason inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because if that object were perceptible without the production of its manifestation, it would follow that it would be perceptible to everyone.
But it is not so; therefore, there is a reversal.
Regarding the point that [objects are known] "only by those who do not themselves know," he says: "But by themselves," and so forth.
Because they are insentient in nature, objects are not grasped by the sense organs such as the eye; rather, it is their status as causes for cognition that is [the case]. (3096)

Since the eyes and other sense organs are insentient by nature like external objects, they do not possess the apprehension of objects in a primary sense; rather, their "apprehension of objects" is merely a figurative designation based on their serving as causes for consciousness. Thus, it might be argued that objects are "apprehended" by those [organs] only insofar as they are ignorant [of themselves], acting as the producers of the cognition of objects. However, this is not the case for consciousness, because nothing at all is done to the object by consciousness such that one could say it "apprehends" the object even while being ignorant [of itself], as the eyes and other organs do.
If it is argued that "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*) is produced [by consciousness], we say no.
Because it is a synonym for knowledge (*jñāna*),

such terms as "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*), "apprehension" (*upalabdhi*), "determination of another" (*paracchitti*), and "experience" (*saṃvedana*) are stated as synonyms; they do not denote a different entity,
nor is it logical for something to be its own instrument (*karaṇa*).
Because of the contradiction of an action directed toward itself,
and because of the existence or non-existence [of the object] in its arisen and unarisen states respectively—
for instance, would knowledge produce itself when it has already arisen, or when it has not yet arisen?
It has not yet arisen, because it arises with the same fate (ekayogakṣema) as its own self;
and it is not logical that something which does not share the same fate as another should have that other as its nature, for that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, it is not logical for an arisen nature to be produced, because there is no further excellence (atiśaya) to be added.
Furthermore, because it would entail the consequence of the cessation of all activity,
the position that [the cause] is "unproduced" is also untenable due to its non-existence;
for the operation of a non-existent thing is not logical, since it is characterized by the absence of any description of causal capacity whatsoever.
Because if there were activity, it would entail the loss of existence;
for this alone is the definition of existence—that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
Therefore, there is no similarity between the example and the subject of the illustration.
Therefore, regarding the passage beginning with "jñāyamānatvam" (the state of being known) and so forth, he says: "Therefore, in this case," etc.;
thus, in this context, the state of being known is what is required for validity.
"Because the experience of an object is never obtained if it remains unknown.

[3097] Now, one might suspect that if cognition is established by itself through self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*), then cognition is valid (*pramāṇa*) by its own nature; anticipating this, he says "etāvat tu" and so forth:
"This much, however, would be the case here even regarding the apprehension of self-awareness."
Because the causes of error exist, there is no certainty regarding its being such [as it appears]. At that time, even its existence as an object is not determined by us,
because through perception based on similarity, the superimposition of something else is possible.

Indeed, it has been demonstrated in many ways that the certainty "this was experienced" does not arise in its entirety merely from experience itself, because the production of certainty depends upon other causes. Therefore, although the capacity of cognition for self-awareness and for being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding an object has been apprehended, it is said to be "uncertain" because certainty does not arise due to the presence of causes of error—such as similarity to what is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), lack of repeated practice (*anabhyāsa*), and so forth.
This is because there is a distinction between the experience and the certainty.
Consequently, there is no fault in accepting that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*) by way of the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa-vyavaccheda*).
As it has been said: "The cognition of the essential nature [of a means of knowledge] is from itself, while its validity is established through practical application (vyavahāra)";
thus it is with respect to validity.
Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, the immeasurable [cognition] is [valid] with respect to its own object," and so forth, he says: "That which arises from practice," and so on.
Just as knowledge arising from practice (*ābhyāsika*) is understood to be valid by itself,
so too some false knowledge remains invalid by itself.
(3100) [That which arises in practice is "practiced" (*ābhyāsika*).]

Just as it has been stated that in some cases validity is determined intrinsically (*svataḥ*) through the power of practice (*abhyāsa*), so too falsity (*mithyātva*) is determined intrinsically for some; and indeed, we observe certain people, such as those with ophthalmia (*taimirika*), who by the power of practice determine the falsity of their cognition of falling hairs and the like immediately upon its arising. (3100)
Regarding this, he says "bādhakāraṇa... etc., in the context of [the verse] beginning with "just as the cognition of falsity [occurs] when there is a defect in the cause":
even when there is the cognition of a subverting factor or a defect in the cause, the aforementioned infinite regress applies;
by that much alone, it is not possible to grasp its falsity. || 3101 ||
It has been stated as follows:
"For you claim that [the absence of a sublater] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because there is no sublater;
yet even this absence of a sublater is held to be another means of valid cognition called 'non-apprehension' (*abhāva*)," and so forth.
"Tad" means "therefore.
Regarding the claim that "this very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is cognized while still in its state of origination," he says: "While in its state of origination," and so forth.

This means of valid cognition is not cognized while in its state of origination, because [cognition] is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*) and because self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvit*) is not accepted [at that stage]. (3102)

Nor can it be established by another cognition, because that [other cognition] is not present at that time, since it too is in an unmanifest state, or else because it would lead to an undesirable consequence.

Regarding the state of its arising, there are these alternatives: is it determined as a means of valid cognition by itself, or by another cognition existing simultaneously, or by one occurring at a later time?

In that regard, first of all, it is untenable for cognition to apprehend itself as "this is a means of valid cognition" by means of itself, because cognitions are non-conceptual with respect to themselves;
nor is the perception of cognition by another [cognition] accepted, because it is admitted that consciousness is eternally beyond the reach of the senses (*parokṣa*);
nor [is it apprehended] by another cognition existing at the same time, because two cognitions do not arise simultaneously.

Nor can it be established by a cognition occurring at a different time; for if that other cognition is not established, its object is not established, and if the cognition apprehending that object is also unestablished because its manifestation has not been manifested, then if one seeks to establish that [second] cognition by yet another cognition, there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress.
Therefore, regarding the passage beginning with "even where there is falsity," he says: "In the Veda as well... and so forth.

Even in the Veda, a subverting means of knowledge (bādhaka-pramāṇa) has already been stated, namely that which consists of inference; by the exclusion of the Self and other [entities] asserted therein, it follows that [the Veda] is not a valid means of knowledge. || 3104 ||
Furthermore, since the human origin [of the Veda] is established, the presence of defective causes must be suspected;
or rather, as in the case of fire, there might be an inherent capacity for false cognitions. Therefore, the cognition arising from the *codanā* (Vedic injunction) possesses defective causes.
And that which is suspected of having a defect does not differ from that which is definitely known to have a defect.
For the Buddhists do not claim that mere similarity (*sādharmya*) is the subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) against the Veda; what then?
This is stated because the categories such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, as asserted by him, are sublated by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*);
this has been established in the *Ātmaparīkṣā* and other works.

Furthermore, since the human origin of the Vedas was proven in the *Śrutiparīkṣā*, or even if they were not of human origin, their lack of authority is possible because causes for falsity could exist—just as in the case of forest fires and the like; thus it is said that their unauthoritativeness is conceivable, and this is not merely a matter of similarity.

It might be argued: "Even if such a possibility exists, how can its lack of authority be established by mere possibility? To this he says: "And that which has suspected defects does not differ from that where defects are observed. That is to say, a statement in which defects are suspected does not differ [in status] from one where they are actually perceived.
The validity of both is equal, because they are alike in their fitness for the practical usage of "existent" and for the negation thereof.
With the words "Therefore," etc., he concludes:
Therefore, it is not tenable that even the Veda possesses intrinsic validity.
Therefore, let it be accepted that there is the state of being composed and proclaimed by those who are ascertained to be faultless.

(3107) It is described as such because "it was composed" (*kṛta*) and "it was proclaimed" (*ākhyāta*). *Ākhyāta* means explained. "Composed and proclaimed by faultless persons" is a genitive compound (*tṛtīyā-samāsa*). Its abstract state is "that-ness" (*tattva*). The analysis of the compound is: "that which is both ascertained and the state of being composed and proclaimed by faultless [persons]."
Therefore, let this be accepted for the sake of establishing the authority of the Veda—this is the connection [of the words].
And the implication is that if this is accepted, then authority would be extrinsic (*parataḥ*); but if it is not accepted, then there would be no authority at all.
Regarding the claim that "one should accept the fact that [the Veda] was composed by someone who is certain and faultless," Kumārila offers this reply:
"Indeed, those speakers who are possessed of passion, hatred, and so forth, protect their own sacred recitation all the more, according to how they are [motivated]. (3108)
"Who is weak in what? Who has recited which section first?
Who would maintain the purity of the accents, and who would corrupt a word where it does not belong?"—for those who are thus intent on seeking out his vulnerabilities are ever watchful. (3109)
How indeed could he not recite the Veda without fault when he is so devoted to it?
(3110) If those men who study the Veda were pure and remained indifferent [to worldly affairs], they would have pointed out that the Veda had been destroyed by others. (3111)
Then, after a long time, having been neglected and corrupted,
the Veda would become something entirely different, reduced to a mere semblance;
for those who suppress the destroyers of the Veda while they are possessed by passion, hatred, and other such afflictions.

The Veda, being protected at all times, shall not lose its own form. For what student would [his] memory, intelligence, and so forth become weak; or who would have studied from whom; or who could cause a deficiency or alteration in the accents, such as the udātta and others; or who, splitting even what is not a word, would recite it as a word? Since there are men among the students of the Veda who, intent and with exerted vigor, are ever vigilant in searching for such flaws in a reciter of the Veda, how could that reciter of the Veda not recite the Veda with due respect?

Therefore, since there is no suspicion regarding the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) of this Veda, what need is there to insist upon its being "declared by one who is ascertained to be free from defects"? This is the intended meaning.

To explain: if those who study the Veda, though pure-minded, were to remain indifferent toward the Vedas while they were being destroyed by others and fail to proclaim them, then it would be possible to suspect that this Veda is something else entirely, having fallen into a state of mere imitation.

However, since those of pure intellect have always protected this Veda by restraining and warding off men whose minds are overwhelmed by passion and other defects and who would destroy the Veda, how could it ever abandon its own essential nature?

It might be argued: "Even if the Veda has been protected by them at all times, nevertheless, since it was completely destroyed during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), it is possible that it later underwent alteration. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And it is accepted," etc. "And it is accepted that the entire world was never otherwise;
no so-called 'great dissolution' is known to exist in an ultimate sense. (3114)

He refutes this with the words "This is not so," and so forth: "Let it be that the reading is indeed identical; however, the realization of the true nature of its meaning does not occur without direct perception. (3115)

For in this way, it is indeed established that there is an equality of the mere recitation alone, but not of the means for attaining the understanding of the meaning; therefore, for that purpose, its status as being composed and transmitted by an authoritative person who is necessarily determined to be faultless must certainly be accepted.

He demonstrates that it is not possible for one who is not omniscient to determine uniformity regarding all regions and so forth merely by the non-observation of a recitation alone—stating "And all," etc.:
"And all persons, as well as all places and times, appear clearly in the mind of the Observer (adhyakṣa) like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand. (3116)
He is capable of understanding even the identity of the recitation; otherwise, however, how could there be disagreement due to differences in place, time, person, and circumstance?
(3117) Here he states the justification for this very point, beginning with "otherwise," etc.
If the reading were identical [in all cases], then doubt or disagreement among people regarding the reading in certain regions and so forth would not occur. (3116–3117)
Regarding the statement "And the entire world is accepted [as such]," etc., he says: "The world is of such a nature," and so forth. Even here, you have no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for this;
it is not logical to assert the non-existence of Saṃvarta merely on the basis of his not being perceived. (3118)
There is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever to prove that the world has always been exactly like this.
As for what the Buddhists describe as the *saṃvartakalpa* (the eon of dissolution), which they characterize as the destruction of the receptacle-world due to the impossibility of further birth;
and as for what the authors of the Smṛtis state: "This [world] was once enveloped in darkness, unperceived, and without distinguishing marks."
By not applying the list of corrections, the text displays this error as *apravattya*. [The verse reads: "It is beyond reasoning, unknowable, and like deep sleep on all sides.
Now, there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that sublates either of these two types of dissolution (*saṃvarta*), by which the world could be established as being always exactly like this.

Furthermore, the non-existence of things is not established by mere non-perception, because even when a thing exists, it may not be perceived in certain cases; thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between the absence of a thing and its non-perception is not proven.

Furthermore—since the Veda possesses intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*), there arises from it a constant certainty regarding the nature of its own objects, and thus there is no delusion; and since, due to its eternity, it is impossible to effect any alteration of its inherent nature, destruction cannot occur in either case according to your own view. Therefore, those who study the Veda perform its preservation in vain. He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "intrinsically" (*svataḥ*): under the doctrine of intrinsic validity, it produces certainty intrinsically.
And since the Veda exists in its own nature and its own meaning, there can be no possibility of delusion or the like [regarding it].
Therefore, as it stands upon a ground free from ignorance, doubt, and error, not even a single young Brahmin would require instruction [concerning it]. (3119–3120)
Furthermore, for that whose root is unknown, even destruction is not possible;
for what kind of destruction could there be for that which is eternal and surpasses even the diamond?
(3121) If it is argued that there is a change in its manifestation, that [objection] has already been refuted in the case of the eternal.
Therefore, even the wise provide protection for this [Veda], though it is fruitless.
The young Brahmin— the infant Brahmin—
has thus demonstrated that its destruction is not possible, independent of its own intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*).
Now, in order to demonstrate that [manifestation] is also impossible because of its permanence, he asks— "Who indeed," and so forth;
the connection is that "if there were a change in manifestation, it would be destruction."
The manifestation of this [is] "it belongs to this," namely, the Veda.
He concludes with the verse beginning "atīndriya" (beyond the senses): Therefore, the seer of supersensuous objects has shaken off the mass of internal darkness.
"Let him who knows the divisions of the meaning of the Vedas be accepted as the author.
(3123) Thus ends the examination of the doctrine of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*).
"Internal darkness" (*antastamaḥ*) refers to afflicted and unafflicted ignorance; its "accumulation" (*caya*) means its mass; he by whom that has been shaken off is described as such.
"Pravibhāgajñaḥ" means the expounder, the author;
"of the Veda" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Thus, it has been established that the thesis (*pratijñā*) is in every respect contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and that the reason (*hetu*)—"because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists"—is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, the proof for establishing the similar instance (*sapakṣa*) has been demonstrated by the passage beginning with "that which is the object of doubt and error," and so forth; this is the meaning of the refutation.

As for the presentation of four alternative positions (*pakṣa*) and the subsequent statement of faults regarding three of them, even there the Buddhist has no concern, for not even one of these four positions is accepted by the Buddhists, since they accept the position of non-restriction (*aniyama*).
For instance— it has been previously explained that both of these are partly from themselves and partly from another;
for this very reason, the presentation of four alternatives is also improper,
since a fifth alternative, namely the position of non-restriction (aniyama), is also possible.

Others, however, describe the meaning of the proposition differently: validity consists in being of the nature of cognition (*bodhātmakatva*), and this is inherent to cognitions themselves, not produced by excellences (*guṇa*), because even in the absence of excellences, the nature of cognition is possible in the case of erroneous knowledge. Therefore, it is said that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*); excellences, however, serve only to eliminate defects, and thus validity depends on excellences for their removal, not for its own acquisition.
This is incorrect,
because it is not logical that validity consists solely in having cognition as its essence,
since that is possible even in the case of erroneous knowledge.

If it is argued that validity (*prāmāṇya*) consists in a specific excellence of cognition (*bodhaviśeṣa*), then one must not say: "And this [validity] is inherent to cognitions alone and is not produced by excellences (*guṇa*), because it exists even in the absence of excellences, as in the case of erroneous cognition (*viparyayajñāna*).

For instance, if validity were intended to be a specific excellence of cognition, then it would be appropriate to point out a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding that very thing being produced by excellences, and not regarding anything else;
yet, by the statement "because it exists even in erroneous cognition," a deviation is shown regarding the specific excellence of cognition being produced by excellences.
What then? It is not that the generality of cognition (*bodhasāmānya*) is produced by a quality (*guṇa*), as the opponent maintains;
what then?
There is a distinction in awakening (*bodha-viśeṣa*),
and it cannot be demonstrated that this [distinction] is subject to deviation because it is produced by qualities (*guṇa-kṛtatva*).

Nor do we accept that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*) on the grounds that it is produced by qualities, such that you would have to establish its intrinsic nature (*svataḥ*) by negating that [extrinsic production].
What then?
Although this particular cognition has been experienced, due to the presence of some cause of error, it does not produce a certainty in accordance with that experience;
therefore, it is established that the arising of its certainty occurs through something else.

Furthermore, even if invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) were possible, one could still argue as follows: that which is called "invalidity" is simply the nature of being a non-cognition; and since this is inherent to cognitions and not produced by defects (*doṣa*), because it occurs even in the absence of defects within correct cognition, invalidity is said to be intrinsic (*svataḥ*). Defects, however, perform nothing but the negation of excellence (*guṇa*); therefore, for the sake of that negation, invalidity depends upon defects, but not for its own acquisition. Thus, this [objection] is trivial.

But Uveyaka says: the validity of cognitions does not consist in their being of the nature of awareness (*bodhātmakatva*); what then? It is non-contradiction with the object (*arthāvisaṃvāditva*). For instance, even when there is the nature of awareness, where there is no non-contradiction with the object, there is invalidity, as in the case of the cognition of silver regarding mother-of-pearl. On the other hand, even without the nature of awareness, where there is non-contradiction with the object, there is validity, as in the case of smoke [indicating] fire. Therefore, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), it is established that validity consists solely in non-contradiction.
And that knowledge arises from its own cause alone, not from another causal complex; therefore, it is said that the validity of all means of valid cognition is intrinsic (*svataḥ*),
because the word *sva* denotes "one's own."
"From itself" means from its own cause;
for, by the latter half of the verse beginning with "a capacity that does not exist inherently," the reason for the negation of the production of an entity from another causal complex is stated:
the meaning is that what does not exist inherently cannot be produced by anything else—that is, by something other than the causal complex of cognition.

It might be argued as follows: since the causes of cognition are common to both valid and invalid cognitions, how could validity be dependent solely upon the causes of cognition? Therefore, validity must be produced by a distinct causal complex (*sāmagryantara*) and not merely by the causes of cognition;
and that distinct complex is necessarily accompanied by excellences (*guṇa*), for the excellences of the sense organs and so forth are its cause.
Furthermore, in the case of verbal testimony, it is established through common usage that the very fact of being composed by a trustworthy person (*āpta*) constitutes the excellence of the cause.
And since it would follow that the Veda lacks authority due to the non-existence of those [conditions],
this is not a fault,
because it is unestablished that [the Veda] is produced by a different causal complex (*sāmagrī*).
For it is not perceived that the operation of excellences (guṇas) functions toward the production of the effect called "validity" by way of a positive injunction;
rather, it is the very nature of the sense organs and so forth, independent of anything else, that produces non-discrepant knowledge of the object.
As for collyrium and the like, their operation lies in the removal of defects, not in the instilling of excellences.

Now, it might be argued: "Even if the intrinsic nature of the sense-faculties and so forth exists when there is invalidity, it would follow that validity arises in all cases, because the causes are complete.
This is not so;
for when there is the presence of defects, a different effect will arise from a different causal complex (*sāmagrī*).

It might be argued: "Why is the opposite not understood—that the very nature of the sense-faculties and so forth, independent of anything else, produces erroneous cognition, whereas the conjunction of excellences (*guṇa*) constitutes a different causal complex that produces non-discrepant cognition regarding the object"?

This is indeed true; however, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is observed that in inference and other means of knowledge, it is precisely the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) which produces validity. Since this is possible in the case of perception as well, that alone is postulated as the producer [of validity].

However, the argument that an effect in the form of erroneous cognition—which does not arise from the nature of the sense organs and so forth—necessitates the postulation of another causal complex (sāmagryantara) is not without fault;
thus, all of this is not free from defect.

To explain: as for what was stated—that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of a cognition consists solely in its non-contradiction with the object, and that this arises from the cognition’s own cause—here there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). For, by our statement that “valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is non-contradictory cognition,” we indeed accept that the non-contradiction with the object is the validity of cognition. However, because of the specific inclusion of the term "cognition," the primary validity of smoke and the like—which are not of the nature of cognition—is not intended; thus, validity as mere non-contradiction with the object is unestablished [for those things], since it is cognition alone that is predominant in the engagement with objects to be abandoned or adopted.

For instance—even when smoke and the like exist as invariably concomitant with fire, a person does not engage in action toward the object until the arising of cognition occurs; therefore, cognition possesses an immediate causal efficacy (*avyavahita-kārakatva*) regarding action, and thus it alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As it has been said: "Cognition is the means of valid cognition because action depends primarily upon it regarding objects to be avoided or acquired. Furthermore, that non-contradiction (*avisamvāditva*) of cognition, which is characterized by the capacity to reach the object, is in fact the reaching of the object itself, since obstacles and the like may arise [otherwise].
And since capacity (*śakti*) is the very essence of things, who would desire its production from something else such that it would need to be negated?
For it is not logical that a property which has not been produced when [the thing] is produced should be its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

And although this capacity is the very essence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because of the presence of causes of error, it cannot be apprehended by those who have not yet realized its effect; thus, it is determined through another [means], namely the effect known as the cognition of purposeful action (*arthakriyājñāna*).
Therefore, it is said that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*) with respect to ascertainment (*niścaya*), not with respect to its production (*utpatti*).
Consequently, the refutation of production from another cause is redundant, as there is no dispute on that point;
for even you admit that the ascertainment of capacities occurs extrinsically.
As it has been said: "The potencies of all entities are established through the presumption based on their effects.

And as for the statement: "A potency that does not exist inherently cannot be produced by anything else"—this reason, which is described for the purpose of negating the existence [of a cause] other than the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), is equally applicable even in the case of invalidity; thus, that too would necessarily follow as being inherent. Or rather, that reason is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*).
As for what was said—

that it is not perceived or possible for there to be an operation of the qualities toward the production of invalidity by way of affirmation— this statement of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) has its meaning unelucidated; it is not understood what this so-called "operation by way of affirmation" actually is.

If it is argued that the activity preceded by intelligence—such as "I shall do this" or "I shall produce that"—is for the sake of bringing about an effect, then such activity is not possible even in the case of the sense organs and so forth.
This is because entities lack the quality of acting with foresight; since all entities are momentary, both intention (*samīhā*) and functional operation (*vyāpāra*) are impossible.
Consequently, because the operation of the sense organs and other factors cannot occur through a positive process (*vidhimukhena*), they would not possess the status of being causes.

Now, if it is maintained that even without the entry of an operation called "action," the sense-faculties and so forth are accepted as causes because they exert influence toward the production of the effect by their mere existence, then this is the same for the excellences (*guṇa*) as well. For no other operation, fixed for all causes in the production of an effect, is perceived or possible apart from the proximity of their own existence. If it is argued that when excellences are present, validity arises upon the cessation of defects, and thus—because it is mediated by the cessation of defects—an operation of the excellences is not possible in a direct, positive manner, then this is equally true for the defects as well.
For instance: even when defects are present, invalidity arises only upon the cessation of excellences; thus, defects would have no positive function (*vidhimukhena*) in the production of invalidity.

Consequently, invalidity itself would follow as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*), since there is no distinction [between the two cases], for defects are never observed to operate directly toward invalidity by first setting aside excellences.

Therefore, since no other causal relationship is possible apart from the positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) of that [cause] with its effect, the causality of defects is equal to that of excellences. Furthermore, as for the claim that the very form of the sense organ and so forth, independent of anything else, produces non-discrepant knowledge of the object— that too is incorrect,
because it would entail the validity of all cognitions simply by virtue of their causes being complete.

Just as the nature of consciousness— being the very form of awareness— is dependent upon the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and thus occurs in every cognition when its causes are complete even in the presence of defects and so forth, so too would there be non-discrepancy with the object.

It might be argued as follows: "In the production of invalidity by defects, validity—even though its general cause is present—is not produced, because it is impossible for two contradictory properties, such as validity and its opposite, to coexist in a single cognition; however, the nature of awareness itself occurs everywhere without opposition. If this were so, then the nature of the sense organ alone could not be established as a cause independent of anything else, because even when that [organ] is present in its unimpaired state, the effect called validity does not arise.
Indeed, it is not logical for that which is independent of anything else to ever fail to produce its effect.
Nor is it logical that something which does not arise even when another thing is present should have that as its sole cause, for this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Furthermore, you ought to explain this: if validity has its causes complete, why does it not arise even when defects (*doṣa*) are present?
If you say it is because the defect, which is a cause contrary to itself, is present; then [we reply]: so be it.
The same applies to invalidity as well;
for at that time, its own contradictory cause—the sense organ and so forth—is present, so let there be no production [of invalidity].

Furthermore, even if there were a desire for validity not to arise out of fear of a contradictory cause in the form of a defect, why would it disregard its own cause, which exists at that time with unimpeded capacity?

For in this way, its own unimpeded power would be manifested by it, if it were to forcibly produce its own effect even when that effect is unwilling to arise. [Otherwise], because its power is impaired by defects, the sense organ would not produce validity; nor would it produce cognition at all due to incapacity.
Otherwise, validity would not be established as being produced solely by the causes of cognition, since it does not arise even when those [causes] have arisen.

Whatever does not necessarily arise even when another thing arises cannot have that same cause as it, just as a rice sprout— which does not arise even when a *kodrava* sprout arises— does not share the same cause;
and since validity (*prāmāṇya*) does not necessarily arise even when cognition (*vijñāna*) arises, this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalambha*).

Nor can anyone destroy the power that constitutes its very nature without destroying that nature itself; therefore, it can also be stated thus: "Let it be understood that the validity of all cognitions is intrinsic (*svataḥ*)," for a power that is intrinsic cannot be destroyed by another.
Thus, it might be argued: it is not intended that the sense-faculties and so forth alone are the cause of validity; what then?

If it is argued that because [the cause] is specifically distinguished by being free from defects, the aforementioned defects do not apply, then it follows that a different causal complex (*sāmagryantara*)— one accompanied by excellences (*guṇa*)— is the cause of the validity of the sense organs and so forth, since freedom from defects is only possible for that which is accompanied by excellences. Consequently, one should not say that [validity] is unestablished because it is not produced by a different causal complex.
If it is argued that the operation of the excellences (*guṇa*) pertains to the removal of defects (*doṣa*) and not to the production of validity (*prāmāṇya*),
that is not so;
for since the removal is a non-entity (*avastu*), it is not logical for anything to have an operation upon it.
For no activity whatsoever is possible with regard to a non-entity, such as a hare’s horn, which by its very nature cannot be produced.
As for what was said—that in inference and the like, it is observed that the three marks (*trairūpya*) themselves produce validity in the cognition that arises—this too is unproven;

for it is not the three marks alone that produce the inference, but rather the qualities residing in the cognizer (*pratipattṛgata*), consisting of being undeluded and having a firm impression of memory.

For instance: even when the three-fold character [of the reason] is present, inference does not arise for a cognizer whose mental impression of the relationship has been lost and who has not perceived that relationship; therefore, it is unproven that only that which produces cognition is what produces validity, by virtue of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
Consequently, the opposite conclusion remains difficult to avoid.
Furthermore, as for what was stated—that the effect in the form of erroneous cognition does not arise from the intrinsic nature of the sense faculties and so forth—that too is an extreme rashness.
For it would follow that erroneous cognition could arise even without dependence on the sense faculties;
indeed, it is not logical for something to depend upon that from which it does not arise by its very nature, as this would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Furthermore, a cognition of two moons and so forth produced by those with ophthalmia and the like does not arise independently of the sense faculties.

Furthermore— if validity is described as non-contradiction with the object, then how is the non-contradiction with the object known in the case of the cognition produced by the Vedic injunction (*codanā*),
such that there could be a conventional usage of "validity" for it by you who are people of limited vision?
For its capacity cannot be determined by those who have not cognized its effect, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Furthermore, since this entire web of arguments was constructed with the hope of establishing the authority of that very Veda for which it is not even well-known, this is merely like husking chaff by one who seeks rice; enough of this digression.
Thus concludes the examination of intrinsic validity and the examination of a person who perceives supersensible objects.

Having prostrated before that Omniscient One, the best of speakers, who proclaimed dependent origination and whose great compassion became his very nature over many incalculable aeons, this *Tattvasaṅgraha* is composed.

Having thus stated the qualification of dependent origination as being taught by an omniscient one, he says the following—beginning with "In this way"—in order to provide a preliminary introduction for the purpose of supporting that point:
"In this way, since the validity of all means of valid cognition is not established intrinsically, no effort is made to prove the existence of a person who perceives supersensuous objects. (3124)

Thus, by the reasoning just stated, since it is established that the validity of all means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) does not arise from themselves alone, a person who perceives supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārtha-darśin*) is proven without effort; therefore, no further separate exertion is undertaken for the sake of proving him. 3124
It might be argued: "How can this be established without effort? To this he says: "The authority of the Veda, too," and so forth.
Since the authority of the Veda is also established on account of a person, and since that person possesses knowledge beyond the senses, its authority rests upon him. (3125)
Otherwise, if the person who is the author were subject to ignorance, doubt, and error, this [Veda] would possess no authority at all, just like anything else.
For by whom was the connection between heaven and sacrifice spoken after having been known?
He must be accepted by others as well as one whose knowledge of supersensible objects is perfectly clear;
"of him" refers to that person.
"Tataḥ" means from the Puruṣa, the agent;
"tasmin" means in that [Puruṣa].

In the phrase "the Veda is the means of valid cognition" (*vede pramāṇatā*), the locative case is used in the sense of dependence (*apekṣā-adhikaraṇa-saptamī*); that is, [it means] "the state of being a means of valid cognition [is dependent] upon the Veda."
The quality of establishing supersensuous objects without error has been stated here with reference to the opposing view;

this is what is meant: if you must necessarily accept the authority of the Veda, then its authority is properly derived from a personal author, such as Puruṣa and others, and not intrinsically (*svataḥ*); and this has already been demonstrated previously.

And if that author of the Veda is one who perceives supersensuous objects (*atīndriyadṛk*), then it is logical that he is an authority (*pramāṇa*) even as an author; for otherwise, if the author were possessed of erroneous knowledge, doubt, and so forth, the Veda would incur lack of authority (*apramāṇatā*) just like the speech of a madman or the like.

Therefore, that author of the Veda who was previously established in the "Examination of Revelation" (*Śrutiparīkṣā*) must necessarily be accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas themselves as a perceiver of supersensuous objects; thus, his rejection should not be undertaken.

For instance, having understood that no human being possesses the vision of supersensuous objects because the eye of their intellect is impaired by the cataracts of defects such as passion (*rāga*) and the like, and thus having lost all hope for the validity of those scriptures perceived by such individuals, a person seeking to understand *dharma* and *adharma* will, like a bird unable to see the shore, surely take the Veda alone as his authority. Or rather, the followers of Jaimini (*Jaiminīyas*), being themselves deprived of liberation due to the poverty of their own virtuous qualities, reject the possibility of one who perceives supersensuous objects—arguing that "all persons are indeed corrupted by passion and the like, as well as by ignorance (*avidyā*), and are deficient in the means to pacify them; therefore, there is no one at all who perceives supersensuous objects. Consequently, they maintain that *dharma* is an object characterized solely by Vedic injunction (*codanā*), not by the senses and so forth; for injunction alone is capable of making known such things as what has been, what is, what will be, the subtle, the hidden, and the remote, whereas no other sense-organ or means of knowledge can do so.
And they provide proof for this:

"That whose form is made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence—which is by nature the absence of the five means of knowledge—enters exclusively into the sphere of the conventional usage of 'non-existence' for the wise, just like a sky-lotus; and the omniscient person has his form made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), since what is to be proven is the fitness for such conventional usage.
Non-existence, however, is established solely through the means of valid cognition consisting of non-apprehension (abhāvapramāṇa).

Now, one might object: "Is not all knowable reality (prameya-vastu) merely this much—namely, the five objects such as form and so forth? And since people in the world are already well-known to know these, the proposition [of yours] is contradicted by common experience. Anticipating this objection, he says: "The denial of being a knower of Dharma," and so forth.
If the mere negation of knowledge regarding the Dharma is what is intended here, by what means can a person who knows everything else be prevented? (3128)

For here, in establishing the authority of the Veda, what is intended to be expressed is merely the negation of being a knower of the self, dharma, and the universe, and not the negation of being a knower of everything denotable by the word "all. Therefore, we do not negate that usage of the term "omniscient" which occurs among people in reference to some person with respect to their knowledge of all things other than dharma and adharma; thus, the sense is that there is no contradiction with common experience.

Furthermore, showing that if even you Buddhists were to attribute omniscience to a person other than one who knows dharma and adharma, it would result in proving what is already established, he says: "And the word 'all'... and so forth.
The word "all" is everywhere intended in reference to what is under discussion;
therefore, since an omniscient being is already established as the subject under discussion, what do we lose? (3129)

Furthermore, he shows that it is this which is under discussion when it is said, "all": "And because [it] is impossible in the case of an object, some effect is postulated even in the case of the word; in that regard, let him who knows all words be called 'omniscient' by name. (3130)

For example, in grammar, when an operation such as an affix or augment is prescribed by a rule like *agni-dṛk* and so forth, since it is not possible for it to apply to the meaning, grammarians explain that by implication (*sāmarthyāt*) it is understood to apply to the word expressing that meaning. In the same way, if you also—on the grounds that it is impossible for anyone to know everything—rely on the fact that the word "all" (*sarva*) within the term "omniscient" (*sarvajña*) as used in your own established doctrine primarily denotes its own form, and thus define "omniscient" as "one who knows the word 'all'," then let it be so; let it be merely by name (*nāmataḥ*). For there is no one who can obstruct someone who assigns names at will, because a name arises solely from independent whim; this is the sense.

Furthermore, even if there is some subject under discussion, such as oil, water, ghee, and so forth, let the omniscient one exist by means of that [knowledge]; he is not thereby prevented from being so.

Furthermore, even if one intends by "all" that which is other than merit and demerit—namely oil, water, ghee, and so forth—and one desires [the Buddha] to be omniscient because he has made all of that an object of his cognition, even so, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Moreover, is he intended to be omniscient through a concise knowledge of the entire world in its general form, or rather through an extensive knowledge of it in its specific forms? Regarding the first position, he demonstrates that it is a case of proving what is already established with the words beginning "existence and non-existence" (*bhāvābhāva*).
When it is said that the entire world consists of the nature of existence and non-existence,
why would an omniscient person not accept this in brief?
Likewise, even by means of the summary of "knowability" and "measurability," [the world's] totality [is established].
If [he is established as] omniscient by relying on this [fact], who is able to prevent it?

For indeed, the entire world has the nature of non-existence because its intrinsic nature consists of mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) and so forth; yet, because it is established as having a positive form (*vidhirūpa*), it also has the nature of existence. Thus, we have described this common characteristic (*sāmānyadharma*)—the state of having the nature of both existence and non-existence—which pervades the entire world. If an omniscient being is established on the basis of such a thorough knowledge of the entire world in that form, even so, it is exactly what we desire. For by this much alone, the status of being a knower of all specific phenomena (*dharmajñatva*) is not proven for anyone, since that is merely a summary.
That very nature of the world as consisting of existence and non-existence is its "summary" (*saṅkṣepa*), in the sense that it is summarized by this;

thus, even when there is full comprehension through general properties such as being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) and so forth, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).

All those who have ascertained all categories (padārtha) in their entirety— both as to what they are and how many there are— are omniscient by virtue of that knowledge, provided they are knowers of those [very] treatises. (3134)

Furthermore, it might be argued that one is established as "all-knowing" through the thorough knowledge of whatever categories of entities (*padārtha*) are determined and taught as being "everything" within their respective treatises—for example, the five aggregates (*skandha*) by the Buddhists, the six categories (*padārtha*) by the Vaiśeṣikas, the sixteen [topics] such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*) by the Naiyāyikas, and the twenty-five principles beginning with primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the great one (*mahat*) by the Sāṅkhyas, and so forth. If this were the case, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for other students who understand the meaning of those texts would also necessarily become omniscient.
Likewise, who indeed would not accept as omniscient even one who possesses discernment regarding the six objects of knowledge by means of the six instruments of valid cognition?

(3135) Furthermore, it might be argued that he who thoroughly understands these six respective objects through the six instruments of valid cognition—namely, perception, inference, verbal testimony, analogy, presumption, and non-apprehension—is omniscient; yet in this case as well, you are merely proving what is already established.
For instance: perception, being restricted to the fivefold objects such as form and so forth, does not have dharma and adharma as its objects;

nor does inference have them as its objects, because inference has as its object a probandum (liṅgin) whose connection with a mark (liṅga) has been grasped by perception, and since dharma and the like are beyond the senses, it is impossible for any [perceptual] connection to be grasped.

Although verbal cognition (śābda) has as its objects all things, both perceptible and imperceptible, one cannot nevertheless become a seer of supersensuous objects through that cognition, because that cognition is non-perceptual (apratyakṣa) due to having an imperceptible object.
Furthermore, it is not logical that a person who perceives through non-perceptual knowledge or through knowledge derived from association should be a direct seer (*sākṣāddarśin*).

Nor is analogy (*upamāna*) a means for [knowing] *dharma*, *adharma*, and so forth, because its object is similarity and its qualifying attributes (*tadupādhi*); as it has been said: "Therefore, that which is remembered, qualified by similarity, or the similarity itself residing therein, would be the object of knowledge (*prameya*) for analogy."

Thus, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) also has as its object another thing postulated because a perceived or heard fact would otherwise be inexplicable; it does not have *dharma* and so forth as its domain, for there is no perceived or heard fact that is inexplicable without *dharma* and the like.

Or, even if we grant that presumptive testimony has *dharma* and so forth as its object, nevertheless, because its nature is non-perceptual, one who possesses it is not established as a direct perceiver of *dharma* and the like.
However, since non-existence has as its object only the absence of a cognizable thing, it is illogical for it to have phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth as its object.

Thus, it has been demonstrated that in the brief proof of an omniscient being, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Now, he states the fault in the detailed proof of omniscience based on the complete knowledge of the entire world, beginning with the words "In particular" (*viśeṣeṇa*), etc.
But for one who imagines that [the Buddha] is a direct perceiver who clearly sees all objects in their particularity,
that imagination of his is both futile and false. (3136) "Futile" means...
It is false because it is fruitless, as it is of no use for the attainment of the goals of human life.
Because its object is an impossible matter, it is false.
(3136) He demonstrates that very fact of its having an impossible object with the words beginning "of one alone," and so forth.
Who is capable of knowing all the atoms, as well as the hairs on the head and body, within a single body?

Indeed, the thorough knowledge of every division of the atoms contained within a single body is already impossible for men; how much more so, then, will be the thorough knowledge of the subtle and other specific details pervading the entire world?
Showing that conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) is a state of delusion, he says: "The means for attaining knowledge of the expansion of all parts and individual instances," and so forth.

[An investigation] being carried out [into such things] is as useless as an examination of a crow’s teeth (kākadantaparīkṣā). The analysis of the compound is as follows: "parts" (*avayava*) refers to hands and so forth; "individuals" (*vyakti*) refers to the *dhava*, *khadira*, *palāśa*, and other trees; thus, they are "parts and individuals" (*avayavavyakti*). These taken together are "all parts and individuals" (*samastāvayavavyaktayaḥ*). One who knows their detailed expansion (*vistara*), characterized by atoms, hair, leaves, and so on, is described as such. The suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent, according to the rule *kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam*.

The proof for that has been set forth; however, it is useless because, being impossible and not having dharma and adharma as its object, it is of no utility toward the goals of human life—this is the sense.
Establishing this very point by means of an illustration, he says: "Just as," and so forth.
Just as the claim that one perceives all things with the eye is fruitless, so too is the proposition of being an all-seeing witness of everything devoid of result. (3139)

By this, it is stated, as appropriate, that the proposition [of the opponent] suffers from the fallacies of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatva*) and being contradicted by common experience (*pratītibādhitatva*).
Now, he demonstrates that point regarding which there is dispute, and how its proof is conducive to human goals, with the words beginning "one's own dharma" (*svadharma*), etc.,
concerning the proof and refutation of one who knows only his own dharma and adharma.
For it is precisely the acceptability or rejectability of the scriptures composed by him that is established [in this context].

Thus, people labor in vain through their zeal for composing treatises and engaging in debates to prove his knowledge of the subtle distinctions of the entire world; such efforts are misplaced. || 3140–3141 ||

The compound *svakīyaś-cāsau dharmādharmamātrajñaś-ca* is analyzed as "he who is both his own [teacher] and one who knows only dharma and adharma"; this is a locative case (*saptamī*). The connection is respectively as follows: for it is through him that the acceptability and rejectability of the scripture (*āgama*) he has composed are established, namely, the establishment of its proof and its refutation.

This is what is meant: if the proponent of the proof establishes his own teacher as one who knows dharma and adharma, then once that proof has been made, the acceptability of the scripture composed by him is established;

and if the opponent refutes the other's accepted teacher as one who knows only his own dharma and adharma, then once that negation has been made, the rejectability of the scripture composed by that teacher whose knowledge of dharma and adharma has been refuted becomes established.

Furthermore, as for the zeal exerted by the Sāṃkhyas, Buddhists, and others in composing treatises or in debate—setting aside the diverse [conclusions] regarding dharma and adharma—to establish whether one who is renowned to both self and others as omniscient and pervading the entire world actually possesses or lacks knowledge of the subtle distinctions existing throughout the universe: that zeal results solely in their own affliction (*saṃkleśa*). In the phrase "in the composition of treatises and in debate," the locative case (*saptamī*) is used in the sense of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*), whereas in the phrase "regarding the state of being the knower of the subtle distinctions of the entire world," it is used in the sense of a locus (*ādhāra-saptamī*) with respect to the zeal.

It might be argued: "If there is no person at all who possesses complete knowledge of dharma and so forth, then how can there be an understanding of merit and demerit in the world? In response to this doubt, he says: "Connected with all cognizers," and so forth.
By excluding perception and other means of knowledge associated with all cognizers,
merit and demerit will attain the status of being cognizable solely through scripture.
Even though the position of the Mīmāṃsā is established by this much alone, that which [is stated] further...
To exert effort in refuting an omniscient being is like killing what is already dead.
Even those who, because the very root [of such knowledge] has been severed and the possibility of knowing dharma has been destroyed,
claim that there are omniscient persons— they have merely performed the threshing of chaff.
