The phrase "being cognizable solely through scripture" (kevalāgamagamyatva) means being cognizable through scripture alone;
although the word "scripture" (āgama) is a general term, it should nevertheless be understood here as referring specifically to non-human (apauruṣeya) scripture by virtue of the context.

By this much alone—that is, by the mere negation of his being a knower of Dharma—even though the Mīmāṃsā position that "Dharma is a purpose characterized by Vedic injunction" (*codanā-lakṣaṇa*) is established, the further effort we shall make to negate an omniscient person is fruitless, like killing one already dead, since the desired result has already been achieved. Furthermore, the effort of the Buddhists and others to establish an omniscient being once the knower of Dharma has been slain by the means of knowledge consisting of non-existence (*abhāva-pramāṇa*) is merely a result of pure exhaustion, like husking chaff for one who desires rice, because the intended result is absent.

Just as one who seeks rice would merely husk the chaff by discarding the grain within it, so too, in the Buddhist and other systems, by discarding the knowledge of Dharma—which is the primary objective itself—one attempts to establish the knowledge of all the subtle distinctions existing in the entire world that are otherwise useless; this is analogous to husking chaff.
Because their root is severed, they are said to be "those whose root is severed," meaning those for whom the primary root—the thorough knowledge of the reality consisting of Dharma—is lost.
The state of being that is reality (tattva).

3144 It is shown that for these [proponents], such as the Buddhists and others who seek to establish an omniscient being, not only is their desired goal unattained, but there is also the occurrence of an undesired consequence: "Directly," and so forth;
because of his direct perception, [he would have] impure tastes and the like.
[If they were so,] they would follow as being self-cognizable; who indeed would then imagine [them]?

Anticipating the objection that "the state of omniscience is inferred from the teaching by the Sugata and others of the reality of the entire mass of objects, and thus the proposition is sublated by inference and the reason is unestablished," he says: "And not... and so forth.
"Nor is there the communication of the meaning of the Vedas, Upavedas, Aṅgas, Praty-aṅgas, and so on."
The word of the Buddha and others is observed; how could he [the Buddha] be omniscient in vain?

The Vedas—known as the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma*—the Upavedas—the *Āyurveda*, *Dhanurveda*, and so forth—the six limbs (*aṅgas*) of the Vedas: phonetics (*śikṣā*), ritual science (*kalpa*), grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), prosody (*chandas*), etymology (*nirukta*), and astronomy (*jyotiṣa*); the sub-limbs (*pratyaṅgas*)—their constituent parts such as verbal roots (*dhātu*) and so on; and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of their ancillaries such as the commentaries (*bhāṣya*) and so forth.

The meaning of these [words] is that which is to be expressed; the "instruction" of that meaning is a statement that establishes it—that is, such a sentence [as this] is not seen to exist among the Buddha or others, which establishes the meaning taught in the Vedas and so forth.
This is because no one is ever seen to compose a treatise that establishes the entire mass of all categories of objects, since all treatises are observed to have distinct subject matters.

Furthermore, one might argue that because we observe the teaching of only a limited number of topics by the Buddha and others, it can be inferred that there are other matters not taught in their own works which they nevertheless knew, given that their power of thorough knowledge is evident; and thus, the aforementioned fault remains as it was. To this, he says: "In their own works... and so forth:
"If it is maintained that even a matter not recorded in their own works was known to them, then all poets would be omniscient, simply because of the composition of their own poems. (3147)

If it is maintained that even a matter not recorded in texts—that is, one not taught therein—is understood by them through the power of inference, then poets who compose narrative works based on their own imagination would also have to be considered omniscient, since they too are seen to possess the capacity for such thorough knowledge; thus, the reason [proffered] is inconclusive due to this lack of distinction.

It might be argued: "The teaching of supersensuous objects is observed in the case of the Buddha and others, but not among poets; therefore, the complete knowledge of all supersensuous objects is inferred for them alone, and not for others. For otherwise, if one lacks the capacity for the complete knowledge of all supersensuous objects, one would lack even the knowledge of a few supersensuous objects, as there is no distinction between the two. Thus, because the reason is qualified by the condition 'being a knower of supersensuous objects,' there is no deviation [of the reason] in the case of poets. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And regarding the omniscient ones," etc.—"and since there are many omniscient ones who teach contradictory matters..."

When all [these teachers] possess equal causes, who indeed could be singled out as the one? (3148) Among the many—such as the Sugata, Kapila, Kaṇabhakṣa, Akṣapāda, and others—who are postulated as omniscient by their respective devotees, when they are the objects of proof, which single one among them can be determined or ascertained as omniscient? For the reason for ascertaining omniscience—the fact that they all teach matters beyond the reach of the senses—is the same for all.
Furthermore, it is not logical to determine that all of them are omniscient, because they all teach mutually contradictory doctrines.

For it is not logical that all those who teach mutually contradictory doctrines should be seers of reality (*tattvadarśin*), because things possess a single nature and thus lack any association with multiple mutually contradictory intrinsic natures.
If it is argued that "only the Sugata is determined [to be such a seer]," he says: "If the Sugata... and so forth.
If the Sugata is omniscient, what is the proof that Kapila is not?
Furthermore, if both are omniscient, how can there be a difference in their views?
If it is argued that both must therefore be omniscient, he says: "Furthermore, if both... and so forth.

Furthermore, it might be argued: "The fact that one's speech is observed to be true even in a single instance allows for the inference of that very person’s complete and unerring knowledge of the reality of all things. To this he says: "In arithmetic and so forth," etc.; for everyone is truthful regarding a portion [of knowledge] such as arithmetic.
No distinction can be determined among the Victors, Buddhas, and other beings.
For among all embodied beings, including the Victors and Buddhas, speech that is non-contradictory is indeed observed in certain instances regarding limited domains such as mathematics;

for it is not the case that those who speak much (or chatter excessively) would have nothing at all that is true in meaning. As it has been said: "In a man who speaks much, there is not even one word that lacks a true meaning."

Furthermore, since there is no discernible distinction among all [proponents] due to their having identical causes, it would follow that everyone possesses omniscience; however, this is not tenable, as it was previously stated that [their teachings] involve instructions on mutually contradictory matters.

Now, it might be argued: "He alone shall be omniscient whose speech cannot be refuted or contradicted by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) anywhere. To this, he says: "By whomsoever... and so forth.

By the very same reason through which omniscience is established for one person merely out of partiality for one's own side, that same reason applies to another as well. [This is true] regarding the polemical arguments used with vehemence in the proof of the omniscient Jina. (3151)
Whatever the Śākyas speak, the Jains employ those very same [arguments].
In that case, since their proofs and refutations are unstable, diverse, and swallowed up by the arising of counter-reflections, how can a definitive conclusion be reached? (3152–3153)
For the very same reason that is employed by the sons of the Sugata to establish the omniscience of the Sugata—

namely, "The Sugata directly knows the reality of all objects because he teaches objects that have not been heard or inferred and are not erroneous, just as one who has directly perceived water and the like teaches it"— this very same reason is presented by the Digambaras to establish the omniscience of Jina.
Consequently, the doubt remains exactly as it was before.

For instance, when the Digambaras present proofs for the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of the Jina, the Śākyas raise these objections: "He is not omniscient because the doctrines he taught, such as *syādvāda* and so forth, are untenable. Similarly, when the Śākyas present proofs for the omniscience of the Sugata, the Jainas likewise raise these objections: "He is not omniscient because the doctrines he taught, such as momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and so forth, are untenable."

And thus, just as a reflection arises immediately following the presence of an object, so too do refutations that stand in mutual opposition to these proofs arise immediately after those proofs. Therefore, how can a determination regarding anyone’s omniscience be made by means of these unstable proofs and refutations, which are swallowed up by the very emergence of their reflections?
It might be argued: "He alone for whom no refutation can be made by anyone in the ultimate sense shall be recognized as omniscient. To this he says: "In this way," and so forth;
thus, when those who are candidates for omniscience have been mutually refuted.
The proponent of the Vedas will slay all those who have been reduced to a small remnant.
Elevating himself, he says: "Just as a certain herb," and so forth;
just as any herb whatsoever that has been touched by the tips of a mongoose's teeth [is effective].
Even when employed by those merely playing, it destroys all snake venom;

likewise, whatever reasoning—whether worldly or Vedic—resides in the mouths of those who proclaim the Vedas, it removes the poison of the knowledge of the "serpents" such as the Śākyas and others. (3155–3156)
What, then, is this "whatever reasoning" [he refers to]? He says: "Of whom," and so forth:

"Who indeed would postulate that person for whom reasons characterized by being an object of knowledge (*jñeya*), being an object of valid cognition (*prameya*), being a real entity (*vastu*), being existent (*sattva*), and so on, are capable of refutation? (3157)
He who imagines that an omniscient being is established by means of a single instrument of knowledge surely maintains that one perceives all objects, such as tastes and the like, with the eye alone.

For he for whom properties such as "being an object of knowledge" (jñeyatva) and so forth—while remaining unperceived as common to both similar and dissimilar instances—constitute subverting arguments, is utterly impossible; thus, he should not be accepted by a discerning person.
For instance, it can be argued: "The Sugata is not omniscient, because he is knowable, cognizable, a real entity, existent, a speaker, a person, and so forth, like a man on the street.
Nor are these [reasons] inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

To explain: one is held to be omniscient through the knowledge of all things; and that thorough knowledge of every object must occur either by means of sensory cognition or by means of mental cognition.

It cannot first be by means of sensory cognition (*indriyajñāna*), because that has restricted objects as its domain; thus, it is illogical for it to have all objects as its domain. For instance, cognitions such as those of the eye and so forth are produced by their respective causes—the sense organs—which act as restrictors, and are therefore of a nature that grasps only restricted objects. Consequently, they are well-known in the world as not transcending the boundaries of their own specific objects; thus, it is not logical for them to grasp all objects. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the various sense organs being redundant.

Furthermore, regarding that which is postulated by the Buddhist—that by means of a single cognition one knows all phenomena (*dharmas*), even those such as taste, form, and so forth, which are apprehended by distinct sense organs—it follows from his own statement, "One knows everything by one; one sees everything by one," that this proponent, the Buddhist, must necessarily understand all phenomena, including taste and the rest, through a cognition that functions by means of the eye as its instrument. Nor can it be argued: "Let there not be a simultaneous grasping of all objects by a single cognition, but it will occur by means of multiple cognitions."

Since multiple cognitions cannot occur simultaneously, and even if they could, there would still be no apprehension of all objects; for the minds of others are not the objects of sensory cognition, and it is impossible for that [sensory cognition] to grasp objects that have reached beyond its range, such as those that are distant, subtle, or obstructed.

It might be argued: "Even if the apprehension of heterogeneous objects by cognitions such as those of the eye is not observed at present, it is still possible that at some other time, someone may have had the apprehension of a heterogeneous object. To this, he says: "By those of such a kind," and so forth.
Whatever kind of objects are perceived by whatever kinds of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) as observed by people at present, they were exactly the same in other times as well.

For the specific determination of the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of entities is tied to their causes; it is not accidental. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that everything could possess the nature of everything else. Consequently, how could a change ever be possible for that which has acquired its own existence tied to such causes? For it is not conceivable that smoke, whose very existence is tied to fire (dhūmaketu), could arise from anything else—this is the intended meaning.
Nor is the position that it [the mental cognition] functions through the knowledge of the mind valid;
for although it has all objects as its domain, it nevertheless lacks an independent operation of grasping objects, because that would entail the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so forth.

Furthermore, since it is dependent on others and has as its object only that which is grasped by sensory cognition, the determination of objects such as those that are distant, subtle, concealed, or the minds of others—which have not been made objects of sensory cognition—would not be possible through it.

It might be argued: "Since we observe differences in degrees of excellence among individuals due to the practice of wisdom and other qualities, it is possible that an ultimate limit of excellence also exists. To this, he says:
"Even those men," and so forth—"even those men who are seen to possess superior wisdom, intelligence, and strength..."
This is due to the existence of slight differences [in capacity], and not because of the perception of supersensible objects.
For even a wise man, though capable of perceiving subtle things, excels other men without overstepping the limits of his own kind. (3160–3161)
For it is never observed that anyone, even through practice, attains the vision of supersensuous objects;

to illustrate this—a man, though exceedingly wise and capable of perceiving subtle matters through his refined intellect, is seen to excel other men only by surpassing their own kind—that is, the natural dispositions inherent to the human species—while still not transcending the limitations such as the lack of divine vision; indeed, no one is ever seen who is actually endowed with divine vision or the like. This is the sense.

And then— the sense is that what is proclaimed by the Buddhists, namely, "With his divine eye, which is perfectly pure and transcends that of humans, he sees beings going to a happy rebirth and going to an unhappy rebirth," and so forth, is simply not tenable. 3160–3161.

Granted that there may be an excellence in all cognitions due to practice and other factors, nevertheless, these [cognitions] excel only while remaining within the boundaries of their own respective objects; demonstrating this in detail, he says: "In sounds accessible to the ear," etc.
An excellence in persons is observed through the perception of distant and subtle sounds, not through the perception of forms and so forth. (3162)

Furthermore, by the attainment of excellence, even the eye performs the illumination of subtle forms located at a distance, but it does not perform the seeing of sound and so forth. (3163) [The compound] *dūrasūkṣmeṣūpalabdhībhiḥ* means "by means of perceptions"—that is, cognitions—of distant and subtle objects; the third case ending (*-bhiḥ*) is used here in the sense of a characteristic (*itthambhūtalakṣaṇa*). Alternatively, there is a reading *dūrasūkṣmopalabdhitaḥ*, in which case the fifth case ending (*-taḥ*) is applied in the sense of a cause (*hetu*), and the suffix *-tas* should be understood as belonging to the group beginning with *ādi*.
But the perception of sound and so forth is not performed by the eye; this is the connection [of the sentence].

Thus far, it has been shown that the sensory cognitions do not transcend the limits of their own respective objects; now, he demonstrates that the excellence of mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is seen precisely through its non-transgression of the objects it practices—beginning with the words "In this way," etc.:
"In this way, a great excellence is observed in the investigations of the treatises, but the knowledge of other treatises is not obtained by that [knowledge] alone. (3164)
Clarifying this very point, he says: "Having known," and so forth:
"Having known grammar well, one's intellect regarding correct and incorrect words is refined; it is not so in determining the stars, lunar days, or planetary positions. (3165)
Even an eminent astrologer is not able to know the correctness of words such as "vit" [in the context of] lunar and solar eclipses and so forth;
likewise, even one who possesses an excellence of knowledge regarding the Vedas, Itihāsas, and other sciences [is not able to do so]. || 3166 ||

One who is capable of directly perceiving the deities of creation and the *apūrva* (unseen force) is not merely a knower of light (*jyotirvit*). The analysis of the compound is as follows: "one who possesses that excellence (*atiśaya*) of knowledge regarding the Vedas, histories, and so forth, which is found in a *jyotirvit*."
By the term *apūrva*, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are expressed.

Furthermore, even when excellence occurs by transgressing the limits of its own object, it does not reach the state of ultimate perfection; rather, it is observed to be limited only by a certain degree of distinction. Demonstrating this, he says: "One who, having leaped, goes ten cubits into the sky," and so forth.
One who indeed goes ten cubits into the sky after leaping...

He is not able to travel a *yojana*, even with hundreds of practices. For instance, if some individuals whose bodies are burdened by accumulated phlegm are initially unable to leap even a hand’s breadth into the air, yet later, through the process of practice, they acquire bodily lightness and become capable of leaping across a space of ten hands in the sky, nevertheless, they would still not be able to fly even a single *yojana* through the path of the air, even with a hundred efforts.
He concludes with the words "Therefore," and so forth:
"Therefore, even by those possessing superior cognitions who have gone very far, it is possible to know only something slightly more [than others], but not that which is beyond the senses. (3169)
"Exalted cognitions" (*atiśayajñānāni*) means cognitions that are preeminent (*atiśayena*) or excellent (*prakarṣeṇa*);
the compound is formed by a *yogavibhāga* (separation of rules) even for the third [case],
and "by them" (*taiḥ*) is an instrumental of instrument (*karaṇatṛtīyā*).
Clarifying this very point, he says: "Of one situated in a single room," and so forth; that perception which proceeds [is as follows].
Its capacity would exist only for that [object], and certainly not for another object within a different room.
And as for those objects separated by great distances—by lands, mountains, oceans, or by other continents and islands—who here could perceive them while remaining right here? (3170–3171)
*Varṣa*—a specific region of the world;
for example, the region of Bhārata is called *Bhāratavarṣa*.
Showing that others as well have placed their own hands here, he says "Nala," and so forth:
"And this [treatise] belongs to both Nala and Ṛtuparṇa, who were knowers of the heart of horses and dice."
While traveling together on the carriage, Ṛtuparṇa spoke these words:
"No one knows everything; an omniscient being is not possible.
There is no single person in whom knowledge reaches its ultimate perfection. (3172–3173)
It is said that the word "saṃvāha" refers to a chariot;
for thus it is heard: there was once a king named Nala.
It is said that, being ignorant of the secret of the dice, he lost his entire kingdom at gambling;
and his queen, named Damayantī,
accompanied him alone as he entered the forest, having been stripped of all his royal power.
Even after he had arrived there, by the power of fate, he was separated from that queen;

with his face clouded by tears born of the intense grief of separation from his beloved, plunging into an ocean of anxiety, and becoming exceedingly emaciated in body as he wandered here and there, he somehow adopted the life of a servant to King Ṛtuparṇa and remained there unrecognized.
And that queen of his, by some means or other, reached her father’s house.
Her father proclaimed Damayantī’s svayaṃvara throughout all lands so that her husband might come there;
this was heard by King Ṛtuparṇa, who thought, "Indeed, there is a svayaṃvara for Damayantī. Upon hearing this, he set out to go there with Nala as his charioteer.
Now, Ṛtuparṇa was an expert in the secret of dice, but he did not know the secret of horses.
Nala, however, was an expert in the heart of horses but was not an expert in the heart of dice;
this was fully known by Ṛtuparṇa, who, having realized that "this man is an expert in the heart of horses," said to him: "O sir, tell me the heart of horses."
Nala also said: "I shall tell you [the secret], provided that you also tell me the heart of dice (*akṣahṛdaya*).
Then this was declared by Ṛtuparṇa: "No one knows everything," and so forth.
Thereafter, King Nala, having learned the heart of dice from Ṛtuparṇa, won back his kingdom once more and brought it home; such is the report.

Furthermore—being omniscient, one must necessarily know objects of the past and the future; otherwise, if there were knowledge of only the present, one would be a knower of a single portion rather than omniscient. Demonstrating that knowledge of the future and so forth is indeed possible, he says: "In the future," and so on.
Direct perception possesses not even the slightest capacity to perceive the future; nor can inference and the like arise without signs (liṅga) and so forth.
Since direct perception arises through the power of the object's own efficacy, and since the future is not yet an existing entity, there is no operation of direct perception with respect to it.
Nor can it be established by inference, because of the absence of a logical mark (liṅga);
for no logical mark known to be connected with a future object exists anywhere, since the future does not yet exist.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the inclusion of an example (dṛṣṭānta) is intended.
The mention of the "future" is illustrative; the inclusion of the "past" should also be understood, since there too, due to its non-substantiality, there is no operation of direct perception.
Therefore, the pervasion of the set of reasons, such as "being an object of cognition," is established.

For this very reason, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the previously stated reason— "because its form has been made the object of the means of valid cognition consisting in non-apprehension" (3174)— is thus explained.
Having thus demonstrated the pervasion of the reasons, he concludes by saying "therefore," and so forth.
Therefore, there is no direct perceiver of supersensuous objects;
rather, he who perceives through the eternal word, he truly perceives.
(3175) This might be argued: not everyone perceives through the eternal word alone.
To explain: Śākyamuni perceives from the words composed by the sage Kanakakāśyapa and others, and another [person] perceives from those as well;
regarding this, he says "this" and so forth, referring to one who, being unable to tolerate this, [relies] on another human-authored scripture (pauruṣeya-āgama).
The cognition of objects beyond the senses is also attributed to the Buddha and others;
since he is equal to that [person] in this respect, your statement lacks authority, and the same arguments previously stated must be applied to the person as well. (3176–3177)

Regarding this—namely, the statement just mentioned: "He who sees by means of eternal speech sees"—the Buddhist and others who cannot tolerate this and think thus: "One does not see everything by means of eternal speech, but rather by what was composed by another person, such as Śākyamuni [seeing] by means of the scripture (āgama) composed by Kanakakāśyapa and others"—for one who speaks in this way, it must be stated that his statement lacks authority (*apramāṇatā*). This is because his statement is the word of that other person, and for the reason that it is equal to the word of any person whose reliability has been observed.
The connection is as follows: it must be stated that the person who composes the scripture is not an authority;
why? By means of the previously mentioned reasons, such as being an object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and being an object of valid cognition (*prameya*).
[Objection: But surely the succession of Buddhas is beginningless, and therefore the established doctrine (siddhānta) composed by them is also beginningless.

Consequently, just as in the case of the succession of those devoted to the Vedas and the Vedas themselves, these two [the Buddha’s teachings and their tradition] are also beginningless and thus free from fault. To this, he replies with the verse beginning: "Of the words of an author and of artificial compositions," and so forth.
As for the alleged beginninglessness of the statements composed by an author, that which lacks the support of the two means of valid cognition cannot establish their validity.
Demonstrating this very point, he says: "Not [the case] with the statements of Śauddhodani," and so forth.
The authority of the words of Śauddhodani does not arise from dependence [on another], for he himself did not perceive Dharma; likewise it is with Śauddhodani and his words.
Just as there is a lack of authority for Śauddhodani and his speech, so too it is for others such as Kanaka and Kāśyapa and their words.
Even if one were to postulate beginninglessness for such individuals,
it does not go beyond the state of being invalid, because it remains situated within the category of lack of authority.

Therefore, even if the beginninglessness of such persons and their statements is postulated, it does not transcend that lack of authority; rather, it remains far removed from it, because they remain situated precisely in the state of non-authority.
Therefore, those who act like Mīmāṃsakas assert that Buddhas possess a commonality of beginninglessness, just as those who study the Vedas do;
however, because their ignorance is not of the same specific nature, they do not attain equality with them.
In this way, validity and invalidity would both indeed be beginningless.

(3182) In that case, even if the Buddhists and others have described the similarity between the Buddha and the students of the Veda based merely on their beginninglessness, nevertheless, validity is not established by beginninglessness alone,
because there is no contradiction in validity and invalidity both being beginningless.
The collective meaning is as follows: the validity and invalidity of those who merely study the Vedas and of those such as Buddha, respectively, would be beginningless;
however, it is not the case that because both are beginningless, either validity alone or invalidity alone is established. (3181)
Clarifying this very point by means of an illustration, he says: "Those which," and so forth.
For those [factors]—the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and their fallacies (*tadābhāsa*), as well as their respective qualities (*guṇa*) and defects (*doṣa*)—are indeed beginningless (*anādi*).
Not all things become equal merely by virtue of being beginningless.
Just as gold, which exists as it is, is a factor in worldly transactions and is without beginning or end, so too is illusory gold; how then could it be equal to that [real gold]? (3183–3184)
The analysis of the compound is: "the qualities and defects of valid cognition and its fallacies.

Now, having avoided the charge of the unestablished nature (*asiddhatā*) of the fact that [the Buddha] has a body made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*), he states the distinction of the Veda from the Omniscient One while establishing the non-existence of the latter:
"Omniscience in the case of the Buddha and others, and the eternity of the Veda—now the distinction between those who claim these two are equal is being stated. (3185)

To those who speak thus— that there is no difference between the two because they are equal as causes for correct practice, since the cognition of supersensuous objects occurs either through the eternal Veda or through the words of an omniscient being— the specific distinction of the Veda is now stated. 3185

For instance: [the opponent] considers that since an omniscient being is not established by even one among the five means of valid cognition—perception, inference, verbal testimony, analogy, or presumption—how could there be any similarity between such a non-existent entity, whose form has been swallowed by the means of valid cognition known as non-apprehension (*abhāva-pramāṇa*), and the Veda, which is a means of valid cognition recognized even by cowherds and their wives? Thinking thus, he refutes the establishment of this [omniscient being] through the five means of valid cognition, beginning with "an omniscient being," etc., stating:
"First of all, an omniscient being is not perceived by people like us at present."

Nor is there any observed part or logical mark (*liṅga*) that could lead to an inference [of an omniscient being]. (3186) First of all, an omniscient being is not perceived by people like us who possess limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*). For the perception of those with limited vision is threefold: sensory cognition, mental cognition, and the self-awareness (*ātmasaṃvedana*) of all minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). None of these three types of perception is capable of making an omniscient being known, because they do not have that as their object. Sensory cognition is restricted to the five objects such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth; therefore, it does not take as its object the cognitive qualities (*buddhi-dharma*) inherent in the mental continuum of another.

Nor [is it perceived] by mental cognition (*mānasa*), because that—by virtue of grasping an object immediately following the object apprehended by sensory cognition—has as its objects specifically determined forms and so forth, just like sensory cognition.

Nor [is it perceived] by self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), because that has as its objects only the present minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) existing within one's own continuum; therefore, by means of that, the mental phenomena belonging to another's continuum or those belonging to one's own continuum but yet to come cannot be known.
Furthermore, since it is precisely the yogic cognition that is the probandum (*sādhya*), the consideration of whether it is grasped or not grasped does not apply here.
Nor can it be established by inference; for the Buddhists maintain that inference relies upon three types of logical marks (*liṅga*).

Among these, since the present context concerns the proof of an affirmation (*vidhi*), non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is not applicable here, nor is the effect (*kārya*), because the causal relation is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*), and no causal relation can be proven between anything and an omniscient being who is beyond all sensory reach.

Even a "nature" (svabhāva) reason does not establish the existence of an omniscient being; for if that [omniscient being] is not perceived, it is impossible to apprehend a nature that is non-different from him. Therefore, a "portion" (ekadeśa) that is observed, well-known, and serves as a logical mark (liṅga)—that is, a property of the subject (pakṣadharma)—is not possible when examined, such that it might lead to the inference of an omniscient being. Furthermore, in establishing the existence of an omniscient being, every reason fails to transcend the three types of fallacy: unestablishedness (asiddhi), contradiction (viruddhatva), and inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva).

For instance, when a reason (hetu) is stated, it must be designated as either a property of existence (bhāvadharma), a property of non-existence (abhāvadharmma), or a property of both; thus there are three possible positions.

Among these, with regard to the omniscient being as the subject (dharmin), a property of existence cannot be established as admitted by the opponent, because that very subject is unestablished (asiddha) precisely insofar as it is the probandum (sādhya); or, if it were established, it would follow that there is no dispute.
For how could a proponent who desires that [subject] to be a property of an existent (bhāvadharma) not desire that argument?
This is because it is impossible to apprehend a mere property (dharmamātra) that lacks a substratum.

Nor is a reason that is a property of a non-existent (abhāvadharma) suitable for establishing an omniscient being, because it is contradictory (viruddha), as it establishes the opposite of existence. Nor is a reason that is a property of both [existent and non-existent] admissible, because it is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

For how indeed could the nature of being a logical reason—characterized by non-deviation from existence, which is obtained through the exclusion of its occurrence in the counter-example (vipakṣa) called non-existence—be experienced when there is no establishment of either the property of existence, the property of non-existence, or the property of both?
Therefore, since none of these three types of partial [reasons] exist as a mark (liṅga), they do not lead to inference; thus, the omniscient one is not established through inference.
He shows that there is no determination of an omniscient being even from verbal testimony, stating: "Nor is there any scriptural injunction," and so forth.

"Nor is there any scriptural injunction that makes known an eternal omniscient being; for how could he be established by something artificial, or even by something non-artificial [i.e., eternal], which is not true? (3187)

The cognition that arises regarding an object not in contact [with the senses] from a word is verbal knowledge (*śābda*). That is of two kinds: that produced by an eternal word and that caused by human utterance.
Among these, the first is not possible because there exists no such eternal scripture (*āgama*) that establishes an omniscient being.

Furthermore, as for what is recited in the Upaniṣads and other texts—such as "He who is truthful in speech, truthful in resolve, and truthful in desire, he is to be sought after, he is to be known"—that too must be regarded as a mere explanatory passage (*arthavāda*).
And as for that human speech which is said—"The Blessed One is the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha"—since that [speech] lacks authority, how could he be made known by that which is untrue?
It might be argued: "We do not recognize an omniscient being based on just any random statement."
What then?
By that very statement spoken by the Blessed One:
"I am omniscient, I am all-seeing; there is nothing whatsoever unknown to the Tathāgata," and so forth.
Therefore, he says "Now, etc. to show that [the omniscient one] is understood from his very word:
"Now, if the omniscient one is recognized by others through his word alone, how can there be the establishment of those two, which involve mutual dependence? (3188)
This being the case, the fault of mutual dependence (itaretarāśraya) arises.
To explain how this is so, he says: "By virtue of being spoken by an omniscient one," and so forth.
"A statement is true because it was spoken by an omniscient one; therefore, how can its existence [as an omniscient speaker] be established?
Without another established root-source, how could both of these be proven?
For instance, the validity of that person's word cannot be ascertained so long as it is not understood that 'this was indeed spoken by an omniscient one.'"
And since the cognition of that omniscient being arises from that very word, there is clearly a mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*);
the meaning is that it does not arise "from another established cause" (*siddhān mūlāntarāt*),
that is, from another ascertained cause.

Now, it might be argued that he is determined to be omniscient based on the words of disciples such as Śāriputra, since it was said by him: "This one, the delight of the Śākya clan, is omniscient. To this, [the author] replies: "But from a statement composed by one who is not omniscient," and so forth;
that is, from a statement devoid of a [reliable] foundation, composed by one who is not omniscient.
Why do they not realize the Omniscient One from their own words?

For there is no distinction between the words of another and one's own words such that the former has not attained the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). We perceive no reason at all—other than sheer stupidity—why Buddhists do not accept the Omniscient One from their own words, yet accept him from the words of another.

Now, suppose it is thought that there have been and will be infinite Tathāgatas, and therefore the omniscience of one is established by the word of another, and that of another by the word of yet another—to this he says: "Many omniscient ones would have to be postulated" and so forth;
for many omniscient ones would have to be postulated in order to establish the existence of even a single omniscient one.
Whoever is not himself omniscient cannot comprehend an omniscient being.

(3191) For one who pursues a succession of omniscient beings in order to establish even a single omniscient being, it would be impossible for a person of limited vision to reach a definitive certainty regarding an omniscient being even at the exhaustion of an entire human lifespan; thus, it would follow that one must postulate an infinite series of omniscient beings.

Moreover—let alone the fact that those of the present day are unable to understand an omniscient being who is not present; rather, even those contemporaneous with him are simply incapable of knowing him because they are not themselves omniscient. Demonstrating this, he says: "This one is omniscient," and so forth.
Indeed, even by those cognizers of his time, it is impossible to know [him] as "this one is omniscient" if they are devoid of the specific cognition of his knowledge and its objects. (3192)
If the Omniscient One has not been realized by someone, then for that person, those [Buddha’s] words lack authoritative validity, just like the words of others, because their source is unknown.

His knowledge is "that-knowledge" (*taj-jñāna*); that which has such knowledge as its object to be determined is "that-[object]-knowledge" (*tad-vijñāna*); and being devoid of—that is, lacking—that [knowledge], they are so described.
Alternatively, that which is to be known by that knowledge is not known by it; that is, they are empty of that knowledge, meaning they are not omniscient.

For one cannot conclude from the mere observation of the body that someone is omniscient, because this conclusion is inseparable from the prior apprehension of a connection with distinguished knowledge.
And that distinguished knowledge has all things as its object and is the means of accomplishment; however,

its having all things as its object cannot be determined without the apprehension of those objects to be grasped by it, for the cognition of "one who possesses a staff" does not occur without the apprehension of the staff.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: For whatever [object] there is an apprehension conditioned by a specific attribute (*upādhi*), there is no apprehension of that [object] in the absence of the apprehension of its attribute. For example, the apprehension of a staff-bearer (*daṇḍin*) conditioned by the apprehension of a staff does not occur when the form of the attribute—the staff—is not apprehended. And for those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*), there is no apprehension of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) as an attribute of the apprehension of the omniscient one’s cognition. This is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), because the apprehension of the possessor of an attribute is pervaded by the apprehension of the attribute, and that [apprehension of the attribute] is absent here.

Furthermore, at that time, for one who is not omniscient and thus cannot ascertain an omniscient being even though he is present, the words of an omniscient person— even if they exist— lack authority because they remain unascertained; this is because there is an absence of the ascertainment of the omniscient being’s cognition, which is the cause for ascertaining the authority of the source,
just like the words of any other person, such as a man on the street.

Now, suppose it is thought: "By thoroughly knowing the various types of mental dispositions, conducts, and so forth of all his disciples, and by means of the miracles of teaching and non-teaching, he wins over the minds of those to be trained and effortlessly demonstrates to them his own nature as omniscience. To this, he says: "Even by all the disciples," and so forth.
Even if one were to corroborate the objects known by all his disciples,
he would not be omniscient, because of the exclusion of objects known by other people;
nor is it possible to corroborate all that is knowable as known by every human being.

There is no meeting with the people residing in the three worlds throughout the three periods of time. Even if one has cognized certain objects known only to a limited number of people present at that particular time, one does not thereby become omniscient, because of the non-cognition of those objects known to other people who are not present at that time.
For one does not become an all-knower through the cognition of only a single part, as that would lead to an over-extension of the principle.

Nor is it possible for there to be a correspondence with the objects known by all people present at that time, because there would be no correspondence with those who are far away or who do not seek [to know].

To this [objection]—namely, that when all people together approach the Tathāgata and ask whatever they wish to ask, the Blessed One explains each at that very moment, and therefore there indeed exists a correspondence with the objects of knowledge known by all men—he replies: "by those residing in the three worlds and the three times."

For a meeting of men existing in the past, future, and present times is not possible anywhere; nor is it possible for those residing in the three worlds consisting of heaven, the netherworld (pātāla), and the mortal realm—or rather, the three worlds should be understood as consisting of the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness. 3194

It might be argued as follows: "If he did not possess the capacity to know all things known by the entire world, then how could there even be agreement regarding a mere portion of what is known? Yet such agreement does exist; therefore, we conclude that he indeed possesses the capacity to know all categories of objects. To this, [the author] replies: "Even one who knows only a little," and so forth.
For even one who knows only a little is able to delude people to some small extent.

Those whose minds are deluded by devotion might grasp [him] as omniscient; yet some, though capable of correctly identifying what has been eaten, what has been thought of, or what object is held in a closed fist through deceptive knowledge, are devoid of knowledge regarding Dharma and other such matters. (3196–3197)
Likewise, some who are skilled in illusions, magic tricks, and the like, delude ignorant people such that they appear to be omniscient.

(3198) For the knowledge of dharma, adharma, and so forth is not established for one merely by possessing a slight knowledge of supersensuous objects; this is because there is inconclusiveness due to those who possess deceptive knowledge and are skilled in illusions, magic tricks, and the like.

For instance: through the application of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, they indeed correctly identify what has been eaten—such as food and condiments—as well as the object conceived by the mind and the substance held in the fist;

yet, on this account, they do not become knowers of dharma and the like, just as certain experts in sorcery display various gardens, celestial chariots, hosts of apsarases, sons of gods, and so on in the sky. Thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anekānta*).

[Objection: But surely in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, Brahmā and others are celebrated as omniscient; for instance, it is recited therein that "Brahmā’s knowledge is unimpeded, as is his dispassion. How then is it that an omniscient being is not established through scripture? To this, he says: "In the Itihāsas... and so forth.
Even though in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas Brahmā and others are celebrated as "all-knowing," in the sense that "his knowledge is unimpeded" and "he possesses dispassion" [3199].

That [omniscience] must also be spoken of only in a figurative sense, like the meaning of mantras and explanatory passages (arthavādas); or rather, it refers to the non-obstruction [of knowledge] regarding the four subjects under discussion: dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa. || 3200 || Dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa—among these four that are under discussion...
His knowledge is unimpeded, yet it does not have all objects as its domain.
Just as there are explanatory passages (*arthavāda*) in the mantras, so too in the epics and other texts, the omniscience of Brahmā and others is to be understood from such explanatory passages;
for an explanatory passage is so called because, while having one meaning, it speaks of another meaning.

Alternatively, because his knowledge is unimpeded regarding the four subjects under discussion— dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa— the unimpeded nature of this [knowledge] of Brahmā and others is specified with respect to these objects of knowledge,
but not because it is unimpeded with respect to all possible objects.

[Objection: But if the cognition of an object were obstructed by that [quality] such as *dharma* and so forth in other cases, how could it be called "unobstructed" (*apratigha*)? To this, he says: "For not... and so forth.

For it is not by mere non-obstruction that [knowledge] is said to have everything as its object; rather, because it is unobstructed even with respect to its own objects, it is indeed "unobstructed" (*apratigha*).

If this is so—if it is called "unobstructed" simply because it is unobstructed with respect to its own objects—then since the knowledge of all persons is likewise unobstructed with respect to its own objects, what is the distinction of Brahmā and others such that their knowledge alone is called "unobstructed" and not that of others? To this, he says: "And this," etc.

And this knowledge that yields its fruit extends as far as the domain of dharma and so forth; however, there is no purpose whatsoever in knowing all things such as trees. This knowledge of what is useful is not obstructed.

Therefore, he receives the designation of "unimpeded cognition" (apratigha-vijñāna). This explains as follows: regarding those factors such as *dharma* that are conducive to the goals of man (*puruṣārtha*), the knowledge of that very Brahmā proceeds unimpededly, and not that of others. To manifest this distinction, it is said that the knowledge of Brahmā and the others is "unimpeded" because it is unobstructed with respect to its own objects; it is not merely "knowledge of what is useful" (*aupayika-jñāna*) for others.

Regarding "the means" (*aupayika*): knowledge concerning dharma and so forth, which are conducive to the goals of man (*puruṣārtha*), is "knowledge of the means"; this continues until [the state] without distinction (*nirviśeṣa*).
And this is a qualification of the knowledge that is effective for the means [to liberation].
Alternatively, he states another position:
"Or rather, that knowledge exists within the self itself, set in motion by the practice of meditation;
it is because of its very non-obstruction that the non-obstruction of knowledge is asserted. (3205)
"In the self" means in the person;
"of that very [self]" refers to that same [person].
Regarding the knowledge whose object is the self:

[Objection] But surely the ten imperishable qualities, such as knowledge and so forth, are recited as belonging to Īśvara; how then is it that he does not become omniscient through his possession of imperishable knowledge? To this, he says: "Knowledge," and so forth.

Even Śaṅkara, who is heard of as possessing ten imperishable qualities—namely knowledge, dispassion, and the eightfold sovereignty—is [included here] because he possesses knowledge through his self-knowledge.

Knowledge is the realization of reality; dispassion is the turning away from sense objects; and sovereignty is eightfold: *aṇimā* (minuteness), *laghimā* (lightness), *mahimā* (greatness), *prāpti* (attainment), *prākāmya* (efficacy), *īśitva* (lordship), *vaśitva* (control), and *yatra-kāmāvasāyitā* (the power to resolve at will). He whose followers possess these ten imperishable qualities, such as knowledge and the rest, is called "possessing the ten imperishables" (*daśāvyaya*).
Among these, *aṇimā* is when, having become a minute body, one wanders through the world at ease, invisible to all beings;
*laghimā* is when, by virtue of lightness, one moves about like the wind;
*mahimā* is when, being honored, saluted, and worshipped in all worlds, one becomes greater even than the great.
Attainment (*prāpti*) means that whatever one contemplates with the mind, one attains—
that is, *prākāmya* (the power of irresistible will)— meaning that one becomes possessed of abundant desire and is able to enjoy sense objects.
Sovereignty (*īśitva*) means that one becomes the lord of the three worlds.

Mastery (*vaśitva*) is that by which one brings all beings, both stationary and moving, under one's control; and one becomes Indra over them. Furthermore, there is the power of determining [one's own] will (*yatrakāmāvasāyitā*): through the knowledge of the Self, one dwells wherever one desires among the various abodes—whether in those of Brahmā, Prajāpati, the gods, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Pitṛs, Piśācas, humans, or animals.
The meaning is that he is "possessed of knowledge" by virtue of self-knowledge, but not by virtue of possessing a complete and exhaustive knowledge of all objects (3206).
Why, then, is Śaṅkara alone called "possessed of knowledge" even when there is only partial knowledge, and not anyone else? To this he says: "For this very reason," and so forth.
For this alone is that knowledge which is the vision of the pure self; that which pertains to the impure and its cause is called ignorance.
(3207) It is so described because it is both "pure" (*viśuddha*) and "self" (*ātman*); the compound [is thus] "the vision of that" (*tasya darśanam*).
The term "having that as its cause" (*tannimitta*) means that which is the cause (*nimitta*) of that vision of the pure self (*śuddhātmadarśana*); what is that? It is the self itself.
When that self, being the cause of that [vision], exists in a state of purity, yet an impure vision of the self continues to occur, that is called ignorance (*ajñāna*), because it is contemptible.

Now, one might object: "If it is admitted that the arising of pure knowledge for Brahmā and others results from the practice of meditation, then what is the cause of this hostility toward the Buddhas and others, such that their knowledge is not likewise accepted as unimpeded and pure? Anticipating this doubt, the author shows the distinction of Brahmā and the others by presenting an alternative view, saying: "But even so," and so forth—"but even so, because Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara have the Veda as their body..."
What omniscience can there be for a human being derived from the Veda, which consists of all knowledge?
Where are mortals such as the Buddhas, and where are the three supreme gods, that one should, out of delusion, hold the view that they too are omniscient by way of rivalry with them?
Because they have made the Veda their very self, they are called "embodiments of the Veda" (vedadeha);
because it is the cause of knowledge regarding all categories of existence, the Veda consists of omniscience.
This is what is meant.
For the knowledge of Brahmā and the others regarding dharma and so forth does not proceed unhindered by their own independent power;
rather,
it proceeds through the medium of the Veda.
Furthermore, you do not accept this [kind of attainment] for the Buddhas and others,
because their knowledge is self-dependent (*svāyatta*).
Moreover, it is indeed logical that the arising of pure knowledge occurs for Brahmā and others through the practice of meditation, since they, as deities, are superior to all people.
Furthermore, because it is recited in the Vedas,
such power as this can never be conceived for a human being, since he is the opposite of that;
therefore, the view that humans are also omniscient is a product of delusion.
This is a deluded view of yours.

It might be argued: "If Brahmā and others are recited in the Veda, then how would it not follow that the Veda itself is non-eternal due to its connection with non-eternal denotata? Conversely, if the eternity of the Vedas is maintained, then it contradicts the fact that Brahmā and others are denoted by the eternal Veda, because they are non-eternal. Alternatively, if there is no such contradiction [in their being denoted], then there is likewise no contradiction in Buddhas and others being denoted by it. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even though [the Veda] is eternal," and so forth.
Even though the Veda is an eternal scripture, there is the mention of the triad beginning with Brahmā;
and because of that [triad's] eternity, the eternity of the Vedas is not impaired.
(3210) "Because of that eternity" means:
Because those [beings] beginning with Brahmā are eternal;
he clarifies this very point with the words "For they," and so forth.
For they (the eternal souls) are eternally endowed with eternal qualities and eternal actions;

since it is possible for them to be designated by the eternal Vedas, there is no contradiction. However, for one who is non-eternal, such as Buddha and others, there can be no comprehension through an eternal scripture.
If the eternity of scripture is accepted, the postulation of an omniscient being is useless;
for [otherwise] it would follow that the relationship between word and meaning is not accessible through eternal scripture, which would entail its non-eternity.
Furthermore, an eternal scripture is not accepted by others;
or, if it were accepted, the postulation of an omniscient being would result in being rendered useless. (3211)
He demonstrates this very point: "Because it makes him known as omniscient"— that is,
because it makes him known as omniscient, the realization of the Dharma is superior for him.
Since the dharma known through the omniscient knowledge revealed by the Veda has been obscured,
only the knowledge of dharma and so forth that is not obscured is specified; thus, the status of being knowable through scripture is not established for an omniscient being.

It is held that the comprehension of Dharma itself is preferable to the mere indication of an omniscient being by means of an eternal scripture. How is it preferable? He says: "Revealed by the Veda," and so forth. For when the knowledge of Dharma arises based upon the Veda, it remains unobscured; otherwise, since worldly existence is uniform, such knowledge would be possible for everyone alike.
However, dharma, though known through the omniscience of the one made known by the Veda, is "hidden" because it is not manifest once he has attained *nirvāṇa*;
even during the state prior to *nirvāṇa*, there is an absence of instruction due to his lack of desire [to teach];
and even when there is instruction, there is an absence of hearing it by everyone, everywhere, and at all times.
He demonstrates that the omniscient one is not to be apprehended through the means of valid cognition known as analogy (upamāna) by stating: "one who is similar to an omniscient being," and so forth.
If someone similar to the Omniscient One were seen at present, then the existence of the Omniscient One could be understood through the force of analogy (*upamāna*).

For analogy, because its object is similarity along with its limiting conditions (*upādhi*), necessarily involves the apprehension of a similar thing immediately following the apprehension [of the first]; its domain is an object not currently present to the senses, such as the recollection of a cow by means of perceiving a *gavaya*. However, since no one similar to the Omniscient One is perceived or possible, analogy does not operate here due to the absence of the apprehension of a similar object.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That for which there is no apprehension of a similar thing is not cognizable through analogy (*upamāna*), just like the son of a barren woman; and there is no apprehension of a similar thing in the case of the Omniscient One. This is a non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Furthermore, it is shown that not only is the cognition of an omniscient being impossible through analogy, but rather, it is logical to understand from analogy that all men indeed lack omniscience; thus he says "men," and so forth.
Having observed that all men of the present day are non-omniscient, the certainty regarding the remaining [beings] as being non-omniscient is established through the analogy of similarity.

Furthermore, wishing to demonstrate that an omniscient being is not established even by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), he first raises the opponent's position, beginning with the words "For the instruction... (*upadeśo hi...*) and so forth.
For the instruction of the Buddha and others concerning the scope of dharma and adharma would not be possible otherwise, if he were not omniscient,
even though [the existence of] an omniscient being has been refuted by means of perception and other [pramāṇas]. (3217)

Regarding verse 3218: He who establishes an omniscient being in this manner through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)—namely, that "this instruction on dharma and so forth by the Buddha and others would not be possible otherwise if dharma and so forth were not directly known by him"—even though it has been refuted that perception and the other means of knowledge establish an omniscient being, he nevertheless maintains that a person who perceives everything is established by *arthāpatti*. The sense is that he maintains what is untenable, because of the reasoning that will be stated hereafter.

Alternatively— [the author] shows that this is indeed inference (*anumāna*) and not presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), because the three characteristics (*trairūpya*) are possible, by means of the words "Alternatively" (*yadvā*) and so forth;
or rather, the proof (*sādhana*) here proceeds as that which is observed in general (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*).
Elsewhere, it is stated that [the teaching] of the Omniscient One is preceded by knowledge,
because it is observed that whatever instruction there may be is preceded by knowledge,
just as the instruction regarding the potencies of *abhayā* and other such substances is of that nature. (3219–3220)
"This instruction regarding dharma and adharma, and the fact that it was composed by him,
allows us to infer that it is preceded by his knowledge.
By the phrase "inferred from general observation" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*), he states the impossibility of [the inference being] one based on specific observation (*viśeṣato dṛṣṭam*).

For when a specific relationship between a mark (*liṅga*) and its possessor (*liṅgin*) has been perceived through direct perception, and that very possessor is later inferred by means of that same mark for the purpose of eliminating doubt, then it is called inference based on what was specifically observed (*viśeṣato-dṛṣṭam anumānam*).

However, since no relationship whatsoever has been grasped between an omniscient being and the teaching of *dharma* and so forth, this [inference regarding an omniscient being] is only an inference based on what was observed in general (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭam*).

For instance: it is observed that, in general, instruction elsewhere within one's own continuum is preceded by knowledge. Therefore, just as the movement of the sun is inferred from its arrival at another location after observing Devadatta’s arrival at another location preceded by his movement, so too the knowledge of the Blessed One, such as Buddha, will be inferred from his instruction on the Dharma and so forth. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is an instruction is preceded by the speaker’s knowledge, just like the instruction regarding the medicinal power of *harītakī* and other substances; and this instruction of the Buddhas and others concerning the Dharma and so forth is indeed an instruction. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). 3219
Regarding this, he states the following reply: "Even otherwise," and so forth.
Since this [proposition] can be established otherwise, this presumption (arthāpatti) is not tenable;
for this very reason, even this inference does not stand as valid.
For the teaching of the Buddha and others can be accounted for in another way as well.

Because [an instruction] seen in dreams and so forth may arise from delusion, and because what is heard from scripture may be false due to [the speaker's] delusion and other factors, the instruction could occur otherwise as well; thus, both inference and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
To explain how they can occur otherwise, he says "svapnādi" and so forth.
As it is stated in the Śābara-bhāṣya: "For instruction arises even from delusion; when there is no delusion, it arises even from the Veda.

In that regard, [instruction] arising from delusion is seen, such as in the case of an object perceived in a dream; [instruction] arising from the Veda is seen, such as in the case of Manu and others. (3222)

However, as for those such as the Sugatas who are ignorant of the Vedas, it is possible that their teaching arose from delusion or for the purpose of deceiving others; this is what [the author] demonstrates with the words "Those who," and so forth:
"For those who are indeed ignorant of the Vedas, [their teaching] cannot possibly originate from the Veda."
Instructional teachings are those produced by corrupt instructors in the world, which proceed either from mere delusion alone,
or for the purpose of deluding disciples, or from delusion not based on that [true reality]. (3224–3225)
"Because it does not have that as its basis" means because it does not have the Veda as its basis.
How is this understood—that this teaching does not have its basis in the Vedas? He says: "If this [were so]," and so forth;
for if this were rooted in the Veda, it would [be known] from the proponents of the Veda themselves.
They should provide instruction just as Manu and others did;
however, because they gave instruction to fools and Śūdras,
it is known that their work is corrupt, being merely a deceptive fabrication like counterfeit coinage.

For if the instruction on dharma and other matters by the Buddha and others were rooted in the Veda, then they would have instructed only learned Brāhmaṇas, as Manu and others did; yet they did not instruct only Brāhmaṇas, but rather only dull-witted Śūdras. Therefore, it is understood that their teaching was conventional—that is, false—just like the practice of using counterfeit coins and the like. (3226–3227)

However, as for those such as Manu and others, since they were knowers of the Veda, their instruction on dharma and so forth is rooted solely in the Veda and not through their own independent authority; this is shown by the verse beginning with "ye tu" and so on:

"But those established authorities such as Manu and others, who are preeminently knowers of the three Vedas and whose treatises rely upon those knowers of the three Vedas, have utterances originating from the Veda. (3228)
The three Vedas, known as the Ṛg, Yajus, and Sāman, are called the Trayī; those who know them are called "knowers of the Trayī" (trayīvidaḥ), and the Brāhmaṇas are so designated.
Those for whom the treatises on Dharmaśāstra and other texts are resorted to by these knowers of the Trayī are described as such.
He states the reason for their reliance on those texts: "Their utterances originate from the Vedas."
Those whose utterances originate from the Veda are described as such.
To the question, "How is this also determined? he says: "Not without having seen," and so forth.
Neither the composition of these texts nor their transmission to disciples is possible without having first seen the Vedic sentences or having shown them to the students.
(3229) "Transmission" (*arpaṇa*) means making [them] known.

Thus, since the omniscient being is not established by any of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he is understood through the method of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*) as being simply non-existent. Therefore, this reason—namely, "because his form has been made the object of the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence"—is established; furthermore, it was previously demonstrated that this reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The underlying point is that the conventional usage of "non-existence" occurs precisely because there is no other cause for it. (3229)

As for those who think: "We do not establish the existence of an omniscient being by pointing him out specifically (śṛṅgagrāhikayā); rather, we establish his mere possibility in a general sense—that there exists some omniscient being, or that omniscience exists somewhere, because we observe the excellence of wisdom and other qualities"—to them he says this, beginning with "nara" (a man): "That 'there exists some man who is omniscient,' or even the proof that 'his omniscience exists'—any such argument employed would be deficient in its thesis. (3230)
The object that one intends to establish is not expressed by this [reason];
as for that which is stated, there is no purpose whatsoever in its establishment.
Since the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) of the reason has already been demonstrated previously, he now demonstrates the defect of the thesis (*pakṣadoṣa*) itself.
When one thing is intended to be proven, yet another is what is actually proposed as the thesis, that is a "deficient thesis" (pratijñānyūna), which is a fault of the position;
and here, it is the omniscience of one's own Teacher that is intended to be proven, not omniscience in general.

For instance—a wise person does not seek an omniscient being out of mere addiction; rather, it is out of a desire for engagement or withdrawal, thinking, "Having learned what is dharma and what is adharma from his words, I shall engage or withdraw. And even if such a person were established in a general sense, he would be of no use to a person regarding engagement, because one cannot ascertain his words without knowing his specific [teachings]. Therefore, that very specific [knowledge] must be established by one desiring engagement; thus, the general proposition is indeed deficient as a proposition, since it is the specific object intended to be proven that is required.
The specific distinction is that "that which is intended to be accomplished" refers to one's own Teacher.
That which is stated by means of this proposition.

Without contacting any specific particulars, one might claim that "there is some person who is omniscient" or "omniscience exists somewhere"; yet even if this were established, it would serve no purpose whatsoever.

He asks "How so? and says: "That omniscience which is asserted for the sake of establishing the truth of his scripture is not obtained merely by the establishment of some general omniscient being. (3232)
If that were so,
the truth of his scripture would be established.
To the question "Why is it not obtained?", he says: "As long as... and so forth.
As long as the Buddha is not omniscient, his word is false;
once an omniscient being is established anywhere, how could [the Buddha's] truthfulness be established? (3233)

For instance, as long as the omniscience of the Buddha is not established, there can be no certainty regarding the truthfulness of his word; nor would the truthfulness of the Buddha’s word be established by the general establishment of an omniscient being, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "in another," and so forth.

If there were another omniscient being, the truthfulness of another word would [only be established] through coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), for between those two there would be a relationship of primary and subordinate.
He asks: "When, indeed, would there not be a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between them? and answers with the words beginning "for in the case of coreferentiality," and so forth.
Co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) means that both of these— omniscience and truthful speech— reside in a single person.
The relationship of part and whole is the relationship of cause and effect;
this is what is meant: when there is a single substratum, truthfulness would be the cause of omniscience, and not otherwise, for [otherwise] there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

To show that even the proof constructed by others for the sake of establishing an omniscient being has been refuted by this very [argument], he says: "That which is called 'all' in this world," and so forth;
for whatever is perceptible in this world belongs to someone.

By means of the properties of being an object of cognition, knowability, and substantiality—just like curd, form, taste, and so forth—even if "mere cognition" were specified, the deficiency of the subject (pakṣa) would result;
for that which is intended as "the Omniscient One" is not established in such a manner. (3235–3236)
If there were someone other than the Buddha who had attained omniscience, what use would that knowledge be for establishing the authority of the Buddha’s words?

Whatever possesses the properties of being an object of cognition (*prameya*), being a real entity (*vastu*), and so forth, is perceptible to someone, just as the form, taste, and other qualities of curd; and since the entire collection of things has the nature of being objects of cognition and the like, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
In this case as well, as before, one must state the deficiency of the thesis and the inconclusiveness of the reason;
therefore, the establishment of omniscience is impossible neither through specific nor through general [attributes],
and thus it is established that there is no omniscient being.
Since that [object] does not exist, its verbal expression does not exist; therefore, no one can engage in activity based on such a verbal expression.

Alternatively, even granting that an omniscient person might exist, a word composed by an omniscient person is simply not possible; for this reason, demonstrating how [your] activity would [otherwise] come to pass, he says: "Having reached the ten stages," and so forth—that one who has reached the ten stages, upon the complete destruction of all passion and the like...
One perceives everything through a knowledge that is like pure crystal;
yet one who has entered meditative absorption and maintains a mental retention (*dhāraṇā*) whose object is all things,
though pervaded by all objects, is simply not capable of teaching.

For indeed, you describe it thus: one established on the tenth stage, through a knowledge as pure as clear crystal due to the removal of the stains of all defilements such as passion, discerns the entirety of the knowable.

Consequently, in that state, while maintaining *dhāraṇā*—the one-pointedness of mind—he is occupied solely with the realization of the object and is unable to teach the Dharma; for no one is capable of performing so many activities at once.
He says, "If, having emerged [from meditative absorption], he teaches," and so forth: "And when he might teach something as a single [entity], like an ordinary speaker."

That which is sung by one who knows only a single part could not be the speech of an omniscient being. For there is no engagement in speech without discursive thought (*vitarka*); thus, he must teach the Dharma while abiding in a mind characterized by conceptualization (*savikalpa*). Consequently, because there would be no distinction between a fool and a scholar in that state, he would not be omniscient; therefore, what he spoke would indeed be the speech of one who is not omniscient.

It might be argued as follows: he does not teach anything at all, because he is always established in non-conceptual meditative absorption; rather, by his sovereign power, there arise for those who are capable mental representations (*vijñapti*) that manifest as the teaching of various dharmas.

As it has been said: "Between the night the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment and the night he passed into parinirvāṇa, not even a single syllable was uttered or spoken by the Tathāgata. For what reason? Because the Tathāgata is eternally in a state of meditative equipoise (*samāhita*). Nevertheless, those who are to be trained through the teaching of syllables and sounds hear a sound emerging, emerging from the mouth, the *uṣṇīṣa*, and the *ūrṇā* of the Tathāgata," and so forth. Regarding this, he says: "While he has entered that meditative absorption," and so on; while he remains in that meditative absorption like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
Teachings issue forth at will even from walls and other such objects.
Through them, human beings come to know all matters they desire to understand,
and they swiftly attain benefits according to their spiritual capacity.
Such things as this, when being proclaimed, shine forth for those who possess faith; but we, being faithless, seek logical arguments. (3243) *Cintāratna*—the wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
This is the collective meaning here: this might appear plausible when described as being without authoritative proof to those who are full of faith;

however, how could those like us—who, by virtue of grasping only matters established by authoritative proof, seek out nothing but logical reasoning—accept this as it is being stated, when it is devoid of authoritative proof?

Furthermore—let us grant for the sake of argument that such a conceptualization might exist; nevertheless, the fact that teachings emerging from walls and the like originate through the sovereign power of an omniscient being remains nothing but doubtful. Thus, he shows that it is not appropriate for discerning people to place their trust in them as authoritative sources: "Of those [teachings] issued from walls and so forth," and so on.
Furthermore, for those [teachings] emerging from huts and the like, there would be no status as being taught by a reliable authority (āpta),
nor would there be confidence in them, [thinking], "By whom were these proclaimed?"— [wondering] whether they might have been composed by the Buddha or by deceivers posing as Brahmins. || 3244 ||
They might have been taught by those playing with distant echoes,
or perhaps they were uttered by invisible beings such as petty piśācas;
therefore, those who consider themselves wise should not place their trust in them.
Everything is easily understood.

This much has been stated by Kumārila as the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*); now, according to the opinion of Sāmaṭa and Yaśaṭa, he states once again the refutation of the omniscient one: "And this," and so forth;
thus, the omniscience of persons is, in its independence, without foundation.
Furthermore, this is considered: how is the All-Seeing One (Sarvadarśin) regarded?

Is he one who knows everything simultaneously or in succession; or by virtue of a single nature; or as knowing according to what is predominant; or is he accepted as omniscient by virtue of his power? (3247–3248)

The simultaneous cognition of contradictory natures, such as the pure and the impure, is never observed by a single cognition; nor are there ever divergent modes of apprehension [for a single object].
Furthermore, who could [perceive] the infinite reality—past, present, and future—successively?
One might be able to understand each [object] individually even in hundreds of years;
however, he who understands everything by means of an undivided intrinsic nature does not perceive the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all things.

Even for that omniscient one who perceives the general form [of things], what is gained by a cognition of another form? An object is not apprehended at all [in such a case]. Therefore, that consciousness which has that single form must be either correct or false.
If there were such a contradiction with what is perceived regarding correctness, it would follow that everything is non-dual.
Consequently, for you, the disciple, the Omniscient One, dharma and adharma, and their teachings would not exist as distinct entities, because their distinct natures could not be determined.
If the cognition of a single [object] were false, then the omniscient one would be mistaken;
his word would not be trustworthy, being like the speech of a madman and the like.
He who [knows] all action together with its causes through supramundane knowledge...
If he is held to be omniscient, he must know [all things] through that which is born of meditative concentration (samādhi).
