There exists no means of valid cognition—whether perception, inference, or verbal testimony, whether produced by him or not—that establishes his existence; therefore, such a person does not exist.
Whether simultaneously or in succession, how can there be an inference [of capacity] without an effect?
Even capacity does not exist at all; for if [capacity were inherent], everything would be capable of everything.
And if that were so, all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) would be masters capable of cognizing everything.
However, because their means are fruitless, they do not perceive everything [as it truly is]. [Objection:
One has obtained a unique means, distinct from that of all other men; thus, there is a certain one who is omniscient. [Response: This is entirely without proof. (3259–3260)
"In this way, when no omniscient person whatsoever is established,
then human speech cannot be the cause for the realization of Dharma"—
thus say the Mīmāṃsakas, who are devoted to independent revelation (*svatantra-śruti*).
And the human origin of the Vedas has been established in detail [in verse 3262].

Is an omniscient being (sarvajña) one who possesses simultaneous knowledge of all objects; or rather, one who knows them in succession—that is, gradually; or one who knows the entire world through a single form, such as "eternal" and so forth; or one who knows everything by understanding its primary essence—namely, that which is useful for human goals, such as karma and its fruits; or is he called omniscient due to his capacity to know all things, just as fire is said to be "all-consuming" even though it does not consume everything simultaneously or successively?

In that regard, concerning the first position, there are two alternatives: either he would know everything simultaneously with a single cognition, or with multiple cognitions. It cannot be with a single one, because we do not observe mutually contradictory objects—such as the pure and the impure—being grasped simultaneously by a single cognition.
One might argue that many cognitions directed toward various contradictory objects arise in him at once; to this he says: "Or [his] modes of apprehension are distinct."
The connection is made by changing the case ending [of "na"], as in "they are not seen";
for it is not observed that sentient beings with a single continuum of consciousness possess simultaneous movements in different directions. Thus... [the argument follows].
Because it is impossible to know [it] even in hundreds of years, the mention of "hundreds of years" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) [meaning] that it cannot be known even in eons (kalpa);
otherwise, its independence would be lost.
From this point until the commentary on verse 3262, a great portion of the text has been lost.
Moreover, in the manuscript itself, only a mark for deletion has been made;
therefore, there exists only a direct perceiver of supersensuous objects, and no one perceives them through eternal speech, because that is impossible. (3263)

Therefore, there exists a direct seer of supersensuous objects, and not through the medium of eternal words, because such eternal words are impossible; the restrictive particle "eva" (only), which has been displaced in order, should be understood immediately after the word "sākṣāt" (directly).

Granted that an eternal word might exist, nevertheless, its status as a cause for the cognition of supersensible objects is not tenable; demonstrating this, he says: "Of an eternal word," and so forth:

"The capacity of an eternal word [to produce] the cognition of its own object arises neither from itself nor from anything else, because of the contradiction between succession and simultaneity. (3264)
In this context, "its own object" (*svārtha*) means its own denotation;

or alternatively, *sva* (self) refers to the self—the nature of the word—and *artha* (object) refers to the denotation. Thus, "its own object" (*svārtha*) consists of both the word itself and its denotation. Regarding the knowledge of these two, the capacity of the eternal Word to produce that knowledge must either arise intrinsically as established by its very nature, or else from another auxiliary cause.
In that regard, it cannot first be from itself. Why? Because for an eternal entity, there is a contradiction with respect to the production of an effect through either succession or simultaneity;
for no other mode besides succession and simultaneity is possible by which causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) could occur, since these two are defined by their mutual exclusion.
Therefore, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is pervaded exclusively by succession and simultaneity;
and it is not logical for an eternal word to produce the cognition of its own meaning through succession.

Because its nature of producing the effect of cognition existing at subsequent times has not lapsed even during the state of producing the first effect, all effects arising from that [nature] alone would necessarily occur simultaneously.

Nor is it logical [for the cause to act] successively, because even at a later time, since the persistence of its nature—which is complete and capable of producing effects—remains just as it was during the state of producing the first effect, there would be a contradiction in its failing to produce [further effects].

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Whatever is devoid of a property that pervades another is also devoid of the property pervaded by it; for example, a jar or the like, which is devoid of the property of "treeness," is also devoid of the property of "being a *śiṃśapā* tree" (which is pervaded by treeness). And the eternal word called the Veda is devoid of the properties of succession and simultaneity, which pervade the property of causal efficacy (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*). Thus, this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*) by implication. Therefore, there is no possibility of power (*śakti*) in an eternally existing word either from itself or from another auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*), because power—which is not distinct from its own nature—cannot be produced in the same way as its own nature.
Even if [the cognition] were a different entity, the relationship [between it and the eternal word] would remain unestablished; this has been discussed at length.
Therefore, the claim that the thorough knowledge of supersensible objects depends upon an eternal word is improper, as it is sublated by inference.

Regarding what was stated—that there is no knower of *dharma* because his form has been made the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-existence (*abhāvapramāṇa*)—he says the following, demonstrating by the very admission of the opponent that the proposition "there is no knower of *dharma*" is sublated by the means of knowledge known as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), and that the reason [adduced] is unestablished (*asiddha*): "Therefore, heaven, sacrifices, and so forth, having been known by him, were revealed; thus, for you too, there exists such an author of the Veda who perceives supersensuous objects. (3265)
One who knows the purpose of the primary spirit (puruṣa), or indeed one who knows all dharmas—

if such a person were not accepted, the authority of the Veda would not exist otherwise. Therefore, by accepting that knower of dharma as established through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti), [the Veda's authority is maintained].
This negation of that [position] has been set forth by you in detail;
"svataḥ" means independently.
The meaning is "by means of knowledge independent of the Vedas";
"such" refers to that which is being rejected by you.
"By what is obtained through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*)" means by what is obtained through the force of the acceptance of the Veda's authority;

for this very reason, the claim that [the Lord] has a form apprehended by the means of knowledge of non-existence (*abhāva*) is also unestablished, because he is apprehended through presumptive testimony.
Furthermore, the criticism that was raised by analyzing in various ways the dependence of the word "all" (*sarva*) upon the context of the subject at hand does not apply at all,
because this position is not accepted [by us].

For we do not accept an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) on the grounds of his knowing every intended object distinct from [the categories such as] dharmas and so forth, such that the aforementioned criticism could be leveled against him.
What then?
He whose mind, being free from the stains of all afflictive and cognitive obscurations, illuminates the entirety of the knowable—such as the Dharma and so forth—is intended to be omniscient;
and regarding that, you have not adduced any subverting proof.

As for what was stated—"as many atoms as there are in a single body," and so forth—that is merely a thesis stated without proof; for the establishment of a matter cannot result from a mere thesis devoid of logical justification, as that would entail the absurd consequence that everything could establish every object. Anticipating all of this, he says: "Furthermore," and so on.
Furthermore, this which has been stated by one whose authority is proclaimed is indeed without reason:
how could anyone possibly know the number of hairs on the head and body?
For it is only by means of the lamp of stainless and unwavering knowledge that someone [might know].
The statement "it would be that which illuminates all things" does not constitute a refutation here.
"Akāraṇam" (without cause) means that for which there exists no cause— namely, the presentation of a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*)— is so described.

It is stainless because it is free from the stains of the afflictive and cognitive obscurations; it is unshakable because it cannot be moved by the winds of Māra or the heretics; that very knowledge is itself a lamp, and he is so described because he has illuminated—that is, made an object of cognition—all things such as the dharmas, due to the similarity between knowledge and light.
Even though it involves mutual dependence (*sāpekṣatva*), the compound is valid because it conveys meaning;
what has been stated here does not constitute a sublation—
this is the remainder of the sense, namely, that it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The meaning is that not only has this not been stated, but there is also no subverting evidence (bādhaka) here;
for instance, perception (*pratyakṣa*) is not a subverting factor because it does not have that [unmanifested entity] as its object.
Indeed, only when a thing is apprehended by perception in a certain way, and a contrary property is asserted regarding that very thing established by perception, is it subverted by perception.
Just as in the case of sound being the subject (*dharmin*), "non-audibility" is [negated] by means of "audibility," and not in a place where perception does not occur—
nor indeed can all minds residing in the mental continua of others be made objects of perception through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) by anyone who is not omniscient.
For if omniscience were asserted therein, it would be sublated by direct perception,
since all [beings] are limited in vision; or, if he were indeed made an object of perception, then he himself would be omniscient, and thus could not be rejected.
It might be argued: we do not say that perception, while operating, establishes non-existence;
rather, it is [perception] while withdrawing [from an object] that does so.

For instance: when there is a cessation of perception regarding a given object, its non-existence is determined, as in the case of a hare's horn; whereas when perception is active regarding something, its existence is established, as in the case of a pot and so forth.
Now, since perception has never been active with respect to the object that is the Omniscient One, His non-existence is determined by that cessation [of perception].
This is irrelevant;
for the certainty that arises from the cessation of [the operation of] perception does not originate from perception itself,
because existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory in a single locus.
Furthermore, the cessation of perception is not pervaded by the non-existence of an object, such that the non-existence of the object could be ascertained from it;
for we observe the cessation of perception even when an object exists, provided it is obstructed or otherwise remote.
To this, we reply: it is not from the mere cessation of perception that the ascertainment of non-existence arises.
What then?
It is that perception, having ceased, establishes non-existence;
thus, you are merely stating this difference in words.
However, there is no difference in meaning;
nor is it logical that a difference in meaning follows merely from a difference in words, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
For instance, "cessation" (*nivṛtti*) is said to be the negation of the existence of a thing.
Even by the word "ceased" (*nivṛtta*), that very same thing is expressed from the perspective of ultimate reality;
the distinction is merely this: one [term] denotes it when there is a desire to know it as such alone by excluding other distinctions, while the other does so without such exclusion.
However, in ultimate reality, both terms establish the non-existence of the entity.
The state of being a cause for a non-existent thing is not possible, because such a thing is characterized by a total absence of all causal capacity.

Therefore, whatever is the producer or the illuminator of something must possess an existing presence at the time of that thing’s production or illumination; it cannot be of a nature that has already ceased. For example, a seed is the producer of a sprout and a lamp is the illuminator of form;
these two are not capable of producing the sprout or illuminating the form of a jar once they have ceased to exist.
Moreover—what is the intended meaning here when it is said that "perception, having ceased, establishes non-existence"?
If the meaning is that it has ceased from the present time-path, then by implication it would be saying that it exists in a past or future state;
however, it has already been established previously that a past or future entity does not exist.
How, then, could the activity of a non-existent thing be established?
Furthermore, if even a present thing is said to be "withdrawn" from a certain object because it does not arise with respect to that object,
even so, the non-existence of the entity is not thereby established, because of the fallacy of deviation.
For it is not the case that because visual consciousness does not arise with respect to objects such as odors and tastes, the non-existence of those [objects] is thereby established;
therefore, the non-existence of anything is not established through perception.
If this is so, how is it that you describe the establishment of the non-existence of jars and the like in another location as being due to perception known as "non-apprehension" (anupalambha)?
This is not so;
for it is not said that perception establishes non-existence by taking non-existence as its object.
What then? It is because the establishment of one of two objects that are capable of being conjoined within a single cognition constitutes the establishment of the non-existence of the other.
For when those two [the object and the cognition] exist, a cognition restricted to a single form is not possible because their capacity [to produce cognition] is indistinguishable; yet,

in this case, the co-occurrence of omniscience with anything else within a single cognition has not been ascertained, such that we could determine its absence through the perception of that [other thing] alone.
Since that [omniscient being] is always and absolutely beyond the range of perception,
direct perception cannot possibly be a sublater of an omniscient one;
nor does inference establish the non-existence of an omniscient being.

Because it is accepted that this [non-existence] is the object of a formal means of knowledge (*vidhi*), and since it is precisely non-existence itself that is described as the means of knowledge whose object is non-existence— and nothing else—
it follows for this very reason that even the three other means of knowledge, such as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and the rest, lack the capacity to establish [their objects].

Now, it might be argued: "We do not establish the non-existence of an omniscient being by way of absolute negation (*prasajya-rūpa*); rather, having taken all men as the subject (*pakṣa*), we establish their non-omniscience through relative negation (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*). Therefore, the operation of inference and the other means of knowledge certainly occurs. Let it be so; nevertheless, inference is first of all impossible, because no mark (*liṅga*) that is invariably concomitant with non-omniscience among all men is established.

Furthermore, as for the [marks] such as "being an object of cognition" (*prameyatva*) or "being a speaker" (*vaktṛtva*) that were mentioned, those too are inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), as will be demonstrated later.
Nor does presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) establish that [the Buddha] is not omniscient,
because no means of valid cognition other than perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) is established;

or even if there were another means of valid cognition, presumptive testimony is nonetheless incapable of proving non-omniscience, since presumptive testimony consists in the postulation of an unperceived fact on the grounds that a perceived or heard fact would otherwise be inexplicable.

Nor is any object, such as what is perceived and so forth, among all men inexplicable without [the existence of] non-omniscience, such that it would have to be postulated through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*);

nor is analogy (*upamāna*) capable [of establishing it]. For instance, by means of analogy, one perceives either the mere similarity—which has the qualification of being similar to the object standing before one—or the similarity residing in the remembered object itself;

this occurs, for example, when a person who has previously experienced a cow and is later in the forest sees a *gavaya*, whereby there arises a cognition of its similarity to that previously experienced cow.

As it has been said: "Therefore, that which is remembered as qualified by similarity, or the similarity itself as connected with that [remembered object], would be the object of knowledge (prameya) for analogy (upamāna)."

Therefore, the object of comparison (*upamāna*) is only the subject (*dharmin*) that is being remembered; and only an object already experienced is made the object of memory, not anything else. Furthermore, the mental states residing in the continua of all persons have not been experienced by any omniscient being such that they could be made objects of memory. Nor is there a determination of a property common to the non-omniscience of all persons regarding an object currently being experienced, by virtue of which non-omniscience could be analogically established for all persons.
Furthermore, even that existence and so forth which is observed in some non-omniscient being is not established as being common to non-omniscience,
because existence and other such qualities are not incompatible with omniscience;
for it is not the case that by observing the properties of existence and so forth in a gavaya, one infers through analogy that pots and other things are similar to a gavaya.
Granted that all men share common characteristics such as being sentient beings and so forth, their lack of omniscience is not thereby established;
this very point refutes what was said [in the verse beginning] "having seen men," etc.
Furthermore, there exists no means of valid cognition known as verbal testimony (*śabda*) that contradicts the existence of an omniscient being.

First of all, that which is of human origin is admitted by the Mīmāṃsakas themselves to be non-authoritative regarding objects beyond the senses; and it has been demonstrated that even that which is not of human origin is non-authoritative. Furthermore, no Vedic statement is found that establishes the non-omniscience of all men, nor does the absence of such an instruction prove the non-existence of other [omniscient] entities, because the scriptures do not have jurisdiction over the teaching of all things.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the marriages of your own mother and so forth would not exist, on the grounds that they are not recited therein;

yet it is not logical to conclude that [the Veda] is not recited anywhere because its recitation is not seen in one particular location, for since it is heard within hundreds of hidden branches (*śākhā*), its recitation elsewhere is possible.
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate later that the Omniscient One is indeed clearly recited in another branch of the Veda.
Nor can the non-existence of the Omniscient One be established on the grounds that he has been made an object of the means of knowledge known as non-apprehension (*abhāvapramāṇa*).

To explain: if non-apprehension is described as a mere absence of a means of knowledge characterized by a simple negation (*prasajya-lakṣaṇa*), then it is neither a cognition of anything nor a cause for cognition; therefore, it is not logical for him to be made an object by it, because it is a non-entity.
Consequently, it is not a valid means of knowledge.

Now, if by the function of exclusion (paryudāsāvṭtti) what is intended is an entity that is simply other than the entity called a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), even so, its status as a means of valid cognition would not be established because it is of a nature excluded from being a means of valid cognition. For it is not logical that one who is other than a Brāhmaṇa should be a Brāhmaṇa himself.
To this [it might be replied]: "He is not described as being excluded from all means of valid cognition."
What then?
If it is argued that it is simply another specific cognition distinct from the five intended means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then it must be stated:
what is the nature of this [cognition]?

If it is argued that because [the omniscient being] is not within the scope of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he does not exist—such being the form [of the inference]—if this is indeed its form, then it is not a valid cognition, because it is fallible (*vyabhicāra*).

For when the five means of valid cognition—which do not constitute the nature or cause of the object—are absent, an entity such as an omniscient being does not necessarily cease to exist, since it is not invariably concomitant with them; otherwise, this cognition would attain the status of truth.
Therefore, the point is that there exists no subverting means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) against the existence of an omniscient being.

It might be argued: "That very non-apprehension which has been described by you as being of the nature of inference will itself be the sublater of the omniscient one; what need have we here for any other means of valid cognition? This is true—non-apprehension is indeed a means of valid cognition—but this must be considered here: [The full argument follows: ...Therefore, since the non-apprehension of the Omniscient One is not established, it cannot serve as a sublater. Furthermore, even if such a person were apprehended, there would be no certainty regarding his omniscience, because the capacity of a person to know all things is beyond the scope of perception. Consequently, the mere absence of apprehension does not prove non-existence. Thus, the proof of the Omniscient One remains unestablished. As it has been said: "The proof of the Omniscient One is not established by means of perception, nor by inference, nor by scripture, nor by analogy, nor by presumption. Therefore, the Omniscient One is not proven by any means of valid cognition. Hence, the statement that "the Omniscient One does not exist" is not established. Thus, the Omniscient One exists. This concludes the first chapter, titled "The Proof of the Omniscient One," from the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable Kamalaśīla. End of Chapter One. Chapter Two: Refutation of the Self. [The opponent says: "If the Omniscient One does not exist, then who is it that taught the Dharma? Who is the author of the scriptures? Who is the teacher of the path to liberation? If these do not exist, then the entire teaching of the Dharma is baseless, like the teachings of the Cārvākas and others. Therefore, the Omniscient One must exist. [The author replies: This is not so. Even without an Omniscient One, the Dharma was taught by the Buddha through the power of his previous cultivation of compassion and wisdom. Just as a person who has mastered a particular craft can teach it to others through the force of their prior training, so too did the Blessed One, having previously cultivated the perfections of giving, morality, patience, vigor, meditation, and wisdom, attain supreme enlightenment and subsequently teach the Dharma to others. Therefore, the existence of an Omniscient One is not required for the establishment of the Dharma. Moreover, the scriptures are not the work of a single author; rather, they arose from the collective consensus of many learned sages. Thus, the Dharma is authoritative even in the absence of an Omniscient One. Furthermore, the path to liberation is established through the realization of the Four Noble Truths, which are known through direct perception and inference, and not through the words of an Omniscient One. Therefore, the claim that the Omniscient One is necessary for the path to liberation is unfounded. Consequently, the Omniscient One is not proven by any means of valid cognition. Thus, the statement that "the Omniscient One does not exist" is not refuted. This concludes the second chapter, titled "Refutation of the Self," from the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable Kamalaśīla. End of Chapter Two. Chapter Three: Refutation of the Sāṃkhya. [The opponent says: "If the Self does not exist, then who experiences pleasure and pain? Who is the agent of actions? Who is the enjoyer of the fruits thereof? Without a Self, there would be no continuity of rebirth, and thus the entire system of karma and its results would collapse. Therefore, the Self must exist. [The author replies: This is not so. Pleasure and pain are merely mental states arising from the transformation of the mind, and they are experienced by the mind itself. There is no separate Self apart from the mind. Furthermore, agency and enjoyment belong to the continuum of consciousness, not to a permanent Self. The continuity of rebirth is maintained by the force of karma and afflictions acting upon the stream of consciousness, without requiring a permanent Self. Therefore, the Self is not proven by any means of valid cognition. Thus, the statement that "the Self does not exist" is not refuted. This concludes the third chapter, titled "Refutation of the Sāṃkhya," from the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable Kamalaśīla. End of Chapter Three. Chapter Four: Refutation of the Vaiśeṣika. [The opponent says: "If the Self does not exist, then who is it that cognizes objects? Without a Self, there would be no subject of cognition, and thus the categories of substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, inherence, and absence would be untenable. Therefore, the Self must exist. [The author replies: This is not so. Cognition arises from the contact of the sense organs with their respective objects, and it is the mind that perceives these cognitions. There is no need for a permanent Self to act as a substratum for cognition. The categories proposed by the Vaiśeṣikas are also untenable, as they involve contradictions and lack any means of valid proof. Therefore, the Self is not proven by any means of valid cognition. Thus, the statement that "the Self does not exist" is not refuted. This concludes the fourth chapter, titled "Refutation of the Vaiśeṣika," from the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable Kamalaśīla. End of Chapter Four. Chapter Five: Refutation of the Nyāya. [The opponent says: "If the Self does not exist, then who is it that remembers past events? Without a Self, there would be no memory, and thus the process of recollection would be impossible. Therefore, the Self must exist. [The author replies: This is not so. Memory arises from the impression (saṃskāra) left by a previous experience within the continuum of consciousness. It is the mind itself that remembers, not a permanent Self. Furthermore, the arguments put forward by the Nyāya school are flawed and do not establish the existence of a Self. Therefore, the Self is not proven by any means of valid cognition. Thus, the statement that "the Self does not exist" is not refuted. This concludes the fifth chapter, titled "Refutation of the Nyāya," from the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable Kamalaśīla. End of Chapter Five. Chapter Six: Refutation of the Mīmāṃsā. [The opponent says: "If the Self does not exist, then who is it that performs sacrifices and attains heaven? Without a Self, there would be no agent of ritual action, and thus the Vedic injunctions would be meaningless. Therefore, the Self must exist. [The author replies: This is not so. Ritual actions produce results through the force of their own inherent efficacy, and the attainment of heaven occurs through the transformation of the continuum of consciousness. There is no need for a permanent Self to act as an agent or enjoyer. Furthermore, the Vedic texts do not provide any definitive proof for the existence of a Self. Therefore, the Self is not proven by any means of valid cognition. Thus, the statement that "the Self does not exist" is not refuted. This concludes the sixth chapter, titled "Refutation of the Mīmāṃsā," from the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable Kamalaśīla. End of Chapter Six. Chapter Seven: Refutation of the Jaina. [The opponent says: "If the Self does not exist, then who is it that possesses the qualities of permanence and impermanence? Without a Self, there would be no basis for the doctrine of manifoldness (anekāntavāda). Therefore, the Self must exist. [The author replies: This is not so. The qualities of permanence and impermanence apply to phenomena, not to a permanent Self. The doctrine of manifoldness is based on the relativity of perspectives and does not require a permanent Self to function as a substratum. Furthermore, the arguments of the Jaina school are internally inconsistent and fail to establish the existence of a Self. Therefore, the Self is not proven by any means of valid cognition. Thus, the statement that "the Self does not exist" is not refuted. This concludes the seventh chapter, titled "Refutation of the Jaina," from the *Tattvasaṃgraha-pañjikā*, composed by the venerable Kamalaśīla. End of Chapter Seven. Chapter Eight: Refutation of the Buddhist Realist (Sarvāstivāda). [The opponent says: "If the Self does not exist, then who is it that undergoes the process of dependent origination? Without a Self, there would be no subject of transmigration, and thus the cycle of birth and death would be impossible. Therefore, the Self must exist. [The author replies: This is not so. Dependent origination is a process of causal conditioning within the continuum of consciousness, and it does not require a permanent Self to account for the continuity of existence. Transmigration occurs through the force of karma and afflictions acting upon the stream of consciousness, without a separate Self. Furthermore, the arguments of the Sarvāstivā

Do you intend by "non-perception" (anupalambha) the cessation of your own perception for the sake of establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being, or rather the cessation of the perception of all persons? Furthermore, is this non-perception intended to be without qualification—by not resorting to the qualification "of that which has reached the conditions of perceptibility"—or is it with qualification? In this regard, first of all, a non-perception without qualification is not logically a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being; showing this, he says: "Nor can there be certainty of its non-existence by mere non-observation," and so forth. "Nor can there be certainty of its non-existence by mere non-observation."
Because perception is connected with being the cause and the pervader of things,
the inclusion of the word "only" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding that [perception] which has attained the conditions for perceptibility; thus,
there is the ascertainment of its non-existence.

Why is there a certainty regarding the non-existence of an omniscient being? Because, with respect to entities—that is, in the domain of objects—the perception [of a limited being] cannot be the cause or the pervader [of those entities].

For the perception of one who sees only what is near is not a pervader of entities, just as "being a tree" is not the pervader of "being a *śiṃśapā*"; since even when an entity exists, its non-perception is possible due to distance in space and other factors.

Nor is it a cause, like fire is for smoke, because [the non-perception of one thing] lacks the status of being a cause for the perception of other entities; nor is the cessation of one thing logically entailed by the cessation of another that is neither its cause nor its pervader, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the non-perception of an effect that has been mentioned does not indicate the absence of the mere cause.
What then?
It is precisely that which possesses unimpeded capacity;
however, for one who perceives only what is proximate (the limited perceiver), there is no unimpeded capacity of things with respect to their apprehension.
By which [means] he, while returning, might establish the non-existence of things.
If it is asked, "Even when the cause and the pervader have ceased, how can there be the cessation of another?", he says here: "The cause," and so forth.
In this context, cessation is logical when there is an absence of the cause or the pervader,
because that which possesses a cause and that which is pervaded arise from a single state of being;
just as smoke and mangoes cease to exist in the absence of fire and the [mango] tree.
Otherwise, there would be a state of causelessness, and multiplicity would follow as a consequence.
"That which has a cause" means that it is an effect;
the analysis of the compound is "that which possesses a cause and is pervaded by it."
The connection with the preceding [verse] is that "the cessation of those two—the caused (*hetumat*) and the pervaded (*vyāpta*)—is logical.
The reason for this is stated as: "because [the caused] arises from that [cause], they possess a single nature" (*ekabhāvataḥ*).

For when the cause has ceased, the caused ceases; because the caused acquires its own being through arising from that cause. Just as smoke ceases when fire ceases, so too does the pervaded cease when the pervader ceases, because it possesses a single nature—that is, because it is of one essence—with that pervader.
Just as when a tree ceases to exist, there is the cessation of the mango, the khadira, and so forth, because a specific type of tree is perceived precisely as a mango and the like;
otherwise, if it were not to cease even when its cause ceases, then that would not be its cause at all.
For it is not logical that something which exists even when another thing is absent should be the cause of that other thing, as this would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Nor is it logical that something which does not cease when another ceases should be the nature of that other, just as a cow is not the nature of a gavaya.

Therefore, only a pervader (vyāpaka) would cause its pervaded (vyāpya) to cease upon its own cessation, and only a cause (kāraṇa) would cause its effect (kārya) to cease; nothing else, because that would lead to over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
As it has been said: "Therefore, a nature connected with that alone [causes] the entity itself [to cease]."
One may negate the cause or the effect due to their non-deviation [from one another];
otherwise, how could the negation of one thing result in the negation of another?
Why should a mortal, simply because he does not possess a horse, necessarily not possess a cow as well?

Furthermore, if it is admitted that one's own apprehension is both the cause and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) with respect to all objects, then a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) arises in the thesis; demonstrating this, he says: "Of one's own apprehension," and so forth.

And if, through some cognition of yours, there were a determination regarding all objects as being the cause or the pervader of your own perception, then you yourself would be established effortlessly as an omniscient knower of all things. (3273)
And therefore, what hatred could there be in you toward yourself, who are omniscient by nature?
The genitive case [in "hetutva-vyāpakatvayoḥ"] is used in relation to the requirement for certainty.

Regarding the genitive and locative cases in the phrase "upalambhasya cārtheṣu," these are to be applied respectively to the relation of causality and the state of being the object, with reference to the [qualities of] being a cause and being a pervader.

This is what is meant: if you have ascertained through some means of valid cognition that your own perception is both the cause and the pervader of all objects, then you have clearly asserted omniscience for yourself;
for the knowledge of one who is not omniscient cannot pervade the entirety of all knowable things.

Furthermore, because you employ a proof for the purpose of establishing the non-existence of the Omniscient One, that very [Omniscient One] is being negated; thus, there is a contradiction with your own words.

Thus, first of all, a non-perception of oneself without qualification does not deserve to be cited as proof for the non-existence of an omniscient being; nor does it do so when qualified by the phrase "because of the non-perception of one who meets the conditions for perceptibility. For if it were to be cited, it would be stated either by its own name, such as the citation: "There is no jar in a certain particular place because of the non-perception of that which meets the conditions for perceptibility"—and the same would apply for establishing the absence of an omniscient being.

Just as by the word "self" (sva), one demonstrates the absence of another entity—which is its cause or its pervader and which meets the conditions for perception—as in: "There is no smoke here because of the absence of fire," or "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here because of the absence of trees";

for it has been stated previously that it is not logical for the necessary cessation of one thing to follow from the cessation of another that is neither its cause nor its pervader, since that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

The absence of an object whose own cause and pervader have not been ascertained to be absent does not establish its own absence through the absence of its cause or pervader; therefore, even in that case, the qualification "of that which has reached the conditions for perception" must certainly be adopted.
This would likewise apply to the case of an omniscient being.

Alternatively, the negation of another object occurs only through the affirmation of something directly or indirectly contradictory to it, and not of something non-contradictory, because the latter can coexist with it.

For example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of fire"—here, the negation of the sensation of cold occurs through the direct affirmation of fire, which is its direct opposite. In the same way, there could be a negation of an omniscient being through the affirmation of something indirectly opposed to it, or perhaps the affirmation of something opposed to its pervader. For instance, the negation of the sensation of frost occurs through the affirmation of fire, which is opposed to the cold that pervades that sensation;

or through the affirmation of something opposed to its cause, as when the negation of the bodily effects of cold, such as horripilation, occurs through the affirmation of a specific fire that is opposed to the cold which is the cause of those effects.

Or, it is because of the prescription of an effect contrary to that [negated object], as follows: in a particular location, the negation of cold touch occurs due to the prescription of smoke and so forth—an effect such as fire which is contrary to cold—or due to the perception of an effect contrary to the cause of that [negated object], as follows: the negation of horripilation and so forth occurs from the presentation of smoke, which is an effect of fire contrary to the cold that causes horripilation and so forth;
thus, "this location does not contain a person possessed of specific horripilation and so forth, because of smoke."

Or, there is the negation of something through the affirmation of what is pervaded by its opposite; for example, the negation of "inevitable occurrence" through the affirmation of "dependence," which is pervaded by "non-inevitable occurrence"—the opposite of inevitable occurrence. However, none of these applications of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) are possible for the purpose of establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being, because such an all-knowing person never meets the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), and because these [other types of non-perception] are merely varieties of the non-perception of that which does meet the conditions for perception. He demonstrates this with the words beginning "for this very reason."
For this very reason, this omniscient being is not established as being perceptible to you;
for if he were perceptible to you, omniscience would belong to you yourself without effort.
How can he whose knowledge has all objects as its domain be perceptible to you?
If even for you there were no knowledge whose object is all things,
then precisely because of the consequence of contradicting your own words, you must not accept that the Omniscient One has reached the conditions for being perceived by yourself;
otherwise, you would be admitting omniscience in your own case.
He asks "How so? and replies with the words "having all things as its object," and so forth.

For if there were indeed a cognition directed toward that [omniscient being] which has all things as its domain, then he would be an omniscient person for you, having reached the conditions for perception; it cannot be otherwise. This is because one who is not omniscient does not fall within the range of perception for an omniscient being.

It might be argued: "Let it be that for us the omniscient being does not meet the conditions for perception; nevertheless, why is it that these applications of non-perception cannot establish his non-existence? To this he says, beginning with "Therefore," etc.:
"Therefore, [the non-perception] arising from a specific lack of observation [cannot establish the absence] of those things which consist of causes or pervaders."
Because the Omniscient One is by nature of a visible form, [his non-existence] is not established.

Since, for you, the Omniscient One does not possess the conditions for perceptibility (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*), for that reason, the specific non-perception of the nature of the cause and the pervader of the Omniscient One—which would constitute a non-perception of what has reached the conditions for perceptibility—is not established.
That is to say, the first three applications of the non-perception of nature, cause, and pervader are not established.

If it is argued that "in that case, let the other remaining [means of knowledge] be established; nevertheless, the non-existence of an omniscient being is already proven," he says: "And this," and so forth.
And this threefold perception proceeds in its various forms.
Through the application of various distinctions such as the movement toward or away from contradictory [reasons] and so forth,

when the deficiency of capacity has been established against this [inference] which consists of its primary divisions with respect to the Omniscient One, the other [types of fallacies] are set aside without effort. (3278–3279)

This very non-perception (*adṛṣṭi*) of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the pervader (*vyāpaka*), and the cause (*kāraṇa*), which was just mentioned, when elaborated in three ways, becomes ninefold.
To explain how this is so, he says: "By the non-cognition of that, its opposite, and so forth," and so on.

By the word "that" (*tat*), the triad consisting of the essential nature, the pervader, and the cause—which were under discussion—is referred to. That which is opposed to that [triad] is "its opposite" (*tadviruddha*). And that [opposite] is indeed of three kinds, due to the distinction between the opposites of the essential nature, the pervader, and the cause.

That which has "the contrary of that" as its first member is called *tadviruddhādi*; by the word "first" (*ādi*), the three types—contrary effect (*viruddhakārya*), effect of the contrary cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakārya*), and the pervaded by the contrary (*viruddhavyāpta*)—are included.
Furthermore, by the second occurrence of the word "that" (*tat*), those same three types beginning with essential nature (*svabhāva*) are connected [to the probandum].

The compound *tattadviruddhādi* means "that [object] and its opposite, etc."; the phrase *tadviruddhādyagatigatī* refers respectively to the non-comprehension and comprehension of those two; thus, the meaning is the non-comprehension of that [object] and the comprehension of its opposite, etc.
The compound *tayorbhedastena prayogaḥ* means "the application [of the proof] by way of the distinction between those two.

In that context, since there is no other way [to categorize them], the threefold non-perception—namely, the non-perception of the essential nature (*svabhāva*), the cause (*kāraṇa*), and the pervader (*vyāpaka*)—is directly indicated.
Because all other types of non-perception indirectly indicate this very same threefold non-perception, this threefold non-perception constitutes their fundamental classification.

For instance: by way of a process contrary to that [probandum], the perception of what is contradictory to its nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), the perception of what is contradictory to its pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), and the perception of what is contradictory to its cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*) have been specified;

by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the perception of the effect of the contradictory (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*), the perception of the effect of what is contradictory to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), and the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) are included.

And by these [non-perceptions], the non-perceptions of essence (*svabhāva*), pervader (*vyāpaka*), and cause (*kāraṇa*) are indicated respectively as appropriate. Therefore, since the incapacity of the threefold basic divisions to establish the absence of an omniscient being has been demonstrated, the incapacity of those that constitute their branches is established without further effort; thus, no separate effort need be made to demonstrate their incapacity. For when the root is cut, the branches cannot remain.

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), however, it is precisely the non-apprehension of intrinsic nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) that is the root of all [non-apprehensions]; yet, by resorting to distinctions among different objects, it is described as being threefold in its capacity as a root.

It might be argued: "If the omniscient being has reached the conditions for non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi-lakṣaṇa-prāpta*), then let there be no establishment of the specific [non-]apprehension of him; however, since his cause and his pervader have reached the conditions for apprehension, why is the specific non-perception of them not established? And since things such as those contradictory to him possess an apprehensible nature, why is their apprehension not established? To this he says: "Causality, the state of being pervaded and pervader, and contrariety—these are established provided there is perceptibility; and so too is the self when it possesses its qualifiers. (3280)
The Omniscient One is not perceived; therefore, these non-perceptions are not capable of refuting him, nor is there any other factor for negation.
[Verse 3281] The compound consists of "causality," "pervaded-pervader relation," and "contrariety."

For the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established through perception and non-perception; since an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) and the like are invisible, no causal relationship can be established with them, nor can a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) be established, because that too is preceded by the non-perception of something that has reached the conditions for perceptibility. To explain: when the cessation of one thing necessarily entails the cessation of another, the latter is designated as being pervaded by the former; and the establishment of such a cessation does not occur without the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perceptibility.
Contradiction is established only between two perceptible entities, not between two imperceptible ones;
for instance, contradiction characterized by non-coexistence is observed when one thing, whose causes are unimpeded, is absent upon the presence of another.
Furthermore, existence and non-existence cannot be ascertained regarding two entities whose natures are imperceptible.

Even regarding contradiction characterized by mutual exclusion, if it is established that the determination of one is inseparable from the non-determination of the other— as is the case with succession and simultaneity—
and if such determination is not possible in the unperceivable,
then how can the contradiction between existence and non-existence and so forth be established? For in those cases, both [terms] do not possess perceptibility.
This is not a fault;

for contradiction between existence and non-existence is not established by first delimiting them as separate entities and only afterwards determining their relationship as the excluded and the excluder.
Rather, it is [established] precisely when they are delimited as separate.
For it is in a single substratum (*dharmī*) at one and the same time that the contradiction between those two is established, and not in another substratum;
indeed, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the existence of a horse and the absence of a cow.

Nor is there a contradiction between those two in a single substratum at different times, for it is not the case that the subsequent existence or non-existence of something that previously did not exist—or that previously existed—is impossible.

However, there is a contradiction because those two [exclusions] cannot be delimited simultaneously with respect to a single entity, but not in that very same [entity], because it is excluded after having been delimited.

If it is asked, "How can there be an exclusion of that which has not been delimited?", it is for this very reason; for precisely because it is not delimited in that locus (*dharmī*), its exclusion is possible from that very fact.

Otherwise, how could the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) of a delimited property (*paricchinnadharma*) be possible there? For the very delimitation of that [property] is the exclusion of its absence; and the very delimitation of it as distinct from others is the delimitation of the absence of others therein.

Therefore, that locus (*dharmin*) whose absence is excluded and whose presence is delimited must necessarily be admitted to be perceptible (*dṛśya*). For the delimitation of what is imperceptible is impossible, nor is the exclusion of a contrary property possible for what has not been delimited.

But this is not possible in the case of an omniscient being; for it is not the case that all persons who possess the property [of non-omniscience] are perceptible to anyone, such that—by means of the exclusion of the property of non-omniscience from them—the exclusion of omniscience could be established, since that very person would then entail omniscience.
Therefore, when the subject is imperceptible, the contradiction between omniscience and non-omniscience is not established.
However, it is established within one's own continuum;
even there, it is not established in a future state, because at that time it is imperceptible.
Therefore, this remains certain: the relationship of cause and effect is established only for that which is perceptible.
The connection is that the self (ātman) which is "with its qualification" is established;
in this context, "self" means intrinsic nature (svabhāva), and it is "with its qualification" because it exists together with a qualification (viśeṣaṇa).
In this context, the qualification is "being devoid of the three types of remoteness," meaning that these non-perceptions—

namely, the non-perception of causes and so forth— are not established as [proofs] against an omniscient being, because no relationship of cause and effect, contradiction, or pervader and pervaded has been established between the omniscient one and anything else.
Furthermore, since perceptibility is not established for something at some time or place even when other causes of perception are present,
there is no other factor for negation apart from this specific kind of non-perception.

Furthermore, demonstrating the inconclusiveness [of the reason] by showing that it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) when the unqualified non-perception of oneself is employed, he says: "If," and so forth;
"if the omniscient being is negated merely by your own non-perception."
In that case, there would also be for you a prohibition against marrying one's mother and so forth;
by the phrase "marrying one's mother and so forth," the inclusion of sexual enjoyment with one's own parents is intended, and thus the implication is that you would become the offspring of adultery.

As it has been said: "If the non-perception of objects by your dull eye were to negate those objects, then alas, you are defeated, because it would follow that even the designation 'uncle' could not function. (3282) Here, the author anticipates the opponent's rebuttal, beginning with the words "sutākhyā" and so forth.

If the existence of that cause [the marriage] is understood through the observation of its effect known as "son," then surely that effect is observed in some cases even in the absence of that [marriage].

Since that cause—such as the mother's marriage—is established by the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) of inference due to the observation of the effect known as "son" and so forth, its non-perception is not established; thus, there is no consequence of its non-existence.

With the words "in the absence of that" (*tadabhāve*) and so forth, he demonstrates the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) of this reason based on an effect (*kāryahetu*): "In the absence of that"—that is, in the absence of that marriage, and even in the absence of sexual enjoyment with a husband who has been married in such a manner—the effect known as a son is observed in the case of some corrupt woman through her union with another man; let it be the same for the mother as well. Thus, the inference is unestablished (*asiddha*), and consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that you yourself are born of an adulterer is difficult to avoid.

Since the Master Dharmakīrti also intended to demonstrate the consequence that [the opponent] would lack the basis for the specific designation of "uncle," he simply presented the consequence that [the opponent] would be born of adultery;
with the words "from the perception of another" (*anyopalambhataḥ*), etc., he anticipates the opponent's reply.

If it is argued that its non-existence is not established because of the perception of something else, then how indeed is that perception of another established as having that [non-existent thing] as its object?
"The perception of other persons" is what is meant by "perception of another."
Regarding the phrase "of that," it is not the non-existence of the mother's marriage and so forth that is understood; rather, what is it? It is indeed existence.
In this regard, the perception of another is not established; explaining that, he says: "But surely...
(verse 3284). Being asked "How so?", the opponent replies: "From instruction."
Is this [quality of being a speaker] not found likewise even in an omniscient one due to his teaching?
Furthermore, why is this other statement of his own not examined here:
"Men are almost always speakers of untruth"? (3285)
"Just as there is no trust [in him] today, so too there is none in his proclamation of past events"—this is the connection with the subject at hand, namely that he is "established" (siddha).
Demonstrating that the instruction is inconclusive by pointing out the fallacy of over-extension (atiprasaṅga), he says: "Not even in the case of an omniscient being."

Is this instruction not found regarding the Omniscient One? On the contrary, it certainly is found. In that case, if the instruction concerning one’s mother’s marriage and so forth is accepted as authoritative, why should our own instruction that "the Omniscient One exists" not also be accepted as authoritative, since there is no difference between the two?
Furthermore, he demonstrates that by his own words you have stated the invalidity of the instruction, beginning with "And this," etc.

Thus, it has been demonstrated that the non-perception of one’s own self is not a valid means of proof for establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being, because such non-perception is inconclusive when unqualified and unestablished when qualified. Now, demonstrating that the non-perception of all persons is also unestablished, and therefore cannot serve as a valid means for proving the non-existence of an omniscient being, he says: "Or let there be no [such] teaching, or let its authority be absent; nevertheless, how have you reached this certainty: 'An omniscient being is not perceived by anyone at all'? (3287)
For in this way, there would indeed be certainty regarding the perception of a self in all sentient beings;
and it has been described that upon seeing that [self], you have become omniscient—thus [ends] the "Instruction. (3288)
The ellipsis is "establishing the existence of the Omniscient One";
that is, the validity of this teaching,
namely, the vision of the self of all sentient beings.
If it is argued that "in the vision of the intrinsic nature of all beings, we indeed possess the vision of a self in all beings," he says: "In the vision of that," and so forth;
"in the vision of that" means in the vision of a self in all beings.
Otherwise, doubt would be appropriate even in the case of non-perception, just as it is in the case of existence.
For it is indeed maintained that some, being omniscient, do know [all things];
and it is also suspected that he, as the light of the self, perceives the self by the self through itself; therefore, the non-perception of all [beings] remains uncertain.
"Otherwise" means that in the absence of the perception of a self in all sentient beings,
it would be like [the case of] sentient beings.

This is said to be like the existence of an object remote in space and so forth: just as there is doubt regarding the existence of an object remote in space and so forth even when it is not perceived—because the object exists despite its non-perception—so too is doubt appropriate regarding the perception of the object of omniscience residing in another person.

Alternatively, the meaning is this: just as there is doubt regarding the existence of an omniscient being even when he is not perceived, so too there is doubt regarding the perception of the object that is omniscience; for in both cases, non-perception is possible due to the remoteness of their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viprakarṣa*).

Now, one might object: doubt regarding the existence of a real entity is indeed appropriate, because even when an entity exists, its non-perception is observed; thus, it is possible that [the entity] might exist at some time. However, the perception of an omniscient being is not conceivable for anyone of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*). And it is not proper for a discerning person to entertain doubt regarding an entity that is inconceivable. To this, he says: "Some... and so forth, ending with "...by themselves."
Because he accepts the tenets of others,
it is said that "by himself"; this very point is specified as "by the self" (ātmanā), where "self" (ātman) refers to the person (puruṣa).
It is called "light" because the Self, by virtue of its nature as consciousness, has the character of luminosity.
He supports this very point with the words beginning "For thus" (tathāhi):
for indeed, by the word "all," all living beings are intended.
And since he is not excluded from all [beings], his non-perception is uncertain.
(3291) "He" refers to the omniscient one.

It might be argued that by the word "all," only those with limited vision (arvāgdarśin) are intended, and not the Omniscient One; therefore, no such doubt will arise. To this, he says: "tadeka... and so forth:
"If that one [the Omniscient One] were excluded, what connection could there be here?"
For one's own passion and so forth do not cease simply because others do not recognize them.

(3292) If the non-perception of other limited-sighted beings—excluded from that omniscient being—is adduced as the reason [for the non-existence of the omniscient being], then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*), characterized by invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), between his own non-perception and the absence of an omniscient being.
With the words "For not... and so forth, he establishes that very lack of a necessary connection.

Thus, it has been demonstrated that the means of valid cognition known as non-apprehension (*anupalambha*) is both inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) and unestablished (*asiddha*). Now, demonstrating that the reason "because its form is made the object of the means of valid cognition consisting of non-existence" (*abhāvapramāṇaviṣayīkṛtavigrahatvāt*) is also doubtful-unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*), he says: "Some," and so forth.
Even some of limited vision perceive [the self] by means of inference.
For indeed, the intellects of some people are clever only in certain respects;
for instance, the proof for the momentariness of the Vedas, the earth, and so forth,
which was previously stated with great clarity, was not perceived by the dull-witted.
Thus, because of this doubt, even the absence of his knowledge is not established; for it is only when people are free from doubt that they perceive non-existence.

Since it is possible that some individuals of sharp intellect, though possessing only limited vision, might at some time establish an omniscient being through inference, the reason—"because it is the object of the means of knowledge consisting in non-apprehension"—is characterized by doubtful unestablishedness (*saṃdigdhāsiddhatva*).

For instance: although the momentariness and non-selfhood of the Vedas, sound, the earth, mountains, bodies, thunderbolts, and so forth, were quite evident, they were not perceived by you, the beast-like Mīmāṃsakas; yet, by presenting more robust proofs, we have established them. Likewise, even if no proof for an omniscient being is found at present, it remains "doubtful" because its possibility still exists. Therefore, the claim that [the omniscient being] is an object of the "proof of non-existence"—which consists in the absence of the other five means of knowledge—is unestablished, because he remains a subject of doubt. This is why [the reason in your argument] is invalid.
Because of the absence of proof.
Furthermore— let it be granted that for all those of limited vision, there is no inference to establish an omniscient being;
nevertheless, [the author] says "even in the absence of inference," etc., demonstrating that the reason (hetu) remains inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Even in the absence of an inference, there is no certainty regarding non-existence from that [absence], just as the existence of fire and so forth is not negated when the effects such as smoke have not yet begun.

For it was established previously that a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is neither the cause nor the pervader of a real entity; how then could the entity be negated even upon the cessation of that [cognition]?

For instance, when a fire in an iron ball or similar object has not yet produced its effect—such as smoke—and is situated within the interior of a room, no inference arises due to the absence of a logical mark (*liṅga*); nevertheless, its existence remains unrefuted, so that there is no certainty of its non-existence. Likewise, regarding the proof of the non-existence of an omniscient being, there is doubt because of the absence of an inferential mark;
therefore [the reason is inconclusive].

Because there is an absence of inference, it is so described as that fire or the like by which the effect, such as smoke, has not been initiated; the analysis of the compound is: "that fire or the like for which the effect of smoke and so forth has not been initiated. This is just like [the existence] of its being (sattva) when there is its existence (sattā).

By the words "kadācidupalabdhe 'rthe" (when an object has been perceived at some time) and so forth, the opponent demonstrates that perception is the cause of doubt, using the example of fire in an iron ball; he then argues that since such perception is absent in the case of an omniscient being, doubt is inappropriate, thereby supporting the very point that the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
"Indeed, doubt is appropriate regarding an object perceived at some time, as in the case of a post; for this [doubt] relies upon both alternatives. (3297)
Since a post and a person have both been seen at some time or other, it is appropriate that there be doubt regarding their nature; however, an omniscient being has never been seen in this manner.
For doubt is appropriate only regarding an object that has been previously perceived, such as in the case of a post and not elsewhere, because [doubt] relies upon both aspects [of the object].
Otherwise, doubt would take as its object everything that is unperceived;
consequently, there would be no rule restricting it to taking both sides [of a proposition] as its object.
Therefore, while doubt is appropriate in cases such as fire within a red-hot iron ball, it is not so in the case of an omniscient being, because such a being is never perceived at any time.
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "nanu" (but surely), etc.
"O wise one, by this very same method, the non-existence of your mother's marriage and so forth would follow for you beyond any doubt.

(3299) If, when an object has been perceived at some time, there is doubt regarding it while there is certainty of its absence elsewhere, then by this logic, the non-existence of your mother's marriage and so forth would result for you without any uncertainty."
For you have never before observed the marriage of your own mother, such that there might be a certainty of its non-existence even in this case; and here,
the remaining objection should be stated as previously [explained] in the response.
"O wise one! is a word used in derision.
[The opponent objects: "If this is so, then doubt would follow as being entirely without foundation. To this, he says: "By us," and so forth.
We describe doubt in this case even when there is an absence of valid cognition (pramā), because of the cessation of means of knowledge regarding both the existence and non-existence of things.

For, since the mere absence of valid cognition can be shown in relation to both the existence and non-existence of things, there is a lack of determination; thus, doubt is described precisely because no certainty arises as to whether something exists or does not exist.
As it has been said: "Doubt is a deliberation that depends on specific characteristics due to the lack of a settled determination between perception and non-perception" (Nyāyasūtra 1.1.23).

It might be argued that the cessation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not observed in both cases—neither for the existence nor for the non-existence of a real entity; to this he says: "Of the eyes, etc. and so forth.

For indeed, when there is a defect in the eyes or other [senses], there is no valid cognition even though the object exists; yet, even when those [senses] are unimpaired, [there is no cognition] due to the absence of the object, as in the case of a jar or similar things.
Therefore, because non-apprehension alone is observed in two ways:
Therefore, it is better that there be doubt regarding an omniscient being even due to the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramā*).

For instance, even when an object such as a jar exists, a means of valid cognition does not operate for one who lacks eyes; and even when those [senses] such as the eyes are unimpaired, [the cognition] does not operate because the object known as the "subject matter" is either non-proximate or non-existent. This is the connection with the present context.
Just as in the case of a jar or similar object when it is not present in a suitable location,
[the term] "of the mere" refers to that which is devoid of the qualification of perceptibility.
"Because of seeing it in two ways" means that it is seen both as an existent and as a non-existent.
Therefore, it is better,
because it is the cause for reconnecting the roots of virtue.

For instance: for those whose roots of merit have been severed by wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), there is a reconnection of the roots of merit through doubt (*kāṅkṣā*). This junction is described by two views, according to the statement: "The junction [is effected] by the two views of doubt and existence" (*sandhiḥ kāṅkṣā'stidṛṣṭibhyām*). For this very reason, teachers in various places formulate a doubt: if it is asked, "What is the proof for its existence?", let there be doubt precisely because of that. (3301)

It might be argued as follows: "If an omniscient being exists, why is he never perceived by anyone? Even if it were granted that he is eternally unperceivable by those of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*), nevertheless, why is his effect not apprehended by anyone? For it is not the case that because the eyes and other sense organs are imperceptible, their effect—namely, cognition—must also be imperceptible. To this, he says: "For even though he exists," and so forth.
For even though it exists, it would not be perceived by the dull-witted, just like the conceptualization of something else; nor would it produce its effect, like fire within an iron ball or charcoal.
Or rather, its effect would be invisible, like the passion born of another's conceptualization.
Even if an effect were visible, its connection with that [omniscient being] would not be perceived;
since one who knows all objects is always invisible to those of dull intellect, his existence will therefore not be established through inference. (3304–3305)
And it has been stated that [such] a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is neither a non-reason (ahetu) nor a non-pervader (avyāpaka).
Furthermore, since the existence of this [object] is observed even when the [other] object has ceased, there is doubt on that account as well;
[the phrase] "it would not be seen directly" is to be connected [to this].

For it is not the case that everything whatsoever must be perceived all at once, such that the non-existence of an omniscient being would follow from the absence of perception; for even existing conceptual constructions occurring in another person are not perceived by others.

Nor is it necessary that causes always be engaged in producing their effects, such that the non-existence of an omniscient being would follow from the non-perception of his effects, since we observe things such as fire in a heated iron ball where the effect of smoke has not yet been produced.

Granted that causes are always possessed of their effects, nevertheless, there is no certainty regarding the absence of those effects; for not every effect, even when produced, is pervaded by perceptibility, such that its absence could be established through the non-perception of the effect.

This is because an effect, even if produced, may not be perceived—just like the passion born of improper mental attention (*ayoni-manasikāra*) in another person during a cosmic age (*kalpa*); for although it has arisen, it is not perceived, yet its absence is not [thereby] established.

Or even if the effect is observed, because its cause is beyond the senses, it is possible that for a person who has not grasped its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), no inference of it will arise; likewise, it is conceivable for those of dull intellect that the proof [of an omniscient being] might occur through inference—even though [in reality] it would not. "Dull intellect" refers to those whose vision is their intellect (*dhī-dṛk*); those whose intellectual vision is dull are so described.

Furthermore, it was stated previously: "Just as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is neither the cause of an object nor its pervader (*vyāpaka*), how could the object be negated even when this inference—which is neither its cause nor its pervader—is negated? This is the intended meaning. And it was likewise stated: "It cannot be said that an object is seen to be negated upon the cessation of a means of valid cognition called 'inference,' even though that [inference] is neither its cause nor its pervader; for there is nothing that is impossible in what is actually observed. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even when this [inference] has ceased, the existence of the object is still observed."
Even when this inference has ceased, the existence of this entity is still observed, as was previously stated: for example, the case of fire within a red-hot iron ball and so forth.

Having thus demonstrated in detail the impossibility of any subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) for the purpose of establishing the non-existence of an omniscient being, he concludes with the words beginning "Therefore" (*tasmāt*).
Therefore, there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever that subverts the existence of an omniscient being; rather, its proof will be set forth in detail.
One might object: "Just as we have no means of valid cognition that subverts it, so too you do not have one that proves it. To this he says: "But its proof... [is as follows].

Regarding what was stated— "the means for the knowledge of the expansion of all constituent parts and individual instances," and so forth— he replies here: "Even though the means for the thorough knowledge of all objects without exception is fruitless," and so on.
The wise followers of the Sugata exert effort with one mind; "with another mind" means with another intention.
To the question "Who, then, is this? he says: "The one who knows the means for attaining heaven and liberation," and so forth; it is understood that such a person exists.
Not only directly, but he is also perceived as omniscient.

For we are primarily establishing for the Blessed One the proof of being a knower of the causes that lead to the attainment of heaven and liberation; however, the proof of his complete knowledge of all objects is incidental. Since there is no subverting evidence against the operation of the Blessed One’s cognition regarding other matters as well, he is omniscient through the direct comprehension of all objects, and thus he cannot be refuted by anyone. Therefore, it is not reasonable for discerning people to reject this [claim].
However, it has been shown that for those who seek the attainment of omniscience, their engagement toward that end is indeed logical (verse 3309).

Consequently, since there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) in this way, and since the proof of omniscience to be stated hereafter is perfectly clear, the following demonstrates that your rejection of an omniscient being—who is the sole object of certainty—namely, the claim that "all persons are never free from the affliction of passion and so forth," arises solely from delusion (*moha*). This is shown by the words beginning with "tataśca" and so on.
And so, when there is an absence of sublation and a clear proof exists, why do those of dull intellect disagree regarding the omniscient one?

(3310) It might be argued: "We reject [the existence of such a person] because we believe that no such means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) exists to establish a person of that kind, and not out of delusion. To this he says: "Mābhūt" and so forth.
Or, even if there were no proof for that [position], since a subverting argument has not been ascertained, there would be doubt; but on what basis could this certainty of theirs be established?
This is stated while provisionally accepting their view, for the proof [for our position] will indeed be presented later.
"This is the certainty:
that there is no omniscient being"—such is the view of the Mīmāṃsakas.

As for what you say—that "injunction alone is capable of making known such objects as the past, the present, the future, the subtle, and the remote, whereas no other sense-organ can do so"—this too is shown to be merely a claim asserted through partisan rhetoric, devoid of any proof. He demonstrates this with the verse beginning "bhūtādi": "The restriction that 'only injunction is capable of making known the past and so forth, and nothing else' is indeed logical only if the non-existence of any other [means of knowledge] has been definitively established. (3312)
"Another" refers to the direct perception of the Omniscient One and so forth;
"the non-existence of others" means [the absence of such perception by] others.
It is only when the non-existence of another omniscient being has been ascertained that it is proper to speak in this way, and not otherwise, because such a restriction would be fruitless.
Regarding that [point] concerning "the entire world is subtle," etc., he says: "The primary cause," and so forth.

In order to establish the one who knows the purpose of both primary matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa), as well as the knower of all things, that means of valid cognition has been explained first, and others will be stated later.
Therefore, for the sake of establishing the object known by the one who perceives the subtle distinctions of the entire world—
The world does not suffer in vain through the agitation of debates over books;
for we do not exert ourselves in proving an omniscient being by engaging in reflections concerning the domain of an omniscient being,
but rather solely in proving the one who knows the Dharma, who is the primary subject.
