And likewise, previously—in the passage beginning with "by that [means] obtainable through presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) and accepted by those who know dharma"—the means of valid cognition called presumptive testimony was stated for the purpose of establishing the Knower of Dharma according to your own view; subsequently, the means of valid cognition called inference will be set forth. Therefore, people are not being troubled in an inappropriate place, but rather in the appropriate place itself.

Regarding the passage beginning with "connected to all cognizers" (sarvapramātṛsambaddha), he says: "Because perception and other means of knowledge connected to all cognizers cannot be excluded, it is not established that merit and demerit are cognizable solely through scripture. (3315)

Since perception and other means of knowledge—which have as their objects things such as *dharma* and are connected to all cognizers—cannot be refuted by mere non-perception (*adarśana*), it follows that *dharma* and *adharma* cannot be established as being cognizable by scripture alone.
Regarding what was stated previously, beginning with "And by this much," etc., he says: "By this much," etc.
And thus, even though the position of the Mīmāṃsakas remains unestablished by this much, the further effort made by others to refute the omniscient one is due to extreme ease [or, rather, folly].
(3316) "Even though it remains unestablished" means:
Because it is established by others— the Mīmāṃsakas— that [the Buddha] knows the Dharma.
Regarding the passage beginning with "But those [who argue] because their root is severed," he says: "But those [who argue] because their root is not severed, etc."— that is to say,
provided that their status as knowers of dharma remains unimpaired due to the fact that their root is not severed.
They say that all-knowing persons are those by whom wisdom has been revealed;
"ahataḥ" (unstruck) should be understood as having the vowel *a* elided [to form *ahitaḥ*],
and "by them" refers to those [wise ones].
Regarding the Buddhist claim that [the self] is directly perceived because of such statements as "because it is seen by direct perception," he says: "By the sense of taste," and so forth.

If the tastes of wine, impurities, and so forth were perceived through a connection with the sense organ of taste, then at that very moment, those [impurities] would become objects of revulsion. [However,
this is not the case for one who perceives them] solely with a mental consciousness arisen from the cultivation of the true nature of reality.
Even those things that are censured in conventional reality are experienced [by him] without being actually reached.

(3319) If it is argued: "Even if there were a direct experience of the taste of liquor and so forth by him, nevertheless his status as a knower of Dharma would not be lost, because he does not incur the state of being censurable," [we reply: one who experiences those tastes and so forth through contact with the sense organs such as the tongue would be censurable according to worldly convention; however, the Blessed One does not experience them in that way. What then? He experiences them by means of the mind, and since that [mental consciousness] has objects that are not reached [by the senses], the state of censurability caused by that is not recognized in the world.
In the ultimate sense, nothing whatsoever possesses the quality of being censurable, because such a state is not fixed;

for instance, that which is censurable for a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) is not so for an outcaste (*juṅgita*). However, although in the conventional world intoxicants and the like are condemned, and one might experience them accordingly, even so, there is no censurability for the Blessed One, because he experiences the intoxicant by means of the mind alone.

It might be argued: "Just as for others, the experience of intoxicants and the like through contact with the gustatory faculty results in the experience of suffering and so forth, the same would apply to one who experiences it through the mind."

This is not the case: flavors and so forth, being experienced through their connection with the sense-faculties such as the tongue, cause benefit or harm to the faculty and thus become causes of suffering and the like;
yet these manifest as causes of suffering and so forth only for certain individuals whose minds are perverted by the influence of unwholesome karma and the like, and not for everyone.

For just as water and the like appear to hungry ghosts (*preta*) in the form of pus and so forth, it is not so for the Blessed One; indeed, because he perceives everything through the mind alone, there is no possibility of sensory impairment or the like. Furthermore, because the Blessed One consists of the five types of conventional activity that are untainted (*anāsrava*), there is no possibility of being under the influence of tainted karma (*sāsrava-karma*). Because he perceives things in their non-erroneous, impermanent, and other such forms, there is no state of perversion (*viparyasta*). For this very reason, even mental suffering characterized by dejection and the like is impossible for the Blessed One, since that [suffering] is born of delusion (*moha*).

And all this objection applies only when external objects exist; however, in the system of the Vijñānavādins, there is no room for it whatsoever. For, since the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) does not exist from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), impurities and the like do not exist at all for them, lest there be the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) imagined based upon them, because [all things] arise solely from consciousness.

Therefore, these do not appear in the vision of those who have internalized the vision of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-darśana*) and for whom all appearances of impurity and the like have been removed; just as hairs and such do not appear in the vision of those with unimpaired eyes when the defects of cataracts and the like have vanished.
As it has been said: "Indeed, impurity, taste, and so forth appear to him through ignorance;
therefore, they are established as being non-perceived, like a second lunar disc."

But how could that brahmin, whose Vedic sounds— existing within his mouth, belly, and so forth— are always connected to every impure place by virtue of his pervasiveness, not be censurable in this world? (3318–3319)

And regarding the passage beginning with "nor [is it found] in the Vedas, Upavedas, or Aṅgas," he says: "Precisely because no statement of the Tāyin is seen that propounds the meaning taught in the Vedas and so forth, for that very reason he is omniscient. (3320)
It is possible that he possesses a state entirely uncommon to all non-Buddhist heretics;
for indeed, one who has studied the Veda through negligence might declare the self and other such things to be false.
(3321) Whatever object exists in a certain way—such as being existent and so forth—one becomes omniscient by knowing it exactly as it is.
Furthermore, the objects such as the self (ātman) and so forth as they are described in the Veda do not exist in that very way, because they are sublated by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
Therefore, how could one who teaches them exactly in that manner be a seer of reality (tattvadarśin)?
Nor can it be said that these things were not known even as false, for they were indeed known just as they were.

For instance: all acts such as the killing of living beings prescribed in the Vedas and other texts are unwholesome courses of action, pointed out as causes for rebirth in miserable states; likewise, by statements such as "There is no being here, nor a self; these phenomena exist with their causes," even the self and so forth are declared to be non-existent. Thus, the Blessed One’s lack of knowledge regarding the things prescribed in the Vedas and other texts is unestablished. 3320–3321.
Regarding the passage beginning with "even though not established in his own treatises," he says:
"The non-dual gate of Śiva, which is terrifying to those of wrong views, was clearly taught as selflessness (nairātmya) for the benefit of those to be guided. (3322)
It is "without a second" because it has not been attained by any other non-Buddhist teachers, as they are all exclusively obsessed with false views of a self;
and all this is a qualification of selflessness,
which is the "gate to the auspicious."
Because it serves as the means for entering nirvāṇa,
"auspicious" (śiva) refers to nirvāṇa for those with wrong views.
Those who possess contemptible views regarding the self and so forth are described as such;
the meaning is that [this teaching] causes terror in foolish people who are attached to false views.
As it has been said: "I do not exist, I am not, I shall not be; nothing is mine, nothing shall be."
Thus, while this is a cause of terror for the fool, it is a moment of fearlessness for the wise;
by this it is shown that for those established in contrary dogmatic adherence, even the mention of its realization is impossible, let alone its actual attainment.
And he shows that it has never before been fully known by anyone remaining on the level of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana): "unfamiliar to those in saṃsāra"—
that which is known as unfamiliar to those in saṃsāra brings about the cessation of all misfortunes.

If poets recognize such a supreme reality— the ultimate mine of jewels of virtue for those engaged in its practice— then who would not consider them omniscient, knowing the purpose of both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa)?
The meaning is that it is "unaccustomed" and "unpracticed" by worldly ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
To the question, "How can it lead to welfare, such that it was taught for that purpose? he says: "Known," and so forth.
When it is "known"—that is, directly realized—it becomes the bringer of cessation for the entire mass of misfortunes characterized by afflictions, birth, and so on.

Even when practiced at a later time, if poets were to realize that very essence which is useful for the supreme human goal—that it brings about specific qualities such as [the ability to compose] on the streets and so forth—then let them too be omniscient. For we do not accept omniscience as being restricted to only one person; rather, whoever knows the reality exactly as it has been described is considered all-knowing, and no other. And since this is not the case for poets, there is no over-extension of the definition.

Demonstrating that by this [argument] what was stated previously—"And among many omniscient beings," etc.—is also refuted, he says: "And this," and so forth: "And this knowledge of selflessness belonging to Vardhamāna and others is of such a kind; for all the non-Buddhist teachers have perished because of their view of a self. (3325)
Those who have stated many things— such as that the *syādvāda* is non-momentary— which are contradicted by perception and other means of valid cognition, how indeed could they be omniscient?
For they stumble even regarding this perceptible object well-known to the Vāhīkas and others.
How can their clear realization of that which is beyond the senses be conceived?
Thus, their lack of omniscience is clearly understood from their association with false knowledge and their teaching of what is contrary [to reality]. (3327–3328)
Just as another person who is mistaken, perceiving a post as a man,

is to be understood through all means of investigation by means of the establishment of reasons, so too is the All-Knowing One (sarvajña) to be known through the correct knowledge of the true nature of all things. // 3329 //
Therefore, in this case, there is no doubt regarding the negative concomitance (vyatireka) with respect to the reason for perfect enlightenment.

As it has been said: if the knowledge of reality were possible for Vardhamāna, Kapila, and others, then let them also possess omniscience. However, since all of these are seized by the crocodile of false self-grasping—the cause of the production of every fault—and are teachers of such things as non-momentariness which are sublated by direct perception and other means of valid cognition, how can their vision of supersensuous objects be considered even a possibility, given that they stumble even over those objects accessible to the understanding of children? For this reason, when it is asked, "Is it not so that Kapila is not [omniscient]? what proof is there?

For in this matter, the following proof can be stated very clearly: those who are possessed of false cognition are not omniscient, just as a person who has conceived the delusion that a post is a man; and Vardhamāna and others are possessed of false cognition—this is a perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory [of the probandum], because being possessed of false cognition is pervaded by non-omniscience, which is the contradictory of omniscience.
Nor is the reason unestablished, since it has been demonstrated through all forms of investigation that they reveal objects in a manner contrary to reality.
Nor is the reason inconclusive due to its exclusion from the dissimilar instances being doubtful; for omniscience is intended here as the state of correctly knowing all objects without exception,
and where there is correct knowledge, there is no possibility of false knowledge, which is its opposite.

It might be argued: "Even if these [words] do indeed reveal a contrary meaning, nevertheless it cannot be concluded from this that they are associated with false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), because worldly transactions can be carried out in another way as well, owing to the diverse intentions of persons. Therefore, the reason is 'unproven due to doubt' (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*). Anticipating this objection, he says: "It is intentional," and so forth.
If the statements regarding "syādvāda" (the doctrine of manifoldness) and so forth were intended [only] figuratively, then what would be accepted as the actual nature of all things by them?
For if it is claimed that these were stated with another intention, even though they contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) such as *syādvāda*, [then the following applies].

Let it be stated: we do not intend to establish the non-omniscience of Vardhamāna and others independently; rather, you—standing in mutually contradictory positions—asked, "If the Sugata is omniscient, then what is the proof that Kapila is not? To this, we state a proof by accepting the difference of opinion among them according to your own view. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*). For instance, if their words are described as being intentional (*ābhiprāyika*), then it must be asked: what is held to be their ultimate (*pāramārthika*) nature of reality? 3331

Being questioned in this manner, the opponent replies: "Because of selflessness, momentariness, and so forth. If it is thus [that these are known], it is because the All-Seeing One perceives directly the true nature of all things. (3332)
"May they also [be valid], because all of them are established through unanimity;

for they did not proclaim a definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) that is mutually contradictory. (33) If one were to say that [the scriptures] speak of a self (*ātman*) and so forth, then a difference of opinion would indeed be stated, and thus there would be no lack of proof (*asiddhatā*)."

He provides the answer with the words "If it is so," and so forth: "It is not our intention to establish that 'this very person is omniscient' by pointing him out specifically like seizing a horn; rather, we speak generally.

If the thorough knowledge of such principles is admitted even for Kapila and others, then you must explain how there can be a difference of opinion between those two, since they all stand in agreement. As for their teaching of mutually contradictory matters, that is established as being of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*)."
It is not logical that those who stand with a single consensus should proclaim mutually contradictory definitive meanings—the ultimate reality.

Therefore, one who desires to accept a diversity of views must state that their words are intentional (*ābhiprāyika*). Furthermore, if this diversity of views is admitted, it should not be asked, "Who indeed is to be determined as the one [authoritative]? For it has already been established that the Sugata alone is determined to be omniscient by virtue of possessing the aforementioned knowledge, and no other.

Furthermore, demonstrating that if one accepts the aforementioned knowledge for Kapila and others, they would necessarily attain the state of a Sugata (Buddha), he says: "Of that which has been established in form," and so forth;
[referring to] that which has been established in form and which pervades all things.
Through the direct realization of reality, they are Sugatas and all-seeing ones.
And for them, in such a cognition, their state as Sugatas does not differ;
because of their possession of this praiseworthy knowledge, this alone is its defining characteristic.
That reality characterized by selflessness and so forth, whose nature (rūpa) has been established and proven through valid cognition (pramāṇa), is described as such;
"of them" refers to Vardhamāna and the others.
"To this extent" means that he possesses praiseworthy knowledge and yoga.

Because the abandonment of all obscurations regarding the knowable and so forth is excellently accomplished through the knowledge of selflessness, he has gone [to that state]; thus, he is called the Sugata.

Furthermore, he shows that even when the possibility of an omniscient being is established in a general sense, it necessarily pertains to the Blessed One alone; thus he says, "Even though such a person might exist," and so forth.
Even though an omniscient being has been established in a general sense as being possible, [it refers specifically to the Blessed One].
The Sugata is established [as such] because of the invariable concomitance with those marks;
"tad" means "therefore."

"Because of the inseparable connection with the characteristics [of an omniscient being]" means because of the inseparable connection with the characteristics of an omniscient being (sarvajña). [Objection: But how can he be established without a specific designation? To this he says: "Even though no specific [characteristic] has been designated," and so forth;
that is, some omniscient being might exist even if no specific [attribute] has been pointed out.

"He who knows the entire world as it truly is, in its nature of being selfless and so forth"—even though this definition of an omniscient one (*sarvajña*) is stated in general terms, when such [omniscience] is observed in a particular person, that specific individual is understood by implication; thus, the mention of a specific [person] is redundant. Furthermore, this definition of an omniscient one is found in the Blessed One alone and nowhere else, because he reveals through diverse means the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the means thereto, characterized by the four truths in their entirety—this is the intended meaning.

For it is not possible to teach an unknown object as it truly is— that is, correctly, without error, and in its entirety— as it has been said: "Indeed, it is difficult to explain that which is beyond perception, along with its goal and its cause" (3337).

It might be argued: "Even if the world is known by him in its true form as being without self and so forth, how is he established as omniscient? To this, he says: "When selflessness has been directly perceived," and so on.
"When selflessness has been directly perceived, no fault finds a footing, because it is contrary to them, just as darkness does not persist before a blazing lamp. (3338)

Omniscience arises from the abandonment of the obscurations of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Among these, the afflictions themselves—such as attachment and so forth—are called the "obscurations of afflictions" because they function as obstacles to seeing reality exactly as it is. Furthermore, the lack of complete knowledge in all its aspects regarding the truth of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, even though it has been seen, as well as the incapacity to teach it, is the "obscuration of the knowable.
Therein, the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions occurs through the direct perception of selflessness;
however, the abandonment of the obscuration of the knowable occurs through the diligent, uninterrupted, and long-term cultivation of that very same vision of selflessness.

For indeed, these afflictions such as attachment and so forth are determined through positive and negative concomitance to be rooted in the false view of a self; they do not arise by the power of external objects, because even when an external object is present, they do not arise without the mental application of improper reflection (*ayoniśo-manasikāra*), and conversely,
they do arise even in the absence of an object when improper conceptualization (*ayoniśo-vikalpa*) is manifest.
Furthermore, it is not logical that something which does not conform to the existence or non-existence of another should be its cause, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
Nor do these [defilements] inhere in a self imagined by others, because such a self has been refuted;
or even if it were granted, there would follow the consequence that passion and the rest would either arise eternally or never cease at all.
Because the self, as the cause of production and persistence, is always present in its unimpaired state,
and because it is impossible for that which cannot have any excellence added to it by others to depend upon them— this has been discussed extensively—

it is improper for these [qualities] to have inherence in anything, since the dependence of both existent and non-existent things has been refuted; therefore, their existence is not bound to an eternal cause.

Nor do they arise from the power of external objects; rather, they are produced by the power of the false view of self (*abhūtātmadarśana*). For instance, attachment to the self does not arise in one who does not perceive "I," nor does attachment as "mine" emerge toward an object that is not grasped as such, provided that object is not apprehended as being conducive to the production of one's own pleasure. Furthermore, aversion never manifests in one who is unattached toward an object that is not apprehended as being contrary to oneself or what belongs to oneself.
Because [hatred] is impossible toward that which does not obstruct one's own interests and which counteracts such obstruction, the same must be said for name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) and the rest.

Therefore, the view of self (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), produced by the repeated practice of its own kind from beginningless time, gives rise to the grasping of "mine" (*ātmīyagraha*); these two in turn produce affection for what belongs to the self (*ātmīyasneha*), and that [affection] produces hatred and so forth. Thus, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), it is established with perfect clarity—even down to cowherds and women—that these [afflictions] are rooted in the grasping of self and what belongs to the self.
The vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is the opposite of the vision of a self (*ātmadarśana*), because their objective supports (*ālambana*) have mutually exclusive forms.

Indeed, it is contradictory for these two to coexist or be identical within a single mental continuum (*santāna*) at one and the same time, just as it is impossible for a rope and the cognition of a snake [mistakenly perceived in it] to exist together.

Therefore, because the vision of selflessness contradicts the vision of a self, it also stands in opposition to passion (*rāga*) and the other afflictions rooted in that vision; this is just as a specific application of fire opposes the specific effects of cold, such as the bristling of body hair.

When the vision of selflessness, which is the adversary of all defects, has been directly realized by that [practitioner], the host of defects such as passion and the like—which are its opposite—can find no footing, just as darkness cannot remain in a place pervaded by light; therefore, through the vision of selflessness, the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions occurs.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: Wherever there is the presence of a thing that is incompatible with another, the latter does not attain its existence there; for example, darkness on a surface of ground in contact with the spreading radiance of a blazing lamp. And there is the presence of the vision of selflessness (*nairātmya*), which is incompatible with the multitude of defects, in a person who has directly perceived selflessness. This is the perception of the incompatible (*viruddhopalabdhi*).

It might be argued as follows: just as there is no opportunity for the view of self (*ātmadarśana*) to arise when the mind is occupied by the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) due to their mutual opposition, so too there would be no opportunity for the vision of selflessness to arise when the mind is occupied by the view of self, since the contradiction is equal in both cases. Consequently, because the vision of selflessness is impossible for anyone, the reason [you provide] is unestablished (*asiddha*). Alternatively, even if the vision of selflessness were possible, nevertheless, despite the existence of this contradiction between the two, an absolute relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) is not established, as is the case with passion and hatred, or pleasure and pain.
Since what is intended to be established here is absolute abandonment, and not merely the non-manifestation for a limited time, the reason is inconclusive;
for even in those who possess unimpaired majesty, passion and other defilements are seen to arise. For this reason as well, the reason is inconclusive.
This is not so.

If the arising of the conceptual construction of selflessness were impossible within the continuum of one whose afflictions have not been abandoned, then indeed there would be no opportunity for the emergence of the vision of selflessness. However, since the manifestation of the conceptual construction of selflessness is established by experience for everyone, and since that very [construction] can reach a state of excellence through cultivation—just like the conceptualization of a beloved woman—it eventually attains the status of direct perception (pratyakṣa) by virtue of having a vivid appearance and grasping an object as it is cognized by valid cognition (pramāṇa). Thus, how could the emergence of the vision of selflessness be impossible?
Moreover—just as in a place enveloped by darkness, there is the possibility of an opportunity for light to arise after some time, why should it not be possible here as well?
Nor can it be said that such a form of contemplation (*bhāvanā*), which would result in direct perceptual knowledge (*pratyakṣajñāna*) of that nature, is impossible for anyone;
for one must state the reason for its impossibility.

To explain: regarding the lack of application toward cultivation (*bhāvanā*), would the cause be a lack of desire on the part of everyone, since the activity of a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*) is pervaded by desire? Or, even though there is desire, does the discerning person not engage because of a failure to fully understand the nature of what is to be abandoned (*praheya*), since it is impossible to abandon a defect whose nature is unknown? Or, even when there is knowledge of its nature, does he not undertake effort for its abandonment because he perceives the defects as eternal, since the abandonment of what is eternal is impossible?

Or, even if they are non-existent, does one desist after realizing their eternity and causelessness, since that which is independent cannot possibly be destroyed? Or, even if they possess a cause, is one indifferent toward cultivation because the nature of that cause is uncertain, for it is impossible to abandon a disease whose origin is unknown? Or, let us assume there is full knowledge of its cause; having realized that the cause is eternal, would a person acting with foresight not exert themselves to abandon it, since a complete cause cannot be obstructed?

Or, even if impermanence [is granted], having realized that the causes of those defects are inherent properties (*dharma*) of living beings, would one not exert effort? For it is impossible to abandon what is intrinsic (*svabhāva*).

Or, if the defects were not intrinsic, would one desist because there is no possibility of a means for their destruction? For there is no attainment of the goal (*upeya*) for one who lacks the means (*upāya*).
Furthermore, even if the means exists, one might fail to practice it due to ignorance of it; for it is impossible to practice that whose true nature (*svarūpa*) is not fully understood.

Or, even if there is full comprehension, might one not fail to apply oneself to cultivation because one considers its ultimate excellence to be impossible—either because excellence is fixed in its limits like jumping, or because rebirth is no longer possible?

Or, even if the destruction of defects is possible through the arising of their opposites due to the attainment of ultimate excellence, might one still not begin the application because one suspects that the defects could arise again, just as the hardness of copper and other metals returns?
In this regard, it is first of all not established that there is a lack of desire [to attain liberation].

For instance: those whose minds are oppressed by the sufferings of birth and so forth, whose minds are terrified of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), and who pray for its cessation for themselves—they, being destined for the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and others, possess precisely this fear of cyclic existence as the cause for their desire to cultivate selflessness (*nairātmya*).

However, those who—by virtue of a particular lineage (*gotra*)—are by their very nature solely delighted in performing the welfare of others, and who, having beheld the world tormented by the three types of suffering such as conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*), are pained by that suffering due to being under the sway of compassion; having cast aside all regard for themselves and accepted all transmigrating beings as their own self, they apply themselves to their protection—for them, compassion alone is the cause for engaging in cultivation. This is because it is difficult to explain the means and the goal when both are beyond direct perception, and [one might ask]: "What purpose does a discerning person have in performing the welfare of others? If this is asked, [the answer is: no.

That itself is the purpose, because it possesses the characteristic of being desired; nor does this entail a lack of foresight, since the attachment to performing what is beneficial for oneself is based on the grasping at a conceptualized self, and because doing what is beneficial for others is approved by all virtuous people and is invariably connected with its own fruit.

Moreover, it was begun here to demonstrate that the absence of a desire for activity is impossible in one who is engaged in cultivation; for even if he were indeed lacking in foresight, how could he be devoid of a desire for activity on that account alone?
Therefore, this alone must be asserted: "No one engages in activity for the sake of benefiting others, because there is no purpose [in doing so]," and regarding that, it has been said:

Moreover, just as some are observed to be excessively habituated to cruelty, delighting for no reason whatsoever in the misfortunes of others and finding pleasure in the suffering of others, so too there are some who are habituated to compassion, delighting in the happiness of others and pained by the suffering of others—even in the absence of any other motive; why, then, should this not be possible?

Nor is there a lack of understanding regarding the nature of the defects, since the host of afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*)—such as attachment, aversion, delusion, pride, intoxication, envy, and avarice—arise and pass away with their specific natures fully known, appearing in forms such as obsession, obstruction, and the exaltation of self and what belongs to the self.
Nor are they eternal, because they are experienced as being occasional;
for this very reason, they do not lack a cause, since that which is causeless, being independent of anything else, could not be restricted by place, time, or intrinsic nature.

For this reason as well, their having an eternal cause is refuted, because a cause such as the Self would always be present, and being incapable of receiving any further excellence, it would be independent of auxiliary conditions.
Because there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence that those things arising from mere [specific] causes would always arise simultaneously;
therefore, by implication, these have only impermanent causes.

Furthermore, even though their cause is impermanent, its nature is well-known, because the collection of defects such as attachment has the misconception of self and what belongs to self (*ātmātmīya-viparyāsa*) as its cause, and because it conforms to the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of that misconception, as was established previously.

Nor can these [passions] be properties of a living being (*prāṇin*), because that very subject (*dharmin*) is unestablished; for there exists no such subject called a "living being" to which these properties such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth might belong.
This is because the conventional usage of property and subject is merely a conceptual construction based on the principle of specific conditionality (*idampratyayatāmātra*).

If, on the other hand, it is argued that these are properties of a living being either by virtue of having the mind (*citta*) as their intrinsic nature or by arising therein, even then there is both non-establishment (*asiddhi*) and inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*).

For instance—one who maintains the relationship between object (*viṣaya*) and subject (*viṣayin*) must admit that the mind has the nature of grasping the object; otherwise, there would be no relationship of object and subject between the object and the cognition.
If its nature is accepted as being the grasping of the object, then it must be said that the object is grasped by that very part of itself which constitutes its own nature;
otherwise, how could it be grasped?
If it were apprehended by means of a non-existent aspect, then the relationship between object and subject would not exist;

for instance, the object does not exist in the same manner that cognition makes it its object, nor does cognition make that object its object in the same manner as the object exists. Consequently, cognitions would be entirely without objects, and this would lead to the undesirable consequence that all things would be unestablished.
Therefore, it is established that its innate nature is to grasp the aspect of an object that is real;
and since it has been demonstrated that the nature of a real object consists in being momentary, selfless, and so forth,
it follows that [the cognition] has precisely the grasping of selflessness as its nature, and not the grasping of a self.

Furthermore, that which has a different nature [from its basis] is established as existing only through the power of adventitious conditions for those who are deluded by its non-manifestation, and not by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just like the cognition of a snake in a rope; therefore, even though the mass of afflictions (*kleśagaṇa*) is extremely powerful, it is unable to uproot the capacity for the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*),
because it is seen to be produced by adventitious conditions.

However, because it possesses the nature of selflessness and is supported by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), the knowledge of selflessness is powerful; thus, even though the contradiction is equal, it is established as the antidote to the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*), whereas the view of a self is not its antidote, because it is the opposite of that [knowledge].

Even for one who holds the position that external objects do not exist, in his view as well, knowledge has the very nature of apprehending selflessness and does not consist of the view of a self, since for him the self is non-existent.

For instance: even if, due to the absence of an object, he does not accept cognition as having the nature of grasping that object, he must necessarily admit it to have the nature of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*);
otherwise, there would be no determination of cognition itself.
Furthermore, that self is to be cognized only in its existing form as non-self, non-dual, and so forth, and not otherwise; for otherwise, the same faults as mentioned previously would ensue.

Therefore, it is unestablished that these [defilements] have the nature of living beings (*prāṇidharma*). Furthermore, even if one imagines that they have the nature of intrinsic being (*svabhāva*) merely on the grounds that they arise therein, their abandonment is impossible because of the lack of necessity (*anekāntāt*);
for instance, the cognition of a snake arises with respect to a rope, and yet it ceases upon the arising of correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*).
Nor is it impossible for there to be a means of their destruction, because the practice of things whose nature is opposed to their own causes is possible as such a means.

For instance: those things which possess the practice of a nature opposed to their own possible causes are subject to the absolute severance of their continuum, just as rice and other grains; and since these [afflictions] such as passion and the like are likewise [subject to such opposition], a means for their destruction is indeed possible.

Nor is there a lack of thorough knowledge regarding that [object], because from the very knowledge of the nature of the cause, it is clearly ascertained that whatever entity possesses an object and aspect contrary to that [cause] is its antidote;
and it has already been demonstrated that the vision of selflessness is the antidote in this case precisely because it possesses an object and aspect contrary to it.
Furthermore, there is no fixed limit to its excellence, as is the case with jumping and other such activities.

Because that which is produced by repeated prior practice does not depart due to its having become one's very nature (*svabhāva*), because each subsequent effort is dedicated solely to imparting a new excellence,
because it has a stable basis,

and because it originates from seeds of a similar kind to those preceding it— such is the case with wisdom (*prajñā*) and the like; however, jumping and other such acts are not so, as will be demonstrated later.

Nor is it impossible for [defilements] to arise in another birth, since the continuity of previous births has already been established. Nor is there any possibility of the defilements arising again—like the hardness of copper and other metals—because the vision of selflessness, which is their antidote, has attained ultimate internalization and is never lost. For in the case of the hardness of copper and so forth, its antidote is fire; since fire is only occasionally present, it is logical that hardness and the like exist only when fire is absent, and that they arise again once that fire has departed. However, in this case, such is not possible.
But this is not the case for the defilements (*mala*);

even when the path has been removed by means of ashes and the like, there is no necessary possibility of the defects arising again, because [the example] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, when wood and such things are reduced to ashes through contact with fire, they do not resume their former form even after that fire is removed; it is the same for the defects—thus, the argument is inconclusive. Furthermore, since the defilements were previously incapable [of persisting] due to being adventitious, how could they have the power to subvert that selflessness (*nairātmya*) which has become naturalized? Indeed, an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) cannot be overturned without effort.

Furthermore, for discerning persons, it is not reasonable to exert effort to abandon or to adopt two things—one to be attained and one to be avoided—without first perceiving their respective merits and defects.
Nor is it possible for a person whose mind is not mistaken to perceive merits in what is defective, or to perceive defects in its opposite, because they are free from error.
Indeed, those whose intellects are not mistaken do not take up a defectless thing as being defective, nor do they regard a defective thing as possessing merit.
Furthermore, the vision of selflessness is never defective,
because it possesses the quality of being free from all afflictions;
for instance, due to the removal of the stains of passion and so forth without exception, there is no affliction resulting from the failure to perceive reality.
Nor is there the affliction of physical and mental torment caused by the outbursts of passion and the like,
nor the affliction of disease, decrepitude, and so forth bound to birth, because of the absence of the afflictions that are the cause of birth;
nor is there the affliction of distaste as in the enjoyment of tainted pleasure, because the flavor of the bliss of tranquility is exclusively non-distressing.
Therefore, it is not appropriate to exert effort for its diminution; rather, if there were to be any effort at all, it should be solely for the sake of its non-diminution,
because the intellect by its very nature is partial toward excellence.
Nor is there any effort to adopt faults, because they are defective by virtue of being the locus of all calamities; therefore, the cultivation of selflessness is possible,
and it is observed that through reaching the ultimate limit of its excellence, it results in a cognition characterized by clear manifestation.
Just as in the case of one afflicted by passion who meditates on a beloved woman—
for him, words such as "I see her with her playful movements" or "Embrace me," as well as bodily activities corresponding to that intention, proceed based on direct perception;
therefore, the reason is not unestablished.

Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) possesses strength due to its having a real object (*bhūtārtha*), whereas the vision of a self (*ātmadarśana*) is the opposite; thus, there exists a relationship of counteragent and opponent (*vipakṣapratipakṣabhāva*).

Furthermore, since passion (*rāga*) and hatred (*dveṣa*) proceed through contact with the unreal grasping of a self, their relationship as opponent and counteragent is not caused by the apprehension of contradictory forms, nor is it due to error (*viparyāsa*), because both are erroneous insofar as they are produced by non-error [in the sense that they arise from the underlying grasping of a self].

Nor is a contradiction between these two established, because both have the grasping of a self as their single source and stand in a cause-and-effect relationship. To explain: when there is attachment to a self and what belongs to a self, aversion arises toward that which obstructs it, and not otherwise. Furthermore, it is not logical for two things that share the same cause and stand in a cause-and-effect relationship to bear the relation of sublater and sublated, just as in the case of fire and smoke, both of which originate from the same fuel, or like the grasping of a self and affection for it; otherwise, there would be an over-extension of the principle.
The non-simultaneous arising [of two cognitions] is due to the incapacity of the mind that serves as their material cause (*upādāna*) to project two homogeneous cognitions at once.

Furthermore, there is no mutual contradiction between pleasure and pain; for instance, pleasure and pain are of two kinds: mental and object-born. Regarding those that are mental, because they are associated with aversion and attachment respectively, they share the same status of acquisition and preservation (*ekayogakṣema*) with greed and hatred. Thus, they possess a contrary nature, grasp a single undifferentiated form of self, have the grasping of a self as their common source, and stand in a cause-and-effect relationship; therefore, a mutual contradiction between them is impossible.
Furthermore, regarding those two which arise from sense objects (*viṣaya*), there is no contradiction because their respective causes are not restricted;

for instance, from the very same thing that pleasure arises, suffering also arises when it is indulged in to excess. Thus, there is no restriction regarding the difference in the causes of those two, but this is not the case for the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) with respect to the other.

Furthermore—both of these [the path and the defects] possess equal strength because they are produced by the power of their respective objects; however, this is not the case for the path and the defects, because the path alone possesses strength due to its having a real object (*bhūtārtha*) as its domain, whereas the defects do not.

Indeed, pleasure and pain are not long-lasting, but the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is not like that, for it is always present and never departs because it has become one's very nature (*sātmatva*), as was stated previously; therefore, there is no deviation [in the rule].
As for the reason why they do not arise simultaneously, that has already been explained.
As for the further claim that passion and the like arise even in those who have ascertained selflessness through the power of inference, that is incorrect;

because it is the knowledge consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*)—which, by virtue of its vivid manifestation, is a non-conceptual direct perception of the selfless reality, and which is non-erroneous because its object is a matter established by valid cognition—that is described as the antidote to the view of self (*ātmadarśana*) by means of its absolute uprooting, not that which consists of hearing and reflection (*śrutacintāmaya*).

Because the defilements have been practiced since beginningless time and have become deeply rooted, their destruction occurs only through the gradual increase of their opposites, not by hearing [the teaching] once;
just as the sensation of cold is not destroyed merely by contact with the form of fire.

Nor is it established that the arising of passion and so forth occurs even when the knowledge of selflessness—which is the essence of what has been heard and contemplated—is present, such that there would be a deviation [in the argument].
For instance— the followers of the Sugata indeed dispel the arisen obsession of passion and so forth by means of the power of mental attention toward the foul and so on;
for this very reason, their possession of unimpaired greatness is not established,
and it is precisely for this reason that the contradiction between these [obsessions] and the vision of selflessness is established.
When that [knowledge] is present, there is a diminution;

for those things which possess the nature of being diminished by the presence of something else, they become subject to total destruction without leaving a trace when that [other thing] reaches its ultimate increase—just as a flame of fire does when overwhelmed by water. Since the defects possess the nature of being diminished by the presence of the knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*), how could they maintain their state when that [knowledge] reaches its ultimate increase?
Therefore, the reason (*hetu*) is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
And because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), there is no contradiction [with the reason].

(3338) Having thus established the abandonment of the obscuration of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa-prahāṇa*), he says— "due to the excellence of direct realization"— in order to demonstrate the abandonment of the obscuration of the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa-prahāṇa*).
And because of the specific nature of direct realization, there is no defect accompanied by latent tendencies;
therefore, omniscience is established through liberation from all obscurations.
(3339) [Question: Of what is there direct realization? [Answer: It is understood to be of selflessness (*nairātmya*), as that is the subject under discussion.

Its distinction is as follows: through many means in many ways, over a long period of time, and in every respect, there occurs the absolute manifestation of the qualities and defects regarding that [object] and its opposite.

For this very reason, even though Śrāvakas and others perceive selflessness, they do not possess omniscience, because they have not abandoned the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) due to the absence of such specific internal cultivation.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That cultivation which is characterized by being respectful, uninterrupted, and long-term has as its fruit a cognition in which the object appears as if held in the palm of one's hand; for example, the cultivation of a woman by one afflicted with passion. And the cultivation of the selflessness of all things in all their aspects by a compassionate person is endowed with the three aforementioned characteristics. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*), because it has been demonstrated that such engagement is possible for a compassionate person due to his state of seeking [the welfare of others].

Nor is there any inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatva), because the clarity of manifestation (*sphuṭapratibhāsitva*)— the property to be proven (*sādhya*)— is established for the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is the subject (*dharmin*) having as its object the selflessness (*nairātmya*) inherent in all phenomena, by means of the reason that it is not touched by a cultivation endowed with the three aforementioned qualifications;
and by this property to be proven, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the aforementioned probans (*sādhana-dharma*) is established,
since the clarity of manifestation does not depend on any other cause.
And consequently, by implication, pervasion by omniscience is also established;
for that very clarity of manifestation of the mind which takes as its object the selflessness and so forth inherent in all things constitutes its omniscience, and nothing else.
Thus, when the general pervasion of meditative cultivation by the clarity of manifestation of the object being cultivated is established, omniscience is likewise established by implication.
Because it is impossible for anything other than the subject as previously described to appear clearly [in cognition],
by this [argument] those faults that were stated regarding the proof of existence are refuted, since the existence of an omniscient being is not what is to be proven.

Since it is established that the subject (*dharmin*), the mind, possesses the property to be proven (*sādhya*)— namely, its state of manifest appearance— in this manner, through the abandonment of the latencies of defects characterized by deficiencies of body, speech, and intellect, which results from a well-established particular direct realization, the abandonment of the two obscurations is established;
therefore, by being liberated from all obscurations, omniscience is established.
It might be argued: "Even if this is established in a general sense, it is not established in the case of the Sugata. To this he says: "And this," and so forth;
"and this is accepted by the Sugata because he proclaimed selflessness at the outset."
Therefore, the Tathāgata stands at the head of all founders of religious systems.
This aforementioned omniscience is accepted as belonging to the Sugata alone; it is established, but not for Kapila and others.
Why? Because of the proclamation of selflessness at the outset.
This is what is meant:

he by whom this selflessness of all categories of things was proclaimed in its entirety at the very beginning through the teaching that they consist of the five aggregates and so forth—he, that particular person established by the logical mark of the effect (*kāryaliṅga*) due to his initial proclamation of the various classifications of the selflessness of all phenomena, is called by us "the Sugata."
By this teaching of his, a stable and complete knowledge of the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, along with the means thereto, is established;

it is on account of this knowledge and yoga that he is proven to be omniscient and an authoritative person (*pramāṇabhūta*). Therefore, it is appropriate for those who desire to practice according to his word to establish [his authority] in this way, and not by means of his knowledge of the number of insects.
However, even regarding the number of insects and so forth, the possibility of his knowledge is indeed established.
His knowledge of reality is firm and complete;

for it is stated as follows: he whose knowledge of reality is established through the teaching of selflessness that accords with valid cognition possesses firm knowledge of that very selflessness due to its teaching being consistent from beginning to end. This is so even within the ninefold scriptural collection (*navāṅga-śāstrapravacana*), because even in teachings concerning the three vehicles (*triyāna*), there is a single coherent purpose (*ekavākyatva*) in the teaching on the truths characterized by suffering and so forth.
From his illumination of the Four Noble Truths through diverse means, his omniscience is inferred;
for he has abandoned that "remainder" characterized by the incapacity to demonstrate knowledge of all aspects,
since one who does not know the qualities and defects of every aspect and is unskilled in their demonstration cannot explain them in such a manner.
Nor is it logical to say that he teaches after having learned from the Vedas, because the [Vedas'] status as being of human origin has been established; this is the intended meaning.
Therefore, it is proven that the Blessed One stands at the head of all teachers due to his possession of superior knowledge.
Therefore, showing that there is no equality with others for the Blessed One, who possesses such an excellence of knowledge as described, he says: "By him," and so forth;
by him, who is endowed with the vision of reality that is in accord with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Others who teach contradictory meanings do not possess the same causal basis;

for those whose speech is confounded by the sublation of their claims through the scope of valid cognition (pramāṇa), their connection with the power of suprasensory knowledge is indeed far removed. 3341–3342.
Indeed, there is no reason whatsoever that establishes their possession of superior knowledge;
for if there were such a reason, it would have to be the very sign (liṅga) consisting of their own words,
yet since those words of theirs set forth propositions contradicted by valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), how could their possession of superior knowledge be understood from them?
If it is argued that even the word of the Sugata is contradicted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: "Connected," and so forth.
It is coherent, possesses appropriate means, expresses the goals of human endeavor,
and is not contradicted even slightly by the two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding matters within the realm of perception.
(3343) "Coherent" means that the sentences are mutually connected through the synthesis of a single purpose, and not disconnected from one another like the sentence "ten pomegranates," etc.

*Anuguṇaḥ* (conducive): that in which a means characterized by the cultivation of selflessness (*nairātmya-bhāvanā*) and so forth is taught as being capable of being practiced; it is not, however, an impossible means, like the instruction to wear the crest-jewel of Takṣaka as an ornament for the sake of neutralizing poison.

*Puruṣārthaḥ* (the human goal): characterized by worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); [the scripture] is the designator of this, and not something whose fruit is a non-goal for humans, like an examination of a crow’s teeth.
[Objection: But surely all of this is also present in the words of Kapila and others; [in response, he says: "Even though [it is] seen," and so forth.

"In what is seen"— that is, in what is intended as the object of perception and inference, by means of these two instruments of knowledge, perception and inference— it is "uncontradicted," because the entity as it has been described exists exactly so.

For instance: it is impossible for the five aggregates—characterized by the cognition of blue and so forth, pleasure and pain and so forth, and the grasping of signs such as attachment—to be anything other than what they are intended to be by others as being perceptible; nor can those things intended to be imperceptible fail to be imperceptible, just as [it is impossible for] those intended by others to be perceptible—such as the configurations of form, sound, and so forth, or pleasure and so forth, or substance, action, universals, conjunction, and so forth—to be otherwise.
Likewise, for those things intended to be the objects of inference proceeding by the force of real entities (*vastubala*), their existence is exactly as it is intended.

Just as the four noble truths— which are accepted by others as not being the objects [of such inference]— are indeed not its objects, so too, by the word "also" (api), it is shown that even for things like the self (*ātman*) which are intended by others to be the objects of inference based on the power of real entities (*vastubalānumāna*), there is no modification even when [the object] is unperceived.

For in this [teaching], having pointed out phenomena such as passion (*rāga*) and their origin, the very vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) is taught as the antidote for their abandonment by way of its opposition to the view of self (*ātmadarśana*) which is their cause; however, unlike the treatises of Kapila and others, practices such as ritual bathing and the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*), which do not oppose that cause, are not prescribed.
It was for this reason that the Blessed One said, "This should be accepted by the wise after examination, like pure gold. Indicating this, he says: "By heating," and so forth.

Just as pure gold, when tested by heating, cutting, or rubbing on a touchstone, does not undergo any alteration, so too the jewel of the Blessed One’s word—when examined through direct perception (which is like heating), through inference based on the power of reality (which is like cutting), and through inference dependent on scripture (which is indicated by the example of the touchstone)—does not undergo any change. (3344) Just as pure gold, which is stainless and free from all defects, does not undergo alteration when tested by heating and other methods, likewise the jewel of the Blessed One’s speech is not altered by direct perception, which resembles heating; by inference proceeding from the force of facts, which resembles cutting; and by inference dependent on scripture, which is illustrated by the example of the touchstone.
Therefore, the intention is that for those who act with foresight, engagement based on such a scripture is appropriate, and not otherwise.
(3344) Showing its similarity to a jewel, he says: "All... and so forth.
The jewel of the Tathāgata’s word, which rises in accordance with the destruction of the darkness of all false doctrines and is not obtained by those with much defilement—
therefore, those possessed of supreme wisdom declare that the Sugata alone is omniscient.
They call him who knows the purpose of both primordial matter (pradhāna) and the person (puruṣa) the best of physicians.
Therefore, the Sugata is omniscient, while Kapila is not; this proof has been clearly stated above, yet it has not been perceived by the deluded.
"Bad judgment itself is the dense darkness; its destruction is its eradication. That whose arising is conducive to that [destruction] is described as such.
By those with many blemishes means by those lacking merit."
"Anantaroditā" means that which arises from the sign (liṅga) consisting of the meaning of the words as they have been stated.
Regarding the passage beginning with "In certain parts such as arithmetic," etc., he says: "As stated from the *Antara*," and so forth.
Even the distinction [of the Blessed One] from false teachers such as Ṛṣabha and others—who merely bring about the destruction of passion—is determined precisely from what has been stated above.

Since the superiority of the Blessed Conqueror of Māra over Ṛṣabha, Vardhamāna, and the rest is established through his possession of the aforementioned excellence of knowledge, it is not proper for you, who speak the truth, to say that "no distinction is perceived. This is the collective meaning.

It might be argued: "Because there is no contradiction regarding certain specific subjects such as mathematics, we say that there is no difference between the two [the Buddha and other teachers]. To this he says: "For who," and so forth—"for what fool indeed would consider [anyone else] to be a knower of the reality of the meaning of all scriptures without exception?"
"Because of the knowledge of eating together and because of knowing only the mother"—regarding the passage beginning with "by that very reason," he says:
"That by which reason," etc. That is, by whichever reason the omniscience of one [person] is established, [the same applies to others].
Because that causal entity does not exist, it does not apply to anything else.
"Tat" means "therefore."
Regarding the phrase "of that causal entity":

even if there exists what is merely a word—namely, because [the opponent] teaches doctrines such as *syādvāda* which have non-erroneous meanings and pervade all objects—even so, because that causal entity (the meaning of the reason) is dependent upon a real thing (*vastu*), and since that causal object does not exist, this reason does not apply to others such as Kapila and the like. For it is only a real thing, by virtue of being dependent upon a real thing, that makes another real thing known, not mere words.
Regarding the passage beginning with "the refutations," he says: "Those refutations... and so forth.
"The Digambaras are incapable of those very refutations which the Śākyas, free from agitation, utter against the teaching of the omniscient Jina. (3351)
"Free from agitation" means they are devoid of impetuosity;
because their engagement with others is solely for the sake of benefiting them through compassion, it does not arise from anger, pride, and the like, as is the case with you.
"Thus" means that he demonstrates the fallacious nature of the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*) and other such teachings taught by him.
Regarding the passage beginning with "there, by those who are unsettled," he says: "That which... and so forth.

That reality which has been established by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) through a proven logical connection (*pratibandha*) is established in the Buddhist system (*saugatasiddhānta*), but not so in other doctrines. (3352)

Therefore, let a definitive conclusion be reached by means of their various proofs and refutations as they have been established, which are sufficient to swallow up the rising reflections [of opposing views].
(3353) "That which... [is as follows:]

Because it is "by means of a proven connection" (*siddhapratibandhena*), the meaning is: by means of a connection characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination (*tadutpatti*), which functions through the power of real entities (*vastubalapravṛtta*).
"Teneti" means "therefore.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of whom [there is] the knowable," etc., he says: "But for the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), however," and so forth;
that is, for the knowledge of all aspects, no [object] whatsoever exists.
Whether directly or otherwise, contradiction [with omniscience] is to be understood through [the properties of] knowability and so forth (jñeyatā).
Knowability and so forth are established by virtue of being excluded from unknowability and so forth;
however, that [omniscience] does not have its characteristic established by virtue of being excluded from omniscience. (3354–3355)

One who wishes to establish the negation of one thing by means of the affirmation of another must establish the affirmation of something that is either directly or indirectly contradictory [to the object to be negated], and not something non-contradictory; for otherwise, the negation of everything would follow from the affirmation of just anything whatsoever.
Furthermore, there is no contradiction—either direct or indirect—between omniscience and such properties as being knowable and so forth.

For instance—when the contradiction between two things is examined, it is established as being of only two kinds: either characterized by mutual exclusion, as in the case of existence and non-existence, or succession and non-succession;
or characterized by the impossibility of coexistence, as in the case of fire and the sensation of cold.

Of these, he first demonstrates that the former kind of contradiction does not apply to omniscience in relation to such properties as "knowability" (jñeyatva) and so forth, by stating "unknowability" (ajñeyatva) and so on.

It was stated previously that the opposition between two things, characterized by their existence through mutual exclusion, consists in the fact that the determination of one is inseparable from the exclusion of the other; however,
omniscience does not exist through the exclusion of knowability and so forth, but rather through the exclusion of unknowability and so forth.
Showing that the second contradiction is also not possible, he says: "Omniscience," and so forth;
"And furthermore, this omniscience does not have its causes complete anywhere."
That which was previously active ceases upon the subsequent occurrence of existence and so forth.

For when something that possesses its complete causes ceases to exist due to the presence of another thing, there is between those two a contradiction characterized by non-coexistence; however, this omniscience has not been observed to have been previously active with its causes complete, such that it could be said to cease later upon the occurrence of existence and so forth.

He asks, "Why has it not proceeded? and says: "In the absence of intrinsic nature," and so forth: "If there is no cognition of its own [nature], that [omniscience] can never arise; for this omniscience would be established as such even prior to its activity. (3357)

If you accept that omniscience ceases when the existence of sentient beings and objects of knowledge is present, then it follows that prior to the presence of sentient beings and so forth, this [omniscience] must have been non-existent and unknowable even by self-awareness. Consequently, since it is devoid of intrinsic nature due to its non-existence, and since it is not self-cognized due to its unknowability, this omniscience does not arise—that is, it does not exist. How, then, could it be said that what previously existed later ceases?
For the arising of that which lacks intrinsic nature is impossible.

Nor is there any basis for establishing the existence of that which is unperceived, because the establishment of the existence of a thing is dependent upon cognition; therefore, the intention is that this results in a contradiction of one's own words (*svavacanavyāghāta*). Furthermore, if its prior activity is admitted, then omniscience is established even without effort toward such activity; thus, its rejection is not logical, otherwise there would be a contradiction of one's own words. Demonstrating this, he says: "Prior to activity," and so forth.
"Prior to its occurrence"—the remainder of the sentence being "provided that omniscience is admitted.
Furthermore, it might be argued: "Even if [properties] such as 'knowability' are not contradictory, they nonetheless lead to the non-existence of an omniscient being"; to this he says: [3357]...
And when there is the prescription of what is not contradictory, the exclusion of something else is not logical.
[Objection: "Since the presence of one form implies the absence of another, the non-existence of taste is also understood from the existence of color.

[Response: But as for the one who thinks: "Even if knowability and so forth are not contradictory with omniscience, speech-actuality (*vaktṛtva*) is indeed contradictory; for, through its indirect cause, conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it cannot coexist with omniscience."

For instance, according to the principle that "one does not utter speech without first reflecting and deliberating," conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the cause of speech; and since all conceptual constructions are intertwined with verbal expression, there is no grasping of the true nature of a thing, because that [true nature] is the domain of non-conceptual knowledge (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*). Therefore, because the true nature of a thing is not fully known during the state of conceptualization, omniscience does not exist [in such a state]. Thus, by the non-perception of the cause—namely, omniscience—which is the opposite of the property of being a speaker, the certainty of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is established; hence, the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

Furthermore, this reason called "being a speaker" (vaktṛtva) is indeed implied by the word "etc. in the phrase "characterized by being knowable, being an object of cognition, being a real entity, existence, etc.

Having raised this objection with the words "this is implied here by the word 'etc. and so forth, he refutes it here as well with the words "those who [assert] the state of being a speaker," etc., regarding one who conceives of that state of being a speaker which is implied by the word "etc. here.
There is a certainty regarding their mutual exclusion due to their inherent contradiction:
if there is conceptualization (*vikalpa*), there is speakerhood; but an omniscient one is free from conceptualization.
For an object is not apprehended by a cognition that is permeated by verbal expression (*abhilāpa*). (3359–3360)

In this regard as well, those who imagine that the Omniscient One possesses the status of a speaker because he conforms to discursive thought (vitarka) do not [accept] that an Omniscient One is possible;
nor is he accepted as such on the basis of the functioning of conceptual cognition (vikalpajñāna).
At that moment, when there is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the state of being a speaker is not established.

(3362) Some maintain that the Blessed One’s status as a speaker arises precisely from the manifestation of conceptual construction; others, however, describe the activity of speech on the part of the Blessed One as proceeding even while he is free from conceptualization, solely by virtue of his previous [resolutions].

Regarding these views, in the first case, if it is sought to prove a lack of omniscience during the state of conceptual construction, then it is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), for they themselves accept that at that stage the Blessed One is not all-seeing.
Now, if it is intended to establish the lack of omniscience in the state of non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*),
then the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*); for in that state there is no activity of speech, since at that time the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) that motivates it is absent.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If it is admitted that there is non-omniscience during the state of conceptual construction, then his word would lack authority precisely because it was spoken by one who is not omniscient. Anticipating this, he says: "The state of being composed by one who is not omniscient," and so forth— "and such a state of being composed by one who is not omniscient is not applicable to him."
Therefore, there is correspondence because it entails omniscience.
Just as someone, having experienced heat, later speaks of it, so too there is non-discrepancy with the object because [the cognition] arises from the experience of that object. (3363–3364)
Therefore, at the time of omniscience, this reason is unestablished; however, at the time of its manifestation as verbal discourse, it would be the establishment of what is already established.
Even though he is not omniscient in that particular state, his [teaching] is nonetheless not composed by one who is not omniscient. Why? Because it is encompassed by omniscience itself.

For this very reason, because it is produced by a conceptual construction arising from the power of the omniscient one’s knowledge, and because it is indirectly connected to the real object, it possesses validity just like an inferential conceptualization.
Regarding this very point, he provides an example, beginning with "anubhūya" and concluding with "tasmāt."
The phrase "because it arises from the power of the experience of heat" means that it arises from the experience of that object,
heat; that is to say, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises through a successive lineage from the experience of that object, heat.

It might be argued: "If the Omniscient One possesses conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), then He would be subject to error; for conceptual cognition is by nature erroneous because it functions by determining an object as being what it is not, despite its own non-appearance [in that form]. This is not so. He would be erroneous only if He did not know the distinction between the superimposed (*āropita*) form and the real (*tāttvika*) form. However, since He determines the object of conceptual cognition as having a superimposed nature, while simultaneously perceiving the external object—the domain of non-conceptual cognition—as distinct and real in its true nature, how could He be said to be mistaken?
If it is asked, "How can one who is non-erroneous superimpose [an object] during the state of conceptualization? the answer is:
no, because he knows the means for the application of words.

Since one perceives no originator of a word other than the superimposing conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), nor does one apprehend a referent of a word other than that which is superimposed, therefore one who knows the means for the application of words—being unable to remain silent without communicating to another the reality as it has been correctly realized out of compassion for the world—constructs, with the desire to communicate that reality, the superimposing conceptual construction as the means for the application of words, and the object of superimposition as the denotation of the word.
This point will be raised as an objection later and refuted;
however, we have stated it here because it arises in the present context.

For this very reason, the inference of passion from the fact of being a speaker is also incorrect, because the production of speech is possible even otherwise; for speech, movement, and so forth are not the effects of passion alone, since their general cause is the desire to speak. And that desire to speak can also occur in one free from passion through compassion; thus, there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*).
If it is argued that compassion itself is attachment, we say no;
for nothing undesirable follows from compassion that is not so named.

However, they say that passion (*rāga*) is the mind’s attachment directed toward objects associated with outflows (*sāśrava*), which is projected by the view of a self and what belongs to a self as being eternal, blissful, and substantial;
and hatred (*dveṣa*) is the aversion preceded by that [passion] toward that which obstructs the self and what belongs to a self;
and delusion (*moha*) is the grasping at a self and what belongs to a self—and compassion (*kṛpā*) is certainly not like this.
Even in the absence of a grasping for a self, that [compassion] arises through the power of habituation merely by seeing specific forms of suffering;
for instance, it is described in the treatises that for those free from passion, loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] have the Dharma and so forth as their objects.

It might be argued: "Even if you were merely proving the non-manifestation of knowledge regarding all objects, there would still be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*); for what you intend to prove is the incapacity to know the full extent of the reality of all things. Therefore, there is neither the fallacy of proving the already established nor the unestablished nature of the reason (*asiddhatā*), since what is intended as the reason is merely the capacity for verbal expression. To this, he says: "The entirety," and so forth.
Even if you were to exclude the capacity for cognizing all things,
the fact that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) remains doubtful would still follow as a consequence.
This is so even if the capacity for speech and activity is accepted as the logical reason (*hetu*).
The fault of "doubtful negative concomitance" (saṃdigdhavyatirekitva) persists;
because there is no subverting proof (bādhakapramāṇa) against the reason in either case when the probandum is reversed,
the reason is inconclusive due to its doubtful negative concomitance.
Now, regarding the position of those for whom the Blessed One’s speech proceeds even without conceptualization, he says: "By means of the wheel," and so forth.
"By means of the process of a wheel's rotation, instruction proceeds even for the Protector who is free from conceptual construction, through the power of the momentum of the accumulations"—
even against those wise ones who say this, [the argument] is not proven.

Just as a wheel continues to spin due to the force of prior momentum even after the activity of pushing with a staff has ceased, so too, some wise followers of the Sugata—namely, certain Vijñānavādins—maintain that while the Blessed One remains with the entire web of conceptual construction having subsided, the teaching still proceeds by the force of the momentum from his prior accumulations of merit and knowledge; against them, the fault of the reason being clearly unestablished (*asiddha*) is indeed recognized.

It might be argued that in this view, since everything is in reality nothing more than the experience of its own appearance, no one possesses the status of a speaker in the ultimate sense. Nevertheless, due to the force of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*), even when another person is speaking, there arises in the world the conceit of "speakership" based on the production of a cognition appearing as such, wherein that other person stands as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). It is precisely this speakership, which is conceptually determined and conventionally recognized in the world, that is intended as the logical reason (*hetu*).
