One might object: "A reason or a subject is not established merely by what is accepted within one's own philosophical system; rather, it must be something recognized by common worldly consensus. Therefore, the reason is not unestablished. Anticipating this, he says: "As for that quality of being a speaker which is considered by the world to be determinative... (Verse 3369).
In such a case, the reason would possess a doubtful negative concomitance (*sandigdhavyatirekitā*).

Here too, as before, the reason is inconclusive because its exclusion from the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) is doubtful. With the words beginning with "nanu," the opponent refutes the lack of proof (*asiddhatva*) that was asserted here regarding the system of the Vijñānavādins: "But by whom [is it claimed] that there is a lack of proof here in this untenable position? (3370)

He thinks as follows: "Only that which expresses what is certain for both parties is a proof (*sādhana*) or a refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), not something unestablished for one side or expressed with doubt, because of the principle that it would require further proof. Therefore, in this doctrine of the Proponents of Cognition (*vijñānavāda*) which is not supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can 'unestablishedness' (*asiddhatā*) be raised? For a refutation does not occur through the mere fabrication of establishment or non-establishment according to one's own whim; rather, it occurs when establishment or non-establishment is brought about by the force of valid means of knowledge. And the system of Cognition is not established by the force of valid means of knowledge, since it has been refuted at length. (3368)
He provides a rebuttal with the words beginning "It is said," and so forth.

It is said: If the state of being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*) is considered an independent probans (*sādhana*), then it would be either "unestablished in its locus" (*āśrayāsiddha*) or "doubtfully unestablished" (*sandigdhāsiddha*).
Because of the doubt regarding this matter, its status as "doubtfully unestablished" is certain.
Therefore, you must state such a proof by way of reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅgasādhana). In that case, the property is revealed merely through scripture;
however, there exists no further means of cognition for establishing its actual existence.

In this regard, there are two possible alternatives: either "speakership" (*vaktṛtva*) is intended as an independent proof (*sādhana*), or as a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgasādhana*). Regarding the first position, the locus (*āśraya*) is not established in its specific form; thus, the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of being unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddhatā*).

Even if the locus is intended in a general sense, as long as speakership has not been proven by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the opponent, the reason remains doubtful and unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddhatā*). This is according to the logical principle that only that which expresses what is certain for both parties constitutes a proof.
Therefore, lest this fault arise regarding the state of being a speaker, you must accept that this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum).

In that case as well, regarding a proof by reductio (*prasaṅgasādhana*), only that property which is established for the opponent through scripture alone—being agreeable when left unexamined—should be presented as the probans (*sādhana*) in order to expose their internal contradictions; it should not, however, be established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because that would be purposeless. Furthermore, since "the state of being a speaker" is not established for the opponent through scripture alone, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished in both ways.
Concluding with the words "In this way," and so forth, he demonstrates the reversal of the meaning in what has been stated by others.
Thus, who would not postulate that [self] for whom reasons characterized by perishability, substantiality, existence, and so forth are powerless to refute it?
In this way, both worldly and Vedic reasoning resides in the mouth of the proponent of the Vedas.

There is no Śākta [practitioner] whatsoever who can remove the poison of the knowledge of fierce serpents. Here, even when looked upon by those with venomous eyes, a dull-witted Brahmin of meager power is unable even to breathe, let alone cause harm.
"But even a sound argument, when residing in the mouth of a proponent of the Vedas, is as unfortunate as a necklace on one's feet; for it is base because of its location.
"Who would not accept that? [the opponent asks].
The word "as a possibility" (*sambhavitvena*) is to be understood as the ellipsis;
the sense is that its possibility is established precisely because no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) is perceived.

Let this matter rest for now—the fact that an unsound argument does not shine when it resides in the mouth of a Vedic proponent is not surprising; however, even a sound argument, when put forward by you, does not gleam due to the defect of its locus (*āśrayadoṣa*).
He asks, "How so? and says: "The non-deviation from fire," and so forth; even the non-deviation of smoke from fire cannot be established.
Because smoke is said by him to exist elsewhere [than fire], according to his view, it would also exist upon the ocean, since it has the same nature as a single entity;
in that case too, if fire were present, what could serve as the basis for negative concomitance (vyatireka)? || 3378–3379 ||

For it is well known even to the intellect of a cowherd’s child that smoke arises in dependence upon fire, and thus its non-deviation [from fire] is established; yet, by you—who describe the ultimate unity of the entire world through its being a "real entity" (vastu) and so forth—it is impossible to establish that smoke does not deviate from fire, because according to your own view, smoke exists ultimately in water as well, since it is of the nature of a real entity.
To this, he says: "In that case too," and so forth, [arguing] that there is indeed non-deviation.

Even in that case, if it were admitted that fire possesses the nature of water by way of identity (*tādātmya*), then water and the like would not be the "dissimilar instances" (*vipakṣa*) when fire is the property to be proven (*sādhya*). Consequently, in the absence of dissimilar instances, what could serve as the basis for the exclusion (*vyatireka*) of a mark such as smoke from the dissimilar instances?
Or rather, why would there not be a cognition of that form, or even a manifestation of its effects such as burning and cooking?
Or, if the individual nature [of the fire] were different, let there be a real distinction between the entities.

(3380) If it is held that fire exists in the ocean in an ultimate sense, why does there not arise a perception of its form and a cognition manifesting its effects characterized by burning, cooking, and so forth?
If it is argued that difference is also accepted, he says: "The self is of a different nature," and so forth;
and since this has been examined in detail in the *Syādvādaparīkṣā*, let this matter rest for now.

Regarding what was stated [in verse 3380], beginning with "by a single means of valid cognition," he says: "That mental cognition which arises through the power of the repeated practice of the reality connected to all things is postulated as the single means of valid cognition for omniscience. (3381)
But visual consciousness and the others do not [function thus]; therefore, why is this said: "Surely he perceives all tastes and so forth with his eye"?
Furthermore, mental cognition consisting of the experience of form and other objects is established.
There is no dispute even with the opponent regarding this much, which is quite clear:
for it is described that memory has as its object color, sound, and so forth, and that in a dream, mental cognition consists of the experience of all objects. (3383–3384)
Furthermore, if an omniscient being were postulated by means of a mental [cognition] whose object is indeterminate, why would he not perceive tastes and so forth?
If that [omniscience] were postulated by means of visual [cognition] alone, this fault would indeed arise.

In brief, the mind indeed perceives taste and the other objects as well. Even where excellence is observed—such as in the perception of distant or subtle things—it occurs within the scope of its own specific object; it would not function like the ear by perceiving color.

Therefore, such undesirable consequences as have been stated by others do not apply to us, because we maintain that excellence resides in the mental [cognition] precisely without overstepping its own object. For,
by means of whatever class of instruments of knowledge (pramāṇas), there is the perception of objects of whatever class.
What is seen by the world at present is likewise [seen] by us at another time as well.

(3389) If it were admitted that the cognitions of the sense-faculties, such as the eye and so forth, possess complete knowledge of all objects, then the aforementioned fault would indeed follow; however, since the Omniscient One is desired on account of his simultaneous grasping of all things by means of a mental consciousness—which arises from the culmination of the excellence of practice regarding the entire reality characterized by impermanence and so forth pertaining to all entities, which has sentient beings and their welfare as its domain, and which has attained the status of direct perception through its vivid manifestation and non-contradiction—it is not by means of the cognitions of the eye and other senses.

Nor is it reasonable to claim that mental cognition is not well-established as having all objects as its domain; for even you have described the memory-cognition regarding objects such as form and sound as being nothing other than mental cognition,
and since the appearance of forms and so forth in dreams is extremely well-known, its denial cannot be made.
Since excellence is desired precisely by not overstepping one's own purpose, you have not brought anything undesirable upon us.

Even for the proponent of knowledge (*jñānavādin*) who maintains that an omniscient being is established by sensory cognition, it is accepted that upon the abandonment of the latent impressions of low birth (*dauṣkulyavāsanā*), there is the attainment of mastery (*vibhutva*) over all cognitions through their engagement with all objects;
for it is precisely the latent impression of low birth that is the cause of restriction in cognitions.
Thinking that if those [defects] were abandoned, how could it be possible for these [cognitions] to have a restricted object as their domain, he says:
"Or else, all cognition would be pure and have all things as its range; for some excellence in the cause is conceivable, and thus some excellence may also exist in the result. (3390)
It is not the case that *āmalaka* trees are observed to have small fruit only in the desert;
therefore, they exist everywhere in that same form according to reality.
Likewise, the scriptural statement that "serpents hear with their eyes" follows from that same principle.

For the karmic capacities of sentient beings are diverse and capable of producing all manner of possibilities. Indeed, because the specific nature of entities is determined by a distinction in their causes, it is impossible to conclude that an object observed once in a certain place must always exist in that same way everywhere. For it is not reasonable for discerning people to determine, based on mere observation, that *āmalaka* fruits—which were found in deserts to have small fruits—must necessarily be so in every location, even when a difference in causes is possible.
Therefore, it is not contradictory that even with that eye, opened by the probe of the power of specific yogic practice, someone perceives all objects. 3390–3391.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of whatever kind" (yajjātīyaiḥ), he says: "Of whom," and so forth.
For, for him, every object situated in the three times appears [simultaneously].
In this way, he is thus fitting to speak of the restricted capacity [of cognition].
The connection [of the words] is as follows: "In that way, with its restricted capacity"—that is, every object appears in its desired form with a restricted capacity.
He says that such [a proof] is fitting to state: "By whatever kinds of means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) there is the perception of objects of whatever kind," and so forth.
Just as it might be for the world now, so it was also in another time.
Even now, the capacity of the world cannot be known by you, who are a mere creature, because all capacities remain undetermined.
Alas, omniscience consists in the knowledge of the capacities of all sentient beings without exception;
yet its establishment cannot be achieved through inference, because there remains the possibility of error.
It might be argued: "We do not say this on the basis of direct perception that [the Buddha] knew it thus, nor that he was so even at another time; rather, we say it on the basis of inference."

Regarding the argument that "whatever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is seen to grasp an object of a certain class must likewise be so at another time, because it is a valid cognition," he replies: "Nor is there proof by means of inference.
This is because, as in the case of the *āmalaka* fruit and others, one observes a specific effect characterized by a specific cause;
otherwise, since the operation [of the cognition] could possibly occur through the grasping of an object of a different class, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "Even those who are seen to possess excellence," he says: "Also by means of the knowledge of supersensuous objects," and so forth.

Even through the possession of the knowledge of supersensuous objects, men are observed to possess qualities such as wisdom and the like, by virtue of their power of learning and other such capacities. (Verse 3397)
There exists a science known as *hīkṣaṇikā* and so forth, which, when well-cultivated, brings about the thorough knowledge of another's mind even in this very life.
Furthermore, there is that object which has not been heard, inferred, or seen in this life.

Men here, possessed by the power of various mantras, serpent-kings, rākṣasas, yakṣas, and so forth, know and speak of the past, the present, and the future, clearly and in accordance with reality. (3399–3400)

"Let it not be that [the object] has been seen," and so forth; nevertheless, there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) here whatsoever, and thus the non-existence of such perception is not established.

Furthermore, the claim that this is "unestablished" because of the perception of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*) is incorrect; for instance, through the power of sciences such as *īkṣaṇikā* (divination), the knowledge of others' minds and the thorough cognition of past, present, and future things is indeed observed among *ḍākinīs* and others.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), Gāndhārī, Prakṛti, and others are included. Furthermore, because of the power of possession by various spirits (*bhūta-graha*) and the like, there is the perception and knowledge of objects beyond the senses; thus, [the argument] is not rejected even in other cases, lest there be the observation of a counter-example (*vyabhicāra-viṣaya*).
Nevertheless, it is not logical to determine the non-existence of an omniscient being merely on the basis of his non-perception;
thus, the non-existence of one who perceives supersensuous objects is not established.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Even for a wise person" (prājñe 'pi hi), he says: "And by the stated manner," and so forth;
that is, once the author of the Veda has been established by the manner already explained.
You must necessarily admit that there exists a person who perceives objects beyond the senses;
therefore, a wise man would be capable of seeing subtle matters, and even while remaining among his own kind, he would surpass other men. (3402–3403)
"By what was said" refers to [the section on] the examination of scripture (āgama),
verse 3402.
He states the proof for this very point: "Just as in its own object," and so forth;
that is, just as the capacity of the ear and other senses is distinguished with respect to their own respective objects.
By means of specific movements, particular conjunctions, and so forth, the same may apply to the mind as well.

(3404) Just as the capacity of the ear and other senses for their respective objects is enhanced by specific movements and by specific conjunctions such as with *añjana* (collyrium), it is likewise possible that the power of the mind is also specifically intensified by a particular cause.

In this regard, he demonstrates the distinction of the ear and other senses produced by the difference in their range of movement, beginning with "For instance" (*tathā hi*): "For instance, forms situated at a very great distance are perceived by vultures; likewise, hidden treasures and the like are perceived by those possessing perfected eye-salves and such. (3405)
He also states that which is produced by a specific yoga: "concealed," and so forth;
the connection is that [the object] is seen by means of perfected ointments and the like.
This third case ending [in *hetunā*] is used either in the sense of cause (*hetu*) or instrument (*karaṇa*).
Having thus established that a specific mode of movement is the cause for a specific capacity for cognition, he says "In this way," etc., applying it to the subject of the illustration.
Thus, through the distinction of their respective states of existence, gods and others may perceive subtle, obstructed, and other such objects, in accordance with the nature of their own rebirth.
"In accordance with the nature of their own rebirth" means:

Their knowledge and vision proceed downward, not upward; thus, according to their respective births and in accordance with their suitability, knowledge arises. Who can prevent this for the gods of the Four Great Kings’ realm and the others?
He also applies the distinction produced by yoga, beginning with "through the practice of yoga," and so forth.
Furthermore, due to the specific excellence of the practice of yoga, it is not contradicted that the mental cognition of yogins may likewise become preeminent in form.

However, if one were to deny such excellence by demonstrating the impossibility of the causes for movement, yoga, and so forth as previously described, then one would be proving what is already established; showing this, he says: "In the case of the deficiency of movement, yoga, and so forth."

If it is argued that there is an excellence in knowledge despite a deficiency in [the means of] movement, yoga, and so forth, this is indeed incorrect; for a fruit does not arise in the absence of its cause.
Just as knowledge of other treatises is not obtained by that alone.
"Likewise, there is excellence when there is a progressive deficiency of those causes.

(3409) As for what was stated regarding the gods—"In the case of things accessible to hearing," and so forth—that too has been refuted by this very [argument]; the intention is that it is impossible to negate such an excellence merely on the basis of non-perception.
Regarding what was stated, "In this way, in the investigations of the treatises," and so forth, [the author] replies: "Nor by a single part," and so on.

Nor is the existence of omniscience asserted on the basis of knowing a single portion [of things], by which [means] heaven and so forth would become perceptible through knowledge of the Vedas and such;
rather, [it is asserted] because an increase is observed through the repeated practice of wisdom, compassion, and so forth.
Furthermore, another excellence is perceived from that [state of] Vardhamāna:

even as mental qualities, these possess the possibility of reaching their ultimate limit through intense practice, just like [the development of] ruthlessness, because they result in the cognition of all objects without exception. (3411–3412)
For wisdom, by its very definition, consists in the comprehension of phenomena (dharmas);
it remains incomplete as long as even a single one has not been fully understood.

We do not, however, assert that the full comprehension of all objects follows from the mere comprehension of a single part—such that you could claim that knowledge of other treatises is not obtained by that much alone.

However, because an excellence of wisdom is observed through the power of practice, it is possible that there is another distinction produced by the thorough knowledge of supersensory objects; therefore, from practice that increases and attains a state of excellence, such [knowledge] is inferred.

This has been established previously, and now it is further substantiated by a formal argument (*prayoga*): Whatever qualities belong to the mind, when there is an intensity of practice, they are capable of reaching the ultimate limit of excellence, just as the lack of compassion in a Vedic scholar who performs sacrifices; and wisdom is a quality of the mind. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

There is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) regarding the reason (*hetu*); for the attainment of the ultimate limit of wisdom—which is characterized by the awakening to the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of objects—is not possible without the complete knowledge of all things.

Nor is the reason unestablished (*asiddha*) due to an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatā*), because the possibility of a specific degree of cultivation has already been established in detail previously;
the word "limit" (*kāṣṭhā*) is a synonym for excellence (*prakarṣa*).
Alternatively, those things which proceed from preceding seeds of a similar kind possess the property of ultimate increase due to the specific excellence of their refinement (*saṃskāra*).

Furthermore, compassion, wisdom, and so forth, which are capable of arising like rice and other grains, possess the aforementioned properties; thus, when they reach full development, omniscience results.

Alternatively, those things which are produced from preceding seeds of a similar kind are capable of attaining extreme growth once specific cultivation has occurred, just as rice and other grains are; and since compassion, wisdom, and so forth possess the aforementioned properties, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
In this case as well, as before, there is no thought that [the reason] is unestablished or inconclusive— that is, that wisdom possesses the aforementioned properties.
The meaning is that they proceed from seeds of a similar kind.
And those things whose nature is to diminish, which undergo absolute decrease in the presence of their antidote— such as the impurities on gold and so forth—
are likewise conceivable in the case of these [afflictions], such as the afflictive and cognitive obscurations.

Those whose minds have abandoned that [defilement] through the teachings as they were instructed become stainless. Or, if defilement were possible for these [beings] who possess the aforementioned qualities, then likewise there must exist an antidote capable of uprooting it completely. (3417–3418)

Alternatively, those things observed to be subject to diminution in the presence of their counteragent are such that they are capable of absolute diminution when that counteragent reaches its ultimate increase, as in the case of gold, impurities, and so forth. Since passion and the like are subject to diminution upon the manifestation of the realization of selflessness and other [remedies], this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*);
thus, the reason is not unestablished (*asiddha*), because the contradiction between the afflictions and the knowledge of selflessness has already been proven.
Nor is it inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because when the counteragent has reached its ultimate increase, the persistence of the opposing side is impossible.
Otherwise, how could that which is incapable of uprooting [an opponent] entirely effect even a slight diminution?
Indeed, even a diamond situated within a mass of blazing fire, radiant with a multitude of clearly flashing sparks, never undergoes diminution.

Nor is there any inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) due to the impossibility of the absolute increase of the counter-position, since the possibility of such absolute increase has been established at length previously.

Alternatively, those things which possess the property of diminishing in the presence of their counteragent are such that their counteragent is capable of utterly uprooting them, just as, for example, a stain on gold and the like; and the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and so forth, possess the aforementioned properties. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Here too, as before, one must avoid the fallacies of being unestablished (*asiddha*) or inconclusive (*anaikāntika*);
by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of the karmic obscurations (*karmāvaraṇa*) and others is intended.
Because it is bound to the vision of reality, an absolute diminution of this internal darkness is understood to occur, just as it does for external darkness;
and when that [darkness] has been diminished, great and unimpeded knowledge arises.
It would proceed with autonomy throughout the entire sphere of the knowable (jñeyamaṇḍala).

Alternatively, those things which act as obstacles to the vision of reality (tattvadarśana) are subject to absolute diminution, just as external nocturnal darkness is; and since the afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa) and the cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa) act as obstacles to the vision of reality, this is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu).
Showing that this [reason] is not inconclusive (anaikāntika), he says: "And of that... (tasya ca).
Of that intermediate darkness,
Or those which, having arisen in a stable substratum, are somehow produced as beneficial, do not require further effort for their continued existence provided no subverting factor is present;
they proceed to the ultimate limit through the progressive intensification of their refinement.
They arise quite clearly, like the purity of gold;
these qualities such as intelligence and compassion, as previously described,
reach their ultimate limit, and in that final state, omniscience is radiant.

Nor is there any deviation [in the rule] here due to jumping or heating water; for jumping does not result merely from the act of jumping, but rather from strength and effort. (3424) Alternatively: those qualities which reside in a stable substratum, which have been produced once by some means or another, and which, in the absence of a contrary condition, do not require further effort for their continued existence, are capable of reaching the ultimate limit of excellence through the differentiation of the intensification of their refinement (*saṃskāra*). For example, the purity of gold and the like; and wisdom, compassion, and so forth possess these aforementioned characteristics. This is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).
The intention is that [the argument] is not subject to deviation here because it possesses a qualification;
for leaping and the heating of water, once initiated, do not continue without depending on further effort and so forth for their subsequent maintenance.

Nor are they based on a stable substratum; for even in this case, since there is a dependence on the qualification "provided there is the operation of seeds of a similar kind," there is no deviation [from the rule] by means of jumping. Thinking thus, he says:
"It is not from jumping alone," meaning that jumping does not arise from jumping alone.
He asks: "Under what condition, then, does it arise? and answers: "Jumping [arises] from strength and effort."

The point is this: leaping occurs when strength and effort are present, but it is not the case that when leaping is present, those two—strength and effort—are necessarily present; for leaping may exist as a stable state even in the absence of them.

This would be so if leaping were produced by strength and effort alone, rather than by leaping itself. If that were the case, then whatever kind of leaping a person achieves through practice, they would have attained that same kind of leaping even prior to such practice.

This is not a fault; because the body was previously impaired by phlegm and other humors, fasting does not occur later as it did before. However, once the bodily impairment has been gradually removed through effort, fasting remains established according to one's strength.
This must necessarily be understood in this way;
otherwise, if jumping were to result from jumping alone, then there would be no established limit to the excellence of jumping.

Alternatively, he shows that there is no deviation [from the rule] by jumping, because even for jumping, its excellence in stability is not established since it depends on specific causes—stating "or if" and so forth:
"Or if, due to specific factors such as the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and speed, jumping also reaches its ultimate limit, this is from its own cause. (3425)
The accomplishment known as "mind-swiftness" (manojavā) is likewise heard of as a valid means of knowledge;
for by its mere thought, the master goes even to a distant place.
Furthermore, the non-existence of that [accomplishment] is not established merely by the fact that it is not seen.
Furthermore, no one is capable of stating any sublation (*bādhaka*) against this point.

To explain: we certainly accept that jumping (*laṅghana*) can reach a state of extreme excellence through the application of a specific power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This is just as the supernatural power (*siddhi*) called "mind-swiftness" (*manojavā*) is taught for the Blessed One; when one abides in that state, one possesses a speed like that of the mind, and for this very reason it is renowned as "mind-swiftness."
Furthermore, there is no subverting means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for this [non-existence],
nor is it proper to reject it based on mere non-perception, as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).

Moreover, even in the case of a physical basis, an absolute distinction in movement is observed due to a specific excellence in practice conditioned by particular qualities; thus, demonstrating that such a movement is possible for the Blessed One as well, he says: "Like a young royal swan," and so forth.
A young royal swan is unable to even leave its own house,
yet through the distinction of practice, it reaches the far shore of the ocean as well.
Just as its movement arises from the distinction of practice conditioned by its environment, so too is this [the case for the yogin].
Why should something greater than that not be possible from such [a cause] itself?
For while in the state of a bodhisattva, one is not capable of attaining such a destination;
but once the sublime meditative absorption (samādhi) has been attained, the Sage would be capable of it.

And just as a young royal swan, though initially unable even to leave its own nest, later—once its wings have developed through even slight practice—flies even to the far shore of the ocean; so too it is possible that another [being] may attain a distinguished state through practice conditioned by a particular support.
If it is argued that it is because of the acquisition of specific wings that he becomes a traveler to very distant lands, and not by the power of practice alone; [we reply:]...

For even a young bird, though its wings have grown, is not seen flying away all at once; rather, by practicing the movement from branch to branch, it first travels a certain distance, and only afterwards, having cast off its fear, proceeds to a much more distant place.

Furthermore—just as in the case of a swan or similar creature, whose movement was previously incapable despite the acquisition of a particular physical basis (*āśrayaviśeṣa*), its movement later becomes specialized; so too, although the Blessed One was previously incapable during his stage as a bodhisattva, it is possible that such a movement [of omniscience] occurs for him later, once he has acquired a particular basis through the attainment of specific meditative absorptions (*samādhi*). It is with this intention that the mention of "practice" (*abhyāsa*) is not intended as a restrictive rule.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: That practice which has as its limiting condition (*upādhi*) a possible specific basis is such that it results in the attainment of an extremely distant goal; for example, the practice of a young royal swan. The practice of humans has as its limiting condition a possible specific basis; this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
He shows that what was stated— "a distance of ten cubits," and so forth— is refuted, by saying "ten," etc.:
"That which one goes by leaping through the space at a distance of ten cubits."
Such a capacity may belong to that cause even when it has moved far away.

By including the qualification "provided there is a stable substratum," he shows that [the reason] is not inconclusive due to the heating of water— stating "of that which is being brought to heat," etc.— for the destruction of water occurs [in that case].
Therefore, because the basis is unstable, for whom could there be excellence in what?

One might ask: "But how is it established that wisdom and the other qualities have a stable basis? To this he says: "Of mental [qualities]," and so forth; for mental qualities, the continuum of consciousness (*cittasantati*) is the basis.
Due to its connection with the basis, that [stream] does not turn back from its activity in any way.
"That" refers to the continuum of consciousness.
"From the occurrence by way of the application of the basis" means that it proceeds through the connection with the basis characterized as the support of the bodhisattva;
this is because a specific basis is intended to be expressed.

For instance: since the existence of other worlds has been established, and because Bodhisattvas—who have made great compassion their very nature—remain until the end of saṃsāra for the sake of uplifting all sentient beings without exception, the mental continuum residing in them possesses an exceedingly stable basis.

However, that which resides in the continuum of Śrāvakas and others does not possess a stable basis; this is because they attain parinirvāṇa much more quickly due to the dullness of their compassion, and thus they lack the effort to remain [in the world]. This is the intended meaning.
If it is asked how the second qualification is established, he says: "As long as... and so forth;
for as long as the flood of qualities in this [intellect] proceeds toward [the object], it proceeds all the more intensely, becoming increasingly luminous. || 3434 ||
To explain how this very point is established, he says: "Luminous," and so forth.
This mind is luminous, having the realization of reality as its very nature, because it abides by its own nature; for the defilements are considered to be adventitious. (3435)
And this has already been explained by us previously;

it has been established that these specific qualities, such as wisdom (*prajñā*) and so forth, are by their very nature the essence of the mind due to their consisting in the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*). Thus, it is proven that because wisdom and the others are its inherent nature, once they have been instilled, they proceed spontaneously by their own force.
If it is asked how the second qualification—that cognition consists of the vision of reality—is established, he says: "The nature of supreme awakening," and so forth.
For if the mind were restricted to having the nature of supreme awakening, then, because its apprehension would be unestablished, the cognition of objects would not be possible. || 3436 ||
Therefore, because it is luminous, the mind possesses the nature of self-awareness;
and this self-awareness exists as a form that is not superimposed.

(3437) For all proponents of philosophical systems must necessarily admit that the primary nature of the mind is indeed self-awareness; otherwise, if it were to be cognized by another subsequent cognition, then the cognition of an object would not be established, as its own apprehension would remain unproven.
Therefore, the primary nature of the mind is simply the self-luminosity of consciousness;
and since that self-nature consists of impermanence and so forth, it follows by implication that the mind is established as being essentially the vision of reality—this is the intended meaning.

It might be argued: "Let it be that the mind consists of the vision of reality; nevertheless, because it is possible for even abandoned powers to arise again through the force [of latent tendencies], the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatā*) of all the aforementioned reasons is difficult to avoid. Anticipating this objection, he says: "When the path has become habitual," and so forth: "Therefore, when the path has become habitual, there is certainly no overcoming of it by those [powers]."
For they were already weakened by defects such as passion and hatred;
moreover, because the Path— which washes away and destroys all [defects]— has become their very nature,
there is no loss of it without effort, and effort does not arise from seeing [its] virtues.
Therefore, the Jina is understood to be omniscient, adorned by a multitude of qualities that are stainless and unshakable, and whose nature cannot be shaken by the winds of defects.

(3440) Since even prior to the internalization of the Path, the stains such as passion were unable to overcome the Path because they were weak due to their adventitious nature, how then will they overcome it once the Path has become fully internalized?

Furthermore—it is not possible for one who has attained the state of self-identification with a quality of the mind to effect its abandonment without effort, just as it is impossible for a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) to abandon his lack of compassion toward women.
Moreover, for one who perceives reality (*tattvadarśin*), effort toward the abandonment of a thing that possesses a quality is not possible;
why? Because of the perception of its qualities.
And this has already been stated before: it is a flaw—a defect.

Alternatively— In order to demonstrate that whatever [reasons] such as "being an entity" (*vastutva*) and so forth you have stated for the purpose of negating an omniscient being are themselves sufficient to establish that very [existence], he first establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the reason "being an entity" and so forth, saying "Furthermore," and so on.
Furthermore, whatever things are clearly visualized appear with perfect clarity once the cultivation is perfected, just like the objects of desire and so forth.
And all phenomena are cultivated for a long time in manifold ways.
The great-minded ones, the Great Beings (mahātmabhiḥ), have established emptiness, selflessness, and so forth as the ultimate reality;
and they have proven that this nature of emptiness, selflessness, and so forth is real.
Because it arises from the cultivation of the true object, that [cognition] is therefore held to be a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa).
In this regard, the fundamental formal argument (*maula-prayoga*) to be stated is as follows:

those things which possess properties such as being real entities (*vastutva*) and being knowable (*jñeyatva*) are capable of being clearly manifested in a single cognition at the ultimate limit of the intensification of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*); for example, a beloved woman, a son, a thief, and so forth, when cultivated by those afflicted by desire and the like; and all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) possess properties such as being real entities. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*), and it is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*).

To explain: whatever is meditated upon, whether real or unreal, all of that is established as having as its fruit a cognition with a clear manifestation (*sphuṭapratibhāsa*) once the meditation is perfected; for example, women and other objects for a lover. And all phenomena are meditated upon for a long time by those whose compassion has become habitual, in their ultimate (*tāttvika*) form. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). By this, it is shown that meditation is pervaded by the fruit of cognition with a clear manifestation, because that clear manifestation does not depend on any other object. To the question, "How is it established that the ultimate nature of emptiness and so forth consists precisely in such a clear manifestation?", he says: "Emptiness," etc. (3441).
And establishing that this knowledge of emptiness and so forth is a means of valid cognition consisting of direct perception, he says: "Direct perception," and so on.
Perception is a valid means of knowledge because it manifests clearly and accords with the actual object,
just like the appearance of blue and other colors arising from the basis of the eyes and other senses.
A clear manifestation can occur simultaneously within a single cognition.
Therefore, let it be understood that this applies to all phenomena as well:
because they are thus conceptualized, like a woman, a son, or a thief, even meditative cultivation—which manifests through the mere power of intention—is not difficult to achieve. (3445–3446)

Because it possesses vivid manifestation, is non-conceptual, has as its object a thing established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and is non-erroneous, this [cognition] is a direct perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*), just like visual and other sensory cognitions.

Consequently, once vivid manifestation—which arises through mere cultivation—is established, the simultaneous vivid manifestation of all phenomena within a single cognition is likewise established. Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is proven: "It is possible for all phenomena to appear clearly and simultaneously in a single consciousness.
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whatever is cultivated is capable of appearing vividly and simultaneously in a single consciousness, just as women and other such objects.
"All phenomena are also conceptualized" is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
Showing that this reason should not be considered unestablished (*asiddha*), he says "desire," and so forth;
for since the possibility of cultivation has already been established in detail previously, the reason is not unestablished.
Having thus established the pervasion by demonstrating that vivid manifestation is invariably concomitant with mere cultivation, he now states the primary logical argument, saying:

"By means of such reasons as the existence of the object, all phenomena are clearly manifested by a single cognition reaching the culmination of cultivation, just like [the face of] a beloved one," and so forth. (3447)

And thus, for whomsoever there are reasons capable of establishing [the existence of an omniscient being] through characteristics such as being a real entity, a sentient being, or subject to origination— who would not prove that person?
[He is one] whose entire circle of objects of knowledge is pervaded by a single moment of cognition.
The perfected one (siddha), the knower of all, who is the crest-jewel upon the heads of both gods and asuras, resides here.

That state which is the culmination of the excellence of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā) within a single cognition is thus described; even though there is a difference in grammatical case, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound because of its capacity to convey meaning.
Those things which clearly manifest in a single cognition at the culmination of the excellence of cultivation are so described;

and he in whose cognition they thus appear is proven to be the Omniscient One—the crest-jewel of all gods and asuras—who, in a single moment of knowledge, pervades the entire circle of all objects of knowledge.
Indeed, those things such as the Dharma were known by you through some [means], even without verbal instruction.
Because they are taught as having a true nature, like the purity of gold and so forth.

Alternatively, those things which are taught as having a true nature are known by someone, just as the purity of gold and so forth are; and since phenomena (dharmas) and so forth are taught as having a true nature, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).
It might be argued: "Since it is possible to give instruction even after knowing [the truth] from the Vedas, your proof is superfluous. To this he says: "Of the Vedas," and so forth.

If the human authorship of the Vedas is established, then [our] proof is not unestablished; for there can be no true instruction regarding what is unknown, whereas [instruction] by a person acting by chance is merely accidental.
Since the human authorship of the Vedas was established previously in the "Examination of Revelation" (*Śrutiparīkṣā*), there is no proving of what is already proven (*siddhasādhyatā*).

Furthermore, one might argue that because instruction is possible even by chance without prior knowledge, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); to this he says: "Of that which is unknown," and so forth.
For it is not possible to speak, as a rule, much that is not contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by chance without having first known it.
The power of mudrās, maṇḍalas, mantras, and so forth, which is beyond the reach of the senses, [is evident] in such things as the liberation from piśācas and ḍākinīs and the removal of poison.
If the stainless knowledge of the Munis, Tārksya (Garuḍa), and others were not direct cognition distinct from what is heard or inferred, how could it have been spoken by them? Furthermore,

regarding this power of mantras and the like to remove poison and so forth— which is entirely beyond the senses— if that were not directly known by the Buddhas and others, then it must be explained how it was spoken by them.
If it is argued that [the Buddha] spoke after knowing [the truth] through inference, he says: "Nor by means of inference," and so forth.
Nor can there be knowledge [of that] through inference, because it has not been previously perceived; for, due to that, the perception of the relationship of a logical mark (*liṅga*) is impossible.

Indeed, an object whose relationship with its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is unknown is not the object of inference, nor can the relationship of any logical mark with such an absolutely imperceptible (*atyantaparokṣa*) entity be ascertained.
Nor has this been stated by anyone else, because the same critical inquiry applies;
nor is it a form that arises by chance or is inconsistent with reality, for such a thing has been thoroughly cultivated.
This teaching has this very [purpose] as its ultimate goal; there is no postulation of another cause.
For it is only when an activity is produced by some other cause that such a suspicion might arise—as, for example, in the case of one whose mind is distracted by thirst while approaching a river.
Likewise, the occurrence of obtaining coral is a matter of chance.

If it is argued that this was stated after hearing it from another, that too is subject to the same inquiry; for even so, the following investigation applies: how did that other person know it? For an instruction of such a kind would not be possible without knowing it oneself. If it is claimed that he also knew it from yet another, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Consequently, if there were a succession of blind men, because none would possess true knowledge, there could be no correct instruction.

As it has been said: "In matters of this kind, the word of a person does not attain the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just as the speech of the blind regarding specific forms [is unreliable].
Anticipating the objection that "this state of non-contradiction might even be accidental, like the carving of a letter by a wood-boring insect," he says: "Not by chance," and so forth.
The analysis of the compound is: "that which has the nature of being non-contradictory precisely through chance."
It may be thought that for one who has set out with the intention of attaining one object, the attainment of another object is merely accidental;
for example, one who sets out with the intention of approaching a riverbank might happen to approach the foot of a tree.

However, in this case, it is not possible that the activity was undertaken with the intention of attaining something else. For, having made the formal promise, "O monks, I shall teach you the Dharma," this teaching proceeds as being solely intent upon the instruction of the Dharma and so forth; it is determined that it is not intent upon any other purpose.
Vāhinī means a river;
vidruma means a coral tree or a sprout.
If it is argued that [the argument] is inconclusive because instruction can arise even from delusion, he says: "Of those with distracted minds," and so forth.
This was not spoken by the deluded who have distracted minds; for this [teaching], though unspoken [by them], is certain and is the supreme means for accomplishing the fruit. (3458)

For it is not possible for those with distracted minds to speak at length a sentence that possesses a fixed sequence, is free from internal contradictions between its preceding and succeeding parts, and accomplishes the goals of human beings;
therefore, it is established that someone has directly cognized dharma and the other such matters.

It might be argued: "Even if it is established in a general sense, nevertheless, it is desired to prove that the Sugata possesses knowledge of the Dharma; how, then, is that proved? Anticipating this doubt, the author, establishing the Blessed One’s knowledge of the Dharma, says: "One who reveals the truth not heard or inferred—that ultimate reality—having directly perceived its nature, is a teacher of such a kind. (3459)
Just as another person who has directly perceived water and so forth might communicate it,
[the Buddha] spoke for the sake of others about that which is true, though unperceived and un-inferred by them,
because its capacity is beyond the senses and unknown to others, through his own certain realization. (3460)

The Best of Sages [taught] the characteristics of the mudrās, maṇḍalas, ritual procedures, and so forth. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: whoever teaches a true matter that has not been heard or inferred must have directly realized the reality of that matter, just as one who teaches water and such things must have perceived them through direct perception; and the Blessed One is likewise [such a teacher]. This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*);
since truthfulness and other qualities have already been established, there is no lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) regarding the reason.
Nor is there any inconclusiveness; this has already been established.
Furthermore, since all these reasons exist in the similar class (*sapakṣa*), it should be understood that they are not contradictory (*viruddha*), for their capacity is known by others.
That whose efficacy is unknown to others— such as a seal and so forth— is described as such.
Regarding what was stated, beginning with "therefore, by means of superior cognitions," etc., he says there: "Therefore," and so forth;
"therefore, by means of superior cognitions that function through the power of skillful means."
"Everything, even that which is beyond the senses, can indeed be known.
Regarding the passage beginning with "of one staying in a single room," he says: "Of one staying in a single room, whatever perception occurs... [3462]

"His power would exist only in that very place, and certainly not in another room"—this you are right to conclude only when there is an experience of the capacity residing in all sentient beings; otherwise, what is the basis for such a determination? (3463–3464)

This has been stated by your honor as being based on mere assertion alone; for it is not possible for those of limited vision to determine that all persons lack the capacity to know supersensuous objects merely because they themselves do not perceive them.
This might be the case: we do not determine incapacity merely on the basis of non-perception;
rather, [we do so] on the grounds of reasons such as being a human being (*puruṣatva*).

For instance: "All persons whatsoever are incapable of cognizing the objects of others situated at a distance and so forth, because they possess the properties of being a person, being an entity, being knowable, and so on, just like myself. To this, he replies: "By the example of oneself," and so forth.

If the absence of capacity in others were determined by the example of oneself through reasons such as "being a person" and so on, then an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would follow regarding the effect [of inference]. (3465)
For if your dullness were thus established, then by your own example, all wise men would likewise be of dull intellect. (3466) [Note:
The word *niścaya* here stands in grammatical apposition with *kārya*.]
In this regard, the reasons are inconclusive because they lead to an over-extension;
for it can likewise be argued: "All persons indeed possess dull intellects, because they are persons, etc., just like you"—yet such is not the case.
For it is not possible to determine that a property (dharma) not observed in one person is absent in all [persons], because differences among persons are observed.

And as for what was said by Ṛtuparṇa—that "no one knows everything," and so forth—he states [the following] to show that this too is merely a thesis asserted by him without any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*): "There is no finality of knowledge in any person anywhere"—this too is cited as mere words, devoid of reason. (3467)

Alternatively, showing that this statement made by Ṛtuparṇa was addressed to persons equal to himself and is therefore not an authoritative indicator because it is not contradictory [to his own position], he says: "Or, having in mind beings equal to himself who are dull-witted and ignorant... (verse 3468). Thus, the statement was uttered by Ṛtuparṇa with reference to those of similar nature who are of impure intellect and dull.
The means of valid cognition has been explained in detail regarding the possibility of an omniscient being, and any sublation previously asserted by others against him has been refuted.
Alternatively, even if that proof of his possibility were not stated:
Its possibility is understood merely through the exclusion of sublation;
for when no sublation is observed and no proof has been revealed, doubt arises, and by that means it attains the status of being possible.
And when that [Veda] is established as authoritative, the restrictive rule is thereby proven:
namely, that dharma is characterized by the Veda alone, which is independent.
(3472) "Svasamāḥ" means those who are equal to oneself, i.e., similar to oneself.
Regarding the statement "it is not seen in the future," and so forth, he says: "And in the future," etc.
And regarding future objects to be known, the capacity of direct perception for yogins would likewise exist; this was stated in that examination of the three times (*tatraikālyaparīkṣaṇe*).
As for "that examination of the three times": [it refers to the analysis of the past, present, and future].

For it has been stated there as follows: "Indeed, all entities whatsoever have entered into the state of being cause and effect, either directly or indirectly. Among these, a present entity is the effect, either directly or indirectly, of the past, and it is the cause of the future."

Experiencing all aspects exactly as they are through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yogins—by means of subsequent pure mundane conceptualizations (*śuddhalaukika-vikalpa*) which, though ultimately devoid of objects, are non-erroneous due to their connection with real entities—take as their object the past and future continuum of phenomena (*bhāvasantati*) consisting of causes and effects, and thereby establish the existence of past and future things. As it has been said: "Yogins cognize that form of the present which has entered into a state of causality, either indirectly or directly."

And subsequently, by means of pure mundane cognitions whose nature is accompanied by conceptualization, they follow the actual past and future continuities of those objects, as well as of their causes and effects, even though [those objects] do not exist in reality.
Relying upon this, the teachings concerning the past and the future proceed.

And this is not accepted by the Sautrāntikas, because they maintain that the Blessed One has direct perception of everything; therefore, showing the desired view according to the perspective of the Sautrāntikas, he says: "Or else," and so forth:

"Or else, through the power of yoga, there may arise for yogins a mental [cognition] that is vivid, resembling what has already occurred or what is yet to be born, and which is independent of inferential signs. (3474)

For just as the cognition of one who sees a true dream—though ultimately devoid of an external object and independent of logical marks or scripture—arises from the power of a particular basis and is non-erroneous; so too, for yogins, by the power of yoga, past or future objects, exactly as they have been or will be, arise with a clear manifestation independent of logical marks or scripture, and that is accepted as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

It might be argued: "Perception is held to have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, yet the past and the future do not exist as particular characteristics; therefore, how is it logical for them to have a particular characteristic as their object? To this he says: "Its own nature," and so forth:
"Because it is a cognition in which its own nature appears, its object is that particular characteristic; and because it is experienced as a clear appearance, it is accepted as perception. (3475)
Therefore, there exists indeed a direct perceiver of supersensuous objects, because an eternal word does not exist; thus, no one perceives [them] by means of that [word].

(3476) Even though a past object and so forth do not exist as a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, it is taught in the treatise that they have the specific characteristic as their object by virtue of self-cognition (*ātmasaṃvedana*); thus, there is no contradiction.

And because it possesses a vivid appearance, it is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*); and because it is non-erroneous due to its non-discrepancy with such a thing, it is non-delusory (*abhrānta*). Therefore, since it is endowed with the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), it is established as direct perception.
Unable to tolerate this, he says regarding the verse beginning with "yaḥ" (he who...):
"The wise have declared that the Sage’s cognition of supersensible objects arises from the aforementioned inference, and not from any other source such as a fabricated scripture. (3477)

The wise followers of the Sugata (Saugatas) have declared that the cognition of supersensuous objects—which is established through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), independent of scripture, and which directly perceives its object—is proven by the aforementioned inference; it does not arise from any other produced scripture. Therefore, since [the opponent] does not accept that [scripture], there is no fault at all. Regarding what was said—"of the words of an author and of artificial [texts]," etc.—he replies with the verse beginning "kartṛkṛtrima... (the author and the artificial).

The lack of beginning (anāditva) is not asserted for the case of a creator or artificial sentences for the sake of establishing their validity, because that [lack of beginning] also exists in the case of what is invalid;
for instance, this is true of the nihilists and so forth, as well as of their words.
And even though the expounders of the Vedas are not beginningless, they possess authority.
For we do not state "beginninglessness" as a probans for establishing authority;
because it would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), as it occurs even in the case of the opposite [of what is to be proven].
Therefore, the objection you have stated is based on a superimposition.

Furthermore, demonstrating that all these objections apply most clearly to you yourselves—who assert the beginninglessness of both the speakers of the Vedas and the Vedas as a means to establish the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of the Vedas—the author says: "Of the speakers and their artificial sentences," and so forth.
Indeed, beginninglessness is asserted for the sake of establishing the authority of the speakers' artificial sentences; that very [beginninglessness] is refuted by us as if in competition. (3480)
The term *vaktāraścākṛtrimavākyāni* is a *dvandva* compound;
therein, "speakers" (*vaktāraḥ*) refers to the commentators of the Vedas.
To the question, "How are they refuted? he says: "Speakers," and so forth.
The speakers are equal to the authors; and the authority of the Vedas depends upon them, because the cognition of meaning arises from the explanations composed by them.
(3481) "Depends upon them" means:
To the question "How is there dependence on the speaker?", he says: "Because of the explanation provided by them.

This means that because the cognition of the meaning arises from the explanation (*vyākhyāna*) given by those speakers, the Vedas' status as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) depends upon them.
3481 And as to what the fault would be [if that were not the case], he says: "Therefore," and so forth;
therefore, the Vedic sentences possess no authority because of their dependence on something else.
Even for those who speak of Dharma while not perceiving it themselves, that [revelation] does not exist at all. Even if beginninglessness is postulated for such speakers,
because they occupy a position of invalidity, they do not differ from an atheist.
Because there is no distinction between that [cognition] being ignorant and its being ignorant of something, everything here attains equality;
thus, validity and invalidity would not exist as beginningless properties.
(3484) "Not at all," [he says].
The connection is with the term "authoritativeness" (*pramāṇatā*).

And since, in this way, the Vedic sentences lack authoritativeness due to their dependence [on others], and all those who proclaim them are unauthoritative—like a succession of blind men not seeing the Dharma—therefore, that which was stated by the opponent, namely, "authoritativeness and non-authoritativeness would thus be beginningless," is incorrect. Demonstrating this, he says: "Authoritativeness and non-authoritativeness would not thus be beginningless."

For only if the validity of the non-artificial statements composed by a speaker were established would there be beginninglessness of that validity; however, since that very point is not established, it is incorrect to claim that both are beginningless—this is the intended meaning.

Furthermore—this equality that we have established between the Vedas and their students on one hand, and the Buddha and his words on the other, was done merely for the sake of comparison; however, there is no actual equality between the Blessed Ones and their words and these [Vedic ones], but rather a great distinction. Demonstrating this, he says:
"Or rather," and so forth—"or rather, this very distinction exists between the Sage and his words."
He himself perceived the Dharma and, being filled with compassion,
proclaimed it; for it has been established that the Blessed One directly perceived and taught the Dharma.

Therefore, the point that "he himself did not see the Dharma" is unestablished; this is the intended meaning. One might ask: how is it established that he spoke the Dharma? To this, he says: "Because [it leads to] prosperity," and so forth.
"That from which the accomplishment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) arises, and from which the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) arises—
that is called *dharma* by all wise men.
[3486] "And of the highest good" (*niḥśreyasasya ca*).
The connection is "from which [there is] accomplishment.
In that context, "prosperity" (*abhyudaya*) is happiness, and "the highest good" (*niḥśreyasa*) is liberation;
such [a cause] is called "dharma."
"Since the attainment of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) is [the result] of that, it is Dharma"—from this statement [it follows].

Let it be granted that Dharma is the cause for the attainment of worldly prosperity and the supreme good; however, how is it established that these words of the Sugata are the cause thereof, by virtue of which he would possess the status of a knower of Dharma? To this, he says: "Because it was spoken by him," and so forth.

As it has been said: "From the performance of the rules regarding mantras, yoga, and so forth, according to the prescribed method, there arises even in this present life [the attainment of] wisdom, health, sovereign power, and the like.
Therefore, the analysis of the compound is: "that which was taught by the Blessed One as the rule regarding mantras, yoga, and so forth."

Yoga is meditative concentration (*samādhi*); by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of mudrās, maṇḍalas, and so forth is intended; thus, it is also a phenomenon of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*).
By the word "also" (*api*), he shows that [this result occurs] in this very life, and not only in the next world.
(3487) Having thus demonstrated its nature as the cause of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*), he says "all... and so forth, demonstrating its nature as the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
From the vision of the selflessness of all phenomena, as revealed by that [vision],
there is the cessation of the flood of afflictions arising from the view of the existence of effects;
the view of a self and what belongs to a self, which takes the form of the perception of a sentient being, ceases to function.
And when there is the conceit of "I" and "mine," every affliction proceeds.
(3489) This teaching of selflessness is the antidote to the view of a sentient being;
once that [selflessness] has become habitual through practice, that [view] ceases. (3490)
And the mass of afflictions rooted in that [ignorance] is eliminated due to the absence of its cause; when that [ignorance] is no longer present, its cause—existence—is not born again.
Through the absolute liberation from that, it is proclaimed as *apavarga* (liberation).
Therefore, the vision of selflessness is the unique gateway to Śiva;
for all non-Buddhist teachers, liberation is desired through the cessation of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), yet as long as the existence of a self persists, the ego-sense does not cease.
Because the efficient cause exists and because the object [of knowledge] is not defective, if that [object] were defective, a contradiction would follow due to its non-existence.

(3494) For it is accepted by all that liberation is the absolute cessation of the continuity of birth, and the means for attaining that is the word of the Blessed One alone; for it is precisely here, and nowhere else, that the vision of selflessness—which serves as the antidote to the afflictions that are the causes of birth—is taught.

Since all other non-Buddhist teachers are intent upon a false view of the self, it is therefore logical that only the word of the Blessed One possesses the characteristic of Dharma, as it is the means for attaining both worldly prosperity and the supreme good; nothing else does.
Thus, the collective meaning is that those who seek the highest good should rely on this alone and not on anything else.

The meaning of the individual parts is now stated: if it is asked how it is established that the flood of afflictions (*kleśaugha*) arises from the view that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryadarśana*), he says: "Self and what belongs to the self," and so forth;
this has already been explained by us previously.

Even if the flood of afflictions indeed arises from the view that the effect pre-exists in the cause, how then does it cease through the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*)? To this he says: "The view of a sentient being," and so forth.
*sattvadṛk*— the view of existence, that is to say, the view that the effect pre-exists in the cause; its *pratyanīkam*— the adversary or counter-position.
This too has already been shown previously in that demonstration of selflessness.
Thus, the view of a self-entity is the root of that.
"Its root is the view of a self because of the absence of a cause" means that there is an absence of the cause known as the "view of a self."
"In that" refers to the mass of afflictions;
"its cause" refers to the cause of that.
The mass of afflictions does not arise because it lacks a cause;
for it is not logical for an effect to arise in the absence of its cause, as that would entail the fallacy of causelessness.
"Absolute liberation from that" means the complete liberation from those afflictions or from that rebirth, by way of never arising again;
as they say: "Liberation is absolute release from that."

Now, one might object: "In other systems as well, the vision of reality (*tattvadarśana*) is taught to be the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), and the ten wholesome paths of action (*kuśala-karmapatha*) are taught to be the causes of worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*). Therefore, how can it be said that the vision of selflessness (*nairātmyadarśana*) alone is the peerless door to liberation? To this he says: "Of all [systems]," and so forth.

For, since the aggregates (*skandhas*) arise from the conceit of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*), liberation occurs upon the cessation of that [conceit]; thus, there is no dispute among any who desire liberation on this point.

Yet, for those of other sects, the cessation of the conceit of "I" is not possible, because they are obsessed with a false view of a self (*vitathātmadarśana*), and because the conceit of "I" is rooted in the view of a self.
Therefore, how could this [defilement] cease when the adherence to a self and sentient beings remains with its causes intact, and when the self—the object of that adherence—is not refuted?

As it has been said: "As long as the mind possesses the conception of 'I,' the continuity of birth does not come to rest; the conception of 'I' does not depart from the heart as long as the view of a self persists.
There is no other teacher in the world than you who teaches selflessness; there is no path to the method of pacification other than your doctrine."
For instance, mental phenomena are not to be removed by being extracted like thorns or the like;
rather,
since they have arisen through attachment to objects as they appear to be, they are to be eliminated by refuting their cause.
If it is argued that "the yogi indeed defiles the self," he says: "By the refutation of that," and so forth.
For instance, that [self], being defiled, must be refuted in the form of non-existence; otherwise, the refutation of it would be futile.
To explain: if one were to adhere to the self as existing and then refute it on the grounds of its being a cause of suffering, [it would be a contradiction].
In that case, the refutation would be entirely purposeless;
for that refutation is intended for the sake of abandonment,
and since the abandonment of that which is inherently eternal and constitutes its very nature is impossible, it follows that the refutation becomes utterly useless.
Nor can their self be refuted by means of the form of non-existence, because it would follow that they would fall into error through their dogmatic adherence to the reality or unreality of the self.

Furthermore, even if it were granted that [the self] could be refuted by some other mode, such as being a cause of suffering, nevertheless, the cessation of the ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*), which arises solely from the view of a self (*ātmadarśana*), would not be logical; demonstrating this, he says: "It is not logical," and so forth.

It is not logical to say "I am not," if indeed that which is called "I" exists; for if it were certain that the knowledge of reality leads to nirvāṇa, then [the denial] would be false. (3495) "It is not logical to say 'I am not'"—thus [it is said].
The meaning is that the view "I do not exist" is not tenable;
"if 'I' were to exist" means if the self (ātman) were to exist.
Therefore, the claim that one who knows reality according to your school attains nirvāṇa is false;

for liberation is held to result from the disappearance of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and since the self remains as an object, the cessation of the ego-sense is not logical—what reasoning supports this?
He concludes with the words beginning "Therefore":
"Therefore, although in other religious systems there is a slight attainment of prosperity resulting from the abandonment of the ten unwholesome actions, it is indeed very minor. (3496)
But the attainment of liberation does not exist even in the slightest degree, because the view of a self-characterizes the mind and the roots of affliction have not been uprooted.
[This is stated] "due to the non-abandonment of the ten unwholesome [actions]. (3497)

The ten unwholesome [actions] are: taking life, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, slander, harsh speech, frivolous chatter, malice, and wrong view; or alternatively, they are recited as: failing to protect others, not giving, lack of service, untruthfulness, unpleasant speech, what is harmful, lack of study, lack of faith, lack of compassion, and covetousness. By their opposites, the ten wholesome [actions] are established.
The loss of those unwholesome states, the abstention from them, and the practice of the ten wholesome paths— this is what is meant by "lighter," because,
being preceded by error, it leads to a swifter downfall.
The root of the afflictions is precisely the view of a self-entity.

He also demonstrates the distinction of the Blessed One’s words by way of their being causes for exaltation: "The ten paths of action which were taught as auspicious by the Protector (Tāyin)—when these are further embraced by right view, they become exceedingly powerful. (3498)
They are "powerful" because their fruits are firm and sublime.
He asks why the others are not powerful as well, and says:
"But those [others] are enveloped by the view of a self (sattvadṛṣṭi) due to their attachment to error;
therefore, they are impure, and from them a pure fruit does not arise. (3499)

Thus, who with a sound mind would say that one sees the Dharma oneself when the Supreme Sage— the teacher of the reality of phenomena— is not seen? For indeed, a perfectly pure result arises only from a perfectly pure cause, not from an impure one.

"Munisattama" means the most excellent (*sattama*), the beautiful one, among the sages (*muni*)— both those still in training (*śaikṣya*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣya*)— thus he is the "best of sages.

Regarding what was stated— "They claim that the omniscience of the Buddha and others and the eternality of the Veda are equal," and so forth— it is said in response: "Of the Protector (Tāyin)," and so on.
The protectors [the Buddhas] proclaim that the omniscience of the Veda is equal to their own; however, we do not accept this because the eternity of the Veda is impossible.
For its refutation has been stated on the grounds of the contradiction between succession and simultaneity.
It is not in any way logical that consciousness and so forth should be its effect [of such a cause].
"Of the Protector" refers to the Blessed One, the Buddha.
For if the eternity of the Veda were possible, then it would be appropriate to say, "And that which is the eternity of the Veda"; however, that very [eternity] is not established.

Having previously demonstrated this through the presentation of subverting evidence (*bādhakapramāṇa*), he now recalls that very same subverting evidence: "Because of the contradiction between succession and simultaneity."
And this has already been explained previously.
Regarding what was said—"An omniscient being is not seen by people such as us at present"—he replies: "Is it seen... and so forth.
"Is it that an omniscient being is not seen by you alone at present, or by everyone? Here, the refutation is set forth in detail. (3503)

"For your non-perception is solitary and subject to deviation; however, the exclusion of all other perceivers is doubtful, and thus it is not a proof. (3504) Furthermore, Kumārila has stated this: "And the conceptualization that 'it did not exist' cannot be established in the same way as its negation. To this, he replies with the verse beginning "nirākaraṇa... and so forth.
The supposition that "he did not exist" cannot be made in the same way as a refutation [is possible]; this is incorrect, because even regarding the past, a refutation of him is impossible.

(Verse 3505) For instance, just as it is indeed possible to effect a refutation of an omniscient being in the past, so too the supposition that "there was an omniscient being" cannot be made; this is incorrect, because even in the past time, a refutation of him is logically untenable.

By the word "also" (api), he shows that [the object] cannot be apprehended even in the two times of the present and the future; for it was stated previously that non-existence is not understood from mere non-perception.
With the words "It might be thought," etc., he raises the proof proposed by the opponent.
It might be thought: "The past time is empty for you, the all-seeing one, because it is time, just as the present time is perceived.
This is not a valid proof, because its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is doubtful.
And this present time has not been ascertained to be devoid of an omniscient being.

The formal argument (prayoga) is as follows: This past time is devoid of an omniscient being, because it is time, like the present time. Since no subverting proof (bādhaka-pramāṇa) has been shown against the opposite of the probandum (sādhya-viparyaya) in that case, there is "uncertainty regarding the negative concomitance" (sandigdhavyatirekitva); therefore, the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Furthermore, the example (dṛṣṭānta) is unestablished (asiddha) because its property to be proven (sādhyadharma) is itself doubtful.
Or, let the example be established; even so, he says "the reason," etc., demonstrating that it is not correct to establish what is desired merely by the observation [of the example].

Furthermore, due to the absence of the causal complex (*hetusāmagrī*), that which is called "past" does not exist at present, like Rāma and others; however, why could it not have existed in past time?
Moreover, what is the connection here [between the two] such that what does not exist now did not exist in past time either?
For it is not possible to infer that because Rāma, Bharata, and others do not exist now, they did not exist in the past either;
