therefore, because of the lack of invariable concomitance (anaikāntya) with Rāma and the others, the logical reason (hetu) is inconclusive.

Regarding what was said—"No single part is observed, nor is there a logical mark (liṅga)"—he replies with the words "of wisdom and so forth," etc.: Having established that wisdom and the rest are the subjects (dharmin), the logical mark has been stated;
indeed, no such mark is seen, nor is existence (sattā) being proven.

By the passage beginning with "ye cāsamānajātīya," the nature of wisdom (*prajñā*) and the other faculties as the subject (*dharmin*) is established, and thus the logical mark (*liṅga*) has been stated; therefore, the claim that "the logical mark does not exist" is unproven (*asiddha*).

Nor is mere existence (*sattā*) being proven; what then? It is a property (*dharma*) called the absolute excellence of wisdom and the rest, and that itself is omniscience (*sarvajñatva*). Consequently, even those faults which apply to the proof of mere existence do not apply here at all.
Regarding the statement beginning with "And there is no procedure for scripture" (na cāgamavidhiḥ kaścit), he says: "But by means of scripture... and so forth.

"However, we do not establish an omniscient being through scripture; for when the previously mentioned inferential mark exists, who indeed would speak of [omniscience] on the basis of scripture? (3510)

For when inference functioning by the force of real entities (*vastubala-pravṛtta-anumāna*) is possible, no one would seek to establish a real entity based on a statement that merely follows one's own whim; therefore, we do not establish the Omniscient One through scripture (*āgama*).
What then?
And that [is established] through inference, as has already been stated above. 3510
Nor is this established—that there is no scriptural injunction whatsoever for the cognition of an omniscient being. Demonstrating this, he says: "But rather," and so forth:
"But if the authority of the Veda is accepted by you, why then is the omniscience of the Blessed One not understood by the deluded? (3511)
The Blessed One, the omniscient one, the best of sages, is indeed clearly recited under the name *Nimitta* in another Vedic branch (*śākhāntara*) by learned Brahmins.

For instance: there exists another branch named *Nimitta*, wherein this very Blessed One, Śākyamuni, is most clearly recited as the omniscient one. Therefore, why is he rejected by you, who, though being fools, nevertheless accept the Veda as authoritative?
Showing how this is recited there, he says: "He who... and so forth.
He who was born as a Bodhisattva, an ocean of virtues, after manifesting himself in a dream as a six-tusked white elephant—
he shall become the All-Knowing One, whose fame is proclaimed everywhere and whose nature is compassion.
He has attained the state of immortality, is pure, and is the father of all the worlds;
his fame is proclaimed with the cry "Vighuṣṭaśabda," renowned throughout the entire universe.
"Having attained the state of immortality" means having attained the state of nirvāṇa, characterized by the cessation of all afflictions along with their latent tendencies;
"pure" [is the meaning].
Consisting of the untainted realm (*anāśravadhātu*):
by this much, the Blessed One’s perfection of his own welfare, characterized by the abandonment of ignorance, has been elucidated.
Now, illuminating the perfection of the welfare of others, he says: "The father of all the world."
The Father— the Teacher of the entire world, because he establishes [beings] in the three types of knowledge and in happy rebirths.
Now, with the words "atha" and so forth, he anticipates the opponent's reply:
"If it is argued that this other recensional branch (śākhāntara) is not accepted as being included within the Veda..."
Therefore, in this case, no basis for [the Veda's authority] is perceived by you except for hatred.

Furthermore, those properties such as accents and so forth, which are well-known to arise from the Vedic revelation, can be produced here [in ordinary speech] as well, since they originate solely from human will. (3515–3516)
With the words "this" and so forth,
he refutes another branch known as the *nimitta* [doctrine] by means of the passage beginning with "in this case."
With the words beginning with "nanu," he anticipates the opponent's reply.
But surely, an authoritative scripture (*āgama*) that is devoted to this [ultimate reality] cannot be found here as something eternal;
for if it were eternal, it would be a mere explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), and if it were devoted to that [reality], it would be non-eternal.
(3517) Thus, [it is] "devoted to this."
To the question, "How is it that one intent on establishing an omniscient being cannot be found? he says: "And if eternal," and so forth.

If this scripture intent on establishing an omniscient being were eternal, then it would necessarily be of the nature of an *arthavāda*; its purpose must be seen as something other [than the literal].
Now, if its status as an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) is not accepted, then by necessity, its impermanence would follow.
Why, however, does its status as an explanatory statement follow if it were permanent? To this he says: "And of the scripture," and so forth.
And since the eternity of the scripture is established, the postulation of that [creator] is useless,
because from it people will understand dharma itself.
"The postulation of that" means...
He asks why the conception of an omniscient being is in vain, and says "since," etc.,
and then "therefore."
He refutes [the objection] with the words "Certainly not" (na khalu) and so forth, based on the eternal scripture (nityād āgamāt).
Indeed, even though this Veda is well-known, it possesses no eternity;
for its fruit consists of cognitions that arise immediately after effort and cognitions that occur in a temporal sequence.
However, this is so provided that the authority of this well-known [Veda] is accepted.
"Since it is also a Veda, its authority would follow even for other recensions (śākhāntara). [Objection:
Although this Veda consisting of the Ṛgveda and so forth is extremely well-known in its own form, nevertheless its eternity is unproven.
To the question 'How so?', he says: 'yat... (Verse 3520)

In the sense of "because," whatever cognition arises immediately after an effort, or whatever is the fruit of sequential cognition, is impermanent—just like a jar or similar objects—and the Veda is likewise; thus, this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).
Furthermore, its lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) and other such defects have been refuted in detail in the *Śrutiparīkṣā*, and so they are not stated here.
"Of this" means of the Veda.

If it is argued that the status of other Vedic branches as "Veda" is unestablished, he says: "That which is to be made known," and so forth; namely, that the non-Vedic status [of those branches] must certainly be demonstrated by you through reasoning.
Otherwise, for you, the fact that he is not mentioned in the Śruti would be doubtful.
(3521) "Otherwise" means:

if it were not made known that he is not [mentioned] in the Veda, then that non-mention of the Omniscient One in the Śruti—the Veda—which was asserted by you, would be doubtful and unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*).
Regarding what was said—that "impermanence would follow if it were for that purpose"—he says: "And let there be permanence," and so forth;
let there be both the permanence of the Veda and its being for that purpose therein.

"If that were the case, why would there not be impermanence? Because of the connection with the meaning of 'perishing' (nāśya). Being thus questioned, the opponent replies: "Because of the connection with the meaning of 'perishing'"; that is, because of the connection—that is, the relationship—with a perishing object, impermanence necessarily follows.
With the words "If it is so," and so forth, he demonstrates the lack of exclusivity (anaikāntikatva):
"If it is so, then [substances such as] clarified butter, wild rice, gold, matted hair, and so on..."
How can things be called impermanent while existing as that permanent self?
Ājya is clarified butter;
nīvāra is a specific type of grain.
"Cāmīkarajaṭa" refers to Agni;
"by him" means by that Veda.
With the words "jāti" (universal) and so forth, [the author] anticipates the opponent's reply: "If the universal there too is eternal, then that too has already been refuted."
If speech were to denote only that [individual object], then the understanding of clarified butter and so forth would not arise from it.
Even if it were to denote that as well, why would the eternality of speech not be lost?
Alternatively, let there be a universal (ākṛti) even in the case of the Omniscient One; therefore, its eternality consists in being directed toward that [universal].

In that regard, [the opponent argues that] a universal (jāti) exists in things such as clarified butter (*ājya*), and since that is what is denoted by the word, there will be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This is incorrect,
because the universal has already been refuted in detail during the examination of the universal (*sāmānyaparīkṣā*).

Or, let it be that there is a universal (*jāti*); nevertheless, from words such as "clarified butter" (*ājya*) which denote the universal alone, no cognition of the individual (*vyakti*) would result.
Consequently, for one who seeks the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) to be accomplished by the individual, the denotation of the universal would be entirely useless.
If it is argued that the individual is cognized by way of necessary concomitance (*nāntarīyakatayā*), [we reply:]...
It is not so,
because there is no remoteness from cognition;

for it is not the case that immediately after the word [is heard], the cognition arises first with respect to the universal, and only afterwards does the cognition of the individual arise through its necessary concomitance.
What then?

In the world, a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of objects that perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) arises from words precisely without any intervention; and it is solely with the desire to communicate those [objects] that one employs words.
Therefore, it is not logical to say that the cognition of an individual does not arise from the word;
for if the word denoted only the universal (jāti) and not the individual,
then, perceiving that it expresses something unrelated— just like an injunction to milk a bull— a discerning person would certainly not act toward the individual based on the word.

Now, if it is accepted that the word denotes that manifested form (*abhivyakti-rūpa*) so as to avoid this undesirable consequence (*doṣaprasaṅga*), then how does the loss of the eternity of the Veda not follow?

Furthermore, even if it were granted that words primarily denote the universal (*jāti*) and that the denotation of its individual manifestation (*vyakti*) follows as a necessary concomitant (*nāntarīyaka*), nevertheless, he shows that the eternity of the entire scripture—even if it were [composed by] an omniscient being—is not contradicted: "Even in the case of an omniscient one," and so forth.

For even in the case of a single omniscient being, it is logically consistent that he may be denoted by a generic term due to the multiplicity imagined through the distinction of his various states; how much more so, then, in the case of an immeasurable succession of beginningless omniscient beings?

Furthermore, even if you do not accept the branch known as the *Nimitta* as being of the nature of Veda, he says "And then," etc., showing that by this very [argument] the fact of its not being stated in the Śruti remains doubtful: "And then, the determination of the meaning of Vedic sentences would occur independently, from the Veda itself or from another, for one whose mind is overcome by delusion and the like. (3526)

Regarding the Vedic injunction, "One desiring heaven should offer the Agnihotra," what is the authority for the claim that the Jina is omniscient? For since the Vedic sentences are eternal and independent, no certain determination of the Vedic meaning arises from them; indeed, this Veda does not cry out, "This is my meaning and not another."

Nor does the ascertainment of the meaning arise for the understander either from himself—that is, from his own self—or from another, namely the expounder; for according to your own view, all people are corrupted by delusion and other defects.
Therefore, even this meaning—"the Blessed One is omniscient" [is derived] from the sentence concerning the *agnihotra* and so forth—is indeed possible; what proof (*pramā*) is there for it?
Not at all; there is none whatsoever.
Regarding what was further stated—that it is impossible for there to be a correspondence between all human cognitions and their objects—he replies:
"Because of the clear teaching of heaven and liberation alone, he is understood to be omniscient due to his thorough knowledge of the primary purpose. (3528)
Of what use is the cognition of a number equal to the grains of sand in the ocean?
Therefore, what is the point for us in the experience of that cognition of an object other than this [present one]?
(3529) As for what was said—that it must be stated as being figurative—he replies with the verse beginning "gauṇatvena" (figuratively).
Even he must be described as speaking only in a figurative sense, because he is like one who knows the meaning of mantras and arthavādas;
thus this rule would be established once the omniscient being has been refuted,
provided that the absence of the previously mentioned subverting arguments has been demonstrated in detail.
The restriction to a secondary sense is doubtful, because the primary meaning is also possible.

(3531) For if an omniscient being were refuted by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then, due to the impossibility of any other [explanation], this [scripture] would necessarily have a secondary meaning; but it is not so, because the primary meaning is also conceivable. Furthermore, it is not logical for an eternal word to be an explanatory eulogy (*arthavāda*), for an eulogy consists of a teaching intended with a specific purpose; and that is not possible in the case of a word devoid of intention, since there is no speaker's intent (*vivakṣā*) [in an eternal word].
Alternatively, regarding the passage beginning with "from the knowledge of the dharmas and so forth under discussion," he says: "dharmādi... and so on.

If the non-obstruction consisting solely of the knowledge whose objects are phenomena (*dharma*) and so forth is described as being accompanied by its fruit, then it is evident that the world has been conquered by the Buddhas.
To explain how it was conquered, he says: "Because," and so forth.

Because it was previously established that, regarding both worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and liberation (*mokṣa*), their unimpeded knowledge together with these [other qualities] is unique and extremely clear;

for since the Blessed One’s unimpeded knowledge of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) has already been proven, his knowledge of dharma and so forth is indeed unique and uncommon to him alone. Thus, by his own words, he would not fail to be accepted as omniscient.

Regarding what was said— "or rather, consciousness [resides] in the self alone"— he says "And that which is consciousness in the self alone," etc., demonstrating that even in that case, since such knowledge is possible only in the Blessed One, nothing undesirable has been established: "And that which is consciousness in the self alone, set in motion by the practice of meditation."
Its non-obstructiveness has also been established by you previously.
"Of that too" refers to self-cognition (*ātmajñāna*).
"Of them" refers to those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones;
"previously" means...
"However much the flood of qualities [resides] in her," and so forth;
but surely, self-knowledge (*ātmajñāna*) was described there as being of the nature of self-awareness (*svavedanā*).
But there is no cognition of an internal active person (puruṣa); how then could there be the fallacy of proving what is already established? To this he says: "For this very thing," and so forth.

For this very thing is that cognition, namely, the vision of the pure self, because it consists in the realization of mere mind (cittamātra) from which adventitious stains have been removed. || 3535 ||
If it is asked how it is established that there is only the experience of consciousness alone, he says: "Unknowable," and so forth.

It has been previously established that cognition has neither the form of the known nor the knower; and that [cognition], devoid of the duality of [subject and object], has been revealed by the Perfectly Awakened Ones. || 3536 ||

By that [means], those of great intelligence became perfected ones (siddhas) possessing knowledge unaccustomed to cyclic existence (saṃsāra); for even today, their teachings shine forth as if presiding over it.
Thus, "previously."
In the examination of external objects,
those for whom cognition is unsuitable and unfavorable to cyclic existence are described as such.
What, then, are those teachings heard to exist through its sovereignty? He says: "By nature luminous," and so forth—"in the mind which is by nature luminous and unstained by the forms of duality."
Who, whose self is not deluded regarding the two aspects, would have a contrary view?

(3538) And when there is the awakening to the selflessness of both, the defects such as attachment and aversion—which arise from conceptual constructions of women and so forth—are completely exhausted without effort. (3539)
This is that supreme reality which the teacher of truth has proclaimed;
it bestows all prosperity and is beyond the reach of Keśava and others,
for its nature is not deluded by the two forms.
The abandonment of the adherence to the grasped and the grasper is the awakening to the selflessness of both [person and phenomena]; thus,
it refers to the awakening to the selflessness of persons and phenomena.

Alternatively—the analysis of the compound is as follows: "duality" refers to the apprehended object and the apprehending subject; its "selflessness" (nairātmya) means its lack of intrinsic nature (naiḥsvābhāvya).
It is "beyond the range of Keśava and others": here, Keśava is Hari, and by the word "others" (ādi), Īśvara and so forth are included.
Now, [the author] asks: why is a pure vision of the self not accepted even by Keśava and others? He says: "For it is known," and so forth.
"For a stable self, resembling a pure crystal, is indeed known by others; yet that [knowledge] of theirs is an error, because of the refutation of a permanent self. (3541)

If a consciousness that grasps a self were to arise from a self, then it would follow that all consciousnesses of every self would arise simultaneously. Or else, if it were not to arise from that [self], then [the self] must be admitted to be eternal.
Then that [cognition] would not have that as its object, just like the mind of another person;
"by others" refers to Keśava and so forth.

Since the self has been refuted in the "Examination of the Self," knowledge regarding it is impure because it is erroneous. Furthermore, as for this knowledge regarding an eternal self that is described by them, does it arise from that self or not? There are these two alternatives. In the first case, all knowledge regarding that object would arise simultaneously, since its cause would be unimpaired. If, however, it is the second case, then that [knowledge] must be either eternal or non-eternal;
in either instance, because it would be dependent upon that self, it could not have that as its object, just like [the cognition of] another's mind.

Regarding what was stated—that "this alone is that knowledge which is the vision of the pure self"—he replies with the verse beginning "grāhya" and so forth: "This alone is not that knowledge, namely, this vision of the pure self," because it is devoid of the characteristics of an object of cognition (*grāhya*), as has been established in detail. (3544)
Furthermore, even if the self is admitted to be of the nature of cognition,
there would still be no apprehension [of itself] because of the existence of a distinction between the seen and the seer (3545).
If it is maintained that this cognition possesses the nature of self-luminosity, [the following applies]:
In that case, self-awareness would be attained and cognition would become perceptual.

(3546) If, first of all, the self is accepted as being insentient (*jaḍa*) by nature, then the knowledge regarding it would be entirely impure; for it has been established in the *Bahirarthaparīkṣā* that, by their very nature, all cognitions are devoid of the distinction between the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*).

Alternatively, if the position is taken that the self is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), even then—since there is no difference between the seen and the seeing—the relation of apprehended and apprehender is untenable, and thus there could be no such thing as "knowledge regarding that [self]. For the relation of object and subject can only exist when there is a distinction between the object and the subject.

Now, if it is accepted that this [cognition] has itself as its object because it possesses luminosity like a lamp, then there would follow the undesirable consequence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*), and the intended non-perceptibility of cognition would be contradicted;
he demonstrates this by saying: "And the cognition would be perceptible" (verse 3544).
Regarding what was stated— "Moreover, because [the Veda] has the Veda as its body," and so forth— he says in response: "And of Brahmā and the others," and so forth.
Furthermore, there is no connection whatsoever between Brahmā and the others and the Veda,

because of their difference, their eternity, and their lack of mutual dependence, just like anything else. Consequently, the claim that Brahmā and the others have the Veda as their body is inconsistent.
Furthermore, the Veda cannot consist of omniscience because its meaning is not definitively ascertained.
Moreover, it has been established that the Perfectly Awakened One (Buddha) is omniscient through his own independent authority;
he is not postulated as such on the grounds of being the "body" of the Veda, like Brahmā and others.
Only if a relationship existed would Brahmā and the others possess the Vedas as their body; however, no such relationship exists between the Vedas and Brahmā and the rest.

For it has been established that the relationship between entities is of only two kinds, characterized by identity (*tādātmya*) or origination from that (*tadutpatti*). In this case, because their difference is admitted, there is no relationship of identity;
nor is there a relationship of origination, since both are eternal and, being incapable of being assisted, lack any mutual dependence.
The connection with the subject at hand is that it is inconsistent to claim that the Veda consists of omniscience;
why?

Because the meaning is not certain, it is only when the meaning is definitively ascertained that it is appropriate to postulate that the Veda consists of omniscience; however, it has already been demonstrated that such ascertainment is impossible according to your own view.
Furthermore, unlike you, we do not accept an omniscient being by means of the Veda.
What then?
It has been established that because his knowledge is self-arisen, the Blessed One himself is omniscient.
And as for what was said: "In some places, the Buddhas and others are mortal."
In this regard, demonstrating that the Blessed One’s being mortal is unestablished, he says: "Five," and so forth.

Because they exist outside the cycle of existence consisting of the five destinies, mortality is not asserted by us for the Buddhas; rather, their manifestation is considered to be such [a manifestation]. (3550)

Cyclic existence consists of five realms, distinguished as hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, gods, and humans; and since the Blessed Ones are outside of those [realms], their mortality is unestablished.
If so, how is it that their birth in families such as that of Śuddhodana is heard of? To this he says: "Their emanation is considered to be such. (3550)
Corroborating this very point with scripture, he says: "In the delightful city of Akaniṣṭha," and so forth:
"The perfectly awakened ones awaken there in the delightful city of Akaniṣṭha, which is devoid of the Śuddhāvāsa [heavens]; however, it is an emanation that awakens here. (3551)

There are gods named Akaniṣṭha; in one part of their realm are the gods named Śuddhāvāsakāyika, for here only the pure noble ones (ārya) dwell. Above them is the place called Māheśvarabhavana, where only Bodhisattvas who are in their final existence and established on the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are born.

If it is argued that this is not established for us because the scripture states, "But here, such a manifestation is perceived through its sovereign power," he replies with the words beginning "by its own independence" (*svātantryeṇa*).
But how can you determine their mortality independently?
It cannot be so through the scriptures of others, for that [scriptural authority] is not established in such a way.
Nor do we assert that they are omniscient out of rivalry with them.
Who indeed would conceive a rivalry between sky-flowers and real things?

(3553) For if you were to assert mortality independently, then it would be "unproven due to doubt," because you possess no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the Lord's mortality, by which his mortality could be established as independent; therefore, you must state his mortality by means of another person’s scripture (*āgama*).
And since that scripture of another stands in the form just described, their mortality is unestablished.
How is it established that these [entities] are like flowers in the sky? He says: "By the absence of all causal power," and so forth.
For it has been proven that eternal things lack any form due to their separation from all causal power; therefore, the Śiva (Tryambaka) and others postulated by our opponents do not exist. (3554)
For Śaṅkara and others are asserted by opponents to be eternal;

and since it has been established that for eternal things there is a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—whether occurring successively or simultaneously—and that the absence of all capacity is the defining characteristic of non-existence, it follows that the three-eyed Lord (Śiva) and others, as intended by the opponents, do not exist at all. Thus, their resemblance to a flower in the sky is indeed proven.
Tryambaka (Śiva)—3554. Furthermore:

"Let Tryambaka and the others indeed exist; nevertheless, because they are so utterly inferior, we do not engage in rivalry with those Blessed Ones. Demonstrating this, he says: "Furthermore," and so forth.
Furthermore, their cognition is inverted due to the view of a self and so forth, whereas that of the Buddhas is non-inverted; this has been established in detail.
Therefore, no rivalry is undertaken with them, because of the vast difference between them.
For who indeed would compete with those suffering from cataracts against a man with healthy vision? (3556) [This is easily understood.

Regarding what was said— that even though the scripture is eternal, it is called the "Veda"— he says in response: "The qualities, actions, the Lord, and so forth, as well as the Vedas, have been cast aside," and so on.
And for this reason, we do not accept that scripture is eternal.
Since the momentary destruction (kṣaṇabhaṅga) pervading all things has been established, nothing whatsoever possesses eternity; thus, all of this that was stated is incoherent.
Regarding what was stated—"one who is similar to an omniscient being," and so forth—he replies: "By means of analogy," and so on.

"The existence of an omniscient being is not established by means of analogy, because it has been declared that analogy is not a valid means of knowledge; therefore, its existence is not established thereby. (3558)
For when existence is already established, similarity is understood; therefore, this proof concerns the existence of the omniscient one.
Thus, there is no establishment [of the subject] through analogy, and the negation [of it] is fruitless.
If you have seen that all men are non-omniscient,

then omniscience would belong to you alone, because of your vision of what is distant and concealed, and because of your perception of the capacity for knowledge connected to the mental continua of others.
For analogy (upamāna) possesses no status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by which a Buddhist might desire to establish the existence of an omniscient being from it;
or, even if it were a valid means of cognition, it would be of no use for establishing his existence.
This is because, when a subject (*dharmin*) such as a cow is already well-known, analogy establishes only its similarity to a gavaya or the like.
Furthermore, the subject (*dharmin*) "the omniscient one" is not established, because according to your own view, that very person is what remains to be proven.

Thus, when the existence of an omniscient being is under discussion as the probandum according to your own position, there is no possibility for an analogy to apply; therefore, its refutation is pointless. The underlying sense is that a negation must be preceded by an attainment (*prāpti*), and since there is no such attainment [of the subject], the negation is invalid.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Having seen men, however, as non-omniscient," he says: "If all men have indeed been seen by you as non-omniscient," and so forth.

For if all men whatsoever were seen by you, then there would be a contradiction of your own words in the negation of an omniscient being. To explain: by admitting the perception of all men, even those who are distant or hidden, and by admitting the ascertainment of the power of cognition belonging to other mental continua, one would clearly have admitted omniscience in oneself; for this involves the admission of perceiving objects that are remote in space, time, and nature.
For such thorough knowledge is not possible for one who is not omniscient;

and since a proof is employed to negate that [omniscience], that very [proof] is thereby negated, which constitutes a contradiction of one's own words (svavacanavyāghāta), just as [to say] "my mother is barren.
Showing that the reason is unestablished (*asiddhatā*), he says: "Even when a person stands before you... and so forth.

"Even when a person stands before you, how could you have the certain conviction, 'This one is not omniscient,' given that you yourself are a knower of things beyond the senses (*atīndriyavid*)? (3562)

If one maintains that the self is not omniscient while being certain that all others are not omniscient, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because even [the self] such as Aja and others would be determined to be omniscient. If it is argued that this is not so because no sublation is observed, then the determination of all phenomena (*sarvadharmas*) must be accepted.
[Objection: But surely, even if [the reason] has been stated, the apprehension of sublation does not differ from the actual observation of sublation.

To explain: when a person is standing before one, it is impossible for a non-omniscient person to ascertain with certainty that "this man is not omniscient" based merely on seeing his body; how much more so, then, in the case of a person situated in another place and time?

If one accepts the certainty that "this [person] is not omniscient" so that the reason (hetu) may not be unestablished (*asiddha*), and thereby accepts the certainty that all others are not omniscient by means of one's own non-omniscience, then, demonstrating that this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) and thus results in the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), he says: "In the perception of one's own non-omniscience," and so forth.
The grammatical analysis (*vigraha*) is: "the perception of non-omniscience in oneself."
It might be argued that while the proof of all phenomena is being established, it is subverted by perceived differences such as [variations in] wisdom; therefore, its proof is not undertaken.
However, since the omniscience of reality (*tattvasarvajñatva*) being established is not subverted by anything, there will be no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
This is incorrect.

Just as a reason does not prove a probandum that is sublated by what is actually perceived, so too it does not prove one where sublation is merely suspected; therefore, the suspicion of sublation is not distinct from the actual perception of sublation. Consequently, even the proof of non-omniscience should not be undertaken, because its sublation is suspected.

Regarding what was said—that the teaching of the Buddha and others is possible even otherwise—he says: "Who else, out of dullness or delusion, would deny that faultless [teaching] of the Buddhas concerning the path to heaven and liberation, which has been established as such? (3565)
The claim that the teaching is based on something other [than direct knowledge] is unproven;

for an irreproachable teaching regarding the path to heaven and liberation cannot arise from delusion. Furthermore, the irreproachable nature of the Blessed One’s word has been established by all forms of investigation as being distinct from that of the insentient.
The meaning is that, at most, he considers him to be no more than Kumārila.
Regarding the phrase "or for the purpose of deluding the disciples," he says: "Even when [the results] are seen," and so forth.
"Even when [the results] are seen—namely, prosperity and likewise the supreme pacification of mental defects—for those who obtain these through it, a supreme delusion has been created by him. (3566)
"Seen" means that in this very life there is prosperity, characterized by such things as permanence, health, and sovereignty.
The connection is with the phrase "attaining";
and "the pacification of defects" refers to the subsiding of defects such as passion and the like.

Then—this is a hyperbolic statement (atiśayokti) meaning that a supreme delusion was produced for the disciples who were attaining [the goal] through the instruction on the rules of mantra and meditation and through their performance of the prescribed practices;
if you consider such a delusion to be [genuine], then you yourself would be deluded, perceiving what is actually non-delusion as delusion. 3566

If it is argued that this [teaching] must have the Veda as its source, he says in response: "And this teaching of the Buddhas does not have the Veda as its source; for that which has been proclaimed by them is stainless, whereas in the Śruti (Veda), it is stained. (3567)
For it is not logical that a stainless instruction should have its source in something stained;
therefore, regarding the phrase "to the foolish and the Śūdras," he says: "for the sake of their own goal's accomplishment," and so forth.
Their instruction is not of such a kind for the sake of accomplishing their own interests;
rather, this entire undertaking is of such a nature as to act for the benefit of others.
Therefore, they are compassionate by nature and consecrated to bestowing welfare upon the world.
Because it is a kinsman that is not bound [by worldly ties], they say that state exists in all things.
(3569) The term "state" (*pada*) refers to the path to higher rebirth and the supreme good, in the sense of being the foundation for the perfection of all virtues.

He shows that it is possible for those very [authors] such as Manu and others— who provided instruction solely to the proponents of the Vedas— to have done so for the sake of deluding them, by stating "those who," and so forth.

For the teaching of those who are under the sway of greed, fear, hatred, envy, and the like, and who are devoid of compassion, would be partial; however, the fact that the Blessed Ones’ teaching extends even to children demonstrates that it manifests their very greatness. This is shown by the verse beginning with "compassion" (karuṇā).
But those who are bound by compassion, who clearly perceive the truth, and who are free from fear regarding all refutations, have given teachings everywhere.
And to whatever extent a person may be corrupted by defects such as ignorance, [they teach accordingly].
In that very same way, compassion proceeds toward those protectors.
The arrival of a married woman at her husband’s house is called *āvāha*.
To the question "What is that song? he says: "In one endowed with knowledge and conduct, in a Brāhmaṇa, in a cow, in an elephant... and so forth.
"The wise perceive equality even between a dog and an outcaste.

Moreover, by you yourself, speaking so loudly and manifestly to fools and Śūdras with a mind arrogant from pride in a false birth, your own great folly has been most clearly revealed here in this assembly of learned men.

For instance: Do your honors, the Brahmins, carry a swelling mass of pride by postulating that there exists some other distinct entity called the universal (sāmānya) known as "Brahminhood"? Or do you do so by observing that your own selves have been consecrated by rites such as the *jātakarman*? Or by relying on the fact that you were born from the womb of a Brahmin woman by a Brahmin father? Regarding these, [the author] shows that in the first case, this is merely a decoration of a sky-lotus, by saying "in hundreds" and so forth: "When the caste has been refuted in hundreds of ways, what is the point of pride in caste? (1.95)
If no excellence superior to that [of others] is established, why is it considered "distinguished"?

(3575) All [beings], being the substrata of qualities such as mastery (*vaśitva*) and having all defilements entirely destroyed, are without distinction in this regard; and if they were joined with that [excellence], they would belong to a different genus. (3576)
If they were to become perfected, then those depending upon them would likewise become distinguished;
otherwise, there would be no distinction at all, as in the case of the hunter and the twice-born.

Furthermore, even if that genus (jāti) were to exist, your pride might be justified only if a distinction produced by it were perceived in its substratum; however, we do not perceive any such excellence. This is shown in the passage beginning with "tadanya... and so forth.

The analysis of the compound is as follows: *tadanya* means "other than those Brāhmaṇas," referring to others such as Śūdras; *atiśaya* means "excellence"; thus, *tadanyātiśaya-asiddhiḥ* means "the non-establishment of excellence over those others.

For instance, we do not perceive any superiority of Brāhmaṇas over Śūdras and the like, whether in terms of wisdom, intelligence, and so forth, or in terms of excrement, urine, flesh, blood, and so forth. Therefore, since such excellence is unestablished, how can that caste (*jāti*) which is supposed to be the substratum of that excellence be distinguished, such that you—who are puffed up with the arrogance of the doctrine of caste—should speak thus: "They would grant it [the Veda] only to the proponents of the Vedas, just as Manu and others did"?

If, however, by virtue of belonging to the Brahmin caste, you were by your very nature the bearers of a multitude of qualities such as self-mastery, sovereignty, the power of irresistible will, and compassion, and were free from all remaining faults, then your distinction would be established; otherwise, how could your distinction be proven, given that even though the connection with the Brahmin caste exists, it is like that of a Brahmin who is a hunter, a fisherman, or a leather-worker?
Regarding the second position as well, he states the fault: "The birth-rites and so forth," etc.;
those which are well-known as the birth-rites and so forth are like other things distinct from that [the self].

For those conventional practices occur even in the case of artificial [beings], just as they do in the case of those who are considered Brāhmaṇas by convention but are otherwise [different]. (3578) Thus, it is "like the others."
Regarding the term "conventional" (*sāṃvṛta*), it refers to those things that exist for the sake of worldly transaction (*sāṃvyavahārika*), such as the act of giving a name and so forth.

Even in this third position, intoxication is not logical; for it has already been stated that there is no distinction whatsoever between the bodies of Brahmins and Brahmin women and the bodies of Śūdras and others, insofar as they are all composed of impurities such as semen and blood.

Furthermore, since even your status as having a Brahmin for a father is itself doubtful, pride is likewise unjustified; demonstrating this, he says: "The past time has been vast, and women are exceedingly fickle," and so forth.
Therefore, even in that case, it is impossible to ascertain Brahminhood.
For among you there is no one who knows supersensuous objects,
nor has even the eternal Veda declared the purity of your lineage.
It is even possible that after some time, one who was not born of a Brahmin lineage might become a Brahmin by birth;
yet, despite your prior status as a Brahmin, it is also quite conceivable that you were born of adultery due to the moral transgression of your mother.
For it is generally observed that women, afflicted by passion and fickle-minded, act in ways that overstep the boundaries of their family’s vows.
Furthermore, you do not accept any person who perceives supersensuous objects, from whom certainty might arise;
nor does the Veda proclaim the purity of your lineage.

Furthermore— not only is the pride of birth unjustified for you, who have not ascertained your own Brahminhood, but moreover, it shows that even Manu and others, being ignorant of [the true status of] the twice-born, gave instruction to those very twice-born out of delusion— starting with the words "Therefore," etc.: "Therefore, Manu and others were also unaware of their [true] twice-born status."
They would not grant instruction to those twice-born men because of the uncertainty regarding them;
"those for whom the twice-born status is unknown and undetermined" is what is meant by that expression,
and [the reason is] "because of that uncertainty."
Because those twice-born ones lack certainty (3581).

Furthermore, he says "the absence of reasoning," etc., demonstrating that the fact that Manu and others gave instruction to us alone is not a cause for your greatness; rather, it indicates nothing but their own dullness.

"Because they lack logical reasoning, because they are incapable of making the meaning of the Vedas known, and because these Brahmins—stunned by the mere recitation of the Vedas—are unable to withstand critical examination;
for this reason, I suspect that Manu and the others must certainly have ascertained [the truth] from some other source. (3582)
The instruction of the Vedas and so forth was indeed imparted by them to the Brahmins.
"Those made dull by the study of the Vedas" means those who have become dull-witted (*jaḍa*) as a result of studying the Vedas (*vedādhīti*).
This means that their capacity to understand reality has been distanced by the study of the Vedas;
"from some cause" refers to this reason.

Therefore, having understood that the Vedas and other such texts lack logical consistency, [the author] shows that Manu and others declared their own words to be established by authoritative injunction (*ājñāsiddha*) in the passage beginning with "The Purāṇa," and so forth.
The Purāṇas, the Dharma of Manu, the Veda with its auxiliary limbs, and medical science—these four are established by authoritative injunction; they are not to be undermined by mere reasoning.
I believe that it was for this very reason that those [wise ones] offered this threat of intimidation against the dull-witted.

How else could there be the status of being established by authoritative command (*ājñāsiddhatva*) for the scripture known as the *Purāṇa* or the "Dharma of Manu" (*mānava-dharma*), other than through mere words? (3585)
"Composed by Manu with its ancillaries" means that it exists together with the six ancillaries (aṅgas), such as grammar and the rest; thus, it is "with its ancillaries" (sāṅga).
"Cikitsitam" refers to the science of medicine;
[it is taught] by that very [science].
This means that you have determined the lack of logical justification for these Purāṇas and other texts, as well as the dullness of yourselves.
3585. "By those," and so forth;
by those who, moreover, have clearly ascertained the logical consistency of their own statements.

The great-souled ones, having thus dispelled all fear, roar their lion’s roar— which brings about the exhaustion of the rut of the intoxicated elephants that are the false teachers— and which possesses the power to convince others and to demonstrate their own [mastery]. (3586–3587)
"Kutīrthyāḥ" refers to the false teachers who are like intoxicated elephants; "siṃhanāda" is that whose nature it is to effect the exhaustion of their intoxication;
"evam" refers to what is about to be stated.
What, then, is this "lion’s roar"? To this he says: "From heat," and so forth.
"O monks, my words should be accepted by the wise after they have examined them—like gold through heating, cutting, and rubbing on a touchstone—and not out of reverence.

Furthermore, he says "And those who... and so forth, to show that it was the Blessed Ones themselves, and not Manu and others, who provided instruction to those who are Brahmins in the ultimate sense.

And those who, because they have cast off evil, are Brahmins in the ultimate sense— having practiced the stainless selflessness [of phenomena]— are found only in the teaching of the Sage. For this reason, the ascetic (śramaṇa) is proclaimed here to be of four kinds.

Indeed, the doctrines of others are empty of true ascetics and brahmins. For the etymological derivation of "brahmin" is "one who has cast out evil qualities" (*vāhitapāpadharma*); and it is only here, within the teaching of the Blessed Sage, that they are truly so, because of the instruction on the practice of selflessness (*nairātmya*), and not elsewhere, due to the absence of the means for the destruction of evil.

Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Right here is the ascetic (śramaṇa), right here is the brahmin; the doctrines of others are empty of ascetics and brahmins. In this context, there are four types of ascetics who abide in the fruits, beginning with the stream-enterer (srotāpanna) and so forth; likewise, there are exactly four types of brahmins who are candidates (pratipannaka) for those same states.
Regarding the passage beginning with "There is a person who is angry" (3589–3590), he says: "A person," and so forth.

It has been established that even such statements as "Is there some man who is omniscient? are not valid proofs, because they are marred by the fault of being deficient in their thesis (*pratijñānyūnatā*). To which specific passage this was established, he says: "niḥśeṣārtha... and so forth.
"For even when the means for the thorough knowledge of all objects is fruitless, the wise followers of the Sugata exert themselves," as was stated previously [in verse 3592].
Furthermore, we do not establish the existence of an omniscient being by first understanding that he is the speaker of [the teachings] and then subsequently practicing them.
What then?
For those who desire to attain the state of omniscience, the destruction of faults is established for the sake of that [attainment] and for the excellence of qualities;

for it is by means of inference functioning through the power of real entities (*vastubalapravṛttānumāna*) alone that the followers of the Sugata apply themselves toward human goals, and not by mere report.
Furthermore, it has already been demonstrated how properties such as "knowability" (prameyatva) can function as a means of proof (sādhana).
As for what you said—that [the Buddha] is "one who has reached the ten stages" (daśabhūmigata)—that too was stated by you without understanding our established doctrine (siddhānta);
for the Blessed One is not held to have merely reached the ten stages.
What then?
It is held that up until the stage of a bodhisattva—that is, through the ten stages—and beyond that, it is the stage of a Buddha.

As for what was said—that "what is sung by one who knows only a portion cannot be the speech of an omniscient being"—showing that this too has already been refuted, he says: "But [the claim] that 'what is sung by one who knows only a portion cannot be the speech of an omniscient being' has also been previously stated [to be invalid] because of its connection with the knowledge of the omniscient. (3593)
Explaining this very point once again, he says: "Just as," and so forth:
"Just as one of limited vision, having experienced objects such as sacrifices and the like, subsequently projects them onto the mind and speaks of them based on that experience. (3594)
And that statement of his does not arise from knowledge of that object;
otherwise, the word of an omniscient being would be the same. However, it differs because of a difference in its cause. [Verse 3595] "One of limited vision," etc.
"One who has limited vision" means one who is not omniscient;

"the arising of the cognition of that object" refers to the cognition or experience of that object such as heat, and the statement whose origin or production (*janma*) arises from that cognition of the object is described as such.
By means of the double negation "not not," he shows that it is indeed the arising of the cognition of that object;
thus,
even that [negation] is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of being the arising of the cognition of that object.
If this is so, what is the distinction between the word of the Buddha and the words of those of limited vision? To this he says: "But it differs because of the difference in its cause.
He clarifies this very point with the verse beginning "samasta" and so forth:
"The cognition of all things has become the cause for this [omniscience], whereas the cognition of even a mere portion of an object remains its [ordinary] instrumental cause. (3596)
"Of this" refers to the word of the Buddha;
"but of that" refers to [the following].
With the words "vikalpa" and so forth, [the author] addresses the objection raised by another regarding the statement of one who knows only a portion [of the truth].
If conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is impossible for him, what kind of intention to speak (*vivakṣā*) could he possibly have?
For, because his conduct has been abandoned, conceptual construction does not occur for him.
Indeed, an intention to speak is impossible for one in whom conceptual construction is non-existent, since that [intention] is a specific form of conceptual construction.

Therefore, being pervaded by conceptual construction, how could it [the mind] exist in the absence of that [conceptual construction]? For there is no possibility of a *śiṃśapā* tree in the absence of trees,
and there is no possibility of conceptual construction for the Omniscient One, because he has abandoned all obscurations such as the afflictions and the cognitive veils.
Since conceptualization (*kalpa*) and non-conceptualization (*avikalpa*) are by nature erroneous, it would follow that an omniscient one is erroneous when those two are active. (3597)

He refutes this with the words "not so" and so forth: "It is not so; for his volition is not afflicted, since he possesses no obscuration or exhaustion [of merit]; but who can prevent that which is wholesome and conducive to the welfare of the world? (3598)

For conceptual construction (vikalpa) is of two kinds: it is afflicted (kliṣṭa) by virtue of being conducive to defilement and so forth, and it is wholesome (kuśala) by virtue of being associated with and originated from non-attachment and so forth.
Among these, that which is afflicted does not exist at all for those who have abandoned the obscurations of the afflictions and so forth, due to the absence of its cause.

However, that which is wholesome is not incompatible even with one who has abandoned the obscurations. Therefore, by whom can that wholesome conceptualization—which is set in motion by the Blessed Ones through the practice of compassion and is conducive to the arising of the welfare of the world—be prevented from becoming manifest? (3598) One might object: "Since every conceptualization is by its very nature erroneous, because it proceeds by determining its own appearance—which is not an actual object—to be an actual object, the manifestation of such [conceptualization] is indeed contradictory for one who has abandoned the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Anticipating this, he says: "And not of that," and so forth.
Nor does he determine that conceptual construction to possess a real object;
for he knows it to be without a basis, being like a magician.
Just as a magician perceives a clearly determined object such as a horse [created by his art], yet knows it to be unreal... [3599]...so too is this person.
He knows that the mind is without an object; therefore, he does not become deluded.

For if he were to grasp that conceptual construction—which is itself objectless—as having an object, then he would be deluded. However, like a magician, he understands it precisely as being the object of that very cognition; so how could he be deluded?

Regarding what was stated [in verse 3600], namely, "But that which is being proclaimed, beginning with 'it,' shines among those who have faith," he says in response: "beginning with 'it'... [and so on]. That is to say:
"But that which is being proclaimed, beginning with 'it,' shines among those who have faith."
"This was not stated by the twice-born in accordance with the subject at hand.
How so? What is that subject at hand? He says that this [statement] is not in accordance with it: 'And likewise, being uncomprehending of all objects, he is not capable of teaching. (3601)
This is indeed the subject under discussion here; regarding that, the great-minded ones have said:
"If there were no capacity for its instruction, what would happen then? Consequently, you must state that there would be no scripture (āgama). (3602–3603)
Regarding this, they say: "Let it be so; have you actually seen him speaking?
If [you say] this undesirable consequence is urged by means of a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum), then if speakerhood were not admitted, there would be no acceptance of the scriptures (*āgama*)."
"But if you accept the scriptures composed by him, then his status as their speaker must be accepted.

Thinking that the opponent will state this very point of his own accord—that "this which I have stated is a *prasaṅga*-proof (*prasaṅgasādhana*) and not an independent argument" (*svātantryeṇa*)—the author first establishes that this present matter is indeed a *prasaṅga*-proof, saying: "And in that regard, they say," and so forth.

Regarding what you have stated—that there would be no capacity for teaching that which is excluded from all objects—we must first ask you: "Let us grant that it has no capacity for teaching; what fault follows from this? Having been asked thus, the opponent himself reveals his answer with the words beginning with "tataḥ" (therefore).

To this it is replied: Even if there were such an absence of scripture (*āgama*), what contradiction would there be? For you have not perceived him speaking, such that there would be a contradiction based on the fact of his being seen. Being thus questioned, you must state by implication the following: "I do not establish his authorship of the scripture by having personally perceived its composition; rather, it is you yourselves who accept that the scripture was composed by him. And that [acceptance] of yours is untenable if his authorship is not admitted."

Therefore, those who necessarily desire that the scripture was composed by him must also accept his status as its speaker; thus, an undesirable consequence is established through this reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga).

Having thus established that this is a *prasaṅga* proof (*prasaṅgasādhana*), he now states the following— beginning with "If it were so," and so forth— in order to apply the point that [the opponent's position] fails to conform to the subject at hand (*prakṛtārtha*).

If such a principle is well-established among those who argue by means of logic, then in a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga-sādhana), the property [of the subject] would be accepted by others based on faith alone;
and if it were established through reasoning, it would become an independent proof (svatantra-sādhana).
And such is the scripture desired by the Supreme One, composed by Him;
due to the momentum of his accumulations, teachings issue forth at will from even walls and other such things, like from a wish-fulfilling gem. (3607–3608)
Therefore, he is designated as the "author" by virtue of his sovereign mastery; it does not follow that his authorship consists in being accompanied by conceptual construction.
But we, who lack faith [in such claims], seek logical arguments.
Thus, this has been stated by one who does not understand the purpose of the *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum).
For the rule is this: whatever property (*dharma*) has been accepted by the opponent based solely on scripture (*āgama*), that very same property is what is asserted in a *prasaṅga*-proof.

In that case, if the opponent had intended that the scripture was composed by [the Buddha] because of his being a speaker (*vaktṛtva*), then there would indeed follow the *prasaṅga* that the scripture is not composed by him due to the absence of his being a speaker; however, he is accepted as the author of that scripture merely by virtue of his sovereignty (*adhipatya*), and not because of the acceptance of his being a speaker.

As for that which you, being ignorant of the purpose of the *prasanga*, have asserted— namely, that the status of being a speaker is established by accepting the scripture composed [by him]— that is incorrect.
Regarding what was said, "of those [sounds] issuing from walls and so forth," and so on, he replies:
"Of those issuing from walls and so forth... Why is there no status as being taught by a reliable person (*āpta*) for them?
When those [teachings] proceed by virtue of his sovereignty—
(3611) for if those teachings did not proceed through his sovereignty, they would not possess the status of being taught by an authoritative person (āpta);
but since it is accepted that they proceed by virtue of his sovereignty, why then should they not possess the status of being taught by him?
Regarding what was said— that there would be no trust in them— it is replied with the verse beginning "sambhinna":
they are free from frivolous talk, violence, and other such despicable matters.
And how could those [Vedas] have been composed by playful piśācas and the like?
For in them, there is no activity characteristic of playful piśācas and such, such as the teaching of base matters including incoherent speech, violence, and so forth. (3612–3613)

That [scripture] is held to be in agreement with the two means of valid cognition regarding its entire subject matter, wherein not even the slightest sublation by those two means of valid cognition is observed;
and that which, even concerning what is extremely beyond the senses, is not contradicted by what precedes or follows.
It is the motivator for all persons in the arising of qualities such as compassion;
it is endowed with all modes of existence; it sets forth right conduct; and it brings about various forms of prosperity for the fortunate ones both in this world and the next.
If this [teaching], which expresses the antidote to the entire mass of latent tendencies and which shatters the gate-panels and city-walls of the city of Nirvana,
were the word of playful Rākṣasas, [then it would be false]. || 3617 ||
Let them indeed be fully awakened Buddhas, since they abide in all those characteristics.
For the nature of a thing does not change merely by the invention of another name;
however, one who applies the designation of an unlearned person to a distinguished one would be censurable by the virtuous.

For if there were an instruction therein regarding the necessity of performing dancing, singing, violence, illicit sexual intercourse, and so forth, then—given that activities such as these are observed among playful beings like piśācas—it might be conceivable that those [Vedas] were composed by them. However, it has been established that this word of the Blessed One is not contradicted by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), is free from internal contradictions, is worthy of noble persons, enjoins one toward virtues such as compassion, and brings about the fruits of heaven and liberation;
how, then, could such a thing be attributed even to a playful being like a piśāca?
If you give even human beings the name "piśāca" (demon), let it be so; for in the act of naming, there is no loss to the actual nature of a thing.
However, the summarized meaning is that you alone, by behaving improperly toward the distinguished Lord, would become an object of reproach for the virtuous.
The meaning of the individual components is now stated: "confused speech" refers to instruction in singing and the like;
"violence" refers to the killing of living beings;
and "debased objects" refers to sexual misconduct and so forth.

"Consistent with the two means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇadvayasaṃvādī*): the "two means of valid cognition" are perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). "Consistency" (*saṃvāda*) with these two is the state of having a meaning that is not contradicted by them. That which possesses this is so described; thus it is called "the doctrine" (*mata*).
"It is certain that [the person] is omniscient regarding that object" refers to the objects of the two means of valid cognition.
The connection is with the phrase "consistent with the two means of valid cognition.

"Virtuous conduct" refers to the celibate life (*brahmacarya*) that is auspicious in the beginning, middle, and end. "The entire mass of latent tendencies" refers to the flood of afflictions (*kleśa*) to be abandoned through vision and cultivation;
[the text speaks of] "abiding in their characteristics" because of that.
Because of abiding in the characteristics of a perfectly awakened one.
Regarding the state of the characteristics, it has been said—as follows: "The super-knowledge has been fully known, that which is to be known has been known;

that which is to be cultivated has been cultivated, and that which is to be abandoned has been abandoned. Because of this, he is called a Buddha. [The list of corrections shows this as *nirucyate* rather than *nirudhyate*; thus,] he is designated [as such]. He knows.
It is more reasonable to conceive that the Veda itself was composed by playful beings such as piśācas and others,
since it reveals improper practices such as sexual intercourse with women who should not be approached in the Gosava sacrifice and so forth; demonstrating this, he says "kāma" and so on.
If unrefined actions characterized by sexual misconduct, wrong conduct, violence toward living beings, and so forth, are manifested through a particular speech,
that [speech] is suspected of being composed by a libertine, a piśāca, or similar beings. (3620)
For such speech is indeed expected from those who delight in such activities.
(3621) [The serpent: "A rogue.
Regarding what was stated— "simultaneously [perceiving] the pure, the impure, and so forth"— he says: "simultaneously," etc.,
referring to the simultaneous [cognition] of contradictory intrinsic natures such as the pure and the impure.
Knowledge perceived by a single cognition is not contradictory, for your cognitions are indeed non-contradictory [with respect to one another].

Even though some entities may be mutually contradictory, they are nevertheless non-contradictory with respect to cognition— that is, with knowledge— because it is observed that multiple contradictory objects can be grasped simultaneously by even a single cognition.
Clarifying this very point, he says: "By way of mutual exclusion," and so forth;
or else, "by way of having characteristics established through mutual exclusion."
Among those [opposites], contradiction would consist in their not existing together in a single location;

it is not, however, their appearance in a single cognition that constitutes their contradiction, since pure and impure things, snakes and peacocks, and so forth, are perceived simultaneously by the eye. (3623–3624)

For the contradiction between entities is indeed twofold: the characteristic of existing through mutual exclusion and the characteristic of non-coexistence. Among these, for those things that exist by way of mutual exclusion, their identity is contradictory;
whereas for those things that do not coexist, their existence in the same location is contradictory.
Nor does their appearance within a single cognition entail that they are identical or occupy the same location;
therefore, there is no contradiction in their appearing in a single cognition.
Indeed, it is observed that even things which are mutually contradictory appear together within a single cognition.
Just as there is a simultaneous apprehension of the pure and the impure— such as a snake and a peacock, which have characteristics existing in mutual exclusion and cannot coexist—
as well as shadow and sunlight and so forth (the word "etc.
including these), if it is then the case that even contradictory things appear in a single cognition without contradiction...
This being the case, one might suspect that pleasure and pain, as well as attachment and aversion, would appear within a single cognition; anticipating this, he says: "Pleasure," and so forth.

Regarding the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth, the fact that there is no simultaneous cognition [of them] due to the absence of causes and their non-proximity is not contradictory; that is what is to be understood.
"That is to be understood" means:

The simultaneous non-perception of pleasure and the other [feelings] is due to their non-arising because of the absence of their causes, and thus they are not present; it should be understood—that is, it must be known—not because of mutual contradiction.
This is what is meant: in that case, the cause for their non-presence is the deficiency of causes, not mutual contradiction.

He demonstrates that even for those things whose opposition is real—and not merely conceptual, like the pure and the impure—they nonetheless appear within a single cognition: "Since blue, yellow, white, and other such distinct forms, though opposed by their differences in location and nature, are nevertheless perceived simultaneously. (3626)
The connection is that they are "contradictory" by way of difference of place and difference of nature (*prakṛti*).
In this context, "difference of place" means being in that place or not being in that place;
"difference of nature" means having a nature such as blue, yellow, and so forth.
Alternatively, regarding the fact that blue and so forth are the material causes [of cognition],
and as for what was stated— "that which has been, that which is, and that which will be," etc.— to that he replies with the verse beginning "by a single cognition," and so on.
"For the Omniscient One has been established as one whose entire circle of objects of knowledge is pervaded by a single moment of cognition; therefore, a sequential process is not resorted to.

(3627) On this point, some of our own fellow Buddhists (*svayūthya*), supporting the position of the Vijñānavādins, raise an objection: "If the entire circle of objects of knowledge is pervaded simultaneously by a single moment of cognition, then the infinity [of things] that was accepted would be contradicted, because there would be a determination of the limit of the objects of meditation through effort."
For in this way, when it is determined that there is no entity other than those entities already mounted upon a single cognition, how could they not be finite?
And it has been said: "Since there is no entity whatsoever other than those mounted upon a single cognition, they are finite because they are known to be just this many."
If it is argued that the defect which exists in the case of the wheel also applies to the position of simultaneous cognition,
this is without substance;
for if the objection is raised while relying on the view of those who maintain that consciousness is formless (*nirākāra-vijñāna*), then everything is incoherent.

For instance: whatever object whatsoever possesses existence, all of that is pervaded by the omniscient consciousness because it is delimited by that consciousness through its mere existence; however, this is not a pervasion in the sense of spatial extension, as in the case of a cloth covering jars.
Nor does the mere fact that objects are delimited by a single cognition entail a loss of their own intrinsic nature (*ātmasvabhāva*).
For if those [objects] were to abandon their infinite nature by virtue of being determined by a single cognition,

then numerous entities such as blue and yellow, whose forms are apprehended simultaneously in a single moment of cognition within a variegated carpet or the like, would neither lose their multiplicity nor would they merge into one another.
Moreover, just as things are exactly as they are, so too are they determined by knowledge and not in any other form;
likewise, the world of sentient beings and the receptacle world is apprehended by the mind of the Omniscient One exactly as it experiences its own existence.

Since the world of sentient beings and so forth is situated without limit in the cardinal and intermediate directions, its apprehension occurs by way of its boundlessness, and not by way of existing within a boundary; how, then, could there be the consequence of its being finite?
One might object: "If you accept the apprehension of the whole, how could there not be an apprehension of its boundaries?
This is not the case.
What is the obstacle here [to this claim] that wherever there is a grasping of totality (*sākalyagrahaṇa*), there must necessarily be a grasping of the limits (*paryantagrahaṇa*)?
For instance: among all those entities that exist, not even one experiences existence with its essential nature unknown to the cognition of the Omniscient One;
rather, every single one arises and passes away with its essential nature known by the mind of the Omniscient One—not even one is excluded. This is the meaning of the "grasping of totality."
And this alone is their pervasion by a single cognition;
otherwise, one would not even have to admit that they are denotable by the word "all," lest it entail the consequence of their being finite.
As for what was said—that because there is no entity other than those mounted upon a single cognition, how could they not be finite due to such a delimitation—that too is incorrect.
For in the position of those who maintain that cognition is formless (*nirākārajñānavādin*), there is no "ascension" of entities into the nature of cognition;
rather, they are made known by it through their mere existence.
Nor is it accepted that entities possess infinity due to having an intrinsic nature that cannot be delimited by cognition, such that their finitude would follow from being objects of knowledge.

However, because it is limitless in terms of the extension of space, the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*) is infinite; and because it is limitless even in terms of number, the world of sentient beings (*sattvaloka*) is infinite.
Furthermore, since there is no limit to their occupation of space, there is no contradiction with their being objects of cognition (*grāhya*) such that they would become unapprehendable.

If it is asked, "How can he be omniscient if he does not grasp [objects] by way of their limits?"—it is for this very reason that he is omniscient; because he does not grasp them as having limits, he is omniscient. Otherwise, grasping infinite objects as if they had limits, he would be mistaken.
For instance—one who perceives what exists as existing and what does not exist as non-existing is called "all-knowing" (*sarvavit*).
Now, there is no limit to the world of sentient beings and the receptacle-world (*sattva-bhājana-loka*);

therefore, perceiving that which lacks a limit reached by travel as being non-existent, while seeing the limit established by the delimitation of omniscient knowledge as being existent, how could such a one not be called "all-knowing"?

It might be argued as follows: "On the view that cognition is formless (*nirākāra*), the apprehension of objects is untenable because cognition is indistinguishable in all cases; consequently, the differentiation of cognitions according to their respective objects (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) would be impossible. Therefore, the position of formless cognition should never even be proposed, as it is always defective."
This is incorrect;

for no division according to specific objects (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) is admitted for the cognition of the Omniscient One, because His knowledge has all things as its object. Since it is accepted that His cognition is not the perception of blue alone, nor of yellow alone, but rather of everything, the objection regarding the impossibility of a determined division is raised only with respect to one whose cognition—being that of a person of limited vision (*arvāgdarśin*)—has restricted objects, and who thus maintains the position of a formless cognition (*nirākārajñāna*), wherein no distinction exists across all objects.

For instance, since there would be no restriction such that "this is the cognition of blue and not of yellow," it would follow that every ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) is omniscient; however, for an omniscient being, this is precisely what is accepted. Thus, what undesirable consequence could possibly befall whom?
Therefore, in the state of omniscience, it is entirely uncontradicted that [cognition] arises through the power of yoga as being devoid of mental aspects (*nirākāra*).
If it is argued that there would be no thorough knowledge of things to be abandoned and things to be adopted through differentiation, we say: no.

For if, when infinite objects appear simultaneously, there were a contradiction in the appearance of objects to be abandoned and those to be adopted; or if, in the absence of such a contradiction, that object to be abandoned or adopted appearing along with others were to lose its true nature; or even if, despite its true nature being unaltered, it did not manifest through differentiation; or if, even when it has manifested as described, no subsequent pure worldly reflective cognition (*vimarśapratyaya*) arises to delimit it—then all this [that you have stated] might indeed be said.

To the extent that the entire world appears, even that object—whether to be rejected or accepted—appears as something whose manifestation is not contradictory and whose essential nature (ātmatattva) does not fall away; it is indeed defined [by its own nature] and is subsequently determined by a pure worldly reflective cognition (pratyavamarśa-pratyaya) arising from the power of omniscient knowledge. Thus, how could there be any lack of thorough knowledge regarding it through such a distinction?
In this way, it has been demonstrated that this objection does not apply to the position of formless cognition (nirākāra-jñāna).
Now, an objection is raised regarding the position of the proponents of cognition with forms (*sākārajñānavāda*);
even there, however, there is no contradiction.

For instance, just as that infinite reality experiences its own existence as being accompanied by infinite forms, so too that omniscient mind, arising through the apprehension of the forms residing in immeasurable things, is indeed not contradictory.

If it is argued that there is indeed a contradiction for a single cognition to possess multiple forms because it is impossible for a single [cognition] to arise by assuming the forms of multiple objects, we say no,
because those forms are unreal.

For if the mental aspects (*ākāra*) were ultimately real for a single [cognition], then there would be a contradiction with its manifold nature; however, since it is accepted that these aspects are merely adventitious (*asvabhūta*) to it, if one objects that the Omniscient One would thus be subject to error because he possesses erroneous cognition, we reply:
this is not a fault, because his knowledge is a thorough comprehension of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtaparijñāna*).
For if one were to grasp the unreal as being real, then one would be deluded; however, when one knows unreal aspects precisely as unreal, how could one then be deluded?

If it is argued that, while grasping aspects mounted upon a non-differentiated cognition and engaging in conventional activities such as seeing with respect to objects that are [in fact] real, how can one be non-deluded? We say no, because of the thorough knowledge of the correct means.
For if one were to discard the appropriate means of apprehension and grasp an object by means of another, non-primary method, then one would be mistaken; however,

since in the position of the proponents of cognition with form (sākārajñānavāda), there is no operation for grasping an object other than the experience of the cognition’s own form, how could one who grasps the object through this appropriate mode of apprehension be mistaken?

Therefore, just like the objects of knowledge, even a single cognition arises by assuming the forms (ākāra) residing in infinite things; thus it is said that infinite reality is pervaded by that [cognition].

And by whichever nature the entities ascend into the self of the cognition, by that very same nature they are delimited by the subsequent reflective awareness (parāmarśacetas). However, entities do not ascend into the omniscient mind as following limited distinctions;
rather, what is the case?
Whatever exists that is experienced, all of that is subsumed [within consciousness],

because the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has unimpeded power with respect to being the objective support (*ālambana*) for the apprehension of all knowledge, and because its domain consists of all objects.

Therefore, since it is impossible for the omniscient mind to grasp the forms of unlimited objects, and because there is no delimitation by way of spatial boundaries through the subsequent pure mundane reflective cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*), how could there be a delimitation such as "there are only this many," which would entail finitude?
Even if a reflective cognition were to arise in the form "nothing exists other than what is appearing," even so, the consequence of finitude does not follow.

To explain: if that which appears were to appear as having an end (*antavat*) in the non-conceptual mind of the Omniscient One, then its infinitude (*anantatva*) would be delimited by the subsequent reflective cognition (*parāmarśacetas*) attained after that [perception];
and through that delimitation, the loss of infinitude would occur.
However, the object appearing in the mind of the Omniscient One appears precisely as infinite, because the power of the Omniscient One is unimpeded.
