Therefore, that which does not appear as something other than that [object] is indeed finite, and its exclusion is performed by the reflective consciousness (*parāmarśacetas*); thus, you have all the more established the finitude of entities—this [objection] is quite trivial.

Furthermore, for those who maintain that all yogic cognition is without an external object (*anālambana*) yet is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) due to its correspondence with reality (*vastu-saṃvāditā*), like the perception of a true dream, the objection regarding finitude has no room at all; so enough of this prolixity.

Showing that even according to the view of those who describe [the Buddha] as omniscient by his own will (*svecchā-sarvajña*), this [argument] is not contradicted, he says: "Whatever he wishes to know, etc."—
whatever he desires to cognize, he knows that very thing by necessity.
Such is his power, for he has indeed abandoned all conduct [of affliction];
he proceeds either simultaneously or sequentially according to his own will.
Having attained knowledge, that Lord, the Sage, is indeed capable through moments and so forth.
With the words "Or rather" (*yadvā*) and so forth, he states that there is no contradiction even in the view that knowledge is sequential:

"Or rather, by means of sixteen moments of consciousness, one knows all that is to be known in its entirety, sequentially, according to the nature of the Four Truths; therefore, one is 'all-knowing' (*sarvavit*). (3630)
In such a state of consciousness, O Lord, even a mere moment (lava) occurs in succession; what need is there to mention a duration of a hundred years?
Thus it is said: "by means of sixteen moments of mind."
By means of the patiences (*kṣānti*) and knowledges (*jñāna*),

there are eight patiences— beginning with the patience regarding the knowledge of the dharma of suffering— and eight knowledges— beginning with the knowledge of the dharma of suffering; thus, because it is stated that "this realization of the truths (*satyābhisamaya*) is distinguished into sixteen [moments]," even a single moment (*lava*) [is included].

A *kṣaṇa* is the limit of time (*kālaparyanta*); one hundred and twenty *kṣaṇas* constitute one *tatkṣaṇa*; sixty *tatkṣaṇas* constitute one *lava*. This is the convention. The word "aṅga" is used as a form of address; "abda" is a synonym for a year (*saṃvatsara*).
Regarding the passage beginning with "by an undifferentiated intrinsic nature," he says: "by intrinsic nature," and so forth.
He who perceives everything through an undifferentiated intrinsic nature perceives the very essential natures (svarūpa) of all entities.

[Objection: But surely, in the treatises, the untainted knowledge (*anāsrava-jñāna*) of yogis is described as having only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, and not the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). How then can the essential natures of entities be perceived by a yogic consciousness whose object is the universal? To this, he says: "Having that as its essence" (*sātmaka*), etc.

That specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa), which is excluded from things that are non-self, non-momentary, and so forth, is here called a "universal" (sāmānya) because it serves as the cause for tranquility and conceptual construction;
and the cognition that grasps it is that which arises through the power of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā).
For the masters of yoga, that very same particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), which is the object [of cognition], becomes manifest.

Indeed, that very particular characteristic—which is excluded from what is of a different class—is called a "universal characteristic" (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) in the treatise because it is the cause of a cognition with a non-differentiated form. Therefore, the yogic cognition that apprehends it, arising with a clear manifestation through the power of meditative cultivation, has as its object only the particular characteristic; thus, there is no contradiction.
How could that which has the universal as its object not be an apprehender of the particular characteristic? It certainly is.

As for what was stated— that "the cognition has that single form," and so forth— all of that is refuted by this very [argument], because the cognition of a yogi has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object.

Now, as for that universal (*sāmānya*) which we have described as being inexpressible through such forms as identity or difference, and which other non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) have postulated as being ultimately real (*pāramārthika*): in order to demonstrate that the claim—that the cognition of a yogi has a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object because it apprehends that [universal]—is unestablished, he says: "That universal which is inexpressible as identical or different and which is postulated by others is not grasped by this yogic consciousness. (3635)
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it should be understood that [the object] is not to be designated by such qualities as permanence and so forth.
Why is there no apprehension of it by that [cognition]? He says: "It is non-conceptual," and so forth.
The mind of the Lord of Yogins is non-conceptual and non-erroneous; otherwise, it would follow that it is overcome by conceptual construction and error when perceiving that [object].
(3636) Yogic cognition is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is non-conceptual and non-erroneous, and thus constitutes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Furthermore, if it were to have as its object a generality (sāmānya) such as has been described, then, because its object would be a conventional (saṃvṛta) entity, it would follow that it is beset by conceptual construction (vikalpa);
and because its object would be a false generality imagined by others, it would result in being beset by error (vibhrama).
Alternatively, if it were to have both as its objects individually, both of these faults would ensue.
Thus, it has been demonstrated that because its object is a falsely superimposed thing, it follows that [the cognition] is beset by conceptual construction and error.

Furthermore, demonstrating in another manner that the apprehension of that [object] follows as being beset by conceptual construction and error, he says: "And the nature of conceptual construction," and so forth.

And that universal which is proclaimed to be of the nature of conceptual construction and is said to be inexpressible— that which has the form of a constant accompaniment— is established as being devoid of intrinsic nature (nīrūpa).

As for this universal just mentioned— which was described as inexpressible, meaning it cannot be designated as being either identical to or different from [the particular]— since it is proclaimed, that is, established, to be the essence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the context of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*).
Therefore, the connection with the context is as follows: "In the apprehension of that [universal], it would follow that [the cognition] is beset by conceptual construction and error.

For instance, since the universal is of the nature of conceptual construction, the yogic cognition that apprehends it would itself be of the nature of conceptual construction, because it apprehends it precisely through identity (*tādātmya*).

Furthermore, since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by its very nature functions by determining its own appearance—which is not an external object—to be an object, it would follow that error (*viparyaya*) is its true nature, and thus it would be beset by delusion.

Moreover, as for the universal (*sāmānya*) postulated by others in the form of a permanent, pervasive entity, that too has been demonstrated in the "Examination of the Universal" (*Sāmānyaparīkṣā*) to be devoid of any real nature; therefore, when that [universal] is apprehended, it most clearly follows that the conceptual construction is beset by delusion.
Regarding what was stated—that action is accompanied by its cause and its fruit—and so forth, he says in response: "Accompanied by causes," etc.
He who knows through supramundane knowledge born of meditative concentration that action is accompanied by its causes and its fruits, is designated as omniscient. || 3638 ||
Previously, its existence was established through inference; there exists such a means of valid cognition for its presence, as it is said: "It exists," and so forth.
Regarding [the passage] beginning with "simultaneously or sequentially," he says: "Simultaneously," etc.
Whether simultaneously or in succession, his knowledge— and likewise his capacity— is revealed through the effect [of his teaching] when he delivers instruction.
(3640) This is easily understood.
Regarding the passage beginning with "one who has obtained the uncommon means," he says: "One for whom this stainless teaching of the selflessness of phenomena is well-practiced," and so forth.
This refers to one for whom this pure instruction on the selflessness of phenomena has been thoroughly cultivated.
Established by all the scriptures and uncontradicted by any means of valid cognition,

she possesses knowledge unsuitable for worldly beings; she is beyond the reach of Keśava and others, yet she is worshipped with their heads according to their capacity by those who are exceedingly wise.
It brings about the destruction of the entire host of enemies that are misfortunes;
it is the cause for the attainment of various prosperities and of nirvāṇa;
and it is the unique means obtained by all persons, characterized by its excellence.
"He alone is the omniscient Lord"—
this [statement] is established with proof by this entire *Tattvasaṃgraha*, which is a compendium of all treatises.

"Knowledge unsuitable for transmigrating beings" means that which is unsuitable (anucita), that is, not innate (asahaja), for those in saṃsāra; that teaching in which such knowledge exists is so described,
as it is beyond the scope of Keśava and others.

This [title] is in grammatical apposition with its own designation; the analysis of the compound is as follows: "duritāni" (sins) are themselves the "arātayaḥ" (enemies), and their "vargaḥ" (group) is a collection; she has the nature of performing the "bhaṅgam" (destruction) of that [collection]. Thus, it means she is the one who brings about the destruction of the entire host of enemies in the form of misfortunes.
The word "cause" (*kāraṇa*) is connected to each [term] as "the cause of the accomplishment of various forms of prosperity" and "the cause of the attainment of nirvāṇa. This is the meaning.
Regarding this, he says "ittham" and so forth:
"When, in this manner, some omniscient being is established..."
At that time, when there is the attainment of Dharma and so forth, the cause is the word of a person;
and it is only the Sugata who is such a person, not Kapila or others.

The intended meaning is as stated previously; furthermore, regarding the fault that was asserted through the conceptual distinction between formless and formed cognition, we have already provided the rebuttal for that as well.
But has it not been said: "Others [hold that consciousness] is with appearance, without appearance, both with and without appearance, and neither with nor without appearance;
yet consciousness does not cognize an external object in any way whatsoever"?
Thus [ends] 3645.
Thus.

Anticipating the objection—"How can it be said that there is no occurrence of faults even when resorting to both positions?"—he says: "(Regarding 'nirākārādi', etc.)—But the consideration of whether [cognition] is formless and so forth is not applicable to the Omniscient One;
for just as your own cognition [is held to be] with respect to some object, so too is the [Omniscient One's] supreme [cognition]. (3646)
Thus ends the *Tattvasaṅgraha*, composed by Śāntarakṣita, which is an investigation into the person who perceives that which transcends the senses.

This reflection on the formless [cognition] (*nirākāra-cintā*) which was previously undertaken by us while adhering to the Vijñānavāda school— now, when a *sarvajña* (omniscient being) is being established by accepting external objects against you Mīmāṃsakas who are attached to external objects, it is in no way applicable for you proponents of external objects to perform.
To the question "How so?", he says: "For just as... and so forth.
Indeed, you must necessarily describe the apprehension of the external object by cognition—whether it be with a form (*sākāra*) or without a form (*nirākāra*);
otherwise, there would be the total abolition of the external object.

And therefore, in whatever manner and by whichever means your knowledge proceeds regarding some object, in that very same way and form will the supreme—that is, the most excellent, omniscient [knowledge]—proceed; thus, this is not a point for objection.
May the abundant merit that has been acquired by me, having attained the state of being the eternal abode of the incomparable splendor of the Jina, [bring about this result].
May the entire world be [blessed] by that Kamalaśīla of radiant splendor, who delights the minds of all people.
Thus ends the *Puruṣaparīkṣā* (Examination of the Person Who Perceives Beyond the Senses). The *Pañjikā* (Commentary) composed by Kamalaśīla is completed.
